It took me a little over 7 hours to 100% this game and I have a lot of thoughts. Thankfully the vast majority of them are positive! Let's start off with the general premise: I absolutely adore it! At first I was uncertain about how well horticulture and Gothic Victorian aesthetics would go together, but they are a surprisingly beautiful combo. 

The atmosphere of the whole game is rather chill and laid back, albeit a bit on the eerie side considering the story being told, but there is no rush to complete your tasks throughout the day. Which is something I really enjoy when it's comes games like this one. 

Gameplay mechanics are very straight forward, person ask for thing, you figure out what thing is then give it to them, and the transaction is done. The only times you venture away from that mechanic is when you are solving puzzles that will help you further the story. The puzzles themselves can be quite easy solve, except for a few of them that the game doesn't give much context on how you're meant to solve them. Something else that can be a bit frustrating with the puzzles is that some of the tools that you use to solve them can be a little off if you don't place them SPECIFICALLY where they're meant to go, which is an easy thing to do, mind you. So that means that you could have the right Idea about how to solve the puzzle, but because your hand was a little unsteady, you didn't place the contraption where it was SPECIFICALLY meant to go and you got the wrong answer. Now you have to wait however long until you can try again and hope you place it correctly this time.

The story of Strange Horticulture is really good in my option, though I do wish as the player we had more freedom in choosing the fates of our clients, but that is a bit of a nitpick since I like having a lot of choices in my games.

TL;DR
All in all, I think Strange Horticulture is a beautiful, relaxing, puzzle game that you can really just sit back and enjoy. Yes, some of the puzzles can be bit tedious, but that's only a few out of the however many that is in the game. All of that said, I can't wait until the release of Strange Antiquities!

[I]Strange Horticulture[/I] is an atmospheric and enjoyable puzzle game in whose DNA you'll find [I]Papers, Please[/I] and [I]Cultist Simulator[/I], but mercifully with the need to work against the clock removed.

As is [I]de-rigeur[/i] in the 'artisan in a small town' genre, you inherit the titular store at the start of the game and nought much else bar a few starting plants, a cat, a shop counter, a pre-loved horticulturist's guide, a map of the game's alt-Cumbria setting and some letters from friends.

Gameplay is split primarily between the shop window and the map. The former is the more [I]Papers, Please[/I] part of the game, with each ding of the bell summoning the next visitor. You'll spend just shy of three in-game weeks here welcoming half-a-dozen-or-so visitors each day. While your libarian friend and the postie will offer the necessaries to move the plot along, the remaining visitors seek your expertise and, ultimately the correct plant for whatever predicament they're in.

Challenge is provided by the fact that the horticulturist's guide is less-than-brilliantly written, and paying attention to extra clues, the process of elimination and trying to best-fit the sketches will help you identify what's what of the almost 80 plants in the game. While I liken it to Lucas Pope's genre-defining dystopian document thriller, you aren't on the clock here and penalties are almost non-existent. Providing the correct plant will confirm its identity (and label it, if you turned it on in the game's options, which I recommend), while getting it wrong will add a chunk to a dread meter.  I never got to filling this fully, so can't comment on what the penalty is if you do. Some visitors will additionally provide queries that can be met in diverging ways. A local suffering from seemingly premonitory dreams, for example, can either be given a plant to render her dreamless or another to make the visions even sharper and clearer. 

Your choices will shape the game's plot and can even influence which of the game's eight key characters make it to the end of the month. A gruesome murder with more than a whiff of the occult about it soon dominates the story and it becomes clear that everyone's plant-based requests are increasingly linked to the endgame. This, for me, is the [I]Cultist Simulator[/I] bit, insofar as the careful linkage together of little scraps ends up adding up to a bigger whole.

A steady stream of letters, clues and a tarot-esque card drawn at the end of each day will steadily point you to squares of the game's map to find new plants and unearth more of the mystery, not to mention some light lore and worldbuilding. Handily, the game checks off letters and clues once their linked discovery has been made. Some nice gadgets that are drip fed to you over the course of the game add some little nuances to the map game. Both the dread meter's ability to fill if you make pointless visits and the need to slow your pace and water your plants if you do get it wrong ensure you think before you click and prevent mindless clicking of the map until the solution presents itself.

The game's hint system also gently holds your hand through any moments you're unsure of, but at no point did [I]Strange Horticulture[/I] feel unwelcomely obscure or difficult. The puzzles are clever but straightforward in their logic and none should leave you scratching your head for longer than you'd like.

All told, I spent about four highly enjoyable hours in the game's charming but ominous setting for the princely sum of £4. Even at £13.50, each hour of entertainment is less than a pint at the local, but at £4 it's an absolute steal. I'm also aware I've unlocked one of presumably a number of endings, so four hours is just for one playthrough and by no means all that the game has to offer.

I certainly look forward both to a future run through the game and the upcoming [I]Strange Antiquities[/I].

Strange Horticulture has proven to be quite an immersive mystery so far. I decided to check it out after having watched the trailer for the developer's upcoming game, Strange Antiquities, which I added to my wishlist as it looked quite interesting.

What I like about Strange Horticulture is the intrigue surrounding everything I do and the people who come in. Identifying each plant and searching for more with clues and the map makes me feel like a real horticulturist or a botanist. I especially love the opportunities when I can go out into the field and explore in search of plants or lore that further fleshes out the game's world and its storytelling. The story is unique in that it does not happen upfront but takes place in the background, which is interesting and proves the world is bigger than me. On one occasion, I happened to trigger the Rising Dread purely out of curiosity since one of the customers who came in mentioned two locations I decided to check out just to see what sort of lore I could uncover. I get that Rising Dread is meant to discourage random guessing, which is a fine mechanic, though when presented with a place to visit for more lore, even if it does not net me anything, I am more than happy building its meter. Even doing the puzzle to restore my sanity was quite fun, and completing it brought me back to the customer who told me the names of those two locations, so I did not mind losing it.

Regarding the customers, I quite like how a handful of them frequent the shop. Each of them feel like figures of the background story I am trying to piece together, and I am already starting to formulate a few theories as to what their roles will be and what will happen next. Determining what the correct plant is based on the dialogue provides more puzzles to work with. I am not always given the name of a plant I can quickly find in the manual, but have been able to reach it at some point thanks to my usage of the game's hints as a tool to help narrow down my search and confirm my hunches based on the evidence I am given.

Ultimately, Strange Horticulture is definitely worth playing. It offers such an intriguing mystery the player is not an active participant in but is invited to be a part of by providing customers with the plants they need, that it is bound to leave you guessing what might happen next. Though I have yet to complete the game, I look forward to its inevitable conclusion and am eagerly awaiting the release of Strange Antiquities so that I may continue to delve deep into this universe's interconnected world. I strongly recommend picking up Strange Horticulture and wishlisting Strange Antiquities if you have not already done so. Not doing so leaves their mysteries unsolved.

This game presents an unique "twist" in guidance-path type puzzles where you are guiding a kitty kat from an entrance door, through a small dungeon laced with dropping floor panels (both controlled and random), tripping floor panels that open doors, teleporting floor panels, and panels that when stepped on will rotate the entire dungeon 90-degrees counter-clockwise.  All of this to get the cat from the entrance door to the exit door in order to move to the next level.  Each floor may/may not have special "pillars" with a symbol on top ("torches", "sheilds", "swords") that cause the four adjacent floor panels to drop in a predefined pattern as determined in a parchment paper pasted on the level.

Using these characteristics, this game is a family-friendly puzzle where it teaches the concepts of "planning ahead" and plotting your course to meet the objective.  It progresses in difficulty during the game but never reaches the point of frustration where you feel the need to "cheat" yet, it still tests your thought ability.  This is a really good casual-style game where you can stop, walk away, and come back to play more...I would recommend this game...going on to play the second game in the series which should prove to be a little more difficult and frustrating...have fun!  Kudos to the devs!

yes i recommend this shooter. honestly for me top down shooter is not my main favorite but this is one of the best shooter i've ever played.

HOWEVER, theres a minor mistake from the dev that almost makes me not reccomend it, it was BECAUSE THE MENU SCREEN CANNOT BE ACCESSED ANYTIME. 
here is the story: 
i was almost stuck forever in this complicated moment: i played it with my daughter in adventure mode, and we left it on the notification that we both get extra jet as stage reward. NOTE: i played as PLAYER1 using keyboard and my daughter AS PLAYER2 using joystick. then......
when we got back and want to continue the game, it was stuck! because the default setting put joystick as player 1! (i set it to player2 before) so what was happening is: we cannot skip the notification to progress the game because it required player2 to press A button! and we also cannot configure the controller button because to open the menu we need to skip that notification first!!!! we even cannot delete autosave data (that was synced with steam cloud) because to do so it also required us to open the menu screen (which need to skip that notification first by pressing A BUTTON ON PLAYER2) . so basically the adventure mode is stuck forever!

Super Retro Fighter looks your average shmup, but IT IS NOT. 

Visuals: 
+ The visuals are gorgeous, its a real eye candy, the glowing atmosphere of the game is just pure nostalgic arcade experience, with vivid colors, and a clean display. The bullets, enemies are clearly visible, the explosions are the best ive seen in a shmup, the popcorn effects are satisfying.

- Right now, the game lacks real backgrounds, they just black screens with some whit dots. Boring. Hope, they will improve on this. 

Gameplay:

There is an arcade mode, which... playes like an arcade mode with 8 very long - impossible - stages. 

So - there is the Adventure mode to go. 
Its a rougelike game loop, u have some lives, u lose them, its game over, u can start the WHOLE GAME from start. 
U can earn a few red crystals, which can be used to afford permanent starting equipment - unlock more life, more bombs, and damage power BUT its limited to 5 (and if u die, u lose a ship and a damage power as well).

In game u can collect blue crystals, and in every stage u can buy a wingman to help u in battle (different styles, gadgets). 

The game is insanely hard after a while. The bosses are just way above the difficulties of the levels, even the earlier ones, and here is a flaw in gameplay loop: u will lose life, and damage while beating a boss... so u get weaker. And its VERY hard to earn more lives, more damage - those are the most dangerous routes, so u probably lose more damage.... so when u encounter the next boss (which is WAY MORE DIFFICULT) u will be probably weaker than when u encounteredthe previous one.... 

What it really means: u only get stronger with 1CC, with perfection, without making ANY mistakes... if u lose some life, u will fall, u will suffer on every level, and there is no way to come back. The game is designed to support 1cc players and punish everyone else. Right now, i think its not their intention to make the game more accessible for everyone.

The main flaw of the gameplay right now, that this game is HEAVILY relies on MEMORIZATION. Yes, Super retro fighter IS A MEMORIZATION game in many stages... but... without the chance to practice the stages. Game over - u start from scratch.... And there are many stages... more than 20 at least, maybe 30, i havent finished it, seems impossible, becouse u cannot try to beat the new stages again, not even in adventure mode. 

I dig the game, the gameplay is one of  the best i ve seen, the atmosphere is great, even the story elements between the stages are interesting, but right now its NOT BALANCED in this state. However, its still insanely FUN, but frustrating as well. 

The content is HUGE compared to other shmups, its NOT YOUR 45 MIN run shmup, the level variety is cool as well, lot of creative puzzle elements. 

I say it: THIS game RIGHT HERE could be a game, that would introduce a lot of new people to the genre, becouse of the beautiful visuals and the very addictive gameplay... BUT the choice of grindy, and punishing gameplay style even on adventure mode easy is designed for a hardcore experience. 

EDIT: I forgot to mention, an earlier version of the game actually had stage select, u could play the previous ones and the actual stage anytime. So, in that regard, the game went the wrong direction.

Rougelike games are nice, but they are not THAT LONG for a reason. 6 - 8 shorter stages, thats it. SRF has more than twenty, and they are all pretty hard - if u actually try to save ur lives and bombs, thats almost impossible to get through thirty difficult stages without mistakes. I love the HUGE content here, its just hardly accessible.

I recommend it anyway for shmup lovers, its my favourite next to Devil Engine, ZeroRanger and Super Hydorah - but all those games are more FAIR.  Only Super Hydorah has branching system like Super Retro, but in Hydorah u can restart the stage, or u can choose a different path on the star system - that route system has more freedom, logic and way more friendly.

This game is a very strong LOVE & HATE relationship.

[b]starlight x-2[/b] didn't really catch my attention around release, I acknowledged its existence and that was that. then I decided to try the demo anyway, and after only 5 very short levels, before even finishing the tutorial, I clicked the [i]add to cart[/i] button, as it made a wonderful first impression.

in a nutshell, it's a [b]sudoku-like in space[/b] with the core elements of planets, stars, light beams emitted by the stars, and asteroids. planets have to be illuminated, but only from certain directions, stars can help with that, while asteroids block light beams. the rule is: [b]there can be only one asteroid and star in any given row or column[/b]. so yeah, sudoku. and no guessing, of course.

11 level packs, each with 50 levels, so [b]550 regular levels, all available from the start[/b], but it's best to follow some sort of order for a smoother difficulty curve. there are also [b]daily packs of 50 levels[/b] for endless entertainment, and there's a bit of an archive, [b]14 daily packs at a time[/b], no need to check in every day if you don't want to miss anything. [b]level states are saved[/b], so progress isn't lost if you quit without solving one.

grids start out at 3x3 for the first tutorial level, the rest is [b]between 4x4 and 13x13[/b] (non-dailies only go up to 9x9), and they vary between easy, medium and hard. it's a very considerate and polite game, [b]no time limit or punishment for misclicks, because there's no immediate error-checking[/b], just like in any decent nonogram or other deductive game. during the tutorial you're kindly reminded that that there situation ain't gonna work, but later it's just a discreet color change in numbers if you place too many of something.

[b]once the correct amount of objects is placed, you might get an 'error detected' message[/b], but I have no issue with that. go over your solution, find the mistake, fix it, done. [b]undo is available[/b], which I didn't find necessary, as you can place and remove things easily.

there's further optional assistance in your quest to infinity and beyond. use the [b]error checker and hints[/b] at your own discretion, as well as the ability to [b]mark cells as 'no star', 'no asteroid' or 'neither'[/b]. markers can be hidden individually and you can drag the mouse to select a line faster without overwriting placed objects. the game is [b]completely mouse-driven[/b], mouse wheel scrolls between placable items, but 1-5 also selects what you want to place without tiring out the mouse.

[b]fun fact:[/b] there are fun facts about various space stuff after every level, so there's a bonus [b]educational value[/b], plus you're slowly unveiling pictures of celestial bodies (planets and such, not pretty ladies you perv).

while the graphics might not qualify as eyecandy, they're functional, the ui is clean and elegant, the music and sound effects are good too. separate volume settings, windowed mode with a resizable window, many languages, metric or imperial measurements, how to play section, a toggle for animations (called graphics, full means animations are on), and some gameplay stats are all available, also while playing.

[b]not much to criticize[/b], I could only think of a few small quality of life improvements. will edit the list if some get implemented:
[olist]
[*]undo, hint, and error check icons don't have tooltips, while the others do.
[*]the restart button should be part of the ui, not just the menu.
[*]a longer delay before the eye/hint message would be nice (and a toggle to turn it off, after 10 levels I'm fully aware).
[*][strike]mouse wheel could also be used to switch between the 5 things to place.[/strike]
[*]the cursor over the grid could show what you're currently holding, a little mouseover effect. it's visible on the left, but still.
[*]clicking somewhere on the border could mark an entire line with whatever marker is currently selected.
[*][strike]clicking on a planet, then the back arrow should go back to where you were before, not the top of planet selection.[/strike]
[*]with such an elegant ui, in-game representation of achievements and leaderboards would look better than bringing up the steam overlay.
[/olist]

I really dislike sudoku (partly because of all the numbers and it's not even a math game), but [b]starlight x-2 is excellent and great value for money[/b], can't wait to see what the developer comes up with next. by all means, [b]try the demo[/b], see if it's something worthy of your time and money (progress carries over to the full game).

This is a decent paper-puzzle-ish game with a solid UI and an initially atrocious title. It was eventually renamed to "Starlight X-2: Space Sudoku", which is a bit better.

Gameplay

This is essentially a paper-puzzle-like experience with a neat presentation. There are 550 levels, plus infinitely more levels, albeit all auto-generated. That means they're all interchangeable, which makes the idea of completing any level set more daunting and less appealing. Unfortunately, that's the main motivation one has in such games, so that made it harder to stay interested. In addition, I didn't find difficult puzzles particularly interesting to solve. Similar to randomly generated Sudoku puzzles, you just follow a rote algorithm step by step, irrespective of level size.

The core puzzle idea is decent for paper puzzles. I don't mean that as criticism; I like lots of paper puzzles, like Slither Link. But when I see 550 levels and know that there won't be any new mechanics, I wonder why this was sold as a video game.

Visuals: In bigger levels, the screen gets cluttered very quickly, at which point it becomes unreadable (similar to solving Sudoku puzzles and writing number clues into every single tile). The devs noticed this and... instead of making the visuals less busy, instead added buttons to hide specific icons like all no-asteroids icons O_o. In addition, the iconography for no-asteroid is a negative image of an asteroid; same for the sun. This is a very unfortunate choice, for the same reason that "don't think of a pink elephant" is a thing. That said, I did get used to this eventually.

UI: The UI is decent, but I wish there were hotkeys. The game requires so much clicking because it doesn't even support a second action via the right mouse button. Things would've been so much easier if e.g. the right click did the opposite of the left click (e.g. place sun and place no-sun). (EDIT: Apparently this feature was actually added eventually. Hooray!) That said, at least the mouse wheel cycles between placable symbols, and clicking & dragging is supported to draw lots of "no X" hints at once. Finally, the hint system is amazing and even tells you if you've made a mistake, but only if you ask. This is something all paper-puzzle-ish games should copy.

Other than that, I found some of the achievements bizarre and yucky. Stuff like "Addicted for 10 days" or "24h playtime", ew.

Overall, I enjoyed this game for a while.

This is more a mixed review than a negative one.

Sometimes in medium difficulty puzzles and [i]rarely[/i] in easy puzzles I wound up with a 50/50 on a single pair of stars but even then that was easily resolved by then filling in all the rote asteroid information.

In the larger-size hard puzzles I found myself switching between star and asteroid logic more often, and sometimes I had more than just a single 50/50 to resolve at the end, both of which I appreciated, but ultimately it still felt like filling in most of the grid did not require much [i]insight[/i], which was disappointing. In larger grids it was also easier to overlook something obvious, especially with all of the light beams filling up rows and columns, but this is a minor complaint.

I don't know whether the logic system is simply incapable of producing truly challenging puzzles or whether the (procedurally generated?) puzzle selection fails to draw out the system's potential, but either way, I didn't feel motivated to progress beyond a sampling of difficulties and sizes ranging from easy to hard and from 4*4 to 9*9, totaling 100 puzzles.

For what is essentially an arcade-styled game that focuses on the completely skill-based gameplay of older retro days, No Parachute is an adrenaline-rush from beginning to end as you guide the most unfortunate gentleman, who fell from an airplane down below into this VERY deep cavern hole without the foresight of equipping a most convenient parachute on him beforehand, through a most dangerous pit that goes down for many miles as you evade a whole assortment of both natural and much more irregular obstacles as you progress through the various layers of the planet itself!

Indeed, this isn't a game that you can easily chill out to and relax, seeing as the action is quick and to the point as you must swiftly evade any and all barriers that, without directing the character away from said danger in time, will result in a most unpleasant splatter of blood and a human pancake smashed all across the obstacle that stopped your progress here! Not just that but said blood marks remain when attempting the same level again as a reminder of where you last failed as well as no doubt being increasingly a more common sight as you make your way into the even more difficult stages with razor-thin obstacles that demand nothing but the absolute best of one's reflexes to fully master this game!

Given how intense the gameplay can be here, even in relatively short bursts, No Parachute isn't for the faint of heart here as it's not just a game of many thrills but can also be quite gory as well as, alongside the remains of blood marks as mentioned before, there is a small 'forgiving' aspect of the game that doubles as a 'punishment' of sorts, by which I mean barely missing an obstacle by having your arm or leg hit it won't automatically fail you as, instead, it will result in said limb being cut off clean and leaving behind quite the splatter of a mess at that!

Whilst that sounds all good, having a safety mechanism that does not result in more frustrating gameplay that has you blaming the game instead where it offers you a 'second chance' of sorts, this does impact your character's ability to move around so gracefully as each limb he loses will impact his ability to move around the tunnel's many obstacles more and more, whereby he will struggle to move much at all by the time he has only his mere torso and head to move around in! So yes, essentially it also acts as a punishment of sorts for not quite making it past obstacles where later levels demand near-perfection for evading obstacles, something that won't be possible to make even with the best of reflexes if you're missing an arm and a leg!

Alongside the main story mode itself, No Parachute also offers an 'Endless Mode' of sorts, which is pretty much the one randomly-generated level that extends forever as you slowly go faster and faster and the obstacles become more complex and difficult to evade alongside the increasing speed, where you have only one live and losing a limb may very well spell the end for your run unlike in the story mode where especially skilled players can get by with the loss of multiple limbs! Definitely worth a shot after completing the main game or returning to it if you decide you want to check it out first to see just how much you'll have improved since then!

Suppose if I did have to offer some criticisms though, the game can feel a tad repetitive before long, with there not being much of any extra 'layers' when it comes to new gameplay mechanics and the likes, since it is purely a skill-based game to seeing just how far you can get down to the centre of the Earth as it were! Alongside that, the retro pixelized graphics may not be to everybody's tastes and attaining 3-star ranks for each story mode level, outside of the tutorial, is VERY difficult and may drive completionists up the wall trying to ensure that each level has that perfect 3-star rank at that!

Otherwise, I would say that No Parachute is quite the excellent game when it comes down to getting that nice arcade experience going, a short burst of fun that also offers some extra challenge for those looking to take the game more seriously here!

Whether or not I recommend this game depends on what type of person you are.

If your only goal is to reach the credits, then I think the game is worthwhile. The game itself is interesting without being complicated, the levels are visually appealing (by pixelated subterranean standards anyway), and even at regular price it's fairly inexpensive. You'll die a lot while you learn each level's layout, which is something I usually can't tolerate, but here I never found it overly frustrating. Sure it's annoying when you die in the same spot for the twentieth time, but since each level is at most 30 seconds long, death is never too much of a loss. All told, you should be able to reach the credits in an hour or two, depending on how good your reflexes are.

If you're the type of gamer who wants to get every achievement, then you might instead end up like me, with 12.9 hours of play time. And I don't recommend that sort of time investment.

Nine of the achievements are easy, and you'll unlock them without trying. The tenth achievement (Underground Superstar) requires you to beat the high score on each level. And the high scores are [i]not[/i] generous. If you lose a limb, you probably won't beat the high score. If you aren't using your speed boost for 80% of the level, you probably won't beat the high score.

For the first several levels this isn't a huge challenge and you simply need to memorize where all the obstacles are. But around the midway point there are two new obstacles you have to start dealing with: 1) extended narrow sequences, which means you have no physical room for error; 2) moving obstacles (ie. spinning fans), which means the positioning that got you through an obstacle on a previous run won't work if you reach that obstacle 0.5 seconds sooner/later.  And that's what took up so much of my time. I went from beating the high score on level 9 after twenty minutes to beating the high score on level 10 after two hours.

Because of how much time I sunk into this game, I also feel qualified to criticize the dismemberment mechanic. How it works is that, depending on how you hit an obstacle, you might only lose a limb instead of dying outright. It's both a funny idea and it's a completely justifiable reason to deduct points from your score. But losing a limb also slows your movement speed, so much so that it will be impossible to avoid most of the remaining obstacles. Which I feel makes the feature ultimately pointless, because instead of being a substitute for death it only delays it by a few seconds.

In short, I like the game and hate the achievements. I wish I hadn't bothered beating the high scores and I encourage you not to either. My dollars-to-hours ratio wouldn't have been as good, but I would have had a happier experience.

Is this game worth it at .99 cents? Sure, why not? But, to be honest, it's not really good and I'm surprised it's rated positively here. It is barely worth .99 cents. It's definitely not worth it at $9.99 USD and not even worth what I paid for it ($3.99 USD).

It took me 40 minutes to beat the game on my first playthrough and that was with taking my time. It took me only 20 minutes to beat the game on my second, even with facing a problem with retrieving a knife from the floor. I think you can probably beat the game in 15 minutes.

The puzzles are too easy. Almost all of them are just about finding the missing object, usually a key. The only other puzzles are putting a picture together, turning some valves, placing knives correctly, & remembering the order of things. The game also has cheap jump scares. There is almost no story, at least not a coherent one.

Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting a steady 90 fps on ultra graphics. The visuals were good for a budget title, but the sounds were very amateurish. You do have full locomotion and snap turning available. I did run into one bug with the above mentioned problem of having problems picking up a knife from the floor. 

Overall, this game feels like a mobile VR port, just with nice graphics. The interactions, puzzles, & scares are all rather basic with no depth. Really the only thing that stands out are the visuals, given the budget price. Buy on a deep sale of 90% or better only. Keep your expectations very low as well.

It's an excellent follow-up to the original Sins of a Solar Empire, which is an RTS classic.  Overall, it plays similarly to the original.  (It's slower and more strategically focused than other RTS classics like Star Craft and Command and Conquer.)  For old fans, it will initially feel *very* similar to the original, as the factions and most of the units from the first game return. 

Nevertheless, this game makes a lot of subtle but meaningful changes to the original that makes it feel distinct.  In particular, the planetary upgrade system is deeper and more intuitive to use.  This game also sees the addition of rare exotic materials, which are needed to build capital ships and yield a number of gameplay improvements.  For instance, exotic materials can be recovered from the wreckage of friendly and enemy capital ships after they're destroyed, which makes wreckage recovery an important dimension of major space engagements. 

This game also improves upon the technical foundations of the original.  It runs smoothly, even when matches reach ludicrously large scales.  Ships now have details like rotating turrets, and textures and lighting are improved.  The UI now scales naturally for modern high-def displays.

TL;DR: Many gameplay issues make this game near unplayable and very much unfun. Not recommended.

[b]First impressions:[/b]
- Menu is a bit lacking. Pretty much no options. The game is way too loud by default and I had to use the Windows volume mixer to turn it down to an acceptable level.
- Song list UI is also lacking. Only shows song name, artist and a short description. Needs at least some sort of difficulty rating and maybe a high score if the song was played before?
- Guitar Hero controllers are supported. However, the support is partial. Since the game is focused on keyboard and gamepad play, the strum bar does not do anything and pressing the corresponding fret buttons is enough to hit the notes. Would be nice to have some sort of "guitar mode".
- The visuals lack polish. The whole game very much has a "first Unity project" kind of vibe to it.

[b]Playing a song:[/b]
Sadly, here's where the game completely falls apart.
- [b]No latency/offset settings[/b] = no way to calibrate for hardware lag (input/display/etc). This means that all songs are off-sync with the visuals and there's no way to adjust it. Come on, this is a basic feature of all rhythm games!
- On top of that, it seems like the game slowly falls out of sync as the song progresses. Pausing and unpausing makes it even worse. This makes the game almost unplayable.
- No visuals or sound for misses or incorrect notes. If you're not paying attention to the "health bar" on top, you'll inevitably end up failing for seemingly no reason. 
- Gameplay area is way too small. I get that the music videos are supposed to be the focus here... but then, why not make them fullscreen, and then overlay the gameplay on top like Guitar Hero or Rock Band does, but with a partially transparent background?
- Scroll speed cannot be adjusted. It's way too slow for how note-dense most of the songs can get at the highest difficulty.

[b]Hit detection:[/b]
The hit engine is very weird in pretty much all aspects.
- The frontend is almost nonexistent compared to the backend. You can still hit notes as they disappear off the fretboard, but hitting them just a bit early will result in a miss.
- Speaking of misses, they sometimes randomly happen for no reason, even if the note was hit correctly - it will count towards the score, but still break the combo and remove a bit of health.
- Anchoring seems to exist in some form (you can hit a higher note while still holding a lower one), but it's a bit random whether it decides to work or not.
- The game accepts hitting just one note of multiple in a chord. Seems weird to me, but could be intentional.

[b]Music choice:[/b]
I don't have much to say in this regard. I didn't know any of the bands featured in the game, but I liked a few of the songs (or at least the parts I was able to hear before inevitably failing due to desync). Looks like they're all smaller artists, which I'm okay with, especially if the game is supposed to be focused on discovering new bands.

[b]Summary:[/b]
Because of all the issues (especially desync and lack of calibration) the game is pretty much unplayable.

Unfortunately, it almost seems like more effort was put into the weird "rewards program" that is featured in the game (which also features cryptocurrency and NFTs for some reason???) than the actual game itself.

Not to mention, it is a [b]paid[/b] game after all, no matter how cheap it currently is - and based on the early access blurb, it seems like the devs have plans for more features but haven't really considered how playable it is in its current form.
It's not a very fun experience at all, and I would definitely not describe it as "fully functional".

I can't recommend this game to anyone, as there are much better rhythm games in the style of Guitar Hero or Rock Band currently available to play - many of them are completely free passion projects made by fans. Heck, you could probably even get a copy of Guitar Hero III for PC for a similar price at a thrift store.

The first self-developed game from Rebuild Games, who mainly do third-party design work on Pokemon games. Metland is being besieged by enemies, and it's up to a crack team of Mets to stop them. SUPER METBOY! has a fascinating control scheme in which the Met you play as bounces around and hops into the air when shooting a projectile. While strange to get used to, the game works beautifully around this mechanic as you use your shots to take out enemies all around the stage and survive waves of enemies. Each wave has a specific number of enemies you need to clear before it ends, and so you have a push-and-pull mechanic in choosing between easier enemies or stronger enemies that offer more money upon defeat. Your choice of Met also impacts gameplay - Metboy himself has a standard straight shot attack, while Metgirl has a heart attack that has homing properties, Metbomber has bombs that move in an arc, and so on. If you manage to complete the game, you get access to a 'special US version' that's harder but offers greater rewards. Those rewards come in the form of Diamonds that can be spent on Chips which alters things like your Attack strength, your HP, and the amount of Gold you get. It's a fantastic game!

Straya is like Far Cry 2 if instead of Africans as foes, your enemy was the fauna of Australia. Ostensibly Straya is a hunting game, but in practice it becomes more of a survival horror game with elements of the small australia simulator genre. The map is larger than Grand Theft Auto 6, comprising the entirety of the Oceanic continent. There are a lot of different kinds of missions, and plenty of animal bounties to seek. There are scary aboriginal things, but they pale in comparison to being literally randomly jumpscared by a two foot wide spider every ten minutes, or being chased by, at one time, a camel, two lizards, a buffalo, two kangaroos, an eagle, a snake, and a spider. Every animal is upscaled and buffed, most animals are actively hostile to the player. Guns are effective, the FAL is probably the best anti-animal tool if you are in a pinch, but in keeping with the survival horror elements, there are no attachments for it. I enjoy hunting with the enfield or shotgun mostly. The game's opening seemed hokey at first, talking about how hard you have to be to live in Australia, but after a mere three hours playing, I can say with authority that the Australian people live in a constant holocaust of anti-human animal kamikaze attacks. I normally hate fishing minigames, but in Straya I had a mission to do one. Normally, fishing minigames are meant to be relaxing, however, a camel, two kangaroos, a goat, and a gator harrassed my character while I was in the fishing minigame. I dared not exit it until I did not see any hostile animals, and even when I thought the coast was clear, a spider attacked me. I would suggest Straya if not for the realism, for the sheer insanity. Stay on the roads, don't go out at night, and always remember, just because you wouldn't eat something, doesn't mean it won't eat you.

It's also a genuine work of expression amidst a zeitgeist of inauthenticity. For that reason alone I recommend it.

I believe the there's just too much shit in this world. Whether it's video games or cereal, there are endless variations on the same few basic concepts. This has made us complacent: we stay squarely in the middle of our comfort zone, scared of the unknown, unwilling to explore the outer rims of this rosebud of life. Well how about for once you strap in, jack off, take a chance and head straight into the danger zone? Welcome to Redaxium, population: you. Perhaps you'll discover yourself there. Perhaps you'll discover that the game sucks. Does it really matter? Only one way to find out.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

I know about the ability to speed up to certain sections by setting a mark; that feature is a) unintuitive in where it decides to place you, b) not explained in the tutorial, and c) unable to skip straight to where you want to let you try a bunch of things in quick succession at a critical point. instead you have to edit these stupid delay values. and on top of that, the way you set the mark to skip to a certain point is by *right-clicking* and this cannot be rebound. finally, there's a little intro thing where another bot pops out when you want to retry, as if the game is trying to force the experience to slow down. think about that: the game whose fun is refinement into an optimized product has major and omnipresent decisions that make the game slow down. I don't know if I'm precisely the target audience, but I don't think an experience with so many seams is going to increase the potential audience. 

this is a frustrating experience that feels like it was made from the ground up on the idea that it'll be more intuitive to have this linear instruction system - but all the most important frustration comes back to that. maybe playtesting went better with that design compared to traditional-style TAS tools; if so, then I suspect this game has two different target audiences: one the concept appeals to, and another the design process was aimed towards. they do not overlap very much.

Love Notes is set in the same universe as Love Bites, with several characters making a reappearance from the first game, though it's not necessary to have played it to understand the story, as it's not a direct continuation. Instead, there are two new main characters (Rachel and Jesse) which the player can choose, both of whom are part of a band whose last gig went seriously awry ... with supernatural consequences.
While they figure out what happened during that gig and deal with the ordinary and supernatural aftermath, the overarching plot scenes are interspersed with the subplot from one of the five available romances, which the player is prompted to choose from a lineup after a certain point in the story. The plot and romance are kept very separate in terms of influence from one to the other, which I didn't mind, as the subplot scenes serve to explore the dynamic between one of the love interests and the main character, as well as the lore of the universe the story is set in.
I played all five subplots, albeit only with Rachel, not with Jesse, and I enjoyed interacting with every romantic interest a lot, as they're all vastly different characters with a variety of personalities. The sprites are lovingly rendered, with beautiful CGs to match (one per love interest and main character, so ten in total), though this is of course also a matter of personal preference. My total playtime comes out at about 6 hours; however, I'm a very fast reader and made frequent use of the skip button on replays (there are two "epilogues" available for each romance, and I wanted to see both). There is no unnecessary padding to the story or subplots, which I appreciate, as more isn't always better.
Overall, I had a great time reading Love Notes, and would definitely recommend that people who liked Love Bites give this VN a chance as well.

- What is with the option that shames you for liking soda? *bursts out laughing* There's nothing wrong with drinking soda.

Edited to add: OK, I've reread this review, and I owe the game devs an apology. My criticisms of this game are wrong. There's nothing wrong with the characters being toxic or morally grey. Having morally grey characters doesn't mean the game devs agree with their characters' actions. My previous review's criticisms were caused by my poor media literacy and comprehension skills. That's not the game devs' fault. 

I'd cautiously recommend this game for anyone who likes villain characters or morally grey characters.

There is one major gamedesign decision, that broke it for me completely: Pitch black rooms.

Even though you get *several* tools to deal with the darkness, none of them give you enough cues to know where the enemy is. And you cannot spam them, because you cannot carry enough energy. Also switching between them takes an amount of time, using them takes an amount of time ... the enemy kills you instantly on sight.

I get what they wanted to do, but this idea of making your game-lifes individuals (not clones of one entity) backfires by not giving the player the tools to value a life (pun by accident). Great game design is enabling the player to make meaningful decissions. 

Ok, this is the major flaw. there are other little things and small bugs I came across which really are not worth mentioning. The game does a great job in condensing the survival alien monster experience into a small package. 
After two hours I was asking myself if I enjoy this game enough to spend more life time on it. The answer was no.

I bought this game recently and had much fun going to the end of its possibilities. It's humble-sized (around 3h for me for 1st playthrough, but please note that I'm pretty experienced in the genre) but very solid in what it does. Solo dev, much respect for the delivered work.

Overall, I enjoyed the game a lot. I initially saw it during one of the summer conferences and was interested by the genre and the art style.
It's exactly what it says it is, stealth elements, light puzzle elements, and mainly adventuring and story-driven, with a heavy dark sci-fi theme that triggered my interest initially. It's also shorter than what I thought back then, during the summer conferences, but when I bought it and saw it was a solo work, I expected a condensed experience. That was conducted well, no feeling of incomplete parts or uncontrolled mechanics.
I played through the game 4 times, partly to see if I could get a deathless run.


MECHANICS AND GAMEPLAY DESIGN

The stealth is moderate but ever present. It goes well with the setting and participates in the theme and the experience. Initially I was annoyed that there existed rooms with no hiding AND no safe beginning (door, etc), but there's a solution to that. I didn't see rooms where the initial placement of enemies would cause an unavoidable fatal encounter, so that's a good point.

The limited room for gadgets was also initially a bit of a hurdle, but there's also strategy for that.

The limited lives of the colonists is a good approach, and so is the respawn at a set point, making sense for story reasons.

A few rooms were frustrating during several playthroughs, until I weighted the decision to use consumables.
The energy consumption is a bit much, but looking back, it sets the challenge bar well, about where it should be. Power recharges are frequent enough between checkpoints to leave strategy options opened.

Overall, the paths options are perhaps a bit too linear. Considering the size of the game it makes sense. The pro of that is that it prevents from feeling overwhelmed by unknown options or feeling unfairly lost. The con is that there are few moments to gain an advantage by exploring, but nonetheless, there are some of them, and they're rewarding enough.

The UI is pretty good, the sound markers are clear, the controls are not overnumerous, controller support is a great addition. The only criticism here is that not knowing what inactive switches will do when activated hurts the strategy planning.

The game options are clearly lacking as there are none, not even sound, display or button mapping. This is lacking a lot in that area.

The save system is... debatable. There is only one save, and it clears after a playthrough. On one hand, this goes with the fact that colonists number is your lives number, so it would not make sense to allow easy reloading. On the other hand, it might clash with the narrative design of having few but key choices. It does not end up breaking the game because it is short, but it'd be a design clash in a longer experience.


NARRATIVE DESIGN, ART AND SETTING

The atmosphere is a strong point of the game. In less that 10 minutes, the immersion is complete, thanks to a short but sufficient tutorial part, and an art style that does an excellent job. The documents found accompany the run at a good pace, including the first documents, helping understanding key points of the situation quickly, then, later, diving into the "how" and "why" some things happen/happened.

The AI speaking also participate greatly in feeling immersed, breaking what would be a lonely experience otherwise, which would carry the risk of feeling disconnected from the events. They help maintain that connection.

The art is gorgeous and 100% hits the target of the dark sci-fi environment. There's attention to details related to the story of where some elements/places are.

The few key choices are interesting.

What may be lacking is a few answers at the end, but we get most of them.


GLITCHES AND ISSUES

I met very few of them, but there are some. None broke my game or my experience, as they are easily avoided after meeting one.

As you have 250 colonists there's plenty of lives if you screw up. The endgame does provide an interesting dilemma for who to save as well.

However, it's a really short game that probably is about two hours to finish for a first play. There's replayability in trying different endings but the game's options only consist of New Game or Continue, and finishing the game deletes your save requiring a new playthrough to see different endings. There's also minimal music in this game (I think only the intro/ending really has anything as the game itself is silent except for ambient sound effects and the short track that plays when a colonist is killed).

If the gameplay still is something you'd enjoy and these negatives don't deter you, then give this one a try.

Warning: this is NOT an rpg. It's a light resource management game combined with a visual novel. There's some parts that were okay, but since the advertising says "flexibility and freedom of TTRPG", I have to give this a not-recommended, because this is certainly not at all what this game is. The devs should seriously reconsider how they pitch this product, because sending people in with false expectations never goes over well. This is especially important for this particular game, because the game it actually is likely won't blow you away either.

To clear things up:
1. The dice rolls they talk about are not really that, they are a set of predetermined numbers for each turn, to be assigned as resources. They might as well not be called dice at all.
2. You can choose some dialogue options during the visual novel sections, but they are largely fake choices that are very inconsequential, all of them leading you back around to the one intended outcome within a paragraph or two. After a while this becomes so obvious that you stop caring about any of the choices.

In short, there is no dice rolling for actions and skills like in a proper rpg, and you have very little agency over your character or narrative direction in the story. This is also made worse by the fact that many of the fake choices you can make, have you think you are choosing a certain attitude or direction (like you typically want to in an rpg), but then the story often just clicks you back into the intended linear narrative and starts describing what your character feels and does and you just sit there thinking "nope, not what I clicked, definitely not what I intended or had in mind", greatly breaking immersion.

The game is also annoyingly PG-12 for a futuristic scifi. Every time that some tension crops up or things seem to take a dark turn, in no time everybody turns out to be cool and friendly and overall too helpful and chummy. Depending on what kind of player you are, this further ruins immersion and tension, or on the other hand, you might just as well call this more of a kids-safe feelgood-game. The writing overall is okayish, and has it's moments, but there's just no sharp edges anywhere, it's pretty dull overall and as the game progresses you start to zone out more and more. (I uninstalled it somewhere in the middle of the extra chapters that come with it, having completely lost interest.) 

So the easy fix here is to tell players what they are actually getting into, in which case I wouldn't have enjoyed it more, but might have given it a recommend for what it is.

TLDR; Looking for an rpg? Don't play this.

[i]Citizen Sleeper[/i] is a well-written visual novel that through simple, yet engaging dice-based gameplay allows players to delve deep into the complicated societal structure of a self-governing spacebase, understand the motives driving different factions and slowly but surely become a part of the community. Even though it’s linear and repetitive gameplay-wise (especially in the late game), resolving the tasks felt purposeful as they lead to good and meaningful monologues (the Sleeper is a born listener, so to speak) allowing us not only to get to know the characters and progress in the story, but also to uncover the relations of power, societal inequalities, and resentments underlying their actions. We need such games, because – very much like Disco Elysium, which was clearly an inspiration for the creators of CS – through a portrayal of individuals they grasp and uncover the structural, political base without jumping to simple conclusions (remaining clearly anticapitalist though, as cyberpunk should be). 

While the storytelling is definitely the strongest asset of CS, the gameplay is also well-designed and gives the player some degree of freedom in terms of following a chosen role. A limited number of dice and supplies required for most actions forces careful planning, especially in the early game: this goes well with the idea of a runaway desperately trying to live to see tomorrow – or rather the next cycle, when the dice reset. The randomness isn’t limiting, as we can find a good use for both high and low dice rolls. The biggest issue comes in the late game, when eventually we have enough resources to stop worrying about survival (hurray) and just start ticking off all quests left. Both the plot and the history of the Eye are still interesting enough to keep the game going, but the dice-based system doesn’t serve as much of a purpose at that moment. The Sleeper does though and the drive to act and help others to achieve their goals, whether it be surviving, escaping or exposing a corrupt leader, is enough to keep the dice rolling and the station spinning for yet another cycle.

Also, you can feed a stray space cat.

I've always found visual novels hit or miss, especially with pacing. Citizen Sleeper hits the mark. The pressure created by the game's time and resource management system keeps you moving forward at a rhythmic pace that never settles.

The setting is gritty, but hopeful. The simple style of the environment art is able to capture a sense of grand scale within the claustrophobic confines of the location. The character's are beautifully rendered, believable, and compelling.

This game is great! I'd give it a solid 9.5/10 for a first playthrough.

* Gameplay-wise, this is essentially the evolved form of a sandbox visual novel, very much in the same vein to me as Disco Elysium. There is no short reaction time based movements or any complex inputs necessary, most of the game is reading and reasoning.

+ The way the gameplay was implemented though, with daily dice, cycles, timers, your body decaying, etc. was all very well done. The game embraces some degree of RNG while still preventing too much frustration, by allowing you to pick and choose where you want to spend your guarantees and where to gamble a bit, all while being well informed enough to allow you be strategic. I think this was one of the best, if not the best, implementation of this type of system I've seen, and makes for very smooth gameplay that does not get in the way of the story being told and instead adds to it.

+ The story and plot progression are very well done, with interesting characters, threads to follow, choices to make, etc. The writing has a distinct style that might not be everyone's cup of coffee, a blend of blunt and somewhat cold, but I was immediately into it, and it was very well executed and consistent in quality throughout. 

+ The music and visuals are amazing. All characters have extremely distinct and well crafted sprites (I love the attention to detail of sprites changing in low-gravity areas!). All the soundtracks are well matched to the current tone of the story and are mixed in and out very well.

+ The game is extremely respectful and inclusive in its perspectives and portrayals of characters and their actions. 

- I think the game is in a way, a bit too easy for its own good. The narrative follows lines of struggling to survive in a hypercapitalist universe, and while you do often have cycle timers giving you anxiety, I really didn't find it difficult to survive or even get rich without exploiting others (as a matter of fact, while actively helping literally everyone in my path), which greatly clashes with the intention of the narrative. Of course, there needs to be a balance between ludonarrative harmony and avoiding player frustration, but I think this balance currently leans a little bit too much towards "avoiding frustration".

- Another balance issue in my opinion is regarding the classes of the game. Interfacing, to me, just felt like simply the best skill to have leveled up a majority of the time, allowing you an easy way to make 20$ per action with any 1 or 2 dice from quite early in the game, and along with initiation and reasoning later on, you can almost always get away with only doing "risky" or "safe" actions instead of the "dangerous" actions often associated with engineering or endurance tasks, while still getting the same or better outcome and benefiting from the best perks. Yes, there are aspects of the skills that can be associated with roleplaying, but leave it to players to optimise the fun out of anything, especially in singleplayer settings.

- The previous two points made me feel little incentive to do another run of the game. I feel like in a way, it was far too easy to see too much of the game at once (both a blessing and a curse, depending on whether you believe in a single playthrough being the ideal number or you want replayability. The class system seems to encourage the latter), because it was easy to 'game' the systems and get a lot of access to resources in not too many cycles. Of course, I could make different choices to get different outcomes, or go for the few drives I failed to complete in the early game, but then I'd just feel like I was repeating so much of what I'd already done for so little unseen content that I just didn't want to go ahead with it. I probably will replay it again in a few years when I forget about the details, but until then...

It does a good first impression, but in the late-game, it wanes off dramatically. Why? Listing some of the points that feel most objective to me:

- Agency over the sleeper switches vastly: In some story parts you get to decide how the sleeper feels and reacts, in others it's like the sleeper is a completely separate character, and does that for you.
- Drive completion: The cycle system is very precise and well thought out, but regarding whether a drive is completed now or not and rewards a skill point, it is not.
- Lategame waste: After completing the sole "main story line", engagement is gone because there is zero urgency and a lot of things feel pointless.
- Dialogue impactfulness: Too much of the dialogue does not influence the story or outcomes enough, and is purely fluff.
- Lack of surprises: No new options/choices were realized regarding new choices or options appearing if opting to do stuff that do not obviously tell the player what they result in. I think that's a huge missed opportunity.

Overall, I think that citizen sleeper does not tie-in enough with the gameplay to make the story, even with its whimsicalness, really float well. It has not fulfilled my expectations overall, hence I cannot recommend it.

The solid soundtrack will keep your attention throughout the games modest stay.

Look for new possibilities in the stars beyond, or see what you can make when you're on the Eye. At first, I found that if I was given the choice about leaving to the belt at any time, especially during the last 3 episodes, I would have taken it. However, the more drives I discovered and the more people I met, it led to me making something from myself. After a time, my operator found it was free for the first time, without the tracker and without hunters looking for them. And if given the chance at that time, I would've left, but the person at that time.... would've hesitated. They were turning a hobble into a home near a noodle shop. They were seeing a blossoming relationship between two former enemies, they were discovering the lush and gorgeous scenery that was the greenway. And with that, it led to tough decisions. It hurt me seeing Lem & Mina, but it helped knowing that they will find something better out there. It was stressful watching bliss leave, but knowing she will do better brought me a sliver of joy. I realized at the end of my first playthrough, I decided to persist through the storm, to be a bit stubborn. Because I had the choice to....after having a tracker in my head and dealing with all sorts of things. I had the freedom to do what I wanted to do, regardless of the consequence. I really enjoyed my playthrough of Citizen Sleeper even though I was desiring a bit more from it. It's a narrative heavy game so there's a lot of reading, but the writing is very well done. At first, I didn't think much of the game, and the first few "cycles", or in-game days, felt confusing, harsh, unwelcoming. But then you realize that this is how it's supposed to feel, as you immerse into this world that words cannot describe. It's beauty lies in its stories, it's characters, between yellow-lit apartment blocks, intertwined in the mass of data which this space station opens for you, bit by bit, sucking you up in a whirlpool of events, all spinning around in "The Eye".

It has been a very long time since a story was so captivating for me, leaving me deep in thought after each questline came to its open (or not so much) end, wandering how my decisions affect the world, the people around me, everything. As threads and paths unfolded before me, I thought carefully about every spoken word, every silent glance... because I actually cared. A lot.

All those friends and foes you make along the way, trying to find your place in this ever-spinning world, they feel almost too real. After a while, you realize they also had to make tough calls, sacrifice a lot to get where they are, that they are surviving, just like you, and that they are vulnerable, sometimes suspicious, sometimes untruthful, greedy... but that actually makes them that much more human to you. This game never forgets to remind you that this world (much like our own) is full of individual people, and they all have a right for a future, even if you won't be there to see it. I will keep this review spoiler-free, so just know that during the playthrough, that world made my soul move to places I have long deemed forgotten. 

Simple text on a screen made me nostalgic, peaceful, sad, angry, anxious, it made me sit in silence, processing, thinking, calculating the possible twists and turns, the outcomes of my decisions. It made me smile both from warmth and sorrow, and made me shed a tear from joy and pain. But what it never did - it never made me disappointed.  

And even if the gameplay might be confusing at first, or feel too limiting - please, give this space station a few more cycles, and you will see that failure sometimes is also a step in the right direction, and sometimes this is just how life's supposed to be, and that's okay.

P.S. The art style of this game is very unique and reminds me somehow of Miyazaki movies, set in cyberpunk future. Turns out it's not only the art style, but the ideas too, for example, of human relations with technology and nature (yes, even in the vast black voids of space). The soundtrack also one of the best I have ever listened to, it sounds just right at every step of this amazing journey.

P.P.S. They even managed to smuggle a cat there, yay! :3

Reditum is fairly basic and has some control issues, like laser reflectors moving slightly out of place sometimes when you rotate, or the problem of only being able to select them when not facing their mirror side. But I like how you can instantly fall onto a block you placed in mid-air by facing the floor you're standing on, and flipping gravity from there. This lets you get into some useful vantage points, necessary sometimes because the map (M) can be quite confusing to look at. There unfortunately isn't a lot of visual variety in the environments, and only one piece of repetitive music. But these flaws for me are discounted by a very clever penultimate puzzle level, which asks you to use the directional blocks in a thoughtful way. If you like laser beam puzzles and block-stacking, get this in a sale.

I am a huge supporter of Revills Games and own all of them loving the original artworks throughout their games and this one is no exception. However some notes on the game-play both positive and negative from 9 hours of game-play so far. 

The positive; the artwork is as usual beautiful and I really loved getting to chose my character at the beginning. Gave it a rpg feel to a solitaire game. That is a very neat addition. Also the mix of game-play within the game (not just solitaire but match 3 and a lite card battler as well)! The soundtrack is good but their is no voice overs. That can be good or bad. I know in Chef Solitaire there is a voice over for the main character which I find was really well done and added to the game but since there is choose your own character at the beginning I am guessing this is why it's just text based. 

There is also lots of cool power ups to buy and as you progress earning coins is not that much of a struggle. 

The negative; I found it frustrating that there was no buying of jokers or wilds. The end game as you go along gets really challenging for some levels and the deck you start out on (the number of cards) just doesn't stretch far enough if what your dealt is bad (and can be numerous times). There is no way to buy more cards to add to your deck as well so your stuck at the number of cards given at the start. Also no re-dealing of the deck.

This brings a lot of frustration to some levels I can assure you. So at times I took a break from the game when I could not get by certain levels due to a lack of cards in the deck and not being able to buy wilds or jokers. 

* There is a power up you can buy that gives you a wild card to use as needed but it has to recharge as you go.  Note that in this game the wild card is actual what most solitaire games refer to as a "joker". Wilds in this game are available (look like goblin cards with designated numbers on them). Those of you familiar with solitaire will understand what I mean by the difference. 

So keep the negatives in mind as they can be frustrating but overall I do enjoy the game and supporting the company. I just really wish if anything could change it would be to be able to re-shuffle the deck (not to confuse the power up for shuffling the cards on the board). That improvement alone would ease a lot of frustration in some levels. 

The prices on Revills Games are always good value for your money so I recommend checking out their library. I have reviews as well on many of their other games. Hopefully you find this review helpful and game on! 🎮

(https://www.lexico.com/definition/the) this is because articles are determiners and also called "function words". but adjectives are not function words. then there is even a special type of article called "zero article", but i would not say zero article is adjective too, not to mention there is no such thing called "zero adjective" existing. in tradition, articles are considered independent from adjective, not just "a special type of adjective". also numerals are qualifiers or determiner. i think numerals can be roughly called adjectives (? but i am not sure), but articles not. because adjectives can be predicate (for example "pretty" in the sentence "she is pretty") but articles can not be predicate. also adjectives can be negative (for example in the sentence: she is NOT pretty) but because articles can not be predicate, it can not be negative neither.

I know I barely started, but this game is really fun! I've wishlisted this since I love the artstyle and the fun approach to learning English grammar. As a second language, it's always good to brush up on those forgotten lesson I was taught back in school.

The grammar explanation is very well put together. It's simple, it has examples, and doesn't ramble. 
It can be daunting at first, but once I understood what I need to look for, it gets "easier". 
I say that in quotes, because before you can purchase a hint item, you'll be clicking and losing stamina if you don't know what you need to find.

In the long run it might be overwhelming to rush through the levels because I'll need to remember so many grammar rules, so I decided to take it slow. There was a review level where you battle for promotion (which I think is a neat idea!).
You can also check your work and compare your performance with other people (though atm, there's not much data collected since it's just launched?)

The music is very relaxing, reminiscent of the jazzy Eat, Cook, Delicious. You can buy more songs with the salary you earned from work. 
I like that the articles you check seem related to each other. They reappear on other articles (I'm looking at you, Judge Smail) which made me invested in the story.

Personally, I love finding the little Indonesian details, like Martabak, and Wahyu the intern. Indonesian gaming is definitely on the rise, but it's always nice to find my culture referenced in a game I'm enjoying.

I do wish I can replay a level to practice my understanding of that particular grammar rule, or for those who are more competitive, an online high score arcade-like section. But boy, that promotion battle was enough to make me sweat, not to mention having to compete with real people!

If you're learning English, try this out! If you're already an English speaker, why not challenge your grammar skills with this?

I'm a little concerned at the spelling and grammar mistakes that pop-up now and then. The game itself needs a good proof-reading, by an experienced editor. However, I must say that the game itself is engaging, for what it is. 

Reporting what you find will definitely help the devs.

Edit:

Having pretty much finished the game, I'm in two minds. It seems like the purpose of the game - to teach core English grammar concepts - is at cross purposes with the developers relative grammatical skill.

Until I played this game, I considered myself to have an excellent practical knowledge of grammar, despite not being able to tell a dangling modifier from a dangling participle. After 9 hours of playing this game; I've not only confirmed both of those facts, but have also come to the realisation that I despise, loathe, abhor and detest having to identify the different parts of a sentence. Fortunately for my continued sanity, the game balances out reviewing documents looking for specific types of grammar (difficult) with correcting incorrect grammar (easier). I was terrible with the former (at least the game keeps you well supplied with candy and coffee from items you buy for your apartment, which help to keep your mood and your stamina up, in turn, as wrong answers can bring both down significantly), however the latter was easy enough for me that I somehow managed to squeak by a pass on many levels I would otherwise have failed. (Oh look, a run-on sentence!) Also fortunately, the promotion fights get easier as the levels progress with the opponent often doing so badly you win even if you only get one or two answers right. That's something I hope the developers don't change as it makes it possible to advance at a reasonable pace through the game. If it hadn't been for that, I would have become very frustrated with this game very quickly. 

Although the grammatical side of the game won't be to everyone's taste, this is still a good game with a lot of positive aspects. The music is very good, the art is interesting to look at and the gameplay is very straightforward with plenty of detailed information for each level. The characters you interact with (plus the player character) are all interesting and have distinct and quirky personalities. Which makes it a little disappointing that you don't get much interaction with any of them. 

The game is a little light on plot and story details as it's focused on teaching the player the rules of grammar. Most of the game revolves around checking grammar in documents, rather than providing players with a realistic life/work simulation or a deep and involved storyline. That said, there is a plot. It's interesting and it runs through most of the levels, however the resolution lets it down slightly as it's very sudden and also very brief. The outcome of the plot comes in the form of a single monologue by one of the other characters that only gives a brief overview of what happens. You also don't get to see any of the other characters after that, so it feels like you don't get complete closure for every plot point or character.

All in all, I found the game to be fun but not in the way most games are. This game isn't about the story, the characters or the daily work/home life simulated in it. They're secondary. The focus of the game is on learning grammar and stretching your brain with grammar-related challenges. I therefore recommend this game for people who are interested in grammar or in learning about grammar, players who consider themselves up for such a mentally challenging game and also players who want a story that's light on plot and the usual game elements that make up a life simulation game, while still being entertaining. 

Because it is entertaining. The aspect that kept me playing until the end of the game was the contents of the documents the player character gets to review. They range from being confusing through mildly amusing to a few that I couldn't stop laughing over. The writing style in the game; from the documents to the character dialogue, down to the descriptions on the shop items, they're all brilliantly done. 

One last note: the game took me roughly 9 hours to complete however I already knew the basics of grammar going into the game. For non-English speakers or people who haven't learned about grammar before, this game will likely take longer.
