Summary: Afterlove EP has a compelling story with an intriguing and complex set of chearacters, but its narrative experience is marred by somewhat clunky gameplay mechanics. It is an admirable first foray into the narrative game genre for Pixelnesia. With the lessons learned from developing this game, I have no doubt their next endeavour will be an even better experience.

[u] Story [/u]
The story doesn't shy away from difficult topics of love and loss. The grief and frustration felt by the main character bleeds into every facet of the story and its cast of characters. You feel not only for Rama, who is trying to move on despite his uniquely unusual set of circumstances, but also for his friends-slash-bandmates, Tasya and Adit, who felt helpless and abandoned after being cut off for a year, effectively putting the band they worked so hard for on a sudden hiatus. The end of the game doesn't show Rama's resolution with his grief, but rather (at least in the good ends) shows the real start of his healing process and reconciliation with his friends.

The three romance options, similarly, each provide different perspectives that help Rama to come out of his shell and move forward. Each of routes delightfully interweaves their unique struggles and experiences within the context of Jakarta, and the story is made all the more engaging for it. Whether it's Regina trying to succeed through less-than-savoury practices in the modelling industry; Satria's orientation as a gay man and the hardships of being a part of the LGBT community; or the overstressed realities of Mira and many youths like her who live in the capital. 

Dare I say, the dark horse in the story is Rama's late girlfriend Cinta, who now supposedly resides in his head. Throughout the game it's never made clear if she actually is taking up residence in his mind somehow or if she is a figment of his grief made manifest. As unsure as her true nature are also her intentions for Rama. At times, it feels as if she wants him to move toward the future with his band and his friends. At others, she seems desperate to nail him down to the shackles of the past.

All the above points makes Afterlove EP's story shine as a captivating story that intertwines the local Jakartan context with the familiar themes of loss, grief, and moving on.  

[u] Gameplay Mechanics [/u]
The mechanics make it somewhat difficult to experience the game's otherwise rich story. The game uses a Persona-esque system where the player can do up to two "actions" each day. This is how the player chooses which character they want to pursue a romance with, and generally which character they want to get to know more. However, the strict requirements of reaching a route's good end leaves little in the way for natural exploration. Furthermore, getting to the good ending isn't intuitive and many players going through the game the first time most likely won't reach it if they are organically exploring the world and interacting with its characters. For example, the street performing activity, while an interesting part of the game, becomes completely superfluous and unnecessary due to it taking up an activity slot would need to be otherwise used on a romanced character to achieve their good end.

A player must actively spend their time on the romanced character and find all of Rama and Cinta's memories first, and leave everything as secondary. Thus, it forces the player to adopt a minmax approach right from the beginning and leaves no room for natural exploration or player autonomy. This limitation goes against the seemingly exploratory layout of the game itself, where you are presented with a vibrant city to explore, yet your options to achieve a satisfactory conclusion relies on denying that very same exploration. With later routes, I found myself doing exactly this, which brought me out of the immersion of being able to naturally choose where I wanted to spend my time and "gameifying" Rama's own mental recovery. 

The text skip system can also feel a little slow. As stated before, a casual player naturally exploring the game for the first time is likely to encounter a bad end, and they may feel dissuaded from trying the other routes if reaching a good end is both unintuitive and slow to navigate through. 

[u] Other considerations [/u]
I was surprised that the game chose to use English voice acting instead of Indonesian though this was not a dealbreaker by any means. However, I feel the game could benefit from a codex-like system, as there are some Indonesian words used when reading in English. If only so other non-native speakers could also appreciate the "Bang Sat" pun. 

Other QoL considerations could include lighter or darker text to indicate whether text has been read before, more save slots, and the game showing the newest saved game rather than just the last slot in the list. 

While the rhythm minigame is technically considered a gameplay element, I am including it here as they do not directly affect the narrative experience. Regarding the rhythm minigame, while fun for the first few times, does overstay its welcome on repeated playthroughs of the game. So I do appreciate the ability to skip it. I did find at times the minigame to be unintuitive, with button presses synced up to the drums or bass rather than Rama's instrument of the guitar.

Over the last five years I have become a big fan of indie games made in Indonesia. This eventually led me to follow Fahmi on social media. I was a big fan of his previous works and he was always kinda my gateway into following a lot of South east Asian developers. Though I never interacted with him directly aside from a few twitter engagements, learning of his passing made me want to heavily follow the development of his final game, his swan song, afterlove ep. I am very proud and thankful of everyone involved for seeing it through and he would be too. Now, to talk about the game itself.
This game is a visual novel first and I think its important for you to know that going into it. The majority of the game is reading. The music game play is a mini game and not the primary focus. Speaking of the music game play, that is where I will start since its the main element that shakes things up from time to time. It is quite simplistic, but polished. Part of me wishes that it was maybe a little more in depth and had more direct feed back for performing well, but it serves its purpose and is still enjoyable. Also, the tracks provided by Indonesian indie band L'Alphalpha are all very memorable and easy on the ears.
Onto the art and music of the game, both are simply fantastic. Aside from L'Alphalpha's contributions there is also a very enjoyable soundtrack that fits the vibe of the game perfectly. A lot of upbeat tracks for the heart of Jakarta and plenty of moody guitar tracks that fit the lead character Rama quite well. The art is all based on the style of a Indonesian artist called soyatu. The art is all very colorful and expressive and you will probably be able to instantly tell anything she ever works on for the rest of your life due to how distinct her artwork is. 
The real meat of the game is the story and characters. One very important thing is that you play as Rama. Rama is NOT a self insert. You have some loose control over his actions but you are not Rama, and sometimes he will act in ways that you may not like. He is experiencing significant grief and stress in his life and sometimes acts irrationally in ways that can be frustrating, You probably would not want to hang out with Rama in real life, at least how he is in most of the story. But its all in service of his story as a man experiencing grief without any healthy coping skills and I really enjoyed that they were not afraid to make him be kinda unpleasant sometimes. The character Cinta is somewhat confusing at first. She is the voice of the lead characters deceased girlfriend in his head, but often the things she says encourage his worst habits. Speaking of Cinta, your feelings on her will make or break the game for you probably, because she talks all the time. Like actually all the time. And she's also the only voice acted character. Watching the memories you find around the map mad me like her significantly more than I think I would have if I were to just have played through the story by itself. The rest of the characters are set up into a few groups. Your band members, Adit and Tasya serve as the primary conflict pushing the story forward. They are by far my favorite characters in the game due to them sticking up for themselves when our main character is sometimes, not that cool to hang out with. They are very human feeling in their writing and even though you spend less time with them individually compared to others, they feel very fleshed out. They really FEEL like old friends. Then there is your Therapist Dr. Santi and the local coffee store owner Kauk mus. They are both characters outside of the games main story events that still play a very big role in Rama's development and I enjoyed visiting both of them whenever they were on the map. The final batch of characters is the friends or potential romance options if you choose to pursue that. Mira, Satria, and Regina. All three of them have unique stories and endings with Rama depending on a lot of factors and decisions you make. They are quite different from each other and have distinct personalities and routes and relationships with Rama as well as the other characters in the story. 
The story itself changes quite a bit depending on your choices. There is a TON of endings, some of them where everyone is happy and some of them that are quite honestly, brutal and depressing. Due to the short run time of the game, this provides a lot of replay value. At its core, the story is about grief, difficulty adjusting to change and the passage of time, and letting go/moving forward. The main two plots are the potential falling out of your band due to friction with your friends over your behavior, and letting go of Cinta and potentially moving on to find someone new. 
I have a few cons to list before I close out this review. Cinta might talk a little TOO much sometimes. I like her, but it is kinda distracting at times from the conversation at hand with how often she commentates. I wish you spent more time with Adit or Tasya individually. I would have liked to see them more in general. Conditions for how to get the different endings are not very clear. I think this is an issue because some of the bad endings are pretty brutal and I think might turn off a new player from trying again if they happen to get them.
I didn't talk about the events in the story much on purpose because I think this game is best experienced blind. But, I did enjoy it very much. It has the heart of a Fahmi game and it felt great to play it finally after following it closely for years after his tragic passing. I was not disappointed at all, had a great time, and I look very much forward to anything these developers do in the future through pixelnesia or as individuals.

I bought clown town 1443 because the developer was in a random unrelated Twitch stream dropping Steam keys out of nowhere. That kind of guerrilla marketing appealed to me and so I decided to purchase the game instead, and that isn't just me coping for not being fast enough to snag one of the keys despite how generous the developer was in giving them.
As a big Friday Night Funkin' appreciator I have a soft spot for games that are basically love letters to Flash classics, and this game is very clearly wearing its Trials influences on its sleeve. There's a bit more to it than just a straight clone, as this game features a bit more depth to its mechanics, such as a heat bar that must be managed. You're free to bump around generally as much as you want, but if you overheat from too much acceleration you temporarily lose control of your vehicle. Crash in this state, and you'll have to restart the level again.
The design of the game is surrealist and dreamlike overall, with ladybugs that poop eggs and meteors randomly falling from the sky, with a final level that isn't. It feels very early Flash in its appearance and gameplay, but there's a competence there behind its simple visuals. It's very difficult in parts and requires some careful timing and maneuvering at times, and some of the obstacles are very devious in their placement, with some levels requiring careful maneuvering while being chased by a creature. However, it is very short. I beat the whole game in under an hour which means if you are twice as bad as me you'll still most likely be able to request a refund. However, I'm only stating that as a measure of the length of the game, and ask that if you do buy the game to recognize it for the short experience that it is, and beating the main game also unlocks an endless mode that will give you more if you absolutely love the core mechanics. This isn't an asset flip or fake scam game, the developer did put work in here and wants to pay homage to a style of game design that has soulful limitations built into its foundation.
The only thing I'd like to note is that for a sequel or update or whatever gets planned to be done with this game, the developer could expand their procedural generation of the endless mode to include terrain. I made it to the mid-800s on my score and it was mostly a flat plain with obstacles randomly placed in different configurations. It is very difficult as well and requires you to adjust to random obstacles on the fly while being chased by a bird, but more variety is always good.
This game makes me feel nostalgic for the old days of flash games as a kid. Will definitely play this more down the road when I can fit a game in on a lunch break.

Breakdown of Pros/Cons of this game:

Pros:
1. Varied gameplay. You can fight bosses, grind for resources, recruit an army of servants to grind for you, use a variety of weapons and armor, build the castle of your dreams, raid towns, explore the world, etc.

2. Great Graphics. Game is beautiful but not overtaxing on system requirements.

3. Great game play - The story moves along and the game holds your hand at first on what to do, then from there its easy to figure out the rest. get basic gear, find nearest boss, kill them, unlock new abilities/gear, build your castle and build out your gear, rinse and repeat from level 1 to level 90. 

4. Great difficulty that scales with online, plus a hard mode for those that want it.

5. Customization - Great character builder, lots of abilities, lots of weapons, lots of items to wear and use. Guns, bows, swords, spears, sythes, blades, etc. Blood types and blood quality are important.

6. Boss Battles - 50 bosses are in the game, every one of them is 100% unique in how they fight, the abilities they use, and how you should approach them. One battle is not the same. Bosses scale with the number of players fighting to keep it even. Hard mode adds additional challenges.

7. Base building - Want a basic plain base, great! Want to make it unique/decorate it? Great. You can do whatever you want. small tiny base, or giant castle with 5 floors. Your mind is the limit.

Cons:

1. Some bosses are very difficult while others are very easy. Dracula has been kicking my butt for a month now and I still cannot beat him but I still play/love the game.

2. Final area of the map needs to be more unique, you get access to it mid-game and when you circle back for end game content you already know what to expect so it feels a bit underwhelming.

3. Servants need to be able to do more than just missions and defend your base, but are a great way to avoid grinding for resources.

Overall:

[h1] V Rising: A Vampiric Masterpiece Held Back by Its Late Game[/h1]

V Rising is an incredible blend of survival, ARPG, and vampire fantasy, delivering an experience that feels both unique and polished. The aesthetic is absolutely stunning, from the gothic landscapes to the eerie lighting that truly makes you feel like a powerful creature of the night.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is its fluid combat. The movement, attacks, and abilities all feel incredibly smooth, making every battle a joy to engage in. The boss designs are top-tier, each offering creative mechanics that keep fights engaging, especially when played on hard mode. The extra ability you gain adds a new layer of strategy, and bosses even shift their tactics when facing multiple players, making co-op fights feel fresh and dynamic.

Beyond PvE, the PvP and raiding systems are excellent. The skill ceiling is high, rewarding players who master their movement, abilities, and timing. Every encounter feels like a test of skill rather than just raw stats, making victories incredibly satisfying.

That said, V Rising struggles with late-game content. Once you've taken down the major bosses and built your castle to its peak, there isn’t much to keep you engaged long-term. The game could really benefit from an infinite dungeon or a boss rush mode, something that lets players continue challenging themselves while grinding for better rewards. A risk-reward system where you gamble loot to push further would add a lot of replayability.

Overall, V Rising is a fantastic game with fluid combat, amazing boss fights, and great PvP. It just needs more endgame content to keep players hooked. If the devs expand on that, this could easily become one of the best long-term survival games out there.

Artists of Fortune: DIstant Worlds is a freemium color by number game that has 20 free images and 180 paid images.  The overall aesthetic of the game is pretty nice, and overall, the game looks pretty polished.

I'll list the pros and cons here:

Pros:
20 free images that are of a variety of sizes, and each have a unique aesthetic artistic quality to them that makes them really nice to look at.
The usual color by number power of the fill bucket is available in this game for those of you that would rather not spend hours working on one image, along with two unique and somewhat interesting powers, including the Rainbow Brush that lets you literally paint in any color while it is active, and the other one which blows up and colors in a selected area of the coloring field.  I don't plan on using any of these powers in my quest to finish all the images.
All paid DLC give a very good amount of content for their price.

Neutral:
Music and sounds are kind of meh for me.  I'll more than likely play the entire game with them off.  Not going to ding you for this, though.
Paid DLC isn't available in a bundle for a small percentage off.  Even if I could buy all 9 DLC for 10% off, I'd do it in a heartbeat.  Not going to ding you for this, either.
Story is kind of bland.  Not going to ding you for this due to the fact that this is a color by number game and not a story driven game.

Cons:
I've found a number of images that don't utilize a large number of colors.  You can easily get a lot more detailed images if you use more colors, and while it would take more time to develop these images, the flipside is that us players get much more interesting images to color in.  Please consider this for future DLCs, especially for the largest images.
Paid DLC is required to get all achievements.  This is a pet peeve of mine, and while I don't mind buying the paid DLC, you might want to consider possibly excluding these in future games as it can be somewhat aggravating for some players.
I absolutely hate the Scientist achievements.  I've found that forcing perfection is never a good thing in any game.
No free XL images.  If you provide just one or two free XL images, I bet you'd get more people buying the DLC.

Overall, a great color by number game, but could still use a little work on the image color variety in the future.  8/10 will recommend.

I've been following and supporting this game/developer for years. I would always periodically check their discord to see if there were any updates and how development was going. When I saw the free demo was out, I was super excited to play. As far as a demo, the game looked decent and I was under the impression that since it was a demo, the full release would be packed with more to do, explore, updated graphics, and complete. After months of forgetting about this game, I saw it released and bought it. I don't remember the price I bought it at but it is currently listed for $20.00 USD. It's been sitting in my library for a while and I just decided to play it today.

This game took me just under 2 hours to play. Based on what the game offers, the play-time, and the anticipation for such a long-awaited game, I would not recommend this game at all.

Pros:

1. Cozy-esque. The game has a specific style which I like. Most games do not have this art style and I commend the developer for her creativity and uniqueness. 

2. The music is simple, but enjoyable. This music definitely fits the vibe/aesthetic of the game and adds to the foresty feel. 

3. Some of the dialogue is cute and unique to each NPC, they each have their own personalities and wishes.

Cons:

1. This game is primarily a walking simulator. Be prepared to do lots of back-and-forth, jumping, and gliding. Most of my time spent in this game was travelling to all of the areas in the map.

2. The quests are lack-luster, repetitive, and unfulfilling. Almost all of the tasks in-game are not related to the main objective whatsoever. You will be running back and forth to complete tasks that give you little-to-no satisfaction or reward. 

3. Filled with bugs and glitches. I've ran into many bugs where upon gaining a steam quest completion and a mail stamp, I was unable to move and would have to re-talk to the NPC to gain movement back. Furthermore, certain obstacles such as rocks and leaves are not able to be walked on, leading to many falls and searching for alternate routes to get up to where you need to go. 

4. Clashing art styles and cheap renders/models. The art style when talking to an NPC is cute and unique. The game itself is lackluster. The models used are cheap and bland with just simple textures over them. This makes the game feel very flat and 'cheap'. Most developers create models with the textures in mind to create a more 3D effect and to add to the realism. These two styles clash with each other and make the game feel incomplete and half done. 

5. Little-to-no story-line and feels incomplete. Most of the quests follow small stories, where groups of NPCs follow a certain story or quest with each other. The overall main objective does not relate to the rest of the tasks you complete, besides the end quest. This makes me feel like my time was wasted doing these unnecessary small storylines as they have little-to-no relation to the bigger objective, which is to deliver the final letter. 

**(Spoiler of endgame ahead, read at your own discretion)**

6. Speaking of the final letter, the ending is disappointing and you are left on an unnecessary cliff hanger. The final task, which is mentioned throughout the whole game, is to deliver a letter to Greg, the bear. After completing every other task and collecting all of the mail stamps, you are tasked to go to the highest area of the map, jump and glide to the new location, make your way up to the top to deliver the final letter. Upon getting there, Greg is sleeping and you are unable to deliver the final letter. You go down to Janet to ask about how to deliver the final letter to Greg and pretty much get a "oh well, can't win them all, good job tho" response. This was a big slap in the face for me, as I spent almost 2 hours aiming to complete this simple task just to have the game leave it on a cliffhanger and incomplete. After that, there's a credit screen and you are lead to the title screen. The final mail stamp is unobtainable and your letter task for Greg remains incomplete. This is a huge disappointment considering the whole premise of the game is to deliver this final letter.

She last talked in the official Mail Time discord in 2023. It has been almost two years of no updates or questions answered regarding the final and most important task of the game. This is a huge disappointment and inconsiderate to the many people who spent their hard-earned money supporting this incomplete and sloppy game.

很棒的游戏，剧情很出彩，可惜卖相不是很好，我第一次看到也觉得很简陋，但是玩了之后发现这游戏大大出乎我的意料，如果对赛博朋克题材不反感，喜欢对社会和正义问题进行思考的玩家千万不要错过，里面一些不经意的选择也能在后面开花结果，可惜游戏应该是因为成本问题导致没做完，很期待dlc或续作
优点：
1.故事真的很棒，人物都很鲜活，很有生活气息，能对话的基本没有无用的人物，而且伏笔巨多，细节很好。里面的冲突也写的很好，有些人也不是朴素价值观中认为的正义邪恶，不是勇者打倒恶龙的童话故事。里面讲赛博朋克那种资产阶级基本垄断，底层人民苦苦求生的氛围描写的很好，也抛出了很多问题，里面不同的人也有不同的看法，甚至没有明显的倾向，你可以做出你自己的选择，证明你自己的意志，可惜就是明显有很多伏笔没能够回收。期待后续故事。
2.平时的bgm无功无过，但是一到关键时刻，尤其是结局，bgm一响直接把情绪调动起来，彷佛玩家也置身于其中，搞的玩完之后怅然若失。
3.这故事你无法左右大局，但是你能做出你的选择，沉默也是一种选择，后面会根据你的选择产生不同的结果，反馈很足，你确实能做些什么，也确实做到了什么，对其他人善意以待，其他人也会回馈善意，真的很不错。里面人也能因为你而改变，互相敌视的人可以放下偏见，幼稚的人能更成熟一点。不过感觉还是为了故事牺牲了一些，由来已久的敌视仅仅几天就化干戈为玉帛，不过考虑到故事仅仅发生在几天之内也无伤大雅。
4.程芳太棒了，太完美了！
缺点：
1.故事明显没完整，快出后续啊！只要能出后续，我什么都会做的。
2.战斗部分做的实在一般，好在难度不高，战斗动作基本全是重复，而且接近动作接攻击我用手柄很容易错过攻击时机，玩的有点难受，特定几场司徒的战斗动画还挺帅的。建议后续士杰战斗直接判定一次就能击倒对方得了，毕竟战斗全是重复，玩多了容易厌烦。
3.存档机制是有点难受的，只有自动存档，好在一般还够用，如果选了不满意的选项一些只要回档几分钟就行了，但是还是不够人性化，而且回到之前的故事节点会直接砍掉原本的存档，建议出一个回到之前的故事节点时产生一个新存档，而不是直接覆盖老存档。

This is a no-BS action roguelike that both doesn't waste your time, abstains from gimmicks, rewards skill and doesn't overstay its welcome. 

Combat is similar to Dead Cells but with a focus on playing a character and their respective playstyle instead of a weapon. Moves are on cooldown and all have uses depending on the situation. Red, the posterboy/protagonist has a short-ranged projectile, a dash, a ground pound that serves as both a gap closer and armor breaking tool, and a super that buffs him. The moveset is smaller than I'd like, but as they're designed well, this is more of a nitpick than anything. The dash is on a really long cooldown, so you'll have to get used to jumping to avoid attacks sometimes. Both enemies and bosses are fair and don't cheat you with gimmicks or cheap hitboxes. The bosses might feel a bit basic for some, but I appreciate that they follow the same rules you do and don't have ridiculous amounts of health even without damage items.

Items are done very differently here compared to other games in the genre. Your main sources of items comes from a chest that may or may not spawn, a shop you can use money to buy from a pool of four choices, boss chests and a combo counter. With the game being a short, easily digestible experience, you should expect to cap out at about 6-8 items per run. Each item will have a passive ability and a flat stat bonus, making even the most unwanted items for your character have some use. If you're tired of playing action roguelikes with a ton of trash items that only have a use if you find the others that synergize with them, you'll feel at home here. There is still decision making to be had, but you're also not waiting the entire game for a chance to get the item combo you want.

Machina Blade advertises being fully skill-based, but that's only partially true. While that is true for the enemy and boss design, the combo/kill counter adds an insane amount of RNG to your runs. A kill counter of 20 will spawn an item, which in a game that has less items per run with each individual one being more impactful that usual, this is huge. The problem is the level generation adds a large layer of RNG to whether you can even get to 20 kills, regardless of your skill to actually get the counter that high. While the gameplay loop of getting to 20 kills for a huge boost in power works in concept, the timer is far too strict, and more often than not you'll lose the combo due to the level generation and enemy spawn RNG than your actual skill. What's worse is that another item spawns at 30, but the combination of the aforementioned issues and the timer going down even faster past 20 means you may never get that far. Dead Cells does this better with there being no timer for your kill streak, but here you're fighting the enemies, your own skill and, most frustratingly, level and spawn RNG. If this is fixed, the gameplay loop would feel even better, but for now it's the biggest flaw in this game's design.

Persistent elements involve starting items and I believe a few more added to the pool, but this game is serious about not diluting the item pool and making each item purchase/pickup feel like it matters. It's a good design philosophy that I'd like to see more action roguelikes pick up. Overall this game is great if you want a no-BS experience and short runs, but it's definitely lacking in content. It feels complete but also feels like the original plan to launch in early access could have gone better. You will likely clear the game within the first few hours, but the gameplay is so solid that you'll keep coming back for more. The asking price is fair considering the light content, but hopefully more is added. If the aforementioned design flaws are fixed, I could see this becoming one of my favorites in the genre. For now, it's got a great foundation.

Been following this one on Twitter for a while now, so I've been excited to get my hands on it.

This game has it where it counts but falls short in other categories.

You can tell the focus was on the core gameplay, which is a lot of fun. The three characters all feel diverse with unique playstyles and satisfying skills & mechanics for each. You're rewarded for performing well in combat and all bosses and enemy types feel fair. That's exactly what I wanted out of this game and it delivers in spades.

Balancing may need some work. I've cleared two runs at this point, one with Red and one with Valerie, and both times were complete stomps. I've barely seen what the third or final boss do because they got melted so quickly. The thesis statement is that "what matters most is your skill", but after getting a couple items it started to feel a lot more like I was overpowering enemies rather than outplaying them. 

The UI is very basic, with some very odd decisions like having no Options or Exit Game on the Main Menu. You need to enter a run and pause the game to access those. Skills do not show their assigned button on the hotbar, which tripped me up a lot at the beginning. The camera could use some work as well: not a fan of having it yanked away towards chests when they're onscreen, and for how much you move downwards to progress in some areas, you can't see very far below your character, which can lead to damage if you're not taking it slow (which the game disincentivizes you from doing, via timed killstreaks). The ability to move the camera and look around would be much appreciated.

There is no story, info about the game's universe, or voiceover. The art and animations are nice, but your only window into the characters' identity is whatever their respective weapons/playstyle are referencing. Same goes for all the items: it's fun to have items that reference other properties, other roguelites do it all the time, but when almost every single item is a pastiche of something from another piece of media, it loses its lustre. But that's mostly just a pet peeve.

There seems to be very little content. There's only the one gamemode that takes you through three stages, each with a respective boss, and then a final boss. So far, the only unlocks I've been getting are more starting items, which just make it easier to snowball. Multiplayer will probably extend your playtime if you can rope some friends in, but I don't see myself sinking hundreds of hours into this one at the moment.

Like I said, it's got it where it counts and it's pretty cheap, so all that in mind, I still think the game achieves what it sets out to do and is worth a buy. I'll definitely be following the game's continued support in the hopes that it can be made even better.

This game feels like a love child between Terraria and Runescape, two of my favorite childhood games. Its pixel graphics are beautifully rendered and surprisingly well-optimized, and the many boss designs are unique and gorgeously animated. Specialized builds are encouraged in this game, and by the end of it I had one each for running, mining, fishing, and combat.

Now, onto the cons of this game:

1. Gear and level progression are very unbalanced. Core Keeper punishes players for playing certain playstyles and forces them to grind missing levels instead of naturally playing the game to not fall behind on the progression curve.

2. Heavy dependence on the wiki to theorycraft any meaningful build.

3. Effort-to-Reward ratio makes some rare/legendary items NOT worth the effort, such as the Soul Seeker. A total of 2800 ingots are required to build this thing and by that time, I had already progressed to the Stormbringer, which was extremely easy to farm for and doubled as a ranged-melee weapon.

For now, I'll tentatively recommend Core Keeper, because despite its frustrating gameplay drawbacks, it is still one beautiful gem of a game. Just...be prepared when chasing 100% achievements.

Constant spawn bugs. We've done everything across multiple worlds and cavlings just spawn on top of us non-stop. Walls: useless. Moat: useless. Traps: Idiotic and useless. I've read as much advice online as I can find. My daughter and I wanted to quit because everytime we build a base it gets trashed no matter what we do.

Class Issues: Honestly in it's current state I'd say it's not worth it. Not because it's a bad game by any means but because nothing is properly balanced. For instance, ranged is the best class in the game with all others being obsolete because getting anywhere near a boss or enemy isn't worth the risk vs the reward. Also defense really means nothing in this game because I did some testing with cheats and I'm convinced the defense stat does almost nothing against bosses. Here's why, all enemies (Bosses included) will always deal 25% of their damage regardless of defense so that means if a slime does 224 damage and you have 224 defense (Likely Not) it's still going to deal 56 damage and since health is harder to increase than defense that's often a good chunk of your health and that doesn't include if you play on hard. The most health you can really obtain is a little over a thousand which sure is fine for most enemies but the boss can and will nearly 1-3 shot you at any given point after the first three bosses. This means sticking away is your best bet and ranger is best for that, mage sucks because mana regen is terrible and you can't really increase max mana too well so it's inherently a nerf, and the summoner is the newest class so goes without saying it's hardly fleshed out enough to be worth it.

World Issues: The generation sucks and I mean *really* sucks. You get little to no or direct hints to where you need to go or what you need to do but after the first three bosses which isn't even where most of the game is mind you, it all goes down hill. They should add more biomes and more bosses having specific bosses for each biome. It already does this but because the world size is so large it generates such a large mass of biomes that some parts can spawn at the bottom right of the map and go all the way to the upper left where the actual objective is, this ties into progression issues. 

Progression: I used the wiki to fight the bosses in the order it gives but by doing this I missed out on a special pickaxe I could have used instead of the one I already had, this is a reoccuring issue within the game. I wanna say about 90% is simply exploring and gathering rather than the story and bosses and as such there's no clear indication where the next ore's are. Especially late game when you have gems and other materials you basically *have* to use the wiki or you'd never know where or how to obtain them. The game took me the entire 76 hours to beat one play through and most of that was mindlessly digging through areas to find what I needed. This ties into how they chose to alleviate this issue.

Scanners: They add craftable scanners to scan the exact location/path the boss takes. But again some of these materials are in biomes you can't access or find because of the horrendous generation of the world. For example, the magma biome, can't mine with a pick but doesn't matter if I randomly obtain a mortar weapon that deals 1500 block damage and breaks everything in the game. That's essentially what happened, I progressed easily only because I found this mortar weapon and all blocks I couldn't break before I could now. I had the highest pickaxe for the boss I beat which I think was galaxite or whatever the one before that is. So after all of that hassle, I finally got the slime I needed to build the scanner only to find out the area I was in, was on the opposite side of where I need to be which was over 2000 blocks away. This is a constant late game. and makes it unbearable for the majority of the game, not to mention the Scarlet Drill is easily better than any pick in the game besides Solarite, just upgrade it with the bench and you'll have the same mining damage with a moment speed buff the pickaxes don't provide.

Early vs Late Game: I honestly prefer early game to late game. Early games just feels fleshed out and easy but can be hard for new players, it's one of those where you feel the progression of you getting stronger and you can see the difference in the damage you take at the start vs later, I consider the early game everything before the opening the wall. Mid/late game however is where all my issues before lie. Defense means nothing, sure you'll see yourself get a lot stronger in damage but your still taking equal to what your dealing. even when one shoting enemies it just doesn't matter because at the end of the day when there's ten of them that deal 150-200 damage each with not even 800 health your going to get shredded anyways even if you built for defense like I did. The ore progression and requirement is awful late game and honestly I stuck with half of my older gear because it was more beneficial than any of the later game armors and weapons there was no incentive to switch. I've played it  for almost over 50 hours (also have the game on Switch and running on MAC via Whisky). It's pretty much Terraria but underground and top-down perspective instead of classic 2D. The Stardew Valley part is pretty much just cultivating seeds and cook what you harvest to get some buffs and health back.

It's a pretty interesting game with fun boss fights (some are quite hard), a several different zones to explore, and resources to extract to craft things and improve weapons and armor as many other games of the like. You can get seeds to cultivate, cook quite a lot of dishes, and make potions and shit, plus you can even end crafting boats and cars, and the weaponry you can find around is varied enough (bows, muskets, swords, magic wands...) so it offers a nice experience overall.

There's indeed some grinding with materials, but it doesn't take too long to get to the automatization possibilities (railways + wagons, drills + hooks + conveyor belts, etc.) so you could end building some sort of mini-Factorio thing to get all the mineral resources, and that may be kinda enjoyable, too.

The main grip of the game imo is that you need to dig with a pickaxe most of the time, since the very beginning. Like, 80% of the time. Almost everything is just solid walls, and yeah, pickaxes and all gear degrade with use, so it may be a bit repetitive in that regard.

Also, the world biomes feel kinda more-of-the-same considering it's huge size, it could definitely use some more quality loot or special zones here and there. They have their own secrets and hidden treasures, and they are nice to explore and solve while beating enemies, but until you get to craft teleport portals it is really extenuating having to get back home to put all the loot and materials in the absolute ton of chests you'll end crafting, then going back to explore again... that's where it becomes quite rinse and repeat until you feel strong enough to take on the next bosses (at least when you finally find their lairs, because it takes A DAMN LOT of time of exploration to find shit).

It's still in early-access and we haven't played since december, tho, so it may have been improved in some areas. If your friend doesn't like Terraria because of its looks and vibes, maybe Core Keeper will do the trick because visually may be more appealing to some people. But if it's the gameplay what they dislike, then it's just Terraria but flat and horizontal, so I would hardly recommend it in that case.

Core Keeper is a sandbox survival game that has all the basics such as exploration, crafting, and combat with a pixel-art aesthetic. Drawing inspiration from Terraria, it drops players into a mysterious universe filled with resources to mine, enemies to fight, and secrets to uncover. The atmosphere is immersive, and the game does a great job of capturing the thrill of discovery.

The core gameplay loop revolves around mining, building, and battling creatures as you expand your underground base. The procedurally generated world makes sure that every playthrough feels fresh (I have already played the EA-Version before), and playing this game in co-op multiplayer is necessary in my opinion. (the world is HUUGE) Whether you’re mining, farming, fishing, or fighting giant bosses, Core Keeper has enough variety to keep you interested in it.

However, the game isn’t without its flaws. Progression can feel slow and grind-heavy, especially when gathering resources becomes repetitive (there is 9 ores that you progress through, which allow you to get new and exciting thechnologies from them -> Terraria). Some biomes lack distinct features, making exploration feel less rewarding over time (especially when you are looking for specific locations in the late-game). 
Combat was one of the weirdest things. (Note: I have played through the main-game in hardmode with no mods) In the beginning I felt like ranged weapons were completely useless but as I progressed further into the mid/endgame even the simplest enemies became so powerful and unpredictable in a way where meele combat was just not viable anymore (which doesnt mean ranged weapons got significantly better btw). While magic-builds are probably possible I just didnt see an easy enough way to pull it off (mana-management). Bosses were the easily the best part about the whole experience. Sometimes at first glance they seemed extremely hard but with good preparation (usually building a boss arena with respawn points) they became much more manageble (could even say "easy" sometimes, since I have a feeling the game wasn't build around the player trying to outsmart certain mechanics.) While I did not really bother about the farming and automation, my coop partner invested quite some time into it and it seemed like he was having fun with it atleast.

Despite these shortcomings, Core Keeper still is a solid choice for fans of survival and exploration games. As already mentioned  I strongly recommend playing with friends (the more the better), where teamwork (mostly in combat and grinding parts) make up for some of its weaker aspects. 
Also in retrospec I would recommend [b] looking into mods [/b] after a few hours to remove some of the frustrating / user unfriendly parts of the game. (example: Autostack into chest button)

Achievements:
Most of the achievements can be completed by playing through the game once and the rest can easily be aquired by using mods (yes, mods do NOT  disable achievements). I would still recommend playing through as intended before getting the last few achievements this way.

[h1]Humans are awful[/h1]
This game is a rollercoaster, not only storywise.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Well, at least we have a full controller support, yay. But that doesn't make the controls good. Although the animations for running, jumping and scratching look nice for an indie game, the controls are wobbly because of that. I often glitched into obsticles by jumping into. But although the game looks super basic and old, I had framedrops out of nowhere. This game is not optimized at all and that sucks.
Additionally, the minigames troughout the story are very lame to play, especially the fights were boring and annoying at the same time, because it is not even fighting but pressing the buttons in the right order intime. 
Also sad is the fact, that we cannot save and load manually. So if you want to play both endings (that are not so different from each other), you have to play the game all over again.

[u]Graphics[/u]
Honestly, the game looks cheap and old. I know it's not easy as an indie developer to afford Triple A-games graphics, but it still looks like being made back in 2010 with assets bought from a shop. It got pretty obvious when we first dreamed. Why do we have low poly trees, but no low poly grass nor rocks? It's inconsistent. But, like I previously mentioned, the cat animations are fine, although I personally didn't like the model itself.

[u]Story[/u]
The main point of this game is definitely the story and oh yeah, I hated every single character in this game, especially the humans. Olive itself is an egoistic old lady who replaced her lost cat with ... me, even gave me the same name and wants me to behave like the old 'Dawn'. [spoiler]And when her old cat showed up, she simply dumped me into the wild, eventho she promised the shelter to take care of me...[/spoiler] But her daugther is even worse and seems to hate cats for a living. It's all neccessary for the story and sadly more common irl than we all want to hear. The story peaked shortly before the ending and we got some heartbreaking scenes that we should always have to keep in mind BEFORE getting a pet. But ... the conclusion that the game gives us, is wrong or at least poorly written, [spoiler]because NO, you don't get back to your abuser who threw you away and just saw you as a placeholder. That's a bad message and 'Home is, where you are needed the most' is simply wrong, Olive never needed us and doesn't deserve cats at all![/spoiler]. So, in my opinion, the story should have ended differently, even if that means, that we don't get a typical happy end after all. Don't get me wrong, every pet deserves a happy end, but the game's 'happy end' is neither realistic nor a good happy end at all.

[u]TL:DR[/u]
The game has important messages and for that alone, it's worth playing (just ignore the ending). The graphics look really basic and cheap and the controls are often wobbly. Get it on sale, 15 bucks is too much imo. 
6/10

This game's story is absolutely brutal almost from start to finish, and it's stronger for it. There are several holy shit moments through the game where it feels like it goes too far, but in retrospect I'm glad that they're there.

There are several big weaknesses and they are fairly big ones:
- the controls are terrible. The cat almost defies gravity with its jumps and not in a good way. You never really get used to this. When the cat turns, it has a surprisingly large turning circle, especially for a cat. The camera sometimes misbehaves and you don't have full control of it at all times.
- at first you get to walk around a house however you like, but in the mid to late game, there are sidescroller sections where you just hold D and alleyway sections with 3 lanes where you press A or D to change lanes. Why? Just give us full control.
- the quicktime events. Oh god the quicktime events. There should never be a point where this game makes you press 4 to 8 buttons in a short timer window to enable some action. It's ridiculous and it's there throughout the game, quite painfully so near the end when you're entering 8 keypresses and wondering why you're doing this nonsensical action.
- The floating text of the cat's inner monologue. This is annoying and pointless, and I'll get to this further below.

I was thinking about these things all through the game and I thought, if the game had any playtesting these would have been picked up. This is a great game that just need polishing. But then I got to the end, and the credits rolled. There were heaps of playtesters. There seemed to be more playtesters than regular devs. Guys, get some new playtesters, they failed you here, big. These were not small issues.

One of the biggest saving graces of the game is the sound design. The music is amazing throughout the game (I especially loved the toilet roll bit). The narrator is consistently great. So great, in fact, that all of the cat's inner monologue bits could have been replaced with either nothing, or the narrator where it was necessary. Most of that inner monologue could follow the rule of much less is much more, but if the cat needed to go get some food, I could have been told about that by the narrator. 

For other things like the paintings, I just don't need or want the cat's moment to moment opinion as floating text while standing in just the right spot. I, as the cat, was not thinking nor caring about that as I walked past. I didn't even care quite so deeply about begging for Olive to love me in my head. I cared more for the cat's dastardly adventure given past and recent events, and any despair I had about Olive could have been much more organic if the floating text didn't keep coming up over and over and over.

Interestingly, I noticed the steam page description and Screen Australia's description are ever so slightly different and it indicates to me that at some point during this game's development, the plot likely changed significantly - this game is not a "wholesome" narrative driven game whatsoever, and it is not about "a cat who becomes the victim of an elaborate plan when a jealous, stray copycat steals her place in the household" at all. To say why is too spoilery, but this probably explains why the game's plot is seemingly overly brutal and ambitious with a few hits and misses throughout.

Despite the game's flaws, it is a fun cat game and I think there needs to be more stories told like this one. With more time in the oven, it could have been something truly amazing.

First, the story is overall well done, with a few questionable decisions, that is let down by a railroaded ending. I enjoyed Spec Ops The Line and that controversial game at least gave you the choice of multiple endings to allow the player to contextualize what had happened in game. A single ending here and while it doesn't ruin the game, I simply don't agree with how it is presented. 

Second, the QTEs are horrible both because they ask even veteran gamers to use button prompts that you will not figure out first try but also because the QTEs kill you repeatedly (trying holding the right mouse button while simultaneously left clicking). Horror games should not kill the player, I cannot emphasize this enough. Leave us at the ragged edge, near death, but avoid murder as much as possible. SWTD forgot this lesson for QTEs and it shows. Ironically the monsters avoid this problem which speaks to different teams working on each section. The very first QTE killed me repeatedly until I figured out what I needed to do and the only other time I had that issue was the 2000s subpar Cliver Barker Jericho trying to jump the gap at game start. This issue does not ruin the game but it sucks the enjoyment/tension right out the window. 

Overall, I like the voicework, the story, the graphics and the monsters. The game is letdown by providing no player agency, we're rooting for Caz you numbnuts, and trying to pad game length but creating try and die QTE sections. A recommend from this horror fan.

This is one of those games where I really wished that there was a mixed review option, but alas, I must leave a negative review in the end. I do have a slight negative bias since I'm not the biggest fan of plain horror and prefer psychological horror with something deeper to it.

I want to start off by saying that I've been fond of The Chinese Room's previous works, so in a way I had slight expectations and familiarity going in. What this game ended up confirming though, is that they really have a specific storytelling style, which is focus on the human aspect and interactions. Telling stories of mundane people without anything deeper to it. 

Now combine that with the horror genre with barely any interpersonal conflict, and you end up having a story focused only on people trying to survive. You can make an argument that isn't that what many horror movies generally are like as well, but with movies there's more of a suspense from not being able to interact with it. Quite often in games, you can be certain that the controlled main character isn't going to die in the middle of it. In this game you also don't get to really make any connections as a player with other characters, so the emotional investment isn't there and it's harder to relate to the emotional turmoil of the main character. I can't say that I was really into such storytelling and the best way to really sum it up is that it was "mundane" without setting up anything.

For gameplay, I'm not going to go that deep since it's about what you can expect if you're familiar with the studio's walking simulator style. Although this game felt more like a parkour simulator. When it came to the more active horror sections, those were actually well done, so personally I think they got that right. Partly gameplay related, but one issue that I had with the game is that at some parts, it felt like you were supposed to act out of game logic, instead of how the character would act in the world, ruining the immersion a bit. I get that it's a challenging balancing act and for most of the game I didn't see any issues, which is why the few select parts really stood out.

For visuals, I'd like to say that they held up to their reputation, BUT...
I'm so sick of the current trend of developers relying on upscaling and ai tech. In this game it quite literally is forced and yet again makes it seem like a crutch fix for poor optimization. It's laughable how as tech advances, visual fidelity continues to go down in games. From the artistic side, the visuals were good, but like I said, it got overshadowed by poor optimization and reliance on upscaling.
As an added note, if you happen to enjoy body horror, then this game has something for you since the grotesque aspects had quite a bit of focus.

All in all, I can't recommend the game unless it really hits someone's niche interests, those mainly being stuck on an oil rig with some sort of an eldritch horror. Personally it didn't leave a lasting impression, even though in the end I'm still glad that it exists. It's just nothing exceptional and hard to justify the full price if you're just browsing for something new.

The aesthetic is probably the coolest part. Control-esque blocky architecture, but with darker surfaces and a lot of cool neon lights, and with some overgrowth kinda like those parts of Portal 2.. it all comes together in a game that's very nice to look at. And take too many screenshots of :)

Performance is pretty decent, with all the fancy visuals my Vega 56 manages to mostly stay above 50ish fps at full 4K, and is always locked at 60 at 75% 4K. (Antialiasing really has to be turned down, it's oddly demanding here - are those just MSAA levels?)

The only bugs I've noticed so far: it's possible to leave no key bound to reset, which makes the "you failed" screen a softlock; borderless mode doesn't support HiDPI scaling correctly (e.g. renders at 2194x1234 instead of 3840x2160).

Overall this is quite a polished, playable, fun game. Where you can see that it's a single developer indie game is in the writing and voice lines (those sound like they were recorded with text-to-speech?) but that's exactly the aspects that are less important for a puzzle game where the concept is the important part and most storytelling is environmental.

Not my favorite game, but definitely deserves more attention than it is getting. It has a "Portal"-like setup but in a horror setting. While the graphics are neat and support the horror setting nicely - they don't really work well with the puzzle character of the game. A large part of the puzzles is the frustrating search for interactable elements. At one point i was desperately searching for a point to target a laser to only to find that a black object that I had never seen before standing without any connection to anything in a dark corner was the correct target... (in the demo trailer see timestamp 7:06)

If you are okay with this search part of the puzzles it is a visually very pleasing standard puzzle game with cubes and lasers and buttons and stuff like that.

I am almost finishing the game, what a great game. I love 1st person puzzlers and this one is very interesting. I have never seen one with a horror theme. One thing I found interesting is that it also has difficulty levels you can choose so it offers replay value. From what I can tell, it seems that the different difficulty levels introduce hazards/traps to the map, the solutions still the same. And the graphics are just out of this world! I think this is the best looking game I have ever played, the reflections on surfaces is so lush, man -  that marble? It looks beautiful. All glassy and reflective surfaces look so good. Nice work.

To be frank, the only thing this game has going for it is its visuals. 

The puzzles, as mentioned in other reviews, are uninspired and easy, with the occasional issue when you get stuck after failing to notice a cube or laser switch tucked away in a dark corner somewhere. The mechanic of having limited steps per puzzle is totally pointless, and doesn't even have any narrative justification. It just makes you re-do the earlier parts of a puzzle if you spend too long wandering around, which does nothing except waste your time - the steps to solving a puzzle are trivial to understand if you've done them once already. 

The narrative is generally lacking. Every NPC is voiced by text-to-speech with stilted delivery and inconsistent pronunciation, the notes have amateurish writing, and the goofy hovering text does nothing but undercut the horror elements every time it appears. 

If you can stomach all that, the game has some pretty stunning graphics to experience. It's blatantly influenced by Control's visual style, but the execution is so good that it would be easy to confuse some TIME BREAKER screenshots for Control itself. But, that by itself wasn't enough to keep my interest.

Time Breaker is a relatively small puzzle game made by one (!) person over the course of 2 years. You might think it'd be a clone of one those prototypes built by following a tutorial playlist on Youtube, but it's not. You can clearly see the creator of the game put effort to create a simple, yet enjoyable experience with the means and skills he had.

First off, i'd like to point out that, despite being built using Unreal Engine 4, the graphics are tweaked to make them better and unique compared to the ones you'd see in other small prototypes and games built using the same engine. Yet, it stays humble and doesn't blow tons of effects at your face in every corner of every rooms.

As for the soundtrack, it's mainly composed of ambience tracks. It does the job well, but having more diverse and "musical" tracks during non-puzzle segments of the game would have increased the immersion into the environments and the story.

Regarding level design, it's obviously the most important part of that type of game and the lone dev understood that. You're not treated like a complete idiot and some rooms will give you a real challenge. The main complaint i'd have about level design would be about one non-puzzle, story-related room being used 3 times but kind of changed a little bit at the same time, which I think is pretty lazy.

The main con and the most obvious one is the lack of polishing. Some small bugs and English typos can be found around, and there's room for small improvements there and around. The creator of the game should have had more people play his game before release, as these problems/improvements could be all fixed in the matter of a week instead of having to update the game every day, but again, it's his first release.

In conclusion, while not being the game of the year, Time Breaker is definitely an enjoyable small game, not without problems, but knowing that it was made by one person that had no prior experience in game makes it look impressive. Definitely an inspiration for other small game devs like me.

I want to preface this review by saying that I veeery rarely play early access games, simply because I don't like playing unfinished games. That means that I don't really know what to expect from early access games. I don't have any other relevant e-a gaming experiences for fair comparisons and I don't really know what is considered "good enough" for early acess.

With that said, here's my review:

This game is SUPER cute and cozy, it has a great playful atmosphere that makes it very fun to vibe with. The art style and graphics are great, but, a game with graphics like this needs to be optimized better. Sound and music are also great and everything works well in cohesion to create that playful atmosphere I mentioned before. 

This game is simplistic, which can be good or bad depending on the context. In the case of this game it is both. 
I will admit that I didn't get that far into the game (first planet only) so I may not have the full picture here, but the building system feels pretty basic at its core. Don't expact full freedom to build what you want, where you want. Constructing and crafting is done either within the zone of your "hubs" or at an "anchor" point, which is a a specific spot on the map in the form of things like a volcano or a waterfall for example.

Even though the game systems are basic, actually playing the game and progressing is kind of a struggle to be honest. Like others have mentioned in their reviews, getting a grasp of what to do or how things work does not come easy to you, and you often have to "research" what you are supposed to be doing or how something works. 
Unclear directions and explanations paired with mediocre UI/UX makes the gameplay way less smooth than it should be. BUT, since the core game systems are not that advanced, you don't feel that jankiness as much as you would in a more complex game.

Overall I would say that this is an alright e-a game that has a lot of potential and it definitely has my recommendation. Hopefully the devs are able to improve it a lot in the coming months! I will be keeping an eye on the updates for sure!

And btw, like others have said, try the demo first to get a feel of what the game is like. 

TLDR: Very cozy and chill game with great playful atmosphere. Simple game systems which feel in place in a game like this, but unfortunately held back by lacking design in many areas. Alright foundation in its current e-a state and has a lot of potential to be great!

I will start off by saying, my friend has set up a multiplayer game as its own dedicated server, so it is always up, and these are my findings as of ~350 hours of gameplay.

PROS
- The pals have nice designs.
- No connectivity issues.
- The progression mechanics do a good job of not letting you progress too fast, but you still feel like everything you do is progress.
- The map is fun to explore solo or with friends and there's a decent number of secrets and collectibles that actually help you along the way, not just collecting for collectings sake.
- The tower bosses are a good challenge.
- Breeding mechanics are fun to play with and breeding pals to get the best passive skills is not an insane grind, although you will grind for it.

CONS
- Building is ass. Everything overlaps with everything, meaning you can't place anything really anywhere. They've created really cool environment structures that would be amazing to tuck a base into, but you can't overlap with the ground or environment walls, so you're stuck building in open fields.
- Bases are still completely broken. If you leave your base, your pals stop working, stop eating, and will starve and depress themselves, making them works half speed, and costing you insane amounts of resources and time to get them back up to speed, only for them to essentially self-destruct as soon as you leave again.
- To piggy back on that point, once you get to a higher level, around 50-55, it can take literal real life DAYS to craft enough of some of the materials you need, meaning as soon as you log off, or leave your base, that stuff stops being made, so I'm currently waiting in my base, typing a review so that my pals (who are 132 hours into making 1000 pal metal ingots, and 300 plasteel ingots, and are still a few hundred away from being done) will continue to work so I can actually make balls (which will probably take a month) to catch the legendary pals.

FINAL RATING
I would give this game from levels 1-45 an 8/10. That being said with the ridiculousness that is the higher levels, and all the issues with bases, my total final ranking would have to be about a 3/10. If bases get fixed to where late game isn't just a waiting simulator, then I will adjust my rating. But as of now, the game isn't worth playing after a certain level, which kills the fun of the endgame.

Reviewed as of 01/03/2025: unfortunately while this game does have some neat ideas, at the end of the day it feels soulless, generic and incredibly grindy and stressful. They grabbed a bunch of ideas from other games such as Pokemon, Zelda Breath of the Wild etc, threw them together, and then didn't focus on refining any of them. No story, no real objectives aside from "get higher level, unlock all crafting options in the level skill tree, beat all bosses, capture all pals". And the road there is incredibly grindy and sometimes downright boring. Constantly you have to micro manage your inventory and your bases. It often feels more like Factorio meets Rust than Pokemon meets Zelda Breath of the Wild. To get better armor, weapons, and spheres to capture pals, you usually need to craft them yourself. For that, you need to micro manage the shit out of your base(s) and your pals to make sure everything gets produced in sufficient quantities. Sooner or later you will also need to spend hours breeding pals to get 4 stars (116 pals sacrificed to get 4 stars which boosts the stats of one chosen pal basically. you need to repeat this process for many pals), to get good IVs (hidden bonuses that influence how much attack, defense and hp they gain per level) and target perks (stuff like +30% attack, defense, workspeed etc). I have probably spend more time building bases, carrying resources, and breeding pals than on exploration and combat. It often feels more like work than playing a game. Even 154 hours into the game I still havn't beaten the last tower boss because I'm not strong enough yet, and there is still a lvl 60 oil rig, and several summoning raid bosses that are even stronger. But I don't feel like breeding specific pals and farming souls and all the other stuff that's necessary to come up with the perfect roster of pals for each of those challenges anymore. You spend 10-30 hours preparing for a single fight that is over in 10 minutes or less if succesful. How is that fun for anyone? I will say this much you can spend a lot of time in this game, and the exploration and even base building is decent if you're into that sort of thing. Many of the Pals can be kind of charming as well. But for anyone who is afraid of games that are too grindy and micro-manage heavy, stay the fuck away from this one.

lies of p is the first souls-like i've played that both successfully leans on familiarity [i]and[/i] stands out as its own unique piece of work. 

the environment is absolutely stunning and varied, dripping with lore that rewards the careful viewer, and changes depending on time of day or where you are in the game progress-wise. with a compelling narrative, it is truly a masterclass in adaptation. lies of p also improves upon the souls formula by providing quality of life updates to NPC quest lines - demystifying progression and alleviating fears of "missing something". the boss designs and OSTs are incredible. i could truly go on all day about how wonderful this game is so i'm going to stop myself there and leave the rest up to you to discover!

with that being said, i do have a few critiques - most of them falling under the umbrella of accessibility issues. descriptions that you have to prompt to appear [i]disappear[/i] entirely too quickly (and i'm a fast reader). NPC indicators on the stargazer menu only show when you are able to progress their quest but not necessarily when NPCs have new dialogue. i missed a good bit of lore on the first play by skipping through dialogue because i thought the game would alert me every time there was something new to be said. the spotlights in [spoiler]king of puppet's[/spoiler] arena are disorienting and there are a few other fights where "dust" is kicked up, making it difficult to read the boss's next move. later in the game, one fight in particular feels completely unbalanced unless you use a specter (absolutely nothing wrong with this - i just like to force myself to learn the dance solo).

all in all, lies of p will be a game that i return to again and again, and i'll be trying to convince everyone i know to do the same. 9/10.

After Elden Ring, I had given up on finding a good game in the souls/souls-like genre, but this one made me believe. My personal take on Lies of P would be that the game is insanely good, barring some minor flaws (considering the playerbase to consist of both veterans and newbies).

[h3]The Pros:[/h3]
[b]1. Story & Voice Acting[/b]
- First, the story, which was super gripping and had me guessing on the motives of the main players till the end of my first play through.
- [spoiler]The DLC tease at the end of the credits has me really exited for what's to come next. [/spoiler]
- Each-and-every NPC is fully voice-acted, and have their own stories which have been laid out mesemerisingly.
- The quality of the voice acting and interconnectedness of each NPC's story with that of P made for really great immersion, and I ended up really caring for each one of them
- [spoiler]The lie system in the gane and the effects it had on the story and ending were also immensely enjoyable[/spoiler]
[b]2. Theme[/b]
- As with all other souls-likes, the overall theme of Lies of P was dark and melancholic, but the setting and lore felt super unique which had me hyped for the gane well before its release.
- This game's the closest we get to Bloodborne on PC, and will surely be a classic in the genre of lovecraftian horror games.
[b]3. Combat[/b]
- Very fast-paced, very smooth, extremely enjoyable.
- I loved the variety of ways we could combine weapons and legion arms to tackle the game in different manners.
- The game really rewards parrying perfectly and overall the implementation of the fast-paced style was right down my alley. LOVED IT!!!
[b]4. Music[/b]
- See, I'm a huge music buff, so whenever a game features good OST, it gets brownie points from my end.
- In the case of Lies of P, I was robbed of all my brownies.
- Really loved all the tracks that we received as collectibles that could be played.
- Also loved the overall music of the game, especially the part right at the end [spoiler]after deciding what to do with Sophia.[/spoiler]

[h3]The Cons:[/h3]
[b]1. Combat[/b]
- I know most of you will be confused seeing this mentioned under both pros and cons, but it definitely belongs in both.
- As mentioned earlier, the combat is super fast-paced (which I loved), but some fights are overtuned which make it impossible to "reflexively" respond to some enemy moves (instead having to respond to visual cues due to the actual attacks being faster than a person's average response time).
- 70-80% of the game felt pretty easy, with random difficulty spikes at some end-games bosses, especially the last.
- All builds don't work well with all enemy types due to the way combat works, and it seems to favour technique (dexterity) focused builds more.
[b]2. Online Elements[/b]
- A bit of a stretch, but I would've personally loved to be able to play this co-op with a friend.

[h3]Summary:[/h3]
I can confidently say that Lies of P hits the single digit ranks among my all-time favourite games, and that's saying something since I've played a lot of games. Overall I really liked the combat and music of the gane, with bonus points for the unique setting and lore. For fans of the souls-like genre, Lies of P is a MUST TRY from my end!

This is a really good Souls-like, and I thorougly enjoyed it. However, for me personally it lacks one important aspect present in many other games of this type, and that is a sense of freedom and ability to explore open locales as the players sees fit. 

Let's start with the many good aspects of this game. In general, Lies of P is easy to recommend to people who, like myself, deeply enjoy the Souls-like genre. In fact, it may be one of the best ways to get into these types of games if you do not have much experience with Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, Elden Ring, and the many games out there that are like them.

Most importantly, the combat is really well-tuned and satisfying. Lies of P's combat system is absolutely best in class among its Souls-like brethren. For me, it even outstrips Dark Souls III and Elden Ring's own combat engine. Only Nioh and Sekiro offer an even more tight combat experience than the one found here. Lies of P's player character does exactly what you want him to when you press a button. Accordingly, the enemies are well-designed in order to be tough to fight (as is part of the Souls-like DNA), but also totally doable to overcome, if you are patient and methodical. The parry mechanic has a tight window, but offers high rewards when pulled off correctly. Unlike Sekiro or Bloodborne, many enemies in this game can be taken out without the use of parrying, but there are a few bosses and low-level foes that practically require it. But you have a number of other options and mechanics to help turn the tide in battle as well. For instance, I greatly enjoyed having a grappling hook arm extension, as it allowed me to yank enemies towards me and position them for the kill as part of crowd-management. This grappling hook is just one arm extension out of many you can use, and they are all great and add spice to the combat.

Furthermore, I think this game has a good length. It does not overstay its welcome at all, and in general feels quite tightly edited. There were no areas that made me think they were an afterthought or of lesser quality than the rest of the game. The developers of Lies of P clearly took a deep look at all the elements that made Dark Souls tick and made those games so popular, and then created their own well-configured gameplay systems to apply to this framework. I very much enjoy games like Mortal Shell, Wo Long, and other Souls-likes, but these games always end up feeling like lesser gods in a pantheon dominated by the From Software Souls games. There are games which stand proudly alongside the games in the From oeuvre, like Nioh, but such games often have certain aspects in which they profoundly deviate from how From Software designs its games. The combat system in Nioh is more like Ninja Gaiden than it is like Dark Souls, for instance. 

Lies of P, on the other hand, made me think that this is the first time I have played a Dark Souls 'copycat' game that works from the same basic blueprint of combat, encounter design, and gameplay structure as the From games, but is not made to look bad in the comparison to From Software's masterpieces. If you like Demon's Souls, you will like Lies of P, full stop. As someone who cannot get enough of this type of game, I am grateful that the developers made a game of such quality as to rival the giants which inspired it. 

There is, however, one fundamental difference between Lies of P and the From games. Nearly all of the games in this genre (from Dark Souls and Elden Ring to Mortal Shell and The Surge) give you large open areas to travel through, in which you can move over and around obstacles relatively freely. Yes, you make your way into corridors within dungeons and such, but in general you are not limited in how you traverse the levels, which are constructed as wide open spaces. Dark Souls rewards you for taking risky falls off of ledges that allow you to sequence break the obvious path through the level, for instance. This freedom was then brought to its logical extreme by Elden Ring, which is one of the most expansive open worlds you could imagine, and which has a jump button to boot. 

By contrast, Lies of P has very constrained levels. Just to be clear, the whole "level folding onto itself" aspect is definitely present here: you will often find your way back to same stargazer (bonfire) via an unfolding ladder or unlocked door. But even if there are at times two divergent paths to take, the game's corridors feel very linear, and there are plenty of invisible barriers that keep you from poking at the game world in any way that was not foreseen explicitly by the developer. In this sense, Lies of P reminds me a bit of games from the early 2000s: if you were to enter debug mode you would see the actual traversable part of the level is only a narrow strip of path, confined by invisible walls. In the game,  you are then kept within this corridor by obstacles that are only a few inches high, like a suitcase that comes up to your knee, or even just a small curb on the edge of the building that prevents you from walking off of it. 

In Elden Ring or Dark Souls, you would just hop over these obstacles. In Lies of P, you are not allowed to stray from the narrow route that was predefined for you. Playing through this game has underlined for me that this sense of freedom is actually quite important for me in these games, and how it contributes to the feeling of adventure and exploration that make me love this genre so much. So in this one sense, I must knock Lies of P a bit. If you are like me, and play these games for the exploration, then Lies of P can fall a bit short of expectations. If, however, you come to Dark Souls for the combat first and foremost, then Lies of P will be sure to satisfy.
