[h1]Lies of P – A Worthy Soulslike with Its Own Identity[/h1]

[h2]A Solid 9/10 – Engaging Combat and Thoughtful Progression[/h2]
Lies of P is one of the best Soulslike games outside of FromSoftware. The combat is weighty, deliberate, and deeply satisfying. Every attack feels impactful, and learning enemy patterns is rewarding. The game's progression systems—Legion Arms, P-Organs, and upgrade currencies—are all well-designed and meaningful, making each level-up feel important rather than incremental.

[h2]A Slow Start, But a Thrilling Finish[/h2]
The early hours are a little slow and easier than expected, but the game ramps up well, leading to some incredible late-game bosses. These fights are challenging, well-tuned, and varied, making for an intense and rewarding final stretch.

[h2]Optimized and Well-Designed, But Visually Dated[/h2]
The game runs [b]smoothly[/b] on PC and feels well-optimized. However, visually, it looks like a polished PS4 game or a late Unreal Engine 4 title. While the art direction is great, it doesn’t quite push the boundaries of current-gen graphics.

[h2]A Great Story with Exciting Hints for What’s Next[/h2]
The story is engaging with some surprising moments, and the way it hints at future content has me [b]excited for the DLC[/b]. The worldbuilding is strong, and while it’s familiar in many ways, it still manages to carve out its own identity.

[h2]Almost FromSoft-Level, But Missing a Little Magic[/h2]
While Lies of P is an amazing game in its own right, it doesn’t quite reach the level of FromSoftware’s best. There’s a certain intangible magic that’s missing—but it’s incredibly close.

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]
If you’re a fan of Soulsborne games, this is an [b]easy recommendation[/b]. It’s challenging, rewarding, and one of the best in the genre outside of FromSoft itself.

Along with leaving its mark on the industry and cementing an RPG subgenre, 2015’s Bloodborne satisfied me so thoroughly that it still stands as the uncontested pinnacle of my personal Soulsborne mountain. Even now, eight years later, I hardly would have expected it to become supplanted; that is, until I sat down to play through Neowiz and Round 8 Studio’s Lies of P. I’m a little surprised to write these words, but I daresay that Lies of P is such a masterfully crafted hardcore gothic action RPG that it could even be said to outdo FromSoftware at its own game.

Lies of P is loosely based on The Adventures of Pinocchio by Italian author Carlo Collodi. Though the game’s narrative is original, quite a few characters, locations, and themes from the literary work have made their way into the game, along with some Easter Eggs for those who are familiar with the story. The story is set in the fictional city of Krat, a large and opulent beacon of the Industrial Revolution, full of lavish opera houses, glitzy theaters, well-stocked storefronts, and craftsmen’s shops. But the city also has its dark underbelly where the poor eke out a desperate existence amid the twisting alleyways and cobbled streets.

Players step into this world as the titular puppet P, awakened in an empty train car by a mysterious ephemeral voice seeking his help. It turns out that Krat no longer resembles the bustling hub of progress it once was. The city’s unfortunate human population has been cruelly set upon, decimated by a painful and deadly Petrification Disease, only to be kicked while already down when the city’s puppets — intricate clockwork constructions acting as a cheap and convenient workforce for menial labor — inexplicably slaughtered their onetime masters in an uprising known as the Puppet Frenzy. Despite being constructed with a fail-safe directive that should have made rebelling against their human masters impossible, the city’s puppets continued the human’s extermination started by the Petrification Disease, brutally picking off those who managed to survive the epidemic.

Writing this review seven hours in, I've got a good feel for the game so far, I've already beaten five boss enemies so far. The combat is fast-paced and flows well. When you're learning it may feel a bit clunky but once you get the hang of it you'll be slicing through enemies with relative ease. Balance is a difficult thing to achieve in souls-like games and I definitely feel they've struck a good balance with difficulty. I've died a few times but not excessively and not to the point of frustration. 
    You can dodge and dash to avoid attacks alltogether, but blocking is also a feasible option. Regular blocks cost stamina and greatly reduce the damage you take and what little damage you do take you can recover if you attack quickly enough after blocking. A perfectly timed block will completely block any damage and can stagger your opponent, or even disarm them if done enough. Larger enemies can be staggered by a heavy attack if they've taken enough damage, and it will prompt you to let you know when, you can then follow up with a critical hit for massive damage.
    There are many ways to spec and customize your character's weapons and abilities. Each weapon has a blade and a guard, each have their own unique ability. Weapons can be disassembled to then be mixed and matched to suit your preference. Your legion arm can wield powerful abilities that can come in handy in a fight, ranging from utility gadgets to a weapon on its own. Weapons can be upgraded and respeced into different stats, so if you find a weapon you like, spec it into whichever stat is its primary and focus your build in that direction.
   There is a small range of stats for you to upgrade as you level up, so you're not overwhelmed with choices and developing a balanced build is a valid option. You can also acquire quartz which essentially function as perk points, there is a large perk tree with many options. Each perk requires a certain amount of quartz to unlock, each quartz you spend towards earning a perk lets you choose a minor statboost granting you even further customization options to spec your character towards. 
    Gameplay aside the visuals are spectacular, I'm playing on max graphics and it is lovely to look at and runs very smoothly. The story seems interesting, I won't spoil anything you'll learn as you play. There are also collectable records which can be played at the hubworld area and these are truly very lovely songs, a wonderful addition to an already great game. I definitely recommend this to anyone who's played Dark Souls, Elden Ring, and especially to fans of Bloodborne. Souls-like games are often hit or miss, and this is a definite hit.

Obviously, this game takes heavy inspiration from From Software titles and doesn't shy away from it. I would even say Lies of P innovates on the genre with the combat, as the inclusion of arms, fable arts, poise/parry system and even the durability mechanic collectively add a lot of depth to the gameplay. Lies of P is probably the best challenging arpg not made by From Software that I've played. It definitely takes a lot of inspiration from Bloodborne as it twists in an adaptation of Collodi's Pinocchio. The result is a game that wears its homage proudly on its sleeve yet still is very much its own thing.

What I really appreciated was the overall tone, linear with just enough exploration level design, and very customizable weapon system (and the combat is quite fun with a particular caveat: see below). There seems to be a robust ng+ system as well for those of you into that.

Nitpicks are too many boss battles had multiple phases. Kinda gets old quick. Fortunately you can summon in an ai shade to help out which I did use occasionally. 
And the combat does favor the parry mechanism, which I generally do lean towards in these kind of games. Maybe it's the fault of the Unreal Engine which generally lacks precision, but there were multiple times its jank costed me an unfair defeat. Not enough to get me to shelve the game but it is notable. 

But the good is waaaay more than the bad. I look forward to what Round 8/Neowiz do with this ip moving forward! 

Also, it runs amazing on Deck. Probably the best optimized game I've played on the console. Rock solid 45fps (one notable drop in one single area that has zero effect on gameplay) at the lower end of mid settings. About 2.5hrs battery on an Oled.

The Plucky Squire is a game developed by All Possible Futures and published by Devolver Digital

The game has some really beautiful environments and the graphics are really well designed and laid out

The game does suffer with some repetitiveness at certain areas of the game but a fun game nonetheless

The Plucky Squire overall, however, is a fun game to play in short bursts and a very good story rich adventure game to play especially if you like creative action-adventure games such as this one!

[h1] RECOMMENDED :) [/h1]

[b] REVIEW SOURCES: [/b]
[list]
[*] None

There are a small few niche cases where The Plucky Squire could end up being someone's favorite game. But ultimately, if you've played even one more decent top-down Zelda-like game, it comes across as lacking substance.

Addressing the elephant in the room: The art direction is amazing, impeccable, insert superlative here. Putting aside that I personally am in love with the Adventure Time, Burnt Toast-like art style of the book sections, there is just so much love and care put into all of the Plucky Squire's environments that you could spend hours just poking around and seeing everything.

And to its credit, the gameplay that is here is generally polished, with no real bugs, soft locks, or glitches to report, at least on PC. Enemies get whacked with a satisfying thunk (with the comic-book words to go with it), and some of the puzzles are quite clever in their execution.

But for a game that has so much charm and heart, it lacks substance. The story is completely linear. The narrator and characters telegraph your direction whenever you as the player are to "figure things out" and the game just hands you the solution - even in Streamlined mode, and even without asking for a hint. It isn't insulting, but it's the type of hand-holding that has the potential to turn experienced players off. It's not that the game is too easy - rather, it forcibly takes the challenge away from the people that play it.

Is the game targeted at younger audiences? Perhaps targeted toward those who have played mobile or casual games up to this point? It's unclear.

Nevertheless, I enjoyed my time with the Plucky Squire. I hope that developer All Possible Futures takes what they have learned with the game's art direction and applies it to a future game that rewards players for coming up with the solution themselves, instead of handing the solution on a platter (or in this case, a text box).

The Plucky Squire is ultimately a good game on the verge of being a great one.

First off, the combat is sleek, and fun. It feels like a mix of A hat in time, and Zelda. I also really like the platforming, and the small exploration aspects, even if it was a bit more linear than I expected it to be. They still managed to make it work really well.

I can understand the puzzles being limited too, but I still wish they would add more funny failed puzzle results, and more creative ways to play around with the word system in general. (I couldn't change the cheese after the giant rat took it in the mountain section for example.) The best puzzles were the ones where I felt really free to experiment, and dig into the mechanics.

The minigames were all fun, but I wish there was more consistency between them, the mechanics are too different for anything to really be developed. Thrash's (unfortunately only) minigame was an odd difficulty spike for me, I feel like it's an extra hard version of what it should be compared to everything else. In fact the lack of an extra hard mode in the first place also confuses me, since the game is supposed to be for Everyone. 

The art is phenomenal, and the best part of the whole game. I cant say anything else that would do it justice. 

The music is good, but I feel like they played it a bit too safe in that department. Nothing really stuck in my head besides the rhythm games where it actually mattered. It still has a mostly cozy adventurous vibe that I like though.

In a tragic twist however, I think the writing was definitely the weakest part of The Plucky Squire. A LOT of things needed more explanation, such as how controlling the book works, how some of the characters feel about being characters, and why they hide it from everyone else. A lot of the side characters are straight up forgettable too. 

As for the main characters, Violet's arc was definitely my favorite part of the whole story. Thrash goes through a similar arc, but it's a more disjointed version. The story should've focused more on him going from a lazy, carefree attitude to a more caring, passionate one rather than going on a tangent about snakes. Also it was weird How he just stopped aiding in combat during the beach level. That makes the whole narrative of them being more involved in gameplay as the story goes on suffer.

Moonbeard's death, and comeback didn't really do anything for the story, He didn't change as a character from it, It didn't contribute to his characterization, and he doesn't even stay monochrome from the after effect. In the credits he just gets his color back. (Kinda shows how forgettable that whole part was,) They also should've gone into more detail about his past brothership with Humgrump, it feels like there's a lot of potential that was glossed over.

Humgrump was almost an excellent villain, but they kind of fumbled him in the end. It looked like his arc was going to be about how he treated his soldiers progressively worse until he saw them all as completely disposable to contrast how the heroes all became closer with each other. Instead he went on to brag about his guards in the last few chapters, instead of replacing them immediately with machines or something. Kinda diminishes his threat. The butterfly narrative wasn't intertwined enough either, maybe they should've called him a worm more towards the start of the story so it would contribute to his denial of growing as a person. The final battle with him should've involved Jot carrying Violet, and thrash out of the book to fight Humgrump together. (possibly foreshadowed with Jot being able to take the pigs out of the book) that would've really tied the story together.

And finally Jot himself didn't really come off as a character at all. We didn't get to see his plucky attitude reflected in his writing, the game just said he was good at it without even making an attempt to show why. Not much else to say there really.

I know it's kinda harsh, but that's mainly because I hope the devs can learn from this experience, and I look forward to whatever comes next!

[h1]My Review[/h1]

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]

A rather fun adventure through which you gain the ability to swap between a world set in a book and the real world. Your on a grand adventure to save the land of Mojo from an evil wizard. You'll find your self fighting in this top-down adventure against grunts and match up against a unique boss in every chapter.

[h3]Puzzles[/h3]

I don't think many people know this about me, but I love puzzle games. This genre is seriously lacking for some solid variety in my opinion of bangers that are worth playing. In terms of this game I'd say the puzzles actually require you to use your brain and think about your options, and in this day and age I can really appreciate that. Also the fact that the devs slip in funny jokes with the word puzzles had me laughing more than once not gonna lie. This game has some interesting stuff in store I think many people will find they cool about this game and come back to enjoy.

[h3]Combat[/h3]

The combat is melee based, but you'll receive new ways to use your sword that makes comboing enemies interesting and keeps combat simple to understand and fun to play with. My personal favorite ability is the sword throw as it lets me keep distance from baddies and lets me move around more.

[h3]Story[/h3]

The story is not something I'd say is gonna win awards or anything, but it most certainly serves the gameplay first and I can't say I'm not all for that. This game has some really cool moments that are quite fun, interesting, and finding collectibles is quite enjoyable and satisfying aswell. As far as I'm concerned the story keeps the games plot at a fair pace and isn't slow in the slightest.
A fullhearted recommendation. This was a great time. Art direction was amazing and the game kept coming with fresh ideas and cool sequences. A very enjoyable experience.

if the first loren game was akin to dragon age origins, then an elven marriage is more akin to dragon age two, for better or for worse. perhaps playing LTAP right before jumping into this one set my expectations too high, as i expected the same sort of quality from this one. i liked the concept; a VN with rpg elements, holy shit what a good concept, what a great way to move the medium forward! but AEM didnt really do that, and id argue it sort of went backwards in execution.

the UI is somehow...slightly worse than LTAP. it was clunky, big, messy-- but it still worked. everything i need was great and easily visible. resistances made sense and easily legible. "critical", "weak", simple words that instantly told you how to tackle enemies. in AEM, it's percentages, which even after reading the tooltip, made it near impossible to know what was effective against an enemy and what wasnt. i liked the tactical thinking i did in the first game, where here i was pretty much choosing which skill did the biggest number. the UI itself is slightly uglier and chunkier than previous games, and i dont know if its due to the constraint of the engine theyre using or what, but nothing looks particularly sharp, it's all got a slight blur to it (im playing on a 24in monitor), which is also annoying in combat. LTAP had this too, to a lesser extent i feel.

the ui being a mess is more obvious in the inventory and shopping screen. important buttons like purchasing, selling, unequipping are small as hell, and navigating it is a pain. maybe if i could make the UI smaller instead of having it scream in my face it would be better? i dunno, overall it's just very loud and in your face. it's not as busy or ornate as LTAP, which i appreciate, but it's still very difficult to navigate. 

on that note, there's also a wild level of art inconsistencies that personally take me out of the game at times. gruff's sprite not being as detailed as the rest of the team, apolimesho using his old sprite despite how critical he is to the story, NPCs with sprites that are just plain sloppy looking and not as detailed as everyone else, myrth's sprites not being cleaned or properly finished...the list goes on, but it just doesn't look good all together. i liked the old style that looked almost comic booky and the stark, black shadows were really unique. it's really obvious when certain npcs stand next to each other in a scene. did the devs just run out of money, did they use two different sprite artists, or what? it just makes the game look incomplete; i understand you dont want to put time into trash mobs or one off npcs, but even LTAP gave all the sprites the same work, even if they did color palette swaps or w/e. it made everything whole, and consistent. i know art is subjective to the viewer, but at the price (though slightly lower than LTAP at full price), i would expect a certain degree more "consistency". hell [spoiler] ashtran shows up and his sprite is just his head from LTAP slapped onto the body of a sprite that gets reused for the ugliest motherfucker of a boss ive ever seen. bruh. [/spoiler]

my last VN before LTAP was hatoful boyfriend, so maybe art inconsistencies are to be expected, but lord it was distracting, and i couldnt help notice it once it kept coming up.

anyway, the story itself was...okay. just okay. i appreciate it being far more grounded than LTAP, it felt more like a set up for the Big Bad Evil in a future installment than of a direct sequel, and that's probably their intention. i found myself laughing and going "what the fuck thats so stupid" or just going "WHAT??" often near the end, like if they just ran out of ideas and were just pulling drama out of nowhere. there wasn't any set up to (MAJOR SPOILER) [spoiler] nathir summoning his deus ex machina of a god to help revive elenor after she gets her soul sucked by jul. HUH? and then ANOTHER GOD shows up to claim elenors soul, and then nathir has to do a challenge to get it back. i know nathirs faith is strong but there was NO lead up to this; nothing that said his faith was so otherworldly it would summon a literal god to his help. [/spoiler] 

and i think that's really my biggest issue with the overall narrative: a lot of character actions are so inconsistent. this felt immediately obvious playing as an elenor who was continuing a romance with rei; the way elenor acted with him, to others, and in the story felt like it was written by varying writers. the way an elenor would flirt and act interested to lydia and nadir despite being in a supposed romance with rei, to the way she would be weirdly callous in dialogue...it didnt feel like the elenor from the previous game. if the game was trying to show that elenor came out of her shell after being a slave to loren, it was doing a poor job at it. elenor in LTAP felt more humble and helpful, the friendly disposition i chose for her made her incredibly more sensible and kind to those around her. this elenor felt...rude, callous. again, maybe this is how she truly is as she's no longer a slave who feels indebted to the amazons, but the discrepancy is wild. there were really some words that elenor was saying that i felt like i was playing like a violently different character. and ultimately, as she was my vehicle during this whole story, i didnt feel like she was getting the kind of character development she deserved.

side note: the quest log still sucks. again, im guessing this cause of engine restraints, but we couldnt have a better quest tracker? something to let me know what i have to do and where to go, instead of just saying the text of the initial quest screen? it sounds dumb to complain, but with how much text is vomited at you i feel like i just forgot what i was doing, and the lack of summary of what i did is not helping, and i had to reload a few times to redo what i did.

anyway, the romance itself was a wild ride. like i mentioned before, this elenor didn't feel like the same in LTAP, and really, so did rei. he wasn't as "gentlemanly" as i would expect, but at the very least it was obvious that he cared for elenor. i didn't feel like the progression for this romance was as fun as previous, and again, a lot of the conversations they had together made me go fucking insane with how out of left field it was. (spoiler for tail end of the romance) [spoiler] elenor suddenly blowing up on rei for mentioning he used to be a better shot before he met her? girl, let him SPEAK instead of getting mad for no reason. why are you so weirdly petty? [/spoiler]. it didn't feel fulfilling, and i imagine the new romances are probably more developed cause they're brand new, but still...i did like at least that their romance was mentioned throughout the game and others would comment on it, but good lord they needed to get a room at times and not be horny freaks..

so, based on this review it sounds like i hated my time with the game, but honestly, i didn't it. again, it was a passable game at the very least, but there were so many small things that make me hesitant to recommend it unless you really, really like the series. there was a game breaking bug i ran into where one of rei's skills would completely crash the game and there was a 50/50 shot i could ignore the message, or just have the game crash and id have to leave rei out of a fight as a result. the over all lack of polish on sprites, the occasional misspelling, or just wild mis-characterization of a character in a scene that would make me wonder what the hell they were on about. but i did like things.

but the overall package, as it stands, needs significant polish. if youre a huge fan of LTAP, it might be worth going through. if you're new, i recommend picking up LTAP on sale and wait for a few more spit shines to this game; i think it can be something good, but maybe i just had high hopes, and a too critical lens to overlook the things i hated. it had its good moments i assure you, but i think it needed more time to bake.

(Id like to start this by saying I don't close my steam games...) A successful continuing of Elenor/Saren's story it is, but a proper successor to Loren it is not. As someone who romances Loren everytime I play the original game, it is strange to not have her here, especially as she is the MC's best friend. The most beloved characters of Loren: Loren, Draco, Chambara, Dora, and Ramas are all gone, leaving us with what I considered the B characters of Myrth, Rei, and the wizard who seemed to be a very different art style that the other characters. The plot was fine, the enemies were meh and I found the fighting abilities of the characters (mainly Lydia) very frustrating. Elenor didn't have much consistency in her character as it didn't matter who you romanced, she flirted with all. Gruff was the only character I really connected with but they were a pretty non important character. Loren did something I think Winter Wolves struggles with, very well. It perfectly walked the line between action, rpg, and romance. The relationship between Loren and Elenor was so well written but Elenor and Lydia falls very flat for me, weather because she flirts with the other characters or because their love has little stake. Overall I was just disappointed with this game and wish WW would let Loren rest and make more RPGs not set in the same world.

I love this game so much, but the pacing of Utopia Shelter is absolutely horrendous and the game's biggest flaw, IMO. It's like the godforsaken lovechild of Labyrinth Zone from Sonic 1 and Space Station ARK from Sonic Adventure 2, but 20+ minutes long and far more tedious.

It marries the old school Sonic design philosophy of "speed is a reward for good play" with modern moment-to-moment Sonic gameplay.

The game REALLY pushes back at you for trying to maintain top speed, which can feel punishing coming from a series where you can hit top speed at the push of a button. Once you get past that and start to utilize the tools and level design specific to this franchise, you can tap into a practically uncapped speed that's an absolute joy.

The combat is more complex than you would expect from a game where it's not the focus, but it's still shallow and runs dry long before the ending. Thankfully it's appearances are brief and let you flex it's parry mechanic, which feels great.

Really fun game with a fantastic sense of speed, interesting story and characters, strong level design with plenty of optional paths and collectables to find, giving great replayability, tight controls that are similar to the adventure era of Sonic games, but much more polished and with a lot of momentum behind the movement. The combat is pretty fun too, if not a bit spammy and sometimes encounters tend to drag on for a while.

My only issues were the aforementioned combat, dashing or other similar abilities would mess up on sections where you're running sideways or up loops, collectibles are SO out of the way and I feel like they could've been integrated into the level better, with some exceptions though, and the last level I feel dragged the experience down at the end. I get what they were doing with a gauntlet level, but having all those cutscenes in between and multiple bosses made it really exhausting by the end, I feel they should've separated some of the encounters to another level.

A nice little bonus was that you unlock the previous game's stages after you beat the main story and they were really fun too, more linear in their design but I feel a lot of them had stronger themes and flow to some of the new stages.

Overall this game is awesome though, I don't have much desire to get all the medals that can be collected through the stages, but I'll definitely replay them a lot cos they're just so much fun to run through.

Sonic Team really should do something similar to this game, they could learn a lot, and that's saying something that an incredibly small team (mainly just the one guy) can make something that I could see being influential to a big development studio.

I didn't think too much of the first two Spark games. The first one was a poorly designed 2D platformer trying to jam together two concepts which just don't really go together, and the second was a decent but not great attempt to translate that broken concept into 3D with similar trappings but much better design to make up for it. Spark 3 is the game that finally irons everything out and gets it right. This game is excellent.

The most important change between this game and 2 is the structure of both the individual levels and the level progression in general. There is now a medal system, similar to Sonic Unleashed Wii, where you are awarded "Freedom Medals" by completing stages, and when you collect enough of them, the next stage unlocks. This is to incentivize you to play the various extra stages which have been added to the various worlds which, early on, gives you an opportunity to try out the speed and combat gameplay styles in both open and linear stages. Combined with the tutorial stages that actually instruct you on each specific mechanic, as opposed to Fark's Schoolhouse from the prior game which threw everything at you at once, you are given a much better idea of how you are intended to play the game and the chance to mold your own specific playstyle. As a bonus, most of the extra levels are pretty fun, being essentially better versions of the extra acts from modern 3D Sonic games.

The level design in general has improved a lot from the second game. Whereas the second game felt very much like Sonic Adventure 2, this game has more in common with Adventure 1, more specifically the beta of Adventure 1 where the level design was even more open than it is in the final product. The levels in this are really big and full of various routes which makes this game a lot more fun and reasonable to route for Speedruns than 2. The big addition to the levels is the grind rails, and they are more functional than grind rails have ever been in Sonic with an extremely consistent way to target and switch rails. This game actually manages to somewhat redeem Rail Canyon from Sonic Heroes by making an actually great expy of it years before Shadow Generations did that for real.

One thing I'm very grateful for is that the level themes break off from directly referencing games like Sonic Heroes and Shadow the Hedgehog by the end of the game. Instead, there's a museum stage which feels like a slight reference to Ground Scaravich's stage from Megaman X6 with its trippy visuals, an airport level which is pretty original though it references Metal Harbor in the extra stages, and a distaff counterpart to Titantic Tower where you have to descend into a massive underground city. It feels like Lake Feperd was carving out Spark's own identity as a series, distinct from its influences, towards the back half of the game. Going along with that, there are legitimate setpiece moments in this game where you pilot vehicles. The opening stage is a car level which is jank in the best ways, and the car comes back at various points and is fun and hilarious each time. In Protest City, there's a really well-desinged shmup section where you pilot a VTOL helicopter and progress similar to the 9S mech sections in Nier Automata or the VTOL levels in Star Fox Zero but faster and with better controls. In the airport level, there's a shout out to the Xenogears Battle Arena, which I never expected to see referenced in anything, where you pilot a mech for a bossfight only with much better mechanics. It's a credit to the developer that all of these are really fun to play.

People who weren't fans of combat in the last game will be happy to learn that combat is entirely inessential even in the levels brought back from Spark 2 that had minibosses. There are combat sections which do wall you off and force you to fight, but there's always a way to skip past them even in the last level. I wouldn't recommend it, though (obviously except for speedruns), as combat has actually been improved from the last game. Not only do you have Fark's moveset from the last game, but you now have additional combos, upgrades, and abilities that you can purchase from the upgrade shop. The combat system feels a lot more fleshed out, and boss encounters are a lot more fun as they're harder to melt now that they have area attacks that you can't parry. Parry has sadly been nerfed in general so you can't bypass level obstacles with it anymore either. While it is sad, the levels are designed around i, so it never becomes an issue. I was very happy to see the Jester powers removed from the levels and added to the upgrade shop instead. Now, there's not a constant question of developer intent towards these powers; they are now communicated a lot better as powers specifically for combat, and the ability to use them at any time is good. Though, I wouldn't be opposed to platforming based Jester powers coming back as temporary upgrades in a later sequel.

The medal system has thankfully been overhauled from the last game in that Speedrun medals are a lot more fun to get, and there are now Explorer Medals you can find dotted around the levels for those like me that like to examine the level design. Unfortunately, I don't like what was done with score medals. While I didn't like getting the score medals in 2 because the requirements where so strict, getting the appropriate amount of points within the 5 minute time limit was a legitimately interesting challenge. I do like the change in this game of locking your score rather than reducing it to zero, but for whatever reason the time limit was extended to an HOUR. Don't get me wrong, if you're looking for the Explorer Medals, you can almost clock an hour (the only level I did was Protest City), but just going for the score challenge you will get the right amount of points long before that. It just feels untested because there's no reason to no get the Diamond Score Medal on every level.

The only other complaint I have is not really a complaint but more of a disappointment. This game doesn't quite reach the spectacle of 1 or 2. I actually like the ending of this game quite a bit, but the big bosses, and especially the final boss, with the fantastic vocal themes and music were so hype that it feels like a letdown even if it's not. Also not really a fan of the new moveset you get right at the end of the game, but it's nothing bad, just underwhelming.

All-in-all, Spark 3 is awesome. It's some of the most fun I've had with a high speed platformer, and I say this with no cynicism: It's better than any 3D Sonic. Like with many fan developers, Lake Feperd has actually surpassed the inspiration in quality, and it's a credit to him. I've also appreciated seeing his journey across the three games, making mistakes and learning from them while not giving up on his style. For the first time, it feels like all the parts of a Spark the Electric Jester game are working together rather than against each other, and it really works with everything coalescing. I'm really looking forward to whatever Lake Feperd can do next with Spark 4 or whatever game he works on next.

Some thoughts for this early access game:
- Upgrades for swimming requires you to equip items that override/replace cosmetics, running around with full scuba gear everywhere isn't optimal (aesthetically)
- Air tanks is a consumable item and diving without them is pretty much impossible, no upgrades for increasing tank-less air and deeper dives seem to drain air faster. Personally I would love a Subnautica style upgrade path instead.
- Doubloon paywall the only way to progress and farming can be tedious (mostly limited to daily requests, weekly tourism and selling junk). Speed upgrade quests also locked behind this.
- Critter interactions could be better, learned likes/dislikes isn't visible and too much requests for furniture, clothes and food. Also a lack of routines and/or hobbies for them

I still have great hopes but someone looking for a PC alternative to Animal Crossing should perhaps wait a bit.

[h3]SNAPSHOT[/h3]
A digging / wave defense hybrid without a lot of longevity

[h3]OVERALL - 6 / 10[/h3]

[h3]PROS[/h3]
+ digging gameplay is fun for the most part
+ a good amount of different tools / upgrades

[h3]CONS[/h3]
- gets old fast
- not a lot of diversity in gameplay
- RNG can have a heavy impact on runs
- set difficulty that is more frustrating than challenging

[h3]FULL REVIEW[/h3]
Overall this game has a lot going for it, but ultimately there just isn't a lot here to keep playing after a few runs. The core game loop is fun in and of itself, but the pacing of the runs are abysmally slow such that by the time you finally get to a point that feels fun you're basically done with the run and need to start over again for the next run.

The excruciatingly slow pace of the game also highlights that the gameplay doesn't change between runs, even with the different "challenges" to alter the parameters a bit. Once you understand the basics, there isn't any meaningful meta progression or any semblance of a story to make the player want to keep going, so there isn't really a lot more for the player to do except play until you're tired of doing the same grind every single run.

I found a lot of the challenges way more frustrating than fun as often times you can lose due to bad RNG. It's one thing to lose a run due to poor resource management or the like, but they all seemed tuned to an exact level of difficulty that the devs intended which leaves absolutely no room for inefficiencies (or bad RNG, for that matter).

If you can get this game on a deep discount it's fun to play for a bit, definitely not an $18 game by any means.

I was mislead, I bought this 2 minutes before the sale ended so wasn't paying close attention, the foggy artstyle and reviews talking about esoteric and confusing mechanics made me think this was going to be something twisty and strange.

It's animal crossing without the crushing financial debt. It's real time, night irl means night in the game, stuff takes a few days to grow, the seasons change as they do where you live etc. It's not the same game as AC by any means, but it's the same bones, if you explained animal crossing to someone this is one of the things they might imagine.

You forage for plants and tools, talk with weird fellas, explore, get tools, slowly fill out a few progression things, and it's made to be played in shorter sessions each day, rather then binged in huge chunks. Nothing seems esoteric or hard to understand, it all feels really intuitive actually.

I very quickly understood the gameplay mechanics, and they feel really nice, the menu's are easy to navigate and make sense, nothing seems poorly conveyed, not knowing everything is the point of *exploring* I planted a seed and poked it, saw it asking for a plant I know and one I didn't, so now I want to try growing the one I know near it  and explore till I find the one i don't... cause it's an exploring game.

I'm not sure how in depth plants cohabiting will be but I am honestly eager to see how that progresses.

If you wanted animal crossing to be a short break from stress to wander around collecting stuff and decorating things, doin a few activities and then stopping for a bit, seeing your island grow as you come back each day and chip away bit by bit, and got sick of the ever increasing debt, fruit farming, event fomo, and sudden stop of the gameplay each day, you'll probably really like this, ESPECIALLY if you are interesting in plants at all, cause I'm getting the impression this was made by light botany nerds who were excited to share their nerdy interest with us plant plebians.

If you don't know what to do, there is an achievement progression thing (think nook miles) to guide you towards small goals, and I assume each day new travellers will be hanging around to talk to, with quests and trades.

The local co-op is a nice touch btw I was just hoping I'd be able to play with my partner, appreciate ya devs <3

Right now, thats the main problem I see in it though. Its usability in some of its concepts is.. soooo poor. Like building and moving things around can become such a hassle when you have to constantly *remove attachments*, which means, remove the things that are above or in this structure first. It creates this boring loop of, let me carefully select each of these chests and signs that I placed on this one storage support so that I can then move it. Very chill Early Access survival crafting game - not much in the way of combat mechanics (at time of writing have only encountered 4 hostile entities) nice mixture of scavenging and adventure with a fairly well built out story.

Overall, this had been a very fun game, as I enjoy games with a significant building aspect, which this game does by way of the airship. It has an interesting story, not only in the revelaing of snippets of the past, but also in following the various efforts forward to find The Cure. The game mechanics surrounding the airship are reasonably sound, so flying around the skies is reasonably navigable. However, there are a few points which I find as detractors from the overall playing experience:

1) The path through the game is scripted: go here, do this, go here, do this. If you want to just build on your airship, you have to progress through the script to get the blueprints you want/need to build more. Secondly, once you've made it through the main story-script - discovered all the wrecked items - then you're at the mercy of random chance in finding data cards while you adventure from site to site, hoping to get that blueprint you want. I feel there should be a Blueprint Trade Station (or some such). After all, there's a Trade Station for memorabalia, why not one for blueprints? At least it would be useful to gameplay in some way, which the Trade Station isn't, in my opinion.

2) Inventory: while I immensely appreciate that all the devices which need to pull directly from container inventories, I've found the inventory sizes to be so profoundly limiting, including stack sizes. This is a huge take-away in my view, as it stands in the way of being able to get fully immersed into gameplay. Are the inventory sized "realisitic"? Perhaps true. But for those who want to take everything not bolted down, and then horde it on their airship, being limited is a detractor.

3) Water mechanism: part of the wrecked items in the game are about being able to collect, store, and use water. Sprinklers also play a role if you want to set up a more elaborate systems of watering your plants (see below where I rant about plumbing). I feel there are impotant/convenient aspect which are missing: 1) pipable (automatic) water filtration; and 2) fresh-water storage. There is the Water Purifier, so why can't there be a similar device which hook into a piping system? In combination with this, there are already tanks in the game, so why are they only limited to dirty water? A tank is a tank is a tank, so a tank which can hold "dirty water" can also hold "clean water". Having a ready source of fresh water, so players can focus on gameplay, would be a huge plus.

4) Recycler: I appreciate having the Recycler, but the placement mechanism is woefully lacking. For whatever reason (bug?) the Recycler is totally in-your-face and won't move away when trying to place it. There is a control panel on it, but you can't actually see it because the whole thing in in your face, which means placing it is mostly random (Murphy's Law says the control panel will be against the bulkhead when you paste it!). Trying to move it is the same. You can see the base, so you know where the sides are, but than means you have a 50/50 chance to get the control panel facing you (or the bulkhead).

5) Trash Can: Along with the Recycler, there should be a trash can. For example, I can only dedicate so many storage boxes to Synthetics before it's rather silly, as there's not "easy" method to get rid of it. So...Trash Cans are a thing!

6) Multiple Airships: I have not played co-op, so I don't know if it's possible there or not, to have multiple airships. In single-player, I would wish for a second airship for the same of "easy mobility". I would have my main sirship as my Home Base, which I could park, and not really have to worry about crashing it into a structure while adventuring. For adventuring, I have a much smaller but still capable airship specifically for adventuring and discovery.  A smaller airship is a lot more maneuverable, and can land in a much more confined area, which would make the ability of having a second airship very convenient for the adventuring aspect of the game.

This now brings me to the two aspects of the game, which I so far loathe.

7) Piping System: if you've done any readying, watching videos, etc, etc about the piping system of the game, you already know it sucks. There's no better word for it, than it "sucks".  All I can recommend for is for the devs to: a) play your own game; if you do this, you'll realise how inadequate and buggy the pipe mechanisms of the game are; b) listen to the players, who are all telling you how much it sucks, and in many cases, offering suggestions on hos to improve it. Using a "snap-to-grid" mechanism, whereas /every/ device using water is in compliance, would mean that every device would be able to connect to pipes, and then transition reasonably well from plane-to-plane so interconnections are possible. As currently existing in the game, the snap-to functionality is limited, and in some cases, whatever plane the game engine determines is the plane you've selected, then you're limited to that, no matter how silly it might be, including if there's no resonable way to go to the next plane to arrive at the desired next connection point. In summary, the plumbing mechanisms of the game need a lot of work still. In make cases, I've build a plumbing system, and the pipes change color all the way through, which would seems to indicate things are good, when in reality, they don't connect all the way through. In most cases, if I rip it all out, and re-plumb it all, then it will work. So the pipt mechanism is "buggy" still, and needs a lot more work.

8) Ballon Core placement: Again, I have to recommend to the devs to "play your own game! Try to place a Core, and you'll instantly see how problematic it is!" If you are playing the game for sake of building on your airship, then you'll ultimately need to add another core or two. In the end, lift is lift, so if you need more space in your airship, then having adequate lift is key. The only way to add more lift is to: a) expand your balloons; and b) add more Balloon Cores. Here's where I've found my second source of Major Frustration in the game: trying to place a new Balloon Core. Being in the perfect place, where you can place the Balloon Core where you want it, is the real challenge. In most cases, I've found being over the desired attachment point is the key, as otherwise, the Core will try to go in the least-logical place, where it won't paste anyway. The game's "selection" of where it moved the Core is absurd at best, which means placing it down where you want it is equally problematic.

In conclusion, the game is quite fun, progressing through the story, and especially the building aspects.  If you like adventuring, discovering strange world, then you'll like this game. If you like building/sandbox games, then you'll have a few frustrations, but will still enjoy the progression in being able to get to the point of building the Airship of Your Dreams.

Also hampered by the fact that game is very poorly optimized. I don't have the best computer in the world, but I can play most indie games on either high or ultra settings with little to no frame loss. For instance, Satisfactory works beautifully on my computer even when I've got thousands of ore, ingots, plates, frames, and so on dancing along conveyor belts on ultra settings. But this game chuuuugggsss at random intervals while set to the lowest settings. My hope is that that is fixed in the future. 

Also feel the pump mechanic for the extractor should be reworked and made significantly less necessary. Either pumping more quickly or less frequent. But that and the rate of whatever the flying critters were called (hatchwing nurseries maybe?) were wayyyyy too frequent to be any fun. 

17 hours got me through all of the content currently available, including researching pretty much everything I found interesting and building a ship that could pretty much function independently from the world by the time I was done. If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.

Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The thing that most surprises me about this game is how much it differs from TPH, which I love playing. There were a few frustrations to start with, mostly because the game world doesn't have quite the same rules. Training seems much faster, for example, and some of the information and controls I'm used to just don't seem available.

Having unlocked 4 sites in the game, I'd say the key difference compared with TPH is each campus is designed from the start to be a long, slow burn. It's easy (and tempting) to make your university big quickly, but you end up running out of money. I'm finding it's better to take time to build up your facilities and staff before unlocking that first star, since meeting the game objectives harder as you go. Along with this, I find there is more strategy to TPC - how many students is the right number and what mix of courses? Reducing the student intake by one or two pupils might mean you need fewer rooms or teachers without greatly reducing fees, which means your campus is more profitable. Conversely, adding a small course (like general education) may mean you need another teacher, but you get much more income. Taking out a loan to build a room for just 1 student may be financial suicide, but the same loan used to upgrade and decorate existing facilities so students earn more XP (and you earn LOTS more cash) can be the right move. It requires a lot of attention - especially at the start of each academic year - to make sure you are set for success.

At the same time, the game has simplified some of the features like managing wages. There are 3 employee types, and all wages are increased with a single button rather than individually for each person.

What I do find frustrating is some of the data and controls. First, I have to mention that sometimes the characters get stuck, and it requires a reload (and according to the forums, crossed fingers) to get them to move. 
Restricting rooms to a specific course doesn't seem to work, so the game randomly allocates courses to rooms across campus making your students complain about the long walk. Since this works so well in TPH, I'm surprised about this and disappointed you can't just click and drag a class from one room to another. But, it does add a layer of thinking, as you try to make sure rooms are available reasonably close to each other. 
Creating an event in the following year is also a bit trickier than it should be. You can access the timetable for rooms in various ways, and there's an option to create an event. But the 'create new event' on the NEXT YEAR tab only seems to work by selecting a room then selecting its timetable. Until you get the hang of how to get to this point, it feels frustrating to be able to do this sometimes but not others. (And this seems the only way to create a welcoming party in the first month of your campus' year, since you don't have enough lead time once the year starts to schedule something in August.)

However, having worked out some of the nuances in the controls and info panels, I find myself enjoying TPC and happy to recommend it.

Another great game from Two Point Studios that attempts to build upon (sometimes succeeding, sometimes failing) the success and formula of Two Point Hospital. You can expect all of the NPCs and radio DJs from the first game to make another appearance here, backed by several new additions that, while not as memorable, are still enjoyable in their own regard. 

To get back to that "sometimes succeeding, sometimes failing" thing though, Two Point Campus does fall a bit short of its predecessor in a number of ways. This game is exponentially buggier and, while nothing was technically game breaking, there were at least 5 times throughout my playthrough where a student would just perpetually freeze in place until I reloaded the map. Additionally, furniture placement would just not work for no explicable reason sometimes. Combine that with a new yearly schedule system meant to replicate a college year, several goals that seem improperly balanced, and an unintuitive new training system and you've got a game with a decently confused flow of gameplay at times.

That said, however, I do think this game IS a step up when it comes to visual fidelity, theme variety, and customization. I love the ideas the team came up with for college courses and I loved how each map tasked me focusing on a single one to break up the repetitive nature of the game. In a lot of ways, Campus feels way more personal than Hospital ever did. It just...doesn't really play as well.

Either way, I liked it a lot and I can't wait for Two Point Museum. My full playthrough (3 Starring all 12 campuses) took about 35 hours, just slightly less than the 45 hours it took me to 3 star all 15 hospitals in TPH.

Was hooked from the demo (which should be coming back soon according to dev comments on forum), this is a first-impression review of sorts so can't say what the end of the game will feel like or how story plays out, but I just played coop pretty much 3hrs straight with a friend, discovering new parts about the exploration, platforming as well as combat dynamics which felt fresh & fun for the entire time.

As a 2-indie dev team made ARPG, the biggest standout was not only the whole beast transformation mechanic (not tied to a single class ability) but just the overall feel, fluidity, juiciness in player animations, hit feedback. When you're surrounded by different beasts circling & flanking you, & you're dodging, charging in with a sword attack or taking aim with your bow, to then transforming into a beast yourself with fluid movement & snappy attack swipes & bites, it's just a rewarding combat loop every second with excellent animations feeding this system where you're not really watching healthbars go down with damage numbers flashing, you're watching these elegant creatures leaping & biting sending their foes backwards from hits, arrows connecting-- It's like the marriage of the best of a 3rd person game with AAA levels of animation quality inside an ARPG system where ingame you just marvel at the chaos of packs of beasts and humans battling.

It's fun solo but even better coop. Even if most of your friends might not be super into ARPGs, I think because of the different feel in movement/animations/attacks & the transformation aspect might make it a good game to pull other people into.

My friend was playing on steam deck & had no issues that they mentioned, I played on a laptop, WASD movement feels really good, there's also an "autorun towards cursor" button (CTRL) which allows you to run a bit like the "point&click" of old, but this is a game where you kind will need platforming, SHIFT sprinting + SPACE jumping (&equivalents on controllers&Deck) not entirely sure how that would translate to some classic click-to-move ARPG controls, there's some actual fun platforming exploration, in coop we developed quickly a system of having one in beast form run & jump to then have the other in human form jump off of a mount to mantle some higher ledges which felt cool (Can teleport to other player if they're in beast form)-- Maybe unintended ways to solve some platforming obstacles, I have a suspicion you'll find later beast forms with higher jumps, or maybe even outright flying ones? You also get environmental obstacles solved with other skills, like elementary attacks needed, fire to burn vines to clear a path, electricity to start up an old machine. Nice stuff to add variety inbetween exploring for loot, enemies, & going from A to B.

Loot seems solid in the first hours, slowly getting more varieties with modifiers, shotgun bows, homing crossbows, explosive bows, poison coated swords, maces, spears, dual-wieldable axes & khopesh swords, armor pieces, not to mention beast loot, from different species (cloaking panthers, fire-breathing dragonlites, hopping electricity spewing beasts--)to collars with stats&modifiers, to ranged spit attacks of poison-fire-electricity variety.
There are some classic skills in roughly identifiable classes here, guardian/paladin types, hunter/trickster/trapper types, healer/buffer types, elemental attack types, I think 4 classes with 3 skill trees each focusing on different strengths-- Personally I decided to be silly & do a custom class since the game allows it, with trickster summon tree & healer (devotee?) skill tree where there's also in the tree another summon, just for the extra chaos.
Maybe too early to tell about story, but decent premise so far, this fantasy-techno setting with an ancient technological civilization that's vanished, you start in this middle-eastern feeling village, with these advanced bracers that unlock your beast transformation skill but then also becomes the driving force to you to figure out how to repair them before they grow too unstable. A good motivating force for the protagonists, & there's even decent voice acting which was a welcome surprise.

Some framerate drops in some bigger areas when the fights get busy with tons of beasts & in coop with both players doing massive attacks all over (40-55fps), but I do have a mediocre laptop and decided to play on ultra settings. i5-11400H, 3050RTX (4GBVRAM), 16GBRAM, Win11.

Controls well, plays well, some nice QoL stuff, map is nice, painting areas you've visited, placed markers give you a dynamic trail to follow, though this being a pretty vertical game you can probably also jump & mantle a lot of areas so not always forced to follow the simplest path. Coop was smooth.
This isn't a AA-AAA+ title, devs have stated it's roughly 10-15hrs for main story, 20-30 if you plan on going for side-stuff or all achievements, which personally I'm fine with, bigger ARPGs with 100+hrs of content with infinite endgame stuff feel a bit intimidating for me personally to jump into, but I understand maybe others feel spoiled for choice with stuff that have massive skill trees, endless loot, combinatorial explosions in possibilities of mixing different abilities & gear & more.
But I think for this price, it's absolutely worth it, I expected this to be 30+/-5$/€/£, getting it almost at half of that, easy choice.

Overview:

Coridden is a hack n' slash featuring semi-open levels all connected to one another. The main feature of the game is the ability to shift seamlessly between your human and beast form with additional options available as you progress through the game and defeat more enemies.

Finishing the main game including all side quests took me around 15 hours on Veteran difficulty, although a couple more hours of fun can be had playing repeatable missions from the main hub.

I played most of the game alone since searching for open sessions using the game's built in multiplayer function didn't produce any results. I am unsure about why I could never find other players to join, it might have been a bug or simply not many people playing the game at the time.


+ The positives:

The combat is fast paced and offers great variety in terms of playstyles and possible builds. It's easy to pick up and the game helps you along by highlighting enemies who are about to attack you. The special effects look flashy and gorgeous while still managing to keep your screen clean and enemy attacks easy to read.

Talent trees are plentiful and offer a plethora of choices for both your human as well as animal forms. In combination with the opportunity to respec your character at any point in the game I never ran out of options to try out. Having multiple forms and variants within those forms to shift into makes for a healthy mix of different experiences, making sure you will never get bored throughout your playthrough. Chances are you might beat the game before even unlocking the final rows in your talent trees.

The world is packed full with little areas to explore and wandering off the beaten path will almost always lead to a reward of some kind. Speaking of rewards, all secret treasures in the game are obtainable in singleplayer with the right build. Reaching certain areas require you to jump off the back of a mount  – when playing in multiplayer this would be your fellow player. However, the game offers multiple summoning skills effectively conjuring an NPC beast companion functioning in a similar fashion, making jumps that normally require another person achievable even when playing alone.

The main story is engaging, albeit a bit slow to get going and a tad tropey at times. The game actively encourages exploration to find log files hidden throughout the world to uncover the mysteries of the post-apocalyptic world you find yourself in. Finding these files always felt rewarding as you slowly piece together what happened in these forsaken lands.

The environments are distinct, each with their own soundtrack, and offer breathtaking views at times. The art style is unique, blending traditional environments with futuristic aspects like bio-luminescent foliage or highly technological wreckage.

The team has been great so far in addressing player feedback and potential concerns, so more bug fixes and adjustments are to be expected in the future.


- The negatives:

At the time of me writing this review the game still suffers from numerous bugs like achievements not being awarded despite meeting the requirements, defense objectives or enemies not spawning correctly, bosses falling off the map thereby preventing you from acquiring their loot and stacked items getting partially lost when transferring them between your storage and your inventory.

Enemies tend to lack variety and the same handful of enemy types are being reused over the entirety of the game with the majority of them being already encountered within the first open zones of the game. Different species do come in variants, however most of them boil down to the same couple mechanics you have been seeing for the majority of the game already. This is specifically noticeable in the middle part of the game where barely any new variants are being introduced. It gets better towards the end again but in between it can get repetitive.

The difficulty of enemies in the world varied greatly depending on the respective zone, but seemed to follow no tangible system at times. The main quest will send you to one zone where you would encounter a significant difficulty spike, only for the following quest step to send you to the next zone featuring much lower enemy levels than the one you had previously been to. This can however be fixed by simply adjusting the game’s difficulty from the main menu any time you run into one of these cases.

You acquire most new shapeshift forms, weapons and attacks for your animal form by defeating enemies. The concept is good, however some of the drop rates seem a bit skewed as of now, leading to some of the weapon types being extremely hard to come by. For example: I finished the game at level 34 and up until level 30 I didn't even know certain weapons types existed since I never got any dropped. Half the game I was stuck using the same ranged attack due to the lack of alternatives and only in the final 2-3 hours of the main game I was suddenly bombarded with more new options to try out than I effectively needed. Maybe I just got unlucky with the drop rates, but this was my experience. Maybe in the future we will be able to purchase animal weaponry or beast forms from vendors as bad luck protection, but as of now RNG is your worst enemy.

The camera in Coridden is fixed and cannot be manually adjusted or controlled. This works fine most of the time, but there are occasions when you end up fighting the camera more than actual enemies. From structures and trees blocking your screen or ranged enemies being able to target and attack you from outside your field of view, I oftentimes felt the desire to zoom further out with the camera or slightly adjust the angle to get a better look at what’s going on. Getting hit out of nowhere by a projectile coming from off screen can be annoying at times, especially when fighting stronger enemies that can dish out significant damage in a single strike.

Some of the controls feel a bit archaic and clunky on mouse and keyboard, specifically when traversing the map. Especially jumping at a diagonal angle can feel very frustrating at times. It works flawlessly on controller, but when playing with M&K more often than not the game locks you to one of your primary axes when jumping despite you pressing two keys simultaneously. Normally this could be easily addressed by allowing players to turn the camera, but since the camera and field of view are locked in this game, successfully jumping at a diagonal angle usually took me more attempts than felt appropriate. Combine that with an instant death if you mistime a jump above an abyss and you have a recipe for frustration. To its credit through, the game does present you with a popup message when launching for the first time that the game is best enjoyed with a controller.


Verdict:

Coridden is a charming indie game with a unique take on an exiting formula that isn’t afraid to try new things. Despite its flaws I had a lot of fun playing the game, even alone, although I can certainly confirm the game is more fun with friends.

Could be hard to believe, but on a personal level, I enjoy this game even more than Baldur’s Gate Dark Alliance series. This game is so much fun and the shape shifting element is not just a “gimmick.” It stands on its own even without that mechanic.
I like the quest board where you can work up your levels before you have to take on the important quest. Also I love being able to change into a creature, I mostly stay in my creature form.

This is a great co-op experience and an impressive release for a small indie team. The combat is good and there are meaningful benefits to working as a team. They've clearly taken a lot of care to smooth out the rough edges that most other co-op games miss. You shouldn't expect AAA levels of polish, but the core elements that matter are all here.

There's still some bugs to work out at the time of writing though. The menus are a bit unintuitive, the key icon on items or actions sometimes uses the wrong input device for the character. The biggest issue is that saves work as checkpoints, so the occasional crash will reset you to the beginning of an area. These are all minor bugs and I'm sure they'll be fixed soon.
An extremely smooth co-op experience with great combat and direction so far.

Do you always play Druids in RPGs? Wish you could carry around that one friend who inevitably separates from the group and gets lost? Perhaps you just have an atavistic urge to grab someone with your teeth and shake them like a ragdoll? Well, this is the ARPG for you!

Having been designed around it as a core gameplay element, Coridden features much better shapeshifting mechanics than most games out there; swapping from human to beast and back again is seamless, and subtle differences in how your character handles on four legs compared to two combine with a full suite of silky smooth quadruped animations (including specialized animations for actions which often get overlooked, such as making a sudden 180° turn or clambering up ledges) to ensure that each beast form looks and feels just as good to play with as the human form does. Plus, as hinted at in my opening paragraph, there are a couple of rarely-explored options available to you as a beast; namely, the ability to carry human players on your back in order to give them greater mobility, and the ability to grab enemies smaller than yourself in your jaws (or, in the case of the scorpion-tailed Scaptor, impale them on your stinger) and drag them around, maul them, or swing them into other nearby foes.

Although you are expected to swap frequently between human and beast forms in order to take advantage of the separate stamina meters and skill cooldowns, it is entirely possible to build your character in such a way as to stay in one form or the other permanently; with twelve human skill trees and eleven beast skill trees, you'll still have plenty of options. Perfect for a duo wherein one player acts as the designated mount and the other as the rider!

Coridden does unfortunately exhibit a bit of "indie game jank," e.g. occasional clipping through environment geometry, and the current game balance is somewhat... less-than-balanced, but it has a solid foundation which only needs polishing up to become something special.

I doubt the voice acting will win any awards :), but the fact that it's there and not cringy is a big bonus in my book.  

One of the most difficult feats to accomplish in an RPG is the creation of a UI that gives the player all of the information they need while simultaneously making it easy to access when needed.  Honestly, the way that this game presents data to the player should be considered a standard for all RPGs.  It's easy to navigate and provides the player with all the information necessary to make solid choices, particularly when it comes to gear, abilities, level-up choices, and many other critical parts of a positive RPG experience.  

Hats off to the devs - excellent work!

Cheers,

Coridden is an interesting game that i picked up for the sake of playing "couch" co-op with my dad when he came over (for some reason PoE 2 doesn't seem to let you do that with both keyboard and controller at the same time- can't tell you why).
--
THE GOOD
--
Turned out to be more enjoyable than I initially gave it credit for, complete with seamless shapeshifting, delay-free swapping between melee and range and skills (and stamina on both beast and human forms are tracked differently encouraging swapping for maximum uptime). The combat can be rather deliberate rather than spamming monsters at you (which is only an issue early in the campaign) and the dodge button actually feels good. (That might have to deal with the next point.)

And rather than suffocating, labyrinthine maps choked full of monsters that make the campaign a chore, they are pretty wide open (which does mean you are holding sprint in beast form, but... you have a sprint - it's not even a dedicated movement skill that you have to waste a socket on). Oh, and the maps have verticality... I legit did not think that isometric jumping puzzles could be anything but obnoxious, so I am reasonably impressed.

And, if you want to say "fuck the campaign, just take me to maps," well... it's got "missions" as soon as you get out of the introduction arena. And if you make a mistake in your build, you get to freely reallocate everything from stats to skill points at your house (which is also protection against sudden and crippling nerfs without needing to farm a few hours on a nerfed build).

The loot's pretty fun since different weapon combinations result in different moves, and your shapeshift is an actual item (that can be target farmed by the looks of it), and each beast type has its own skill tree and attacks.
--
THE Not-So-GOOD
--
It does go with the more traditional diablo 2 style skill tree rather than the skill web (so pick one skill, and max it out.... rather boring design), and doesn't appear to have "supports" for skills (as far as I can tell)...
But you get to multiclass in from level 2 onwards. And, unlike Path of Exile... I don't see this game getting a lot of post-release support. There's no monetization - just a single purchase. Don't get me wrong not having scummy monetization is a good thing, as is being cheap while polished, but it does mean there won't be a financial incentive to continue to push out new updates and leagues and such, unless they start selling expansions, which does not look like what they have planned.
Oh, and some of the jumping puzzles are actively impossible with the keyboard, while being trivial with the controller.
Moving Downwards also has *severe* vision limitations.  And moving down screen is really, really common. Some camera versatility would be useful.

There's a main storyline and also repeatable side content.  The big twist of this game is that your character can shapeshift, and there's ample incentive to do so frequently, as both human and animal forms have separate energy bars that deplete as you attack.
Overall, it hits all the standbys of the genre and does a great job at implementing the things that make it different.  The rough bits, which drag my rating down to only an 8 or 9 out of 10, are things like 3-D features occasionally interfering with the camera, a lack or variation in the repeatable missions, or a slightly clunky inventory system.  The skill trees are also a bit disappointing - Everything has 6 ranks, so you're spending most of your time on incremental improvements rather than actual new things, and don't gain new abilities nearly as often as you might expect.

This game is incredible. It is a very small dev team and a fairly small game, yet for the price this game is absolutely a gem. 
    Before I give game feedback I want to note how wonderful the dev team is. They are actively taking feedback and improving the game from their discord. Furthermore I messaged them one week before the release of the game when I was playing the demo with my wife to let them know that while it was an excellent demo, the out of stamina noise was painful and was hindering the experience. They fixed it by the full release (purchased day 1, the demo was that good.)

Pros -
1. Fluid and engaging combat. The combat is the shining star of this co-op game. It was designed from the ground up with the shape shifting mechanic and playing with your friends in mind and it does it flawlessly. I rarely give anything a perfect score in a game. That being said, no ability goes to waste in this game, they are all impactful and every action has a reason to do a playthrough with it.
2. The shapeshifting. There are very few games that let you turn into creatures. I have been hunting for good shifting games since being a fan of the Animorph books as a kid. I have never found one that does it this well. you have equal value between being in creature form and human form and both feel excellent.
3. The story. The story may be a little basic for some but for me its clever and engaging. I especially appreciate that allot of the sidequests give you an option to turn them in if you already have the item in hand. I am also enjoying experiencing the story as it unravels. It has entertaining twists and developments.

Cons -
No game is perfect and I would feel bad to not discuss the bad with the good, but don't take these as super harsh.
1. The inventory management. The biggest downside by far is that in some ways this is a rogue like and that means loot. Organizing the loot and upgrading gear is by far the most annoying part of the game. That being said you dont absolutely need to engage with it that much and the devs are actively working on improving it.
2. The voice acting. Frankly, its just dull. Some places it even is old school ps2 levels of funny. It doesn't really take away from the game at all but I will say it can be delivered in a bit of a harsh manner from time to time.
3. The exploration isnt the most rewarding. Allot of the gear you find will be under leveled or not have upgrade slots which are fairly important.

Overall I am currently giving Corriden a 7/10. But I want to give it an 8/10. I am holding back because I havent finished the full game and I suspect its going to prove very short. That being said it has allot of replay ability and is one of the best coop experiences currently available!
