This game is very fun, there is a ton of creativity and heart behind this project and I'm very excited to see what comes next for the future of this game. To further explain to you what this game is like, i will create a detailed pros and cons list below

PROS:
Combat- combat is very fun and feels great once you get used to it. using a combination of bestial forms, as well as cyber inspired medieval weaponry like axes, swords, hammers, spears, crossbows, bows.

Forms- In this game you will collect beast forms from slain enemies, each form has its own load out and levels independently from the human form. Each beast specializes in different elements and mechanics; Fire, Electric, Poison or you could go with a more base specialization such as; Bleed, Health, Stealth, Defenses.

Co-op- this came features both local and online co-op and is an absolute blast. with a party up to 4 players large it makes you feel like you are playing an old school Gauntlet game. There are different AOE buffs that can stack and apply party wide translating into some very silly progression. For example, when traversing my first co-op play-through, I speced into an electric archer style of play, with homing missiles and ranged barrage attacks. one of my friends specked into a stealthy beast form giving him the ability to stealth and dart around the battle field leaving trails of poison. and my final friend specked into a tank. i mounted my beast form friend like a little mounted turret while the tank took agro letting us demolish our foes.

Mounting- as per the last pro, i mentioned mounting. i thought this was a super cool mechanic, allowing you to mount your summoned creatures, or a friend that is in beast form. it unlocked a whole new angle to play the game from.

Progression- The games progression feels quite good, i never felt too powerful or too weak, despite completing every side quest i stumbled upon. levels are meaningful as they only give a small portion of attribute and skill points that you must thoroughly consider where to put.

Respec- Now take what i just said and ignore it entirely, because you can respec everything that levels at any time, for very cheap. this lets you play around with everything with no real downside. I love games with respec mechanics

Gear- The gear in the game is all super interesting, made true by the socket system. Gear consists of; Helmet, Chest, Main Hand, Off Hand, Ranged Weapon, Beast Form, Collar, and Breath Weapon. All portions of gear can be augmented with Diablo style sockets that alter and add properties to the weapon.

Augmenting- augmenting/forging/crafting is incredibly intuitive, as someone who often struggles with processing numbers in rpgs. its quite simple and augments can be changed out at the forge. there are also secret sequences you can find through out your journey in Log Books. placing the augmentations in that order on any bit of gear will grant even more power to the player/beast form.

Skills- The skills in this game consist of passives, auras, and actives. each one feels pretty good, and each one feels powerful when building into it. some of the animations are very fun for it as well.

Art- I absolutely love the art direction of this game, a combination of fantasy, post apocalyptic, science fiction. that tickles my chest. all the flora and fauna look like if Tourok and Avatar ad a love child. Great job to the devs for blending all that together so naturally.

Music- From what i have heard of the music its pretty good, nothing to in your face. in my opinion its a little too subtle and i often found the music over shadowed by the sound of combat.


CONS:

Camera- The camera angles are... questionable at time. i spoke with the Dev team about it so hopefully it will be fixed with haste, but at the time of writing this review i have to apply this note.

Move-Set- This may just be a personal gripe, but all the weapons have basically the same move-set. Axes, Hammers, and Swords both one-handed and two-handed have the same move-set. Spears, and Halberds have differing move-sets, but in the future i would love to see more animations for different weapon types.

Buff/Debuff Timer- as of right now there are no displays or indications of active buffs or debuffs aside from stuns. If they do exist then they are to subtle to notice in the vibrant world. in the future id love to see clear buff timers, maybe displayed at the top of the screen, and more noticeable effects for things like bleed, poison, shock, scorch, ect.

Run Time- I'm sure this is an issue only now, at the launch of the game,  but the game is fairly short. I completed it and a grand majority of the side-quests within around 16 hours. Normally that would be a fine amount of time for an ARPG style game to complete the story, but as of right now, there isn't a whole lot to do after the main quest ends. This is an issue that I'm positive will be solved in the somewhat near future.

Beast Forms- there is only one down side to the forms, and this is a personal gripe and more than likely wont apply to most people, but in the future, i would love to see more diverse skill trees for the forms, as of now i feel like many of them are the same with the same moves flavored with a different element.

Skill Points- Right now the current level cap is 40. i know this will change in the future, but as of right now I don't feel like i have enough skill points available to really complete a full load out for any skill tree as i only get one skill point per level, perhaps a consideration for 2 skill points per level would feel better.


Overall i would give this game a very solid 8 out of 10.

Still very early on in Coridden, 5 hours as of this review, playing with a friend, and it's been a blast. First of all, this is a game to go into with the expectation that it's a 15$-20$ game by a small indie team, and the level of polish will understandably not be able to match up to larger developers.

In terms of features, the game plays from an isometric view where enemies encroach into your view from offscreen, often in large hordes to attack. Every player has a melee button and a ranged weapon to use, as well as one equippable creature form at any time with a melee attack and interchangeable breath attacks.

There are 4 classes to choose from, as well as a customizable class that lets you pick and choose from the skill trees of multiple classes. Each class has 3 skill trees to select abilities and passives from. In addition, each [i]beast[/i] form has it's own levels and skill tree, and an option of 1 additional skill tree with various elemental or additional powers. Altogether each player has access to up to 5 skill trees at any time to pick and choose abilities from. There's a tremendous amount of depth here and I've only just scratched the surface.

Combat is fairly fluid with what feels like a soft lock on system. Changing forms during battle is encouraged with the stamina system. Attacking and using abilities uses up stamina. When stamina is fully depleted, switching forms gives you a full second stamina bar to drain while the other refreshes. Combat does not feel too challenging so far, but offers enough diversity to be enjoyable.

Loot so far feels fairly simple, but enjoyable. There's a handful of weapon and ranged weapon types to try, and some quests reward more unique types. Higher level creature forms and ones with different appearances are discoverable when killing enemies.

The creature forms, the main selling point for the game, all feel fairly unique from each other, while sharing similar features. I've only discovered 4 so far, but my co-op partner and I have favored different ones. Theirs sprints faster and features fire and physical attacks, while mine had an enchanced leap, keeping it agile while firing off electrical attacks. You are also able to mount a fellow player in creature form (or summonable mount) and attack and cast abilities from their back.

Again, you won't mistake this for a big budget game, as graphically it's fine, but nothing to write home about, and voice acting is sparse with some curious voice direction (potentially AI driven or enhanced, but I am not well versed enough to say for certain). I will credit them for the creation of a lot of what seem like unique assets and models though.

As a final note, Steam Deck compatibility has not been verified as of this review, but my co-op partner is playing on Deck and has encountered zero issues thus far.

[b] First off: [/b]
The game itself is amazing, it's not the most amazing game I've played, but it has more heart than many games I have played before and as of late is among my top 10 favorite games with just the impact it's made so far. I think the devs did a wonderful job on this and I appreciate the fact that they were able to bring this out and give this game life.

[b] Shapeshifting: [/b]
The shapeshifting mechanic is probably one of the biggest parts that I was excited about, though at first I was a bit hesitant too. The ability to switch to and from forms I thought would take a while, but no massive animations, no excessive flare except the first time you transform to a form. It's like a little "Congrats, this is your new shape, take it in." fanfare, then you change immediately.

My hesitation mentioned earlier was I was afraid the shapeshifting mechanic would be a sort of "You can only stay in this form for so long before energy/timer runs out." but no, it's just use your form as much as you like. It's a breath of fresh air, and the beast form usually is good for traversal and moving quickly. Yet your human form is just as useful and some abilities can be layered between forms, such as switching to human form, slamming down a healing field, switching to beast, and using that to tank with the beast's defenses and strike down particularly tough enemies, giving you the option to play with some of the strengths of both.

[b] Forge/Alterants: [/b]
The forge is also another amazing system. Get a piece of armor, weapon, beast collar, or even a beast with an Alterant (enhancement) you like but don't like the gear itself? Take it out for cheap, store it up for later, find something you love, and improve it by putting in the Alterant. It even affects beasts themselves, so you can make a beast incredibly strong and capable, and because Alterants can be taken back out, it means that your build isn't lost if you find something better or more appealing. This is a massively appreciated feature that I absolutely love, and the fact that beasts themselves can have them is a gorgeous mechanic choice. It should be noted when you take out an Alterant, you do need to still forge the item after it is removed so it's confirmed removed.

[b] Combat: [/b]
Combat feels very good, dodging doesn't take up energy, so you don't get punished for using up all your energy trying to avoid attacks only to have nothing to strike back with. Instead dodging is encouraged because of this so it gives you time to recover your energy mid fight while keeping the defensive. It's not too potent of a dodging mechanic, but just enough so you learn and can still enjoy the game. I can say in most cases if I mess up on a dodge, it's my fault.

The fact that both human and beast form get a type of ranged attack is amazing too. I absolutely love it and think it's amazing. I don't feel completely forced to one form or another just because my enemy is a bit out of melee reach. And lastly, the fact that melee movement (turning while attacking) actually has impact (such as some forms will use their tail more if you're turning while striking) is a beautiful touch.

Being able to grab enemies as a beast is even more amusing if you're bigger than them. However if you are smaller, some of them may do the same to you. It is both hilarious and terrifying to have a Houndra rush up on you, grab you and slam you around on the ground before throwing you against the ground leaving you barely breathing. After being mauled by a Houndra myself I couldn't help but imagine it saying "Puny god".

[b] Mobility: [/b]
Mobility is absolutely great, running, dodging, strafing and moving around feels more alive and fun. Small things here and there give something beautiful. I found myself in a beast form chasing my tail and just having a bit of a laugh. That simple dual stick (Move and Aim independantly) mechanic while moving adds volumes of expression to movement and function. It's simple but I absolutely love it and it comes in handy and makes me actually have to aim for ranged attacks.

But once again, shapeshifting comes into play. Just barely failing to hop up on a ledge even at full sprint jump in beast form? Shift mid jump to human form and hold jump, it will let you change to human and get that little ledge grab and pull yourself up when you couldn't get up somewhere in human or beast form alone. Again, a great touch that I was absolutely impressed by.


Onto the main and honest honest issue I have with the game. Saying this ahead of time, I would rather make simple suggestions if I see a problem or at least be somewhat positive where possible.

[b] Main issue: [/b]
The camera is probably the biggest issue I have here. When having to do some dangerous jumps, it can be very difficult to see where you're going and plan your jump ahead at full sprint as a beast depending on where you are. If turning the camera can't be done, then a suggestion could be controlled zooming of the camera or zoom tied to the Sprint button so when you hold it down it zooms out especially in beast form. If possible, an option to control said "sprint zoom" distance a little bit if manual zooming can't be done.

This can also hit hard when you have longer range attacks with a bow/crossbow/beast ranged attack, and it's hard to see where your opponent actually is.


[b] Final thoughts and statements: [/b]
This is an absolutely beautiful game as said before. I can see the work and effort and ideas poured into it. A little bit more polish could help, but I love this so far. To the devs and those who helped in the game, for those who supported it, if you read this, I want to say say this:

Thank you, To the devs for making this game, for the supporters who helped the devs keep working on it. I hope that you'll keep that passion and those ideas at heart in the future. I hope money and fame doesn't blind you. I hope that your success continues, and finally I hope that you all have a wonderful time both now and in the future.

Conclusion: even if the game feels a bit unfinished and unpolished, it introduces some new staff in the isometric RPGs genre, and some of them are funny. I think the game is probably not worth playing alone, but in couples, it is great. In my view, it is great for relaxed and easy-to-understand upgrades and a relaxed pace of going through the camping. It's decent but has lots of problems.

Good:
-Soundtrack is well composed and sounds excellent
-Map is large and expansive
-System requirements are light, game will run below minimum spec (I have tested personally)
-Game is mostly well polished in terms of UI and graphics with only a few flaws.

Bad:
-Lot's of grinding and resource gathering doesn't always feel consistent
-Some content isn't easy to figure out
-Game is too expensive for what's given, I recommend it only if it's on sale for at least 33% off. I'm likely to remove this as more content is added to make it actually worth $29.99.
-Game is too easy after health upgrades, you'd have to be braindead to die to anything unintentionally even with damage set to maximum

Some suggestions for gameplay:
-More consistent ways of resource gathering, such as drills like in Slime Rancher 1 and make resources area specific, maybe a hybrid approach would work where you'd find resources and a drill would provide a ton of the resource but over time. Or potentially ways to scan for items using the map or a new upgrade.
-More enemies/hazards should be added and a difficulty slider to make the game actually feel like a challenge. Existing Tarr and damage settings could be linked to this.
-Add more consistent guidance throughout the game on how to progress
-Add ability to make waypoints on the map to allow players to mark important areas
-More slimes need to be added. Slimes that are based on elements is an idea I came up with, similar to Pokemon. And also more rare slimes, potentially spawned by scripted events or just extremely low chance or specific situations.
-Less focus on decorations/non-essentials and more on story/gameplay. Not everyone cares for cosmetic features, you already have more than enough especially in the latest versions of the game.
-Add underwater gameplay and more water based features. For a game where a significant portion of the map is water, the Slime Sea isn't much more than a trash can for Tarrs or items you don't need.

Technical things:
-Add higher LOD settings, distance detail is far too low even at max settings and it's obvious.
-Add MSAA back, Slime Rancher 1's 8X MSAA clearly looked better and it's easy to add to this type of game engine and graphics API. Please do not go towards the current trend of bad AA tech and upscaling like TAA, FSR, DLAA etc. which all look terrible.
-Game still stutters even on the strongest of PCs, and even worse on low end systems. Although this has gotten much better since launch.

Although Slime Rancher 2 is an ambitious take on its predecessor, it fails to deliver any meaningful changes over the original.

Slime Rancher 2 is the sequel to the highly praised slime rancher, a game all about collecting slimes and farming their valuable Plort on the market. 
Gameplay mostly follows the same formula of its predecessor, with different areas to explore each home to a different set of slimes to capture. Gordo’s, largo’s, corrals, gardens, chicken coops and slime toys all make a return. The ranch, albeit aesthetically very different, functions roughly the same with multiple areas to unlock to house new slimes. Characters from the first game also make a welcome return to tie two games together. 

The game has a few new features, like upgrades no longer just costing money, but also resources gathered from the world, although these resources can no longer be obtained using harvester. Instead, you collect them yourself. Also, slime science is unlocked from the start, giving you access to hundreds of cosmetics to decorate your ranch with. And as can be expected, the game has a multitude of new slimes to collect and take care of on your ranch. The world, rainbow island, looks great and is far less linear than the world of the original. It is clear a lot of time was put into making the world feel far more interesting to explore. Personally, I thought the colour palette of the game at times was a bit too soft, but it fits the style of the game well.

Sadly, that’s where the positivity for this game ends for me. Yes, the world has gotten a face lift, and the new slimes are a welcome addition, but this game just doesn’t do anything that differently compared to slim rancher 1. Drones are missing from the previous game, and the game really doesn’t have much of a story. There are no major new mechanics, other than a few weather effects that have a minor impact on the world. I hoped this game would make ranching more interesting, with perhaps different climates too keep your slimes happy, new corrals or corral upgrades or new ways to combine slimes together. It doesn’t have any of that, while cutting a lot of the features the original had. Yes, the game is in early access, but it has been for two years now, and the end doesn’t seem near at all. Most of the time and effort has been placed in more ways to customise your farm and a new shiny world, but very little effort was made to make the game mechanically interesting. I’ve put around 50 hours in the original, but this game can hardly entertain me for more than 10 hours.

If you are new to the game, please just buy the original on sale for a few euros, before considering this game. Preferably, wait a few more years so this game has some time to become engaging. And if you must, consider buying it on sale.

This sequel presents major improvements to its predecessor. Better sound, more interesting ways of finding slimes (weather), different ways to harvest plorts, new slimes and slime catching methods, new lands, new methods of finding resources, and upgrading your tools is tied to the crafting system. It does not alter its core loop too severely, so it will feel like a continuation of the original game.

My only problem is the amount of progress I make in the game is minimal. In the game, you leave the ranch, hunt slimes, procure resources, and unlock new territories. Then you return, feed your slimes, deposit or sell plorts, and continue the process.  Each time you complete this cycle, you increase your money, build new expansions, craft new items and upgrades, and more to increase your revenue stream and make it easier to explore the lands.

But in Slime Rancher 2, the amount of "progress" I make feels insignificant. I can never seem to find the right blueprints/treasure pods, the right resources don't appear in the correct places can't be found. It took me at least 10 hours to find the first energy upgrade, 20 to find the jetpack. Jellystones love popping up at different points when they respawn, so its hard to find 10 to create another Finery Repository.

This issue becomes glaringly obvious in the Grey Labyrinth, where doors are locked by plorts belonging to Slimes that do not appear in the area. If you are clever you will find the right slime in a jar and feed it, but it sure feels difficult. Also, you need 1000 Shadow Plorts to unlock every "treasure pod" in the area, which are acquired by firing objects at the Shadow Slimes - 1 plort per collision/touch. So... you'll be spending a lot of time at this.

It's a great game, but just thinking about the tasks makes it difficult to play it for any more than 3 hours a day.

Other than the fact this kind of just feels a little like a copy of Slime Rancher, it's different enough that it's still fun to play, even after having played Slime Rancher 1 (if you have) It also allows you to be fairly familiar with the mechanics. The only things that are notably different I think should be disclosed if you HAVE played slime rancher 1, is the fact that resources are gathered throughout the land with your Vac this time around, instead of through the machines you craft in the lab place, there are no helper drones (yet), and you can't buy upgrades anymore- well, you still have to buy them, but you also need resources and, like, parts specific to the upgrade. Which is a little annoying, but it does add some-... enrichment, to the experience. Feels a bit more compelling. Very good game, and even if you've played the first game, I still think the second is worth playing. Just be sure to do some research on it before hand, because while the mechanics are similar, enough of it is different that you should look more into it, maybe even before buying (and maybe buy it when it's on sale, lol).

Ah, yes, a park that keeps business hours in the post-apocalypse. Sounds like the company where a friend of mine works.

But while running to my workbench for the umpteenth time because I was missing  one lousy microchip and that is the only place you can craft it, I simply stopped, said "I don't want to do this anymore", closed and uninstalled.

However, I was slightly disappointed that some structures lacked an incentive to upgrade—for example, the barrier dome over infected plants, where the first level was sufficient. I also wished for more explorable areas beyond what’s visible from the rooftop. While elevators provide access to different sections, the helper robots couldn’t use them, forcing you to haul materials up manually—at an agonizingly slow pace! An upgrade to improve their speed would be a great addition. Hopefully, the developers plan to expand the world and refine some of these mechanics in future updates.
I played a bit longer to unlock achievements, but the main story wraps up fairly quickly. Unfortunately, some achievements seem to be bugged—I painstakingly placed all the roof patches but never received the achievement, which was pretty disappointing. 😞

I also wish the cooking system provided more guidance on ingredient combinations for recipes. Additionally, better recipe organization would be a huge improvement—perhaps sorting them alphabetically or by category. While drinks have their own tab, everything else (desserts, simple ingredients, and main dishes) is lumped together, which led to a lot of unnecessary scrolling just to find what I wanted to cook.

Pros:
- Recruitment system and headquarters mechanics are extremely satisfying.

- The story was much better than expected, by the end of the game I ended up really liking some of the characters that I originally hated. 

- War mode is also much more enjoyable than expected (first few are boring and slow but the war battles later in the game are amazing).

Cons: 
- At endgame, there are multiple story missions where there won't be save points until after an hour.

- When you reach a higher level than enemies, they start giving like 1% of the exp that they usually would. This means that random encounters will inevitably become tedious and pointless at every area, which is a frustrating time-waster in areas where you need to constantly backtrack (especially the final castle and library, I almost quit the game when needing to go through that area because this).

- The stat scaling for characters drastically change between levels. Some characters like Iugo remain consistently great throughout the whole game, while characters like Mio have worthless stats for her first 60 levels but then suddenly shoots up at the end (when Mio is level 50, many of my level 30 mage characters have higher physical attack than her). Milana is also somewhat similar, she is a mage with garbage magic stats but decent physical stats until she hits around level 55 at which point her magic stats start shooting up. This means that many characters that you get early on are not even worth using until the end of the game.

I really want to like this game, there are some genuinely good things about it. But I feel like for every good thing, there's another that just makes you sigh or groan.

The writing and overall story is pretty good, for the most part. While you recruit a large number of characters, only a handful have an actual effect on the story as a whole. But I really have to say, Lian is the absolute worst character in any game I play, I cannot stand her archetype. She adds absolutely nothing except to maybe antagonize Nowa for no reason, she is insufferable. As a contrast, however, the Empire characters are all very interesting in my opinion, and when you get to learn more about them, it's a nice change of pace. The voice acting is also well done for each character, no matter how small.

A knock against the game though is the sheer number of mini-games present; it really feels like this game was the victim of design creep. Off the top of my head, I can list dueling, army battling, card games, beyblade, egg hatching, racing, kingdom management, goods trading, cooking battles, fishing and I'm sure I'm forgetting some. Many of these mini-games are required to play if you want to recruit all of the characters.

As far as gameplay goes, it's a mixed bag. Most normal fights you can just hit the Auto button and not worry about it, then for bosses they take a bit more thought as they sometimes have a certain gimmick. It would have been nice to figure these out myself through trial and error, but the game almost always tells you what they are. However, the mechanics of combat itself leaves something to be desired. You almost never use magic due to how scarce MP regenerating items are, and magic takes up a comparatively large amount to use, as you don't have much to begin with (my mages are close to lvl 40 and have roughly 300 MP, and spells typically cost 40+). 

And then there's just a lack of polish overall. Item management is a nightmare with only 30 item slots until you hit midgame (it can be expanded though), and it also includes equipment as well as restorative items and food. You can only save at save points (though some would consider this a plus). There is a massive amount of backtracking necessary. The encounter rate can be confusingly high at times. There's no footstep sound when you run, and your movement speed is, at it's default, unbearably slow. When you rest at an inn (which are ludicrously expensive), you only restore the HP and MP of characters in your active party. The list goes on.

If you're a fan of old-school RPGs, you'll probably like Hundred Heroes. I've never played Suikoden myself, so I don't have nostalgia for it. But it's certainly clear that this game is an homage to old-school RPGs. My biggest hang-up though is that there's a decent amount of modern-day polish that I feel is missing. I'm giving this a recommend purely because I know that there are some people who absolutely love this kind of game, but as for myself, I'm about halfway through it right now, and am unsure if I'll see it through to the end.

Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes - 2024 Review - The Spiritual Successor of Suikoden, does it meet expectations?

To start this review off I will say I am a huge Suikoden fan. I remember seeing Suikoden II being announced in a Game Informer magazine from Funcoland, and so I marched down there (begged my dad to drive me) and used my lawn mowing money to buy Suikoden I and II. From there I fell in love with the series and played all except the Japanese only release on PSP and Suikoden Tierkreis on the DS.

Whether we as Suikoden fans love this game or not, the reality stays the same: this is the ONLY reason that Konami woke up and decided to remaster Suikoden I and II. If this revives the series, this game is what we should thank for that. So even with its bugs on release, we must appreciate what it has done for us as fans.

The development of Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes was led by Yoshitaka Murayama, the legend, the creator of the Suikoden video game series by Konami. Murayama had directed Suikoden and Suikoden II during his time at Konami, but left the company in 2002 shortly before the release of Suikoden III. Sadly right before Hundred Heroes was release, we were all hit with the news that Murayama had passed away. It was funded by Kickstarter and it was the 3rd highest funded video game in Kickstarter history. Original release date was said to be October 2022 before being delayed. The game was then set for a 2023 release but was delayed to 2024. Finally then being released on April 23, 2024.

Art Style:
I'd say the strongest part of this game, the art style is another beauty. Once again we have another 2D Pixel style that is merged with 3D backgrounds. Like the original Suikoden games, I love the detail on the characters and combat art. The bosses and enemies are done well and don't feel regurgitated throughout the game. All in all a job extremely well done, absolutely succeeded in making a vibrant and living world.

Cast of Characters:
I know the original plan was to release DLC for each of the 3 major characters in this game. I will say I do hope that is the case. While I really enjoyed the character interactions and the growth they had, I felt like I didn't really know much about them. Specifically Marissa, she felt very hollow, with a past that was mentioned but really not further explored. Similar to games like Suikoden or Chrono Cross, when you have more than your average characters, its going to be hard to make them very deep. Such is the case in Eiyuden, but it was to be expected that not every character would have a backstory or plot point. The issue more so is that some characters were just downright useless. Yet I did like that some of the characters you recruited in the very beginning actually could last till endgame. There were some characters who were trapped behind mini games that I am never usually a fan of.

Gameplay:
Oooof, gameplay. I think the best way to do this is to just get the technical errors out of the way. There were several bugs when this game released that really affected the gameplay. It took a while for them to be patched, while some still haven't been touched. As for the bugs that have been fixed, I can look past, but there was some specific ones that really affected my rating. Anyone who has played Suikoden knows the Combo system. Basically specific characters can have combos with each other, which may make weaker characters actually worth using if they have a strong combo with another. Eiyuden brought that system into its gameplay except.....its just about worthless. I am not sure if it was meant to be this way, but the damage % is a mess. Combos did less damage then normal attacks. It just didn't make a whole lot of sense. I also felt like the magic system was a bit off. Late game you get a mage who was phenomenal, but for a majority of the game there wasn't a single person who could put out good magic damage. I enjoyed the "gimmicks" in boss battles that added an extra factor. The 1v1 battles as well as the war battles were very similar to Suikoden II in that they felt almost staged. There really was no "losing" but more all for story purposes.

Soundtrack:
I remember at a certain point in this game thinking "Eh this OST is not bad, nothing special" then I got to the first 1v1 battle and "Flag of Brave" kicked in. From there I felt like this was a very underrated soundtrack that I have added to my playlist. The final fights music is unbelievable. The two composers who worked on these tracks were Motoi Sakuraba (best known for his work on the Tales Series, Golden Sun, and Star Ocean) and Michiko Naruke (best known for her work in the Wild Arms Series).

Story:
Now one of my favorite games is Suikoden II, absolutely love how they pull off war and political drama. Hundred Heroes first half feels almost like a lesser copy of Suikoden II unfortunately. Some of the bigger plot points felt a little lackluster at times due to the way they were dealt with. Now the second half of this game felt like a whole new experience. I thoroughly enjoyed the second half and the pickup of the pace. Which is a shame because by the time I got to the end I was actually really bought in on the story and wanted it to continue. I am very much looking forward to seeing this story continue as it sounds like this series will be moving forward with more games.

Overall:
I think I overhyped this game with expecting it to be on par with the Suikoden Series. Unrealistically I wanted it to follow the Suikoden world when its a different series and cannot do that. With all that said, this is not a bad game. If the bugs were fixed and the damage was balanced this would probably have gotten a 4 out of 5 stars. Very interested in seeing what comes from this, whether its a sequel to Hundred Heroes, Suikoden III and IV Remastered, or maybe Suikoden VI?? Wake up Konami!!

Absolutely loving this game!  I didn't even know about it until one of my Youtubers was playing it ^^  I was looking for some kind of building game that gave you freedom to build but wasn't so resource grindy, and this is it!

The building is a great combination of freestyle with grid-snapping that makes it easy to place, adjust, edit, and experiment.  Most of the floors and walls can even be chunked down to smaller sizes for more design and placement options!  And I love the ability to explore islands and see how wood and stone buildings were created - it gives you ideas and a solid place to start so you can see how things might go together as you create your own.

It's very intuitive!  

Most of the structures you see can be learned so that you can build them yourself.  The exception seems to be shipwreck-type structures and lore-type structures, which is a bit unfortunate.  The shipwrecks are just normal wood, in-game logic suggests you ought to be able to craft them.

Although it takes a bit of practice to be able to fly well, I find most of the movement and actions to be very intuitive, and the ability to chain actions together whether building or fighting is sweet.  I experienced a few moments in game with some unique movement actions based on the environment, and it was just incredibly satisfying and thoughtful for a game that's still in early access.  (One example was sliding through a tight squeeze in a cave.)

As I've seen in other posts online, the game does tend to crash on me randomly and for no reason, but it hasn't been so frequent to really impact my play.  I've gotten into the habit of saving often.  If you have a lower end computer, you may have more trouble.  I'm hoping the devs will stabilize the game as they work on it to eliminate this problem.

All in all, this is a very thoughtfully crafted game, and it's incredibly satisfying to be able to construct your own buildings, design your own mini island, and to fly your home around.  So unique!!  It takes the stress out of a game where travel and exploration is key, as you know you're always close to your home to regenerate or drop off supplies.  

11/10 highly recommend this game!!
100 hours in and I am still completely hooked.  This is one of my favourite games of all time.  it is the most peaceful and satisfying game that I have ever played.  Try it, you won't regret it!

So far I loooovve the game even though it's still Early Access. Definitely has potential but even as it is now it's so wholesome and fun to play. 

What I Enjoy:
- The flying/kite mechanic of the character makes me feel all "wheeeeee!" and it's so fun! I especially love the gusts of wind that you can use to go faster and zoom to flying islands to.
- Love the animals! So adorable, and the resources you can get from them are useful. Would I like more added? Definitely yes, so hopefully more will be added and I can make a flying zoo.
- The aesthetics of the game are awesome. Looking forward to a little bit more explanation of the lore or the culture there in the future, because I have so many questions.
- Cooking! Having cooking mechanics in games really adds some good stuff to games and it's useful for getting HP/stamina up when doing combat. 
- I love building and flying, so having both an island that you can build and sail around is so freaking dope!
- Really like the idea of making your own island in the island creator. Haven't messed with it much yet.
- The 3 terrains that are currently available are cool and have their own vibe, which I appreciate each one. Looking forward to more being added as well as availability of certain resources that are hard to get.

What Needs more work:
- Some glitching of resources and the set home part of some islands still need some work. One island I have has it set to home inside a rock cliff so anytime I appear there I get stuck, and I am unable to fetch out the animals that are sent to "home". It's an early access game that recently released so looking forward to when they do fix those things.
- The combat is cool and it definitely gets harder the more you get into the game which I do struggle a little bit with. Mainly it's me lacking the skills, but I think it may also just need some more work to smooth it out. I haven't checked to see if the difficulty can be changed but it didn't take long for me to feel a little overwhelmed since there's those big mushroom tentacles, increasingly harder enemies, and the terrain can also make it much hard to hit the nodes depending on where they're placed. 

As it is now it definitely needs some work, but as long as the devs keep updating and adding things and making bug fixes to the game like they have been doing so far I do think it's worth it. Some people think otherwise, but this is just my opinion.

Overall a good game. I think there are some missing elements that would turn this game from good to great.
After about 1-16 hours, or after passing through the first rock storm the game gets a bit repetitive. Fighting the same 3 enemies gets a bit too bleak and the world begins to feel a little dead. 
Here are a list of things I think would improve this game:
- NPC's, The mystery of the world begins to fall away, but the introduction to other NPC's would vastly change this. This could be small tribes, traders, explorers or even pirates. Which brings me to the next item.
- More in-depth and variety of enemies. Improving, upgrading weapons is pointless since there's never any enemy progression, but if they included harder and harder enemies, including human enemies, pirates, factions that chase you down and try to board you or something like that I think the need for combat progression would increase players returning to the game. 
- Difficulty: Now I understand the peaceful ascetic and I'm all for it at times, but the introduction of a hardcore more maybe, where you need food and water to survive, and you lose gear or level progression upon death would increase the replay value. Forcing players to use the extra tools picked up, require back up gliders, clothes for death runs, etc..
- Crafting & Comfort: I think creating a comfort buff would push players to focus a little more on creating a better home, push players to use the decorations to increase comfort levels instead of just a visual ascetic would increase the game play as well. 
Island habitat: I think larger islands should have some type of predator, something that would balance the eco-system.
Story: I would enjoy some lore aspects. Deserted towns having notes left behind, or NPC Questlines.
Combat: Should be more difficult, there's a lot you can do with the glider aspect, but overall it should be more challenging and require different strategies to defeat different enemies, or at least some puzzle to unlock islands. 

Overall, this game has a lot of potential and introduces a fun easy environment but gets too repetitive and feels too empty at the current state.

I tend to play at a very slow pace, playing more for escapism than action. I really love the art style and the fact that even in the beginning the player can build a basic home with an inviting atmosphere with just a few resources. And the unique and very beautiful artstyle ensures that allthough Aloft may fall under the tag of "cozy", it never feels too cutsy, kitschy or sugary sweet. 

The progression of the game is very much up to the player and I appreciate being able to take my sweet time, without feeling the pressure of a quest list or any urgency of not getting anywhere quick enough. 

The game mechanics feel very intuitive to me. At no point was I tempted to refer to any outside sources because I felt at a loss or didn't understand how a goal might be achieved. If something can't be done yet, the answer usually isn't more than an island or two ahead. Still I don't feel like the game takes me by the hand. The lore enfolds quite naturally throughout the game with intuitive and artistic symbolism and visuals. There seem to be no underlying morals implied in restoring the ecosphere, a refreshing take on the matter. Helping the islands to thrive again feels just as natural as building your home or trying new skills. I like that a lot.

So, 3 D Chess this game is not, nor are fighting skills or an aptitude for strategic skill tree developement required. There is a little combat, because nothing good comes for free. But most of the time you will enjoy tending to your animals, growing your favorite foods or lie in the meadow until you feel utterly at peace. And then there is the flying of course. You can soar through the skies, as if you were made for it. An absolute thrill in my book.

I'm going to recommend this game, but there are some key things to keep in mind when deciding if this will be an enjoyable experience for you:

1) It is VERY casual.  There is almost no survival aspects.  You never need to eat, drink, cook, or do anything.  Food gives you very minor buffs, nothing you'll ever need or want to bother with most likely?

2) The building is "ok" at best.  Other games have done a much better job but it works and I haven't encountered any issues.  Basically you can place anything almost anywhere, no support or structure needed, just build whatever you want.

3) Combat is extremely basic and a bit janky.  Enemies will have an attack animation, if you are within range you get hit.  When you swing, if they are in range, they get hit.  There is no "impact" or good feel to the combat so look elsewhere if that's important to you.

4) The "gameplay loop" is pretty basic.  You have 3 main tasks:
- Explore random islands and loot them, they start to repeat so this gets pretty old fast
- Kill 1 or more "infested mushroom" boss type things to cleanse the island.  This uses the janky combat so it gets old pretty fast but is easy.
- Restore the ecosystem for islands by chopping corrupted trees, planting/placing/repairing a few things and done

5) The tech progression is very off.  It feels almost random outside of the main "things" you click on to unlock major story progression items.   I found myself having a crafting bench unlocked for a very long time that I couldn't use because I didn't have another required part unlocked.

awesome game. cozy survival. great solo. better with friends.

Pros:

- Beautiful environments and breathtaking scenery

-The gliding feels very smooth and enjoyable to just fly around endlessly all over the place and driving islands around is a lot of fun. 

- The resource crafting is a nice fresh take on traditional crafting methods used in other survival games and felt a little more intuitive because you play a dead by daylight skill check style mini game during the process and its not just click and boom its done.

- The building mechanics are pretty fluid and closely resembles something along the lines of grounded's building mechanics where you need to place down a blueprint/frame and then physically build the piece afterwards. This comparison is not including the handy gnat in Grounded that enables you to fly and build simultaneously as you cannot do that in this game.

- Animal care taking is very simplified which I'm neutral on as I would enjoy a more complex system than simply feeding and petting my animals every once in a while whenever its not on cooldown, but I also understand some enjoy the mechanics the way they are and also don't want an emphasis on spending time caring for animals and would rather explore so I leave it up to you to form your own opinion on it. Its not a large problem by any means.

- The music soundtrack is amazing. Whether its in combat or relaxing and farming on your island, the music is great, really enjoyable to listen to, and it isn't too loud or overwhelming.

Cons:

- You and your friends must each have their own islands. This was not an issue for me personally as my friend and I enjoyed having our own island to build our own style of house, farm, etc. and visit each other to see one another's progress. I know some will want to share an island with their friends so it would be best to inform you now that it simply isn't an option unless you are okay with only playing when your friend is online and designating an island between yourselves to always use together. 

- When I say this, I don't mean the combat needs to be difficult like dark souls or anything like that by any means, however the combat does feel a little too easy. Most enemies go down in 3 swings of a sword or less and this becomes especially so once you unlock the sharpening station. This allows your tools and weapons to pretty much all become 1-2 shot kills. Beyond this, the enemies are very easy to dodge even in groups as your melee has longer range than theirs does and the ranged troops just run away from you whenever you get within 5ft of them. There are other troops that fly and such but they feel like they have little to no impact in fights and are easy bow fodder.  

-Performance is a little rough around the edges with a lot of stuttering when flying into new areas, but it is obviously an early access title and this is to be expected as I'm sure they will fix it down the line. If that's a deal breaker for you, I'd suggest waiting some time and maybe checking again after some updates, but I found it to not take away from the overall experience.

I really liked the "boardgame" style planet surface. You can make groups of 2 bastards and run them in different directions, and you will be looking at road blocks (the actual fps parts), seeing what enemies are there, adjusting who pairs with who, what equipment they get etc. It's got that satisfying "min maxing" aspect. "This roadblock is a bunch of yellowbellies with shields so I'll take Rawhide (they can shoot through the shields). Behind that is a mind control satellite (converts some enemies to allies), I'm going to drop it on this harder roadblock with a ton of enemies. Then I can bring Hopalong cause the roadblock is all critters and Hopalong spawns a health pack for each critter he kills" etc.

 Then there's all the equipment mods. They can really help offset a bastard's weakness, or turn one's strength completely OP. Homing throwing knives? Check. 6 round sawnoff shotgun? Check. Explosive chain gun? Check. Chance to not consume the bastard's Ult on use? Give it to Smokey and constantly light everyone on fire. 

There's been discourse recently about good and bad character design, and this game has amazing character design. Every one of the 13 has a totally cool and unique look, weapon, personality, and ult. Space Western let them think of some awesome stuff. Smokey is a skeleton who's always on fire, and he fucking loves beans. Kaboom is a ghost who blew him self up and (you guessed it) throws dynamite as his weapon. Since he's a ghost, or living mist or whatever, he can float on water (which is usually poisonous), no fall damage, and his movement and sprint are silent. My favorite is Hopalong, a snake duke, with snake dreads, a silky gravely voice, and he uses a lasso. This lasso completely stunlocks an enemy and does intermittent rising damage till they die. Just make sure there's no others around since you're kind of a sitting duck (snake). But while your constricting them, you can still duck, and move slowly to reposition. I then realized I could use my prey as a shield which is always funny watching the enemies kill their own try to hit you. His ult is to stun all the nearby enemies so that can be used proactively or reactively, and then you can start killing the group of kyotes or whatever one at a time, even not worring about damage cause of the aforementioned health packs critters will drop. You will even start realizing good combos of characters, like Hopalong and Smoke. Smokes sets enemies on fire and they take dot damage, then you can switch to Hopalong and lasso them so their held in place taking that dot fire damage as well as the rising lasso damage. 

There's almost a kind of imsim vibe to the game as well. Enemies have hearing so you can sneak around, if shoot from hiding in the weeds, they'll shoot where the sound came from, a couple characters can convert enemies into allies, I've nocked enemies into the poison swap, there's a decent amount of destructible cover (especially in the last biome) so I've absolutely just unloaded with my bombs/Gatling gun/shotgun to clear paths and sightlines. 

The campaign was a fun story, and had some gameplay twists along the way. It went on a bit too long (I beat it after 25hr on medium difficulty) but that was probably partly my fault for exploring each planet I landed on 100% and then later waiting for the Princes to arrive so I could kill them for Infamy. 

I definitely want to go back and try harder difficulties or the challenge modes.

So, I don't normally do reviews but this one deserves it.

Firstly, loads of promise, can be fun when things work, and is generally a decent time.

Now the not so nice bits:

1. Difficulty Spikes:
Going from Easy to Normal (not what they are called in game) is, from personal experience a very big jump. In easy you get really good ratings on most designs and is pretty easy to beat out the AI on contracts, allowing you to spend time further refining designs and modifying components to eek out the best performance for each role your tanks need to fill. Going to Normal however feels like the AI has reduced research times, no maintenance costs to contend with, no design times to wait for and no engineering times to wait for. For example I've made numerous saves per run so I can back track if things don't work out, however upon reloading a much earlier save the contract type evolution changes or the AI is already on a MK.2 variant before I even have the base version of the tracks or hull. This means your designs, which are now being more "fairly" rated, cannot compete with the AI's designs. Note this is not me saying that AI designs have a rating boost but that they have a design that better fills the requirements while you have just gotten to the point of being able to start meeting them.

2. Maintenance Costs:
While I understand these and they make perfect sense, with a reduced budget, higher wages and higher maintenance costs  overall, coming into Normal and trying to keep up with the AI and contract demands is really really tight. Every building has  a maintenance cost, and every upgrade increases this cost again. Even with all the admin upgrades to reduce these costs and without hiring any more workers, you can still be looking at 150K gold per month when you are struggling to fill contracts, and that's without upgrades to anything else. As mentioned in the section above, if you struggling to keep up with AI designs, purchasing some of the research lab upgrades or for the design bureau or engineering lab, can help but now you higher maintenance fees. Now you are not only losing contracts, you're failure condition is coming at you much quicker. If you can keep pace excellent, but now you have to make sure you get those contracts and are constantly creating new component designs to meet demands.

3. Engineering:
This one might be the biggest issue, for me personally anyways, as the time constraints and the massive number of alterations that are required. For example: You've got the 6 and 4 cylinder engines as the Brits, but you may have to have 6 versions of the 6 cylinder and 2 of the 4 cylinder for different designs, however you have to wait up to a month for these to be done, which means overall you could be looking at up to 180 days of waiting, before you finally have something that works for 1 contract and by then a new type of classification has come out. But now this issue is on everything. Hulls, weapons, tracks, engines, turrets. Everything.

4. Research:
So you 1 research slot and 3 different categories. Each piece of tech in the categories takes progressively longer and longer to research, pretty standard. However as mentioned in section 2, the AI always seems to be ahead. I've had all the focuses added on to speed up the research, I've had the breakthrough lab on and my first administrator attached to boost the speed and grant a chance to instantly unlock it. However as stated there is no way to know which contract type will come first, or if the AI will generate a contract for that tank type after researching it. For example, I had already got all the research for Exploitation type tanks done; tracks, hull, engine, even the bits from later researches that provide good bonuses; still haven't had a contract generate for it...

Overall it's a bit of a mess. At the time of typing, I've done 5 or so runs in Normal difficulty to varying degrees of failure.
I either don't have the parts researched by the time a contract comes round or the AI is on Mk.2 variant for the contract before I've seen the contracts. (I've done runs in easy and I am now just sitting on a piles of gold by the end of era 2)
I didn't even mention that the research of components unlocks more components that you need to for the engineering alterations or the trophies being reverse-engineered further unlocking more parts for those alterations. Or the fact that contracts a fewer with the difficulty increases.

NOW. I'm not one to write a review and not leave some suggestions.

For the difficulties, I'd suggest leaving the starting resources and gold the same as easy. At least going from Easy to Normal, this gives the play a chance to mess around a little and find their footing against an AI that is more on the ball. A little wiggle room to get things wrong means a player can still make a few mistakes but make it through the games quirks.

For maintenance costs, I'd suggest changing how much they increase by, now if we are doing the option listed above, then this may not be as necessary but if the changes to the starting resources and the like stay as they are this would also be a viable option.

For engineering, this one is the option I'd like to see the most. The more copies of something you make the quicker the engineering turn around time. For example if I'm making 6 copies of the same engine for different contract requirements, the time should either linearly or exponentially reduce with each subsequent iteration. My engineers know this engine and how to fit components like a race Pit-stop crew at this point, why is still taking a month?
The other change I would like to see with this as well, is upon the completion of the research, the first component is designed by the player and that becomes the default option. Right now it makes one with whatever tech the devs have deigned to attach, when the research is done, instead let the player design it and that becomes the first accessible one without having to wait for the engineering time.

For research, there are 5 slots listed but even in ERA II to you have access to 2... so making extra slots available for purchase would be a good alternative, then remove breakthroughs for both players and AI, this levels the playing field and means that players need to be more strategic in the selections but can buy an extra slot in each era (max 2 slots in era 1 and max 4 slots in era 2) to attempt to catch up if they selected the wrong technology. It would also allow players to research companion technologies within a a more reasonable time frame, as again you have 3 tech trees with no crossover unlocks (ie, you don't unlock the tracks with the hulls currently).

Ultimately, we are going to have to wait and see as there are still menus and mechanics that haven't been implemented yet. I know there is a page where you can see the budget breakdown of the nation, so does that mean we can tweak how much goes where to speed up research or reduce production cost/time, and so on. I do hope they don't over complicate the mechanics too much and I do hope that some of these suggestions are at least looked at. In the mean time I am going to go and start a 6th run and record which contracts appear when, get as far as I can, do a seventh run and see if I can use my guide to stay a float.

Best of luck to you other would-be-Tycoons!

A very fun take on the development of one of the most influential (and terrifying) machines to ever cross the battlefield. From the first ever British Mark Is to the Mark Vs, the French FT-17 (which coincidentally was also the first tank used by the American Expeditionary Forces when they entered WWI), the St. Chammond, to the German A7V, a pillbox on tracks.

Based on the type of tank needed you'll be creating designs based on historical fact, the needs of the nation, or the outright outlandish. Just be aware that every design has it's flaws and limitations. A tank with a purely machinegun armament and light armor won't do you any good vs tank on tank engagements; and a tank with a singular fixed cannon won't be much use against the infantry wall tactics of WWI.

If I did have one gripe about the game is that though there are various battle difficulties one might face, 7/10 times the battle is of an 'Extreme' difficulty in which case several tanks (especially the earlier ones) will fail most of the time.

Still a work in progress

Currently it's a fairly light business sim with a reasonably simple tank designer bolted on. Hasn't currently got a huge variety of tanks but you get the depth from trying to optimise the components.

Though, its very grind for the early stages of interwar. Its very fun to create your own "beautys" and I played for 99 hours total on this game, since I had unlimited ways to create French tanks have more additional guns.

There's a lot of things to like about Trail Out. It can be a lot of fun. But it already has plenty of good reviews. It deserves a few bad reviews that point out its flaws. And it has three major flaws. The first 2 flaws a lot of other racing games also have:

[b] 1) The upgrades for your car are meaningless. [/b]

They may make you go a bit faster or survive a bit longer, but they actually make no difference in whether you win or lose, because the computer racers upgrade right with you. They always go faster than you, no matter what upgrades you install. When you get a new class of cars that are better, so do they. There is nothing you can buy or upgrade that will make you faster than the lead cars. No matter how fast you go or how much of a lead you have at any point, the computer rubber bands the other racers so that they will always catch right up to you by the final lap.

[b] 2) The races are completely determined by the computer. [/b]

You start every race in last place and the same few cars are always ahead: either yellow, red, usually at first, and then black or blue later in a longer race. Usually, it's Frank in the yellow far ahead. Ivan is always last or close to it. Every single race, this is exactly the same. After completing the campaign, a special character unlocks in a black car that is faster than anything you can buy or upgrade. Because you are always behind, the only way to win is to let the computer rubber band/slow the lead car so you're close to it, which almost always happens in the last lap close to the end, which it's obviously programmed to do. Then, you have to count on the lead car crashing or skidding or having some accident determined by the computer. 

 Winning is literally about redoing races over and over until the random chance works in your favor - the computer randomly makes the lead cars crash and you can zoom by. And this is how you get first place: it's random chance when the computer sabotages the race for other drivers ahead of you.

[b] 3) This game is supposedly about crashing into competitors, but it constantly punishes you for any contact. [/b] 

Crash into too many other cars and your car is destroyed quickly. Even small crashes can randomly destroy your gearbox, nitrous or engine, making it impossible to win. Crash into anybody too hard and they take minimal damage while you go flying through the windshield in a cut scene and end up far behind them when you finally reset.

Speaking of resetting, no matter how hard you knock competitors off the track or into obstacles, it basically does nothing. They instantly reset and are right back next to you within a few second.

The best strategy for winning a race is to never bump into anybody if you can avoid it. And for a game that's supposed to be about massive crashes, that sucks.

This game is adorable, yes; it is also the kind of game to go to after you are done with Overcooked, another game that is about cooking, meeting goals and you have only so limited time. However, I have two major complaints, one more crucial than the other.

Let's talk about the more problematic one. The keybindings and controls are awful (I play with a controller). As a solo player, the constant tapping using the controller's buttons is giving me hand cramps from overusing my thumb. I hope the developers listen to this and change it to something similar to the Overcooked style. If you are chopping or preparing the cloud or hearts, just let your character continue the work on its own without having to repeatedly tap the button. It strains my muscle so much after a while. Also, the keybindings are very awkward. You dash with A, pick up and drop with X, and chop, punch and throw with Y. It may not sound bad just from reading, but as you start playing the game, it becomes an actual problem. There have been so many times I just accidentally threw my finished cake off the platform into space and have to restart as a result. I would recommend changing the bindings to chop, punch and throw to be on X, pick up and drop to be on A, dash to be on B; which if not the same, then very, very similar to the bindings for Overcooked 2. (I also do not understand why Y is cancel/return on the main menu, most games do B instead. Most games also use A as select, this game uses X.)

The second complaint is a minor one, which is online co-op. The game has so much more potential if the developers invest in online multiplayer. Thanks to Remote Play Together, the game is not limited to couch co-op, but still, high ping may be the detrimental point to a player's enjoyment.

I do think the controls are a little finicky and need to be refined, and I would love if keybinding was something that is added to the game in the future, as I find the controls a little unnatural. It would also be nice if a proper online co-op mode is added, since remote-play can be laggy at times.

Where overcooked is scattered and panicky, this is more focused. I'm assuming some of these levels are easier with more players, but if you're only playing with two like we are, it can be *really* difficult to get three stars as you get into week 3. I think the difficulty scaling needs a little work, or perhaps the timer needs some adjusting. As it is, it can be really frustrating and make us want to quit as opposed to continue playing.

All in all, I'm really liking this game, and I hope the devs continue to refine it and add more levels. I think it could be a really promising entry to co-op games, it just needs some tweaking! Excited to see more in the future.

    +Funny in-game achievements, and even more adorable BUNNIES to unlock makes you want to play more!
+Upbeat and catchy in-game music
+Did I already mention the cute and adorable BUNNIES!!!?

Cons (minor):
-The upbeat and catchy in-game music can be a bit repetitive
-Throwing ingredients in the game can either get stuck in some odd places, or disappear into an abyss if throwing past the bounds of the level, which can be a bit frustrating when time is about to run out
-On the later levels (Week 3), it can be difficult at times to distinguish between the chopping, mixing, and baking machines. -Needs more dessert varieties and combinations

Overall, Turn the Line is a super-fun and addicting "chaotic co-op" game to play with family and friends! I'm eagerly waiting for whatever creative new levels, desserts, achievements, and BUNNIES the developers will come up with next!! Great job, devs!

The "this is all a game" aspect of the story has always been the weakest part of the Breaker series and it feels like that here most of all, where nothing has real stakes and any kind of logic or reasoning for what characters do breaks down when you realize it's all a game. Why are the character portraits avatars and not the actual player behind the gunpla? Why is so much drama being made over what is essentially a game demo? Why are they meeting inside the game instead of in real life or through a different service when they know that the villain can spy on them as long as they're logged in? 

The pro-AI propaganda aspect of the story comes from a specific character who is an AI, and said character becoming the focal point of the story. The antagonist wants to erase this AI character while the protagonists want to keep them around. Right away you can see where they try to make it look like AI is good and not a wholly destructive technology, as the characters use emotional appeals like "but she's our FRIEND!" instead of a logically-supported argument. AI in real life can easily fake emotions, and there have been many cases of AI services using that to manipulate the users into spending more money and developing a codependency for the AI service. All cases that this game would like you to believe don't exist, and for that I believe the game should be rated M or AO.

Normally, when I feel like giving a "mixed" review, I would go for not recommending it with certain caveats, but here, I don't think it's a hard "No". The writing is acceptable, even if at times rather uninspired and lacking depth. It isn't straight up bad, by any means. The plot contains some intriguing twists and turns, but ultimately it doesn't deliver a thoroughly satisfying experience. Additionally, the frequent shifts between perspectives can become frustrating, especially if you are not playing in one continuous session. I'm not opposed to the idea, it's a neat gimmick, but I do think it was done way too excessively. 

Overall, to give you an idea, Sovereign Syndicate is to Disco Elysium what Greedfall is to Dragon Age. It’s a solid shot at the formula with some good foundations. Is it anywhere near as great as its obvious inspiration? Not even close, but just because it’s not as great doesn’t mean it’s not a decent game on its own. You could definitely do worse.

I play Open World Survival Crafting games. [i]Lightyear Frontier[/i] is a farming simulator which is outside my normal genre. But a lot of great OWSC games include farming elements ([I]Valheim, Subnautica, Raft[/i]). With everything else the trailer showed, I figured there would be enough points of commonality to be worth a shot.

[i]Lightyear Frontier[/i] turned out to be an excellent little cozy time-waster. I was able to sink into it and lose hours of my life in a very pretty (if not very deep) world where I was constantly engaged but never stressed. I loved the world design and the lush, colorful environments. The resources and tech trees are simple but still fun to pursue. I rarely had to seek an answer to something online, and I never encountered a bug.

I am not a fan of the folksy farming aesthetic that I should expect from a farming game. But here it was offset by the sci-fi trappings. For example: the AI in the orbiting satellite has a southern drawl and uses words like [i]skedaddle.[/i] 

I appreciated the lack of Survival mechanics. In every OWSC game, those quickly become tedious. Once you beat hunger and thirst, constantly being pulled away from the fun stuff to deal with them becomes a chore I wish I could turn off. Sure, part of me missed being able to use my crops (like [i]Valheim, Nightengale[/i] and [i]Raft[/i]) to make ever fancier foods, with my character eating far better than I do in real life. But it was a good trade.

I love base building and decoration. In [i]Lightyear Frontier[/i], you don't design your base but you do decorate it, with increasing coziness levels that offer very nice perks. 

I really appreciated some of the choices. For example: I usually don't like animal husbandry in games because caring for animals becomes a chore and I hate the feeling that pets will starve to death if I spend too much time doing the parts of the game I enjoy. So I loved that the game provides an "animal sanctuary" where you can store your animals in an NPC's care if you just don't want to deal with them for a while.

The story... is? Maybe? Not really. But in this game, I'm strangely okay with that. My character came here to homestead, not pursue some epic quest.

One note: I have severe problems with motion sickness in games. [i]Lightyear Frontier[/i] is designed with accessibility in mind, including multiple FOV sliders. But beyond a certain point, those create bad fishbowling. I cannot play this game first person. However, I've been able to play for hours on end in third person without any trouble.

This is one of those rare narrative-driven games that lingers in your mind long after you finish it. From the start, I was drawn in by its incredibly well-written story, which constantly kept me on my toes. I thought I had a solid grasp of what was happening early on, but I was very, very wrong, and I loved that.

The voice acting is phenomenal, elevating the emotional weight of every moment. Each performance feels deeply considered, making the story even more immersive. The world-building is fascinating, and the way it slowly unravels kept me eager to see what would happen next.

That said, I do wish there was more to the gameplay beyond walking and talking. While the traversal "puzzles" involving floating sigils add some variety, they didn’t resonate with me as much. Perhaps I missed some of their symbolic significance, but I couldn’t shake the feeling that the interactivity could have been expanded.

And honestly? Playing 1000xRESIST has made the game I’m currently playing (Dragon Age: Veilguard) feel so much worse by comparison. The writing in 1000xRESIST is sharp, layered, and full of surprises, whereas Veilguard... well, let’s just say it doesn’t have nearly the same impact. It really highlights the difference between a game that takes risks with its storytelling and one that plays it safe.

Even so, 1000xRESIST delivers a gripping, thought-provoking experience. If you enjoy story-rich games that challenge your expectations and leave you with plenty to think about, this is absolutely worth playing.

Every once in a while a game comes out and tries to push the boundaries of video game narrative design further than what has been attempted before. Undertale in 2015, NieR: Automata in 2017, Disco Elysium in 2019 and a few other titles distanced themselves from the rest and even after years of iteration manage to feel unique. In my opinion 1000xRESIST falls within the same category, and will be remembered by those who played it as a reference point for future attempts at experimental narrative design in video games. 

The tragedy it narrates is a personal, societal, global and universal one. Its characters exude personality despite their homogeneity through perfectly directed voice acting. Its cinematography and score wouldn't feel out of place in a movie. And more than anything, unlike many other Visual Novels, 1000xRESIST always asks itself how its gameplay can go beyond moving the player from a voiceline to another and twists it to fit and enrich the narrative. I would go as far as to say 1000xRESIST could not exist as anything other than a video game, which means it took all the advantages provided by the medium and made them its own.

As many masterpieces, it's not a perfect game. Without spoiling much, the mid-game cut from a plotline to another was jarring, at least initially. I also found the final hours to be a bit repetitive in terms of concepts explored, though it fits with the direction of the second half of the experience. Even with these caveats the second half is impressive (especially in certain scenes), while the first half and its gut-punching personal drama is one of the most moving gaming experiences of the past few years on its own.

This may be the best written game I've ever played. The ways the story's themes are layered and revisited are masterful and the presentation of each scene is amazing. I don't like the term "walking simulator".  I feel it's a pejorative used by people who are allergic to story.  That said, this game is a walking simulator.

Don't get me wrong, it's worth playing.  It swings big, and hits more than it misses.  It tells a rich, multi-layered story about love and pain and betrayal, from an immigrant family  struggling to do right by their daughter, to the end of human civilization, to multiple generations of a post-apocalyptic sci-fi community, exploring the roots of their society's disintegration and the ways in which hurt people hurt people.  At its best it takes a grand, ambitious story and repeatedly makes it personal, taking immense trauma and making it small enough to stab you in the chest.  There are some unforgettable moments, and the game's vocabulary slowly worms its way inside your brain and takes root.  Hekki Allmo.

At its worst, the game is about slowly navigating large and sparse maps to space out the game's few dialogues, or bouncing back and forth between time periods in a sort of 4-D hunt-the-pixel puzzle until you find who you need to talk to to progress.  It's fully linear, with some side-quest achievement hunting that doubles your play time for very little value if you're trying to interact with all the interactibles.  It would have been a fantastic game at half its length, but I spent chunks of time wishing that there was a run button before remembering I was already holding it down.

On balance, a qualified recommend.  Go in expecting to just interact with the main story, and possibly the clearly outlined side objectives, without worrying about peering into every nook and cranny; and be prepared for a bit of a slow unroll regardless.  But if you take that experience for what it is, the story is rather remarkable.

Also, AFTER you're done, watch the game's "Hekki Allmo" trailer video for a really poignant rendition of a song that I don't think is actually ever sung in the game itself.  It's not a huge spoiler, but it hits so different after you encounter the in-game lyrics and understand their full context.

What lies beyond a story retold by shared memories meticulously selected to the myriad of copies of yourself? 
Keep them going by assigning them functions and keeping them in fear so they stay in line and society might endure.
At what cost?

What this is about isn't up to you. This is, explicitly, about generational trauma. Motherhood. The fear of letting go. The mistake of letting too much go. About the effects a lack of communication can have. It's about Hong Kong, the protests in 2014 and 2019, and the people who are forced to leave their homes behind due to similar situations. 

It punches very hard, and bites very sharply, and I'm SO glad I played it.
