If you combined the sci-fi futurism of Yoko Taro’s [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/524220/NieRAutomata/] NiER: Automata, [/url] the introspective quest of Lowis Lowry’s [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Giver] The Giver, [/url] the theatrical and abstract level design of [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/231200/Kentucky_Route_Zero_PC_Edition/] Kentucky Route Zero, [/url] and the grounded, Asian-Canadian immigrant story of [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1491670/Venba/] Venba, [/url] you’d have a game that looks something like [i] 1000xRESIST. [/i] On paper, none of these things should work well together, and yet somehow sunset visitor 斜陽過客 knocked it out of the park with their first game. Incredible voice acting, emotional performances, and really great writing. 

Nevertheless, [i] 1000xRESIST [/i] is one of those games with a somewhat niche appeal. If you hate “games like this” – games that are light on gameplay, where you mostly just walk around and talk to people to experience the story – you will likely not have your mind changed by playing through the 10-12 hour main story of the game. If you play [i] 1000xRESIST [/i] hoping for a game with deep combat systems, dense skill trees, or complex dialogue options with dozens of branching paths and a morality point system, those hopes will not be met by [i] 1000xRESIST. [/i] However, if you are compelled enough by the elevator pitch of “ambitious, experimental visual novel where you re-live the memories of a clone-God,” I cannot recommend [i] 1000xRESIST [/i] highly enough. Every time I thought I knew where the story was headed, a new story event would happen that threw everything that preceded it back into question once more. Can’t wait to see whatever this team does for their next project.

I don't usually review games but I wanted to do something, anything, to increase the visibility of this masterpiece. That said I will start with the bad, since there is so little of it:

Gameplay beyond (tbf many) dialogue choices and some light platforming is barebones. In the future would love to see them weave more game play into the narrative. if you don't already like visual novel type games, it might be tough to get through all the writing.

Amazing: Some of the best writing I have experienced in any medium ever. Out of the books I read, movies and shows I've watched, and other great games I've played in the last year plus the beginning of this one, this might have the best writing. It so expertly weaves its themes of inter-generation trauma, immigrating, rebellion, parenthood, memory, and connection with smart, funny, and often poetic writing. They also mesh the themes in every aspect of this new interesting sci-fi world and just throw you in it, with a confident inclusion of modern HK history and culture. 

You would think that using all the tools they are to tell this story (a complex sci-fi world, writing that doesn't hold your hand, and cultural references), the story would be hard to understand. YOU WOULD BE THINKING WRONG. The word smiths (Pinki Li and the writing team) here do an excellent job of pacing questions and answers in a way that you are always learning something new or getting a reveal at the right times. While in the beginning you will be confused, the dialogue can feel random and almost like a bunch of non sequiturs, but just trust the story. It is all explained eventually in way that is not condescending to the player, but also not so obscure that you need to watch an hour of youtube videos to explain whats going on (except for [spoiler] what Jiao's secret from chapter 1 is [/spoiler] but honestly that didn't need explaining). 

The writing as well is combined with beautiful visuals and camera work, excellent voice acting, and a sound track that NEEDS to get on spotify.

Anyways, everyone should buy and play this game.

A very captivating narrative game. Beautiful soundtrack. Interesting stories that intertwine and compliment each other. Complex characters, relationships, and development. Can be incredibly confusing and mind-bending at times, but by the end of it all I think they wrap up the story well.

Something I didn't like that was really noticeable was how stiff and janky the animations can be. The characters have no facial movement during conversations so there's no expressions of emotion, which would go a long way to enhancing the experience. Animations can look awkward even in important cutscenes, which detracts from the moment and can sometimes look comical when the tone is supposed to be solemn.

The graphics are quite poor in some instances, with textures looking like games from the early 00's and the environments feeling oddly barren and devoid of detail.

The dialogue options are also annoyingly vague (à la Mass Effect, but worse). But it's not a huge deal because the protagonist is very much her own character, despite the choices you can make.

The ending I chose initially caught me by surprise in how abrupt it was. After taking some time to read people's discussions and think through the themes of the story again, I understand now why they considered my ending (and 5 of the other 7 endings) the "wrong" choice, despite me thoroughly believing in mine. There's a good reason the game is titled 1000xResist. It expresses lessons that can be hard to swallow, but crucial to remember.

Listen, I'm shook. I tried writing this up and make it approachable and easy to grasp, but screw it. I think the pretentious version is what I want to leave here, so this is what you'll get: 

I just played through this story and I haven't experienced anything like it. It's not Theatre, not Performance and not Literature, but a game that utilizes strengths from all of those and inherent strengths of the mechanics they lay out and manage to explore that relatively small set of features so thoroughly, via a maximalist story where every part of it manages to be given thorough time without ever boring you but bringing you deep into its so specific set of characters and memories to let you live something else for a while. I've cried and I've laughed, I've been tense for hours, and now I mourn that it's over almost as much as I mourn the choices made by my favorite characters within. 

This is not THE future of games, but one way that games can convey experiences in ways that no other medium can. The closest thing I've played/read/experienced was a little game called "Paradise Killer" but really, this is a tribute to nothing in games except itself. It deserves all the praise it getting, and it actually deserves even more. GIve them your money, now. And please take more of mine.

I decided this year, to start going into games blind again. To not be curated a list of "What's good" and "what's trash" - and to play games with the purpose of completing them again.  I won't spoil any of the game - or it's story, I'll simply tell you this is an experience. It's beautiful, and it is clearly something built with love and with disregard to what may or may not sell. This is one of the few "art games" I've played that is, unquestionably, art (as opposed to mere entertainment). Beautifully and very intentionally written, and it speaks on multiple levels -- there is a lot of symbolic breadth/depth here. It is a sci fi story, it is also a psychodrama, it is also a meditation on attachment and trauma and on healing, and of course it also deals with systems of power and oppression. I do think the work is at its best (artistically) when the specific object of reference is more difficult to pin down [ie., when it feels most poetic, less tied to the concrete narrative]; nonetheless, part of the message that the devs want to articulate here is that this work cannot simply remain lofty and abstract, removed from the suffering of the world. We must ultimately return and ground ourselves in reality. 1000xRESIST articulates itself beautifully, and it is clear that the writers know how to make use of symbol in a way that overcomes the precise confines of language and rationality. Not to simply just glaze the devs here, but this is really some high level shit. It is truly a rare achievement for the medium, one which I did not expect.

This game should be included among discussions of the few other great artistic/experimental/narrative endeavors in the medium of videogames: Disco Elysium, even Planescape: Torment, and others come to mind. I couldn't help but compare it with DE after finishing, as DE has long been my favorite "narrative" or visual-novel sort of game since its release. While 1000xRESIST is certainly more lacking in gameplay elements, it really surpasses something like DE in its writing. The scope and clarity of the vision here is just really impressive. Of course, the two are also doing very different things -- DE is much more tightly-focused narrative, and it accomplishes its aim very well -- but nonetheless, this game is just monumental in what it manages to tackle in 15-20 hours. I really love it, and I am so grateful to have had this experience with it. Thank you to the devs for making this. 

Also: it is a bit slow going at first. If you're not hooked by the first few chapters, try to get at least to the middle of the story.
While the gameplay is somewhat shallow, the story is among my favorites in gaming.

Pros and cons are down below) If you want to see a video review, this game is the 2d (out of 3) that I discuss:
https://youtu.be/zMQY_676fFM

Pros:
1. Combat. Combat is the main pro and the main reason to play this game. It's a VERY DIFFICULT game, please keep that in mind. Mechanics are pretty close to dnd system. You got stats and abilities which affect the probability of a successful attack or skill check. Weapon that you use affects which stat is gonna be used. Armour you use may increase your stats. Overall, you have to optimize your build to make your strengths stronger and get through the game. I'm a person who always plays on the highest difficulty level no matter the game. Here I got destroyed XD, lowered the difficulty and got crushed again >.< So I was playing on the lowest difficulty which humbled me a bit. Now this happened for several reasons: dice rolls being more unforgiving than in dnd, time pressure on higher difficulty levels which makes it impossible to play through the chapter if you don't know what you're doing and million icons and effects and stats and abilities and weapons and armour and herbs and booze and encounters and other things (you get it) that it's practically impossible to finish a chapter on the highest difficulty right off the bat without getting used to the mechanics. All that (in MY opinion) makes the game very fun and worth replaying but if you read all that and it didn't sound like fun to you then this game might not be for you, please read more reviews and do more research before spending your money. The challenge of the game is a part of the game.
2. Visuals. They are pretty :3 what else is there to say. Each armour set looks different on the character, there are many different enemies with their unique animations. It's not that important, but it did play a part in creating and enjoyable experience.
3. Pacing. The game has 5 chapters only (each takes around 4 - 5 hours to beat on the lowest difficulty if you succeed 1st try) and they all feel different. Not only enemies and bioms are different but the game introduces new mechanics to keep it fun. 2d chapter introduces vehicles, 3d - ships, what you do in the 4th affects the 5th. Loved it. Moreover, at the end of each chapter you get lore points that you can spend in the lore shop to make your initial loadout stronger and also lets you unlock new classes to try out.

Cons:
1. Lag, there's a very annoying input lag that doesn't really affect much but is just really frustrating. (basically when you click for your character to attack, they won't do it right away so you start wondering if there's an issue and clicking different stuff and then it works and it's just weird). There are also other bugs but I haven't encountered anything game breaking. For example, there was another annoying thing that made a certain class scream over and over again but they fixed that literally the next day I finished the game lol
2. The rng is relentless. The game is difficult and it is a part of the game, yes. But it's still so frustrating seeing 95% of success and have your roll fail >:[ rng sometimes makes it feel like nothing you do matters but it's a temporary frustration. Still, I felt it often enough to mention as a con here.

Overall we got 7.5 Inconspicuous sheep out of 10.

Thank you for reading my review <3 Hope you have a nice day and fun gaming!

Every single thing I wrote here is somehow related to the emotions of this game. And that's what this game is about, really. The game itself is merely a medium; a vessel. It just so happens that for this particular story, for these particular emotions, this vessel is the most potent one.

Before I finish, there's one thing I wanted to talk about. When I first started playing this, I felt this... fatigue. Almost all characters have some unusual pronouns or have something LGBTQ-themed to them, and that's just the norm in this world. If there are two things I've learned over the years about time loop stories, across all mediums; it is that they are tragic and they are the deepest form of horror one can experience. How many loops would it take before you go mad? How long before the people around you and their repeated samey responses and dialog starts to just feel like NPCs? Even those closest to you, those you love, your friends and family will start to not feel like real people as they do the same thing. Over. And over. And over. And. Over.

This game leans fully into the horror of being stuck. The mystery of why and the maddening journey trying to figure out how to escape. The terror of seeing everything go horribly wrong and being stuck with that memory. Sure you loop back, you reset everything, but who do you turn to to process that feeling? How do you talk about the emotions caused by an event that only you remember happening? How does it not drive you to the brink of sanity?

This game is an emotional journey from start to finish. I took my sweet time with it and probably made it take longer than it should have to get through to the end. The writing may not be to the taste of some but for those willing to engage with it and meet it on its level, it will stick with you. I won't go so far as to say the game will change you or anything but it will have an impact. Normally I try to write my reviews immediately after finishing a game, for this one I had to take a week to process the emotions it left me with. I smiled, I laughed, I cried... I cried [b]a lot[/b].

You'll maybe throw up some simple buffs, you'll use your strongest attack, and you'll heal when needed. There's a couple of mechanics encouraging chaining of combos and at least one major fight requires paying extra attention to enemy abilities and timing but like I said the combat isn't the focus. More than anything else the gameplay is about piecing together the story and solving the narrative puzzles.

I wish I could say more on the game but I fear spoiling too much if I do. Play this game, it is well worth the time and emotional investment. And maybe avoid looking too much into fanart and stuff until you finish the game. There's some later reveals you might accidentally spoil yourself on. It won't hurt the narrative getting spoiled but it takes some of the intrigue out of the mystery. Don't make the same mistake I did!

With clear influences from its RPGMaker predecessors, In Stars And Time soars above them as a piece about mental health and its effects on others from a place of deep understanding. It's hard not to talk about this game without comparing it to another similar title, Omori, which also deals with similar topics surrounding mental health, but I can't help but feel ISAT pulled it off better with more specificity and nuance. And this isn't even mentioning how natural our main protagonist, Siffrin, and his friends all interacted with eachother, having conversations with eachother that I could absolutely see myself having with my own loved ones.

For a game that's based around looping the same stretch of time over and over, I never felt like the pacing was ever stagnant or boring. And this is especially true for  the character development as, even though you're repeating a lot of the same things, there still manages to be significant development with each loop! 

In Stars And Time pulls off the magic trick of having a huge, fleshed out world with extremely limited space, which only then gets pushed into a crescendo of emotions that left me bawling my eyes out by the end. The silly doodles on my screen had me thinking about my own experiences,  how I've been treated and treated people in the past, how I've been in very similar positions before, and left me feeling grateful for it, for the people I consider a family at this point.

I highly, highly recommend this game, one that now has a special place in my heart, and I hope in yours too.

[quote][i]This is the [b]39th[/b] review of the Steam Redlight series, a series where I purposely seek out negatively or controversially rated games on Steam to see if they're as bad as the Internet says they are. It's accompanied by a video review that can be found [b][url=https://youtu.be/ayV3tMygSHI]here[/url][/b].[/i][/quote]

[b]In summary, I can only recommend Succubus with Guns if it were on sale, and as a numerical score I’d rate it a 4 out of 10. It being closer to a five than a three.[/b] The game is visually strong and the Endless Mode is enjoyable, but comes up short in terms of story, audio direction, and is further weighed down by some deeply repetitive, frustrating, and occasionally game-breaking buggy gameplay.

[h2]Introduction[/h2]

In Succubus with Guns you play as a nameless protagonist who has got a hell of a way with her sway and a bunch of visible skin to help you smack the shmeat. No sexual content though, so the imagination will have to do for some of you. The bit of story setup in this game is that a ritual has gone wrong, and for reasons that are unbeknownst to us, our protagonist has to go and kill hundreds if not thousands of enemies across six different realms (stages) to right the wrongs of some ne’er-do-wells. The six unique realms feature several waves of enemies that spawn once you clean up the current wave, with the last wave being a biome-specific boss.

The enemies in this game vary from healthy to extra thiccc, some being melee, some being ranged, and some enemies in both of those combat types capable of doing [i]big damage[/i]. Each level in the Story Mode contains a new weapon to add to your arsenal, some additional health, as well as ammo for your weapons. The weapons you have access to include a sword, several different bullet-based firearms, a rocket launcher, and a plasma cannon rifle beam boomer blaster. While ammo seems scarce in some levels, you can conserve your ammo by using your melee attacks or by hitting headshots for extra damage.

If you happen to die, you’ll be given the ability to respawn by picking up some bushy red balls if you aren’t playing on [b]Hard[/b] mode. You can pick up to ten during your respawn timer and each one you pick up represents 10% of your health; you can pick up as little as one or as many as ten. The game does have a stamina meter which limits your melee attack frequency in addition to your sprinting and jumping capabilities.

When it comes to Endless Mode (EM), you fight an endless wave of enemies that spawn at some randomized frequency. Each kill gives you resources you can use to purchase ammunition, additional weapons, or buildable items like turrets or traps. EM does have an auto-save function and you’ll be able to start from your last checkpoint if you wanted to keep racking up the score to place on this games’ global leaderboards.

For those who care about achievements, it took me a little over four hours to get all of them, but those who are better gamers than I could probably get them in three. The additional game time comes from other endeavors.

That’s about all we need for the foundation, so let’s talk about what I liked.

[h2]The Good[/h2]

The most notable commendation I’d have to give this game was the enjoyability from Endless Mode (EM). EM is [b]way[/b] more exciting, challenging, and fair than the default Story Mode. While EM isn’t perfect, it’s the reason I spent more than just the bare-minimum amount of time in this game, and that’s driven largely by the leaderboard aspect. At first, you have to strategically engage enemies until you build up a considerable amount of buildables. Even when you think you’ve monopolized murder, a group of very healthy units will spawn to reset the playing field, keeping EM consistently engaging and challenging.

The other worthwhile mention for me are the graphics — whether they’re premade assets or not. The lighting is excellent, the [s]titty bounces[/s] animations are smooth, and overall the game is easy to enjoy visually.

That’s about all the mentionables here, so let’s look at what I liked a little less.

[h2]The Ungood[/h2]

The weaker of my criticisms come from this games’ story. The game does give you a couple of cutscenes without much dialogue to explain some of the motivations of [i]anybody[/i] in the game. From here, it just seems like the Succubus wants to take the opportunity to engage in some casual genocide of the other six realms. For the most part, [i]I get it[/i], the focus isn’t on the story. But… it’s here, and it doesn’t do a lot for all the questions I have. We’ll revisit the story in some later criticisms.

Another thing that I found less enjoyable was the games’ audio direction. I don’t consider the sound effects to be that poor, but the music is incredibly lackluster if not downright forgettable. There’s at least one very quiet song that plays and if it’s the same as the title screen’s you’re listening to this singular, quiet song for just about your entire gameplay duration. It’s disappointing there’s no change in music between realms or bosses. Also, the Succubus randomly says these lines, [i]”I love you”, “Oh”, “I’ll never leave you”[/i] (plus some others) without reasoning and sound are poor in recording/playback quality. The randomization does lead to some comedic timings, like when you deliver a shotgun slug to the head of a zombified waifu and the Succubus follows up with an [i]”I love you”[/i].

Lastly, the gameplay brings up some concerns. I’ll only talk about a few for character count. To start, the AI is easy to manipulate. If you aren’t dealing with any ranged opponents, just hop on a vertical platform and lay down the law since they don’t really jump. Unfortunately most bosses succumb to the same type of exploit. If you’re into melee combat, just continue walking backwards, briefly stop, strike, and resume backwards walking. You’ll avoid most melee damage this way.

Another gameplay element that mixes with story is that some levels force you into specific weapon paths, such as being forced to use the sword with no explanation, even though you consistently keep your guns and ammo for all but two levels (including the sword level). These types of inconsistencies could be explained away by some general writing, but instead you’re left wondering on the conditions of the level that are the exception to the regular gameplay experience. As a side, the plasma weapon is unique to Story Mode, while a bow and arrow is unique to Endless Mode. These two weapons are unavailable in the alternative game mode, and I’m not quite sure why.

Lastly, there’s a game-breaking bug that you can encounter when you shotgun a downed enemy. By shooting the shotgun at an enemy that’s prone, you have the chance to knock them beneath the surface where you can no longer hurt them with any weapon. If you’re playing in Story Mode, this means you [b]can no longer complete the level[/b] and will have to restart it. This did happen to me twice, and you [i]should[/i] be able to avoid this by just [i]not[/i] doing [i]that[/i]. A more minor bug is that in Endless Mode, if you close the purchasing window too quickly after buying a buildable, the resources will be consumed and you won’t get the buildable since it takes a second to enter your inventory. This one can be overcome by just waiting for an extra second, but could lead to some frustration if you don’t understand what happened.

[h2]The End[/h2]

That’s about all I’ve got. I think this game is a perfectly acceptable $5 game considering one of the two modes is enjoyable, but $15 really raises the expectations for this game and a lot of them just [i]aren’t met[/i].

UPDATE (July 18, 2022): The developer has made a variety of updates to the game and I'd encourage you to read the release notes to determine if the below issues you're most concerned about have been resolved.

Bjorn (FKA "Cloud Island," which I found to be a much more appealing name) is a 2.5D side-scrolling action RPG with a unique visual style and fairly simplistic mechanics. Unfortunately, in its current state, Bjorn is riddled with technical, mechanical, and design issues which make it more frustrating than fun.

To put it succinctly, I would describe Bjorn as a game in which the art direction far exceeds the technical output. It has a very striking appearance, with low-poly models, fantastic lighting, and a tilt-shifted lens effect which gives everything an interesting miniaturized look.

The technical issues are many, however:
- The game seems to launch with the volume at 0%
- Various display resolutions don't seem to display correctly - on my 4K monitor, 4K and 1080p worked correctly, but 1440p did not. Additionally, the resolution picker box would sometimes render empty
- Numerous issues with audio playback, primarily sound effects instantly playing multiple times, each overlapping the previous effect
- Hitboxes and collision are all over the place, making attacking a specific target very difficult and unclear, and hits would often register numerous times even within a single strike
- Copy and dialogue is riddled with errors - I get the sensation the developer may not be a native English-speaker
- Key and mouse presses often seem not to register - this is especially problematic when it comes to attacks, as the combo system doesn't seem to work consistently
- UI could be made dramatically more clear - switch the health value to a bar, move other values to lower priority, add backgrounds on subtitles and change text to white or a similar neutral color, add mouseover effects to menu options, etc.
- Gravity settings seem to be a bit off - the player character will leave the ground even upon walking over a bridge

The game's mechanics also require some refinement:

- Combat needs to flow more smoothly - as it is, it's unclear to me how it's intended to flow. Enemies come at you in groups and will attack relentlessly, and this plus your slow-to-register hits means you almost never have an opportunity to strike back without getting hit
- Attack registration and combos need to be much more clear - I couldn't tell how to begin a combo, when a combo ends, if there's some sort of cooldown between swings, etc.
- Level design is fairly unimaginative - a series of floating platforms which you traverse left-to-right. The only obstacles generally seem to be gaps or trees, both of which are oddly-placed and trivial to overcome
- Story could be delivered in a clearer, more coherent way - right now, it's fairly obtuse

Truth be told, it's a bit difficult to assess the mechanics while there are so many technical issues.

Assuming the developer patches up some of these issues, I'll be happy to revisit and reassess my rating. As for now, Bjorn is a beautiful game with a lot of issues, so I probably wouldn't recommend it at its current price.

This is the railroading game I’ve been waiting years to play. As it stands now, even in the Early Access state, Railroader has so much to offer and a lot to do. Its primary aim is to simulate railroad logistics in the Transitional Period, covering everything from yard switching and freight to passenger service as well. Don’t go into this expecting in-depth operation of locomotives—the controls are simplified in order to make the overall task of running a short line much more approachable to a wider player base. And that’s completely fine by me, as this is a video game at the end of the day.

When it comes to the equipment itself, there are a wide variety of steam locomotives to choose from, as well as a couple of diesel engines that serve as more of an “end game” acquisition. While I enjoy operating the different steam engines, I’m certainly looking forward to using more diesel down the line (I’m a diesel guy after all).

Highly recommend picking this up if you’re a railroad nerd!

This game is the game I've been dreaming about! I've searched high and low for a fantastic immersive experience for trains and railroading. Not just to relive my childhood fantasies when my dad had a model train set, but to really experience in some way, of what it's like to actually be a Railroader.

Unlike other train games I've experienced, you don't need to figure out difficult menus about how to operate the trains or make them move on their own. This game allows you to do that, but with less difficulty and more simplicity. Yet, it retains a sense of realness to it that I've yet to find anywhere else! Similar to one of the other amazing games I love, Derail Valley, this game features coupling and the ability to not only control your trains, but to take and pick up orders for them. The difference between that game and this one is that it's even more simple. The game sends you a various variety of cars that you pull to and from stations and towns.

This game isn't just about getting money and operating trains however, it's about operating your own railroad. Hence the name, you are the president of your railroad, and you buy and sell and transfer goods to and from various industries. You even make repairs to the main line. The setting is pretty much what saves this game, really. It's set in Warsaw in 1905, and it just feels really authentic. Granted, I've never been to Warsaw, and I'm not Polish, so I can't tell how authentic it is, but it feels like it was made by people who understand this period in Poland's history, the culture, the politics, the population, etc. It really felt like a glimpse into the past, albeit with magic and demons. I also really enjoyed the inclusion of the Jewish community, which gets quite a bit of the spotlight, with "Kabbalah" being branded as their own secret school of Thaumaturgy. Not something you see in many games.


Unfortunately, other than the setting, the story is kind of lacking. It starts off pretty promising, and some of the side quests were interesting, but I found it didn't really ever grip me. The characters were fine, but the writing and voice acting were a little iffy and made it harder to connect with them than it should have been. The story doesn't really feel like it goes anywhere, and this was mostly evident in act 3 when I'm supposed to make a big choice between 2 options, that will decide how the climax will play out, and I found I don't really care either way. If there was a 3rd option, to just walk away from this conflict, I'd have 100% chosen that. It just doesn't do enough to make it [i]personal[/i], you know? I was just kind of wondering why I am even involved in any of this.
To make matters worse, this game does what I consider a very big no-no in RPGs. It sometimes take control of your character away from you. Basically, the idea is, you have a Flaw (as all Thaumaturges do) that kinda pushes you to act a certain way. Choose the option connected with it, and you feed the Flaw, making it stronger. In the lead characters' case, this Flaw is Pride. Now, I didn't really make a conscious choice at any point between giving in to my pride or avoiding it, I just chose whichever dialogue option felt right to me at the time. I did often choose myself above others, because... like I said, it was kinda hard to connect with the characters, so I mostly cared about growing my own power. This resulted in choosing the "Pride" dialogue option more often than not.
As the game progressed and my pride grew, dialogue options started being locked out - with the caption "Your pride is too high to choose this option". That's fair. I don't really [b]like [/b]it, but I get it, and I typically had other options, not just the Proud one, so I could manage to say or do the thing I wanted to.
This changed in act 3. Suddenly, things just happened. I wasn't given a choice. The game just said something like "Your pride chose for you" and made me do things I didn't actually wanna do. Suddenly my character was acting in ways I didn't agree with, and it didn't feel like my character anymore. I was now just going through the motions, playing with the mechanics - performing combat, interacting with objects, etc - but I was not really role playing anymore. I did not appreciate that at all.
I think one of the biggest examples of where this really harms the narrative is one scene where a character died because of a selfish choice I made earlier in the game. I was there, watching him die, and... there wasn't even an option to apologize. My pride was too high for that. I could only basically mock him and say something like "well that's what you get". 
That's not what I wanted at all. That was the first time in the game, maybe even the only time, where I saw serious consequences to my actions. It kinda made me rethink things. It made me want to do better and make up for my mistakes... but the game wouldn't let me. You were a proud a**hole at the start, so you're a proud a**hole till the end. Why? Have they not heard of character development?
In contrast, one of my fondest memories of any game, ever, is from my first playthrough of Mass Effect 3. I was playing full Renegade, until a scene where a former crewmate stands up to me and basically says "I'm not letting you do this, you're gonna have to shoot me". I decided not to. The first time in the whole trilogy where I didn't choose the renegade option, because the scene and the character just got to me. It felt right, it was a moment of growth, and I let it change how I played the rest of the playthrough.
Meanwhile, the Thaumaturge puts you in a similar position, but doesn't give you the option of growth. You've chosen who your character is, now sit back and watch.


One other issue I've got is with the combat. Not the system itself - it's fine. It's not great but it's serviceable, and building an arsenal of demons to choose from was kinda nice. The issue is rather with... who you fight. It's like the developers made this combat system and then thought - "wait, we don't really have any reason for combat to be in this game". The result is... you fight drunks. That's almost exclusively it, at least in acts 1 and 2.
You walk into a bar as part of an investigation - a bunch of drunks show up and say "we don't like outsiders here" and a fight starts.
You try and get onto a carriage to travel to another part of the city - a bunch of drunks show up and say "that's [b]our[/b] carriage!" and a fight starts.
You question a kid about a murder he was a witness to - a bunch of drunks show and say "why are you talking to this child? are you a pedophile?" and a fight starts.
F*cking hell. You can't go anywhere in this city without a bunch of drunks showing up and starting a fight. Why was this necessary? At first I thought it was just because I'm starting out, these are the low level fights and the combat system is just being introduced with easy enemies - but no, like 95% of combat in this game is against drunks who start a fight for stupid reasons. It just feels like a complete waste of time.


To end this review on a high note, I'll mention some other things I [i]did [/i]like, other than the setting which I already stated is the best part. I enjoyed the soundtrack, I enjoyed some of the ideas and themes in the story very much, I enjoyed the diversity of demons who come from a variety of different folklore, I liked the fact your actions do have consequences that feel significant (I would have even considered doing another playthrough with different choices if I could be bothered to beat up every single drunk in the city again), and I thought it did a good job of building up a mystery and slowly unfolding it (though, sadly, the mystery is solved quite a while before the ending, and then the game just... keeps going).


It's a decent game, it feels like it was someone's passion project, and I definitely appreciate it for what it is. However, it's flaws are quite significant and do often impact the experience negatively. In the end, I do recommend it, but it's certainly not for everyone.

And if you think the Pokémon comparison I opened with was kinda silly? Well, the game itself acknowledges it - There is a point where you're asked to make a wish, and one of the dialogue options is "to be the very best, like no one ever was".
Thaumaturges are just Pokémon trainers. I said what I said.

Can we all agree that this is the kind of game we want?

Deep story, meaningful choices, an incredible atmosphere—plus, I get to summon spooky Slavic demons to settle my problems. What’s not to love?

As a Polish person, seeing 1905 Warsaw like this is magical. The city feels alive, full of history, grime, and people who all have their own agendas. The characters? Phenomenal. Every conversation feels like a high-stakes mind game, and the voice acting is top-tier.

Combat is a mix of strategy and mystical smackdowns, and the moral choices hit just as hard. The Thaumaturge feels like The Witcher met Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines at a dark alley dance battle.

10/10, would haunt Warsaw again.

Pretty decent game. The story is engaging and gameplay is good enough. Battles mostly not challenging (at least on medium difficulty), but that's not a con IMO
And the most appealing part of the game is it's setting. There are not many other games which sets somewhere in early XX century Eastern Europe and are not strategy games.

Oh and as a side not I would mention, that setups to some fights that happens during exploration or some side quests reminded me porn movies. Like a few slightly random lines of dialogue and BAM! straight to the action

At its best, it's a decent RPG, with lively characters, dialogues, and situations. Locations look amazing, full of love for old Warsaw architecture. I never imagined that mud on the cobblestones can look so alive and diverse, you can almost feel it squelching and slipping under your feet.

It's not always at its best though. Combat is an unbearable chore that doesn't bring neither fun nor tension, just a mindless repetition of the same actions vs identical opponents, that can't be sped up, nor bypassed. Whatever mechanics there are outside of combat, they fail to impress just as well. You just tolerate it as much as you can.

Overall, the game is a bit iffy and mediocre, but if you're in the mood for some authentic Polish stuff, it's well worth it.

The more I think about it the more mixed my feelings get. I loved the atmosphere, the story was intriguing and I appreciate rpgs where the role of combat isn't a major factor. Pride options come up in dialogue but other should as well and feeding the pride flaw should have more consequence then it takes the wheel sometimes.

I gave this game a try because of the setting and unfortunately it couldn't really capture me for longer. The combat looks interesting at first but quickly turns a bit stale later. I wouldn't say the story so far was bad but it also didn't make me keep engaged personally. All in all I wouldn't say it's a bad game but try it at least out for 2h! It's enough time to see if the game clicks for you.

I really struggled to cross the finish line on this game. There are things I love, and things I don't. Do not take this review as an out-and-out rejection of it. If there was a "recommend under specific circumstances", I'd choose that. As it stands, I imagine more possible customers will leave dissatisfied than satisfied, which is a shame, as with a bit more polish and better design The Thaumaturge could've been an RPG I play every year.

Conceptually, this game should be a slam-dunk. It's about an early 20th century wizard solving mysteries in Poland before the fall of the Romanovs. The design team, Fool's Theory, will be working on the Witcher remake, and Witcher vibes are pretty strong here. Technically speaking, the detective parts of the Witcher and its sober grounded slavic drama is what makes that game series so beloved, so producing a condensed version of that formula that focuses on quests and dialogue is very clever and forward thinking.

But Fool's Theory, true to their name, fumble the ball in a few areas.

The biggest problem is the game is terribly optimized. This is to be expected of a AA title I suppose, but it's shocking how much the game struggles to not leak memory. From afar, the levels look very nice, particularly the mud, water reflections, and clothing textures, but hair and faces are very poorly done. Some characters have wide disturbing mouths, particularly the protagonist when he smiles. The lighting also fights against the character models in certain places. The game is very muddy and simple, despite how taxing it can be on your system.

Next is the story which feels like it moves at lightspeed but is slow as molasses at the same time. I'm somewhat surprised I beat it in 32 hours. Mechanically, the story plays like your standard Witcher game. You're presented with a number of side-quests that each toe the line between the natural and supernatural, where the world of man and spirits blurs, all pivoting around a central storyline the consequences of which don't fully reveal themselves until much later.

Perhaps it's the localization, but it doesn't all flow together neatly. Characters all deliver sobering and sarcastic lines, which feels true to the source, but not every joke comes across. In some instances it's clear the developers wrote a cultural joke that the translation team didn't even bother to translate. For a game that's mostly about dialogue choices, it's very hard to speak with intention when those intentions aren't always clear.

Next, the actual gameplay mechanics are frustratingly stiff and shallow. Every area presents you with a number of "clues" you can unveil with your witcher-sight button. Story progression is gated by finding a certain number of clues until you unveil a deduction, after which you can talk to a sign-posted NPC and open a dialogue that moves the story forward. You are also limited by your salutors, the "spirits" that the main character collects like Pokemon. On more than one occasion I encountered quests I couldn't complete because I needed a certain salutor at a certain level. Oh, also side quests are limited by the act you're in, and some can be missed entirely. If you don't play with a guide, it's very possible that you'll soft-lock your way out of certain storylines, and not for trying.

Combat also is interesting, on paper, but vaguely flat. It runs on a Persona-style turn-based combat system with all sorts of stacking debuffs and buffs that don't work well together and don't really matter. The key to victory should be using the right salutor on the right target, but again, if you don't happen to have the right salutor you can still just faceroll enemies away. The long attack animations that play over and over again also drags the gameplay to a crawl. On top of it all everyone in Warsaw is weirdly keen to kick your ass in an early 90s video game sort of way that doesn't always make sense. It was so hard for me to finish the game because I dreaded getting into another alleyway fight when all I want to do is buy a box of goddamn donuts.

The voice actors are a mixed bag of average, and no one can decide what sort of accent, if any, the characters should have. You will hear british, french, american, russian, and hispanic accents thrown in haphazardly, and they will all slur pronunciations of Polish nouns full of chaotic consonants.

It's bad, but the entertaining kind. So I don't count that as a flaw.

The music, is pretty good actually. There aren't many tracks, but they do the job well.

The last thing I can say, and the last good thing, is that the monster designs are very interesting and unique. This is going for Witcher vibes, so expect a veritable grab-bag of Eurasian beasties you can corral into your roster.

---

Look, if the game is on sale, I recommend a buy. If Fool's Theory puts out another game (not necessarily the Witcher remake), I'd give it a look. Even if it's only a demo or trial run.

So far I'm disappointed - the game doesn't seem to do anything demanding graphically but seems to run incredibly slowly. I suspect it takes a good desktop PC to make this game playable.

I'll update this review if I change my mind, but I'm not optimistic.

Great atmosphere. I loved it from the beginning. Whole game (except prologue) takes place in 1905 Warsaw under occupation of Russians. Poland did not existed during this time period.

Mechanics are pretty simple - you look for clues using your powers. Talk a lot. Many of dialogue options have some consequences. Some quick, some will kick you much later.

Turn based battles are satisfying. You can play a lot with your build. Changing abilities is free and available before each fight.

If you're looking for a lot of action - skip this one. If you're looking for captivating plot, credible characters, and atmospheric world - jackpot!
Excellent graphic and intriguing story. I enjoy this game

A very well made RPG with captivating plot, good writing and very unusual setting. Really well made, it punches above it's double-A status and looks almost on par with triple-A titles. Combat is a bit simplistic but still serviceable. This can be forgiven though, as it's certainly not the main focus of the game though, story and characters are. Thaumaturge is not Disco Elysium, but it's certainly one of the "thinking man's RPGs" which it inspired.

For best results, set voiceover to Polish, you will not be disappointed.
Creepy details where choices matter. It's easy to pick up and start playing without many complicated mechanics.
Don't miss out on this if you like mystery, deep and engaging story, noir, or isometric games in general. Highly recommended!
I love this game. It's not completely free, but still has a good wizard/detective feel. I'd recommend it to any fan of crpgs, the Witcher, or Raidou Kuzunoha.

10hrs in and I am enjoying this Role Playing Game (RPG) set in 1905 Poland within the Russian Empire. This is a fictional, linear story, with side quests. Setting within a historical setting, with some historical themes like the social, political, nationalistic, racist and class tensions of the times, and historical characters such as Rasputin and Tsar Nikolas 2. 

The protagonist Wiktor is the prodigal son of a wealthy Polish man. The game follows Wiktor's adventures and the player has some choices dialogue, where choices matter, and it can be fun to play with the option "PRIDE" and be a rude arrogant elitist... or try alternate paths to reduce tensions. The side quests and exploring the world give more experience and more character development points, so the player is rewarded for looking around. The turn based combat has been a bit of a button smash for me, working out what are the better combinations for what challenges. I'm slowly getting better at it. The protagonist Wiktor has a personal salutor (like a folk spirit or demon) he can call on in combat and to manipulate NPCs in dialogues if he has enough information from using his special sense, a bit like the Witcher. The Salutors are a bit like pokemons, where Wiktor is looking to capture more to do his will. The voice acting for Wiktor and Rasputin is very good. Other characters are hit and miss. The childhood friend Andreyc is wild and you can make some choices you would or would not do in your own life - this is a mature RPG game after all - play with it.

A decent RPG in a setting in a novel setting - 1905 Warsaw. There are some hat tips to Bramstoker's dracula, and Reasputin has premonitions of what will be the Titanic and WW1 battlefields. Rasputins magnatism is shown and it makes more sense as to how he could have infiltrated the Russian court, in a time where people still considered superstition and the supernatural as somethings not yet to be ruled out.

Gameplay is essentailly, explore, investigate objects, interview NPCs, have a brawl, acquire a new pokemon salutor, and progress the story or side quest. The cut scenes, music, backgrounds, characters, mystery, intrigue, mystical elements, architecture and world building, are all very good, Mature themes such as the supernatural, drunkeness, dug references, prostitution references and political repression are there, adding to a more beleivable world to explore.

Edit: found the combat boring after a while and not adding to the story much.

Fantastic game!

The story was intriguing with plenty of choices affecting how things proceed - both your actions and words matter, making it a truly unique experience and allowing you to replay the game with vastly different outcomes.

All the characters had memorable personalities and backstories, even those only playing a role in side quests (of which there were plenty too!). Wiktor made for a great protagonist with all flaws attached. The occasional humour in the dialogues gave me a good chuckle too with Abaurycy stealing the spotlight more than once.

While the fighting mechanics might have been a bit repetitive, as well as some animations, the salutors greatly made up for it - amazing designs, both in their looks and sounds! Not all of them are equally as viable as others and I ended up using the same strategy almost every time, but it didn't really take away from the overall experience.

In conclusion, I absolutely recommend this game, enjoyed every second of it!

First time not recommending a game mostly on the basis of sound. The voice acting, sound editing, the jarring echo effects- it is abysmal. And I want to enjoy this beautifully crafted setting and this interesting time period in European history but then someone decides to talk, and I want to pull my hair out.

Realistically, how many diary pages and secret letters are people throwing on the ground? It just seems absurd. I know it sounds picky but all of this is immersion breaking.

The main storyline is interesting enough but has some questionable turns. I definitely did not enjoy the way you were introduced to it as if you should know everything there is about thaumaturgy from the get go. 

I was looking for a Disco Elysium like experience and that is why I was excited to check out this game and although a similar noir vibe is definitely in place and the setting is well executed (kuddos to the artists), this game just did not deliver in my book.

A great game. Very unusual. Very deep in some moments. I really love the combination of real life history plus magic and ghosts. And I do love Poland. SO YEAH- I LOVE The Thaumaturge. It is important to state that it is great to be playing an RPG where the character is a white male with a complicated personality

I was drawn to this game because it seemed like something in between The Witcher, Baldur's Gate 3, and Supernatural, and I wasn't disappointed. The combat isn't quite as refined as those bigger games, and as such can get a little tedious, but the overall enjoyment of playing far outweighs that. I love that this game is so very un-american in style, culture and tone, and isn't written to pander to a wider audience. I could absolutely see this world getting adapted into a TV series.

It is quite a shame. The premise of The Thaumaturge is promising and, for video games, the writing is competent and the game starts rather strong without dumping a gallon of lore onto you with long intro sequences narrated with endless lines telling you of some generic conflict. Our protagonist Wiktor Szulski (with "W", as he insists on) isn't feeling well and in contrast to many other games in this budget range we see it immediately; reddish eyes with violet eye sockets and sweat all over his face. Wiktor is a thaumaturge (the word derived from Greek and meaning as much as miracle worker who draws on magic to influence the physical world) and as of late his abilities seem to fade and weaken, so he seeks a healer In a remote village who himself has been witnessed doing miraculous healing. 

If this isn't already intriguing add the early 20th century set in what is nowadays Poland, which was partly territory of the Russian empire at that time, at the beginning of the Russian revolution. So expect protests, revolutionaries and militias, in short political unrest and turmoil with the region on the brink of civil war. This is unique and I don't recall any other game with that exact setting. No being exact the same thing but the closest thing you get is probably the brilliant Disco Elysium. And The Thaumaturge does have its fair share of similarities with Disco Elysium because there's a lot to read. And I mean *a lot*. Still not quite as much as in Disco Elysium and also with less choice and consequences. But as with Disco, your options in dialogues increase the more clues you find in the environment to confront characters with. For a more streamlined experience the game tells you if a dialogue option is locked-out due to a missing clue. This doesn't mean you can't progress but you may barred from a certain decision or path. Often you can exit dialogues, though, and keep searching for missing clues to increase your dialogue options later.

The environment offers good fidelity but the muted colours and desaturated tone might not be everybody's cup of tea although it fits the setting. Interior decoration, clothes and hairstyles look accurately fitting to the period and monster design is grounded on Slavic folklore, as much as you expect from former The Witcher developers from Poland.

To summarize what we've got on the positive side of things: Good storytelling, unique setting with plausible execution and intricately detailed quality monster design.

I will ignore stiff animations and weak NPC face fidelity because some of the greatest games ever made don't excel with their graphics but with their gameplay and/or story. Those games' flaws are comparably small and few to the strong points and are perceived as a minor annoyance at worst but nothing that would break the game and stop you from having fun and playing it. Unfortunately this is not the case with The Thaumaturge.

This game's biggest flaw, which ultimately made me stop playing by ALT+F4 out of the game, is its combat. And no, it has nothing to do with the difficulty in case you thought I rage quit out of the game. It is, in short, its tediousness and lackluster 'punch'. Pair this up with an incredibly boring skill tree and many, many mandatory fights and soon you'd be dreaming of Disco Elysium's non-combat stance. But let's go into detail why The Thaumaturge is another example of a ruined experience by the lack of focus on what you're good at as a developer.

First of all, there are so damn many fights. Unusual for western cRPGs is the lack of options to avoid combat. This is not to say *every* fight is mandatory, but more often than not you simply can't avoid it. Wiktor can't sneak, can't do stealthy take downs and sometimes, when you think you can bypass some NPCs you get locked into a sequence and a dialogue menu. And often this is just a facade because no matter what options you pick, combat is inevitable. But, I hear you interject, isn't it fitting for the setting that tempers stopped being resigned and became explosive with people actively looking for a fight? Fair enough, but then at least make the combat fun. When you make combat a main gameplay pillar of your game with a ratio of at least 50% of what you'll be doing, it's better be fun, engaging and impactful.

Combat works in turns. Your and the enemies' turns are determined by your action's speed. So it's possible to make three quick but weak punches before enemies have their turns. Or you go a slow but strong punch but get stabbed, shot at or punched before it's your turn. Most attacks will impose status effects on your or your enemy, with your typical damage over time or status effects like the chance to completely interrupt an enemy's attack. The combat is transparent and offers full visibility on the enemy's next action (unless certain enemies have an effect that's hiding it) and how fast it's going to be and how fast your attack will be. You also have those Salutors (think of them as monster pets who fight for you and have different strengths and abilities). Those are the pros.

I wouldn't say the combat mechanic is conceptual bad. It's the execution that drive the stake into the game's heart. For instance, animations are way too long and drawn out. Hits lack a satisfying punch to it; there's little sound and little particle or animations effects emphasizing a hit. It might be realistic but we're dealing with monsters and thaumaturgy, and for the sake of a satisfying and fun fight I'd take a little less realism. There's no pop, no cracking sounds, no sound of big slashes or busted or burst bones or anything. Guns sound weak and so do punches. People drop and that's it.

Now enters the poor skill tree. If you are thorough with your exploration and only do a little side questing you get so many skill points you can't even distribute them all because you're gated by the main plot. For hours I had 10 unspent skill points because I was already maxed out at that point and could only skill further once I progress further in the story. You get so many skill improvements/augmentations (e.g. you can augment your quick punch so it interrupts enemies, you can augment another punch to reduce an enemy's damage, etc.) but only very little actual skills you can use in combat. I have like fifteen skill augmentations but only four skills actively to use in combat with Wiktor (the Salutors have their own set of attacks and give you more variance the more Salutors you have). But it never feels satisfying. At some points you get human companions but they act on their own and intricate attacks with synergy effects are difficult to pull off later in the game. 

Difficulty-wise it manages quite well, confronting you with enemies applying more status effects on you or hiding their own next actions. Still you get the numbers game, however, and enemies get more and HP. But so do you, which doesn't mean the game gets more difficult but fights drag on even more. Especially when you don't fight two but three people at the same time and another group of three guys coming in waves. It feels like it just never ends.

I wouldn't mind a few but meaningful fights that keep you on your toes and where every hit and punch looks and feels great. I wouldn't even mind the game's flawed combat when it was used more sparsely because the developers have clearly more talent in characterisation, world building, dialogues and story. But why do you shoe-horn this almost seperate (combat) experience that keeps you from the good one over and over and over again and stretch them longer and longer. If people want to have combat this is fine, but give the players more options to avoid it.

With that being said (and I also ignore the somewhat lackluster exploration when you constantly snip your fingers with a right mouse click to highlight interactive objects and certain items only appear when you do so) it is not a game I can recommend unfortunately.
A massive bait and switch between the opening of the game and the core of it. A waste of time and awful characters.

The lore, setting, vibes, and characters are very well done. The combat can get a little repetitive but it tried something new/interesting so points for that. This game also gives you a wide dearth of choices and rewards/punishes you for them accordingly. A really good RPG.

It is good if:

You like a nice lore and nice stories.
You like Constantine.
You are fine in walking around pressing one button to reveal clues and read a lot.
You like easy combats in a turn based style like a deck builder game.
Cut scene after cut scene does not repeal you.
You are fine with bugs especially turned around the character movements and passing through some walls.
You are fine not being able to say something to someone because you do not have enough points to reveal an information or you did not go to a particular place before and you won't be able to go there anymore at the moment of the discussion.
You may miss things to be done as you are moving in the story without being told that is a no return point. (You can still load a save on this one but you may have to redo a couple of things then...)

I won't recommend to always follow what the game indicates you to do first. Since there are path or actions you won't be able to take.
There are real choices that have incidences. But you are not always able to make them the way you would like and it would have been possible by the script presented. Not sure if it is intended like that or if another type of exploration would have been possible before.

I am not into reading much in game. I prefer action in general and/or more strategy. But since the lore is great, and the story appeal, I continue playing and give it the thumb up.
Good story although it would have been nice to draw conclusions rather than have them drawn for you.

The dialogue interactions had unexpected consequences and encouraged me to make the smartest choice, not just the most colorful dialogue option, which set itself apart from most of these kinds of games. I got around 40 hours of gameplay out of this but I took my time to get as much as possible, but I think it's more than worth the price.

All I will say in regards to this game is that I thoroughly enjoy it. If you want a more in-depth review just check the top reviews there are several that say what I would with far more eloquence than I'm capable.

Urrrggh, I really struggled with which way this recommendation should go.

There was a lot I didn't like about this game.
- Most of your time is spent running backwards and forwards across the same few locations, mostly doing almost-irrelevant busywork. I uttered the words "PLEASE let that be my last time here" way too often.
- I was expecting there to be meaningful tradeoffs to the acquisition of new flaws, to make character progression interesting - but no, it's all upside, and indeed effectively mandatory.
- What character progression there IS is, IMO, poorly designed. Early on, you earn skill points super fast, and progress along the tracks at a rate that makes it look like you'll easily max all the tracks by the end. But then later on it slows RIGHT down, and you discover late on that it's not possible in one playthrough to earn enough XP to maximise all the tracks, or even ONE track if progress them pretty evenly. So your choices are to become a jack of all trades/master of none that fails ALL the hard late-game skill checks, or to take a random guess at which ones you think will be important, and end up also failing medium ones in a couple of the dimensions in order to pass hard ones in the others. And there's no hints given to you that this will be the case, nor any respec option when you realise you got it wrong.
- With the one flaw that's actually gameplay-relevant - your starting one - you either want to push it a lot, or not at all. Moving from low Pride to medium closes a bunch of doors, and moving from medium to high opens a bunch; being medium is the worst of both worlds, but you don't really get warned about that either.
- The combat is simple, repetitive and easy.
- The voice acting is very inconsistent - lots of jarring accent changes/mispronunciations/incorrect emphasis.
- The ending was possibly the most disappointing I've ever experienced (and I played Mass Effect 3 before they patched it ;-). I can't say too much without spoilers, but in short, my character's faction wanted to set the world to rights, they achieved "maintain the status quo", and were bizarrely happy about it while I stared at the screen going "wtf!?".

Given all that, you're probably wondering why this review is a positive recommendation - and I'm finding it frustratingly hard to articulate that beyond "somehow, despite all of that, I still had fun". The story is interesting, I liked a lot of the writing, and there's just something about the fundamentals of being a thaumaturge that's unique and feels good. Like, if you step back and look at it dispassionately, "follow a trail to three objects, click them, and use the dialog option that unlocked" sounds pretty dull. Yet, somehow, it really WORKS. The way you get special insights from these objects that nobody else could, piece them together to figure out a secret someone thought impenetrable and use that against them - it somehow makes you feel clever and powerful despite it being trivial gameplay. So ultimately, despite feeling like I just wasted a lot of time, I have to apply the maxim "time you enjoy wasting is never wasted time" and hope that you'll enjoy wasting yours too! :-D

It's a good game, though it would be tough to recommend it to everyone. For me, the biggest advantage of this game is its original setting. The game is set in early 20th century Warsaw, and the city looks really great. The characters, environments and collectibles feel real and authentic. There are also references to historical events and figures, which is a plus for me. Polish script and voice-acting are done really well, as they reflect the language of that era. Also, the concept of a "folk demon hunter" is appealing to me. What's more, some of the demons' designs, like Bukavac or Lelek, are sick. The story is interesting, and I wanted to unravel it to see where it will lead the main character. The latter, Wiktor Szulski, might not be as interesting as Geralt, but he was appealing enough to me. When it comes to the flaws,. Probably the biggest to me is the fighting system. It's really weird. You fight a group of enemies, you shoot each other with guns, which sometimes do less damage than a punch, and after the fight your enemies usually get up. Graphics on close-ups are also kind of mediocre. The side quests, usually, are also quite simple and standard. Though, I have to admit that some of them were interesting. Finally, usually you have just an illusion of choice. No matter what answer you pick, the outcome will be the same, but paraphrased words will be used. Of course, choices matter during key events. Overall, I enjoyed the game, but I'm not sure if the game will appeal to foreigner, as its biggest advantage, in my opinion is its early 20th century Warsaw atmosphere. It's not very expensive, and you can get it on sale, so if you want to try being a Polish demon hunter, you can give it a go.

I will preface this by saying I got this cause steam said in its like others you played tab that it was like Littlewood, a game I loved and played through multiple times, So I know i'm not judging it fairly on its own merits, but this is how it was presented to me and i feel others that it might present to need to know. Now I haven't completed the game yet, but I can see where the like Littlewood suggestion came from, it has very similar gameplay loop of start a town from nothing, build up your town by using up your energy on daily tasks, slowly unlock more features as time goes on and your town grows. light farming and building while having to use lower materials to upgrade to better ones. 

These similarities at least at the moment feel surface level at best, like someone looked at Littlewood and said that was neat, lets do that in space, without any of the heart. The Npcs are soulless cutouts, all of them have like one quest (a few as of yet don't even have quests) and then they just repeat the same 1-2 lines everyday, again unfairly comparing to Littlewood where each npc has a distinct personality, their own wants out of the town, you can hang out with them, flirt with them ect. The town building is equally flat, you can place things however you like and build roads and walls, but you have one road option and one wall option (preface there may be more later and i just have not unlocked them). The little scraps of story are something, but not really compelling thus far.

Its been 3 hours and I don't really feel like I did anything of substance, wake up, talk to new colonist, get new building, place new building, add one new thing to the routine maybe, go to bed, rinse repeat. In and of itself isn't a bad thing, like I said the gameplay loop is very similar to Littlewood, but it lacks the push Littlewood had. You can go up to the NPCs and talk to them everyday, it won't change a thing, they will still just say the same stock phrases. There are only three areas, at least at the 3 hour mark, one of those areas is a really shallow combat dungeon that you press one button and nothing will ever hit you, and one is a big open space that you only go to for like four quests thus far and it just sits there, other then that you are stuck walking around your base. Compare again to the varied locations in Littlewood where you could realistically plan a whole day around going to the forest for trees, or the mines for rare minerals, or town for buying stuff and a fishing trip.

In conclusion, This really feels like it should of been early access, a lot of the basics are there, it just doesn't go much deeper then that. My opinion might shift if i play it more, but right now I have to say i don't feel like its in a state to be worth the price tag I paid of 20 CAD. I say if you are looking for something that you can just turn your brain off and build for a bit, I'd say it will do that, but wait for a sale. If like me you were drawn to it by the like others you played suggestion, I'd say don't get your hopes up and know what you are going into. For me personally If i was talking to my past self, I would have to give it a not recommend, tho i do acknowledge there is something there that could net someone, Just Steam set me up for an expectation it just could not live up to, and that is completely on me.

I'm very on the fence about recommending this one.  I got some mild enjoyment out of it, and if you'd like a Mars aesthetic for a farming game, maybe buy on sale and check it out.  I did have a bit of fun with unlocking new buildings and exploring the different minigames for a few hours.

But after 7 hours in, I am on day 36, and as far as I can tell, my only remaining objective is "keep playing until day 200".  I don't think I want to do that, without any hints of anything else to look forward to.

There are some other design choices I especially feel aren't optimal in this type of game:

* Equipment upgrades mostly only mean I run out of energy more slowly, i.e. my reward for advancement is I get to do MORE repetitive chores in a day if I choose to.

* Thoroughly filling out my recipe list actually seems to make me less profit, because complex ones just take more time but don't seem particularly more valuable.

* The dialogue trees feel a little clunky to navigate. Some things are insufficiently explained (like a quest I didn't know was aimed at the park building), sometimes I keep opting out of a quest because I'm trying to make the dialogue display faster and click the decline option, sometimes I feel punished for talking to someone because I get a 5-step set of instructions I can't opt out of.

There are several things I had trouble figuring out how to do.  I couldn't find a wiki or forum for the game, not sure if it doesn't exist yet or if "Mars Base" is a little too common a phrase.  

Anyway, if you go in with patience, persistence, and not-too-high expectations, you might find it to be a reasonably fun little game.

Great idea to use MIDI keyboard in a rhythm game, but the whole thing just doesn't work for me.

I diagnose the problem as follows. The way I use MIDI keyboard is usually to play music -- I have a melody or chord progression in my mind, and I directly play it. I don't think about what key I'm gonna play, I just play it.
This game, however, requires me to look at the screen, see what note is coming, then play it on my keyboard. In my mind, I have to turn what I see on my screen into some melody, and then play it. It just doesn't flow well for me.

Or from a more phenomenological perspective, MIDI keyboard for musicians is like a lively tool, or an extension of their body. They don't "gawk" at a MIDI keyboard, they just skillfully play music with it. This game requires people to "gawk" at their MIDI keyboard, so it can't possibly work.

Let me use another analogy to really illustrate the problem. There are typing games where the screen shows you a word or a sentence, and you need to type the word in a given amount of time. Sounds like a fun way to kill some time. However, imagine a typing game where the screen shows you *where to type on your keyboard*, instead of what you need to type. There's an outline of the keyboard on the screen, but no letter on that keyboard outline. Sometimes a key turns green, and you need to think "what letter is it?", and then hit it on your physical keyboard. In such a game, there would be absolutely no flow, it would just be confusing.

So how to fix the problem? In short, show players the *musical content of what to play*, instead of the physical action to play it. One possible solution is to use this "Watch and Play" method: the game gives players a hint on what *musical content* to play, and then the player has to play it. A rhythm game that does this incredibly well is Rhythm Doctor -- this is a rhythm game that flows so well it can even be played by a blind person.

Overall, I think the idea of integrating MIDI keyboard in a rhythm game has a lot of potential, but for now there are major problems. To solve the problem the game probably needs a big rework, but it is a fixable one.
