Against my better judgement, I have completed each level in this game and have acquired the gold in each individual level. This is my assessment of this game:

1.5/10

Story:
While there is a story displayed here in the description of the game, there is no story given in game. There are level selections from the main menu that you chose to play. Each level you play as an unnamed soldier that runs and guns through the level to collect a pile of gold. Each level has their own map, but no contiguous story attached.

Gameplay:
As said before, you play as a soldier that runs through the level, shoots the bad guys, and collects a pile of gold. The gameplay can be best compared to ARMA 3, but stripped bare to its most basic elements - third/first person firefighting, an inventory system, and infrared/night vision modes.
The inventory system gives you a whopping 6 inventory slots. You will only use it to stache ammo and grenades, as there is no reason to carry weapons with you. Each throwable can be stacked, ammo can be stacked. There is no way to pick up ammo from enemies. The only way to retrieve ammo is by looting it from random tables with preset items strewn across it in a very not so pretty fashion. There is a slot for a backpack, but in my experience playing, there is no way to either loot or craft a backpack.
Speaking of crafting, there is an entire crafting system I assume is not implemented that I found by accident by pressing the M key. As far as I found, there are no items to pick up off of the ground or from enemies, so I could not craft any items during gameplay.
You have 3 meters at the top left of your screen:
- Stamina
- Unknown meter A
- Unknown meter B
Stamina regenerates extremely slowly. Unknown meter B seemingly drains over time. I'm unsure what Unknown meter A does.
You are a bullet sponge, and you'll never know how much health you have left. The screen will go fuzzy, and then you will flop over and die when you absorb enough damage. There is no indicator other than the fuzzy screen that will tell you that you are low on health.
You can blow up tanks with land mines, when they decide to work. Otherwise, you can blow them up with grenades. Otherwise, you can blow them up with other tanks after the game RNG rolls to decide that you hit them.
Speaking of tanks, you can use vehicles in this game.
- The Fighter Jet:
Will explode on contact with anything, and is useless except for transportation. You will NOT be able to combat anyone in the plane. You will fly it at top speed and then promptly receive constant incoming damage from unavoidable missiles and a constant barrage of machine gunning from behind until you either explode or eject from the plane. Upon ejecting, you'll free fall like a piece of paper until you either hit the ground or press F to open your parachute. There is no warning, you must KNOW the button to open the parachute. Good luck.
- The Tank:
Moves at the equivalent of walking speed. The reload speed for shells is painfully slow. The tank shells can only blow up vehicles, and will not kill enemy soldiers unless they explode from a nearby vehicle. The machine gun will decimate soldiers, but you'll never figure out it's the Spacebar key until you visit the training level. It will never explode with you in it, because it has a ton of health and nothing will threaten you inside of it, as other tanks only barely dent your health.
- The Car:
You will move at the speed of the jet, and you will not be able to brake unless you use the handbrake which you'll never know is the Spacebar key until you visit the training level. If you do not use the handbrake, you will slip and slide as though you were driving on ice. Due to the awful physics in the game, you will go flying in the car if you hit anything sloped, and also flip around if you hit a wall or an enemy. Yes, that's correct. You cannot run over enemies. They are solid as stone if you attempt to drive over them. It's awful when they break your momentum. You also cannot fix your car when it's lifted off the ground or flipped upside down. It is stuck forever then.

The guns that are available in the game is as follows:
- Machine gun
- Machine gun, but more ammo?
- Pistol (Desert Eagle quality)
- Sniper

You'll always kill an enemy instantly if you headshot them. The sniper will kill on body shot.
There is a First Person Mode, if you press the Z key. It is completely unnecessary, and you won't use it. If you do, and if you even attempt to scope in to shoot, you won't be able to see where you're shooting after the first shot, as the recoil on the gun throws your reticle all over the place.
In 3rd person mode, the reticle does not accurately show where your bullets fly.
If you die, you will respawn at the beginning of the level, and the level will not respawn vehicles or enemies killed. Some levels require vehicles, so you will end up restarting the level anyways, and restarting the level anyways will respawn enemies and NOT enemy vehicles. Huge oversight.
There is no way to heal in this game. You will "heal" over time, but I can't tell if you really do or not, because if the screen gets fuzzy, it'll unfuzz, but then immediately fuzz up again when an enemy shoots me.
Enemies have hawkeye accuracy, and they will NOT miss. Enemy tanks have the worst accuracy and sometimes do not shoot downwards, until they decide they have master accuracy and will hit you with every bullet killing you instantly.
There are no markers for where to go. You will be walking around for a while just trying to figure out where the heck you're supposed to be going. Sometimes it's possible to just drop out of a plane directly atop of the gold and win instantly. Either it's extremely hard to win or extremely easy, no in betweens.


Graphics:
The graphics in the game are stock, and I have no doubt about it. The mountains clip into themselves, and some just aren't even on the ground, and you can walk underneath them. All duplicated assets appear identical to each other. Water will simply stop existing where the developer decided they didn't want to put water anymore. Some levels will have identical assets to other levels, and some levels will have flat expanses of land that will simply cease existing. The quality of the textures are not so great. There were many levels I got stuck in and had to restart the mission.
Animations are janky as all hell. When you kill an enemy, their head will spin around constantly as they're on the floor. When you die, if you were pressing a direction, your camera will stop and you'll see your body flip around all over the place and roll about on the floor. Ragdoll physics gone wrong.
Broken vehicles are simply vehicles with a black texture over them to "look burnt". It looks awful.
Sometimes, my grenades simply do not explode, resulting in them just disappearing.
The win screen is a static image basically saying, "You got the gold, you win!" and then back to menu. No fanfare, just an achievement.
In each level, your only hint on what to do is a text box asset telling you loosely where to go in broken English.
The main menu is garbage and bare minimum, the level select screen bugs out the Credits option, the Credits option does not work and only shows Valkeala Software and then stops working.
Animations on your character look extremely funny.


Music/Sound design:
Repetitive and boring. There is more than one track in the game, but the track loops constantly and drones on. It is not cool or enticing. One time, my music didn't even load, so the level was played in ultimate silence.
The sound of the machine gun is awful and it will be the only sound you hear in the game besides your own gun, since all enemies use the machine gun.
There are pretty much no other sounds or music in the game.

Solid port of a pretty good board game.

Dune is a worker game - if you have played games like Lords of Waterdeep you will be familiar with the basic mechanics. You start the game with a couple of workers ("agents" in the game parlance) and have the ability to acquire one more. Board locations are colored and you have to play a matching card to send an agent there, and if an agent is already there you can't (in most cases) send one of yours there.

It is also a deck-building game, where the main gameplay deck for each player starts off with 10 crappy cards and you buy cards over time at the end of every turn - and destroy cards in your deck now and again - to make your deck better.

The basic gameplay is simple but the game is a lot of fun, having a complex enough strategy where you will be thinking through your turns, but not so complex that the AI on hard mode is completely handicapped. You will still win many games against computer players, but you will lose often enough to keep yourself entertained, and if that isn't enough for you the multiplayer is very robust.

Well implemented deck builder with a tight, tight game play loop in which you have 10 rounds maximum to build out your deck and are fighting for resources with up to three other players in addition to  trying to out-manuever those opponents in realizing game-board opportunities and reaping the benefits of being victorious in superior-force conflict.

Every turn involves making interesting, nuanced choices made against challenging constraints.  The choices you make during your turn are nuanced because the number of turns you will have is limited, so you won't be able to do everything and will need to focus on whether you should attempt to accumulate victory points in the short term or  pursue a more long-range strategy. Your nuanced strategy will be affected by the special abilities associated with the Dune universe character you choose to play as when the game started.

The dynamic aspects of the Dune story (factional conflict and lore) are well-represented in the game play loop as well.  Fans of the recent Dune movies will be rewarded as various characters and locations from those movies appear within the game.

The game implementation is solid with challenging solo-play against challenging AI opponents and a bunch of fun on-line modes, including asynchronous multi-player and several challenge modes. 

Definitely recommended for fans of the original board game, Frank Herbert's original novels,  or just people who want a good, fast, well implemented deck building worker placement game to challenge themselves with or play with remote friends.

I found this game via Reddit, of all places, and was initially skeptical because it looked like Risk of Rain 2 at home. However, after having played it for a bit... oh my Lord, if you go in expecting Risk of Rain 2, you are in for a RUDE awakening.

Firstly, the movement. It certainly takes a bit of getting used to -- rebind your dash from Alt to something else, by the way -- but once you get it down MAN is it smooth. Jumping to and fro without a care in the world, searching across land to land for trinkets, and the fights are certainly something to behold.

That said, I have a few nitpicks.

For one; this game is VERY grindy. Unlike other rougelikes such as Risk of Rain (overall), Ember Knights, etc etc, you're given a starter character with two starter weapons, and that's it. You have to play through -- and likely die in -- multiple runs in order to get *one* of the unlocks, let alone any of the rest, especially if you're running solo. I haven't even actually unlocked any of them because I don't have the luxury of friends that own this game, meaning I'm on my lonesome to fend against the encroaching robot army.

For two; there is one enemy type that I genuinely don't enjoy, and that caused me to stop playing. Minor spoilers, fair warning. [spoiler]Within stage two you encounter enemies I call "Scissor Wisps", since they remind me of Lesser Wisps from RoR2 and look kinda like a pair of scissors. These things are actually just unfair.[/spoiler] Allow me to explain; your survival hinges entirely on your movement, especially in the early game. You can fly, you can blink, you can dash, all of which very important... important enough that [spoiler]adding an enemy with a hitscan effect that not only damages, but [i]disables your movement abilities[/i]? Especially in later runs, it is nearly if not literally impossible to kill these things when there are twelve of them on top of the fifteen other enemies you're fighting. These enemies [b][i]need[/i][/b] to be nerfed in some manner, be it less health, a different/lesser effect, or some other method. "Getting good" simply is not possible against enemies that are quite literally guaranteed to disable your only method of avoiding attacks.[/spoiler]

That said, the visuals for this game are AMAZING. I absolutely love the cel-shaded vibe that it's got, and it almost gives me Borderlands vibes for the two areas I was able to visit thus far.

IEH2 is hands down the king of the idler/incremental game genre. If you're a fan of this genre (trimps, kittens game, almost a hero, CIFI, universal paperclips, Clicker heroes, etc.), if you remember old "Kongregate," if you've ever been to reddit/incremental_games: This game is for you. I've played them all, some for many weeks/months. This is the only game I've played for years.

The game has six classes. You start by playing/progressing these classes one at a time, but gradually you end up playing many of them at once passively, with one hero active. Each hero provides it's own buffs/resources/strengths to your team. You need to have all heroes leveled and invested into in order to succeed with certain challenges. There are bosses to beat with your solo heroes. There are boss challenges to beat with your whole party. By tabbing between your active and passive heroes, there is always plenty to manage, and when you learn more about the game, it seems there is always something to be doing to get stronger.

The game has a battle progression system that is rewarding. There are power spikes which automate previously tedious tasks, and create a new desire for new automation when your task priority progresses. There are additional difficulties of each zone which increase enemy level, hp, damage, defenses, and rewards. 

The game is incredibly well balanced. 

The game has a very active discord. 

The game's depth is unrivaled. You just need and want to upgrade ... everything.

The game has unlimited "New Game Plus" (world ascend).

The game has a built in "nitro" system, which allows you to unlock the ability increase game speed (this comes naturally with progression) to allow you to blitz through previously tough barriers, which will then create new barriers to topple.

I want to dispel/discredit the negative reviews of those who have claimed this game is "pay to win," or destroyed by premium currency. This is totally bogus, and only reported by people who zero/minimal experience playing the game. There are dailies which give hundreds of currency each day, and only take a few moments to do once you get a bit of progression under your belt. There is an INCREDIBLY small/insignificant "money only" reward from one of the bundles, which is (not an exaggeration) less than 1 percent of my total epic coin gained over my total game hours. At first glance, the ability to purchase "nitro" (consumable currency that speeds up the game speed) is pay to win, but you learn very quickly that you can create nitro as a resource in the game, making it an infinite resource. After a bit of progression, you will have permanent nitro going all the time with no money spent, and the concept of spending money on nitro is obsolete. The epic store gives you huge quality of life unlocks which are something you get excited about purchasing with your daily currency. IU can't say this enough - this is a different vibe from predatory mobile games. You passively do your dailies each day and every few days you are rewarded with a new feature that you get to choose which will help you progress wherever you are in the game. These purchases are not "double your power forever" type purchases. They are to automate certain processes which make your life and time in the game easier and more effective. I would encourage anyone who does play the game for a long time to make a purchase or two to help the dev - they've certainly earned it from me. 

One slight downside is that the game has a bit of a slow burn start (first couple days may feel slow in contrast with some other games from this type of genre). Once you start rebirthing and gaining exp multi, the game pace and tasks pick up immensely. Soon, you will unlock a feature to auto rebirth, and progression picks up substantially from there. Trust me - stick it out for a bit.

If you like these types of games, give this one a shot. You won't regret it.

Rogue Waters is a pirate themed tactics RPG which combines turn based combat with roguelite mechanics.

After being betrayed during a quest to find a magical gemstone, captain Cutter must recruit a new crew and take revenge on his former captain, Blackbone. 

[h1]Gameplay (medium quality)[/h1]

•	During each run, you’ll navigate through a map which uses a node layout similar to other roguelites. Nodes include normal and elite fights against enemy ships, random events where you’ll make a choice and receive rewards or penalties, shops where you can buy or steal new items for your ship and crew, and shrines where you can heal wounded crewmembers or repair damage to your ship. Each run will end with assaulting a fortress, which sometimes includes a fight against Blackbone himself.

•	Combat encounters are divided into two phases, starting with ship combat, followed by boarding the enemy ship for a hand to hand fight on deck.

•	Ship combat involves three rounds of cannon fire where both sides will attempt to weaken the other before the main fight. You can kill enemy units to reduce the number you’ll have to fight on deck, but as they’ll try to kill your crew, its often better to destroy their cannons first. Both ships will have modules equipped, which function like relics in other roguelites, providing passive bonuses such as increased health, damage, armour, and movement range. Modules can also be destroyed, so you’ll need to decide how to prioritise your attacks.

•	Combat aboard the enemy ship functions like most tactics RPGs, with the area divided into a square grid, and each character being able to move, attack, or use a special ability on their turn. The player can win by eliminating all enemies, or maximising the fear gauge by over-killing enemies – dealing more damage than their remaining health, which also triggers a brutal finishing move animation.

•	Base damage of attacks is relatively low, but most attacks have a knockback effect. This means the combat system is built around taking advantage of opportunities to get bonus damage by knocking enemies into each other, walls, spike traps, and other hazardous tiles such as fire and blight (poison). But the enemy can also do the same to your crew, so positioning is important. Some tiles contain ropes, which let you swing across several tiles to get behind enemies. You can undo moves back to the start of the current turn, if you make a mistake or think of a better plan.

•	Unlike most other games, your whole crew can participate in the battle, but you’re limited to how many can be active at once (which can be increased or decreased by ship modules). When one of your crew is knocked out, you can replace them with another crew member on your next turn. A KO’d unit is wounded, which reduces their maximum health in future battles. However, if your whole crew is knocked out during the same fight, you’ll lose the run.

•	Between runs you can recruit specialists, who are your main crew members. They can level up and gain new abilities, increased health, damage, armour, and movement range. Spearmaiden can hit two enemies in a line, or throw the spear. Grapplers can grab an enemy and throw them in any direction. Cleavers can hit three enemies in adjacent tiles. Witches can teleport by swapping their position with an enemy or an ally. Musketeer can fire a high damage rifle, but they take a turn to aim so I don’t find them that useful.

•	Your crew also contains mates, who have no special abilities, and are primarily an expendable unit who you can use as meat shields to protect your specialists in tough fights.

•	Cutter also has the ability to summon a sea monster. The Kraken will use a huge tentacle to crush multiple enemies in a line, and two other monsters are unlocked as you progress through the story.

•	There are a few different enemy types who mostly use similar weapons and abilities as your crew, while Blackbone is the only boss enemy. This feels like the main area where the game could improve. The setting would allow the developers to add some monstrous enemies with unusual abilities, to provide variety to the combat. For example, a random event where half a dozen giant crabs board the player’s ship.

•	The first couple of runs can be quite tough, even on normal difficulty. Enemy ships can severely damage your crew in the first phase of combat, and they’ll have lots of active bonuses from modules in the second phase. However, you’ll earn currency from successful and failed runs, which lets you buy upgrades to get stronger in future runs, making higher difficulties winnable.

•	Increasing command points, which determines how many times you can fire cannons during the ship combat phase, is essential. Destroying enemy cannons before they can fire, so your crew can enter the main fight at full health, while also taking out their more important modules, can make the main combat much easier. You can also buy better cannons and modules, and equip more of them on your ship. You can increase the number of specialists and mates in your crew. And you can increase the power of sea monsters.

•	There are a couple of ways you can exploit tactical loopholes to make some fights significantly easier than they should be. They aren’t really problems, but I can’t imagine the developers intended players to do the following things.

•	When stealing items from shops, you’ll enter an extraction combat mission, where you don’t have to kill all the enemies, you just need one crew member to reach the exit tiles. However, if your crew has a witch, all you have to do is swap places with an enemy near the exit, and you can often escape on the first turn without fighting at all.

•	If either ship has an equipped module which applies blight to all characters, you can enter battle with just one mate at a time and let the poison damage slowly kill enemies for you, while minimising damage to your crew.

[h1]Story (low quality)[/h1]

•	Each successful run advances the story. Quests relating to weakening Blackbone and his army are fairly interesting, but the ending is a complete anti-climax designed to allow the player to keep doing more roguelite runs.

•	Combination of pirates, magic and monsters feels similar to the Pirates of the Caribbean films (but without the slapstick humour).

•	None of your recruited crewmembers participate in the story.

•	Voice acting isn’t great, but I’ve heard worse.

[h1]Technical (medium quality)[/h1]

•	It took me 16 hours to complete the story, and a further 10 hours to win a run on the highest difficulty. As this involved winning another 10 runs, the lack of variety became much more visible.

•	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes, or framerate.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

Rogue Waters is a fun tactics RPG which fans of the genre should enjoy. I think this game can be described as a “hidden gem” because it doesn’t seem to be getting much attention from other reviewers. However, as a roguelite it lacks variety for long term replayability, so I would recommend buying it on a sale.

Rogue Waters has good moments and shows potential, but the lack of game content drags it down. This clearly wants to be XCom with pirate themes, but falls short in every regard - the game plays like early access or technical demo, which shows the potential, but never becomes the "full game".

Base building - there are 4 buildings in the base, and I've unlocked the second sea monster with no signs of there ever being more buildings or an expanded tech tree to unlock for future runs. Like others have said, after 10+ hours I've unlocked most upgrades, which kinda makes side missions useless. The XP and costs increase exponentially, to the point where it takes 19k xp to level a specialist, but an outstanding run on heroic2 may produce 5k xp. That's 4 runs to get one level for lackluster upgrades.

The specialist classes are rather uninspiring, they mix 3 random talent trees, which are not entirely random. For example the musketeer can not get any toughness upgrades. So once I get specialists and do well on a run, there is no reason to rotate them by leaving them to heal wounds. This means every raid is the same. 

Where this game shows potential is in the ship to tactical combat transitions - there were tough fights where I had to sacrifice crew, modules and cannons to get through to tactical combat. This "barely getting through" is rewarding, as understanding the system and mechanics is what wins those fights. 

The AI in tactical combat is quite good - once tier 2 abilities are unlocked on enemies (such as armor debuff and push), the AI can stack enough damage to kill of a specialist character in one turn if I make mistake. But the naval AI is atrocious - it randomly picks targets without any clear strategy in mind - it rarely if ever "finishes off" a cannon or a module, leaving some with 1 hp, and wasting shots on another module that it will clearly not destroy outright. 

The enemy ship setup seems random and weird - I can't tell how it is related to the "stakes" of raids. I have seen ships with a single 0-5 damage gun. I've seen other ships with 5 guns. I've seen ships where I can ignore everything and just kill the 4 crew members with cannons without even going into tactical combat. 

After 10 + hours I still have trouble understanding what the "gold" is used for in raids - the ability to buy cannons comes really late, so most events that give you a choice of "rare cannon" or "150 gold" are useless. 

Wounds and wound healing is very poor - most events give wounds to "mates", simply because there is more of them than specialists, but the lone "temple" event also offers to heal a wound to a random crew mate, which most often is the mate. This means the "heal wounds" choice is also meaningless. 

So far I have seen 3 enemy factions with 2 tiers of abilities, with random modules on a ship buffing the enemy crew. There is not enough enemy variety to keep the game going into 40+ hours. (I remember how you were fighting sectoids and mutons for dozens of hours in XCom and that was fun).

Despite how it looks, this is a very complex and punishing survival game. You go from hoarding coconuts as your only source of food to eventually farming vegetables and keeping livestock. You go from sleeping on a crappy bed of leaves and having monkeys stealing your belongings, to eventually building your own house with a shed and a nice bed. 

The mechanics constantly surprised me with how in-depth they are. You might think you hit the jackpot when you find a few banana trees but your character will start getting depressed if you force them to eat literally nothing but bananas for days. If you try to live off coconuts too much you'll get diarrhea. It's actually possible to make certain animals go extinct if you keep hunting the same kinds over and over. 

Rainfall is super important for your consistent water source but it's totally random whether it rains or not. I didn't realise this until I went over a month in one game without any rain. At first this seemed really harsh but I think it's better for gameplay as it teaches you not to rely on one source of water/food/protection etc and to constantly be thinking of ways to diversify or to prepare for emergencies. 

The only thing I struggle with in this game is repetitiveness. There are different characters or even custom characters that work slightly differently but ultimately you are still in the same jungle with the same locations and same animals and same research tree. So I'll have a lot of fun playing a game for 10~ hours then die stupidly because I lost track of time in the middle of the jungle and couldn't find my way home or something like that, but I need to wait a few months to try again otherwise it feels too same-y. I wish the dev would come out with more iterations of this game like medieval fantasy style so I can swap between them :)

So the only reason I'm giving this game a good review is because I got it on sale, and I think it's worth the sale price, I don't think it's worth the full price though. This is maybe a $5 quality game.

Pros: Simple concept and interesting mechanics. Multiple goals, and steady game progression. Fun little Easter eggs and side tasks from visitors.

Cons: Very bad late game balance of mechanics.

So your troops can get stressed and fatigued, and when these attributes get too high, you can't train your troops. As you play, you unlock stuff that reduces their stress or increases their stamina, but the problem is you unlock all of that stuff, and then there is no more. You have 12 troops, all of them completely stressed and fatigued, and you only have 4 facilities that can fix that, each only allowing one troop to use it per day. What's more is 2 of the facilities are for stamina, and 1 is for stress, and 1 is for both, and it really shows. Stress is basically impossible to deal with if you have a fully upgraded base. All of this could be easily fixed if you could just upgrade the size of the facilities to hold more troops.

The actual campaign you fight when the 12 weeks of training is over is cool, but the balance seems really off on that too. Basically all the stats you train besides shooting are inconsequential to the mission. Any stats gained from the mission are so small compared to training stats that they feel pointless. The M.O.D.s you can assign to troops are not very good, because they take a lot of effort to get, and they all have downsides bad enough that is basically cancels out their good sides. I imagine this was intended to encourage the player to diversify so you have several skills that have different roles to fill in combat, but the problem is their up sides are also so niche, they just don't have any particular benefit. I had better luck making all my troops basic infantry than I did trying to assign specialties.

Lastly, the training point system gets obnoxious at the end. unless I'm missing something, you have to spend all your training points to finish the training week. There is one way to spend them all at once, which is going on a group run, but if you send a single soldier to do a single thing, the option to spend your remaining points is gone, and you now have to meticulously spend all your points waiting for soldiers to finish their training. The best you can do is send them to the flag pole, which sends them to all 4 training sections once automatically and spends 4 points. There are some facilities that only allow 2-3 soldiers to train on them, and if you set more than that to auto train, it will spend your points and they will not do the training or get stats. Another way to reduce stress and gain stamina is to not train your troops, but if you are forced to spend all your points every day, the only way to not train your troops is to meticulously train a single troop well past the point of full stress and zero stamina so the others can catch a break. And if you do this, you can expect to spend what feels like 10 minutes doing nothing but micro managing a single guy to spend all your points.

Suggestions: Make some stats have a bigger impact on the mission, like maybe strength can add to your troops health, or intelligence could reduce reload time, or just something more tangible than what's there. Have more options to reduce stress and restore stamina. Have an option to end the day, and instead of having troops only regain stats from doing nothing, have them regain stats based on the number of training points left, that way there is no downside to having more training points. Nerf the downsides to M.O.D.s so they are at least a little more appealing.

First of all, This game is fantastic. If you were looking for a roguelite-dungeoncrawler game with some slapstick sprinkled on the top, this is the game for you. This really just feels like Monthy Python and the Holy Grail was made into a video game, and I love that!

There are tons, and I mean tons of weapons you can bash your way through the tower with, because literally everyting can be a weapon. From pointy daggers, to comicly large Sledgehammers. Hell, you can even use vegetables to brawl with. There is so much replay value it's unbelivable.

There are companions to meet in the tower, so that you won't be alone. They are very well done and all have an amazing character. You already know the game is good, when a turtle standing on two legs with nothing but a wooden club can become your BFF.

Throughout the tower you will face various challenges. Monsters, traps, puzzles, tasks and riddles. The tower definetely won't ake your stay easy here.

There are thousands of hilaurious ways to die. Being crushed by an anvil, eaten by a monster or falling down the abyss, this game ain't easy and it will defientely tell you that, the moment you enter the tower. 

There is also a cool "hidden level" at the end of the deungeon, if you choose to take on an extra challenge at the end. 

The game also features a town, where you can by a house, become a citizen, build a fabulous statue of your glorious self and sell your equipment to a merchant, so that you may buy it again sometime, anytime you please.

The game also thrives with attention to detail. The artstyle is very beautiful. Hundreds of dialogues and amazing voice acting. Nice sound effects and good background music. Lots of callbacks to the older games aswell, weapons armour and the secret treasure room. the Enemy design is very good as well

That being said, I'd also like to point the things out that aren't as great. 

Now, it is incredibly important to remember,that this game is still in early access, but I'd still like to point them out. The combat can feel very repitive. You don't really do much else than just clicking your left mouse button. Heavy attakcs for example would be a nice addition I feel, that would definetely spice the games combat up just a tad bit. Also ranged weapons like crossbows would be a nice addition.

Another Issue I have is that there is very little armour and helmet diversity. This is espacially frustrating, because the devs managed to make a great job with the weapon diversity, there is literally doezens of different weapons and more are yet to come. 

But with the armour... More often than not, you just end up with the same armour over and over again. There is very few different chestpieces, let alone helmets and the only thing that mostly differentiates them from each other, is the colour. I'd like there to be added a lot more armour and helmets in the near future, ESPACIALLY, Knight Helmets. Helmets with a visor or a fully closed helmet for example. 

Now obviously, the devs will add more helmets and armour in the future, I'd just like amount of gear to protect your hero with to be bigger. becaus there is also a lot of defferent shields, just not as much armour.

But I genuinely feel, that this is the only major complaint I have about the game. Not being able to look like the badass knight, that youre supposed to be. Because the only like actually heavy steel gear that isn't peasant clothes or a barrel that you clad yourself with, makes you look like a Village Guard from Monthy Python. 

There are some bugs here and there, but they are literally being worked on, as I type this, so I decided not to talk about it.

That would be it thus far I feel. This ame is very good. It's addictive, it's funny and It's a challenge. Lovely and unique characters aswell, that make your stay more entertaining. The perfect combination for a game like this. I can definetely only recomend buying it.

Wow, what a game.

Don't know if all the problems mentioned in other comments happened to get fixed right before I started or what, but the game's performed perfectly for me through 50 hours in.

The setting is a war-torn land trying to rebuild itself after the wars have moved on (at least until you become a solo army and wipe out the lingering elements yourself).

The main gameplay loop is designing and running your village, building your people houses and places to work and making sure that your community's functional stats all stay in the green. As your village gets humming along, you spend your free time protecting the land and conquering territories. This involves defeating a particular zone's base of enemies, with a fun boss fight at the end, and also setting up a major community service building project as a PR move (re-building a bridge or a watchtower). 

I had fun with the combat, especially once I got my hands on my first sword, for which the animations are well done. There's fun parry mechanics you can unlock, and you can adjust difficulty sliders for enemy damage output and health, and for things like parry timing (and tons of other things, including plenty of non-combat related stuff). So you can make the combat exactly as challenging as you like it.

Your reward for conquering territories is unlocking the ability to craft better tools, weapons, armor, and buildings for your village. The whole loop's all well designed, and quests (both main and side) help shepherd you through the process so that everything flows really well.

And along with those quests, there are other RPG elements, of course, with skill points to make you better at everything from use of different weapons, to crafting or harvesting materials, to running your village well. And it all feels like just the right amount of things to do for the pacing of the game and its passing seasons. (The best part, in my opinion.)

If you're looking for a slow paced world to escape into for a bit, this is a good one.

Having played enough to have a rounded opinion of the game (in Early Access -February 2025) I feel I can give a useful REVIEW of the state of the game.

Firstly let's look at what is GOOD:

+++The theme and the general idea. Building a village is Sengoku period Japan is a great idea and the game gives you a genuine sense that you are in this world. 
++ Building your own 'dynasty'. The game creates a good sense that you are (somewhat slowly) building a microcosmic version of your own empire.
+The game creates quests and regional unlocks that players must overcome to progress and unlock technology and buildings.

Now, rather than look at could be labelled bad, we can look at what is MISSING and what needs IMPROVEMENT or fixing - the opportunities:

---The game has NO GRAND VICTORY condition or greater purpose. The game would triple in value if it had one or multiple victory conditions (the player can optionally set from the start menu) that require significant development, resources or power to ultimately work towards. Such as defeat a great enemy, build imperial roads between all regions, conquer all regions by building small forts in each one, reach and maintain a large population target, etc. Having a victory FMV for 'winning' would be very satisfying and add real purpose to gameplay and shake of that sense 'what's the point of this?'. Simply refuting the idea of victory or win conditions with "but this is sandbox game" will kill all of this great potential and for absolutely no good reason.
--options for unlocking technologies need to be more flexible or randomised rather than 'complete objectives 'a' and 'b' in region 'y' to produce a bronze sword. This limits replayability. While I agree there needs to be an incentive to complete regional objectives these should only be bonuses rather than critical technologies. Advancing your dynasty level alone feels like it is enough to unlock these and not cause any harm.
--Villagers can only be assigned to one workstation or field. This is incredibly limiting. You can have a dedicated farmer and six small farm fields easily managed by one farmer but they can only manage one single plot and cannot do anything else. There is no reason why the option to allow villagers multiple fields/stations could not be included. They are limited to a maximum workload already.
--Autosaves are continuous. I look at my autosave list and see dozens of unnecessary save files. This needs to be limited to just a few files like you would see in every other game.
-- There are fixed loot boxes in the world that once looted never refill and remain empty for the rest of the game. These need to respawn a few items after each season to make it interesting.
--Boss camps never respawn enemies. Once you clean out a boss camp it is permanent and they remain vacant for the rest of the game. It would add value if a few of the enemies respawned after a season in these locations just to make it more interesting.
--Villagers need to be reassigned from their list of allocated tasks on a work station to special projects which makes good sense and creates good opportunity cost dilemmas in the game. However when you reassign them back to their original workstation all of the production amounts have RE-SET TO ZERO require annoying micromanagement. Click, click, click , click, etc. And you will likely have forgotten how you had fine tuned their tasks before they left. This needs to be fixed. Just annoying and unnecessary.
-- A recent update mentions how you can name buildings. This is a great idea but actually the most important aspect of the  game CANNOT be renamed. There is a menu called the 'job' menu that is incredibly DISORGANISED. This a haphazardly arranged list of all of the jobs where you assign your workers and essential to gameplay. Each workstation is labelled 'field1' or 'workbench 3'. It really is a necessity to be able to rename these labels to for example' iron workstation' or 'wheat and gobo field' so that you actually know what task you are re-assigning your worker to. This makes the game a bit of CHORE. The list of workstations NEEDS to be actually organised into a coherent list based on the type of workstation- such as all of your fields together in the list instead of a random mess. Terrible and in its current state IMO lowers the rating of the game.
-Not enough NPC quests for rewards in the game. There needs to be more to make it worth interacting with NPCs and create a more responsive and interesting game world.
-Not enough danger in the woods. The game would benefit from roaming enemies such as looters (they don't need to be hard to kill but make travelling out of your village area slightly more risky). This could be a game start option you could turn off if you didn't like the idea.
-(limited spoiler)  There is a quest in the game where you can court with an NPC to become your spouse. As soon as you talk to them the game already labels them your spouse before you are even married. This needs to be re-named to 'suitor' or something else. 
-You have the task of special projects building bridges but this seems an unnecessary task when the river water is mostly ankle deep and easily crossed. It would better if you could NOT cross a river without a bridge being built and make it more relevant and purposeful. "I need to cross that river, I'll have the satisfaction of building a bridge so that I can"
-Some special regional projects require a large amount of resources and probably too many making it tedious to complete them. No need to make the quantities so high.

OVERALL this is a game that really deserves to be worked on by the developers. The game is still some way from being worthy of being called a '1.0' version in February of 2025. Fix these issues, do some much-required polishing and add more content and the game will be well worth a HIGH rating.

Thank you for reading.

As an on-going "work in progress" game, this is really good. 
Developers are actively working on it, listening and interacting with players, updating quite often, (1 week ago since last update) without overdoing it with hotfixes on a near daily basis. 

The gameplay itself, is as you expect it from other Dynasty games, a classic "rags to riches" story, but with a lot more costumization options, in terms of both buildings, decorations, gardens, temples and much more, and it keeps the style of feudal Japan very nicely. 

The village management system itself, is also quite amazing.
Lots of different crops, recipes, more adults per house, easier to find settlers, but with a much larger chain of crafting than other dynasty games. 
Sake as a good example, need to go through multiple steps, before you can even make it. 
Boil the rice, ferment the rice and finally brew the Sake.  
This allows you to set up a lot more jobs for your settlers in just 1 building. 

The liberation system is a breath of fresh air in Dynasty games, having to both build special structures and actually go out and seek out combat and remove warlords from the regions, is a nice touch and gives a great option for a break from the grind of gathering/building.
Combat is fluid, though quite stiff in a few of the animations, with a bit too long "pause" before allowing followup attacks, mostly on 2 handed weapons such as the naginata. 
Bows however could use some realism work, there's zero arrow-drop, it's basically a laser beam, just aim and shoot a target 200 meters away with no challenge, the arrow auto-corrects itself, and curves upwards and gives a realistic flight pattern, but where you point, is still where you hit. 
Stealth is non-existent, even though it looks like it is and definitely should be. 
You can crouch down on a cliffside hiding behind bushes and send an arrow in the face of a bandit, and immediately all other bandits around your target, knows exactly where you are, quite sad for sneaky play.
The hunting system however is great, and stealth actually works well there.

Even though there's lots of stuff to find and explore, i do feel like it's a shame that we can't actually rob that many places. 
Other dynasty games, have chests in houses, random items laying around and such, i'd love to see that here along with a reputation punishment in case you get caught stealing.
But in general, i just want the option to grab random things i find. 

The story, though there isn't much of it yet, is already interesting and realistic for it's time, i'll not go into details on the storyline, but it's good so far. 

Graphics however, in terms of the overall world, plants, weather and buildings is quite nice. 
But characters and animals is quite lackluster for todays standards. 
10 years ago, it would have been ok. 
Character customization could also use a LOT more options.
As an example: Female character have 3 skintones, 3 faces and 2 hairstyles.

Hopefully this is something that will change during developement. 

But all in all, it's a great dynasty game that brings more excitement than others and by far have the best combat system among dynasty games, i mean it's not even a competition.

[u]Pros:[/u]

Buildings can be upgraded to provide more storage, crafting spots, sleeping spaces etc by adding furniture to them rather than needing to build a new tier on top of them.
- The combat is decent and reasonably intricate, although a little unresponsive.
- The map is much larger and much more alive than MD, with multiple villages to build in different regions, and various goals and quests to complete.

[u]Cons:[/u]
- Performance is still a big issue. Stuttering, fps issues, very noticeable freezes when changing areas or moving towards/away from large villages. I can't decide whether the latest update made this better or worse. Performance is not good.
- There is no dynasty element to Sengoku Dynasty. You can marry and have a child but that child never grows up and is currently little more than an accessory. Villagers also do not marry or have children, so your villages do not grow organically, with families.
- Villagers are all essentially identical. They don't have an age or any stats or skills. They are just either male or female - thats it. And most look exactly the same due to a lack of hairstyles, body types and faces.

Development seems to be quite slow on this title, but hopefully it will continue at a better pace in the future. I think it is worth buying now, but only if you can tolerate the fps problems and frequent freezes.

Sengoku Dynasty Review - A Game with Great Potential, but needs Work

     I've only put about 12 hours into this game, and while I'm giving it a thumbs up, it's more for the potential I see rather than the current state of the game. If the developers continue to invest time and effort, this could turn into something truly special.

     That being said, Sengoku Dynasty needs a lot of work. The first few hours are fun- the world is visually appealing and the concept is engaging-but the experience quickly becomes repetitive. The durability of tools and weapons are frustratingly short, and the return reward for gathering resources is underwhelming even with higher tier items. Not to mention you can't repair, you just have to bring lots of additional weapons/tools along to complete you tasks. Combat mechanics also feel unpolished, with animals glitching out and exploitable spots where you can take down anything without real danger. I would like to point out that some of the finishing moves in combat against your foes are pretty awesome, and make you feel like a real Samurai. 

     Building your dynasty should be the most rewarding part, and while the architecture, the layers of crafting and different decorations are beautiful, the villagers leave much to be desired. Managing them feels clunky, often leaving you scratching your head and saying WTF out loud. Your villagers seem content doing craftsmen work, sucking up resources and mooching off of your hard labor, rather than our there gathering resources and being productive members of society. Leaving you, the Dynasty Lord-doing all the grunt work. It begs the question: why am I the ruler if I'm the one swinging an axe?

     Overall, I'd rate Sengoku Dynasty a 6.5/10. There's a solid foundation here, and with proper updates, balancing, and AI improvements, this could become a fantastic game. But, as it stands, it's more of a promising work-in-progress than a fully realized experience.

[b]Things I love about this game:[/b]

The building
This is the thing I've always wanted in games where you build. You can walk up to a place you've already made, and just upgrade or swap things out like you're doing a renovation! It simplifies so many things, saves resources, and makes building enjoyable. There's no, oh I have to destroy this to build it again but with different materials and times that by how many times there are material improvements. You can just walk up, swap material, or change that wall into a door or a window, or get rid of it entirely. 10/10 on this devs!

Naming
I love being able to rename houses, makes it super easy to place people or work out where on you map it is. They did miss allowing you to rename your traveller outposts, but I think that'll be fixed soon. 

Combat
You can disable this if you don't like it! But if you do like it, it's interesting and does require patience. There is a stamina bar, and if you run out of it, you are 100% a sitting duck. In this way it kinda reminds me of Souls games, but definitely not to the same intensity or degree.

Settings
Super customisable! If you've played ARK before, it has almost the same amount of customisation of the settings for the world, which is amazing.

Heir System
 This is WIP but the road map looks and sounds good as long as the devs deliver on it. This would pair really well with a proficiency and/or a trait system (see my list of what I'd like to see from the devs for an idea of what I'm talking about)

Marriage
 The quest is straightforward task-wise without being Skyrims walk up and lets get married, and it has a nice level of complexity in completing the task. Does my guy want to be romanced with flowers, food, wine, and a 5000 dowry plus elite clothing? Yes. Is it hard to get? Technically no. Is it going to take me a while to achieve it? Yes! Is that a bad thing? No! I 100% approve of a longer marriage quest! You have to earn and romance your chosen partner, and you have to earn the heir, and it is very satisfying (and funny for my friends watching me grumble about my partner having expensive tastes) to do so!

Mounts and/or beasts of burden, please! 
Horses were around in this era, but they were expensive. It'd be a great mid to late-game addition to get around. The map is big and it takes some time to get around, especially when quests send you hither and yonder. They could have some penalties/costs to them as well to make them an interesting element to the villages e.g. fodder, water, bedding with some side bonuses e.g. fertiliser, transport, money/breeding, bonus to farming if more advanced tools are introduced. 

Livestock
I understand that eating meat was seen as bad/unclean during this era (depending on the predominate religion in the area) but some were sneakily eaten on the side by nobles or the desperate. I could see this affecting the karma system mentioned in the update roadmap. They could be an interesting element for food, and money, and affect the future karma system. Maybe some npcs get a negative opinion of you, and this effects future interactions.

Proficiency
I'd love to see a proficiency system, mostly for the npcs rather than yourself. E.g. a refugee joins your village and you assign them to be a woodworker for 2 seasons. During those two seasons they'd gain expertise or proficiency, which will dissuade you from changing their jobs. This way your village slowly gains skilled labour. Let me preface this review by saying that despite my positive recommendation I in no mean intend to trick you into thinking this is a good game. This game has a lot of untested elements and unimplemented features that make this game rather unfun to play if you are trying to enjoy it "as a game". However, I am fully serious when I say that it is probably the best two dollars I have spent in recent memory. 

What I can say is that, like every other reviewer here, if you go into this game expecting an *actual game*, you will be disappointed. Some positives I can initially point out is that this game, to my knowledge, has completely unique assets and isn't just a asset-flipped game. The goals of the game are rather ambitious and it does have some unique mechanics for an early-dev's game. That being said, this game boasts many flaws. Firstly, upon our first launch it seemed the "fade-in" effect of the game did not trigger and made it so that we were in a black void with the text "Almost ready" and a single red light, which we later figured out was the sun, that pierced through this darkness. Eventually the text and screen began to warp ( pictures depicted in the discussions under this game ) and we had to quit the game. The game doesn't format to different aspect ratios making it in some cases impossible to close the settings menu. The games movement is as if you are drifting on ice and becomes especially inconvenient on higher slopes as you get sent flying backwards at rather quick speeds. If you are not constantly jumping you will eventually clip through the floor, which because of the instant saving feature, means that your progress is entirely moot as you spawn back in the void and you have to start over. Day length seems variable to our knowledge, with it occasionally skipping entire days, but for the most part every day lasts 15-20 minutes, meaning to beat this game, you need to spend 24 REAL LIFE HOURS to get to the ending. Building has no rotation feature so you can only place walls in one direction ( along with some occasional model issues with placing them, most notably with door walls ). The crafting recipe for the crafting station and the walls are also the exact same, with walls supposed to be crafted when placing the items on the crafting station, though this does occasionally glitch out and make it impossible to craft another crafting station. Some crafting items ( rope and wheat, only one of which has a working crafting recipe ) can be picked up into your inventory and become completely useless, no longer able to be used for crafting or removed from your inventory. Eventually all passive entities ( crabs and birds ) will be completely gone ( usually before day 5 ) as either the random movement of the parrot sends them of the map, or the crabs clip through the floor. A good number of features in the trailer ( to our knowledge, farming, torches, and beds, the latter of which is required for an achievement ) are not available in the actual game, and farming is particularly interesting because you can make farm plots and get seeds but you cannot place the seeds. You also can only get rid of ONE item from your inventory, being the crafting station after you place it, so once you fill up your 5 slots with non-crafting stations, you cannot get any other items, with any items you attempt to pick up instead being deleted out of existence as it tries to go to an empty inventory slot that doesn't exist. Eating food restores your visible hunger but not your actual hunger, with any gains immediately being lost when hunger next ticks down to the number it would've been had you not eaten at all, but hunger does not kill you, and instead keeps going down past zero ( going into the negatives then infinitely looping between 0 and -100 as it constantly ticks down ) Some food also eventually stops increasing your visible hunger but does not leave your inventory space, making the item useless and permanently removing another one of your slots ( not that food did much in the first place ). The enemies spawn in the air sideways and do not have a bottom texture, nor do farm plots. When reading the book, you also freeze in place, including in the air or other precarious places you should not be. The achievement "Build the walls" is unlocked by making a farming plot, and the achievement "Kill a living" with a picture of a crab is not unlocked by killing a crab, though an item for crab meat does exist in the game. The LAST things I can reasonably think of is that essentially all playable content and all locations can be discovered within about the first 2-3 in-game days, which for a game that is about surviving 100 days is not ideal for keeping the game interesting.

This game is truly uniquely bad in ways that only an abandoned unity project by an early game developer could be, and it has such a charm to it that I cannot possibly give it a negative review. This game DOES have an ending cutscene, which is why I have any playtime over just an hour testing, and it was honestly such a surprise. It was moments like this and the fact that all assets were handmade that truly painted the picture that this wasn't some lazy cashgrab ( especially with a price of 2 dollars ) but was something that someone was truly dedicated to for a time. I think the developer behind this game is truly ambitious and if they choose to keep exploring game development could help make incredible things. I think looking back at this game it at LEAST deserves 1 good review, not because it is necessarily a good game, but because it does have some passion behind it and has been such a fun little rabbit hole to dive into.

TLDR; if you play this expecting a game, you will be thoroughly disappointed, but if you play this to dissect it ( preferrably with a friend just as invested ) it can be rewarding, and because of this I think this game deserves one good review

TLDR: buy it on sale.

7 hours into this now and the more I see the more I like.

Pros:

- Good balance between playability and realism. The game feels like a simulation, but without the DCS level switchology and manual reading. You can get to the fun quickly while also having a believable, realistic experience.

- There's a decent amount of vehicles to play around with already. T-64s, M1s, BMPs and much more are all playable.

- There's a lot of missions and they are modifiable once you complete them on default settings. This adds a lot of replayability. I didn't count them all but there's got to be 40+ and you can switch the default vehicles for other models in their class (switch T-72s to T-55s or Leopard 1s, M113s for BMPs, etc.). You can switch ammo too (3BM15 for 3BM22 on a T-72M, for example). There's also a campaign that appears to be setup for replayability (some randomness built into it).

- Graphics are decent and the game performs well enough on my mid-range system. I can play at max settings @ 4K and 30 FPS with no hiccups. This is in full-screen windowed mode. If I use pure full-screen (not windowed) the FPS goes as high as 60.

- No crashes so far.

- 5 maps to play on IIRC.

- Good audio. Gun firing, ammo reloading, and engine sounds are all on point. Decent voice-acting for the crews too.

- Has enough content now to easily justify $30. It's a bargain. If you love war sims, you should give it a shot.

- Good combined arms feel created with helicopters, artillery, CAS and infantry.

Cons:

- No mission editor or multiplayer yet. Co-op is coming though, so I'll just be patient.

- No commitment to PvP. I can understand that the developers need to focus on creating an awesome single-player and/or co-op experience, but man would PvP be fun in this! I'd probably give up on my unhealthy relationship with War Thunder if this had PvP.

- Environment isn't destructible. Maybe they will add that later? Driving a tank through fences has no effect on them, for example.

- AI is still a bit wonky. Your platoon-mates will occasionally get stuck on trees, so you'll need to switch tanks in order to get them on the right track. 

If you have a passion for war simulation like I do, you owe it to yourself to at least give GHPC a trial. 


Can't wait to see what the devs add next!

[h1]71/100 A Unique VR Experience That Excels in Its Trope[/h1]

+ Behemoth Fights are peak
+ Cool Zipline
+ Story is good.
+ Cool quality of life
+ Looks incredible

- Was hoping for a more RPG experience, like the Walking Dead, unfortunately it was a one through story.
- Some bugs in the beginning
- Game's story is decently short

[b][u]GAMEPLAY[/u][/b]

The game centers around you, Wren (m warrior), navigating a cursed land using blades w/o the sorcery. You get a cool grappling hook though and it has so much utility. My favorite thing about the game is the mobility. I loved zipping around like Spider-Man. It was so nice and so clean. 

The arsenal of weaponry was super fun, my only complaint being that it seemed a little inconsequential to get a game you like as you get story items of each time in the game. So even if I preferred another blade style, I was basically at a loss if I gave up my story related weapons.

THE BEHEMOTHS ARE THE MOST FUN FR! Seeing them tower above you and having to wrack your brain to fight them was so fun. I really wish they were more. <3 I had fun with each one fr, except the last one because I played this game so early there were some game breaking bugs. 

The weapon play is okay, but in the beginning everything felt incredibly unwieldy. I thought that was the vibe they were going for, but a later patch had made the weapons far more wieldable. So that's fine. The team is very active to player feedback. 

[b][u]SOUND DESIGN[/u][/b]

The voice acting is solid. Wren's character sounds nice.

The clinking and clanking is pretty nice. The music fits the world. There isn't a ton of hopeful tracks. One of my favorite is the track at the end. It makes me think that there is going to be more to the game. Most of the tracks are heart racing battle drums and tense, fast-paced strings.

[b][u]STORY[/u][/b]

Behemoth's plague the land wrought with a darkness that corrupts the mind and body. You play as Wren, someone defiantly attempting to rid the world of this plague. The plot is interesting. Not super complicated or crazy, but it has some fun twists and turns. I do really enjoy the lore and learning more about what was before all of this disease destroyed the land and kingdoms there once was.

[b][u]THE WORLD[/u][/b]

The world used to be this sprawling fantasy empire, full with might and gods aplenty. Where you play is naught but a ruin of that. Very interesting hearing some of the lore, but they never dive too deep into it. This is one of those worlds where I think they were testing this game before they did an INCREDIBLE amount of world building, but they do enough to make it not feel empty imo. They don't talk a ton about who the enemies are, for example. Like they're just random bandits and witches that worship the behemoths or have been corrupted by the darkness. 

I, for one, would love more content on the world. The ending seems pretty positive for the hopes that there may be some world building or history shaping even.

[b][u]VISUALS[/u][/b]

Probably the best game I've seen visually on VR besides Blade & Sorcery. They nail the snowy mountains (The LODs look incredible and like you could actually travel to them.) Some of the visual effects when you're on behemoths are super impressive too. I played this on max settings with no issues at all. But if you're looking for an insanely convincing desolate snowscape in VR, this is the game.

[b][u]MULTIPLAYER[/u][/b]

None, sadly. But It never even hinted, so no points deducted.


[b][u]CONCLUSION[/u][/b]

So, the game was pretty hyped for me. There were some disappointments when I finally got my hands on it, but almost all of those were bugs that were fixed in the same week. Sometimes things just happen. So I only deducted points for how short the game is. I finished it in probably 9 hours on Max Difficulty. But the devs keep hinting at something more, so I really hope they deliver, because the game was so good. I could easily play more if they added more content, or a boss rush mode or something to keep me playing afterwards. The game unfortunately doesn't beat Blade & Sorcery in sword melee combat, although the mechanics are still great. But what it lacks there it makes up for in mobility and the Behemoth fights in general. I enjoy the enemy variety. It is definitely one of the better VR experiences.

Note, that my issues with this rerelease isn't with the games themselves, but rather how the rereleases were handled.

Imagine releasing a glorified emulator with encrypted ini files and bin/cue files (So good luck getting a fan translation of the game working with the official release, so you can actually read dialogue), not offering any sort of official English translation, and hardcoding resolution options that only go up to 1080p (Which don't really integer scale properly with 240p/480i outputs, unlike something like 1440p).

For all the flack people give Nintendo for their lackluster rereleases, at least they give you the option of reduced flickering/strobing effects, which absolutely is a massive quality of life improvement for many retro games. The most that I can really say about this compilation in particular, over just buying a Saturn copy, making a dump of it, and using an English patch, is that it has achievement support, and they fixed the lag issues that were on the Switch release.

There really needs to be more effort towards finding original source code for properly enhanced ports, rather than emulation, where outside of community efforts, they end up coming off as massive cashgrabs with less effort put in than even compilations from 20 years ago like Sonic Mega Collection. Literally, that compilation is almost old enough to drink alcohol, and we still see emulated rereleases of old games lacking incredibly basic improvements.

EDIT: By the way, the online leaderboards are completely broken.

A fantastic shmup, and personally my favorite game of the Cotton series, finally now with an affordable and fine way to play it!

Even the emulation issues I noticed from the unpatched Switch version of the physical Saturn Tribute compilation seem to be fixed here, which is also really nice.

- The language warning on the store page is half-false. The emulation shell's menus and the game's menus are fully in English. The story text in the game, however, is not in English. While the story is funny (and is worth playing with the English fanpatch for that), no Japanese knowledge is really needed to play the game. And really, everyone who's interested in this should have expected this anyways, considering this is a pretty basic re-release of a Japan-exclusive game. Not a huge issue for me since I know what everyone is saying, too. And if this bothers you that much, there's a full playthrough in English on YT, and the fanpatch is down that way.

This is a bad PC release.

Basically this is just the Japanese Sega Saturn rom built in with a proprietary emulator. I mean this is not bad per se, I would rather have more old game legally accessible this way than not having them.
The problem is when you encrypt the rom itself, preventing the pc gamers to mod it in any way (in this case I wanted to apply the fan’s English patch, since the company behind this game didn’t even bothered to translate the game dialogues to English). And not only that, encrypting the rom also prevents me to play it legally on my own Sega Saturn, not sure what is the problem of the company with that. Maybe they want to limit their own proprietary emulator to play this rom? Anyway there are much better ways to handle that (like checking what rom is actually being loaded) and even this is stupid because there are much better performing Sega Saturn emulators freely available on the pc if anyone would have the idea of playing other roms on it. Sega themselves release the roms not encrypted in the mega drive collection.

With a release like this I don't recommend it, unless you really want to play this game legally and cheap (and have a decent performing pc). Otherwise just buy an used Sega Saturn copy you will be much better served and you will have much less headaches.

To comment on a review posted here by another user who was a developer on the original game, the full credits from the original game are actually included here. Just as in the Saturn release, you must finish the game to see these original credits. The credits accessible from the main menu only acknowledge those involved in producing this re-release.

Guardian Force is a port of the Saturn version on a new engine so it can run in modern systems. It also comes with a plethora of improvements, including a rewind option (extremely useful to try bullet patterns), free play and quick save/load. Really, it runs pretty well but it suffers a few issues the affect other STG ports, especially the input lag that makes dodging the heavy ordnance quite cumbersome, especially since the tank hitbox seems a bit uneven. There is also a slow mode you can trigger with the shift key but I've yet to find its purpose other than to cheat through some bullet patterns. Also, the control scheme by default is weird as hell and I recommend changing it to something that may suit your style better.

In my case, rotating the turret was all piled together between a button and a trigger in the Xbox Controller. By mapping left rotation and right rotation to the triggers and shot to A or B you can least get a partially more modern control setup but that's just me. Thankfully you can remap controls in the game's contextual menu. (There is an in game option menu but that one let's you control credits and lives as well as the difficulty.)

Anyway, presentation and music wise this game's awesome. The story is not much clearer than "enemy empire wants to conquer all" but you seem to be descending into the underground and it really reminded me of the insane Mahou Daisakusen premise. Either way, bosses are all presented in text with names that are mostly metal as f*ck (The Unforgiven, Maverick, Gold Rush, etc.) and the soundtrack is also extremely good. I wish they would put a soundtrack DLC in FLAC/mp3. I mean, sure, it's not Radiant Silvergun or Soukyuugurentai (also, I hope this one gets ported too!) presentation-wise but it's high up there.

The mechanics require you to pick up different items that change what the turrets shoot (from a yo-yo type of weapon to missiles, machine guns and lasers) and be mindful of powering them up with the crystals you pick up along. Dying will power the weapons down and you'll lose the side arms (usually missiles) but you can usually recover faster unlike, say, Gradius or some older STGs where you might as well initiate restart syndrome. A lot of big enemies and mid bosses are timed so you are encouraged to make short work of them, bomb and aim at weak spots to get those juicy score bonuses. By the last missions you'll be assaulted from all directions by heaps of bullets so you'll need to put the 8-axis rotation turret to good use while you take refuge as the auto-scrolling stage strolls along. Easier said than done, even though the game hands you over 10 credits with 3 lives each by default!

All in all, I love seeing obscure Saturn games brought back to life in the style of M2 ports so I really hope more are brought over. Of course, the price is probably a bit steeper as is the case with most STGs so either consider it on a sale or get it if you have a buddy to play the 2-player mode, which is really enjoyable.

Recommended!

My feelings about whether the original or the remake of Riven is better are, well... themselves riven. Both of them are wonderful experiences. They are also flawed in differing ways, and regardless of the technical limitations both face, there are things gained and lost in both from their creative/puzzle/story aspects. Regardless, I wholeheartedly recommend both.

That's the gist of my review, really. Below are the messy details...

As of my current hardware setup, the most efficient way to travel through the age of Riven is through the Steam release of the original. With the remake on my 3070, the time it takes for each island to load is about the time it would take to change out a CD, an ironic echo of the 5-CD release I first played the game with.

The lore of Riven in the remake is more compact. It takes much reading outside the original to make complete sense of what's going on, but I believe the changes in the remake streamline the important information into the game significantly. In terms of a self-contained game, the remake is more coherent of itself.

The changed puzzles overall make for a fairer difficulty. The original's puzzles are almost impossibly difficult, but figuring out how everything connected in the original was more of the fun of Riven for me. Knowing the solutions off a guide and meeting those solutions and my understanding why in the middle - seeing how organically cohesive everything was - has been fascinating. For me, that is the unique replay value of the original Riven. Arguably, that's really esoteric, and I welcome the argument that the remake as a puzzle game overall flows better.

Part of that flow in the remake comes from not being limited to a point-and-click interface. Exploring Riven in real-time and especially VR has been a dream of mine for years. It's absolutely cathartic to do so. The original falls completely short in this regard. That said, where the remake pales graphically to the original is some tiny nuances in some of the pre-rendered animations of the original - little details that are some of the most memorable parts of the game. I don't mean changes in the puzzles at all - just graphical/artistic things that lose a lifelike, minute fineness from the original. I would argue though that other details like the textures and some other scenery-based changes/additions overall are more lifelike in this remake. For the most part, where the already compelling "naturalistic uncanny valley" artstyle of the original isn't matched, the remake has elements that look even more attractively convincing.

The sound design of the original, while lower quality and technically limited to choppy soundscape transitions, has more nuanced personality in my opinion. This goes back to the hair-splitting degree of fineness in little moments of the original. They might seem pedantically pretentious to bring up, but those little elements are at the heart of what I carry with me from my experience of the original.

Speaking of graphics and nuances in the original: no 3D rendition will match John Keston's live acting as Gehn in the original. I believe the same can be said for all the other iconic performances. I feel even Rand Miller's acting as Atrus is more convincing in the original. It's definitely a gravitational pull I feel away from the remake.

All that to say, it's impossible for me to value one over the other. Both games feel like two different, surreal lenses of the same mystifying world. At best, for someone new, I would recommend them start with the remake, and if they're still interested go for the original. Otherwise, Riven - as a collective of both iterations of the game - stands among my favorite games and most formative artistic experiences.
