Disclaimer: Huge original Riven fan here. 

Now that this is out of the way, let’s move on to the remake review.

I didn’t have huge expectations from the remake, mostly because there isn’t really too much to improve on the original Riven. What I’d really like to play is a “Masterpiece” Riven, meaning the same pre-rendered gorgeous graphics, but upscaled to a greater resolution, which sadly is not possible due to the original render files having being lost for decades now. AI upscaling may help in the future. 

I found the remake’s graphics pretty good, but in my eyes they don’t match the original’s atmosphere and details, not by a long shot. They’re great for 2025’s standards, but not for ’97’s standards I guess 😛.

That is for the environment graphics. The 3d characters are not just bad, they’re downright, subjectively awful. They’re so bad that sometimes they made me laugh out loud (I’m looking at you pajama guy at Tay)! What were you even thinking Cyan? 

The voice acting is for the most part the same from the original, but due to the awful models and acting of the new characters, the overall experience isn’t getting much better. 

The music is also mostly the same from the original Riven, which is great news (I have been listening to the soundtrack for two decades now, it’s so relaxing and calming, I absolutely love it). The “bad news” is that Robyn Miller’s new music tracks, while good on their own, they don’t really match with the Riven’s atmosphere or with the rest of the soundtrack. This is particularly notable in the new underground cavern, at Boiler Island. I have been following Robyn’s work over the years and this new track(s) feel like an outtake from his movie’s soundtrack (The Immortal Augustus Gladstone), which I also listen from time to time, but doesn’t really belong to the Riven soundtrack. In other words, the new music is not bad but it’s anti-climatic.

My other expectations from the remake were to visit new areas or even new ages that wasn’t possible in the original. Did the remake met my expectations? Yes and no. 
- I always wanted to visit Tay (who didn’t)? The remake did provide us with extra content here, but honestly there was much to be desired. The new Tay content is limited to a short 5 minutes walk (if you reaaalllyy take your time, like I did), meeting several copy-and-paste NPCs, nothing to do really other than look around the environment. I was kind of disappointed. 
- Age 233: We knew that there probably wasn’t too much to see in this age, but still the new content is so minimal that it was disappointing. And actually, the extra stuff added on the outdoors, didn’t make too much sense to me. 

Let’s talk new mini-areas: This is what I was mostly excited about, and Cyan here kind of delivered. I loved the fact that we could see some familiar places from other angles etc. Although not many examples here, I can’t complain. There are some additional walks in the village, some new underground places, some different point of views here and there, etc. 

Now, let’s talk puzzles and relevant area changes: When I read that there were new puzzles added to the game, I was excited. What I didn’t know back then though, was that most of the new puzzles added replaced other major and classic Riven puzzles. I was actually shocked when I first arrived at Jungle island and didn’t find the ball waiting for me or the frog silhouette at the cave. I then thought, why on earth did they remove such core elements from the original and these are also my thoughts now, after 35 hours of gameplay. 

I’m not saying that the changed puzzles are bad, what I’m saying is that they’re worse than the originals. Furthermore, the overall difficulty of the game has decreased, which is sadly a global trend in the game industry nowadays. Maybe because people’s focus is more limited, or because game developers believe that people’s patience and/or intelligence has decreased over time… I don’t know, but the fact is that most games now are easier than what games of the past used to be, and I consider this a bad thing. I would also say it’s a bit insulting as well. 

New puzzles are good, but old puzzles were much better. They shouldn’t change those. While the new star fissure puzzles and the travel-between-domes flow for example is a good idea, it doesn’t work at all practically when in-game. In the original, after we unlocked the domes, the linking books inside were a shortcut to travel between parts of Riven. With the new mechanism, there’s so much to do inside the star-fissure, that this “shortcut” logic doesn’t make any sense anymore! So, almost every time, I preferred taking the long way rather than the dome “shortcut”. So, not only did we loose the previous dome puzzle which was excellent, we also lost the shortcuts. 

To make things even worse for backtracking, they decided to cut the bridge between the Dome and the Crater islands. I’ve heard there might be technical reasons, but I really can’t believe that they couldn’t surpass these problems.

The submarine “puzzles’ were simplified - aka they’re now straightforward and boring. 

The new mini-area under the lake, was a great idea but with pure execution. Up until now, I haven’t really understood what this underground level was good for! It looked like it turned on and off the heating, but I  still don’t know how that helped me complete the game, and this is what I should call bad design by definition. 

Furthermore, there’s a lever now that lowers/elevates the bridge connecting the Gehn’s temples (the two main parts of the Dome island), and up till now I also don’t know what this level is for. Why elevate this bridge in the first place? If there’s an answer, I haven’t been able to find it, in-game or online. 

Regarding the new animals - puzzle, while not bad in retrospect, it was very frustrating too me because it took me a very long time to realize that I actually needed this magnifying glass I was carrying around and had completely forgotten about that I carried, because the “inventory” UI is honestly bad. Having to carry around anything else other than books, is so non-Myst by the way. The only other case (if I’m not mistaken) where we had to carry something in the Myst series, is the stone tablet in Myst 5. And don’t even get me started on that 😞.

I could go on and on with the changes on the environment and the puzzles, but let me sum this up: I would be more happy if they just added new stuff to see and more puzzles to solve (even if they weren’t super-great), as long as they didn’t change the original areas and puzzles. 

Dear Cyan, you knew this was coming: Fans loved the original Riven and you knew that there was gonna be a backlash from old players if you changed core gameplay, and well, here it is. You made Riven a little more worse than it was, but that’s ok for me because I have experienced the original many - many times and will again in the future. It’s only a shame for new players who may never get to try the original in the first place, and this is sad. 

I know I have been mostly critical, but still I really did enjoy the remake. For the most part. Not you 3d models, I hate you with all my heart.

Riven (1997) is my favorite PC game before 2000. I own a signed print from the creators, the anniversary Myst book, etc. etc. Super fan - and was more excited for this game than any of the Myst remakes. That out of the way, there's a lot to love about this remake, but also a few head-scratchers. 

The best thing, in my opinion, is there are many nooks and crannies to explore that I wish I could have in the original. The village is much more fleshed out, there's hidden caves, walkways, paths, and overall there's just more to SEE. I wish it had been pushed further in a few places, though. 

The big elephant in the room is the 3d models, which still remind me of the awkward End of Ages days. They are very stiff, lifeless, the lips don't match, and simply break the immersion. Unfortunately, immersion is what made the original so special, so while this is pretty at times, it's also pretty distracting to have cold puppets staring into your soul. 

There's 3 big notable changes in gameplay. 

1. New area involving the domes. There's a very cool concept being explored with the domes this time, but I wish it had been pushed further and actually served as a more efficient fast travel mechanism. 

2. Jungle Island's animal puzzle has been completely redone. While the end result is the same, the method to solve it is different. While the changes are fresh, I wouldn't say it adds any more depth when compared to original method.

3. The marble puzzle is tweaked. Maybe people were complaining about the original massive grid, but that has been scrapped and replaced. Again, not sure if this is any better this time round. 

Overall, I would describe this as a linear step. It wasn't worse, but it wasn't better. The 3d people are cancelled by the environment, and the puzzle changes seem unmotivated. That being said, I think if you're a Myst or Riven fan, it's worth exploring again. But don't get your hopes up that it's gonna be this incredible upgrade from the original. It's just alright, and maybe could get you chatting with someone who is new to this world. If I feel a Riven itch however, I'll just play the original. 7.2/10

[h1]Story:[/h1]

Set on a fictional island(Lingshan Islands) in the South Pacific(Close to China but no...The enemy is Korean), we are taking control of Nomad "a US Marine equipped with the powerful Nanosuit". But what is Nanosuit? It's a technologically advanced suit that grants enhanced strength, speed, invisibility, and armour modes.


[h1]Game Mechanics:[/h1]

Unlike the other games in its time era. Crysis comes with various game mechanics. 

◘CryNet Nanosuit 1.0: The core mechanic, the Nanosuit, revolutionized FPS gameplay. You were able to seamlessly switch between different modes as in:
•Strength: Increased damage and the ability to lift heavy objects. (you can't flip tanks and vehicles like our Chief😔)
•Speed: Enhanced movement speed for quick traversal and evasive manoeuvres.
•Armor: Increased resistance to damage.
•Invisibility: Become nearly invisible to enemies.

◘Open Worldish: The game does offer a degree of freedom in how you can approach combat and exploration. You could choose to stealthily infiltrate enemy camps, engage in open combat, or utilize the environment to your advantage.

◘Destructible Environments: Environments were highly interactive, allowing you to destroy foliage, collapse structures, and utilize the environment to your advantage in combat.


[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]

Pros:

+Groundbreaking Graphics: Crysis was(still is) a visual masterpiece for its time, pushing the boundaries of graphical fidelity in video games.
+Innovative Gameplay: The Nanosuit provided unique tactical options and encouraged creative players' expression.
+Immersive World: The lush tropical island setting was beautifully realized and provided a sense of scale and exploration.

Cons:

-Demanding System Requirements: Limited accessibility for many players at launch.
-Story: Not particularly memorable or innovative. [spoiler]You will have to read books and comics in order to fully understand the lore[/spoiler]
-AI: Enemy AI could be predictable and easily exploited.

[h1]Conslusion[/h1]

Crysis, a 2007 landmark, redefined FPS visuals with its demanding graphics. The innovative Nanosuit gameplay, while showing its age, remains influential. A must-play for FPS fans, though be prepared for outdated mechanics.

Crysis Remastered brings back one of the most iconic FPS games of all time, delivering the same sandbox-style combat, open-ended gameplay, and cutting-edge visuals that made the original a legend. While it may not be the groundbreaking technical marvel it once was, it still offers an exhilarating shooter experience that holds up remarkably well.

The Nanosuit remains the heart of the game, giving players an incredible range of tactical options. Whether you want to go full stealth with Cloak Mode, tank bullets with Armor Mode, or sprint into battle with Speed Mode, Crysis lets you approach every encounter your way. The open-ended level design is fantastic, allowing for both careful, tactical approaches and all-out chaos. Unlike many linear shooters, Crysis gives you freedom—every fight feels like a unique puzzle to solve.

Visually, Crysis Remastered does a great job of modernizing the game, with improved lighting, enhanced textures, and new graphical options like ray tracing. While it may not be the mind-blowing PC benchmark that the original was in 2007, it’s still one of the best-looking remasters out there, especially in its lush jungle environments.

Gunplay is still satisfying, with punchy weapons and destructible environments that make combat feel dynamic. Blasting through buildings, using explosive barrels, or picking off enemies from the treetops keeps every encounter engaging. The AI, while not perfect, still offers a decent challenge, forcing you to adapt and strategize.

The remaster isn’t flawless—some bugs and AI quirks remain, and the later levels (especially the zero-gravity alien sections) still feel less polished compared to the brilliant first half of the game. However, if you’re here for that classic Crysis experience, the sandbox combat, gorgeous visuals, and freedom of choice make this an absolute blast to revisit.

Whether you’re a long-time fan or a newcomer, Crysis Remastered proves that great gameplay is timeless.

Rating: 8.5/10 – A beautifully remastered classic that still delivers incredible sandbox FPS action.

I mean, where do I start...? The game is good dumb fun. It's as blocky and as "simple" as Wolf 3D, but it has none of the finesse of Wolf 3D's fire management where you have to carefully stun-lock the right enemies in the right pattern to survive.

The level design is... ok? Sadly, some levels massively overstay their welcome and go on for way too long. I also got lost more than I do in Wolf3D or even something like Supplice. Make of that what you will.

The repetitive "themes" and visuals in those huge levels don't help much either. Shorter, tighter levels would have benefited the game a lot.

It's visually pleasing for the most part, but the gameplay is a lot closer to something as simple as Catacomb Abyss with extra visual bells and whistles (detail is entirely visual, the action and player-monster interactions happen on one fixed block level, like Wolfenstein, for 99% of the game).

The level editor is the game's biggest asset and strength, as it even supports importing your custom textures in a large-size "tilemap" image, so you can go wild with what you can do theme-wise.

Let's be clear here - this game is neither Wolf3D, nor is it Heretic or Hexen. It's decidedly a lot more Catacomb Abyss, so very much on the simpler side of things.

However, the overall package is presented well, it looks pleasing to the eye and it plays in a very... non-offensive and relatively fun manner (and given the downpour of HORRIBLE 'boomer shooters' we have on Steam, that's honestly an achievement).

The game is also attractively priced (another advantage over a large number of boomer shooters that cost more and play a lot worse), and it's good enough to get the blue thumbs up, so there you go!

Exploring the dev's portfolio, I also discovered the same dev did retro-modern remakes of Apogee's Secret Agent, Crystal Caves and Monster Bash, and I've already bought, thumbed up and played almost all of Secret Agent, so maybe look into those as well, as an added bonus.

I play a lot of deck-builders, especially the rogue-like kind. I really like this one. It really brings a bit fresh to the genre the samurai aesthetic is a more or less unexplored theme for this. Completing most levels i have encountered is not too difficult, but if you want to complete the extra side objectives it can get pretty tricky, the game doesn't require you to do so right away, you also don't have to successfully get every side objective on any given map in one run, so you can retry them to get meta-progression points. This game has a really interesting way of incorporating movement and positional awareness into the game completely allowing you to say shoot in and land a hit and then use movement cards to scoot back out reducing the incoming retaliation. There are definitely cards that give a payoff for you maneuvering into an ideal position before using them.

All in all i think its a fantastic game and a great building point for new games in the genre the few things i would like to see are: 

a DLC/Sequal/Update that adds some multiplayer to the game a lot of game sin the genre are starting to embrace that playing card/board games with friends on the internet is a like-able thing and this game really puts off that vibe of being a "Board game" and a "Card game" at the same time as still also firmly being a video game. Games like Hellcard and across the Obelisk prove that the multiplayer formula for these games when implemented well can really make the game play super fun.

A little-bit stronger of a theme for each character, they are all neat and fun to play but they don't really leverage enough uniqueness in thier play strategies since any character can kinda grab any other colored card. I'de like to see thier starting deck and desired cards have a little more nuance and impact on how that run will go. If you look at The new Ninja turtles splintered time roguelike, sure you want all the upgrades you can have but there are certain ones that match up perfectly with certain turtles strategies (on hit for Michealangelo, Master strike for Leonardo, tool activation for Donatello etc.)

It would also be fun to have some longer maps where  you really get to build your deck for a while ... the current maps especially the ones that require turn limit clears can feel short and like you don't really get a chance to engage in the deck-building as much as you'de like .... it kinda feels like you just have to take every movement card you can to run around the map quickly ... maybe some bosses that guard teleporters so there is more than one intelligent way to solve the crossing the map problem.

Within the setting you have created, maybe a phased map or two where you have multiple objective to complete the map but some of them are choices and you don't have time to do both then once complete providing you with a new set of multiple objectives you cannot complete all of. Making each play through on a map a little more fresh, so that you aren't only replaying the maps for the harder side objectives but also to see how different the map plays out if you make a different story decision.

A general feel for what the game is like: this game gets challenging. Fast. Those moments where you're going lightning fast require near-perfect maneuvering. You crash, because no one is near-perfect on their first rodeo. You try and try again, maybe you get a little farther, maybe you make that one nasty turn, or maybe you crash right at the beginning of the level trying to get that first near-miss boost. Multiple times in a row. You crash at the middle of a level. You crash going through a boost at the wrong angle. You crash into a wall because the way you were turned caught you off guard. You crash trying to squeeze between a couple trees. You barely miss the timing for a rotation wall. You crash on that one rock you've managed to avoid every run until now. You crash inside of a narrow tunnel. 

You will crash, you will crash and you will crash again.

But there comes a time where this doesn't happen. Seemingly at random, that one run where you feel like everything is going your way appears before you. You fly pasts the boosts at top speed, twisting and turning around each nook and cranny and for a fraction of a second you eye that black and white striped wall - your ticket to freedom. You fly straight into that damn wall and you say, 'finally', as you sit back in your chair a champion. You did it. You completed the gauntlet. Congratulations.

But that's only one level. And you only got 2 stars on it. Shit.

I usually play multiplayer games solo, or with close friends, as I'm not normally a fan of PVP / asymmetrical COOP where you have to play with random players unless you've got a full team of friends to play the game with you, but I took the plunge with this one as I love the Ayuwoki theme and couldn't resist. I'm really comfortable playing with randoms in this, because the interaction is controlled through the ability to select pre-formed phrases like "Hello", or "Have you seen the creature" that your character says, but can give away your position to the Ayuwoki.

So at the time of writing, there's one environment - the mansion. Two to four players take on the role of the survivors, and one person is the Ayuwoki (so you need a minimum of three). You can't choose to queue as either - the Ayuwoki is always selected at random.

The survivors have to escape the mansion by solving puzzles to find items they need to escape the house, but even though all puzzles are always available to solve, the ones that reward the player with the items are randomised. Each survivor can run, walk or crawl (the latter being the quietest movement) and can pull out a lantern to help them see, but will make them more visible to the creature. They also have a special ability to help them, such as being able to roll and dodge, or turn invisible when crouching and staying still.

The Ayuwoki has the easier time. If you play as the creature, you can see clearly, or lope extremely fast on all fours, and can attack players. Hitting them several times will down them, forcing them to crawl around until another survivor helps them back up, or you can execute them with an 'ultimate' move every 2-3 minutes or so.

The environment also plays an important role - survivors can open and close doors, but the Ayuwoki can only break them down, requiring several hits to do so, so this can buy you time as a survivor. You can use purple wardrobes to teleport to another part of the mansion, yellow wardrobes to push over to get in the way of the Ayuwoki (I've heard you can hide in them too), and dropping rats whilst the creature is chasing you will force the Ayuwoki to stop and eat them. There are also pickups like health, energy drinks and oil to refill your lantern, not to mention eerie 'webbing' than can hinder your progress if it's closed, but will open to let you through.

The art style is fantastic but I appreciate it might not be everyone's taste in a horror game. I'd describe it as a cross between World of Warcraft's visual style and an enchanted Disney castle with it's cartoony feel, and with it's cheesy classic horror soundtrack it is a bit of a cliched setting, but that's not an insult, I love it.

There is also a progression system, but it takes a lifetime to level up (I've got over six hours at the time of writing this and I'm still level one), and I think it's mainly because there isn't a big enough population to get public games going regularly yet. Sometimes I've sat in the lobby for around 20 minutes to get a game, and once you're in the game, the game doesn't tell you if people quit or if they're killed. This week I ran around trying to 'solo' the game not bumping in to anyone, and given how quickly the Ayuwoki can cover the mansion, it can't have been coincidence. If you choose to leave the game, you don't get XP for what you've done, you get nothing. The game has also crashed on me twice during a game, forcing me to quit and lose any XP I would have got, so things like that are slowing down my ability to level up.

They've now added a season progression bar, so you can see what you get by levelling up (I think it's just cosmetics for the survivors or the Ayuwoki). You don't need to buy these new cosmetics with real money, it looks like you buy them with in-game currency which they've not added yet, so customisation is currently limited.

One final thing I'll say (as I appreciate this review is getting rather long) is that it does feel like a single player game with a multiplayer mechanic. What I mean by that is that there are lots of puzzles which aren't obvious at first glance, meaning you're forced to spend time to work them out whilst being hunted, and these take time to do, particularly as there's no way to communicate with other people on how to complete them, even with the pre-formed phrases. You also need to spread out to find these puzzles (as the mansion is procedurally generated) and minimise the risk of a massacre, so for a large portion of my experience I've not really seen or interacted with others. But once you know how to complete the puzzles, you can do them in seconds.

All being said, this game is simply so much fun, and as someone who is both a fan of Michael Jackson (the Ayuwoki) and the horror genre, this is a win-win game which has so much potential to be a real classic.

On the surface, Poppy Playtime is just another mascot horror game. It has all the staples: Colorful murderous mascots, an evil corporation with subterranean lairs, jump scares, and, of course, glitches. Back in the game's early days, I wouldn't even touch it with how over-monetized the initial launch was, though they did thankfully pull back from the more egregious examples.

But with chapter 3, and ESPECIALLY chapter 4, it's honestly become one of my all time favorite horror games. The game was made by a studio mostly known for art and animation, and it shows, with great and memorable set pieces, great character animation, and stand out voice work. The toys are also a highlight- they all feel like they could've been real 80's-90's toys, with theme songs, beautifully drawn posters, cut outs, and, of course, very silly names.

If you like horror games for the scares first and foremost, this probably isn't the game for you. But if you're more interested in memorable moments, solid atmosphere, and some interesting takes on classic mascot horror tropes, then I think you'll have a lot of fun with it.

I hate to be the first to post a negative review and ruin that sweet 100% score but there's a slew of issues that prevent the game from deserving the score imo. Pre dusk just didn't cut it for me, so i can't recommend it in good conscience hence the negative review. I'll disclose the issues both for warry buyers and also as feedback for this developer as it is their first project. The main thing that's problematic in this game for me is the difficulty curve. The game has a good and gradual increase in difficulty throughout the first 3 levels and up till that point i was gonna recommend it but that all changed in the 4th level. Suddenly the game just spiked with these 2 minute long sections of tight jumps on a timer paired with unfun mechanics. This game does the instant kill spike pits/walls which is doable in most levels but in the 4th level the gaps between the spikes are tiny and jumps suddenly require near pixel perfect inputs. 

Where i was breezing through the game at a steady pace initially i just hit a wall here. I don't want to make it sound like a skill issue as most of the steam discussions also mention this 4th level, so i'm not alone here. The 5th level isn't equally bad but still far from perfect. The final boss is also a huge jump in difficulty whereass previous bosses were fair and even quite fun. I gave up here and watched the ending on youtube since i was already fed up with the game at this point. The game's lenght would normally be a bit of a problem but i'm glad it ended there as i was getting fed up with the game at this point. The level design just wasn't fun anymore at this point with too many instakill mechanics. The levels were also very random from an immersion point of view. From a swamp straight into a dessert and right back into a rainy castle.

The whole game felt inconsistent due to this, as did the story. The writing was very poor even putting some context in brackets as a 4th wall break in one of the dialogues. This completely pulled me out of the experience and what was there just wasn't very good. It's pretty generic and some things come out of nowhere like at the very end where [spoiler]a character died because reasons?[/spoiler] There's also this whole talk about some secret that the MC sets out for but then he suddenly looks for his parents after some random NPC told him about that? It's just bad and there's no payoff or satisfaction from the narrative. The combat did give some joy especially the earlier bosses but there's still issues with feedback both visually and audibly.

Speaking of audiovisuals the game's music is pretty solid albeit generic. Sound effects are good and the artstyle is also nice despite being basic. It gives some limbo vibes, especially in the 1st level but later levels remind me more of Feist. Unlike feist though the controls are not as responsive. The character does react almost instantly most of the time but other times it doesn't do what you want it to, especially the super jump (glide + double jump) which doesn't work sometimes. There's also a very apparant issue with input buffering where if you press jump while in the air or falling your character will immediately jump again once you hit the ground. This can make you bump your head into spikes or cause other annoying problems. This also inputs if you die, so as soon as you respawn you will jump. The last one isn't annoying but it just shows that this is a prevelant issue and easily identifiable.

What's also identifiable is the fact that this game's file size is absolutely huge despite the basic art style and short lenght. At 16+GB this really should not be the case for a game of this sort. Some optimization in this regard is definately recommended for future projects. However credit has to be given where it's due as the performance and load times were superb. Appart from the input buffering issue (which feels more intentional by the dev as a mechanic) there's no real bugs either. So on a technical level the game is well made. Then finally there's the price and for this price one really can't complain. I would have recommended it despite how basic the story and gameplay is but that difficulty spike is just too much. Try to set up with some playtesters for your next project to help identify these sort of things.

Remember that desolate corner of the arcade where dreams went to die? Ah yes, the coin pusher machine, where you’d toss in your life's savings (in the form of quarters) hoping for a shoddy keychain or a sticky hand. Well, welcome to the digital version of that heartbreak: "Old Coin Pusher Friends."

Instead of genuine, tangible disappointment, now you can amass digital trinkets. And guess what you're using to play? Coins that look so ancient, you'd think they once paid for a T-Rex's parking ticket. Honestly, these coins look like they’ve witnessed the invention of fire.

Land a special item and - bam! - you hit the jackpot, allowing you to reclaim all those relics you’ve haphazardly chucked into the digital abyss. That's if, of course, you don’t utterly bungle it. And speaking of chaos, random menaces appear just when you thought you had your coin-throwing PhD. They might boost your earnings or rob you blind. It's like the digital universe's way of saying, "Gotcha!"

The game's title isn't just trying to butter you up with that "friend" bit. You can actually team up with online players! Or as I like to call it, "strategically mooching" off others' skills. Cough, I mean, forming valuable alliances, of course.

But wait, there's more! Fancy a personalized touch? Integrate your VRoid Hub character. While they won’t give you any pep talks or moral support, they’ll stand there looking as dazzling as a disco ball.

In conclusion, grab your granny's antique coins (or their digital counterparts) and dive into "Old Coin Pusher Friends." Will you conquer the digital realm, one ancient coin at a time, or go broke in both reality and virtuality? Only time (and coins) will tell!

The following oft repeated hint from the games sums things up nicely:
 "Follow the right sequence or it will take too long to complete this level!" 
First off the bat - it simply isn't true (in casual mode there is no timer and no move limits; although this can be changed if you want more of a challenge). And some of the other instructions were oddly phrased too.
But it does actually hint at a key point; this actually a match-3 game you have to think about at least a little.

I bought it mostly for the different game types: Match 3, Solitare, Mah Jong, Spot the difference.
But actually found the match-3 puzzles the most enjoyable. Which in an era flooded by generally dreadful ad-heavy mobile match-3 games was a little bit surprising.

There are quite a lot of clever mechanics here, many of which I'd not seen for many years, or at all. I won't go into details, but they genuinely make this a puzzle game in places, rather than just match-match-match over and over.

As an example, if you ask for a hint you aren't simply given a move you can make, but a general strategic goal you should be aiming for next.
Both the mah-jong tile match and the solitaire games have a 'bank' where you can store one tile/card meaning with a little thought and planning they are hugely more solvable than normal.
There are no massive power ups or chains of explosions here. It's more focused on using your noggin and using what you have to best advantage.

I genuinely enjoyed playing this all the way through and may well return to it in another game mode to see if it still works as well.

If, like me, you enjoyed match-3 games back in the day but are jaded by the endless copy-cat unplayable mobile versions then I can definitely recommend giving this one a try.

Perang Laut - Maritime Warfare is a game based on naval expeditions between the 15th and 18th century in the area that is now modern Indonesia. You basically play as one of the multiple regional powers to attempt to achieve hegemony in the islands.

Now, from the screenshots, one can already expect that this game have neither graphic nor good english pronounciation. But this is not the thing I'm going to nitpick today.

Like any good gamer jumping to a new game, the first thing I do was to look for in game options; music/bgm, VSync/windowed mode, etc. Which was unfortunately not present on the main screen. Oh well, I can live without that.

Then I jumped to the tutorial. First steps are okay, but once I started getting into building my own buildings and sending out my first navy, things started to get.. weird. In my first tutorial run, I followed the tutorial, clicked on the research button and the resources button, all good. Though there are no explanation on what the resources are and finding where these resources are produced is another problem in itself. But no biggie, I'll still follow up on it.

Then comes the part where I get to build my own buildings. Nice. First time I did it without problem, good. Job done. Then I get to send out my first navy. Selected a couple of ship, although there are no option to switch back and forward between ships, I theorize that since there are a limited type of ships, when I've switched between them all, it'll go back to option one. This logic works. Now I can switch back to my first ship type after scrolling through ~12 others. Unsophisticated, but if it works, it works. Then I try adding men, wood and rice to my armada. Again, the button only adds resources, can't find any indication that you can take them away. Fine, you can cancel navy building process and go back to the first scene. No biggie. Except I pressed escape instead of back, which threw me out of the current session. Should've read and remembered that better.

And I restarted the tutorial again. Baby steps, done, now let's build that building. But.. I can't? Oh, I'm missing wood. Alright, let's wait until the city stocks up on wood then. 18 turns later and a rebellion which saw a city previously under my command now a new kingdom, I still haven't got my wood. Where could I have gone wrong? I quit the session, restart the tutorial again, and same result. That is until the Xth time, I somehow get to see the city management screen where I can see if I want to export wood or not. In my hesitation, I clicked on it, which finally stopped the city from exporting precious, precious wood, so that I can build my building. Finally.

Now, back to navy-ordering. Ships selected, men ordered, rice loaded... and there are -28k wood that I can load? Oh well, let's try that nonetheless. After randomly pressing somewhere around the "Go outside" word, I finally got my first navy out. Yay! Now let's click around on it.. wait, why's my navy gone? Alright, let's make a new one. Click on city, click on shipyard, designate ships, rice and men, and oh look, the wood situation is finally under control. Good then, second try. Second navy. Not clicking around and follow the order "send the navy to Sriwijaya".

At that instant I regret not retaining any memories of classes in pre-modern Indonesia. I know Sriwijaya is nowhere near Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi, or Papua, but I still scroll around nonetheless. Oh, it's a coastal city on north Bali. Duh. Alright. Click, click, ship moves and when it reaches Sriwijaya.. it disappears. What?

At that moment, around half an hour have passed. At this point I can still ask Steam to give back my €5.60-ish euro because... this game is a burnt on the outside, but raw in the inside. You can still stomach the appearance, but the gameplay and the tutorial does barely anything to help you understand the game. Not only basic options are missing, but basic functions such as zooming in and out and moving around the map are not even discussed in the tutorial. This might be okay for experienced gamers (we can try the classic WASD, if not, arrows, one of them should work), but for a total beginner (including the horrid lack of guides)?

Perang Laut - Maritime Warfare is Sengakala's second game and judging by its first game and an article written by the devs for the Historical Games Network, at least one of them hast to have some interest in the history of Indonesia, which is something that is sorely underrepresented in video games. Unfortunately this game does not do this history justice. The spectrum of what the devs wanted is huge and respectable, but how they approach making the game needs major overhaul.

And since I'm not shy to rub salt on wounds, you'd do much better to spend the normal price of this game (€10) on an old copy of Tradewinds (sadly no longer available on Steam afaik). It might not scratch the same itch as what Perang Laut might try to do, but for a game that now is of legal age, Tradewinds is (unfortunately) a much better polished game.

It’s hard not to recommend a game for just $1. However, as a sequel, Toree 2 feels like a bit of a mixed bag.

The game sticks to the same formula with nine 3D platforming levels, but the gameplay has evolved, leaning more towards the fast-paced "gotta go fast" style of 3D Sonic. The first eight levels follow a new formula of extended linear running, with frequent boost pads to keep up the speed. It's not bad it's just not really to my taste. There's also not a whole lot of challenge here and the game is considerably easier than the first. 

The themes for the levels in this one are cool and more dynamic than the first game. There are also a couple of new boost pad/gizmos but they aren't particularly revolutionary and don't really add any new tech. The dark/sinister/weird vibes that develop throughout the first one are weaker here too, it all seems a bit rushed.

What is nice though is the variety that can be found at the end of the game. After 8 rather linear speedrun platforming levels we get a pretty fun little boss fight and 3 bonus levels. These Xmas-themed bonus levels are particularly interesting  as the first two abandon the speedrun style and create Mario 64 style hub levels. These are a welcome change and what I would've preferred to see more of.

Overall if you enjoyed the first it's still worth the dollar and is a very pleasant half hour of platforming.

Toree 2 is still a fun time, but not as good as the first game. The level design is more direct and not as intentionally breakable as Toree 1, and therefore I found it a lot less fun to try and route for the speedruns. Also, the final level was a letdown compared to the first game, and the final boss didn't belong in this type of game. If anything, the extra levels that were added post-launch showed a lot more promise with different, and more open, approaches to to levels design, although the speedrun mechanics didn't really belong in those.

Still recommended, but don't play it over the first one.

Space X Collector is yet another of literally thousands of 2D retro platformers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere.  This one is 3D rendered, but badly, and looks to have been coy + pasted from a basic Unreal Engine platformer template.  It's a very shallow, lazy platformer, instead of dedicated level design, the "developer" here just made an endless jumper where you have to keep jumping up along a series of procedurally generated platforms to see how high you can go.  It's incredibly shallow shovelware with no serious value or merit for PC gamers.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the 1990s.  It's unclear why the developers weren't able to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets for the game, and also irrelevant... what matters is that this looks bad as a result of their decisions, a compromise PC gamers shouldn't have to put up with.

The controls and game handling are notably very floaty and imprecise.  It's janky and unsatisfying to play... and any experienced gamer will tell you, the handling, responsiveness and general gameplay feel of the control scheme must be well polished for this kind of game to succeed.  Unfortunately, this is something the developer seems to have phoned in, with little to no apparent gameplay testing or polish done.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.

Some of the defects in the game can be attributed to the choice of using the GameMaker Studio construction kit/toolset.  This is a very poor quality toolset favoured by amateur developers as it's cheap and requires little in the way of development skill, but unfortunately has very limited capabilities.  Just as you can't make a silk purse out of a sows ear, you can't make a great video game if you use a terrible engine.  GameMaker Studio is most commonly used to make retro pixel shovelware and cash grabs.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected in the general public reception.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the game all-time peak player count was only ONE player.  That's right, only one person ever played this at a time.  When I played this for the purposes of reviewing it, I equalled the peak player count for the game.  OUCH.  The only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in the game is to be expected.  Gamers just didn't take this low quality game seriously, and for good reason.

Space X Collector is relatively cheap at $1 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

Hey all,
I don't think I've ever taken the time to write a review for steam but this game made me somewhat equally parts angry/semi-happy that I just had to say something.

To keep it short, yes I do not recommend it to most 2d horror lovers. 
Reason being because of quality of life issues, some nonsensical puzzles, and no fast-forward/skip on text/cutscenes while playing the game. Those are cardinal sins (imo) while playing a 2d horror game. If you want to know more feel free to read below I'll try and keep it short. (Keep in mind all of this review is during the early access 10/12/2021)

(Proceeds to not keep it short)
[b]Pros:[/b]
~ The different art style was very eye catching in my opinion, and I was pleased to see this take on 2d characters for a horror game vs other somewhat similar (type rpgmaker looking) games..
~ The length of the game was decent for what I got, keep in mind there were some puzzles (okay for me like 1 puzzle), that required some research, or backtracking. Your mileage may vary (YMMV)
~ The game is in Alpha/Early access and plays quite well with no bugs that I can see, or experienced currently.

~ The controls mapped well, for me using an xbox controller, not counting me needing to add an extra for the D-pad.
~ Music and sound effects were on point for moments of tension or straight out scary factor considering it's a 2d horror game. This is definitely one of those games you will want to wear headphones for, or have no background noise so you can get the FULL experience if that's your thing.
~ This game was excellent about letting the user know when they were about to need to high tail it! And I had fun doing those sequences because I got hyped ahead of time instead of frustrating surprises. (Yes some surprises are fine, but the chase sequences....who likes that?)
~ The story itself was well done, and different from what we normally see in these types of horror games (imo)... 3d,2d, or otherwise so it was refreshing. 

[b]Cons:[/b] (still this is all based on the early access):
~ Like I stated above, the game has a horrible habit of making you watch every slow text output from the characters....I'm assuming to elicit the type of atmosphere for that moment, but that should be up to the person watching it. 
I personally get the moment when it's tense, why can't I skip the text to either continue the storyline faster or get to the action? This game does not allow it.
~ Going with the above not being able to make text go faster, the game also forces you to watch (text)cutscenes you've already seen...aka you cannot skip cutscenes. In most horror games, the player knows they are going to die, or maybe they want to collect some achievements which also is a big thing in some modern 2d horror games.... Why can't we (I), skip these long (already viewed) cutscenes?

~ There are currently about 20 endings in the game, but I decided not to even pursue going out of my way to see all of them. Why? Because of what I stated above, it's too slow to go through old events, and read the text you've already seen.
~ Wording on puzzles: One of the meats of 2d horror games are their puzzles. Like most adventure/puzzle/horror games you have to keep picking stuff up and/or collecting clues to solve an upcoming puzzle. Something that left a bad taste in my mouth is that there was a puzzle that required you to move pieces in specific spots based off a nearby clue that may have been worded incorrectly. In the wording of the puzzle it seemed as though something needed to be placed in one spot, yet the provided solution given by the offical devs said it was put in another spot, that did not make sense in the clue. I don't know if that was an oversight or on purpose, but there are some other small situations like that in the game, that may make initial puzzle solving tedious.

~ This is more of my opinion (again...like all of this), but the current GAME is too short (for what I'm greedy for). We (aka myself, and future players) need more content to flesh out the story. I wish there would've been more of everything cause I did enjoy the flawed stuff of what I got. Yes...I would've personally paid more for more story and gameplay :)
~ Not being able to save anywhere is a huge con/taboo for me anytime nowadays regardless of the game genre. 
This isn't 1998/9. I could care less about needing to find a save point to make the tension high and all that other nonsense. Just let me save the game anywhere, so I can quit as need be, or right before a tense moment. Yes I understand that bugs may occur if you allow saving during scripted moments, but I also understand that you (as the dev), can also block those saving moments as need be. So give folks options in these types of games. My personal opinion has always been, in the game options, for horror games saving options: allow save anywhere/autosave, or save at save points. If some folks just have to have that save at save points... give it to them, but let the other folks who time is a commodity for, save anywhere.

~ The last one may be more of a me issue (like all of this) but I could not use the d-pad for movement. I had to use a third party program: xpadder to program the keyboard arrows to my xbox-one wireless controller for movement, so that might need to be looked into unless it's just me.

Regardless of all of my opinionated opinions. I did enjoy the game after I got the (what I think is supposed to be the last?) ending.
Since the game when I'm reviewing it is still in early access, it could change later, but till then I won't recommend it to the folks I know, but if you've read till now. I (since I don't know you random reader,) think you should try it out, as it's a good game so far.

The characters are interesting in their own right if you take the time to talk to them and read their diaries when you have the opportunity to. This is absolutely my thing but I can't recommend it, which is sad because it could be a solid 8/9 with a couple minor tweaks.

The biggest problem is the game not being sure if it wants to be golf game or a golf puzzle game. The puzzle formula requires a bunch of specific tweaks to the standard golf rules, and this game implements about half of them which makes it extremely frustrating to play. The biggest issue is the driver hitting with so much force that the shot prediction goes outside of the camera range, which is a huge thing when you're tightly bound to a par that you're required to hit in order to not instantly lose the (3+ hour long) run. On top of this, there's several course layouts that require you to use items in order  for you to be able to finish them at all - if you don't have the items or make the mistake of saving and quitting out of the hole after you've used one (which restarts the hole but does not refund the items) game over.

The devs have tried to mitigate this with an equippable pin system, but the pins are so horrifically lopsided that you're at a supreme disadvantage if you don't pick up the one that allows you to free-aim the shot prediction and the one that lets you sacrifice any card for +2 par on the hole, so have fun rerolling until you get one of those two and then desperately hope you can pick up the other. This also leads to a lack of agency since it always makes it advantageous to take the map route that will give you random cards over a shop or money, as the cards can be pawned for +2 regardless what they are and you're going to be doing that A LOT to beat some of the longer maps.

tl;dr : Devs, if you're still working on this at all please make the free-aim a regular feature, unlock the camera and take a second pass at the map generator. There's a good game here but it's completely hamstrung by being broken.

I can't bring myself to recommend Legends of Dionysos to anyone, it's too bland. I wasn't expecting anything groundbreaking, just some sidescroller slop I could enjoy for a few hours and I won't even get that. I REALLY enjoy this genre so it's a shame. If this is something you're looking for I'd redirect you to Withering Rooms which is arguably the best I've played. The Gamplay here requires you being a mix of everything, swapping between Weapons to fight. Fairly similar to Guild Wars 2 where Weapons have specific Skills for each one. So if you're an 'Archer' and an Enemy gets on top of you, you can use the Bow to slide away, switch to Staff to blink and gain more distance, then to Shield to heal, then back to the Bow.

What are the Issues?
- Traveling is a Chore and every map/arena is too big. Squeeze everything down a little. When Waves spawn in Arenas you practically need to go kick an enemy in the head to come towards you. Enemies need to just start moving towards the Player as soon as the Wave spawns. The Portal Home should also have a 'Return Portal' similar to many ARPGs like Diablo.

- Unable to hover over anything. You can't read any Skill Descriptions or Stats. My assumption is that STAM/STR/DEX/INT directly scales into Shield/Sword/Bow/Staff, which if true it's incredibly lazy.

- Leveling up (the main aspect of the game) only nets you increased stats. Armor directly scales with level so anytime you level up your armor is immediately outdated. 

- No Talent Tree whatsoever, so the only 'spec' in the game is trying to focus a specific armor type which have affixes like "of the Knight/Mage" to give TINY extra bonuses to STR/INT.

- Animations and Movement are janky.


What I'd WANT from a game like this is:
- Weapon/Armor Sets at specific Levels (7, 13, 19, 25, etc) that give bonuses (or Skill boosts). Look at how MMO's or other RPGs handle this system, it's not new Armor at every level.

- A Talent Tree (gives something for Leveling up). This can help make the 'build' that Players want to use.

- More Skills, and the ability to form a personalized Build. There should be Weapon-specific, and NON-specific Skills.

This is a great, portable (DRM not required) MIDI generator and visual sequencer. If you have a DAW (recommended) or other synthesizers, you can send MIDI out from Midonous and program interesting, evolving patterns, melodies, and pure chaos. Benn Jordan (the Flashbulb guy) worked on this.

This non-linear midi sequencer is only available here on Steam, which doesn't suit some people and I can sympathize with some of the arguments/opinions, but only to a certain degree. I don't (relatively) care that Midinous is a on Steam only thing, I have countless plugins on different computers, many standalones, a huge list of browser web apps/software and even many more different stuff, so what? and therefore it doesn't bother me as long as it is useful and functional.
Especially since it's also a matter of taste and should be considered individually; some people prefer a grid-based thing like this one, while others find everything in it a bit fiddly and less appealing.
For those interested, I mostly use Midinous for experimenting and generating soundscapes/textures. I often use my CMI V from Arturia as a standalone paired with it and so far I have been able to achieve some very nice results, like the thing I did for a friend who needed very special atmospheric background music for his art exhibition. 

When it comes to hearing a reference of what the program does without any other software, than there is an internal standard synth with several different waveforms: sine, square, triangle, sawtooth, ramp etc.
So one approach would be to open Midinous and choose new colors for that user interface and according to your current feeling, select a random bpm and generate your first structure of MIDI data and listen to that with the internal synth. 
If you kinda like what you hear, try to change a few notes here and there and play with the possibilities of how the patches can be connected, then open a music program like: Arturia Pigments, Wedge Force Hydro, Initial Audio Sektor or AudioThing SX1000 and let yourself be surprised by what suddenly happens. Or you can synch it like I did once with Ableton, or the DAW of your choice like Reaper, Bitwig or Logic.
And a little advice for those of you who are still quite inexperienced with but eager to learn such things, take your time, be patient with yourself, work with the manual and have fun while you learn and try things out. 

I can definitely recommend Midinous if you want to create complex sequences or if you just want to experiment with sounds and audio design in general.

But there are 3 things about the game I don't like:
1) some objects are "mis-labeled": a "flashlight" is drawn as a lantern, a "brush" is drawn as small paintbrushes in a coffee cup, the "cup" looks to me like a trophy, etc.  Not too many, but this game could be gone thru slight translation adjustments.
2) your progress within a scene is lost as soon as you return to the main menu.  However, completing a scene unlocks the next scene.
3) there is a store (I dare you to find it!) where you can spend some money to get some other cat/dog; perhaps the idea was abandoned by the developer as I couldn't find a way to earn money!!!

The bar above the object's "name" represents the progress made within the scene, NOT a timer... so no rush to complete the scene.  Once completed, you can replay any of the 4 scenes.

I bought this game while on sale at 70%; even at that price (around $3), it feels overpriced.  I did not encounter any technical issues, but because it feels like an incomplete game, especially compared to many other hidden object games, I simply cannot recommend it... unless you get it for free.

[h1]Garbage Writer who Derailed their own story in the second half[/h1]

[h2]tl;dr This guy is basically another Yanderedev. He needs to Get A Fucking Proofreader.[/h2]

I'm going to abridge this review because Steam has a character limit.

The first half was written beautifully. The story was set up about Blite. Learning to love themselves. One with the destructive impulse to lash out at their repression, the other maintaining a smiling façade to hide their other half away. The doomed negative spiral continuing until they have a literal near death experience, and only then does a glimmer of hope show itself.
Blayk and Nite starting to repair their relationship was what got me invested in this game, and my investment in the characters and wanting them to be happy and together was the core of wanting to see this story through to the bitter end.

The [strike]Pokémon[/strike] Ahoki, collectibles, combat, lore, or other details all only worked because the core characters were people I wanted to root for, decorations for Blite themselves.

So what happened? He focused on those decorations and the writing went to shit.

[h2]Trans fans[/h2]
He made (both of) the main characters transgender, but does not explore how their character is affected by this other than vaguely alluded to parental abuse and a generic resolve to "not run away from their past anymore". Character traits, even minor ones, are not purely cosmetic sprinkles; especially since Blayk and Nite inhabited the same body, you could have explored how their identity affected their relationship in the past and present. This potential is squandered.
In addition, he didn't even listen to his trans fans when he had the opportunity. One of them had issues with the way the "Photo dialogue" between Marmot and Blite was written, but he [b] refused to listen to it at all[/b]. I don't think he's stupid enough to believe he owns the Transgender Experience™ in [i]our[/i] universe, but he definitely believes he owns [i]Blite's[/i] transgender experience.

[h2][i]Sloppily handled story beats[/i][/h2]
[list]
    [*]Zyra openly tells Marmot Blite's biggest secret when asked why they seem to talk to themselves a lot, despite him being a total stranger and her having no reason to share something so personal.
    [*]Inclusion of the Nullflower motif to represent persistence despite that not being a theme in the character writing at all -- you can't just include surface level motifs to communicate character, you have to write them that way. Zyra does not come across as persistent in the face of pressure, she comes off as hostile and guarded. 
    [*]Characters talking in dialogue scenes where they are not present in the party
[/list]

[h2]WHAT THE FUCK WAS THAT?! Or, Everything wrong with GodBlight[/h2]
It was well foreshadowed that Blite themself was some kind of eldritch diety/proto-god, so it was no surprise that they ascend into full god form during the bossfight. 

[h3]Visually lazy design[/h3]
So what does that God form look like? A chain-tentacle abomination straight out of Lovecraft's nightmares? Something that had a lot of chains in the design due to that being a major motif and, ya know, the main aesthetic of their powers? Nope, its just them but [i]naked[/i] and with [i]scythe arms out of nowhere[/i], shackles hastily slapped on as the author realized "oh yeah, I forgot to put chains in this design". I have never seen a design so inconsistent with earlier motifs or so uncreatively lazy.

Congratulations, Loverde, you somehow managed to make seeing Blite naked disappointing. That is a feat

[h3]Butchered character[/h3]
Out of nowhere, Blayk decides to knife Diana and team up with Marmot to destroy Charcoal and betray Ahokau. This is completely inconsistent with their earlier character of someone who lashes out but decided to try and get better, and there is ABSOLUTELY NO DEVELOPMENT towards a villain arc of any kind. 
They were just hijacked by the author to force a villain protagonist without any buildup or quality writing. 
Nite might deal with issues by lashing out, but this COMPLETELY contradicts their earlier efforts to genuinely build trust. And what explanation does Blayk give for agreeing with all this? Their world is a hellscape with "Abusive parents, shitty world leaders, retaliating nature..." 
It makes sense for them both to snap here. But the reader is given no indication as to what convinced them to betray Ahokau, nor was their character ever inclined to EVER be okay with death lasering innocent people. So when they snap in THIS manner? NO!! If you wanted them to side with Marmot, ACTUALLY DEVELOP THE CHARACTER IN THAT DIRECTION!!

I suppose it’s fitting that it ends with them ripped apart into separate bodies and an arm hacked off on the both of them. Their characters were figuratively butchered, so you literally butchered them to twist the knife.

[h2]Fan feedback - GET. A FUCKING. PROOFREADER.[/h2]
A recent interview the developer gave made him realize that some fan feedback he was given was inconsistent with his own plans for the character, and incorporating it was why they were so inconsistent. This is technically true, as fans don't have access to all of your Secret Plans and as such make different reads into characters than what you intended.

However. THAT IS ON YOU. If people are making different reads than what you wanted, then the onus is on you to change your writing so the message is clearer. Fan feedback is not the reason your work failed, it is YOUR failure to decide what feedback to incorporate and how. 

He resolved to never make any changes in his next project. THAT IS HOW YOU NEVER GROW. Plans change all the time, and there is no shame in deviating from them if a better way presents itself. Just make sure that the end product is consistent from start to finish instead of containing every impulsive scribble that went through your head.

The best way around this is to GET A PROOFREADER.  Take your script for [i]Malice[/i]. Give it to someone to read. See what feedback they give. AND THEN REVISE YOUR DRAFT.

Is to [i]Colin McRae Rally[/i] what [i]Super Woden GP 2[/i] is to [i]Gran Turismo[/i]. Sublime handling and great track selection, with just the right amount of arcade polish to keep it snappy and moreish.

The game is enjoyable and does nothing inherently wrong, but it also fails to introduce anything truly new. The gameplay aligns well with expectations for a top-down arcade racer, striking a good balance between control and visual flair. The car selection is satisfactory, though the limited variety of liveries feels restrictive. The tracks themselves are engaging and complement the gameplay nicely, leaving you wishing for a free-roam mode akin to what Art of Rally offers.

The realistic art style is serviceable and maintains clarity during gameplay. However, the distinction between countries often feels superficial; environmental props are reused excessively, with only occasional country-specific structures. These unique elements are frequently repeated across multiple tracks within the same region, which detracts from the sense of variety.

On the technical side, the game is stable, and I encountered no bugs during gameplay. However, playing on a super ultrawide (32:9) monitor results in menu glitches, likely because the developer optimized only for standard ultrawide (21:9) setups.

While the game is fun for arcade racing fans, its biggest issue lies in its positioning relative to Rush Rally 3. Aside from the top-down camera angle, there’s little to differentiate this title, making it feel more like an extended DLC or a mod than a fully justified standalone game. This is especially notable given the identical pricing, which forces players to choose or pay twice for largely overlapping experiences. The design choice to separate the two games may stem from technical constraints, such as overhanging trees in Rush Rally 3, but the result still feels like an unnecessary split.

To truly stand out, the game would benefit from more attention to its environments to make each location feel unique. A simple and impactful addition could be a tilt-shift camera effect, which would enhance the aesthetic and give the game a distinctive visual identity. Considering the ease of implementing such a feature using readily available Unity assets, this could be an excellent (and hopefully free) post-launch update.

Overall, while the game feels like a slightly modified version of Rush Rally 3, it is still worth picking up on discount for fans of Art of Rally or similar games. However, at full price, it struggles to justify itself as a standalone title.

For those of you who grew up in the early 2000s with either a LiveJournal, an online role play community, or both....this game will absolutely hit you in the feels. I'm not just talking about nostalgia either. This game tells the story of friends who found solace in a Live....er....LIMEJournal roleplay community. You'll have your IRL bestie....the mutual that you met through your IRL bestie....and online romance??? YES! As hard as this game hits you with the nostalgia, it will absolutely hit you in the feels as you build your relationships. And depending on how into the online world you were during this time, it will hit you even harder. You will laugh, you will cry, you will cringe, you will have a good time, you will have a bad time. All in all, it will be absolutely worth it. 

The fine people who worked on this game knew exactly how to capture the feel of growing up in the LJ / RP era of the internet. Everything, including the pixelated transitions between websites is perfectly recreated to bring you back to the 2000s. And even with how emotionally invested I was in this, I found myself most impressed with how these people were able to succeed in recreating what the internet was like for some of us in the early 2000s, for better and for worse.

But even if you didn't grow up with a LiveJournal, this game is still one of the most emotional stories I have ever experienced in gaming, with game-play mechanics that simplify the online interface style of gaming in ways that make it one of the more easily accessible online interface simulated game-play.

This game does deal with heavy topics. Some of these topics include assault, bullying, descriptions of explicit violence, gaslighting, and varying degrees of depression and anxiety. So be prepared mentally if these are topics are not easy to handle.

All in all....incredible game. Would strongly recommend. You'll get more out of it if you ever had a LJ account and/or got involved in online roleplay. But even if you didn't, this is still worth it if you are into story driven games.

[h1]Casual puzzle game about shooting cannons, sometimes in the right order[/h1]

On the fence here: this is a flawed, casual puzzler.

Your task: click cannons to make them shoot the targets. Only one cannon can be interacted with at the time, so it takes several seconds before you can shoot another one.

First, shots just make tunnels with walls disappear (if the target is shot as well) and thus make way for other cannons. Later, you get to rotate bullet deflectors and tunnels to make your shots reach the targets. Never during shooting though, and there's infinite ammo, i.e. infinite retries. Only one or two levels require a specific order and it's unclear whether that's by design or not.

Eventually, (almost) every level can be completed by clicking stuff until it works. The puzzle is to do it fast enough not to fall asleep in the process; I am only partially kidding.

[h1]Technical stuff[/h1]

Volume sliders for the mystifying (but oddly monotonous) music and sounds exist separately. There's no windowed/fullscreen switching, though the regular alt+enter works for transporting the window from screen to another monitor.

There are some bugs:
- If you shoot a cannon and direct the bullets back to your cannon, it will shoot perpetually as the bullets fill the cannon while it tries to empty itself. This causes a soft-lock that requires a level restart to continue.
- To remove walls, a constant flow of bullets is required from the cannon to the target. Level 50 (and possibly 47) has such long bullet paths that their stream fails to remove the walls they pass through. Failing that, you'll need to restart the level and try again.

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]

It's not a bad game, nor is it expensive. Yet it's not a very fun game either.

It can certainly waste a bit of time, taking me some 90 minutes to complete, plus minus 15 min (hard to estimate exactly because of the wall bug in level 50 that kept me in for half a dozen tries). At least all achievement worked in the end (but the game froze with painful broken sounds at the ending screen with typos, shown after lvl 50).

It could swing either way but with the lack of polish I am going with Not Recommended.

Once in a lifetime you'll come across a game that truly captures the history and cultural distinctions of the modern world the way a person can subjectively perceive it through our guided field of perspective. I have to admit, I had my doubts when I first learned of the game. After all, Battle Brigade? Will this game even be good? How ignorant was I to even have these thoughts. Little did I know I was about to indulge in what may have been the best 2 hours and 21 minutes of my life. The game started out strong. The opening scenes enticed the audience with a captivating enigma. I was so taken aback from the next-generation animation that I almost didn't even realize the underlying symbolism in the ongoing scenes. It wasn't until my twenty sixth viewing of the game where I finally got my bearings together and was able to focus on the gripping and labyrinthine stratagem. The underlying analogy for 19th century distopianism and the evangelical deviation of typical orthodoxy was enlightening to say the least. Just when I thought the game could not get any better, the increasing conflict before the climax began. I could not believe the complexity of the story as the main bee protagonist, Bellza, struggled with the everyday endeavors for a quintessential bee such as the consistent up- hill altercation of the fight against misogyny and the fiscal synergy of opposing interplanetary dynamisms. There I was, gripping to my chair as the conflict of the game began. I was so enticed by the game that I felt as if I was both practically and relatively apart of the game. This is a special kind of high that not even the strongest of drugs can give you. Was I part of the game? Am I inside the game right now? This game will leave you questioning existential nihilism and the objective skepticism of our perceived valuation of anthropological existence. At this point in the game, I was fully intoxicated by the avant-garde animated art style. That's when the plot finally aggrandized and I was completely stupefied. You could have lived a thousand years of isolation trying to predict the plot twist and you would never even scratch the surface of what actually transpires in the game. I was so bewildered that I actually had to pause the game so that my existential crisis didn't dive too deep inside of myself. Even pausing the game was surreal. It's almost as if life paused with the game. I felt as though I had actually become a cinematic tangent quantum. The effects are still wearing off and I haven't been able to watch the game in several years. I spent the following seven years afraid of what outside of my house actually looks like. Every single day and night I live in misery because I became fully aware that happiness is never achievable. I realized that human life has absolutely no meaning and that no matter what I ever do, it is of complete unimportance and in years from now, no recollection of my existence will prevail, meaning that if I died years ago, died now, or die sometime in the future it will not matter whatsoever to anyone. But, then again, the fact that I'm living doesn't matter either so I might as well stick around for awhile, living in complete isolation, condemned to a life of traumatic memories and a completely corrupted sub-conscience. Plan Bee literally ruined my life. 10/10

Honestly a surprisingly cool and deep game. It's like if Phasmaphobia had a bastard child with Viscera Cleanup Detail that was raised by the SCP foundation.

The premise is you're a crew of 1-4 players sent to clean up an area, you're usually given basic tasks. But each area also has an distortion (what the game calls it's version of SCP-like creatures) or two haunting it. You have to document and learn about them over the days of doing your tasks, while also exploring and learning the map, and then the final two days are setting up to capture or remove the distortion using everything you learned. You get money for permanent upgrades to your stats via buying furniture and decorating your apartment at the end of missions, but during missions you get a budget to spend on equipment thats delivered during the mission for immediate use, and what you don't spend gets taken out with you for furniture after.

The neatest thing is any way you change the map during a mission, such as installing cameras, installing doors, installing alarms, removing obstacles, repairing equipment, etc, carries over to all future playthroughs (or replayythroughs) of any mission at all that takes place on the same map, allowing you to, over time, change a map to give you the advantage.

One great thing I like about Cuphead is the access to being able to rebind inputs on a gamepad (or keyboard, but I use controller in this case). I didn't enjoy the original controls and rebound them to my liking to make it a more comfortable and enjoyable experience. I've managed to play through it multiple times using these controls and have loved every minute playing it (less when it comes down to S ranking everything). 

This leads me to my [b] Main [/b] problem with this game...
The controls you get are the one's you're stuck with.

At first I thought it wouldn't be too much of a problem and I'd get used to them, but I didn't want to continue playing if I won't enjoy the controls. I did try keyboard controls and my only comment on them is it's like talking with your hands (the Italian way), but you're hands are upside down and stuck in a crowded train. When I was trying to shoot air-bound enemies, I kept going to use the right stick to aim without moving and could only sort of do it when I rebound LT to stop, then use the right stick to aim. It worked, but the problem is something like this would've been preferred in the game as standard (this could just be down to personal preference though, but wanted to mention it anyway).

One small nit pick that isn't to do with rebinding controls, but is to do with how the game controls (and probably would just have to get used to it) is the jumping. It feels off for some reason and I'm not sure how to put my finger on it other than the arc that you jump doesn't feel either consistent or feels too sudden with faster angular movement mid-air. Apart from that, actual control of your character feels pretty good.

On a side note, after defeating one of the bosses (The one with the propeller hand and throws the floating bombs), there really wasn't a great deal of feedback onto how far into the fight I was. There didn't really feel like there was anything showing how well I was doing and how close I was to defeating them. I've been around since the beta tests back when the game ended for act 3, there was no faction and philosophy systems, and the devs hadnt even come up with act 5 or thought of adding in roguelite features.
