Been really giving this game some honest love and attention for a while now and I'm really torn on what kind of a review to give.  It's difficult to say yes or no.  Best way to put this is, if you're experienced with hockey team management games and have a good working knowledge of how a hockey team's front office works, I would definitely recommend it.

However, if you're a rank novice to this world (and most people are), it's a definite pass because documentation is SORELY lacking.  You'll get frustrated REALLY fast and want a refund.  This is a highly complex game and yes, it's impossible to provide details on how every little nuance works, but at the same time, when you're looking to get answers to simple questions like, "how can I look up/follow up on trade offers I've made that haven't been responded to yet," your only real option is to go to the FHM community forum and start weeding through everyone else's questions, gripes, release notes, and banal jokes and comments about the great team they put together.  And as anyone who's ever gone down this path before knows, there's an art to finding that just-right phrase or combination of words that will give you the precise answer you need to a particular question.  Then, when you've exhausted all the possibilities, throw your hands up in resignation, and start a new post to ask a question that's already been asked before, like all other forums you run the risk of getting shouted down by forum regulars because you didn't "SEARCH THE POSTS BEFORE POSTING!!!" and get immediately directed to the post that has your answer, which never showed up in your searches.

So now, after all this verbosity and consideration, I'll stick with this game and probably play it some more, but as a final yes/no, I just can't recommend it. I know for a fact that I'm only experiencing about 50-60% of what this game can do, but I just don't have the time to devote into doing deep research on how to play it.  Considering that most Steamers probably aren't hockey GM experts, my recommendation would be to start out with Eastside Hockey Manager first instead to get a feel for the genre.  It's an older game with a lackluster interface and a lot less bells and whistles, but at least it's intuitive enough that you don't need to spend more time trying to figure out [i]how[/i] to play the game than actually playing it.

I like this game a lot. In my mind, this is the version of FHM that finally eclipses the last EHM that was released, even with the 1.5 beta enabled. It's a bit buggy (ENABLE WEEKLY AUTO-SAVES!!!) and I've had a number of crashes, especially during the 2D sim portion of the game, but FHM 7 was patched up pretty quickly so I wouldn't let that deter you from purchasing this game if you are a fan of the genre.

The budget system is a very nice addition, and I would imagine if you play in lower-revenue leagues, would present a different facet of gameplay in terms of balancing your scouting and development budgets. The new scouting reports are rife with information that can help you discern between a draft-day bust and a draft-day gem; I picked up a guy in the 7th round that had great mental stats that my scouts reported favorably on, and he ended up being rated as a 4.5 star potential guy after a season. Conversely, a guy I drafted in the second round has completely flopped down to a 2 star potential guy. Those are the kind of features that keep me immersed in a GM sim.

FHM also does statistics and attributes much better than EHM. The difference between a solid 1st line forward and a franchise forwards is much more noticeable, as it should be. I love EHM to death, but Chris Tierney scoring 70 points in a season is one of those EHM things that likely wouldn't happen in FHM. There's also a section under 'Team Stats,' under your league's main page, that allows you to sort all the teams in your league by the aggregate of any specific attribute you would like, which makes evaluating where your team is at skill-wise very easy. 

And this is just a review of the run-of-the-mill, modern day, quick-start league. You can do so much more than that in this game. Historic matchups, what-if scenarios, individual player experiments, this game is the best sandbox hockey simulator that's ever existed for my money. Try beating Canada as Russia during the '72 Summit Series. Take over the Quebec Nordiques and tell Eric Lindros's dad to piss off. Become Julian BriseBois and win a Stanley Cup without cheating the salary cap lol. The possibilities are endless. And the gameplay, I think anyways, is now at a level where these kinds of challenges don't sound tedious anymore.

3. This may be difficult, but the way that advanced stats are moving forward in the NHL, a few more stats wouldn't hurt. xGF and xGA stats would be awesome.

First let me stipulate that there is a lot to like about FHM8 and for someone who has supported the franchise since FHM1 but has more often than not been a harsh critic of past iterations, I am slowly being won over with this current effort. That’s not to say I believe it is a perfect 10, but for the first time I can clearly see that the evolution of this franchise is now showing the promise we all desire. 

So to that end, if you are looking for a deep & engaging hockey fix, the plethora of gaming options provided by this game will be sure in some fashion to scratch that itch. 

Perhaps you are frustrated with the current direction of your favourite club and think you can do better, or maybe you want to change the course of history via its historical play, or perhaps want to create your own hockey universe, and climb the managerial and coaching ranks from Junior through to the Pro ranks and cap it off leading your chosen Nation to possible World Cup and Olympic glory.Whatever the approach you want to take, you will do no wrong picking up this years offering. 

Admittedly while I’m still not a fan of the current 2D game play or of it being particularly helpful in setting tactics and strategies, there is no denying it is slowly evolving in a positive fashion. Maybe it is just not my cup of tea in its current form.

Insofar as the Developers and FHM community is concerned. Everyone involved in this franchise has proven over time to be wonderfully engaged, extremely responsive and very helpful to both newcomers and seasoned pros alike. So I'm confident in saying you need not have any concerns on that front whatsoever. 

To conclude,  if your are at all harbouring the urge to test your hockey managerial and / coaching mettle, in my opinion this is a very worthwhile buy.

While some of the changes and improvements were nice, this is yet another inch forward priced as a full game. Started playing FHM 6 last year (it was cheap bc it wasnt recent) and fell in love with the series. This one raises that love so much. The ability to build arenas, see your scouting spread, and the budget system all make this feel like such a rich and unique game. It gives you a lot of control over your team in every dimension.

The AI trade system is a little broken. For instance, shipping off Eichel only gets you Tkachuk and a 4th, but teams will trade multiple picks and a prospect for a worse prospect. In my first campaign, Florida traded Barkov to Detroit for a low-tier prospect and a 3rd. As a Wings fan, I loved it, but it's not very realistic.

Considering this is only the 8th installment, this is a pretty good development pace. I would love to see more visualization of line strength. For instance, putting a ranking by each line kinda like Daily Faceoff does for teams' lines each day. Also, a college system needs to be established. Even if the rosters are just fake players except for NHL picks, something to create it as a viable alternative to the CHL needs to happen. A lot of top picks are taking the college route, and few USHL players are making that jump once you're two or three seasons in. Overall, good game. $40 is a little steep, but for me it's worth it.
Not perfect, but by far the best PC hockey simulator yet created.

I think that, overall, it is a good game. I'm just going to focus on the things it can work on.
- The filter resets every time I leave the page (to examine a player, for example). It is very frustrating to have to redo the filter every time. This is a surprise, as OOTP23 does not have the same problem. Do the devs exchange notes? I jest, but it really is annoying. 
- There's no easily accessible Trading Block tab. I would like to access who around the league is on the block, and the existing path is not intuitive, especially for new players.

This is a wonderful improvement, but a suggestion for the historical game, the ability and preference to play only one goalie, prior to 1965-66 when it was mandated, that Junior and senior goaltenders be brought out of the stands on the rare occasion of a goalie being injured. I do wish that the trading could be improved. Sometimes the AI makes unrealistic salary dumps. FHM8 GREAT Game for Simulation, I am awaiting the line change aspect to the game it is long overdue. its going to make the game even better hopefullly you will be able to interact during the game with line changes that impact games, 
trading for a great face off player, while protecting a one goal lead will help that team in the def zone late in games, which will give them the advantage to clear the puck down the ice. Right now you have to rely on the AI to make the matchup changes, which is not very accurate.

You can control your NHL team but you also have the option of being hands on with their minor league affiliate. To start of I have to state that i'm not a big hockey fan. I know close to nothing about tactics, squad building, or even individual player types. That said, I enjoy playing FHM (along with OOTP) despite not being a fan of either hockey or baseball because as a general management gamer there's a lot to keep me occupied which i'll get to but nevertheless there's still a lot that FHM does badly that ultimately lead to me not recommending it. Again I have to stress this: My review is based on me being a fan of sports management games in general not as a hockey fan in particular which means that my rec is based on whether you should buy this as a sports management fan first and foremost and not as a hockey fan first and foremost.

To begin with what the game does right: Having the full plethora of not just NHL players and foreign player but also future players is a big draw for me. I enjoy taking over a rebuilding team and drafting real live players and future superstars like Connor Bedard or Berkly Catton. It definitely adds that extra bit of realism that makes it more engaging. Moreover, being able to find a hidden gem in one of the numerous foreign leagues is super satisfying.

Another thing the game does well is stat keeping. Being able to track what every player and team is doing is super cool and while it doesn't quite match up to OOTP its still immersive enough that I can lose myself for hours just simulating and tracking how my players do stat-wise.

Unfortunately thats pretty much it for the positives. IMO there's alot more negatives than positives starting with:  Scouting is an absolute joke. I discovered FHM with FHM7 and while disliked the game I still thought if they improved the scouting it would make it very enjoyable indeed. Unfortunately FHM8 did not improve this at all. They introduced a monthly scouting budget points system that changes based on the team performance but this was a negligible if not completely irrelevant change. Basically if you hire enough scouts you'll still have a complete knowledge of regions and players, and will have a negligible effect on your overall budget you don't really have to do any kind of balancing. I sorta get why this is kinda hard for them to get right, but IMO the real enjoyment of these games (FHM and OOTP cause OOTP has the same problem) is the difference between being a building team and a win now team. And having a scouting system that prioritizes one over the other is something that I would like to see more emphasis on. 

In fact just to add to this I really do believe that the primary joy in this game is to be found in how one manages the contrasting team builds. The win-now. The rebuilding. And the balance or just so-so. Right now these distinctions just aren't defined enough. I've had too many saves already where i've gone from a rebuilding to so-so to win now over the course of one or two seasons simply because i've figured out how to win the game (hint: have a lot of two star rated players on minimum contracts and a few well payed but not over payed 3 star or plus  rated players. The AI will always commit big money to 4 and 5 star rated players meaning that the rest of their depth is just crap and you can be a perennial playoff team just by having more two star third and fourth liners than the AI.) Again, all of this is without me knowing anything about hockey tactics. Every save I start I literally just randomize the tactics and let the AI handle lines. All I focus on is making sure I have more two star players than the AI. This is basically mixing two criticisms into one but my overall point are A) make it harder to build a losing team into a wining one and make it harder to keep a winning team together and B) either make the AI smarter or make two star players less effective in the game.

Howling Village: Echoes (Inunakimura: Zankyou) is the official game to the 2020 J-horror film Howling Village (Inunakimura), which is directed by Shimizu Takashi and features Miyoshi Ayaka. The game was originally released in mobile platform in 2020, and now it is ported onto NS and PC. (The porting is bad though, the game even tells you to TAP the screen rather than CLICK.)

It's basically a point&click puzzle game with a linear story-telling. The game features 6 main characters, each one has its own route, and each route has its True Ending. The True Ending to a route is always blocked at first, you should play other routes to unlock it (like 428: Shibuya Scramble in a much simpler way). The game makes you feel like you have many choices and options, but in fact you don't. In order to clear the game you must play each route and each chapter in a certain order to unlock the True Ending. Like I said, it's pretty linear. As for the "more than 50 endings" they claim in the store page, well, it does have that many endings, but most of them are just meaningless Bad Ends. The game only has ONE TRUE ENDING, and you can't ever miss it.

By the way, the translation is very bad. Grammar errors and misspellings are everywhere, but above all the confusing tutorial translation is the worst. I was misled by the English tutorial first, only did I switch to Japanese can I realize how ridiculous the translation is. So I'll put the correct tutorial here: In the route selection page, a blue chapter indicates you have clear the True Ending to it. A blue-gray chapter indicates you have yet to clear the True Ending BECAUSE it is blocked, you can only unlock it by playing another chapter whose top right corner has a INCOMPLETE sign. After you replay the chapter with INCOMPLETE sign and trigger the right thing, the INCOMPLETE sign will become COMPLETE sign, and the once blue-gray chapter will become blue-red, which means the True Ending has now been unlocked. Clearing a chapter with Normal Ending or True Ending will grant you 5% progression, as the progression grows new chapters may be available, and once the progression becomes 100%, the epilogue will show. 

Now back to business, the game is a horror game, it has many cheap jump scares, most of which are not scary at all (I mean, not all but some of the jump scares still got me). The whole game is giving me a low-cost feeling. Maybe it is a good mobile horror game, but also a bad PC horror game. It reminds me of Tsugunohi, which I think is even worse than this one.

The most notable thing in the game is its plot. It's quite obvious that the game's plot has many connections to the Howling Village movie and shares some common ground with The Grudge (Ju-on), which is another famous J-horror film directed by Shimizu Takashi (There's even an Easter egg to Ju-on in the game). The game's plot is in a typical Ju-on style, 6 characters, 6 inevitable deaths by the same curse that cannot be lifted, 6 stand alone chapters intertwined in the end, all in one infamous haunted place created by the agony of many deaths. I think the game even has a better plot than the movie. It's a pity a good horror story like this is wasted in such a low-cost mobile game. Hana is especially a remarkably terrifying J-horror figure, just like Sayako in The Grudge or Sadako in The Ring, but Hana even doesn't have a proper CG in the game, leaving all things to my imagination.

Although you can play the game without having watched the movie, I strongly recommend watching the movie before or after playing the game. And if you have already watched the movie and rather like it, consider this game a must-play. Because the game answers some questions to the movie. Like when I watched the movie I wondered [spoiler] why did the men from the company abused the villagers? They could just kill them, abuse is clearly not necessary.[/spoiler] After playing the game I found the answer to it:[spoiler] Because the company director blamed the curse of Inunaki for his wife's death, so the abuse to the villagers is his way of revenge. [/spoiler] So the story of the movie is making much more sense now.

In a word, this is a good mobile game, not so good on PC, but still worth playing, especially for J-horror movie fans.

这游戏名字叫做《犬鸣村：残响》，是2020年清水崇执导的恐怖片《犬鸣村》的官方游戏，[strike] 没错，就是三吉彩花都救不了的那部烂片 [/strike]。这游戏原本是手游，现在则被移植到了NS和PC上。（而且移植得相当烂，日厂传统艺能了。）

游戏玩法是个point&click解谜。6名角色6条线，每条线有一个真结局。真结局一开始是锁定的，需要打其他角色的线才可以解锁（可以把玩法理解成一个低配428）。尽管这个游戏会让你产生一种自由度很高、分支剧情很多的错觉，但实际上这是个线性得不能再线性的游戏，因为解锁真结局需要按固定顺序来游玩章节。至于商店界面说的50个结局，绝大多数都是毫无意义的BE，这游戏真结局只有一个，不可能错过的。

顺便一提游戏英文翻译非常糟糕（[strike] all your base are belong to us[/strike]）。而最令人发指的就是教学都能翻得牛头不对马嘴，搞得我还切了日文版才搞清楚教学讲了啥。顺便把真正的教学放这里吧：在章节选择界面，蓝色的章节表示已经通关了真结局，蓝灰色的表示未通关真结局且真结局已被锁定，解除锁定的方式就是去玩另一条路线上带有INCOMPLETE标志（英文版）的章节，在该章内成功触发某个事件后该章的INCOMPLETE标志就会变为COMPLETE标志，然后原本那条线的蓝灰色章节就变成了蓝红色，表明真结局已被解锁可以打出来了。每通一个真结局和普通结局游戏完成度+5%，完成度升高后会解锁新章节，完成度100%后出整个游戏的真结局，然后就通关了。

言归正传，作为一个恐怖游戏而言，本作存在大量很low的jump scare，其中绝大多数都不恐怖（不过也有少数几个恐怖的）。整个游戏从头到尾充斥着一种廉价感。能看得出这游戏是一个优秀的恐怖手游，但绝对不是一个优秀的PC恐怖游戏。这让我想到了翌日，而且其实本游戏比翌日还要强一点。

本游戏做得最棒的地方，其实是剧情。这个游戏的剧情不但和电影版有很多联系，而且还带着浓浓的咒怨感（这游戏有一处咒怨的彩蛋，就是村长和夫人的名字分别叫刚雄和伽耶子）。且游戏的叙事结构也与咒怨非常相似——六个主角，六个注定的死亡，六条相互交织的叙事线，全部被一个诅咒之地联系了起来。我觉得这游戏的剧情可比那烂片的剧情要好太多了。很遗憾这么优秀的剧情却被浪费在了一个廉价的手游身上（这剧情要是拍成电影或者做成步行模拟游戏都很棒啊，偏偏就做了个点击手游，我该庆幸这手游好歹是买断制的吗）。我特别要提一下这游戏里的女鬼担当，Hana酱，她的形象真的太棒了——和服少女+缝合怪，天真的面庞+邪恶的肢体，形成一种绝妙的反差感，一眼就能看出这是只有日本人才能设计出的怪物形象。比起伽椰子来我更喜欢Hana这种类型的女鬼，伽椰子有点太露骨了，Hana这种克制感就很棒。但是Hana酱甚至连一张清晰的CG都没有，实在非常遗憾。

尽管没看过电影也不影响玩这游戏，但我还是建议看过电影再来玩或者玩完再去看电影。因为游戏和电影剧情有一定关联，游戏也解释了一些电影里没有解释的剧情。比如说我看电影的时候就奇怪[spoiler] 为什么电力公司的人要虐待村民呢？明明只要把村民杀了就好，并没有虐待的必要啊。 [/spoiler]然后玩了这个游戏我才找到了答案：[spoiler] 因为公司经理认为自己的妻子死于犬鸣村的诅咒，所以出于为妻子报仇的心理而虐杀了村民。 [/spoiler]这么一来就解释通了。

总之，作为手机上的恐怖游戏很棒，作为PC上的恐怖游戏就没这么棒了，不过还是值得一玩的，尤其是对于日恐电影粉丝来说。

'100 Hidden Cups' is a hidden object game set in a surreal environment. While the black-and-white hand-drawn graphics are decent, they don’t quite match the quality of other games in the series. However, the accompanying soundtrack does a good job of enhancing the atmosphere and drawing players further into the surreal setting. The game challenges players to find 100 hidden cups, offering a rewarding experience for completionists with 100 Steam achievements.
The game is brief and only took me about 5 minutes to complete and unlock all the achievements. Its single ending and automatic save feature make it simple to pick up and play without worrying about saving progress. I would rate the difficulty at around 4 out of 10 because some cups do not look like cups at all. Without a hint system, you may find yourself resorting to random clicking to locate the last hidden cup.
The game is described as "a difficult adventure for the eyes," and it certainly lives up to that description. Compared to other games in this series, however, this one does not live up to expectations. If you have never played a "100 Hidden" game before, I would not recommend starting with this one, as it may be very frustrating.
I purchased this game during a sale for 0.49€, which initially seemed like a fair price. However, after playing it, I found the experience disappointing even at the discounted rate. Given the game’s short length, lack of polish, and simplistic art style, the regular price feels completely unjustified. If you are still intrigued, I strongly recommend waiting for a deep discount before buying it.
Overall, '100 Hidden Cups' is a decent game to play during a short break, but it is definitely not the best in the series. There are several hidden object games on Steam that are not only better than this one but also free to play.
If you’re struggling to find that last cup or simply want to watch a playthrough, feel free to check out my full game playthrough video here:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=knybMTrdSFE
If you enjoy hidden object games, I would recommend trying out a free game on Steam called "Mushroom Cats." It offers a charming and lighthearted experience that is definitely worth checking out!

[b]Smushi Come Home[/b] by [b]SomeHumbleOnion[/b] takes the classic exploration / adventure platformer genre, and uses it to create an experience that is cozy, wholesome, memorable, and enjoyable.

The visual aesthetics of the game are clean, recognizable, and of good quality. 
Each chapter feels distinct, and features a good variety in gameplay elements — new abilities, new characters, new types of puzzles, new means to navigate the map, and new things to collect — which all help keep the player engaged throughout the game.
The soundtrack of the game varies between relaxing and upbeat, creating a light atmosphere that is propitious to adventure.

The game also features hidden objectives that further extend and enhance the gameplay experience.

[b]Smushi Come Home[/b] is overall a good quality, wholesome, and accessible exploration / adventure platformer game from [b]SomeHumbleOnion[/b].

This is a solid roguelite in a similar vein as Dead Cells or Rogue Legacy with a cool sense of style and a morbid sense of humor.  It is really for people who are into platforming and 2d combat with hard-hitting bosses.  And the workplace drama is great.

The game itself is fun to play.  You start each run from the beginning each time, like a rougelite.  And while you can choose the level path you take, it is always the same choices in the same order to change floors each time.  While that may seem limiting it does lend itself to making builds, as you know which bosses you will be facing and in which order.  

The builds have a lot of room to explore in them.  There are a wide variety of items to unlock in terms of basic scythes, spells, and cool-down "cloak" abilities.  In addition to that, there are three skill trees to build through each run focused on offense, defense, and spells.  All of these things are given to you randomly as you proceed through certain checkpoints in a run, so it stays fresh.  Though the randomness can make it hard to pre-plan a build.

Fair warning, I am writing this review after getting the "Finish the Game" achievement.  According to steam about 3% of players actually get that.  I can sort of see why. I purchased this game expecting a good roguelite experience but after a couple of hours playing this I'm really disappointed with what I got. Regular enemies hit way too hard, there is no countering or blocking of their attacks, there is a stun mechanic which works okay if you're just fighting in a 1vs1 but when you get into an area with multiple enemies it's actually better to just move along to the end of the level to get to the elevator unless you're stuck in a challenge room where you have to kill them to progress. Dashing seems to work okay, but it oftens puts you way too far, or when fighting bosses not far enough, and also has a cooldown so you can't spam it. Killing enemies also has little to no benefit since they don't drop currency you need, they MAY drop a healing orb or some item but it is not guaranteed and so far there is no indication that you can increase drop chances. So you can waste your time and get hit and lose health, or you can just move along and ignore the enemies.

The combat is really what makes or breaks a game like this and this one is very poorly designed. It's a 2D game where you're expected to fight in horizontal and vertical axis, but there is no diagonal movement. So you can be fighting enemies on the ground, have enemies above you attacking you at range and if you try to do a vertical attack, and they happen to move slightly to the side you miss and are just waving your scythe around the air doing nothing. Regular attacks don't lock on to enemies, so fighting bosses that move around a lot is a chore. It's just not fluid combat, and it completely ruins the experience for me.

Meta progression is also virtually non-existent. You get one currency for meta progression but it mostly unlocks cosmetics for the base hub, it can unlock new weapons but there is no option to choose what weapons + spells combo you want to take at the beginning of a run. You're stuck with only the basic scythe, which there is no way to upgrade permanently outside of the runs and you MAY get offered something at the beginning of a run via a contract but it seems to be RNG based. So, loads of weapons and spells but no way to guarantee a base loadout you can take on a run to try to get better at it over time. It's all RNG drop based. No way to upgrade your health, your defense, your curses, your base weapon, your unlockable weapons and spells, why even bother having meta progression then?

There is a level up system that gets you permanent unlocks for runs, but most of the unlocks are worthless. Curse re-rolls and elevators so you can skip the levels and go straight to the boss fights (with no upgrades to damage, health or mana from the start by the way). Between that and getting the feeling that running is better than fighting, why is your game encouraging me not to play it?

[h1] TLDR: 8/10 The definitive Jelly Car game. Not only does it have a ton of brand new levels, challenges, and abilities, every original level from the past games are remastered! Sadly though, the requirements for 100%ing the game REALLY start to drag after a while. [/h1]

[h3] Actual Review (No Spoilers) [/h3]
Pretty sure this is the best possible version of a JC sequel we could've gotten. This is one of the most classic mobile game series and I remember playing all the old ones growing up. The car definitely controls better on a controller than it did with mobile controls. You will definitely need the extra help because some of these levels are pretty brutal. It's hard to make soft-body physics consistently enjoyable, and I think JC is one of, if not the best implementation of it as a main feature. It does feel like a really annoying hindrance at times (aka, for any of the dev time challenges), but it has a surprisingly high skill ceiling.

As far as completion goes, there is a LOT of content and unlockable stuff. This is both a blessing and a curse, because each level has additional challenges to complete. Some of them are unique, but most are a selection of a couple different generic challenges (collect letters DKC style, complete a level backwards, etc) but all levels have at least the beat the dev time trial.

The time trials are pretty much the ONLY major complaint I have with 100%ing the game. Some levels are pretty easy, but oh my god there are some absolutely infuriating time trials. You'll be leagues ahead on some levels, only to get stuck trying to drive up a bumpy surface. It's literally just about timing and lining up correct angles, but soft-body physics are just not conducive to consistency and precision. There's also a co-op world, which you bet also has time trials. As if one bouncy car wasn't enough, you now get two chained together. Good luck! At least playing the co-op world normally is still really fun. The actual achievement list is pretty easy too, besides the skull levels which you'll be stuck on for a while.

There is also a community level hub which you can check out as well, it's got some really amazing levels that make clever use of game elements. I'd definitely recommend this game even if you didn't play the originals back in the day. 8/10

I stream obscure indie titles. It's what I do, at megateamup.com. I scour Steam for new releases that not many people have heard of, or will hear of. I paid money for this. I wanted to like Sit Down, Please. I really, really, really, really wanted to like it. Here's why I didn't.

Dialogue heavy is an understatement here. This is more of a visual novel than anything else. USE THE "FAST" STORY MODE IF YOU PLAY THIS GAME. An entire completion of this game took me 4 hours, a large majority of which was spent staring at the same interrogation scene and reading line after line of redundant dialogue. Every character says the same thing multiple times in different ways. There is actually an interesting story here, but you're going to miss the trees for the forest, if that makes any sense.

As far as gameplay goes, there really isn't much. There's one minigame where you keep a heart pumping and keep a body cool. The gameplay changes into a guitar hero like rhythm game at the very end, and there's a huge difficulty spike that brings everything to a grinding halt.

If you're the developer of this game and you read this, please don't mistake my negative comments for a personal affront. You clearly put a lot of effort into this and you have nothing to be ashamed of. You had something really interesting here, but you wholly missed why people who make visual media opt for a "show, don't tell" approach. Hours of looking at the same chair, lightbulb, and heart machine was not the way to go on this one. The characters talked about so many interesting scenes, and we didn't get to see any of them. Fatigue set in quickly from all of the reading that needs to be done to fully digest what's going on.

I can't recommend Sit Down, Please in its current state. More variety in gameplay and more showing of what was going on would have went so far to make this worth it, but it just wasn't. Take note of games like Papers, Please, that slowly introduce new gameplay mechanics in order to keep things fresh and interesting. This just doesn't do that, or really anything but make you tired and sad.

[b]ultimaze[/b] is a simple-looking puzzler with [b]200 labyrinthine levels[/b] and a ton of different mechanics (portals, keys, switches, disappearing tiles, block-pushing, magnets, springs, ice, bombs, etc.). levels are unlocked one by one, but there's a [b]skip level button[/b], so you can keep progressing if you get stuck on one. skipped levels weren't marked initially, so after a while it was problematic to remember what you hadn't actually solved, but a patch eventually took care of it.

[b]no move limit or timer[/b] on the levels, but there are [b]a few timing-based mechanics[/b] and a time limit can be set on custom levels in the editor, so I guess it's possible that some regular levels also have a timer (didn't try them all). [b]undo works from a fail state[/b], so if you happen to step on the wrong thing, no problem. [b]you can only carry one item[/b] for the most part (there's an item that extends the inventory), stepping on another replaces the current one and whatever you're holding can also be dropped.

controls aren't rebindable. wasd/arrows to move (can be held), space/shift to drop or activate an item, 'z' is undo (can also be held), 'r' is level reset, esc toggles full screen. the menu is always visible and can be navigated with the mouse. there's a handy [b]block guide[/b] that explains what everything does, but level names usually provide a hint on what needs to be done. a [b]level editor[/b] is also available with its own guide. no workshop support, level codes have to be shared.

it doesn't look or sound flashy, no music at all, but there's a volume slider for the effects, a player speed setting (always nice) and a brightness slider to make the background less blindingly white. windowed mode offers various sizes as well, but [b]there is no exit button[/b], have to switch to windowed mode and close the game like that, or press good old alt+f4.

while it might not look like much, [b]plenty of content, great puzzle variety and a low price make it an easy recommendation[/b].

There are not a lot of games that focus on indirect control as the core mechanic, and SoFG is probably the best one out of all of them. All the things you'd expect to be wrong with a game of this scope to budget ratio are there, from crunky UI to unevenly available information to arcane sub-sub-subsystems that might decide the outcome of your game if you haven't seen them before, to very uneven feel of quality between different playable elder gods...

But then if you're looking at this title, chances are at least some of the opacity, abundant complexity and plentiful soft failure states are actually a draw rather than a drawback for you.

The game has a number of subsystems that interact with each other. Plagues cause death, death can be used to spawn ghasts, which will enshadow the countryside, enshadowed locations corrupt their rulers and heroes with more shadow, at which point they will start ignoring the spreading plague.

However, the game is also full of heroes and rulers who will by default fairly easily undo anything you put into place. The key to winning the game is often two-fold - picking a core strategy early (which means learning enough about what they all are, which will take a while), and running distraction tactics until your core strategy completes.

You have a number of agents and evil god powers that are all able to make the world a little bit worse, but none of them will be enough to win the game on their own. Instead, the game essentially is about building out a self-growing engine of corruption and decay into the game world's independent systems.

Assassinate a ruler? A heir will take his place. Instead, steal a personal belonging of theirs and use it to engineer a scandal in a neighbouring kingdom, making war between them that much more likely.

Drive a local town into madness? The clerics and heroes will soon fix it. Instead, mask and hide the growing abyssal fish-people cult until it begins spilling over into new towns and you can curse entire family bloodlines.

Amass an orcish army and break the human kingdoms into dust? There's more of them and they will destroy you armies once they become notorious enough. Unless of course you have a secondary orcish horde ready to take over the now-abandoned lands of their slain brethren - and those of the razed human kingdoms, too.

Try to remove a ward against shadow a religious movement placed? They will place hundreds more. Instead, manipulate signs of prophecy to place your own minion as their prophet, and slowly turn the religion into one that spreads shadow for you instead.

The game has a stupid amount of options and eventually it makes it really fun to engage with the game, being able to pick from your vast array of tools to sculpt just the outcome you want. Until that happens, you're kind of stuck picking things up to try them out and learning that hey actually they don't do very much on their own at all, and that the process for finding out why they failed or what they even do is pretty obtuse. But, you know. Some days all that feels like a plus. Maybe today's that day for you?

PROS:
-Great artwork (character portraits, sprites, etc)
-Great music for each area

-The 8 secret spots give neat rewards that are very helpful and not game breaking
-Simple battle system

CONS:
-A lot of grammatical errors (too many commas when it should have been periods, misspelled a few things, etc). Feel like things should have been proofread before release.
-Font used for telling where you are/using ability in battle is way too dark and can barely see it.
-Quite a few spots where you can walk where you normally shouldn't be able to walk on (ex. first forest area on Kathleen's path, there are 2 spots where you can walk behind a big tree and then be able to walk out of bounds)
-Most areas only have 2 enemies. One area has 1 enemy and the last area has 3 enemies. I feel like they could have been a bit more creative with adding more monsters to fight. 
-Speaking of enemies, I noticed some enemies palettes are used more than once, though all but 1 are the same palette. Only one enemy was used at a different point in time and they took the time to change the color of it to make it seem a little more unique, whereas the rest are the exact same and just a slightly different name. Not as unique.
-One of King's abilities, War Roar, says it gives you Atk/Def buff to everyone, but it only gives attack.
-Speaking of buffs, when used they have a chance of missing. Never seen a game like this where buffs can miss. 
-No credits at the end of the game. To most that may not seem like a con, but when it comes to giving credit to people who worked on this, it should still be added and feels kinda disrespectful for not even recognizing who did what.
-As cool as the rewards are for the secret rooms, you have to walk every single tile in every dungeon/forest to find said rooms
-As of right now, the dlc is just extra cash for the devs as it does not give you the walkthrough. 
-States the game has over 15-20 hours of gameplay, but after collecting everything and walking pretty much every tile and talking to every npc, doing every sidequest, and finding any bugs I can find, I was able to beat the game in 10 hours. 
-No character progression in terms of character development
-Each character only learns up to 6 skills

As much as I enjoyed the game and am currently working on a playthrough on youtube to showcase the game, as it stands right now I cannot recommend it as much as I would like to. This is one of those games that could have been great, but ended up being very ordinary due to bugs and the laziness of the game devs.  EpiXR Games UG are the ones who made all the AERY games and they have used the same soundtrack for all of them!!! In the AERY games, none of the achievements work, but at least for the first time, they do work in One Last Memory.
This game is a walking simulator with narration about an old man and his memories and all the life changing events of his life.  The story is pretty ordinary and I guessed what would happen in the end.
This game's redeeming feature is its gorgeous graphics.  There are 6 chapters and each chapter was a different environment.  Some of them were stunning.  There is no combat involved.  You just pick up floating diamonds which represent memories which narrate the story.  There are also secrets in each level which are red floating diamonds.  They are harder to find.  A couple of the levels require keys to open a door/gate and these are blue diamonds.  Each collectable has a matched coloured aura, so they are fairly easy to find.  The secrets are sometimes hidden down tunnels.
The downside of each level is that there is no save.  If you quit halfway through a level, you are reset to the beginning of that level.  Some of the levels are quite long.  Level 3 was 90 minutes for me and I still didn't find everything!  Some of the levels are quite convoluted and it is easy to get lost.  A checkpoint is essential as not everyone has an hour to spare.
The soundtrack was annoying to me because I've heard it too many times!!  It was very loud and drowned out the narrator's voice.  I turned the sound off but I could still hear the 'loud thumping' of the person's footsteps, so off came my headset.
*Bugs*  There is a bug towards the end of level 4.  I entered the tunnel to pick up the secret in the cavern and I couldn't move to get it.  There is also some sort of bug at the end.  You just get a black screen and then can't exit out of the game.  I used Esc but that didn't work.  I had to Ctrl+Alt+Del out of the game, so not a good finish.
Overall, I did enjoy the game because it was peaceful and there was plenty of eye candy.  I was just disappointed that the lazy devs didn't source another soundtrack.  There definitely needs to be a checkpoint in the middle of every level and the bugs need to be fixed.  I don't have much hope that will ever happen.
Interestingly, they are releasing a reimagined version of this game in June 2022.  It looks like there is combat in it.

In its current state, I cannot for the life of me recommend this unpolished game.

There's a lot of work that needs to be done in both UI and the barely defined gameplay departments, from minor patches to noticeable bug fixes. Starting with the former, there are some graphical glitches at draw distance that can be seen depending on where you aim. Plus, there's the annoying footstep sound effect that makes me wonder if the unnamed protagonist had shovels below his shoes or something and resulted in me having to change the volumes in game though not by much since the narration is associated with that as well. There's also no indication for the movement controls anywhere, so much so that it took me a bit to notice that I could run and jump with the controls I've learnt from other first person perspective games.

For the latter we can start mentioning the soul-crushing lack of mid level save state. I learned this the hard way after resetting Act 4 because I couldn't get past an invisible wall to get the last collectible for the level, attributing it at the time to a load error. Since at the time of writing this such bugs haven't been fixed, not only can't you get all of the achievements, you have to beat each level in one go, no questions asked.

Furthermore, we have what happens at the very end of the game. Without spoiling anything, once you are entering what I assume is the last cutscene after going through the final act, the game goes into a loading screen and just stays there without going further. No number of button presses, pausing nor prayers worked, leaving me to close the game and getting a menu glitch where the start menu was on top of the pause one. What a fitting finale to this 4 hours long run.

Having said all of the above, there's still some positive aspects to it. There's the tragic tale and the slow rock and new wave soundtrack which separately got me different kinds of enjoyment but not always fit together leaving me wondering if the people working on them talked to each other before its integration. Most importantly, the nature setting made this one of my most recent screenshot heavy games to date. There must be at least 200+ in my folder, many worth of being wallpaper candidates mind you. I just couldn't help myself considering that apart from that the only gameplay noteworthy were the secrets scattered around each level, which weren't difficult to get aside from the exceptioned one already mentioned.

But in the end, not even the screenshots nor its cheap price can make me overlook all its problems. I suggest either waiting for a series of patches or giving another game a chance.

I'll start out by saying that Andalia is definitely a bit rough around the edges, and I was pretty skeptical when I first saw this game, but I'm very happy that I stuck with this game!
I'm not gonna list every pro and con, but here's some things that I think are important to know, and aren't immediately obvious just looking at the store page.

Pros:

Six entirely distinct factions (!!!). Having this many factions, each with their own units and buildings, is something you very rarely see in an RTS game, let alone a game with a single developer and a price tag like this!
And it's not like the number is so high because factions don't have much to offer. Every faction has a unique theme, and around 9 units each (Necropolis has a lot more if you count the skeleton variants they can only get through magic!).

The game has so much passion put into it. Every unit and building has an unique model and textures, and with the amount of content this game has, that's very ambitious. The game has an official discord server with a small community, and you can find the dev there, sometimes playing the game with the community, and always open for feedback.

Multiplayer is something that many players take for granted, but it takes a lot of time and effort to implement something like that, so it should e recognized that this game has a multiplayer that works well. Even you don't have a friend to play with, you can join the discord, where you can find people to play with, and the ai for the game actually knows how to to put up a fight, so that's another option.

At the time of writing this review, the game still receives updates to many aspects of the game. Some are smaller than others, but the constant additions, balance changes, and quality of life features really add up over time!

Cons:

The gameplay is slow. There's a setting to increase game speed, which I'd highly recommend you use, but even then, the game has a lot of different resources you have to manage, and a lot of time will be spent building up your economy.

The game doesn't have a quirky artstyle, and the graphics are can be pretty plain. There's a ton of maps, units, and buildings, each with their own graphics, but there's few of them I'd really call beautiful, even if there's a few I do enjoy. The style is definitely nothing to write home about, but at least I can say that the game has a consisten style.

The gameplay experience is mostly bugfree, but it could be a more polished experience, and lacks a few quality of life features that you'd see in bigger games, but the game still received patches aimed to improve on these aspects, so eventually this might not be an issue, but for now there's still room for improvements.

No More Heroes 3 takes some steps forward and some steps backwards. Even in just the shiny new engine visuals, some scenes look stupid good while others make characters look like they're made of clay. And I think that's the highlight of the vibe here: It's good, but boy is it bad at times.

Multiple weapons and multiple playable characters are gone. One beam katana, one character. New Game+ exists, but for what reason? By the time you clear the base game, you've already unlocked everything. Only reason that sticks out is maybe you want a harder difficulty run.

The open world is back. I know totally gutting it made NMH2 feel a little empty, but this open world is only slightly better than NMH1. You will crash into invisible walls and uneven ground geometry. The only reason you drive is to get to the next objective and there is nothing else happening in the world.

Chores are here again, and it's fine. I don't think they're as painstakingly bad as previously, so I'm good enough with them.

I think the bigger chore here is getting through some of the dialogue. There's a lot of good dialogue but sometimes so much fluff is injected into a conversation that it kills all pacing the moment was building. It's like having a pizza in front of you but having to sit through a real-estate sales pitch before you can eat a slice.

The first few boss fights are harder than the later ones. Some boss fights in particular are egregiously bad.

The main unlockables are special power-up chips, that are actually kinda cool but unbalanced, and t-shirts. Stop forcing t-shirts as a rewarding collectible. I think the majority of players find a t-shirt that they love and don't plan to change out of. At least that's how I felt about it.

Most of all I really miss the boss fight as a reward for clearing an area of enemies. Splitting the fights into random areas of the map feels like unnecessary padding that doesn't reward a boss fight. Feel like this is the worst of the game by far.

So what's good? Suda's style, the combat feels good even if limited, the music, and the off-the-wall goofy s**t the game throws at you constantly. It's really catered specifically for NMH fans, but even then, this game can be a hard sell.

There are times when I wish Steam had a "mixed" rating. This is one of those moments.

In terms of combat, it is even more simplified than what was present in 1 and 2. 
The story is all over the place. Some scenes are solely just Takashi Miike glazing.
Outside of a few bosses, most of the boss fights were lame as shit.

I can tell this has a lot of love from Goichi Suda himself. Maybe there's something I'm not understanding with this game... but, this really is a downgrade when compared to the likes of Travis Strikes Again.

At first glance, Conundrum is a short and fairly easy pixelated puzzle/platformer.  You are presented with a series of rooms with switches, boxes, and gates that must be navigated through to proceed through the complex. It uses the standard keyboard/mouse combinations (WASD, run, jump, interact).

There is no save function so if you exit the game, you will start from the beginning. I finished my first pass through in under 45 minutes so the lack of save on exit was not a big deal.

Once you have achieved the first ending, a series of new paths open up and things become more interesting and a whole lot more complicated. When you exit and restart in the first room, these new paths remain accessible. What first seemed like a really short game expands as previously hidden areas open and new challenges are presented. I would encourage players to work through the optional endings just to see how much bigger Conundrum is than it first appears.

With the exception of one timed platform sequence, the puzzles are not hard and most involve a combination of platform jumping and box climbing.  For the most part, the platforming does not require precision and I had few issues. In a nice change from some other games, boxes are stored in your inventory and positioned and stacked with a single key. So, no running around while trying to hold onto a box. The boxes defy gravity so you can do some serious climbing with just two of them! In an optional area, you will also get to practice your evasion skills but the only penalty for being caught is a respawn and some retracing of steps. 

As I attempted to get the last two achievements, the lack of a save function became an irritant. Retrying sections towards the outer edges of Conundrum meant backtracking countless times (unless I was willing to leave the game running). 

I recommend this game to those who like fairly simple exploratory puzzlers with a twist. I've enjoyed the experience and am still finding new things as I aim for 100%. Gamers who pursue multiple endings will definitely get their money's worth, as it takes time and an attention to detail to discover the hidden features of Conundrum.

Conundrum is a first-person puzzle game which takes large inspiration from games like Portal and the Talos Principle. Starting off simple enough, the game takes you through a set of test chambers manipulating buttons, switches, and boxes to get to an exit. It's all standard stuff, until you reach the game's ending 20 minutes in, unlocking a Glitch Visor. Here is where the game becomes something special.

Developer Nogam uses everything in the toolkit and more to make the most of the space given. With the help of the Glitch Visor, the player is asked to deconstruct the levels in the first 20 minutes and use the items, world, and design to find various hidden exits. The love of secrets and hidden mysteries are apparent, and each new discovery and hidden passageway is not only crucial to finding the ultimate exit, but enjoyable when you realize the world doubles back frequently on itself. 

While I love everything introduced, I wish there was more. More mechanics, more room types, and more on the presentation side. There is little to no music and some of the endings blend together narratively because they boil down to one way of escape over another. The voice acting doesn't help this, as I wish they got even a robot voice to deliver lines as opposed to the accent-heavy mess that exists now. Additionally, basically the final puzzle in the game is a joy to gather the clues to solve for, but the actual solution is nonsensical, and I wish had way more direction that compares to how well the rest of the game directs the player.

Overall, Conundrum is an impressive effort from this developer and I'd love to see more attempts at breaking the mold and pushing the narrative further.

Richard West and the Golden Mask is a Boy's Own adventure in the vein of Indiana Jones.  It was great fun and a very enjoyable adventure.  It is quite short to complete as most players only take 1-2 hours.  Don't take any notice of my time as I have an incredible gift of dying far too much.  Lazarus is my middle name!
Richard West is an archaeologist and the location of the fabled Golden Mask was finally discovered.  He must be Superman in disguise because he is quite athletic and able to jump large gaps and never seemed to tire.
The game has 3 chapters and each chapter takes you deeper into the temple.  There are artefacts to discover and well hidden keys to claim to open the door to the next level.  Each level has its booby traps, puzzles and mysteries to solve.  The booby traps were my nemesis, especially the rotating scythes.  Each level has about 3 checkpoints, so if you die, it goes back to that.
This game requires quite a bit of dexterity and strategy to overcome the pits and traps.  A couple of the segments were timed whereby you pull a lever and you need to complete an obstacle course in time.  It is quite doable as I stayed alive long enough to complete them!
Graphics are basic poly, so very minimalist.   It did suit the genre.  Some parts of the temple were beautiful and quite realistic.
Music was suitable for each occasion.  Dramatic when you have to run; spooky when you're in a dark maze and sometimes just silence.  Sound effects like footsteps, crackling of the torch, the closing of doors and other traps were well done.  The groan when Richard died (usually by breaking his neck) was heard too often my end!
I got over half of the achievements, but one was not to die in the game.  I obviously didn't get that one!  Another is to complete the game under an hour.  
If you want a fun, short game to test your reflexes...and want to be superman....this is it.  Recommend for kids 10+ as the only violence is Richard dying.  Watch your step!

One is the pacing. Especially in the tutorial but later too, you just sit there waiting for the dialoge to finally progress, because there's no skip button. A "story-driven RPG" as it says on the steam store page, this is absolutely not.

A bigger issue is the enemies. They're too bullet spongy. Sure, so are you, but having to shoot at an enemy for what feels like a full minute is just awful. It feels like all you have is a water gun and while the "Dart" enemies, the most basic ones, are one ply toilet paper and shredded in half a second, the rest of them are stacks of glossy paper.
Your gun also has about the reach of a water gun, and the "bullet speed" of one. The reach s abysmal but even if it was more, you'd hardly hit anything but stationary targets. Not helped with aiming is that your shots go below enemies. Sometimes they still miraculously hit but would it have been so hard to just adjust the plane the enemies sit on a tad downwards so you don't actually always shoot under them and want to compensate by aiming higher which you obviously can't?

Another small issue, that annoyed me greatly, is the radar. See, it's your normal circular radar sitting in a square box. If an enemy or objective is outside the range displayed in the box, its symbol is drawn at the edge of the box. So far so normal. Now the issue is, 99% of the time the symbols not in range sit in the corner of the square.
From what I can see, they didn't place them like any other game, where they'd place them at the intersection of an imaginary line from you to the target and the box edge. Instead, it seems to be that they took the area currently displayed in the radar. If the thing is directly in front of that area, it gets placed on the upper line, directly to the left of that area, left line, and so on. Anything outside of that gets placed in the corners. Assuming the radar box was 10x10 meters, that means anything in front of you that is more than 5 meters to either side gets placed in the corner.
Allow me to demonstrate: https://files.catbox.moe/idsj4x.png
This also means the radar is very finnicky. Thanks to how perspective and distance works, if your target is far enough away, moving your mouse a tiny bit means it falls out of that "scan area" again and mostly jumps from corner to corner.
I mean, look how much I moved the view so that the green target icon jumped to the other corner:
https://files.catbox.moe/1lp5g5.gif
This thirdly means than no matter how far an enemy is away, it canmove quite quickly on the radar if it's not in a corner, giving the wrong impression of being right next to you.
Yea, much text and illustrations for such a small issue but damn did it irk me. How do you even make such an error?

finally, he shield should recharche way faster when no enemy is around so you don't spend most of your time ingame waiting for the shield..

A buggy, roughly translated adventure that can definitely be enjoyed AFTER its bugs have been patched, and the game gets playtested by anyone but the buyers. To start off, you play as a butler apprentice proving his worth to a questionable looking Egyptian heir. Fortunately, you're not alone, as you have the help of the maid sisters and the ever-watchful chief steward to keep you in line. It's a simple story that has its charm and humor, and it's fully voiced, so bonus points to them. As for the gameplay, it revolves around collecting items, fishing, and playing a bunch of other mini-games as the days pass by. You gain points for performing well in these games and tasks and, of course, lose them on failure. Nothing too crazy, but it's fun enough to at least play it out to see what the game throws at you next.

The only truly positive thing to note here is the art, interactions, and scenes. The hentai and art are amazing and carry this game HARD; I would buy the game for the art alone at its price. As for the scenes themselves, they are all fully voiced, and that goes for the rest of the game too.

Now onto what brings this game down: the bugs and translation. The translation is, as mentioned, rough. You'll notice it in every other sentence, and for the most part, you can still understand it, but sometimes I have to double-read a line just to make sure I got it all. The translation can be overlooked, but what can't be are the bugs. I had CGS stuck on my screen, which required a restart, and a failure to load a BGM theme that kept appearing, which also required a restart. Lastly, I had my save files overwritten with what I can only assume to be dev saves as it came right after an update, resetting my progress. (Also, I never even got any Steam achievements, so more food for the devs.)

Overall, I'd wait a bit for some patches to be rolled out, or a sale. Regardless, if you can look past its very real faults, the art makes the game an excellent addition to any collection, and for only 5 dollars? You can enjoy the company of an Egyptian loli in ALL its beauty.

A spooky first-person dungeon crawler with a retro aesthetic, Lunacid is a great game with a large game world to explore. RPG elements are present in the stats you can upgrade when you level up, giving you freedom over your build, whether you want to focus on melee combat, ranged combat, mobility or spellcasting.

The gameplay of Lunacid isn't particularly complex, but then first-person games are rarely especially complicated unless they're gritty realism survival games. As you'd likely expect from a first-person game, combat isn't all that deep either. But whilst you'd expect dodging to be limited with a first-person camera and weapon strikes to be fairly basic, there's also the added fact that the game entirely lacks shields (or at least does from the first half of the game, as I haven't completed it yet), relying instead on the use of your weapon stats for blocking. Ranged combat does feel a little overpowered at times, though there are sections of the game (not counting the start before you even get a hold of a ranged weapon) where you're pretty much forced to use a melee weapon or spells on account of visibility or enemies being immune to normal weapon damage. And even then, some enemies do shoot back at you or move quite fast.

Graphically, the game is stylistically retro, so it certainly won't be winning any awards in technical capability. It's aesthetic is on-point though, reminiscent of the less cutesy aspects of Spooky's Jumpscare Mansion (but given Akuma Kira also worked on that game, it's hardly surprising). The design element of the graphics is amazing and when combined with the soundtrack and environmental sounds, Lunacid really impresses. I think this is really what makes it stand out compared to the games of the era its emulating - modern sound design and aesthetics appealing to contemporary tastes. As well as of course modern technical abilities in the ways of frame rate, controls and resolution and such.

Control-wise, this is where things are a little frustrating. Rebinding requires editing a text config file - which you can access through the in-game menu, but it does tab you out to edit it. Items are not accessible via a traditional hotkey system, but rather have to be scrolled through, with fairly odd default keyboard bindings. This of course is a controller-friendly method, but it does diminish the experience slightly on a mouse-keyboard setup. I can let Lunacid off for this, being an indie game with a small team.

Character creation is... almost infinitely free (not counting stats/class options). Not that any of the aesthetic side matters much, being a single-player first-person game where NPCs only speak directly to you and not to each other. As such, though there is an extensive selection of available pronouns (yay, non-binary representation!) and fully customisable player appearance through the allowance for custom-made character portraits, none of it actually means anything (your pronouns aren't actually used at any point in the game). The most meaningful option really is the ability to choose whether to hold weapons left-handedly or right-handedly. The reason I say near-infinite though is that there isn't an option (that I can see) to input custom pronouns; the player's visible hand will always appear grubby, pale and human (even though even some of the default portraits don't match up to it); and despite everything else being customisable, one thing you can't tweak is your camera height.

All in all, this is a fun and sufficiently scary game that I very much recommend. There's plenty of content, it does well with the spooky atmosphere without relying on cheap jumpscares (unless you count enemies sneaking up on you), the gameplay is simple but fun and the aesthetics are great. A solid 8/10 game (nothing groundbreaking or spectacular, but still enjoyable with flaws that can be easily overlooked).

Lunacid is an incredible dungeoncrawler-RPG from an era long past, offering an unforgettable, but sometimes flawed experience full of references to FromSoft games.

Positive:
+ Music
+ Artstyle
+ Environments & Atmosphere
+ Lore
+ Incredible Weapon, Spell & Enemy Variety
+ Breaking different parts of enemy bodies to weaken or disarm them
+ Lots of rewarding secrets in the levels, tons of missable, optional, well-hidden areas
+ No handholding
+ Some emergent gameplay

Negative:
- Combat is very basic and gets boring after a while. Enemies are never dangerous because they deal very little damage and have extremely limited movesets. Bosses are damage sponges and take way too long to kill while never being interesting encounters. A parry and a dodge ability would do a lot for this game, with slightly more complex enemies to balance it out
- Leveldesign is a mixed bag. Half the levels are pretty good, but the other levels are just mostly empty maze-like hallways and rooms full of enemies
- NPCs are just... ok. There's not much dialogue, they don't have a lot of personality, and their questlines are too short and simple

Overall, this game is an awesome experience I'd recommend to any fan of dungeoncrawlers and FromSoft games, but it sometimes left me a little frustrated, imagining what it could have been with better combat, levels and NPCs.

The good:
-Solid first person action RPG gameplay with tons of weapons to find, spells to learn and experiment with, along with some light platforming. Enemies provide a challenge and nice design variety. Progression is largely gated through stronger combat encounters, but rarely feels unfair. 
-Combat itself features nice feedback, with weapons feeling snappy and sound design making it clear when weapons are effective and when they aren't.
-The atmosphere absolutely nails the moody and Gothic PS1 aesthetic it's going for, with a top-notch synthesized soundtrack. Even features an in-game manual to complete the illusion that it's a long-lost classic from the 90s.
-Level design is sprawling and maze-like, with frequently unlocked shortcuts. World design is interconnected and features a variety of settings that feel unique. Absolutely captures the FromSoftware feeling of world building and level design.
-Loads of secrets that almost always reward your exploration and experimentation with new weapons, spells, useful consumables, NPCs with quests, and optional areas.
-Game length feels just right for this type of game and price point. Not an overly short game, but does not overstay its welcome.

The bad:
-Combat is pretty basic and a bit clunky, sometimes clinging to its inspirations a little too well.
Most basic enemies have pretty limited move sets and AI. Only a small handful of bosses and mini-bosses.
-Weapon and spell balance isn't the greatest, discouraging experimentation once you find something overpowered.
-RPG features aren't as robust as later FromSoft titles, leading to “builds” feeling samey. 
-Lore is somewhat obtuse, even more so than the games that inspired it.
-Lack of in-game map feature will undoubtedly be a turn-off for some, especially in the more convoluted and maze-like dungeons. I got lost frequently in some areas.
-Some of the more obscure secrets feel pretty inscrutable. Many solutions aren't well-telegraphed in the game itself and will require outside help like guides and wikis.
-Minor polishing nitpicks like sporadic spelling errors and the occasional menu bug.

Conclusion: Lunacid stands tall next to the games that inspired it. It perfectly captures the feeling of games like King's Field, Shadow Tower, and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, with a sprinkling of modern flavor from games like Dark Souls and Elder Scrolls. It retains many of those games' rough edges as well, and will probably not win over anyone who thought those games were too unforgiving or cryptic. Still, it will appeal to anyone who loves the darkly fantastic and mysterious worlds in those other games.

Using spells in innovative (but probably intended) ways made it feel like I was out-smarting the game. The levels are diverse, crafting a desire to explore, which is rewarded by many hidden areas to find.

Make no mistake, the game is fantastic, but it's not without its flaws. The slow combat can be a definite deterrence for some, and the enemy AI does it no favors. The player power creep is a little too exponential, with enemies going from sponges to fodder way too suddenly. I found the backstep mechanic to become obsolete after a few levels. An additional boss or two would also help the pacing.

If you think you wouldn't like Lunacid, you probably wouldn't. If you think you would like Lunacid, you'll love it.

[h2]In search of a grim but very charming gaming experience? Look no further.[/h2]
I want to preface this review by mentioning that I haven't played any of the Fromsoft games Lunacid has been inspired by, so I will review the game on its own merits.

[list][*] Aside from the completely useless pronoun selection at the beginning of the game which absolutely doesn't affect any dialogue and was apparently only added as a kneejerk reaction by the devs to "own the chuds", I don't have many qualms with Lunacid.
Lunacid is a first-person dungeon crawler set in a giant underground maze of temples, caves, crypts, forests and more inhabited by the dark creatures born there and those that were exiled into the depths. The main "story" hook is finding a way to escape and there's not much more than that, but the game employs the kind of ambient storytelling that feeds you tidbits of the lore at a steady pace via books and the environment, allowing you to piece it all together yourself, which is something I enjoy in games.
[*]The areas themselves are varied and feature a lot of secrets, but some of them could've needed a little bit more exciting vistas in my opinion. But I understand that the devs went for a gloomy, almost oppressive vibe with many of the locales and thankfully, none of them overstay their welcome too much.
[*]Combat is rather simple and doesn't really evolve much throughout the game. You charge up your attack and try to damage the enemy without getting hit yourself. Expect a lot of kiting, especially during the very few boss battles.
The spells are varied enough to stop them from being boring. You got utility spells that let you create your own path, spells that don't affect gameplay too much and exist purely for lore reasons as well as your tried and tested combat spells, which were not created equally as a very few really outperform the rest.
[*]Lunacid's OST really surprised me. Some of the BGM reminded me of Silent Hill, Castlevania and even Ocarina of Time. There's a lot of variety here and every song is a perfect fit for its respective area in my opinion.
[/list]
[h3][b]Conclusion:[/b][/h3]
Apart from the combat staying rather simplistic throughout the whole game, I enjoyed my time with Lunacid and will be on the lookout for more games of its kind.

Seriously, I probably would've kept trying if there was a map or no permadeath.

This is an anti-lemmings game, in which you have to destroy all the robots in each puzzlestage.

The puzzles themselves aren't that good, there is generally a lot of ways to cheese them and I think quite a few of them have a lot of noise (in the sense that they can be solved trivially  but there are still a lot of unused stuff). I'd say that's sloppy design but I actually like that. I think some alternative ways of solving the puzzles are actually by design and I kinda like it when you get different ways of solving a puzzle. Only, the puzzles themselves are too easy. Besides the noise and cheese, even when you solve it the intended way, it only takes at most one or two attempts to know how to solve them. I think this idea could be developed further, into a longer and more challenging game.

You also get introduced to new mechanics every now and then, which is both good and bad, but in particular the first puzzles after the first appearance of a mechanic are kind of tutorials so when that happens that's a free stage.

For its price, overall, its a cool, short but fun and challenging game. The effects, the variety of skins and trails make this game very polished. Would recommend if you like games like Geometry Dash and Celeste.

The game sure ain't polished:
* The skin resets to the default one after reopening the game. Not that it matters since the game is so short.
* For a "speedrun action game" it sure is weird there's no try again button after completing the level. You have to go to the menu and then reenter the level.
* There's no turn-off music button in options. You can turn it off but there's no imidiate way to do that. Honestly it's kinda exhausting to listen to the same song over and over again. Same as with skins, options reset after reopening the game.
* You can't exit the level you're playing. You have to complete it or exit the game.
* The coolest skins are unlocked at the very end so there's no time to actually enjoy them.
* I can't get the achivement for beating every level under 50 seconds tho I have achivements for beating each level individually. Kinda sad.
* Speed tiles are *saturated* yellow and slow tiles are *desaturated* blue. Where is consistency?
* There are no transitions between levels.
* Some levels are kinda boring. Just pressing right arrow.
* Some levels have some unnecessary red tiles.
* Every level has the same background so I feel like I am playing the same level each time. Just change the color, it ain't too hard.

It's not like the game is bad, just unpolished. I liked it regardless

-A good variety of loot and builds to try out and upgrade

Negatives:
-A somewhat large emphasis on RNG, especially in the early game (or in the late game with a sub-optimal build). You have damage variance, crit variance, and chance to miss. There are ways to mitigate some of these, but in ladder mode you often won't be able to and you just have to accept defeat or attempt reloading the stage (reloading the stage doesn't refresh the rng seed).
-Acquiring Set bonuses in ladder mode is very unreliable, because you have no inventory there other than what you have equipped. Sets usually have 3-5 pieces, so you're stuck having to wear bad half finished sets in hopes you find the other pieces later. This incentives ignoring sets and just sticking with 'generic good stuff' instead.
-Despite normal mode having loot carryover as a feature, it is not balanced around this at all. If you carry over your gear you will annihilate everything; nothing will pose you any threat. It's quite strange because you have the option to minmax a set of gear and upgrade it over multiple runs, but you never have any enemies that compete in power with it. It's like getting ultimate equipment without anything to use it on.


All in all for 4-5$ you'll probably enjoy it for several hours, just don't go in expecting a long-term roguelite experience.

Base Wars is a unique strategy concept, it feels mechanically similar to RTS games like Age of Empires and Starcraft but packaged in a turn based format. I'd describe it as chess without a grid.

Online games are easy to set up and the map editor is very in-depth. There are some missing extras like a full singleplayer campaign and a replay system, but those are claimed to be coming soon. 

If you aren't a fan of turn-based strategy games, you will not like waiting in Base Wars. Mechanically the game is beginner friendly but it takes a while to get used to planning moves and positioning units, which means new players tend to take a long time to play. Your first games will probably take an hour, but after that curve games take 15-30 minutes. 

If you are a fan of turn-based strategy games, then you should try Base Wars out. It's been a blast to play and I'm constantly running into new strategies and tactics. If you don't have friends to play with (or even if you do) then I really recommend you join the Discord. The discord community is very small (like 5 people as of now) but that's the best way to set up multiplayer games. The dev is also active there and has been open to feedback.

I know that's not particularly helpful, but then again, this isn't a particularly deep game.

It is more or less a Match-3 game (in broad terms), where you must move your protagonist (a cat samurai) across a grid, surrounded by enemies and as you pass by or end up concluding your move sequence adjacent to a sufficient number of enemies, you will destroy them and remove them from the board.  Some enemies will randomly become "angry" and if you end your turn adjacent to them, they will injure you (and you only have a certain number of hit-points/hearts per level).

Obviously, as the dozens of levels go on, you will receive some special powers (e.g. a potion to quell all the angry enemies on the game board) that are each usable once per level, and some enemies will require two hits to destroy, etc.

There's even a few boss-fights with a variety of special conditions that you must contrive to bring about with your movement and attack patterns in order to beat.

It's not a terribly difficult game (on average difficulty.....there is a harder difficulty with less health), and I only died a handful of time over dozens of levels, and almost always on a boss fight.  The achievements are more-or-less easy to get and you will ultimately get almost all of them just through a normal playthrough (although there is one for killing a huge number of opponents where you will just have to avoid beating the level even when it's in your sights and deliberately stick around killing non-specified opponents rather than the ones the level wants you to slay, just so your can rack up a high enough number of kills).

So, it's certainly not anything special, but it's a fun way to kill ~8 hours if you're in the mood for a palate cleanser between harder, more intellectually demanding games.

I played this game on stream, if you want to watch my initial impressions, the archive will be linked at the bottom of the review.

Overall, this game has cute graphics and a really interesting concept that is unfortunately executed poorly.
You will expand your island town and recover crystals that are found throughout the world below.
Exploring the continent below entails common survival elements (but let me be clear: this is not a survival game) of exploring for resources to collect and gather to expand you island town.

The interesting part is that the island town sort of acts like your skill tree/you RPG progression. Which opens up interesting opportunities for not just build craft, but optimizing how you place your buildings to enhance your theory crafted build.

The problem comes in with the design of the continent:
Firstly, the game relies heavily on what I call "BS" design. Nearly every single death I had in this game was at no fault of my own unless you consider "I had no idea nor any indication that would happen". Such as very normal looking wooded boxes exploding randomly, getting spawned in lava, or mushrooms suddenly becoming sentient and poisoning so severely that I die long after the threat was defeated.
The game winds up heavily teaching me to just use my pea-shooter because using my sword results in immediate death.

Secondly, the world itself becomes rather dull rather quickly. As an overworld, it works well enough to help move you from point A to B, but there isn't much to do besides explore dungeons, but dungeons don't much different from the overworld other than being dark and somewhat linear. There are no stage hazards and combat becomes very repetitious very quickly. For once, I feel like this game would benefit from some of the randomness found in rogue-like design, but unfortunately it lacks those surprises and thus stagnates rather quickly.

So, as I said; it's cute charming art, with a cool concept, but unfortunately executed poorly.
