Do you miss Ultimate Soccer Manager '98? Have you been looking for a great game with all of those features, a game that's immersive and gives you total control of your club? So have I. But I've stopped looking...

BECAUSE SOCCER BOSS IS IT!!!!!!!

No unnecessary twaddle -- no cute prelude animations in which you have to meet every person on the staff one by one. If someone needs to tell you something, you get an e-mail. 

Close to EVERYTHING is statted out for you. All players have a large number of ratings so you can make informed decisions, and the interface is so clean (and colorful) that you DON'T get swamped by the stats. Matches are top-down and easy to follow, with NO annoying repetitive play-by-play, allowing me to do the annoying repetitive play-by-play announcing myself. (You can even skip the match play and just get the results if you wish.)

The game is close to perfect. One caveat -- if you have never played a statistical soccer sim before, this is NOT your starting point. While there is some guidance in the form of a *very* limited tutorial, there is no documentation. 

One thing that might be a turn-off to some is that all of the players are fictional. I did NOT find this to be an impediment; believe it or not, it makes the game more realistic. In some other soccer sims, you'll right away look to acquire Pele, Maradona, Beckham, Messi, etc., because you already know who the great players are. In Soccer Boss you'll need to figure out not only who the greats *are* but which players may *become* greats (Soccer Boss has a stat for training potential to help you find the young players who are worth the time/money investment).

To reiterate, if you're looking for the replacement for Ultimate Soccer Manager '98, THIS IS IT!!!

10/10

ADDENDUM: The programmer, sadly, has passed away. The only thing that's missing in Soccer Boss is the ability to make small tactical position changes, that is, to instruct a player to play slightly back or slightly to the center of the pitch, etc. That can't be added now, but this is still an OUTSTANDING game regardless.

[h1]This is where I'll leave my heart.[/h1]

Every time I come across some amazing story, I'm afraid that it was the last time, that I'll never find something that can embrace my soul so much. I'm not saying that the stories that come my way are bad. Not at all. They are interesting, they arouse emotions in me, they entertain me, intrigue me and so on, but they are not able to get through my skin, flesh and bones to reach the core. However, the "Royal Order" proved to be more than capable of doing this.

[h2]This game is excellent in every way.[/h2]

To begin with, this is an exciting story in which, importantly, there is an opportunity to build a romantic relationship. This is a visual novel, but it doesn't consist solely of text, images, and choices. It also allows you to upgrade your character using other methods and think strategically. In addition, the game has different difficulty levels, which makes it even more interesting, although, I admit, I did not take the risk and choose the most difficult level, since my weak heart would not have survived a large number of deaths, and it was already faced with a sufficient number of them.

Yes, some characters in the game die. Basically, these are not the most significant characters that appear in the story as a "shadow," but I would be lying if I said that it didn't hurt me to lose them, because every character in the game became dear to me. I wanted to know their stories and not know their deaths, but alas.

It's also worth noting that this visual novel is beautiful, in all terms of beauty, but at the moment I'm talking specifically about visual. I was especially attracted to the chibi drawings. It's adorable, but everything else is beautiful too.

Actually, I can talk for a long time about the advantages of this game, but I don't have enough space, so I'll just say one thing: for the first time in my life, I'm meeting a story that absolutely meets my desires. This is exactly what I was looking for, and what was worth looking for. It merged with my soul and now it will stay with me forever. I thank everyone who participated in the creation of this masterpiece.

But I would be a bad review writer if I didn't point out the cons, but I hasten to assure you that they don't really exist. How come? Well, first of all, there's something that I personally would like to see a little differently, let's just say, but it's nothing more than a matter of taste, so it doesn't count. Secondly, there were probably some flaws or mistakes in this visual novel, because no one and nothing is perfect, but I was completely engrossed in delight, so I didn't notice anything.

Well, and thirdly, it wasn't enough for me. Actually, with each new week, I thought that the game was about to end, but it went on and on, and it delighted me every time.  But, anyway, when the story ended, it still wasn't enough for me. I've enjoyed every second of this game, but I would give it even more of my time if it were possible. I'm interested in knowing some details, something that happened after the final scenes or even before them, I would like to read about the fate of some characters, even those who were mentioned only once, and then only in one route. Oh, I would like everything, but I perfectly understand that the developers simply did not have the opportunity to satisfy all my desires, they gave me enough, so this is also not a con.

I am grateful that "Royal Order" happened in my life. And I just hope that this is not the last delightful story on my way, but in any case, this is now my favorite story, which is second only to one animated series that became a part of my soul when I was a child.

Love to all.

Netherspace is a beautifully crafted retro-looking shooter game with quite a funny twist in most of the interactions that take place between the two starring heroes.
There is great variety in terms of what the player can choose to invest in per playthrough, as the many ship's stats prove to be a major factor in choosing a personal gameplay style.
The teleportation and shield mechanisms are both vital for survival and the ability to move at double speed when not firing gave me a good choice of defenses without which it would be impossible to reach the game's ending, so kudos for nice variety in that area.
The ship's weapons have separate ammo each and up to four can be equipped. They each have their strengths and weaknesses, whether it is in terms of ammo, ammo recharge rate, fire rate, hitbox size, damage and certain special weapons even have spread and their bolts teleport along with the ship.
What I enjoyed most, other than the direct gameplay, was the beautifully written script.
Both heroes are interesting and the presentation of the plot after each defeated boss and upgrade screen, exclusively through the dialogue of the protagonists, worked perfectly for me.
In the end, I've had fun with this little game and see no reason not to recommend it to shoot'em'up and retro-looking games lovers.

Foreword:  I own Disgaea 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and D2.

Disgaea 6 is a downgrade from Disgaea 5 in almost every respect.  The price you pay for 3D-modelled characters is downgraded gameplay and graphics.  The graphics using the gamepad have a pause between each square, even when held down, so that the movement of characters is jittery.  So much so that I can't play it for more than a couple of hours without getting a headache.

The writing is funny as always (well, funnier than Disgaea 4 anyway), which is why I bought the game despite the warnings in the negative reviews.  Well, the reviews were correct.  Simple things like retaining your place in a 2000-item list are completely missing from the game, and have not been corrected in at least 4 years.  Same for the "Try On" option in Rosen Queen, where it should retain your place in the character list, but in D6 it resets to the first character *every time*.  Why is this critical?  Say you want to give your character 30 mana potions...you have to scroll down 500 items EACH TIME you want to select the next mana potion.

The scroll speed in D6 is either too slow or too fast - Disgaea 5 was just about perfect in this respect.

The attack animation option to "Skip" the animations no longer lets you see the animation the first time, then skip it thereafter.  It skips it every time, so you either have to watch every animation over and over, or you get to see none of them.  This is a downgrade from D5.

D6 doesn't tell you which rarity of items you have acquired without going to the Records NPC.  There is no way I can remember if I got a Common, a Rare, or a Legendary item on my own for every item in the game.  In D5, when you looked at the items on an NPC, if there was an item of a rarity you hadn't acquired, it would say "New" next to it.  Not any more.  Again, this is a downgrade.

The Quests can be repeated, and you can select ALL of them this time - so why even have a selection screen at all?  Why not just do it automatically?

It seems like all the quality of life components of D5 were removed and replaced with an auto-battle / auto-leveling system.  There are quests associated with the auto-leveling system, and also with auto-exploration of items in the Item World.

Even simple things, like the voice of Lucky Boards, haven't escaped downgrading.  In D5, Lucky Boards sounded like Gremlins from the movie of the same name (using Howie Mandel's voice).  In D6, not only are the voices of Lucky Boards in the bass vocal range, the lines are unbelievably phoned-in.  It's just awful.

Look, I love the Disgaea series.  After looking at the large number of negative reviews, I waited for D6 to go on sale, and if things were as bad as the reviewers say, I wouldn't be wasting so much money on it.  It definitely wasn't worth it, even on sale.  If you want to know the D6 story, go watch a story video on YouTube, don't buy this game.  I sent an email to NIS support in the hopes they might come back and fix it...but this is 4+ years after release, and D7 has already dropped (with even more negative reviews than D6).  I'm not holding my breath.  The fact that playing this game literally gives me a headache should be the biggest warning for people with similar visual issues.  This game is not complete, despite the name, except for being completely broken compared to D5.  I'd rather go back and replay D3 than play D6 any further.  That depresses me, and I fear for NIS' survival.  I hope they look over the negative reviews for D6 and D7, and look strongly at D5 as a role model when they go to make Disgaea 8...if they survive that long.

[h1]The Only Thing Worse Than the AU is a Negative Review[/h1]

[h2]Story[/h2]

Rather than a typical demon lord story, this game has the player characters tackle a government conspiracy involving a fantasy version of the United Nations, which has more power over member states than the real UN for some reason. The majority of interactions consist of Versailles coming up with a conspiracy theory, Jack dismissing it out of blind faith towards the Atlian Union, and Versailles being proven right. I felt that interaction being overused towards the middle of the game, since I find it ridiculous for Jack to still believe in the AU after one of their commissioned scientists literally spilled the beans on them and connected them to a mind control zombie virus. Even if he was indoctrinated through his school and parents, his unwillingness to entertain any suspicion made him really unlikeable for a large chunk of the game. The good news is that Jack does get development, albeit a bit late, but the bad news is that Johann is left as the least developed despite being the protagonist. He's supposed to be bland and uninformed for the sake of receiving plot exposition from other characters and being a self-insert, but it doesn't make much sense for him to be like that when his family is supposed to be closely connected to the Himmelland royalty.

There are several endings to the game, with two of them being bad endings where you don't even get to finish off the final boss. As for the four proper endings, I would have preferred Jack or Versailles getting the leadership role in the president endings, since they have the most personal conflicts with the Atlian Union and are more knowledgeable about politics and current events than Johann. Johann doesn't seem like the type of character to have that kind of leadership ambition, making the non-president endings seem more in-character for him. For all of the endings, I feel like there are some plot threads that need more focus. In the president endings, we don't know how Johann intends to use his newfound power, since he could fix a lot of the flawed policies that screwed over a lot of member states. Additionally, the king of Himmelland warned against letting Versailles keep an important plot item, but we don't actually know the consequences of letting him use it, aside from maybe someone evil stealing it from him.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

For the most part, the battle system is well-balanced and follows a very basic turn-based formula. Everyone has defined roles, with Johann being the fighter, Jack being the healer, and Versailles being the mage. Though the endgame gives way too many powerups to Johann compared to other characters. Also, maintaining buffs in long battles gets harder in the end because Jack has to handle both healing and group buffs. I kind of wish there was a fourth party member who could handle dedicated buffing.

In the mid and late game, random battles can deal heavy damage to the party, but at the same time, it's possible to wipe them out in one or two turns, essentially turning the gameplay into a "he who strikes first wins" contest. This can make it hard to conserve MP, which makes things difficult in the midgame when enemies don't drop much money, but easier in the endgame when the party can easily farm MP items.

Bosses in the endgame also get really tough, since they can use most of the player's favored buffs and debuffs against them. It becomes important to immunize against both stat debuffs and ailments, though it's also possible to cheese a lot of fights with Jack's final defensive skill.

The mapping of the game is easily the worst part though. Most maps are extremely bloated in terms of space and can take a long time to navigate, and the size of each new map seems to get bigger as the game progresses. This is especially bad in dungeons, which use random encounters with low fleeing rates, meaning the long navigation and high encounter rate can make it a slog to dungeon crawl. It got to the point where I simply gave up on opening chests in the final dungeon, since most of them did not justify the effort to find them. IMO, big bloated maps are only advantageous if the player can dodge encounters, and even then, they only need to be big enough for dodging.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

5/10

Gameplay Mechanics: 7/10
Narrative: 7/10
Graphics: 6/10
Sound and Music: 6/10
Replayability: 8/10
Innovation: 7/10

Three Kingdoms: Hero offers a turn-based strategy RPG experience set in the legendary Three Kingdoms era, delivering accessible gameplay with a focus on tactical battles. Players command their forces on grid-based maps, using maneuvers like flanking and ambushes to outwit opponents. While the core mechanics are enjoyable, the battles can sometimes feel repetitive, and the strategic depth may not satisfy players seeking more complexity. For its approachable yet modest gameplay design, it scores a 7/10.

The narrative provides a functional retelling of the Three Kingdoms saga, centering on the alliance of Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei. While it captures key historical moments, the storytelling remains straightforward, lacking the depth or emotional weight that could make it more compelling. Narrative earns a 7/10.

Visually, the game’s cartoonish art style is serviceable but doesn’t stand out. The character designs and environments are clear but lack the detail and polish seen in more modern titles. Graphics score a 6/10.

The sound and music are similarly unremarkable. While the period-inspired tracks and battle effects are fitting, they feel repetitive and don’t leave a lasting impression. Sound and music earn a 6/10.

Replayability remains a highlight, with character recruitment, random growth attributes, and plenty of weapons and equipment to collect. The level editor adds even more variety, earning replayability an 8/10.

Innovation is modest, with features like the military stratagem system and trap placements offering a few fresh twists on the turn-based strategy formula. However, these ideas don’t always reach their full potential, earning the game a 7/10 for innovation.

In summary, Three Kingdoms: Hero is a solid but unexceptional strategy RPG. While it delivers fun tactical battles and replayability, its simplicity and lack of polish hold it back from standing out in a competitive genre.

If you're a 90s kid who was completely mesmerized by the likes of Solar Winds and other mysterious space exploration games, if you love some light role-playing elements and especially resource collection towards building your own spacecraft, this one might definitely be for you. Starcom: Unknown Space expands on those ideas and manages to incorporate plenty of fitting game mechanics. Got it from a slight -20% sale and after 16+ hours and maybe close to being halfway through, wouldn't have regretted had it been a full price.

I consider this a game in the vein of "good classic game design", but in a way that doesn't make it feel dated. A good majority of game time is spent flying through space, finding unknown areas to explore with a decent amount of fighting in between. As a guideline, you usually have either a mission, or a problem for which you're trying to find a solution or just a clue, so you rarely have to just fly blind looking for something to do, but you could do that also if you wanted. This means the game is very much an open world for the player to discover, but it doesn't feel empty or shallow like some other open world games I'm not going to mention here. The exploration and fighting is nicely paced because finding stuff is frequent, and putting it to use in the shipyard and the quite extensive research screen are what give the player a sense of achievement and even momentary power trips, if the ship designs are good enough. While the R&D parts are some of the coolest mechanics in the game you don't have to design your own ships - the game already includes plenty to choose from if you prefer it that way.

While the game is open world, pretty much everything that happens is bound to the semi-linear story. To me this is a good thing because it means everything is hand-crafted. If you don't want to solve a gripping space mystery about the echoes of an ancient fallen empire by going through a story like that and would rather have something procedurally generated, this one might now be for you.

Now for me, just like lifeforms on a planet, a game such as this either thrives or dies according to the suitability and strength of the atmosphere. This one has a strong one, constructed with world building and a fitting, enigmatic ambiance both of which begin on the second you click to start your first game. The atmosphere gets maintained by a beautiful and calm musical score that not only fits the game like a glove but also reacts to changing conditions, like enemies approaching.
Bigger titles could actually learn a lot from Starcom; giving the player a strong start can hook the player from the first minute. The opposite can easily be achieved if you prolong unnecessarily.

Starcom: Unknown Space feels like it was written by someone who is a fan of Star Trek (exploration, encounters), Stargate (travel, mystery) and Babylon 5 (diplomatic conundrums), but while it draws influence from them it manages to build its own little universe and story and stands completely on its own. The writing is superb, witty, incorporates hard science concepts and manages to hold a good balance between serious and humorous.

An absolute gem of a game I will be returning to at some point despite the (assumed) inherent lack in replayability.

This is a really great game for the money! At its heart, it’s a space exploration and combat game where you pilot a starship that you can modify—or even build yourself. The entire game is text-driven, but the writing is well-done, making the narrative engaging. The graphics are solid and on par with current (2025) gaming standards.

Combat feels fair on the normal setting, though some battles can be challenging. Learn to save (F5 is your friend) and recover (F9), as it will save you from unnecessary frustration. One feature I found particularly useful is the ability to add notes to the map, which helps with navigation and remembering key locations. Trade isn’t overly complex, making it accessible without feeling too simplistic.

At times, it can be unclear where to go next, but when that happens, I simply wander into space and discover a new star system. Shipbuilding took some time to get used to—I expected to preview future designs before committing to them, which would have helped with long-term planning. However, in the end, I didn’t rely on the pre-made layouts much. It still would have been a nice feature for strategic planning.

Overall, I find Starcom: Unknown Space captivating, enjoyable, and sometimes hard to walk away from. If you’ve ever played Wing Commander or Freelancer, you’ll appreciate this game’s strong story-driven approach. It’s a great mix of exploration, combat, and adventure, and I’d definitely recommend it to fans of the genre!

I get that there's very little traction in this game, so I'll leave this review for the developers so they can address the game's flaws.

This game isn't worth $20. There's a bunch of flaws that keep it from being a stable game. I like the look and concept, but it's fairly unplayable at it's current state.

When you're in your house (where you start) it's so painful to look at. I don't know what the problem is whether it's lag, or the camera trying to fix itself against the edge of the screen but there's something it's running into (This seems like the case), but it's like the game shakes constantly. Once you go outside, it gets better (still not completely gone though), but it's awful indoors. In the trailer, it shows it happening in other indoor sections as well.

The text in the game is incredibly slow in some places, then it speeds up occasionally out of no where, only to go back to being slow again. Why? It's rough watching every word come out and not be able to speed up the text. I read fairly fast, so making me read something slowly is torture.

Next thing is also something slow... It's battles! Oh my goodness!! It took me 16 turns to finish the first battle, and I barely won before running out of MP. It's incredibly unbalanced. I don't think any battle should take that long. With that, the text going slowly during the fight, and the attack having an animation that plays, this fight took me about 10 minutes.
A little bit later, I was in a trainer battle that the enemy had a "summon" of a human? that was 2 levels higher than my dog. My dog proceeded to destroy him which made no sense after the first couple battles. It was level 8, my dog was level 6. After I demolished them, my dog then gained 3 levels, making it level 9 when the enemy wasn't even that high... What? I fought 3 long grueling battles and only gained one level earlier, then this happens. Still seems very unbalanced.

The story doesn't seem very enticing either. Maybe it's because it happened out of no where and the dog can talk, or maybe it's because the game goes into more detail about eating dinner than it does what a summoner is, but it feels like it's bogus, and it ruins the immersion. 

Like earlier when I was discussing the indoors issue, the camera is locked. It moves around to show you if there's something in the way, but it's very jerky. It wigs out if you go around a building or a corner, and you can't spin the camera even though you have to go south a lot.

The collision with the assets are hit and miss. At the farm, you can walk through supposed solid objects, but the smoothing of the land walking upstairs makes it so you can't walk up to the platform unless you find the sweet spot. This doesn't feel at all polished and it's like you didn't even check the game for bugs.

Lastly, the reason why I quit instead of giving it a full hour like I normally try to do: the game uses your character telling you that you can't go in a direction as a blockade to other areas by saying it's either too scary or not your current task... okay, sure, it's a linear game that makes you go home over and over. The problem I have is that when it does this; if you were holding the button to move when the character runs into the "blockade"... which you 100% of the time are, your character keeps going for either a second, or doesn't stop even when you leave that text. This doesn't seem bad until you realize your character just passed the point of the obstacle, and now you're softlocked while the game continues. You're locked either running straight forever into whatever wall you reach, or you're stuck standing where it stopped you, unable to do anything. This is a major bug that caused me to revert to my last save, which was literally like 2 minutes before that, but this happens every time you try to go somewhere you aren't supposed to go. I just didn't care enough to continue to find bugs for a janky game. 

I don't feel like you should be charging anyone for this game... it honestly feels like you should pay people to test your game so it could get better with some work done to it. I don't expect anything to be fixed since this is over two years old and there hasn't been an update in over two years, but maybe this will help people not make the same mistake as I did by buying this

Clearly, the developer made so much money hodling BTC that they don't need to work on this game anymore, so I'd say don't bother buying it.

It uses Maslow’s hierarchy elements and even knowing and understanding that I couldn't feel what the main character might've been experiencing. 

I know this is a short (bite-sized) game and expanding the story would undo that, but it lacked the connecting factor to empathy or relatability. 
Without these two elements, it strips the game of essential thought-provoking psychological impact. That is what creates and makes this a psychological horror experience. That point where we (the player) connect with the main character's realization. That's when it becomes terrifying. 

Alas, that didn't happen.  

There's a good atmospheric narrative in there. Perhaps a different tone, delivery or mix of both would've helped. Of course this is all a "maybe". This might be the best method, and I'm just made out of stone. 🤷‍♀️

On to gameplay. "Please Comply", if you don't there's no game.  There aren't any "other options". No magical door will appear, no ladder will drop from the ceiling. If you want to continue playing, you need to comply. 

In essence, this is a walking simulator, where you walk around a small "square" room. There is no actual gameplay or puzzles to solve. 

As you comply, you will be asked to do certain tasks that will strip what is meaningful to "you", until you are left with "nothing". It breaks the person until there is nothing. This is the [psychological] horror of the game and method. Back to my point, that "second hand" terror wasn't there. 

Unless the bigger picture (which would be a BIG STRETCH) is that the horror comes from feeling nothing (as the player) towards the character. Then again, that would be horrific, but mostly to those around us, that "know" us, and that’s just going down a complex rabbit hole I highly doubt this story was aiming for.

In the end, I still felt detached from the character and the situation. It's unfortunate because it fails in the storytelling and in what ultimately should've been a jarring and terrifying experience. 

The game includes easter eggs (achievements too) and different ways to get to the ending, but you'll still get to the ending.  

I'm torn in a recommendation standpoint. I've seen much worse but at the same time, it's not unplayable. "The Red Exile," is a first-person survival horror game that introduces roguelike elements through procedurally generated maps. Players are tasked with performing an exile rite to eliminate a relentless pursuer before falling victim themselves.

Pros:
- Dynamic Replayability: The procedurally generated maps ensure that each playthrough offers a unique experience, maintaining player engagement. 
- Adaptive AI Antagonist: The pursuer's AI learns from the player's actions, increasing the challenge and tension as the game progresses. 
- Perk System: Players can unlock and equip various perks, allowing for diverse strategies and personalized gameplay. 

Cons:
- Repetitive Environments: Despite procedural generation, the limited variety in room designs can lead to a sense of monotony over time. 
- Simplistic Mechanics: Some players may find the core gameplay mechanics lacking depth, potentially reducing long-term engagement. 
- Technical Issues: Reports of bugs and performance issues, such as crashes and input lag, can disrupt the overall experience. 

In conclusion, "The Red Exile" offers a fresh take on the survival horror genre with its roguelike elements and adaptive AI. However, repetitive environments and technical issues may hinder the experience for some players.

-Battles are really unbalanced, but there are difficulty levels and encounter rates to suit your grind preference.  I enjoy a hard game, but don't necessarily like battles every 2 steps, so it was fine for me.

The Bad:
-The game has frozen on me a number of times.  Not crashing persay, but it will get stuck on a screen/menu/map and while you can hear the sound effects as the game still runs, your actions don't reflect on screen.  This could be due to the sheer amount of events running on the game at any given time.  With that said, my rig runs most modern games on High settings  at 60+fps, so I shouldn't be having this issue. Even with the performance options on, it still does this from time to time.  The game does have an autosave however, so you're not really missing a lot of progression. -Some of the plot objective are not intuitive when it comes to keeping the story flowing.  There were a few places I got stuck at, because the objective wasn't really clear, which required me speak to every NPC in order to get back on track.  If that wasn't it, then I had to explore several maps to trigger progression.  Whereas some events automatically progress the story where you least expect it when you're trying to explore the area or talk to story characters.

With that said, this truly is a passion project and it shows.  The number of hours that had to be dedicated to this game shows in the quality and storytelling.  For this reason alone, I recommend it.   The story is coherent and touching, the environments are beautiful and the characters have depth.

[h1]A Few Steps Forward and a Few Steps Back[/h1]

[h2]Story[/h2]

Gaia's Melody 1 already had a decent story and worldbuilding, and the sequel expands on a lot of backstory and world history. As a consequence, this game is much longer than the previous, which is both a good and bad thing, since some arcs, such as the school arc, feels like filler, while others feel relevant to the overarching plot concerning the Gate. The epilogue quests are definitely one of the best parts of the game, since it gives proper time to wrap up various plot threads and prevents the pitfall of having rushed and unsatisfying endings.

As for the dialogue, I noticed that the characters don't speak in as childlike of a manner anymore, which makes sense because they're older. Additionally, Choko doesn't use the speech patterns of the Usagi anymore, which is a nice attention to detail that shows how much traveling the world has affected her.

The game also finalizes several characters' romance arcs, and while these are well-written, I do feel like giving Akira a canon pairing does render the previous game's choices irrelevant to some extent if the player was shipping her with someone else. However, it's still necessary to give her a canon partner sooner rather than later because she's going to show up in Endless Melody. That said, there are some sussy bits with the age gap for some of the couples, such as Bawr x Yuina and Tara x Ryuan (FBI open up?), though this is only noticeable if you read the guidebook.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

I complained about the balancing in the first game and sadly, there are only minor improvements at best. There are still characters like Kari and Kasumi who have such low HP that they're not viable against enemy skills that have high enough damage formulas. It's also very grindy to make sure everyone is strong enough for story challenges, since the game doesn't have any shared EXP. There is an accessory that can cause EXP that was supposed to go to Akira go to someone else, but you don't get it until the final dungeon, which is too little too late.

As for damage formulas, I noticed that they aren't very consistent. Skills that cost about the same amount of MP seem to do very different damage, even when you consider stats and elemental weaknesses. This also applies to enemy skills, where an enemy can deal scratch damage with one skill and OHKO with another. I'm not sure if this is intentional or if the skill damage wasn't tested properly, but it does lead to a difficulty curve that feels like a sine wave. Maybe it would help if the damage formulas were also written in skill descriptions?

As for the party meta, Doken and Zephyr got nerfed to put them closer to the level of the other characters, though Doken is still one of the most consistent damage dealers even if he can't spam his ultimate skill as easily. However, due to the enemies having inconsistent damage, bosses are best dealt with by having a fast character like Tara to keep them stunlocked. Basically, the game's balance feels just like modern Yu-Gi-Oh, in that your win condition is to keep the enemy from taking any action.

The game has some new features, such as a difficulty setting and an improved version of the previous encounter setting. For the difficulty settings, Boost mode increases EXP gain and lowers enemy stats, which can make the endgame grind less tedious, but it still feels like a band-aid solution to the overall balancing issues. Hard mode multiplies enemy stats and lowers EXP gain, and it would take massive amounts of grinding to catch up to them. I suspect hard mode was meant for NG+, since the multiplier can't make enemy stats go beyond the stat cap. There's also a neat little art collection that functions as a collection sidequest that spans the entire game. Unfortunately, the game also lost some features, such as minimaps and the bestiary. The former was crucial in figuring out where to find story objectives, so this could make it tricky to avoid advancing the story too far. As for the bestiary, it seems to have been replaced with a scanning feature, but scanning the enemy doesn't give very useful information at all and it might as well not even be a feature.

Edit: Minimaps are implemented now, along with objective markers. Also, hard mode was rebalanced.

The combat animations in both games tend to be very long, even if you hold down the examine key to force the game to make the animations faster. Additionally, I personally don't like having characters move all over the place randomly, since this could make it more annoying to check on their states or figure out if an enemy is covering up another. IMO, it would be better if the characters returned to their original positions at the end of each turn so that it would be less disorienting.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
6.5/10
The story has some sussy bits and filler, but it's still very well-written and it's satisfying seeing the characters get their happy endings. Unfortunately, the combat is still not much better than the previous game and I'd go as far to say that this duology has some of the worst combat I've ever seen in an RPG Maker game. Overall, I'll have to give a barely recommended score to the game once again, since a game really shouldn't neglect its [i]gameplay loop[/i].

It all started when I decided to get RPGMAKER MV on steam. In my head, I thought it would be neat to use: Everything I need to make an epic RPG adventure of my very own. Well, it's a $3 game that's 20% off for launch, so I can't really complain, but I can't recommend the game. 

See the trailer? That's the game. Like, the entire game. There's only one enemy type, there's only one arena (the 5 stages are just that arena with that one enemy type in larger waves as stages progress), and Phi doesn't have any sort of complex combos or growth to mix things up.

The worst part is how the game controls though. It's [i]incredibly[/i] floaty and unresponsive. Phi has acceleration to move, so she starts at a slow walk from neutral for a moment before going into a full run (you can dodge into movement to skip the acceleration time). I cannot put into words just how bad this acceleration feels. There's a jump button, but Phi only jumps directly upwards with no forward momentum, and there's no enemies that are aerial, or that jump, or are tall at all, or that have sweeping or projectile attacks to jump over, so it's actually useless. The basic attack string is only three attacks, which includes that long spinning attack you see in the trailer. You cannot dodge cancel out of attack animations. Control just feels bad, bluntly.

Also, it's worth noting that there's no control rebinding of any kind. The controls setup is relatively standard, so it's fine, unless you don't have a controller or a QWERTY keyboard, in which case you're totally out of luck.

Otherwise, combat just doesn't have much to it, since there's only the one enemy type (with one attack, by the way). You can hold shift to do a knock-up/jump to do an aerial combo, which can be used to keep enemies off you while you focus the knocked-up target, but it's completely unnecessary. There's a counterattack that has relatively strict timing with pretty much zero payoff. You're better off just spamming basic attacks. There's a heavy-hitting wide-area special attack which you don't need at all since there's never enough pressure to call for it unless you just sit around letting the enemies spawn on purpose. There's a super mode that you can activate when below 50% HP, that changes up your attack sting a bit, but you'll never need it if you pay attention at all.

Also, I beat the game in 0.3 hours with all of the achievements (I have 0.4 now after going back in to double check the jump and the options), which included replaying a stage and letting myself get hit so I could be low enough HP to activate the super mode. Yes, I skipped the story, which could be great, could be terrible, I literally have no idea, but it's not what I came for here.

Look. It's only $3, so whatever. If you're curious about it, go for it I guess, but I seriously can't [i]recommend[/i] it. From a gameplay perspective, there's really no reason to play this game at all over any alternative you can think of.

Also, it's worth noting that the game tries phoning a server when you first start it up. Not sure what for, but I don't think it's a particularly good look. Unity games do the same thing (which I don't like either), but you can tell they're at least contacting Unity addresses, whereas this isn't a Unity game and I don't know what the IP address it was sending to is.

City of Springs is a solid action adventure game, centred on Val, a scrappy (heh) protagonist trying to survive in a post-apocalyptic and dystopian city dominated by clockwork machines. It blends exploration with an easy to grasp tower defence combat mechanic that is snappy and feels natural in its setting.

The visuals are gorgeous and immersive, the quests are charming and the setting breathes love and attention for detail. All in all it's hard to believe that such a small company managed to release a game at this level of quality. At this price, it's an absolute steal. Having given the game a try, I can happily say it's worth four times the price.

An old school style dungeon crawler, with some light overworld and battle resource management.  Challenging, but not unfairly difficult.  Brisk as well, clocking in between 10 - 15 hours for a single playthrough with NG+ after that. REMEMBER:  This is styled on old PC DRPGs.  That means status buffs on your party, with debuffs and negative status effects on enemies is imperative.  Do not expect to brute force your way with simple attacks.  Learn to use fire and poison properly, manage your battle resources, and always have a tank and a healer in your party at all times.

Good luck, Quester!

Cleverly designed, perfectly addictive, and criminally overlooked.  I wasn't expecting this unassuming game to be one of the best dungeon crawlers of the last few years, but that's what it is.

At first I was a bit mystified by the terse interface and seemingly chaotic combat, but once I figured out what was going on (hint: read the manual), I was hooked.  Exploration is gradual, but rewarding.  New campsites and purification upgrades increase your range of exploration, scattered miniboss encounters raise your team's level cap when defeated, and new questers and equipment expand your strategic and tactical options with new skill combinations.  It's hard not to keep playing for just one more turn.

I do wish that party members were a bit smarter about targeting enemies; most attacks will target the enemy with the lowest HP, even if it's about to die anyway from dots or AOE, which leads to some wasted attacks.  Still, that just means that planning your attacks efficiently is part of the game.

Very charming, quirky, rather Japanese-feeling dungeon crawler. Remember when 'weird' Japanese games like Katamari Damacy started getting English translations? You can experience the novelty of that moment with this game!

Clearly takes from classic 80s games like Wizardry in terms of dungeon crawling, but with a unique auto-battler spin. Your moves come with priority numbers (higher -> executed sooner) and you stack them for each character, press 'fight' and hope the characters hit the right enemies. There is no targeting system and player characters choose their targets randomly. Some attacks can hit multiple times, or multiple enemies in the same row, and these are very nice to have. The other thing to manage is hate: attacks and certain special abilities generate hate, and high-hate characters get targeted more often. 

Characters unlock multiple abilities as they level up (1 ability per 10 levels). Characters are divided into classes that break down to Magic Damage Dealer, Physical Damage Dealer, Tank, Debuffer, and Healer. The main fun to be had is in finding characters whose abilities complement each other, and building a team around them. You can build some really quirky combinations (a team built around a tank/healer who heals the party for a small amount each turn, say).

There's no story to speak of, but hey! Use your imagination and picture all those quirky anime characters supporting each other, building combos off one another's moves... 

Incredibly fun as a podcast game due to the autobattler-ish nature of things. If you enjoy grinding, this game is rather grind friendly.

The absolute best thing of this game is that it's an indie in the early-2000s sense. Picture yourself as a young gamer, buying a random game CD from a convention and booting it up. This is the sort of game you might find. When you complete the game there's even a QR code to get your own game completion stamp! It's utterly charming.

Quester is a prime piece of doujinsoft, inspired by early 1980s PC Engine dungeon crawlers in a way that is so earnest it almost brings a tear to my eye.

Authored and illustrated by Kazushi Hagiwara (BASTARD!! - Heavy Metal, Dark Fantasy -), this is a game that will appear alien to you unless you either know the general tenets of the source material or are willling to let yourself discover a long-lost branch of a genre that, in the West, is best represented by your DIablos and your Wizardrys. 

From the way the screen is partitioned to the way combat works, Quester strikes a very interesting balance between vintage (but efficient) design sensibiities and modern quality of life. Combat will arguably be the trickiest bit to figure out, as it requires you to select your every party member's action along a *timeline* represented by an orange number in each action's selection window. That number determines when any specific action goes off, helping you piece together a "timeline" of attacks that will unfold automatically after you've selected every move and pressed "start battle". 

Once you figure out how to "program" effective combos in this system however, the rest of the game is actually quite generous: the resource management is light, fleeing battle is always possible (at the cost of your main resource) and a full loop clocks in at around 25 hours if you take your time to look for cracked walls, stock up on food and maybe level up an extra party member or two. Party members which are, by the way, either found inside of green crystal bugs or whenever you discover a new bonfire/fast travel point.

The game's only real penalty comes in if you actually get careless enough to let a full party wipe happen: in which case half of all food you've collected during your current 10-day stint will be lost, along with a significant amount of "Materials" - the resource that lets you upgrade your weapons and level up.

Oh yeah, there is also a story - but, much like a lot of the game's mechanics, is minimalist and sort of streamlined. You'll find logs explaining bits and pieces of it every now and then, all of which are very neat and shed morsels of light on a setting that is overall quite interesting. That said, the game's "linear" story isn't really the focus of the experience, and that is perfectly fine. 

Also, if you're wondering whether to get this one or Quester OSAKA: the differences between them are, essentially, the same as those between DOOM 1 and DOOM 2. Take that as you will.

Quester is a fast-paced turn-based Dungeon Crawler that has you lead a team of the titular Questers on an odyssey through the post-apocalyptic ruins of the Tokyo Underground. With a tight gameplay loop that lets you focus on exploration and finding new gear, you build up your party and take on bigger challenges to keep exploring the dungeon. Your goal each 10 days is to find enough Food to support your party, but while you are out there you also want to be on the lookout for breakable Walls, keys to unlock Gates, treasure and little bugs that have kidnapped potential party members. With each run you reveal more of the map including the positions of new Base Camps that takes your runs deeper and deeper into the dungeon.

Running into Monsters triggers a battle which lets you use your party's gear and skills to deal with them which resolve in a deterministic priority queue (e.g. actions at priority 40 always go before actions at priority 30). This predictability lets you set up your favourite combos and blast through most random encounters while needing to switch things up based on your available resources during boss fights. There are a lot of conveniences like a 100% guaranteed escape (even from bosses) and automatically healing party members after fights (though there is a Fuel penalty for KO'd members). Avoid wiping if you can, it can be a bit punishing if you lose half your Food on the same run when your 10 day cycle ticks over :P

Overall, I had a blast playing this game and immediately purchased its followup Quester: Osaka to continue the adventure! It's worth pointing out that this game features a New Game+ system that can make future runs more challenging and let you run into different characters or gear to explore the full scope of the game system.

If I had a few points of criticism they would be:

- Its clear that the game was machine-translated for English and while that doesn't hinder your experience in a major way you will often run into gear and skill descriptions that are a bit off. For example, some items have the Strength+ trait but there is no attribute called Strength (maybe they meant Vitality or Melee?) and others that have the Defense+ trait but there is no matching attribute (there is one called Guard). There are also multiple message boxes where you see colour tags which have not been closed which might be a result of running a JSON file through a machine translator and importing it back into the game. You do eventually get the hang of how everything works but it is clear that a better localisation is necessary.

- The mid-game can be a little friction-less if you luck into a good combination of party members and high-tier gear. The game lets you "farm" treasure caches which can be exploited to find gear ahead of the intended curve. Luckily some of the later encounters in the final two regions pressure you nicely with the last boss being a decent challenge unless you are kitted out properly. This is something that its followup Quester: Osaka does a lot better so its good they took feedback on this.

- The UI while stylish in its presentation does fail a bit when it comes to Inventory menus. They give you sort options, however, Weapons of all types have the same icons and colour (despite a rarity system being in place) can only be distinguished by their name which gets a little cumbersome at endgame when you have 16 pages of items to shift through. This game is the story of single father Henry Hughes and his daughter Enid plus Henry's best friend Joseph who is an important link between past and present.  Henry's wife has died and he is a busy park ranger and has to raise Enid on his own.  This is their story.  
Henry has Alzheimer's Disease and can't remember why Enid and him have been estranged for so long.  The narrative is an retrospective journey into Henry's mind about the past and what an emotional rollercoaster it is!  Henry's mind is in a dreamlike psychedelic state and his memories are unlocked by tangram puzzles.
In the real world, you collect fragments of their past.  You experience the day to day struggle of Henry and see the many mechanics used to jog his memory.  For example there are post-its all around the kitchen explaining what each object was and how to use it; there was a corkboard with instructions for the day and it was very emotional to see messages of how he was loved.  Tangram puzzles and post-it stickers are real life techniques used to alleviate symptoms in patients with AD.
The game is really a walking sim collecting glowing boxes which represent Enid's paintings which jog her father's memory.  There are about 9 chapters and be aware that there is no chapter select at the end of the game, so be sure to check everything in both worlds before going deep into Henry's mind.
Warning:  there is a bit of a head bob as you walk along, so I reduced the camera sensitivity and that helped a bit, but I had to play this in short bursts.  Another warning is that there is photosensitive issues for epileptics and those with eyesight issues.  There are areas of whiteout representing Henry's cloudy mind and some very dark scenes where he gets lost.  One other thing is that there is a chapter where there is music involved, so you have to follow the sound.  Music is actually an aid for AD sufferers and calms them.  But it is difficult for deaf people to hear the music in this chapter.
Other things you collect are clinical notes or letters.  These are very educational about the disease and were a real eye opener!  This is where I felt the reality of what I was playing really hit home.  The loss of memory and cognitive behaviour; the confusion and frustration and then the eventual disassociation from the world showed what a terrible brain disease this is.  When Henry descended into darkness and the ice world representing his frozen mind, I just wept for all the people with this horrid condition.
I am not the sooky type but people of my vintage know others who have this disease or who have died from it.  And as I played, fear gripped my heart that I could end up like this.  I've witnessed the impact on their families and the heartbreak of seeing a loved one become a shell of who they were before.  To me it is the total humiliation of a human being, but it does bring the best out of others.  I applaud those working in this difficult field.
The music in this game was sublime and evocative in particular scenes.  The last chapter's music was exceptional, which is where I totally lost it!!!  The graphics were bright and colourful and went through the seasons.  The man who played Henry was really, really good, but the lass who played Enid had a very strong Spanish accent which was a little difficult to understand at times.  There is also positive LBGTIQ representation here for those in that community.
The game was made with great love and with the desire to educate others and raise awareness about AD which they succeeding in achieving.  Be aware that you will shed a tear or two as this is an immersive experience.  Now I'm heading off to tend to my broken heart....sniff!  Please support this game for AD sufferers.  8/10

Recommended with caveats.

The game starts with a warning about photosensitivity- this is important for people with photosensitive neurological conditions and some vision disorders. There are flashing lights, areas of extreme brightness or darkness, and sequences where the screen will  white-out making it hard to see where you are moving the character. 
 UI contrast is not so good- white text or icons that get lost on bright or light colored backgrounds.

There are very few settings to adjust things- no colorblindness settings, no UI scaling, no UI contrast settings, no resolution options, no VSync on/off. The game is locked to 30 (31) fps, and the camera can be a bit jerky at times.

The voice overs do not always match the dialogue text on screen in English. A few words missed here and there, nothing that changes the meaning of what is being said- the native Spanish version is much better, if you are fluent in Spanish.

That all said:
The music is fantastic- moody, charming, calming, energetic, dark- changing to suit the scenes and story well.
The art styles are quite good- both the comic style used in cutscenes and the stylized almost psychedelic style used in the playable game world.

The puzzles are tangram-style puzzles (fit shapes together to fill in a space, but not classic tangrams) and logic puzzles that can feel a bit trial and error at times. Which was fine for me- it suits the theme and context of the game. Confusion and uncertainty go with playing an Alzheimer's patient- you are seeing the world through his eyes.The puzzle difficulty progresses at a reasonable pace- some are quite tricky as you go on.

[b] "Alpha Snowflakes" be advised[/b]- there is a strong LGBTQ+ theme that runs through the game. Not with the main protagonist, but with his daughter Enid (who is not the protagonist- not sure why "female protagonist" is in the user-defined tags, but LGBTQ+ is not.) If LGBTQ+ stories trigger you- you'll want to avoid this game, it might upset you. :)

Th story seems to be well researched as far as Alzheimer's symptoms and treatments go, and what someone with the condition or someone caring for a person with the condition may experience. The game is quite surrealistic at times- I have family members who had Alzheimer's and eventually passed from its effects. I found it both enlightening and concerning that this *may* have been what the end of their lives was like- wandering through a confusing world filled with things they could not understand, created in their on minds, and could not escape from. Yes, the game made me weep for them many times.

TL;DR- the game has some Accessibility issues. It can be an emotional roller coaster if you know or are related to anyone with Alzheimer's. The UI and controls are not great, but the game ran quite well on an older gaming desktop, no crashes, no stutters, but expect it to feel like what it is- a port from an older console.

I did enjoy the experience, even though it was quite emotionally draining at times. Buy on sale, and know what you are buying before you drop $$$ on it.

I am giving this game a massive thumbs up, but there is absolutely no point in my attempting to review it. One word describes the experience though. Immersive. To immerse yourself in it is the only way to 'get' it. Reading about it will not do it. 
Thus, the below wall of text is not a review, but may explain the thumbs up.
I got lucky. I bought an early version of this game in the 1990's (BC3000). It was a time of my life when I needed to take some time out and basically lock myself away for a few weeks.  I had this CD with this game on, a printed manual and a PC.
I read the manual, which is what you did in those days, and I spent those weeks figuring out the game and learning to enjoy it more and more. It sucked me in. There was absolutely nothing like it. 
I got to the point where a screen full of numbers would translate in my mind to my troops running to defend my ship, I could see my engineers running down corridors to fix damage and effortlessly switch to a screen to check my inventory of parts while managing fighters and planning an escape strategy from a fight I had gotten into that I probably could not win, hoping I could pay for the parts I would need to fix her up. To give one example of a possible situation among many... many... 
And it was all huge fun, totally immersive and challenging and rewarding. This game is massive. You can read other reviews of it there is so much to do, but there is that one thing you need. Immersion.
Eventually I had to spend my time doing other things, I forgot about the game, then one day I realised I had lost the CD, and there wasn't much hope of getting another copy. It was never a popular game.
Then sometime later I discovered that it was available for free on the internet. So I downloaded it and got it to run but realised that it would just eat my life so I had to leave it to one side.
Even more years later and  I am so glad I have it on steam, well this evolved version of it which seems like an improvement from the few hours I have in it.  I start it up and I am instantly back in the seat. The 'obtuse' interface makes internal logical sense and is intuitive once you really know the whole game, even 30 years later. It is like an old friend. 
I start to play and then I realise, I am in that other universe. Immersed. if I don't step away from the computer, my friends and family may not see me for weeks. 
There is no other game like this, that I know of, and I play a lot of games.
If this small sharing of my experience with the game makes you think it may be worth your time investing in it then I say go for it. You may find the most immersive gaming experience you ever had. There's a cat in the game that is grumpily sitting next to a glass of wine, contemplating drinking the whole thing in one go. That cat is now me after playing this game. 

It's clear that the devs wanted to make a unique puzzler game that featured cute and iconic cats. They succeeded in illustrating some iconic and cute cats. However, the game itself is a nightmare. "Matching Cats" asks you to match cats, yes, that's true, but what it doesn't tell you is that this is an amalgamation of blind puzzle tile sliding and memory, with required single-card flips for EACH SPACE. The result is something that feels like you have to brute-force two potentially enjoyable genres of game at the same time, spending an absolute unnecessary amount of clicks to move one card to where you want it to go. I've had to break up my playtime of this game not out of enjoyment but because it's absolutely infuriating to have to input so much for basic movement, tile by tile, instead of being able to click any tile not adjacent to the current selection, or being able to slide a tile through, say, multiple empty spaces instead. I committed to 100%ing this game and I don't feel like it's worth it.

The pluses are really the cats they included in their illustrations. I think the devs made some good choices in which cats to include, selecting images that feel iconic and differentiated enough - for the most part - that the matching part feels fun. I definitely found myself referring to different cats by different made-up names or pertinent descriptors after a while. "Mafia cat," "dancing cat," "Walter making you a deal," "Goofy Walter," "lil orange boi," "alien," "void (puff)," "sad birthday cat," "salad," and similar names feel very familiar and intuitive after a while. Again, I do think the selection and illustration choices are the one good thing in the game.

My overall review: If you want to waste your time, if you want tendinitis in your clicking hand, and if you want to forego any amount of actual mental effort or stimulation in favor of simply mindlessly flipping cards even if you already know where their match is, go ahead and play this. Otherwise, I'm gonna recommend you steer clear and find another cute cat puzzler.

Everything is for Humanity is a very neat looking horror game. Sadly that's about it. I take it back, the voice actor you hear in the trailer is pretty solid. Outside of that, this game is a hard pass for me. I'll break down why, but maybe you're scraping the bottom of the indie horror barrel like I am and just really want to try it anyways. Which hopefully you find something redeeming in this game. 

- Most of the visuals of this game look great. I suspect it's the stock assets or asset packs and the game engine (I forget which one at the moment) does a lot of heavy lifting with great volumetric lighting and reflections. However, there's a lot of made assets, characters, and animations that are pretty janky. It wouldn't be a problem if some of the rough assets weren't in a world of high quality ones. The mismatch makes it jarring. 

- The horror elements are mostly nonexistent. Getting chased happens a little bit in this game and that part can be scary, but I literally just sprinted around the threats. I don't even think I saw one of them? The AI and pathing is also pretty rough here. I hid in a room right in front of a monster, closed the door (didn't lock it) and it just went to the door, shrugged, and gave up. 

- The saves are annoying. So I completed a whole area of gathering stuff and wiggling around a threat. When I got the next cutscene, the game didn't make it very clear I had to leave in a hurry. In fact, I thought I'd be immune to the problem given the circumstances, but nope. I died. Had to go back through that process of finding the items again (which they're not randomized thankfully) 

- The puzzles are either obscenely easy or obnoxious because the instructions aren't quite clear. I actually soft locked myself because of it. You can (easily) brute force some of the puzzles and one of them has the dreaded Resident Evil Village puzzle. I won't get into what exactly that is, but if you know, you know. 

- I also got softlocked because there was a mechanic I wasn't sure how it worked. I saw an option to do something...so I did it. I was confused as to what exactly that was doing, but while I was wandering around I found a monster. The game then told me to do the thing I was doing, but you apparently can only do it once. I couldn't move, the monster wasn't attacking, I just stood there, stuck. This would usually not be enough for me to rage quit, but while I was getting annoyed with the game when it had some silly puzzles and a weird story. 

- Ah the story. So...I have no clue what's going on here. Now it could very well be that I'm just too dumb to know what's going on here, but I feel as if there's all these neat scenes/levels, but there's no explanation as to what's going on or why. The game just kinda throws things at you and expects you to accept it. It doesn't feel very character driven and it's just there enough to explain where you are, but that's about it. 

Hopefully you get enough out of this to make an informed decision if you want to try it yourself. I personally am not interesting in completing it, but maybe you are and you know what? Good on you! There's some nice visuals and imagery here, but I'm particularly picky with my horror games.

There aren't many good roguelikes, specifically in the vein of Slay the Spire. Astrea gets the closest to being as good as StS, but falls short in a few areas. I'll point them out, and if they aren't dealbreakers for you, I'd recommend you buy this game.

First, the UI is very pretty, to the point of distraction. It's very easy to miss dice you could possibly roll. True, if you hover over the end turn button any dice you might be able to use will wiggle, but you get used to clicking it (or the spacebar) to end a turn, and there are no speedbumps to ask if you're sure you want to end turn.

Dice actions also have abstract images with simple color patterns. They don't always speak to what they do either. Much of the game is about throwing complexity upon complexity, which is why Astrea isn't as good as StS. Too many developers confuse complexity with quality. Astrea is one of those titles where you're often spinning plates to perform even the most basic of functions, and you don't always know how certain dice interactions will play out until they happen. All this to say, the abstractness of the dice works against the flow of the game.

Unlike other deckbuilding roguelikes (or perhaps, like too many bad builders), Astrea frontloads a lot of the skill based on your choice of character. There isn't much in the way of "working with what you're given", since each character has, more or less, a single build that works. Too many character options are simply weak compared to others, or outright bad. Some builds feel as though the developers were afraid of a character being too strong, so any small gain you may have in one area is shackled with an innumerate flaw. The character Sothis is the crown jewel of this amateur design, as much of the debate over characters will attest.

That said, I did put 61 hours into this title and beat the game (the true ending) with each and every character, unlocked every relic and die, and max-leveled every oracle.

For things I like, the art is good, it's just much in the UI. Sound design and music is good, this is one title where I've wound up listening to tracks outside of the game, it's quite enjoyable. Despite how much spinning plates you do, and the narrow builds, the game is not as bad as Ballionaire, Chrono Ark, and similar titles in this genre. As I said, it's not StS, but it's the closest in terms of quality.

The mechanics, while overly designed for some, do work more often than not. When you get a successful build going, it can be very satisfying to down bosses on the harder difficulties in a turn or two.

So if any of what I said didn't sound like a dealbreaker, then by all means I highly recommend Astrea. I know I will be looking forward to future games by this dev team.

This game is really, really fun. It's pretty unique for a "deck" builder, it has a lot of variety within each Oracle, and it's very smooth/responsive. 

The art style isn't quite my thing, mostly due to some things (especially enemies) looking a bit too much like a blob of color without much depth at times due to the way the shading and outlines are done. It's good, just not my favorite style.

There are a lot of builds you can do for each Oracle, some with more risk than others, and they do genuinely feel significantly different. More impressively, most of those builds involve mechanics entirely unique to each Oracle. There's a ton of effort that, depending on how loosely you define a "build" as separate, results in dozens to potentially over a hundred separate builds, and there's enough overlap and synergy between them that you can mix and match without everything feeling completely useless to each other.

It sounds like a dumb complaint in a game about Dice, but I think a few of the later Oracles are a little too RNG-based. Specifically, Sothis and Austra feel very different to the other Oracles. Sothis causes your dice to trigger twice, but it only happens a certain percentage of the time. You can control that percentage to some degree, but it's an integral mechanic to him and it can be very frustrating when it works against you. Austra focuses much more heavily than other Oracles on random damage. Most of the time, aside from the deck-building elements, the only RNG is the dice rolling, so it can feel bad to play those Oracles when you're used to having fixed amounts of damage at fixed times.

The game's biggest drawback is that the endgame feels a little more lackluster than similar titles. There's tons of replayability on the Oracles and their decks - the devs really put a TON of effort into that - but the variety in enemies is much less, the variety in maps is essentially non-existent, and I would have loved to see them come up with some crazy bosses to match the crazy dice bags you can build (there are a few unique ones, but you're going to be fighting the same bosses A LOT as you start playing the game). Also, to the best of my knowledge, they haven't added Leaderboard of any kind yet, even to the Daily Runs. I would love to see some more community aspects like Leaderboards, Custom Run setups, and maybe some more tweaks to add in extra variety to each run as far as enemies/layout/bosses.

I've played A LOT of roguelike deckbuilder games. StS opened the gate for me and since then I became obsessed with the genre. After putting 150 hours in Astrea, unlocking everything and beating the hardest difficulty with every character I can say that, afterStS, no other game felt as satisfying as this one. 
-  The massive amount of thinking that you need to do every turn is unparalelled. The order of everything matters and you have to take into account many factors, specially all your blessings and the enemy's abilities, to figure out how every dice you play will work out.
-  The deckbuilding aspect is so well polished and balanced, you have at least 4 or 5 viable builds with every character (there are 6 of them), so you never feel that you are obligated to go with certain build to beat the game. In that regard Astrea is even better that StS, as there are no "must have" dices or blessings to beat the game at all, the strenght of every blessing or dice you get offered as rewards depends entirely on your current build. 
- It has the same thing as StS where you find certain blessing that interacts well with some of your dices so you decide to make a build based on that alone. And as there are tons of blessing and dices, the amount of possible options is very, very high. It's very common to discover along the way some of those interactions for the first time, which makes every run feel pretty unique.
-  There are not as many enemies as in other games of the genre, but each of them is very well designed and makes you think hard how you can adjust your play to beat them, specially when it has something that counters some important aspect of your build.
- You can have up to 2 sentinels (companions) that add to the general complexity, as you can use them to improve your build or cover some weakness of it.
- The pathing has a lot of interesting options and forging dices feels really good.

All in all, congrats to the devs for making such an incredible game. If you are a fan of this genre, Astrea will defintely scratch your itch.

When first looking at Super Roboy, I didn’t find the cartoon graphics particularly appealing and had concerns that the game would be too kid-focused and easy. While the story didn’t capture my interest, the option to skip all cutscenes is a huge quality-of-life feature I wish more games included. Some dialogue must still be skipped manually, usually at the start of a new area, but overall, the game respects player time. The dialogue itself is family-friendly rather than overly child-oriented, which is probably the best approach given the game’s chosen art style. I also appreciate Roboy’s unyielding optimism in a world that is clearly falling apart. More importantly, the environments are distinct, and both enemies and backgrounds are easy to read. Since visual clarity directly affects gameplay, this is a well-executed design choice.

The gameplay is where Super Roboy truly shines. I was surprised at how confidently designed the game is, especially considering it's the developer's first listed project. Roboy starts with the ability to jump, shoot, and aim, gradually acquiring new abilities as the game progresses. While this is standard for Metroidvanias, what sets this game apart is the sheer speed at which new abilities are handed out. This rapid progression keeps the gameplay engaging, ensuring that Roboy is constantly evolving. New abilities are unlocked by defeating enemies and bosses, then purchased with crystals found in the environment. The upgrades are easy to use but feel substantial, significantly enhancing movement and combat. By the end of the game, you genuinely feel like a Super RoGod.

Combat and movement feel responsive, making deaths and platforming challenges fair. However, menu navigation feels clunky on a keyboard, as “E” is used to confirm and “C” to cancel, which is an unusual and unintuitive setup. A notable strength of the game is its difficulty modes. On Hard mode, enemies don’t just have inflated health; instead, they become faster, more aggressive, and fire additional projectiles. This approach makes them more mechanically interesting rather than artificially tougher, which is something many games fail to achieve.

In terms of content, Super Roboy is packed with variety. Enemy types are diverse, each with unique abilities and status effects that impact Roboy’s combat capabilities in meaningful ways. Some status effects limit Roboy to a single projectile, while others disable the explosion effect of the Target ability. These mechanics keep encounters fresh and exploration engaging. The game also features a solid roster of bosses, most of which become more difficult when they reach half health, adding more attacks and moving faster. Due to the way ability progression works, some bosses may seem too difficult at first, but returning after acquiring new upgrades makes them significantly easier.

Level design is functional but rigid, with most rooms feeling rectangular and boxy. While this makes traversal straightforward and prevents unnecessary obstructions, it also gives the world a somewhat clinical feel. Some players may find it lacks the organic charm of other Metroidvanias. However, exploration improves as Roboy gains abilities, with later skills revealing secrets on the map and improving fast travel options. This makes 100% completion very approachable.

One aspect I was less fond of was the inclusion of puzzle rooms, which are required to collect all the crystals needed for upgrades. While none of them are so complex that external guidance is necessary, they aren’t particularly gratifying to complete. They serve as a minor speed bump in an otherwise smooth experience. On repeat playthroughs, I don’t think they will add much value.

Overall, Super Roboy is a surprisingly well-made and satisfying Metroidvania with strong progression, excellent combat, and a generous difficulty curve that rewards player skill. While the level design is somewhat rigid and puzzles aren’t my favorite addition, the strengths of the game far outweigh these minor drawbacks. I’m excited to see what the developer creates next.

The skill unlocking mechanism is quite unique, adds a ton player choice as you make your way through the world. The movement is extremely crisp, enemy balance is fair (albeit with some difficulty spikes if you enter an area under leveled), the skill system is unique, the map layout isn't punishing, and by the end of the game once you have unlocked enough skills and leveled your stats high enough, you are flying around the maps at light speed instantly destroying everything in your path. 

Boss battles are pretty good, some of them are great, and only a few seemed a little underwhelming. Of all my deaths there were only handful of them that where I thought "That was some BS". The rest of them I could only blame myself. It's light on the questing which is fine by me. A bit light on the platforming challenges for my tastes, but that's the only major downside of this game I can point out. 

Overall, great experience and worth the money.

In a world of early access titles, it is somewhat refreshing to see something release in such a complete and polished state.  This is a game I am glad I came across, because it is absolutely beautiful so far.

To sum it up, while this may look on the surface like some kind of Mega-Man analogue, it plays much more similar to a classic Metroid.  The controls are snappy and super responsive, there are a variety of abilities to unlock and choices to make on how you improve yourself, combos to work through, etc.  Like any good Metroidvania, your agility with the controller determines your success here.  The story is very interesting so far, and is more of a post-apoc style theme than I was expecting.  The music is beautiful.. it is somber and almost sad, but it fits this story really well.  It's a bit of a mystery still, with some very sad overtones.  I actually think it's poetic and beautiful.

The difficulty here is not like Dead Cells or Astral Ascent.  This is going to be more akin to something like Hollow Knight or Ori (though I think the controls here are much better than both Hollow Knight and Ori).  This is also not a roguelite or anything.   It's a classic Metroidvania where you move around the map unlocking doors, beating mini-bosses, collecting items, etc.  You move to different biomes as you go.  Saving is performed at key locations where you find a save spot, much like Hollow Knight.  If you die, you go back to that save... so it can be frustrating if you die sometimes, but it's never more than a few minutes (or hasn't been so far).

This is one of the more relaxing Metroidvanias I own, and I'll happily be playing it.

Oh, an important note... I am playing this exclusively on my Steam Deck and it works beautifully.  So while the store listed Steam Deck compatibility status (as of the date of this review) is "Unknown," I can assure you that it works fantastic.  In fact, this is one of my go-to games on my Steam Deck now.

If you like Metroidvanias, want something somber and relaxing, perhaps a change from the super hard challenging roguelites (I love those as well), then this is a great choice.  And after all, I really do believe the developers should be rewarded for releasing such a well polished game out of the box.  Well done to them.
