Steam is full of sub-par match 3 games, many of which try to sell you on the naughty ecchi images or an enormous amount of unnecessary features creating massive clutter. Fortunately, in my never ending quest for something I can play while on my breaks with one hand holding a sandwich, and my other on the mouse, I have found FishWitch Halloween. 

When you play the first level, you might notice that it resembles a bit like Clover Tales by Five BN Games. However, unlike Clover Tales, FishWitch Halloween doesn't market itself as 'free to play' and then nickle and dime you with the in-game monetization required to unlock packages of crystals that is an in-game currency to recharge certain abilities, as well as play games without having to wait for the energy bar to recharge itself over real-time. Nope, FishWitch Halloween does it right by just charging you a nominal one-time price, as it should, and then let you play the game to gain gold, which in turn is used to unlock ornaments, which also give you crystals that are used to recharge your abilities.

PROS:
- Visuals are 'just right'. They are crisp and colourful, but not overbearing.
- The levels and puzzles are well designed and are not overly frustrating.
- The UI is simple and not cluttered.
- Tutorial and in-game help is useful.
- Definitely a game I can play 15 to 30 minutes at a time. Great for work breaks.
- Good background music that isn't overbearing. 

CONS:
- None really. Perhaps the lack of different modes.
- The background music is randomly played. So you may listen to the same one three times in a row. My original review stated there was only one background song, but I realized there are actually more after playing over two dozen levels. 

SUGGESTION:
- Definitely needs a game mode that allows players to play forever, until there are no more moves left, or not enough time left. 

CONCLUSION:
Ultimately, FishWitch Halloween deserves two thumbs up. It's fun and easy on the eyes.

[b]secrets of magic 5[/b] plays almost exactly like the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/453780]first[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/713430]second[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1351250]third[/url] and [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1467060]fourth[/url] games in the series, so my review will be very similar as well.

beatrix, victoria's student from som4, is back. I was hoping she'd turn evil and breathe some life (and narrative) into the series again, but it wasn't to be, they're just watching over the school while the boss is away. so all the dialog is about [b]mandatory decorations[/b], just like in som3. the devs went with the 'every item has a bunch of variations' approach, which I first saw in [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/388450]spooky bonus[/url] (I think), so you can buy something, then change its appearance at will.

there's still [b]very little difference from the previous games[/b]. typical match-3 action on [b]100 levels[/b] unlocked one by one, matching 4+ tiles creates various power-ups destroying stuff in different shapes, and there are chests and keys to bring to the bottom, the latter to unlock more of the level. one change is [b]created power-ups can't be clicked anymore, they have to be swapped to trigger[/b]. the swap doesn't need to end in a valid match, but they're a lot less useful now and a lot more annoying on levels where they're completely walled in. great job on changing something for the worse for no reason.

even though you learned and upgraded everything in the first game, then again in each sequel, [b]you start with nothing and have to unlock all the power-ups yet again[/b]. understandable from a gameplay perspective, not so much otherwise. and after re-unlocking all 4 early on, there's not much else going on, only a few typical mechanics get added to the mix. [b]no spiders or imps this time[/b] either, but new things include portals, cannons and snow blocks affected by gravity, plus [b]multi-screen levels[/b]. just click an arrow to switch between boards.

[b]relaxed, challenge and timed modes, the middle means a move limit[/b], no star rating once again, but there's a scoreboard for every level after completion. and there's a [b]second layer of difficulty[/b] regarding the amount of obstacles and power-ups: [b]casual has fewer obstacles and more power-ups, expert the other way round[/b].

[b]same lovely and varied tilesets and backgrounds with fitting music.[/b] the decorating screen went back to 2d, thankfully, with much nicer-looking objects, but the background here is not as good as the loading screens. well, it's not good at all. separate volume settings, windowed mode, custom cursor, tutorial and match hint toggles, in-game representation of achievements and some languages. there's also an on-screen keyboard when you type your name. accessibility and all that, but it covers the ui buttons and can't be closed for good, so type, close keyboard, click ok. lame. also, [b]ui buttons can be pretty unresponsive and any and all keypresses advance dialog[/b], making alt+tabbing and taking screenshots problematic during conversations. never been an issue before, again, great job.

[b]optional hidden object, jigsaw and tile-swapping levels[/b] are also new. there are 8 total, the skip button needs some time to charge, hints are available. tile-swapping is just that, jigsaw is jigsaw, new pieces appear as you move them from the bottom and mouse controls are floaty and uncomfortable. hidden object scenes are in 3d, and the guy from som4 was either fired or learned a lot because these look a lot better (only 15 years old instead of 20). the camera can be moved by clicking and holding the arrows on the side, not that great, but no penalty for frantic clicking.

since it's pretty much the same as the other games, which are among the better match-3 titles on the market, I can only say the same about this: [b]worthy addition to anyone's collection, unless you don't want more of the same[/b]. though at least the other kind of levels and a few new mechanics provide some much-needed variety, so even with the issues ([b]the board can bug out[/b] too, 2 tiles overlap, leaving an empty tile, only restarting the game fixes it, though it only happened in windowed mode), I'd say [b]this is the best entry since som2[/b].

Lockes The Thief is a fun and challenging 3D stealth platformer that puts you in the shoes of Locke, a rogue who must stop his former allies from unleashing a dark force upon the world. The game has colorful graphics, smooth controls, and varied levels that test your skills and wits. The game also has a catchy soundtrack and some humorous dialogue that add to its charm. Lockes The Thief is a Goldilocks game that hit the sweet spot in several ways.  Its mechanics were not overly complicated, and I felt I didn't need to invest a huge amount of mental energy in order to play it well.  They were, however, detailed enough to keep me engaged throughout the entire game.  Its difficulty matched its mechanics.  Lockes The Thief isn't overly challenging, but just challenging enough to make me consider different strategies when I died.  One of the bosses took me about 10 times before I figured out how to beat him, and when I did, it was very satisfying.

The narrative isn't overly complicated, but it gives you just enough story to keep you hooked and interested in the characters.  The game doesn't give any overbloated backstory about its world and its cast; it gives us the basics that are told in a way that makes you love the protagonist, Lockes, within minutes.  Lockes fits the big-hearted, anti-hero persona well; he exudes a charm and swagger that makes me hope to see him in future games.  

It lacks polish in, IMO, ways that are fairly insignificant.  But where it lacks in polish, it more than makes up for in charm.  I really enjoyed its bright, cartoonish style.  I loved sneaking around and yeeting unsuspecting enemies.  I loved that it kept me wanting to play without demanding too much of my mental energy.

I've gambled on many indie games under $10 and I usually wind up disappointed;  Lockes The Thief definitely did not disappoint for its modest price tag.  If you're looking for a more casual action RPG style indie that succeeds in capturing the basic elements of what makes a game fun without too much pomp and circumstance, then I would recommend this game.

[h2]Notoris: The Goblin War Review[/h2]

When this game was put up for review, I was quite intrigued by it. The main reason is that I never played a game that falls under this genre. I always wanted to give this genre a shot but ended up procrastinating. Although it seems pretty interesting, it also looks like it’s a bit complicated. The genre I am referring to is Strategy + Turn-based combat. 

So, this basically means this is the first game I played in that genre. The first impression is supposed to be the best impression. Let’s see if this game managed to impress me and maybe help me gain an interest in this genre. Oh, and this game was apparently made by a group of students. Would be cool to support passionate start-ups! (Totally not saying this since I am also about to become a dev myself 0.0)

[h1]About This Game [/h1]

[h2]Storyline [/h2]

If I am right, the game doesn’t possess a narrative aspect as far as I know. You can play as three different characters namely Havie, Colmac, and Mika. I played as Mika! Each character has their own set of 5 battles that possess their own mini-plots. I am pretty sure these battles have no relation with any of the IRL wars or something. I mean, duh, the game has elves and goblins. 
[h2]Gameplay Mechanics [/h2]

As I mentioned in the introduction, this is the first time I played a game that falls under the “Turn-based combat” Genre. This means that I need someone to literally spoon-feed me at least the basic how-to-play info. I was very disappointed when I found out that this game literally throws you into a battle with no tutorial of any sort. I had no clue what to do and was just randomly clicking stuff trying to figure out what my next move should be. I would’ve appreciated it if they at least added a textual tutorial or something basic. It’s not fun playing a game that is hard to figure out. I mean, if their target audience are those players who have prior experience in playing such games, then I see no problem. But a game should be friendly to players of all kinds, which this game lacks. I hope they implement a tutorial after seeing this! ^^

This automatically makes me the wrong person to play and review this game. Well, there’s no turning back now. Here’s everything I learned about the game:
[list]
[*] FIRSTLY, I wanted to get this out of the way. Basically, in the settings, you can change the game’s volume level, yeah? I basically muted the Master Volume since I play music on Spotify while playing games. The issue here is that when I re-launched the game, it wasn’t muted. After going to the settings, the game automatically muted itself. Look into this bug!
[*] The core gameplay revolves around what I assume to be the basic turn-based combat gameplay. You make your move, end your turn, then your allies make their moves and then the enemies make their moves. Sounds pretty simple yeah? But I still had a hard time figuring out how the game actually worked. 😅	
[*] Basically, when it’s your turn, you can choose from a total of four possible actions: Move, default attack, skills, or ending your turn. Each action (Except ending your turn) uses up a portion of your energy. If I am right, a character becomes useless once you use up all of their energy.
[*] Each character is unique since they possess different skill sets, strengths, and weaknesses. Melee characters obviously have a much lesser attack range when compared to ranged allies. Considering all the factors above, it’s pretty evident that a lot of planning is required before you make your move. 
[/list]

[h2]Visuals & Audio[/h2]

The game’s UI design is pretty basic. It’s not very polished and looks a bit low quality. Some text elements on the screen stand out and look awkward. The assets used are somewhat low-poly. This basically means that the game shouldn’t be heavy. But for some reason, I get a lot of FPS drops. The problem continued even after reducing the graphics to medium. They need to optimize the game so the players get a smoother gameplay experience.

The Aural aspect of the game is pretty decent. The only issue is the settings problem I mentioned in the gameplay segment. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Simple eye-pleasing visuals.
[*] A total of 3 characters to play as. 
[*] Each character has 5 battles that vary in difficulty and troops. 
[*] You can choose different approaches whenever you play a level. This adds a lot to the game’s replayability. 
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] The game isn’t well optimized.
[*] UI can be made better.
[*] You might encounter bugs and glitches here and there.
[*] The game lacks a tutorial of any kind. There are no tips or hints either!
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game lacks polishing. I am sure the developers could improve it with a bit of tweaking. It is playable in its current state. But yeah, steer clear from this game if you’re new to this genre since it doesn’t help you at all during your gameplay. Is it worth its base price? I guess so since the game isn’t that expensive. It’s nice to support passionate student developers!

[h1]An Adorably Whimsical Collection[/h1]

[i]Slide Stories: Bucky's Quest[/i] is the third collection of slider puzzles by [b]Remix Games[/b]. It contains six slider puzzles, which are [i]animated[/i], and can be solved on five different difficulties levels: 3x3, 4x4, 5x5, 6x6, and 9x9. As you solve one puzzle, the next becomes available. This sequence of unlocking puzzles allows for a story to unfold with our heroes, Bucky and Shin. I enjoy the subtle storytelling that this setup creates.

This game includes a few helpful options for solving the puzzles. As previously noted, there are varying difficulty levels, allowing puzzlers of different skill levels to play and solve the slider puzzles. You can choose any size at any time: you can start of with the easiest or the most challenging (or anything in between): it's up to you! You can play through all levels (which I enjoy doing), and play them time and time again.

Once you're working on the puzzle, other options are available. One is to look at what the completed image should look like. This feature is particularly helpful with the larger count puzzles, when you are trying to figure out where in the puzzle the characters should be standing (or lying down, as the case may be). This beats setting up a bunch of the puzzle only to later discover your rows or columns are off by one (and having to shuffle everything over).

Another feature is to number the pieces. This is also especially helpful on the higher count puzzles, as smaller pieces may look quite similar to other pieces, and it can be tricky to figure out which ones go where (this is particularly true, I found, with puzzles 3 and 4 on Pro difficulty). In my experience, I've used this feature once I'm nearly done the puzzle and am struggling with a few similar-looking pieces.

Finally, there is a undo option, which undoes your recent moves by sliding the pieces back in reverse order. Early on in a puzzle, this option serves as a simple reset, rather than undoing a few moves.

As mentioned at the beginning of this review, the slider puzzles are animated. They aren't [i]fully[/i] moving pictures, just small parts. This, too, helps with figuring out which pieces are neighbours to one another. With that said, I found the motions to be a bit too quick and rather nauseating. I suffered from this problem with the second collection, [i]Slide Stories: Bonds & Memories[/i]. The first set, [i]Slide Stories: Neko's Journey[/i], does not have this problem. The animations are well-balanced in that first collection. I've noted this previously with the second collection, and I'll note it here as well: I wish we could freeze the animations. That would be a nice additional option to have, especially for those who are prone to motion sickness.

I should note, too, that there is a single track that plays throughout the game (on the menu and puzzle pages). It's perfectly suited for the adventure being told through the puzzles. I have also mentioned this in my other reviews for this series: though the single song is nice, I would prefer a bit of variety between puzzles. Nonetheless, the music perfectly captures the feelings of the puzzles and their story.

I enjoy this game, as I did the others. I do wish there were more puzzles to solve. Six isn't much, and there is room on the game's interface for a few more. I recommend [i]Slide Stories: Bucky's Quest[/i] to all who enjoy solving slider puzzles. This series has a nice twist with the animations and overarching story told through the puzzles. I hope to see the company make more of these collections in the near future.

Gameplay: This is a story drive JRPG. You'll explore the world while fighting enemies. The combat system is a bit of a fusion of persona/old-school JRPG and a quick timed mechanic to score an extra attack once a weakness is hit. You'll gain additional powers as you progress. This is an RPG maker game, so the quality for the battles is pretty limited but the creater did a great job with what they had. I found both the exploration, story and combat all worthwhile investments of my time. 4/5.
Story: So first off, as an amateur author myself, I'm always drawn to RPGs for the story. And I enjoy it even more when that story is something new, something I haven't seen before. Elohim Eternal takes the biblical mythos and weaves in a story of supernatural yet futuristic elements together. I don't want to spoil too much of it and my only comment would be to stick through the intro sequence when they're dropping lots of biblical verbiage, it all pays off. I am more than excited to see a sequel come out. 5/5.
Music: Classic JRPG fare, but it fits so well. Everything was enjoyable, but not as memorable as a Nobuo Uematsu. 4/5.
Graphics/Art-style: So this is an RPG maker game and you can see this is where the game suffers the most. With that said, the maker did a great job with what he had. Enemy designs are unique and interesting, the maps are well-done and this is a tier above many other RPG maker games but certainly don't go in expecting super graphics. 4/5.
Fun-factor: I had mistakenly turned off the battles at the beginning (yes, you can choose to play only for the story if you so wish) and I turned them on about 2 hours in and went back, fighting all the enemies I missed on my first go through. I don't generally do that and found the combat system interesting, but what really kept me going was the story. Fantastic job there and I cannot wait to see where it continues in the next entry. 5/5.
Overall: If you like JRPGs, especially old-school ones with a different story that will draw you in, this game is right up your alley. 4/5.

Yes, I will recommend this- with some caveats.

This is not a HOG like an Artifex Mundi game. 
I would call it more of an interactive visual novel.
If you are hoping for a big AAA-type production- this is not it. 
Solo dev with a little help from some friends- set your expectations accordingly.

Interesting mix of art styles- Minecrat meets anime meets detailed pixel art. 
Really nice music.

No voice acting- if the sound the Charlie Brown teacher makes annoys you- well, that's what you are going to get for dialogues. Dialogues are also all in text (good for HoH and deaf players, but read on, please...), so you can mute the game and play silently. But if you need scalable text for any reason- you can only zoom in or out to scale it, and some zooming in will cut the text off of the screen due to where it appears, usually with no way to have the character repeat it if you couldn't read it all. (Some dialog will repeat, but most of it will not.)
Again-  
[quote]Solo dev with a little help from some friends- set your expectations accordingly.[/quote]

Can be played with a mouse only- LB, RB, scroll wheel. So good for anyone who can only play with one hand.
On the downside- some of the scenes are very dark, and the colors are a bit muddy- people with low vision or color-blindness are not going to have an easy time with this game. Some items are very difficult to detect simply because the contrast between them and the surroundings they are in  is close- they do not stand out and tend to fade into each other. 
There are few settings options- nothing for brightness or gamma, no accessibility options, 

The mechanics are similar to "No Longer home" by Humble Grove, though no keys needed- you control zooming in and out, and rotating the scene with mouse-only. Lots and lots of clicking- a short enough game to play in one sitting, but playing in shorter sessions may make your eyes and fingers happier.

I will say the hidden objects you have to collect become more difficult to collect as the game goes on. The difficulty progression with finding and collecting these items goes from "Super easy" to "OMG my eyes are bleeding from trying to find these things!" at the end. 

The end of the game was not what I expected- the story was not terribly deep throughout, but it did have enough depth to make you want to know more. But at the end it just dropped out, and you watched it instead of being part of it. The castle section and final scenes seemed rushed, or cut back. Solo dev- so funding and time could have been the issue, but it wasn't the most satisfying ending for me. It left me wondering "What the heck?". The ending was a bit of a let down for me. 

It was a good game, though. Not a great game, but good for killing time, and one character will likely be vaseline and tissue material for some gamers who like big-chested anime girls, lol. Just don't expect any bouncing- the NPCs are static images- they do not go "boing-boing" across the screen.

Was it worth the price? For me, sure. (Keeping in mind I paid the release price, which was 10% off.)
But I can afford to buy all the games I want. If you are on a tight budget and are wanting something you'll get a lot of time out of- maybe not. Little replayability in this game- once you go through it, you know the story and where everything is. There is level selection, though. So if you miss a collectible along the way, you can replay a level to go back and find it. 

Interesting enough for me to recommend it, but I must also be honest about what the game is like- it's not a big dollar production, don't expect it to look or play like one. But it's a decent little game made by (mostly) one person. I support solo devs and small indie/independent studios when I can and when the devs aren't total jerks. I had some contact with this dev both here on Steam and on their social media account via DM- they were very approachable and responsive when I reported a bug to them (very quick hotfix that squashed that bug, too). They treated me nicely and respectfully- please do the same for them if you have any contact with them. 

(edited to remove paragraph about broken achievements- the dev pushed another quick hotfix- and all achievements trigger correctly now. Dev is responsive and fast with fixing reported bugs.)

UPDATE: I am finding some SERIOUS bugs a week after launch. I am sure they will be fixed but at the moment a real game cannot be played because these bugs screw all the calculations (which are the foundation of 18xx games). I might reverse the review to negative if they aren't fixed in a few days.

Original Review:
You should know what you are getting with the 18xx games. This is pretty good, both as a client and as an entry in the family of games, including elements that are questionable if you are a purist but are pretty nice if you like your board games to have replayability and some minimum degree of asymmetry, and I am referring to the pre-game draft of assets cards. Also the theme is great and enriched by the Korean war elements.

Buyers beware: there is NO single-player or versus-AI mode. This is a multiplayer only game. *As it should be.*

UPDATE: Developers appear to have abandoned this game while there still some important gameplay elements to adjust and some bugs to squash. Still playable, but I no longer recommend it as a purchase.  My original comments are included below.

_________________________________________________________________

Pretty exciting to see a developer making an 18XX game for PC along with AI! Any 18XX fan should consider purchasing this game in support of the developers for that reason alone.

But, my current review is as follows: This would be the type of game someone who played their first 18XX game a few weeks ago might design - an homage to 18XX but not quite right.

Everything "works" more or less, it's just that the game's Korean War rules are so all-encompassing in the strategy that you are really forced down a limited number of strategy paths. I wonder about the replayability because of that issue. Games feel too similar, even by play #2. Your choices are: Invest heavily and early in the North or heavily and early in the South. Or a minor variation of those two. That's it.

Also, the game provides too many build points. It's too easy to connect everything in a big hurry. The board develops much too quickly and this contributes heavily to the "same-y" feeling. It becomes a station placement game very quickly because all the best routes are built early, and even worse, the board halves itself permanently early in the game due to the war. Thematic, perhaps. Fun? No.

The privates are much too strong by nearly any 18XX standard. And since they are drafted there is no auto-balancing feature normally provided by bids.

There are more issues too, but I think the above are already more than enough reason to avoid this game.

Some improvements suggestions for the DEVELOPERS:

i) During play it should be clear how much each company made in revenue during its last run.

ii) When preparing to lay track, it should show coloured track lines to indicate what the current "best routes" are for the active company. It would make deciding upon track builds much easier.

iii) Remove the game pause when the little trains graphics are activated. Players should not have to wait while that animation takes place.

iv) During revenue payout, it should show the potential amounts below the "Dividend" and "Keep" Buttons. For example, under Dividend it would say $58 per share and $106 to the company.  This information is vital for companies that want to upgrade locomotives and it's not good to force the player to have to click around to calculate that information for themselves.

v) During a stock round, each company should graphically show which players own stock in each company and how many shares they own. It should ALSO show the last revenue that company recorded during its last operating round.  This information is not always easy to see and so including it on the stock market will improve decision-making.

I understand it works for a smaller map, but not sure how I feel about it after only one play through but its intriguing for planning and strategy.

All in all I enjoyed playing it and will convince my friends who enjoy 18xx as well to get it.  It certainly is a good basis as far as bringing the tabletop games to the PC.

Finishing Fleshport took me about 9 hours, but I'm very slow and check every detail twice. This game had me hooked from beginning to end. The characters are both unsettling and charming.
The design in some parts of the game are confusing, with doors that are hard to notice and details that are easy to miss. There was one puzzle in particular I could only figure out after interacting with every object and smooshing my face against every wall. There are also some bugs, especially with the chase mechanics, but nothing game-breaking. I fully recommend this weird, weird game.

First of all: Do not save the game while you are being chased. This may cause the game to crash any time you try to continue the game and if you only used one save slot, you will have to restart the game. I had to restart the game which was annoying but in my second playthrough I remembered not to save while being chased and everything went well.

When you upload a game to Steam I guess it's a bit of roulette. Regardless of an indie game's quality, there's a chance that not many people will discover and play it. I think the thumbnail art for the game looks both boring and weird. The trailer also does not do the game justice. 

Overall, I am very impressed with the game. I only have some minor things to criticise. I don't really understand the lore but I have ADHD so it might not be the game's fault. Aside from the game crashing maybe 2 or 3 times in my second playthrough, I don't remember encountering any bugs. I believe the game only crashed due to me speedrunning through the dialogue since I had already read it all in my first playthrough. I think the music throughout the game is fine but it's a bit boring and could be a lot better. Some of the tracks have a sharp high pitch sound which I find painful. At the same time, most of them are very interesting. 

My least favourite area in the game is the syringe area - I won't spoil anything. It took me a very very long time to work out how you are supposed to survive Preoria there until I realised in one of the rooms, you had to go near a trap first and hope she gets trapped before going to the item in the room. I hacked the health in the game just to survive this one area. It's basically almost the end of the game but I have no problem with the other areas in the game. My only other area annoyance is with how dark the laboratory is. I did a bunch of zigzagging to get around objects there.

The game has some secrets although I wonder if some things are a red herring that is intended to make you think there's more secrets than there actually are. For example an X on the side of a building but I have no idea what to do there so maybe it's not a secret.

The game has a decent atmosphere and interesting story from what I can understand. Visually it's both hit and miss - some things look better than other things in the game. Generally I do like the way the game looks. Preoria, Shaye, Pugsly, the dolls and that butcher are my favourite characters and I think they look better than the other characters in the game. Shaye is very cute. Nipsy reminds me of Frank from Donnie Darko (even though Frank isn't pink) or Gummo. I haven't watched Gummo, but I've seen a character from that movie who wears a bunny hat. 

The game has a kind of New Game +. I haven't finished the New Game + yet but it has a few cool things in it. Playing the game again after your first time should be a lot faster because you know what to do. This game is very speedrunnable.

I hope the developer makes more games.

Nice new game from Inu To Neko developer who is famous for making games that have a lot of different loot items, crafting and some complex mechanics. The games mechanics usually are not explained fully so it takes some tries to understand how they work (even for those that had english translation), but these complex mechanics still make the game worth it.

Their games are usually simulation games. There were simulators of blacksmithery, ring maker, farm, hotel, dungeon explorer, caravan, goods store and some others. This one seems to be about an explorer girl (or at least it seems like this, maybe we are exploring a tower with several floors and fixing it, I am not quite sure). Edit: finally translated the description from the store and apparently we play as tower repairer, so exploring the tower, gathering resources, repairing it.

This time it's more of an idle game where you just progress through the map linearly and clear slots either using time (idle) or mana (active). You get 1 mana back after clearing each slot. Eventually you get tired and start progressing slowly so should press a Rest button to go to the next day.

I am still trying to understand some mechanics because I barely know Japanese, but I see that there is crafting, customizing a map that is being explored by merging two of them to transfer and upgrade traits, allies with passive abilities, using items that charge while you progress through the map providing different effects, subquests that provide extra items, shop where you sell your loot, shop where you buy some things, orbs that provide boosts to some stats and extra abilities, some other exploration minigame where you destroy rows to get loot. Overall it again looks quite complex and interesting as most other their games.

Too bad it doesn't have English translation (and I doubt it's coming as it never came for most of their later games). Even having just skills and items translated while leaving the story in Japanese would have helped immensively.

PS. some person in one of the negative reviews that are visible to me complains about not being able to close Subquest screen, you close it with right mouse button. Another person complains about tiredness not being displayed, but you can obviously see when you are progressing too slow and can press Rest then, there is no need to actually see the number.

They just either help you get more unlocks, or kill people in extravagant but underwhelming ways that ultimately amount to nothing.

Other than that, the game is alright brain fodder, can be cathartic, and has potential to be actually good rather than just a guilty pleasure. Seems to be an abandoned project though.

As for the main character, I was more than pleasantly surprised to discover that she could actually be supportive and kind to him and not be punished for it. No forced choices where I have to choose between 'fight him' or 'bite him', as I find in more recent otome games. These two facts above were the reason why I decided to write a review and recommend this game to anyone who might be interested in the same things I am. [strike](I'm usually too shy to write reviews lol)[/strike] 

As for the things I didn't like about this game, they aren't a lot, but they were enough to almost ruin my day. First, the ending. It was so rushed, I was surprised when the screen took me to the main menu. A well-written universe such as this one requires an equally thought-out ending. I didn't mind the gruesome parts of the story one bit, but I assume that most readers want to feel rewarded in the end and spend some time with the love interest. In the Master's route there was almost no romance, which was very disappointing. [strike]And of course, no erotic scenes either (sadly).[/strike]

One other thing that I really didn't like was the fact that getting a good ending depended on the random choice of selecting between H2SO4 and H2SO3. 'Well, I'm sorry, Master, that you don't love me, but I've had my chemistry classes years ago!' As a fellow dev and writer, I wouldn't dump jargon from my discipline into a story and make it into a crucial choice that would determine the ending. I ended up really sad when I discovered that my first ending was a normal instead of a good one.

Anyways, this game is still precious to me, mainly because of the dynamic between the Master and the MC. I rarely find relationships such as this in otome games anymore, so I'm still grateful.

Madrid Noir is an interactive VR experience telling the story of a young girl named Lola as she pretends be a detective around the city of Madrid, during the summer she lives with her weird uncle. As the story unfolds and clues reveal themselves, the stakes are raised dramatically and there is a great on-foot chase sequence. The story is super cute, with a lot of very nice animation to match the excellent voice acting.

For those that haven’t seen a VR experience before, they’re pretty straightforward. They will almost always be less than an hour’s worth of narrative content where players engaging in the story through minor interactions. These often are things like pushing buttons or pointing items at the action. Sometimes these are optional, but I find they help add to the sense of presence of the films. Madrid Noir, for example, had a scene where we had to aim a flashlight in the dark to help Lola find her way before it would proceed to the next scene.

It’s worth noting that this particular experience did require players to stand so that players could turn in the directions the experience wanted us to be in, to see the characters. I find this kind of setup to be demanding and rude towards its audience- Snap rotation is a standard across almost all of the VR industry, so I don’t know why a developer would choose to exclude the feature when it means the difference between a seated or standing game. Accessibility matters, even in VR, people!

I really did adore the experience, however. Lola and her uncle were great, and I love the animation style so very much. This wasn’t the studio’s first VR experience, as they have previously produced Battlescar and Gloomy Eyes. I can tell Madrid Noir was made by a team of professionals, and I am hoping for more along these lines of quality. Recommended.

Madrid Noir is a VR-exclusive... thing. It calls itself a movie, but since the set is 3D and it occasionally needs your input, I wouldn't call it one. It's also hard to call a game since it'll carry on without you doing anything for the vast majority of the run time and the interactivity is very limited even when it is present. To me, it feels most like some kind of small-production stage play that involves the audience. It's about the same length as a lot of plays, has an intermission, and most of the scenes take place in sets that look an awful lot like a stage. It certainly has a lot of aspects of games and movies as well, but I think it's easiest to say you'll enjoy it if the idea of a 45 minute play is appealing to you. 

Unsurprisingly, there's almost nothing to talk about in terms of gameplay. You get to move objects around to progress the story a couple of times, but otherwise your interactivity is limited to choosing where to look and throwing objects around without being acknowledged at all. It does at least look quite nice, though. The sets are very detailed and the cartoony art style fits the game well. Although it obviously draws heavily from the noir genre, many scenes also evoke classic cartoons. 

Does it benefit from being VR-exclusive? Yes and no. It's fun to be able to look around and it definitely has some setpieces that would be nearly impossible to reproduce on a real stage, but there's also nothing that stands out as specifically requiring VR. It might have been a little bit less immersive as a regular non-VR game, but I suppose it would have been harder to justify the price tag that way. 

Lastly, the story. It's hard to say much about this without getting into spoilers since the story is so short. The protagonist tells you about the summer she spent in Madrid with her shady uncle. She starts trying to piece together what he's up to, and eventually noir things happen. It has a couple of clever moments and is generally well-told.

I dont usually write Reviews for indie games, but this "thing" rubbed me the wrong way a bit too much.

So what is "CADE PRIME"?

- A quadruple [b]Assetflip[/b] bunched together.
- It literally uses the demo levels of the Assetpacks linked below as the entire games content
- Green
- a complete mess


Assetpacks (Appear in this order in the game with pretty much zero changes to the levels themselves.):
1: https://www.unrealengine.com/marketplace/en-US/product/advanced-puzzle-constructor
2: https://www.unrealengine.com/marketplace/en-US/product/first-person-puzzle-template
3: https://www.unrealengine.com/marketplace/en-US/product/ultimate-fps-puzzle-kit
4: https://www.unrealengine.com/marketplace/en-US/product/puzzle-logic-system

1, 3, 4 have playable Demos on the store page, which is the stuff that is in this game. (which means, you can play 3/4 of the game for free, in way better graphics, if you really want to give this a go.)
2 has a video of what appears in this game, but in green: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=450TtZhl0Js


[h1]That aside, lets get into the other stuff that this game does not have:[/h1]
- A menu (Esc closes the game)
- Graphics options
- Sound options
- Keybindings
- Mouse settings
- Loading and Saving
- any artistical direction
- selfmade content

or to put it in different words: it doesnt even have the most basic functionality you would expect from any game.


[h1]The things the game has:[/h1]
- sometimes First Person Gameplay, sometimes 3rd person - depending on which assetpack you are currently playing.
- wonky physics
- a soundtrack which definitely doesnt belong into a puzzle game, but rather into a club
- red/green/blue boxes you have to move around... which you cant distinguish from each other because everything is green.
- a mix of different UIs, if there is one (each assetpack has its own)
- sometimes it has a crosshair, which is really useful when aiming
- different mouse sensitivities depending on assetpack
- the most basic puzzle gameplay you can imagine... because it is made up out of demo maps that were meant for developers.


[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
I stumbled upon this thing by accident, when I was scrolling through the store frontpage instead of playing Final Fantasy 14, like I should have been doing instead... would have saved me this "experience", but at least I can warn others now - so it has had something positive after all.

I played through the entirety of this thing and I still have no idea what the purpose of a game is that is made from Assetpacks that were given away by epic for free at some point and where the only content is the demo maps of said assetpacks that everyone can just download for themselves... for free.

Nothing in this game fits together, it lacks the most basic things, it looks like garbage in comparison to what the Assetpacks should look like... I just dont know who is supposed to play this.

[h1]I highly recommend to play any other (actual) puzzle game instead of this, its a waste of time. (If you really want to try this, get the free Assetpack-demos, they even look better.)[/h1]

EDIT: If you dont believe me, remember: you can refund within 2 hours of playtime or 14 days after purchase, whatever you will reach first.

An incredible project where everything but the OST was done by the solo developer Achromi. The game has a big world with tons of secrets both big and small, and the game has a great sense of discovery.

The story while simple is told without words, instead using symbols for nearly everything, down to the menus. This leads you to experimentation to learn what everything does and I love that.

While these aspects are great, some things bogged the experience down for me. First off, while the spritework is good and there's a detailed world, the two tone graphics made it to where there's clarity issues in what exactly to do in the game.

Another issue is while there's a general mantra of "if you can enter a dungeon, you can beat it", there's an optional mini dungeon that has an item that not only is very convenient, it's required to not make one dungeon not obtuse in a way that while matching the games of old felt out of character for this game.

And if we're talking about this game, we do need to bring up the combat. The weird momentum slowing down was something I never got myself. And while letting go of a button to attack wasn't bad for me, the fact it's an option setting should say a lot about this initial design decision. I also just think the combat is not fun enough to engage with, so I had more fun playing with the lowest combat setting.

Despite my negatives, the positives do shine out. And while my own playthrough was only 8 hours, there's many more secrets to discover, as well as an over 100 puzzle nonogram mode that's just baked into the game. I don't hate this game, but I wish I liked it way more than I do. I personally am curious in the second game by the developer, as I think Havenlocked can improve on the negatives to be a standout game.

Link's Awakening coded with some questionable control design decisions (preserving forward momentum after swinging your sword, swinging your sword after *releasing* the button being the default), and not super well-made picross/nonogram puzzles that are annoyingly needed for 100% achievements.

I will update this review if the developers actually listen to their community and change the game for the better. Unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game in it's current state. The hook is this game is co-op Hades although it seems the developers didn't take any of the right lessons from their inspiration. 

First and foremost, the first major balancing patch was nerfs across the board (in a PvE game? Why do game developers insist on sucking the fun out of their games) with no noteworthy buffs. The reason I found online was "too many people are clearing the game on higher difficulties". So the solution is to just blanket nerf everything to cater to the smallest percentage of your audience? Nerfs simply should not be a priority in a PvE game. This is consistently proven time and time again whenever this happens in a game.

Second, the game has great variety in terms of weapons, spells, and boons, but unlike Hades, there's clearly a lot of builds that are under-powered and it's much harder to find builds that actually make you feel powerful. There needs to be some major balancing rework to make it so even a "bad" run can feel fun and like you have a shot (again Hades does this very well). There are obviously busted and extremely powerful builds, but even average to okay builds should feel like you have a fighting chance. 

Third, enemy health is egregiously spongey once you hit the water area and beyond. It's the point where fights can DRAG on if your build isn't doing the ideal damage output. This is especially noticeable on higher difficulties. 

Fourth, the difficulty options. Frankly, they're just not fun. The affixes aren't great and create SO much visual clutter at times it can be impossible to tell what's happening especially if you're playing co-op. Enemies become damage sponges even more so than before too which makes them even more tedious to fight. Affixes aren't a bad idea but forcing you to take on up to 4 at a time on higher difficulties is a joke especially with how much visual clutter the game already has you dealing with. On top of that, Exploding Mushrooms is atrocious and sucks the fun right out of encounters. And let's just collectively agree to remove No Resurrections on bosses (including Arthur like c'mon big dog) because it's just artificially making the game more challenging in a way that isn't enjoyable. Too much comes down to straight luck on these higher difficulties because of the affixes. Also, the way difficulty is done is far inferior than the Heat System in Hades. They already copied the hook of Hades so I'm not sure why they didn't copy arguably one of the better systems in Hades for difficulty. 

Fifth, co-op balancing. It's awful. Enemy spawns are too high, attacks and affixes clutter the screen to the point where I've seen upwards of 90% of the map covered with attacks. One solution in my mind would be to increase the size of the maps depending on player count to allow for the increased enemy spawn rate and affixes. They could even zoom out from your character even further if necessary to accommodate such a change. Also, the difficulty differences between playing solo and co-op are night and day. It's horribly over-tuned for co-op and needs some major reworking. 

Sixth, one nitpick I have too is the way that skills/boons upgrades currently work. The first upgrade gives you a major percentage boost, but every one beyond that the gains are much, much smaller. Why? It makes upgrades start to feel worthless after a couple of upgrades as the gains are so trivial compared to how much the enemy health balloons in each new biome.

Overall, this game has a ton of potential as it does play like a co-op Hades would and it can be incredibly fun to play, but there are too many things holding it back and in it's current state it's impossible to recommend anyone play this over the far superior Hades 1 or 2.

So, seeing some folks dismiss it as just a co-op Hades/Hades II feels like a medieval slap in the face.  Sure, the House of Hades might have whispered some inspiration in its ear, but this game has its own story to tell, its own rhythm, its own thing.

And that "thing" is Arthurian legend, but with a delightfully twisted spin.  As a massive Arthurian mythology nerd, I'm all in on this reimagining.  It gives the whole questing and slaying and dying (it's a roguelike, after all) a real sense of purpose.

The gameplay?  Chef's kiss.  I'm hooked, line, and Excalibur, and I can't wait to see what the 1.0 release brings.  So, here's the breakdown: If you've ever thought, "Hades is great, but I wish I could share the pain with a friend," then this game is your holy grail.  If you're a roguelike aficionado craving a fresh challenge, consider your quest fulfilled.  New to roguelikes and curious what all the fuss is about? This is a fantastic place to start your (many) glorious deaths.  And finally, if you're like me, obsessed with all things Arthurian, and you haven't already added this to your library... well, what are you waiting for?  The Round Table needs you!

How lucky are we to have so many good AA games coming out that the biggest complaint against this one is that it is somewhat derivative of a certain greek mythology roguelike game.

+ More weapons
+ I like the idea of flipping weapon nodes to change the functionality of the weapon.
+ I like the arthurian setting
+ Multiplayer (absolutely huge, a massive selling point for me, and the enemy scale-up feels in a good spot [compare to ravenswatch which has *horrible* multiplayer scaling])

- I wish there was more *there* there in terms of exploring the setting, characters, voice acting, etc. 
 - I also think it's somewhat unreasonable to expect the level of polish that grecian underworld simulator has from a smaller studio with significantly less budget.
- Blessings that do not directly impact damage feel bad to take and don't feel like they have enough bang for their buck
- It's impossible to increase your odds of getting the more-fun blessings until your first win. This wasn't a problem for me, but more novice players may not stick around long enough to see more-fun talents.
- Dodge and companion boons feel somewhat superflous, and not really build-enabling or build-making.

TL;DR: Good gameplay, multiplayer a huge +, doesn't have supergiant level of polish but IMO doesn't really *need* to. I do hope more resources are invested into VA and world-building as the game gets closer to launch. I also help more builds become viable and feel good to play.

One final note: Sorry devs, there are way more round-table knights in arthurian legend than currently represented in the game. I'm gonna need to see some more of them. You made your own bed on this one.

[u] Pros [/u]
[list]
    [*]The weapon upgrade options can make a weapon play completely differently increasing the build options.
    [*]The sword in the stone upgrades can completely change the way a weapon or spell plays, further increasing the customisation available in an individual run.
    [*] I really like the toggle-able abilities present in the skill trees and the weapon trees allowing you to adjust things, e.g. you can choose to add an additional dash charge or an additional mana charge and can toggle this between runs.
[/list]

[u] Cons [/u]
[list]
    [*]I would really like a way to increase the chances of a particular fae appearing. When you have a build in mind to test out, or are hunting certain blessings it can be really frustrating if you do not see that fae at all until the third biome. I have had runs where I have blown 7 re-rolls across 3-4 banners and not seen the fae I want.
    [*]The random rolls of the corruption options can sometimes just end a run. Running water back to the luna blossom when there are exploding poison mushrooms all over the blossom or the water as an example. Also I really dislike blessing seals, I do not mind ultimate seal or companion seal as these abilities generally are supplementary to my builds, but if you make a build around a particular synergy or fae interaction then again having this removed can sometimes end a run.
    [*] Balancing - Some weapons and spells need balancing and I would like it to be buffing the ones that feel underwhelming rather than nerfing the ones that work well. I would also like to see the spells get some kind of upgrade tree similar to the weapons. Some of the spells are excellent right out of the gate and others are left somewhat underwhelming until/unless you get certain sword in the stone options.
[/list]

At its core, SWORN is a Hades clone. If you liked Hades (or Hades 2), then this game will give you more of the same. That being said, SWORN brings its own flavor to the table and creates a unique and enjoyable experience. Even in early access, the game feels complete and enjoyable, certainly worth its current price tag. If the developers continue the path, the game will be a shining gem within the genre. 

Done well: It feels rewarding to invest both deeply in a single Fae or to mix and match different ones into a unique build. The spells feel great to use and can even be improved mid-run to create some viable and really cool abilities, becoming your primary source of damage. The weapons all feel different and most are really fun. Secret shops can have more than temporary buffs, making them almost always worthwhile to check out and invest. Meta progression moves at a good clip. 

Done poorly: The curse mechanic can be overly crippling, taking away the buff on you light attack when you have a light attack focused build can end a run if it occurs late. This gets especially bad when boss curses start to get included. Some enemies can feel a little cheap, like there is a laser enemy in the third biome that shoots in a sweeping arc that hit you almost from the edge of the screen. Current gameplay strongly favors quick or ranged builds, where melee weapons with slow movesets almost force you to exchange health you cannot afford to lose.

Had a Recommend previously but have changed after playing higher difficulties. Seals are one of the most insanely anti-fun mechanic I've seen in a game. Building around a particular style of fighting then having all the Blessings for that style negated for a room is bonkers. Even beyond that, some of the other Corruptions are so poorly thought out (no Resurrections; e.g. even with 4 full rezs in pocket, you just lose if you go down) truly make me question the design philosophy of the game.

In general, so many of the design decisions make me feel like I must be drunk. Why are there so many single doors so that you are completely at the behest of RNG? Getting meta-currency single doors multiple times in a row feels awful. Why is a meta-currency that only unlocks cosmetics an option that can pop up with single doors? So many of the Blessings from gods are useless for certain weapons/attacks because they don't scale. There is also the sense that the game copied so many of the aspects of Hades, but skipped some of the quality of life improvements that Hades made.

There is a good game in here somewhere but I'm concerned that the finer details that make Hades great will be what makes Sworn misses and leaves it a let-down.

TLDR: It's a co-op Hades clone, fun but with some downsides. After going through all of the difficulties, this game does not want you to play with friends. The later difficulties lock you out of your build, and the devs are nerfing the options players like to pick.

The game is fun as hell and better with friends, unless you plan to go past the first two difficulties. Each difficulty past the first adds random modifiers to make enemies stronger(good), players weaker(good), stage hazards(fine-aggravating), or stopping you from using the build you've invested into(anti-fun).

- Questionable Corruptions: These are added modifiers on higher difficulties. Some like stats, death explosions, regenerating, or speed are good, but others are just frustrating. The innate stage hazards are manageable, but the added ones from corruptions on later difficulties get infuriating. The incoming number of them scales with the group size. On paper it works similar to the standard party size difficulty, in practice it discourages from playing with friends. Often due to bad RNG, a small boss room with hazards and attacks to dodge is now 80% covered in poison while meteors rain down. Most games scale with party size by adding enemy stats/increasing the amount of enemies, this one adds more screen pollution.

- Terrible Resurrection System: Most games have a bleed out timer to get someone up, or the team must wait for the room to clear to come back. In this, if a player goes down, someone must spend their own money or health to res them. Which is fine in games like Gunfire Reborn, but you make very little money in this game. With the newly nerfed healing from abilities, the health cost is hard to afford also. If you cannot afford the cost that scales with EVERY TIME any player is downed, everyone on the team must lose 25% of their max HP. As an added bonus when a shop rolls around, the surviving player is rewarded by being the only one too poor to purchase anything. Real good way to introduce your friends to a new game. 

- Anti-Fun Seals: There are many ways other games in this genre have shown that weaken the player without taking away fun(Raising shop prices, reduced healing from rest zones, less options offered when powering up, time trial, less effective innate buffs, lowered max HP, less XP rates, etc). This game ignores those entirely to pick this god awful option. It locks out one of your main abilities. The major downside is the majority of builds and weapons rely heavily on ONE of their TWO moves. Having the wrong one sealed randomly guts any enjoyment you were having. Now you get to hit souped up enemies with a wet noodle.

- Nerfing Devs: Right away the devs nerfed the options players enjoyed along with all forms of healing. Instead of buffing weaker or clunkier options, they gutted the highly picked ones.

As I am approaching 400 hours, perhaps it’s a good time to leave a review.

I’ve often been asked, what’s the deal with this game, there’s no action, no combat, what’s there to it? Anything at all? Simply put, there is magic of wind and sail. You pull on the winches, all the pieces of canvas start catching wind. Then comes the unmistakable creak of wood together with the sound of strained rigging as the boat slowly comes to life and starts splitting the waves. This either speaks to your soul on a sort of primal level, or it just... doesn’t.

Sailwind is a sailing simulator lite. I’m calling it “lite” because it’s got all kinds of simplifications going on under the hood, but there’s also sufficient complexity to keep one occupied as you learn the ropes. And the winches. And points of sail (also, people who have actually worked on a sailboat say it’s legit, so who am I to argue about the sim side of things?). 
And there’s quite a bit to take in, especially if (like me) you’re coming from the more arcadey side of things, used to all kinds of simplifications and conveniences. Well, the old adage is true - no use peeing in the wind. Learn to adjust your sails. So I started from scratch, learning different types of sails and how they fare against the winds. Learned to appreciate all the classical methods of navigation using the tools provided in the game. 
While the planet Sailwind is set on isn’t Earth, same principles still apply – establishing your position by dead reckoning obviously still works, but you still get to determine longitute and latitude using the basic tools such as the quadrant as well as through comparing local noon time against the set time on the chronometer...
But, I am probably getting too technical here. 

The basic idea for the game is this: you start with a simple boat on one of the game’s main archipelagos (your choice of local flavor and dificulty). There isn’t really a set objective to the game, but it’s generally understood that you will be making your fortune by running cargo delivery missions between the islands. Simple. 
You trudge along, slowly accumulating money and the know-how, moving beyond just fulfilling your own basic needs of food, drink and sleep. Then it's time to pick on more and much bolder tasks (you start by delivering small packages of mail and dairy products vs. hundred of pounds worth of cargo - enough to challenge your ingenuity as you struggle to fit all of this on your tiny boat, also bearing in mind that it doesn’t go under the first bigger wave coming your way). 
With time, your starting capital will grow to let you do your own trading, looking up the local prices to maximize profits. This money will then buy QoL stuff for your ship, upgrade its sails, tweak the masts and rigging, try something diferent, then you buy extra tools, fishing rods, furniture... and gradually the boat turns into your floating home where every item has its place and purpose. It's a rare thing when a game captures this feeling of "ownership," and it's both genuine and meaningful.

But we're not finished yet. Slowly, you’ll work up the courage to leave the relative safety of the starting archipelago and set out to the open ocean. It’s a rite of passage in itself, being out there at the mercy of the elements with nothing but the sun and the stars to guide you. You keep your fingers crossed in hope that you packed enough provisions (after all, such a journey can be measured in weeks). You see the monstrous waves, towering above, and that cozy boat of yours feels nothing more than a chestnut. The struggle is as real as it gets. Then (hopefully) comes the first Land Ho! moment as you spy a little dot on the horizon. Absolutely extatic. It’s only a game, but you can still feel some of the same magic as the sailors of old. Even a sense of pride if it pops up where you were expecting it.
And it’s only the beginning. The game world is sizeable enough and from now it’s the oyster at the palm of your hand.

With that bit of a dramatization done, let’s get a bit more specific. The game is still considered early access with a single dev. This needs to be said so that you set your expectation as straight as they need me. In its current state, the game offers plenty of stuff to explore (including secret and not-too-secret islands), a good selection of boats to try out as well as plenty of options to customize their sail plan, making your sailing experience as simple or as complex as you want it to be. Or perhaps you’d like to recreate a historical rig you’ve seen in a book that captured your imagination? Chances are, you can; and this is the de facto heart of the game for a lot of folks.

What else needs to be said, the game has a pretty active modding community that is also super friendly and helpful, if you care to come over to the Discord channel. There are bugs, some of them get squashed, some have been with us for some time and... we've kinda gotten used to them, but updates are coming (at the author’s own pace) and there’s a roadmap of more goodness to come. I'm telling you this to help set your expectations straight on this one, because it doesn't need false advertisement. The game really is one of a kind (perhaps slightly untrue as of January 2025, there’s been some recent accouncements, yet Sailwind still benefits from a major headstart in terms of development), but bear in mind – it's still in early access, solo developer.

Just recently completed a successful cross-ocean voyage in the game (Fort Aestrin to Dragon Cliffs - in the Brig with its default rigging), and so feel I can now write a comprehensive review.

For along time I had always been wanting an age of sail simulator with a first person perspective, where you get to start at port that you can explore, eventually board your ship, and navigate the high seas. Finally, here is a game that successful fulfills that desire. For those who are looking for this type of experience, I can't recommend this game enough. 

As other reviewers have noted, the experience of being on the open seas with no land in sight for (in game) weeks on end, the whole time attending to your sails, wind direction, and heading, braving storms, trying your hand at old-school navigation (quadrant and sun compass is what I sued), and kind of just hoping your doing everything half right...let's just say when you finally hit moment where you actually spot the landmass you were hoping for (especially, as in my case, after missing Happy Bay on that maiden voyage), it provides a unique sense of accomplishment and satisfaction that I don't think any other video game has ever delivered for me. To get this same experience, I recommend definitely do some outside research of the game (don't just use the in-game guides,. This game has an active community on the internet to teach you in-depth skills on how to properly sail and navigate), learn the necessarily nautical and sailing terms (you don't necessarily need to know what things like "running beam reach" means to play this game, but I think it helps with immersion). Take your time to do this research while you try to get the hang with everything and before you do any serious sailing. It will make the initial learning curve difficulty of the early game more enjoyable. It did for me, a least.

One big caveat. I went into this with game more of a desire for a "flight simulator on the high seas" experience. I wasn't actually too keen on the survival mechanics (hunger, thirst) and the need to engage with a cutthroat mercantile economic system to build up to the bigger ships through grinding. In fact, those mechanics made me hesitant about purchasing this game at all, though I'm glad I eventually did.

One of the big reasons I made the jump is because I found out I could bypass those mechanics by uploading my save file to that site that lets you edit saves, in order to give myself infinite funds. This allowed me to immediately buy the true sailing age-of-sail ship I wanted to simulate (the Brig) and made food and water management much more manageable. I'm sure some players in the community might frown on that, but honestly this game already has enough rewarding challenges in it in terms of learning to sail and navigate successfully, which i think strict resource management system detracts from. I do hope the developers will consider giving players a bit more natural freedom in the game in terms of whether they want to engage in the merchant and survival systems. In any case, I still highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a solid high seas sailing adventure!

This game really scratches the sailing itch for me. It's really the first that perfects the experience by balancing time and fun. Sailing between locations takes a fair bit of time, unlike pirate games, but you can get there in one sitting, unlike sailing sims. This is a slow-paced game, but it's amazing. There's no music, but the waves and creaking of ship lines are a melody in themselves. It is such an amazing feeling to finally see lights of civilization after wondering if you made a navigation mistake, or to make your first landfall at Oasis after a few days at sea. It's even more amazing to make it to another set of islands after 10 days. When you first see land on the horizon, it's glorious. 

The physics can be a bit wonky at times, but they're really fun and make the whole experience unique and better. Stacking cargo just right is satisfying. Navigation is appropriately semi-difficult, depending on your skill with a map and compass, but it's fair. 

I would recommend keeping pen+paper notes to sketch islands and their docks for your own perspective. The maps in the game don't show a ton of detail, so it can be easy to confuse a couple of the small islands. (This is not a problem to be fixed, though, in my opinion. It would be nice to have a way to edit or draw on maps, but this is also why it helps to have some paper in real life. 

Suggestions/ wishes: I would like to see the land more fleshed out with things to do, people to talk to, or something else. Someone even had the idea of buying land and customizing it/ a home, which would be neat. There really needs to be something between the small (ex. Dhow) and "medium" (ex. Sanbuq) ships. I think that these new ships should cost the current price of the "medium" ships, because that's not too expensive. This would add a lot more longevity to the game. As it stands, jumping from the Dhow to Sanbuq is too much and really makes the game end quicker. 
A way to tow ships would be nice. A bit more life via more npc activity would be nice. Sailing really is the focus here, though. Some say there's not much to do once you've bought a bigger boat (I also suggest not rushing into this for this reason.) and sailing around the ocean a few times, but the dev has added uncharted islands. 

I would say it's a complete-enough game to purchase for the price. There are some frustrating bugs, such as when waking from sleep in the Dhow, you might get dropped off the back of your boat and have to swim fast to get to it. Another bug is that my ship once got teleported onto the dock. Sometimes you'll pick up a piece of cargo by mistake and ruin your perfect stack, but outside of having a "lock this box's position" option, it's hard to avoid.

I recommend starting in Al'Ankh (default) for an easier break-in. DO NOT underestimate ocean crossing to other islands. It can take 2 weeks or so. (alcohol makes you tired quicker, so you can sleep more.)

What an INCREDIBLE game! I played on the Demo when it first came out with some friends so much, that we could 100% without the killer touching us or even hunting us in the first place. When that got too easy, we made up our own rules like "No shutting doors" or "You must slam the door/turn on a radio to bring the killer to you every 2 minutes" so we could keep playing while we waited for new content. 

That was a few months ago, fast forward to today, after some months away we came back to new game mechanics,  new maps, new fears, new vehicle, new characters, and new ways to collect items, run/hide from the fear and even ways to get rid of the fear all together! Also A STORE!!!

We ended up playing for 4 hours on stream, and had such a blast! Though we do have some suggestions of how to make it harder for those who have played it for so long that the challenge is lost, and some ways that user experience for new players could be better, and even thought up some new fear ideas that would translate well into the game. This game is amazing and so worth every penny. 

I will say I see some people who have reviewed the game saying the content is boring or that they grew bored after 12 minutes. I think with this game (like any co op game) it matters who you play with. If you are playing with people who you have easy fun with, work together or even just fuck around, you will have fun. This game not only is a fun challenge to play solo (with the killer chasing you as you try to find the gem) It is also a less challenging fun game with friends (Assuming you all get along).

TIPS FOR BEGINNERS 

~Use doors to your advantage! You can both block the fear from getting you by slowing it down (as it needs to open the door) and slam them to draw the killer to you 

~The bus is your best friend, when being chased, get on it and close the door, it takes extra long and therefor you and your friends have more time to hunt the crystals

~There are hidden rooms and keys and puzzles in the map! Just be careful what you remove from the map, you might just remove something that you need for these rooms and the puzzle!  

TLDR : 10/10 An amazingly fun game, where you and your friends play against an AI (fear) that is trying to attack you while you try and find all of the gas cans to escape. Maps filled with hidden rooms, locked doors and even a puzzle!

New fears

Able to see what resources you've put into the bus throughout the course of the game

The ability to search the dropped loot box to pick out what resources you want to grab out of it instead of the whole box

The general aesthetic and style of the game is I would say overall good. Lots of interesting stuff visually going on throughout the game, and the soundtrack is great.

The story starts off pretty interesting but doesn't really follow through all that well and is a bit all over the place. The ending is ehhhhhhh.

However, the main issue with the game IMO is the core gameplay, which is the combat, which is what you will be doing for 80% of the game. It starts off simple enough. A bit button mashy with the enemies being rather basic and easy to deal with. And then as time goes on.............it doesn't really change much. There are a ton of upgrades and "new" enemy types, but at the end of the day the gameplay largely remains the same, uninteresting. If any of you have played the game "Guacamelee", Imagine that, but with the color mechanic completely removed and a bit sloppier over all.

Playing this, I am reminded how much I love combat-centric games where you can press any button in any order and it does something different even if you don't intend for it to. The difference here is you would have to be a bit more up close and personal but that doesn't take away how fun it is to beat up some of my mental problems or the type of people I dislike, like 'antisocial creep'.

It may be me but I can never get tired of this type of game, as long as I can see what I'm doing and the enemies aren't too sponging to defeat. This isn't the case here at least on normal difficulty. I'm not one to challenge myself with harder difficulty but if you want there's an option for it if you want to compete with yourself.

As for the story, I like how this game discusses problems like awkward relationships, friend betrayal and the survival of keeping your job. All of this is extended especially when our character is an immigrant trying to adapt to another country, learning its language and culture which is an issue you don't commonly see in video games. I'm thankful this game showcases problems people may not think twice about so they can witness the struggles people may have to face with these challenges. 

When it comes to the gameplay you'll find you would have to make decisions on whether you want to spend your currency earned on completing missions on new stuff that will enable you in combat capability like no combat button press or attack enhancement like adding freeze or damage number to your attacks. Or stuff outside of battles, like taking language classes so you'll be able to understand other NPCs or you won't be able to have a full conversation with them.

If you're someone who mostly cares about the combat or you are a story-driven person both of those are possibilities you can take away from this game and feel pleased with the experience to conclude from.

Combat can just as easily be precise as button-mashy, and if you're watching the screen you should have no problem getting through the game easily. Movement itself is fairly smooth and responsive in combat, as well as the combat area constrained, you'll never be too far from an enemy so combat goes quickly from one to another and the player usually has the option to be completely healed between combats at no expense to the player.

Between chapters, an *also* gently-psychedelic cutscene barely exploring the character's life difficulties, but no concept is explored too far as to over-focus on it other than the drug element, which gets a pass for being a passive gameplay mechanic.

The key, albiet only true sell the game has is it's style and possibly soundtrack.
If you're into the style of the game's presentation, buy it on sale. 
It's not worth $15, but it might be worth 5-7.

Welcome to Pill Baby.
