Ok, I played this game just when it launched, so these are my "first impressions", don't take it as a complete review, and take into consideration that being an early access title, I evaluated it in its crude state.

[b]Note: played on Linux with Valve Index, not Windows.[/b]

[h1]What is this game about?[/h1]
I got it blind -- didn't know anything about the game, I just saw the very cheap price and decided to take a chance. It seems to be a short survival horror game, not much unlike Slenderman. It is said it will have a story with three chapters (one map per chapter). Currently there is no story and only one map for you to play on.

[h1]What's good[/h1]
- The map they've made is a good one. A night map in a rural area, with some scattered houses. Good weather environment (rain), well made terrain if a bit primitive. The river waters look like sand, not water. The size of the map is small.
- Your hands are visible and don't penetrate objects. Instead, they behave much like in Half-Life: Alyx and this is a big element for immersion, few games have it. Very noteworthy.
- The configuration options are done via the TV in a bedroom, it's an immersive way to do it.
- The monster is creepy and well made too.
- Environmental sound in general is well made, although minimal because it's a bare environment (e.g. no birds chirping because it's night, and the likes).

[h1]Configuration options[/h1]
- Currently, it seems there is only one option and it's the level of detail. There is no smooth turning option, game uses snap turning.
- You can also select three levels of difficulty when starting.
- There are no comfort options and the only mode of locomotion is smooth locomotion (which is the one I prefer anyways). 
- Speed: Your character moves at unnaturally fast speeds, even though it would be adequate for a more arcadey game, in the case of a survival horror it is not immersive, it seems like you're driving sonic around. Or maybe add it as a configuration option.

[h1]What can be improved[/h1]
- More configuration options, specially comfort options.
- More populated/detailed environment.
- More noise/ambients.
- Doors sometimes move in a weird way
- Objects are not interactible. The physical hands are so good that the fact that they can't move anything other than doors is contrastingly bad. There are many half-opened drawers and you can't do anything to them. There are cupboards, fridges, closets, etc. and they are just immobile objects.
- Even the doors you open by clicking on them instead of grabbing and pushing or pulling.
- You can't turn off the camera you're carrying. This does not make sense...
- I think the camera should not be the only way to see in the dark. There should be a flashlight, even if it is also a hidden object to find later. A situation where a person at night would take a camcorder but not a flashlight or any other light is not believable.
- It is clear what is the winning criteria (you have to find the 5 orbs/souls), but not the losing criteria. It's based on time? Being in the same area for too long? Having not evaded the monster? I only saw the monster when I died, not sure if it chases you. And I was stuck at the terrain anyway (near the borders of the river).

[h1]Preliminary conclusion[/h1]
As I said, this is not a finished product, so I won't conclude anything about the game. It might turn out good, it might turn out bad. As it is not, it's a simple search for hidden objects in a small map, at night, without a flashlight.

I also hope the developers plan a multiplayer component, that would make the game much more enticing.

There's no neutral recommendation option, so I am recommending the game for now because I believe the developers have the potential to make something quite fun out of it. I hope they continue working on the game.

The game is very well made for what it is. The AI unpredictable and terrifying, the environment is very well made and immersive, and the sound design is on point. Currently there is only one map and one mode for game play, but that is more than enough to justify the price (there are also 3 difficulties... nightmare being the hardest, and it is a very hard challenge). There appears to be 3 maps, 3 story mode chapters, and 4 classic modes on the way as well, but the price will increase as the game gets expanded, so I would suggest getting it sooner rather than later. The game initially gave me Slender vibes, but the more I played it I realized that it is almost the opposite of slender in terms of game play. You have to frantically look around to see where the enemy is coming from in the dark woods, and making the decision of lowering your night vision camera to run faster (which your night vision camera is the only way to see in the darker areas), or keep looking at the night vision camera and risk getting caught by the enemy because you are moving too slow, makes this game so much deeper in game play than other horror games like it. So rather than trying to not turn around in fear of the enemy killing you, like in slender, you are actually forced to keep looking around and be aware of your surroundings to win. I found this to be a very refreshing take on this style of game. The game is well worth the price and I will be watching it very closely throughout its early access. Looking forward to future updates. Cheers

You can view my review & gameplay here: https://youtu.be/4TOflhL-HWg

This is a budget-priced mini horror experience similar to Slender man type games. There is only one mode and one map available currently. You basically look for 5 blue balls in the dark around a decent-sized map in the dark while using a camcorder to help light the darkness while a monster lurks around. Collect them all before it gets you basically is the game.

Tranquil Cove is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting variable frame rates from 90 fps to 45 fps. However, it didn't really effect gameplay. The pop-in that occurred occasionally effected my experience more. You do have full locomotion (head-gaze based only) and snap turning available. I did not experience any serious issues or bugs during my short playtime. 

I thought the visuals looked nice for a budget game. The sounds were okay, but I think there could have been better spatial audio to help let you know when the monster was nearby. I could only hear the monster when it was basically already too near for me to do anything. The VR interactions were all very basic & could be more polished. Overall, though, it's a nice little game for the asking price. 

[b]Rate 6.5/10. I paid less than $2 USD, so I feel I already got my money's worth. If the devs deliver on their EA promises, this price will be a total steal in the future.[/b]

As a player with 4.3k hours in Project Zomboid I heard MANY times that this game was going to be the "Project Zomboid Killer" during its release, and back to 2023 my thoughts were: "If this game is meant to be a PZ Copy, its destinty is failure", so I didn't pay much attention to it other than what I saw during streams (I didn't like what I see during that time to be honest). Now it is 2025, and somebody recommended it again a couple days ago, so this time I gave it a try so let's deep dive into my impressions.

First of all, I'm really glad that HumanitZ evolved into its own personality and is definitely NOT A COPY of Project Zomboid (while it has similar things of course, it is a Survival game with Zombies). If you play this game thinking this is a 3D Project Zomboid made in Unreal you are going to definitely be frustrated as it doesn't offer the same but more "beauty".
Some of the most noticable differences with PZ:
- Special zombies/Infected. While most of the zombies are the traditional slow romero-like zombies, some of them are different, from runners to some toxic ones, and some of them that on death something happens (I died because of this, I don't want to spoil, discover it yourself). In my opinion I would compare the Zombies with 7 Days to Die but COMPLETELY more blended into the game, they fit much better to the whole atmosphere.
- Zombie animals: not much more to say about this, PZ doesn't have them and will never have them.
- Bandits NPC and other NPC's such as traders with Quests. Until B43 in PZ we won't see this kind of things.
- A more focused Gunplay experience. 

The bad things
Probably one of the most important points to make here is that none of this "bad" points are actually BAD things that destroys the experience, those are just things that can be improved IMO or are current bugs.

- The camera: so my biggest problem was with the camera, mainly in big buildings or around cities. Around cities the problem is that as the walls doesn't dissappear whenever you are close to a tall building, you can barely see what's going on. Inside big buildings what happens is that the camera tilt effect allows you to see your character all good BUT you can barely see anything that's not close to you. The Review Critic: HumanitZ – An Empty Sandbox of Repetition
HumanitZ attempts to carve out its place in the overcrowded zombie survival genre, but instead of an identity, it delivers an experience that feels half-formed. It presents itself as an open-ended survival game with flexibility, yet ultimately boils down to a repetitive cycle of resource runs, respawning enemies, and barren landscapes.

The Good:
Multiplayer Exists – Unlike Project Zomboid, you can jump in with friends out of the box, but don’t expect thriving public servers. Most are password-locked or nearly empty.
Base Building Potential – You can construct a home base, but without automation or meaningful NPCs, it feels more like a chore than a rewarding long-term goal.
The Bad:
Lack of Identity – It borrows ideas from other survival games but never fully commits to any. More scavenger-sim than action or exploration, it lacks the chaos and emergent storytelling that make other survival games shine.
Repetitive Gameplay Loop – Expect to run the same supply routes, fight the same enemies, and loot the same locations with little variation. Resource respawns can be disabled, but then you’re just left with a world that feels even emptier.
Barren World Design – The environment lacks character, with open spaces blending together into an uninspired blur of trees and roads.
No Meaningful Social Gameplay – Without good NPCs to interact with, the world feels lifeless. You’re surviving alone in a world that doesn’t care if you exist.
At best, HumanitZ is an early-access framework for a better game. At worst, it’s a soulless loop that fails to justify its place in the genre. 4/10

Taking this shovelware seriously as if it was a genuine attempt to make a game, it doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the 1990s.  It's unclear why the developers weren't able to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets for the game, and also irrelevant... what matters is that this looks bad as a result of their decisions, a compromise PC gamers shouldn't have to put up with.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but I wasn't able to find it on the app stores.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes "Join Rush Attack / 加入突袭" might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in the game is to be expected.  Gamers just didn't take this low quality game seriously, and for good reason.

SokoRamp is an indie puzzle game take on the original Sokoban, but suffers from insufficient innovation: the ramps, switches, and keys don't make this game feel less tedious than the original.

Level design is disappointing. Levels are tediously big, with par moves reaching 100-200 moves, which can make even the optimal solutions feel deeply unsatisfying. There's a strong sense that the level designer wasn't skilled enough to make shorter or more compact levels sufficiently interesting or challenging. In addition, levels are often not satisfying to solve when not trying to optimize moves (because just solving them is not sufficiently challenging), but also not satisfying to optimize due to their absurd sizes. It doesn't help that even those optimal solutions mostly don't feel elegant or insightful.

The level progression sucks. Solving a level only unlocks the next one, so you're often stuck. There's no level skip, no choice between unlocked levels; instead, the game expects you to bang your head against the most recent level that was more challenging than average. To add insult to injury, the game is too unpopular to have a walkthrough, so the progression system isn't just unpleasant but an outright disaster.

The par system is once again unsatisfying in comparison to the best-in-class implementation of Dungeon and Rooms. For instance, it's deeply annoying trying to optimize a solution you did a while ago, when you don't have access to a replay of it. And the par counts are just way too strict for such high numbers - Dungeon and Rooms had most levels <50 moves (though with bigger move sets); this one has levels where you have to make 121 moves perfectly to get gold.

A proper sequel to what I considered to be a game with a very solid base game mechanic.

Coming off as a mix between Snake and Break Out, it captures their respective arcade addictive nature in (usually) short bursts of gameplay. After each round you're inclined to play it again to either go for achievements, unlock the different modes or just try to place better on the leaderboards than your peers. At no point did I feel any semblance of frustration rather a sense of accomplishment after improving.

On the presentation side, there's a wider variety of skin customization now. Not only blocks and palettes are customizable like in the first game but the snake itself is as well (which you might wanna take into account for some of the achievements). The main track also changed to a more jazz-like tune and I personally prefer it over the old one. Menus now have their respective tracks as well and they are not half bad either.

Back to the gameplay, one of the added features was the inclusion of different modes. They include a more chaotic chaos mode, an endless mode where the board just keeps expanding and a combination of the two. They were actually really fun to play for a while and they have their own leaderboards as well so you could prove your skill in them as well as in the classic mode. In short, having the option to play different modes makes the gameplay loop more engaging.

Side note regarding the endless mode, its achievement took me a very long session to earn and that wouldn’t be much of a problem if the game didn’t start chugging and slowing down after a while. In fact, the run was 2 hours long according to the game but in reality it lasted for 443 minutes. Maybe not many people will see this as a problem unless they really get into it and it might have to do with my setup but I’ll mention it regardless as one of the only gripes I had with the game..

Lastly, whileI don't have much to say about the multiplayer mode since I couldn't play it much, the one time I did I had some connection issues during some rounds. It was a while ago so by now it must have probably been fixed. Apart from that, I can see the mode being attractive if you're able to find someone else to play with. Too bad the game itself already has a very reduced audience no matter how many times I’ve tried sharing it.

To sum up, even if you didn’t like the first game this one will most probably grab you for a while so you should give it a shot as it’s pretty cheap. I find it a good option to play it during work breaks or in the background to pass up the time so it’s accessible time wise. With all the added content mentioned above I have to give my huge props to the dev and I haven't even mentioned the flavor text that comes up depending on your score.

[b]threaded[/b] is a link-a-pix puzzler. basically numberlink but the result is a picture, not just a bunch of lines connecting numbers without leaving empty squares. very few of these on steam and this is one of the better ones.

[b]80 levels[/b] are available, sizes vary between 15x15 and 40x40 and they are all unlocked from the start. 8 got added a few days after release, so there might be more later. each starts with a riddle, so you can make an educated guess about the goal. each page of level select looks differently, as they represent different themes (there's a bunch of animals among other things, sadly no wombat), but I still [b]wouldn't mind level numbers and page numbers[/b] there. also, [b]selecting a solved level resets it without confirmation and removes the solved image from level select[/b], dick move.

a quick [b]mandatory tutorial[/b] teaches the rules and the [b]mouse-only controls[/b]. it's straightforward stuff, click and move the mouse to draw a line (or click individual squares if you want), there's even a counter that shows how long it currently is. you can't have multiple unfinished lines on the go, but going back on your selection is possible and a must in a line-drawing game. right click anywhere removes the whole line.

[b]zooming is also possible[/b], might be handy on larger levels with small squares and numbers. both the mouse wheel and clicking the +/- icons work, though with the ui moving around as you zoom in and out, clicking isn't really a good idea. similarly, clicking the mouse wheel is a more comfortable way of moving the zoomed-in grid around than clicking the arrows on the side. there's also a magnifying glass and its surprisingly powerful effect is added to regular zoom, which is as neat as it is overkill.

the [i]fill singles[/i] button is an excellent quality of life feature, as it saves you from clicking all the 1s, it's just busywork anyway. would be better if it was instant but you can keep drawing while it's happening. the [i]show miscolored[/i] button lets you [b]turn off mistake highlighting[/b], which is another nice feature. it's on by default, no problem with that (and if you make a mistake within the same color it won't help you anyway, as per its name), but [b]turning it off doesn't stick, have to click it every time a level is loaded, really annoying[/b]. if you get stuck (you won't, it's all very easy), the [i]solve line[/i] button does what it says, but it's on a quick cooldown.

I mentioned riddles on startup, but there are also [b]trivia questions after each level[/b], connected to the image you just created. it's a bit random but there you go. there's even some extra info after, not just correct/nope, but [b]the amount of clicking to get through all the end-of-level stuff is a bit much[/b]. at leeast everything's skippable.

nice graphics, good enough music, a lot better than I expected. settings, also available while playing, include separate volume sliders, resolutions and windowed mode, some languages and a [b]timer toggle[/b]. it got patched in upon request to hide the way too big and incredibly distracting clock in the corner. the game can handle multiple profiles to keep track of progress separately and [b]individual mid-level progress is saved[/b] as well, quit and continue as you please. [b]dark mode would be a necessary addition, boards are pretty blinding[/b] with all the whiteness at the start.

it's a [b]mostly good adaptation of a classic puzzle type[/b] with almost all the necessary functionality and some surprising additional features. it won't take long, even the biggest levels can be done in a few minutes and the whole thing shouldn't take more than [b]5 hours or so[/b], but it's fun and relaxing. if only they fixed the mistake highlighter and added dark mode. [b]achievements are also buggy[/b] if it's something you care about.

Threaded does nothing wrong. It's a chill, quaint, cutesy puzzle game that I'm almost sure I've seen somewhere else. If you're familiar with Picross or Paint By Numbers, this is a similar style, but even easier. Every stage is a pixel art of an animal or object colored in a sort of embroidery thread style. The puzzle is solved by filling in lines of thread noted by the amount of blocks required to complete the thread. Threads number anywhere from 1 (just literally clicking the 1) to 12 (making long threads that make you think critically about surrounding threads. I'm able to blaze through puzzles fairly quickly, especially with the convenient buttons to auto-fill single blocks (which saves on tedium) and Solve Line which will randomly solve a line or two for you (though there is an achievement for completing a number of levels with out this). Completing the level reveals what the art is and usually a trivia question usually related to said art. This is definitely "Your Mom's" or "Your Dad's" Puzzle game as the trivia will often pertain to facts that would be rather old compared to much of the Steam audience. I only guessed right about the Speedy Gonzales voice actor because I saw the name "Mel Blanc" countless times as a kid watching Looney Toones, and those shows were ancient by the time I started watching them.

The simplistic gameplay and cutesy art style won't hold my attention long enough to complete this. This is a problem of my personal taste rather than any issue of game design, so anybody looking at this game saying "Oh, that looks cute!" or "This could be fun" should probably enjoy this. The music is chill,  performance is solid and controls are perfect except for a couple moments where i didn't quite drag where i want....but I also was going fast, which is not the point of this game.

Threaded would make a great gift for an older game player or players looking for something that is cute, but not too cute and not too challenging either.

[h1]QUICK FACTS[/h1]

Type: H-RPG
Developer: Eugor Evol
Publisher: Otaku Plan
Price: €3,99
Est. playtime: 1-3 hours
Censorship: yes (patch available at publisher’s website)


[h1]THE GAME[/h1]

[b]MECHANICS[/b]
Lust & Magic: Chisalla in a Flower Basket (L&M) at first glance looks like a classic JRPG, but is in fact mostly a puzzle game. While the controls are similar, your MC has no stats and doesn’t need to fight any enemies. Instead, the majority of the gameplay consists of exploring a dungeon, solving puzzles and collecting treasure items (which serve no other purpose than completing an achievement). Solving the puzzles progresses the main storyline.

Controls: keyboard and mouse

[b]STORY[/b]
You play as a young researcher (name of your own choice), hailing from the steampunk city of Lucia. At the start of the game, a storekeeper named Garion tasks you with researching a strange magical stone. This leads you, Garion and his ward Maria to the remote village of Eta, where you soon find out that magic hasn’t quite left the world yet.

[b]QUALITY[/b]
L&M looks good. That’s pretty much the best that can be said about it; the quality of the artwork is really nice. The next thing that stands out is that it’s really, really short. You can probably wrap up the entire thing within the hour.  Completing all the puzzles and objectives – particularly the treasure collecting – will take you a couple of hours more. The puzzles themselves aren’t very difficult, but do require thorough searching and attention to detail. 

As usual with this publisher, the (machine) translation is passable, but at times difficult to understand.


[h1]THE GOODS[/h1]

[b]SUBJECT[/b]
The lewd in L&M is a small collection of scenes, featuring the four women as well as the MC. It looks like the devs tried to slip in a single scene for some of the major trope in the genre (tentacles, urination, stuck in the wall, etc.).

Keywords: [spoiler]fluids, forced, straight, tentacles, urination[/spoiler]

[b]CONTENT[/b]
About 10 scenes, consisting of a few mostly similar-looking images each.

[b]ACCESS[/b]
A few scenes are part of the main storyline; the rest requires you to complete a subquests and/or be at the right place on the right time.

[b]QUALITY[/b]
As said before, the quality of the artwork is excellent.


[h1]VERRO’S VERDICT[/h1]
I’m not sure what to make of L&M. It seems as if it’s not a complete game, but rather the first chapter of one, or perhaps a proof of concept for something bigger. While the story is neatly wrapped up at the end, you’re left feeling that it could – and likely should – have been something more. For example, at the start of the game you learn that you have the ability to read the mind of NPC’s by pressing A, but afterwards you hardly ever get to use the feature again. Which begs the question: why was it in the game in the first place?

Still, for the quality artwork, the puzzles and the modest price, I’m going to give it a hesitant thumbs up. If you’re up for some light-weight puzzling and treasure hunting with a few quality scenes as reward, this one may provide you with an entertaining evening.

The tutorials are the other. They just info dump everything on you and feel quite stilted. You are able to easily skip them though, so that's nice. The levels also feel pretty easy for the first third-[i]ish[/i] of the game, and hard af for the last few levels. (Oh, and the level complete screen should say "Level Mastered" if you did the mastery goals though (but it's not that big a deal)).

The models and artstyle are [i]noice[/i], the music is space-y, the physics are floaty enough to be believable without feeling too game-y, and the puzzles iterate upon the mechanics quite well. It would be nice to have more levels, but for $3 this is a fun puzzle game.

There's a handful of typos (most notable the Aprentice Space Architect achievement misspelling "Apprentice"), but they're mostly minor and don't affect the game too much (though magnets saying they pull when they actually push is fairly severe). Also noticed that crushers claim to increase mineral storage without actually increasing it.

Lastly, there's too many achievements imo. You don't need one for mastering every single level, instead have 2 or 3 for mastering different amounts (e.g. master 5, 10, and 15 levels). The ones to restart the game and destroy buildings feel like filler too (as does constructing only 5 buildings).

So yeah, solid 7.5/10. Would be 8.5/10 without the following issues: Lacking keybinds for buildings makes it tedious enough for me to remove .25 points, the multitude of typos takes off .15, and the remaining 0.6 is removing for how short it is combined with the front-loaded tutorials being a bit annoying.

But, I'd still say to get it even if you aren't super into puzzle games. It's a simple, fun, space-themed puzzle game that I enjoyed.

I was excited for this, and wanted to like it - I'm a huge fan of Metroidvania's in general. Ori is one of my favourite games of all time, the world looks fun and mysterious and the overall vibe certainly felt like I would enjoy this, but the early stages have put me off wanting to explore further.

The central mechanic so far is whether or not you are inside the light, and you can only attack while inside the light, but enemies are all over the place in the shadows too, leaving you defenceless in many areas - stepping into a beam of light and actually being able to attack feels a little disconnected from the visuals, leaving me feeling like I was in the light, but unable to attack for a moment before it seemed to catch up. 

Combat feels frustrating and is (at least in the opening scenes) limited and unclear, the shadow that attacks for you seems to visually engulf your character when attacking, and the animations don't make it clear following the 'boof' whether you successfully attacked on time, or got hit yourself, or both, especially when more than 1 enemy is in melee range, as happened often in my limited play time.

The resource for healing, and seemingly also for unlocking new abilities, are floating orbs, which are found in the world as well as from defeating enemies. They run away from you, often into un-engaged enemies, and do not adjust their height based on the terrain, often leaving them unobtainable as you chase them away, outside of your reach. 

Besides the combat, the game offers little to no visual feedback in many other areas, leaving the player feeling directionless. I appreciate not being hand-held every second, but some additional indication could be helpful.

Early on, I came across a Rift that spawned basic enemies to kill, under a spotlight that sways back and forth. As I killed the enemies, I saw no apparent change on screen, and after 3 or 4 kills, left assuming I either didn't have the tools to pass yet, or that they were infinitely spawning. 
Backtracking, I found the first available upgrade which required 80 orbs, at a cost of 10 orbs per heal, needing to sacrifice the resources of 8 healing potions in the early stages of the game while combat is still so limited by light, and the enemies so abundant, felt a bit much. 
On returning to the rift, killing 1 last enemy, the rift closed and allowed me past, so some indication of X/5 required would be useful here. Maybe the rift grows duller, or more fractured as the enemies spawn/are defeated?
I did make it as far as unlocking the ability to 'charge' some light, that is to say power up in the beam so you can still attack when you step back in the shadows, however again the lack of visual feedback left me at a loss. Was it time-based, or successful hits? How long does it last, How many attacks can I make? With no indication on screen I was often left chasing to finish an attack just as the charge ran out and the enemy instead hit me as I had suddenly become defenceless without apparent warning.
It's a minor complaint, and it may just be personal preference, but the 'chime' that sounds every time you charge in the light set my teeth on edge a little, and given how often I anticipate needing to do this throughout the game, this heavily affected my decision not to proceed.

Overall the game looks amazing, the aesthetic is great and apart from the frustrations with not being given enough visual information, appreciate the minimalist UI. 
It's possible that later upgrades further into the game resolve these issues, or maybe this game just isn't for me, but with the experience so far as it is, I'll have to refund and give this one a miss.

I am recommending this game because I understand as a small indie developer a single negative review could be very harmful to the game. There is definitely passion put into this game, but this review I am writing should be read carefully for anyone who plans to purchase this game.

I played this game on stream and quickly began to feel annoyed with it.
The game is unfortunately very obtuse in its design, and also begins to ask way too much out of players way too early.
The game lacks any sort of real tutorial on game elements. For example the first bomb you come across is never explained. As a curious player, I walked up to the bomb, pressed the action key, and exploded and died. That was behavior I somewhat expected, though I was curious if you can move the bombs or just ignite the bombs. However, my intuition here was completely wrong. Because the bomb had exploded just after I pressed the action key, I was under the assumption the bomb must be lit using the action key. This is incorrect. There is a pressure plate that ignites the bomb. Fortunately I figured this out fairly quickly. However, what it taught me now is that when a pressure plate is next to a bomb, it will ignite the nearest bomb.
So a few levels down the road, I became very irritated when I stepped on a pressure plate and 2 bombs exploded, 1 that was right next to the pressure plate (makes sense) and then one a few tiles away (why???). This makes no sense to me.

The problem I see in this design is the puzzle design doesn't want you, the player, to think about it's puzzles. It wants you to know what you are doing, and to perform it quickly. With the timer and step counter at the top, always present with no easy way to retry a level, it feels like a strict teacher standing over your shoulder while you do a test, and then slapping your hand every once in awhile, but not explaining why it slapped your hand. Did you do it wrong? Why did you do it wrong? Who knows. This teacher doesn't care to explain.

Maybe this game is fun later, but it's high expectations from the very start of the game, to the lack of explanation, and inconsistent game logic made it nothing but an unfun, frustrating event. I feel sorry for the Dev, because the last thing I want to do is write a review like this, especially for such a small indie game. Unfortunately this is the reality, especially when the game is commercial. This game needs way, way more work, and the dev really should consider what their first time players will experience with this game. If they want to go the "intuitive" design route of game design, then it is absolutely imperative that game logic is consistent and makes sense (for example, what does a pressure plate have to do with a bomb? They aren't connected by a wire, so why would I assume a pressure plate would set off the bomb?). However, I think plainly explaining concepts through a tutorial is a better way to go for this game. Regardless, the dev really needs to consider making sure players understand their game clearly, otherwise I suspect player retention for this game will be low.

It can be seen as a bit of a prequel to Sunless Sea and Sunless Skies, taking place many years later in the same universe.

The game itself is a visual novel, with a bit of dating simulator which also turns into a bit of a murder mystery. The writing is delicious, the characters are deeply interesting, and the way the murder investigation is performed is creative but the qualities as a game is rather lacking. It is ambitious and I certainly recommend it for the atmosphere and the imagination, but not everyone will like it as the game it actually is.

From the terribly shallow surface this game may seem like just another pixelated indie platformer, but underneath the basic presentation is a gleaming treasure trove of brilliantly-made levels that feature intuitive layouts, fun level gimmicks, a surprising amount of charm and theming, and (most importantly) tight, satisfying platforming.

Switching between black and white is such a simple mechanic to base the entire game around, but Cat Box Paradox manages to make full, extensive use of it, resulting in later levels feeling like a brilliant dance of frantic colour-switching splendor. It's extremely impressive to see just how much mileage is gotten out of this one simple mechanic.

Ontop of the confident simplicity of the levels themselves is also a few extra challenges, mainly completing the level without getting damaged once (which is simple but genuinely hard to do sometimes), and collecting the elusive Mons. There's only one in each stage, but they're hidden in genuinely clever spots that make for fun and challenging detours. And to fully complete a level, you'll have to do both at once, and despite all the frustrating hiccups that you can make, I never feel mad about replaying stages to perfect them when the stages themselves are so well-built and fun.

In conclusion, the reviews don't lie. This is seriously a hidden indie GEM, and while it can be recommended to just about anyone who likes platformers, I think die-hard enjoyers of the genre will get the biggest kick out of the ingenuity and challenges of this one.

[h1] A true masterpiece. [/h1]

And unlike many people, I don't use that word often, if at all. Only a few games truly deserve such praise in my opinion. So when I say KCD2 is one of them, then you can be sure I was truly impressed by what I saw. KCD2 is basically KCD1, but 5 times better. That's why you can refer to my KCD1 review and multiply every positive I pointed out by at least two. Everything is bigger, better and more entertaining than before. Steam forces me to cut every review in half every time I want to praise or criticize a game, so I'll try to be as brief as possible, although this games deserves at least an essay on how great it is.

[h3] Story [/h3]

One of the greatest improvements I've seen. KCD1's story was decent, but it was mostly just... there. It did what was necessary, provided what was needed and wasn't filled with logical errors and stupid discrepancies. It wasn't something to write home about though. But now? Now we have a proper great story to rival and surpass many other of my beloved games. Absolutely no spoilers here though. You have to experience it for yourself. You'll love these characters, dialogues and overall storytelling.

[h3] Role-playing [/h3]

Another greatly improved aspect. There are so many ways to finish [i] most [/i] quests that even giving one as an example would eat all the space I have here. You can talk your way out of things, you can sneak, you can fight, yada yada yada, all that other RPG stuff (true RPG, not starfield, veilguard or elden ring). But there are also soooo many details and non-obvious ways to finish most of the quests, it honestly stunned me, and it still does. It looks as if the developers thought of almost everything, so if you use your imagination and deviate from the given objective while using logic, more often than not you will find that Warhorse have thought of that, and such things can even influence dialogues during this and further quests. NPCs remember what you did, they comment on it, they comment on what you do, how you act, how you're dressed, are you smelly or drunk, etc. TES games had things like that, but they pale in comparison honestly.

[h3] Music [/h3]

Another great improvement. KCD1's was decent. KCD2's is great.

[h3] Combat [/h3]

You guessed it, another big upgrade. It's smooth, it's not frustrating, it's easy. Honestly, too easy for my taste. Master Strike once again solves everything. Maybe Hardcore will fix it, but I didn't like KCD1's Hardcore, so I'm not holding my breath. But even like that it's still highly enjoyable, and you [i] can [/i] lose if you're too cocky. Also, only swords have Master Strike now, so that's something. Turning off indicators is a fun way to make things more spicy, but I had to use a mod for that.

[h3] Open world [/h3]

Yep. Again. Another big step-up. Just riding through the forest is interesting in this game, and this is the greatest praise I can think of. Games like Witcher or Bethesda games rely heavily on POIs such as caves, castles, monster lairs, etc. Almost none of that here. Does this make exploration boring? It doesn't. Because so many space that would be empty in any other game is filled with random encounters (the best I've seen in games so far too) and neat little discoveries that are also sometimes referenced by NPCs, but play no real role in quests.

One example here: there was this wine merchant's wagon I found that crashed near a small river. I took some wine for myself and left. 10-15 hours later I was tasked with tracking down some bandits, and one NPC said that I can find them near said wagon. Since I already knew where it was, it was easier for me to navigate and find those bandits. This will be even cooler when Hardcore is released, because such landmarks will help you find things when you can't see your position on the map. This was neat in KCD1 as well, but here it's much more detailed, and almost every NPC during most quests will give you clear enough instructions to find things you're looking for without relying on a map or even compass.

[h3] Interface [/h3]

Didn't think I'd praise something so trivial, but here we are. The only other game I can think of that impressed me with it's unique interface was Persona 5. Here, it's also uniquely stylish and authentic. It was also improved from a practical point of view, you can access your horse's inventory from the same place as you own, for example. 

[h3] Graphics [/h3]

Also not something I praise often, but holy moly, this game is absolutely beautiful (and well-optimized!). I fully expected it to be just like KCD1, maybe slightly better. But it surpassed every expectation I had. It's at least as beautiful as RDR2 (kinda sad that a 2018 game is the one I'm comparing this one to, as most new games are far laggier, and at the same time far-far uglier and technically inferior to RDR2).

[h3] Issues [/h3]

Surprisingly, almost none. I had a few bugs, but 95% of them were visual. No broken quests. The only big issue was when I needed to chase an NPC, but didn't have the best horse, so I had to try ~20-30 times before I actually caught up with him. If my horse was at least a little bit slower, I'd have to reload an earlier save and find a faster horse to be sure. This was a story quest too, so bummer. Still, I caught the guy, so that's something. I just wish it wasn't a flat out "You lost" screen when I failed, but rather an alternative development for the quest, as is the case in many other quests, but oh well, can't have everything.

Other than that, the game has some minor issues, but that's all they are. Minor and negligible.

I'd also like to point out that realism in this game is not that tedious. Many people criticized RDR2 for such things, but I honestly think that RDR2 is more tedious than KCD2 in this regard. Almost no 10 minute horse riding, easy access to fast travel, animations aren't as slow. It's also much easier to access Savior Schnapps than in the first game, as well as food. It may not be for everyone, but I'd say that it should not stop you from trying the game if that's what you're afraid of. And if that's still an issue... mods exist. Don't like to rely on them to make the game playable, but it's not like that. The game is fully playable for a casual player, far more than KCD1 was. It's just extremely easy to install mods, so just know that you have that option.

[h3] Summary [/h3]

This is a great game, and one of the greatest RPGs I've played in a long while. It may not be for everyone, and that's a good thing. More games should be "not for everyone". This is what AAA games are supposed to be. What every miserable small indie company like ubisoft wishes to have. A game with soul, made by people who love their work, people who have something to say and show. This is probably not only my Game of the year, but rather "Game of the last 4 years", since the last time I fell in love with a game this much was when Ghost of Tsushima released, and when I played Persona 5.

Also, much love to Tom McKay and Luke Dale. Not only are they great and passionate voice actors, but great human beings as well, and I love every moment of their presence in-game, on social media and in game-related materials. I love these guys <3

[h1]Tired of Games That Feel Like Theme Parks? Good.[/h1]

[h2]Kingdom Come: Deliverance II isn't building another thrill ride. It's building medieval life, unfiltered.[/h2] 

Forget your power fantasy medieval romp. This isn't about slaying dragons and becoming a god-king. This is about being Henry, a blacksmith's son caught in the messy, muddy, and often mundane reality of 15th century Bohemia. And somehow, it's utterly captivating.

[i]Example?[/i] I hopped on a random wagon just to get across the map faster. Expected silence, maybe a canned "farewell" when I hopped off. Instead? Two guards chatting about the price of ale, then about some weird noises they heard in the woods.  Then BAM, Cumans ambush us. We fight, we win, we keep riding. And they just keep chatting. Like nothing extraordinary just happened.  [b]That’s this game.[/b] Life goes on. Chaos happens. It’s normal here.  And that’s the weirdest thing -  in a game world designed to be ungamey, that normalcy feels genuinely groundbreaking.

And you know what else is surprisingly un-gamey?  It actually works.  Right out of the box. No need to immediately dive into graphics settings and wrestle with DLSS, FSR, XeSS just to get a playable framerate (my rig’s decent, but not NASA-level, and it runs smooth as butter).  Remember those day-one patches the size of small countries and praying you could actually start the game without crashing?  Yeah, Kingdom Come: Deliverance II seems to have skipped that memo entirely.  It’s polished. Stable.  Dare I say it feels like a game from a bygone era, you know, when games launched polished?  Almost suspiciously so for a modern AAA release. Maybe they actually playtested this thing before unleashing it on us. Imagine that!  It's kind of refreshing.

Most games throw epic quests at you every five minutes. Kingdom Come 2 throws life at you.  Chores, conversations, the occasional bandit attack. And it doesn’t hold your hand. [b]You will get lost. You will make mistakes. You will spend hours just trying to figure out the alchemy system[/b].

[i]Combat?[/i] It's clunky. Unforgiving. [b]You will get your butt kicked.[/b] But it also feels visceral. Panic, desperation, the weight of your sword.  [i]Saves?[/i] Yeah, they’re limited. Annoying? Sure. But also [b]makes choices matter. Makes you think twice before picking a fight with a group of armored knights.[/b] It's not convenient. It's consequential.

[h2]Kingdom Come: Deliverance II isn't trying to be fun in the traditional game-y sense. It’s trying to be something else.[/h2]

[h1] [b] A Masterpiece of Historical RPGs[/b] [/h1]

[h3] [b] 🔥An RPG that rivals even The Witcher[/b]  [/h3]

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is a beautifully crafted RPG set in medieval Bohemia that can hold its own even against titles like The Witcher. It’s one of the most immersive RPGs I’ve ever played.

 [h3][b]📜 Story & Characters[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ The story is excellent and epic, featuring historical figures that are well-written and full of depth.
✔️ Even though the characters aren’t real, they feel alive and important, making you genuinely care about them.
✔️ The game's script is written at a very high level of quality.
❌ The occasional predictability of the story bothers me a little, but that might just be my personal perspective.

[h3] [b]🌍 World & Immersion[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ The world feels incredibly alive, from forests and villages to bustling towns.
✔️ It’s not quite on the level of Red Dead Redemption 2 for reference, but it gets impressively close.
✔️ NPCs have believable routines, adding to the immersion.
✔️ The random NPCs that interact with you while traveling or can give you quests are also very well done.
✔️ Czech voice acting is a fantastic touch for Czech and Slovak players, making the experience even more authentic.

 [h3][b]🎮 Gameplay & Exploration[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ The game is addictive, with engaging combat, activities, and minigames.
✔️ Side quests are diverse and creative, on par with those from CD Projekt Red.
✔️ The game features two maps – the first is smaller, while the second is larger and more detailed.
✔️ Arriving in Kuttenberg feels as grand as stepping into Novigrad in The Witcher 3.
✔️ The city is huge, full of life, and packed with atmosphere.
✔️ The dog in the game is very helpful this time, although it can sometimes get in the way during combat.
✔️ The save system is also improved, and the game saves more frequently, so you don't need to carry as many saviour schnapps with you.

 [h3][b]🎵 Soundtrack & Atmosphere[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ The soundtrack by Jan Valta is phenomenal, pulling you deep into the world.
✔️ The music is world-class and enhances every moment of the game.
✔️ I’d say the nature sounds are the best implemented.

[h3] [b]💘 Romance & Relationships[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ Romance is well-executed, comparable to The Witcher 3, Cyberpunk 2077, and the Mass Effect trilogy.

[h3] [b]⚔️ Combat & Challenge[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ Combat is smoother than the first game, but also easier – it doesn’t feel as challenging.
✔️ The combos in the game are good, allowing for engaging and strategic combat, even when outnumbered.
✔️ Option to improve skills with trainers and training is a great feature.
✔️ The large castle battles are also very well executed.
❌ Enemy balance needs improvement, which could be fixed in the future or through a Hardcore Mode.
❌ Kutná Hora Tournament felt too easy, lacking a real sense of achievement.

[h3] [b] 🛡️ Equipment & Inventory[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ Armor and weapons are beautifully designed.
✔️ More weapon variety, including crossbows and hand cannons.
✔️ New inventory system allows you to create three different gear sets (e.g., civilian, stealth, combat) and switch between them quickly.
✔️ I appreciate the wide variety of items, such as food, materials, valuables, treasure maps, books to learn from, and so on.
❌ It’s too easy to buy high-quality armor from merchants, removing the excitement of earning it through effort.

[h3] [b] 🛠️ RPG Mechanics & Progression[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ Extensive perk system lets you customize your character based on your preferred playstyle – whether stealth, melee, or ranged combat.
✔️ The game rarely restricts your approach, allowing for freedom in completing quests.
✔️ I appreciate that the developers added the option to be a blacksmith and craft weapons, horseshoes, and more.
✔️ I appreciate the communication options and dialogue choices with NPCs in the world and story. The reputation system is also well-implemented—how you behave in the world affects how people, including guards and others, treat you.
✔️ The character progression from the ground up is well-designed, making you feel a real sense of growth and development by the end of the game.
❌ It bothered me a bit that when you go to the bathhouse to wash and clean your clothes, it doesn’t wash all sets of clothing. For example, if you're wearing civilian clothes, it won't clean your armor, etc. So, I had to go to the bathhouse three times in a row to get everything cleaned.

 [h3][b] 🚀 Performance & Optimization[/b]  [/h3]

✔️ Excellent optimization on both PC and consoles.
✔️ Warhorse Studios sets an example for modern developers, proving that a game can run smoothly without relying on DLSS or Frame Generation.
❌ There are some bugs, glitches, and issues, but nothing that would break quests or progression (they will be fixed in the future).

[h3] [b]🎯 Final Thoughts[/b]  [/h3]

Despite a few minor bugs and glitches, the game is an absolute masterpiece. These issues will likely be fixed over time, making the experience even better.
I’m excited for the upcoming DLCs and future projects from Warhorse—there’s a lot to look forward to!

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II had me hooked from the start, I can't remember the last time I was addicted to a game this much, let alone a HUGE game that can easily take 100 hours to beat, depending on your playstyle and exploration. 

This game's biggest strength is undoubtedly the world. Everything just feels real, and I had so much fun just exploring the map, seeing everyday life in 15th century Bohemia. Even simple villages in the countryside have so much tiny details and practically every village is unique and different. 

The other strength of the game is the freedom of choice you have. You can decide almost everything with diplomacy, violence or thievery, but also a lot of the time the NPCs and quests will acknowledge if you've completed the required objective (like, say, acquiring a quest-related item before you were told, or dealing with a group of bandits beforehand). Similarly, there are a lot of reactions to your character's current looks and attributes. NPCs will react if you're dirty, covered in blood, not wearing any clothes, even wearing stolen clothes.

There's a lot more I can praise, like the writing, the visual design, the music, but I'd also like to mention a few criticisms that will probably really affect a new player's overall enjoyment. 

First off, the combat. Enemies are still way too good at countering you, from the very first fight in the game, which results in a very weird difficulty curve where the beginning is brutally hard but once you unlock Master Strike and get some perks going, you're unbeatable. There is very little reason to use any melee weapon besides swords. Making master-strike a sword exclusive and limiting the angle of attack for non-swords just seems like a very weird decisions that limits your options in a game where you're already doing the same thing for 90% of the time.

The other big issue I have is the pacing of the game. A lot of the story missions are extremely linear and can railroad you for hours, which is a stark contrast with the open-world freedom you have for most of the playtime. And honestly, some parts just suck from a gameplay perspective (I am NOT looking forward to serving wine for 30 minutes again on a second playthrough). I also did not enjoy a lot of the "follow NPC that delivers exposition" moments and wish more of them had the option to skip forward to the actual gameplay. 

Lastly, the crime system in this game is a bit weird and doesn't always seem to make sense, but I dont know if this is a bug or the devs are trying to emulate how unfair the medieval legal system would be for a low-born peasant. I was accused of murder despite only ever killing bandits who attack me first and that soured my whole experience a bit.

I know I wrote more negative stuff than praise, but I really love the game and hope those criticisms will be addressed somehow to make the game even better. It's really up there, a near perfect game, just needs a few more tweaks and fixes.

I'm having fun so far, but I really dislike the save system. You have to craft an item to save,or sleep in a bed, but there are multiple parts of the game where you just simply can't do either of those things for an extended period of time. This will result in you either 1. having to abuse the save and exit system or 2. spending 4 hours replaying the same super difficult segment

It's also decently buggy , visual bugs, stealth is really whacky and inconsistent, had some NPCs glitch out and not perform actions and whatnot. 

But despite the bugs and the sometimes annoying difficulty, the fantastic story, writing, and graphics / animation are enough to make this easily one of the best AAA titles I've played in a while. I really don't like these types of games usually so it's kind of strange that I enjoy KCD2 so much. 

In summary, it's a little bit janky, the combat kind of stinks (it does get better as you level up), and there is an overwhelming amount of mechanics. However, all aspects of the game work together and create a piece of art that is overall worth recommending and playing, especially considering this launched at the now-forgotten $60 price point. Wait a minute, does that make this a budget title, then, if it's not $70 or $80?

You ever play a game and think, “Wow, this is exactly how things should be?” No cheap tricks. No easy victories. Just raw, unforgiving reality. That’s Kingdom Come: Deliverance II. This isn’t some fairy tale where you’re handed a sword and magically become the chosen one. No, no, no. This game makes you earn it. And that? That’s just beautiful.

Let’s talk about Henry. Some nobody blacksmith’s son. No divine prophecy. No secret bloodline. Just a guy who loses everything and has to claw his way up. Sound familiar? He doesn’t get special treatment, he has to fight, bleed, and suffer to become something greater. That’s how the world works. The weak? They stay weak. The strong? They take what’s theirs. Henry? He adapts. He learns. He survives. And when he finally becomes a warrior, it’s because he deserves it.

Swordplay in this game? Oh-ho-ho, it’s real. You don’t just swing and hope for the best. No, every strike, every block, every counter, it’s deliberate. It’s skill-based. And when you master it? You don’t just win. You crush your enemies. You dominate them. They beg for mercy, and you decide whether they get to keep breathing.

And let’s be honest, there’s something deeply satisfying about watching your enemies panic when they realize they’re outmatched. That moment? That’s what real power feels like.

Bohemia. 15th century. A land torn by war, corruption, and ambition. And guess what? The game doesn’t sugarcoat a damn thing. The world doesn’t care about your feelings. You walk into a noble’s court looking like a peasant? They treat you like dirt. You get caught stealing? You don’t get some slap on the wrist, you get beaten or executed. Actions have consequences, and I love that.

And the attention to detail? Oh, it’s obsessive. The way people react to you. The way armor slows you down. The fact that you actually have to learn to read? Now that’s commitment. You can smell the dirt, the blood, the sweat. It’s immersive in a way that most games wish they could be.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II doesn’t hold your hand. It doesn’t care if you whine about difficulty. It doesn’t care if you’re used to games where you get handed everything on a silver platter. You want to be a hero? You have to earn it. And when you finally stand on the battlefield, armor shining, sword dripping with the blood of those who doubted you?

That’s the moment. That’s the power. That’s what separates winners from losers.

✨ Kingdom Come: Deliverance II - Full Comprehensive Review ✨

KCD2 is an open-world RPG that completely immerses you in medieval times. The world feels alive, the combat is deeply satisfying, and the game provides an incredible balance between realism and fun. It improves on almost every aspect of the first game, making it an absolute must-play for RPG fans.

🌍 A World That Feels Truly Alive 🌍

The game does an incredible job of making the world feel authentic and lived-in. NPCs have routines, react to your actions, and their struggles feel real. You’re not just an observer; you’re a part of the world. If you get dirty, people react differently to you. If you wear noble clothes, they treat you with respect. Every small detail adds to the immersion.

The historical accuracy is another standout feature. The food, clothing, architecture, and even the way people speak feel like they were pulled straight from the medieval era. You’re not just reading about history, you’re living in it. Even small details like real medicinal herbs with their actual properties make the world feel richer. While it’s not 100% realism, the balance between historical authenticity and gameplay mechanics is handled perfectly.

⚔️ Satisfying, Skill-Based Combat ⚔️

The combat system is hands down one of the best aspects of the game. It’s not just about stats, it’s about skill. Timing, movement, positioning, and reading your opponent’s actions all play a role. Even after 55+ hours, there’s always something new to learn, whether it’s perfecting counters or unlocking new combos.

What makes combat even better is how it ties into the world. Bandits roam the roads, and deciding to engage them or avoid them is entirely up to you. You can also loot fallen enemies, but the game makes it feel realistic. You don’t just throw everything into an infinite bag. You need to sell different items to the appropriate vendors (blacksmiths for swords, tailors for clothes, cobblers for shoes, and more). Not every village will have all the ones you need. Bigger cities will have more variety, but even then, travelling around the city takes time since everything is so well-detailed. This forces you to explore and visit different towns, making the economy feel grounded and rewarding.

Even though combat is challenging, it never feels unfair. If you get overwhelmed, you can always retreat, and your environment matters. Fighting in tight spaces makes battles harder, while open fields give you more room to maneuver. You gotta stay on your toes.

📈 Progression That Feels Natural and Rewarding 📈

KDC2 nails progression. You start with nothing and have to build yourself up, whether it’s through alchemy, trading, hunting, or combat. Everything you do levels up naturally. Selling goods increases speech, carrying heavy items levels strength, and practicing alchemy improves your potion-making.

The perk system offers tons of customization, letting you tailor your character to fit your playstyle. There’s always something new to unlock, but it never feels overwhelming. Every perk has clear descriptions and fun little details that make leveling up feel engaging rather than just another menu grind.

🎭 Freedom of Choice in Combat and Role-Playing 🎭

What’s amazing is that combat isn’t the only way to play. If you focus on charisma and speech, you can talk your way out of fights or dress and act as a scribe to avoid combat entirely.

Even if you enjoy fighting, the game never (really) forces you into battles. You can run away, set ambushes, or manipulate enemies into surrendering. This flexibility makes the game feel truly open-ended, allowing each player to craft their own experience.

🏹 Deeply Engaging Side Quests 🏹

Unlike many RPGs where side quests feel like filler, KDC2 treats them with just as much care as the main story. Each quest feels meaningful, with real consequences. Some side quests even connect in surprising ways, acknowledging past choices you made. It’s not mind-blowing in terms of long-term impact, but it’s still more detailed than most games, making the world feel connected and reactive.

⚖️ A Perfect Balance Between Realism and Enjoyment ⚖️

While the game is deeply immersive, it’s not overly punishing. Yes, there’s an inventory weight system, but you can expand it through perks and your horse’s saddlebags. Yes, NPCs react to your appearance, but it’s not so strict that it ruins the fun. The game gives you realistic systems but keeps them enjoyable by adding just enough gamification to prevent them from feeling tedious.

🎲 Unexpected, Emergent Moments Keep the Game Fresh 🎲

One of the best parts of Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is how things don’t always go as planned. You might run into unexpected enemies, have a simple side quest turn into something much bigger, or get caught in completely random events. The game doesn’t script every little moment, and that unpredictability makes the world feel alive. Sometimes things just pop off in the wildest ways.

🔄 Incredible Value and Replayability 🔄

At 55+ hours in, the game still has so much to offer. The fact that it can hold your attention for this long without feeling stale speaks volumes. The combination of satisfying combat, immersive storytelling, and player-driven choices makes this a game that you can keep coming back to. Based on what I’ve experienced so far, I assume that even after finishing the main story and side quests, the emergent gameplay and combat system would still give it incredible replay value.

Not to mention, the sheer fact that you can play differently each time adds to the replayability. Maybe one playthrough you embrace chaos, looting and fighting at every turn, while another time you choose a peaceful path, relying on persuasion and diplomacy. The game supports a variety of playstyles, making each run feel unique.

For those who love open-ended RPGs, this game is an absolute must-play. The developers put genuine passion into making it polished, complete, and engaging from start to finish. Unlike many modern RPGs that release unfinished and rely on patches, KDC2 delivers a fully realized experience from day one!

🏆 Final Verdict: One of the Best RPGs in Years 🏆

KDC2 is, without a doubt, one of the most immersive RPGs in recent years (other than BG3 of course). The combination of realistic combat, meaningful choices, historical accuracy, and rewarding progression makes it stand out from the crowd.

The last time a game held this level of attention was titles like Valheim, State of Decay 2, Tears of the Kingdom, Baldur's Gate 3, and Breath of the Wild. If you’re looking for a rich, immersive RPG that will keep you engaged for hundreds of hours, Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is worth every penny. It just hits differently.

This medieval life simulator will test your patience, skill, and ability to avoid getting arrested for wearing stolen armour. Whether you’re fighting, trading, or just trying to remember which NPC you accidentally insulted, this game is a true testament to immersive RPGs. 😍

Now go forth. Thy kingdom come, thy purse be full, and may your pockets always be just light enough to run from the guards. Amen. 😂🙌

ORIGINAL REVIEW: Unfortunately, this is a perfect example of a game that's more fun to talk about than to actually play. It's full of dozens of absurdly intricate systems and features that sound good on paper (and build up hype in the gaming press) but end up making everything a complete and utter slog in practice:

Does it sound really cool that there are extremely detailed minigames for every possible action, from making potions to smithing weapons? Yes! Do I actually want to painstakingly mix a bunch of herbs for the nineteenth time when I'd really rather be making actual progress? No! 

Do I want to tell all my friends about the dynamic reputation system that even factors in whether your clothes are dirty or clean? Yes! Does it actually feel good to lose thirty minutes of progress because I forgot to wash my face in a horse trough before starting a speech check? No! 

Would someone be impressed if I told them the in-game economy has prices rise and fall depending on what you buy and sell? Yes! Is it actually fun spending ten minutes riding to another town just because I sold too many swords to the trader in the town I live in and now the prices have bottomed out? No!

The whole game is like this. It's essentially impossible to do *anything* in this game in a straightforward way - no matter how seemingly simple some task is, you are almost guaranteed to be stopped in your tracks by some minor issue you didn't think about that takes ten or fifteen minutes to fix. I'm sure life in 15th century Bohemia was actually filled with this sort of tedious busywork, but as someone who has other priorities in life beyond reliving the thrill of moving a bunch of flour sacks over and over again, it makes this one pretty much impossible to have fun with.

After desperately awaiting KCD II and even buying a new gaming PC just for the game, I can confidently say, after completing the main quest and a large portion of the side quests, that it is definitely not a disappointment. In an era of half-baked releases, plagued by terrible performance, game-breaking bugs, and frustrating roadblocks, KCD II shines like a beacon. On ultra settings, the game runs buttery smooth (around 140 FPS), even in scenes with many NPCs, such as the city of Kuttenberg. While Rattay in KCD I caused frame drops and instability, Kuttenberg is the complete opposite. The overall polish of KCD II is truly remarkable. During my first playthrough, I barely encountered any bugs—just a few minor graphical glitches, like flickering shadows or a twitching belt—but overall, the game is in an outstanding state.

The game world is stunning and invites exploration, while the side quests are engaging—sometimes amusing, sometimes absolute highlights—that further enrich the world. The main story picks up right where KCD I left off, expanding on the conflict over the throne between King Wenceslas and King Sigismund in a meaningful way and bringing it to a conclusion. Hopefully, this won’t be our last encounter with Henry and his companions, as I already miss this fascinating group of characters.

I can confidently say that Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is a masterpiece and a game that truly saves the AAA industry. The world is incredibly immersive—every single NPC has their own life, making it feel like a real, living world. The open world is massive, split into three regions, and does an amazing job of making you feel like you’re actually living in medieval times.
The graphics are excellent, and the dialogue choices and interactions feel endless. The writing is top-tier, and the story is an absolute masterpiece. While some side quests can be a bit dull, the majority are really well-crafted and engaging. Henry, the main character, is both likable and funny, which makes the experience even better.
Alchemy is a huge part of the game, and it’s actually really fun to learn. Combat, at first, feels a little weird, but once you unlock some skills, it becomes super satisfying. That said, there are some bugs—staircases can be frustrating since you sometimes can’t go up them properly. There are also a few combat bugs, and some quests might break, forcing you to reload. However, considering this is a brand-new release, there are fewer bugs than I expected. Sometimes, combat can feel off because of these bugs, and there’s an issue where your first attack doesn’t register properly unless you “activate” your weapon swing first, which seems like a bug.
The save system is a mixed bag. You can only save when quitting the game or by using a special item, which can be frustrating if you want to save before a tough quest. It’s something to get used to, but I personally don’t love it.
Overall, Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is an amazing game and, for me, a strong contender for Game of the Year.

What I said above stands as this game is really the continuation the first game needs for the whole story to feel complete from a story perspective.

As far as gameplay goes, my only minor gripe is that the difficulty isn't really there for a game that I think could highlight that difficulty. If you have a means to funnel enemies, you're kind of unkillable which doesn't make a whole ton of sense. I think the "Godmode" nature of Henry in KCD2 isn't as extreme as KCD1, but it's still there by the 50 hour mark (could be sooner if you actually focused on getting there). Ultimately, the godmode nature stems from 3 "problems" if you wanna call them that (and I'll add a solution to each because just complaining is lame).

1. Money is incredibly easy to make. Since bandits and a lot of enemies gear is dependent upon what level you are, eventually all bandits have really good gear and just trouncing baddies will make you have more money and stuff to sell than you can possibly do anything with. This is generally OK given money sinks like trainers exist, but without any sort of town builder DLC that KCD1 had at some point - you become filthy rich pretty easily and that's not even considering how insanely rich you could get stealing. Combine all this with repair kits being relatively cheap, a very strong tactic early on to become filthy rich insanely fast is just repair everything you find and sell it - you make more than you spend by a mile.

SOLUTION: My thought on how to solve this is 2 fold. 1 is to just implement some more money sinks like settlement building, spending money to improve companion's gear and tie to the main story, etc. 2 is to overall lower the amount of money you get from selling stuff. If I can clean out a merchant with selling 1 or 2 pieces of armor without even haggling, that's a bit extreme. I'd say a more advanced solution is that if you're selling tons of armor to the same people that over time you get less and less money (as the supply goes too high), but that's fundamentally solved by just wait -> sleep -> wait -> sleep, which if you don't have any time constraints present you can abuse. Economics in RPG's is awkward, but just lower price of selling stuff and add a big money sink that isn't training and it'd be fine.

2. Enemies, compared to Henry, die too easily when they have the same gear as Henry. If I'm in full plate armor and 7 people can wail on me for a good 20-30 seconds, 1v1's vs enemies with heavy armor should be terrifying (and thus rare). I feel like a big reason 1 is a problem is because 2 is a problem. Enemies are too weak without ANY armor (dead in 1 hit), so tacking armor on them becomes necessary which then becomes necessary to give to the player to be sold, etc etc. The best example I can give about this: [spoiler] at the end of the game where I maybe killed 100+ enemies in groups of 10 or so at a time without really any difficulty. Few to none of them wore armor and I could tank 2 hitting me while killing one with consumables on me. [/spoiler]

SOLUTION: Just make these kitted out enemies far more rare and make their armor really noticeable to the point you don't just use a sword all game and need to swap out to a hammer or piercing arrows/bolts from time to time. A lot of this is just tweaking quantity. I don't mind owning unarmored fools and being a badass knight, but when I'm owning other badass looking knights, it's a little awkward.

3. This is kind of a problem mixed with a solution. . . Remove master strike. Honestly, the reason fighting other knight armored individuals is lame is because of master strike. If I'm unable to swing to get any of the cool combos against people with swords because they'll masterstrike me -> I'm only ever going to masterstrike them and it's boring...and anyone that I can do combos on die in 1 combo or in just 2 or 3 hits (even fully armored). The fun of the combat system, to me, is the perfect parry->strike back and forth, similar to fighting in games like Chivalry (ignoring the swing dancing in those kinds of games). Master strike removes any back and forth and just makes the fight very simplistic in logic...

Does the enemy have a sword? Wait and masterstrike.
Does the enemy not have a sword? Do a simple combo and win... or wait and masterstrike. 

--- TL;DR / In Conclusion ---
