Punch and Dash use a stamina meter

Shoot uses bullets, of which you'll have to reload, but you can reload infinitely

Bombs are limited and can be regained by picking up more or dying

Slow time uses its own meter is shares with another ability to see hidden objects


Now the gameplay is okay, it's just not great. 

For instance, shooting is extremely basic. You get one gun to shoot from that fires one bullet at a time. You do extra damage for head shots and can detonate bombs by shooting them, but that's about it. There's no charged shots or multishots or any other kind of trick-shot, No different guns or different ammo, just a pistol that shoots normally. You do have to lead your shots since bullets aren't super fast like in most shooters, but that's about all that was interesting. 

As for bombs, I never did get a handle on whether there was a special trick to throwing them, so they would often get in my way since they can also hurt the player. Melee was okay, in that it was a single hook, but enemies would deal a good amount of melee damage as well, so this would be best for enemies on your tail that can be taken out in one hit, otherwise, bigger enemies can occasionally add an extra blow while dying. 

The melee also takes up a lot of stamina meaning you may not be able to dash after using it. Now, the dash is fine. In fact, it has a neat ability where if you ram into an enemy, it stuns them. However, it can be annoying to use dash to runaway since you can't dash backwards, especially since a lot of areas are small hallways where you'll be chased by skeletons with swords that take quite a few hits. In which case you can slow down time and walk back, if you've unlocked it at that point. 
The time slow ability is pretty good besides some issues with reloading while it's active and continuous shots.

Starbase gunship is basically the old Beachhead game in space. :)  You can even call it "stationary FPS". As a gunship that must defend the starbase under assault by a drone fleet until the starbase can be evacuated, you alone must hold back the tide when a variety of ships, from scouts to fighters, from torpedoes to cruisers, assault your position, seeking to either shoot or kamikaze into the starbase.  Fortunately, you can take the points you gain during the previous attempt as amount of cash to spend to improve your ship to better your chances for your next attempt. 

You have up to 4 weapons available: laser, mass driver, missile, gatling. Laser has the best range, but is weak (relatively) compared to other weapons. Mass driver has good range and does huge damage, but requires a bit of a lead. missile requires lock-on and may not turn fast enough to intercept when launched close to target. Finally, gatling gun requires a LOT of lead, but it puts enough volume of fire to saturate an area. However, its range is very low. You need to unlock weapons other than laser, as level 1 laser comes with the ship. 

You can also buy additional armor for the starbase, as well as a repair kit that kicks in when it has suffered 50% damage. 

Finally, you can add to yourself generator upgrades (which helps with the energy drain by each shot fired, giving you longer sustained volleys), as well as some single-used nukes that wipes out enemies on screen. Provided you have enough "teran cash" (which is your final score when you finish the game, you can then use to upgrade the ship for your next attempt). 

In mission one, you are to defend starbase Omicron against 30 waves of drone fleet attacks. Each wave is composed a little differently, from scouts and fighters to torpedoes and cruisers. Scouts don't have weapons except for their kamikaze warhead. Fighters do have lasers. And cruisers have long-range laseAnd in one of the last waves, you'll also see a carrier that will keep launching fighters. Also keep in mind that sometimes, one of the torpedoes may have a nuclear tip, and definitely don't let that his the base. However, you do have a "radiological scan" to spot those when they happen. 

THe ultimate objective is to survive for 30 waves, thus fully evacuate the starbase, hopefully without any penalties like losing one or more of the freighters evacuating with refugees. 

With three levels of difficulty, while the game does get a bit monotonous, it is still exciting, if a bit shallow.

If it was possible I would give this a mixed review.  Like it's pre 2K predecessor, it has so much potential, but it only partially delivers on it.

Pros - The players, player maker, outfits, venues are done very well.  The game itself plays very well, like many 2K  products it is solid.  The progression methods that I've seen so far are good.  It's a fun game to play, and just like real tennis, sometimes it's appropriately frustrating.  Career mode has lots of venues and is very similar to previous TopSpin products.  Difficulty modes are appropriate and you switch between them at any time to adapt play.

Cons - Player progression in Career Mode is...odd.  For example, after a season and a half (on hard mode) the least AI level that my player will face at Lvl 7 is roughly level 17 in the bronze qualies and 21 in the silver qualies.  It's like they missed an entire bracket of competition for the beginning Career Player.  This problem can be adjusted through the difficulty mode (for example, if I play an exhibition tournament with players on lvl 30, I'm competitive), but do I really want to do that, then ratchet up the difficulty later?  So if I don't want to change the difficulty setting (which is appropriate), I'm looking at probably 4 seasons before I'm capable of being competitive in a qualifier and "really" start my player progression.

The shot bar is excessively difficult to anticipate, for example, I would expect it to be difficult to time a hard shot that puts me in a defensive position, but I would expect that a poor shot coming from my opponent (especially short) would be an easier put away winner.  Mostly this isn't the case, and it seems inconsistent.

It is a single developer game, so we should not expect the production quality of a a Triple A studio, yet, the game lacks many things we would consider basics in any game. It feels more like a prototype/demo or an early access than a a complete game, that is how it is being sold as.

So, after let's go to the point and start with the good and bad points, and what would make me change the review to a positive one:

- The AI is completely braindead. When you most see how bad is, is in city assaults, where you must capture and hold an area until the enemy runs out of reinforcements or a progress bar is completed. You can see both allied and enemy AI roaming around ignoring the objetive area while ignoring each other, just waiting for you to take action.

- The management feels lacking. While you can train your soldiers, research new equipment, and upgrade your facilities, it is not fun, and more like an annoying chore you must complete to get anything else than an M4, or the basic grenade and medkit. Adding more variety to this first tier, for example, the AK-47 and the MP-5, would make early gameplay more entertaining and dinamic, rather than waiting for "days" (cycles) to the research to complete, just to have the option of playing stealthy.

- While the enemy variety is not the most amusing ever seen, it feels enough, the problem lies in your own troops: you have access to multinational operators, ranging from the most known like US Rangers, Seals, or Green Berets, the British SAS or the German KSK, to other less known or directly making their first appeareance in a videogame (not counting mods), like the Spanish FGNE, or the Australian SAS. But, and here comes the but... they all feel the exact same. Yes, the SAS can call an airstrike, and Green Berets have support of local troops, so theorically you can deploy 12 operatives instead of the 6 members team, but... there is literally just a MARPAT, the arid and regular AOR uniforms, a diving suit, a Gorkha in 2 camouflages, AUSCAM, the woodland Flecktarn (despite being a desertical enviroment), the US Woodland, and... Multicam. Taking into account that there is special forces from France, Spain, Germany, Netherlands, Latvia, Russia, United Kingdom and United States, in the end, it feels they all are a simple name change for US troopers. Even if they are not in use anymore, a DPM or MTP would make the British forces way more interesting than a generic Multicam, same with Spanish or Latvian.

- There is a severe lack of armament. There is only 2 pistols, both the exact same, only 1 SMG (whose model and icon have absolutely nothing in common except that they both are MP5's), 2 machine guns (again, with problems of the icon and model not matching), a single sniper rifle, and 5 assault rifles, which 2 are the same, but with and with out supressor. 

- Same happens with the equipment, having 2 grenades that are the exact same thing, yet you need to research the second one, and, having many different vests, that are basically the same, but with different camouflage pattern. 

- The ship assault are not fun to do, as the "planning mode" (visually similar to Door Kickers) is poorly made, trying to make a single room entry a pain, and working better to just select all your operatives, and throw them into a corridor where braindead AI is waiting with out taking cover, hoping for the less bad result. 

- The map campaign is pretty bad-looking, reminding more to an early Total War game (see Medieval 1 or 2, Shogun 1 or Romer 1), or to Mount & Blade, per se, it is neither good nor bad, is just a visual preference, but, I would prefer to at least, see curves though a river course rather than a straight line with small bumps of dirt trying to hide it.

- There is no "post game", once you finish a campaign, it simply restarts, no congratulation message, no credits, no nothing, just a campaign restart, although you keep your team and researchs, so I guess it is good to do the same unfunny missions again and again with out unlocking nothing new?

- The guns sound is not the worst I have ever heard, but, if it possible, please... change the AK-47's sound, it is really annoying, especially when everyone except maybe your operators, are using them.

- There is a bug with tracer ammunation, where they go across every possible object, until they exit the map, add the fact that once detected, the enemy AI will not stop shooting until you kill them, and you get a really annoying situation where you do not know if you are under fire by an unknown enemy, or it is just the same bot that spotted you 5 minutes ago that is still shooting.

Although I have said pretty bad things of the game, I did like the idea of having a some sort of new Jagged Alliance game, although more based on Special Operations rather than managing a mercenary group, but, I miss many of the great management options those games had, or, if the game is supposed to be more action, and less time worrying about training tropps, or managing every aspect of the group, the current options hinder said action more than making it an interesting feature. If there is further updates correcting at least the bad AI, and adding more maps (you literally have like 7 or 8 different maps only, with out counting the 3 different ship models) and correcting some of the most severe problems, like the lack of deep management (or its presence), and some variety in weapons and equipment, especially among the enemies, as it seems they only have AK-47s around, I would probably change the review to a positive one, as the game itself, does not have bad ideas, just executes them a bit poorly.

It's rough. A ways off from the level it could be but, it's still a really cool game imo, and has a feature set I've been really dying to see in a game. But it crashes a fair bit and has bugs.

The GOOD:
Really cool feature sets that basically let you run your own GWOT. similar to a mount and blade over world, you have an aircraft carrier that you can navigate around, and find target you want to hit. Theres also a fairly simple simulated economy of the fake country your operating in, and more stability to the economy means they can afford more security, which also helps you win the war. It's like the old breach and clear games but with A LOT more inspiration from the more modern Door Kickers series, with the troop movement and stuff. I'm really impressed with how many different things Applesauce incorporated here. 

Then there's all the different management stuff, training your guys, hiring on new people (permadeath for them too), purchasing equipment for them, upgrading the boat, upgrading your helicopter, researching gear, finding targets, and maybe more. None of it is very in depth, but there just so much that it really does help get you wrapped up in the campaign and adds an XCOM style of depth.

The BAD:
Animations are pretty janky, the graphics are quite low quality (not that graphics matter THAT much) but worst of all, is the controls, which are fairly buggy. Sometimes your character wont move and you need to unselect then reselect them to issue a command they'll respond to. And the path markers get SUPER cluttered, making it really hard to make precise runs effeciently. The game world also doesn't seem all the large, only a few points of interest on it. And then there's the crashing which f'd me over a few times, losing a fair bit of campaign progress. Always seems to happen on the campaign map.

The MEAT AND POTATOES:
If you like Door Kickers, and like me, have always wished it had a deeper campaign mode, this can give you a pretty good taste of it.. but its not nearly as polished as DK. It does feel like an early access title, with very basic menus and UI, and an experience that feels like a first version, waiting for more content or DLC, but sadly, I highly doubt anything is coming (seems ultra dead, which is a shame). But, still well worth the 10$ price tag imo, and I think its a hidden gem in the milsim/tactics game genre, that if nothing else has some really unique campaign mechanics I'd love to see adopted in other games in the future.

Underrated game IMO. The meta part is great, helping to rebuild a region overrun by insurgents. In a way it feels like building up my own town. It has a dynamic economy system that's directly hindered by pirate ships and insurgent patrols until you take them out. Then more cargo ships and trucks will safely arrive at their destinations and earn more money for the city (which also serves as your money for buying things).

The micro game is well done too. Squad members can crouch or go prone like an FPS. You can safely open doors by having one guy go prone and aiming straight in, with two others crouched on the sides to cover the left & right pie pieces. The tutorial will show you how to pre-plan the orders of several squad members and then execute the plan all at once, but I've found most things perfectly do-able without using that feature.

Capturing villages from insurgents can be tricky at first, but isn't bad once you learn a couple tricks. First, get to the capture area and hold Shift so your squad constantly faces your mouse cursor, then move the cursor in slow circles to monitor all directions and take out any enemies that get close. Second, watch for enemy artillery smoke and immediately vacate the area once you see it (use double-right-click to run, don't walk). After the artillery is over, make your way back in and continue capturing. And third, any friendlies in the area won't help capture, it's up to you to bring your squad there.

After every battle, you'll probably have a couple guys that need to spend some time in the infirmary healing up, and a few other guys who have some training points they can burn at the shooting range. In both cases you just watch & wait, no minigame to play, but you can speed up time.

The new weapons and armor you can research might be a little underwhelming compared to what you'd normally see in an RPG. But you do get some boosts from them, so they're still worth it, just don't expect too much. Training up individual stats seems to have a more noticeable effect.

Rarely do I bother to write a review, but I feel like this game deserves one. I gave it a few runs and a fair shake, but the game balance and RNG can be incredibly brutal. I normally don't really mind that in games, but I feel like this one just really does not click with me.

Unlike most of the recent reviews, I've not really run into any performance issues aside from a bit of minor lag here and there.

Let's start with the good:
Aesthetically unique and beautiful. Graphically it can be a little busy, but I do think it has a wonderful amount of character. The colors are vibrant and lovely, the animations have a kind of shadow puppet vibe? It's very cute.

The neutral:
The music is... fine. It's just fine. I turned it off to play to my own music after my first run.

The bad:
Alright. Here we go. I wouldn't have written a review if I didn't have Opinions.

1. The RNG.
Absolutely brutal RNG sometimes--the equipment that drops, the skills you get... it could end up that you're through the first area and you just don't find anything that's particularly helpful. Having some early weapons drop with absolutely crippling skill debuffs like a whopping -40 accuracy and -2 movement and finding absolutely nothing else helpful, or just finding absolutely no ranged weaponry whatsoever... building a character for magic attacks but finding no reusable skills. I found it quite difficult to get an alright build off the ground.

2. Enemy summons.
They can act the turn that they're summoned, resulting in some absolutely brutal snowballing. In a game like this, where action economy is king, the enemy summoning several allies and completely bloating the action economy feels incredibly difficult to recover from, especially when each enemy that gets summoned has the potential to shank you twice, or completely cripple you with debuffs. I would probably suggest not allowing enemy summons to act the turn they're summoned, or move the summons to the very end of the initiative track, at least. I've run into several infuriating fights with enemies rolling 22+ on initiative, summoning several enemies, and then absolutely dog-piling one single character before I could even act to do anything in response.

3. Unclear interactions.
I cannot, for the life of me, figure out what the heck is up with tall grass. My best guess is that I can't target things inside tall grass with ranged attacks? It would probably benefit from an explanation somewhere.

4. Movement.
Occasionally, movement on the hex tiles is slightly blocked by enemies, making you unable to click on certain hexes in your movement range. Additionally, you cannot move through your allies, resulting in some incredibly awkward placement on maps.

5. Spirit points/SP.
You can only regenerate these at campsites, but in later areas it feels like every freaking enemy has some way of draining your SP. Going back to the aforementioned magic-based characters finding nothing reusable--there are some reusable spells that cost turn-regenerating resources to use, but occasionally you will build a character for magic but are only able to find magic spells that cost SP. Enemies draining SP when it's already such a limited resource (you use it to reroll your level up stat bonuses and skills, too! It's very important!) makes this resource scarcity go from Feels Bad to Absolutely Infuriating.

6. The spirit system.
I'm... logically okay with the spirit system, but... and it could simply be because I'm fundamentally misunderstanding how to play the game. That's possible. But it seems like the game encourages you to play without spirits because you unlock more achievements/skills for defeating certain enemies without spirits equipped. But there's no way to get more villagers? So once you lose your villagers... I don't know? I have yet to do a run using spirits because I feel like I'm supposed to be going spiritless to unlock more new skills. It just seems like a very odd system. Not my favorite approach to meta progression.

7. Slow pacing.
The characters walk in a straight line, and I feel like I would almost prefer if it just skipped from one node to the next. The walking in-between makes the game feel bloated and slow. There are too many loading screens that require me to click to proceed.

8. Sluggish UI/annoying UI design.
I'm not a big fan of the menus, either. I wish I could drag and drop accessories into the slots, and I often click an accessory and miss the secondary prompt to actually equip it. I don't need to watch XP being allocated. The level-up screen takes a hot minute to show up, as well. Resting takes quite long. Just a lot of small things that add up to making the game feel quite bloated.

9. Winning feels sluggish. Losing feels sluggish.
I've not really had a single fight where I felt like I was really powerful. It often feels like I'm chasing highly mobile enemies around on the map, with a distinct lack of ranged options at my disposal. And when I'm losing, it also feels like a frustratingly slow death march where I know I can't win but the enemies draw it out as long as possible. I really cannot explain why, the pacing just feels off no matter which end of the win/lose spectrum you're on.

Now it might sound like I hated the game, and that's... not strictly true. I think there's the basis of a good game in there, but it really does need a bit more polish and love to get there.

Recommended with a caveat: it will ultimately either upset you or anger you after you play this for a while because you'll realize that there's a lot here and so much potential but due to reality of sales and finances it'll probably never reach that potential with all the polish and the jankiness smoothed out.

So much of the game is damaged just from the dodge mechanic. 

Timing your dodges to an attack, managing your distance, and placing your strikes is good enough and possible. But dodging more than one attack on screen is too difficult for how often it happens.

Most of the enemies can throw more than one projectile at a time and sometimes at different speeds. With a dodge interval of 1 full second, you're going to dodge the first one and get hit by the second. Sometimes, you will manage your distance well enough to dodge both of them, only to get hit by the third attack the enemy is winding up. The dodge propels you about 1/4 of the stage's length, which can often land you into another attack that you can't dodge out of because of the dodge interval. You may dodge away from an enemy and their attack, and then be chased by a projectile that you can't dodge because of the interval.

Since dodging is the only way to avoid taking damage, as there is no crouch or jump, you will most of your time and die a lot trying to find ways to survive an enemy's attacks and less time attacking the enemy yourself.

A lot of this game is good and solid with a nice art style, cool looking characters with interesting attack patterns, and good music, but the dodging makes the whole game so much harder. I'll give it a 6/10.

So this is pretty solid rhythm game, but I do have some reservations with giving it a blanket recommendation.

The core gameplay is a sort of hybrid of a twin-stick shooter and an inverse Mai-Mai, with notes coming in from the edge of the screen that you collect at the center of the screen by pointing an analog stick towards and pressing the trigger on the same of the controller. As an added wrinkle, there's collectable power ups that kinda feel like they came out of an Amplitude game, but overall the core game loop is simple and pretty well executed.

As for the setlist, it's pretty good IMO. There's a bent toward almost 80'ish pop and ambient pieces that feel pretty unique for a commercial rhythm game, and while there's not many tracks, there's a plenty enough of them to justify the games relatively cheap asking price.

On the more questionable aspects of the game, I have issue with the games visuals. On the subjective side of things, there's some aspects of the visual design that I really dislike, like the games choice of fonts, so I hope there's some theming choices added in the future. As a more objective complaint, though, the game's default gameplay presentation make me HORRIFICALLY ill, to the point that I'm running to the bathroom after a single chart. Turning off all the visual options in the menu helps but it doesn't quite entirely get thing under control thanks to the game's fatal flaw that exacerbates the whole situation: atrocious performance.

I've been playing exclusively on a Steam Deck, and as the game's optimization stands the Deck can basically can never hit 30fps in gameplay, with normal gameplay sitting at ~25fps with regular dips to the tens, even with turning down all the few visual options the game has, which is absolutely mindboggling considering what the hardware is capable of. To the game's credit, it actually plays okay at those low framerates, and if it didn't exacerbate my issues I wouldn't complain too much.

However, since framerate is an issue for me, I've been spending the last couple of hours messing with engine config settings trying to get stable performance that without making the game look like garbage, and I think I've got a something acceptable now:

By going into the game's AppData folder and editing GameUserSettings.ini to set all the scalability groups settings to 0 and the resolution scale to 80%, I can lock the game at 40fps at the OS level with a fairly minor hit in image quality, which does actually help tremendously with the queasiness, even if it doesn't eliminate it.


Anyways, despite how much of this review is dedicated to negative criticism, I do honestly recommend it overall. It's a fun and fairly unique rhythm game that's a good fit for portable devices and it likely won't bother the average player. I just hope there's some added options and performance optimization down the line.

Reviewer's context: I play way, way too many roguelikes/lites. Got a taste for it with ADOM and Brogue, moved onto BoI, Spelunky, Enter the Gungeon, and many, many more. Most played game by hours is currently Slay the Spire, followed by Binding of Issac and Deep Rock Galactic.

At the very baseline, NecroBouncer does what it says on the tin; it is a twin-stick arena fighting game, with passive items, active abilities, and roguelite progression. And if that's enough for you, then this will serve. But I think the devs could do more.

Primary of my complaints: there's an opening cutscene about how the bartender wants you as a...whatever you are, to go bounce for them for their bar. And instead of taking the time to try to build upon that world at all, you may as well have slept through it for all it matters. There's this thinking that the gameplay loop makes the game, but it's only one pillar of the gameplay experience. I purposefully bought this game thinking that there would be a world to explore, parts of the "bar" that would be interesting to learn about/uncover. None of that actually matters, as it turns out. The only time you see the "bar" is when you encounter it as a shop, and otherwise it is as generic of a melee-focused top-down arena fighter as you get.

The rest are polish/game-feel issues:
- The concept of hit-stop is fully non-existent, your attacks are just an animation that passes through everything, making anything that took damage blink once. No good audio cues, no hit-stop animation.
- The player's hurtbox is too pixel-exact, and doesn't account for the fact that the players are humans, and thus think in a 3d mindset; the very top of the player character's head, and a fair portion of the upper body do count as part of the hurtbox, which strikes me as a little illogical, given that we move around in 3d.
- Bosses are rather dull, due to the "fully invincible except for certain parts of the fight" mechanic that doesn't really make any sense. The first few times to learn the pattern, and then since you can't do anything else _but_ dodge, it loses my interest immediately.
- Movement is a bit too stilted for a melee-based arena fighter, and dodge rolling, while helpful, feels imprecise; I could not tell you where I was going to land once I started, which clashes a little with the "relic hunt" arena
- The AI really stupidly just stands there, once spawned; if the response to this is that the enemy are drunks that need to be ousted, a) then animate them as such please, and b) once they are aggro'd, they should present some kind of consistent threat. Having them suddenly stop chasing the player removes me from the moment very quickly. If this is artificial easing of the fight, it feels bad and needs to be re-considered.
- That there were only three possible starting archetypes felt really, really bad; the fact that you could only start with one kind of body with its one ability really turned me off. I understand that you needed it that way to center level up upgrades on, but with basically no choice, it felt really bad.
- Finally, the least of these issues, once you've completed your objective, the room exit immediately opens up, and if you were standing on the exit, say goodbye to anything you hadn't picked up yet in that room, as you're off to the next one. No choice to delay moving on.

To be fair, this isn't a 0/10 review:

- The game turns on and off with ease, and doesn't take up a lot of disk space for what it does, and it appears to be not buggy at all, which is nice
- The abilities are interesting to play with, once you can get them
- The metacurrency concept of achieving certain goals before acquiring a piece of metacurrency feels better than "just grind the game's deaths until you win". This forces the player to learn the mechanics, and allows for a sense of accomplishment.
- The pathing tree and legend are very neat, clear, and easy to understand. No scrolling necessary, it feels really good to use.

Ultimately, as it is, unless the devs really re-work this game, it just feels like yet another middling game to throw onto the heaping pile of top-down arena shooter/fighter roguelites that are currently flooding this market. You have to do something really meaningful to stand out, and not having any real NPC interaction at all puts a big damper on it for me. As it stands, I will be submitting for a refund shortly after this review posts.

Certain things seem intended to tick the player off, too, like the pillars. They'll get stuck on walls frequently, and you'll never be able to get them all into place before the timer goes off. The same could be said for the Crystal rooms. Relic Rooms are THE WORST. Imagine the worst traps with perfect yet desynced timing, and you have the rooms you need to get through. The worst thing, though, is the room clutter and spike traps. As if keeping track of everything happening onscreen wasn't enough, you have to keep track of slightly different grey tiles that can damage you while you're trying to artfully combo a bunch of enemies, and the clutter just makes getting around and actually landing or positioning right a nightmare.

Then we have the relics. Oh boy. Only slightly better than Issac if you know what I mean. You get to choose 1 of three, but one might be corrupted, though your hand WILL sometimes be forced to choose the corrupted one due to how... Either self-debuffing or just plain stupid some of the relics are, like all the ones that add # of clutter clutter based on _ when clutter is already an annoyance. Yes, there are sets of relics that would act like builds.... IF they ever came up in the right order, and, oh hey, look at that. Relic pool bloating going up per run, too, making that impossible when randomness is in play. Ugh.

Then we have the standard moveset. The melee can DELAY, NOT RESET enemy actions, so, if you were unlucky enough to have something charging a moment before you hit them, you're going to get hit in the next milisecond. The ranged is actually what SHOULD have been the main attack, but no. It's a piercing wave projectile that takes a limited energy meter to cast. The same one that you do your far more powerful abilities with (zap bouncer does far more damage than 3 waves, but they cost the same amount of energy).

Then we have the map. Yeah. Map. Mhm. Totally have a choice here guys. Totally not just going to go for all the relics because they do important things sometimes, if the right ones come up. Nope. Was the room choosing totally pointless? Yes, except when you want to avoid Relic Hunts.

Last gripe is that the game seems like it fights itself on whether to give the player XP or not. Remember those pillars and crystals? The way they work seems to force enemy spawns, yet.... The point of the room is to stop them from spawning, but, you want them to spawn so you can level, but then leveling is capped to once a room, and there's a downside of Zombies spawning out of corpses if you linger too long, as well as a level cap that you WILL hit in zone 1...

I definitely do NOT recommend this game to anyone else.

[b][u]GAMEPLAY[/u][/b]
The gameplay in Steelborn is a mix of exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving. The player must navigate the game's open-world environment, which is filled with enemies, traps, and hidden treasures. Combat is fast-paced and satisfying, with the player having access to a variety of weapons and abilities. The game also features RPG elements, such as leveling up and skill trees, which allow the player to customize their character's abilities to suit their playstyle. The puzzles in Steelborn are challenging but not overly difficult, requiring the player to use their wits and observation skills to progress through the game.

[b][u]STYLE(GRAPHIC/SOUND DESIGN)[/u][/b]
The graphics in Steelborn are impressive, with detailed environments and character models. The game's art style is unique, with a mix of sci-fi and steampunk elements. The environments are diverse, ranging from desolate dungeons to futuristic cities, which adds to the game's immersive experience.

[b][u]PROBLEMS[/u][/b]
While Steelborn has some positive aspects, it is not without its problems. Here are some of the most prominent issues with the game:
-Repetitive gameplay: While the combat in Steelborn is fun and satisfying, it can quickly become repetitive. The game's enemies are fairly predictable, and there is a limited variety of weapons and abilities to use against them. As a result, some players may find the gameplay to be monotonous after a while.
-Lack of direction: Steelborn's open-world design can be both a blessing and a curse. While it allows for a lot of exploration and discovery, it also lacks clear direction. Some players may find themselves wandering aimlessly without a clear objective or sense of purpose.
-Thin story: While the game's setting and lore are intriguing, the actual story of Steelborn is fairly thin. There are few characters to interact with, and the game's main questline is relatively short. As a result, some players may feel that the game lacks depth or substance.

Tips it would be good to know from the start i have found:
As you are searching around always look out for items with 3 teeth (stars) - they make significantly better weapons and armour so always try to have everything 2 or 3 teeth grade
Fires - you need to build big fires to last the night while you sleep (or things will get you after the first couple of levels) - the trick to building fires is watching the circle that goes around the side of the fire pit - start your fire with bark and 3-4 small sticks - you will notice the circle goes around and goes past a point labelled M - this means the fire is big enough to take medium sticks, once you throw a few of those on it gets to a level to take large logs and a few of those should max out the ring and get you a good night's sleep! Also the extra long sticks can be grabbed at each end and snapped into a small and medium stick.
You can also collect arrows you shoot that miss their target so definitely easier to go looking for them than making new ones all the time
Last one - you can leave liquids in your mortar and pestle so if you make a health potion and dont need to drink the whole thing then sip it and just keep the rest in the vessel for later

While it isn't without its flaws, Song in the Smoke is criminally under reported and underappreciated. At the time of writing, there are only 23 other Steam reviews. Oomph. The development team deserves better. This game is a well produced, functioning full length product with plenty of features. For these reasons along, it is a positive rating and well worth trying. 

Everything that follows may sounds negative, but Song in the Smoke is still an enjoyable VR experience of which there are far too few. Fighting the animals is a ton of fun. Being chased by the dinosaur sized animals is a ton of fun. Taking in the large forests in the twilight light, firefiles scattering through the air, is a ton of fun. 

If you liked the art of S&S, you should be at home here. It runs fantastic on a 4790k and 2080 Super. It has some of the largest environments that I've encountered in a VR game. Boneworks had giant street and building interiors, but they were mostly empty rectangular spaces. Subnautica has large waterways but, when I tried it, they were plagued with assets popping in once close enough to the player. Here, there are giant forest areas with many nooks and crannies to explore. The colors are vibrant and lush. Ok, it isn't super detailed, but I assume, like S&S, the developers were balancing style with VR performance. Both S&S and Song in the Smoke are masterclasses in the ethos of doing more with less. It felt like a mix of Turok and open world Zelda. 

There are lite, lite story elements. Personally a weak point. Dropped immediately into a caveman doing his thing. Your mission is collecting hidden orbs per zone and then fighting progressively harder animals. After you collect orbs, you're treated to a brief cinematic. There are also hidden power ups. 

The biggest flaw is its clunkiness, which is likely the result of being ported from the PSVR. Inventory management is more smooth and intuitive in PCVR first games like HL:A or Walking Dead: S&S. For example, there are two quick slots for inventory, but they're seemingly bound to specifically the left or right hand versus shoulder location. While you'll access them by reaching over your shoulder, if you reach your right hand over your left shoulder, you'll pull out the right hand item. It can be confusing until you realize what is happening. There are other nagging object and inventory interactions. New instructions are floating tool tips that can be easily missed, such as if you are in active pursuit of an animal. 

Between tracking down the orbs, you'll have to survive. Frankly, I liked S&S's or the Forest's survival balance better. There is no stamina meter. Instead, you'll progressively become hungrier and sleepier. The survival elements were on the tip of being overbearing. For example, you basically need to eat a couple pieces of meat or fruit each day. However, most of the animals only drop one piece of meat per kill, and the act of harvesting the single meat usually takes half the day cycle (it fast forwards). Unlike S&S or the Forest, where I could stockpile plenty of food materials during the day and then prepare meals to last several days, I basically just kept my head above water each day. It ended up being faster to skip harvesting meat and grab berries or mushrooms on the fly. 

Physically crafting each item, like knives, arrows and campfires, is really neat. Still, like the one to one meat experience noted above, crafting is one to one also. While quick, you will be hand crafting each and every arrow you use (unless you take time to find the hidden caches). After building your 10th campfire (which has to be rebuilt at least once or twice in the night), the experience starts to drift from game to chore. Plus, items tend to wear out really fast. The starting bow broke on the second or third hunting trip. Each item has an independent quality level, but you would be forgiven for overlooking that detail while scavenging. There is simply a lot of upkeep.

The initial impressions of the game are very favorable. The crafting is satisfying and discovering new crafting recipes while exploring is great. You search for the required three items while trying to gear up and getting pumped to face your strongest foe yet.

Then the game keeps repeating the same thing. Location after location  you're doing the same thing. Create camp, hunt local wildlife and gather local resources to upgrade yourself to next tier. Move to next area and repeat. Creating a storage sack is often very important but each storage is it's own thing. You're always starting with stuff on your back when moving between areas and all your previous work becomes moot. Having a Resident Evil style universal storage sack would be incredibly welcome and cut back on the repetitive tedium of the game.

The last areas are very disappointing. Boss of the second to last area is nothing but a walking target, offering no resistance.  Last area is very arduous and frustrating.

You need to feed yourself, keep warm and for some reason keep away the dark. Hunger is great and easy to handle. Staying warm doesn't seem to come into play until closer to the end of the game which feels like a missed opportunity. Cold snaps could have been a great thing.

Keeping away the dark... it's not about the darkness. A magical floating goat that people usually call Wendigo will haunt you at night. It causes massive damage, clips through walls and can't be fought off without light. Game wants you to explore at night for upgrades but the Wendigo actively encourages you to hug your bonfire at night.
I would recommend not building a bonfire at all but to simply have a torch in your inventory at all times. When the menace wakes you up at night, simply smack your torch against the wall to light it and it will go away. You have to do this twice a night to keep him away but you will save a lot of time fetching firewood each day.

Repetitive and stretched out nature of the gameplay combined with the awful Wendigo mechanic is the reason why I'm giving this negative review.

This is THE BEST representation of the early VR Survival genera! Crafting is intuitive, making good use of motion controls to keep immersion high. Status effects such as cold, tired, hungry or bleeding, are shown subtly as a few floating HUD icons like ice-crystals, sleepy-eyes, or blood-drops. The fear can get pretty real as there are many dangers and encounters to avoid or conquer. The upgrades feel useful and rewarding by covering areas like larger-packs and higher armor/weapon stats. Keeping all your "meters happy" includes managing hunger, fatigue, temperature, and light-sources. Item management includes having enough firewood or light, with deadly consequences if neglected. Campfire system is unique that it requires a "pyramid" mix of timber using sticks, medium-Sticks, and logs.
This game is absolutely immaculate in my opinion. The story reaches deep into the human experience and gives you a subtly spiritual journey as you fight for your life. Love it!

All around great VR survival game: cool setting and atmosphere, good looking stylized visuals, smooth difficulty curve and addictive gameplay loop. The only weak parts are awkward melee and teleportation climbing, but even that is tolerable.
In my opinion, it is one of the best games that came out in the last 2 years.

You play as a lone hunter in beautiful prehistoric environments that get more a more hostile as you progress. Stylized visuals look almost as good as Saints and Sinners, and later levels have those breathtaking vantage points where you can see almost whole map from high above. Forest sounds and realistic lighting with pitch black nights create thick atmosphere of wild nature and sometimes primal horror.

All interactions are designed for VR with intuitive item crafting and building. Gameplay loop is addictive, you constantly have something to do as you hunt and gather to get better equipment or explore the land to progress in the story. Song in the Smoke never leaves survival phase for base building like many similar titles do. You are a hunter, not an industrial builder: food will always be scarce and nights - dangerous if you do not prepare enough wood for bonfire before dusk.

Archery is deliberately slow: bowstring draw speed is limited, stopping you from becoming an arrow minigun like you usually do in VR archery titles:) And there is huge difference in damage between hitting a heart and anything else, further encouraging accurate shots. Melee is weightless and not very enjoyable, but it's usually only used to finish wounded animal with 1-2 hits to the head or block enemy charge.

The campaign is quite long for VR and will take about 10-20 hours to finish depending on chosen difficulty and your playstyle.

Wow, what an underrated gem. You are a cave-person / native trying to survive and level up your equipment as you face increasingly dangerous animals in the prehistoric wild. It's exciting (& creepy at night), challenging (with a good difficulty ramp), uses VR mechanics (vs. simply being a survival port), great sounds (crank it up), and has a unique art style. I hope more serious players give it a chance as it is completely worth the journey.

Octomaze is a charming and engaging casual puzzle game.

You play an octopus whose tentacle reaches to the far corners of a maze to collect goodies, whilst avoiding obstacles and badies. The concept is clever, as octopi are know for solving mazes in real life.

The game is very well produced with professional graphics throughout, and has amusing animations in keeping with the theme. The music is a short loop, but is soothing and includes pastoral sound effects.

Gameplay involves numerous features including switches, moving walls and bombs. These are introduced gradually, so the game is very easy to learn. These features add much variety, and the game has many levels that will provide hours of fun.

TLDR: An improvement in every way to VBFI, which was already among the very best games on steam with opt in 18+ content. Well worth the price if it at all interests you. 

Long version:

In relation to Venusblood Frontier:

An evolution of the game system from Frontier, but shares no story threads or characters from the previous game in the series. You can freely start with this game.

Notable improvements:

Much better UI and explanation of mechanics. Pop up explanation of you hover to skills, every gameplay screen has a “?” button that explains the screen.  

a max of 18 vs 18 battles rather than 6 vs 6, and units can generate resources outside of battle, making better use of the large cast of units.

more units, skills, items

Unit deployment, Map movement, and choke points, making defense tactics a thing

Higher resolution, better overall art quality

A longer, arguably better, story with more scenes


Best parts:

Unique and fun gameplay: Unlike 99% of sexually explicit games on steam the gameplay is not some barebones RPG maker game, cheap knockoff of a better game, a brainless “puzzle” game, or a visual novel with no gameplay at all. But even if it does not appeal to you, the developers don’t have such an ego that they won’t let you skip it.

Play as you want: Easy mode literally comes with a “I win” button for every fight that you can use at any time. Hard mode will force you to learn every minutia of the game to be successful. NG+ includes difficulty modes than even those who can beat hard can’t succeed at. Every story scene in the game can be instantly skipped if you just want the gameplay. Every story scene in the game can be read at any time in the extra menu once you reach it in the game.

Huge amount of content: hundreds of unique units you can use to fill out your army, each customizable through equipment and the hiring process. 2 distinct routes with many different ending scenes. A long story that is probably better than you would expect from a game of this type.

Worst parts:

Can be intimidating at first:

Lots of mechanics in the game, and, for better or worse, the game does not hold your hand drip feeing your tutorials on each one. I highly recommend you do not play on hard to start if you are not familiar with the series and/or don’t want to spent a lot of time in the beginning learning all the mechanics.

Wow. I am shocked. This visual novel is good. REALLY good. What looked like a simple VN turned out to be something great. 

[h1]Story[/h1]
While the story does have a focus on romance, another focus is Isabella and the demons that she face. Our protagonist tries to talk to this girl he has fallen in love with, only for something to prevent him from doing so, whether it is something like a lack of confidence or Isabella leaving before he gets the chance to. What seems like just a shy girl that is too scared to talk to people turned out to be something more. 

[h1]Talking about Porcelana[/h1]
From the moments she appears and the different ways the protagonist describes Isabella using similes and metaphors, I can tell that Isabella is a mysterious but interesting girl. What is hiding behind that face that shows very little emotions? After learning about how Isabella was like in the past from Camil, it makes me wonder what caused this change with how she acts. Moving on to the chapters, none of them felt drawn out. Each one is given enough time and doesn't feel like filler.

Once you finally learn about Isabella's past, you finally learn why she is shy and distant. Let me just say that is not for the faint of heart. It is just a reminder that not everyone is has a happy life. Some people are living through painful lives and no matter how hard they try, they can never find any form of happiness. Learning about Isabella's past made me tear up a little. No one should have to go through what Isabella did. Unfortunately, the protagonist learned about it after "that" scene happened. 

After I witnessed "that" scene, I hoped that there would be some way my choices could change the ending I just witnessed. Then, this VN surprised once more as I was able to [spoiler]write a letter for Isabella. After I wrote a letter, a different choice appeared. Giving the letter to Isabella results in the protagonist getting the courage to talk with her more. In the end, I was given a satisfying ending where the protagonist was able to get to Isabella in time. This was such a great ending. I am glad that the protagonist and Isabella were able to get a happy ending.[/spoiler] After everything Isabella has went through, seeing her [spoiler]cry tears of joy when the protagonist convinced her to continue living[/spoiler] is a satisfying scene.

[h1]Negative(s)[/h1]
- The characters other than Isabella? Yes. Most of them either felt underdeveloped or had no development at all.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
I cannot believe how good this VN is and how little attention this VN has. Porcelana tells a romance story that looks harmless but can be heart wrenching and depressing. The story will make you feel like you are on a roller coaster of emotions. Once again, I cannot believe that I enjoyed this VN so much. How does this VN have very few people playing it? If this VN interests you in the slightest, then I highly recommend that you purchase it. You will not be disappointed. If Pandita Studio makes another VN, then I will not hesitate to buy it when I can.

- Startup "tips" every time you start a puzzle cannot be disabled. By level 8 the game literally explained to me that "[url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2828059081]The horizontal lines are called rows[/url]". I'm speechless.
- Store page advertises "griddlers with no pen and paper!" like yeah we understand the concept of computers yes? 
- Three mistakes = instant game over. Painted a line over the wrong row on accident? That's 3+ mistakes, game over, start the puzzle from scratch. You already have the stars system in place, why force game over?!
- In-game coins, bonus coins mechanics, a shop to buy extra mistake-chances and hints, and generally more crap you never asked for in a game like this.
- Poorly picked font of white characters on a light-gray background in a 1024x768 window (or in blurry fullscreen) makes it seriously hard for the eyes.

I seem to have exhausted Steam's entire supply of Picross games at this point. This is the first title that I'm gonna have to skip because of how badly made it is from every perspective.

Full disclosure: I got this on sale for .49 cents USD for the theme. It was on sale around Valentine's day, so why not, right? Well, I'll admit these are not my favorite type of logic puzzles in the first place, though the tutorial to make sure you understand how to play was fun.

It's the color scheme that isn't. The wee white numbers on the light grey background had me squinting. The font style also had me guessing if I was looking at a 1 or 7. Add in this company's three key system that they won't let you turn off, and it was soon a frustrating slog.

You can try to forgo the keys and grind for coins for power ups, but it just frustrates the heck out of me that this wasn't set up with a casual relaxing play in mind. You either have to restart at every mistake to get your three keys, and good luck realizing you made a mistake with the wee numbers, or grind for coins to buy those power ups for hints and to undo any mistakes. 

Not my cup of tea, and nothing I'd recommend to try for your first try at this logic genre.

I really wanted to like this game, the characters are really charming, and I found myself constantly enjoying at all the Otaku culture references in it, but the main gameplay loop is just incredibly shallow.
When I purchased this as a maid cafe game, I was expecting more depth in that “Maid Café” part—learning your regular’s preferences, learning new recipes and making up dishes with the maids, figuring out how to make different kinds of coffee and setting up collaborations with other shops. Sadly, none of that is present. Instead, you’re given a simple interface to select compatible maids for each shift day, press A when customers want to order and when they want to pay, and delivering dishes from the counter to them. There is no cooking mechanic for the protagonist (The button that says improve cooking merely gives a small boost to your kitchen staff). 
All maids are identical beyond appearance and numeric parameters for Waitressing/Cooking/Cleaning, with no niches or gimmicks that you may want to play around, and all the “dishes” are reduced to a different sprite, without any name, recipe, ingredient requirements, preferences or price. The coffee-making mechanic is incredibly underutilized, appearing only on 14 of the over 50 days of the game (You only get a chance to make each coffee exactly one time).
There is a boutique and a hair stylist in the game. The former exists only for story events and the latter is either bugged or is a small visual gag and nothing else, the maids and the protagonist’s appearance cannot be customized by the player in any way.
The cafe, too, cannot be personalized in any way, the furniture store besides your café will only grant you 2 tables across the first couple weeks of the game, with no other use after that, and the florist to the right of it exists only as part of the gift giving mechanic.
There is a gift-giving mechanic, but just like the rest of the game it is INCREDIBLY shallow; none of the maids have any preferences (Gifting a makeup set will give the same result to a Chunni Otaku and to a Gyaru) and they also don’t have any distinction between gifts and will react in the exact same way at being given a box of chocolates as if you give them a cleaning/cooking/service instruction manual.
For the dating mechanic, you can only go on dates with the maids on some specific days (the game main story has a tight schedule) and the phone that you use at the start of the game only exists to receive some messages during the story, there is no way to start a conversation or go on a date after the shift, and your protagonist (that again, you can’t customize in any way) doesn’t exhibit ANY personality beyond the first day of the game.
 Your cafe's popularity isn’t determined by your performance, but by a single button in the break room which can be used with the money destined to “cafe expenses” collected during each day (Which has no other uses than to press this button, there is no need to pay rent or purchase ingredients).
Some other reviews might suggest that this game could work as a visual novel, it could not. The main gameplay loop, as shallow as it might be, butts in every single day of the story of the game, being a mandatory

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio (with some lazy "wings" to fill the pillar).  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes Solitaire TED and PET might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Solitaire TED and PET has the farcical price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

Unfortunately, Hello Goodboy just wasn’t for me. However, the gameplay felt more like a children’s educational game—honestly, it reminded me of something like Dora the Explorer turned into a game. While the story itself is cute, it wasn’t what I was expecting. I love story-driven games like Florence, where the narrative is balanced with interesting, interactive gameplay elements, but Hello Goodboy was missing that spark.

Most of the game involved advancing the story by hitting the spacebar, with only a handful of simple puzzles sprinkled in. There are multiple endings, but I didn’t feel motivated to replay it and see them all. I think this could be a lovely game to play with a younger child, but for me, it just didn’t hit the mark.

I enjoyed Roman Wars, although I have to confess that it isn't quite what I expected. I had hoped to build a deck over time that evolved as I progressed through the missions (think System Crash or Cardpocalypse). However, more than anything, it reminded me of a single-player Dominion (the tabletop card game). 

There are ten scenarios, and you will be building your deck anew in each one from the same selection of cards. The choices that you'll make in terms of what to buy (and what order to buy it) will depend on the scenario that you are playing and the strategy that you've chosen. Therefore, the game felt to me more like a puzzle game, although there is certainly still a deck-building element.

The game is tricky, and I still don't know how I beat some of the missions (even using the bonus cards). Building up to 10 gold in that final mission was absolute brutality, but I guess that brutality is par for the course when it comes to ancient Roman combat. A quick tip: if you upgrade one of your structures and it is destroyed, you will draw and be able to play the [b]upgraded[/b] version after it cycles back through your deck. This can make upgrading structures a good investment.

I'll be the first to admit that I really do love this game; I've been around the community since it was first released into EA a few years ago. I've played it on and off in that time and have been able to accumulate a relatively good couple hundred hours. That being said however, I cannot recommend the game to anyone in it's current state. 

There are a few reasons for this, the first being that depending on your region, it is going to be rather difficult for you to get into matches. For for the moment, you are more likely to find more consistent matches without alot of waiting time on relatively few of the NA as well as few of the EU servers. This is can be attributed to the dwindling player count in the last year or so. The second reason is the near radio silence on the roadmap from the developers within the last year or so as well. This was mainly due to an ongoing legal battle between the developers and their publisher, from which I've heard has been somewhat resolved at this point. The third reason is the toxicity of the relatively small community within the last several months as well. The community forum have been a place where new ideas/concepts go to die, even recommendations which might not necessarily be implemented soon, but just open for discussions. I will say that the developers do have a discord that they attempt to shunt the playerbase too for most of their updates, but having those posted to their steam page are growing increasingly scarce. 

Overall, I would say to wait until the full release of the game. I'm really hoping that there are some fixes to the content, mechanics, movement, armor/gun balancing as well in this full release too in addition to some better moderation of their community forums. If you want to pick it up and try it out, be my guest, but know that it is currently in an unfinished state and that the player numbers are dwindled to the point where they are rarely topping 100 players on the weekends. I would love to see this game kick off again, but for the time being, it's just not for me.

This is not a recommend/don't recommend as much as a 'i don't know how i feel about it'. It's not a bad game, it's not poorly written, it has enjoyable moments, but i found myself rather frustrated and conflicted with a lot of things as i was playing it. So let us go over some of them.

Matchmaking ROs with other npcs. This has always been a heated topic of debate, some like it some don't. I do not enjoy it, and while i normally wouldn't bring this up as it's ultimately a matter of preferences, one specific match made me side eye this game. Ryan, if not romanced, can get with Heather, MC's rival. Now it wouldn't be all that weird, if the game didn't point out that Heather is basically MC's copy, in body type, in skintone, in hair, in eyes, 'could pass as mc's doppelganger' as the game puts it. Even more comical is one of MC's dialogue options being 'they look good together'... which i genuinely am not sure how to interpret? like girl wdum they look good together she has YOUR face. It's honestly a questionable match all around that i'd laugh at if it wasn't so sad.

And now for the romance itself. 
	The way the game is structured makes it so one RO starts with a massive advantage over the other two. Because the Devil is constantly around MC to help her and tempt her into giving away more of that precious precious soul, he gets the most screentime and relationship development. He's the one to support MC, he's the one to tempt MC, he's the one who'll try to get to know MC and understand her better, he's the one to witness MC's moments of brilliance and failure.
	On the other side Ryan and Cris barely have any screen time in the 1st half (with maybe one appearance per chapter). All of these scenes i found to be on the lackluster side, with them exchanging a couple of sentences with mc then in a 'duty calls' fashion going on their merry way to do their own thing. Realistic? Sure. But in the context of a romance game it doesn't make them particularly intriguing, and having to hit on them once per chapter for crumbs of possible reciprocity is hardly riveting romance content. For fairness' sake i will say that towards the 2nd half of the game if you choose to pursue them, they very much become the focus of the show while the devil takes the farthest backseat possible with only the occasional mention so that you don't entirely forget about the crushing promise of eternal suffering in hell. 

I say all this, because playing the game for the first time i found myself questioning Ryan and the whole election plotline in general. I did not understand his inclusion as a RO. I thought the election was out of place and yet another manifestation of CoG's undying love for rebellion/revolution/government overthrowal plots. Hell i barely saw him in my game, it really felt like he came to shake mc's hand twice to ask her to vote for him and that was the extent of his screen time. I swear a Temu commercial i was unlucky enough to see once was more memorable than that. 
	Furthermore, i did not understand why he, a 'rising politician from a fabulously wealthy family and movie-star good looks', would be interested in our random passerby MC. For comparison let's take Pirate's Pleasure, the author's previous IF: MC was from the get an established pirate with her own ship, crew, reputation and i could see why the governor would take interest in her, recruit her and subsequently try to wife her up. But what reason does Ryan have? MC is a nobody at the moment of their meeting, and remains basically a nobody for the majority of the book (not counting the whole 'is an aspiring Broadway star'.. because who isn't). I wish more text was invested in laying some groundwork for his romance otherwise it really feels like MC is just strongarmed into volunteering for his campaign for a chance of romancing him. 
	His selling point is that he's this good dude with superman looks (and the game does not miss one opportunity to mention how much of a white knight and prince charming he is every single time he is brought up in the text, which.. i got it the first time you needn't beat me over the head with it), but we barely get to know him in the mandatory scenes that he does have before being yeeted into the ether. Now, his actual romance route, should one choose to pursue it, is decent enough, very sweet and cheesy. Although for all that talk of knightly courtship, i don't think the game quite managed to deliver and amusingly, for most of the story it still felt like some kind of long con to win mc's vote/public support.

Cris, as mentioned previously, suffers from the same issue. Thought his status as a romance option and presence in the story i at least found believable. He's MC's neighbor, they sometimes cross paths and talk, unless you don't romance him in which case they stop crossing paths and he disappears never to be seen again except for the few moments game deems it important to reminds you he's now hooking up with your roommate. 

Davin the devil, to the surprise of nobody, was my favorite RO. As i said, because of how much time mc spends with him and how many interactions they have, even if i started as a hater i ended up liking him the most.
	Now, Davin's romance also made me wonder why he of all people would become invested in MC. Unromanced, Davin will show interest in the librarian npc, a man knowledgeable and powerful in his own right who can easily handle Davin's devilish nature and be his equal. Mc in contrast is just the usual naive mortal who has no idea what she's dealing with. Well the answer we get from the devilman himself is that mc's willpower is so strong that even he cannot help but be in awe of it... A dubious claim, strong 'she's not like other girls' vibes, but unsatisfactory as i found it at the very least some explanation was given.
	Of the positives, i was pleasantly surprised to find out that even with a low %rel stat, after refusing all of his offers, i was still able to successfully romance him and achieve a happy ending (though with how many people said they had trouble getting Davin's romance i wonder if i just lucked out or really am that much of a smooth operator lol). There was a sense of freedom of choice to his route that i didn't get with the other ROs, where i felt like i had to agree with them or pick specific behaviors to get anywhere (mind you i didn't codedive idk how true that actually is code-wise, there was just this *vibe*). And while i won't gush much over his romance, i did genuinely find the writing of it to be lovely.
	Of the not so positive, i found the conflict in his route to not be much of a conflict. He says he can't be with mc only to almost kiss mc in the next scene and fully succumb to his feeling in the following one and bam now they're together forever. There was so much potential for angst and drama that ultimately just went nowhere. Guess they can't all be Adam from twc. Another letdown was the branch where you give your devil away to another willing soul, which i expected would lead to a dramatic ending more so if you're romancing Davin.. but no, nothing came of it. One sentence about how he now doesn't talk to mc and that was that. Rather anticlimactic, that whole affair. 

Ultimately, im giving this a thumbs up because i do think that this IF has better written romance than a lot of HC entries of late, i just wish the author went a bit deeper with it because the potential is very much here.

Have you wanted to be a top musical star or actress on Broadway, or date the devil? Any and all of your wishes can come true after a magic spell goes wrong and you find yourself with your own personal sexy demon who is here to do your bidding. For a price, which is your soul. You can go along with him to overcome obstacles and vanquish rivals, or steadfastly refuse to join in the deadly game, or have romantic liaisions with people you meet on the block you live in in 90s New York. You can help save the area being overcome with dot.coms, or be foremost among those who want to gentrify the slum where you live, turning out the many vibrant characters that give the Village such character. The choice is yours. Then there is the small matter of your soul, and the choice is still yours when you meet people who can help.
This IF game has plenty of choices, some fabulous characters to meet, and recreates a small part of 90s New York so well you can almost smell and taste it as you play. Given the amount of choices you have, there are many different endings which allows for plenty of play throughs if you like finding all the endings, and there are achievements to earn too! Do you want to be tempted? And how much would you give to vanquish your enemies and achieve the success you were born to have? There is only one way to find out. IF games give you the best value for money because there are always so many choices, and so many "what ifs?".

After seeing the player guiding an arrow in the trailer, I was interested in trying this indie action game from developer Enoops. I'd never played anything else from this studio, but the guided arrow reminded me of a combination of the Slayer rocket from Perfect Dark (on the Nintendo 64) and the bullet-following camera after shooting a shot with the sniper rifle in either Sniper Elite or Max Payne.

Although the mechanic itself was somewhat enjoyable, everything around it was pretty uninspired. The encounters were repetitive and often involved killing zombies that were simply standing still and presenting no threat. Making matters worse is that your character "resets" to a position where he is aiming slightly to the right. Therefore, you will always need to either move the cursor to the left prior to shooting or immediately after releasing an arrow.

There was one encounter in the game that was actually quite difficult, but only because you'll need to memorize the order in which you need to dispatch enemies to cover your scavenging partner. Some of the enemies move faster than you'd expect, and others don't move at all despite their proximity to your partner.

Unfortunately, I can't recommend The Story of Archer. Guiding the arrow is a neat enough mechanic, but what surrounds it needs a bit more substance.

Serious Sam: Siberian Mayhem is a standalone but from the gameplay perspective an add-on to Serious Sam 4. It has a new story, new enemies new weapons and new special-items. Additionally it has some survival Levels. For me a must play for every Serious Sam fan. The game runs fine and was for about 8 hours pure fun.

I have been a Serious Sam fan since the beginning. When I say from the beginning I mean literally from the beginning. My cousin got a copy of Serious Sam: The First Encounter and me and him played it Co-Op on a 56k Dial-up. Never got to play The Second Encounter until some 15 years later. I played through the series HD Editions and loved almost every second of it. Hated the jump pads of Second Encounter but grew to love them because the give and take of the flow of combat remained the same.

What I witnessed playing this game is a butchery of Serious Sam to a degree. When I played SS3 and there was soooooo much hate for it I didn’t understand. SS3 is great. It's a nice combination of linear push & pull spawns Vs. overwhelming the player to the point where it's not exhausting....When SS4 came out I realized there was a certain art to Serious Sam games. When I say there was "A Certain Art," what I mean is the developers had a knack for using the spawn system to essentially create a "Push & Pull," between the user and the game. It was very linear but at the same time every time you started to feel you were pushing forward the spawns would double or amp up and become more creative which would force you back another 100 Ft. It never felt unfair...or like the game was overwhelming you because you had ALL the firepower to overcome it. The gadget mechanic is fine but it feels like it’s the modern SS games over rely on them. 

I want to like Serious Sam 4 & Siberian Mayhem but I cannot. I am going to give the modern Serious Sam & Siberian Mayhem a thumbs up because they are still super fun to play Co-Op but it feels like that is strictly how they are balanced. Playing them solo on Serious went from being manageable to completely absurd and un-fun with Serious Sam 4 and Siberian Mayhem UNLESS you use gadgets, which is fine but when so many of the large scales rely on you using those gadgets it starts to lose its identity. 

Co-Op is still amazing without gagets.... I had as much fun as I did some years ago on a dial up connection. It's so much funner with someone else. It's almost like the game was designed with Co-Op in mind.

I love Serious Sam 4 and Siberian Mayhem as a Co-Op experience but solo it really stunk. Find a balance like the classic Serious Sam games and stop focusing on completely overwhelming the player and find a fun combination of pushing the player back than allowing them to push forward, then pushing them back again. Something has been lost on this franchise and I'm not sure if it will ever be regained but I truly hope it will because there is definitely a market for a game that has the kind of gameplay as SS1 &2 had.
