The game is buggy and missing tooltips.  The gameplay is extremely RNG heavy and unbalanced making the game unplayable without giving you a clue what you might be doing wrong or how to fix it.

The game appears to give you a massive amount of space to build in but the vast majority of that space actually can't be built on.

1) First of all, the energy system is very annoying.  You have to wait for energy for everything and the fast forward doesn't work.  This makes trying to figure out the extremely poorly documented features an exercise in frustration because the buildings aren't expensive but require energy which discourages exploration.

2) If you try to fast forward the game will randomly pause instead.  Fast forward is extremally buggy and will randomly change speeds from no fast forward, to a bit faster, to extremely fast if you're lucky (except if you're on an adventure at which point it makes the adventure unplayable).

3) There are very few tool tips.  The customers show an icon showing what you need to stock but there are multiple items with the same icon so it's of limited help.  The stats don't give you a clue what they're supposed to do.

4) Everything is super RNG.  Want to get your party going?  Better hope that you can get more then two elements used.  Want to cook food for your guests?  Better hope that the ingredients show up.  Want to sell food to your guests?  Better hope that you can hire workers.

5) Building explanations are non existent.  Why would I want a Shared Room or Private Room (or any room for that matter)?  Why would I want a hall, seated hall, or large hall?  Do any of these rooms improve energy regen?  Give more gold?  This wouldn't be nearly as bad if the buildings only took gold so I could try building them and scrapping them if I don't like them but they require energy which appears to only regen in real time and the fast forward doesn't work correctly.

6) Adventures are forced to end prematurely wasting all the energy and gold spent to go on them because there are no matches on the board.  There is no auto reset of the board or warning that you're out of matches and you're out of luck.  You have to manually check every possible option before abandoning the adventure and wasting the energy which is real time.

7) Fast forward does impact the Adventures as it vastly speeds up the opponent's action bar and there's not way to turn it off while on the adventure so more wasted Energy and gold.   You can see the animations go super fast.  I don't think it's consistent but I only ever had the energy to do a few adventures so I don't know for sure.

8) What do stats do?  Body seems to increase HP but what about Soul and Mind?  Once again missing hover text and explanations.

9) Stat training is a very stupid thing to do.  You end up facing mobs with more HP then you have and attacks that do 22 damage vs your 1 or 2 damage.  This is the point that I quit playing.  I increased body, mind, and soul and nothing increased my damage.  This could be a bug in the hover text but I didn't stick around to check.

10) The shopping interface is awful.  The ingredients are random but they don't show you how many you have or how many you need for current orders.  Instead of having a nice clean interface with how many you have, how many you need for the queued jobs, and what you can buy they have a multi tab inventory with what you have in stock and the jobs on a separate screen.  In order to see what you have in stock and what you can purchase you have to scroll through both long lists and make sure you check the correct tabs for your inventory.  The inventory is in alphabetical order while the list of items you can buy are not which adds to the frustration every time you go to stock your inn.

11) The game doesn't give you a clue how much you need for wages and doesn't allow you to reserve gold.  This leads to situations were you miss calculated how much you needed and were short so the game randomly fires people and doesn't tell you.  You then need to figure out who was fired and how to recover.  If all your workers were fired and the RNG doesn't give you the option to hire more workers this round you need to fire everyone and wait for the buggy fast forward to move you to a new day where hopefully the RNG will start to let you rebuild from the accident.  This is not a fun mechanic.

This is a game that's easy to get a lot of hours on because you need to leave it running in the background to get anywhere due to the broken fast forward, energy system, and RNG.  I tried to give it a fair chance and I regret purchasing it as the game quickly gets to be unplayable if you experiment and the energy system is horrible. Despite a very interesting concept, this is simply a terrible game.  You take the role as a Record Label(At least, I think you do.  You're not given the option to name it or many of the functions associated with being a record label, but you do manage bands.  Kind of.)  The problem is, nothing really seems to work as you might expect it to.

When you start a new game, you're instructed to "Scout" for a new band to sign.  Then you're forced to wait a number of weeks for the scouting results to come in.  You're presented with 3 band options, each with 4 members.  Each member of each band has a skill rating ranging from 0-100 and a future potential rating using the same scale.  Naturally, you'd like to compare the stats of one band versus another.  You can, but in the most aggravating way possible.  To see a band member's stats, you have to flip their display picture over.  But you can only flip over the display pictures of one band at a time.  So instead of being able to conveniently shift your eyes from one band to another, you have to repeatedly flip one band's pictures over, hope you memorize their stats and then do the same to the 2nd band.  Lather, rinse, repeat.  Quality of life is for losers, apparently.

Whatever, you pick a band and you sign it to your label.  They start out costing you $0 per month, somehow.  So now what?  Each band will have 2 songs already written and you can choose to have your band "Plan Album", "Plan Show" or train their skills.  Every action costs a minimum of 70 energy(your energy is capped at 100.)  Playing shows increases your bands reputation and fan-count, but also immediately causes your band to cost more per month.  Planning an album can be used to compile already written songs(that part is important) and make some steady income, but there is NO WAY TO MAKE YOUR BAND WRITE SONGS.  Seriously, I played this game for ~20 in-game years and the 2 bands I managed wrote a total of 6 songs via random events.  And even when you do manage to release a 1 song "album"(with that snail's pace of songwriting, that's all you'll ever manage), the game doesn't track past performances at all.  There's no monthly charts.  No competing bands in the world.  Nothing you'd expect from a management game.

So I got bored of sending my band to random gigs around the world and noticed I could try to recruit individual band members to replace the mediocre drummer.  I found a new drummer with a 70-90 potential.  When I went to hire him, I had $294k in the bank, it said it would cost $3500 to hire the drummer and $4700 to fire the old drummer, but the "Confirm Change" button was grayed out.  No explanation was given.  Competent games would suggest that band morale or chemistry wouldn't allow it, but those traits don't exist in this game.  So I'm forced to "Reject Candidate" on the obvious upgrade and move on.

And I moved on by uninstalling the game.  The mechanics are broken.  The gameplay loop is nonexistent.  The user interface is awful.  Even for $2, this isn't a game worth your time.

Good concept but there just....isn't that much there, and it progresses too fast yet also way too slowly at the same time.

I had the same band for 5 years and they only made 5 songs, but I could have a gig in Australia for tens of thousands of people. And there are MONTHS where you do nothing but press E (next week). When you initially sign a band, it shows you a skill bracket that they can max out at (up to 99 I think), but that disappears once you've signed them. So if you want to replace a band member, you can't compare them unless you can remember the skill bracket (which once you have more than one band, is really difficult). I also couldn't find any way to replace a front man and I had issues with a few of them. And there isn't a tour function, just singular gigs (or at least it didn't come up for me).

I also found it weirdly hard to find the information I was looking for because of the UI set up and how loud most of the graphics and fonts are. Like, you can only view member info by clicking to flip their "info cards", so you have to click each member before practice to see how much they increased their quality. Same for the signing of bands, you can't compare all members of each band against each other, just see one band's members at a time.

So yeah. I just wish there was more to it. If you want a game you can complete in a couple of hours max, this is it. Don't expect much more unfortunately.

[b]daydream mosaics[/b] is essentially [b]jewel match nonograms[/b]. hardly surprising, as they share a developer responsible for some stuff there and pretty much everything here. and they're very much commendable for [b]adding a new game mode upon request[/b] (even if it took a year) to make things work like in a proper nonogram, and not only providing it for the latest 3rd entry, but patching it into the first two games as well.

there are [b]108 levels[/b] divided into 3 chapters, levels are unlocked one by one, [b]going up to 25x25[/b] (or thereabouts, nothing bigger than that), each with multiple colors. solving a layer or even just a few lines might help with another one, so make sure to switch around if you can.

it looks like all those style over substance efforts with no basic functionality, but even in its initial form this was better, as [b]it has mid-level saving[/b]. and of course [b]numbers get crossed off one by one (sometimes, see below), the timer only appears on the level complete screen and no guessing is necessary[/b] after a patch fixing a few iffy levels, though [b]there are power-ups (sometimes)[/b] to help you out if you want, hidden under random cells. [b]no way to reset/restart just one color though, only the full level.[/b]

so there are [b]4 game modes[/b] now. in [u]relaxed[/u] mistakes are checked and revealed but no level reset after a few, [u]normal[/u] is the same but the level fails after 3-5 mistakes, and [u]advanced[/u] is again the same but highlighting a bunch of cells doesn't stop after the first mistakes, so make a few in one selection and you're toast, plus in this mode numbers only get crossed off when the entire line is solved. [u]freestyle[/u] would be the bee's knees, with [b]no mistake counter/highlighter and no power-ups or hints[/b], but unfortunately [b]clues don't fade out one by one here, as they should[/b].

[b]controls are abysmal as well.[/b] left click to color a cell, right click to mark it, right click also clears cells in freestyle mode. it should be left to color/remove color, right to mark/remove mark, and maybe the current one as an alternative method. dragging the mouse over multiple cells brings up a cell counter, always handy, except [b]marked cells are overwritten if you drag the mouse over them[/b], big fucking no. it doesn't work like that with other colors, so dragging a white line won't interfere with yellow or whatever, 'only' within the same color. and if you start dragging with left click and leave the current line, the whole selection gets canceled, while doing it with right click marks cells all over the place like a drawing tool.

the overall presentation is very jewel matchy, [b]crystals collected on levels unlock cosmetic sanctuary upgrades[/b], the local equivalent of castles. settings, also while playing a level, are separate volume sliders (music is nice but very repetitive), different looks for tiles, a help screen explaining the basics (literally the first word is 'guess' in a game involving no guessing), a windowed mode toggle with a smaller, non-resizable window, custom cursor and the really useful 'mask revealed pieces' toggle. basically, it hides solved layers, so they won't interfere with figuring out the current one. with up to 6 colors things can get messy, though there's also a 'colored number background' toggle. the unskippable dev logo after the loading screen wasn't a good idea and [b]the divider after every 5th cell is barely visible when they are filled[/b].

there are better (and worse) values for money, but even after all the extra effort, [b]sadly, it's not something to recommend[/b]. most players should be fine with what's on offer here if they enjoy all the other subpar efforts for some reason, and as I said, [b]with mid-level saving it's still better than about 96% of nonograms on the market[/b]. something like [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1207310/]the gizmos series[/url], close but no cigar.

I had beaten Blue Fire a while back and saw this new expansion that was also a stand alone game, and I have to say, at the low low price of FREE, you just won't find a 3D platformer of this caliber anywhere. 

I could go on about the actual Blue Fire game, but let me just speak about the stand alone Void Maker game, since that’s why you’re here. Sit back and settle in, this one meets the word count for that 6th grade English final. 


PROS:

The character movement. Controlling the character just feels fun. It feels as good as if Super Meat Boy finally got made into a good 3D platformer. Quick, snappy, very responsive, and easy to control the character with a high skill ceiling but easy to pick up intuitively. Genuinely the best 3D platformer character-controller I’ve seen from an indie developer. Hat in Time feels sluggish and uninspired compared to this. Void Maker can stand on its own separate from the main game with no story or progression due to this movement, it feels that good. 

A very in depth level creator that I admittedly have not sunk my teeth into as much as I should, though it is extensive and very powerful. Like Mario Maker but 3D and very expansive. It is a straight up way to practice 3D level design on the scale of nearly making your own game in a user friendly way. It has the ability to create levels with even metroidvania style elements, where as you progress you unlock the various movement mechanics and unlock the next challenge. Or just start with everything and fly through the pure platforming challenges. I’ve dabbled with it and it definitely seems like it will let you create nearly exactly what you want, and anything not in the game yet has the potential to be added due to the….

Developers support and engage with their player base. There is an active discord that you can join from the home screen. The community is small right now from what I’ve seen but definitely has the room for competition.

It looks good. This is a personal preference but the game looks great. It’s no AAA Unreal 5 rendered game, but it has a simple beauty that also clearly conveys through color and art the information the player needs to intuit the meaning of unknown objects. Big red spikey thing? Prob gunna kill me.

The music is great. Again, preference here, but it has a calming atmospheric lost-soul sort of vibe to it. Makes me feel nostalgic, which I like when I’m playing a modern old school 3D platformer 

User generated content. I keep coming back daily and finding new levels to play. Not all are the best, just like with Mario Maker, but honestly there are some gems. And beating a level with .45% completion rate and getting a world record is SATISFYING. 

The devs are still supporting it. The last update listed on their Discord was 5 days ago. They are committed to this and I don’t see this passionate team stopping until this expansion is as polished as can be. 


CONS:

The current menus for the Browsing Levels in the game are very bare bones and a bit buggy. I have gotten a few records that did not show the next time I logged in on the stages I got the records on. 

There is no Personal Stat screen or character screen. Skins to unlock or customization, or even just a personal page that tells you stats like all deaths and all the levels you’ve cleared would be great. Like in Halo, everyone loves their Service Record. 

The community is small. There are not, at the time of writing, too many content creators for the game. Both creating content like on YouTube and creating Maps. There are a handful of very good level designers though. I personally have not found the content list to be small enough to complain though it could be an issue if you get super addicted.

Unless you’ve played Blue Fire and memorized the icons, you won’t know what powers you are starting a level with. Currently, how this is shown is by listing the icons of the items that grant movement abilities, and highlighting the ones that active. This doesn’t convey to you what they do unless you already know their meaning. That being said, 7 seconds of pressing buttons fixes that. Still this could be fixed with the next point… 

No tutorial level. This is a free game, not every player will have an understanding of how Blue Fire works as many are coming here to try out BF before buying the main game. I personally would not have thought that my third jump came from holding and charging the Attack button to get a spin attack in air, but it is vital to know this for several of the player made levels. 


This is clearly an early version of the Void Maker game but my god is it so worth your time. It is one of the only games I can pick up and just spend 10 minutes trying a level or 3 hours playing on accident. The actual game is smooth and mostly bug free. The user interface outside of the game play could use some polish but I would be shocked if any of my concerns are even valid in a few months with how fast they are updating and patching the game. 

I love indie games, and this one takes the cake as the most fun free one I’ve played on Steam. It’s criminal that it is not more widely known.

This is one of the laziest executions on what could've potentially been one of the coolest UGC platformers. Blue Fire is an amazing game and when I first heard about it I was told there was a level creator, which is technically true, but it's a completely separate game. I don't think making this a free spin-off that has to be a separate download did it any favours on any front, considering that the paid full game has WAY more reviews. Not to mention that this being a separate executable means that any changes made to the core has to be manually updated for both titles, and I don't even need to make that a hypothetical. You can't even set your Windowed resolution here, whereas you can in the main game. Considering they made this a separate game, you'd think they go the extra mile to trim down some of the RPG aspects of the game and de-clutter the existing menus? Nope, you still get to see an inventory menu with hundreds of empty slots, a useless progression menu that shows all the Quests and Voids in the real game, and the start pause menu being the same without necessary functions like a restart button where the REAL pause menu you're supposed to press is on Select instead of Start. I am not much of an artist so I have not tried the actual tools yet, so I cannot comment on the state of that, but some of the levels I tried were pretty good. Unfortunately, the discovery is pretty bad so it's hard to find good levels that capture the essence of the original game. You can only view random(?) highlights, newest, and top levels. The majority of the top levels are either tech-focused challenge levels or super casual levels that don't give you all the items, so anyone trying out random Voids to see if they want to buy Blue Fire won't get a good impression of the great mechanics of the game. The overall package is a fumble, but you can have fun with it if you dig really deep.

It was only after I had written on another review that VS was among the games where I had gotten every achievement that I got back and realized that wasn't true. Adding new achievements with updates should be punishable by law. It was also then when I realized that I had not written a review for it either, which felt weird, considering I enjoy writing reviews for games I spend a lot of time with and it is also the OG game that got me (and probably most other people) into the survivors' genre. Now I've FINALLY gotten all the achievements (again) and, writing this review, I also end not having put down into words my opinion about it.

As I've mentioned, I've written reviews for other survivors games but had not done so until now for this one. This means that my opinions now has been shaped by my experience with those other games in the genre and could've been different in retrospective. That's why I want to begin then with what I'm positive hasn't changed; 

Vampire Survivors is a very enjoyable game. 

It is simple, it is fun and it cuts to the chase. The premise is quite simple, you kill mobs, you gain experience and level up, you choose a weapon, you choose an object that lets you evolve your weapon and you rinse and repeat a thousand times with very small deviations over several maps and runs until you become a walking god that decimates everything you set your eyes on. A power trip can totally be the reason you should be playing this game.

It might sound boring and, while feeling a tad repetitive from time to time -hence why I've gone back and forth with several games in the genre over the span of several hundred hours-, some of us get a surprisingly rewarding experience out of it.
The best comparison I can come up with is that you could think of it as an idle incremental game that isn't entirely idle.

Now, I do NOT believe Vampire Survivors is the best in the genre. It does not have the most elaborated graphics, the best looking maps, the most enjoyable sound design or the most ingenious mechanics. Some of its competitors do those things better or even shine in some of those aspects. But it is true that Vampire Survivors shows charm, respects the player, has some fine humour built in and for the ridiculous price it is commonly sold for should absolutely be recommended. 

I remember reading that poncle, the creator, used to be a programmer for online gambling houses and decided to use his knowledge about quick gratification for better uses thsn separating people from their money. The fact that he has studied how much and how often the player/user should be rewarded with a dopamine hit might be enough of a selling point. 

To summarize, this is a game that if it clicks for you you'll have content for days and for a very nice pricetag. It is the OG and it is a very decent game, so adding that to everything that I've mentioned explains why it should be treated and respected as such.

Vampire Survivors is fun for the first 15 minutes of gameplay per run. After that, it's just brainlessly standing around, looking at an epileptic drone strike hitting your eyes as you proceed to play the dullest version of dodgeball I've ever seen—to the point where it feels like getting hit in the face by an actual scrotum would be a more fun version of dodgeball.

If they capped this game at around 15–20 minutes per run, it would have been a great semi-idle game to play while chilling. However, because of the longer duration, it just goes stale, even in "Adventures" mode.

Overall, it's fun for a bit and worth having a look at but not something I'd recommend in the long run for more than a couple of hours as a passing fancy.

Vampire Survivors: A Perfect Blend of Mindless Fun and Strategic Depth

Vampire Survivors has quickly become a breakout hit, and for good reason.  Its simple premise – survive hordes of increasingly powerful enemies – belies a surprisingly deep and engaging gameplay loop. What truly sets Vampire Survivors apart, in my opinion, is its brilliant scaling of difficulty and the fascinating duality it creates between luck and skill.

On the surface, the game seems incredibly accessible.  You can easily pick it up, choose a character, and let the auto-firing weapons do their work.  Early runs often feel like a breeze, a satisfying power fantasy as you mow down waves of bats and skeletons.  This makes it perfect for those times when you just want to unwind and switch off your brain.  You can lean back, let the game play itself to a certain extent, and enjoy the satisfying visual spectacle of the ever-increasing chaos.  Luck plays a significant role here; a fortunate early weapon or item drop can drastically alter the course of a run, leading to unexpected and exhilarating victories.

However, beneath this veneer of mindless fun lies a surprising amount of strategic depth.  As you progress, the difficulty ramps up significantly.  Simply relying on luck will no longer cut it.  This is where the true brilliance of Vampire Survivors shines.  You're forced to start thinking strategically about your build.  Which weapon complements another, creating a devastating synergy?  Which passive items complement your preferred style of play?  Do you focus on area-of-effect damage, single-target DPS, or a combination of both?  Suddenly, every level up becomes a crucial decision.  You're weighing the pros and cons of each option, carefully planning your build to maximize your chances of survival.

This blend of luck and skill is what makes Vampire Survivors so addictive.  Even when you have a seemingly perfect build, a string of bad luck can still lead to a crushing defeat.  But conversely, even with a less-than-ideal start, skillful play and smart decision-making can turn the tide of battle.  It's a constant push and pull, a dance between chance and strategy that keeps you coming back for more.

Whether you're looking for a game to play while listening to a podcast or a challenging experience that demands careful planning, Vampire Survivors has something to offer. It's a testament to clever game design that such a simple concept can offer so much replayability and depth. Highly recommended!

This game is just wow. It's a great way to experience all the games from the classic Sonic era. The challenges are fun and it's nice that you can choose between an anniversary mode and a "classic" mode. I'll explain why the brackets later. 
The story mode also adds opening and ending animated cutscenes that tie the story nicely. You can also play other characters that weren't in the games originally (Tails in Sonic 1 and Sonic CD, etc.) You can also play as Amy, but she'll cost you 10 bucks, as well as Knuckles in CD, as both are locked behind the Plus upgrade.
There are some issues tho. First off the physic engine is not the same as the actual classic games as these are a port. This leads to some parts of the game not running as smoothly as they were intended to. Also the soundtrack from Sonic 3 & Knuckles was changed (likely due to copyright issues with the Micheal Jackson company. You can mod the game to add the original soundtrack back, tho) and the prototype OST was used, however the audio quality feels lower and more compressed compared to the other 3 games.
Coming to the classic mode, the main issue with is that they're not the actual classic games from the Megadrive, but rather a cropped version of the anniversary mode with the lives system added back (since they've been replaced by the coin system in anniversary mode, an in-game value that allows you to retry special stages or buy items from the museum, and you got infinite lives). Therefore the physic remains the same as well as all the issues it brings. 
The mirror mode is nice as well as the boss rush.
Another complaint I have is that the character selection screen could have been better, you're given the choice of selecting a character and a few teams (Sonic and Tails and Tails with Amy or Knuckles), having the ability to simply choose if you wanted to play solo or duo and make you choose WHO you want your duo to be formed by (like Knuckles and Amy for example) would have been much better. 
Also SEGA, removing the original classic games from Steam to force people into buying this collection was a scummy move.

All and all, I still think this is the best possible way to experience the original classics, and apart from some flaws (nitpicks or majors) this is a very enjoyable game. Anyone looking for a good side-scrolling platform should buy this.

Also for the love of God SEGA, please release a Knuckles' Chaotix remastered for PC. I don't even care if you do as a separate game from Origins, just give us the chance of playing it.

The rest of this review will just be about the Gamegear games I care about. It's really the only reason I wanted to buy Origins. The ones I don't mention are either very uninteresting or just bad. What I can say overall about them is that it sucks that we didn't get the SMS versions of Sonic 1, 2 and Chaos. Sonic 1 8-Bit I'd say is a pretty good game. It's not designed like the Genesis games though, instead being a more standard platformer with straight-forward levels instead of ones with multiple routes to explore. Jungle Zone may be a little frustrating if you can't do precise platforming and Sky Base honestly hurts my eyes with its seizure inducing-lightning. I would also say it has the best soundtrack out of the 8-Bit games with it containing more bouncy and catchy melodies. 

Sonic 2 8-Bit has not aged well. It has some good though still linear gameplay but quickly devolves to unfair old-gamey level design, especially with all of the tubes unfairly punishing you and making the levels confusing. I also personally don't like the music as much with this one. I'd say skip it once you start experiencing too much frustration.

Sonic Chaos is an alright game. Finally is the level design trying to be like the Genesis titles with multiple routes to explore and goodies to find. My biggest issue with the game though is that the levels are tiny. They usually span 20 to 50 seconds, and I was even able to get through Mecha Green Hill act 1, ( The fourth zone by the way ) in only 17 seconds! This is also where they try to mimic the physics of the Genesis games with scripted slope going up walls segments. It's a nice attempt I'd say but pails in comparison to the real thing. I should also mention that this game is abnormally laggy compared to the other games for seemingly no reason. It doesn't make the game sluggish but instead just overall slower paced. The soundtrack is good with a few great tracks and some average ones ( I wish this was the SMS version because I much prefer its Gigalopolis theme ;( )

Sonic Triple Trouble is actually a GREAT game, getting close to being as good as the main Genesis games. It's still 8-Bit but the level design here is much bigger and longer than Chaos', the attempts to mimic the physics are more prevalent and much cooler and the sprite-work is very impressive for the hardware. It also even has zone transitioning cutscenes like how Sonic 3&K has. The music is also really good though I'd say not as catchy as Sonic 1. I have nothing bad to say about it, don't overlook this one!

Sonic Blast is... not bad just because of the visuals. It looks horrendous yes, but the controls also might make this one of or if not the WORST controlling Sonic game. It feels like you're permanently on ice/Luigi physics and your air control is very sluggish. If you didn't have a double jump ability then it'd legit be unplayable honestly. The level design of the game is also a massive step back, being linear again and very simple with it not even having a lot of platforming. Blue Marine is especially infamous for its insane pipe usage that basically requires you to have a map of the acts open if you don't want to prolong your suffering. The ONE good thing that I can say about this game is that the music is really good and quite memorable actually.

You're meant to spindash around the place which can quickly lead to chaos due to how fast you actually can go. [h1]A flawed but enjoyable collection of classic games[/h1]
Sonic 1, 2, 3 and CD are some of my favourite classic 2D side scrollers of all time, and are still just as fun to play today as they were on release.

Sonic 1 is more basic and slower compared to their sequels, but has plenty of platforming and secrets that make each playthrough unique no matter how many times you play through it. The game is simple enough for anyone to pick up and play while having enough mechanical depth for experienced players to figure out new ways to experience the game every time, setting a strong foundation that would only get better with the sequels.

Sonic CD is my least favourite of the games in this collection, but still a fun experience throughout. Focusing more on exploration, this game features time travel to the past and future. Destroying the robot generators in the past creates a Good Future that is free from Eggman's influence, otherwise the Bad Future is one where Eggman takes over Little Planet. The level design can get very sloppy, and this game is a great showcase of how pathetically easy and anti-climatic the final boss is when you're given rings for it.

Sonic 2 remains a timeless classic that takes everything good about the first game and made it even better, while ironing out the original's flaws. This game laid the foundation for level design in the series, with higher routes being faster but harder to stay on, with the lower routes being slower and the penalty for making mistakes. Levels are much faster, the spin dash was added, and the finale is quite tough especially for first time players which makes finishing it all the more satisfying.

Sonic 3 & Knuckles is one of the greatest side-scrollers ever created, so much so the original release needed two separate cartridges locked-onto each other for the originally intended experience, combining one epic adventure from both games. New abilities, elemental shields, bonus stages and the largest zone count of these games make this the longest game to play through. But it's worth it for the immense sense of speed, amazing soundtrack and epic climax that wraps up the series perfectly.

Sonic 1, 2 and CD are mostly based on their mobile remasters that added widescreen, with lives being replaced with a new Coin system which can be exchanged in the museum for various extras such as remixed music from other games in the series (loved the inclusion of the Generations remixes), bonus illustrations and bonus videos. One coin can also be spent to retry special stages if you fail them. The spike pit in Mystic Cave takes you to Hidden palace Zone instead, a cut zone from the original release. Tails & Knuckles are now playable in Sonic 1 with their signature abilities.

These games still hold up today and are well worth playing. However, this remastered collection has some baffling design decisions that hold this back from being as good as it could've been. Previous releases of Sonic 1, including the 3DS and mobile versions, had a Spin Dash toggle to allow you to play with it off to match the original Mega Drive version, or on to match the sequels. You can't turn this or the newly added drop dash off in this version; even playing Sonic 1 in Classic mode forces you to play with this ability enabled. While good additions, they should've been optional or disabled by default in Classic mode.

The only way you can play with the original lives system in this collection is to play in the 4/3 aspect ratio even though 1, 2 and CD on mobile had widescreen and the original lives system. The mobile versions of Sonic 1 & 2 also had a level select that allowed you to replay any level you want after beating the game when this version removed this feature. Sure, you can use the Time Attack and Ranking mode to replay any level you want, but your emeralds don't carry over so you can't replay levels in super form.

Sonic CD has some weird quirks of its own that make this part of the package feel less polished. Both the US and JP OSTs are present though it defaults to the US version and you have to switch it manually from the in-game menu instead of the options. Menu options for the spin dash toggle and the OST selection take you to the 2011 menu and is not consistent with the rest of the game's presentation.

If you're replaying special stages for Time Attack to unlock hidden extras, you can't exit out of them from the pause menu. If you mess up, you have to complete the stage to give it another try when every other version let you quit to the stage select. And no, you still can't play as Knuckles in CD unless you buy the Plus expansion when this absolutely should've been a standard feature that comes with the base game. On the bright side, the vocals for You Can Do Anything and Cosmic Eternity have been restored.

Understandably, Sonic 3 had some of its music replaced due to copyright issues with the original Michael Jackson compositions, so the music for Carnival Night, Ice Cap and Launch Base are instead taken from their prototype and Windows 95 versions of the game. Personally, this doesn't bother me too much; even as someone that's used to the original MJ tracks, I actually prefer the prototype tracks anyway. My issue with these tracks is that they sound awful in this collection and are not nearly as good as the Mega Drive prototype versions of these tracks except for Ice Cap Act 1.

All the games (except CD) also reset the music whenever you obtain a 1-UP or coin when this never happened in previous versions, and Sonic 3 & Knuckles has various audio issues not present in the Mega Drive version. I even ran into a game breaking glitch in S3&K where having the lightning shield and falling in the water covers the entire screen in white making it completely unplayable until you restart the level, which was an issue at launch that still hasn't been fixed to this day.

As for some of the new content additions to this collection, there are a series of Challenges to complete. These play similar to the ones in Sonic Generations - you're given a task to complete and you're ranked based on how quickly you can complete them. Some of these are actually pretty tough to get the S rank on, and it feels so good to finally master them after many tries. Sadly, this mode is far too generous with granting coins for completion - I ended up with far more coins than I could ever need.

I really loved the new animated cutscenes at the start and end of each game. One of the best things about these games is how they tell a compelling narrative at the time of their release with zero dialogue, and these animated scenes take that one step further by showing what happens that lead up to the events of the games taking place. Some of these are really funny and charming, while staying true to the spirit of Sonic's coolness and edge that defined the series from the very beginning.

My Sonic bias may be showing a little bit here, but this collection isn't terrible by any means and is still a good way to experience all 4 titles. There are far worse collections out there - it's just a shame that these aren't the definitive versions of these games as it's lacking some of the QoL features present in other versions, and the original versions should never have been de-listed as there's still an appeal to play retro games exactly as they were, flaws and all.

I'm conflicted on this one. Despite its flaws, I can still recommend this collection [b]IF[/b] you've never played these games before or don't have the means of accessing them. If you already own other collections featuring these games such as Sonic Mega Collection Plus or the now de-listed SEGA Mega Drive Classics collection, do not pay full price for this - wait for a sale. If you're still not happy with the way these games are represented in this collection, mods can fix some of the issues and it is compatible with the fan de-compilations.

improvement in a few key areas to better reflect the intensity of the sport.

Tackle Sound Effects – Right now, tackles sound soft and lack the impact you’d expect from a brutal, high-speed sport. A more aggressive, bone-crunching sound design (similar to modern contact sports games or arcade brawlers) would enhance the experience. Adding variations to the tackle sounds could also prevent them from feeling repetitive.

Metal Ball Sound Effects – The ball itself sounds dull and lacks the weight and sharpness you’d expect from a heavy metal object being thrown at high speed. It would be great to hear a more distinct metallic clang, thud, or ricochet when it bounces, hits walls, or makes contact with players. This would add to the visceral nature of the game.

Half-Time & Full-Time Titles – The current presentation of these moments feels a bit basic and lacks the dramatic flair that would match the game’s fast-paced, futuristic aesthetic. More dynamic visuals and sound cues (such as a stadium announcer, crowd reactions, or intense music stingers) would help make these moments feel more rewarding.

General Audio Balance – Overall, the mix could use some tweaking to make key actions (like tackles, passes, and goals) more prominent while maintaining an immersive stadium atmosphere.

I think with these improvements, Speedball 25 could feel even more intense and immersive. Hope this helps, and looking forward to seeing how the game evolves!

Too many glaring issues to recommend this.

-Even though the game listing says "Partial Controller" support, it's more like non-existent or broken. You can't use the controller for anything else except while driving the cars around. I just took a spin with the Early Access release of Carnage Cross, and I'm fairly impressed. As of the time of this review, the game consists of a sampling of a handful of vehicles and maps, but there doesn't appear to be a complete, cohesive campaign.

The game wears its influences on its sleeve boldly and proudly: this is as pure a Twisted Metal 2 homage as you're going to find. As someone who's intimately familiar with TM2, I'm always on the lookout for another quality vehicular combat game, and now I've got fairly high hopes for Carnage Cross.

The essentials are there: the vehicle movement feels good, with nice variations for each vehicle type (I love the addition of drifting - very satisfying), the essential weapon types and special attacks are all there (some of them are even direct references to TM2), characters all have the bizarre, strange backstories made familiar in TM2, and here they're even showcased with similar voice acting and comic book-styled portraits. Additionally, the levels feature the wacky touches you've come to love from TM2: the Statue of Liberty shoots lazers from its eyes, a rogue 747 gets disappeared by a bolt of lightning, monolithic snowballs careen across your path. The developer has hit a lot of the essentials for a game like this and it's fantastic to see.

That said, there are definitely some things that need smoothed out:
- Camera angles need work for some of the vehicles - I couldn't see over a few of them, making shooting and tracking targets quite a chore
- Level design needs more variation and character. Right now, all levels are generally some variant of a large, flat plane with a smattering of obstacles littered about - I'd love to see buildings, vertical elements, ramps and gaps, etc.
- Audio needs some adjusting - the actual sound design of the levels, vehicles, and weapons is grossly overpowered by the music, even with the music turned WAY down
- Overall polish and refinement - menus are a bit ugly, performance could use a bit of help, and the usual EA bugs and glitches are fairly easy to find
- Of course, completed campaigns and a cohesive story mode, at the very least

There's a lot of promise here. If enough character can be injected into the game, the levels can be infused with more intrigue and variation, and the game can be finely polished, this will be one to watch. For now, it's an enjoyable, brief demo, but don't expect too much more as of the time of this review.

I so, so badly want to be able to give a recommendation for Void Heart, but it has a few glaring issues that really suck the fun out of the experience as it stands.

Void Heart is a 2D shooter with roguelite elements in the vein of Scourgebringer or Black Future 88. It's got a beautiful aesthetic, and the pixel art and sound effects are well-executed, cohesive, and pleasant. The core mechanics aren't bad, either - it's your usual blend of procedurally-generated levels, power-ups and stat boosts, and suffering through numerous deaths as you gain enough power to progress further into the maze.

Unfortunately, the aforementioned issues begin to crop up quickly:
- Enemy logic is braindead. The vast majority of enemies simply move towards the player with standardized bursts of fire, aside from a few enemies which attach to walls in an equally uninspiring manner. This simple logic means enemies easily get caught on terrain, or conversely, all just home in directly on the player, crushing you to death ad nauseam.
- Aiming and the aim animation are a bit perplexing. It appears that you can only aim while firing, which makes predicting trajectories ahead of time impossible. Compounding this is the fact that you auto-target enemies and can't break this auto-targeting to aim wherever you please, begging the question "why am I allowed to aim where I please at ANY time, then?"
- Initial guidance/onboarding is a bit vague - you're led to a teleporter that's unusable until you traverse a few more rooms, acquire a key, and then have to make your way back to said teleporter. I'm not sure what the intent of this initial set of rooms is, to be honest.
- The UI could use some cleaning up and clarity: the health numbers are far too small, gun icons are unclear and look too similar to one another, and the dash recharge icon needs to be much more prominent. Oh, and all menus should be usable via the keyboard or the mouse, including the start menu.

There is a lot of promise here, and with some updates, this could be a great game. Even spending some time refining the enemy logic would go a long way.

I'll revisit this review if and when the developer releases any updates.

To see the final scene, I had to watch a video prepared by ChochKlah who I know from the reviews here. All in all, Trance is a game that does many things well and has beautiful ideas but in terms of mechanics, it needs some development. Although the story is not told detailed, I can easily talk that I followed the story with interest and the world created pulled me in. I think Pantoy Games has a good vision and I am looking forward to seeing their new works in the future.

Trance is a 2D platformer with an emphasis on "exteme difficulty," as per the game's own description. Unfortunately, its difficulty manifests via mechanics that are more frustrating than fun, and I found myself uninterested in further attempts after less than ten minutes of play time.

The pixel art is beautiful, the narrative is fairly cohesive, and the overall presentation is quite nice. Sadly, the level and enemy design are masochistic, and not in a way that motivates the player to try "just once more." Poorly-telegraphed enemy attacks (that are often so quickly chained together as to be unavoidable), completely unforgiving platforming sections, and difficult-to-parse foreground and background artwork all combine to create a gameplay experience that's an exercise in frustration.

There are right and wrong ways to do "uber difficult" games - relying on cheap shots, poorly-balanced enemies, and janky platforming sections are all wrong ways, if you ask me. The core game design would need a rework here to become an enjoyable experience worthy of repeated attempts.

Hey I’m Corthos and I’m a member of The Indie Game Collective I’ve played this game a bit ago and I wanted to give my thoughts on it. I’m not going to copy and paste my script either so if you want my full thoughts watch my video on it.

For me the best part about the game is the graphics. The graphics are depressing and I like it. It’s gloomy areas with little to no color fits this game a lot more than filling the game with bright colors would not work. The muted color filter change for each level is good enough. However I’m the type likes to focus on the gameplay elements the most and I have to say while in concept the game is simple with its controls, the game’s difficulty all over the place. The combat works as intended including all the upgrades you get, but fighting the bosses can get annoying when you realize sometimes they do not target you, they attack in general. Confused? Let me try to convey it to you the best way I can. The third boss flies on a carpet and throws daggers and dashes toward you. This boss is likely to float around throwing daggers in a way that won’t endanger you at all and when the boss dashes to you, eventually, it’s easy to dodge. At the same time the first puzzle is really hard to do. To fix this just add a play back machine so the player can hear what they need to do to match the tones. The other puzzles are easy enough to figure out what you need to do to solve it.

What is stopping you from doing nothing or running away to get back to full health. I've finished enough routes I think to review the game overall, although I intend to play more of the game and finish all routes. 

Music: First of all, the song "Dream Eater" alone was almost enough to make me buy the game. I know most trailers show off the best bits, but in this case, it definitely lived up to the excitement felt in every bit of the boss fights. The music throughout is great, and I loved that each boss had their own theme (with lyrics!) If you're not a fan of rap, know that I think the technical skill of the performers transcends genre preference. The overall ambient music is great too, and I love the music that plays in the churchyard.

Combat: SWC's combat is styled to be slightly clunky in a retro, Silent Hill way; you cannot run and shoot, you must stand still, and the camera perspective switches between 3rd and 1st, adding to some disorientation. This means there IS quite a bit of an initial learning curve... but once you learn it, it feels *very* good, and extremely satisfying. Normally, this style of gameplay isn't really my cup of tea; but fortunately, in place of difficulty levels, SWC has instead a variety of accessibility features, which run the gamut from a beneficial aiming drift, pure auto-lock aiming, to infinite health recovery. After a good deal of frustration in the first level, I played through the game with the lower end of aiming assist, and felt that it really made the game much more enjoyable for me, while still providing an adequate challenge. Having specific options that I can control as a player feels MUCH better than simply having one "Easy" mode. 

Aesthetics: The character designs are ON POINT. I cannot get over how hot everyone is in really interesting ways (the Duchess and Chamuel especially). I also greatly enjoyed the fixed camera, and felt that it really added to the anxious atmosphere. I wouldn't say this is a pee-your-pants super scary game, but there is definitely a constant tension, and those sensitive to gore and violence will definitely be disturbed by the demon designs. I personally was made strongly nervous by the grimy, rusty feeling of the Aquarium level, and also by the entirety of the Crypt. 

Story: The setup of the story is VERY strong, but this is probably where the game struggles a bit. From start to finish, my first run only took about 6-7 hours, so it's not very long, especially when you consider how much of that is spent in combat/exploration. There are quite a few characters who I really wished I'd gotten to see and learn more about, especially Chamuel, Dream Eater, Beloved, and Lucy. At times, it really felt like I was only being given a taste of a full story that I would KILL to read more of. If the developers ever decided to do an expanded edition, or a sequel, I would absolutely pay for more. Out of all the cast, Darrel and Oakley (and Mimi!) probably have the most balanced story arc, as they're generally comedic in tone, so the shortness isn't as distracting.

TL;DR Definitely worth the price, absolute recommend, my only warning is that it might leave you wanting MORE!

A phenomenal survival horror experience before even getting to the outstanding narrative. Sorry We're Closed has all the classic hallmarks done well. Clunky combat that's just unwieldy enough to make you dread trying to take out an enemy, puzzles with odd solutions, and plenty of unnerving atmosphere. But what really makes this game special is its world and characters. I've never played something so openly and joyfully LGBTQ in the horror space like this, the closest I can think of at all is the also-excellent turn-based RPG Ikenfell and that is completely different vibe from this. The complicated feelings on love and change as you explore deeper into the Duchess, the multiple difficult choices you make that do have a massive impact on the narrative, and a sense that these characters are actual people and not just NPCs really do make this something special. The sense of humor present is fantastic too, with little touches like Michelle's bedside entertainment or any time you interact with the post-man. For a PS1 aesthetic game it's pretty gorgeous too, the bright neon colors set against Silent Hill style rust and decay is a bold choice that works out well. Repeated playthroughs are a must here from what I can tell and I'm glad the game is a relatively trim 5-6 hours to make that easy. 

My only real issues are 1) resources are dealt out maybe a little too generously, with the combination of the weak point based combat and plentiful ammo I never found myself hurting for options, and 2) as much as I like the soundtrack overall, the lyrics during boss fights take away from the tension a little bit. This isn't like Alisa or Tortured Souls or even Silent Hill (in combat or puzzles), this would probably be a great introduction to survival horror but super experienced players might be let down by the difficulty. I know as someone that doesn't have much experience in this genre outside of Signalis and more action-focused ones I appreciated it, but again, someone looking for a challenge solely on gameplay might want to look elsewhere. But those are absolutely nitpicks in what is as of now an incredibly slept on experience that really is unlike anything else. Mouthwashing and Silent Hill 2 Remake really grabbed the most eyes in 2024 but don't let Sorry We're Closed pass you by.

There's no surprise that this game might be my GOTY for 2025 already. The art style alone sucked me into this world. CB's art is striking and the models each have this unique flair that makes each character feel real. They all have their own movement quirks alongside their visual that makes me feel at home in this nightmarish alley neighborhood. The atmosphere is a masterpiece for this game. The game isn't scary per se, but it is uneasy.

Uneasy because Love is hard. Love is everywhere in this game. Not in the "everyone has a match or dating sim" kinda feel, but in a grounded, realistic manner. Whether that's through heartbreak and grief, or understanding that differences can bring you together. This game explores how family ties can jade your perception of love, how material and fame can corrupt, and the most intriguing aspect: religion. 

The mythos of demons and angels and the great divide are explored in juxtaposition to modern vices and society. The writing and explanations as to how and why the world and its inhabitants function feel real. The characters each have their own dialect and tone when talking that you quickly learn and adapt to on the fly. Darrell is a douche but still a lovable idiot. Chamuel is misguided but understandable. Marty is adorable but knowledgeable. I read and clicked on every interactable object or person to see what they could possibly say or do. 

Add onto this the third eye mechanic, which allows you at the press of a button to change the world from the demon *silent hillian* world back to reality and seeing what it really looks like. There are puzzles and hidden environmental storytelling in these flips that explain more to the story than that is told to you. It all has this style that feels refreshing yet familiar. I've yapped about this before when it comes to the recent trend of PS1 styled survival horror games that are a dime a dozen now. It's a style that was innovative for a time, but now more so has become like how pixel based games were in the early 10s. It's on the later half of the spectrum now where games are becoming less copying the graphical style and mechanics to evoke that nostalgic feeling, and instead using it as a baseline with modern philosophies to create something truly original. The sound design, the cinematography of the cutscenes, the exaggerated color grading all coalesce into something that I can't stop thinking about since I played the demo (and immediately bought after).

As a game Sorry, We're closed is on the shorter side, but that's a good thing for this game. Coming around the same length as the original RE or SH, my play through only took around 7 hours to complete the Lucy ending (the most work needed out of the 4 different endings). It follows a simple loop. You start the day chatting it with the neighborhood, helping out the locals or just catching up. Then you head over to a dungeon with its unique mechanics and fight demons before fighting a boss. Afterward, you cool out by talking with the demons and angels of the Hotel and unravel more of the greater plot. I joked with my partner that it reminds me a lot of Persona. At first, I didn't think I would like it as I thought it would be a more direct story of chaos until the ordeal was over, but having the brevity to get to know the characters and world around you was satisfying.

Combat is easy to learn, and maximizing the heartbreaker system can make the game for a survival horror vet rather tame. I never really struggled with resources and would often waste water just to top up my health to pick up another water, over using it while in danger. The soon to come Hard Mode and NG+ will def make getting those other 3 endings more fun to get with the added challenge.

I don't usually play indie games, so my perception may come with a bias born of ignorance.

According to public "how long does it take to complete" I am about 1/3 through the game and I feel I have seen all the different variations of gameplay that I will experience up until the end.

The pacing of the game is very good, story intense sections alternate with "dungeon crawling" sections with puzzle elements. For "completionism" or as a part of the plot there is backtracking, but it is done in a way that cannot be seen as "time-padding to hit a mark".

Writing: characters are tri-dimensional, there are distinct personalities and motivations that clash or cooperate along the traced plot. Pivotal moments can lead to a different outcome, which is not obvious and it invites the player to go through the game again to explore the possibilities. It feels sometimes to be in a tumblr fanfiction environment, but this stays as an aftertaste during the gameplay and doesn't negatively impact the unfolding of the story.

Gameplay: puzzles are ok, not too hard to require a video guide and not too easy that you have to move and move a crystal into the energy socket while the game is telling you what to do. FIghts are a throwback to tank controls of first RE titles without the obnoxiousness of endlessly respawning enemies and aiming uncanniness, the code doubles as a way to look around which is a very nice way to experience the environments. 

Graphics: odd one to list I guess, but the artstyle is consistent and portrays a vision over the technical limitations (2-person team!!). Strong hints at Araki's drawing style; probably the face structure of the humans was kind of repetitive. The colour scheme is gorgeous in both levels and character design, I especially enjoyed the protagonist's pink coat popping up against the terrain/environments/other characters like a "you are here" circle integrated in the flow of the game.

If you feel concerned by the "LGBTQ+" tag and the current social media shitshow of woke against non-woke, don't. The writing is sensible, you are not shoe-horned into someone else's issues a-la-Veilguard. All characters could have been gender-coded in any other different way and the game would still be good.

I don't think the tag LGBTQ+ is suitable for this game even though some aspects of the game reflect this, but the good point is that the game doesn't stress this issue but it goes deep into discussing what love really is. Species in the game, despite having a human-like form, aren't human so they have different definition and value for love, and the story focuses on this topic as the protagonist goes through the adventure to discover her own answer for love. I like this plot very much because it's unique and doesn't cheapen all the characters. The play time of the game is a bit short but it offers some replay value because it seems that the game offers more than just one ending depending on your choices along the game. Considering this price, this is a good choice for an approximately 10 ~ 15 hours of thrilling and nostagia.

I had a lot of fun with this game, although "Sorry We're Closed" definitely [i]feels[/i] like an indie game. Visuals alternate between stunning and janky, the writing is clever at points and clunky at others, and it's easy to break the enemy AI by just standing in weird places. I was disappointed to discover that the different narrative choices were fairly...[i]unsubtle[/i] about what was considered moral or correct by the game. Yes, I know, financial greed is bad.

All of that being said, when I take the game as it is — as an urban fantasy fable about pursuing love in spite of heartbreak — as well as a very personal game made by just two people — there's a lot I found incredibly charming. I love the way combat feels; it's snappy and satisfying landing a long chain of hits with the pistol. Monster design is universally grotesque and fascinating. I love the little rat monster in a Hawaiian shirt.

It's a relatively short game — I got my first ending after 8 hours, and subsequent playthroughs took me about 4 hours each — but as a result, it's easy to replay and test your different choices. Even knowing an ending is going to be bad, it's fun seeing [i]how exactly[/i] dramatic irony will kick the protagonist in her ass ([spoiler]My personal favourite is Clarissa's ending. It's so goddamn silly[/spoiler]). There's a pretty respectable amount of hidden dialogue and story beats that I only stumbled upon on my third or fourth runs.

If you like the vibe of the game from it's trailer, give it a shot. If you like picking apart smaller indie titles and examining where all the seams are, you should also give it a shot. If you like being scolded by tall gender-ambiguous demons and/or putting them in their place, you should give it a shot. And if you like rat monsters in hawaiian shirts, give it a shot for at least the first 2 hours. You'll find him next to the hotel kitchen.

disaster gays dropped into a colourful, scarred world between heaven and hell. with no choice but to dive face first into peril, wearing their precious, broken hearts on their sleeves. fueled by a mix of desire and yearning, against all odds with spiteful persistence.

queer horror shaped by the contemporary conditions of that very survival: unstable employment, lesbian yearning, colourful attire, pop tunes & a visible tiredness of sanitized queerness coming through refreshingly direct and crass. and that doesn't only extend to the narrative; its sound design is a remarkable feat. every rattling, gurgling, bonecrunching sound is extremely crisp, creating a very tense and threatening atmosphere. along with the vision denied to me by the fixed camera angles, it would align in a cursed constellation that would make me feel those gnarly sounds right inside my bones.

for all the twisted dynamics and explicit ongoings, i found it most touching during quiet and reflective moments, be it sitting in a car, talking about what lies ahead while a catchy song lowkey plays on the radio and the wind blows through our hair, or hearing about the conundrums loving demons & angels find themselves in due to the roles assigned by their makers, in the church of all places. every relationship is complicated by factors outside of their control that need to be considered and overcome, paralleling external with internal struggles in a way that feels grounded in complicated queer experiences, yet heightened through supernatural struggles. sometimes they might not always strike the exact nerve amidst their messiness, but it is noticable they always come from a place of struggle and wish for things to be different, for cisheteronormativity to cease.

if you wanted to summarize its overarching thesis into one sentence, it could fittingly be one of its very own quotes. it is not only the essence of how the game feels, but stands as a powerful statement against these grim times we live in.

[i]i will no longer let fear suspend my existence. are you ready to do the same?[/i]

I am a huge fan of the first game you guys made, already 25 hours in just listening to the music over and over, and guess what, the animation still gets to me too. It's not a good comparison because it's a different experience, but I found that you didn't put as much love into the animation here, this game has a lot of static drawings, and very little animation to elaborate on the scene - also, not nearly as many metaphors. Strangely, I think the last game had more to say with no words, where this game had a lot of dialogue, but much less visual storytelling. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) Taking into consideration the short run of the game, I think the narrative design and the concept were interesting, it's just so hard for me to start a game and end it 30 minutes later, it takes 30 minutes for me to warm up to the story, you know.

(+) Any visual novel with unique art is a big plus for me. If it was any other developer I would say you did a decent job, but it does not compare to the first game you did, I thought it was so beautiful, so I wish you did a bit more here with the metaphors and visual storytelling.

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

(?) I felt like I didn't spend enough time with the main characters, their interactions were the most interesting to me. When it comes to visual novels, it's always nice if the devs can create some narrative forks that have more impact, that helps with the replay value and the player has more time to reflect on the experience. The visual storytelling was not nearly as enjoyable as the previous game, it was okay, but I think you can do a lot better.

[b] Overall Thoughts: 6/10 [/b]

I mean I like what you guys are doing, I just think it has to be a little bigger and more complex, I want to see more internal grief from the characters and more animation for that visual storytelling. For the price, it's fine the way it is, but I also don't want an interesting story to blast right past me. I am a fan, but you have to give me something more substantial.

[b]ufotofu: hex[/b] is a palindrome-based matching game. think of words like racecar, madam, or the lyrics to weird al's [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gAfIikFnvuI]bob[/url], replace letters with colors and that's what you're doing here. I never played the original mobile game mentioned on the store page but this has hexagons, making that one obsolete and this infinitely better, yet still disappointing.

there's a [b]really inconvenient tutorial[/b]. 3 pages of looping animations, can't pause, no idea how long each one is, gotta wait for them to start repeating, lame. the mouse is the most comfortable way to play but keyboard and controller are also available everywhere. always nice, especially from a mobile port, but [b]keys aren't rebindable[/b] (q/w/e/a/s/d and space). dragging and clicking individual tiles both work, can go back on your selection, even hold the mouse for a few seconds over it to cancel the whole thing.

[b]3 game modes[/b], have no idea about the differences besides board size and turn limit because they went with an [b]always unfortunate text-free interface[/b]. lazy at best, even if it's creative and actually takes more effort, useless at worst. not to mention they could've ticked all 100+ supported languages for interface on the store page for better visibility, not just english. there's text in the credits, not just names, so I guess they went total honest instead of ticking everything, gotta respect that.

anyway, there's always a randomly selected tile, gotta create the longest palindrome from there, then click the line of tiles on the bottom to confirm it. points for you on the left and the non-numeric turn counter (why? it has numbers on level select) gets reduced, and you're shown a summary of your achievements once the run is over. the 3 modes offer 5, 10 and 10 turns (no, not even 15) and as I said, no idea what the 3, 4 and 5 means. bigger boards, yes, but it's not the minimum length for a palindrome, as I first thought, nor the number of available colors, as I thought next, a sort of easy/medium/hard thing. either way, [b]can't have more than 3 of the same thing in a row[/b], gotta mix things up.

and funnily/sadly enough, [b]mixing up is what they failed to do[/b]. no leaderboards, local or online, no endless mode, no challenges or campaign, nothing. [b]no timer[/b], you either play a [b]5-turn or a 10-turn game[/b] on a random board and that's it. [b]the game saves after every turn, quit anytime and continue later[/b], so there's that. and an on-screen save indicator (often missing) and a run in progress is marked on level select as well.

colorful presentation, as you can imagine, didn't like the audio, very basic settings, but they're available while playing. only separate volumes, resizable windowed mode, and a cursor toggle to change mouse to gamepad. or something. text-free nonsense, you see. it took away the cursor but moving the mouse still moved the selection. if keyboard and mouse work simultaneously, why would a controller need a toggle? might be something else, whatever. [b]no colorblind settings in a color-based game[/b], well done, but every color has a different shape at least, should be enough.

bottom line, [b]there's no meat on this bone[/b]. good idea, controls are mostly fine, but would've been better if they went for clarity instead of a gimmicky text-free ui, and added more and longer ways to play. I lose interest in endless/random games after an hour or two of random sameness (still recommend worthy ones, of course), in this case it was about 10 minutes. 10 turns instead of 5? wow, total game-changer... and the only one here.

even as a relatively rare take on matching games and a low price (I paid half price during the first discount ever 2 years after release), [b]it's not worth bothering with[/b]. [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1595020]otteretto[/url], another game with the same idea, is not done too well either, but maybe there is (or will be) a third, more enjoyable attempt at this.

A summer vacation love story. Who hasn’t fantasized about having one? An innocent short romance, that lasts as long as the vacation would and then never to see each other again, becoming an endearing memory forever lodged in the crevices of the mind, sometimes surfacing about that cute person or perhaps that first kiss that was simply magical is forever etched into your heart? That is the basic premise of 7 Days of Rose, or so was how the protagonist Michael hoped it would go: to meet a cute girl, escape his parents a little bit and have a picturesque recollection.
Like the premise, this game is pretty brisk. Over the course of a week Michael interacts with this girl that he meets, named Rose. Is she toying with him? Rose is so certain of herself, high in life, leading him by the hand while he gets constantly embarrassed by his parents every chance they get to tease him, either by public display of emotions or poking fun at him. Soon darker realities crept in, like how tourists turn their gaze away from their own realities from home or the areas surrounding the popular spots, there is always just underneath the surface waiting to make themselves known.
The protagonist himself isn’t anything to write home about, the parents can be a little too comic relief at points, but Rose’s story can get dark really quickly and treats a very delicate subject that wouldn’t just go away with the power of a summer teenage love but it would take a long road. It is a good thing that the protagonist admits he isn’t equipped to help her the way she needs to, but offers to be by her side and help her as much as he can and doesn’t give an overly tired of “all you need is to find your one true love, love will fix it all”. 
It is possible to archive a bad ending and it isn’t a very pleasant experience for people who suffer from mental health, so viewer discretion is advised. Rose’s parents are verbally abusive, calling her names in public by the end of the story that may lead to said bad ending if the relationship with her isn’t in a good level. While this game isn’t overbearing depressing, the darkness is foreshadowed enough that isn’t hard to tell. If you think the subjects might upset you, it could be a good idea to pass on this one.
Graphic and sound wise it is very consistent, with nice sprites and beautiful background art. This game is a very standard affair, nothing that makes it stands out for the better or the worse. As a short adventure for an evening play it is adequate, with enough hooks to keep the player imagine the world continue going after the end of the story but also a solid conclusion. Some of the lines can be a little rough to get through and at first Michael can be a hit or miss with the player but it is a work from a promising small group.

TRIGGER WARNINGS:
- Depression
- Verbally abusive parents (Rose's)
- Suicide (potential)

I learned about this game through the Kaiji subreddit. I was interested to try out an indie game based around the series. After finishing a playthrough, I walked away with extremely mixed feelings. In many ways, I think this game successfully encapsulates the spirit of indie games, both the pros and cons.

On the one hand, this game has an impressive amount of care and passion put into it. Despite the simple art style, the game goes above and beyond when it comes to the animation quality. It's got so many moments that made me think: "They didn't have to add all these animations, but doing so added more charm to the game." The game also didn't disappoint in the game mechanics aspect. As a game designed around gambling, it would have been easy for the dev to simply use the familiar mechanics of something like blackjack or poker and create a story-heavy experience with cookie-cutter gameplay. Instead, the game came up with its own flavor of poker to create an experience unique to this game, and they didn't stop there. One game acts as the "centerpiece" for the core of the gameplay, with additional smaller gambles also being involved. The variety on display is remarkable.

The one aspect I wasn't expecting to leave an impression was the story. While the characters and world didn't grab me from the start, this was the type of story where I felt attached to everyone by the end, which is a good sign when dealing with a game where some of them might not make it to the end. The story does a decent job of raising the stakes over the course of the story and making you feel the weight of the lives of you and your loved ones in the gameplay. The game does a great job at making you think twice about going all in when running out of chips means your sister dies.

Nothing about the game feels like it was tested through a focus group. It really does feel like the passion project of an individual making what they want to make. And that's where the game's biggest strengths and weaknesses lie. While the story and gameplay are completely unique, they can also be quite unrefined at times. Sometimes the game feels too easy while other times it feels frustratingly unfair. The game does not hold your hand when it comes to the explaining the finer mechanics of the game. It took me several games before I realized you could hit the sub-menu button to bring up a player's bio so you can read what the status effects and special skills do. I almost missed the fact that the game has equipment stores that let you change your party's equipment. If I hadn't bought one by accident, I would have been playing at a much bigger disadvantage since the upgrades are so useful.

This is the kind of game I would recommend playing blind. I played the game blind myself and found it quite immersive to take the gambling seriously. Since I didn't know what was going to happen, it made the character deaths and survival that much more significant. If you're interested in a unique experience, I would recommend simply playing the game yourself and not reading the following spoiler text. The pros definitely outweigh the bad. 

[spoiler]Most of my mixed feelings come from the game's ending. I have to commend the writer for making such a truly contemptible villain and stealing away your protagonist privilege to face them in a brutally unfair death match. By removing your ability to save, you are given one chance to play a perfect round of poker against an opponent stronger than anyone you've faced up to that point. Usually the best strategy is to stack up all your chips into a single player, but anyone that runs out of chips here instantly dies. Never have I felt a game more effectively convey despair and hopelessness than in that final battle, though perhaps other players managed to get the true Kaiji experience of watching that despair turn into hope. Even though it is wholly unsatisfying to have the game end unfinished in defeat, in some ways it feels like playing another playthrough would ruin the story. I think the bad ending where the villain wins helped me to understand what the story was trying to convey. When you lose to the final boss, it's hard not to feel like you were cheated by the game. But then you remember that the entire game is about cheating at poker. Whether the game cheated or you cheated, it doesn't change the fact that you lost. Though it is perhaps a cynical lesson to take away, pointing out the unfairness of your situation doesn't save you from it. There is no power in pity if your opponent doesn't pity you. Just as they say in Kaiji, the only way to survive is to win.[/spoiler]

This would maybe make sense if it was limit poker, but as it is, all you need to do is dump all your chips to a team-mate, maybe win one hand, then fold until the round is over. As you might expect, this makes all the poker segments non-games. The minigames were fun, though.

Very early on in the [i][u][b]story,[/b][/u][/i] you are told to make a choice that feels very weighted. The text stresses that you have only one chance to pick what you want to do.
