It's no secret that Cellings is heavily based on the cell sequence from Spore. But that's what makes it such a cozy experience. It's a fun little time-waster that feels like its own game. But what I like most is that it celebrates its inspiration, and if you enjoyed the early stages of Spore, then you'll have a very similar experience here.

What makes Cellings so fun is that the devs took more than just the cell stage from the [i]release[/i] version of Spore (I'll get to that in a bit). Along with the same type and amount of customization from Spore, the game also changes the further you progress. You start as a blob, whose goal is to eat whatever it can to grow. When you evolve, you're given an intricate customization menu where you can design and evolve your blob further, by adding combat capabilities - or, interestingly, beautifications to make them charming to other cells. You can rotate your cell, add new parts (including appendages), and build and optimize them for your intended playstyle. Immediately, you might be thinking about the creature/tribe sequences from Spore, and that is exactly what it is.

From the customization menu, you're thrown back into the world. You leave your culture/nest/homebase(?) to either attack and consume other cell forms, or mine and present them gifts in the form of rarer elements found in the world. Once you've got enough evolution points to move onto sequence three, the game starts giving you base building options. At this point in the game's lifespan, only a few of them are worth getting (if you're playing a pacifist route); unless you provoke other cell forms, you wont need towers to defend yourself.

At this point, you'll need proteins to keep evolving and unlocking customizations and even forms for your own cells. This is where the game's [i]3rd person shooting gamemodes come in to play[/i]. By entering the arena in your map, you can compete against other cell forms for proteins. Although a bit laggy and possibly in need of some balancing (teleporting enemies and weak attacks if you don't invest heavily into damage during the customization), this is extraordinarily trippy but stupidly fun, and deserves to be its own game mode in Cellings.

In short, Cellings may borrow heavily from Spore, but it's a stupid kind of fun that, through a unique hybrid of gameplay mechanics and designs, is a neat time waster. I hope to see it evolve and worked on.

Cellings is a creative sandbox game where you can create your own cells and compete against other species in an abstract procedurally generated world. The game is inspired by the classic Spore, but has its own unique style and mechanics. 

Pros:
- [b]Interesting and colorful world.[/b] The game is visually striking, which creates a sense of immersion in a microcosm. The world is filled with a variety of species, resources, and events that make you explore it with curiosity.
- [b]Flexible and creative cell editor.[/b] The game allows you to create your own cells with different parts that affect their characteristics and behavior. You can experiment with different combinations and colors, and share your creations with other players via Steam Workshop.
- [b]Diverse game modes.[/b] The game offers three game modes: Journey, Dimensions, and Cell Editor. In Journey, you go through the full evolution of cells over three generations, adapting to different environments and interacting with other species. In Dimensions, you fight other cells in three arenas: Deathmatch, Duels, and Protein Wars. In Cell Editor, you can freely create and test your cells.

Cons:
- [b]Unfinished and unstable gameplay.[/b] The game is in early access and has many bugs and issues that prevent you from enjoying the game. Some of them are: poor optimization, crashing, bugs with physics and AI, low online, lack of balance and progression, boring and repetitive gameplay.
- [b]Lack of content and feedback.[/b] The game has little content and feedback to keep players interested and motivated. For example, Journey has no clear goal or storyline, Dimensions has no rankings or rewards, Cell Editor has no tutorials or hints. Also the game has little community involvement in development and does not take their wishes and suggestions into account.

All this is helped by an incredible cast of characters and some of the best written dialogue I've ever experienced in a game of this ilk- or hell, any game at all. This is further bolstered by fantastic English localization, and that can not be understated.

Oh yeah, it also plays like Hollow Knight meets Sekiro and it absolutely kicks ass. Gameplay is extremely satisfying and feels like a joy to master, the biomes immersive, the boss fights brutal and inventive, and the art direction, music, and sound design are all stellar. Nine Sols stands out to me as a game that is surprising in how it twists itself around. 
It is an artistically lovely game to look at that will not pull any punches with violent content and theming, it has a very digestible difficulty curve that will not hesitate to beat the crap out of you when it's time to test what you've learned, and never ceases to pull new rugs with the story, slowly drip-feeding the series of events that led to the introduction.

Our protagonist Yi is not only beautifully animated and a delight to control, his slowly expanding arsenal and skillset is effortlessly fun to master and tinker to a playstyle. The combat does not make a good first impression, and a issue I do have is the lack of recovery frames that will make you eat dirt if multiple attacks come close to one another, but at some point with the upgrades and new abilities, suddenly, it all clicks, and from there fights become great fun. The mix of a versatile tag-talisman that injures enemies with the multiple ways you can parry nearly every attack by the end of the game create a greatly satisfying combat where you constantly dance on the devil's door. There is a decent variety of enemies that keep the campaign fresh as you progress, and even late game some mooks can be dangerous if underestimated.

The general level design is varied and generally enjoyable to explore, thanks to an easy to read map and convenient shortcuts, but I did find some areas way better than others, and some in particular, to avoid spoilers, were more confusing to progress in and had annoying trap-ridden layouts. I found all the possible loot, upgrades and intel in the game and I will say some of it is hidden away in corners that feel like a practical joke. Not a dealbreaker however, overall I'd say for the grand part of the experience exploration is rewarding and very fun. 
I also found the small pavilion hub area very comfy, I always appreciate when hubs reflect progress in the game too, and this one delivers in stride.

There is also a very strong focus on the characters and the setting of the game, and while there is no real voice acting, the writing does a good job of making clear the stakes and their situation. Yi is a surprisingly engaging character despite his abrasive nature at times due to very concise moments and the mystery of his true intentions keeping a tension whenever he interacts with any NPC or boss. The bond he builds with some characters also feels genuine and earned due to it requiring you, as a player, to bother with it across multiple hours of playtime.
The game makes great use of your investment with these NPC's in key moments, creating some genuinely impactful set pieces that feature the best tracks of music in the game. 

In short, I would definitely recommend Nine Sols to anyone looking for a moderately hard game with a great character-focused narrative, I had no idea what I was getting into and left very satisfied with it.

I'm pretty borderline on if this should be positive or negative review. This game has a pretty good combat system and story but I felt like some of the flaws really took away from the overall experience. As a TLDR, I think if you are really looking for a parry-based metroidvania you might enjoy this game but there also might be some annoying parts that you might be able to overlook or they might take away from the experience. 

One of the major issues I had with the bosses was how little would change in-between phases. All the late game major bosses have at least 2 phases and the 2nd phase is almost an exact copy of the first phase except there will be 1 or 2 additional attacks or stage hazards added. It makes the fights feel very tedious since you are either dying to the new phase 2 attacks which then requires you to get the phase 1 down again just to retry the phase 2 attacks or tanking the hits and just doing a second run through of phase 1. When everything is flowing and you've learned the attacks, the bosses feel really enjoyable and rewarding to fight but the middle section where you are learning phase 2 just isn't as enjoyable. It also doesn't help that some of the bosses are given run backs to the boss that is just a bit to long or there is an enemy between it (mainly just mini bosses that do this but still) which makes fighting the boss slightly annoying.

Another issue I have is fights including multiple enemies. It is very common that if you miss 1 parry and get hit, you'll end up getting chained into other hits immediately from the other enemies without any chance to react. This gets even worse when there are stage hazards as if you get knocked into one of them you will respawn into an enemy already doing the attack they had setup meaning you will lose a ton of health.

The last issue I have is with teleporting between nodes unlocking so late into the playthrough and only being usable from the main hub. One of my favourite things when playing metroidvania's is finding a new ability and going back to a place you saw earlier that clearly required a new ability to get through. With no ability to teleport, it feels very tedious to go back to those locations and a lot of the time it wasn't worth going back to them. Even when you do unlock teleporting, they still made it tedious by requiring you to go back to the main hub and then teleport to another node from there instead of just allowing teleporting from everywhere to reduce the amount of loading screens.

I would still like to point out some of the great things about the game. The parrying and attacks all feel really crispy, the sound design is great, I'm a big fan of the art style and the movement always felt really responsive and clean. All of these things make the game feel and look awesome. A bunch of the bosses felt like they had just enough difficulty and learning curve that you are constantly making progress on the boss and the finish line always feel within reach. 

Overall I enjoyed parts of this game a lot and I think if you are looking for a parry-based metroidvania you might really enjoy this game however I do feel the flaws of the game hold it back from being amazing.

Souls like comparisons are drawn but that's just the mechanic that you loose money upon death, which  is punishing, because money is used for different upgrades like health and so on. I expected more from this one really, even more when it sits at 95% positive.

For me, this game crosses the line between difficult and frustrating. Here is why:
- No invulnerability after being hit, or even during the stand up animation after being knocked down. This means that you can be easily killed while not having control of the character. Add to this the absurd damage some enemies inflict, and the result are some delicious situations like a (multiple phase) boss one-shoting you at 80% health with a two-attack combo, or dying to a minion that shoots you multiple bombs, because all of them hit you at the same time.

- The talisman mechanic leaves you way too exposed. When fighting multiple enemies you have to be extra careful when using it, but even in a boss fight, when using it right before the boss attacks in order to do the waiting behind them, they'll still turn around and hit you, which feels unfair. You charge that ability by doing perfect parries, so the extra difficulty of executing it right feels a tad too much for me. Not to mention you lose the charges if you do it and the enemy dodges.

- The bloodborne mechanic of droping your stuff when an enemy kills you is specially horrible here, since you get a lot of money from chests, and in case of death before retrieving your stuff, the effort of getting the money back killing enemies feels unbalanced.

Aside of that, the usability of the map doesn't help either:
- Doesn't show closed paths, which leads to false positives when exploring / trying to progress through the story.
- Shows the locations of some NPCs, but it does not for others.
- Doesn't allow to add marks.
- You have to zoom in and out all the time to inspect the different areas, which feels clunky.

There's no "next objective" info in the menu or any other help in order to figure out where to go next aside from some dialogues, so the fact that you have to rely on the map to figure out your next destination (and the lack of propper fast travel) makes it worse.

If you don't care about these things that make the experience frustrating for me, then you're gonna have a great time.

Finally a Metroidvania where you can actually follow the story and where its not all one big lore-fest where you have to watch 20 hour long videos on Youtube to understand the story (hollow knight, all Dark souls games :)). 
For the rest a really good Metroidvania, on the top of my list in this genre together with Blasphemous.

Nine Sols is an action-packed and incredibly satisfying souls-like metroidvania. These genres go hand in hand honestly. We saw Hollow knight take the world by storm ages ago and now we finally have a competitor in Nine Sols. Whilst the movement and combat at the start is quite generic and simple, similar to Ori 1, every main boss's defeat still feels like a grand achievement and every ability unlock results in new ways to absolutely demolish enemies with precise parries that just feel amazing to pull off. The parry system is most easily compared to Sekiro and feels just as good as Sekiro. At multiple points in the game it feels like it all clicks and everything works in tandem like this boss was specifically designed for you to feel like a badass and for you to do exactly what you've just done, which is the most I can ask from a souls game; the final boss especially is like souls boss fight perfection it's incredible.

Nine Sols has close to flawless gameplay. However, I have a large issue with how the story is presented. 95% of the game, possibly more, is shown through dialogue boxes, pretty much like a visual novel. Maybe it's just how my brain works but, I could not get insanely invested in the story this way, i'm playing a metroidvania souls game, not Persona 5. I could tell enough of what was going on for the ending to pull on my heartstrings a bit but I think a second playthrough is needed for me to fully dive deep into the lore. What's frustrating is the very few minutes of cutscenes are stunning, they are extremely well made but we're only blessed with those for like a couple minutes in the start, middle and end of the game. The way the text bubbles and character models pop up is just so Club Penguin-esc you know? Maybe it's just me. If you just like gameplay you can enable hold to skip and just play the game but that's no fun I wanted to know what I was doing.

Despite all that, big recommendation from me if you love either genre, this gives Ori 2 a run for their money for metroidvanias and that game is stupidly good.

Great game. The combat takes a couple of hours to click, but when you get in the rhythm of it, it's a blast. The bosses are mostly great (the final boss was a bit too frustrating, though...). Awesome music and it has a very unique visual flavour. Hollow Knight is an obvious inspiration here, but Nine Sols really does its own thing in the end, and it's way, way, way more than  a copy. The real cutting edge factor here isn't actually the game's action or art style -- it's the story, which is a very surprisingly cool piece of sci-fi/fantasy from a very different perspective. Quite a few memorable characters and Yi, the main hero, has a very distinct point of view and personality that gets revealed over the course of the game in a compelling way.

If like action games and you're curious about this one, go for it...definitely recommended.

[h1]Nine Sols is the best metroidvania I've played since Hollow Knight.[/h1]

Where to begin...?

Nine Sols is a 9/10 video game that deserves [u]every penny[/u] of its $30 price tag. 
It's Hollow Knight meets Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice.
The art and music is stunning, the gameplay is snappy and feels [i]good[/i] to master, and the bosses are ruthlessly challenging -- which makes memorizing their attacks and giving them a thorough beatdown [b]all the more satisfying.[/b]

[h3]There were a couple of (small) gripes I had while playing[/h3]
   1: The fact that you have to watch a boss's animation [u][b]every[/b][/u] time you start the fight over when fighting them [i]can[/i] get a little bit grating, on occasion. The biggest offender for my whole playthrough though was the first boss - a major roadblock, if you're not fully comfortable with parry timings yet. I wanted to hop straight back into the fray; not watch this dude scream again for another 4 seconds, [u]especially[/u] after 20+ attempts.

   2: There is a stealth section in one part of the game. The section is dark and visually muddy. Yi is crippled in both health and movement speed and [i][b][u]CANNOT DASH[/u][/b][/i] - tripping and falling over if you attempt to. This is exactly as [i]fun[/i] as it sounds. (It is thankfully made up for by the fact that the respective Sol is a fantastic fight, but dear god, I hated the prison.)

   3: justice for my girl Goumang,, she deserved better,, all that buildup and a sick character design wasted on a piss-easy fight: it's the [b]only[/b] 1-phase Sol fight, and you don't even get to fight *her* - just her pair of souped-up fodder enemies. 
I don't think it even took me more than 3 attempts, and one of those was a fumble on my part since it was my very first time playing with a controller (I mixed up my dash and parry buttons [i]frequently[/i] on that first session)

Okay. That's EVERYTHING bad that I personally have to say about this 36 hour long experience; one (1) crappy room, one (1) especially underwhelming main boss, and some wasted seconds every time i Got My Ass Kicked by a Horse (because of Skill Issue).

[h2]Now let me say why this game is living in my brain rent-free[/h2]

1: The Writing. 
  The story, while arguably nothing [i]groundbreaking[/i], absolutely hits you in the feels when it wants to. Especially for the True Ending. Yi is a lovable asshole; definitely one of my favorite protagonists in recent history. While the beginning may be a little confusing on your first time through with all the terminology and information getting dropped on you, going back for a replay with later knowledge adds an extra level to it all.

2: The Gameplay
  These bosses go hard as hell!!! There's a reason one of my biggest complaints is that Goumang got shafted; I honestly just want [u]more[/u] boss fight content. Red Candle Games nailed it on their first foray into the Soulsvania genre, and I genuinely do hope this [b]isn't[/b] their last, whatever comes next. The charm-system that got basically lifted straight from Hollow Knight does it one better, IMO, allowing for even more playstyle customization. And my only comment on the platforming is that there could've been [i]more of it[/i], honestly.

3: The Art
  Everything about this game - from the unique 'Taopunk' aesthetic, to an OST that gets your heart pumping during tense fights, to the snappy and satisfying sounds of nailing a chain of parries and retaliating with a beefy talisman explosion - it's honestly just a great time, all around

...I shall keep myself from yammering on any further, at risk of spoiling anything else.
Do yourself a favor and pick the game up! Whether you decide to wait for a sale or not; it's worth it.

Every penny spent is well worth it. Alongside Hollow Knight, this has become one of my absolute favorites on Steam.

This game has a captivating story that hooks you from the start. It makes you curious as to what has happened and what will happen. The gamplay is well thought out and the movement responsive. I'd give 9 Sols a 10/10 if not for the 3rd phase of the final boss fight which absolutely tanked my glowing enthusiasm for the game. As someone who has scored near flawless victories on Sword Saint Isshin and Orphan of Kos, I feel I'm not being overly melodramatic when I say they kinda went a tad too demanding with the end boss. Which wouldn't have been so bad if the devs either let me start right from phase 3 after defeat or made phase 1 and 2 faster to burn through (like Isshin) so I'm not so frustrated when the unrelenting and difficult to read and react phase 3 kicks in.
I did swallow my pride after 5 hours of attempts and put on easy mode to finish the game. But that did sour an otherwise phenomenal experience. 
So yeah, play 9 Sols. It's great even with that big caveat.

I bought this game expecting a quick Metroidvania, I was pleasantly surprised with what I experienced.

Gameplay 10/10: The combat makes this game stick out from other metroidvanias. It's smooth quick and intuitive. The focus on parry creates a new experience I don't find in other metroidvanias. 
Soundtrack: 9/10: Majority of the soundtracks were amazing, I still have some of the main boss themes added to my spotify.
Story/Characters: 9/10 : Enjoyed all the characters and backstory going on, ended up rereading all the story logs found across the map before finishing the game. 
Maps/Exploration: 8/10: Most areas were enjoyable, I think my main gripe was the minimap and some connections between zones that are easily miss-able from a glance view. 

I recommend this game if you want a new experience compared to most 2D scrollers, especially if you find it on sale.

[spoiler] I do wish there was a bit more content post game or the possible unlock of a hard mode with more hidden content. There was a few instances that felt that there missing content due to devlopment but overall it did not spoil my enjoyment of the game. [/spoiler]

Now that I've 100% this game, I mostly stand by my initial thoughts. The combat gets better as game goes on, but there are a few nitpicks for me. 
1, that directional ground parry is annoying. It led to me sticking to the air most of the time because it was one less button input I had to think about most of the time. 
2, why does mid-air dashing not exist at the very beginning? Early game combat is so tedious without it, and while natural progression would suggest you get it towards the third sol, you can get it before beating any boss, so... 
3, some bosses (last boss mainly) have moves that start the same way but string into different endings, which was tedious to learn, especially since the dodge for some options get you damaged in others and it never felt fair to me.

(Original Thoughts)
If you're okay with hitting your head against a wall constantly while playing a game, I'd heavily suggest this game.

First the positives: The game is gorgeous. The characters, story, and lore are all amazingly done. The themes explored are really good. I'm loving the exploration/world, with a lot of really fun parkour sections.

The negatives: The combat is... tedious at times. Most enemies are damage sponges, many move way too fast for me to parry their moves (edit, you can parry, but it's a tedious learning curve and really ramps up at one point), there's so much you can do during fighting that I constantly jumble my inputs. Skill issue, I know. And I am slowly getting better at it. But it is a pain sometimes. (even after 100%, I still occasionally jumbled my inputs, since there's just so much you can do in battle).

The game also does not explain things well. The "first boss" I thought was the only option, with the story pushing me towards them even though they're infinitely easier after beating two other bosses first (And the other two bosses are easier in my opinion). Upgrades aren't always clear. And some things were taught in the middle of live combat... made it hard to actually read and learn stuff...

Overall, if you're looking for a challenge and love metroidvanias, I'd suggest this. If you're a more casual player, you'll probably want to pass.

[Spoiler Zone!]
I really, really love Shuanshuan. He's a wholesome little boy, and I love seeing how much he learns and grows with the people around him. The ending almost made me cry for this poor boy.
Kuafu is such a silly man. He gave me hope for the other Sols! I love the friendship that Yi and him have, and I love seeing him and Shuanshuan get along.
Chiyou is quite whimsical. I love the concept of "war machine capabl of killing a bunch of things but just wants to read and have fun instead." I also love how Chiyou valued his brother until the end. I got scared when I first killed Xingtian because I felt so bad, but I'm glad he survived and was able to have some final moments with Chiyou.
Goumang is the sassy bird-cat of all time. Despite her rudeness to Yi, I loved seeing the story behind her! Opticberries are interesting, would eat.
Shennong is Mr. Alcohol. I loved learning about him and the apemen, and being able to go back to the tutorial areas and see what has changed, how it was in the grand scheme of things. Shennong may be a rude person, but he's got a good heart.
Yanlao is an old old senile old man. He kinda had his death coming. But at least he was happy with having kept his antiques in check.
Jiequan pissed me off. He really threw Yi into prison and tortured the everloving crap outta him. But he wanted to keep his clan's honor, and I can admire that.
Lady Ethereal was, by far, my favorite character of all time. I'm a sucker for themes of mental illness. I loved seeing the story behind soulscapes, seeing what Lady Ethereal endured. I loved seeing her misery, I loved seeing her responses. I loved the boss fight, it kinda reminded me of Abnormality Dancing Girl. Everything about her and her story was absolutely beautiful. I'd replay it forever.
Fuxi and Nuwa I first took to be bastards. to be fair, Nuwa was extremely snarky, and she seemed to be ignorant. This toned up more when I saw the Fuxi had the Tianhuo virus because I thought she was *really* being ignorant. Seeing her soulscape was interesting, seeing that Eigong tried to give Fuxi treatment (I don't even know if she genuinely tried considering her story) and how much Nuwa cared about Fuxi, even in his last moments.
Ji's story was very fun to see! Seeing him around randomly from time to time was interesting. I was intrigued by the scene where Jiequan talks with Ji, since it's not very common that two Sols interact with each other (there's obvious exceptions--Yi and Kuafu, and Nuwa and Fuxi). I loved seeing Ji finally be able to rest. The music in that room genuinely has a hold on my heartstrings. Also, I love the random record in the back. Very unusual, but it's pleasant to listen to.
Eigong really had me going. I thought things would be simple: get her Sol Seal, be over with it. Seeing the recordings was shocking, to say the least. The Evolution recording is also very whimsical, I love how it is in fact canon that the solarians evolved from cats. Knowing that Eigong caused the Tianhuo virus, and after trying to find a cure, instead gave up and used Tianhuo in her favor makes her seem incredibly scummy. And she is. She knew everything was going wrong and used it to her advantage.
The Shanhai 9000's were all amazing (this includes Shanhai 1000, too). I loved their different personalities, seeing them pretty closely relate to their regions, the little details. I loved the story behind the "defective" Shanhai 9000. It genuinely broke my heart when it died, and how the enemy even had a different variation just to be Chien. It was a truly unfortunate story, but I'm glad Shanhai found Chien.
Abacus didn't mean too much to me throughout most of my playthrough. He gave information from time to time, great. Someone adjusted his sentiment value, cool. But when Eigong tore through and damaged him, I, once again, almost cried. It hurt me to see this being who had offered us nothing but help and guidance be damaged and having to shut down. It still pains me to even think about that. The care he shows as he's dying really ties it all together.
Heng was amazing. I loved seeing her care for her brother, wanting to always be around him. I loved seeing their differences in how they viewed the world, I love seeing how different they were. Even more, I loved seeing their final communication. Truly knowing Heng passed so long ago, that Yi is only just now reading the messages she left, knowing the sorrow Yi has for not being able to see her again, it evokes some feelings in me.
Finally, the endings. I got the "bad" end first. Honestly, seemed quite fine. I failed to realize the flower was Heng and had to have it told to me (through a tenor gif, but I digress). I was interested in how Penglai looked, seeing Yi's chamber, and the apemen.
Today, I managed to get the true ending. Eigong, a true bastard and scumbag in her acts. I was taken aback by the fact she literally took her life to fulfill her goal, as she saw Tianhuo as the future. I was heartbroken seeing Shuanshuan's tantrum, and his emotions. Kuafu, still acting like a silly friend until the end. The entire ending sequence left a scar in me. Shuanshuan crying as he learns from Yi that he will in fact, not be joining them on the Pale Blue Planet. Kuafu's understanding, yet still holding sorrow that his friend will die this way. The Tianhuo virus infecting the Primordial Roots and seeing them wrap around all the dead Sols's positions, around the Four Seasons Pavilion. Yi pulling the arrow back, picturing his reunion with Heng, through death. The after-credits scene, seeing Shuanshuan, Kuafu, and the apemen. The resulting title screen, of their new civilization and their adjustments back to the Pale Blue Planet. This ending cut through me, and I love it with all my heart.

Thank you, Red Candle Games, for making such an amazing game with such a touching story.

This game is truly excellent. Barring a few minor nitpicks (rare times when hitboxes feel larger than they ought to be, one wonky parry in a bit of optional content, small things like that), the game is pretty much perfect. Gameplay feels very good. It's too difficult for my tastes on standard difficulty, but it has a story mode that lets you adjust incoming and outgoing damage percentages that should make the game beatable by basically anyone.

Music is a standout that feels very different from just about anything else I've played. The game is also a feast for the eyes, with very tastefully done backgrounds, excellent character and enemy design, and really nice comic book style interludes in some scenes. Voice acting is minimal, but used to good emotional effect when it occurs.

The real standout, however, is the story. I strongly encourage anyone who plays this game to be sure to do all the optional side quests, as they have spectacular character development, and add deeply emotional moments to the closing acts of the game. I don't want to go into detail, as I think the game will hit harder going in blind, but I will say that during the end of the sidequest chains and the scenes prior to the final boss as a whole, I started crying so hard I had to stop playing for a couple of hours because I couldn't see the game and my hands were shaking too hard to play.

If you want a game with solid gameplay, art, and music, with a truly spectular story filled with emotional gutpunches (in a good way), this is at the top of my recommendation list.

Nine Sols is a strong metroidvania with fluid combat that feels amazing to master, which I heartily recommend to anyone looking for a stellar combat, parry-focused gameplay challenge, and doesn't mind skimping a little on narrative aspects.
Unfortunately, the visual world design starts to become dull due to the prevalence of mostly metallic structures throughout all districts; this contrasts with its greatly crafted world, which is not only easy to get through, but gives you some freedom on how to progress and from where you can traverse each district.
The OST ranges from repetitive to outstanding, depending on the boss and New Kunlun district.
The game shines in boss design and in making you feel, especially from Lady Ethereal onward, like you're the best at anything you've ever played.
Despite my many failed attempts to enjoy Fromsoft games, I finally get the feeling that so many people chase over; I started the last boss on a Tuesday and only on Thursday, four hours of gameplay later, did I manage to beat it. The exhilarating flow state you can achieve when you fully read the true ending fight is unbeatable, and dearly reminded me of Nightmare King Grimm in Hollow Knight's DLC.
Funnily enough, most other bosses probably took me under 10 tries. This is not to say they were worse or didn't leave me feeling accomplished — the galactic docks fight left me feeling like a god for parrying every single mirage, and the twins fight leaves you with such a feeling of superiority for outmaneuvering two enemies at once — but there is a considerable difficulty spike from previous bosses to the last one. Either way, all of them have imacculate designs.
I don't have much to say about the narrative; the preceding story is interesting, with heartwarming moments between Yi and Heng, but that's most of the extent. Yi's development is nice to see, but you can find arcs on stoic protagonists that learn through the mistakes they made that they might not be a great person in other games that focus on delivering the narrative, like Yakuza and Disco Elysium — insane comparison, I know.

To most citizens of the Velaya galaxy, Empress Adèle's abdication came as a surprise. Heir to the Crystal Throne is her eldest daughter, Love. Sheltered from the realities of life, the young woman has hitherto shown more interest in pop culture and carefree pursuits than in intergalactic relations and diplomcacy.

[i]Blood Nova is her coming-of-age story[/i], one that sees her rising to the occasion when suddenly she and her royal sentinel Kel find themselves the only survivors of a bioweapon attack on the lighthouse where they resided before her coronation ceremony. As their distress signal remains unanswered, it is the Princess herself who must produce the antidote that could save her best friend's life.

The game transports you back to a different era of science fiction. It made me think of what it must have been like when [i]Neuromancer[/i] just came out and transformed the genre with its stark depictions of body modification and the fever-dream experience through highly advanced technology. [i]Blood Nova[/i] features pixel-art backdrops in various shades of purple, and in its world, diskettes and cartridges are still in wide circulation. Combine this with ominous beats and spherical sounds, and it puts you just in the right mood.

As we navigate Love through the hazardous environment, we find ourselves immersed in a world that surprised me with how alive it felt. Unlike many other video games (or even movies and literature), there is no detached info-dumping to bring you up to speed. Instead, glimpses into the wider lore and political realities flow seamlessly from the narrative itself and make you [i]imagine[/i] what the world was like.

In the beginning, our world is the Looping Vale. We don’t yet fully understand the lighthouse's official role within the galactic society, but we quickly learn that the release of fungal toxin was possible because it was produced as a bioweapon in its laboratory. We learn that members of Velaya's Nine Houses sell their deadly creations to warlords. The setting blends cyberpunk aesthetics and esoteric mysticism, with lore becoming relevant as you solve the problems at hand.

You care because of the human quality of the events. War may cause a refugee crisis, but it’s the fate of a little girl that is at the forefront of your agenda. Don’t be fooled by the low-budget production—nuanced writing and gripping artwork leave no doubt that this was a passion project. Genre fiction is often frowned upon for generic prose, but it can be elevated when creators find the exact off-beat words to make scenes come to life. [i]Blood Nova[/i] delivers many moments of this variety. You’ll vibe with the lighthearted tone and fun characters, and you might even argue that the happy-go-lucky demeanor of the central protagonist is integral to the story. Love’s youthful disrespect for tradition ultimately proves to be her greatest strength and the quality that makes her worthy of the future she’s destined for.

As you may have guessed, the gameplay is story-driven to the core. Instead of actively moving around your surroundings, you solve puzzles by clicking on visible objects and combining your findings. For many players, this might not be enough to feel fully invested, and that’s fair. The game is decisively old-school, and you must be prepared to experience it more like an interactive short story. While limited in your options, the solutions to puzzles can get quite involved. Admittedly, I got stuck a couple of times and had to consult a walkthrough to continue my space-operatic adventures.

The plot is driven by mysteries that thrust themselves upon you: Who is behind the attack? Why did the Empress abdicate? Who is the mysterious girl people keep mentioning, and where is she now? These questions form the overarching narrative arcs, while operable tasks keep you occupied in each chapter. I particularly enjoyed how Love begins to lose touch with reality as magical elements creep into the mix. You live through her rite of passage as she meets an oracle amidst the pink dunes of a distant planet, recollects the meaning of star signs, or deciphers enigmatic broadcasts sent directly into her mind by an unknown entity. Then again, there are more immediate threats, culminating in an over-the-top showdown where the various villains reveal their true faces in delightful action-movie fashion.

For fans of story-driven games with retro aesthetics and thoughtful writing, [i]Blood Nova[/i] is a gem worth exploring. If you are into cyberpunk or space operas, I'm sure you'll love it’s a poignant tale of growth and rebellion against oppressive traditions. Provided that you don't mind its laid-back and somewhat static gameplay.

Deluge is Riggy2k3's latest endeavour in RPG Maker, and I can safely say that it is most certainly his absolute best even though I've never seen his previous works (finished or not) - Deluge is just that good.

[b]Graphics[/b]
Deluge uses at least 90% RTP graphics with a few nicely original looking sprites and system graphics thrown in for good measure. Dialogue windows do away with the system set textures entirely and are instead represented by translucent black speech boxes. The RTP that is here is mostly unaltered, but there's a decent amount that has been recoloured or darkened to fit with the game's tone and it all works brilliantly in the game's favour.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay in Deluge mostly revolves around completing simple puzzles and defeating enemies in a very straight forward version of RPG Maker 2003's default battle system. The gameplay in Deluge isn't innovative and doesn't strive to do anything terribly new, but what it does do is expertly executed by a man who claims to have no released full games under his belt.

Much of the game is spent solving puzzles in the small village of Figaro. This involves going from house to house looking for keys, but also determining how to pacify inhabitants that you come across and how to locate the evil minions that you have to defeat to ultimately move onto the final big baddie of the game.

The default battle system doesn't do anything too new, but Riggy2k3 set it up in a way that is really enjoyable to play with. There is no "attack" command, and the skills you have in battle are largely dependent on who or what you are fighting. For instance, when you run into a panicked villager who wants you out of their home, a "pacify" skill will be added to your arsenal that you can use to try and deter them from fighting you. You also pick up a cool summon ability that lets you add zombies to your party mid-battle to help you out. The summon ability? Essential! You'll find out why!

[b]Story[/b]
Pretty straight forward, but I won't give away the bulk of it since you discover it from playing. The gist of the story? A scary grim reaper has ventured to the village of Figaro where he has risen several skeletons from the dead and has tasked them with eradicating the entirety of the village's population. You are one of those skeletons, and you are awarded sentience by your master before he sends you off on your way. The path that your skeleton takes is pretty interesting as he discovers memories of his past life and ultimately decides to forge his own path that may or may not coincide with his master's bidding.

The story in Deluge isn't super deep, but it is very well written and the overall narrative is excellently crafted.

[b]Sound[/b]
This game has amazing sound! The music in the game is all original and super fitting (and it's not ALL creepy/scary as you'd expect), and every track fits into each given scene very well.

The sound direction though, that is where this game really shines. There are so many unnerving moans, whispers, and ambient environmental sounds throughout this game that are placed PERFECTLY. No sound is mismatched with any given scene, and the ambient stuff is all tremendously atmospheric and immersive. Riggy2k3 definitely has an ear for sound direction and it shows marvelously in Deluge.

[b]Atmosphere[/b]
The general atmosphere and vibe in the village of Figaro is dark, dreary, eerie, mysterious, ominous, and so many more things. I feel like I covered this enough with the visuals and sound, and I don't really want to ramble and repeat myself. The atmosphere in this game, with the sort of emotion it will evoke in players, is extremely engaging and immersive.

[b]Overall[/b]
Riggy2k3 says that this is his first finished game. I call him a liar because this game is amazing. It only takes you somewhere between two to three hours to complete, but I easily could have played a full length game like this that sees you go on a larger overall quest to stand up against the evil entity who raised you from your grave. Deluge is awesome, and if you've got a few bucks that you're willing to part with, it is absolutely worth grabbing and giving a play through. Well done, Riggy!

Deluge is a unique RPG that draws you into it's world through an expert use of retro visuals, atmospheric audio, and consequential choices. It is not common that an indie game of this duration (2 hours or so) gives you the complexity to to choose alternate paths and to face time based consequences, which is something that makes the world of Deluge feel alive. You feel pretty raw if you make a mistake, and wanting to see if you could do it better is never far from your mind.

The combat is JRPG fair and be quite difficult at times. It feels a bit more like Rock, Paper, Scissors, and the unique levelling mechanic means you can't grind your way past challenges. 

The inability to save wherever you like may be a bit of a turn off for players with a lot of at home responsibilities, but the play through is quick enough that so long as you leverage saving when you can you should have a good time.

Overall, the world is interesting enough to draw you in and the gameplay adds challenge and replayability to keep you coming back. A steal at the price.

Warning, contains some spoilers; Review based on Version 1.2






Overall:
Deluge is a short, narrative-driven game made in RPG Maker 2003 about a small town called Figaro.  Over the course of the game you begin to unravel the history of the town and the game world and gain an understanding of who the characters are, who you are playing as, and how it all fits together.

You play as a freshly risen skeleton, one that has been given sentience by its master; a litch/dark entity called Ganglim.  You are given the task of clearing Figaro of Human life and are left mostly to your own devices for a good portion of the game.

Game Mechanics:
There are not a lot of custom game systems in Deluge, and the ones that are are seamlessly integrated into the game so you don't notice them.  Most of the game play in Deluge is puzzle based with several fights through out the game.

Some of the puzzle's, in older versions, were not quite advertised enough and took a bit of thinking to figure out how/where to start.  More nudges have since been added.


Audio:
The game shines here.  The audio design and production in this game are top notch and the audio creates the perfect atmosphere.  All music in Deluge is custom.


Battles:
There are few battles in Deluge, at least compared to most RPG Maker games.  Battles can be tough, at times, if you do not have any items and each fight has a few ways that they can be resolved.  Deluge includes a "Pacify" mechanic similar to those used in Undertale-like games so there can be different story events based on choices during battle.

None of the fights feel unfair, but some do take good strategy to beat.


Writing:
The story of Deluge is one of discovery.  You start off knowing very little.  As you explore the game you will find books of all shapes and sizes that help you to fill in the past events and you will find cut scenes that will show you flashbacks to your former life that explain who you are and what happened leading up to the start if the game.

Deluge's story is one of the Human condition and it is very well paced and written.


Level Design:
The game takes place across a single town; Figaro.  There are several buildings and several other connected maps.  Most are well designed, there are just a few issues here and there on the ones that I am calling "not well designed"; they are still very well built.

This game includes a "door" indicator similar to other 1997-2001 era games, such as FF7, to tell you where exits and entrances are.  Progress through the maps are done via keys, so there is a natural progression through the town until you find the Skeleton key, which then opens up most of the game map for exploration.


Balance:
The game is balanced to be on the more difficult side; not Dark Souls level hard, but also not your typical "Normal" either.  If you don't use your skills and items in battle, you'll be seeing the graveyard a lot.

Item placement and amounts are almost perfect, unless you really get rolled by an enemy, you should have enough of everything to deal with the fights given that you get fully healed after most fights.


Overall Deluge is a banger of a game and short enough to complete in one sitting.  Everyone should buy and play this game.  My review score is a 9/10.

The Dead Prince's most obvious points of comparison are Hitman Go (and its follow-ups Lara Croft Go and Deus Ex Go) and Thief: The Dark Project; the former for the actual mechanism of play, the latter for the larger-scale strategic movement patterns it evokes. Unfortunately, despite this sounding good on paper, The Dead Prince also encourages tedious and repetitious play, something that its inspirations did not suffer from.

Chief among these is the decision to have each 'level' actually be a series of three in sequence. While the game does provide a lives system, giving you three retries before starting over from the first stage each time, this feels to me more like a bandage over the problem of having such marathon puzzles to begin with. The other big change relative to the Go series is the introduction of abilities for the player character that can be fired off in accordance with both a recharging mana bar and a counter of how many enemies you've killed so far in the current level.

Combined, these changes cause The Dead Prince, in my opinion, to feel less like the tightly-wound puzzle dioramas of its inspirations, and more like it doesn't quite know what it wants to be. The worst offender is the 'Skip Turn' button -- in Hitman Go, you're required to make a move on every turn, and being able to change the timing of the guards' paths is a precious opportunity afforded only by certain pickups. In this game, if there doesn't seem to be an obvious path forward, you can simply wait most of the patrol route out. The fallout of this decision becomes obvious, as levels have turn count objectives that stretch past 150 turns, and later stages are filled with enemies to the point where the obvious solution is often to just find one safe spot, pass five turns, and then pick them off in sequence. While there are some more inspired moments, usually near the ending of individual stages, where the level design shows the promise of requiring creative ability use, most of the time I spend about as many turns waiting around as actually doing anything, which is the worst part of any stealth game.

On a less severe note, the art is very charming, and the music serviceable (although I would have also liked to hear more than one track in-level, especially as the stages wind throughout several different areas), and the flip side of my criticism above is that the game should not be particularly *difficult* to complete, although perfect scores are an often infuriating exercise in replaying 100+ moves from scratch due to a msiclick. If you must have more grid-based stealth puzzles in your life, you should play The Dead Prince; but I can't recommend it in a vacuum.

[i]To be completely honest, I haven't seen enough of Velone to write a proper review. As a huge fan of Zachtronics and Opus Magnum in particular, I was pretty excited when this popped up in my queue. I'm sad to say it's not living up to expectations. Here are a few notes from my ~2 hours' gameplay.[/i]

---

- Ads on the main menu in a paid game, not a great look. This is probably the publisher's fault, but it's pretty distracting.

- Art style is unsettling. Intentionally or not, the whole game feels cold and sterile. A little more color and detail in the core UI elements would go a long way.

- Tutorials are vague and unhelpful. Mechanically deep games need to give the player time between lessons to practice and internalize what they've learned. Velone rushes you through a brief and incomplete description of its basic tools and then throws you to the wolves. 

- Programming is a serious chore. Despite containing an almost 1:1 copy of the Opus Magnum programming interface, Velone fails to recreate even half of the functionality. Instruction hotkeys (unlabeled, of course) require you to place your cursor over the desired program slot, making them practically useless. The only method of deletion is to drag things off-screen, which is tedious and unreliable. There's no visual feedback for invalid instructions or collisions between pieces. Honestly, it's all a mess in this department.

- "The Palette" - this MONSTROUS menu contains all of the pieces the player needs to build their solutions. It's unlabeled, disorganized, and it takes up a whopping 1/3 of the screen, completely swallowing up anything on the board beneath it. Totally unnecessary.

- Bugs, bugs, bugs. There's no way to manually save a design in progress, and backing out to the main menu (the only way to change settings, by the way) results in a deleted design about 50% of the time. Menus and game pieces are unresponsive, things get stuck on top of and under each other, and sometimes the entire UI just decides to call it quits.

---

Velone is gonna need some major changes to pull me back in. I'm crossing my fingers that a few timely updates can bring it more in line with other games in the genre. For now, steer clear.

Unpolished and confusing, I'm afraid, with tutorials that do not actually explain the game. Sins that could be forgiven, perhaps, were it not for the inclusion of advertising in the menu. Advertising! I paid money for this: I should not be beset with further demands for money within such a thing. Advertising, and the experience of the thing I am made to tolerate ads for is... simply not that good. Perhaps it would have been worthwhile to spend more time with Opus Magnum to truly understand what made it Work before making a version that... does not.

For games like this, it's important to be able to create and change your designs with as little friction as possible, but a rough control scheme and poorly tacked-on systems make doing anything a chore.

Positives:
- Puzzle mechanics feel like a natural expansion of Opus Magnum
- Consistently great art & sound design

Interface issues:
- Text is extremely small & has poor contrast
- Default keyboard & mouse hotkeys are obtuse with no options for rebinding
- Poor use of screen space (parts palette covers half the board, no labeling on programming tray icons)
- Hard to remove placed objects & instructions

Game issues:
- Tutorials do a poor job at teaching mechanics and interactions
- Energy collection sequence serves no purpose other than to be annoying

There is a legitimately great game underneath the UX disaster, and I'll certainly be following updates to see how it improves in the future, but I can't justify purchasing this in its current state.

To prevent this, stock up on food before you reach Saturday, there's a bug that breaks the only shop after you complete a minigame (which you would do to get money, to buy stuff from the shop). So keep that in mind while you play to prevent that annoyance. The second thing is that for a game that has 10 different endings, why in the HELL can you not skip the cinematic credits after the first time? It might be an oversight or something but it really did get on my nerves while grinding all of the endings out. These issues can either be minor annoyances or major headaches depending on how you approached the game, so that would detract from my theoretical scoring of this otherwise extremely charming game.

This is one of those games you wish you could  give a thumbs "neutral". It's not bad. In fact on paper it has everything a city builder should. There are a handful of annoying mechanics like how the upkeep of your produced resources takes into accont what you spent that month on research, buildings, and building upgrades. More than that, though, my biggest complaints with this game are more abstract and have less to do with the mechanics themselves, and more to do with how they come together with the overall design to produce an engaging experience (they fall short in this regard). There isn't much motivating the player at any interval. In the short term, things like production shortages are obfuscated by bad mechanics, which makes these short term obstacles moot. You don't really know when you need more of something unless it's one of the resources run through pipelines. That was fun to balance, but sadly other resources don't get similar treatment and so you are left without much to manage in the short term, which leaves you gazing at medium and long term objectives that leave much to be desired. 

Sure, there's plenty of resources and production chains to manage in the middle of the game, but why? What benefit do I get from managing them? This question is ubiquitous throughout the experience. For example, this game has temperature mechanics, which presents a survival mechanic, as does another well known city builder, "frostpunk". Yet the treatment here is very different. You don't know when temperature changes are coming. They aren't broadcast in any meaningful way before or during. They're just "there". You don't know how long they'll last. You see the snowflake icons, and upgrade the insulation of your houses and then move on as quickly as you noticed the problem. Though there is a temperature mechanic, it might as well not be there. It doesn't add very much at all to the player experience. This really gets to the heart of the problem. The game doesn't tell you about what to expect if you keep playing, but even if it did, I suspect it would not do so in a creative and fun way. Instead it'd be more likely that the player would miss these cues altogether because of how forgettable they are. Why do I want to expand into ever increasing production chains and expand across the ocean floor? There is no sense of purpose here. 

Sure in the story there is a thematic reason for all this, but this is a videogame. I need something more than an impassionate voice telling me to keep going because I am contributing to this thing I have no direct experience with. Again, this story might as well not exist because the player doesn't interact with it in a meaningful way beyond completing the game's production chains. Give me a way to lose and maybe give me multiple paths to victory, if you'd be so bold. At least give me multiple ways to lose. As the player, if anything of the sort existed in the game, you'd never know it, and that's really the problem here. This all may sound really bad and you may wonder why I'd give it a thumbs up. It's because this game has much of what it needs to be a good game on paper, it just fails to come together in the end. I can't knock it too hard for that, it's still worth $8 on sale. The critical commentary owes moreso to the fact that it is an example of wasted potential. When you boot up Aquatico, you have every reason to get excited in anticipation of what is to come. It presents itself as the total package. Unfortunately, though the game may be as deep as the abyss which surrounds your colony, your adventure never feels as though it never hoes beyond the shallow reefs. 5/10

For the most part, I played this game in co-op with my wife and son.  At the outset, my son got a little concerned when we had to build our first houses to sleep in that night.  To quote him (He's 20 and I'm 40+), "This seems like it's a very tedious and grindy game". 

But then something changed.  We gained a follower - an NPC we could give orders to and have tend to things at our base automatically.  After a few more followers, it became very obvious my son had demonstrably mischaracterized the game because just about 20 hours in the game, we had a crew of 10 followers (companions) that were bustling around the little town we had built and were constructing buildings, gathering food, gathering wood, and doing other various tasks while we focused almost exclusively on expanding the territory and making it safer.

There is also a story that the player(s) go through that is quite interesting and entertaining with custom quests and fully voiced dialogue, abet, some dialogues sound like it was AI generated and there is no randomization of idle chatter between NPC's, if one NPC comments on how well your town looks, they all will as you run past them.

I believe the AI in this game is something they could polish up and become a very unforgetable game.  The combat is also unique and seemingly modeled after some VR sword/shield games with the way in which you control the direction you swing your weapon. 

The "Army" system in this game is both it's greatest strength and currently it's greatest point of issues.  To say you can have an Army is an overstatement, but you can have a platoon or more followers all equipped in the same gear you're equipped with.   Even more, not only will they fight for you, you can give some basic orders to have them harvest a cotton field or loot bags from a recent fight and then have them return to base and automatically sort all of that loot into their correct containers most certainly showing off that my son had entirely mischaracterized the game.

But this system is plagued with pathing issues in higher-end areas where it seems there has been less polish on pathing meshes leading to stuck followers and considering how much time is required to earn enough renown to hire just one of these followers, essentially losing a follower to a pathing issue is quite a critical ordeal and the only way I've found to get them unstuck is to simply roll back the save.

On normal settings it took a little over 200 hours for the 3 of us to beat the game.  At which point we found there is no real ending yet and simply there is just nothing more to do when you reach a point of liberating all of the villages.

There are a few other systems that I found very interesting.  Bandit migration was one of the most interesting systems I've seen in a game so far.   Essentially, as you ignore a sector of the map, bandits increase patrols in that area, and if left long enough, they will establish a base which increases patrols in neighboring sectors which will also increase the likelihood they establish bases there too.  This gave rise to some truly dynamic gameplay that I've not yet seen before in a game.  As we began to clear the map and push the bandits further and further south, we found the stronger and more unified they got.   As we pushed them into the lower quadrant of the map, we found we needed entire squads to deal with the near relentless barrage of patrols on the roads to push further and further to the last 2 villages.  This is where the game really became fun but it sadly didn't last as long as I had hoped.

All in all, this game is a solid 7/10 and I'll be willing to give a few more points once the bugs are ironed out and promised end-game content is added and expanded upon.  This game has the potential to be a 10/10 game.

Bellwright is a fun and frustrating game, but not in a bad way. It gets you thinking. Too many of these survival style games in the past have just been about collect resources and the pew pew. This has been a flaw in other Snail Games titles. Donkey Crew seem to have been able to break that mould a little. Whilst it is still in Early Access, there are plenty of positives and the direction is good. 

Some of the issues that I've experienced are of my own personal opinion. Village management can be cruel, especially in the early game or if you grow too quick. As you can't allocate villagers to a specific job, just a generic role. The priority system isn't the best and will assign a rank 4 crafter to a crafting station with multiple queued jobs that have higher ranked jobs, forcing out a better crafter. This can slow things down or leave gaps in other crafting stations. As it stands this is probably my biggest gripe as it can become quite a headache at times.

The AI can be quite frustrating too, whether the AI voiced dialogue (which to Donkey Crews credit they have said they will address later on in production) which is very Janky (some npc's even change voices) or combat on Bridges where your militia just stand still and take arrows from bandits to the face.

Progress currently feels very sharp and there isn't a real curve to it. it's gradually then goes up a cliff, then goes gradual again and then another sudden cliff. This may just be because it's in Early Access, but at a certain point you become reliant on granite to allow the research of key buildings, but then it's pretty much useless after. My hope is that this is because they will eventually introduce stronger fortifications, but they aren't here yet.

Storage. Storage is great. But only to a certain extent. You can designate Storage buildings to only accept certain goods. This is great until you want to split up things like Medium and Heavy armours or clothing. But overall, it's pretty easy to manage making routes in your village/outposts more efficient.

So that is pretty much how Bellwright started, we've recently had a large patch introduced to build on mechanics. The River Dock, Roads, Prosperity and (sadly) decorations.

The river dock was certainly something the game needed, running from one side of the map to the other with your army in tow, wasn't exactly fun. Whilst it does need some tweaking, it's a move in the right direction. Roads are a freaking blessing, although being able to add a travel point to them like the base roads would be even better. Prosperity is a win and a loss. It makes the villages much more useful other than a source of villagers for your own village or renown. However, it does need more work as it heavily relies on migration bandits and reclamation parties to thrive, something some players may not want on.

Decorations I thought, at this stage in Early Access at least, was a wasted exercise. There are more important things to work on at this point of development rather than a pretty weave basket. 

Overall the game is fun, but a little frustrating. 7/10 (pending on future improvements)

Hi folks just a quick review for this game.

This survival/settlementsim/kinda Mount and Blade mix is just the right approach to define the rpg genre imho.
First things first: This isn't Skyrim where you head for quests and becoming stronger and stronger.
The lifeline of this game is your village together with you combat abillities. That being said you need to enlist npc's to get your village going. Hire specialists to research certain techs, to build certain stuff and to accompany you on your never ending quest to cleanse the land of Bandits and Brigants. 
This together with Mount and Blade combat system plus The Elder Scrolls like leveling system brings you a unique feeling of managing your settlement, playing rpg and classic survival mechanics.

But you need time to develop. It took me several hours to progress to the next tech-tier and even much longer to the last tier not to mention how long it took me to get every research done. 
Though I do like the pace of the game.
It's like: 
1. manage your population 
2. manage your recourses 
3. manage your food supply 
4. get equipped 
5. go for a fight 
6. get your warriors ready to liberate a city and watch the fight unfolding.
Very satisfying. :-)

There are some things which need to get addressed like the menues. In theory you don't need to walk to a workshop in order to sort out what stuff is gonna be produced and what items you choose to que. 'cause you may manage everything through the menues. Some stuff is really hard to find or to laborious to get to so I rather walk up to the certain workshops anyway. 
The combat is more like M&B but not anyway near it. 
Other than that Bellwright gives you a comprehensive experience for an AE-game. I didn't encounter any bugs or at least as I'm aware of so I do(!) recomment it. 
Besides the potential for Bellwright is outragous. New quests, new buildings, new items and what not. So it stays interesting where the developers will take the game in the near future.
Did I mention that your settlers will build any kind of structure anywhere on the map for you? And that you're able to found dozens of outposts throughout the map?  ^^

I'd say don't hesitate and give this game a try ;-)

Bandits get more difficult the more you kill them.  Logically thinking the more bandits you kill and more prosperous the villages are, the less reason that bandits would get new recruits.  The less recruits and the higher level you become,  the easier they should be to kill.   Buildings are twice as hard to move once placed since you first have to remove every board and they hammer it back in place.   Logically that makes sense, but if they are going to use logic there to make moving buildings so difficult, then they should also use logic with bandits.   The more bandits you kill the easier it should be to kill them, but Bandit camps spread at a zombie infection rate across the board with more camps and they get much better supplied and have more troops that you can not keep up with them.  I understand entering new areas would have harder bandit troops, but when you have been in areas before and those bandits keep getting stronger, that does not make sense.   Also, After killing the main Lord in the first part of the game and after the reclamation unit goes out to recapture a village, the reclaimed troops defeat the same troops that killed the Lord (boss).  So the troops that no longer had a lord and was from the base that was cleared out (no armor or weapons left) is now stronger than the Castle itself was to defeat.  That makes a lot of sense, lol.   After killing the Lord (boss) things should be much easier not more difficult and definitely  not near impossible to defeat troops that are out trying to reclaim one village.   Again, theoretically the new troops would have to first protect their reclaimed base (castle) and then only have a few troops to send out to reclaim a village.

Bellwright can best be described as if Medieval Dynasty and Mount & Blade had a child.

It is a 3rd person light action/rpg with settlement building, colony management and fighting baddies by yourself or with your companions. And I have to admit I find the game very intoxicating for some reason!

It is not a fast paced game by any means. Crafting, researching, skill book reading, building, traveling etc takes real time. You have to take the time to craft, or let your villagers do it for you.
The game is also naturally paced by these mechanisms, as you cant just go all John Rambo, liberating the land with your wooden club and tattered clothes.
You will have to research proper gear, level up both yourself and your companions. Kit up in proper armor, smith weapons that deal damage and build up an industry that can feed and tool your army.

Once you get the grip of it, you start snowballing!

The game has a way of guiding your expansion and activities by increasing the amount and strength of enemies the further south you go on the map. And that is also where you find the resources you need to evolve your settlements.

For a game that is in early access I do find it very much playable, and I am enjoying it immensly.

The negatives I have is mostly technical as of now, which are:
1. AI voiceovers. While it is better than having no dialogue, I hope the developer puts the effort into making real dialogue. There are several quests where you find peoples dead relatives, and their response is absolutely emotionless.
2. The AI companions seem to stop or get stuck when ordering them around or calling them from afar. It would be very helpful to be able to fast travel with them instead of having to walk them across the map.
3. The army manager is useless, and my companions cry about being hungry and bring their harvested resources with them. They should offload goods and stock up/eat before joining the army/party.
4. The list of craftable objects in workshops is to tight and narrow, even with filtering it only shows 4-5 items at a time. That might be a "me-thing".
5. Fast travel signs should be possible to build inside a village once it is secured, as I hate having to run unecessarily to the quest givers in the towns, and then all the way back.



I am sure I have some more nitpicking to do, but in total I would still recommend this game.
It takes some getting used to and figuring out the limitations and quirks, but once you get past that the game is enjoyable.

Simple but fun, fastpaced action.  Reminiscent of Pac-man's mechanics but with breakneck speed, avoiding enemeies while collecting all items in a stage, but lacking any ability to become the hunter, which I missed.  I kept trying to lure the enemies onto the bombs after running past them to set them off, which would have been such a fun way to give you some way of dealing with them, but that does not work.  Perhaps an idea for a sequel?

Clearing all the items is highly satisfying, and the high speed makes every moment engaging, and adds to the sense of accomplishment pulling off precise manoeuvers.

The central concern with a game like this is if the controls are tight enough and the game runs well enough to pull off the necessary manoeuvers at the high speed your character moves.  It seems to be a solid yes on that front--I had a handful of times I was pretty darned sure I died from lag, and a few dozen debatable instances, but overall it ran very well and the controls felt precise and responsive.  My laptop is new but solidly midrange, so I think it should run fine on most systems.

The pixel art is pretty, the music is good, but it does randomly cycle between two songs on each death/victory, which I found a bit annoying over time...just when I'm getting into the groove it changes, and as I came to prefer one song over the other I'd sometimes suicide until I got it before trying another run.  An option to choose which song plays would improve things greatly, imo.

I also wish it didn't auto progress/restart on every death/victory, having a moment to breathe without closing out the game would be nice.  A little victory or death splash screen with a button to restart or return to menu would improve the experience greatly.

The biggest drawback imo is that there are only 20 levels, which I beat in 2.2 hours, and since all of the reviews are after 2-3 hours of playtime, I'd guess that's average.  I don't think there's much replay value.  I got it on sale for a very good price, so I'm happy with my purchase, but I think 12.99 might be just a bit too much for 2-3 hours of content, so my recommendation is more to wishlist and wait for a sale or get in a bundle if possible.

My first impression after watching the trailer was that I'm going to get terrible motion sickness from playing this, since the screen seems to be moving so fast. Still, I decided to give it a go.

And boy, am I glad I did!

It's ridiculously adorable, fun to play, has an actual plot with character development and... surprisingly intricate lore. Yeah, I didn't expect that either. But now I'm in love with Squidlit, and while I normally don't like sequels, I'd really like to revisit Squishu at some point (there's a previous game, just Squidlit, so at least I have that).

The gameplay is great in its simplicity. You attack by double jumping, and you also have a headbutt dash which doesn't deal direct damage but helps knock enemies back. Each level has its own set of enemies, its own music, and sometimes even a bit of a gameplay change, such as getting a space shooter section or having most of the level be underwater, which totally switches your controls around (in a good way! You're a squid, swimming comes naturally).

Every level also has a... FPS section. It's not as well done as the rest, mainly because Game Boy resolution and 3D don't really mix, and there's less variety. You literally pew pew baddies in a maze, like a crappier version of Wolfenstein 3D. On the plus side, you collect EXP, and you get to level your FPS character - Skwit Skwot - to upgrade her spells. You also have to manage your health and mana levels, so it's not completely bland.

The game also has some really cute and weird attention to detail. For example, pressing down makes you go ^_^ ! Which doesn't have much purpose (that's how you save, and that's about it) - but it's very cute, and other characters react to it - either by doing ^_^ themselves, doing their own version if they're not a squidlit, or petting you because you're so cute. At some point, Skwit Skwot gets her hands covered with grape juice, and when you approach her for headpats, she says "sorry, I can't pet you now because my hands are all sticky". 

To wrap this up - if this game actually came out during the Game Boy Color era, it would've been a hit. While I wouldn't call it a masterpiece by modern standards, it has enough of this warm magic that just makes you smile, and keeps you playing.

[b]Super Squidlit[/b] is the colorized sequel to [b]Squidlit[/b], and it's as charming as ever. The big improvement over the first game is that it's longer and more varied. The first game is really short, and only somewhat made up by the achievements.

The platforming is here to stay, and Plip has gotten a new dash ability which literally opens up new heights as well as new ways to deal with enemies or avoid them. There are also first person shooter sections, which I actually quite like. The game is advertised as "Strives for total accuracy to Game Boy Color hardware!". Given that [b]Tyrannosaurus Tex[/b] exists, the first person shooter on a game boy color is not unfeasible. Heck, [b]Faceball 2000[/b] exists for the OG Game Boy. Anyway, these sections aren't actually as unplayable as some may tell you. The game does actually provide an option to play with modern controls, if you have a controller that is. I played without, you have to hold a button to strafe or left and right or the camera will turn instead. You can also lock onto enemies. The weapon selection only goes forward which is only a minor inconvenience. Overall the controls are adequate. The gameplay is a little repetitive, not much enemy variety, though there are a few "gimmicks" to try to spice it up, such as an autoscroller, or a falling section that uses this first person view or a boss fight. I actually liked these FPS sections so much, I'm craving for more stuff like this. However, what I did find "unplayable" is swimming controls. The swimming is similar to any old school game like [b]Super Mario Bros.[/b] except when "jump", you swim in a given direction. You can swim up, up-right, up-left, and down. You can face down-right and down-left but can't actually swim in that direction which is kinda awkward. Moreover, in order to attack the enemies, you have to turn around, which is also awkward, and the shot goes in upward trajectory (if you aren't aiming straight up/down that is). Works the same way as in 2D platforming sections but it's just so clumsy. I did not find the entire swimming level and it's boss to be much fun. I think modern swimming controls would've worked greatly. It's a squidlit afterall, not a fat plumber.

With longer runtime it's more likely for unpolished moments to creep in. I already mentioned swimming mechanics, and the first person shooter sections are somewhat devicive. Then there's the final boss in the FPS style, where the difficulty is actually finding the boss and approaching them from behind. I was actually quite confused on what to do until I figured it out. Still though, overall [b]Super Squidlit[/b] is still a good game, there are few issues to speak of compared to the rest of it. It's quite enjoyable and a worthy successor to the original.
