As cute as [b]Sugar Shack[/b] could be, and as interested as I was in the world tile placement, I rage quit and returned this game within 45 minutes because [i]you can only carry one thing at a time[/i].  

The premise is that you signed a contract with the Devil and now have to rehabilitate a broken-down maple syrup tavern in Canada or purgatory or something.  There are loads of interesting world customization options plus a restaurant to run, and everything about this would be perfect for me if [i]you had a backpack[/i].  Heck, I'd even settle for [i]Fruit Bus[/i]'s stupid two-items-at-a-time mechanic.  

Instead, you get a basket that carries multiple items (but only a set number of item types)... but picking up and moving that basket [i]counts as your one item[/i].  So you're just running from bush to bush, carrying one berry at a time to your frozen basket in the middle of the hexagon, and then nipping back to the shack to unload your produce.  It is the single dumbest inventory system I have ever seen.  Seriously, what cocker spaniel approved this?

Anyway, I guess I'd recommend this if you don't mind carrying one item at a time and are particularly interested in town building and annoying the Devil.   But I don't actually recommend this one; it's been a few months and I'm still mad enough to write this review, and while I remember some cool or otherwise promising things in the first 45 minutes, my main takeaway was that the inventory was designed by the same Devil who manages your contract.

I reached a part where I needed to find a 5-digit code to a rotational lock, and I couldn't tell whether I was doing the puzzle correctly or incorrectly. The instructions in the game are written in English, but sometimes the instructions are unclear (like the use of the words "Counterclockwise", "Anticlockwise", and "left" interchangably. I didn't get far in Deranged, and I feel like some small updates would really improve the game. At $3, you're getting more game than you're paying for. But it might not be enough to leave you feeling good about it.

While it isn't bad by any means, I just think for me personally the whole climate change and pollution theme is sort of done to death in indie games. Having played this for a good amount of time, I must admit that it deserved the DMCA, and I kind of can't believe it was still published - it really is just an inferior ripoff of Loop Hero. I can't even say the serial numbers were filed off, b/c the game is [i]still[/i] called Loop Odyssey when you fire it up - only the Steam store and game launch splash page were changed, not any of the internals or the name of the running program. The graphics are nearly identical, but with less resolution and polish, and the conceit is nearly identical - you wake up with amnesia and must fight your way through a time loop to vanquish the Unknown Big Bad.

Really, the only thing that's different is the main type of "idle" gameplay - which is more akin to a baby's first programming logic game than the tile-placement of Loop Hero. However, this is also much worse - you can't alter the map to your needs, you can only explore in the dark, micromanaging every step of the way. You can't even really idle until about 500-1000 loops in, and that assumes you happened to hit the time saving powerup as soon as possible, which is NOT a safe assumption. The game simultaneously wants to to explore the tiny map in full so you can plan your route, and actively hinders you from doing so until you've perfected a loop of your current 9-square area, and you need to beeline to the next time extension spot (fireflies) without knowing where they are.

The basic mechanics of "get more efficient at tasks the more you do them each run" and "take different actions with NPCs over runs to get branching stories and actions" were intriguing, but ultimately hamstrung by the rest of the game. I think if the map was fully revealed, or significantly easier TO fully reveal (say, doable in 3-4 loops right at the beginning) this would actually have been an enjoyable game despite its many flaws, since you could easily plan ahead and try new actions. Also, being able to interrupt your current loop, add actions, and continue rather than having to fully restart when you haven't reached that action yet would be a massive frustration reducer.

It's alright. Stuck in Time feels more like a programming game than an idle one, so consider trying it if you're a fan of both those styles of games. That said, it has a lot of flaws, so maybe get it on sale.

The core of the game is very solid. Setting up the foundations of your loop and then tinkering and experimenting with it to maximize its efficiency is fun and rewarding if you're the sort of person who enjoys optimizing things. There's also many upgrades and unlocks that can cause you to reroute your entire path to take advantage of some new resource, so you're encouraged to keep revising your loops even as you approach the end of the game. Your success feels more due to how well planned your loops are than how much grinding you've done. You still need to grind quite a bit - it's an idle game, after all - but an efficient loop makes the grinding relatively fast (for idle game standards, at least).

However, outside of the core mechanics the game has a lot of problems. The interface just isn't good enough to support the hundreds of actions you'll be performing in late game loops - editing existing loops is clunky, you have no good tools for debugging loops, and it's hard to figure out what instructions correspond to which actions once the loop starts running back and forth over itself. The only interesting screen is the first one, all the others are very simple in terms of routing through them, and the overall progression through the world is quite basic as well. Exploring new areas involves repeatedly running entire loops just to reveal a handful of tiles at a time.
The biggest problem is that grinding isn't interesting. Most of your grinding, particularly your familiarity levels, is something that happens invisibly in the background while you do other tasks. And when I say "invisibly", I mean you have to really go out of way to check it and it's generally unclear how much any individual familiarity level is actually helping you, so you don't get the dopamine rush from seeing a number go up that usually compels you to keep playing idle games. The method for actively grinding things is, in almost all cases, grabbing a bunch of mana potions and then interacting with something until the loop ends. This is also boring, since it means you approach grinding pretty much everything in exactly the same way, even using a nearly identical loop.

I enjoyed Stuck in Time, but that's largely because I'm the type of person who really likes shuffling around instructions to try and make a system slightly more efficient, and despite the fact I liked playing it, I have to admit that it's quite flawed. I'd say it's still worth checking out if you like the concept, but maybe not at full price.

Cold Verdict is a short visual novel about a group of strangers trying to escape from a killer's maze. It's reminiscent of the Saw movies, and mostly involves the characters piecing together why they are there.

The story is easy to follow, involving a tragedy that happened in the past, and as you play, everyone's part is revealed. There are a good deal of choices throughout, and every character can live or die, so I appreciated that choices matter in that respect. As a visual novel, the writing is decent and every character felt unique and had their own personality.

The music is very good and immersive; dark ambient tracks that build suspense. Each track was great and really fit the mood.

As someone not really into the gore, torture, etc., that the Saw movies are known for, I can appreciate that Cold Verdict isn't gratuitous in that respect, but I think this will disappoint people looking for a bloodier, grittier experience.

Overall, I enjoyed the game. It was a nice way to spend 40 minutes, and it was a fun experience.

This is a VERY cheap game, that doesn't ask much of you, doesn't take much of your time, and by the creator's repeated admission, doesn't have much in the way of top-quality art. Indeed, though I came here for the animations, a lot of them were rather stiff, repetitive, and had some "off" parts like the gums of the cyborg girl; usually, they just use teeth and something about that red stuff in her simulated mouth bothers me when it's animated.

It's good and recommended for how cheap it is. If you like simple games that make you work for a half-decent fap with good artwork to look at but no complexity or much inherent fun in its gameplay, get this. It's like, less than 1 USD, literal pocket change, and the developer seems like they could really use the money and provide some half-decent art for the saking price, along with the variety.

If I had one major complaint it's that the gameplay tries to be unique: combine two separate game systems into one. However, it clearly hasn't managed to succeed in marrying and fusing the concept in a way that's fun and interesting.

It should have been an Asteroids Shooter, or a Qix reveal game. You should have revealed more of the board through destroying enemies or getting their pickups, the player's movement should have been greatly limited from this free movement, and the enemies need to start shooting back or be more of a threat.

The game doesn't really give you much incentive to shoot or gather power-ups and money aside from convenience. The gallery is basically just a more expensive, inferior version of the animated scenes, not that there's some interesting stills like transparent tops for those into that. The two styles just haven't been combined in interesting ways and that makes me not want to grind the gallery, as easy as money is to come by.

If I had to tell the developer one thing, it's that the art and the asking price is fine. However, they need to take pages out of Deep Space Waifu or the classic Gals Panic! series: do one thing well, than combining two things poorly.

P.S. 99% Reveal is too tedious, especially with the corner areas and how it can be difficult to see remaining areas without a flashing indicator or extreme color change from the rest. Make it like 90% or 95%, or make a power-up that gives you more field reveal for a temporary time, to incentivize shooting enemies.

Anyway, this is getting to be long and this game doesn't deserve that much attention from me. Good luck with your next game, developer, I'm sure it'll be fine if the art remains the same or improves in the meanwhile, but not if the gameplay continues to be lackluster.

This is a very very skeptical answer...
I usually go for the better option when I'm on the fence, but this just gets to me in a bad way. I went into this thinking I was getting a creature collector game, and this is not one in the slightest. It's okay for what it is, which is a RPG, but I have problems with the format. There's a lot about this game that I want to discuss that may change your minds if you were looking into it, and this would be the perfect example of a neutral option for recommendations. I'm not doing pros/cons because some things others would see as pros I hate, and some cons I like for this game.

There's no aspect of you collecting. You get robots, sure, but not in a sense where you can go out, collect a ton of them, then form a party based on what you would need in the situation unfolding. It's more like a RPG with creature collector elements. There's weaknesses and buffs against types, and that's what makes it feel like a creature collector. 
I'll explain this more so you can completely understand...
- You get a robot to fight with in the beginning of the game
- You fight a TON of NPCs with a robot of their own
- You then save up enough to get a voucher to get another robot, which there is always 4 choices for, but almost never the same choices
- You can only get 1 robot per junkyard. I'm 3 hours in and have just gotten my 4th robot. That brings the tally up to one robot per hour of gameplay excluding the first one you get to be able to play
That is NOT a creature collector format in the slightest.

This game is VERY linear. It blocks you from going places with NPCs constantly (and by constantly I mean EVERY FEW STEPS), or gives you the runaround with fetch quests to unlock a door or other slow progressing options. There's no run option, and driving is just as slow as walking. They give you the option to heal your party at these healing stations that are a bit more reasonable to get to, but then charge you more to use a healing station over going to a workshop and getting them fixed there, so since money is fairly scarce, I've always opted to walk to the workshop to heal, which usually needs to happen after EVERY FIGHT. This causes a bunch of boring walking back and forth, and there's no item to equip to move faster or to use to teleport you to the workshops to make this trip one sided either. Going back to locked areas, I can understand locking people out of places to keep them from stronger danger, but this isn't even the reason. Everything I've run into so far has been able to be beaten by low levels if you have type advantage, which makes sense because if you couldn't, you would be softlocked by battles once the enemy had type advantage over your party since you don't get a wide variety to switch between. You can't walk past a single NPC fight, they block you from progressing until you beat them. This is EVERY SINGLE FIGHT. So the playthrough consists of this;
- Get a robot
- Fight one of the 5 enemies otw to the next set of buildings. Earn around 10g
- Go back to heal because if you don't you'll lose the next fight. Costs 5g
- fight the second fight. Earn around 10g
- Walk back to heal. Costs 5g
- Fight the third fight. Earn around 10g
- Find a chest with an item that can heal you so maybe help you not walk back once once you get an item to also restore your stamina
- Walk back to heal. Costs 5g
I think you can see where this is going. This game is 95% walking slowing to go heal or get into a forced fight, and once you fight the NPCs once, that's it. They're now just there to get in your way as you walk slowly through the areas to try to progress your missions. There's one NPC in every town that you can "Train with", by which I mean you can fight them over and over; this is the only way to grind. There's no random encounters, so if you got a lopsided team because you didn't understand type effectiveness for this game, then this is the only way to get your robot to be better, and that's only if you can beat the NPC by them not having type advantage over you.

I think this needs a "What Can Improve This Game" section. This is for improving this game without changing it's format (If it was more fixed it so you didn't have to heal after every fight, that would mean changing the entire game, so I'm not going to be discussing things like that)

- Running! Please give us faster movement
- More money per fight OR make healing stations as affordable as Workshops (this also stems from having to move so much so slowly)
- Items of equipment for faster movement
- Get rid of fetch quests that serve no purpose (Having to walk back across the map to get a battery to leave after walking across the map to leave to begin with was just stupidly frustrating, especially since there was nothing that happened besides dialogue that could've been completely avoided, making the entire trip take double the time)
- Give us faster movement! 
- Let us activate NPC battles between sections instead of locking us into every single fight, then have them be able to be fought multiple times. This would get rid of having to have so many healing stations, cause less walking back and forth, and give people the option to grind (if they want to) with multiple battles instead of just one per section. This would be the biggest thing that could fix the game in it's current stance IMO. You could still have necessary battles, just not make every battle necessary. That could also give a bit more exploration and control into the linear aspect of the game.
- Did I mention faster movement yet?

The game was decent. It took me about 2.4 hours to clear my first pass. This was me playing with rampant save scumming as I tried to get through each week without burning too much spirit energy. I discovered that each monster you face has different results when you face them with different partners. Some spirits can be defeated by your partners without using your own power and still leave behind monster food. Those are really the golden ones and the paths you want to find because spirit energy regenerates really slowly and if you rely only on that, you won't get much food.
This is less a game and more of a visual novel so it lives or dies on its story. The story isn't that interesting though. Not much really happens. You run around with the other Scoobies and fight monsters. Kurokami is probably the most fleshed out of all the characters but even she doesn't receive much characterization. The plot is pretty much what you expect: a demon or whatever forces you to hunt down monsters to feed her. The writing is bare bones and that's a problem for a visual novel. I'll probably try to play through a second time to see if I can get a 'good' ending (or maybe I did get the good ending, I don't know).
Anyway, game is decent. If the concept looks appealing to you and you want to burn a few hours then give it a try but this isn't a game that I would be recommending to my friends.

[h1] How to play the game - Tips  [/h1]
- To start go to the emails and check the boxes so you can meet the monster mentionned in it. 
- There seems to be no more than one monster per place. You don't need to kill each one to get it's food.
- Every round there seems to be at least a place where you can develop your experience so you can fight Kurokami-sama when the time comes. It seems once you used it it isn't interesting to go back in that round (every round in 10 days)

- [b] You don't need to use your skill everytime![/b] That's why choosing your partner is mandatory. Refer to the guide for more infos. 
- Sometimes you have a mini game, you just have to click as soon as you see a signal, too soon or too late and you're dead.
- For some monsters you will have to ask around. Generally monsters mentionned in emails cost 1 actions and those you ask around cost 2 actions. But it is not a rule. 

[h1] My opinion [/h1]
So all in all I did 2 rounds until now. It is kind of repeatitive in its mechanics but there are new monsters and places every round and the story seems to start after round 2. The visuals are very nice and the game is enjoyable for it's price. I am not sure yet how much it is worth as a Visual Novel or if listening to my partners thoughts will have an impact later.

TLDR: This is a JRPG with life simulation elements, not the other way around. Ignore the Steam page headline that says "Life simulation RPG", change your expectations, and you may well enjoy it. I'm glad I didn't get to refund it, even if I was unhappy at first.

I would definitely buy it on sale, however, because the publisher's behavior doesn't scream that they wanted to give the game the refinement needed for its AAA-status.

Now, for the more comprehensive notes:

I'm actually glad I waited to play this long enough to be ineligible for a refund, because the first bad impression would've stopped me from playing what lies between a good and great game for my tastes, even though it could have been more.

It's strange, because in many ways, after playing the game thoroughly, it really does feel as though, in some parts, a lot of effort and joy was put into things like the aesthetics of the world and its worldbuilding, the character portraits, the music, and even a good part of the writing.

Much of this is contravened by many other things, however, that suggest that some people either didn't like the work they got, or, more likely, that the game was rushed by investors who wanted an expensive game out without the refinement required for a good experience.

Whatever the cause, this manifests as:

-Very limited character customization; hair color and eye color, and that more or less seems to be it, much in contrast to practically every other "life sim" out there.
-Animations and choreography is often without variety, choppy, or otherwise janky, (They don't even have moving mouths!) and appears as though it was made in a rush. In the context of rushing, this makes sense, as you usually only make animations when the models have been made, which is later in the game cycle, where the suits may have become impatient. I've lost count of how many times the wacky "shaking my head" animation has been used in an already highly limited repertoire of animations.
-Almost every character seems to have the same "base" shape with certain alterations. Namely, that everyone seems to have a pretty wide set of hips, including the males.
-Very little voice-acting, mostly triggered when you go near an individual and hear them comment on something, or even just say "Hello" or "Have a safe trip", which, despite being homely, doesn't change the fact that having no voice-acting in dialogue is very suspicious for an AAA game in 2024, especially at the current price.

Weren't it for the textures in some places being surprisingly detailed, I would be easily convinced the game was from, say, 2010.

So why, in that case, do I actually quite like the game?

-Where the game lacks in model and animation variety, it manages to create quite a few individual storylines that, while not very charming at first to me, became more and more interesting as more characters were added, while the depth of the stories seemed to get deeper and touching on various serious subjects, rather than becoming diluted as more characters were added.
-Continuing on to this, while I must admit I was much less impressed by the very beginning and the last 1/10th of the story, between there it had only gotten more and more interesting, and touching on some pretty real subjects, whether or not I agree with the writers' conclusions.
-The music, as far as I'm concerned, is absolutely phenomenal. I would have to write an entire new review for the soundtrack alone, but I can say that the peacefulness of the homestead track, the ethereal/lonely feeling of the Quietus track, and the various environmental tracks ranging from excited combat-music to somber ruins-wandering music... it's just right up my alley.
-And finally, the worldbuilding and the beautifully designed environments, such as the glowing trees and crystals on the homestead, or the white granite buildings of Nemea flanked by clean water and cherry blossoms. There's a definite charm with hearing the nighttime tracks (each town + homestead have daytime and nighttime tracks) play in a rather fantastical environment.
-The combat has some satisfying moments, even if it's not that amazing overall.

For me, at least, it always takes a while to warm up to a game and start really enjoying it. I was sad and would have likely refunded the game when I first tried it. But not being allowed to do so, I committed to it, and I really enjoyed the experience.

However, and I really must stress this... it really could have been much more. If I see this as a "good, sometimes great" game, then if they introduced modding (lol, good luck) after fixing all the above issues, it would have been a "great, sometimes fantastic" game.

I don't have the biggest hopes for this franchise or the above wishes, given the reception and, frankly, "throw it out and forget about it" attitude that Square Enix seems to have taken with it. I wish to be wrong on at least one of those counts, though.

Solid, straightforward, but short point-and-click adventure. 

As I understand, this game is the sequel to “Nelson and the Magic Cauldron” (without The Journey) which I unfortunately skipped, so the beginning was a bit confusing and some story parts flew over my head. Playing in order seems necessary, as there is little to no recap given here.

The ‘puzzles’ aren’t exactly complex, so if you’re looking for a challenge, this might not be the adventure for you. This one’s more to unwind, with pretty clear solutions and little frustration. 
There is one odd (and unintentional -I would assume-) misdirection right at the start of the game though (minor spoiler):
[spoiler]In the first scene, a character tells you that a recipe / list of ingredients is found in the castle. There is no list - whatsoever. By the time you can enter the castle, you will probably have most of the ingredients already. Once you've found every ingredient (it’s a little unclear), speak to the first character again to resume the game.[/spoiler] 

You can fast-click through conversations (which is always a lifesaver when you have looping dialogue) and fast-travel via the map. I would have wished for the possibility to also just walk faster, but there is no option to do so, as far as I know.

The voice acting is amateurish, but doesn’t distract too much imo ( I played in German, so I can’t judge the English version). 
One big flaw for me is the font choice however. It’s frankly just really bad. It was annoying to read and I can’t imagine how bad it would be for people who are visually impaired in any way. 

The humor didn’t hit for me either, it’s a bit juvenile. If you watch the trailer, you can pretty much guess the tone of the game, so you’ll see if it’s your cup of tea.  
You can also see the art style. And since art is subjective, I won’t comment too much on this. You can easily find the interactive objects and I thought the switch-up in the final chapter was pretty neat.   

[b]tl;dr[/b] overall the game is fine. 
It was made by a single developer with little budget (kickstarted), which is quite a feat.

One of the better games in the cosmos 9 bundle, mostly by default, but, yeah.

As for the bundle as a whole... it really feels like a game jam that they're making you pay to play. Half the games are either tech demos or just feel... unpolished, and they're all a bit too far on the short side to be particularly engaging. And there's no real cohesion between the graphical design or the controls meaning the whole "console" gimmick doesn't really hold up. The whole set is definitely a bit overpriced and even at the 50% off price point I can't say it felt worth the time I spent with them all. 

If you do have to get any games in this pack, Triga is probably worth full price, Linelith and IFO are pretty cool albeit a bit underdeveloped and probably worth it on sale, and maaaaybe Tendy and Frequency Dissonance are worth it on sale but those are hard to recommend otherwise, and the other four are either too tedious or too underdeveloped to be even worth your time, so I'd give the bundle as a whole a pass.

I really love the graphics on this game since they are so unique and charming. And as for the puzzles, they're all cute and relatively quick. After each row TENDY moves, the other entities get a turn so to speak like a puzzle rpg kind of. However, the catch is that the moves you don't lock in (you can lock a row or the first column to make sure they are where you put them) get randomized, so you have to logic your way out of it! There were only a couple levels where I found trying to figure out a way to best the randomness annoying, but that was probably due to me not doing it the intended way, ha. Overall I loved it!

Very cute little sokoban puzzler with a "robot instruction" gimmick similar to Robo-Rally.

You get a 3-turn instruction machine, which holds 3 instructions per turn, and there are 3 types of instructions. You can lock a single turn or one instruction in each turn to reduce the randomness enough to accomplish all goals in a level.

This emphasis on "instructions" rather than "moves" is a really clever way to make the player distance themselves from the puzzle. While you are setting your instructions, you get a view of the level's start and goals, which allows you to properly plan. The randomizer encourages you to think about what moves are "necessary" on which turn.

Quite good! Some more puzzles would've been nice - there's only 15, 18 if you count alternate solutions - but also the game doesn't outstay its welcome or get frustrating at all, so I finished it feeling very satisfied.

One of the more immediate aspects that interested me in TENDY was the visual presentation. The artstyle is very reminiscent of claymation, and the way everything has a sort of idle animation while standing still adds to this being my favorite game in the CosmOS 9 bundle, visuals-wise.

Thankfully, this game is not just a looker. The way you have to manage 9 total rules to beat every level is cool on its own, but the rules are actually randomised, and you receive them 3 at a time. The game gives you the ability to either lock 3 rules to one of the 3 "steps" in the level, or to lock 1 rule in each "step", and it's this strategy element that really stood out to me in this game. It's also very cleverly built, with how there's always a way to guarantee you'll always receive the correct rules to beat a level.

Add the fact that you can make some direction choices throughout in this game and you have a very fun and pretty puzzle game. Thoroughly recommended!

However, you can lock a row or the first column to ensure a function is present when you need it.

For each puzzle in TENDY: Robot Gardener, you select nine actions you think you'll need, and then the game randomly shuffles them into three sets of three actions apiece. You can perform a set's actions in any order, but must complete one set before executing the next. The twist is that you can lock one set, or one action in each set, to guarantee three actions total. That is, the locked actions aren't randomly shuffled.

I have some reservations about this system. In many cases, I was able to progress with minimal restarts by locking the first set of actions to guarantee early critical goals, then selecting actions for the remaining (randomized) six to maximize the chances of being able to finish the job. I suppose you could spend extra time trying to find the lock configuration that guarantees victory 100% regardless of randomization- which apparently exists for every puzzle according to the game- but I was rarely motivated to do so because it often felt like that would involve tediously analyzing various random outcomes. I'm not sure the puzzles are worth that much effort for how simple they are. Strictly speaking, I might not even call them puzzles without the game's main mechanism obfuscating your efforts. Generally it felt more efficient to tolerate a bit of uncertainty.

There are at least a few puzzles that want you to lock one action in each set, and I found these more rewarding to solve cleanly, without any uncertainty. I wonder if I would have enjoyed the game more were this your only locking option. Incidentally, I never saw much use for locking the second or third set of actions, though I may have missed something.

I also feel like the concept could have been developed further. There are only three action types; you're always limited to three sets of three actions; you're pretty much always locking actions in one of two ways (as far as I can tell). This really seems to limit the puzzles' depth.

Overall, part of me thinks there's potential here with an interesting concept, but the other part of me feels like it's a roguelike deckbuilding mechanism shoehorned into the puzzle genre, and I'm not sure whether it's a good fit.

Go in with the right expectations, as it's short and minimalistic, but it's a decent effort and while nothing in it is noteworthably good, nothing is really bad, either, except for the story. I liked the mood, so it gets the thumb up, but there's room for improvement, especially since it's a little too short for the price, so what content it has needs to be better to make up for that.

Graphics are alright and make good use of color and lighting, but look a little asset-switch-y and a lot of areas seem too empty. The ending seems unfinished due to being presented as roughly sketched still images which simply doesn't fit the rest of the game and cannot convincingly be considered a matter of style, but is very obviously a matter of means. Sound is okay, could use some more unsettling background noise and while poor voice acting might end up being worse than no voice acting, I suggest giving it a try and adding them for the few spoken word parts the game has.

The puzzles focus too much on finding keys or lock codes and are too easy and generic. They work as a way to direct you through the locations, but as the only gameplay element, they are too weak. Not a fan of automatic item use, either, but I'd argue it doesn't make much of a difference since the possible points of interaction are limited anyways.

The story is where the game lost me. A woman who's hardly even a character having been killed as the personality and background motivation for some guy is such an overused and lazy trope it makes it hard to care about what is going on, especially since the reason she got killed is just as uninteresting and clichéd and way too obvious way too early anyways, so the reveal at the end seems weird and unnecessary. The game is also a little confusing and reluctant when it comes to letting you know who you actually are, what your relation to the other characters is and what you are looking for.

So there's a lot to improve, but it's probably best to use the feedback for the next game. This one's more or less mediocre, but likable, so I recommend it with a heavy grain of salt. Know what you're getting into and you can have a harmless hour or so of clicking through a moody puzzle game.

[h2]TLDR -[/h2]

Spider Man Miles Morales should have just been a DLC for Spider Man Remastered. It has less than 1/4 of the content from the original game and is sold and priced as an entirely separate experience. The movement system is identical, and the combat system is more entertaining, however, in my opinion, less complex. The story also feels rather rushed and unmoving compared to the original entry. 

[h2]Pros -[/h2]

The UI improvements compared to the OG game are stellar, and are really well done.

Miles combat abilities are extremely entertaining to me. The finisher system being its own thing tied to the combo system instead of being tied to your ability to regen health is in my opinion, a massive improvement.

Miles' Animations are very entertaining and flashy.

Same level of frame stability as the OG game, this game runs quite well on higher graphical settings besides the random graphical flashes. It's the same engine, so the optimization is very similar to the OG game.

[h2]Mids -[/h2]

Most the combat system and the movement system is directly copied from the OG game. Those who played the OG game will find the combat very familiar in this game and absolutely slaughter the early - mid game enemies. 

The music dosen't feel befitting of a superhero game to me, good tunes, but not fitting.

[h2]Cons -[/h2]

This game is INCREDIBLY short compared to the OG game, which itself, didn't even pass the 1$ per hour of enjoyment rule. This one VERY much doesn't pass that for the current asking price of 50$. At 5 hours in I've already gotten to the 60% mark of this game. There are also no DLC to pad out the content. Final thoughts after beating the game - A casual playthrough of this game will take about 7 - 10 hours at most. compleationist will take at tops, ~15 - 30 hours to get everything in this game done. Even acheivements.

Weak story compared to the OG game. Very weak. Spoilers for certain charachters and parts of the game - [spoiler]Miles and some of his rouges gallery just... Get powers for no reason out of nowhere. Miles is constantly put on a higher pedistal than Peter in terms of power scaling. Despite having been given Spider powers via the same method as Peter he develops the same exact powers as Peter and far more than Peter. Miles' "Venom" powers, on top of having an unoriginal name and not relating to the symbiote at all as far as I can tell; are never explained at all in this game. Peter litterally loses to Rhino for no reason in the intro and Miles takes him down instead. Phin invents "Programmable matter" in a run down store and it's glossed over like it's NOTHING. How did some 15~17 year old girl with very little resources make something that top scientists at Oscorp and even Parker / Otto themselves were struggling with? Nuform is never explained. How was it made? What even is it? Why does it make people sick? The Tinkerer's chase is bassically the same chase compared to the Shocker from the prior game. Despite being a normal human, the Tinkerer showcases unexplainable superhuman durability. They are not wearing any armor beyond a face mask and some armor plates on their arms. The final boss fight against the Tinkerer has very dissapointing dialogue to me. Tinkerer's powers over Miles the entire game make nearly no sense. Especially the amount of hits she lands on Miles. Story: The game follows Miles Morales as he navigates his new role as Spider-Man, filling in the shoes of fellow Spider-Man and mentor Peter Parker. The narrative is like many of the films, with Miles struggling to balance his personal life with his superhero responsibilities. The characters are well-developed, and the story arc is engaging, with a mix of heartfelt moments and high-stakes action. However, the story is noticeable shorter than the previous Spider-Man game lacking some depth.   
8/10

Game play: The game play is fluid and dynamic, with a variety of new abilities unique to Miles, such as his venom powers and camouflage. These add a fresh layer of strategy and excitement to combat and stealth. The web-swinging mechanics, a hallmark of the series, are as exhilarating as ever, feeling fresher and more refined from the first game. New skills and gadgets make meaningful improvements to combat and stealth and are true to Miles’ abilities.   
9/10

Graphics and Sound: The graphics are stunning, with detailed character models and a glistening, snow covered New York City. Being developed for the ps5, the game takes full advantage of ray tracing and high-quality textures, which looks amazing but comes at a great performance cost. The soundtrack is energetic, featuring a mix of hip-hop and orchestral music that complements the urban setting and Miles' character.
9/10

-Specs: Laptop with RTX 3060, AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, 16 GB RAM, 2T M.2 SSD
The game was mostly played at 1080p with visuals set to medium/high and ray tracing off with DLSS set to ‘quality’, causing frame rates to sit around 65 fps with jumps into the 70s and lows to 50. 

Side content: While the game is shorter than its predecessor, it's densely packed with content. Side missions, collectibles, and challenges provide ample opportunities for exploration and skill mastery. The side missions and collectibles feel a lot less ‘grindy’ than the previous Spider-Man game with more quality and less quantity. The addition of mission replayability is much a welcome feature allowing players to replay favourite missions in an instant.
9/10

Conclusion: Spider-Man: Miles Morales is a fantastic addition to the Spider-Man game series, offering a fresh and exhilarating take on the web-slinging superhero. While the story is short and lacks some depth, it is still an immensely enjoyable ‘coming-of-age’ story which includes many epic and heartfelt moments. Add in the exhilarating gameplay, stunning visuals and enhanced replayability and you get an unforgettable Spider-Man experience. 

Overall: 9/10

There are rather a lot of... "mechanics" which I think is what made this tricky for me. You've got a dodge, double-jump, a parry (and for the love of God use the parry, for your own sake - [b]do not leave it to the final boss like I did[/b]), rhythm, combos and buddies. The buddies are... something. I was over-reliant on these for most of the game until I started playing solo, using them as a support system instead, which worked out far better. I like the concept of a buddy system but for me it was more of a hindrance, an extra "step". Regardless of my criticism though, I highly recommend this game. It's a guaranteed good time, especially for rhythm game enjoyers. 8/10.

I don't usually write reviews, but hoo boy this game put me in a chokehold and has yet to let go. We're now 2 years out from the game's release so at this point most everyone who wanted to buy this has probably already bought it, but for anyone like me who has had Hi-Fi Rush on their radar for a long time but not gotten around to it yet, consider this your sign. I always knew I was going to like it, but I was wholly unprepared for just how much I not just like but love this game.

I have some very minor gripes--mostly little QoL stuff that would be time-savers when trying to complete challenges or get achievements, but they really are peanuts compared to everything this game does right. If you like rhythm games, buy this; if you like character action/hack-and-slash games, buy this; if you like fun in general, buy this. It's $30 USD for a game that could have easily been full-priced with none of the annoyances and scummy practices of modern big-budget productions. Just a really, really well made game made by a bunch of people who were really passionate about the thing they were making, and it's such a relief that Tango got pulled from the jaws of death at the last minute and lives on.

The music is awesome regardless of whether you're playing on streamer mode or not--so much so I went back and bought the original soundtrack. I actually prefer the streamer mode music if I'm being honest. The gameplay is tight and extremely satisfying with a lot of visual and audio feedback when you parry, land combos and traverse the world. If you're not the best action-game player, you can get by just fine with the basic combos, but the skill ceiling is plenty high if you decide you want to really dive into the ins and outs. It's not DMC5 Dante high, but still high. Even just walking around is enjoyable; the whole world--the movement of platforms, the blinking of lights, the cartoon-y squashing and bulging of background elements--is animated to the beat of the music, and the art direction is colorful and vibrant without being an overwhelming mess, and it doubles as an aide in keeping you on-beat.

The characters are neat visually and the writing for them is legitimately pretty funny with a lot of meta gags, niche references, and recurring bits that don't overstay their welcome and are, at worst, charmingly cringe.  It's clear that there were cuts made to several parts of the game due to time and budget, but they get creative about patching those holes and they lead to some of the funniest parts of the game. The story is nothing groundbreaking and the foreshadowing has all the subtlety of a cyborg rockstar hitting you in the face with a guitar, but it's presented with so much earnestness and fun that I didn't really care, and personally was so attached to the main crew that when the game did decide to dial back the humor and let their characters have emotional moments, they hit. 

Once your first playthrough is wrapped up, there's still a lot of do. Aside from the epilogue quest of sorts, there's multiple new game modes, a new difficulty, tons of costume unlocks, and of course there's a long, long list of challenges to check off separate from the achievements (though there's a lot of overlap). I've had a lot of fun just challenging myself to 100% the game well after finishing off the story.

There's just a lot to love about this game, and knowing a sequel is apparently in the works makes me extremely happy. My brain tells me this is like a 9, maybe 9.5, but in my soul this game is a perfect 10.

It honestly saddens me to write this a bit; I want to cheer on Hexadrive in their first proper solo effort; there's clearly a lot of production value here, it's all very pretty and stylish; and the implication if I'm understanding all this correctly seems to be that this is the 1st part of a plan to make a MOBA called "Star League"; a kind of gameplay foundation which makes a lot of sense when you know that context; you go out to defend against waves of enemies coming through lanes to destroy your core, you push up to fight turrets to eventually take down the enemies core (in the form of a boss fight), and the combat is a big 3d interpretation of moba combat with long skill cooldowns, an emphasis on energy (mana) management and even an item shop when you warp back to base...
If this was a moba it'd be a unique starting point... but it isn't a moba, it's a PvE "Tower Offense" thing and... maybe the later missions resolve the issues listed in the rest of this review but, in all honesty the 1st hour of this game has been nothing but a slog to get through...

 The onboarding is abysmal with some text-box tutorials that honestly don't really teach you how to play the game that much while also saying a lot about using your ingame currency for per-session upgrades and the fact you need to use that currency to buy the mechs for AI teammates in a session....it's a bit weird but once you get in-game and finally start playing it....it becomes incredibly tedious. Well I say that, the gameplay itself is actually okay, a neat, if a little stiff, take on moba combat and cooldowns and shopping for items in a 3d space where the concepts of up and down are also a thing.

However there are 3 Central issues that basically ruin anything this game is doing alright:
1: The rate of getting resources to buy items is glacial: at least in the 1st maps I played that fun feeling of fighting enemies, getting resources, and powering up your character is just nothing which stops you from feeling any substantial sense of strategy or growth or basically anything at all. It doesn't even seem like the enemies are dropping the resources for your shop or at least not at any substantial rate, they are however dropping cubes that you use to power up a passive rate for your shopping resources...it's a very unsatisfying system.

2: The enemy cannot handle the concept of strafing: be it minion, boss, or turret, strafe and shoot and you'll win any fight eventually; and because you don't spawn minions naturally (although yes you can go to a mysterious hidden poll that isn't on the map nor really explained and it will spawn 1 small wave of minions) this means, at least as far as the turrets are concerned, this behaviour is somewhat intentional otherwise the game would be impossible; so most of your game is just hold strafe and left-click until eventually the high health turret dies. It works on the boss too, your only danger is time investment....this is beyond boring.

3: The balancing between single-player and multiplayer is abysmal: Because of the weird "buying AI" thing that kinda discourages you to and with the game making no real mention of it, on my first match I went into single player alone, and it was a slow slog of just waiting to eventually kill these turrets that feared the concept of the a and d keys. It took a lot of time, eventually by the end I had some starter items, I was high enough level to have an ultimate ability, and slowly but surely over the course of about 30-40 minutes or so killed the boss with incredible strafing skills. Then I went in a multiplayer match with 1 other human and 2 AIs. It took 8 minutes, we never had to go back for items; we just strafe killed every turret and the end boss and we were done before we even got our ultimates....Both matches were not fun for very different reasons.

Look I want to cheer on Star League if and when they make it; I mean there's a cool traditional moba meets flying anime mech hybrid here that could be really cool to see one day, maybe not necessarily my thing but I'd be happy to see it and give it a go... But this thing, this format....it just isn't fun. It's clearly not low effort, I mean playing that 1st map multiple times had different layouts and stuff and that was kinda cool but....it was so boring......it was insufferably boring on my own, and then immediately tediously simple with others... Sorry Hexadrive, I want to cheer you on but I cannot in any good conscience recommend this game to basically anyone, at least not in this form, sorry :(

The problem arises when you realize that you can't reliably automate aether until late game, long after you are required to grind a TON of things to get there.   Overall the flow of progress needs work.  

It's a cute game bogged down by needless extra grind, not because you need to grind to set up your automatons, but because everything you need to unlock comes from villager quests that ask for a TON of resources.  

Example: So you build this big automation to fulfill the quest, and then you never need anything near that level of production for your own personal use.  So you end up having all of these scattered productions across the map that are all at full capacity, just looping waiting for you to use a few of that resource.  An example of this is to unlock the ability to craft scouty sparks and hauling sparks from your workstation, you need to turn in 180 rocky sparks and 120 carry sparks.  After finishing that quest, I now have a dedicated automation making rocky sparks that I will never use more than 10 or 20 of.   There's just no reason to automate this except for the quest.  Many quests are like this. There needs to be a better balance between what you use to build with, and the quantity you need for quests.

My other complaint is that half of the automation buildings need to be built on specific locations (ancient spots of some sort) and these are sparsely scattered around the map, most of the time not near the resources you need them for, wood and stone.  This means that if you get a bad map seed, trying to work around these locations becomes tedious and not fun at all.   You can't modify the terrain at all, so if these sites are wedged too close to the edge of a cliff, too bad, you can't use it.  The game would be 100 times better if they got rid of this ancient site building location requirement altogether.

The games that started it all! Your first experience with the Creatures games will involve shuttling cute little "Norns" around, trying to teach them words and the skills necessary to survive on their own in their simulated little worlds. But once you spend some time with them, you'll realize that the "virtual life" engine goes way deeper than the veneer of cuteness -- these games intentionally allow you to peek behind the curtains and play around with the underlying "genetics" and scripts that make these little creatures tick.

Creatures 1 is a simpler engine with fewer words and items to interact with, and somewhat less intelligent Norns. But don't be fooled: there is plenty to explore and a ton of fun to be had guiding these Norns around! Be wary of unfamiliar plants, and unless you know what you're doing, try to keep your Norns away from the Grendel, for both of their sakes!

Creatures 2 introduces a bigger world space, smarter norns (well, kind of...), many more objects, some new tech, and a new species: Ettins! This entry is also where community-created content really took off back in the day, and there are plenty of new breeds (my favorite are "Kai Norns" and "Boney Grendels"), genetics (look up "Canny Norns" if you want actual smarter Norns), and injectable objects (check out creaturescaves.com or creatures.wiki) to keep you coming back for new and totally emergent gameplay experiences. (There are also a ton of community-created mods for Creatures 1, but not nearly as many as Creatures 2 overall.)

One last, hugely important warning: both of these games are very difficult to run on modern PCs, and it may take a ton of troubleshooting and testing in order to get them fully working. (Like right clicking on all of the EXEs and selecting 16 bit colors, etc. Tools like "DXWnd" might also be able to help.) If you don't have time or patience for that, you might be better off going with Creatures Docking Station and the Creatures 3 Steam DLC.

Creatures: The Albian Years is a compilation package that includes Creatures 1 and its standalone expansion, Creatures: Life Kit #1. This collection provides an opportunity for both new and nostalgic players to experience the origins of the Creatures series. Let's delve into a review of Creatures: The Albian Years.

Creatures: The Albian Years faithfully replicates the gameplay mechanics of the original Creatures 1, offering a virtual pet simulation experience with genetically engineered creatures called Norns. Players are tasked with caring for and guiding these adorable creatures, ensuring their well-being, and observing their behavior as they navigate their digital ecosystem.

The game's genetics system, which was innovative for its time, remains intact in Creatures: The Albian Years. Breeding and genetic manipulation allow you to witness the hereditary traits passed down through generations of Norns, adding a layer of depth and experimentation to the gameplay. It's a joy to observe how Norns evolve and adapt to their surroundings.

However, the user interface and controls may feel clunky and outdated compared to modern games, requiring some adjustment and patience. Additionally, the steep learning curve and lack of clear objectives might be overwhelming for newcomers to the series. Without proper guidance or tutorials, understanding the intricacies of the game and effectively caring for your Norns can be a daunting task.

Creatures: The Albian Years includes the expansion, Creatures: Life Kit #1, which introduces additional content and features to enhance your gameplay experience. The Life Kit offers new objects, environments, and toys for your Norns, expanding the possibilities for interaction and enrichment within the game.

Furthermore, the collection allows you to access the Creatures Community, an online platform where you can share and download user-created content. This opens up a wealth of additional genetic breeds, agents, and modifications created by the passionate Creatures community, extending the longevity and variety of the game.

Graphically, Creatures: The Albian Years retains the charm of its original release, with its pixelated art style and colorful environments. While the visuals may not match modern standards, they exude a nostalgic appeal and create a distinct atmosphere within the game's world.

The sound design, consisting of delightful chirps and cries from the Norns, adds an endearing touch to the overall experience. However, the limited variety of sound effects can become repetitive over time.

Creatures: The Albian Years serves as a nostalgic trip down memory lane for fans of the original Creatures game. It faithfully recreates the core gameplay and genetics system that made the series a beloved classic. However, newcomers may find the outdated user interface and steep learning curve to be off-putting.

The inclusion of the Creatures: Life Kit #1 expansion and access to user-generated content through the Creatures Community add value and extend the gameplay experience. It allows for further customization and exploration within the Albian world.

If you have a fondness for retro games or are seeking a virtual pet simulation with a unique genetic twist, Creatures: The Albian Years is worth considering. Despite its technical limitations and learning curve, it offers a charming and nostalgic journey into the origins of the Creatures series.

Everything from the little [i]whoosh[/i] of moving a piece, to the adorably anthropomorphized designs of the tiles, to the compact minimalism of the game’s interface, is perfectly calibrated to make for an exercise in absolute delight. 

I will say that it’s not particularly hard to hit a wall with the learning curve here (it took me a solid 6 years of consistently playing just to go from getting occasional 768s to occasional 1536s), and that some might consider the game overpriced, particularly if they’re not as into just fiddling with the perfectly tuned mechanics again and again, as they are into constantly reaching new skill levels at a frequent pace…. but considering all the years and all the time I’ve spent playing this, whether I was at home, at school, or just out and about, I thought grabbing this here was an apt way to show my appreciation for all the pure, bite-sized fun I’ve gotten from playing around with this game for so many years. 

Another excellent version of a downright wonderful game.

Multiversus could have been the perfect F2P fighting game. When it first launched, it was fast, felt great to play, and was full of charm - a great visual style, a fun and funny varied character roster and lots of potential. The developers clearly couldn't keep pace with the live service content machine - the same thing that kills so many live service games, and they decided to pretend the game had been in Beta and removed it from stores for a year to work on things. 

The problem is, when it came back it was actually worse in literally every way - the gameplay was slowed down and felt like you were underwater, they made the economy significantly worse and took away your resources and choices from the original launch, they took away a bunch of your rematch options and post-match stats to keep bad players from realizing how poorly they were doing, and despite taking away a game that people had paid $100 for a year to work on things, the content slowed down immediately afterwards again so the team could go back to trying to make fundamental mechanical changes again to reverse the damage they had done. 

It's no surprise they're pulling the plug on this game, but it is an absolute shame - they had the perfect template for something special, but WB and PFG made the wrong choices at literally every potential junction. Too slow to update, while shooting itself in the foot with every patch. This was one of my favorite experiences of the generation at its initial launch, but as it dies a quiet, unmarked death, I can only remember it as one of its biggest disappointments instead.

Ever played that flying game in Wii Sports Resort and thought "I'd love a whole game of this"?

If so, this is it.

The game is cute, the characters have fun personalities and Mika is a likeable character from the start.

Unfortunately I couldn't get used to the camera sensitivity, it was too fast for me even after changing it in the settings, and I got motion sickness from playing the game. Flying didn't feel fun, and even though it makes sense because of the story progression, it just wasn't what I was expecting -- it was more like gliding rather than flying (I only played until [spoiler]the light broom upgrade[/spoiler] though, not sure how that changes with the other upgrades). I ended up requesting a refund for it.

The game is overall fine. I spent almost 8 hours trying to 100% the game, and I'd say by the end I'd probably have given it a neutral rating if that was an option. 

I'd say my biggest grip with the game is probably the writing. There's a lot of painful and cringe dialogue for most of the characters, and they're all almost entirely forgettable. I don't even remember most of their names. The two "villain" characters are just cartoonishly evil, and incredibly one-dimensional. I get that this is probably supposed to be simple kid's game, but that doesn't mean characters have to lack depth.

The rest of the game is otherwise fine, the delivery aspect is an interesting concept, although I feel the execution is somewhat lacking. There's dozens of deliveries, but not much variety to the debuffs that you have to account for. Either the parcel is fragile, and/or you can't get it wet. I feel like more could have been done to switch things up, like impacting flying mechanics based on weight or shape, or something like maintaining a parcel's temperature or humidity. Just anything to help keep things fresh. They didn't even particularly use the timed delivery very often. 

As for the controls, I didn't find it particularly fun to fly around, just passable. The vast majority of the broom's move-sets are tied to static objects on the map, like launchers, windtunnels, and vortices. The actual broom doesn't have much it can do in of itself. other than a fairly weak dash that gives you a small upward lift (which you can only use when on the ground or when touching a special static object) or a weak dive.  I actually found it more productive to unequip the broom and just fall and try to catch myself by re-equipping it. So I never ended up even using the dedicated button for diving that much, even for the races. It just doesn't give enough downward momentum.

Overall, it didn't really overstay its welcome. The game to me just feels like a prototype, one with a lot more potential than is displayed here.

You move using a rocket on your fist that regains fuel slowly over time, when on ground, and when going fast, which encourages you to move fast and learn how to play smoothly. And you also have a small course correction tool that aids you in that.
The challenge so far for me is in being able to precisely go where you want, using enough fuel - thinking of the best place to bounce / land, particularly so on sloped grounds, and also being patient enough you don't fall down.
And it's all really fun! Really love how bouncy you are, how fast you can go, and the balanced power the rocket can give you.

My only concern would be the content - after you beat it, what is there to do?
Well you'd want to get the achievements, and then try speedrunning a bit or maybe even mastering the game so you can practically smoothly fly around everywhere. But then what?
Well thankfully the dev(s) have plans for more levels, and some way for user generated stuff, like steam workshop.


Regardless this is a really fun, rather polished game with great difficulty that reminds  me of other great difficult games like getting over it, and jump king. I really do enjoy playing this game and therefore recommend it, but I want you to know what you're getting into.  Nothing is wrong with the code, the gameplay, or the visuals.  The problem for me lies in the very concept of the game.  The Wratch's Den tried to blend roguelite elements with base building, and the result was unfortunately not very fun in the end.  The point of building [b]anything at all[/b] is so that it lasts (or until you can at least sell it, in the case of real estate agencies).  This conflicts with the game's roguelite traits, as you literally [i]can't[/i] make your base last forever, because the invading heroes will just keep on coming and keep getting stronger.  The Wratch and his army literally cannot improve fast enough to keep up.  From my perspective, it's pointless to put time and effort into building a base (and therefore making it [i]yours[/i] ^^) when the only victorious outcome for you, The Wratch, is to find the Gems: or die at the hands of your enemies trying to defend the home that you've literally built from the ground up with your minions.  However, the rectifying factor for me is the price.  I purchased The Wratch's Den when it was on sale for $0.18; a completely acceptable and fair price for the quality of game that I received.  

So?  Don't expect more than $5 worth of entertainment from a $5 product.  However, The Wratch's Den is a good game.  Significant time and effort were obviously put into making this game, and I can always respect that.  I also respect the devs for pricing their game right.  Give the devs a couple cents if it's on sale and the price of a coffee if it isn't.  That's the least they deserve.

The bell mechanic itself is an innovative take on the death-bombing mechanic, one that takes precision to leverage to its fullest. One can draw a parallel to the collectible UFOs from the Touhou game of the same name, in which survivability and points are trade-offs when deciding how to make use of them. Not very friendly in terms of accessibility. Retro-themed or not, that's no excuse to:

* Throw in a lot of button mashing games, enough that I went and bound single and multiple button turbos via Steam's controller profiles. My days of playing Smash Melee and/or Mario Party are long gone, and I have low tolerance for thoughtless inputs/mashes.
* Have several tests where one must quickly identify colors of similar shades, some of which are mild or even imperceptible to me. I'm red-green colorblind and it got in the way more than once.
* Put in a mandatory sequence of ~9 randomized button presses while a very annoying tone plays (unless changing the difficulty from Original) within a 5 second timer every time a game is failed. While trivial for me to perform, it wasn't trivial for my SO, and between having to do this and having to watch every game's intro every run, there's many games where you spend more time doing this than playing the game! There's even a Steam thread where someone brought this issue up and the developer was entirely unsympathetic, claiming that's how retro games are...which is a load of bs.
* Have several cases of "Gotcha!" where if you haven't played the game before, information you're not privy to will have you dead man walking, such as off-screen obstacles where you need to be in certain positions or speeds yet have no clue beforehand that that's the case.
* Balance is all over the place, with some games being trivial regardless of difficulty setting and others being difficult even on Easy.
* The boss of Story's second chapter induced motion sickness on me. Its one of those 16-bit era first person dungeon POVs, with an awkward camera and generic walls. You can't skip boss fights, so this hard-locked me out of getting to more content for over an hour, until my SO was able to get one successful clear.

And this is only having seen the first 60 of 100 games.

Its not for hating retro - I grew up in the 8-bit and 16-bit eras, and have been exposed to and enjoyed games that predate those eras. But most of those games don't go out of their way to annoy like this game does. And if you're thinking this is more of a WarioWare style game, the pacing is wrong for that too - controls are not intuitive without hints enabled, game intros/outros take too long, and ultimately its less about reaction speed and more about filler.

I'll probably attempt to finish due to sunk cost, but I don't anticipate enough changes happening to make this a positive review in the future.

Regarding the developer's comment:

1) At the time of this review, I have seen 60 games. Of those, I can think of several off memory that rely on button mashing (jungle escape, cat dinner, baseball, race with water hurdles) where the main point of the minigame is the speed of the mashing. There are others where it can be argued, such as the tortoise/hare race where a preset order of keys need repeated, that mashing may or may not be present.

3) The problem is when I want to play original difficulty without the added tedium. My experience is that the "cheat code" sequence is both time wasted, and in the case of the partner I'm playing with, very stressful. But if I don't pick original, letting them play the Easy half and me the Normal/Hard half, then we can't share the experience.

To borrow a comparison from a well known game, think of L-canceling from Smash Melee. It was already correct to do, it wasn't hard to do, but it must be done since failing to do so doubled your landing lag. In essence, it made players do extra inputs that had no purpose other than to be mandatory, since anyone decent at the game wouldn't mess them up.

Your cheat code system is just like this. Listen to an annoying sound while inputting arbitrary presses, and even if I mess up, there's enough time to do it again...except for players who aren't so fast and get screwed over by such a system existing. It serves no purpose other than to gatekeep and/or waste a player's time.

6) I have since found that the game does not handle mirroring well unless I both turn off G-sync and force 60 FPS through Nvidia Control Panel. If I do that, the framerate is more stable, at the cost of having to change it back whenever playing unmirrored on my main monitor. While G-sync is not something you have control over, there should be a setting in the options for setting a frame limit, and ideally for toggling V-sync as well.

I hate not recommending a game by a small dev and I did have a bit of fun, but there's some fundamental problems with the game's design and marketing that make my review feel more like a warning.

All the store page videos make it look like WarioWare with lots of short mini games. Most of DUCK is that and these microgames are pretty fun. Even when things get difficult, the original mode gives you an opportunity to enter a cheat code to replay and easy mode just lets you retry it regardless.  

Then you get to the boss levels. They generally feel like really polished game jam submissions, but some are way too long. I paid 8.99 hoping for a game with fun, brisk mini games, not a 2D forced movement precision platforming level that requires you to memorize a very specific route through a pretty large level. So much trial and error, just too frustrating. Another boss game is a first person labyrinth where you collect some stuff, which the dev assures us it can be completed in under one minute in the discussion boards. It certainly takes a lot longer when you don't know the layout and have to memorize it, although once I figured out the audio hints it was a lot easier to blow through.

Nobody who purchases a product expecting microgames wants to spend so much time figuring out mazes or being frustrated by a level that requires so much memorization to get through the somewhat strict time limits, although the easy mode setting is very forgiving compared to the original mode. I guarantee this game would have closer to 100% positive user reviews if the extra long boss games were designed to be shorter.

Most people are better off avoiding DUCK. It's worth it if you like WarioWare, just expect it to not be very fun sometimes.

One of the most influential works of art in the modern age. Find the Sunbed presents you with a compelling story that asks the real questions. It captures our innate desire to conquer the unknown. It musters our innovative minds to overcome obstacles that it itself creates on our way. This is more than a game. It is an experience. A one in a lifetime at that. But let's return to the beginning for a moment. The game starts very humbly. We are not given any sophisticated quest of saving a kingdom or our beloved ones, we are simply tasked with finding an everyday object, the titular sunbed. But why do we need to find it we don't know. It is one of the more profound questions the game asks us. Why? Why do we strive so much to find the object that we can easily live without. Why do we sacrifice hundreds of lives in a pursuit of a simple piece of furniture. This, of course, is a commentary on our species as a whole. It describes the human nature of destruction for one's gain. It describes what leaders of empires were ready to sacrifice to gain resources. It describes, what we, simple citizens are ready to sacrifice to gain something. For some it might be their family, as they spend more and more time at work, for others it might be their health, as they wither in the pursuit of fame and glory. Throughout the whole ordeal, what this game reveals to be, the player starts asking himself, is it worth it? Is the sunbed even real? What will happen with me when I finally reach it? Will I finally be happy? This questions slowly sink into his mind until he finally confronts them at the inevitable end and only then he is able to draw conclusions from the whole journey. What is left of him then is something more than a man. A man becomes something more enlightened. Something that grew out of the primitive shell of a human mind and began to understand what the universe truly is. 

In other words, this game is a masterpiece and you need to play it.

[h1]A decent stealth assassin or maybe a puzzle game[/h1]

[i]The Psychoduck[/i] is a remake of the now-removed [/i]Psychoduck[/i], with slightly better graphics and improved UI.

In the game, you are a duck who collects crowns, worn by herons, so the psychotically logical thing to do is to kill them and take their precious belongings. But since herons can fly and they are guarded by frogs, you need to be sneaky about it.

[h1]Increasing complexity[/h1]

First few levels teach you to approach the heron silently ('shift' for sneaky mode) and to avoid the gaze of the frog guards. Running, while faster, will more easily get you caught and lose, restarting a level.

It takes a bit of time to figure out how the sight of the frogs works. They see pretty far towards sides, but only a bit towards north and south. Then, it's often possible to pass a guard at a daring place. In mid-game it often offers a couple of approaches, and as the levels get larger they become more non-linear.

Tutorial screens welcome new mechanics every few levels, including boxes to push, bushes to hide in, a distracting device to lure guards, and some travel and block mechanisms to bolster level design. For full completion, one needs also to be on the look out for snail shells, which are sometimes hidden away from the path. If you miss any, you can always return to find them using a handy level selection screen.

[h1]Small annoyances[/h1]

The line-of-sight of the frog guards caused me two kinds of grievances, one neutral and one frustrating.

First the neutral one: the levels sometimes have enough space for you to sneak riiight past a guard, above or below, in a way that's probably intentional given that there usually was another clear path to success. This way, it's possible to sometimes skip small or occasionally large portions of the level.

The frustrating one is that initially it's hard to know how well the frogs see, causing many level restarts early on. A sight cone like e.g. in the excellent [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] games would've been useful for this purpose, though admittedly it would've made the game way easier. Still, this would have fitted the first tutorial levels nicely.

This remake introduced icons to show guards off-screen, a handy feature that I applaud, since in the first version it was easy to walk into a guard without realizing before it was too late.

[h1]Just long enough[/h1]

The game mechanics are exciting only for a couple of levels. Good that the game is only 50 levels long, or it would have needed something more going for it. I think this was pretty much a perfect length for the game.

For me, the completion was about 2h 40min. Price is quite fair, particularly on sale (I got it for €1/-50%), so it's a good enough recommendation for me.

As a longtime fire emblem fan, all I have to say about this game is that it is great, at times bordering on amazing, especially for the small development team. It deserves to be recognised among the best SRPG games imho. 

The good:
-Tactical combat is both accessbible and much deeper than fire emblem, requiring constant smart use of units and their positioning and active abilities and cooldowns, which they get from both their classes and equippable items.

-Amazing class variety, each unit can upgrade their class twice with 3 choices each time. While there is a shared pool of classes between characters, each individual class is genuinely powerful and made me excited to use it. 

-On hard/veteran difficulty, it is a genuine challenge and very difficult to complete optimally, with all side objectives met. The difficulty curve itself is good, punishing for mistakes but also very rewarding of tactical play. 

-The campain has a lot of choices you can make which influence what rewards and characters you get for your actions. 

-The campaign is lengthy, taking me about 40 hours to finish on hard difficulty. 

-The overall writing and characterization of characters is great for the genre. Especially in the second half, there is real tension and made me want to keep seeing 'what happens next'. Most characters feel more like real, layered persons than most fire emblem quirky characters. There are no anime tropes but rather realistic midieval ones. 

-The music is great and has some amazing themes like the main menu theme. 

-The visuals are good enough for in indy game. The character art itself is the highlight. 

-The developers are very active and approachable/friendly in fixing the post-release bugs, of which there aren't many. 

-Imho, the overall quality for the price is great. 

The bad:

-My main gripe with the current release is that the last quarter of the game felt rushed and stale gameplay-wise to me, not living up to the first 75%. It relies purely on the tension of the main narrative by that point and on large-scale battles. However, there seem to be no more side objectives or collectable rewards like there are in earlier chapters. Also the support conversations drastically reduce in number, as well as that there are no more real changes in how to outfit your units past the 70% point. 

-There are some balance issues between classes with some clearly being better than others, but there is no way to respec your characters into different classes. 
 
-Ther are mostly minor post-release bugs, which are being worked on. 

-Being unable to restart the chapter instantly from inside the chapter is a bit clunky. There for some reason is nu 'reset' button, instead you have to go back to the main menu first to restart the chapter, then sit through the pre-battle story again (though it is skippable). 

-There is no voice acting outside the narrator. Which I can understand for the small budget, but similar small budget games like Sympohy of War at least had a few in-battle lines for each character which added a lot of extra personality and immersion. 

Overall rating: 8,8/10 (amazing for the price, teamsize and genre). If the last quarter of the game had the quality of the first three, it would be a 9,5/10 for me. If the bugs were resolved and some element of voice acting was added, it would be a 10/10.
