One of the best turn based games I've played in a long time. If you are a fire emblem or battle brothers fan this game is a fantastic combination of them.

Positives:
*Overall plot is very solid while there are a stumbles along the way for a first game I can say it blows most of the genre out of the water.
*Dialogue is well above where I expected it to be. The characters have fairly distinct and strong personalities with their own wants and morals. Even better the recruitments aren't weird like many other series, everything from Those Who Rule flows reasonably well
*Length is a solid 20 chapters and when I got to the point when I started thinking I hope this doesn't go on too much longer it wrapped up the story. I would say depending on how deep you want to dive into Min Maxing or restart because of deaths it will take anywhere between 20-40 hours
*Combat was definitely a challenge at the highest difficulty. The game can throw more reinforcements at you than you think that you can handle but played well you definitely can. AI is fairly solid which is a huge plus.
*Dev has been very responsive to the community and has been adding QoL upgrades/bug fixes like an absolute mad lad.

Negatives:
*More content in between chapters, side quests, or conversations has been marked on and the dev has told the community that it will be coming in the next series of patches, so this will likely not be a negative for long.
*The level of character art fluctuates, you can tell which artworks were done first and which were done last as the quality is transparent. Not a big deal but it might annoy some players
*Objectives in combat are usually reach this point or kill all enemies, and survive for most chapters. Would be nice to have a defeat enemy boss for a few of the chapters.

There is perma-death (which you can toggle off at the start of a game), but also if any one of your 3 main characters dies, that ends that tactical battle and you have to restart the game and re-fight that entire tactical battle all over again. I would prefer either a "better" more standard save system (and let the player decide how they want to play (e.g., save scum), or an option (like the toggle  of perma-death off or on) to toggle off or on the "hero's death ends the battle" to the "hero's death doesn't end the battle" and they are just knocked unconcious like all the other mercs in their team, lol.

Really great game. If you have ever played Fire Emblem or enjoyed any TRPG, this is a no-brainer. I've been playing since early February 2025, I see a lot of negative reviews - many about bugs (and from January). I'm into chapter 8 -- have not had a single bug, crash or instance of that. I think the developer is really hot to fix and put out updates here. 

Game is fairly difficult - with plenty of options to dial up or down. Permadeath on or off. Casual, medium, hard modes available from the start. I'm playing my first run through no-permadeath, medium. I win every mission but it's not a cakewalk. 

The underlying mechanics have what I would say is a sound foundation. You have a handful of classes (defenders, strikers, healer, archer) which upgrade at least once into a more specialized or hybrid role. Also a handful of weapon types each with their own niche or role. Shields in this game are pretty clutch (offering basically some temporary hit points which refresh rapidly). It all works very well and I think lays the groundwork for more if there are ever DLCs (free or otherwise) or a potential sequel that has non-human combatants, mages and such. Although, that said, I'm probably not even 1/2 point in my first playthrough. 

Missions have some variety. I've seen games with more but a lot of games with less. It's not always kill everyone, there are stand your ground, escape missions (and I've only played 8, I think 20+ is the overall number). 

I played this exclusively on the Steam Deck. It works but there is not currently official support and there is plenty of hard to read small text. I also think the UI is not necessarily clunky, but is an area where improvement(s) could be had. That said, it plays perfectly fine As-Is on the Steam Deck, even without official support, and I generally am not crazy about using the track pads to get around -- but it works.

This is so damn good, I could not put it down. It's in fact so good, that i did not even finish the game (yet), i just had to recommend it. Sure, neither graphics nor art design are anything like Baldur's Gate 3, Wartales, Xcom or Banner Saga, this is, obviously, a lovable indie game, but the tactical combat, the mature writing and this constant flow of achievements (level ups, new abilities, new classes, new weapons with new possibilities, new members to the party etc.) just kept me going and going! Also: no bugs, no freezes, no stuttering, no clipping, nothing. This runs smoothly. Can this be the new norm please? 

Regarding game play: sure, dialog and fighting, fighting and some chatter, then fighting, that's mostly all you do but, again, damn, do i enjoy this: fighting has all the best elements of similar tactical strategy games like Banner Saga, Expeditions: Rome, Fire Emblem, Wartales: good positioning and remembering the abilities of your squad is key, here similar also to Xcom although this game does not really have any management (of a base, a camp or something): after a fight there's banter between the (really) well-written squad members, there's some dialog to move the intriguing story forward and then you can better your equipment if you have enough money. To some that may seem minimalist but it really works in that nothing distracts you from concentrating on the varied battlefields and new tactics. 

Room for improvement: 
- more customization would be nice (armors, coloring, appearance on the battlefield). 
- In a well written, character-driven story like this a silent customizable hero wouldn't make much sense, but if there's a sequel I'd love the option (if the writing continues on this level or even get's close to Shephard in Mass Effect). 
- There's some story interaction between some members of your crew but there could be more, I especially miss interactions on the battlefield and, like the bonds in Xcom between soldiers that share fight experience side by side, consequences for those decisions: Marcus and X are always side by side? Give them defense plus 3 if that's the case in future battles. Y is not chosen for a battle the third time in a row? Give him plus 5 Attack for the next battle because he really wants to earn the respect of the commander - or something like that.

All in all: amazing game!! Buy it, have fun, gift it to friends that love the genre (or this mix of a mature story and really good tactical combat)

Edit: Finished the game, i stand by my judgement: an awesome and satisfying game from start to finish. Now the sequel please.

If you are a Fire Emblem fan, particularly a fan of the older games, you'll probably have a good time with this one. It makes some innovative changes to the genre, and the moment to moment gameplay is very satisfying. This game allows you to create some builds from promotions and item choices that create an overall much more interesting build path than seen in the FE games. I highly recommend playing it with no permadeath on, however, as there is no in-chapter saving system at the time of this review. Other than that, the usability of some areas is lacking, but it's not enough to severely damage the experience.

There is a lot of room for improvement and I look forward to a sequel that addresses some of these issues. Some of the levels can get tedious as you move your big army of units forward together. In general, the level design is a step down from the mainline FE games. The unit portrait art is fantastic, but the unit promotions don't look all that interesting. The story is passable, but not good. The diplomatic intrigue of FE games is there, but it's missing the strong characters of FE. The soundtrack is amazing.

Overall, this definitely scratches the traditional older Fire Emblem itch.

Really enjoying this game so far!  I'm a long time Fire Emblem fan, and this does a great job of providing a very similar experience on PC, while also innovating in a few distinct ways.  The creator has implemented a very cool flanking system in addition to using a hex grid which I think has enhanced the strategy overall.  I'm about 4 hours in and definitely looking forward to playing more.  I've been collecting a lot of my thoughts so far, which I'll include below.

Good:
1. Windowed mode works very well and I like that the game allows me to select the exact dimensions I want.
2. Really like the flanking system. Makes positioning my units even more interesting and strategic.
3. Nice artwork. The characters and environments look great, especially during the dialogues.
4. Enjoying the music so far, and seems fitting for each situation.
5. I like that alt shows all enemy range, and that I can click on enemies to see their specific movement and attack zones.
6. Zone of Control feels really impactful and I love using it strategically to limit enemy movement and protect my support characters.
7. The shop and forging feels significant.  So far forging weapons has been more cost effective than buying upgraded ones, but time will tell if that continues to be true.

Quality of life improvements:
1. Enemy actions start almost immediately after the player's final action.  It would be nice if there was a bit of delay or transition.
2. Dialog boxes and character models are increased in size to the point that their heads get cut off when using a wide screen monitor or using windowed mode with widescreen dimensions.  I was able to work around this by setting a narrow window when starting the chapter from the main menu, then expanding to my desired size.  When doing this, the dialog box and characters shift to the left side of the screen which is a mild annoyance. In addition, the dialog only advances if I click in the area of the characters and dialog box, but not to the sides of them.
3. Would love to be able to see enemy movement with alt even when in the middle of a characters turn
4. I was initially very confused about attack order, as sometimes it seemed like certain enemies were attacking out of turn.  Once I studied the characters in more detail, I learned about the "First Strike" ability some characters have.  This might be worth including a tool tip, as it was frustrating to me in early levels (particularly the first training battle).
5. Sometimes left click closes tip boxes, sometimes right click.  That seems inconsistent.
6. For shield and weapon benefits, what counts as "facing" an enemy? Is it the front three hexes, or only the one directly in front of my character?
7. Perhaps add an animation or indicator to show that reinforcements are coming from buildings, etc.
8. It would be nice if mend and heal effects could just be targeted with a mouse click on an ally, just like weapon attacks, instead of have to select the ability first.
9. It would be nice if after moving without performing an action, a single mouse click ended the players turn and went to the direction facing stage, instead of having to click the end turn icon.
10. Skirmishers don't get a second movement after opening chests.  Not sure if this is intended or not.
11. Slyker's character model for the dialogues looks slightly too big compared to the others, particularly his head.

My feelings on this game are complex. It's difficult to write this review. I've enjoyed the game in spite of its bugs and oddities. And the developer appears to be very responsive on the forums. Unfortunately, the game is currently plagued by a number of bugs and painful design decisions. 

[b]NB: It is important to add here that the dev has been very active responding to bugs and issues. The fact is I can't stop playing this game, in spite of the bugs and issues. I give this game a cautious thumbs-up after 35 hours. [/b]

Those Who Rule is a labor of love. It's a simple game, with a very solid core of tactical combat. I appreciate that the dev focused on fighting - you aren't taming animals or picking herbs mid-combat. The game wears its Fire Emblem roots on its sleeve, but does - I think - a better job of making the "rock / paper / scissors" more fun. Very few character builds have hard counters, so you aren't constantly juggling the correct weapon. The resulting combat is fun and surprisingly deep.

The writing and art were professionally done. I applaud a solo dev for paying for real content rather than throwing AI slop at us. The story is fine. The minute-by-minute dialog is actually... quite good! Some characters have real personalities in quick vignettes and it's nice that the developer eschewed standard anime tropes.

Maps are different enough to feel fresh, and don't have too many gimmicks. There are a few maps that are pretty severe difficulty spikes (CH7 and CH15 come to mind). One or two maps have an annoying addition - like rescuing villagers - but you can actually safely ignore that as long as you hit the objective. 

Kudos to the dev for a deep, thoughtful, tactics-forward game!

Unfortunately, there are negatives.

The UI in the game is [i]atrocious[/i]. To shop, you need to access two menus, back out to view your, access a different menu, and access a sub-menu. Information you need is hidden behind several sub-menus. Information about your character's proficiency is not available on the buy screen. Upgrading equipment is yet another menu dive. There's no reason for this; the game is not a ported console game. 

The poor UI shows up again in battles. You can't see information about characters - weapon skills, class info, even active skills... unless you mouseover them and enter yet another menu. If you want to see attack range, it's another menu. You get no notification when a character dies, so if you look away for a moment (say, to get the cat off the table) and look back, you could have lost characters. There's no way to access a roster. No battle log. I found myself ignoring the tactical information because I just couldn't be bothered diving into menus.

I have found several softlocks where I was unable to select any character. Even hitting End Turn did not work. I had to alt-F4 and restart, which fixed it.

The major lock I just experienced was in a mission where you have to rescue a character. That character is [b]not marked as essential in spite of being essential.[/b] You cannot leave the stage without that character. In my game, he died around turn 4. At turn 31, two hours later, I was ready to leave the stage victorious... only to discover that the dev had failed to mark that character essential. I should have had a gameover when he died.

[b]Finally, and this may sound petty, but... the worst issue is that [i]there is no way to restart battle from inside a battle[/i]. You have to wait for your turn, right click, menu to Main Menu, click Restart Stage, and then skip through ALL of the dialog again. The skip dialog button only works on some dialog, btw. It is actually slightly faster to alt-F4 if it's the enemy turn. I am in attempt number 28 for Chapter 15 and I am giving up; it takes nearly two minutes to reset the battle.[/b]

Overall, this is a cautious thumbs-up for this game. It's a very, very good tactics game marred by a UI that actively discourages you from engaging with the depth of the game. The responsiveness of the dev (a solo dev!) is wonderful, and I look forward to whatever is next.

Fun little fairly-straightforward turn-based game.

Beat it a bit under 30 hours.

Mostly well done, but some of the dialogue seemed out of place (modern-day/real-world words/slang/humor).

My biggest grip is the save feature (or lack there of). 

The game consists of basically 2 modes - 'between battles' and 'in-battle'.  
Between battles, you manage your crew inventory, and can shop (but it's very limited).  You also watch conversations between your party members.
In-battle, it's standard turn-based fare.  Pick your units, set your formation, start your turns. The the CPU does the same.
The battles themselves can last 20-30 minutes or more.  And the only option to save is actually "save and quit".  At the main menu, you have basically 2 options - Restart a chapter or Continue(if you did a "save and quit").  So there's only 1 "save" slot, and it's not like a traditional save system.  In otherwords,  a single miscalculation can cost you your 20-30+ minute battle because you have no practical way to save every once in a while.   And a single core character's death means Defeat (game over, restart chapter)

For under $20, it's a solid deal and worth picking up if you like this sort of game.  I'm glad I grabbed it.  But don't expect too much depth or variety.  There's a lot of story and a maybe a time or 2 where you have a dialogue option that may change the outcome.

This is one of the best tactical turn-based strategy games that I've played in a long time. As many other reviewers have pointed out, if you like Fire Emblem and Final Fantasy Tactics, this is likely a good fit for you. I've only played ~10 hours and I felt compelled to write a review because this game and its developer deserve to be recognized for an outstanding product. 

Combat is exciting and challenging and the side quest system within levels is very fun. The gear system and forging are also cool and bring back memories of the FE weapon triangle. I absolutely love the 1h + shield vs 2h weapon choice. It's genuinely meaningful. A huge plus for me, due to zone of control, archers are really good, unlike other games in this genre. In fact, the entire zone of control system is very effective in creating tactical combat. There are lots of classes, which I have not had enough time to evalualte, but will allow me to replay the game over and over again. Overall, this game has a ton going for it and I can't recommend it enough.

There are a few areas for improvement that I know the developer is already attempting to address. Class balance is an issue. Some classes are just better than others. Level design is pretty standard, but more than suffices to create a difficult experience. I'm playing on hard mode with permadeath and it is challenging. I've also had a couple of crashes, but nothing worth detracting points for. 

Finally, the developer clearly loves this game. They are incredibly responsive and continue to try to refine their product. I love what they've done with this game so far and am excited for the continued updates. This has been worth every penny and I recommend it to all of you!

i like doing things my way, so customization is always a plus for me. heres a couple related details that would have made the purchase decision easier for me:
- your units gain promotions at level milestones. promotions add extra class abilities and weapon proficiencies. two promotions, each with 3 options. there's 6 starting classes with 9 possible combonations each. you can't change them on the fly or anything but its a fun system and the promotions are well thought out imo. i found it hard to choose. good stuff.
- weapons can be improved with forging, you can improve weapon accuracy and damage but its fairly expensive and money is pretty limited. most weapons can also be further customised by adding up to 2 upgrades which can be freely swapped out and moved around. these can be simple buffs or huge impact game changers.
- you can equip up to 3 weapons, a shield, and 2 accessories, which range from bandages and rings to misc items that do all kinds of different things. you can swap weapons in battle freely before you take action. before too long i had a rogue backstabbing through 2 people at once with a 2 handed polearm. its neat.

all these things combined make your squad highly customizable. if youre into these games, this one hits the spot.

Some critiques that I have of are:
- Story is ok but the choices are too few and not that consequential as far as I can tell, except for the last one which was a biggie but felt unsatisfying and didn't do enough to make me feel the weight of my choice.
- Similar to choices, the story is quite linear, it's 20 chapters with no side missions, there are side objectives but for my run through I rarely didn't do a side objective except for the odd case of failing to keep 1 of 5 allies alive.
- I didn't run into any game breaking bugs but in dialog the tops of peoples heads was cut off for the entire game.
- Some ui choices could be better in particular the info/inventory/forge menus, they really don't need to be 3 separate things and it was annoying to have to exit one to look at the other. 
- There are some turn based chapters but there is no turn count indicator, so at least once the end of the chapter surprised me. 
- There is no info on the class tree, so I forgot which lvl 10 class I needed to pick to set a character up to get a certain lvl 20 class.
- Given there aren't any side missions I found myself usually picking the same group of characters for every chapter, they got stronger which made me even more likely to pick them for the next chapter. At one point I thought to take a weak one along to try to grind them, but they were weak enough that I had to coddle them and really force certain situations which wasn't fun. I also started the grind late enough that they didn't ever get to the point that they were an adequate level before the game ended, so it was ultimately a waste of my time to grind them at all.
- Due to using the same group of characters for every mission (and save scumming to avoid perma death) by the time I got to the last few chapters I felt really over powered, so they could maybe do a better job of level or difficulty scaling. 
- They use ai for some background images which feels unnecessary given they already have someone to help with character art assets.

My general comments and critiques:
For the record, I've done two playthroughs, and both were on veteran/permadeath.  

-The first half of the game, especially, is phenomenal-- the side quests and bonus objectives on most missions are EXTREMELY fun and rewarding.  I wish that all the missions had this.  

-The final third of the game feels a bit rushed and uninspired-- there is much less thought/considerations given to the missions, no side quests or bonus objectives.  Just units on a linear path with "kill everything" orders.

-Do the support conversations do anything mechanically, aside from add flavor?  I'm not sure that they do.  And likewise, do weapon proficiencies do anything other than allow you to use certain weapons?  I'm not sure that they do either (Illyana's personal skill excepted).

-The world is bigger than it needs to be for the purposes of this game, unless sequels/expansion content is in mind.  I thought that Zoltan was going to be the big boss, but nope--we don't even get to fight him.  Just about the entire game takes place in Fern and is just a story of rebellion against Fern's ruling class.

-Enemy units never use special active abilities.  This makes the game easier, for example, knowing that an enemy Paladin will never use the 100% hit "Smite" ability on your units or that an enemy Sniper will never attempt to "Dead Shot" your guys.  It'd more of a challenge if enemies would actually use their active skills.  Similarly, enemy units never carry more than 1 weapon and they don't weapon switch.  This makes the game easier, not having to anticipate such possibilities, the way that you have to in Fire Emblem.

-At the Promote screen on every 10th level up, it would be nice if I could also view my character's stat growths when selecting the class I want for them.

-At the normal "Info" screen for each character, it'd be nice if it also displayed the current amount of used (and available) Weight rather that just displaying the amount of total Weight.


My tips to new players:
-The "Blade" class is pretty OP, especially once you get those big multi-target weapons (Greatswords and Polearms) and ways to give your units bonus turns (such as Stilleto, Blade Surge, or Elk Effigy).  My Illyana and Edward were able to solo entire armies with good positioning-- they can end up basically getting to 100% evade.  Just be sure to boost their STR with the Strength Ring on levelups, where possible.

-The recruitable "Finn" becomes OP after you babysit him for several levels.  Be sure to equip him with stat growth accessories from the beginning (especially the one that gives him +10% to all growths).

-The scariest enemy units are Rangers and Lionhearts.  

-As there is no Magic in this game, the Defense stat is really powerful.   The key is to never let your guys get flanked.

This game cant be compared to my summer car, so disregard reviewers that do that. My Summer Car is an authentic experience of being a young male finn in mid 90s rural finland, and you get a really detailed recreation of the Datsun 100A you get to build and customize at a very detailed level, the engine itself requires you to actually get it to know and it takes a lot of real time effort getting the thing to run correctly. You have none of the fidelity of vehicle simulation in this. I guess most people dont play MSC correctly (no mods, no premade saves, permadeath, only way if you ask me) anymore because "rural looking area where you can do some stuff" isnt what MSC is (just) about, the life sim is secondary to the car maintenance sim. This game has lower fidelity of car maintenance simulation than some car "games" for DOS, abstract percentage for health of engine, wheels, suspension, you use repair points from a "repair kit" item that can repair both engine and radiator, wheels and suspension.

It is absolutely not where you will find the charm in this, it is elsewhere. It is better compared to Eurotruck simulator, or Motortown, with some very janky Fallout New Vegas inspired setting and side-gameplay and some kinda unpolished and sparse late 00s/early 10s stalker mod levels of gameplay depth and experience. The game does feel like a passion project, though it really needs some polish, even for jank.

This game is slavjank, it feels very much intentionally so. The world doesnt feel very slavic, though, more like if Fallout: New Vegas was made by The Long Drive dev and that life of Boris guy. It is a strange mix of dully shaded assets intended for two second survival jank flips. There is deformable terrain and an economy that is very easy to find extremely profitable niches in that never disappear because the game economy never really varies. You can drink beer, but you dont get drunk, you can piss, but you dont die if you dont pee, and there is no penalty for peeing the wrong place, like on cops or into the face of a homeless person. There are cigarettes, they do nothing, you dont even really need to sleep, you cant really die from hunger even on longest hauls.

Also if you want to get into any of the fnacy stuff, you will need to kill a dog, it is not like in Postal 2 where you can throw a dog treat to non-violently pacify a dog. Kinda sucks, that part.

Where the game really shines is in its atmosphere, it feels less like a trucking sim or a car mechanic sim, or even a post apocalyptic RPG and more like a Life of Boris "that totally happened" slav-themed tall tale generator, set in a world that reminds me of the desert in Xavier: Renegade Angel if it had an MDMA comedown hit too hard. It is a fun walking-with-wheels simulator, you can do whacky stuff, there is a bit of a physics puzzle element to trucking and salvaging the other vehicles you want. You need to explore to figure out things because the wiki cant keep up. The dev seems friendly any nice.

Cant wait for the dynamic economy to become a thing, also I would wish the game was harder, much harder, the updated engine you start out with has way too good performance both thermal and torque-wise. I would wish cigarettes, alcohol, drugs, etc had actual addiction and actual uses to it. I would wish parts wore out faster, I would wish I could take apart the engine. I would wish the fuel economy was wood gas and ethanol based instead of fossil fuel because fossil fuel extraction just doesnt make sense in an apocalyptic world. I would wish travelling the roads was actually dangerous, I would wish I actually took damage and died from crashes, I only just recently dsicovered that mesh of truck can even be deformed and it wasnt after tumbling for hundreds of meters down a mountain, or head-on collission with speeding truck, or slamming into a lightpole at 100+ km/h, it was from an NPC car lightly tapping me on the corner of my truck after I backed out unto a road and didnt see it slowly approaching me.

There are no raiders, the cops do nothing but look intimidating, even if you ram their cars out of this plane of existence nobody comes to even give you as much as a small fine of 100 slaverian dollars.

There are many things I would wish with this game, because for now it is just a mostly fun but very barebones low-fidelity half-sim physics based trucking arcade game set in a kinda delulu life of boris inspired post apocalyptic desert mountain island world. I give it 3/5. Will keep playing.

Played it first a little after the launch, loved the idea a lot, idle/clicker with the strategy aspects (map exploring, "conquering" tiles for resource bonuses and so on), basically got it to 100% at that time, since there was not much to do, but conceptually it was sound enough for me to recommend it, but we are to talk about what happens now, aren't we. Also, I will be focusing more on madness that is tier 2, as tier 1 is basically sit and watch the game play by itself.

The gameplay on base level somehow got worse. You don't see what you are going to research until you unlock the branch for the said research, which is fine for the first playthrough where you don't exactly know your stuff, but gets annoying really quick, as well as the unreal requirements to unlock them in tier 2 (40+ single type units available (have also seen posts for 100+)), it's practically impossible on most map layouts, which can be rerolled, but, to be fair, it isn't fun to waste time on this). 

The map is also feels like a downgrade, now it's more or less veeery budget level Civilization game, where you have to actually conquer tiles, upgrade them, "interact" with different civilizations, which, again, is almost impossible in tier 2, as you spend most of you time dealing with crises (more on that later), civilization interaction also adds a 35% bonus when you try diplomacy with them, and add temporary crisis chance when they are hostile to you, and you have less and worse prompts on what to do with other civilizations and villages, all I see is some improvement for research speed and everything else is basically a debuff.

Crisis mechanic itself is the same since the beginning, but at this state of the game feels untested for new stuff and is utterly unbalanced, earlier it was more of a hindrance that enables some variety in a clicker game, which is dependent on how "aggressively" you improve. As for tier 2, well, it's basically almost a softlock most of the time, for me at the very least. I didn't have that much of a chance for crises to happen, but when I try to deal with one, two more spawn, and it's not like you can avoid them, since you have to conquer the map and get improvements (which raise the chance of crisis happening) for your own civilization. And for the first run on tier 2, if you don't get some ultra op hero, that gives unreal bonus to your damage, you are done, I had to deal with 10+ crisis in a span of  around 30 minutes (maybe even a bit more, didn't actually watch the time, basing it off of default duration of crisis) just to get debuff that disables building anything during crisis (go figure), and practically lost all progress in 20 seconds, then to get back to level I had before and lose it again practically the same way, when I can't even defeat this crisis fast enough.

Which brings me to combat. As I said earlier, you can't do anything during crisis on the first run of tier 2 (at least closer to the modern era) as you don't deal enough damage. During the aforementioned crisis "softlock" I had tried to defeat them just to find out that I do no damage to them (using all units I had), WITH military fully researched up to my current civilization level. Maybe, just maybe, if you have all heroes that somehow only add damage and amount of units you can have at a given time, you can deal with this, but then there is no point in having other bonuses on your heroes.

[b] Just to clarify, maybe these problems with crises that I faced were my shitty hero and ascension setup (although I had all damage boosts and resource generation from tier 1 applied) but everything else still stands. [/b]

I can't recommend this game in this state, when (at the time of writing) the exponential growth in difficulty and gameplay loop being "hope that you get lucky so that you can unlock branching tech without selling your soul to Mr. Satan himself, hopefully to, then, get a hero that gives you a bonus that can actually help in this hell, get 2-3 researches done, hope that you don't have a crisis fiesta, build half a building upgrade when there are no impending crises and then hope that you don't die on next era breakhtrough crisis, rinse and repeat".

A small but truly atmospheric game with a lot of potential. The mood, lighting, and sound effects weave together to craft a haunting tapestry that is best experienced in the dark. Hearing the War-of-the-Worlds-esque horns that bellow from the mothership blocking the sky above your farmhouse is one of my favorite details, as it blurs the line between cool and creepy. Beyond War of the Worlds, I think it's also clear that the game takes inspiration from the movie Signs. The game does a great job of capturing how the charming serenity of the countryside slips away when the suns goes down, as trees and vegetation morphs into towering shadows and blackness that can swallow you whole. The feeling of isolation alone is incredibly ominous, and again, the sound effects really sell it: the rustle of leaves as you wade through cornstalks, branches breaking under foot, wind howling. Now factor in that the natural landscape is littered with alien creatures hell bent on hunting you down... There's two kinds of extraterrestrials: ferocious humanoids with a horrifying penchant for crawling on all fours (best to avoid tall grass in this situation because they can easily sneak up on you) and the hulking monsters that linger around points of interest. They force you to constantly choose between fight or flight. Having to make those split-second decisions is nerve-wracking and constantly at play. All in all, I enjoyed playing this, and I'm really looking forward to following both the production of this game and the studio itself. Many games by small developers show promise but don't deliver; this is not of those games. Abduction is bite-sized horror that's worth experiencing for yourself.

There is potential, and the premise is interesting. You walk around talking to everyone with different characters, mapping out what kind of relationship the characters have with each others. The goal is to determine who is going to be the murder victim, rather than the killer, and then be that person at the time of the murder in order to free your soul and escape the time loop.
The execution is lacking. The characters walk around very slowly, which is annoying due to the time limit. A run button would be appreciated-. And even when you discover the right person and get freed, you still go back to the start of the loop. That might have worked, if it was the next day and you had to figure out the next victim, as if everyone would get picked off one by one by the killer, but it is literally the same day and the same mystery. Finding out the murder victim was actually very simple (spoilers): Once you get out of your house, just keep transferring to the next person available, and it's the last one. There's little logic involved and no need to talk to anybody, as the murder happens automatically. There could have been some prerequisite puzzle that needs to be solved, before a murder can happen, so you couldn't just try every character to see if they die. Maybe the murderer couldn't find a gun, unless you provide him with a one. Or maybe he doesn't want to kill you, unless he's been told that you know too much. After all, you're the soul that wants to get free, so you should earn it.
Note that one of the endings includes killing the dog, and you even get an achievement for it.
The English translation is lacking and has some inconsistencies, which is kind of a huge deal when everything is text based.

Pelissä on potentiaalia, ja alkuasetelma on mielenkiintoinen. Pelissä kävellään ympäriinsä ja jutellaan kaikille eri hahmoina, jotta saadaan selville, minkälaiset suhteet eri hahmoilla on toisiinsa. Päämääränä on selvittää, kenen on määrä tulla murhatuksi, sen sijaan että selvitettäisiin kuka on murhaaja, ja sen jälkeen olla tämä uhri murhan aikaan, jotta sielu vapautuu ja pääsee pois aikakierteestä.
 Toteutus on puuttellinen. Hahmot kävelevät ympäriinsä erittäin hitaasti, mikä on ärsyttävää rajallisen ajan vuoksi. Juoksunappi olisi arvostettu. Ja kun lopulta saa selville oikean hahmon ja sielun vapaaksi, palataan jälleen alkuun, kuin mitään ei olisi tapahtunut. Tämä olisi toiminut, jos olisi seuraava päivä ja pitäisi päätellä seuraava uhri, kuin heidät kaikki napsittaisiin yksi kerrallaan, mutta on kirjaimellisesti sama päivä ja sama mysteeri. Murhatun löytäminenkään ei ole mitenkään vaikeaa (juonipaljastus): Kun pääsee talosta ulos ja jatkaa vaihtamista aina seuraavaan saatavilla hahmoon, niin oikea vastaus on viimeinen. Ei sisällä minkäänlaista logiikkaa eikä tarvitse puhua kenellekään, sillä murha tapahtuu automaattisesti. Olisi voinut olla jonkinlainen pulma ratkottavaksi, jotta murha voisi tapahtua, jolloin ei voisi vain vuoron perään kokeilla jokaista hahmoa ja katsoa osuisiko nyt oikeaan. Ehkä murhaaja ei löydäkään asetta, ellei sitä anna hänelle. Tai ehkä hän ei haluakaan tappaa, ellei hänelle kerro, että tietää liikaa. Sinähän se vapaaksi haluava sielu olet, joten se pitää ansaita.
Huomatkaa, että yhteen loppuun pitää tappaa koira, ja peli myöntää siitä jopa saavutuksen.
Englannin käännös on melko kömpelö ja sisältää ristiriitaisuuksia, mikä on merkittävää, kun kaikki perustuu tekstiin.

When I started the last main section of the game, I honestly thought I had to be sequence breaking, but no, the game's required path really is that hard. There are no difficulty options; the ability to slow the game's speed or to have more broom stamina would be welcome additions.

By the two hour mark, it took me dozens of attempts for each bit of progress, requiring perfect flight lines and momentum conservation, with certain death if I deviated from the developer's intended (but not visibly marked) path. When that area thankfully ended, so did the game, abruptly, even though I'd thought the main story was just getting started.

The in-game maps and switch puzzles from the demo did not appear in the rest of the game. You do not collect any new abilities either, although there are environment-specific effects which can help or hinder your flying.

I encourage everyone to try the demo, and buy the game if the fun you had was worth the price, but be warned that the additional content is more like a Meat Boy-style precision gauntlet instead of the Metroidvania feel of the opening area.

Cursed broom is a nice little platformer with a unique mechanical gimmick. The main path is shortish, and I haven't done much hunting for optional collectibles outside of the tutorial area yet - I guess you can sink a good deal more time and tries into those.

The signature mechanic is the eponymous Cursed Broom. This artifact can fly, but only by building momentum, by wall rebounds, or by environmental boosts. The game could be more verbose in guiding you here - especially the rules of momentum left me confused, and in consequence, some passages felt a little janky, perhaps because there were other intended paths. The wall rebound on the other hand makes for some really interesting interactions - it means the direction you fly (left or right) matters, and you can use obstacles to your advantage by bouncing off of them, occasionally multiple times. Again, what you actually need to do (keep the glide button pressed and just switch directions) could be clearer right away.

The artstyle is clean; What you see e.g. in the trailer is what you get, so you'll know right away whether it's your thing or not. The latter part of the world felt kind of bare to me, while earlier on there are nice little details in the level.
The soundtrack is catchy and a big plus in my book. It carried the length of the game nicely.

A small nitpick: with the option to quit with and without saving, I'd appreciate a warning for the latter. Together with the demo, this led to me playing the sewer level three times over - not a big deal, but easy to avoid IMO with a warning, maybe one that you can opt not to show after the first time.

Cursed Broom is an absolute delight for anyone who loves a mix of magic, humor, and pixel art. 

This game may look simple, but it’s packed with charm and offers way more than meets the eye. The pixel art is stunning and full of detail—you can instantly tell the amount of love poured into the design. 

Each level is varied and makes exploration genuinely rewarding. Mastering this stupid broom is part of the fun, and each level introduces new puzzles and obstacles that make great use of the broom’s “curse.” The controls are precise, and the mix of light puzzles, platforming, and hidden secrets keeps you hooked. It’s perfect for a quick session or hours of play without getting boring.

The soundtrack complements the atmosphere beautifully, setting the mood without overpowering the experience. 

All in all, it's a must-play for fans of pixel games and indie gems. If you’re up for a charming adventure full of spells and puzzles, Cursed Broom is a magical journey worth taking.

[h1]Not Those Orcs[/h1]
[h2]Story[/h2]

The good news is that there is some more individual characterization for some of the Scrap Springs Division party members, since many of them suffered due to the ESA's tyranny. It's a good way to handle both the macro story of the ESA and the micro story of individual characters, and motivates the player to fight the ESA even harder.

Chronus-13's interactions with the party are weird, since it doesn't seem to mind at all about being ostracized by everyone and it generally acts as a medium for Zeron to communicate with everyone else. This might be intentional, since Krax likely didn't want it to develop too much free will and run off with the important Molarian data. Personally, I would have found it more interesting if Chronus did have more agency and question which side it wants to remain loyal to, since it is essentially treated as a tool even by the good guys. It would add a lot more weight to [spoiler]its digital death in the ending of the game[/spoiler].

As for the macro plot, we get more context about how Carol Everson [spoiler]got blamed for the Raxion II incident, and how Novus went along with the ESA in framing her. We also get to see how the ESA propaganda works due to the news networks framing the story to suit the country's agenda, which is eerily similar to the real life war on terror. Personally, I think the news segments are a good way to show what each country or faction expects their citizens to believe. It's also a good callback to the optional NBN event in Origins, where the player themselves could have been easily suckered by the pro-Novus documentary[/spoiler].

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

The game is mechanically very similar to Origins. However, there are some new additions that greatly affect the balance.
* First of all, there are both one-time and respawning enemies, and taking advantage of the latter means the player can reach the party's power ceiling much more efficiently.
* Shops now have an accessory that can grant a passive speed buff with a power penalty, with the latter not actually mattering due to how power cost scales to max power anyways. This is an excellent placeholder until the user can learn the temporal acceleration passive from their own skill tree.
* There are now robot party members, who use an entirely different skill tree. They cannot benefit from the brain drain series of skills nor can they use the more broken non-robot equipment, but their ceiling is incredibly high due to their threadripping skill tree, which can grant them three actions a turn. They do have some weaknesses though, since they require specialized synthetic healing methods and they are very weak to electricity by default.

Like before, every humanoid character has very similar skill trees, though due to the higher enemy power ceiling, it becomes even more obvious that the Technician class is the best one. They have power/charge regen as well as passives for power attack, making them excellent at pretty much every role in the game, though their best role is to refill the party's power/charge as required. While their OPness is somewhat acceptable in this game, in the main "Suikoden"-like game, they will definitely need to be nerfed to prevent the player from just running through the game with a party full of infinitely recharging Technicians. The only non-Technician class that stands out is the Combatant, since they have group buffs that surpass the generic support drones.

As for enemies, the first dungeon of this game is more beginner friendly than Origins, since it's smaller, has mob sizes of 1, and has a boss with an easy alternate win condition, which makes it doable on normal. Afterwards, you get access to the shop to properly prepare for the real challenges of the game. However, enemies also require you to learn the electric and antimatter damage types, since many of them will easily tank Matcon Scythe attack spam. Fortunately, if you have the brain drain series of skills, you can easily farm enough knowledge points to learn every damage type you might need.

One thing that really tips the scales in the favor of the player is that shops have almost all available equipment tiers available from the start, instead of unlocking progressively. This means if you farm enough money through criminal skills or Blackjack gambling, you can make a fully decked out team before the first true boss of the game and clobber them even on very hard. Shops for humanoid equipment are also fairly frequent, though robot shops are much rarer for some reason, so make sure to take full advantage of the latter before making any story progress. The only things truly locked behind story progress are [spoiler]the far futuristic weapons in Time's Eclipse, but you probably don't need them for beating the final boss[/spoiler].

As for the infamous Doppelganger armor, I think something like this should be locked behind challenging late game sidequests, since it seems like something that is too strong to simply be buyable from the start. Additionally, the temporal acceleration passive should be similarly difficult to obtain, since increasing the characters' speed in an ATB game gives a huge advantage. Combining these two can completely break the game in half due to the player gaining a massive turn advantage even on the highest difficulty.

Tactics battles are mostly the same as before, though I do find some maps easier to deal with than others due to the available space to maneuver in. One thing I did notice is that for some battles, you have more control over your units' starting positions than others, which can be bad if the game starts off your allied units facing away from the enemy. Also, like before, tactics battles do not have the same extremely high preparation ceiling as regular battles, so I stuck to normal mode with these.

One new addition are cyberspace battles, which are basically regular battles but with a more limited skill tree and item loadout. This time, the skill trees have even less individuality and a fairly low ceiling, so I stuck with normal mode for these.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
[i]ORC: We have supply issues because of the ESA's crackdown.
Also ORC: We sell almost every tier of equipment in the game. Have fun.[/i]
7.5/10
The story is much better than in Origins and you get a better sense of what's at stake for those who fight against the ESA. I do wish Chronus-13 was more fleshed out, since it feels like the story couldn't decide if they wanted it to be a tool like the fully robotic party members or if they wanted Chronus-13 to truly be a main character. As for the gameplay, the way shop progress is handled, or lack thereof, makes it hard to find the balance between being underpowered like in Origins's first dungeon or grossly overpowered like my fully equipped team. Maybe it's better to treat this as a preview of the main game's potential power ceiling.

That said, I felt that some things could have been improved:  You spend more time shopping to outfit your 7 member party that the game almost feels like it's a shopping simulator.  Why can't you see what equipment your charaters have while comparing what the vendor is selling is a mystery.  Yes it shows you how the stats would change, but I can't remember if party member #5 of group 2 has an antimatter rifle or a graviton pistol without backing out to look. Fair warning, while it's a fun game, it's VERY short for traditional RPG fans.  It's also a bit harder than what you may be used to in the early game, even on normal difficulty.  Not unreasonably so, but it definitely doesn't hold your hand or pull any punches because it's the beginning of the game.

Star Shift Origins was a tech demo, conceptually.  Even shorter than this, and actually a little easy.  Star Shift Rebellion is proof of concept for this dev team.  And it's a darn good concept.  It isn't going to revolutionize RPGs, but it's got enough old school in its DNA to be familiar, while inject enough fun and interesting takes on a lot of staples in the genre to make it new and exciting.  There are no glaring issues of any kind (or at least none I came across), and while the story is a LITTLE Saturday Cartoons villain-y, it's pretty adult in it's presentation.  People do die, and graphically, and not just to be edgy.

There are some things I think could do with some improvement, but overall I have no actual complaints, and nothing I noticed needed any MAJOR rebalancing... EXCEPT: giving the MC "Brain Drain" on the class that can automatically regen their version of MP is ACTUALLY broken.  And while it takes a heavy investment on another character, having 2 of them that can rocket through skill trees is actually a little absurd.

The good:
+Story
+Leveling (very non-standard approach, love it)
+Combat
+Soundtrack
+Art

Cons:
-Full access to every possible piece of equipment (except the LITERAL endgame weapons) from the very first "town" with an INCREDIBLY fast and easy way to make the money to buy everything actually makes the game very easy.  Paired with the ridiculously fast "leveling" you can do with the MC and you can actually cheese the game super hard without meaning to.
-Explanations are pretty much non-existent.  If you're a RPG veteran, other than minor adjustments to systems you're familiar with but are called something else, there's no major hurdles to get over.  However, this is NOT for players new to the genre.
-Gear is not very well explained, and since it takes pretty hefty "exp" investments to make a character specialize in a weapon, you can absolutely waste points.  And past a certain point, combat encounters are hard limited, so you can easily mess that up.  It's not going to "ruin" a character, but it does feel wasteful when clearer indicators on what stats do what could easily make that avoidable.
-Short.  I mean REALLY short.  Origins, this teams "first" title in this... trilogy? was shorter, but, again, for vets of the genre, this is going to feel like a set up than an actual game.  I don't think this is a negative in that it's BAD, just that it's definitely going to be something that, understandably, would keep some people from spending the money on it.
-The "strategy" layer.  It's not bad, but it's INCREDIBLY easy, and I was NOT expecting that.  It makes sense, it'd be a shame to be stuck in one of those combats when you actually can't affect anything about them outside of what orders you give in the combat itself, but I don't know if it's possible to fail all but 1 of them, and that 1 it would still be difficult to fail it.  I tend to enjoy games that mix genres, but because it feels like it's only included for story elements AND to be able to claim it's MORE than just an RPG, I think it would be better to remove those elements and focus that time and effort on the RPG part of the game... OR make those elements more integral to the game by using some kind of systems that either tie back to the other parts so there's payoff in some respects (story choices give you more or less units, or stronger/weaker ones, etc.).  It doesn't actively hurt the game in any way, but it definitely feels like it's ancillary rather than essential.

I know I laid out some pretty long criticisms, but they're HYPER specific, and despite the fact that I have criticisms to make, I really don't think anything I'm giving feedback on harms the game in ANY way other than diverting attention and focus away from the other elements.  Which I think are actually very well done, again, considering the fact that it's an indie dev team.  I enjoyed Origins and was happy to leave a positive review.  I enjoyed Rebellion and am happy to leave a positive review.  And I'm eagerly looking forward to the 3rd title and expect more of the same.

There is a seed of an interesting game here.

- "Attack" enemies by spelling words using letters from a grid.
- Earn experience points by creating valid words; the amount of exp earned can be increased further by purchasing various perks from the skill tree (see below).
- Leveling your character awards skill points, which can be used to purchase perks from any of 3 different skill trees.  
- Defeating enemies (called "guardians" in-game) may also award runes, which are used to purchase upgrades, which are separate from the aforementioned skill tree perks.
- Defeating enemies also grants a chance to award gear (weapons, armor, etc...), which may be equipped on your character.
 
[hr][/hr] 

I find the core game loop of the game appealing, but as it stands, the game is far too unpolished to be enjoyable.  This really should have been released into Early Access first.

[hr][/hr] 

Here are some issues I have with the game:
- There are many instances of misspelled words, which is ironic given the fact that this is a word game.  
    Some examples:
      - Right on the main game screen, the upgrades button is misspelled as "ugrades".
      - In the upgrades screen, there is a section marked [b]Inentor[/b].  I assume this should say "Inventory".
      - Also on the upgrades screen, in the Guardian Upgrades section, I see the following text: "[b]LV 1: uardians hae 10% decreased .[/b]" 
- Exiting from the upgrades screen via the Home button presents a popup box that contains a Cancel and Okay button; above these buttons is text that says: "[b]    er e      [/b]"  
- In the skill tree page, moving your cursor over any of the skill icons will provide a popup with brief description of that skill.  This is fine.  However, sometimes the popup won't go away at all, even after leaving that screen, going to a different screen, starting a new round of play, etc...  The only way to make that popup go away is to exit the game completely then relaunch the game.
- Occasionally, during play, random letters will change to blank tiles.  The way I get around this is: click on the blank tile, which adds it to the word I'm currently spelling, then erase that letter from my word, at which puts the 'blank' tile back into the grid, but with the proper letter now visible.

[hr][/hr] 

More subjectively, I'd personally love to be able to use my keyboard to enter letters rather than having to use the mouse for everything.  I'd also like to see various resolution/windowing options.  Right now the game simply plays in fullscreen.

As mentioned earlier, I like the idea of the game and I want to be able to enjoy it.  However, I cannot recommend the game in its current state.  It's fairly janky and could use some QoL improvements.  I will keep an eye on the game and will update/change this review if the quality improves significantly.

Look. It was $3 on sale, and when its not its $8. As a reminder, I measure a game based on the number of hours I spend playing the game. If I can get $1 per hour then its a Top Tier game. So, kinda hard not to reach even 0.50$ an hour. 

Anyway, the good:

Music - excellent. Wide variety and all ... futuristic? I loved it. 

Voice Acting - Really good. The voice quality and acting quality left nothing to desire. 

Art - Its .. unique. It feels like it was made in some old-ass engine, but its fine for a top-down shooter. 

Controls - This is the first thing I noticed out of the gate. its wierd and i expect it will be difficult for a lot of players. You can press C to cycle through various modes, i think 4, at will and youll eventually land on one you like and are familiar with. 

Gameplay - So.. there is a certain linearity to it which I dont like. The map is basically a series of pathways and in some cases, if you have the right jet pack you can short cut here and there. I picked the shadow class and ran around with a small army of robots that I started off with following me, then figured out I could put them on hunt and follow them instead. There is crafting but I didnt do any of it except interface with the various tables at least once. I did apply upgrades to the Jetpack and my gun but its super simple and straight forward. Loot is odd.. some things you just need to touch, other things you get near and then have to press T to loot. A lot of the time I felt like i had no clue what i was doing, what my skills or weapons were doing etc. I did have access to a stealth via TAB, but wasnt sure what its purpose was, though it did save me from dying once. Levels are standard RPG fare.. with attribute points that you apply to various categories. Each level appears to unlock a new skill for the class you picked at the start of the game. 

Story - not bad, not great. I did actually take the time to listen to it instead of skipping which is encouraged by the typing out of the story text as its narrated to you. Its your standard crash landed gotta survive and escape fare. The only people I saw were ones trying to kill me but I suspect from dialog that there are friendly settlements somewhere. 

At $8 i figure your getting 4 hours of gameplay (im guessing here) which gives it a C grade. At $3 your getting an A grade game. 

Thats my two cents. I could refund the game if I felt like it, but im choosing not to because I want to support the effort and it cost me very little.

Lensed Night Sky is probably my favorite Touhou fangame, and I mean that with absolute sincerity. This is a seriously fun take on a Touhou roguelike, leaning way more into the genre than Touhou 18 / 18.5 did. The writing is humorous, the art looks good, it's generally presented rather well, there is a plethora of items which can all help make really interesting builds, the music's good, and the character cast is fairly unique. Sumireko and Chiyuri & Yumemi are odd choices to have as playables (alongside Reimu of course), but they're really cool! Chiyuri in particular is such a little shit, I love her.

This game is hard. I suck. I got to stage 5 on normal once, and recently finished the game on easy. But this is in no way a criticism, as I feel the sheer difficulty combined with the crap ton of items just adds extra replayability to the game, which is cool!

Lensed Night Sky also has a bunch of endings! Every stage, and every boss, has a unique ending specific to the character you're playing as - this is yet another thing which adds to replay value. I really like the character profile stuff in the menu, alongside the fact that you can just. Read the endings. And the ingame dialogue too, actually. Genuinely a really nice touch to have all of that available from the menu!

Spoilers for stage five/six:
[spoiler]Stage 5's... lack of existing, really, was cool. It felt foreboding. And then the reveal with the earth. Seriously not a turn I had expected the game to take, but it was awesome! Yorihime is a tough fight, but her theme is so damn good. This is also when I understood why Keine and Akyuu were portrayed the way they were. Akyuu commenting on your number of losses was pretty funny. Anyway, stage 6. I didn't expect Yukari. But I can't say I was overly surprised, either. The stage itself is rather pretty, I like the way the background is done. Reimu's portrait art changing was cool. The whole Yukari fight was cool. I was expecting a Necrofantasia or a Night Falls ~ Evening Star, but instead we got something better. Awakening From Fantasy ~ Immaterial Dream is a wonderful song. I didn't realize it was an Eternal Shrine Maiden cover until a good way through the song, and the part with the Maiden's Capriccio motif was so fucking cool. I think this is by far my favorite song in the game so far, it's seriously so good and I legitimately don't have words to describe my feelings on it. So damn good.[/spoiler] 

As of right now, I've only cleared the game as Reimu, so I'm unsure how the other characters' dialogue beyond stage three is. But, I really dig it. The characters are all written accurate to their canon selves (okay maybe except Chiyuri but this is infinitely funnier), and stage 5/stage 6 especially are rather impactful.

Please, play this game. It is seriously so good. It's got charm, it's got a cool visual style, it's got nice music. It deserves to be so much more popular than it currently is. Thank you for continuing to work on LNS, devs. This is such a cool game and I can't wait to see how 1.0 will be.

First of all, there are two primary things to know about this game:
1) This is an H-game, with a lewd content patch located here: https://aura-dev.itch.io/star-knightess-aura-patch
2) Despite being an H-game, this is a really unique RPG where resources are finite and careful planning is required if you are attempting to beat the game without corrupting the protagonist. It is unironically one of my favorite RPGs, and I would play it even if it didn't have any H-content

On the H-game front, the essential premise is that this is slow burn brainwashing. If you lean into the brainwashing or fail to win a "good" victory, the protagonist (name Aura) will slowly transform from a nerdy girl with a pure heart to a horny, incredibly evil, basic bitch. 

The game has three primary phases: Roya, Aura's mind, and Earth. In Roya, the protagonist tries to save the fantasy world from the demon king. It is an RPG that is intentionally difficult due to limited resources, However, you can commit lewd actions, which will make the game easier, but also progress the brainwashing further. After finishing a day in Roya, either by doing an action which requires until the end of day to progress, losing a fight, or manually choosing to end the day, you progress to Aura's mind.

In Aura's mind, you control one of the primary antagonists and can use corruption points gained in Roya (from lewd actions, evil actions, using a special power called "Star Knightess" or simply many days passing). These corruption points get used to slowly brainwash Aura. The early items are things like slightly improving her feelings to someone or slightly decreasing her interest in books, for example. Changes start small and slowly build up over time.

Finally, in the Earth phase, you will see the effects of the changes in Aura's mind.

Most of the rest of the review will concern Roya, which is the primary part of the game. As previously mentioned, the game isn't the typical RPG maker fare. A "pure" playthrough, where you never commit any lewd actions in Roya, or spend corruption points in Aura's mind, is possible, but is very difficult and requires several playthroughs of experimenting. In chapter 1, your options are limited, but starting in chapter 2, there are many possible builds that can work for the game. But for your first playthrough, the expectation is you will be using at least some corruption to benefit yourself.

While the game does fit into the corruption genre mold, unlike many others in the genre, it isn't of the "protagonist gets raped until they like it" mold or whatever. Instead, lewd stuff in Roya is mostly transactional. Aura has a lewdness score, and can't take lewd actions above her required score. Usually taking these actions get you a benefit, such as gold, items, or stat increases. On the flip side, you might be forced to take a lewd action if her willpower (an in game resource) is low enough. A slightly different version of the scene will play out if you are forced to take it. Lewd actions also typically come with corruption. Above a certain threshold (that changes as you play the game), you will lose the game if corruption exceeds that point. As such, you need to spend corruption during the Aura's Mind phase if you aren't playing a carefully constructed pure playthrough.

The game's writing is generally solid by normal standards, but for H-game standards, the writing is phenomenal. The character writing is good, with characters having fairly distinct voices that are emphasized well in dialogue. Characters generally bounce off each other pretty well, and have some scenes where they particularly shine.

Generally, I recommend this game highly if at least one of the following is true:

1) You are looking for a fairly deep resource constrained RPG where every item is precious and routing better routes is king.

2) You are looking for lewd slow-burn brainwashing where the heroic protagonist becomes evil.

On the other hand, if you are looking for a quick fap, or a casual game that doesn't require much thought, then this game probably isn't for you.

I'll go into more detail below, but the TL;DR is that this is a very fun (and surprisingly challenging) RPGMaker game with a focus on corruption fetish that shouldn't be skipped if you're into both of those things.

You play as Aura, somebody who was chosen to be isekai'd into a Star Knightess to defeat the Demon King. Her first attempt doesn't go perfectly, and now she has the succubus/demon Lucelia inside of her head. During the day she goes about her non-isekai life of going through school, acing every test, reading horrible light novels, and other such things, and at night she is transported to Roya to help finish the demon king off and save the world. The school scenes are purely visual novel, and only happen in certain conditions, the Roya segment is the main part of the game and where the RPG combat takes place. However, whenever you swap between these two (by dying in roya, or doing something that causes time to pass) you instead play as Lucelia, and have to invade Aura's mind to corrupt her into a bitchy bimbo NTR'd kinky cheerleader... you know how this type of thing goes.

Where the game gets interesting, however, is the synergy between all three of these sections. Your main goal in Roya is to defeat the demon king and save humanity, but you definitely won't be able to do that all in one night! Playing as Lucelia is inevitable and common, and requires you to interact with a bunch of different parts of Aura's brain. These are surprisingly varied, and come in the form of a series of rooms that all interact with eachother. One room might focus on her appearance, and making her prefer to wear high heels or take off her glasses. Another room might affect what she derives happiness from, so you can make her desire popularity while caring less about helping other people. Aura is the most affected by this during school, which are mostly VN/corruption scenes. However, it also starts leaking over into Roya, giving a cavalcade of debuffs... but intriguingly, buffs as well. A big part of what makes Star Knightess Aura enjoyable to me is that the game is pretty difficult, and by engaging in the corruption mechanic you can actually make your life a lot easier if managed right. You've seen the trope of "blow a couple guys in a back alley to make five times the gold" in a ton of other corruption-style games, but on top of that you can also get stat buffs and lewd spells from reading books written by particularly horny wizards. For example, one gives you extra magic attack for every point of [Lewd Knowledge] Aura has, so it's a pretty solid strat to start off the game degrading her morals as fast as possible via drugs, stimulants, and speccing into giving her fetishes. This all generates [Corruption] though, which is the main resource in the Lucelia sections... the more you have unspent the faster it goes up, and if you get too much she instantly dies and your game is over. So you can't ignore corrupting Aura, but you can do it smartly... I'm assuming it's balanced so people can do the classic "purity runs" of games like these, but there is a time limit set by how many times you die or pass time.

The writing is hit and miss, but in the right areas. It's clearly self aware it's a very trashy isekai setting, and is even poked fun at occasionally... I do find a lot of the characters annoying, but at least with Aura it makes you feel a tiny bit less bad about corrupting her. While the dialogue is very over the top and trashy (not in the horny way), the way the gradual mind control is written is honestly very solid and a good reward for paying attention to the character's interests! It turns out Lucelia is also somebody who is isekai'd named Alicia (Aura is pretty airheaded to not notice with names like those)... she's also her former best friend, which makes it easier to tug at her mind in more ways than one. So while the sex scenes happen mostly in Roya, [imo] the most horny content actually takes place in the real world, where you see Alicia tempt Aura into vapid and horny avenues while her brain is unknowingly being altered. While I found myself more aroused at the situation than caring about any of the characters, I also started to feel bad when things in my playthrough went really south- so maybe something's actually here in the writing and i'm not giving it enough credit. I definitely found myself enjoying these brain altering/real life segments more than the actual sex, but maybe that just speaks to my sensibilities...

In short, this game is fantastic if you're looking for a fun fetishy time where gameplay is actually well integrated into the kink you're interested in. The more you die in Roya, the more Aura gets corrupted, but that allows you to take hornier avenues to power up faster, but that can be a slippery slope... sure, test scores going down and caring more about fashion than books might not affect fighting ability, but now Aura gets sooooo booooored when reading, including those important stat books that give you new bonuses. Yeah, you now have an ability to distract humanoid creatures with your assets, but you're now used to wearing high heels on your armour, causing agility to be reduced for all stat checks. I find myself an equal amount horny and invested in the game systems while playing Star Knightess Aura, which to me is what all h-games should strive for. And if you're somehow this far in the review but aren't interested in the horny aspect of it... well, it's one of the better RPG Maker games i've played, even if it's on the basic side!

I've played the game for over 50 hours during its early access, including a full pure run. I (obviously) enjoyed the game, but also understand that it can be hard to get into.

It's a game that requires you to take it seriously. If you plan to fastforward through all dialogues, and ignore all of the mechanics, you're going to have a miserable time. The game can be surprisingly difficult, even on lower difficulties, and unless you like losing (makes more sense with the Restoration Patch) it's easy to bounce off of the game, or yell at the game for being unfair.

However, if you do decide to take the game seriously, it's the most in-depth RPGmaker game I've ever played. Every quest/encounter can be solved in multiple ways and mechanically the game is very non-linear (though the story is linear). The areas are meticulously crafted (unlike the generic dungeon layouts you see in many of these games) with well-thought out encounters. I originally started playing the game for its story and themes, but that diversity is what made me do multiple playthroughs.

But again, there is a lot of text to wade through, especially early on (Put on Instant Text in the options, you'll thank me). And the game's difficulty and complexity can be daunting at the beginning. I think it's certainly worth it though.

I played this on another platform when it was still being developed and was blown away by how well designed the gameplay was. It has a really creative spin on traditional turn-based combat that is not only challenging and refreshing, but also works very well with the narrative. This is probably the only adult game that I've ever played where I've enjoyed playing the prudish route, both because it's challenging and because the characters are written so well that it's more fun to engage with the story by making a good faith attempt to act as you think the characters would.

This game will be best enjoyed by people who genuinely like when games tell them a story and provide character development. It will help, but is not necessary, if you're familiar with the isekai trope in anime. The main character, Aura, is smart and creative, but also overconfident and self-righteous. It's refreshing that she doesn't feel more like an archetype than a person, and doesn't fall for obvious tricks for the sake of advancing the plot in a certain direction.

The day to day mechanic where there's an emphasis on solving the world's problems as quickly and efficiently as possible while minimizing corruption takes what would ordinarily be relatively boring grinding and making each small battle into a cost/benefit conundrum. Yes, you can defeat this group of monsters, but will you take so much damage that you need to spend precious items or let the day end at the cost of corrupting you a bit more? On top of the whole cost/benefit thing, the battles are actually just very well designed and engaging even on their own merit. Most are challenging and require the player to figure out an ideal strategy that minimizes losses, and that strategy may require the player to obtain a skill from elsewhere before the battles are cost/time-efficient to win.

The objective of Save the Llama is to create a safe environment for your llamas by meticulously cramming as many hilariously-voiced booming, buzzing, pew-ing, and zapping anti-UFO towers you can fit on a single platform. The llamas will reward your obsessive over-engineering by only periodically being abducted by that one fast-moving ship that keeps evading the wrath of the Tesla megastructure you built on a rotating gear in the middle of the desert.

STL is easy to pick up and play and won't punish you for abruptly taking a break or for losing your favorite llama. Maps can be restarted at any time if you end up feeling like 6 windpump guns on a train is safer for your llamas than 4 catapults on a cog, even though the right answer is always all the Teslas on an anything. Perk points will help you squeeze more out of your preferred anti-alien strategies as the game progresses and gets more difficult.

I'm outside of the target demographic for this (I'm a straight man), but its definitely pretty solid so far (only the prologue and chapter 1 are out right now). 

A few things to decide if the game is right for you:

1) This is an otome game. Otome games are ones where a female protagonist has (usually) male romance interests with the romance taking a primary role in the story. Currently there are two male leads to romance, but it seems there might be some secondary ones added for later chapters. 

2) This game is dark/edgy, and the protagonist can be outright villainous depending on how you play her.

3) The RPG elements are enjoyable, but not particularly deep. On the positive side, combat is nontrivial, and losing battles is very possible, especially if you make decisions that force you to get into difficult fights. Also the game isn't grindy, with random encounters giving little XP, and most of the stat differences coming from equipment. On the other hand, there isn't a whole lot of customization available, at least as of the end of chapter 1. Outside of some possible bonus equipment with minor stat buffs, you are basically using the characters you are given without customization.

4) The writing is strong, with engaging plot and characters.

5) The presentation is superb. The Steam pictures and gameplay video aren't cherry picked; the game is gorgeous throughout the entire game, with regular CGs, and good combat animation.

Let me preface this that this is an untapped genre that is rarely explored. There are seas of otome games, but rarely ones with rpg elements where there's actual gameplay. 

If we're judging this game by that criteria, it does the bare minimum as an rpg, but it does that aspect decently. Gameplay is the frontal aspect of any game, and the silent kingdom delivers to the minimum. For example, I was craving an in depth gear system, but shops and item drops were very rare, I rarely had a chance to experiment with weapons, armor and accessories. This is my biggest complaint of the game, while the rpg element is there, it's not very fleshed out and seems like an afterthought. Please lucky cat, please make items and gear a more prominent aspect like other RPGs games.

There definitely needs to be a mini map to navigate certain sections. And as others have mentioned in the reviews, maybe a difficulty option would benefit. I very much enjoyed the combat system and it's rng, but others may not have. An easy/normal option maybe? I rather have a more difficult option myself.

Game would definitely benefit from an overall "quest list" feature that other typical RPGs have, a few instances I lost track of what NPCs interactions I had.

Now onto the aspect I absolutely adore, the story, character art and choices. For anyone familiar with typical otome games, this game has like 3x the standard CG art, and let me tell you the art is GORGEOUS. There's a lot of shitty Western otome ripoffs on steam, but the art is on par with some of the big Japanese hitters I've played. And I can't stress enough how often you get hit with a CG art piece, an art cg gallery viewable in the next update would be pretty dope.

The story is an absolute hit, and without spoilers all due respect fuck you lucky cat for making us make that last decision to progress the story. Brilliant narrative.
