[h1]A Brief Review of HyperLeague Heroes[/h1]

[i]HyperLeague Heroes is terrific fun.[/i] I started playing at the end of December. As of this writing, I am about 500 hours in. I picked up the game just before a holiday event ended. The event unlock is still a member of my current team.

The artwork appeals to me, along with the variety of villains, heroes, and monsters you can choose to form your line up. My playtime is predominantly idle but I do go active periodically.

The game has many options that allow you to strengthen your characters and build up your team. Leveling up, upgrading your base, perks, fusions, battle formations, and gearing up feel meaningful; that is, when I make decent choices, I can get some pretty impressive advancements and progress. Well… for me. I am not the greatest player. You won’t find me passing you on the leader-boards or anything.

One last observation—I find it encouraging that the developer consistently revises and updates the game. If you like idle or auto-battle games, I would recommend giving this a go. I certainly have had a blast so far.

Its a decent idle game, but it isn't what I was expecting from reading the store description or even the intro cinematic.

If you come into the game ignoring anything else but the fact that it's a nice little idle game, that instead of paywalls, subscriptions and a real money shop, you simply buy in, then you will not be disappointed.

The opening cinematic was fairly decent and gripping, demons from space are invading Earth, and alongside contemporary modern soldiers, super heroes are doing their best to fight back the invaders with the end goal of defeating the demon king. 

So I was expecting to be able to build my dungeon delving team from a wide roster of heroes and perhaps even regular forces, and inbetween runs build up my home base, and this is where the game falls flat.

Any enemy you defeat, becomes available for recruitment – which is awesome!
However, this is seemingly the only way to gain new units.
So, instead of a roster of heroes...I had the default starter hero (you don't get to pick), a thug wearing a balaclava, wielding a knife and aptly named shanks, a giant bipedal sewer rat in the news for murdering people, and another people murdering monster, a giant snail, as my team of 'heroes'.
Straight away, the entire theme of the game is thrown out the window as if it was nothing but an afterthought and UI dressing.
The current roster of units is fairly small, with just 28 units; 20 of which are villainous minions such as mobsters or mutant animals, 5-6 are super heroes, and 2-3 are super villains (I'm not sure if ghast is a hero or villain).

Yep, that's it. That's close to the total number of enemies you can fight, and that's what you have to recruit from.
So if you want to build a team of super heroes, and stick with the games premise, well, you get a handful of people to choose from...eventually.
Each unit is assigned a cost value to recruit (and therefor upgrade). Specifically the 'hero' units range in cost from 500,000, to 354,000,000; the cheapest unit costs 10,000 as an example.

Base building is also completely non-existent. If you wanted to build up The Avengers/Vought tower, you are out of luck.
The 'base' upgrades are temporary, minor, 1 hour long buffs. Yeeep.
Things like, every 10 floors, heal 10% health, or to increase the drop chance of materials from enemies by x% for an hour.
Other things you can do at your base include;
:Training a unit – once every 2 real life hours you can train one of your units, by clicking really, really fast. Click fast enough and you get up to 4 levels which is hardly exciting when level milestones for your characters seem to be every 500 levels...
:There is a merchant that sells consumables, but he is useless as the currency traded at the merchant is needed for the ONLY useful progression in the game outside of earning XP, fusing.
:Fusion chamber – sacrifice one unit to boost the stats of another. Costs crystals. A tonne of them. Only worthwhile non combat thing to do, totally invalidates the merchant because why would you waste precious crystals on consumables? Interestingly enough, you can use the fusion chamber to give your units new perks, which could be fun to play around with much, muuuuch later in the game when you have literal billions to spare to buy the different units and create unique teams.

When it comes to the idle/clicker game side of things, Hypeleague Heroes doesn't even come close to matching (honestly, even learning from) juggernauts of the genre like Clicker Heroes or Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms), but there is still a fun and interactive idle game here even if it is incredibly basic and lacking in depth.

There is one issue however, that has almost tempted me to thumbs down review the game, and made me heavily consider refunding – the store page brags about an in game leaderboard, however progress clearly wasn't wiped on launch, so the devs/early testers have an enormous lead over even day 1 buyers that totally takes the fun out of chasing high scores.


Overall, even though this review was pretty scathing, I still recommend the game as is to fans of the idle genre. For people who are drawn in purely by the idea of running a super hero league, I'd look elsewhere.
There is enormous room for growth in this title and I hope the developers can put in the time and effort to bring out it's unrealised potential.

Hyper League Heroes  V2.7   WORKS ON STEAM DECK  

The game is a mixture of several IDLE / RPG / Puzzle games all in one.   Most of this in the MANUAL tab. (Rebirth is extreme end game) 

If you enjoy progress and beating mobs while trying to determine what you can do to maximize your teams capabilities and speed up your leveling, this game has more depth than ANY game I have played to date.  Some simple, some insane and complex.  You can play, selecting which hero attacks which villain, choose when to use your super powers, and potions, OR select auto. (This is further adjusted in Tactics in the CREW screen where you can tinker who you want to attack and how you want them to use their abilities (Think Soda Dungeon 2 scripting w click options super easy) 

Stage 1 (Starter)  you have a tree of heroes that will become available after reaching certain goals. These heroes can but Fused / Merged (in Facility) to make a tougher / stronger single hero.(there are combos of merging different heroes to make a more powerful 3rd type of hero.
** Singe + Wolf = Werewolf (watch stats before you merge, they can differ depending on which one is more powerful and faster etc. ((This is part of the madness endgame))
You can go straight into the Tower Climb ( in Battle) but I suggest doing a Loot Rush (in Battle) first (20 min cool down between runs)  *(as of 2.7 it resets to lvl 1 every time you close the program, if you can get past 100 lvls the 2nd time you run it during the same game play it starts at lvl 100. Gear Scales based on the lvl your completing. ** Reminder watch your time and be sure to leave on a 10 level when asked, )

*** IMPORTANT:  REMOVE GEAR AND CHARMS BEFORE MERGING ! ! ! 

Stage 1.1   with the Loot Rush, you have to understand how long it take your to clear 10 levels. IF you do not click "RETURN TO BASE WITH LOOT" (this happens every 10 levels) you will lose 1/3 to 1/2 your prizes. Those are super important, those are where you will get most of your Fusion Gems plus Phoenix Gems (Needed to Reset Fusion Costs back to base) Make sure to right click gear that you want to keep because you can only have 50 in your inventory the rest are converted to gems @ 5/each (they actually add up fast which is good, because your going to need a LOT of them... so many.... :)  ) 

Stage 2:  Story / Leader Board - Good to test your heroes but more important because this is where you get your charms for things like +20% Healing, Stun Immunity, Open Chest Automatically (SO important and game changer)  These Charms can be combined and will make more powerful charms,  It can be a bit of a grind but you are getting materials so its a win win. 

Stage 3: Tower Climb - #1. You can start it and walk away, once your heroes reach a level they cant beat in the time or are killed it will go back to the closest lvl 50 (50,100,150,200,etc) and start again, so you might end up grinding lvl 51 a lot if your unlucky ;)   
#2. You can play, along and play the mini games that will pop up and also select which zones you go to next vs it being random. Helpful when your trying to get to that next check point.  
This is where you will get the bulk of your resources needed to craft potions, gear, charms, stat upgrades etc. 

Stage 4:  #1 - Base Upgrades: These take ORE, which is randomly dropped in Tower Climb. These will be a HUGE source of your heroes power and capabilities, as well as giving you more time in Loot Rush, meaning higher levels / better gear. 
#2 - Dojo Cave: You can boost your characters levels automatically every 2 hours for XPS or play a click mini game no cost. 
#3 - Wanders Cave:  Another place you can get ingredients, these cost gems (Loot Rush)
#4 - Craft:  where you can make extra healing potions or Invulnerability Potions (my favorite) 
#5 - Loot Hunters:  You get a gem every hour your heroes are playing the Tower Rush (another place to get random ingredients) 

Stage 5: Eventually you will get into actually looking closer at your heroes. Each hero has 3-4 upgrade options, Attack x3 / Speed x3 / Defense x3 / Ability. One UNIQUE aspect of the Heroes is that they have attack speed effected by Fusion with faster heroes, merge a hero with an 8 speed with a hero with a 4 speed and the fused hero will have a 6 speed (then with another 4 speed = 5, then another 4 speed = 4.5, then 4.2, 4.1, then finally 4)  This can be done to an even quicker speed if you upgrade the speed x3 on the 4 speed it becomes a 2.8 attack speed.
*PROTIP recruit 5 sewer Rats, upgrade their speed to 2.8 then merge them with another rat you have NOT boosted the speed on. This Rat will have an attack speed of 2.8, then you will upgrade its speed on the character screen and it will now have an attack speed of 2. (you can see where this is going, resource sink)

‘Shores of Loci’ is a 3D jigsaw puzzle of sorts in which you will be building little islands full of life and detail to the point that they look like little dioramas and then those little islands become real-sized ones once they are finished. It is well worth mentioning the level of detail that has gone into these puzzle islands as it really is incredible, like holding a small piece of land in your hands and feeling like a god as you build the islands back together. It’s slow-paced, relaxing and shouldn’t give most puzzle fans much hassle as there is a hint system in place once you hold don’t a piece for long enough.

While there are only 4 worlds it will take you a good hour or so to get through them all and by the looks of things there are more to come in the future. I would have liked it to have been a bit cheaper than the current £11.39 asking price, but I think the amount of effort that has gone into the models still makes it worth the purchase.

I recommended this game for the sheer artistry it able to offering me. And I'm always had a soft spot for something unique in such department (art).

But we are talking about video game here, So the presentation and being "artistry" alone doesn't cut, So how's the gameplay you may ask.

Well, Lets jogging back into your memories a bit, Remember first time you play something like Lego or Jigsaw, or perhaps building a sand castle or clay? Yeah, This game gave you that kind of moment back to you again. But this time in a VR and you can inspecting detail on each of piece of puzzle in a way that only VR could offering to you.

Shore of Loci is about you picking pieces of "puzzles" and figuring about which go where, Simple as that. The best part is when you are realizing that your "pieces of puzzle" are getting much bigger, much grander and more elegant as you are progressing through the game.

So this is where a little Con start to kicking in, The gameplay are just that, You are fix in one room scale position, Doing a 3d Jigsaw puzzle, Finishing one stage and transfer to next, Rinse and repeat.

So the best way to experiencing this game, is not to rush, you are to enjoy "things" each stage could offering you, The BGM, The beautiful scenary, The puzzle and most important "Time" that you are willing to spent and feeling like a little kid again.

And the price tag is in my opinion the best , Not too much, Not too little. The Dev could made an extra by releasing a DLC for the soundtrack alone too.

I voted Shores of Loci for the Sit back and relax-award with, in my opinion, good reason. The game is essentially a puzzle. Not just any place, mind, but a series of places, grouped by different architectural styles and surroundings. The places are even inhabited by, well, some sort of inhabitants, going about their business.

The graphics are gorgeous! The controls are simple. The pace and the places are relaxing. Coming back here every now and then is a bit of an antidote to hectic life in the real world. A pocket-sized vacation, if you like.

Shores of Loci is basically a 3D jigsaw puzzle game using completely three dimensional puzzle pieces that naturally fit together (versus the traditional jigsaw puzzle pieces). You'll have to look closely at the puzzle pieces from all sides to find connecting roads, bridges, pillars, etc. in order to connect them to each other. The game currently consists of 4 themed world levels and it took me approximately 2.5 hours to complete the game. 

There is a hint system in case you get stuck, but I recommend not using it if at all possible, even if you're stuck. The hint system did not work on the last level, so you will have to just learn to look at the pieces closely. I will say that while I did enjoy the art style and the game in general is beautiful to look at, with flying birds and swimming dolphins in the background, the visuals overall were a bit too low resolution and a bit muddy looking (devs did put this on App Lab for Quest). I also enjoyed the sounds of the game. The game has a soothing soundtrack and nice ambient sounds. 

Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting steady 90 fps. I did not experience any serious issues or bugs (other than the hint system not working on the last level). I think that there is a lot of promise but some of the game's core mechanics are just frustrating. I bought this game for me and a friend and we compared our experiences as we played through it. We concurred on every point. I would for sure recommend this game if the checkpoint system and the jump boost mechanics were altered a fair bit. Let me explain:

1. The checkpoints are single-use and have a very long timer cooldown. This is frustrating if you're a medium-ability player because (especially for reasons explained below) you can't predict how the mechanics of a jump might go, so you end up waiting for the checkpoint meter to refill because that saves you more time in the long run. It's frustrating for a low level player, because you have to keep resetting your checkpoints every time you fall off. It's frustrating for all players, becuase if you forget (froget?) to reset the checkpoint, dowwwwwwn you go again.

2. The jump boost mechanic is really unreliable. Both my friend and I concurred here too. It's very fiddly and you're never sure whether it will work. Hence, you loiter around waiting for your checkpoint meter to refill because you don't want to jump and risk resetting. Neither of us were in any way tempted by the time trial mode, as without checkpoints the unpredictable boost pads would ruin it every time.

But the game has some good points. It's got a very chilled out vibe, and depsite the frustration I never got properly mad at it or anything. I like the aesthetic and it's clearly somebody's labour of love. The core rocket jump game mechanic is pretty sound and I could quickly get into a rhythm when jumps didn't require boost pads. If the developer were to: a. fix the boost pads and b. overhaul the checkpoint system, perhaps by making checkpoints unlimited use and shaving a few seconds of the reset, or even just adding set checkpoints, I think this game has a lot of potential.

In short, I can't recommend this game (yet), but I did still make my friend play it too. Good effort developer; don't give up!

Finished this yesterday and overall I'd say I like it.

The combat mechanics are really solid, having to do a balancing act between regular attacks, skills and MP regeneration made the combat consistently engaging, I was playing on Normal, but even with that the regular encounters never felt mindless. I'm not too familiar with RPG Maker so I don't know how much this deviates from the usual, but it felt pretty unique to me at least. The areas you explore were all right, pretty standard but definitely not bad. I wasn't a big fan of most of the lategame sidequests(with one exception) since they felt kinda short and didn't tend to move the characters forward or even let them interact all that much, the main story locations were generally good though.

I generally like the cast of characters here, the main cast are very enjoyable and I really enjoy the dynamic the have with each other, their interactions were generally the highlight of the game for me. All of them are queer which is generally something I like and I feel it's handled well here, their identities are all important to their character and come up a quite a bit, but they've got plenty going on besides that.
The side cast fares a bit worse unfortunately, I'm not big on Lillith, she feels a bit too generic to me. I like what the game was going for with her interactions with Freya, but I just felt like the execution wasn't all there. Ruthea is also not great, I like her when she shows up, but she really needed more screentime. Despite being important to Freya's backstory she only shows up a couple times which makes the resolution between them feel a bit undercooked.

As for the general plot, this game is really going for something more character centric which I like and it's well executed, but the general plot beats are pretty generic, basically just a compilation of fantasy tropes. I can't say I found this world or most of the major events all that interesting, the interactions between the main party was the thing keeping me engaged, not so much the story around them.

The game tries to have comedic moments pretty frequently and these are a mixed bag to me, generally it's great when it's not relying on reference humor or memes which is unfortunately pretty often. Still got a good amount of laughs out of me, but also quite a few groans.

Visually the game looks pretty good, not blown away by the pixel art, but it does look pretty nice. The OST is also really good. I did notice some performance issues during battles in the late game side quests, the laptop I played this on is pretty old so maybe that's the reason, the issue was also generally resolved by quitting to the title screen and reloading so it ultimately wasn't that big of a deal.

Overall I'd say I definitely have my issues, but I still had a very good time with this and would recommend it if you're looking for a good indie RPG.

The Game Of All Time ∞/10

Plot:
It starts off with a charming little cutscene that explains the game's plot. Shrumblo, the blue robot, was going out on a walk as he usually does, but being the doofus that he is, he stumbles upon the lair of the red magical immortal Grumblo and enters it.

Gameplay:
There is no escape from Grumblo and his lair, so now your goal is to lure Grumblo into the moving spikes. Every time you do this, you get a point added to your score, and Grumblo gets stunned. The higher the score gets, the faster Grumblo will chase you. You also have the ability to boost with your rocket boots. The boost has a meter that will run out if you use it too much but will refill when you're not using it. The boost will also instantly charge when you get close to Grumblo. If Grumblo or the spikes touch you, you die. There are four spikes in the game. one moves like a DVD logo at slow speeds. One goes up and down at medium speed, one goes side to side at medium speed, and one goes around the borders of the room at fast speeds. There is an extra game mode that has two Grumblos instead of one, although in this one, only one of the Grumblos will get faster as you score points. The gameplay is really addicting and replayable, especially since there are trophies for you to unlock for each game mode. You get these trophies by getting a specific score. These scores are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and I'm assuming that the last one is 100 since I've still not managed to get there yet. The game did an amazing job of feeling like an arcade game and is also simple enough that anyone of any age could pick up and play.

PC Requirements: Pretty much any PC could run this, and don't worry about having to wait a day for the game to download since the game size is pretty small.

Music: The music is public domain, but it still slaps though. I love the upbeat tune of the menu, representing how Shrumblo must've felt on his walk, and don't even get me started on the theme that plays once you start playing. The game's theme starts off with an epic piano and drums before the violin comes in, making everything sound complete. It truly represents the showdown between Shrumblo and Grumblo and how Shrumblo's fate is sealed, so his only goal now is to try to survive for as long as he can.

Character Design, Art Style, and World Building: Shrumblo and Grumblo's design can be summarized pretty easily. "Simple but effective". I think the reason for this is because of the childlike nature of the art style. The art style is really reminiscent of a children's book. It also explains why Grumblo doesn't appear as a typical demon but is still evil-looking enough to get the message around that he is a demon. The simple plot of the story also helps convey the idea that this is a children's book. The world-building is also very interesting. It makes you ask questions like, Why did Shrumblo decide to go a different path for his usual walk? Why does Grumblo want to be left alone? Who built Shrumblo? What kind of world is this where robots and demons coexist? Did Grumblo eat Shrumblo? These are the questions that keep me up at night.

Conclusion: Go buy the game.

[u][b]Clarent Saga: Chronicles[/b][/u] is a subpar and amateur linear novel with turn-based JRPG battles interspersed between the scenes which is something that I've never seen before and is an innovative concept that adds a bit of engagement to the novel and helps break up the act of reading.

Overall, I don't recommend it because the combat system falls prey to the age-old pitfall of the genre where battles require very little strategy and can be won by simply dealing as much damage as quickly as possible, the story is prosaic, ill-conceived, and relies far too heavily on deus ex machina moments to advance the plot, and many of the characters feel pointless because they have very little relevance outside of their one chapter in the limelight where they are used as a medium for a deus ex machina moment.

Note: this review is current as of v 1.0.4 released on 23 June 2023 which is the latest update.

[hr][/hr]
[quote][b]S U M M A R Y[/b][/quote]

- The gameplay is standard for the JRPG genre and incorporates some nifty mechanics to add depth while there are many questionable design choices;
- The replay value is quite low since the game is a completely linear novel, although the cheat menu does allow you to recruit the humanoid boss characters and face extra, stronger, bosses;
- The graphics are made up of vibrant and stylish 16-bit pixel art sprites for the characters but shabby art assets for the enemies;
- The soundtrack is composed of unremarkable and uninspiring 16-bit fantasy adventure songs which are heavily inspired by the early [i]Final Fantasy[/i] titles; and
- The story is a typical tale of good versus evil which suffers from the flagrant overuse of deus ex machina moments to conveniently provide a solution to the party every few chapters while the huge roster of 14 characters makes most of them feel pointless outside of their one chapter in the spotlight.

[hr][/hr]
[quote][b]R E V I E W[/b][/quote]

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The gameplay is based on the 8 and 16-bit JRPGs of old but adds a few neat mechanics in an attempt to modernize the combat system and add some layers of strategy to it such as being able to "break" (stun) enemies if you hit their weaknesses enough times, swap characters mid-battle, or use "Boost Points" to multiply the power of your next action. Lamentably, the Boost Points undermine and negate any strategy that the other mechanics add because it lets you win battles through sheer damage and brute force alone.

All types of armor can be used by any character which means that there is an objectively "best" set for each role that you want to fill and begs the question of what the point of most of the equipment is since some sets are simply better than others and strictly worse options only serve to add unnecessary bloat to the game. Furthermore, characters can have any other character's class as their subclass (with some exceptions) which grants them access to that class' spells, skills, and equippable weapons.

Both of these elements combine to homogenize the characters that you get in the first half of the game into their predisposed role (fighter, mage, or hybrid) and make them indistinguishably interchangeable from others who also fill that role which begs the question of what the point of having so many characters is when they can each do the same thing that every other character can; however, the most baffling part is that all of the characters in the second half of the game completely overshadow those from the first half in terms of raw power, versatility, and because their class can't be used as a subclass by anyone else.

Each chapter starts you in an interlude area where you can change the difficulty and access the tutorial, shops, and BGM player, as well as a cheat menu where you can give yourself levels, gold, or subclasses that you don't normally get access to during the game, recruit characters early, recruit the humanoid boss characters, and fight in battles of various level ranges for extra gold and experience. These features are completely unnecessary since the game is already extremely easy to begin with, especially since you have access to it from the start when it would served better as a post-game reward.

The game also has a number of other perplexing design choices such as all equipment being available for purchase from the start which is both overwhelming when you first view the shop and removes a sense of progression from the game, barely getting enough gold to outfit more than four characters which partially renders the swap mechanic moot, and having random surprise and preemptive attacks despite the narrative often mentioning one or the other which is contradictory.

[h3]Graphics[/h3]
The graphics use colorful and great-looking 16-bit pixel art for the named characters and humanoid bosses but bland art assets for the enemies and non-humanoid bosses. The novel portions of the game are overlaid on a pure black screen which doesn't help set the scene or provide an atmosphere, especially since the writing doesn't describe everything in very graphic detail.

[h3]Sound[/h3]
The soundtrack is conventional for the fantasy setting and adventure theme and fits game well but is otherwise middling and unmemorable. You can access the entire soundtrack via the interlude area between chapters and there are a huge selection of songs but they are so forgettable that I couldn't tell you if all of them were even used in the game or not.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is a banal tale of good versus evil that is told from the perspective of one character but is atrociously crafted due to the complete overreliance on deus ex machina moments that provide conveniently apropos solutions to the party's predicaments at every major impasse. And this doesn't just happen once or twice, it happens every few chapters which feels downright contrived and amateurish and had me constantly rolling my eyes.

The characters outside of the starting four seemingly join the party for no genuine or believable reason and having an inflated roster of 14 characters means that most of them get very few lines outside of the chapter in which they are introduced where they play pivotal role as a result of their deus ex machina moment. If you don't actively swap who you use in combat then you might even forget that some of them exist until they have a random line in a later chapter.

The writing is adequate and is descriptive enough to paint a reasonable visual in your mind while the dialogue is competent as each character has a distinct personality and their more pronounced (or annoying) traits shine through the script; however, there are a few typos including some misspelled character names which is somewhat embarrassing.

[h3]Miscellaneous[/h3]
The game has a number of bugs which range from harmless visual ones to more severe gameplay ones such as the inability to steal items since their count doesn't increment properly (sometimes causing the item menu to display that you have zero of an item) as well as possibly being unable to steal from bosses unless you just need a really high agility stat.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Overall, I don't recommend it because it is a very rough amateur production which is severely lacking in the story and gameplay departments and has a copious amount of incomprehensible design choices. That being said, adding battles to a novel is a fresh idea since they act as a relatively entertaining diversion from the reading but this concept is unfortunately executed very poorly.

Perhaps the characters could have been split into separate parties and the story was told from different perspectives, eventually culminating in the merging of these stories, or the story could have focused solely on the four starting characters and their growth and development rather than inundating you with needless characters who feel more like a showcase for their class and most of whom get very few lines anyways.

Nightmare of Decay is a very good and simple horror action game and a good resident evil clone; okay let's talk about the story. A young man is at home watching the news about the recent disappearance of a young woman who vanished without a trace just like the other 10 people before her, the only common link to them is that they all suffered from nightmares. The young man can relate as he too has been suffering from nightmares, figuring that watching the news is only going to make his nightmares worse he decided to have some dinner and go to bed, but after laying down to sleep he then wakes up in a strange Mansion filled with horrible monsters and the undead, but this doesn't feel like a simple nightmare as he must traverse the strange nightmare realm in order to escape.

Now let’s go into the likes, the gameplay is very good it's a simplified version of Resident Evil, solve some puzzles, scavenge for resources and fight monsters nothing too complicated while still being very enjoyable and a bit challenging for first time players. The weapons were good each one was devastating with their own feel, you get your standard pistol and shotgun, also a Magnum, but after beating/doing some challenges in challenge mode you get more. The puzzles are good nothing too complicated with very simple answers if you're paying attention. 

The challenge modes was good although horde mode could be a bit of a pain, but I do like that there's an option to not have the cultists appear as they have weapons and if you're not careful they can take huge chunks of your health, anyway the challenge modes were a nice distraction after beating the main game, but there is a slight problem with one mode, but that’s for dislikes. 

The enemies and bosses were very good each one had their own unique, but traditional looks, like there zombies and zombie dogs, but we also get unique bosses like haunted armor and one boss that was quite a funny reference to a certain movie. The graphics were very good with a great classic old school feel with its uses of colors, designs and overall aesthetic. The levels are good, the mansion is a bit diverse and simplified with each room being distinct that keeps you from getting lost.

The story was good, it’s pretty simple you're trying to wake up/escape from this nightmare, it also does a good job giving hints that there's more going on than this being just a simple nightmare like when you talk to the different NPCs and read the notes, the story does a good job in setting up for a future sequel.

The characters were good while there's only two real characters, the main character and a cat, with the others just being window dressing/just to give a little bit of back story on what might be going on they were still all very good. The atmosphere was good nice and spooky, while not being too spooky as you wander around the mansion for the first time playing the game and dreading what's around the corner.

The game also has plenty of very good references to other works of horror and other stuff like besides Resident Evil; we have character cameos from Silent Hill and one particular movie reference that I was quite surprised to see. The notes were good as it helped the game’s story and atmosphere while painting a picture of what might be going on. I also really like the price for the game its more than fair. Now is the game scary, honestly yes at least for the first playthrough, where you're wandering around and dreading what's behind the next room. Also the game can be quite gory, heck there's even an option where you can turn up the gore factor.

Now let’s go into the dislikes. There's nothing really to dislike about the game although I will say there was one bug that happened to me where the game just kind of crashed on me, but only happened to me once and that was during the escape dungeon mode. The hoard challenge could be pretty annoying especially with the dog enemies as they can be quite chaotic and run around. Now there was a problem with challenge mode and there's this mode called randomized mode where it randomizes items and enemies only problem is after beating it I was expecting it would unlock something like infinite health items or infinite something else.

Okay with that done Nightmare of Decay is a very good and simple horror action game and a good resident evil clone; it has very good gameplay, very good graphics and very good enemies and bosses. Now I definitely recommend this game if your fan of Resident Evil styled video games then this is definitely for you and I honestly hope the makers of this game do a sequel.

[h1] [b] [i] A passionate, low-budget homage to the first Resident Evil [/i] [/b] [/h1]

[h1] [b] [i] ★★★★★★★★☆☆ [/i] [/b] [/h1]

Nightmare of Decay is an excellent example of how to pay tribute to a beloved game or a franchise while straying beyond mere inspiration into the realm of straight up copying the original content. The game is unafraid to parade around the fact that it was not just inspired by the first (and to a smaller extent, the second) Resident Evil game to the point of featuring pretty much the same exact setting, many of the same puzzles, the progression, and the gameplay. The thing is - it is done so damn well that you won't really care. Nightmare of Decay treads the line between inspiration and plagiarism with all due grace and elegance and ends up being a nostalgic call-back to a very different era of games, it the best way possible.

[h1] [i] “Looks like the nightmare has claimed yet another victim.

Many have been brought here against their will only to meet a terrible end one way or another. No one has ever managed to escape alive!

I wonder how long you'll be able to survive for...not long if I had to make a guess...” [/i] [/h1]

Nightmare of Decay is a humble game, small in scope, but as you can easily notice from the overwhelmingly positive reviews, the little it does, it does extremely well. The premise? One dev decided to create his own Resident Evil 1 in a pixel-art graphics and played from the first perspective and mixed in a few elements from Silent Hill series, Amnesia a few other popular games falling into the horror niche. The result of this predictable concoction is a comforting survival horror shooter you will likely blitz through in a couple of evenings. While it won't surprise or shock you with anything you haven't seen before in other, sometimes much older games, Nightmare of Decay manages to deliver that addicting "check-list" gameplay you won't want get away from until you reach the inevitable end, in much the same way as it was in the first Resident Evil or Silent Hill games. 

The developer's biggest strength are his humble, realistic, yet sufficiently high-enough aspirations. Nightmare of Decay is not a breakthrough in indie horror by any means, but its every single aspect is polished to perfection. The pixel-art graphics are amazing, the combat feels punchy and impactful, the exploration is rewarding and the loot and difficulty is balanced in a way where you always have just enough ammunition and healing items to feel carefully optimistic but not overconfident. The game is also just long enough for it all to not get boring or stale, but if you want more (which you very well might), then you also get two extra modes: an endless horde mode and a random dungeon generator, which means you'll be able to get your fill of the game's humble but fun combat. 

Honestly, with the incredibly low asking price, Nightmare of Decay is nothing short of a steal. While it is a small project that in many ways blends together the most recognized and prominent elements from famous horror franchises, it delivers just enough of its own unique essence to sate that never-ending hunger for a good old-school survival horror game.

I will generally recommend this game as it is clearly well made, and had a lot of love poured into it. It's a fun experience until you get into the later game, and I'm sure if you get comfort from repetition, then this game is for you.

That being said, I have to say that the roguelite element of it is a real detriment to the overall enjoyment of the story (and this game has many narratives). Resetting after long runs just seems like more of a punishment/frustration, than any feeling of accomplishment/advancement, and resetting in order to go through it all again to get one chance at one of the other narratives (briefly if you are in timer mode, as you are likely to fail first time). It therefore seems interminable to go through so many rounds of the basics, just to get one more crack at the end of one of the narratives.

Don't get me wrong, I think the fixing and "mechanics" of the game brings the same amount of joy as "Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes", but imagine if in "Keep Talking", you always restart at the most basic level again, have to work your way through 6 rounds of the easy stuff again, just to continue with the more engaging stuff. As other reviewers have mentioned, the permanent upgrades don't seem to add a lot to making that experience smoother. I feel like if they just incorporated "punishment" into the learning-mechanics (like "Keep Talking"), rather than also rogueliting your way back to zero (i.e. just have one punishment loop), it would have been a better game overall.

As it is, I played in timer mode, until I realised exactly how many times it was likely for me to re-do the end phases, and decided to restart again in non-timer mode. This way, at least I could eliminate one punishment track (running out of time), which did allow me to enjoy the game more and get to the end of at least the main narrative (at least, the first time).

Sadly, after doing that, I didn't feel compelled to do it all again, something like 7 separate times, just to complete all the narratives. Its the kind of game you just go to YouTube to watch the endings on, which is a bit sad. Would have rather done it myself, if I had infinite time on this earth.

Anyway, if you are super into roguelikes, then this game is for you! If you are luke-warm to the constant resetting, I would advise non-timer mode so you get a little less punishment. If you are medium to dislike on Roguelikes, give this one a miss.

Here's the thing. Despite not being german, I love repetitive game loops where I do menial tasks to fulfill jobs. Adding a rogue-like element to that makes it even more charming. If you like that PLUS a challenge, the frantic mode of this game is gonna be perfect for you. If you're more of a coward like me, you'll still like this because it has a more relaxed mode that's not timed. But honestly, even if you DO like a challenge, I recommend starting on the non-timed mode just so you start getting a solid feel of what each repair job entails and get comfortable with being able to diagnose the issues without having to double-check basic things.

There is a tutorial in this game. It will teach you the basics of moving around your repair shop, but it will NOT explain how to do any of the repairs. That's what the manual is for, dummy! You better like quickly browsing through it and zeroing in on the info that you need. Most jobs you can cross-reference at your leisure without messing them up, but there are some fixing tasks that are very demanding time-wise. That's what makes even the non-timed mode challenging.

You think you've gotten the hang of things, you're comfortable taking on the more challenging jobs, and then BAM, your fun gets ruined because you stumbled onto a melting reactor or a pipe bomb and as you try to read through the manual for what to do, the ship's exploded on your face. Or you forgot which client kills you on sight.

Random pros: The rogue-like upgrades for runs are fine and useful. The art is charming. There's a lot of content and it's a very fulfilling feeling when you start memorizing some of the repair jobs and you feel a sense of competency over how nice a fictional sci-fi mechanic you are while sometimes just hosing shit out of a toilet.

Random cons: Some of the instructions in the manual can be worded in a very confusing way. It's not fun trying to sit and memorize the manual, so you'll likely end up learning as you go and cross-referencing as you fix, but since the jobs are very random and the more challenging ones come up later, you will likely end up ruining a bunch of runs when the time-sensitive jobs you haven't had a chance to practice before pop up late run. I REALLY wish there was a practice mode where you could select the specific jobs you want to redo.

All in all, if you like job simulators, easy puzzles, or a timed challenge, I'd highly recommend this charming game.

The game has so much going for it. It's an interesting premise and story (what I've experienced so far). It has style for days. You can tell the devs put some heart and soul into it. The need for the grimoire/manual is pretty neat. The puzzles are pretty well thought-out, on the whole. 

I think my issue with this game is it's repetitive nature being too linear, and the rougelite nature being more of a slog than something exciting or challenging or varied for each new run. There's obviously only a set number of different puzzles that can be in the game (they can't be procedural like how a roguelike/lite can make a level procedural). Over the course of doing run after run, the repetitive-ness of those puzzles really detracted my enjoyment. Risk of Rain 2 or Project Zomboid make me excited to start a new run after failing/dying. This game made me just want to close it and play something else instead of doing the same things again for another hour or two to get back to where I was. The few upgrades didn't seem to make much of a difference, so the runs all started to feel *really* the same after a while.

I absolutely love this title's style and music and vibe, and wish that I wanted to play it more. If it weren't a straight roguelite, I think this game would be a huge hit. Or maybe, if the roguelite elements were actually cranked up a little to somehow make a bigger difference to the upgrades or choices ... so runs didn't feel the same. But I get that this game is how it is. It's a roguelite with a limited number of puzzles. It's also finished (i.e. not Early Access), so there's no expectation that's going to change. 

That's okay - it's just not a game for me. It's super cool, and I think it's fairly priced. So, thumbs up for those aspects even if I don't recommend the game to my past or future self.

That being said, I don't think it quite holds up to what other roguelikes have to offer in terms of raw replayability which is a defining trait of the genre. 

Though the gameplay is fun, as a roguelike veteran it doesn't offer enough challenge or gameplay diversity to keep me engaged. I never felt the need to experiment or change up my playstyle as Cramit's core moveset is just effective enough to deal with most scenarios. After beating Archmage Cramit for the 5th time with the same build I'd been clearing rooms with an hour into my run, I started to get bored.

Upgrades also don't change up gameplay enough for each run to feel different. Most are just stat upgrades or another method of dealing damage. This leads to most runs feeling the same. More randomness in terms of level design and enemy encounters would also be a welcome addition, as these start to get predictable fast.

To be honest, I was slow to warm up to the MC in this game, as it felt I was being railroaded onto a certain path with preconceived opinions. However as you get into the story the options to develop your character, what they believe, and how they think become more varied and the decisions you make do carry consequences and influence how the game pans out and what sort of ending you get. You are sent on a mission and as you investigate the circumstances you find yourself in you are allowed to change your mind if you want. Without revealing any spoilers, your character grows and matures because of their experiences, but this is no child growing up, its an intelligent 25 year old adult who has grown up apart from society and is faced with social and political views they did not know even existed until confronted with them. How they cope with the contradictions to everything they have been taught, and carry out their mission is up to you. There were several developments I did not see coming that could be described as throwing a spanner in the works. You will need to play the game to find out.
Most of the options and choices presented to you are reasonable, and only a couple of times did I feel that my MC was being forced to act differently from how I thought they should behave, and i was relieved that the option to change my mind was present up until the finale. The writing itself is solid, intelligent, and the author keeps up the air of expectancy and tension right until the end. There appears to be far more to read than in the usual IF games, I've done one run-through and while it did not take 6 hours (I had to leave the game at one point without shutting down) you will certainly not be able to race through it like you can with the young adult IF games. If there is a category for adult fantasy and magic, this is where this game would fit. Yes, you can romance some of the characters, and I think there may be an option for the obligatory sex scene or two, which you can simply ignore if you are already juggling too many schemes to further complicate your life.
There are plenty of opportunities for a rematch to further expose the parts of the story you have not yet discovered and explore the other pathways you ignored. One nice touch is that at the end of every chapter you are given the chance to replay it, or go on to the next one so you can rescue the bad click that took you somewhere you didn't want to go. I think this is something most fans of this genre appreciate.
Despite the slow start, I have enjoyed this game and am off for my second run-through, and if you try the demo and like it, then you can expect to enjoy a game that does not seem rushed at the end, and has an epilogue to tie up the loose ends. Another nice touch.
Incredible story with intricate characters. Choices are very impactful and branching.

They say that the key to a good story is to focus on characters: "Interesting characters can carry a weak plot, but the reverse can never be true."

Stars Arisen, however, manages both. The very lore of the world glides with its' characters, making for an immersive, impeccable experience that captures your full attention, even to minute details. It's a full coming of age story laced with magic, betrayals, and a carousel cast of unreliable narrators, which will have your Starchild measuring their own judgement against their trust in other people.

Stars Arisen is very unique in its' player-led experience, and even choices that shape the MCs' personality will have grand consequences to how the narrative is displayed. Will you play the lost heir, vying for their stolen birthright? Or the timid child of a hermit fumbling through a destiny bestowed upon them? It's an amount of nuance and choice that's frankly remarkable, and speaks to a level of back-end writing that goes unsung.

Fallen Spirit is an art-style micro-adventure that sees you helping a fallen star get back home. There is no spoken story, no guide, or help, its just you teleporting about working things out for yourself. It instantly reminded me of ‘Eclipse: Edge of Light‘, it’s got a dark, but neon blue light world all set in a cave with falling rocks and crumbling platforms. But you are never really in any danger here, nor is there a challenge, but there is a wonderful 20-40 minute adventure here filled with magic and mystery with some low-poly, but nonetheless beautiful graphics. While it did take me a long while I was savouring each scene, each area and taking it all it. You could easily rush through it in 10 or less. For me, this is what indie VR games should be like and for the money, it is super-easy for me to recommend it.

Amazin’ George is a frustrating experience. Despite my best efforts I was not compelled to finish the game and I am okay with that as I think most people would probably put in less effort than me. 

As far as this gameplay goes it is… fine. Doing mazes is a legitimate game and Amazin’ George does it pretty well. The mazes are varied, and they are quite maze-like, so the goal is achieved. That being said they are quite frustrating. First off, I wish there was a directional arrow. I do not think this would eliminate the challenge of the game and could even be used to trick the player into following the wrong path, but knowing where you need to be is super helpful. I have done corn mazes before, and you always know where you are supposed to end up, it does not hurt the experience it merely gives you a level of guidance. The arrow could be time-based and only show up at the last 5 minutes or something, it could be an item, or you could use the 3d environment to your advantage and make a tower to use (I had one in a corn maze before). Without this guidance, it is slightly more frustrating. Speaking of frustration I was never 100% sure how the balls of yarn worked. All right so I get that they can occasionally get you treats very simple, but then they can also give you a speed-up that is supposed to be bad as it gives auditory feedback that it is bad? It can make things more difficult, but that is not always the case. Not only that but it feels random as when I move sometimes it just moves me in random directions. It feels sloppy and frustrating, but don’t worry once you reach level 3 I had them stop working altogether, not even a sound would play. Speaking of things that are not clear and frustrating, what are rabbits and frogs for? Do they do anything or do they just frustratingly block your path? I was not able to interact with them and that was annoying as they got in my way. The enemies are way too hard to avoid, a lot of the time there is nowhere to outmaneuver them and they generally move faster than you as well and so I just ended up just giving up the treats to get past them, and the sharks are even worse because they made you restart the level. Speaking of sharks though level 4 was one of the most unpleasant gaming experiences I have had in quite some time, the reason being that jumping is just outright scuffed in this game. I don’t understand how it works, it seems like it needs a running start of at least one space, but does not always work, and sometimes when you do not get a start you just jump anyways and it feels too quick and slippery to respond properly. Then there is the issue of distance it just is not clear, I could easily make a jump in one spot that is large, but a small jump was impossible. This made level 4 terrible because if you jump in the wrong spot or jump (or don’t) when you don’t mean to you have to start the whole level again after a shark wrecks your day. It just felt gross to play. Lastly, for gameplay, I need to discuss the reason I stopped playing. I intended to at least get to the DLC for this game but chose to cut it short as I think any sane person would do. When I got to level 5 I paused the game, funnily enough, my cat was pawing at me for a treat and I needed to eat so I just got up and went to go do that. 12-13 minutes later I get back to my desk and realize that for whatever reason despite the message that says, “it’s Paused, meow!” (with that capitalization mind you), the timer had been going down and I had maybe a minute left, well I had all the treats I needed so it was not a huge deal and when I timed out on level 3 it just finished the level because I had enough treats, so I was not worried. Anyways I should have been, because when the timer finished I failed and went back to level 1. An hour of work wasted, yes there is a save feature, BUT this is inconsistent and just outright an error that can’t be ignored as it ruined my experience immediately as I was not saving, 1 because I intended to finish it in a single session if I could, and 2 because I did not need to I was doing fine. If this would have happened on level 3 I would have had no issue as it was consistent and I could learn from it, but this was out of the blue and was caused by a menu lying to me and saying that it is paused. This soured me so much about this game, yeah it is pretty boring and has some issues, but this is unforgivable. I did later return to check out the remastered version and sadly even after the update the gameplay is no different and I was running into the same issues that made the experience frustrating, in fact, I was really displeased to see how I was struggling more and how I had to retry level two a few times to try and pass it. This game just isn’t fun take my word for it.

I hate to be that guy but the story of this game kind of sucks. It is done in a kind of rhyme style at the beginning of levels, and it doesn’t flow well and I was never gripped by its narrative. If anything, it felt like a waste of time. It was inconsequential to the gameplay and never really added to the experience.

The UI had some issues. First, I did not know I could change the game volume until I quit to the menu. When I start up the game and it gets right down to business, I immediately pause to try and find options to change the volume, and they are not there. So I play the game until I am quitting and exit from the menu to find that there is a main menu and I can adjust settings from there. Even odder, in the remastered, it has no menu to go to you can only save and such at the end of levels. And better yet, the only way to quit either version of the game is to exit full screen and close the window or alt-F4. Why is everything hidden, convoluted, or missing? And get this, when you start the game a second time it starts you at the beginning so if you want to load your game you have to skip the initial dialogue, exit to the menu, and then load it. This is fixed in the remastered content, but the remastered now lacks a volume option so 1 step forward 2 steps back I guess. This kind of simple stuff shows disregard for the user’s experience.

The Music is thematically fitting, but from what I listened to is limited to 2 songs and a sped-up version of 1 of those songs, so get comfortable with repetitiveness. Sound effects are also limited and are very simplistic. So there is nothing to praise in the sound department.

Artistically this game is a mishmash of 3d environments with largely 2d pixel assets and it is fine. If you like that older style of games I think you will appreciate it. In the update, the game is brought to the graphics of the sequel which has more of an N64 vibe, and honestly, I think they are worse from a stylistic sense, but if you like it you can freely switch between the two. 

I wanted to like this game, I hate to be so critical of small devs, but lying about my experience to make someone happy is worse. Even for the pennies I paid for this game, I don’t think it is worth it, it was just a frustrating experience. I wish I could say the update done after the second game’s release made things better, but as far as I could tell it improved nothing (and in fact may have broken more things). It’s disappointing because this game feels unique in its own right, but unique is not always good.

Alien Rogue Incursion is one of the most frustrating experiences I've ever endured. Here's a list of issues I have with the game that I've noticed in my short time playing it. 

- Grabbing items off of one's person is lacking in sensitivity to the extent where I cannot grab the motion tracker or ammo without actively looking at where my hand is going, otherwise it comes up empty (not ideal in high intensity scenarios as you would imagine). 

- Items don't always deposit back into your inventory when you release them and I cannot for the life of me understand why. I'll release the grab button in the exact same manner for the exact same item and sometimes it ends up back on my person and other times it lands on the floor with an embarrassing thud. 

- The Aliens are bullet sponges

- Hand movement is sluggish and always feels slower than my actual hand movements leading to a strong sense of disconnect between myself and the player character.

- This is personal preference but I'd prefer disembodied hands to a full body render as whenever the body moves it usually doesn't move in a similar manner to my own, thus creating a disconnect. There's a reason Half Life Alyx used disembodied hands, not even Valve could figure out a way to make that look good. 

- Little to no build up to the first Alien encounter so any tension that might have existed was completely deflated. Pacing in general feels very rushed frankly. 

- The Aliens spawn on an infinite timer that's about as consistent and predictable as the sun rising in the morning. This kills any sense of fear or tension and results in the Alien threat serving as a nuisance that's preventing me from exploring. In a flatscreen game this would be bad, but in VR that issue is exacerbated. VR games inherently favour exploration as scrounging for items is a far more involved process than simply pressing the "E" key on an item to add it to your inventory. The aforementioned sluggish hand movement also makes combat with the Aliens feel like an absolute chore.  

- The game attempts to hide its loading screens in gameplay which on paper sounds like a good idea. VR is all about immersion after all and hiding the loading of a game in order to allow the player to keep full control of their character should help retain immersion in the game. The problem is that loading causes obvious slowdown and freezes which break immersion far more severely than any loading screen ever would. 

- Lines of dialogue would bug out to the extent that my character would respond to a question around 5 minutes after it had been asked. Multiple times. In a row. 

- The main character simply won't shut up. When I was carrying around a quest relevant item, whenever I dropped it to have both my hands free for something, she refused to stop reminding me of the object's existence despite it being A LITERAL FOOT AWAY from where I was standing. This was the straw that broke the camel's back for me. I can take jank, but I refuse to be talked down to. 

There are things to like here. As someone who likes as much world interactability as possible, the amount of objects I can pick up and mess around with is impressive. The computer terminals and the PDA are intuitive and true to the world. The hacking minigames take advantage of the VR medium quite well. The issue is none of these positives outweigh the sheer slog that is playing the game. I'll give it another try when a major update hits but until then I cannot recommend this game.

Pros:
+ You can tell the devs were obviously heavily inspired by Alien Isolation and really wanted their title to fit in its universe - the atmosphere and environmental art direction is spot on with Alien's retro futurism.
+ Single player, story driven, survival horror experience, unburdened by shoe-horned in multi-player mechanics, loot drops, card systems, leveling systems, and other unnecessary trendy game design fluff.
++ Xenos are an actual threat and aren't a horde of punch-able zombies - do whatever you can to not let them get close - plant grenades at choke points, fight from positions where you aren't easily flanked, sometimes even running is a viable option. Do yourself a favor, set it on hard and every battle overcome will feel like a great accomplishment. This setting also makes the alien lore of its lethality faithful - "the perfect organism."
+++ No corporate merc enemies/gun fights - easily the most boring encounters from prior alien games so glad it is omitted less I get flash backs of Aliens: Colonial Marines. This needs to happen in Part 2 also.

Cons:
- While many wished for "Alien: Isolation with gun," VR does make it less accessible to the masses, but that's just how it is. That being said, it's a great VR entry title for Alien super fans.
- A dismemberment system really would have added to the visceral nature and added more interesting game play, ie only explosive ammo can immobilize xeno movement and reduce combat effectiveness rather than relying on a bullet sponge stun effect. Half-xenos crawling towards you still murderous has always been a cool thing from early alien games, even in the sprite based era.
- There are some scripted ambushes/encounters time to time that feel cheap.
- Is there a weird copyright preventing Alien games from modeling the film correct weaponry or what?! Too many recent Alien games have overstepped creative liberty altering the very iconic props we've all wanted to handle. "M4A1/2," "M41A Mark 2," "M41A2," etc etc, no thanks. I haven't seen a correct variant in an Alien based FPS since AVP 1 and 2.  Even the Defiance comic book this game is based off of rendered it correctly. Also would like the motion tracker and its UI to resemble the one in Aliens as it is a military model, not an improvised device that was kludged together like in Isolation. Re-skin option please?
- Need m240 flame unit badly. Could be used to block and purge vents hostiles are coming from.
- Add the VP70 with the movie correct firing sound as an alternate side arm.
- Need Remote sentry guns.
- Smart gun, 'nuff said. Part 2 probably?
- Add USCM helmet since there's a hat system in place, complete with pull down, functional eye piece.

VR games are still in their infancy as far as I'm concerned, as multiple tech issues and compatibility quirks can often get in the way of them functioning as well as intended. Such is the case with Alien: Rogue Incursion, a game I truly wanted to love. I'm a big fan of the Alien franchise, and being fairly new to VR and also a streamer, I was hoping this would be an excellent fit for my channel. It turned into a laughable tech nightmare for 75% of every session, and for a game that probably should have only taken me two streams to complete, I went for maybe 5-6 streams and I still haven't completed the game, because the game simply won't let me complete it.

I was soft locked out of an elevator that takes me to what I assume is an end-game area after dying in said area and respawning at the save point by this elevator, and I can only hope that this is fixed for others in the future so that they do not have to go through the pain of basically being brickwalled by this bug. I normally wouldn't write a review longer than a few succinct sentences for a Steam review, but I'm so annoyed by what just happened with this bug and how it entirely bodied this playthrough to the point of it being unplayable that I feel the need to air my grievances. I'm adding to the noise, but hopefully it helps someone else down the road.

The soft lock bug mentioned above was not the only problem I encountered with this game. Sometimes it would freeze. Sometimes clipping would be atrocious. I had a difficult time seeing over my own body in the game to find any of my ammo, which doesn't seem right. I had multiple issues getting this to run with some of the overlays I use specifically for streaming, and had to tinker around a lot with settings to make this work properly. I know that this is a specific to streaming, but when no other VR games seem to have these issues, I have to mark it as a negative for a game. The "SteamVR/OpenXR" error that pops up constantly, while seemingly not mattering in the long run, is like a warning to all that should be heeded. It's fixable, but if you plan on using some kind of overlay software in tandem with this game, you're going to have some weird issues. My system is sporting an i9-14900KF with a 4090, 24GB of VRAM and 64GB of uh other RAM, so it's not really a slouch. On a Meta Quest 3, Rogue Incursion seemingly ran like garbage, even after finely tuning my settings. I don't have this problem with other games, but somehow this one was a consistent issue. 

Control schemes for the game, while immersive, were fairly clunky as well, and I can't imagine playing this on any difficulty harder than the easiest one, or maybe just normal, because of how clunky and broken everything felt. And again, I did find enjoyment in the game when it worked - the environments, sounds, all of that was PERFECT. There is truly something to be loved here for a fan of the films, and if you're one of the lucky ones to have no issue running it, then you should consider buying a lottery ticket tomorrow. Because of a buggy mess presented in a well known IP package, I cannot in good faith recommend Alien: Rogue Incursion as a smart buy at full price, as it feels like a borderline slight to such a beloved franchise.

What I'm working with: Quest 3 wireless on at Ryzen 7600x, 32gb DDR5, RTX 3060 (12gb). Of note, I think this is below the minimum specs for GPU. But maybe the 12gb VRAM helps. I also overclocked it a little as well.
Technicals: Tried to play on low settings due to GPU concerns, but it was terrible. I bumped it to mostly medium and it played well. Only stuttered a few times like with decontamination gasses and such. 
Unlike pretty much all the other SteamVR games i use, this one wants you to launch through Virtual Desktop (which I fortunately had) set up in VDXR (a setting in VD you can easily select). You can play through SteamVR but don't have access to in game menu with this method.

Gripes: Overall, this was a very enjoyable game despite a few moments I wanted to give a negative review. The biggest  flaw was when I was in one wing of the facility near the end off the game, went to a save room as it was getting late, came back to play later and I was stuck in one area with doors to the wing closed and locked and the elevator at the other end of the chamber closed and locked. No way forward or back. Only choices were to 1)Start the game over, 2) Hope an update comes out eventually to fix it, or 3) contact Servio support. As I was near the end of the game I didn't want to start  it over. I also wanted to finish it soon. So I contacted support. To their credit they responded fairly quickly (check your spam folder). They basically gave me a save file to start me in he same area (with ample supplies thank you). I took it from there and just finished the game.
Another frustrating flaw was map waypoints near the end. The map had served me well up to later on in the game. But then I had to get a couple things for the ship. One was easy to find on the map. After I obtained the first thing, the waypoint was still marked at the location I came from. I didn't see any other waypoints so I looked back in the area I just was at. Wasted time and limited resources with nothing to show, so I searched more through the map including different areas and levels and found the location of the other thing needed. Shortly after this I had to go to a different area but again the waypoint remained from a previous spot, but the door was closed/locked to this area so I had to go searching around on the map to find a way. 
So the map was useful 90% of the time, but the other 10% could send you in the wrong direction. It would also help for them to label some of the bigger areas of the handheld map such as: medical wing, warehouse, garage and so forth. Don't need every room and closet labeled. 

Enough with the gripes. Here's more useful information/suggestions.

Weapons: Pulse rifle (99 rounds, 4 mags), pistol (6 rounds, 32? total), shotgun (8 rounds, 30? total). Reloading isn't too bad but an take a little practice. Sometimes misreads my loading actions (usually because I'm frantically doing it). Aiming is good. Just get the retacle approximately lined up then it mostly autoaligns to help the am. Some other shooters it's difficult to line up the sites while holding the controllers in the air, but this game does it well. Sounds reasonably good.

Enemy: Good aspects-AI pathing is very good. They don't always just go for the direct path. Sometimes they'll take the ceiling or wall and approach to your side or behind (I tried to keep a wall to my back and not stay under an open vent). Sometimes you'll hit them and they'll retreat and come back at you a moment later, possibly from a different angle. Usually they'll come at you in 2s or 3s. But  there are a few times you have to fight more. You do occasionally have to deal facehuggers. If one gets on your face, pull it off with and grab your pistol, shoot it with one round. I made the mistake unloading the pistol into one.
Bad aspects- The spawning frequency could be annoying as others mentioned. I think it was good to constantly have to stay on edge to keep in spirit of the IP, but  they need to make some changes here. I do think sound played some role as knocking over a bunch of boxes or using the welder seemed to attract them so that makes sense. Otherwise they need to vary the frequency of enemy spawning. 

Story: nothing amazing but it was engaging. 

Movement/grabbing/etc: generally fine, but  trying to grab an item out of a bin/box was nearly impossible. I usually just dumped the contents on the floor to pick up. Sometimes the arm/hands would get caught up in things, but this was a minor problem. 

In summary, I loved the meat and potatoes of this game. If you enjoy Aliens games then you should be satisfied. If they fix a few more of the bugs it would be an even better experience. I think they'll learn a lot from making this game and come out with Part 2 with a better start.

This game really captures the spirit of the Alien franchise. It is a sci-fi horror thrill fest and I couldn't stop playing. There are some amazing and unexpected plot elements. The addition of a semi-useful Android companion (story/battle mode) is a nice touch that relieves some brief tedium in the early game. There is a lot of tension and suspense throughout. 

Yes, it's on rails; yes there are pre-determined encounters (some you can't avoid dying from the first go-round while fumbling for your pulse rifle); and you have to fetch and place for the most part but it's a good balance with the atmosphere. I also had an issue where every time an Alien came on the screen it would freeze for about a second and when there were multiple Aliens it just crapped itself. This was especially frustrating about the middle of the game when it disconnected, froze, and crashed often just as all hell was breaking loose. I did quit a couple of times because there was nothing I could do to resolve it. This is a shame because you need that consistency and fps at the moment of conflict and it really takes the fun away.

I don't know if they are going to get to make Part 2 but I hope they do and I hope they improve on one or two elements of the game that detract from the experience. I definitely recommend it for a sale price. And watch for future patches.

[h1] Intro [/h1]
I had to spend a bit of time after completing the game to figure out whether I wanted to leave a recommendation or not. That alone might make it sound like I should give it a negative but I believe the pros do outweigh the cons due to the game's more story focused structure. Can't explore everything so I'll try to keep it brief to the things that stuck out the most to me.


[h2] Pros [/h2]
[b] Design: [/b] Character portraits, overworld models, combat animations, all of this and more were pleasant to the point that I want to branch out to other HD-2D style games just to see what they look like. Only thing I'd liked to be improved is the artistic design of the maps, some of them felt too plain and forgettable when effort was clearly put into the forementioned designs.

[b] Soundtrack: [/b] Not every track is golden, but there was plenty enough for me to groove to in my chair during combat or just sit back and enjoy while listening to the story progress.

[b] Story: [/b] I liked it. The characters interactions throughout the main story did a pretty good job of keeping me engaged and wondering what's going to come next, who will be revealed as a rat, should we take a pragmatic or moral approach and so on. Throw in the Scales of Conviction system for deciding which route you take and you have a pretty unique way of listening and responding to the world's events. Sometimes it'd be a bit cliche or cartoonish level of good vs. evil, but nothing I haven't seen or couldn't handle.

[b] Characters: [/b] More neutral towards most of them outside a select few that drive the storyline, but the game doesn't bore you too much with the ones you might not be interested in so it's up to you whether you want to care or not. That said, the downside is like what I said in the story section; some of the folks are a bit too one dimensional for me to agree with in most, if any, circumstances. Some of the English voice acting can be a bit dispassionate so heads up.


[h2] Cons [/h2]
[b] Combat: [/b] Really mixed about this as a con, but I've got to put it here. Does this mean the combat in this game is terrible and there's no way to get better at it? No, but heavens does this need some fine tuning and a half to not be so rigid in how you can approach the levels.

The general idea that you should maximize your positional gameplay so you don't allow yourself to be flanked sounds fine and dandy until it clashes with some of the enemy types. I cannot express how much I DETEST the enemy support units in this game. Let them get too comfortable for a round or two and they will force a reset.

"Oh, well you should stop complaining and just go for them right?" Yes and no. Go in seeing red and the melee attackers will kill you before you get within striking range.

"Okay, so don't rush them and just take your time turtling?" Eh, it depends on the map, as you don't always have time to set up the "perfect" plan due to all the moving pieces and how easy it is to overlook something. Plus, if you're too passive you'll set yourself up for the enemy to corner/surround you and give you no room to work with. Definitely think that for how many units this game has on the field at a time, it could stand to have more open maps to work with.

Worst part? You have very little idea how interactions are going to go. Other games like Fire Emblem and XCOM give you a solid idea of how an interaction can go or how a group of enemies may react to your units. Here? You will never know how much an enemy with hit for, their hit rates, who their target preferences are beyond "I can kill this unit now," if your 4 units will be able to kill a unit, etc. There are some aspects like certain characters skills and their upgrades that can help alleviate the pain a little, but it boils down to praying the AI and RNG debuffs work in your favor at the end of the day. Fun when things go well, but man did I get some out of control resets.


[b] Difficulty: [/b] Play hard mode at your own risk. I had a crisis of gamer identity at one point due to how overtuned some of the chapters felt. You can be outnumbered, squished together like the underleved sardines that you are, while the enemy sits at a premium vantage point with stronger stats across the board and is a misclick away from snowballing you. I'd have liked this kind of challenge more if the units you commanded had abilities that could turn the tide easily without having to wait 3-4 turns to charge up (the "mana" system in this game is tied to your unit's turn, so some abilities can take a while to use without dedicated support). Throw in the limitations the game puts on your upgrade system to make it unnecessarily expensive and you have a tough experience ahead of you. 

I've heard Normal mode and below isn't too bad beyond the occasional butt slap difficulty spike, so do with that what you will. Other folks even claim it makes the game too easy and that playing Hard mode is the best way to experience the game the first time and for all subsequent runs. I stayed with Hard mode all the way due to my pride (thank you Fire Emblem, Persona, and XCOM), but get ready to rage at times until you figure a cheese tactic or luck decides to grace you.


[h2] Closing Thoughts [/h2]
Overall, I'd say give the game a try if you're looking for something different that can be both challenging and relaxing. It might not be a groundbreaking game and it's definitely built for being played multiple times, but getting it for $24 on sale was well worth the price. Enjoyed the game enough to give NG+ a try and see if I can't fall in love.
