Kojima's first independent experience. 2015, [b]Kojima left Konami[/b] after MGSV. They didn't even let him accept the award he very deserved so. For the first time in years, there was no work ahead of him. No office, workers, computers, or resources; the man lost everything. 30 years in the industry, but no chance. Banks? Didn't trust him. Publishers? They didn't understand. Even his own family was against his idea, but if he going to continue creating unique experiences, it has to be on his own terms. He already had an idea that he was compelled to.

A studio that produce AAA games doesn't come in cheap, and Kojima didn't wanted to settle for less. [i]We know you're renowned, but you don't have actual results. [/i]It took him a little while to find a banker that's a fan and trust his vision for a loan. With the studio formed, with a logo that thrown on a paper - because they didn't had any computers - Kojima started to contact with western publishers. [i]You are crazy. [/i]What they told to him, because there was no pitch.

[b]You might think it's crazy too, I won't judge. But hear me out and be honest, Death Stranding is out for years and we know how the game is. If you were an investor, and some guy rushed in your office to pitch you a game where the main emphasis is connecting people together while delivering cargo, would you gave him the green light? I don't think so.[/b]

Despite all the circumstances, out of all game studios out there, there was one studio that was interested with the journey to independence of Kojima, despite being one of the largest game company out there. They understand he didn't want his creative vision to be touched with. A studio that known for getting smaller studios beneath them to create games that exclusive to their systems. But despite their authoritarian and strict policies, they didn't hesitate once when Kojima asked for help, and they basically gave him an empty check for him to pursue his dream.

[b]On December 16th, 2015; a day after Kojima's contract with Konami has been officially ended, Kojima Productions has been officially announced alongside with a strong partnership from Sony.[/b] 

He didn't had a studio to work with, because landlords didn't felt to settle with a company that didn't even produced anything yet. So he's settled for a room he was able to borrow from a friend and turned it into an office for himself and his three team members. He kept his independent endeavour a secret from his family, until the success that he was looking very forward to. But unfortunately, [b]his mother passed away during development.[/b]

He was just 13 when his father passed away, so his mother was a single parent that struggled to see the end of the day. Hideo, being very protective of her, stopped pursuing his dreams after finishing high school, and studied economics to be safe - a choice that satisfied everyone except himself.[b] But he never stopped dreaming.  [/b]He satisfied his active imagination through other forms of entertainment, His parents, encouraged his interest in movies; they would sit Hideo down to watch a movie together, and discuss the themes and direction with him. He was lonely and isolated and he still carries it to this day, and television was only thing to let him cope out of this.

[i]What helped me get through that period were movies and books. This was when I discovered the power contained in entertainment  and stories. I decided that when I grew up, I wanted to work in a job that would allow me to create these kinds of stories. [/i]He was determined to become either a film director or a novelist. Unfortunately, at that time, these seen as [b]significant risk.[/b] After his father's passing, financial concerns became unavoidable, adding to the mental burden his mother carried as a single parent.

When he first encountered video games, he realized they could offer a new way to create film-like experiences. The potential of this emerging medium was undeniable to him, ultimately steering him toward a career in the gaming industry rather than filmmaking. However, with the market oversaturated, publishers losing control, and competition among home consoles intensifying, the video game industry crash of 1983 unfolded. His friends and professors thought he was out of his mind and urged him to reconsider. 

[i]It was only my mother who told me that I could do whatever I wanted to in life. She was the only one. The ghosts in the game — maybe my parents are one of them, seeing me in this world. I wanted  to have that kind of metaphor, that within you, you’re connected to the people that passed away.[/i]

Hideo opted for an existing engine to avoid extending development by months or years. Seeking the right fit, after visiting several studios, they arrived at [b]Guerrilla Games[/b] to assess the [b]Decima Engine[/b]. Impressed by the team, Hideo was deeply moved when managing director gifted him a wooden box containing [b]Decima’s full source code—no contract, just pure support.[/b] 

[i]I always feel lonely in society. There are so many people who play games feeling like that, like they  don’t belong in this society. They don’t really feel comfortable. You’re all alone playing the game. And you’re trying to connect this fractured society by yourself. The world is beautiful, but you’re small, just a tiny speck. You feel hopeless and helpless and powerless.[/i]

That deep sense of loneliness ties back to his childhood. Leaving Konami brought those memories rushing back, finding comfort in knowing others, even fictional ones, felt the same. He wanted players to experience that feeling, inspiring Death Stranding’s online features, where they can see footprints, hear echoes, and leave helpful tools for others. Hideo’s childhood also inspired oceanic environments and massive sea creatures. His father pushed him out to sea in a boat—a terrifying memory that stayed with him. Another key influence came in 1970 when he attended the Osaka World Expo. For the first time, he saw people from different countries and witnessed a blend of ancient cultures and cutting-edge technology under the slogan [i]Progress and Harmony for Mankind.[/i] This vision of a future where technology unites humanity left a lasting impact on him.

While the internet had connected people like never before, he saw increasing fragmentation and isolation. He wanted to offer a more positive way to connect people—without competition or co-op combat. Instead, the game’s online component would focus on helping unseen players work toward a shared goal, a concept that became the [b]Social Strand System. [/b]

His team was skeptical. They pushed back. [i]But no one plays games to help others. Players want to stand out, to be the strongest. [/i]He wasn’t surprised. [i]A new concept is always hard to explain. Even with stealth games, my first opponents were my own team. [/i]Their doubts grew when they learned the gameplay centred on delivering packages and reconnecting a desolate world. Traversal mechanics would add depth, but no one grasped his vision. Frustration mounted as they kept asking, [i]Where are the guns? Where’s the combat?[/i]

[b][i]No. This is about something different. It’s about walking and experiencing the world.[/i][/b]

Well, Death Stranding leaves me with mixed feelings. And this is the longest review I’ve ever written.
If I had rated the game after the first 20-30 hours, it would have been a 9/10. However, after 200+ hours, my score is 7.5/10. And that’s still an overrating.

[hr][/hr]
[b]The Good[/b]
First, the positives. Death Stranding is a highly cinematic game with a decent story and well-written characters. It feels like a Japanese take (vision) on a Fallout post-apocalyptic world. The graphics are stunning, especially in terms of character realism. The acting is great and emotionally engaging. The overall visual concept and storyline, at first impression, are quite unique and create a strong atmosphere. There are no major flaws that make any particular aspect stand out negatively. For an open-world game, it delivers a solid performance and has a unique MMO element to it.

[b]The Bad[/b]
I still think it’s a solid game worth playing—I wouldn’t have spent 200+ hours on it if it weren’t. My critique actually comes from the fact that I do like this game. But when the story becomes boring or the world feels empty, you start noticing flaws—and there are some. 

[b]Storyline[/b]
The more I played, the more I realized that the story wasn’t as unique and mystical as I initially thought. In fact, it follows a very standard structure: good guy, bad guy, save the world. The plot feels somewhat cliché and predictable. As the story progresses, major logical gaps appear. I would say a major issue is that, due to the game's heavy focus on characters, it never truly feels like a world-shaking event is happening. What initially seemed like a unique approach eventually became quite generic and boring, mainly due to a poorly written storyline.

[b]Characters[/b]
The characters are well-written and well-acted. However, as the storyline progresses, they all become increasingly annoying. The game constantly over-explains every single detail through dialogues and monologues, as if assuming you are infantile.
The exaggerated politeness and niceness of all the characters make their interactions feel artificial and fake, creating a sense of monotony as well. Well, I understand Kojima’s idea behind it—about friendship and helping people—but the execution falls short. To trigger an emotion, you need to create an emotional connection first. But you cannot do that if you stay on one emotional level the whole time.

And then there’s Higgs. His constant need for approval, combined with his teenage-like behavior and forced attempts to be 'cool,' make him not just a terrible antagonist but ridiculously unbearable. I played the whole game on veteran difficulty but switched to easy mode during Higgs' fistfight, simply because I couldn’t stand listening to him any longer.

[b]World Design[/b]
The game pretends to be realistic, yet it presents the entire USA as a place you can cross on foot in 40 minutes. But that’s just a weird detail. The bigger issue is that the world feels lifeless—there are no people, no real locations, no real action and no points of interest. It’s a localized story centered around just five characters, pretending to depict world-shaking events.
As for the environment, the designs of bridges, vehicles, and other structures feel completely impractical. It’s as if whoever designed them had no real understanding of engineering. On one hand, Kojima created a great realistic walking simulator; on the other, the vehicle physics are the worst I’ve ever experienced in a game. There are great ideas and concepts, but their execution is often flawed.

[b]Co-op with no Co-op[/b]
Concept-wise, it’s unique. You feel the presence of other players helping you, and the game would be much harder without player-built structures. However, it breaks the narrative—over time, the overwhelming number of structures makes the world look utterly bizarre, turning it into one big wasteland.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
At first, delivering packages is appealing, but over time, the gameplay becomes extremely repetitive. Timefall is annoying. Enemies are annoying. Traveling is annoying. Replacing broken items is annoying.
I broke the intended concept of progression and built roads before progressing the storyline. What was meant to be a challenging walk turned into a one-minute ride for me. The problem is that you can do this. On one hand, Kojima forces you to watch all the unnecessary animations, while on the other, he gives you the option to break the game’s intended experience. 

[b]Animations[/b]
Normally, I wouldn’t even mention this, but in Death Stranding, it’s a big issue. The sheer number of unskippable animations is simply insane. Out of 200 hours of playtime, I’d estimate that at least 50 hours were spent watching unnecessary animations. Every battle begins and ends with a 10-second cutscene you cannot skip. Every safehouse entry and exit is animated. Every delivery involves an animation scene and a process with four different summary screens. At first, it’s a wow effect, but over time, it drives you crazy.

[b]Overall Design [/b]
This is a subjective matter, but I personally don’t like the game’s design aesthetic. It lacks detail, features a sterile environment, and the latex outfits don’t fit the themes of decay, destruction, or the end of the world. They simply feel out of place. The melancholic soundtrack didn’t appeal to me at all.

[b]The Ending – The Peak of Annoyance[/b]
By the time I reached the ending, I was already extremely frustrated and just wanted to finish the game. But then… a semi-controllable 30-minute cutscene plays, where Amelie explains everything all over again, as if Kojima thinks you still haven’t got it. Then, an unskippable credits sequence. After that, another 40-minute cutscene, followed by another 10-20 minutes of unskippable credits. Kojima forces you to sit through all of it. Well, if it had been impactful, tragic, or meaningful, I wouldn’t complain. But it was predictably boring, with everything already said throughout the story.

I truly hope Death Stranding 2 doesn’t repeat the same mistakes. The game has the potential to become great.

Death Stranding is a singular experience. There's really nothing like it, and I really love it, but I also know it is not for everyone. And somehow, it's a refreshing, meaningful experience.

"Make America whole again" sure feels different in 2025. Overall, I really enjoy this game. When I played the original, I was confused and not too impressed. Playing the Director's Cut, I'm still confused, but I enjoyed the gameplay a ton more. To me, the game is the best when it focuses on connecting people. I personally lose interest when the game starts talking about the beach and all that it entails. But overall, a fantastic experience!

I hated parts of this with a passion and I will also definitely play it again.

The world and its characters are nothing short of mesmerizing and draw you deep into a devastatingly dark beautiful place. Surrounded by a melancholic soundtrack, you travel from one desolated area to the other, protecting your fragile cargo and your fragile self. 

I actually really enjoyed the main gameplay loop - just making your way across rough terrain, gradually eased by little helpers like vehicles, better equipment and streets that you really learn to appreciate here. If you enjoy the repetitive elements of Stardew Valley and the likes, you might like this too.

However. Parts of this game made me want to pull my hair out. The UI is insufferable. A large portion of the texts and dialogue are bloated and unsubtle beyond sense and some characters are so overacted and overdramatic that it makes you wish for the extinction to get on with it already. Not to mention the, without exaggeration, THREE HOURS of ending cutscene beating down on the sad corpses of plot points that were weak starting out and dead after the first three cutscenes. The world building overall is not terribly logical, but I think that's all right when it's more about art and atmosphere.

It's been a few weeks and some of the images still haunt me. The little tortured smile that Fragile does; the nightmarish fights when you get too close to a BT; a man searching for his family so they can die together... I would have missed something had I never played this. 

TL;DR: Play this if you enjoy some gorgeous atmosphere and gameplay that's for once not shooting stuff (mostly). Be prepared to suffer, but it's worth it. Do skip the ending cutscene beyond the first half hour though.

The sound and music in the game are simply outstanding. They play a crucial role in setting the mood, enhancing both the eerie horror elements and the lighter, fun moments that are so characteristic of Kojima’s style. The auditory experience is as captivating as the visual one, drawing players deeper into its mysterious world.

From a gameplay perspective, Death Stranding manages to blend horror with moments of pure fun in a way that keeps you constantly on your toes. The mechanics are innovative and engaging, pushing the boundaries of what a game can be. Every twist and turn in the story feels meticulously crafted, with each character adding their own distinct personality to the narrative.

Visually, the game is a marvel. All models and textures are beautifully rendered, and there are no visual bugs to take away from the experience. Every detail contributes to a cohesive world that is both immersive and engaging.

In summary, Death Stranding is a testament to creative ingenuity. With its groundbreaking gameplay, exceptional sound design, and rich storytelling, it stands out as a truly special title. Hats off to Kojima and his team for delivering a game that challenges conventions and offers a fresh, exhilarating experience.

Death Stranding was the newest creation of game designer Hideo Kojima, he created that series after his nasty break up (getting fired) with Konami. Hideo Kojima was the creator of the legendary Metal Gear Solid series which helped solidify the stealth video game genre. After some drama Kojima was having with the company he was working with which was Konami and after people discovered Konami is apparently kind of a s,hitty game company they decided to fire Kojima and prevented him from receiving an award at the game awards for Metal Gear Solid 5. Later on Kojima formed his own game company and they revealed their new game project which is a game called "Death Stranding".

...and when the game released it was polarizing and divisive

If you have ever heard of Death Stranding before I am going to assume you heard what people describe what this game is like, you probably heard that Death Stranding is...

"A glorified walking simulator"
"Delivery/USPS worker simulator"
"Tedious and boring"
"Weird"

Most of that is true, for starters a lot of the game is "walking" and the main goal of the game is to deliver packages to people in bunkers. You do get things in the game that can help you traverse delivering things a lot easier in the game such as tools like hanging ropes, ladders, and you can even build structures like bridges, post boxes, and ziplines. Eventually you are even able to create and ride vehicles in the game, but still I would personally say a lot of the game still is "walking", but there are moments where you can drive a bike/truck to make deliveries much faster. The parts where I would say you probably could not use a vehicle to deliver a package is when the game sort of presents either terrain too difficult or too much of a pain to drive through such as a section of the map with a ton of rocks for no reason or a mountain you need to climb that is too steep to drive over.

The concept of the game when its described to people makes it sound like this game is really "stupid and c,rap", but the way I like to look at it is it's more of a "hiking simulator" as you get some tools a hiker would probably use on their trips like climbing anchors, energy drinks, and spare shoes since you walk a lot and they deteriorate over time. I would personally argue the main core of the game is trying to traverse the difficult terrain the game presents you on the road to the destination you need to deliver. The weather is also a major gameplay mechanic, the rain is weird in Death Stranding because when you are in contact with it you will age rapidly which is why the main character wears a special suit. The rain also effects the packages you carry, the rain droplets makes them rust quicker so you need to move through the rain as fast as you can and also carry special repair sprays to remove rust.

The over all theme of the game is the importance of "being connected to others", the main goal the main character Sam Bridges is trying to achieve is "reconnecting America" after its fall during the Death Stranding incident and also trying to rescue is sister. The way Sam reconnects the country back together is by delivering packages to bunker cities throughout the country and then connecting them to something called the "chiral network". The chiral network is also a game mechanic in the game, it allows you to place structures in the region that bunker city is located at and allows you to use structures placed by other players.

The game does have combat and even stealth, although I do have issues with how it handles enemies in the game. There is basically two main types of enemies in the game the terrorists which are called MULES and a ghost enemy called BT's (Beached things). The enemies in general are never much of a threat and are generally very easy to avoid or deal with and the enemy sections are kind of sparse. The terrorists whenever I had to go past one of their camps I could either run or drive past very easily usually unless I mess something up. Once I had an encounter with the terrorists randomly in the game, I didn't have any weapons but my fists and they had guns, but I managed to beat the c,rap out of them with only my fists which was like I think 10-16 terrorists all of them I knocked out cold. I don't like how the game handles the BT's either, certain sections of the maps in the game have spots where they always have BT's located in. The way you usually avoid the BT's is by sneaking past them by crouch walking past the area and holding R1 to hold your breath when that prompt shows up on screen. The BT sections are always raining, so every time you run into those sections you are moving slow while your packages are getting damaged until you leave that zone. You can kill the BT's but I never personally really felt like doing it as I just saw it's kind of a hassle for me to do it so I just sneaked past them. Killing the MULES however isn't advised because dead bodies in this game turn into bombs which can explode and result in a game over so you need to take those bodies to an incinerator before that happens. If you do manage to get caught by a BT for whatever reason what happens is a certain section of the ground underneath you will turn black and goo human looking monsters will spawn underneath it trying to drag you down. If you manage to escape the section that has been turned black those goo monsters will go away, however if they manage to drag you down the goo monsters will drag you off to a certain part of the map where the game will summon a mini boss. Those mini bosses are pretty cool, the game only forces you to fight them like once in the game as an actual boss fight. You technically don't even have to fight the mini bosses, you can escape them just by leaving the area they are in making them kind of pointless and it's what I usually do because fighting is kind of a hassle.

I think the major issue with the enemies in general is that they are more of a "hindrance" or "nuisance", enemies exist in this game purely just to slow you down and inconvenience you making them kind of a pain when you have to go through enemy sections. The game is very easy in general, I died like twice in this game once is when I fell off of a cliff by accident and the other was at the boss at episode 9. When you die you don't restart at checkpoints you start as some sort of spirit and you need to fly back into Sams body and when you revive you revive at the same spot where you died typically. The main character is immortal so he can die as much as he wants. When I revived on that boss fight I died on the boss had the same amount of health before I died.

Do I recommend this game:
I do, if you like SIMs and running/driving/riding around with stuff that needs to be picked up and delivered.
I do not if you rather play an action RPG and loathe the repetitiveness of doing similar things many times.

About the gameplay:
It's a SIM, and not so much a fast-paced RPG action game. You will be travelling from the East-coast to the West-coast, in an imaginary post-apocalyptic (USA-ish) country, building a (digital) network. Assignments are being picked up by means of some communications pillar, which are scattered all over the country. Some assignments are mandatory for the game to progress, others are for you to pick and choose, depending on your preference. You are a "(trans)porter", moving items from A to B. How you do this, will be up to you. You will collect 'likes' for every properly executed assignment. More 'likes' will promote you, each level with more incentives. Building structures, and/or contributing to finalizing someone else's structures, will give you 'likes' as well. 

What I like about the game:
- The protagonist is the actor in The Boondock Saints, Charmed, and - of course - The Walking Dead, Norman Reedus. 
- The graphics are stunning.
- There's quite some humor hidden all over the game.
- A never seen before tool: "BB". A fetus in a container that will warn you against your biggest threat: "BT".
- Many ways of transportation. Walk, drive, ride. You choose.
- The 'Likes' you can give to structures built by other players, which is 'kind of' real-time/online.
- Some assignments are time-based, some volume-based. All are quality-based (so if you slide from a mountain, you could damage the goods and you will get less 'likes'). 
- The storyline is interesting. Not going to write a spoiler, but the afterlife plays a significant role.
- Other players may 'snatch' your vehicle, if you leave it unattended. Just like in real life. Oh, and the game itself will do the same.

What I do not like about the game:
- Does not have a built-in option to play on wide screen, like 5120x1440. I had to manually change some HEX code in the EXE itself for it to work. Come on guys, you can do better. (but the graphics are even more stunning now) :)
- The AI. Opponents are not all too intelligent and too few in numbers. 
- Travelling long distances, without even encountering any challenge, other than the rugged landscape itself.
- Many dialogs are endless. You could click them away, but then you will miss the essence of the story.
- Building roads is a pain. You need loads of resources, which you won't be able to carry in one go. So you will be travelling back and forth, just to build a small piece of road. Next piece, rinse and repeat.
- After a while, the game becomes very repetitive. Pick up something at location A, take it to location B. Again: rinse and repeat.
- The last two chapters made it obvious that the designers were out of ideas. Good story, but for that, I'd rent a movie.

Conclusion:
It's a SIM and not an action RPG. You may like it, you may not.

A very quaint combination of Hogs Of War and Worms, two very beloved games I hold dear to my heart (both in childhood and adulthood), whilst adding some new quirks to make it its own unique game! This is Wardudes, the game where ragdoll based army militia men battle it out for the victor's spoils. Definitely is a well thought out game. As mentioned, it takes the dark, edgy humour of Hogs Of War (and name-calling inspiration from various regional Hogs inputs) and the destructible terrain aspect of Worms (as well as a couple of functions such as the teleport mechanic). But in order to add its own spin on things it has entities like sharks, destructible cameras and rat bombs, to name a few.
I have been playing it on and off during its early alpha days, so I've seen some major improvements in this game, and therefore would like to recommend to anyone who loves the turn-based strategy genre.
Just a few things I'd like to address; if you have a less beefy computer, then you'll have to reduce some quality settings in order to get some smoothness in gameplay; I'm hoping that can be fixed in the future.
This game is also quite sweary-scary to put it in an advisory term - swearing is found a lot in this game. So if you're a little younger, just be very aware of that.
And, finally, they plan to add so much more content to the game in the future as far as I know, such as a story mode. So this game still has plenty on the table to offer.
But all in all though I hope to grind with some more Wardudes in the very future! And I'm looking forward to seeing what more this game has to offer, as we head into its next phase.

I have to say, for a visual novel that I did not enjoy for the first 30 minutes, not only the story got so much better, I actually fell in love with the lore and the characters to a point of obsession - thank you Roi, I will eat anything you give me, and I don't care what the devs say about you because you are a treasure, and nothing less than a psychotic gentleman. Now, I think there are some consistency issues with the writing and the pacing of the story, some of the routes have very blunt and short responses, and then you follow the Roi's path and it's all philosophical, mysterious, intense, and thought-provoking, like the writing got brilliant all of a sudden - it's like I am playing a different game. You know what the problem was for me, all of the abrupt deaths at the start because they tried to give me metaphors before I was able to interpret them - but once you have a better grab on the lore, it makes more sense. I actually like narrative games where the character can die constantly, but I think you don't want them to feel sudden and cheap, I only like those that feel earned. 

Also, in order to understand the impact of some of the endings you need to know what happened in a different ending, so your experience may change based on the order you unlock them. The game got so sad sometimes I felt bad playing it, in a good way I mean, but still, it will take me days to recover from the melancholy. It actually has a pretty decent amount of content for the price, at 3 hours I got about 80% of the content, with a few missing endings which I currently am unable to locate. 

So much gorgeous art in this game, I don't think the trailer and even the first half of the game shows it, the only lacking parts are the backgrounds, but it's understandable, I guess you have to cut corners somewhere as an indie team. All of the cutscenes and the ending art is so beautiful, I want to use it as desktop backgrounds or something, please make some steam profile covers and maybe an art book. The soundtrack was mostly ambient and conservative, however, I think you manipulated the effects better than I expected in a $5 game. One question though, with all of the cool art in the game, why the main menu looks so meh in comparison, you do all of that work but you don't care to make a great first impression.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) I think the writing in this game has moments of brilliance, nuances, attention to detail, and is actually very emotional in some paths. It was not consistently good across the whole game and I think some of the random deaths took away from it. Again, I like games where you can die a lot, but I think it needs to be used more strategically so you do not interrupt the story, the deaths have to be earned, if that makes sense (and some of them are, just most of them are not).

I want to make a separate note for the world-building and the lore, while the game is not that interesting at first, I think the overall story has a lot of thought-provoking themes once you get a better idea of what is going on, very unique I would say. We pretty much have just 4 characters, but all 4 have interesting motivations, and I enjoyed that I could not tell for sure if I could trust them or not.

(+) The art in the game is absolutely gorgeous, especially the occasional character interactions and those endings. Overall I really enjoyed the unique look of the world and the character design. If I had to nitpick one thing, I wish the backgrounds and the main menu also had the same look to it, or at least something close to it.

(+) Decent amount of content for the price. I didn't do everything in the 3 hours, I imagine 4 would be enough with a guide. Pretty fun to collect achievements if you are into that. 

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Pacing [/u] - I don't mind the idea of constant narrative deaths, but I wish they were used more strategically. Those in the early game seemingly tried to push some metaphors, but you kinda need the context behind the lore of the game to get much value out of them. I like some of the deaths in the game when they were earned, but you didn't need as many of them to get the point across, it just made me restart the game constantly. 

As I mentioned the art was really good, I only wish the main menu and backgrounds were similar to the cutscenes. 

[b] Overall Thoughts: 8/10 [/b]

I'll levae a positive review for now, but the game has some serious gameplay issues that really hinders the fun it could be.

This is an obvious homage to Yie-ar Kung-Fu 2 (YAKF2). Not the first one, but its sequel that was released for the MSX and got some horrendous ports for the Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum. The game even uses the font from the original Brazilian MSX model (The Gradiente Expert) to make its homage more obvious (I'd prefer if it used YAKF2 font, but oh well). So I'll compare it to the game it is trying to homage, while also mentioning overall features of the game.

Like YAKF 2 , each level is compromised of a few screens of enemies, and then a 1 on 1 fight against an enemy. Unlike YAKF2, instead of fighting the same enemy, you have some platform sections, arrows flying at you, guys trying to beat you up, background hazards and stuff like that, which adds some variety to the game. Also lke YAKF2, you'll reach the boss with your health depleted because of those initial screens, which will feel the fight is unfair, but that's how the game was and I see they tried to do the same here. The game is very generous with the extra lives too.

Alas, fighting the enemies feels unfair as hell, as they have way more resources than you, and you will have less health than then because you were fighting goons and jumping arrows before. It was like this in YAKF2 too. If you die on this fight, you don't have to start the level again, you now can try to fight the enemy with your full health.

The game uses 2 buttons (unlike YAKF2 that only used 1), one for punches and one for kicks. You jump pressing up which wouldn't be a problem if it wasn't by the fact you can change the height of your attacks by pressing up or down at the same time (or a few frames after) you press one of the attack buttons. This WILL make you jump by accident sometimes. Someone suggested a jump button would be better, and the dev added the possibility to jump with R3 or L3 which not only is weird as hell (Why not one of the trigger buttons? We didn't need them as extra attack buttons that do the same as the face buttons), but also doesn't eliminate the main problem because there's no way to turn off UP as jump, so even if you want to use L3 to jump, you'll still jump accidentally while trying a high attack.

And you NEED the high attacks because, like in Kung-Fu Master (Another game this is at least giving a nod to), on the initial screens of each level you may need to kick or punch enemies (arrows, etc) at the right height. Which is DIFFICULTY AS HELL with this control scheme.

So you may just try to defend by pressing the opposite direction (like in Street Fighter) but then... your character gets confused if he's supposed to defend or just change direction and move back. So defending on the initial screens is a mess. 

Soundwise I really disliked the game. The music didn't do anything to me, and many of the sound effects are your typical stuff made with BFXR (or similar) which plagues so many indie games, with some grating sound effects (The menu sfx is awful, and I could completely live without the tape loading sfx on the intro. It's ok for nostalgia sake the first time, but it's REALLY annoying the 2nd time you load the game)

For the positive points, the gameplay *is* good if you can get around all the problems I mentioned above. There's some timed attacks and jumps you need to learn which is pretty cool.  The game has lots of secrets where you need to attack certain areas of the background to get extra power ups (Again, pretty much like YAKF2). Figuring out the patterns for the enemies is fun (though that guy with the whip and the lion... Jesus Christ is that hard). The graphics are solid for this kind of game.

With some small adjustments, the game could be awesome. For right now... I'd say is "above average". It's not bad, it will give you memories of Yie-Ar Kung-Fu 2 if you've ever played it (including its frustrating trais).. and for the price range (it seems it NEVER gets a discount, even on sale periods, which is a bummer) you can have a solid, if flawed, game.

[b]edit:[/b] the game became free in may 2022, guess it was easier than patching it up.

[b]axiallis[/b] is a mouse-based tetris-like that has you placing tetrominoes, but [b]creating lines only awards extra points, doesn't remove the lines themselves[/b]. the goal is to prolong filling the board for as long as possible, but you can fill areas blocked from the top, since pieces aren't falling from the sky. the current and next shape are visible, leaderboards available for some optional competition.

click any available spot to place the current tetromino, keep clicking the arrow to rotate, then place with right click anywhere, left click on the big button on the bottom or space. [b]no reason to omit keyboard controls[/b], wasd/arrows and something to rotate would work just fine, but sadly [b]space is the only key that does anything[/b] (and enter to confirm your name).

interestingly, [b]pivot segments where pieces are rotated remain available after placement[/b], and that's where the big money is. placing a tetromino's rotaty bit over another's pivot awards more points, doing it a third time is even more beneficial. the latter also creates a so-called super axis, which lets you place another tetromino on top of it. no points for doing so, but it can be used to get rid of an ill-fitting (or non-fitting) piece or plug a nearby hole.

reaching a certain amount of points unlocks the next level, meaning you can potentially fill multiple boards in a single run. the numerical requirement is only shown on the game over screen, but you can ballpark it based on the lines filling up on both sides of the board. even if the goal is reached, the current board has to be finished, then come the stats, then instead of a new game you get to carry over your score and time to the next level. [b]no time limit, but playing quickly is advised if you care about points.[/b]

really nice presentation, loved the music, too bad [b]it's lacking in functionality[/b]. no settings in the main menu, a single audio on/off toggle in the pause menu while playing. you can also change the music there. no windowed mode or resolutions, alt+enter only makes a non-resizable window, so it's useless, gotta edit the registry for such things. [b]no toggle for the timer[/b] either, but it's not that intrusive, and the [b]tutorial[/b] is only available from the main menu, not while playing.

[b]it's pretty good overall[/b], if not as good as some other point & click tetris-likes, and since it could be better in certain areas, I'm glad I picked it up at 75% off when it cost $4 at full price. half price would've been still reasonable, but instead of patching it, the developer made it free, so it's a moot point.

Game Review: "Tyrone vs Cops" – The Ultimate Sprint-for-Your-Life Simulator

⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (4/5)

If you’ve ever wanted to experience the heart-pounding, sweat-dripping, adrenaline-rushing thrill of running for your life without actually leaving your couch, "Tyrone vs Cops" has you covered. This indie masterpiece combines parkour-style movement, GTA-level police aggression, and the kind of chaos that makes you question your life choices.
Gameplay – A True Test of Your Reflexes (and Your Sanity)

The game drops you straight into Tyrone’s sneakers, and buddy, you better start running. The cops? Oh, they don’t believe in due process—they come in hot like they’ve got a quota to meet by sundown. You’ll be sprinting through alleyways, vaulting over fences, and juking like a prime-time NFL running back. The movement is smooth, but the learning curve? Steeper than Tyrone’s rap sheet.

Power-ups include mystery snacks, which somehow make you faster, and crowd distractions, like throwing a random cheeseburger to send a hungry mob into a frenzy. There’s also a shopping cart escape option—because nothing says "high-speed getaway" like riding a busted Walmart cart down a hill.
Graphics – Picasso on a Budget

Visually, the game is… well, let’s just say it’s charmingly rough. The animations have that “indie game jank” feel, but honestly, that just adds to the chaotic energy. Character models are about as polished as a potato, but when you’re too busy dodging tasers, who cares?
Sound Design – A Symphony of Sirens and Screaming

The soundtrack? Nonexistent. The sound effects? Absolutely perfect. The game treats you to an endless loop of police sirens, angry yelling, and Tyrone’s panicked breathing, which really immerses you in the experience. Every once in a while, an NPC yells something ridiculous like, “Bro, just give up!” or “You ain't built for this life!” which is both discouraging and hilarious.
Story – Who Needs Plot When You Have Chaos?

There’s technically a “story” here, but it’s about as deep as a kiddie pool. Something about unpaid parking tickets escalating way out of control. But let’s be honest—you’re not here for the lore. You’re here to see how long you can last before Tyrone gets tackled like it's the Super Bowl.
Final Verdict

"Tyrone vs Cops" is stupidly fun, frustratingly hard, and absolutely hilarious. It’s a game that doesn’t take itself seriously, and neither should you. If you enjoy games that test your reflexes and make you laugh at their sheer ridiculousness, this one’s a must-try.

Yeah, this is really good.

It's Hollow Knight + Quake, with just as much charm and technical skill as that formula warrants.

The graphic are all voxels, the music is all bleeps and bloops, and it doesn't matter. It's all done with so much technical precision that the game feels fantastic to play.

In soulsgame style, it shows more than it tells. Enemies have gimmicks you have to sightread. NPCs drip feed the lore to you, and keep a lot back.

On the flipside, there are regular Serious Sam style battle arenas. Guns all feel technical and interesting in a very Dusk/Blood West/boomershooter renaissance way. You unlock upgrades and soft progression that you can farm for, but it's not essential. There's also difficulty scaling that is both fair and dynamic---easy mode gives you hints before it straight up turns the numbers down.

It's staggering that one person made this thing, especially given how polished, bug free, and above all big it is. Other reviews are clocking in at around 15 hours, and I believe them. There's a ton to explore here, the biomes are all tight and atmospheric, and the difficulty does a very good job of scaling at your pace.

Frogmonster is a gem. Buy it at full price and then buy whatever else this dev puts out.

Edit: You should absolutely drop the difficulty if you stop having fun, lol. I made it to the false finale before scaling back from classic to easy, and easy is normal in most other shooters, just with the twist that it'll scale back a little if you're getting absolutely shreked. There's a few fights that are endurance contests more than anything else, and having to do them on classic would've made me quit. I've generally been a "souls games shouldn't have difficulty options if the developer doesn't want them to" person, but this made me completely change my mind. I don't know a souls game that wouldn't be improved by having this kind of dynamic 'easy' mode.

2nd Edit: Good god that difficulty is not messing around. Even on easy I think this is the hardest fps I've ever played, and a big part of that is that you're not ever only doing two things. Even in a purist technical fps like Serious Sam 1, you're generally just juking incoming fire, kiting charging enemies, and picking a target to focus down. In Frogmonster, you're doing all of that, eating mushrooms to manage the cooldown on your poison immunity, constantly rotating weapons to manage the low ammo caps, adapting to the 6+ phases on your average late game boss, shifting priority between ammo recovery and offense, and doing *precision* shooting on small targets rather than blasting a horde (or while you're also blasting a horde, depending on the boss.) This all makes the boss fights super memorable, but even with the difficulty downscaling from losing a bunch of times in a row on easy, they're still massively sweaty.

3rd Edit: Yeah, I'm not bothering with that final fight. 90% of the way through the health bar is good enough for me. It's long, which makes it tedious to repeat, and the crescent spam pattern is a second phase only pattern that kills you if you can't memorize it, which means you have to repeat it a bunch of times to memorize it. The second to last boss is a real high note though (apart from the phase that you're supposed to lick and then dash away from, despite there being no other point in the game when you need to do this with anything.) Overall, I strongly recommend Frogmonster. I've washed out of other soulslikes right at the end (Sekiro, Lies Of P,) and they're still good games, so don't let the lack of completion put you off. I just don't have a lot of patience for games that require you to play perfect. Frogmonster is still very much worth getting, and if you like a challenge I understand that there's a bunch of endgame content after where I stopped.

An outstanding look into the future of shmups! Takes the Touhou formula into something very uniquely special with its abstract fantasy setting and exquisite world-building discoverable due to the scanning mechanic. Despite it's advances into the potential of the bullet hell genre, it's actually very easy for a bullet hell! It makes this a great introduction for new players that would want to explore this genre as it's quite forgiving with it's amount of lives as well as bullet patterns which make this very approachable for something of this caliber before getting into the harder difficulties. The cast of characters are great! The playable characters all have unique special attacks and their perks that are worth a try although Empitts is hands-down the easiest character to do a full run with as she gifted with bonus lives and the best balance of speed and utility. The bosses and the enemies are unforgettable with their surreal appearances and multi-media visual style that tell vast stories with their looks alone, which applies to the boss spell cards as well. (When was the last time I've seen rotting teeth being used as projectiles in a bullet hell? Let alone any game!) Learning about each of the colorful characters and their settings throughout playing the game and unlocking journal entries is really fun and worth a look into the vastness of this universe's themes of mortality and time. The music deserves a shoutout for being wonderful and a PERFECT match to this colorful visual style. My favorite songs being the Stage 2 Boss Fight (Audrey), the Extra Stage, and the nostalgia-inducing beauty that soundtracks the Journal pages. I can't recommend this game enough! Despite a bug here and there, (nothing game-breaking as far as I found, just some visual or input hiccups.) as well as lack of controller support and volume options, this game is absolutely worth it! It's supplied with a lot of content to chew on despite being an arcade bullet hell. I'm endlessly excited to see what Ethereal Airport does next to add to their already diverse collection of indie games. Check it out!

There is *great* detail to every book cover in the library, and for a second, I even thought that some of the books might be real ones. You get a glimpse into your customers personalities, into what their lives must be like, and it's great- It's just a glimpse. you don't get to learn anything too deep about anyone, just like you should. You're just a librarian, and the game shows that perfectly. 

However I can't bring myself to recommend this at all. It feels like nothing but wasted potential.
 
The game feels great at making a setting, and gives you a lot of info for everything to feel more "real": there are flowers in another room. you get paid on the 20th. no eating or drinking in the library. rules, details about the place, it's all there.
Yet all you do at your job, is click a card to scan it, click the books on the counter in any order, and return the card. 
If someone returns a book past the due date, you are not the one to spot that. the game tells you they're overdue. the game does not allow you to do anything that isn't reporting it, and everything that is out of place is *very* highlighted in red. You have one job- and the game does it for you. It feels very passive. everything feels very automatic. Someone wants to make a card? you need to check the returns box? you only ever have one option to click, and sometimes it feels as if you were just clicking a button for the story to proceed- except... there's no real story. 

It kind of feels like the game does not actually know what it wants to be. It's a little bit "Papers please", while missing the entire core of the pressure of working, it's a little bit "casual setting", at the same time there are strange mysteries, (maybe even some very light horror?) elements that pop out of absolutely nowhere, some crime mentioned, for no reason.

Morph King is exactly what it seems to be, and I mean that in the best possible way. 
A stylised, easy to understand but hard to master twist on Chess. Don't let the cute animations and sounds trick you though - there is plenty of depth here, and it hooked me surprisingly fast. 

You control only one chess piece, but it changes type each turn (Rook, then pawn, then queen and so on). Thus, the game provides a simple premise, but it get complicated fast as you have to calculate many enemy movements, your upcoming chess piece types and of course the normal movement and board tactics.

There are two modes: Endless and Bullet. The former is a classic arcade style high score chaser, while the latter challenges your fast thinking skills to see what you can score in a minute. And given the type of game here, a tactical turn-based board game, these modes are very different experiences.

If you like chess, but want something fresh and a change of pace from the classic game, this is your game. A great value, smooth and addictive experience, and I'm curious to see the highscores some may manage. But the above really is the whole game... So, if you're not a board game fan, this naturally won't appeal. Personally, I find I have little time for Chess, so this is a much better option.

I've only played two of the Search All series of hidden object games - this one (Christmas) and the free game UFO. This game has a single large monochrome scene in which 80 candy canes have to be found; parts of the scene are animated. There is a zoom function (essential for this game as the canes can be very small and indistinct against a detailed background), and a recharging hint facility which indicates an area in which a candy cane is located. There are achievements for game progress, but they do not appear while the game is running, only at its end.

I thought that the scene was well drawn and sufficiently detailed to make finding the candy canes quite difficult and challenging in a good way; in the end I had to use the hint facility to help locate the final two canes. My game play represents one playthrough.

My reservation about this game is the method it uses for moving the viewpoint around the scene; instead of clicking on the background and dragging the viewpoint across the scene as most games of this genre seem to use, and which allows controlled slow movement while searching for hidden objects, the Search All series uses directional arrows at the edges of the scene. These are triggered by moving the cursor onto one of the arrows, but controlling the speed or amount of the movement is very difficult. This makes detailed methodical searching much harder. In Search All - Christmas, the candy canes are small and hard to spot, and the background is detailed, so the lack of an easy method for slow careful searching is serious. This didn't ruin the game for me, but added an unnecessary level of frustration.

This is a kind of unique game that looks like an old Zelda clone but is actually equal parts light action RPG and Sierra-style deliberately unfair adventure game. The puzzles take a ton of figuring out but nearly all of them make sense once you connect the dots after finishing them. 

It is definitely an old school game for good and bad - you will need to level/money grind at points and the Sierra style adventure game aspect can make itself known when you need to restart after 10+ hours of gameplay. It is possible you will make mistakes in Chapter 1 that will render Chapter 2 unwinnable, but in the same sense as a Roguelike game this actually makes sense in the greater scale of things - each run contributing to your overall understanding of how to solve the puzzles of the game. Basically you could spend 100+ hours playing Chapter 1 alone and still have entire areas in the game that you've never seen.

I particularly enjoyed that very few items are just vendor trash and all have secondary or exploratory uses that might not be clear at first.

It is largely bug free and the dev is highly responsive with fixing bugs and providing hints for the puzzles. All total progress wipes are a product of the deliberate design decisions which makes them brutal but you lose progress for a real reason.

The music is nice, but the gameplay is not very expansive. It is not a huge barrel of fun, at most makes for a somewhat limited idle game. If you like the aesthetic, you'll enjoy it. You don't even need to wait for a sale, it's $2.

By the barest margin, I do not recommend this game to other people. The setting and premise are unique (You play as the invading force, rather than defeat them) and the art style, while looking a tad amateurish, is charming in its own right, akin to a crayon drawing come to life, but the game-play has some serious strikes against it.

I found it a tad strange that the player characters don't get any EXP until all three party members are in your ranks. If that decision was made as a technical thing, then fine; I don't expect RPGMaker to be that perfect. What irks me the most (and ultimately decide to not recommend the game) is the fact that the bosses and other scripted fights have an ungodly amount of HP. 

The player characters' health varies around 25 to 40 points worth, which is appropriate for low levels. The fight with Inventor Verne and subsequent fights were just bullet sponges, with HP in the low 300s and high 400s. I tried using clever tactics to beat Inventor Verne, like using Dill's solar slap and Tyler's trailer park move to stun him and make him bleed to supplement the damage I was dealing. Was costly, but felt appropriate given the scenario. The next major fights (Kid in the library and the brothers Gym and Lunch teacher) were the same deal, with no common enemies in between them to help me level up any. Finally, I gave up when the bathroom fight had me go against an opponent with more than 500 HP. I stopped playing after that.

You have an almost-wonderful game on your hands, but please, [i]please[/i], lower the HP of the enemies. More health does not equal more engagement.

XenoTown is an RPGmaker game that takes less than ten hours to complete. It does the Earthbound thing but with a completely different style and perspective: you're an alien invader here to conquer Earth, and you pair up with a misfit Earth kid (and a germaphobic robo-toilet). You place mind control goggles on people after battle to make them friendlies, and your ultimate goal is to mind control the principal of the local school.
There are no random encounters which is nice. Maybe the creators planned for random encounters then later took them out, because the maps are laid out like a game with random encounters would be: lots of long empty hallways and mazes. To compensate the game throws a lot of items your way (mostly found by digging through trash or going to vending machines).
The setting is a small American town called Pinewood in the 1990s. Like Earthbound, but more down-to-earth and at times cynical in an authentically American way. Your earth child companion is a misfit/bully. You have to fight his drunk, abusive father.
I got it on sale and you should too, if you have an evening or two to kill, liked Earthbound, and aren't expecting too much.

I can only recommend this with reservations. There's good and bad, but the bad can mean the game feels a bit tedious.

Positives

The art, music, and story are all really fun. It has an Earthbound vibe, and they created a game that pays homage while also finding its own identity.

Negatives

The biggest problem is the dungeons. It feels like they were designed for a game with random battles, but the game only has battles at pre-planned locations. Therefore, you end up walking through long, empty corridors. I saved a lot because I didn't want to have to walk through empty hallways again if I died.

Because there aren't many battles, it feels like the developers decided to make the battles longer, much like Cosmic Star Heroine did. However, CSH had an interesting battle system with interesting decisions. The battles here find you simply repeating the exact same actions over and over.

Worth it!

I had a lot of fun playing the game. It's simple and quirky. The best part is the style: the music, the humor, and the graphics all working together to create what I think might be best described as an Anti-Earthbound. Pineview is a gross place. The people are weird. It's full of homeless vagrants and humor that goes far, but I never felt like it went too far.

I felt like there were some balancing issues with some of the abilities: solar slap only felt useful in the beginning, the tentacle attack felt really expensive for what it does, the defense boosting ability that one of your party members gets felt really weak for how expensive it was, and I never used the big heal you get at the end because the first heal you get does plenty of healing (it works really well) and your characters just don't have enough HP to warrant a bigger heal for such a high cost. 

I'd have liked to have seen a larger variety of equipment, but what's there works; the game is only about 10 hours long, and I felt like the rewards and the equipment you could buy were well balanced. I just like the option to customize my characters, and there's very little of that in the game. Which is fine. The game leans more into story and art than mechanics, and it was a really fun little story that I'd love to see expanded. 

There are no random encounters. The game is very railroaded; I don't think that's a bad thing because it delivers on what it sets out to do: tell a funny story with some emotional pull. It's simple in a good way. 

The game is pretty easy once you get the hang of it: most of your damage is going to be dealt by causing status ailments: bleed, gross, and burn. Bleed is the big one, but you could rely more on burn and gross if you wanted to buy the items that cause those (they're all different kinds of bombs). I didn't use the "bombs" until the end of the game, and they weren't necessary; since the game is so railroaded, you're always at the right level to take on a enemies, so levels are more about changing the way your characters work than overpowering weaker enemies. I just used the bombs to add some burn damage to speed up some of the later fights.

Fights are long in this game, but there aren't a ton of them. I'd say there's just the right amount. 

Overall, a great project especially for the price. Remember to save. Learn the economy. Enjoy the ride!

I had initially purchased this game because it looked like a great little homage to Earthbound and was available at a very fair asking price. There is a lot of charm to what I experienced, but as an RPG it really fell flat on some critical areas which were enough for me to warrant a refund.

You play as an alien on a mission to conquer the planet by defeating humans and mind controlling them to serve your boss. I enjoyed the art, music, story, and dialogue. 

There are a few big glaring issues for a game like this: 
- You get zero experience from the things you defeat, and have no way to level up your characters to get stronger. This is likely a bug, but the developers are unresponsive and the games nearly been out a year, so I don't think a fix is planned.
- There are no random encounters or generated enemies in the overworld to fight. There are only pre-scripted, one-and-done fights that offer very little resources and again, zero experience, when defeating.
- The boss fights have an insane amount of health, and due to the lack of equipment (EVERY STORE IS CLOSED THAT SHOULD SELL GEAR) and the lack of increased stats from leveling up (again, due to ZERO EXPERIENCE when defeating enemies) you are forced to engage in a battle of slowly whittling down the enemy health in between spamming healing items you got from a vending machine, which is not sustainable given the limited amount of resources you get from the limited, pre-scripted encounters.

Don't support this game until the developers start supporting it too.

In the ever-evolving landscape of gaming, there are few titles that can seamlessly blend creativity, problem-solving, and fun as Hello Engineer does. Developed by Tiny Build, and set in the same universe as the popular game Hello Neighbor 2, Hello Engineer is an innovative multiplayer puzzle game that challenges players to build intricate contraptions and solve problems using physics. The game is a perfect example of how entertainment and education can come together in a way that captivates players of all ages. This essay will explore how Hello Engineer stands out as an amazing experience in the world of gaming.

At its core, Hello Engineer encourages creativity. The game is centered around solving complex puzzles using a wide array of building materials, including motors, wheels, and engines. Players are tasked with constructing vehicles or machines to navigate obstacles, transport objects, and reach designated goals. Unlike many other games where the objective is straightforward and linear, Hello Engineer allows players to experiment with various designs, making the process of creation both challenging and rewarding. This level of creative freedom encourages players to think outside the box, fostering a sense of innovation as they come up with unique solutions to in-game problems.

What truly sets Hello Engineer apart is its integration of physics-based gameplay. Every machine or vehicle that players build is subject to the laws of physics. The way objects move, the force of gravity, and how components interact all contribute to how successful a player's creation is. The game does not simply reward players for the aesthetic quality of their designs but for how well they work in a practical, real-world sense. This creates a deep sense of satisfaction when a player's creation works as intended, especially after multiple attempts at refining and tweaking their design. The process of trial and error in Hello Engineer is not only engaging but also teaches valuable problem-solving skills. Players learn the importance of testing their creations, adjusting designs, and persevering even after failure.

In addition to its creative and educational value, Hello Engineer shines in its multiplayer aspect. The game is designed for cooperative play, allowing players to team up with friends or other online players to complete tasks. This multiplayer mode adds an exciting social dimension, as it requires collaboration, communication, and shared problem-solving. Working together to build and navigate contraptions adds an extra layer of enjoyment, as players must coordinate their actions and use their strengths to achieve a common goal. The ability to work together while still exercising personal creativity makes Hello Engineer a truly dynamic gaming experience.

The visual and atmospheric elements of Hello Engineer also contribute to its charm. The game’s cartoonish art style, set in a whimsical world filled with strange robots and colorful landscapes, creates a lighthearted atmosphere. Despite the technical complexity of the puzzles, the game maintains a sense of fun and adventure, making it accessible for players of all skill levels. The engaging environment draws players in, making the experience feel like a delightful adventure rather than a task to complete.

In conclusion, Hello Engineer is a truly amazing game because it combines creativity, problem-solving, and multiplayer fun in a way that few games can. Its emphasis on physics-based gameplay, collaborative problem-solving, and imaginative design sets it apart in the gaming world. Whether you're a casual gamer or a serious enthusiast, Hello Engineer offers an experience that is both entertaining and intellectually stimulating. It stands as a testament to how games can push the boundaries of what is possible, all while providing endless hours of fun and learning.

[h3]Good[/h3]
[list]
[*]Does not bother you with reading dialogs/watching cinematic/making story-related choices. Game makes you do what it is supposed to: play.

[*]No billions of useless stats like elemental resistances. 

[*]No ambiguous stats like strength, which gives whatever stats devs thing it should, just raw direct stat hp/dmg/crit increase on level up.

[*]Moving in a turn based games is a big mistake that does nothing, but consumes time. This game understands that perfectly.

[*]Sound is good
[/list]

[h3]Bad[/h3]
[list]
[*]Do you use your players' CPU to farm bitcoin? Why does this game loads it so hard?

[*]Lacks skills description. The first tutorial encourages you to hover over hero stats to read info. Okay, I hover over a stat and what do I see? "Shields affinity". Perfect! Don't dev understand, that no one in the world knows what it is? Especially in your game, please care to add some meaningful description.

[*]What is corruption? Dare spend some time to write proper description instead of spending time for writing useless text in notes that are found in the game, which no one reads anyway.

[*]Character treating mechanic from Darkest Dungeon (that gladly they got rid of in 2nd part of the game). I already have 6 chars to manage, I don't want to put them to treatment for every 2 turns and manage another 12 to play with meanwhile. Also, the idea of "world turns" which pass only if you embark on a quest is stupid itself, why can't you just skip it?

[*]Clerics do nothing, their only heal spell could be cast only every 3 turns because of exhaustive mana cost. They just chill on the backline, skipping turns the rest of the time.

[*]Moving through dungeon rooms is boring and should be instant.

[*]Craft is meaningless, you just combine potion with items to get the same potion with slightly randomized stats.

[*]No inventory system, just potions and some ugly looking charms with pointless stats, like +1hp.

[*]Game looks like early alpha in terms of interface

[*]Animations are very slow, pauses between turns are too big, need a slider to make this 5-10 times faster.

[*]Why promoted units has worse stats (initiative) than their former version?

[*]Augments are destroyed upon extraction, this is a bias of 90s games that does nothing, but makes them more grindy and not fun, it should be freely removed from character with no penalties
[/list]

[h3]Bugs[/h3]
[list]
[*] Some potions are not working, it is said they should e.g. heal 16% corruption, but consuming them does nothing. Also, the overall idea of corruption is again stolen from the darkest dungeon and exists only to stop you from playing your party and create another one for several turns. This is literally a counter fun feature, and mistake of DD game, that unfortunately spread to other titles.

[*]Characters just hit/heal for 1 dmg if there is an enemy 2+ level above them present on the battlefield.

[*]Any full HP character regardless of build, even tanks, could be one-shot by the same or even lower level enemy at the 1st turn of the battle.

[*]Martyric sacrament skill does nothing but sets caster hp to 1.

[*]Enemies on the map may not disappear after you defeat them, resulting in endless fights.

[*]Character can disappear from party upon mission completion. Yes, full hp one, not dead.

[*]If enemy is killed by ranger's (marksman's, they don't even know how their characters are called, and have different names in different menus) intercept skill, the battle is stuck, because dead unit will try to perform action that was intercepted ;D

For players like me, Norland is pretty discouraging due to the randomness of events. Why did all my peasants survive in a battle and the lord died? Why did I get -10 relationship from the hunt event? I reload and get a different result. The problem is I do not want to save scum, I want my actions to have a predictable effect.

Here is how different CRPGs matured. They had random hit probabilities. Newer games (e.g. PoE) replaced this with crit probability. You still have randomness, just less randomness.

Some other games (e.g. Crusader Kings) show probabilities of different outcomes. This gives me less control, yet at least I know the risk and can calculate if I want it.

Also, this is not transparent how long each action takes. I set education action, and it hung for several days. I cannot say if this is some sort of deadlock or just long education, and the game does not give a hint. The hunting action can actually fail and provide a negative relation bonus if another character is busy, this is IMO just a UI problem. Of course, I can free another character from his current task, I just was not expecting this to be a problem.

The game design "losing is fun" may be ok if the new game gives you a lot of replayability and you can improve with every playthrough. It makes little sense to play another game hoping randomness will favor you more.

This games was a fun little game. I definitely recommend picking up this game and playing it for 3 big reasons:

1. It's short.

The biggest reason why I don't play games now that I'm an adult suffering from chronic time deficiency is that *they're too damn long*. I've played games where 20 hours in I still haven't reached the middle (I loved that as a kid tbh), and I've also play games I really wish the devs had fleshed things out a little more, but Gem Worlds sits right in that happy satisfying length where I'm not fatigued by the presentation of a new challenge.

2. It's relaxing.

It's a turn-based game so you have as much time as you need to think about your next move. I do like games that require reflexes and skill, but when I'm done playing a good game of Smash Bros I'm sweating and my hands are shaking. This game is not like that. There's an odd satisfaction to the sound effects plinking away as you walk towards a new part of the map.

3. It engages faith in a normalizing way.

There's a tendency within games to look at trust in the divine as a kind of "unique character quirk" or even a "limitation". The story in this game feels different--it normalizes a faith-engaged perspective, which as a person of faith I find refreshing.

A very flawed and beautiful game.

The entire point of the game is frustration that you can't make sense of basic language. You'll spend the lion's share of the game just trying to fill out your dictionary to give meaning to the dialogue; the game is super short and the dictionary carries over between each play through. It also has an excellent interface that is not nearly as confusing as it sounds it would be. 

A catch-22 concept, because it's doomed to be too short to stretch it's wings to give all the work put in it's proper payout without forcing superfluous vocabulary. This gives way too many words such limited usage that you'll be mostly guessing, a fact acknowledged and celebrated by the opening of the game. This also means when you've hit your personal bedrock of logic and vocabulary, and inevitably crack open the steam-guides dictionary piggy bank you will find more layers of context to the story; either a pro or a con depending on how you view external information.

The story is incredibly simple, and in retrospect there are so few lines of dialogue that I feel tricked by it having such an emotional impact on me, but something about needing to piece it together yourself in the most literal sense made it very impactful.

This isn't a game I'll ever be able to play again, but I feel like I'll think about a lot.

Be aware that a lot of the negative reviews aren't reflections of the game, but rather a giant skill issue on the reviewer's end. This game is exactly what it is, as advertised, and it was a phenomenal experience. Hats off to the creators. Creating a cool story with multiple endings in a simplistic language is certainly a challenge, and they nailed it.

But I'd like to address some of the negative reviews and why their biggest problem with the game is that it's not dumbed down enough for their posters:

1. "It's a cypher, not a conglang!" Obviously, genius. It shows that in the videos/images in the store page. There's no universe where a game makes a conglang and provides no translation (the whole premise of this game) while maintaining the attention of unmedicated ADHD gamers long enough to actually enjoy the game/story.

2. "It's frustrating so I uninstalled ten minutes in." I'm confused how you thought that ten minutes of playtime was all you needed to learn the language enough to understand it. Hell, I finished the game in less than three hours and you can refund up to two. I'd take this review so much more seriously if they uninstalled after an hour and a half, but it's always the people who can't manage enough dopamine to try a "difficult" task for longer than a YouTube short's worth of time that post this crap.

I imagine this game probably works better in Japanese where "words" can have multiple meanings or can be used to express concepts more seamlessly than is possible with English. Funnily enough I actually tried that with a few words where I just typed the romaji instead of English and it worked surprisingly well. 

I didn't expect the simple "vocabulary" to remain like that the entire game, meaning that the sentences never become any more verbose, and frankly I fail to see how one can find gratification in a story told with so few words. Trying to learn a new language without a translation is already hard enough, but trying to learn a language where each sentence is limited to three words is even harder. Technically this is what infants go through the first time they learn a language, albeit without the arbitrary restriction on sentence length.

I think most people who play this game probably won't enjoy it, but this concept could definitely work with a different execution. Alternatively this could just be a me problem and this game isn't suited to my tastes.  Something which definitely could use improvement is the UI. "Ordinary" puzzle games have always been my cup of tea and this time was no different. However, what was different, was the puzzle style or genre of the game in question, one might say.

With an autistic person's worst nightmare, we have to live a week in a cozy apartment and through dialog, repetition and good ol' language immersion you have to understand the very things around you. Little by little you learn new words and the everyday conversations open up more and more, until in the end, you have vowen yourself a beautiful story of your own imagination.

On my first playthrough(I did 2 and that was enough for me, explanation later), it took around 2-3 hours with a bit of rushing and guessing. I didn't quite grasp the story fully but the cinematics told what words couldn't tell and that was nice, as I wasn't totally lost. I enjoyed used time and would say that It was worth every penny.

[h3] Quick spoiler warning or something I dunno.[/h3]

[spoiler]How about my 2nd playthrough? After completing the game I went to the community page to get more clues about the story and found out that the minecraft enchantment langauge wasn't just any random language, but it had meaning! Before I said that the gameplay loop was an autistic person's worst nightmare now I can confidentally say that this will be an autistic person's wet dream. [/spoiler]

[spoiler]BY HAND I started to decypher letter by letter each rune, or what ever they are, and it just got me into a flow when half an hour passed, then a second, third... until I came to the realisation that there must be an easier way. After I had decrypted around 70% of the letters I wired up a python code(took one from the internet) to decypher them more efficiently(yes I read that someone had posted something of a translator in a post but where's the fun in that?). After around 3 hours had passed in total of my translating journey I was almost done. And boy, was it worth it(Did an all nighter and gonna sleep during the day). In the end I was more surprised that how many of the words I got correct or atleast almost correct on my first playthrough(maybe 40-70% of the important ones).[/spoiler]

[h2] The bad and the conclusion[/h2] 

After I had translated the game nearly fully, its ugly side began to pop up. The story WAS NOT WHAT I HAD  THOUGHT AND I WANT IT BACK I WANT IT BACK MINE WAS SO MUCH COOLER.... Like in real life as a child, life was so much more colourful and enjoyable than it is after taking the redpill. Secondly, if you had to use imagination at first in order to get the story to be even some sort of cohesive mess, after translating the game it got even worse.
