From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio (with some lazy "wings" to fill the pillar).  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes Knight Solitaire 2 might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Fans of Amiga classics like Flashback or Another World will instantly feel at home with this game and will know exactly what to expect. Anyone else needs to read the full review to decide whether or not it's for them.

First of all, the graphics do a fantastic job of capturing the 16 bit era. Lovely detailed sprites and backdrops really invoke a sense of nostalgia. The same is true for the sound effects. 

The gameplay is also strong with an intriguing plot that pulls you in. For much of the game, your objective is not clear - you just know you have to keep going and escaping the dangers you face. As you progress, you uncover little clues which prick your interest further, before you finally uncover exactly what is happening. Plotting is well-paced and tight.

The game itself is a puzzle-platformer that will be instantly familiar to older gamers - pixel perfect leaping, precise timing to escape hazards and lots of use of switch mechanics to unblock the way forwards. There's nothing revolutionary here, but it's all really well implemented. 

BUT (and it's a big but), you need to be patient because throughout the game, you will die a lot. Touch water? You die. Mis-time a jump? You die. Fall too far? You die. Don't run fast enough.... you get the picture. Thanks to the game's plot, mechanics and liberal use of save points this never gets too frustrating, but if you're type of person who hates frequent (often hidden) deaths, this isn't the game for you. Personally, I enjoyed it - each time you die, you learn how to do better next time and the game somehow never feels unfair, even when it is! I was completely addicted and played it until I uncovered the whole plot.

The other thing to be aware of is the playing time. The game is very short (the frequent deaths are partly there to mask this). The playing time logged at the point of this review(around 3 hours) is how long it took me to complete the main game (although not to complete all achievements). It's not a long game by any stretch of the imagination and once you know what you're doing, you can probably play through from beginning to end in around an hour. Still, I'd rather play a short, well-put together game like this than one which feels drawn out and becomes a grind to play

I was a huge fan of the original Discolored and highly recommend it.  This second one, not so much.  The first game felt intuitive and, although switching colors constantly became a tad tedious, it made sense and the story flowed. Discolored 2 just left me cold... no sense of wonder or victory at the end. There is a comprehensive hint system which I needed to use more often than I am used to...  not for puzzle solutions but to help me figure out where I needed to look next.

The game (in Safe Mode) felt like a grind... one puzzle and finding one hidden object after another, without a sense of direction or purpose. The puzzles themselves were fairly easy, once you figured out the mechanics. The inventory key mapping felt clunky and I was constantly left-clicking or right-clicking by habit (which was not correct in this game). I finished the game and discovered I did not have access to 17 out of 45 achievements in Safe Mode. For those who are not achievement driven, this is no big deal. But, for me, it was oddly irritating.

So, I decided to give the Standard Mode a try.  An hour in, I am am under attack for the third time.  I am in an elevator shaft and I believe that my way out requires fighting wonky controls with a power saw that takes longer than the enemy lets me live. Any residual fun factor has disappeared entirely and the quest for achievements is no longer compelling.

The game has multiple save slots (I used 10) which is very handy if you need to circle back.  In safe mode, most achievements are story-related, with two groups of collectibles (radio transmitters and donuts) that are easy to miss if you are not examining each area thoroughly. 

So, would I recommend this game?  Perhaps to two kinds of players.  (1) Safe Mode is great for those who don't care about Steam achievements and don't like to game under fire. (2) Standard Mode is for those with lightening quick reflexes and who function well under pressure. Note that completionists will need to play the game between 2 and 3 times -  once in safe mode and twice in standard mode. You need a perfect standard mode game (no captures and restoring a save point before a capture is not an option)  and at least a partial standard mode game with failures (getting caught multiple times).

I can't give the game a thumbs down. It is well designed and executed with an interesting story line and a diverse set of puzzles.  For the right gamer, I'm sure it is a lot of fun. I experienced no bugs and the art and sound track are impressive. But, it was not developed for the same target audience of the original Discolored.  This departure by Godbey Games was a bit of a disappointment to me.

An added note: Having escaped the elevator shaft, I am now well on my way in Standard Mode. This version is how the game was designed tp be played and the 'gaps' in Safe Mode are filled in and things flow much smoother. To the developer's credit, they have provided clues and slow the enemy's timing after a certain number of failures. In some cases, there are milestones in your encounter and the game is saved so you don't have to always start from square-one after a death.  The challenge is rarely about 'running to escape.'  You need to assess your inventory and the environment.  Then, quickly use the resources available to survive. In some cases, there are brief QTEs which are very fairly timed. I have accepted that it will take me multiple deaths (and 'try again' screens) to make it through each area, but it is still enjoyable as I figure out how to outsmart an adversary. I have no aspirations for a perfect game so I am relaxed and glad the developer has given imperfect gamers a fair chance!

My philosophy is that honesty is kindness so I always give brutally honest reviews. With that said, here is what I think.

Story

There isn't really any story. Your cow dies in the beginning and you are told to talk about that with the king and there is a heavy religious theme. That's about all the lore, unless I am forgetting something. Is that a bad thing? Not necessarily, not all games need FNAF level lore. However, this game could be improved with a bit more background information.

Graphics

I have nothing to exactly complain about. It looks like an attempt was made. It doesn't look like Forza Horizon 5, but it is not the worst graphics I have ever seen in a game I have played.

Music

The main theme is fine but some of the music is annoying. I definitely suggest the music to be improved.

Bugs

99.99% of the time, the game works perfectly fine. There is just the extremely rare occasion when you freeze and have to quit the game and come back because you are unable to move, but due to the rareness this isn't too annoying. There are also other very minor bugs I will tell the developer about.

Controls

At the beginning of the game I couldn't interact with anything. I kept pressing E to interact like a lot of games and learnt after talking to the developer that the correct thing to press was spacebar. The main problem with the controls is there should be a menu telling you what they are. As far as I could see, there was no menu for controls. The other problem was that running only worked with left shift. It should be able to work with right shift since trying to walk with WASD and using left shift is uncomfortable.

Gameplay

I thought the gameplay was fine but it gets boring after a while since you can just keep pressing attack and using items. Of course, sometimes you need to strategise in order to just survive but generally spamming attack works. You need to make sure all your guys are at a decent level. 

Items

There are a lot of items which is cool but there are so many that you will barely use any of them.

Summary

I like to buy games with no reviews so I can give feedback on them. This is the best game I have ever played that had no reviews at the time I played it, so that's a positive. It's not much, it's a little boring and empty, but I think it has potential and it is a good attempt, that's why I have given a positive review. I will follow any news on this game.

Nothing too big, just click the burger to get money, use this money to buy buildings (then highlight the $5 building you start near), then use the money now to upgrade. I would like to recommend this game because of how much promise this game has but I simply cannot. There are so many things missing in this game that the dev team seems to no care about that really ruins the game.

Here are the things missing or things that ruin the game. (From Most to least necessary.)

-No Right Click to manual attack. Allow us to right click a unit to attack it just like in every other RTS. It is extremely annoying for a Tank to be targeting a infantry squad 800 Meters away when there is enemy tank throwing shells at it. Allow us to command units to hit certain things in RTS mode. 

-No Autosave. There should be an autosave function in the map screen. Maybe once every 10 months? Let's be real we all save scum it is just how most of us play. But to constantly have to go out of our way to manually save every battle is tedious and you tend to forget to save if you're in a high intensity conflict. I lost days worth of fighting because the enemy decided to cheese and destroy my developing army and set my stabiliy to 0%. I would like to relog and sort the units to get the best infront but nope have to go back to the start of the entire war.

-Cannot backlog units in battle. There should be away that units can retreat from the battlefield and go to the bottom of the spawn queue. If a tank has no ammo it is completely useless so being able to swap it out for a fresh unit could spice up gameplay. It also fixes the issue of losing a tanks and having to waste a slot because you have to keep the crew out of battle to keep the squad alive.

-Vehicle AI. I think the Devs know this but they really seem to not be targeting the real issues about it. Vehicles have a tendency to collide with other vehicles to get somewhere rather than going around it. Vehicles love to get caught on rocks, trees and buildings to be stuck forever. Vehicles will do a full 360 turn if told to directly move back instead of just reversing allowing for more time to be shot. Finally, vehicles have a tendency to target standard infantry over other vehicles or RPG guys leading to many preventable vehicle damages/deaths.

No minimap on map screen. The World is quite a big one with a lot of island and it is easy to get lost in the black void of unrevealed terrain. Yes you can press F to go back to your capital but that takes you back to the beginning of your search and most people don't know about the F Hotkey. A simple minimap can fix this.

-Lack of Modding Support. The reason why people think this game has some potential is the customizability this game could have. There is a reason why games like Arma 3, Cities Skylines, HOI IV and Rimworld still last to this day and make large money because of its community creation support. You have a workshop, yes, but it has barely anything on it. You need to allow people to do anything with the games format. A map editor to make new campaign maps (where you can recreate real conflicts or fictional ones) allow for total overhall mods that changes the games theme (Star Wars, Warhammer-40k, WW2, More Units mods among others) as soon as you unlock the full range of customizability, this game will rocket.

-The RPG. 3 things I will briefly mention. Why is it only the RPG? It is so weird seeing a Democratic country using a RPG-7 when it's mostly a Socialist weapon. We need some Western Anti-Tank like SMAWs or the M3 MAAWs. Along with other types of rockets like single shots (AT4, RPG-22, NLAW) or Surface to air. (Javelins, Kormet, Milan) Second, the sights on the RPG are atrocious for any range apart from >50M. We need a RPG Mod version of the RPG so we can attach specialied scopes onto the RPG so it can be used in FPS mode. Finally, what is up with the projectile? You can have it aimed perfectly on flat terrain at perfect range and somehow the rocket will overshoot the target. Yes, real projection is often unpredictable but in the game it is predictable that the rocket will overshoot every time. You may want to fix the Z angle on the projectile movement.

-Lack of heavy small arms. I already mentioned Heavy Anti-Tank but what about other missing heavy weapons? There a 3 LMGs in the game. The RPK, the M249 and the L86. These work well as infantry support weapons but what about heavy machine guns. The PKP for Socialist, PKM for African and the M240B and/or MG3 for democratic. Weapons that can pin down vehicles. Not only HMGs and HATs but what about Manpads? (Stingers and Iglas.) Something that can swipe air units out of the air that isn't a vehicle.
 
I feel as soon most or all of these are fixed then I can give it a positive review but for now, no bite.

[i]Sweet Collector[/i] is an adorably cute puzzle game in which you are tasked to arrange a set of given shapes on a grid, with the condition that in the end no spot remains uncovered and no piece is left behind. It's basically the same gameplay as [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1369340/Cats_Organized_Neatly/]Cats Organized Neatly[/url] / [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1597730/Dogs_Organized_Neatly/]Dogs Organized Neatly[/url] (which belong to a different developer), but this time the cats and dogs are replaced with mouth watering cakes and sweets.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2749624536
Each new piece is presented with a short and hilarious text at the beginning of the level when you first encounter it, and is then unlocked into a collection that can be accessed from the main menu. All the drawings are very sweet and the pieces all have unique animations while being idle, or when they are picked up / dropped.

You don't have to be a genius to complete the game, but I'd say that the difficulty ramps up steeply starting as low as level 12-13. As you progress through the game, the grid becomes bigger, the pieces also grow in size and take weirder, longer or bulkier shapes, making their placement a more complex process. Finding a solution is most of the time a matter of trial and error - after all, it’s a “find-the-developer’s-solution” kind of game, and there’s close to 0 logic involved. Also, the grids are not designed in a way that lets you eliminate most of the incorrect placement possibilities.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2749624482
The game runs and plays fairly well, but if I were to complain about something that would be the interface. When you start a level, the pieces are scattered around the grid, and for smaller resolutions it can happen that one piece is positioned by default too far out and thus not displayed on the screen any more, making it inaccessible. The grid also has quite a big area in which the pieces can’t be dropped, which makes removing pieces from the board sometimes uncomfortable - you have to try dropping them several times until you find a working spot.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2749624507
Despite the charming art, this is not a kids game - the writing is full of funny puns and references that younger gamers probably would not understand. Also in terms of difficulty / complexity, the gameplay could prove to be a challenge for younger audiences.

With its 100 levels, it has enough content to keep you occupied for a few hours. If you get stuck, there is no hint to mark the incorrectly placed pieces, but the levels are skippable.

Star Sign is a pretty alright game trough and trough. It has simple controls that are easy to grasp but hard to master, and fun to swing around. The environments are pretty charming with sweet and clamming sound that enhances the setting. With the biggest flaw of it being the level design. 

The level design is both confusing and repetitive. Confusing in the sense that sometimes when you think you have done every single path that the level has to offer, you don't advance because there is another area you have to go trough, but have no idea where to go or direction. There are big beams of light in the sky you could look at for direction for a path, but when you done all of the paths in you're line of sight, it hard to find that one more path/light that could be up way high in the sky. Objectives could defiantly be made more clearer.  The level design is repetitive in the sense that it make you do the exact same challenges. It's fine for the first level, but the second level is almost identical in terms of challenges. Jump from vine to vine with no challenge or gimmick obstacle in you're way, Hop in a tornado and reach for the furthest vine over and over, slingshot from platform to platform from very long distances and such. I feel like it never grows to be more interesting   or even more involved then it's stale swing to swing set of vines and grind ropes. 

I also have to point out that the checkpoints are very few and far between. Sometimes minutes apart. I personally don't mind the challenge of less checkpoints, and I do appreciate the options of extra challenge difficulty trough no checkpoints and the fun idea of the floor is lava, which is really cool! But I feel like the game would benefit by having a easy difficulty for those who are having a hard time with the long stretch of level design without a checkpoint. 

(UPDATE: The dev has since updated the game  to be more customizable with how you want to tackle difficulty in the game. If you want more checkpoints, but same amount of jumps, you can do that. If you want to have the normal amount of checkpoints with more then 2 jumps and aim assist, you can also do that as well. Allowing the player to mix and match however they please. The fact you can do this is just awesome to see!)

With that said, the other aspects of the game are pretty good. Namely the controls and movement. The controls are easy to learn since they are only four actions. Jump, swing, slingshot, and sprinting. You get quite the feeling for swinging around pretty fast that you feel like you are in absolute control over.  You can speed up you're swing and momentum jump  with the sprint button that acts like a boost while you swinging. The way in which you can control you're speed/control is pretty flexible depending on the trajectory of you're swing. The slingshot is a pretty good option for movement too from a standstill if you don't have that much space on the ground, or to make you very own way above the skies without need land or rocks above you. It's a pretty cool  detail that opens up the approach you could go for. 

While the level design is pretty repetitive, the game does allow you to grapple onto any surface and or terrain there is in the entire game. This can allow you to use the movement you learnt and apply it to the path you see fit. You could follow along the path, or take a slight shortcut if you climbed up the floating island and skip all the vine climbing, or even cutting trough all of it and making you're own path if you think you can. You can even use the terrain  to save you're self from a dangerous fall if there is a wall nearby. It really opens the door  and can even make a playtrough unique.

The world does a pretty good job in making you believe in it's dreamlike qualities. For example, in the first level, there are the normal nature things you find out in the woods, trees, ponds, vines, mountain and such. But when you get to the next level, all those things get re decorated to fit the theme of that sky-box. Which is pretty neat, but noting note worthy by itself. Expect for the fact that music accompanying the levels really fit whiten the floating landscapes and feel right at home. It's nice, sweet, calming, and flowing with peace.  The type of music you would fall asleep to, hence it's dreamlike qualities. The music does the heavy lifting for it's world design and presentation. Though a issue I have is sometimes the game would go very quiet and nothing would be playing, which makes for awkward silences where music would be well welcomed. But sometimes, as you make you're way trough a certain path, the music would come right back while you were swinging and taking in the local surroundings which is a really nice feeling. I appreciate the detail to more dynamic things like that. But could be implanted in a more fitting way where the silence would be not existent.  

Overall Star Sign is a mostly well made game where you can defiantly feel the passion and love trough playing it. While the level design could be better in displaying you're objective and the variety, and the lack of easy mode could be a turn off for some players. Everything else is pretty good. Not amazing by no means, but gets the point across pretty finely. If the game play and screenshots appeal to you then I say I would recommend it, but wait for a sale.

I think the checkpoints could stand to be more generous, and I find myself unsure where to go now that I've gotten at least one light pillar in each of the cardinal directions from the central hub of the first level, but the vibes are extremely good in this game. Antivine is an adorably cute and charming tale of Senshu who was born without branches on his head and has to wear false ones all his life to fit in with his community.  Senshu is bullied, mocked and rejected by others in his village as they regard him as a freak.  It is only his devoted parents who accept his uniqueness, especially his mother who constantly showers him with her love.  [spoiler]At his 16th birthday, his mother dies and he is left alone.[/spoiler]
Senshu struggles with his difference as his desire is to become a Treeman like everyone else and bear fruit for his community.  Only the Mountain God has the answers to all his questions, so off goes Senshu on his quest. On his way, he meets a little girl Mumei (like Mummy!) who has lost her memory and carries her in his backpack to take her home.
Game play is to click on the path where you want Senshu to go and you switch between him and Mumei to get to the exit.  The puzzles are fairly easy...I only needed the walkthrough once towards the end where the difficulty ramped up.  I found the music to be lovely, switching from tolling bells, flutes, piano and orchestral sounds.
Graphics are mixed with monochromatic hand drawn cutscenes for pertinent parts of the story, but the diorama graphics are bright and crisp.  Traversing through the dioramas, you have to dodge carnivorous plants who will chomp on you and hungry starfish who grab you with their antenna.  There are cute cactus plants who were having a snooze until you wake them up and they march off (with sound effects!).  There are not so cute coloured balls who are not friendly at all!  There are plants that rotate to help you get to a difficult spot, shy vegetation that act as lifts and plenty of pressure pads.  You are even able to manipulate the moon which affects the level of water as it waxes and wanes.  There are also little carts that are moved by wind funnels.  So lots of innovative ideas to get you from A to B.
When you finish the game, the achievements on the main menu tell you which ones you have missed and how many deaths you need to make.  I am an expert in dying, so I got those achievements very easily!!  You can even go back and play a particular chapter from the menu on the main page which is very handy.
There is a drawback to this game.  As others have stated, there is poor English translation that can affect your immersion in the game.  This ranges from blatant spelling errors and bad grammar.  It is obvious that no QA was done in this area which could have been fixed by an English speaking native.  Depending on your personality, this will either annoy you or you will just brush it off.  I felt the end in particular was lost in translation and it felt rushed.  I actually wonder if they are hoping to make a sequel to this game.  If it is as good as this, I will buy it if they get an English translator.  This is certainly a game that children can play as there is no blood and guts and will help them learn strategy.
Overall, Antivine is a lovely example of an evocative narrative-focused puzzle platformer which takes around 2-4 hours for clever people and longer for the dull of brain (like me!).  It is a story that many of us can relate to.  Points deducted for lazy translation.  7.5/10

[b]disclaimer:[/b] I helped with testing off-steam builds before release but bought my own copy when it came out.

[b]quest for cathay kingdom[/b] is a unique take on the usual mahjong formula. it's based on the [i]rivers[/i] variant, something [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1161360/]shisensho solitaire[/url] does exceptionally well on steam, but in this game [b]only the top tiles are available[/b]. you can, however, [b]switch adjacent tiles[/b] (right click), and match-3 elements let you [b]remove 3 or 4 tiles in a straight line even if they're not on top[/b], as long as they're the same suit, in sequence, etc. double-click the first and the last to do so, possible combinations are described in the menu.

levels start with a [b]limited number of moves[/b], running out means game over, but [b]only switching tiles counts and extra moves are awarded[/b] for certain things. the goal is to have fewer tiles left than the number of columns, so if the board is 9x6, the level ends once you have 8 tiles left. there's a counter for remaining pieces, but [b]the game doesn't indicate if there are no valid moves[/b], you have to 'declare defeat' when you reach this conclusion by yourself.

[b]no hint, undo or shuffle buttons either[/b], but other mechanics include [b]betting coins earned from levels[/b]. it's only possible during the first 90 seconds after starting a level, that's the only time the clock is relevant and you can click it anytime to turn it off. [b]coins are used to buy specials (joker tiles) and moves[/b] and betting can increase your money faster. moves can also be sold for coins and all this and more is explained before certain levels.

[b]4 game modes[/b] are available. the [u]cathay[/u] variant with all the bells and whistles can be played with or without a story (cutscenes are skippable), [u]waterfall[/u] does away with everything but switching tiles, so just match tiles from the top, and [u]match & sequence[/u] only allows removing a sequence of tiles next to each other, but has coins and specials.

[b]the story consists of 16 levels[/b], increasing in size and difficulty. doesn't sound like much but you probably won't breeze through all of them on the first try. [b]the other game modes have 10 levels each[/b], but of course tile placement is random and level select lets you replay unlocked stages, so it acts more like a size setting than anything. the game also creates save files to go back to, which I find completely unnecessary, that's what the level select screen is for.

graphics are fine, there's a light and dark mode for the tiles, audio is fitting, some really nice tracks to listen to, but [b]the tutorial font is a bit hard to read[/b] and the [b]pop-ups for the dev's previous game and newsletter are really annoying[/b]. they should put both images in the corner instead of constantly moving them on and off the screen. further settings include separate volumes, windowed mode with a resizable window, some languages and story text size.

Fascinating really. I played around with 4D Toys before, and having a basic understanding of how to think about 4D really helped a lot here. 4D Toys uses a really good tutorial-analogy that lets you play around in a 3D space and shows you how a person in 2D would perceive things there. You can then use this understanding as a jumping off point to think about how you in your 3D view of the world perceive a 4D space. (you can find a good demonstration video on youtube)

Cake4D sadly does not have a tutorial of that quality. Here you are given several Mario-esque jumping challenges, each is first solved by a bot playing the game for you (highlighting the buttons pressed for each action) and then you are left on your own to try and repeat that. It does not explain what the different vision modes (R, F, G and T key) are for or how to understand them.

In short: R is normal reality with a XYZ coordinates. X  is blue & left-right / Y is green & up-down / Z is red & forward-back. The fourth dimension is pink. You can slide along this direction by pressing Q and E, which will noticeably shift the world. Alternatively you can use the vision modes F, G and T which each swap one of the three coordinates with the 4th one.

It is a bit of work to wrap your head around this, but once you manage to do just that the experience is quite unique and definitely worth the asking price. I would suggest to play each level not just until you bump into the solution but try to understand how this 4D space is actually structured. How each platform and door you see corresponds to what you see in the other views. I would say that is where the actual value of this game lies. The jumping around is bland to be honest, but it is the right tool, a very simple and intuitive tool to understanding the world. And that is priceless.

Just when you think you've seen it all ... "Game City" comes along and shatters all hope that might have remained.

"Game City" is neither a "game" nor a "city". It's also certainly not about "parkour" unless you cound mindlessly jumping from one cube to another as "parkour". 

The "game world" consists of a skybox ([url=https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/vfx/shaders/free-skybox-extended-shader-107400]free Unity asset[/url]) and 341 identical untextured cubes floating in space. The "player model" is simply an - also untextured - capsule. That's it. There's no user interface, no goal, no nothing - you jump from cube to cube until you fall down or get fed up. The warning "English language not supported" on the Steam store page is hilarious as there's no text in the game at all.

Everything screams "my first Unity project" and this is cemented by the fact that the bulk of the game's install size is occupied by assets used for the default Unity project scene. None of them are used by the game, though, but the scene is still there, just 10,000 meters away from the player. 

Why is this on Steam? This is a project you'd make as your first attempt at moving a character in Unity and then delete once you've got the hang of it. You certainly don't release it as is on Steam and ask almost 9 bucks for it. What's going on here? This is by far the worst offender I've reviewed and the bar was already four floors down the basement.

It seems the "developer" even realized all this when he wrote the game description:

A sad recent trend has been popping up lately - asset flippers taking code found on Github for free and releasing the compiled "game" on Steam for money. To the flippers this is even better than having to pay for an asset from the Unity store. For people like me who hunt asset flippers it's annoying because the assets in question aren't always that easy to identify. Still managed to do it, though, heh ...

Anyway, "Stapel" is such an asset flip. It's simply [url=https://github.com/telecoda/stack]Stack[/url], a very bare bones game someone named telecoda put together to, as they write, learn Unity. They also released it on the Google Play store but it's been removed by now. The code is from 2017 as well so it's likely long been forgotten by the original author.

All "Quickbobber" did here was clone the repository and compile it with Unity. No change has been made and so the "game" opens in a 480x800 window as it was apparently designed for rather ancient mobile devices. There's a resolution option in the equally ancient Unity launcher but it's overridden by the game code.

The "game" itself is an extremely simple clone of the successful mobile game "Stack" by Ketchapp. There are countless free clones of the same game (which is also free) so there's really no need for another one, especially one that's not one iota better than any other.

Oh, by the way - this is also in violation of the MIT license which, while granting the right to do whatever with the code, has to be included with the game. It isn't.

Do yourself a favor and don't buy this crap.

This is easily one of the best games I've played in a very long time and might be one of my all time faves now.  It's hard to even pick a place to begin with singing this game's praises.  As a long time Pokemon fan, it completely blows the entire series out of the water in my opinion, ESPECIALLY the most recent titles.

The game absolutely oozes with personality and charm.  The art direction is a very pleasant and easy on the eyes cartoony aesthetic.  The Beasties all look great, plenty of cool ones, cute ones, weird ones, whatever your taste is you'll likely find plenty to like.  The writing is wonderful too.  The characters are all a lot of fun and very extra in a way I very much enjoy, and the things they have to say range from cute, to hilarious, to even poignant and thought provoking on occasion.

The music totally slaps as well, so much so that I just today bought the digital soundtrack.

You might go in thinking that the whole "volleyball" thing is a gimmick, but no, honestly!  It's very well thought out and incredibly fun in my opinion!  A bevy of options for strategies both offensively and defensively, and it always feels great when you make a risky play that winds up swinging the matches in your favor.  The interplay and teamwork between Beasties is awesome, and I'm sure the more tactical minds out there could spend hours putting together very powerful teams with crazy synergies.  Just a boatload of simple to learn, difficult to master strategic fun for both casuals and sweats!

The Beasties also develop relationships with each other as they play together, which is not only cute and fun, but opens up even more strategic options as they can teach each other tons of moves and unlock various "super moves" based on the nature of their relationship.

Also, if you're a fan of hunting shinies like myself, you'll almost certainly have a great time doing so in this game.  Even from the beginning you get some tools to make finding them more manageable, and it only gets better the deeper in you get.  I started a "shinies only" file and am well on my way towards getting a complete "shinydex".

In short, if you're a fan of creature collector games, I can't recommend this title enough, especially when it reaches 1.0.  It's honestly the most fun I've had in the genre.

It also has pronouns and stuff so the gross anti-woke cringe lords won't come anywhere near it, which is always a win in my book.  : )

This is such a special experience, even in Early Access. The writing is great- efficient and evocative and emotional, with a well-realized world and a story with twists. But for me, the standout feature is the way that the Beasties interact with you and each other, which is miles away from any other creature-collecting game I've ever played.  Just the change from "capturing monsters for your collection to fight battles for you" to "recruiting animals to your team to play sports with each other"  is so positive and heartwarming and so good. 

Beasties love to ball. Toss a ball in their direction and they'll start keepy-uppies at a moment's notice. The wild encounters use slightly weird and inefficient tactics, because they're not playing to win, they're just having fun. Each Beastie has a unique 'recruit condition', because you need to show them something specific that makes them realize that playing for your team might be fun. And when they aren't playing matches for your team... they go home, and hang out with their friends. They form relationships with each other, they form a community. It's so wonderful.

And that's Beastieball!

Growing up, I've always had an attachment to the creature collector genre. Big Pokemon fan but lately, I've been craving something that can stand out from the Pokemon system per se which can also give me the satisfaction of caring for my team and completing a "PokeDex" of sorts. I found Beastieball right before it was released and the gameplay intrigued me. Volleyball with little creatures that you can assemble as a team? Splendid!

Once I finally got my hands on it, it clicked like clockwork. I LOVE the way Beastieball puts its own spin on the formula. The type system is simplified to three here, Body, Spirit, and Mind where a "super-effective" attack is based on how high a beastie's defense stat is towards that type. Each Beastie (so far) seems to have their own kind of moveset and archetype to make them stand out without relying on attack types. Because of this, you can craft your team in a lot of ways easier, in my opinion, when compared to other games in the genre. Even while in early access, this game has a Battle Frontier in the endgame which I really appreciated.


The artstyle looks really charming and the characters all look pretty good. I like their personalities and the social system where you can meet with the coaches (gym leaders) and spend some time with them is a nice touch! Speaking of personalities, I adore how the beasties have unique traits too and how they react to things you do both in-battle and while just walking around the world. The little moodles that pop-up along with the relationship system among the beasties just give them so much more character and I had a really fun time immersing myself into the game as it did.

Now, this is still in early access so there are a lot of things unfinished. Some beasties don't have animations yet and some have their sketched poses as their current ones. There are also some bugs that I've run across but they provided a bug-reporting tool in-game for these purposes. The game also runs slow at times when I Alt-Tab and return to it but I've only run into this in like three times during my playthrough.

All-in-all, one of the best creature collectors I have played so far. I look forward to the full release and I will definitely follow this game on the road leading to it!

I have played nearly every goddamn monster catcher under the sun and they all invariably had the same issues - they had little room for strategy (a common issue with PvE games that try to also be balanced for PvP), their stories were mid-tier at best, and for the most part they're just a few degrees of separation from Pokemon.

So when I say that this one is so far ahead of the curve that you could pretty reasonably say it's the first good game in its genre, I am only SLIGHTLY joking. The moves and abilities are crazier, there's no stat RNG to encourage eugenics, natures dictate actual creature behavior instead of stat growths, battles have significantly more freedom and the way monsters form relationships with eachother is something I never even knew I wanted. It makes complete sense, you're a coach for a team, not just a master and their army. This is the first monster catcher I've played where battles both felt satisfying and rewarding to be GOOD at, as well as the first one in a while where I bothered to headcanon personalities for my squad, and believe me that is a fucking achievement with how jaded I am about these games. My singular complaint is that EV training hasn't been nuked from orbit and replaced with freely-allocated stat points, but it is MUCH more straightforward here in that the game doesn't HIDE THE FACT IT EXISTS.

I could go on about the music being just as good as in Wishes' previous games, I could go on about how the daycare equivalent is about sending a team to another player's game as an overworld encounter, I could go on about how the story is Really Good and about the sports industrial complex instead of another goon squad - I just want to end by pointing out that, as of this writing, there are THREE (3) negative reviews. One of them is a joke. The OTHER two complain about "DEI" and the fact a main character is trans. That is effectively a 100% positive rating, and frankly I can think of few games more deserving of that than the one that restored my faith in its genre before it was even finished.

Eden's Last Sunrise is an interesting game that deserves more attention. It's one part Final Fantasy Tactics and one part visual novel.

Society had a major split 200 years prior to the start of the game. One faction used modern technology to take to space and forge a new life, while the other stayed on the planet and embraced magic. The beginning of the game sees the space faring faction detecting a potentially life-ending wave of energy wiping out their distant satellites, and deciding its time to contact their long-lost kin. In true visual novel form, you choose whether to play as the space faring people or those who stayed behind at the beginning. From there, each route splits into two more a ways in.

The combat gameplay takes most of its queues from Final Fantasy Tactics, but notably adds a cover system and an aggro system. The cover system effectively changes how you think about positioning, while the aggro system allows for MMO style tanking and riskier positioning with those who can reduce their targeting priority. The game also features an action point system, with each character (typically) getting 6 action points per turn. A standard attack costs 3 points, moving can be done once per turn for a single point, and defending is always available for 2 points. Stronger attacks can cost more, while certain attacks and utility abitliies may cost less. This usually means a move, an attack, and a utility ability or defense per turn, but could also means two or more attacks in a turn if forgoing movement. On top of this, you have a solid number of classes to mix and match abilities with, covering both magical and high tech options. There is also a tension system, which allows for powerful limit-break like abilities, but I found that most of these were either not that impactful or took too long to build to show up outside of the longest couple of battles in the game.

The combat is enjoyable, but it unfortunately doesn't quite hit the tactical heights of the best in the genre. I found the majority of the moves I used to be damage with some minor status effect rider or healing moves, with pure status effects and debuffs not generally being worth the action points when alternatives are available. For example, there's nothing that feels impactful in a similar way to Time Mages in FFT. There are a couple of abilities to speed up turns, but they only speed up the next turn as a rider effect on a heal or as a high tension cost ability that just didn't come into play. Similar things could be said about hard control abilities and other utility focused skills. Further, the difficulty is a bit odd -- I found once I'd learned a few essential abilities hard mode was quite easy, but expert was annoying. Enemies on expert are not only at a substantially higher level than you, but they also get an additional action point per turn. This means that most enemies can move and attack twice in a turn, which just felt bad to me. It was still doable once I got rolling, but I found I preferred just having the game be a bit easy rather than constantly feeling like the computer had a weird advantage.

I really enjoyed the character writing. While I did find some of it to come across as a bit amateurish, the cast is quite likable, has good development, and are all quite distinct from one another. This is bolstered by each character having an affinity rating that is increased through optional social scenes.

My biggest complaint about Eden's Last Sunrise is that, much like many visual novels, it expects you to play multiple routes to unlock the good end. I liked the gameplay and story well enough for a single route that took 25-30 hours, but not enough to playthrough a couple more times given how many excellent games are sitting in my backlog. The ending I got did a good enough job of wrapping up character arcs, but the conclusion to the existential threat was unsatisfying. I still enjoyed my time with the game, but it did drop my final opinion of the game a bit.

So, my recommendation for the game comes down to this: If you like doing multiple routes in a game and New Game+ type options, and are interested in the genre, then definitely give Eden's Last Sunrise a go. If not, I think it's still worth playing, but it does depend on whether you are willing to move on with a bad end or are happy looking up the good ending.

This is the story of a teenage girl who must use her wits and one strange alliance to deal with the awful fate she has been handed - being married to her uncle. This visual novel does away with the main pet peeve I have regarding other visual novels, which is the characters standing in one place while the dialogue suggests they are doing some sort of action not depicted. In this VN the events are usually written while no character portraits are present. Speaking of the character portraits, they are drawn in a style similar to the developer's previous games. I've read the VN five times already and only received two different endings. While I can't recommend this to everyone because of its dark themes, I will recommend it to anyone who is even a little interested.

A delightful, emotional, story-driven game with light JRPG and shoot 'em up elements.

The presentation is simply superb, boasting beautiful pixel-art graphics, sombre music, and a fair smattering of evocative, poetic prose. On this basis, the game is an easy recommendation, and the developer, easily praised! Great work!

The gameplay, on the other hand, excites less enthusiasm. The RPG mechanics are quite shallow, and the balance of combat... the tools given to the player and the enemies... feels all over the place. For example, enemies capable of inflicting status effects are infinitely more bothersome than those who are not, and pickpocketing is an infuriating dice roll unless one happens to pick the class that can [i]simply ignore it.[/i]

Actually, granting the player the ability to dodge every direct attack may be at the root of these issues — the mix of avoidable and unavoidable damage in the game as it currently is simply feels awkward, at least to me. At any rate, though, combat is so easy that this is all easily overlooked. Though, on the subject of difficulty... (As the section below covers NEW GAME PLUS, it is of little concern to prospective buyers; however, I hope Jack Astral himself stumbles upon this!)

[b]Challenge Mode[/b] is unlocked upon the game's completion, and serves to increase the difficulty and add some additional lore items to find. Splendid idea! Alas, its implementation pleases me very little, indeed.

To address the elephant in the room, it's... not challenging whatosever. In fact, the differences between it, and Normal Mode are not clear to me at all. Or was it that I picked a different, stronger class?

Secondly, despite being a dedicated NG+ mode, Challenge Mode does nothing to alleviate that the bulk of the game involves easy puzzles, separated by cutscenes. [i]Lots[/i] of cutscenes, with underwhelming functionality around skipping through them! Between that and the low difficulty, I found my second playthrough to be an unfortunate drag.

One final topic, and my greatest pet peeve with the game: Backtracking!

While backtracking in a game like this is perfectly fine, and the game's design facilitates it well, the [i]interactivity[/i] of the world serves to undermine its immersion! There are so many characters whose dialogue ceases to make sense past a certain point in the protagonist's journey, and it's jarring to see them remain while certain other NPCs move on. [spoiler] Why does the protagonist ignore the fading spirits found earlier on in the game, when they interact with those in the Sky? [/spoiler] [spoiler] Why does that one Dark Spirit reply to Vesper, long after their departure? [/spoiler]

While this is a most petty complaint, it is exactly what I would expected a game like this to excel at, not to mention being something that I hope could be addressed with a relatively small effort in an update :)

In conclusion: I salute thee, Jack Astral, stranger though thou art, and thank thee for thy work. [b]I recommend this video game.[/b]

A melodious platformer that doesn’t overstay its welcome.

[b]What is it:[/b] A platformer that looks and sounds amazing, and prefers to be enjoyed, not to be plowed through. It mixes in a bit of precision, a bit of puzzle, a bit of hidden object, and a bit of metroidvania.

The story: Symphonia is the land that music built. Unfortunately, it’s also the land that music forgot. A long time ago, four musicians combined their talents for magical music to build a perfect land, beautiful and bountiful. But with Philemon, one of the four founders, gone, debility, dismay and distrust caused the other three to isolate themselves, leaving Symphonia to slowly decay. One day, Philemon is brought back. Can he traverse the treacherous terrain, rekindle the old friendships and bring back the orchestra for one more concert?

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3417873272

The gameplay: This is mainly a platformer, with running and jumping as your main tools. There is no fighting, and for most of the time, no rush, you’re free to take your time and plan your route. The main goal is to keep progressing to the right until you catch up with each of the three former musicians. It is possible to fail, though, since there are deadly spikes and bottomless pits, but there are very frequent checkpoints, and failing simply puts you back a little bit. Along the way you can collect hard to reach musical notes, hidden aura shards, or defeat more challenging optional sections holding memory fragments that give you powers, or letters detailing the backstory. Some of these collectibles require a second visit since they can only be obtained with a special ability not yet unlocked, like slingshotting from special pads, or an enhanced bow that you can use as a slinghook. There are 3 and a half chapters, a shorter intro teaching you the controls and the goals, and one environment for each musician, each with its own theme and mechanics. At the end of the last chapter there’s a long chase scene which is the only one that really tests your speed and reflexes.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3417877616

The game isn’t long, it is possible to finish it in under two hours, if you’re not trying to get the collectibles, but it does have strong replay value. Other than going back to collect all the things you couldn’t get on the first pass, collecting memory fragments unlocks Philemon’s “memories”, which are optional skills you can enable or disable, and these affect the gameplay in major ways. You gain the ability to alter the game speed, slowing it down if you're not nimble-fingered, or speeding it up if you're a professional precision platformer player looking for a real challenge. You can unlock double jumping, all catapult, all bounce, a shadow chase mode, or even turn yourself invisible. Each of these modes make for a very different course through the game. After you beat it once with the default mechanics, you can try it again with the all catapult mode, that makes many sections a lot easier, but it makes other sections very tricky. Same with the all bounce mode. You can try to beat the shadow chase mode in which you must always keep moving. You can try to beat the hardcore mode, in which you only get a few lives, and if you lose all of them you have to restart the whole chapter. Or even with the default mechanics you have to go through the levels once more, since it’s impossible to gather everything the first time through. Although not a very long game, it does encourage repeated playthroughs.

Did I mention that it looks and sounds amazing? It really does. You have the ability to just play the violin whenever you feel like it, with one of many lovely improvisations to listen to. At the end of every chapter, when you finally catch up to another musician, you play a minutes long duet, and an extra long concert with all the band members (and an accompanying orchestra) at the end of the game. There are different environments for each chapter, a glassy greenhouse full of plants, the countryside with its string meadows, a shiny brass palace with a darker underbelly. A true work of art. Well done, Sunny Peak!

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3417872939

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Easy to moderate, for a platformer, with only the final chase scene being more demanding.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 3.5 chapters, 4-6 hours to finish once, 5-10 hours to get 100%, but you can keep replaying it a few more times with different modes to get the full experience. I for one spent 30+ hours in it, and I’m not fully done with it.

[b]Level design:[/b] Good. Each screen adds something new, a new type of obstacle, or a new combination of moves to try.

[b]Quality:[/b] Excellent. Good levels, good music, good looks. Configurable controls. Good settings. Cloud saving, good achievements. Three save slots. Fast and responsive.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] Yes. May seem expensive for a not very long platformer, especially if you compare with how much playtime you get out of Celeste for the same price, but it’s not just how much the buyer gets for the money, also how much work was put into the product.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] Doesn’t require too much speed and precision.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] The chase sequence.

[b]What would make it better:[/b] An option to have checkpoints in the chase scene. More save slots. More secrets.

The platformer genre is over saturated and as such it is difficult to stand out from the crowd.  Symphonia caught my attention as I love classical music and I play a string instrument.  It is a novel setting that stuck to a tried and true formula, rather than trying something different.  Ultimately, the game would have been better served by trying something ‘different’.  I would have preferred to have sections, where you have to move to the beat of the music and/or use your instrument in ‘boss battles’.  The notes you collect could mean you can perform different and more complex songs/ moves to defeat your enemies and would make the collectibles more relevant. 

I found the controls and movement mechanics to be counter-intuitive and frustrating.  There were sections in the game when I wanted to move a certain way, but was unable to.  For example,  in a section of the woodwind level, I wanted to double-jump to the next two ‘cymbal’ swings and then double jump onto the platform, I could not do consecutive double jumps, I could only do one in the sequence.  I know it would have made the sequence easier which would go against the grain of the difficult tag, but this gameplay decision and others like it, does not make sense to me.  I understand that people have different playing styles and unfortunately, Symphonia does not suit my style of play.  I did not bother finishing the game, as I play games to have fun and I found this game to be tedious and frustrating.

I cannot recommend this game for the average gamer.  It’s a shame that the developers did not incorporate different difficulty modes, to make the game more accessible for the average gamer (a large target audience) as I found the elements they incorporated did not make the game easier - e.g. what is the point of having a double jump if I cannot use it how I want to. For all those wondering, yes I did pass that area, by saving the double jump for near the platform.  With that being said, I’m sure there are plenty of gamers out there who would enjoy this game and the challenges that it provides, but that was not my experience.  I would prefer to give Symphonia a neutral rating, but that is not possible. I opted for a negative rating, as my experiences were ones of frustration and tedium, no doubt other people will have vastly different experiences and opinions to my own and their reviews will reflect that.  I hope the devs take the constructive criticism on board for their next game, as Symphonia shows they have a lot of talent.

In fact i didn't even make much use of the double jump outside of snagging optional collectibles along the way. This is because while symphonia is definately a game belonging in the precision platformer category, it doesn't require pixel perfect inputs or quick reflexes. There's a lot of mechanics that give you some breathing room and the checkpoints are very generous throughout. Most section aren't even THAT difficult only requiring a handfull of tries at most. The hardest platforming is found in optional side rooms that are exactly that, optional. I played through the game and got every collectible in the main rooms and some of the side rooms however i was left satisfied to leave it at that. The main rooms have a perfect challenge rating that is never overbearing and honestly ridiculously fun.

The platforming mechanics in general in Symphonia are top notch, which is ofcourse very important in a precision platformer. The character responds exactly how you want and there's a nice preservation of momentum that can sometimes lead to certain death if you cannot keep it under control. The game keeps adding extra mechanics at a steady pace and there's even a sweet chase sequence at the end to put all your skills to the test. Most of these mechanics come from your own skillset that expands in metroidvania fashion but the environments play an equal part in adding variety. This is one of the things symphonia does best, as it makes sure that no two sections feel the same. In the end a blend of perfect challenge, smooth controls and great level design create a varied & fun experience throughout.

What's also very consistent throughout is the thematic of musical instruments. Like an orchestra the game is divided in 4 sections namely strings, woodworks, brass and... strings? Yeah it's unfortunate that percusion didn't get it's own part but there's enough percusion related things like drums that serve as bouncing pads. Still each region does a lot of things to make it tie in thematically. From drafts of wind in the woodworks section, which was the highlight of the game for me, to the gliding rails sections of the strings and the mechanical platforms of the brass. Each section has it's own gameplay flair as well as strong visual identity. The visuals in symphonia are outstanding with incredibly detailed environments & vistas or crisp & colourful assets. They are further brought to life with great sound design & ambience and last but certainly not least an orchestral score befiting of the setting.

Music in symphonia is really good! I've always liked orchestral music from movies and obviously games but this game made me wanna see a live orchestra perform whatever, it doesn't even have to be from something i know. Just the sheer grandiosity of an orchestra is something i need to experience and this game gave me a wakeup call that i really need to do this before old age ruins my hearing hah! Regardless i gladly picked up a copy of the OST with my purchase and while all of that combined was pricey for only 5 and a half hours worth, i thoroughly enjoyed my time with symphonia. The game was a very polished experience both in terms of gameplay & presentation but also on a technical level. No frame drops, bugs or crashes and near instant loading/respawn times. 

The only minor issue with the game is a rather archaic level select that can be annoying if you're looking for 100% but not enough to detract from an otherwise incredible experience. The experience is great with the basic experience but if you wish to do all side rooms you'll even be rewarded with snippets of lore and lots of challenge modifiers. The lore won't really add up to a narrative masterpiece but the modifiers can get crazy, there's also a few sweet achievements related to speedrunning which add even more replayability if you're into that. If you're up to the challenge this is a bargain but even without I'll gladly recommend this game at full price, moreso at a discount and especially if you want to do all side content.

The limited time system really makes you have to plan carefully for each day which adds a really fun and addicting challenge to the game. I often found myself playing way longer than I meant to because I was motivated to get something done. 

Cons: There are some things that are a little difficult to figure out, which is possibly a pro if you like having to find stuff yourself. But also there are parts that give you a lot of info on what to do, so it's kind of a pro/con either way. 

Also, and this one is more for me, but I don't like games that just kind of assume you're a straight dude. There is enough customization options for me to feel like it's my character to make, but then all of the posters and art are scantily clad women. Upgrading one of the areas in your cell just increases the posters of scantily clad women on them. So, overall, fun game and do recommend, especially if the cons I listed aren't something you mind. [h3] Think of Rhapsody as a visual novel rather than a JRPG, It’s better this way. [/h3]

The battles, at least on the normal difficulty, are - there can be no other way to describe it - significantly broken in favor of the protagonist’s party. 

The team members gain EXP extremely quickly. It is not unlikely to raise a level 1 character five levels with a single victory. It may be justified by the fact that completing several side quests demands raising certain party members to their 30s or above. Nonetheless, it keeps the mains grossly overleveled for the remaining part of the adventure. 

[h3] Let me derail the current train of thought here for a while. [/h3]

Every major member of the party has a certain side quest that is completely optional. Rhapsody indicates it only at one place and in a rather indirect way, therefore it is not unlikely for some players to finish the game without even being aware that said quests existed in the first place. Nonetheless, the only reward for completing them is the game’s lore and maybe saving a life or two, so not a big deal, right? 

[h3] Now back to the original idea. [/h3]

The overpowered primary party. From the midpoint of the story on, my main tactic was to skip the Coronet’s (Rhapsody’s protagonist) turn, put the spellcaster in the middle of the battlefield and use the area-sweeper that instantly destroyed every enemy. Rince, repeat.  

Furthermore, the dungeons can be infuriating. First, they are all made up of the same, one-screen segments: an intersection, vertical and horizontal corridors and turns. While not unusual for a jRPG game, all the rooms use exactly the same template with only minor objects that differentiate one room from another. There are also teleporters and long, mazelike sequences of dungeons that can span across several levels and lead to an empty room with no reward at all. Later in the game, these same assets appear with an extremely lazy blue, yellow or red overlay put on top of them to indicate the location’s element.  To make matters worse, Rhapsody provides no map at all, making it exceptionally easy for the player to get lost, constantly pestered by annoying, meaningless battles with feeble enemies as the party struggles to find their way.

Speaking of which, the encounter RNG mechanism is a mystery, and a terribly inconsistent one at that. The party can easily travel through the entire dungeon floor without a single battle, or they can have two fights inside a single room, one just a few steps from the other. This manages to be annoying regardless of whether the player is scouting a new location or grinding those side-characters to meet their quest demands. 

Luckily, there is an extremely convenient item that instantly teleports the team to the world map, although some of the dungeons prevent the party from using it. 

On a much more positive note, the defeated enemies have a certain chance of joining up with the protagonist’s group. As far as I know, there are no dedicated capturing mechanics like in a traditional monster collector, so it remains entirely luck-based. Furthermore, the ‘core’ team is both unique and extensive enough to make the entire monster catching entirely optional. It is a welcome feature, nonetheless.

[h3] Now then, since we’re already somewhere halfway through my ramblings, let me take you all the way back to the beginning. [/h3]

The game starts with the protagonist, Coronet, trapped in the darkness running away from a monster chasing her. Just as it is about to capture her, the prince appears, kills the monster and saves her. Then, just as she is beginning to swoon, she gets bonked on the head and wakes up.

Could I ever ask for a more charming twist on the ‘JRPG hero waking up in her room at the beginning of the story’ trope? Don’t answer. It was rhetorical.  

This scene perfectly showcases Rhapsody’s wonderful charm and the sense of humor. 
I’d go as far as to say that it was the primary factor that kept me finishing the story despite all the annoyances encountered within. The writing in this game is marvelous. It is whimsical, light-hearted and also extremely heartwarming. Think of it as an entire season of Slayers! packed into one experience. It also successfully turns into something deeper, more solemn and meaningful for a moment or two.

[h3] Coronet is a wonderful person. [/h3]

The progress she makes from the time she needs to be saved from the dragon by the prince to when [spoiler] she slays dragons to save the prince [/spoiler] herself feels so natural I’ve only noticed after it had already happened. And, in contrast to the more contemporary narratives, it does not feel one bit preachy. 

Coronet is stubborn, innocent and extremely charming, and so much more than just a girl on her quest to get the prince. She changes, grows up and discovers one or two important truths about herself and the people surrounding her. Who, especially Etoile – Coronet’s lifetime friend and rival – are astonishingly fascinating individuals capable of displaying some unexpected but also very welcome depths of character when the time comes. 

[h3] The game’s art is exquisite. [/h3]

Rhapsody gives most of Square’s 2D games run for their money without breaking the sweat. The backgrounds, character designs, animations – everything is astonishingly stylish and crammed with wonderful little details to marvel at. Even the repetitive dungeons. The pixel art is top notch, especially with the optional CRT filter applied. The only stumbling block here is the fact that Rhapsody runs in the original PS1 proportions with no option of stretching it to fit the modern screens.

Ironically, for a ‘Musical Adventure’ the sound design is rather mediocre, and the English arrangements of the game’s songs are – at least in my opinion – atrocious.

[h3] Come for the feels. [/h3]

The game’s mechanics are far from perfect, and the tactical options during the battles are rather limited. Dungeons are unnecessarily labyrinthine and irritating too. Finally, Rhapsody’s story is far from being original. And yet, the tones, moods and the proportions in which they are evoked make this tale an emotional masterpiece. 

As always, do with this whatever and, as always

[h3] Try to have a wonderful life. [/h3]

Really fun and challenging physics based racer that reminds me a lot of Lonely Mountains: Downhill, and a bit of Trackmania. Its early access right now, but with the content it has could have been considered a full release i think.

There is 5 vehicles which all handle differently, iv'e still not made up my mind which is my favourite yet. I think the azimuth possibly is the best all rounder, but i always end up using the whirli a lot, as its awesome for jumps. There's 7 tracks i think, but two of those are restricted to the explorer mode for now, the others you can play in all modes. currently there is Trailblazer, freestyle and challenge mode.

I had tons of fun with the challenge mode, where you have to drive through the middle of huge rings that have been set up. This starts of fairly easy and then ramp up considerably with the harder difficulties. The challenges were all very well considered and unique that i always felt i was having to improve and learn new skills and techniques along the way while trying to progress through them. I really felt a sense of achievement beating the harder tracks, even tho my patience was tested on occasion, ha. I have not beaten them all yet, but there are well over a hundred of them. 

I also really enjoyed the Trailblazer mode. You can race your friends here or you can race against the clock and other players on the leaderboard (you can download player ghosts). Its a checkpoint style race across the map. The levels are really very big and have multiple routes to learn and sneaky track skips you can search out. like lonely mountains its physics based and you can find yourself crashing a lot on your way through the levels, having to restart at checkpoints often, especially if you take more daring lines like grinding a log surrounded by water. With each crash you restart the checkpoint with the time you had when you passed through it, which lets you experiment a lot with which lines might be quicker.

The last mode is Freestyle and its all about planning routes to fit in lots of tricks on boards, ramps, rails, and drops on the way to the checkpoints. I have not spent as much time on this mode as yet, was distracted enough with the other ones. The trick/stunt system is fairly decent, you get slides, spins, grinds and darkslides, pulling off tricks fills up your points meter, which is also your boost meter, so you have to manage that as while you are boosting you are also biting into your score you have been racking up at the same time. 

Its early access tho so i guess that means more content is planned, I'm not at the point i need new content but i wouldn't say no to new vehicles, modes or maps. 

Easy to recommend if you like games like Trials, Trackmania, Lonely Mountains and those types.

Fun gem of a game with humble beginnings on itch.io, [i]absolute[/i] steal for $2 on the summer sale, and I'd still say worth the full $11 price for what's there:
[list]
[*]Simple rally driving with boosting, jumping, and tricks (drifts, spins, grinds).
[*]Car can get wrecked if it impacts too fast: can sometimes be easy to pull a Redline and obliterate yourself into a wall with a bad drift, or botch an aerial/grind and fall to your death. For this reason, the game also has a car-reset key to place you on the track again.
[*]Logs/Rails/Edges can be grinded, however it doesn't snap you to the grind, so if you're not careful you can very easily fall/pop/spin off a rail.
[*]The soundtrack is decent, one or two meh songs, but several that groove hard.
[*]8 stages with 3 game modes: Track race, freestyle, challenges
[*]Track race is just as it sounds, race the level start to finish. Game currently has no looping tracks, they're all hand-made with a beginning and end.
[*]Freestyle is for most trick points thru the track, also earning time as you trick across checkpoints. A few maps are also "park styled", with no start/finish, just open space for tricking.
[*]Challenges ("Exploration") let's you free-roam a map, and from menu select hand-crafted challenges for the stage. These involve doing jumps, grinds, aerials, through rings which have physical collision with the car. The expert challenges are basically flagellation, only for the type of player who gets all gold medals in Pilot Wings 64, or all platinum times in Blast Corps.
[*]Modest selection of car types, with paint color schemes unlocked from challenges.
[*]Global leaderboards for game modes, race against the ghost of your personal best, or against anybody else's record on the leaderboards
[/list]

At just under 2 hours (with about 15 minutes of that getting briefly lost) Darxanadon is a somwhat flawed but charming  metroidvania, who's strengths primarily lie in the overall aesthetic, visual world/ boss design, and the classic thrill of finding gear in the far reaches of some poison cave, or far flung castle. 

The most appealing thing here, for me, was that barring a few moments where you very clearly should -not- be traversing an area without a specific upgrade (the poison cave leaching your HP if entered with no preparation comes to mind) you are able to tackle the game in a relatively free-form sequence. I found myself fighting what I -assume- was a later-game enemy relatively early on, earning what seems to be the best sword before some of the similarly powerful armour, and -any- of the magic spells. 

I even found a magic candle late in the game, never finding a use for it after having already struggled my way through a dark cavern I think it was intended for. 
There's something really cool about that. 

Don't go in expecting a complex combat system, or an in-depth story/ loads of hidden secrets, and If you have fond memories of NES/ 80s-era fantasy adventure PC games I think there's a good chance you'll find something to enjoy here.

I was pretty underwhelmed at first, bounced off, took a break, came back, bounced off, took a break, came back one last time, and it clicked. im not sure if thats a mark against the game or just my mindset at the time. 

Regardless this both does and doesnt feel like a successor to Hyper Light Drifter. HLD is a better *game*, the combat is better, and the gameplay is a little tighter. Solar Ash on the other game NAILS the movement, the exploration is also much better (but that might come down to my brain just having better 3d navigation than isometric) and the story is actually really good and fairly resonant if youre willing to go and look for it (doing all the npc side quests). Both games excel in the art department, and aesthetically they match very well. 

my only complaints are that the combat was very shallow (although some enemies had some novelty to them) and sometimes its hard to figure out where you are in the world (a proper in-game map would have been appreciated). otherwise the game is very solid! I can definitely recommend this to anyone who is looking for a 3d platform exploration game that has a little combat.

Much like Hyper Light Drifter (HLD) which is a top down action puzzle platformer, Solar Ash gets it's kicks from exploration, puzzles and some basic combat. The view is switched up to third person this time and most of the game is about quick traversal. Much like HLD, Solar Ash has a unique story and characters that are interesting and exciting. The game can be completed with relative ease which is a change from HLD which challenges reach the extreme. The game does have a higher difficulty but is still relatively laid back by comparison. The art style fits the universe that Heart Machine has created and is colourful and vibrant but also grim in places and stands out on it's own. I got relatively 9 and a half hours out of the game without playing through Hardcore and beating the the timed achievement. I whole heartedly recommend Solar Ash, the price point is a bit higher for the time to $ ratio so I would recommend picking it up in a sale instead.
