[h1]Review written after clearing almost half of the puzzles and achievements.[/h1]
[h3]I'm also a twisty puzzle fanatic, who was driven to get this game![/h3]

[i]Before I go into detail about this game, I will say that at least one of the puzzles are bugged. Specifically, I "solved" the Windmill Cube halfway through making progress, and it may or may not be the only shapeshifting puzzle that suffers from bug.[/i]

Who Shuffled My Shapes? is basically a PC game in the vein of everyone's favorite (or least favorite) childhood toy, the Rubik's Cube. It was made by the same devs behind the famous (and free to play) Coloring Pixels game, which I spent countless hours on for my casual playtime. I found out about this game through Coloring Pixels via its "bonus" book, looked into it, and figured it was up my alley since I love Rubik's Cubing. Not only does it feature the structure and functionality of said puzzle, but in total, there are twenty puzzles based on it of different shapes and sizes - Many of which are based on real, physical puzzles you can buy in a store.

When you start a puzzle, it automatically shuffles itself. Drag a side like you would an actual Rubik's Cube to move around its pieces, and attempt to solve it. There is an undo button which I think is very helpful in case I mess up a move combo, or algorithm, to solve a specific part of the puzzle. There is also an in-game timer, which I think is not TOO helpful, but goes by how quick you can solve it through the game itself (Occasionally, I can solve a physical Rubik's Cube in about a minute).

Though, be warned that getting all of the achievements may require you to solve every puzzle in the game. And you WILL need to learn how to solve the Rubik's Cube, as well as its easier and of course harder variations of it. You will need to look online for a good solution, especially on YouTube. But hopefully you can learn plenty from the Rubik's Cube when going through this completionist route. Speaking of which, while I'm learning how to solve the cube in the most optimal way, I had the idea of doing it on this game, especially when there is an undo feature present in case I screw up or want to analyse certain moves I make on it.

However, the game suffers from a few inconvenient flaws. As I said above, the Windmill Cube is bugged while I tried solving it - It eventually registered as a solved state. I hope the devs one day put some heart in this game more and fix this bug. Another slight problem (and not as harsh as the first one), is trying to move sides on some puzzles, especially the mirror puzzles. The clickboxes are precise and don't seem to hit the side I want to turn (just attempts to turn the an adjacent side it thinks I'm clicking on and sliding). Might be an issue trying to speedrun these puzzles if I may.

This is a simple game copying the puzzles of the Rubik's Cube category, and would be an excellent quickie if it weren't for the bugs I mentioned above. But still, I fairly like the state of this game right now and will try playing some more should I not get driven away from my nitpicking.

Dave's an interesting little game for the loot goblins of the world. I would describe it as plate spinning the game. It has two distinct play types depending on if you're in the water or out of the water. It isn’t a game I would say is for everyone, gameplay is not exactly difficult if you have a little bit of patience I would say as I only died once (outside of scripted battles).

Music and SFX are good with a few unexpected tracks you can get near the end. The gameplay loop is… fine, nothing I would write home about but the game slowly layers new things to do until you have about 4 or 5 layers, then starts removing most of the necessity from previous layers. It is a little strange that only the top layers of the diving area have different layouts and everything else is static but it didn’t really detract from the overall experience.

As mentioned it’s a bit of a loot goblin, collectathon type game where the overall goals of the game tend to be 'collect all the things whether it be 3-star fish, rare weekend catches, weapons or [spoiler]farm[/spoiler] upgrades. I found it a little exhausting after the third set to have yet another thing and another thing added to the list of collectables.

But they're all optional so you can engage or ignore them as much as you want. The meal enhancement system is also kinda weird. Since you're regularly gaining access to new recipes with a better baseline value, is rarely worth going above level 3 or 4. It’s a weird calculation of trying to figure out how many meals would you have to sell of this $340 item to make up the cost of sacrificing 50+ of that item to enhance future sales by $80 (hint: over 200 more in this case). 

Additionally either it wasn’t clear and I missed it or it wasn’t said but the one thing I had to look up online was [spoiler]why my level 20 branch manager couldn’t use all the ingredients. Apparently it's based on the manager's cooking skill value which didn’t make intuitive sense since the manager isn’t the one cooking anyway.[/spoiler] Once I looked it up, everything was golden though.

Regardless, played it for 60 hours well past the 'ending' and enjoyed the vast majority of it. Well worth the investment if its something that looks like its in your wheelhouse.

9/10 game for the first 10ish hours. Then it drops off.

For the opening hours, the pixel animations, humor, diving and sushi gameplay are great! 

But once you reach the [spoiler]sea people[/spoiler] you get flooded with fetch quests, chores, grinds, and notifications. At this point it's perfectly fine to:

A) Quit, or

B) Ignore a lot of the content. Most of it isn't even needed for achievements.

E.g. You can ignore:
- notifications on your phone
- eco watcher quests
- [spoiler]the farm (except the story crops)
- the sea people quest board
- the sea people minigames (except for earning trust for the main quest)[/spoiler]
- all of the dialogue at this point. Especially if Dave is alone, as he'll just be stating things you can see, e.g. "The stakes started moving. I must avoid them."

Be prepared to be frequently forced to arbitarily end your runs early in order to progress the story, and expect to run into a lot of things that you can't interact with until the game lets you. E.g. The urchins, bubbling rocks, and seahorses.

And be prepared that some things you would expect to be able to interact with, you can't. E.g. Even bombs won't let you kill crabs, or break wood.

Also be prepared that combat will start to feel samey. All big enemies can be beaten by [spoiler]"dodge, shoot as it moves past"[/spoiler]. Though bosses change this up.

Some quality of life improvements would be appreciated like:
- making the [spoiler]Sea People[/spoiler] Necklace a permanent (non-charm) effect
- reducing the need to swap weapons for mining
- adding a way to enhance dishes faster, like an "enhance all" button
- adding a way to send all fish at once from [spoiler]the fishery, to save interacting with 7 nets[/spoiler]

This game would feel amazing if it cut down the arbitrary gating, and reworked some of the mechanics that feel like chores (maybe to optional post-story content?), so that it was streamlined 10-20 hour experience.

This is my second time finishing this (first time being the DS version and also dabbling in the untold version), but i am reminded why i like this style of Dungeon Crawler. Unlike Wizardry-like games that is hard wired into RNG everything (from equipment drops, to stat increases, with even chances at your map being destroyed and perma death), the mechanics of the EO games is more absolute (stats are clearly displayed, boosts are shown, there is no hidden mechanics, gear is unlocked in the shop through selling monster drops monster drops, and the classes are simple to understand). 

All in all it's quite new player friendly despite being very hard in the beginning and towards the end of the game, going into the post game. All you have to do is just explore and make your way down, very simple but fun concept.

The map controls moving over to pc takes a little getting used to but they somehow made drawing on the map relatively painless either through the right stick on your controller + triggers to select things, or preferably just simply using the touch screen on the steam deck or mouse to draw since they worked in kb and mouse controls. Exploration and drawing out maps just becomes fun to do (6th stratum not withstanding since that's the obligatory bullshit map selection that every dungeon crawler has at least one of).

Combat-wise.... since its the first game you can maybe tell the balance a little wonky and they they did not quite get it right until the 3rd game. This one heavily relies on defensive buffs to get through the latter half in the game to the point where its near impossible to fight the super bosses without a tank (though possible with some timing and rng jank) and completely impossible to beat the 6th sanctum boss.

Progression-wise there is some growing pains to start which is as expected when you are going into it with a lvl 1 party and no real skills to your unit's name. Without going through spoilers, the difficulty of the first boss is actually quite interesting since you have to kill it fast or else get swarmed. Which is a mechanic you don't see much in other EOs until much later sanctums. After that one part though you'll find that progression becomes much easier as you start to unlock more hard hitting skills, and just going into encounters blind becomes easier from the 2nd sanctum going forward, to the point where you can just fight the FOEs as you come across them.

Difficulty is as you'd expect from a dungeon crawler though a QoL feature added, was the ability change the difficulty whenever you want outside of the dungeon between: 

- Expert - The OG EO1 difficulty. I wouldn't call this difficulty fun since it forces you to over-grind and be more party specific to survive, but if you want the OG experience (or just to beat your head at the wall to get the final achievement) then have at er. 

- Basic - It's hard but not overly so. Highly recommend playing it on this setting since it gives you the feel of the OG EO1, but won't punish you if you aren't running a Medic/Tank through most of the game.

- Picnic - Makes everything die in a couple of hits. I don't recommend progressing on this difficulty since imo it takes away the fun of the game. It is excellent however when you need to level up units since you get an exp boost, or for runs through the dungeon with a collection squad that you no longer need to keep pace with your main team to not die in the later stratum.

All in all, play how you want and have fun with it, i know i did.

I spent a couple of hours playing this game, got up to the 11th wave before being defeated: I don't think what I saw hugely merits a re-play, but it might do if more updates come later, and I've definitely found worse uses of two quid in my time. This is essentially a tower defence style RTS: you build up a base, and troops, and steadily larger waves of enemies come at you until you're defeated. The theme is (with exceptions) sci-fi, and the enemies are very much grub/swarm style aliens though your own forces include a lot of alien/demihuman/robot creatures (and an utterly bizarre array of 'heroes'). Between waves you can upgrade units, and also you should take forces out to "hunt" the docile versions of the swarm enemies, which cover the rest of the map. This, and minerals, are your two important resources: you get additional troops randomly dropped at the end of each wave, but can make some droids of your own as well.

The good parts of the game are mostly in the technical competency. The game handles its RTS-style build very smoothly, few major movement complaints (once or twice a unit got left behind when I moved a group), and the balance and buildup felt reasonable. The graphics were likewise smooth, and mechanically it was fine. So the basic structure was well executed. There were elements of the look that could be improved – the fonts are at times very boring, and the button to buy a hero is not in English (not sure what language the script actually is).

I think there were two or three big areas that could have pushed this from "this is fine" to "I'm actually invested in this game" for me, and they're connected by the theme of worldbuilding. Firstly, physically, the map is a featureless grey plain with your base in the bottom corner, and the developers clearly have the necessary skills to find some assets on the unity store, possibly add some elevations or impassable areas, and just make it something other than a flat grey square to wander around, and things might feel a lot more interesting. Given that you have to micromanage the hunting parties between waves, making it a bit more interesting is pretty important.

Second, and also not technically complex: the single biggest failure of the game is in the narrative design, which is to say that there isn’t any narrative design. And it looks like it has the capacity for one, too – you’ve got various humans and demihumans dropping on a space colony that’s manned by robots and being attacked by bugs, but why? What for? Is this planet strategically important, are there citizens you need to protect? Are you as the player representing the military, or a company, or the galactic government? Do we know anything about these aliens that we can apparently extract resources from but also are swarming to kill us? It would take very little effort to add a few descriptions that get across the feeling that the scenario is interesting and quirky rather than arbitrary. This is doubled down on with the heroes. What’s up with the heroes (other than that they’re probably all pre-purchased assets bundled into this on that basis)? Why am I in a sci-fi game but can hire a knight or a vampires or a pirate? Who ARE these people? I don’t say this to say it’s bad that there is this bizarre array of heroes, but if they’re going to be there then they should be individually named and get some little biographies or something which would again turn it from “this is bizarre” to “this is a fun mash-up setting”. I do get that English might not be the devs’ first language, but honestly this would make a world of difference.

Third, and finally, as a bigger set of thoughts: this game is built like an RTS, and I can't help feeling that to really improve it should have the courage of its convictions and become something more like one. If the game set a win condition for the game so players have something to build towards, and utilise a more detailed map by making resource gathering more interesting (wider array of enemy huntable monsters, limited gatherers per mine and not having them all at base), then it could be quite a fun RTS. Most of the technical groundwork needed to do this is already in the game, and it could go from feeling just about worth two quid to something easily worth double that with a bit of depth added even with very few mechanical changes.

Anyhow: if you want a competently built but narratively kind of a void RTS-tower-defence to spend an hour or three on and do a couple of runs of, this will provide you with about that amount of entertainment. It does have the technical execution level of something rather better, and I hope the devs look at improving or building on it.

This is a great game for listening to podcasts. Top-down tank combat with rogue-lite elements is a great idea, especially when it involves hot-swapping tank turrets on different hulls. The anime girls act as the crew--each favoring different playstyles like high explosive rockets, smaller caliber magazine weapons, armor piercing weapons, or a mobility focused ramming playstyle. There's no such mechanic. Also, I haven't played the demo but it features a line of sight system. What is in the game now is just a flat circle of visibility with you being able to see everything inside it. I get it's an arcade-y rogue-lite top-down shooter but having it as an option you can either enable or disable would go a long way towards pleasing both audiences.

In the end this game is a barrel of fun that is easily worth twice its asking price. I'm definitely trying to find more games like this, if anyone has recommendations please let me know.

This is another fantastic mystery/light puzzle narrative adventure from one of the best in the business. It's a crying shame that these games haven't gotten more attention, as they are amazingly well-crafted and do a superb job of supplying authentic "slice of life" narratives and characters within a very clever puzzle framework that seems clearly inspired by Return of the Obra Dinn.

You spend most of your time just perusing through the materials provided in each chapter, with the goal of identifying the exact dates of the various journals. It's probably best to think of yourself as a research assistant that needs to supply an accurate chronology from a wide variety of disparate raw materials. These include everything from fully professionally composed songs, to voice-acted radio and television interviews, to letters and other forms of written materials.

Through these items, you get a fantastic sense of the characters and culture involved and develop an investment in not only the main characters, but the supporting players involved at various stages of their lives and careers. You're also expected to do a bit of external searching to solve the game's clever puzzles to arrive at the correct dates. Players of Sheinman's previous games might find it a bit more difficult because you have to input the full dates yourself (there are no "multiple choice" elimination games here.) However, I found that the puzzles are designed in a way that greatly reduces the need to brute force solutions, although I will admit there were a couple journals that I did need to do a bit of guesswork on, but it's usually easy enough to eliminate a significant range of dates and reduce the number of attempts that are made.

For anyone who has any interest in detective stories, the Pop Culture of the '90s, or just plain well-crafted worlds, I cannot recommend Riley and Rochelle highly enough. And give the other games in this "series" a try too: Rivals and Conspiracy! are both available on Steam and well worth the purchase price as well.

A mystery box of 22 indie games ranging from 5 minutes to about 1 hour in length - most of them have a narrative twist or a unique take on the gameplay deconstruction. Almost every game here has a theme of self-discovery, introspection, or self-reflection, even when the game is not a visual novel (most of them are), there is generally a story being told as you play. You don't get to choose the order in which you discover the games, but you can skip them once you see the title artwork. With that in mind, the game hub gives you a reading with the tarot deck, in my example, I believe it says "you will play all the bad games first".

I guess you could say most of these have a feel of a student project, but I would argue that some of them come from very talented individuals that were pushing their creative limits - perhaps 8 games or so, very thought-provoking, very immersive experiences. Ironically, I do recognize some of my favorite developers here who made more substantial games, but this package does not have their best work, perhaps something they made prior to getting all that dev experience. But I guess it's all part of the journey, most devs don't make high art on a first try, what I see here are a lot of great ideas, that are not fully realized, in some cases. 

Now, $25 for these, I don't regret paying for it, but I am not going to go detective mode and count how many of these can be found on the internet for nothing, it's not very relevant to me, I support small games when they deserve it anyway. Even with some awful and potentially broken games here, I think the good half pulls it together, granted these are very small experiences, something you generally would not pay more than $1 to 5 per game individually, so it's very much a package for indie rats like myself that see every brick as a yellow block of cheese. I assume all of the hub art is original to the actual package, given the art style, so if nothing else, it's a nice presentation, like a big gift of mystery indie games, you just don't know what you going to get, maybe it will be unique, maybe it will be very compelling, or just absolutely awful and unplayable. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) While nearly half of these games are probably not even worth my time, the better half really sold it on the heartwarming and creative adventures. Individually they are nothing too special, just some really sweet games here and there, nothing huge, just something to kill a few hours, with a few compelling themes.

(+) I did enjoy the hub presentation with the cards, like opening a gift on xmas, I guess I just like opening loot boxes.... ummm, that came out wrong, I just like that feeling of not knowing where the game will take me, and you just don't see as much of it unless you dig in the darkest corners of indie gaming. 

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Nitpicks[/u] - a few of these games have strange interactions or maybe bugs (hard to tell), but it's unclear how to advance. Also, I wish you had achievements for finishing games as well.

[b] Overall Thoughts (as a whole package): 7/10 [/b]

I actually love buying game packs specifically with a single hub, it kinda reminds me of when we would get demos on the CDs, I just like that feeling of discovery, otherwise, I would never try some of these games. I would say maybe 60% of the games were relevant to me, most of them are very simple, but some have very compelling stories. Not sure about $25, if you love small indie games, you probably will find something you like, maybe get it on sale, whatever feels more comfortable.

Cartomancy Anthology is a beautiful compilation of 22 games connected to each of the Major Arcana cards and allows for further continued use in single card or past, present, future three card pulls. Overall, the deck is very inclusive (lots of LGBTQA+ and pronoun affirming narratives) and beautiful for daily mindfulness and self-reflection. Overall: 4.5/10

Individual game ratings:
The Fool: The Fool is about opportunity, potential, and new beginnings which didn't feel as though it was translated well into the game. Overall the storyline and changing allegiance felt altogether unimportant and uninteresting (though the dog, Soliloquy, somewhat made up for it.) 3.5/10

The Magician: This is one of the more beautiful games with a genuinely beautiful narrative as well, while short that really pulls from the meaning of the card even though it is primarily visual. 5.5/10

The High Priestess: This game contains many dot based puzzles that you must complete in order to perform tarot readings for the people of the town before making your way to the High Priestess. While the writing wasn't particularly engaging and felt somewhat unmemorable, the puzzles were challenging, and the game played on the traditional intuition meaning of the card. 4.5/10

The Emperor: One of my favorite games in the collection both in managing to encompass the meaning behind the Emperor card and in the artistry and gameplay, I really enjoyed exploring the world after awakening from my reality in order to serve a dish based off of a combination of emotions themed around each of the day's meditation poems to this powerful divine masculine energy to determine whether or not I would be worthy of being sent back to my reality. 6/10

The Empress: This is a straightforward, yet somewhat challenging puzzle game using gardening to grow and weed out flowers. Overall, the card represents birth, nurturing, and maternal femininity. While the game showcased this through growing sunflowers, the main storyline was one of manipulation and collecting glass shards which didn't tie in with the theme. 4/10

The Hierophant: This game really didn't have much at all to do with the prompt tarot card signifying religion, learning, teaching, and collective groups. This is one of the more lackluster games of Angela He's and feels like it was just pulled from something she was already working on rather than inspired specifically for this anthology. 4/10

The Lovers: I really appreciate the emphasis on self-love and shadow work with this card rather than using others to dance through life and fill an internal void. 5/10

The Chariot: The Chariot game was one of the longer games that, again, was really more visual than anything as you move past obstacles that slightly slow you down if you hit them and collect other objects (fossils and gemstones) that are seemingly meaningless at the end as you ride off on a path in your chariot towards an impending storm. 4/10

Strength: This game is about getting annoying letters in your inbox and taking our your frustration on them by punching them. This short temper is actually the opposite of what the strength card represents: strong will. Also, the actions for punching for each of the hands is a bit delayed and overall not consistently receptive which makes it nearly unplayable. 2/10

The Hermit: This card is all about self-reflection and internal work, so it's fitting that the game takes you through the main character's memories linked by photographs. The message is very clever and beautiful despite the execution being somewhat juvenile. 4.5/10

The Wheel of Fortune: The Wheel of Fortune card traditionally asks that you remain optimistic and have faith in the universe, destiny, and luck to take care of situations in the best way possible to allow you to be on your most abundant path. I really appreciated the use of various semi-luck related (a combination of random weather, time of day, use of lure, and a timed skill bar for rarity) varieties of fish waiting to be caught, cataloged, and given to the town grandma to help her and those in need. A really genuinely charming game while a lot of spirit. 6/10

Justice: While this is one of the more mature storylines that clearly follows the theme of the card, the musical mechanics when acting as an all-seeing oracle seeking truth are very finicky and it overall felt very draining completing the story. 4/10

The Hanged Man: While the tarot card is traditionally about sacrifice and feeling stuck in a situation and the need for patience, this game takes that to a whole other level by often requiring you, the cashier, to sacrifice some of your own organs when you can't guess what combination of items the customer wants in order to make quota for the day and guarantee customer satisfaction, because, after all, the customer is always right. 5.5/10

Death: While I can appreciate the message about change and letting go that heavily relates to the theme of this card, the monochrome visuals and ability to only move forward being the entirety of the "game" made it more of a visual meta-experience than anything. 4/10

Temperance: The card of temperance is about finding balance and moderation and is a card of peace and patience. Fittingly, the game involves making potions that you have to balance with the right ingredients in order to acquire ingredients for yourself to make a potion that will create a lasting legacy. The concept, gameplay, and pettable capybara making this a really cute game to play. 5/10

The Devil: This game is also really more of a visual novel that doesn't really have much to do with the tarot card which is all about control, limitations, restrictions, and the shadow self. In fact, the game doesn't really have much if anything to say at all. 2/10

The Tower: This game is more of a horror based short story explaining the inevitable fall of the tower and destruction, change, and chaos encompassed in the Tower card. 3/10

The Star: The Star is a card of renewed hope and faith and a sign of blessings. The game, on the other hand, is less hope and faith filled, and more about the journey of shapes and water and their desire to be understood hidden amongst lengthy text that tries too hard to be profound and philosophical and just ends up being pretentious. 3/10

The Moon: This game reminds me a lot of Arise: A Simple Story in terms of the water manipulation and glowing orb collection elements that help give the ebb and flow of the tide in relation to the moon rather than focusing on the misunderstanding, illusion, deception, intuition, imagination, and spiritual elements of the card. Overall, it's a relaxing puzzle game. 4.5/10

The Sun: This is a cute little game where you play as a little sun with sun rays for lives as you jump around different islands following the beat to help shoot away all of the dark infected inhabitants. This card is traditionally one of positivity, optimism, freedom, and fun and the game does exude that. While there's no really story and the controls aren't the most responsive, the game is cute and one of the more visually pleasing games in the collection. 4.5/10

Judgment:  Taking a cool twist on what the Judgment card is supposed to mean, you play as Rhad who has been transformed into a scarecrow awaiting judgment in the Garden after dying and must judge others while he waits to find out his fate. Overall it's a really wholesome game that plays a lot like Death and Taxes, but with the ability to have more intimate conversations with the fruits and vegetables you might plant in the garden before making your decision. This card is all about new beginnings, choices, redemption, and renewal so the narrative feels very fitting. 6.5/10

The World: This final card is one of completion, but ultimately the game is draining to complete and many of the mechanics  special effects simply don't appear to work. You play Eon who was split into 4 animals each with different skills. 2.5/10

I have been very excited for this collection and so far the games are very fun! One major issue im running into is weird vsync stutter on moving objects on screen, so far the fix is to disable full screen optimizations but this has only worked on the main client excluding individual games that so far all seem to have similar issues.

So I never leave reviews but this project really deserves some love! I don't remember how I found this game or why I bought it (I'm not even that into tarot!), but I have no regrets because it's probably the coolest thing I've ever purchased on Steam. If you're someone who appreciates game design as an artform and the experimentation that indie games allow for, then this shouldn't be overlooked. 

These games are meant to be experiential rather than gameplay-heavy. Every one of these bite-sized experiences won't be for everybody (there were certainly a few I put down early because I didn't enjoy their genre), but every one of them will make you think. I was also under the impression from some of the other reviews that this would be far buggier than it was; really, there was only one game in the whole bunch that was buggy to the point of being unplayable. 

Special shoutouts to my top five games, in no particular order: The Emperor, The Empress, The Hierophant, The Hanged Man, and The Magician.

After trying out all the cards, here's a list of some notable games without spoilers (treat it as some kind of personal ranking):


[b] S tier: [/b]

Empress - overall great puzzle game, level difficulty is just right, concise story and to my surprise there's also voiced lines

Fortune - this fishing game is just adorable to its core, also it's made by only one person, it's really impressive, I just wish that my luck wasn't so bad that it took me so many tries just to get the correct weather I wanted

High Priestess - cute art and story, the puzzles are quite challenging and I appreciate that there's an optional easy mode, do also note that you need a mouse to play the game

Emperor - I'm probably biased because I love cooking games, but I still think it's great because even though the game is short, the story and message are still solid, and definitely need some thinking to interpret what the emperor desires

Hanged Man - I just find the concept of this really interesting, you have to combine ingredients to make an item for each customer, which then you also have to interpret each customers' demands carefully as they are not the most direct orders, probably one of the games where I really cracked my brain juice hard thinking what the customers actually want, I don't know yet if there's any "true endings" to this game though, as the game just loops you back to Day 1 at the end


[b] A tier: [/b]

Judgement - one of the visual novel-ish games that took me the longest to clear since there's a lot of dialogue, the (main) characters writing are genuinely great, but there are some bugs in the game (not major, thankfully), and I felt that the ending was too abrupt

Temperance - charming potion brewing game (also there's a capybara!!), although it took me a while to realize how the gameplay actually works

Lovers - it's like a dancing dating simulator, you do get to dance with everyone and then make your final (and only) choice at the very end, so it honestly doesn't feel as if there's any consequences if you flopped, but I still enjoy it overall, the characters are charming


[b] "Crying because it looks great, but unplayable" tier: [/b]

Sun - this is a personal reason... I'm terrible with platforms, especially in 3D. I know it's not even a platform game, it's a fun and cute shooting game... but I barely got passed the beginning area just because I couldn't make certain jumps. The art looks super cute though. Maybe because I don't have the right setup, I'll try again when I have the time. 

World - genuinely, the concept of the game sounds so interesting, it's a visual novel game where you can change your character's personality based on different scenarios and see how it changes the stories. Problem is that the core mechanic (changing personas) just simply doesn't work.


Overall great anthology that I would recommend experiencing, 7.5/10

Amazin' George 2 is a fairly standard JRPG but the things it does well are all excellent and the things it fumbles on are minor and easy to overlook.

Story:
The story follows old school JRPG conventions where there is a simple starting goal (in this case find your master) that takes a while to solve, and then there is a twist that sets up the final portion of the game. The dialogue is told through poetry and it lends a lighthearted feel to the story. This is nice for a change as too many rpgs have high stakes serious storytelling.

Gameplay:
The gameplay is fairly standard. You move around local maps with visible enemies you have to fight (I think they are limited and don't respawn which is nice), and you move around an overworld map featuring all of these locations where you get RNG fights similar to Final Fantasy or Dragon Quest. The combat system is turn based featuring abilities, items, guarding, attacking, and fleeing. A nice quality of life feature is that fleeing works 100% of the time so you aren't stuck in battles you don't want to fight. Each local map has treats which are the game's currency scattered around so you get to collect them as you clear the area of enemies. This actually helps the level design as it is fairly fun to collect it all (even though most of your currency is still gained from turn based combat). Throughout the course of the game you end up with four party members, but for the majority of the game you will be controlling two characters. This all works and the game feels fun.

Graphics and Sound:
The graphics remind me of the PS1 era of games and it seems to be heavily inspired by Final Fantasy. For an indie game these are surprisingly well done. The textures have enough detail and the art design has made each area feel distinct. The soundtrack feels very warm and bubbly. As I said in the story section this game feels very lighthearted and the music really lends to this feeling. Nothing feels better than a catchy tune after you win a turn based battle and this game has a pretty decent one.

Bugs:
As of the time I am posting this review (2/15/2022) there are a few bugs still in the game. One of them is a chest that gives you nothing when you open it and Japanese characters appear in the popup text box. Another is well known where one of the party characters will become more and more offset each round of combat (this doesn't prevent anything and is just visual) which is funny when he gets so far offscreen in a boss fight that he may as well have went to the Moon. There is also some text that seems to reference unused mechanics like the ability to use fireworks under effects in the menu and something about changing a map to dark theme or something of this nature and neither actually exist ingame that I could find. Also it seems that I cannot get the starting the game achievement so perhaps that broke sometime between version updates. With that said there are no game breaking bugs or anything that would ruin your enjoyment of the game. 99% of amazin' George 2 is very well polished in that respect.

Value:
I was able to get around 3-6 hours or so of playtime for $5.99 at the time of writing as my out of game time is a little bit higher than my playthrough actually was ingame. I would say this is pretty fair value for the price you pay and the experience is enjoyable enough especially if you like JRPGs already. While it is already worth it, a content update adding another hour or so of playtime would be very welcomed. It is good to support indie developers and the creator of this game definitely made this out of passion for the genre.

Overall:
Amazin' George 2 is a fun lighthearted romp through a classic JRPG style story with all the twist and turns and gameplay that genre entails. Well polished with appealing graphics and music, and 3-6 hours of solid gameplay this is an easy sell to anyone interested and reading this review already. Especially so if this game is on a sale as $5.99 is more than fair. Definitely check this one out!

You farm resources and go craft higher level gear.

Repeat for ever.

If you die, you make a new character and lose your equipment but keep your inventory.
You die a lot. Get used to crafting yourself new gear. Always dismantle your highest found level equipment.

I dropped Lost Ark for this... 

You probably wonder why I made this statement. Well World Seed has all the things you would probably enjoy in all those f2p/mobile "mmo" games. Character progression to infinity, builds, random (kinda) gear drops. Some exploration. Co-op dungeons/bosses. But it actually is free to play on the web version, and it does not gate you with stamina refreshes, pay to get more powerfull gear/characters etc. You can play as much as you want, whenever you want.

You start from the center of the map, get some gear drops to increase your item level. Then you go out to the higher level areas, get higher level gear, and repeat. It is grindy. You will not reach the crazy hundrends of thousands dmg/item-level fast. And I must admit it might get repetive. Not sure, I still have lots of fun on my fourth area. Combat is automatic, your character(s) trade blows with the enemie(s) untill someone retreates or dies. There are some elemental effects you can have on your gear, but it is simple. Better numbers result in victory. If you die you lose your character, and whatever he is wearing. And start with a new one of your choice again. It is not that bad, early game at least, because you can get some materials and craft the gear pretty fast again. Unlesss you had some mats laying arround in your bank (you probably have). There are no character levels, everything is about gear. There are coop dungeons for special loot also, but you will probably spent most of the time exploring and grinding gear. 

This is all I have experienced so far, and allready loving the game. It will be my chill farming, rpg game. And it can be totally free if you want to, I chose to purchase it on steam to support the dev. Personally got tired of the time gating mechanics of the f2p model games, and their shenanigans to get me hooked. This game fits like a glove on that place of my steam library. And will gladly spent money on it again, as long as I play it.

Really looking forward to see where the development of World Seed will get it.

This was a nice wholesome experience and a perfect break between other major visual novels. The game is about 3 hours long and has a very cozy and relaxing Christmas atmosphere. It's mostly slice of life and romance. There are some moments of drama in here but it's relatively minor and resolved pretty quickly every time. There are no choices, but I would have liked separate routes for the two heroines. 

The visuals are the highlight of this VN, the quality on display here is way better than what I typically see for indie non-Japanese VNs. The backgrounds in particular are really good and some of them are gorgeous enough to be in top-tier Japanese VNs. The main characters' sprites are all well-animated, which is even more striking to see in an indie VN. The Russian voice acting is decent enough and the music fits the atmosphere.

There are some issues with the game, however. The translation is rather mediocre, with occasional grammar errors and janky sentences, plus a few typos. A few times it was a bit hard to figure out what was happening. Overall, it's readable enough if you're willing to overlook these problems, since the story isn't too complex. There's also a calendar in the game that's displayed occasionally, but it displays the wrong month (January instead of December) and conflicts with the text. 

The ending was rather abrupt and I almost expected an epilogue. The game also just froze on the final image, and even after the credits were mentioned and the final song was played, it doesn't send you back to the title screen automatically. There are also a number of technical shortcomings. This was built on a custom engine instead of Renpy or one of the other established engines, so it's missing a bunch of important features that I'm very accustomed to in VNs. The options menu is very barebones here. These are some of the missing features:

1. There's no gallery to view the CGs after you finish the VN.
2. There's no "Do not cut voice after clicking" option like most other VNs. So if you move from a voiced line to a non-voiced one, the voice gets cut off immediately instead of continuing to play.
3. There's no backlog to view previous text.
4. There no voice replay button to repeat the current voice.
5. There's only one save slot. This combined with the previous issues mean that it's really annoying to view any previous text that you may have accidentally clicked through, or a voice that you want to hear again, since you only have one previous save to rely on.
6. There are no options to adjust text speed or transparency, so you're stuck with the default speed.

Final conclusion: The excellent visuals, voice acting and the cozy Christmas atmosphere are the main draws of this VN. However, the translation could be improved quite a bit, and there a number of essential technical features that are missing here which hampers the experience.

Castillo: Shattered Mirrors is an awesome mix of a Retro FPS, voxel based graphics, and a level progression reminiscent of Super Mario 64. You have a small hub world where you enter various portals around the the hub, looking to collect shards needed for progression. And progression works great, I love the system they have and feel more games should include it. Gameplay wise the game works well. I feel this is a good point to mention I had 2 very different experiences while playing this game. First day I streamed it we encountered numerous bugs, lots of audio issues, strange bullet trajectory problems, and multiple hitbox issues with enemies. Turns out the Dev was watching the stream, and overnight, fixed almost every issue we encountered. That to me, is absolutely amazing and is so rare to see in game releases. Major kudos for that. Second day was a much more enjoyable experience, and the game, while simple, was just plain fun. Not to mention it has one of the best soundtracks I've heard recently, from metal to synthwave, everything is catchy and enjoyable. 

The graphics might not be for everyone, but I found them a nice change of pace and worked well for the aesthetic the Dev was going for. The one issue I had with this game, was its cost vs length. The game took just under 4 hours to beat (despite being told I missed a couple secret levels, but I can't imagine they add too much to overall game time) So $10 seems like a heavy ask when a lot of similar Retro shooters are priced $2-$5 for more content. However, I did receive a message from the Dev letting me know all his plans for the game in terms of free DLC, and I'm not sure if they want to disclose all of it, but there is a lot, which would more than double the game time. I feel once all that is included, it will absolutely be worth the cost. The game also includes a level editor which can add endless replayability if the community is strong. Also includes a separate demo mode called Flashback. and I LOVED this mode, everything is much faster paced and played more akin to Doom, despite the experience only lasting about 10min. I will say, the entire campaign IS planned to be able to be played with this mode, which is awesome and something to look forward to. 

Overall, I can't help but feel like this should have been an Early Access release for half the price, and maybe increase it once all the planned content has been released. That being said, I still have no issue recommending it. Its still fun, its unique, and has some replayability in the campaign with the "choose your next weapon" system that locks you out of the weapon you didn't choose. But absolutely what impressed me the most was how fast the bugs I encountered were fixed, and gives me complete faith that this will turn into a MUCH bigger and better game in the coming months/years.

Finger Football (FF) is an arcade game of turn-based football, played in real-time with limits to stop time-wasting. [/tr]
ːmanaː There are 5x game modes: One player, two player (local), tournament, penalty shoot-out and a free-for-all mode. 
ːmanaː Choose from 35x international teams with individual attributes of: [shot] power, time [to shoot] and aim [accuracy].
ːmanaː Select from 5x starting formations.
ːmanaː There are no microtransactions in the PC version, but currency must be earned to play most single player variants and to unlock a good portion of teams and most of the starting formations.
ːmanaː Single player has five tournament types with varying degrees of entry fee, rewards and game time.
ːmanaː As well as teams, local two player mode allows sides to choose day/night stadium and game duration.
ːmanaː Penalty shootout against the AI lasts for five kicks only with the player alternating between shooting and goal-keeping.
ːmanaː A free-for-all mode sees both sides forego taking turns and wind-up their shots to shoot as soon as possible.
ːmanaː Matches consists of five large counters on each side. Played on a fairly small pitch taking turns to push the ball or other counters to get the ball in the opposition net. Counters can hit opposition counters or be positioned where required.
ːmanaː All matches can currently be restarted if the end result isn't favourable.
ːmanaː Apart from currency the only notable counter is the number of victories earned in during the lifetime of play.

[h2]Warning - Asset Flip![/h2]

Dejavu Games? I certainly had a deja-vu when looking at the game's screenshots - surely this is an asset flip?

Actually, it's [i]two[/i]: the game itself is [url=https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/templates/packs/finger-soccer-game-kit-45611]Finger Soccer Game Kit[/url] by Finalboss but slightly modified by also implementing [url=https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/tools/modeling/stadium-crowd-generator-203643]Stadium Crowd Generator[/url] by AiKodex. The latter exclusively to make a short intro animation of a full stadium before the game starts ... which, during the actual game, is never seen again. At least the "developer" added some (working) Steam achievements.

But it's still an asset flip. Just because you managed to buy a competently made framework asset and add a few lines of code to implement achievements doesn't make you a game developer. While the game is playable and doesn't even look terrible, it's not [i]your[/i] work. The template was also made for mobile devices so don't bother looking for a way to customize resolution, controls or anything - there's none. It's also pretty obviously just a template to add your own ideas to - while rather fleshed out there are some parts where you go "hm, shouldn't there be more?".

"Finger Football" isn't the worst game in the world and for the low price you'll maybe even find some fun here. Just keep in mind "Dejavu Games" - whoever that may be - didn't actually create any of this and doesn't deserve your money.

This game builds upon the first one in a way that is fun and interesting, with a lot of unique mechanics to make it worth playing. The puzzles are not too difficult but figuring them out is still fun.

Hook 2 is follows the same theme as Hook but with a few additional twists (pun intended).

The basic premise is to extract the rods and hooks when their extraction path is clear.

Early on, the puzzles are somewhat simple but it's when you get towards the end where the real fun begins. You're forced to complete the puzzles in a 3D space and coupled with the monotone colour scheme, this can make tracing lines and their respective toggle buttons that bit more challenging and rewarding. The new mechanics for connecting the toggles to the rods and hooks add another welcome dimension to the puzzle series.

The game is relatively short (only takes an hour or so to complete the whole game) but it is an enjoyable casual puzzle game, without feeling frustrating.

The game's method of introducing new mechanics is quite clever. Rather than include guides or instructions on how to utilise new mechanics, they're all presented in a simplified puzzle to demonstrate their ability. Once you've clicked through, it's time to utilise it (and all others) in more varied puzzles.

The only issue I have is that it's far too short, however, for its price (AU$3-$2.50), it easily covers the hour or so of game play you'll get out of it.

Overall, highly recommended. I would also advise you purchase and finish Hook first, if only to prolong the experience. Hook 2 is somewhat more of the same but with a number of new mechanics which introduce new twists on completing the puzzles.

Covid Simulator is visceral.  It is detached.  In as much as it is possible for art to reflect reality, Covid Simulator has reflected the darkest nature of modern human impulse.  

Covid Simulator is also the most realistic simulator ever created.  Sheer genius in its simplicity: it reduces human beings experiencing the office work environment during the pandemic of 2020-onward to their most fundamental productive units.  Paradoxically, the inhabitants of the simulation are gifted with a sort of perverse free will, where their decisions have potentially catastrophic consequences to the larger collective, and potentially to themselves.  The decisions are made nonetheless, perhaps or at least seemingly at random, and what unfolds is a vision of collapse from every angle: total and complete collapse.  

As in life, it is temporarily possible to stave off the collapse through adequate preparation, but the impulse to ignore some apparently mundane element which may drive spread under certain conditions for the sake of maximizing profit is too great to resist.  Slowly the workers are decimated, and then dessicated, as the workforce succumbs to the disease at first in dribs and drabs and then in torrents.  

Masks help, but people take them off to eat.  Vaccination helps, particularly against Delta, but less so against Omicron.  You can institute quarantines or work in shifts, but your efforts will only limit the spread so much.  And the most important thing is your score (profit) and you have to maximize that.  

A sense of eerie foreboding pervades the music, and it instills appropriate dread and vexation as you wield the lives of the inhabitants as tools of your own personal aggrandizement.  At first I found myself speeding through the days, unable to bear witness to the folly I was driving.  That is, once I realized I could increase the speed.  Prior to that, the inhabitants bumbled along placidly, almost blissful, taking off their masks (safely) to eat lunch, chatting about their city name and sports team, or blithely generating profit at their workstations.  I tended to slow down a bit at night and reflect on the splendor I had granted these beings, through the purpose I provided them.  

Eventually things began to get ugly.  And no matter what I did, I could not get the level of infection to a place where I could manage it.  Even with the entire office pro-vax, masking, and working in shifts, there was no way to eliminate the risk of exposure.  Even worse, my profit was tanking.  Even when a level of herd immunity was achieved, with most of the infected remaining asymptomatic, there was no way to ensure an increase in profit.  While the infection of the workforce was certain and therefore a known quantity, the uncertainty around profitability left me feeling empty and desperate for a way to turn the red number green.  In truth, playing in a way where that was the only important thing to me was the most difficult road to travel, yet I strode on into the face of my workers' destruction.

I bought this game on a whim, being familiar with the urban legend it's based on, curious to see what direction they'd take it. I imagine a lot of people buying this game will be doing so for a similar reason, for the title alone. Obviously, this is a fanmade interpretation of Yeah Yeah Beebiss, as it is in reality just a copyright trap (look up Yeah Yeah Beebiss if you want the context here.)

Anyway, it's a simple NES style game. Overall, it's a fun game, although pretty light on content - and the difficulty in reviewing this game is that I don't know if to class that as bad or suiting, given the bootleg NES vibe it's going for.

With that said, my biggest gripe with this game isn't a style criticism, but rather the control binding issues. It's bound to WASD for movement, when I would've preferred to use arrow keys. I thought I could fix this problem by plugging in a 360 controller, but unfortunately on a controller the game uses the left stick instead of the d-pad. Allowing d-pad input for an NES-style game seems like a no brainer and should be the default setting.

As for the game itself, it's a simple game that is probably best enjoyed in short bursts - but there's no way to save, so if you want to complete the game you'll have to do it in one sitting. I guess this makes sense given the NES style, but it is a little disappointing because I probably won't have the patience to finish. There are 100 levels, but it is really just the same 10 stages palette swapped, and the first two are very similar. So far I've played to level 25.

The game consists of going around and zapping the enemies called "Evils." You have to kill a specific amount within a time limit. The time limits don't get harder with each palette swap, so do that ten times and you're done. There also isn't much enemy variety, with there being four types in total (one is just an alternate version of the most common enemy.) This is too bad, as adding more aggressive time limits or enemy variety over time would've been an easy way to spice up the same stage layouts.

Still, platforming around the level works well and is pretty fun to get the hang of. Most of the fun of the game comes from learning to efficiently navigate the stage layouts, which are filled with challenging jumps and obstacles.

At first the game seemed quite challenging, until I realized I could just hold down the zap button, since the attack stays on for an unlimited time and doesn't slow down your character or pose any other disadvantage. I can't tell if this was intentional or not, but either way the zap attack feels a little bit unsatisfying and I wish there was more "oomph" to it. There are also boss battles: these seemed difficult at first too, until I realized I could simply jump, strike, land on the roof next to the boss and repeat, and never need to touch the ground where the obstacles are. Again, I have difficulty telling if this was an intentional decision to mimic the style of NES games or was an actual oversight.

Sometimes the enemies can spawn in right where you're standing, although this can at least be avoided by staying off the ground so feels like an intentional mechanic. It mostly happens in the first two stages which are entirely flat.

I don't have much to say about the music, which are 8-bit renditions of public domain tunes. I feel like they could've created something dark and slow to go along with this artstyle, and the chiptune sound would lend itself to that particularly well, but this is fine too. The snippets of The Nutcracker feel particularly out of place against the gloomy aesthetic though. I do really like the artwork, both in the game and in the boxart/manual.

Also, although this is a nitpick, the game player itself also has some small bugs: for example the Credits button actually goes back to the Main Menu.

It's still an okay game, and definitely something I would play when I'm bored and want something quick to boot up and get into, but I would recommend getting it on sale if you're interested.

Bad Faith is a rather short, approximately 3 and a half to 4 hour long kinetic visual novel set on an isolated island, home to a strict, all female community. Early on it is made abundantly apparent that the island operates under very strict rules and deviation from community standards results in very harsh punishment. The story follows a girl named Magda, someone who once violated the community's standards and very nearly received the harshest penalty one can face, exile from the community.

At its core, this is a story about the darkness of human nature. It is a reflection the damage that can be caused from a variety of different ways. The story presents instances the harm one can cause when one physically harms another person. The damage and negative perception that can result when one uses their authority and status to bully another. What results when one changes with time and breaks their trust in a significant way. Even if one does not directly do something that is harmful, but refuses to be supportive and is indifferent to the troubles that one is going through, when they refuse to be there for you and are bothered by your issues. All these various forms of harm can ruin people's lives. They can lead to depression, anxiety, and can leave lasting emotional harm that some may never recover from.

Bad Faith has fantasy elements and deals with existential threats and horrors in the similar vein of Saya no Uta. It is very Lovecraftian. The game, at parts, creates a very atmospheric setting that truly is quite creepy. At times, I felt the dark atmosphere (along with the backgrounds of nature) reminded me of the feel of Higurashi, another dark story. However, I do not feel the story always excels in this aspect. While the writing is good overall, I do not think it is exceptionally great. I felt like Magda had some great dialogue but some of her dialogue felt mismatched with her character, like some lines were written for filler without any real substance.

While I write about how the story is a reflection of the darkness of the human ego, I do have to ask myself at the end of the story, "What really was the point?" What I mean by this is, there is no real explanation as to what is up regarding the mysterious being that is introduced into the story. Without spoiling anything, the mysterious character has a big impact on the story towards the end and I do not really understand the significance of it. I suppose perhaps the being represents the human subconscious which is a cool interpretation. I suppose the ending can represent the damage careless people can cause. But I just don't understand how the rest of the community suffers as a result of the actions of a few. I suppose further that this can be a result that one who experiences harm may lash out at others beyond who hurt them. To me, this just felt like a typical dark story. The End. If that's what you want, then that's what you will get. It isn't bad per say, I just don't know if I would consider this a "great" dark story that is good for the sake of just being a dark story.

I struggle to find a deeper meaning in this story. The story is cool but I feel like it lacks a lot of depth. The story sets up a lot of lore but a lot of it is hidden and never revealed to the player. A lot of the sprite work felt very animated and was overall, really good, but the game barely uses them and I feel like the characters were pretty underutilized. I would have liked to see more of the world, but really all that is presented is a small carve out of this tiny isolated community. 

Overall, I liked Bad Faith and I can certainly recommend it for its cheap price tag. It is an entertaining read that depending on your preferences, may provide you with a really satisfying ending, the reasons for which I will not hint at to prevent spoilers (although many other reviews have sadly hinted at it a little too strongly in my opinion). For their first visual novel, I believe this is a solid start for Mado and I hope to see more works from them in the future.

Bad Faith is a solo developed VN which was made in under a year. It oozes charm from every single aspect, from the dynamic character sprites with numerous poses and facial expressions to the evocative use of sound effects to the impressively eerie soundtrack.

The presentation for this VN is also worth praising. All of the main heroine, Magda's, thoughts are depicted in a standard textbox, but the dialogue for the other characters is displayed in speech bubbles, which makes the VN look kind of like a comic book. It makes the presentation that little bit more lively and dynamic, and the speech bubbles help break up the text into bite-sized chunks that makes you want to keep reading.

I'm very fond of aesthetics of this VN in general. It uses filtered photo backgrounds, rather than hand-drawn backgrounds, which is something I've always liked. It makes me feel nostalgic for the When They Cry VNs,. The frequent use of the NVL textbox, meanwhile, and some of the text effects (changing fonts and font colours for certain characters, text that progresses faster/slower based on the speed a character might be talking, text which auto-progresses to the next line when a character gets cut off mid-dialogue, phoenetic screams and some repetetive sequences as Magda's mental state deteriorates) reminded me a little of Fate/Stay Night.

I haven't really touched on the plot, but I found that very enjoyable too. The main character, Magda, is a failgirl who is very anxious and #relatable. She's trying her best to be good, but she's stuck living in a cultish commune on an island that's full of girls who despise and mistreat her, and her true feelings will often slip through the cracks despite her determined attempts to be 'normal'. Magda's inner narrative goes between thoughts of "I just want everybody to be happy, I just want to live a peaceful life" to "I wish all of these horrible girls who keep tormenting me would die horrible deaths" in a way that feels very believable.

There's some pretty unpleasant bully characters in this story (as Magda is a target of bullying, she needs people to harass her), but even these characters are fleshed out. While we mostly see the story through Magda's point of view, there are a few scenes that depict the bullies away from Magda, talking to their own friends and generally living 'normal' lives. During these interludes, we discover that these bullies aren't one-dimensional charactes who exist solely to torment our troubled heroine: they are multi-faceted characters who are capable of being kind and compassionate to their friends...

They just don't regard Magda as being 'worthy' of their kindness or compassion, which makes their petty cruelty towards her hit even harder.

The world building in this story is pretty light, but it doesn't matter. The cultish world the girls inhabit isn't really the focus here: it's the interpersonal relationships between the characters. The main plot details Magda's slowly unravelling mental state, and it focuses on how prolonged mistreatment and ostracisation from one's peers can damage a person and lead them down a dark path.

The atmosphere is very unsettling, the story moves at a fast clip, all of the characters are nuanced and interesting, and the presentation is good. I can't recommend this highly enough. The VN does have a few technical problems (hovering over the quick menu can result in the menu labels like 'save' and 'load' being stuck on the screen until you hover over them again), and I think the third act wraps up a little too quickly after the slow and carefully constructed build-up in acts one and two, but that's not enough for me to mark this VN down.

This review may be a bit bare bones but I'm not much of a review writer and also try to avoid spoilers. 

It's a good, well crafted game. It's quite an engaging story, but also really dark. It's about bullying, ostracism and sects (and also moral hypocrisy and self fullfilling prophecies), and what effect they can have on people. It's themes are heavy, but the game does them justice and delivers them without pretentiousness or banality. Situations and emotions portrayed feel real. Bad Faith also delivers the atmosphere of anxiety of being judged very well. It's also not a very pleasant story - it is grim and can be very brutal, but it does serve it's purpose. 

The overall writing quality is good. Dialogues and internal monolgues feel natural, descriptions flow well, pacing is good - we get quite an ammount of details to get immersed, but not too much so it doesn't drag. Characters feel alive and are characterized well. They do feel like they are actual humans living their lives and forming a community. What the game does well about bully characters (which are usually portrayed over the top comically evil all the time) is that we can actually see them being somewhat likable from other peoples point of view (which is what makes them effective as bullies). 

The art is very pretty. Common and creative usage of CGs and sprite shenanigans also makes it feel more dynamic than many other visual novels. There are some minor visual glitches, but it's nothing too serious. As for the sound effects, sometimes they work TOO well.

Worth trying out!

[h1]FoxMania: The Quest To Review All Fox Games On Steam![/h1]

[i]Conditions for inclusion:
[list]
[*] -The player character must be consistently a fox; the fox must not be merely a skin or a character optiond

[*] -Must have 100% working Steam achievements

[*] -Must not be a visual novel
[/list][/i]

[b]Game #28: Path to Gaea[/b]

This is a short, yet excruciatingly slow, turn-based puzzle game. There are 25 levels. It took about 2.5 hours to beat the game, and about 4 to achievement hunt it.

Puzzle design is OK, with a few good moments. The puzzles are based on parity. You can walk between squares on a 2D board. Every time you move, enemies also move. You can kill enemies by moving onto them from the side, but some enemies are invincible because they share the same parity as you, meaning they'll always be on the wrong square and you will never be able to catch them. So you'll have to figure out how to avoid them, or kill them with a projectile attack.

Early levels have spikes which rise and retract on some spaces every time you move, but in an unintutive pattern that you'll have to follow closely to avoid getting impaled. Later levels have some new enemies with more complex behaviors, and some objects you can interact with.

If you're going for 100% completion, the game has some "hidden object" elements to watch out for, which I found to be a nice addition.

The game is decently pretty, which I feel is the main appeal. This feels like a newcomer's first Unity project, using store-bought assets and all, except they've taken the time to actually polish the game to make it look and feel nice. I can really appreciate that. I also feel like this might have been conceived as a touchscreen-based mobile game to begin with, but it's a decently pleasant one.

Too bad the game is just so slow-paced. Most of the game is spent watching the fox slowly trot from one square to another. It made the game so unpleasant to play. If the game had about twice as many levels, but moved about twice as fast, I think I would have been very happy with it.

4 / 10. I'd give this a neutral vote if Steam had one.

What a delightful game!  Space Station 52 is a very creative murder mystery that is presented in a point and click format. The art is unique, the voice-overs are well done (I especially liked listening to the main character) and the story is interesting enough to make you want to keep playing.

You control Edward Locke - a space maintenance guy who arrives to find his predecessor murdered. You then loop through areas of Space Station 52 to look for evidence and meet/interview potential suspects. There are puzzles and quite a few 'find and use' exercises which range from simple to head-scratching. For me, a pencil and paper were necessary (which I never mind, as note-taking while gaming is an old habit).

There are collectibles in the form of evidence, doodads, and moxie. Evidence is uncovered by clicking on specific hot-spots and by conversing with suspects. Doodads and moxie are 'earned' by clicking on specific hot spots and then used to purchase items in your apartment. While there are more than enough doodads available (I ended the game with several hundred above what I needed), moxie is a different story. I don't believe you can miss any if you want to fully populate your apartment and achieve the status of 'hoarder.'

The game auto-saves regularly and has a crazy number of slots for explicit saves. Hot spots are easily revealed and instructions are clear on most puzzles.  I ended my first game missing one piece of evidence and about 30 moxies. So, being the Type-A gamer that I am, I immediately replayed in order to find what I'd missed. Replaying means starting your collectible counts from square-one but the game goes faster if you've made notes on puzzle solutions and remember some of the more quirky inventory uses. Most players are likely to miss two achievements that are unrelated to hot spots. Without the developer hint in the Steam discussions, serious luck is needed to stumble upon them.

I highly recommend Murder on Space Station 52. It is obviously a labor of love by a small development team and they did a remarkable job. I hope to see more from Made From Strings in the future!

I have to say that, although there is a slight learning curve and some luck required (There are wildlife that go around attack players randomly as an "Anti-afk measure" in a game where it easily takes more than a single session to get anywhere.) the biggest issue is the lack of protection for you once you've passed the point where that becomes an effective threat.

You see, it takes maybe a few hours to pass that first hurdle if you have a good starting position, but there is really no way to stop a more advanced player with a full military from simply killing you, and this problem becomes even greater when you realize that there's no easy defensive option either, walls take a literal day to construct, and even with them up you still require defensive structures and soldiers to defend them, but even if you do, you can't be online 24/7 constantly watching your base.

Which means that an opponent could simply wait for you to go offline before attacking, although again, it takes a substantial amount of time relative to setting up your economy, leaving plenty of time for them to simply attack you when you can't defend yourself, the issue here is that there's literally no reason for them to leave you alone, when they attack you they give everyone else on the planet a de-buff which makes them gather slower. 

They also gain resources from destroying your buildings, for instance farms give ants which are an important resource to build the standard soldier unit and are an incredibly limited resource, which means that not only do you have no functional defense against them, but due to the current game balance any rash action to make defenses or units cheaper would simply favor them, as they're already more economically advanced and therefore more capable of using any advantage that is given.

Not to mention that, while planets themselves are controllable, giving larger players a reason to immediately kill any smaller players which seem to be growing in size/power, smaller factions take up space which larger factions need, which means that not only are they rewarded for it, but it becomes necessary after a certain point of growth, as the starting worlds fill up and players with older empires become more powerful, it will become less and less possible to do anything without dying, making this game's balance unfortunately unsuited to new players, in my opinion.

In a world full of Metroidvania-ish platformers, there's no reason to play one with so many self inflicted wounds. It's possible that the game gets better at some point, but it's hard to imagine. I've played for a little more than an hour but feel like I've accomplished almost nothing. It's a terrible first impression. 

The game doesn't teach you any important controls or interactions with the environment. You're going to learn everything by trial and error, but failing often won't give you a hint of what to do. What's the item you just picked up? Who knows!? Want to find power-ups? Attack every wall! 
The game punishes you for basic interactions. Exploding red blocks or skulls that come to life do little other than force you to perform basic travel through block walls more slowly. The red blocks in particular a terrible fun stopper.  Their existence is counter-intuitive in a game that practically demands you try to destroy every wall. The red blocks explode and damage you very easily. To get around some of them without damage you have to attack them at a range in a way that feels a bit like kiting.

The game's jumping isn't great. There are some minor mechanical issues. There are a number of "headbanger" leaps where you need to jump short to avoid hitting your head. The reaction from these 'headbangers" is not player friendly. Jumping and hanging wall can be difficult if there's a ceiling because you'll bounce way down if you tap it. 

The bigger problem is the jumping philosophy. Jumping in a game can be used as a challenge where it matters if you fail. But sometimes it's just a way to get from place to place and it shouldn't be difficult. Unfortunately, some games feel the need to make nearly every section with any jumping a challenge even if you have to travel the area multiple times, and these sections will have close to one right path which requires correct jumps from each platform. These jump combos aren't terrible the first time, but when the game does the same thing over again or forces you to run the same precise room to explore, it's a drag. The developer has spent extra work making routine sections of the game less fun. 

The first point where I'm wasting too much time is a large room you have to cross back and forth over several times to reach the top. If you miss a jump, there's a good chance you'll end up back at the bottom. You probably won't take damage (or much damage) so the penalty is time. If you try to explore the room, there's a good chance you'll have to end up back at the bottom of the room wasting more time. If you decide to go back and explore a previous room, you'll waste more time crossing it. these rooms with mostly one correct path and easy to miss jumps do little but suck time.

I've seen games do jumping worse, but when I'm backtracking because I can't figure out how to tackle the first boss the bad travel jumping issues are magnified.

And the first boss was the last straw. The game gives you little hints on how to damage the boss. Other enemies could be damaged the same with close range and long range weapons. The boss only works with close range. There's no indication of where the spot to hit is until you hit it, it doesn't have any color changes and it's the same kind of bone as the rest of the boss. It takes a lot of work to get to the point you can hit this spot, but since the long range weapon makes you think it's not a hitbox for anything there's plenty of reason not to try. The only reason I tried is because I had fought the boss for several lives and not done a point of damage, and then ran back across the map looking to see if I missed power-up, and then came back, and wasted more lives stabbing and shooting everything in the room from until something finally ticked.

I quit when the boss then came up with a new move that made the already slow task less fun without a desire to spend more time on it.

I'm honestly puzzled by the number of games like this that make the first boss difficult. You want the player to feel a sense of accomplishment. This game doesn't do that. As a bonus, the game won't dump your gold count for a level when you have to "continue', but it will if you quit the game because it's so hard to correctly store a number. The game is practically encouraging you to give up before your'e invested.

I also ran into serious performance issues on a machine that runs modern 3D games fine in 1080. I've run Cyberpunk in 1080 on it without issue. It should be able to deal with a primitive pixel platformer. Jumping in many cases would slow down the game during a longer jump. Because this would usually happen without enemies on screen, I wasn't until I tried the game on another system that I was certain this wasn't just bad jump physics.

There's enough skill shown in the parts of the game that work to be good, but the developer has shown little need (via the game play) to help the player understand the game, or recognition of elements that conflict with core game play. It's like playing an old 1980's NES game where all the important details are in the manual but you don't have the manual. And also like a bad 1980's NES game that punishes you because it can with arbitrary dangers and routine path jumps that are difficult.

At the moment, it's hard to recommend this game at any price but especially $15. I'm not sure it's beyond fixing if the developer is willing to significantly reconsider the new player experience and make the game more intuitive. It would require believing that there's a problem and being willing to make serious changes to the presentation.
