Everblade is a fantastic hidden gem of a game. While it certainly has some rough spots, there is more than enough polish elsewhere to make up for its shortcomings. 

The main factor Everblade has going for it is variety. The game is divided between a hub area and 9 levels which generally unlock in sets of 2 or 3 (plus a final level). The level themes are diverse and range anywhere from underwater ruins to a church and graveyard crawling with undead. 

Beyond the aesthetics, each level has a unique feel as they all focus on different mechanics. You'll be dodging plenty of boulder and riding along on the wind in the mountains, jumping between falling tree branches and swimming around thorns and poison in the swamp, and mostly solving puzzles while trying not to drown in those underwater ruins I mentioned. Several of the levels are even broken into two distinct segments, such as the desert level which first has you platforming across the desert while periodically dipping into water to avoid heatstroke and later has you fighting your way through a trap-filled pyramid. The underwater level does go on for a bit too long, but otherwise the levels stay fresh and interesting from beginning to end.

Secrets are another aspect Everblade excels at. There are a truly *ridiculous* number of breakable walls and hidden passages in this game. If a wall looks even a little bit suspicious, chances are high that you can break it or crawl through it for a prize or a challenge. While many of these secrets result in relatively minor amounts of treasure or a 1up, there are also plenty which grant more valuable prizes in the form of skill coins, max health upgrades, lore books, or minigame portals (which in turn unlock another upgrade when you find and complete all of them). The hub area itself also has plenty of hidden paths to gradually uncover as your skillset grows. If you get a sense of satisfaction every time you find something hidden in a video game, chances are you'll love Everblade.

Level progression and backtracking is handled rather well here too. The path leading to the boss of each level tends to be straightforward, but finding every permanent upgrade hidden throughout a level is rarely going to happen on your first run through it. In fact, it's outright impossible to do so in a single run for all except the final few levels as many of them have paths you can only reach with upgrades found elsewhere. Thankfully, Everblade does several things to make backtracking fun instead of tedious. Each level entrance has a marker to let you know if you've found every important item inside it. Doors and other shortcuts remain permanently open across visits, with a path leading to the later areas of a level almost inevitably right near the start. Lastly, you can leave a completed level at any time with the only penalty being the loss of half the treasure you obtained on that run, which is likely to be next to nothing if you're focused on seeking out missed upgrades. What this all means is levels are long enough to feel like satisfying challenges on an initial clear while having enough permanent shortcuts open up along the way that you rarely need more than a minute or two to reach any part you want to investigate while backtracking.

The combat system itself is decent. You have a standard slashing sword combo alongside a set of 3 weaker, regenerating throwing daggers for ranged attacks. I found myself relying on the daggers most of the time as most enemy types can take quite a few hits and often deal plenty of close-range damage. This does mean combat can feel tedious early on if you like to play it safe, but it picks up in the back half once you get more utility between decreased cooldown on dagger regeneration and elemental daggers which let you freeze most enemy types or leave behind fiery damage areas. Enemy placement is also handled well, with enemies often positioned in locations where they can make effective use of their attack patterns rather than being haphazardly tossed around.

While combat in Everblade generally falls under "decent if unremarkable", the boss fights are more noteworthy. To begin with, every single boss and miniboss has its own combat theme. Many bosses are immune to dagger attacks, so learning how to dodge their attacks and when it's safe to get close enough for a few quick sword slashes is vital. This isn't to say that daggers are completely useless for these fights though, as many bosses summon in weaker enemies (which can drop valuable health) or shoot destructible projectiles and daggers *definitely* come in handy against the bosses who don't have immunity. Bosses also have enough health to put up a good fight without having so much that the fight drags on. Furthermore, most bosses either have a fixed pattern they change up in some way around the halfway point or pull from a large enough pool of potential attacks to ensure the fights feel satisfying and tense from start to finish. The only boss I didn't like was the one in the mountain level, which was a neat concept for a sort of 'summoner' fight, but the execution was a bit tedious.

With all that said, it's time to get around to discussing some of those rough spots I mentioned. To begin with, the visual language of Everblade has some issues. For example, the castle level has plenty of thin, grey, rectangular platforms whcih look like they should crumble beneath you and, while they do disappear upon contact, it turns out they're bounce pads. You can jump up most walls, but the walls you can't jump on have a thin line of green moss which blends in so well with the environment that it took me a moment to understand why I couldn't jump on some walls. These visual issues are rarely a problem other than the first time you encounter something, but they do mean otherwise simple mechanics can sometimes feel oddly confusing to understand.

Treasure and 1ups don't feel valuable for most of the game. The inclusion of a lives system in the first place is a strange decision, but it's made especially pointless when there's a hidden 1up you can farm in the castle (one of the earliest levels) within 30 seconds of the entrance once you open a shortcut; I spent a good chunk of the back half of the game hovering at or around the maximum of 9 lives thanks to how easy this and other 1ups were to obtain. As for treasure, it's virtually everywhere and finding hidden treasure can in and of itself be fun, but the only things you can use it for are a skill reset token, a single max health upgrade, dirt cheap consumables (you can only have 3 copies of a single type at a time), and passive items which all either go away upon death or do something upon death (you can also only have 1 passive item at a time and they are all so expensive that it makes more sense to simply save for consumables).

Lastly, Everblade does have something of a U-shaped difficulty curve. The reason for this is nearly all of the skills related to exploration are found in the first 3 levels in the back half of the game. The result is you spend the first few levels getting a tiny handful of skill coins for permanent passives and a few max health upgrades and then the number of health and skill upgrades you can find skyrockets once you get these new skills, making damage largely trivial until near the end where the game starts becoming balanced around the assumption that the player has found most of the health upgrades. It would have made sense to distribute these upgrades more evenly across the game.

When all is said and done, none of Everblade's issues are particularly severe. Ultimately, Everblade is a wonderful game full of plenty to like from start to finish and I'd say it's easily worth the asking price. And if you're still on the fence, I strongly recommend checking out the demo as it lets you play through the entirety of one of the early levels (it certainly did a good job of convincing me to take a chance on this game at least).

This is a real hidden gem, I can't believe it's only got as few reviews as it has. A wonderful pixel adventure, you play as a mage on a quest for revenge.

The bosses and minibosses all have interesting designs, if fairly simple patterns to remember. But this is not a game focused on challenging bosses, the focus is on the bright and wonderfully detailed environments. The levels are always bigger than you think, full of secrets and treasure ala Shovel Knight, but with a focus on shortcuts and puzzles. You'll unlock new abilities that will open the path to even more secrets and treasures. If you like exploration focused games, this is def one to check out.

You start off with simple sword slashes and some magic daggers for ranged combat, but you will gradually unlock spells and new attacks to mix things up. Enemies can sometimes be challenging, but are often placed in ways to make you consider your platforming. Most enemies also don't respawn, so it's easy to backtrack if you think you've missed something. A death will restart you very close to where you died, but after you lose all lives you must restart. Shortcuts and items found remain in your possession though.

There are also fun minigames to find and unlock for even more treasure. In between levels you find yourself in a hubworld which is just as full of secrets  of its own. Everblade is overall a really great action adventure game, if you like metroidvania games consider giving this one a try, even if it isn't a true metroidvania. It's such a polished and fun adventure, with a unique feel of it's own that it really deserves a bigger audience.

[h1]Wellington's [url=store.steampowered.com/app/1874220/GO/]GO[/url] mixes elements of brick breaker and pool in a relaxing minimalist package but lacks thoughtful strategic design.[/h1]

Break the whites and bounce off on blacks. Some pieces move, most are static.

With a mirror effect on screen edges, most of the 100 puzzles are either easy one-shot solves or fall into the trial-and-error category. You can let some levels run for 2 whole minutes and just watch the ball bounce off randomly until it clears all the pieces. Coupled with the occasional glitch, this makes solving puzzles rather unsatisfying.

For the tougher levels, I would have liked to see my last move's position before attempting another correction.

Go presumably took strong inspiration from Kamibox Games' more polished [i]Okay?[/i]. Okay is more musical and has more diverse elements (such as strings that make sounds but don't disappear). Go relies on screen mirroring to solve its puzzles while Okay does not. Yet the similarities are otherwise striking beyond coincidence, both in terms of concept and presentation.

[h1]Positive[/h1]
[list]
[*] Nice minimalist aesthetic
[*] Relaxing
[*] Very affordable
[/list]

[h1]Negative[/h1]
[list]
[*] Puzzles can get solved by accident with the ball going off-screen without limits in ways that were clearly not intended
[*] No options to reset progress or replay previous puzzles
[*] Ball occasionally passes through solid blocks
[*] Derivative of another indie title without improving the formula
[/list]

honestly I didn't have the heart to give this game a thumbs down since a lot of love was obviously put into it, but I don't think I'm going to play it for too long. Consider this a "meh."

Pros:
-I love the way level-ups are handled; you can put points into a few stats, and level up individual skills.
-GREAT spritework, and I also like the aesthetic of the drawn art.
-Tactics are solid. One of my pet peeves is when a TRPG boils down to "one-shot the enemy before they one-shot you", and this game doesn't do that. 
-I like the story. There isn't too much and you get right to the battles, but the characters are all written well.
-Good soundtrack, which seems to take its inspiration from Final Fantasy Tactics.

Cons:
-Movement is weird, it is often unclear why you can or can't move to a certain square. Height info isn't displayed, but occasionally you just can't make a jump that looks completely doable and it throws your whole strategy off. Plus since you can't rotate the board, there's a lot of terrain behind trees and ledges that you just plain can't see.
-Monsters just sit there until you get within the range of one of their attacks. This means that in battles where you are outnumbered, there's a whole lot of time spent each round cycling through the non-turns as each AI unit waits.
-I really feel I've seen everything this game has to offer after only two hours. Each unit has like 8 skills and four passives, so there's not a lot of build variety at play here.  To me, build variety is like THE THING for TRPG's.
-I just plain do not like the whole "two types of damage" mechanic. FP acts as BOTH HP and MP for some characters and it contributes nothing fun to the strategy. 
-Some UI trifles, for instance how unclear it is to determine which unit you are targeting in regards to the turn order display, and that (playing on controller) the same buttons do different things in different menus so I accidentally ended a unit's turn too early a few times. 

Conclusion - If you love TRPGs and you're in the market for one, this will probably hit the spot. It isn't nearly as deep as Final Fantasy Tactics, or even some more modern takes like Fell Seal, but I'd suggest giving it a shot if you're curious.

FAFH carries obvious touchstones to the Tactics Ogre series and FF: Tactics, but stands out from these and other tactics games by approaching the genre in new and refreshing ways that made me want to keep playing the game well after its touching epilogue.

FAFH emphasizes team building. Many tactics games (Fire Emblem, the two series listed above) can be broken open by creating a hyper carry character who you dump all your experience points and stat boosting items into. FAFH doesn't allow you to do this because experience is shared between the team, meaning everyone levels at the same pace, and the enemies scale with your level. So rather than bulk up, say Gabriel to solo levels with dodge tanking, you have to consider your party as a whole. The game also allows you to view all of the skills and traits after you complete the first stage, so right from the jump you can start theory crafting and building your team. In some runs, I made Gabriel and Claster tanks, in others Crim, sometimes Simon can be a monster who shreds armor and does major damage, others he's a fantastic support. Every character not only comes with a starting kit to fill different roles, but also can be played in multiple ways, so replayability is deeply rewarding for those who want to try different combinations of team building.

FAFH also innovates with the addition of Agile/Endurance units. Endurance units work in classic SRPG fashion. They have a standard HP pool and a TP (mana) pool. Agile units, meanwhile, have a MUCH larger TP pool, and their TP acts as not only how they use skills, but also as their health. This forces you to play around balancing big swinging attacks or support moves that can drain Simon, Gabriel, and Graff's effective HP. Tanking, pulling enemy aggro all becomes much more important. This system emphasizes control, rather than simply trying to DPS down everything. It can be difficult to wrap your head around right away, but trust me when I say it's more intuitive than it sounds and is one of the features that drew me really deeply into this game in the first place.

Finally, this game is story and character driven in ways that are very refreshing. By keeping the cast small, FAFH is able to give some really deep exploration of its characters while also telling a story that is engaging, but doesn't hold its player's hand. It leaves room for players to draw their own conclusions about the world, while giving a satisfying and engaging ending to the core narrative of the story.

The fun thing with these are ranks 1-3 does 'stronger' and rank 4 does a bonus effect which was exciting to look forward to earning.  Stats are gained on levelup, some via the character automatically and some are distributed by the player.  Again you can pick health / dmg / speed to fill the role you want.

Then there is magic focused (everyone else),  and every mage has mana shield.  aka you must hit them and drain all mana before killing them, and mana shields have innate armor?  Anyways, was a tad miffed to have 3 mages, one being a healer, and 2 endurance characters.  However one of those endurance could 'partner up' and become 1 unit with someone else. 1.  Gabriel is obviously a female, but Gabriel is a male name.  Should be "Gabrielle" or something similar.

They fail to speak up in cases where they 100% would have said something if they understood their language, and what they say often sounds very odd given their level of understanding.

(Another Spoiler)

3.  After watching the scene after the final battle, we see a figure run up from the bottom of the screen before everything goes to hell.  I assumed that this represented a last-ditch effort to save the character who sacrificed themselves, but that plot hole is never resolved, at least 2/3 through the second play-through.

By far the biggest body count is held by Graff with his Barrage skill, which is able to mow down enemies by the handful. After that, the other characters are lucky if they can kill a single enemy each.  I almost never end up using any of their skills.

Bad:

This game is a party-based Tactical RPG similar in many aspects to Final Fantasy Tactics Advance. Characters run a fixed class, but points gained from leveling up can be distributed into varying attributes or leveling up skills, allowing for gameplay styles. There is no standard equipment, but characters may equip rings providing passive bonuses. Some of these bonuses are simple stat growths, but most others are more unique, such as granting a stacking buff every turn that increases the equipped character's skill potency for their next skill.

My favorite aspect of the game so far is how it isn't afraid to provide characters interesting abilities early. So far there doesn't seem to be any environmental interaction, but skills are still very unique. One Guardian character, for instance, may partner up with an ally, sharing their tile and allowing the Guardian to take the damage of any attack hitting that shared square, or allow any such attack to be countered by the guarded character. Passives that can be unlocked affect a character's playstyle greatly, and are extremely impactful in their effects.

There are also some quality of life features or aspects unique to this game among the genre, such as a shared EXP system, or items taking up a Supply resource that is also necessary to to craft the aforementioned rings. And there are still yet others I haven't discussed. One important one is that different aspects of the difficulty may be altered to the player's convenience at any point.

The only gripes I can say I have with the game is that the control scheme takes some getting used to, and that both dialogue and animations start out very slow. These are minor gripes though; the former just takes time to grow accustomed to it, and the latter can be changed somewhat in the Settings menu.

I've also heard this is the Developer's dream game, so congratulations to them for its release! It is a very worthy addition to the SRPG genre.

Short version:
Cozy on the outside, a bit cut throat on the inside. If you enjoy meticulous money making ventures with a side of relationship sim, you will likely have a wonderful time with Potionomics. Just, don’t let yourself get burnt out.

Long version: 
I demoed Potionomics at PAX West 2024 and waited until the definitive edition with full voice acting launched. For the vocal performances alone, I think it was worth the wait. I recommend playing on PC if you can; I played it on a Switch at the con and I could tell it was struggling a bit.

Some of the criticism I’ve read purports the potion making grows tedious and the time management overly stressful. I loved this game, but honestly, valid. Whether the game intended to or not, it calls for a shift of mindset after you’ve sufficiently fallen into the rhythm of things, from hustle to...CAREFULLY DELIBERATE hustle. 
The first few hours of gameplay were fast paced, but then gradually morphed into a loop that incentivized me to act slowly, tactically. And I enjoyed that! In hour-long doses. 
It’s a game where I could have burnt out if I didn’t pace myself. It’s the closest simulation to what I think an actual, modestly successful small business owner must feel like; a little tired but proud of their achievements!

I do have some suggested improvements for the devs should they decide to continue to refine Potionomics. The game is great as is! Though if a few quality of life improvements were made, I do think it would tip Potionomics to the next level.

STORY & CHARACTERS
The characters are largely where Potionomics shines the brightest. The world of Rafta felt authentically diverse, and there was a good balance of Heart and Humor. I genuinely loved Sylvia’s absolute rizz whilst hitting on the instantly loveable, romanceable cast. 
The voice acting amplified the expertly written character dialogue tenfold. The core story isn’t particularly deep, but in the true spirit of a quality dating sim, I found the individual character stories to be truly excellent. You instantly know what each character is all about, only for them to surprise you with a new side to themselves later on. I was grateful that the post-game offers an “endless mode” in which I was able to see each character’s story through.
Biggest suggestion: dialogue history. Accidentally skipping through dialogue happens and it's a bummer when it does!

GAMEPLAY
Potion Making: 
This being a core game-mechanic, removing friction here would go a long way. My biggest suggestion of improving the potion-making workflow would be macros or some way to save previous ingredient combinations. The most tedious part of potion making is hovering over every ingredient, on almost every page, every time. On one hand, while it's cool I began to memorize certain ingredients, I wish it was easier. Yes, the filters do definitely help speed things up. But it is still quite a chore, overall. 
If you could rely on a “potion ingredient history”, it’d allow you to perform less inventory scanning each time. It could fill your cauldron with what you have on hand, then the player can supplement any potential missing ingredients from there. Other improvements could include:
- Indicator of what positive/negative qualities are present in the current brew
- Visual indicator on potions in your inventory that have already been aged
- Further inventory organization, would love to set aside potions meant to be saved for adventurers and what ones I can allow myself to just sell without thinking about it 

Deck building and negotiating: 
It’s fine! I enjoy the visual and auditory design of this portion. It’s another part of the game where you can see the strength of the vision; you truly feel like a cool, hustling witch, and watching the different patrons and friends come through help make Rafta feel alive! 
While I technically never struggled with the card playing portion, I can’t say I was able to pull off satisfying chain reactions/combos very often. The act of switching your cards around isn’t great either. There’s enough friction that while I’d LIKE to experiment with deck builds more, setting up your deck beyond swapping in and out a few cards isn’t worth the hassle.
The best feature that could be added here is a way to save different deck builds and easily switch between them. Similar to the history/macro idea in potion making.

Time Management and Over World: 
It felt well balanced to me! Some mild quality of life improvements could help, but nothing that jotting down a few notes can’t solve. 
- Shopping cart for Ingredient Boutique would improve tedium
- Some way to see how much time is left on your brews while in town

All in all, I found Potionomics to be a rewarding experience and a delight on the eyes and ears at all times. It deserves a lot of love. Great work dev team!

When i started this game, i was cautious about the direction this game was headed, but i decided to bear with it, and i'm glad i did. This is a fun management/card game/romance sim novel.

The story is about Sylvia, inheriting her Uncle's potion atelier shop, and the overwhelming debt that came with it, and with the assistance of a magical talking owl, she signs up for a tournament for the best potion shop in town for a huge cash reward to pay off the debt. There is a set time limit to get your tasks done, and that time will be divided between making potions, selling your products, and hanging out with your friends.

Potion making is fairly simple but complex, you might think you can throw anything in and hope for the best, but all the ingredients have select values to them, and each potion needs to reach a certain threshold on their values before they can be made. Early on the potions are simple to make, but down the line when the values get bigger, they can have negative or positive traits to them that can help improve or devalue the end product. I spent plenty of time trying to get the most out of each potion so they would give back alot of gold to pay off for more ingredients or shop upgrades, and therein lies part of the fun.

Potion selling is a whole different game, you try to barter with each customer to increase the value of your product without them losing all their patience, and you do this with playing barter cards. If people have played "Slay the Spire", they will feel right at home with this. Each card you play costs a certain amount of patience, and when letting the customer have their turn, they could either shield themself to reduce your effectiveness, or deal stress or debuffs to you. How stress works is you have a percentage meter, each percent is related to the chance you have on each draw, to draw a Stress card, which will harm you in a number of ways, mostly by adding to the percent value. Having 100% stress will knock you out for the rest of that day. You can recover from stress from either playing stress reducing cards, sleeping for the day, or hanging out with your friends.

Spending time with your friends is also hugely important to this game, not only do you feel connected to each person, but most of these friends offers a service to help you out, from buying and sending adventurers out to look for ingredients, and buying new cauldrons, to upgrading the size of your shop to sell more, even trying to adjust the following days sales bonus to select items of yours to sell. As you rank up with each person, some time passes by and you can unlock more cards to help your sales pitch, by raising the base price of the item, shielding yourself from stress related attacks, drawing more cards, lowering the cost of your cards, even using your stress for a bigger interest attack. Each individual person can be given a gift to raise their relationship quicker, but they all have their likes and dislikes, so its always best to remember who likes what. Now before i said i was uncertain with this game and that is because of each of the relationships of said individuals, for example, you become friends with Mint at the very beginning, i thought nothing much from her, until she mentioned she was raised by her "two fathers", which started to raise flags in my head, another person I don't think the game even mentioned their gender and i assume they left it to the players imagination. There was even some less questionable people, like a person that is strictly vegan, or a person that prefers natural remedies than the alternative. All of these made me think at one point this was made for DEI in mind, but i pressed through to see how outrageous it would be, and the good thing is this, it is not forced or in your face every two seconds like most other modern games, each person cares about themselfs and keep to the fact that this is a game and not a political message. Each person has their strengths and pains, and it helps you understand each person, eventually letting you get to the point of romance. At the start of the game, aside from the difficulty level, it gives you the choice of if you want to seek romance with one person only, or the whole cast if possible, so you can choose the one you care about the most, or go wild and gaga for the lot of them. I personally went "One Love" since it felt right, and chose the cauldron maker. Note that being in a romantic relationship doesn't effect the progress of the relationship from levelling up, so you can "just be friends" and have the same progress as the rest, it is only for visual flair.

Overall this was a fun experience, and i'm glad i pushed through despite my worries, some battles were tricky at times making me question my approach and made me consider different play styles, and what i would consider a quick game and leave, ended up being me beating the whole game within a week or so. Regardless it was fun, each person, good and bad, has witty humour and interesting animations, but i can understand if people are nervous with the characters in general.
While i myself had fun, if you are on the ropes on getting this game or no, i recommend getting more info in the form of youtube videos and the sort.

Alchemy, Romance, and High-Stakes Potion Making—What Could Go Wrong?

If you're looking for a game that combines alchemy, romance, and high-stakes potion business life simulator, Potionomics is here to answer that bizarre prayer. It's like if Breaking Bad met The Sims, but with more cuddly monsters and fewer meth labs. A highly unique blend that will leave you simultaneously thinking, "How did I end up here?" and "I can’t stop making potions!"

You play as Sylvia, a novice alchemist who’s tasked with saving her late uncle’s potion shop. And what better way to do that than to turn your humble little cauldron into a high-stakes business empire while romancing a bunch of quirky characters? It’s like if your local pharmacy decided to throw an awkward dating sim and a time-management game into the same cauldron—and then poof, it’s magic. 

The instant million dollars of debt made my real life student debt feel not so bad !

WARNING: This is NOT a chill game. You WILL be skill-filtered if you expect to take it as such.

You’d think this would be a chill game like PotionCraft, HELL NO. This game has a heck of a lot of features:

-Deckbuilding for haggling (around 90-110 different cards for a 20-card deck)
-Relationships with 10 different NPCs for new cards and discounts
-20 potion recipes (that you actually use during adventures)
-200 ingredients, with different traits and values
-10 traits for potions (5 negative, 5 positive)
-Aging potions for extra value
-Gardening to duplicate rare ingredients by sacrificing other, more common, or less useful ingredients
-Customizable shop for aesthetics
-Customizable shelves, barrels, cauldrons, and displays (all of which have a tangible effect on your gameplay)
-Different shopkeepers that provide services (ingredients, marketing, enhancements, adventuring, investing, lootboxes, fuel, shop upgrades, equipment upgrades)
-Autosell that can sell your surplus or help you sell if you can’t do it in person
-Custom orders with timers and specific traits 
-Sending NPCs on adventures, where you have to give them potions for them to succeed (all 20 potions have a use here)

Keep in mind, you juggle all these on a timer. You get 9 days between competitions and 6 time segments per day. It is surprisingly stressful if you don’t get a grip on the day-to-day and week-to-week cycle.

Other good things about the game include:
-Most interactions are voice-acted
-Really good animations and expressive characters
-Cute and interesting designs
-REALLY good soundtrack
-Some characters are really cute (you WILL simp for demon mommy)
-Gameplay is solid—you have a lot to do and can choose not to do some things if you don’t like them. Since you have three ways to sell potions: haggle, autosell, or custom orders. You also have three ways to get new ingredients: adventure, treasure boxes, or investment, so even there you’ve got options. The economy is not too hard, especially once you use Luna’s advertising. It’s by design, so you use your time to get better rep with NPCs and earn better cards to beat the final boss.

As for cons:
-Crashes/freezes, especially during travel
-Can’t save or quit during exploring or haggling (annoying, since you have to Alt+F4 to leave during haggling if you messed up your deck or potions)
-The story is nothing to write home about—sweet, but okay-ish, serviceable.

As a final point, it’s worth mentioning that the final boss is tough as nails compared to the rest of the game. But this is mostly a skill issue. If by day 40 (20'ish hours) you haven’t figured out that you need to upgrade your cauldron, use the best ingredients available, age your potions, and have a good deck by interacting with NPCs, then you’re just bad at this game. Mori is a love letter to those Newgrounds and Kongregate classics you spent your formative years of life mastering. I had the pleasure of exploring the enemy juggling and damage dodging complexities of Mori on it's Itch.io release. I'm pleased to see there's even more polish here to shine.

The game never takes the player for granted, it is engaging off the rip and compelling mechanical interactions are added constantly as the story arc unravels. Beyond the initial challenges implemented, you will need to be sure to look out for check points on at least your first run. In subsequent trials you are able to set your own limits with personal bests. What will be your highest multiplier? How much damage will I take? How many bullets can I keep? Will I 'Burn Out'?

While I wish there were more custom touches, like a personalized high score tracker, and a more dynamic soundtrack, where Mori truly excels is in the smooth gunplay and in the quick movement of it's flick-heavy gameplay. You're able to accelerate to the brink of your limits and adjust just as appropriately.

The mechanical design and distinguished pixel-art style show off a promising game developer, and separate Mori's flame into a kind of kindling of its own. It's definitely among the best two dollars you'll ever spend.

[b]blocks are all single letters and they fall really fast.[/b] arrows/asd to move them or make them fall even faster, but [b]placement is irrelevant[/b] and tiles fall from different columns, so there's often no real need for movement at all. [b]words are formed by clicking placed letters anywhere to match the current category.[/b] there are a bunch of [b]special blocks[/b], some explode, others slowly fade and have to be clicked to see what letter they hide, ice blocks can be used multiple times, etc.

besides the why-is-this-so-fast speed, a major issue on release was the game couldn't be paused, but esc to do so got patched in after a few days. until then you were either playing or could click the house icon to instantly abandon the game and go back to the menu. [b]presentation is very basic[/b], settings only include separate volume sliders besides the two toggles. [b]no windowed mode[/b] and alt+enter only makes a non-resizable window. the list of found words can be browsed in the menu.

Reus 2 is a fantastic city builder puzzle and a very impressive sequel. It both retains mechanics that made the original Reus special, but also improves the formula by adjusting mechanics that were less gratifying.

The progression is a little more simple, but feels rewarding for strong play. The idea to break up ages via progression is a great and rewarding design choice that allows the player to succeed while not having much unlocked. It allows for more success while unlocking higher tier biotica, actions, and abilities.

Several new giants and biomes have been added in addition to those returning, and they are unique and well characterized. Allowing the player to choose which giants to start with adds another layer of replayability and complexity in the early portion of a planet.

The creative new ways to string together biotica combinations is interesting and an upgrade over the already strong preceding system; Using a wide variety and range of tags allows for more complex and less strict ways to achieve significant score. This, in combination with the switch from a time-based system to a action or action/point-based system make the game less stressful, though it remains engaging and challenging at times.

Each separate score value is also a currency that is used to purchase additional actions or abilities. While all of the purchasing options can be a little overwhelming at times, but the addition of complexity that adds to replay value and the game's challenge.

I would highly recommend Reus 2, especially for fans of the first in the series. The updates are have added even more flavor and interesting mechanics, and I am excited to see how the game continues to progress.

It's a rogue-lite, after you finish the game on normal you can access a harder mode and the boss rush, but the difficulty does not change much. There are a lot of unlocks, granted most of them are not very relevant. I think the game needs higher difficulty scaling to really take advantage of it, it gets kinda too easy after you beat it on hard, it needs more bullets and patterns for enemies per mode. 

For a "ninja" platformer with $8 tag, it's not that bad, even though I think it has a lot of room for improvement - I mean, it's not going to compare to Cyber Shadow and The Messenger in terms of overall feel, but you know, it's 1/3 of the price, and it still hits that retro itch for me. I actually think the gameplay mechanics and power-ups are pretty fun, that said, I think the developer needs to work on some of the character frames, and the enemies will need at least 2 patterns so you not just killing everyone with a spear, perhaps some homing attacks, or maybe enemies that can teleport toward you. I beat the game on my third attempt, it's not too difficult, and the run takes about 40 minutes (on a first try).  I would like to see some enemies that run toward the character with the blade, maybe even doing some jumps because right now it's too easy to abuse the ranged skills. 

I won't go hard on the rogue-lite design, if anything it just needs more stages. I think some of the unlocks are too grindy, people will burn out on the game way before they have a chance to use them, and by some, I mean most of them. Like honestly you could probably cut the requirements in half and it would be okay. It makes no sense if the shop spawns in the first 5 seconds of the level before you have any gold. The stages could use more variety in terms of RNG sections, seems like they only have a few. Since the character has a relatively nice set of mobility tools, I would like any potential new stages to use the verticality more, and I think you can make the platforming a bit harder as well.

///

I don't actually mind the rogue-lite events and how you implemented the power-ups, the only issue right now is that the game is a bit too easy and too short to get a full effect out of them. For example, what is the point of gold upgrades, like you barely even getting a return on them, if at all. Pay 50 for a 5% to double in 40 minutes, like I am not sure if that even climbs out of the negatives. Seems like there is a nice variety of random challenges, I just want you to make them a bit harder, personally. Like, instead of killing 3 static enemies with no damage, put the player in the middle, and make him kill like 3 waves of enemies, otherwise, it's a no-brainer, there is no risk.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) So I think the movement mechanics and the power-ups are good, but you need to work on the frames a bit. Most of the time the game is very fair, not many cheap deaths, but I still would like to see more patterns for enemies so it's harder to abuse the spear. 

(+) I like what you doing with the event variety, the only thing I would suggest is to make them a bit harder, have some risk vs reward going on. 
For the price, I think the stages look okay, I actually think the platforming gameplay is decent, that said, I would like you to do more harder platforming if you make any new stages - just to utilize all the movement mechanics. For example, you put all of those hit-resets, and spear jumps into the game, but you don't take full advantage of it, most platforming sections are very short. 

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Loop mods [/u] - you have to go beyond increasing damage to make the higher difficulty fun to replay. Put more enemies, give them more bullets, more attack patterns for bosses. 

[u] Frames/Animation [/u] - when the character climbs on the spear, I wish you would skip or speed up the climb frames and go straight into the jumping charge, the pause feels a bit awkward after you press the A. When you doing the dodge-roll, I think the character should recover a bit faster. Maybe a bit more control in the mid-air when you attack, just a little faster with the movement. The edge grab probably should be automatic if you hold it toward the wall, and I think you could make a little animation for wall sliding, at least some dust to show the movement. 

[u] Enemy Patterns [/u] - first of all I would like to see maybe a few enemies that go toward the character or have an ability to teleport toward the character, just so you don't find yourself 100% safe killing everything from the distance. Most enemies in the game don't have a way to damage you from a spear distance, perhaps you could add a few different patterns or attacks, maybe give some enemies triple projectile, a different angle or homing missile. 

[u] Upgrade balancing [/u] - I think it would be cool if the spear always did 10+2 on return, but maybe reduce the return damage upgrade from 10 to 5. The shield recharge is pretty OP, maybe it could have 3 uses total, and each upgrade would add more charges.

[b] Overall Thoughts: 7/10 [/b]

A bit underdeveloped but I think the game will be decent with a few updates. I would like to see some upgrades to the character frames and the enemies so you can't spam your spear the entire run, don't be afraid to make the game a bit more challenging. If you add more difficulty modes where enemies would fire more bullets, that would help too. Right now there are a lot of unlocks, but the game already got too easy so, I am done for now.

Watashi Suzume is a neat little visual novel that is best experienced blind, so I won't bother touching on details here, I'll try to only share my overall thoughts on the game.
The game is well crafted, with pretty visuals and appealing storytelling and writing. On top of the pleasing story It also tries to "game-ify" the genre by introducing a couple of mechanics that in theory should make it more interesting to play. Unfortunately these mechanics are only used sparingly to the point where they don't make a significant enough impact on either the story or how I played the game. 
It should also be mentioned that while impressive, for the first project of a small team, there are some small nitpicks I would like to go over. For starters I did encounter a few grammatical errors on my playthrough (I got the True ending btw), which didn't take away from the experience but they are noticable on a game that is 99% reading. The visuals, while very pretty, should also be criticised for how inconsistent they are. Backgrounds, CG's, sprites and even the Main menu art have such different artstyles to the point where they feel like they were done by different artists. Because they were. I don't want to put shame on the team, this makes sense for a small studio that mainly got art from commissions, however I believe that with better communication the difference wouldn't be so noticable. Lastly I would like to mention that the main conclusion of chapter 9 felt very..... ehhhhh. This kinda enters spoiler teritory but [spoiler]the game really had a very interesting plotline going on, that I was more than excited to see how it would conclude... but unfortunately those expectations were shattered when that conclusion was *in a big nutshell* "friendship is magic and the bad guy is no longer bad". Just... for what I would consider the main antagonist of the game, and someone that you are chasing after in all the chapters that came before it, those last moments felt very weak. I understand that they play a big role in another character's arc and that the overall theme of the story leaned heavily on these messages, yet I didn't enjoy it that much personally[/spoiler].

Other than these few issues, however, I can say that I pleasantly surprised with the game. I didn't really know what to expect with it, so my expectations where pretty neutral, but in the end I can say that Watashi Suzume is an enjoyable little story that's definitely worth the price it asks.

I played this game alongside a few friends where we each acted out the characters. Reading the story out loud with other people was a fun experience, and I think helped me in catching a lot of things I wouldn't notice had I read it to myself. This review will try to be deep and informative as possible while staying succinct and not spoil any major plot points. It'll be organized as such:

1. Story (the overall plot concept and structure, setting, and pacing)
2. Characters
3. Assets (art, music, and misc. features)
4. Final thoughts/Conclusion

[b] STORY: [/b]
The concept of the story is great. I liked the slice of life style of storytelling circling around a large mystery. The town of Seishin Tekina feels lived in and was nice to explore and learn about. It had neat history and locations, and captured that small coastal town vibe. The growing relationship between Shouta and the other characters was fun to watch. The only glaring issue I had with the plot structure was the fact that it's split into a sort of 2 act structure, but the climax of the story ends with the first act, and then the second act comes in and happens. It made the second act feel dragged on because it introduced a new problem suddenly after the main conflict was resolved. This was a recurring issue where information was given when it was relevant, rather than being brought up prior and being made important later. I think it could have flowed better if the conflict of act 2 was introduced around halfway through the story, and developed alongside the plot revolving around the baseball cap guy. That way the story could have its climax and resolution closer together, rather than having the story feel like its overstaying its welcome. The act itself was enjoyable, however, and really portrayed a lot of different sides of the characters. It's just the order the problems of the story are introduced. But the ending of the story wrapped everything up nicely.

[b] CHARACTERS: [/b]
There were some characters I enjoyed and there were some I was indifferent about. Shouta fit the bill of your average VN protagonist. I liked his growth throughout the story, but sometimes he was annoyingly dense. But that's just how VN protagonists are at times. The cast of side characters like Akira and Urata had fun interactions and it was enjoyable seeing them on screen. They fit their roles nicely. Keiko was also a great character to interact with and watch her grow. I honestly found Ayumi annoying at times. She's very standoffish as a character which is part of her archetype, but I was having trouble vibing with it. Even after learning about the reasons why she was like that, it didn't change my opinion much about her. I felt she didn't grow as much as she could have being the centerpiece of the story. Ironically, the character that acts as a parallel to her, Chloe, was the character I enjoyed the most. She starts off a bit standoffish as well, but we see a lot more facets of her personality simultaneously with her sarcasm and humor, and enthusiasm for the supernatural. All that stuff was shown through interaction with other characters, while Ayumi's characteristics were told through her giving exposition about her backstory. And at the end we see Chloe fulfilling Ayumi's character arc in her stead, with her opening up and learning to make friends. I thought this was very well done. Chloe best girl.

[b] ASSETS: [/b]
This is a start up project by a small studio, and I think that's very important when it comes to judging quality of the project. Assets are expensive and can be difficult to find the right artists or musicians. The music in the game was good. It did it's job and fit the scenes. I think there was only a couple times where I felt a certain track was playing for too long at a single time. The art was nice too. The big issue was that the artstyle wasn't consistent. There looked to be at least 2 or 3 different artists for sprites, which is really noticeable when multiple characters are on screen and they're all drawn differently. It's nothing that took me fully out of the game, but it was noticeable. I really liked the investigation mini game. Added a lot of player interaction and was something I found was very unique for this medium. The sparrow button, which would pulse and you could ask Ayumi how your and her's relationship status is, I felt was actually detrimental to the game. There was several times when I could just interrupt a serious scene with Shouta breaking the flow of conversation to ask "Hey Ayumi, how we doing?" and then the scene would just continue on as normal afterwards. It broke the flow of a lot of scenes. We don't need a button to ask how the relationship is doing, the story itself should show us. Plus, there was a couple times where the button glitched and would get stuck in its animation, causing it to pulse after every line despite not being clickable. Those moments did take me out of the story, unfortunately.

[b] FINAL THOUGHTS: [/b]
Watashi Suzume is an enjoyable VN and a commendable first project for an upcoming indie studio. It has its flaws and issues that are to be expected for a first time project. But the overall quality shows a lot of promise in the team. There's great ideas and a knack for making authentic interactions between characters. Refining some of the edges and if the team takes all the feedback they've gotten to heart, I think there is a lot of potential in Shamrock Creations, and I look forward to seeing their future projects.

[h1]Circular Reasoning[/h1]

[h2]Story[/h2]

The main character is Prince Eldar of Onnya, who seeks to prove himself worthy of the throne by research the legend of the hero and finding a way to defeat the legendary villain. At first, he's a spoiled brat who cares more about the glory of solving the legend than his actual duties as a prince. In a twist, [spoiler]his research causes him to learn of many truths that were censored by his government and how his kingdom actually perpetrated many injustices against Llooan and the zsagni. Thanks to his travels teaching him more perspectives, Eldar now actually gains a purpose as a royal, making this a roundabout way of becoming a worthy king. However, he also put himself in a position where he might not be able to gain the political power needed to bring justice to Onnya's victims[/spoiler]. This game's aesop seems to be that although people have to focus on their duties, sometimes it's alright to indulge in one's own wants and needs if their current life isn't working out for them. This can be partially seen with [spoiler]Yvlor, who spent so long trying to be a perfect hero that he didn't know how to balance his love for Nyo with his duties. That said, I wish we could see more of what happens when Eldar returns to Onnya in the ending, since his aunt and cousin are implied to be running the country into the ground, thus potentially creating interesting consequences for Eldar's decision[/spoiler].

The game also features a time loop where some people can remember past lives, some living beings are forced to be immortal until the loop restarts, and some enemies are unusually powerful while dropping Breach Chunks that can kill immortals. This also causes a religion to form based on the idea that destiny must be preserved, or there could be unpredictable consequences that will destroy the world before a new loop can start. This ties into the main aesop somewhat, since [spoiler]the only way to break the loop and allow the civilization to properly develop is to stray off the beaten path of destiny[/spoiler].

Unfortunately, the time loop does unintentionally make Lue less sympathetic, since [spoiler]she's a chronologist and therefore would know Jovla can be trusted based on previous time loops, yet she treats him as a mere vagabond that Eldar shouldn't associate with. Maybe this was an act meant to hide her status as a chronologist, but it still seems unnecessarily mean of her. Maybe the point is that even with her prior knowledge of time loops, she was never able to overcome her overprotectiveness of Eldar[/spoiler]?

As for Jovla himself, I'm not completely satisfied with how Eldar reconciles with him. Eldar screws up Jovla's chance to get an important answer from a ghost and never really apologizes for it or attempts to make up for up. By the time Eldar does mature enough to possibly revisit this issue, [spoiler]it turns out Jovla already knew the answer all along, making the entire issue moot[/spoiler].

For the most part, this game isn't about attacking and dethroning god or fighting against tyranny. It's basically a research project to solve mysteries surrounding the legend of the hero and the time loop. In a twist, most of the explanations are way more mundane than expected, but will almost always lead to a new clue. The time loop in particular [spoiler]is caused not by some nebulous demon lord, but by a powerful witch exploiting the save/load mechanic on a meta level in order to undo Yvlor's suicide. This does lead to some unexplained plot threads, like how the loop restarts despite how Eldar is not guaranteed to meet Yvlor in every loop. My own assumption is that Nyo cannot maintain Yvlor's crystal prison forever, which means the Hive unfairly blamed Eldar just because of circumstantial evidence. On the other hand, it's possible Lue's chronologist memories apply to Eldar's usage of saving/loading, essentially resulting in miniature time loops[/spoiler].

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

The damage balancing is okay for the most part, though lower HP characters will get oneshot in the final boss fight even at full HP. This is balanced by the final boss sometimes not targeting the party.

Every character has a unique way of learning a new ability, with Eldar learning from maestros, Lue learning from mentor crystals and spell usage count, Jovla learning from new weapons, Laric reading recipes, and Qibayn finding inspiration from regular foes. In terms of character tiers, I'd go with:

1. Eldar - Has TP regen equipment to spam his TP skills easily, including his healing skill.
2. Lue - She has single-targets, AOEs, and strong heals, making her very versatile. Her only flaw is that her skills take long to grind to their full potential [spoiler]and she leaves after the Keeper boss fight[/spoiler]. Personally, I think she's a very close second to Eldar.
3. Jovla - Has a double hit normal attack and a buff that stacks with Eldar's group buff. However, his evasion buff can prevent affected characters from receiving heals/buffs and his ailments are generally less meta in this game because enemies will either die quickly to regular DPS or bosses resist those ailments. He has no TP regen, but his normal attack heals 20 TP if he lands both hits and his 40 TP AOE is stronger than Eldar's 60 TP AOE.
4. Laric - They're dependent on ingredients to use their skills, but their normal attack and HP are high to compensate so that you can save ingredients if needed. They can also set up group regen to make healing overall more efficient. IMO, red herbs are somewhat more scarce than other ingredients out in the wild, and most of his best recipes depend on those.
5. Qibayn - She has stronger single-target spells than Lue and learns skills more easily, but her only healing spell has an exhaustion penalty. She also cannot do AOEs without using a special consumable first, and by the time she sets that up, Eldar and Jovla will likely defeat the enemies with their own faster AOEs. Her spells come with ailments and deal good damage, but again, regular enemies die before the ailments will actually matter and bosses tend to be more resistant, giving her less overall utility than Lue. IMO, it would be better if her spells came with weak but irresistible debuffs. Unfortunately, [spoiler]she replaces Lue in the final stretch of the game, creating an artificial-feeling difficulty spike. I generally prefer difficulty spikes that are based on enemies becoming more complex than the party losing power and/or versatility[/spoiler].

The game's mapping philosophy is designed to make maps look bigger than they really are. While most games will just use regular walls, this game makes walls out of boxes, pots, and other obstacles to close off parts of the map that you shouldn't be able to access. YMMV may vary on this, since while it prevents the world from looking small, the amount of stray boxes everywhere starts to look excessive after a while. At this point, it's practically a safety violation. TBF, the NPCs seem to be humorously self-aware about the placement of obstacles.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

7.5/10

I liked uncovering the secret history of the setting and the aesop about balancing self and duty, though there are moments that make Eldar and Lue come off as more unsympathetic than was probably intended. The time loop story is surprisingly cohesive, but there are a few details that needed more elaboration like [spoiler]loops where the journey stops prematurely[/spoiler]. As for the combat, every character has their own strengths and weaknesses, but there is a tierlist that becomes very obvious [spoiler]when Lue is replaced by Qibayn[/spoiler].

[i]I Am Your Beast[/i] is a stellar FPS that nails everything it sets out to do. The ex-special forces solider trying to escape the  needless killing of the military industrial complex is a compelling story, and it plays out through short conversations over communication channels that provide a nice break from the killing. The combat isn't too difficult; you'll probably only die a few times, if at all, during the campaign if you're experienced with FPS games. The real challenge comes from mastering you capabilities and completing levels in faster times. That being said, [i]I Am Your Beast[/i] is still an incredible experience as a casual play because the narrative is compelling, the combat is so smooth, and the music is incredible. The difficulty not being crazy also makes it more approachable. 

There have been many games over recent years that are leaderboard-centric, with short levels that encourage you to speedrun and master the abilities at your disposal; this is easily the best of those games that I've played. Games like [i]Neon White[/i] come to mind, but the story there is.. well not good, and in games like [i]Ghostrunner[/i] the challenging difficulty creates a barrier to entry. [i]I Am Your Beast[/i] has the compelling story, is stylish, and is easy to get into but hard to master. Additionally, it's clearly made with a lot of love as the developers have added many new free levels post-launch. Plus there are challenges for each individual level to provide that extra carrot for those who end up loving it. I highly recommend [i]I Am Your Beast[/i], it's the best FPS game I've experienced in a long time.

[h1][b] TLDR: A rush of a game. Fun combat and witty story create a simple yet empowering action FPS. By far the biggest negative for me is the lack of meaningful, long-term content to enhance replayability.[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Adrenaline rush gameplay
➕Good music
➕Variety of combat approaches
➕Good traversal
➕Lots of levels
➕Good narrative - funny dialog and voice acting

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹”Lazy” achievements

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Enemy pathing/AI can be annoying - often missing an enemy stuck in a tree somewhere
➖”Bonus” objectives as a requirement to continue
➖Could use online elements, like leaderboards
➖No real incentive to complete S ranks/bonuses

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative/Length) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
About ~35 levels in total for the story part. All other levels are optional. The full run though for all story levels will take a bit over 3 hours as each level takes 1-2 minutes to run a single time, with repeat runs being required to progress (bonus and S ranks required). 


[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [8/10] [/b] [/h1]
Super fun combat. Very satisfying to obliterate forces with a variety of guns and explosives. The throwing element adds an awesome component that allows for some truly fun combos. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Performance) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | Windows 11 installed on SSD 

[h1] [b] Audio – [8/10] [/b] [/h1]
Awesome soundtrack. Good voice acting, good sound effects. Solid. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Since all achievements are pretty much given from the main story, the only reason to replay is to get better scores, but with no online component, there isn’t even a way to show scores to others or compete for better times on a global stage. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
I Am Your Beast (IAYB) is a pure rush of visceral combat that makes you feel like a bada**. It combines twitch FPS with a story similar to the Borne Identity series (but doesn’t take itself seriously). It also reminds me a bit like SUPERHOT from a gameplay perspective, just with no time stop elements, or even Metal: Hellsinger, one of my favs. 

While the gameplay is fun, the main story will only take you around ~3 hours to finish. Unfortunately, there’s little incentive to replay this beyond chasing high scores. With no leaderboards, ranking system, or meaningful unlockables (aside from a few achievements), it ultimately feels like a wasted effort. 
Aside from the main story, there are challenges to do, and 2 additional after-story level bundles to play, so there is more content beyond the small 3 hour investment. Still, I do wish there was more to do, at the very least the game could definitely use leaderboards and/or rankings. This is by far my biggest complaint for an otherwise great game - IAYB just lacks long legs or tools for player retention. As of this review I have finished the main story and the afterstory levels, but am having trouble to find incentive to play more. 

I did also run into some very annoying AI “Bugs” where sometimes the NPCs during kill-all levels would just be stuck in a wall. This caused me to spend excessive time jumping around a small empty level looking for the soldier stuck in a bush or something. This happened quite frequently. 

Overall, IAYB is a great game and I enjoyed it. I would strongly recommend to check out Metal: Hellsinger if you are interested in this game. You can also read my review for that here: https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/1061910?snr=1_5_9__402

I have played Jump King for about 80 hours and have beaten all the levels. I have also played some of the custom maps made by the community. Therefore, I am writing this review with this in mind since the game is inspired by Jump King.

This game has a lot of potential, but with some major flaws that if fixed/changed, can make this game shine.
This game is NOT an early access game, but it surely does feel like one.


[h2]The first major issue is the name of the game, the main character and scenario.[/h2]

The game is not just borrowing from Jump King, it is almost copying everything from it. I get that it is a game inspired by it, but it is almost a clone of it.

My suggestion for this is to change the name to something more unique along with the main character. Create some identity for this game itself to set apart from Jump King.


[h2]A second issue that I had with the game is the physics.[/h2]

Don't get me wrong, they are actually OK, but they can be well improved. The ledge of the platforms is slippery for example, so you don't land very well on them. And it would be a nice touch to have some grace period for the next jump.

What I mean by grace time/period is that for example Jump King remembers that you pressed and held jump again after being in mid-air so that when you land, you immediately start charging the next jump.

It does not need to be exactly like jump king, maybe just a second of grace period before landing is good enough. Because when you are going fast from jump to jump, you may press the jump button a millisecond before landing and it will not start charging the next jump. By doing that you can start walking and fall off the cliff by accident.


[h2]Another issue that I had is a small one and related to the menu and options.[/h2]

The main menu is too empty and there is no background. There are no options for settings for example. Only after you start the game you can access the a pause menu where you can go to settings.

The settings does not let you set the volume for audio, only allows you to mute or unmute the music, sfx and ambient sound.


[h2]Lastly, here some other improvements that can help the game shine.[/h2]

Add some lore/story for the game. Other characters also would be interesting.

The background of the game sometimes obscures the platforms, so maybe changing the art style a little bit (which would help making the game more unique) would contribute to that.

Add a level maker feature that allows the custom levels to be made and shared with the community.


[h2]That being said, there are very innovative things this game does.[/h2]

For example, having to get the key and throwing it at a door adds a new layer of difficulty. This can be surely more explored, by adding more items and mechanics that make this game unique. Maybe some puzzle area where doors open or close depending on where you put an item. Idk, there are many ways it can be explored.


[h2]Summarizing[/h2]

Again, the game has a lot of potential. It is not a bad game and It does some things very well, but there is a lot of room for improvement.

The game can really shine if it becomes more unique and less of a Jump King clone.

I am looking forward to seeing this game being a success.

[h1] A game with a world to enjoy [/h1]

I really like this game, and I dare say it is one of the most expansive and free turn-based RPGs that I have played, the world and the side quests engaged me so much that by the first time I got to explore the sandbox world, I just couldn't stop and did everything I could before advancing the story. 

   This, I believe is because the side quests actually seem fitting for the world, it seems reasonable that your character would be trying to help, and it feels meaningful to help these people in their daily lives, even if its just a fetch quest or a kill X enemy quest, it didn't feel like just another chore for power ups.

  The diversity in weapons and skills also added replayability and diversity to the game, which made me play two full playthroughs with different weapons (my first was 90 hours long with fists, and my second was 50 hours long with swords), and start a third playthrough that I will touch upon a little later. I should mention that you can switch weapons from the equipment menu freely, I simply chose to focus on a weapon type.

   Skills are divided by weapons and schools of martial arts, having 6 types of skills (simply put they are normal, strong, special, and finisher attack, movement skills, and one buff/debuff/utility skills), which you can equip 4 of each that share the cooldown within their types (so, if you use a finisher, all your finishers go on cooldown too). And, since you can mix and match your skills from different martial schools, you get a lot of flexibility within each weapon type.

   I also really enjoyed the story in my first two saves, first playing half blind and then playing to try and get a perfect ending and some achievements. There are quite a lot of side quests, some of which are bigger and basically plot lines within themselves, which made it interesting to pay attention to what people said and explore the world. You also get to discover a lot of companions, many of which can be missed if you don't do their starting side quests. So, in a playthrough where you are immersed in the world and trying to complete what you find, it is a great experience. I personally really like the characters and the relationships between them, and how some companions give advice to your protagonist if you have them in your party and thus affecting how things develop, or how occasionally they get power ups because they got to learn from the events happening in the story (there is no party limit by the way, so you can keep everyone around even if you are not using them in battle).

[h1] My one complaint [/h1]

  However, when I chose not to engage in all of these story lines, in my third playthrough, is where I found myself disappointed in the game, because it did not feel like there were consequences to not helping solve a situation, or letting another character live. I will exemplify in the following paragraph with some spoilers on a side quest. 

   [h3] [b]This is also my main criticism and feedback to the developers.[/b] [/h3]

  [spoiler]For example, in one of the big side quests you need to help one of the Three Geniuses of the era (Leng Wuqing) stop a pirate invasion which threatens the land. This pirate invasion is being orchestrated by another of the Three Geniuses, (Lou Fuzhao) who serves one of the main antagonistic sects in the game (Tianlong Gang). While doing the quest, one of the towns in the coast gets permanently invaded by pirates and the residents there die, and although you kill Lou Fuzhao and stop the pirates from further invading the mainland, the village remains occupied for the rest of the game. So, if you did not do the quest, you would imagine that Lou Fuzhao survives and the pirates invade the mainland, right? Wrong, in the current state of the game, if you just ignore this quest, the pirates never invade that town (so the residents stay alive and you can go buy whatever little things they have) and Lou Fuzhao never shows up again, even during the main story even where you invade and destroy the Tianlong Gang's headquarters.[/spoiler]

   This is the kind of lack of consistency to my failures that made me stop playing in the middle of my third playthrough, because my "lazy" playthrough didn't seem to really show me many different scenarios, beyond the natural developments of not having those extra companions' advice to help guide the protagonist (companions connected to missed side quests), which really bumped me out. However, I don't think this would be true for absolutely all of the story, namely there are two Villains that you kill in a side quest that I have heard mention of showing up further in the story if you don't kill them, although I stopped before seeing that happen.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

   [b]This complaint/feedback aside, I really really really enjoyed this game, and I would thoroughly recommend it to anyone who enjoys turn-based RPGs. I even daresay it is on par with some of the top titles of the genre, such as Chrono Trigger.[/b]

There might be too many things going on and not enough focus applied to the meat of it, but that's just my guess with my little play time.

The UI is aggressively bad. If it's not pretty it should at least be clean. This is hard to look at and decipher. The clouds aren't immersive they're smudges. If that pixel mobster doesn't quit blowing smoke at my face then this confusion is going to turn into frustration. Everything should be one font. Different fonts for different screens? Cool. Six different typefaces for the main screen (Kill the rat, End turn, Italy level 1, Money menu, Card descriptions, and the helvetica letters over pxel art cookies that are the POIs)? Oof. 

Also there are a bunch of tool tips and tutorials, however the're embedded and competing with all the other clutter. I don't know what order I should be clicking them and it's tiresome to learn stuff out of context and have to experiment. I don't mind when games ask you to fail to learn, but from what I've seen from everything else I don't know if this will be worth that effort. There are video tutorials, but none tell me how all these mechanics the game is throwing at me relate to each other or the win condition. I like complicated games, and I like that some things have minigames, but I am in the weeds here. I don't need it all laid out for me, learning is part of the fun of complex games, but I would at least like to know what I'm getting into.

Criticisms aside, I think there's a gem under all this. There are a lot of mechanics at work here, a lot of systems to jump into. I don't think I could come up with something like this and the dev has clearly put a bunch of work in. I'm all for supporting indie devs, and there are some ideas I really like here. So I'm not gunna ask for a refund. I'm going to check back in on this in a few months and see where this goes.

A dark fantasy RPG with a gripping plot and tight combat that will keep you on your toes for the whole journey. It's a game in which the gameplay is as truly gripping as the plot, in which you'll carefully plot every move, manage and ration your resources wisely, and take every step carefully to avoid the certain doom that hangs over the cast. Think of Darkest Dungeon but with a traditional JRPG structure.

Highly recommended if you love challenging and well-tuned RPGs!

NOTE: I played and completed a non-Steam version of the game.

An exceptional game set in a seemingly doomed world, providing a very likable cast of characters with conflicting flaws and issues. The overall plot is exceptional as you try just to survive while uncovering more about this world and pushing the characters forward.

It's rare to find an RPG cast of characters I like this much, rarer still for their own motivations to shake up the plot this much. I didn't expect to find so much heart in a dark fantasy, it was a very welcome surprise.

Combat is very survival based, kill or be killed. Don't expect your normal escalation of power, as new gear and powers are more about fine-tuning your play style rather than getting big upgrades. You also need to break foe's guard gauge to help you damage them, which can be a learning process. 

Ultimately I think the battle system really supports the dark tone and story, and it makes battles very tense, but also incentivises you not to take combat lightly. I think it makes combat slightly less enjoyable and more nail-biting than some other RPGs, but given that it supports the world the story takes place in, I can't really complain much. 

The game also has multiple endings and seems to alter the plot based on choices or character actions. I'm not sure exactly how this works but it's a very neat touch. I'll have to go back and replay more of the game to see if I can get a handle on how everything changes.

Overall a high recommendation. I wish more RPGs put this much effort into characters, story and world.

Instead, it's given no regard at all, the suspension of disbelief is taken for granted until it's savagely torn through by the main characters and stampeded over with all the nameless NPCs that stand there and tell you random facts and gossip about the game's world.
