[h1]Praying for More Supplies[/h1]

[h2]Story[/h2]

As you can imagine from the game's title, the story is pretty bleak, since humanity is inevitably going to die to the Miasma/Fog. The constant despair has done a number on the overall mental health of human society, making otherwise good people more desperate to uphold social order. This can be seen with Mia, who wants to save humanity, but is unable to maintain order among a panicked population, causing her to resort to desperate methods to save as many people as she can. On the other hand, Aeyr rejects utilitarianism because of how poorly he was treated by society, but this also means he has little regard for anyone outside his circle of friends. For most of the game, the two are friends who are trying to reunite with each other, but the player can see that their opposing ideals will eventually make them come to blows.

The game has four endings and I got the one that requires the two leads to stay in-character, which requires more effort than having them act out of character. I suspect this "Resolve" ending is supposed to be the true ending, but I never got around to getting the other endings. I don't know if this is true of the other endings, but I wish there was more follow up for Luke, Trill, Amalie, Reyson, and Serra.

Edit: Turns out there is no true ending and each ending has its own trade-offs.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

The combat system gives the party three actions per round, and anyone can use up any action. However, all characters have an SP bar that regenerates at the end of every round, which means it's more efficient to spread actions among all characters if possible. Though I usually end up having Aeyr use most of the actions per round because he's the only one who can heal without items. However, the actions per turn can be hard to plan around due to how the UI doesn't display buff/debuff duration.

Most of the character skillsets are balanced and useful, but some of them have very RNG dependent proc rates. This can be a problem for Mia, since she needs to proc Branded on enemies in order to use some of her skills properly. Serra's Oracle abilities are an even more extreme case, since they grant very powerful buffs, but applying them isn't an absolute chance. This is in contrast to Trill, who gets more situational and weaker buffs that are guaranteed to proc.

Every enemy has a set of weaknesses and resistances, which can be viewed from an analysis menu in the middle of combat. This makes it easy to keep track of such information the moment it's discovered and adds a layer of strategy when it comes to swapping out equipment in the middle of combat.

At first, the damage to the party members doesn't seem too bad, but you'll soon find that it's difficult to hoard supplies, due to the item cap being at 10 and the lack of inns. While there is a traveling merchant, I find that the merchant doesn't show up very often or predictably. This can make resource management a lot harder, since it's easy to use up too many items in a tough battle, you can't save up supplies in preparation for long dungeon stretches and while you can find a lot of items on the ground, you won't be able to pick them all up or return to them, making the resource situation unpredictable. IMO, this limitation wouldn't be so bad if there weren't so many respawning enemies, making it hard to backtrack while maintaining supplies. As a result, the gameplay feels like a bizarre combination of a JRPG and a stealth horror game, since it becomes necessary to dodge roaming encounters in order to avoid running out of supplies. To be fair, EXP is scaled to the characters' level compared to the enemies', so it's actually fine to skip some encounters. Plus, the flee rate seems to be near guaranteed unlike other games.

The game mainly relies on save points, and while they are spaced out adequately, it would have been nice if the player could save on the world map somehow, since entering an area could trigger an event. In a game with a lot of "points of no return," saving on the world map would go a long way in making the player feel more secure.

For some reason, the game has a difficulty setting, but only after you already beat the game once. I personally would have preferred having it available from the start, since I'm the type of person who likes to use the lowest setting on random foes to save resources while using the highest setting on bosses to test the limits of my party's abilities.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
8.5/10
I really like the clash of ideals in the story, since I feel like many people (at least in my Twitter feed) simulataneously feel despair towards their fellow people's hypocrisies, but also have a moral code that makes them feel obligated to support utilitarian (of varying kinds) outcomes. The gameplay is a mixed bag for me, since the resource situation feels a lot more stressful than in other RPGs due to how unpredictable it can be to resupply. It's still mostly balanced on the default sliders and the EXP curve makes up for the resource situation somewhat, so it's not quite as hard as it initially seems.

The most obvious thing about this game is that it is incredibly, incredibly grimdark. The world is in the middle of a slow-motion apocalypse, but there is no Chosen One around to save it, so everyone is resigned to futilely pushing back the encroaching doom until humanity is finally snuffed out.

Now, I say [i]grim[/i]dark instead of dark because, well, the existential horror of the setting doesn't seem to actually [i]weigh[/i] on anyone that much. The cadets training to be the last bastion of defense against humanity's inevitable destruction still make time for petty high school cliques and bullying, and despite their leader being borderline fascist the protagonist is able to get away with petty pranks and constant, flagrant disrespect for authority -- until suddenly he can't and he's going to get EXECUTED for backtalking the king, but actually don't worry his friend in high places pulls strings to bail him out because we can't actually have consequences for the protagonist, it's not like this is supposed to be a dark story or anything.

...Let's back up so I can explain the plot. The world is being consumed by a supernatural mist called the Fog that spawns monsters and slowly kills everything it touches. There used to be oracles who could see the future, but after the Fog appeared they all lost their powers -- except very recently, an oracle suddenly delivered a prophecy that a revenant would bring ruin to the world. One of the two protagonists, Aeyr Wilder, becomes that revenant after dying to a monster and being resurrected, whereupon everyone decides he's actually an insane demon wearing Aeyr's face and has to be killed, despite all evidence to the contrary. You can probably see where this is heading: it's a self-fulfilling prophecy because Aeyr decides that if everyone hates him he'll become the monster everyone thinks he is. Meanwhile, the second protagonist and Aeyr's only friend, Mia Alacruz, becomes leader of a band of refugees she must lead to safety after they are cut off from civilization by the Fog.

The writing is characterized by some pretty extreme tonal whiplash. Once the plot gets moving, most of the main characters do treat the situation with the gravity it deserves, but Aeyr and his team never stop acting like quippy, juvenile, and unreasonably optimistic YA characters. It makes it really hard to take Aeyr's claims he's oh-so-oppressed seriously when he doesn't act any different from your average real-life teenage brat. The Big Shocking Reveals are similarly edgelordy, and almost universally revolve around everyone being Stupid Evil or just plain stupid. As an example: The fascist commander discovers that humans become immune to the Fog if implanted with magic artifacts, and moreover that willing subjects have a 100% success rate while unwilling subjects have a 99% failure rate. Instead of [i]telling people this[/i], in which case she should logically have a queue the entire length of the city, she keeps everything a secret and continues torturing unwilling subjects for no reason. Why? Why would anyone do this? This isn't even necessary evil, this is just plain stupid evil.

The story is overall framed as a conflict between individualism (on Aeyr's side) and collectivism (on Mia's side), and though the developer claims there is no "true" or "correct" ending, I see a very clear bias towards Aeyr: Aeyr betrays Mia first, but Mia forgives him and this is brushed off by the narrative; when Mia betrays him later (for a much, much better reason), that's treated as an unforgivable offense. The story is also incredibly misanthropic: the masses are consistently depicted as selfish, overemotional idiots who never listen to reason and descend into panic and violence at the slightest excuse, and anyone who tries to be any kind of ruler is inevitably corrupted by power and forced to commit crimes against humanity to appease these monsters. (Also, hive minds are bad.) There are a few token attempts to claim Aeyr bears some of the blame for his ostracization by being a childish raging asshole to everyone constantly, but this never goes anywhere, while Aeyr's accusations that Mia has become a fascist (by, uh, not wanting civilization to collapse) are proven objectively correct by the narrative.

There's also a disturbing degree of monarchism throughout the whole thing. Both of the two societies we see are ruled by bloodline monarchs and are shown to fall apart as soon as they die because no one can conceive of any other form of governance. One of the monarchs is shown to be evil and the other incompetent, so it's at least not depicting monarchs as objectively better, but did we really need this? I get that monarchies are a staple of fantasy settings, but if you want to provide social commentary on modern society you need to accurately reflect modern society. Vanessa is already the de facto leader of Asala at the start of the story so nothing would have to change by making her de jure, and making Vergio a democracy would at least lend some credence to the claim they're a slave to the masses instead of their emperor being the only monarch in all of history who places the peasants' desires over his own.

Additionally, I feel I should note: The only dark-skinned characters are the magic mutant people with psychedelic hair, and the characters list their dark skin in the same breath as the impossible hair when talking about how they're Weird and Other. This is a bad trope and fantasy authors really, really ought to know that by now. Dark skin is a normal human trait and should be treated as such.

The whole story ended up feeling very post-hoc to me. Its argument appears to be, "Taking it as a given that people are terrible, asking people to make sacrifices for the greater good is wrong." Except, uh, no, I do [i]not[/i] take that as a given, nor should I. People are not inherently unreasonable and do not inherently desire fascism, nor does every single person in a society fall to mob mentality when it strikes. There were German citizens who fought and died opposing the Nazis. Donald Trump did not get a majority of the vote -- nor did Hitler, I feel I should point out since everyone loves to trot out that he was democratically elected. Humanity is not a monolith; "society" or "the collective" is always made up of individuals who make their own individual decisions, and it is not fair to lump everyone in with an evil vocal minority.

It's a shame, because I feel there is a lot of value here. On paper, I think the story is a very good one -- the struggle between collectivism vs. individualism is an important question, as are questions of what to do in the face of existential risks and how to balance ideals and reality. The story is very genuine, and I found parts of the Judged and Tired endings genuinely touching. But it just crumbled in execution, largely I suspect due to the creator's overwhelming bias towards individualism; the story was supposed to weigh it against collectivism, but it could never do that fairly. Maybe that is an intractable problem with the way we tell stories, which present an inherent divide between The Main Characters Who Matter and the The Background Characters Who Don't? It's hard to care about the collective when they are a (literally, in this case) faceless mass that speaks in one (whiny) voice.

Well… picking up random games from my wishlist paid off. I expected this to be Anonymous Agony levels of self-masturbatory teen power fantasy…
But it’s not – sure, the protagonist is an ass-hole, but he gets some consequences from it. He’s also not all that powerful, despite what the dream sequence might have suggested to you. He’s a kid with bad upbringing living in a world currently going through an apocalypse.
Speaking of the apocalypse, the story is dark – humanity barely ‘survives’ in a land covered by demonic fog. The fog kills you if you go too deep into it and there are also monsters living in it. There’s some fancy torches burning with a blue fire and protect humans but they aren’t exactly mobile… also some prophecy says that a revenant will destroy the world. Add to that knights being chosen in a fight to the death and it gets pretty grimdark.
You don’t just control the edgy edgelord Aeyr though – you get many party members from different walks of life(and races). The game switches point of view between Aeyr’s party and his childhood friend’s party every chapter, showing you how they both grow and change. I’ve found Mia’s chapters to be harder – she and her party have no healing skills and there’s very few items to go around at first. 
Speaking of items that mechanic is weird – there are backpacks all around the world… but you can’t see what’s inside. And you have an item limit… and SOMETIMES the backpacks disappear once you examine them, but not always. I have no idea how that works. Still, you can get yourself locked if you aren’t careful with health management at first… because AT FIRST shops are rare and backpacks are too. At the later parts I started ignoring backpacks since I was always well-stocked. The balance needs some work I guess.
The art style is edgy, maybe slightly childishly so – store screenshots show you exactly what you’ll get; things like a crucified dude that buffs enemies or a half-bug dominatrix. Some people will hate it, I loved it. Kinda reminded me of Black Souls and GOING TO ALICE.
The combat is tactical… explaining it would be hard since basically every character has extremely unique way of fighting. Luckily the game has a guide you can access at almost any time to read those mechanics. Could have used it during battle but unfortunately that’s not an option. I liked the combat, though sometimes I felt like certain party members were useless for an entire chapter, just to regain use later. Once again – balancing(mostly of resistances of enemies).
Well, what else can I say really – a good, well written grimdark fantasy. A bit edgy with a few typos, but I had fun. I have a few questions like how do i get other endings, but I’m not sure if I’ll get an answer… but that’s what I get for playing games with at the time of writing one review lol.
10/10 – hope I can kill God in the sequel… or in some secret ending lol

This game is not worth more that $3.00. It is an adorable little city builder, but there are no quality of life features. There's not even a settings page: No way to change the mouse sensitivity (It's different from your desktop sensitivity somehow), no way to disable to voice-over or the music individually, no way to change the keyboard bindings. As far as I can tell, there are no key bindings. This entire game is played with the mouse and the escape key.

I don't think the game even understands itself. It states that you are rebuilding a war-torn town, but you just start with a blank slate. No war-torn town just holding on by a thread, just 6000 money, 400 wood, and eight people that I guess just exist. Buildings don't even consume resources: it costs 600 wood to build a sawmill, and then from that point forward it just gives you 400 planks every minute. It is impossible to balance your resources, because the game consists of nothing but gains.

IMO: Don't waste your money on this game. You'll get more from drawing a city on a piece of graph paper.

Edit: I just read the full description for this game at the bequest of a commenter, and learned that there is one keyboard shortcut built-in: pressing the 'r' key brings the last built building to your hand, rather than you returning to the menu to select it. I have no way to test this as I already refunded the game, but based on the description other games do it better. Most games will have you hold the shift key to place multiple buildings, because building a dozen of one building shouldn't require a dozen keypresses.

The Good:
-I am personally a fan of the art style, i know not everyone is but chances are if you clicked on this game you're not one of those people regardless. There are some things i feel need to be cleaned up (the rain is seizure inducing) but otherwise i do feel like there is a pleasant feel to the art.
-When you are walking nearby points of interest there will be a faint "ghost"-like imagine on your screen that shows which direction you need to walk. I liked this as i found myself walking through the forest and wondering where the hell the town was at.
-Walking into buildings is seamless. You click onto the building and you're inside without loading screens. This may not be the case for everything such as dungeons but unfortunately i was unable to make it that far. So lets talk about whats bad.

The Bad:
-The font is borderline unreadable. I know they're trying to achieve a certain aesthetic with the font but if i need to slow down my normal reading speed to read dialogue between my character and a towns person that is not a good thing. It makes interacting with people/things a tedious task rather than an enjoyable one.
-Click to move. Some people may enjoy it, and ive played games in the past, Runescape for example, that do click to move pretty well. This isnt one of them. You dont have to take it away but WASD movement should be an option or honestly the default.
-Zero guidance. I hope this is just the case because its Early Access, and I dont necessarily need any hand-holding but i need some sort of instruction on what i should be doing at least to start. There is zero explanation on what to do, what any buttons are (had to spam click all the buttons on my keyboard just to see if any of them even do anything), and anytime i walked through the forest i had little midgets run at me, jump on my head, and take away my health with seemingly no way to defend myself. 

Quality of Life Improvements:
-Show keybinds and allow players to change keybinds. This one is pretty self explanatory. 
-Character Customization. Let me name my character and design how they look. Again hopefully this is just this way because its EA, but a game like this definitely needs to allow the player to put themselves in the world and not just play cookie-cutter premade characters the devs made up.

TL;DR The game has the right idea and seems like they have some good ideas still to implement (skill-trees and such). If you have $10 to throw at it go ahead and check it out and support development, but dont expect a finished game.

Finally finished part one and am excited to play part two when it is released. Few things I thought could be improved or suggestions for part two:
- The main thing that I found odd was the level difficulty from one to the next. In some ways it is quite nice that after a harder level you get a little respite with an easier one, but it does feel like you aren't progressing through the game when you aren't getting to use more of the things you've learnt through earlier levels. So, I'm not saying don't have easier levels popped in (especially ones more about story as they are fun), but it would be good to have more of the tasks and difficulties in the levels as you progress so you feel the challenge and feel like you are getting better at the game as you go. I think that would be important for part two.
- I'd like the menu screen to select the level you want to be easier to use, as I have to use my touchscreen to get it to swipe right and it is a bit clunky even doing that. A simple arrow to the next list would probably suffice.
- I like the quiet and creepy sound effects etc but would be nice if the music could build a little more suspense, especially on racier levels.
- For part two, I'd like to maybe see some more items that have other effects, rather than just gems to collect.
Hopefully these comments will help to shape make the rest of the game a great experience for players.

Finally, just wanted to say I'm not a huge PC game player and was worried I wouldn't be able to play it well, but I found this one easy to get in to without making it too easy or boring, so great job Jelliebox! Bring on part two!

While the game features impressive graphics and an eerie atmosphere, the overall experience is marred by numerous bugs and performance issues. Frequent crashes make it difficult to play for extended periods, and the gameplay itself can induce motion sickness for some players.

The AI is lackluster, with enemies often acting in predictable, uninspired ways or not acting at all. The needs you to kill 400 zombies to progress the story and similar mandatory tasks feel tedious and repetitive, making the game more of a grind than an enjoyable challenge.

Some parts of the game are very dark, and you don't always have a flashlight, which can make navigation frustrating and add to the overall difficulty in an unpleasant way.

A particularly frustrating issue is the erratic mouse behavior. Despite playing with very low mouse sensitivity, the cursor sometimes randomly turns 90-180 degrees, making navigation extremely difficult and disorienting.

"AFTERLIFE - Killing Death" feels like a diamond in the rough. It had great potential, but the developer seems to have skipped the final finishing touches needed to make it truly shine. While the potential for a good horror shooter is evident, "AFTERLIFE - Killing Death" is currently not worth the investment. Hopefully, future updates will address these issues and refine this unpolished gem.

A fun off-the-wall game (Sort of Jazzpunk + Serious Sam if you need points of reference) that manages to be a decent sort of old-school FPS as well as a decently funny game. The gameplay isn't particularly deep, but the random weapon swap (a bar counts down to your swap once you start firing) keeps you experimenting and using guns that would normally be tossed aside for a standard machinegun/shotgun pairing. The Slide-kick is gratifying and becomes incredibly useful for some of the harder areas once you learn to use it right. The difficulty is kind of all over the place. Mostly a decent balance where keeping quick and aggressive works, though there were significant spikes and once particular perspective shift that makes a certain section much harder than it would otherwise be. 

Not every joke lands, but I suppose that's somewhat expected for a Mel Brooks style "Try everything you can think of and see what works" style of comedy. The throw away gags that NPCs in levels say and the goofy mission objectives/descriptions managed to get chuckles consistently, and some of the late-game plot made me smirk and laugh from time to time.

Gun Ugly runs about 2-3 hours depending on difficulty/skill and is well worth the $5 it runs when not on sale.

Oogy: Can You Help is a wonderful addition to the indie game scene. Its soundtrack will get stuck in your head for hours! The storyline, dialogue, and characters are whimsical and unafraid to be cute, although they're not without a darker undertone and a satisfying sense of mystery. Each card was clearly designed with care, with frequently hilarious flavor text and pitch-perfect illustrations. I liked how everything in the house has come alive, from lamps to earmuffs, each imbued with personality, leading to some real moral questions as one decides whether to drain their health or give them a good clean. The game mechanics itself is pretty clever, easy to pick up, and ripe for expansion. It'll be interesting to see some of the new features that are in the works: it's a tricky business trying to make sure a card game is balanced, and there appear to be a weekly stream of improvements. For instance, I like the recent addition of being able to remix your opponent's deck, and I'm curious to see what the new customization features will be like: I imagine someday there will be online multiplayer! All in all, Oogy's world is definitely one worth immersing yourself in--I recommend giving it a try!

Found this game randomly on YouTube, played the demo and then bought it. Lets make no mistakes about it. This is a remake of the original Ninja Gaiden for the NES. Character names are changed, but that's what this is. I grew up playing the original so seeing this hit me too hard in the nostalgic feels for me to pass up. The game is good I must say. Not perfect, but nothing that I think would keep me from enjoying the game. I heard this was developed by a single person. If that's true, this is quite an impressive effort and I'm reviewing the game based on that information. I will update this review if I need to. 

Pros
Graphics are actually really good. Music is all remixes from the original game. All good. (Release the soundtrack please.) Controls are responsive (See Cons for a big issue though) and I like the addition of the double jump/glide mechanic. There's also a kick and a downward air slash that's not in the original game. 

Neutral
Difficulty - Feel like the difficulty ramps up a little hard. First stage is easy, second stage..., not so much LOL. It's not too bad, but it's noticeable. Also, when you die you have to start the stage from the beginning. But if you die on a boss, you start from that boss thankfully. Also, time is a little bit of an issue. Try not to spend too much time on any area, just try to keep moving and you'll be fine. Again it's not too bad but something I noticed. I died twice already because time ran out.

Cons
The biggest con by far is the fact that this game only supports analog controls. You cannot used a D-pad. I urge the developer to add this as soon as possible. The people that would be interested in a game like this are people that played the original at a time where there were no such thing as analog controls. I can still play the game of course, but there are times where I'm facing one direction and I let go of the analog stick and it turns me around and I'm facing the wrong way. You might say that this is a problem with my analog stick and you might be correct, but I really shouldn't be forced to use it. There are also a few glitches, like getting stuck on or in a wall. I've also gotten stuck on an invincible wall and after jumping, I can then pass through said wall. It doesn't happen enough to ruin the game. Just annoying. Lastly, there was a collectible item that somehow got moved into the foreground a little bit. When this happened, I was unable to pick it up. So it looks like some objects can move into the 3rd dimension, but the hero we are controlling cannot. This only happened to me once so far though.

Overall, I recommend this game. It's fun, challenging, looks good, sounds good and for $4 or $5, I definitely think it's worth it.

I own and fly several drones, have 100s of hours in other sims such as Velocidrone, Liftoff and Liftoff Micro Drones with my favorite being Liftoff due to the balance of realistic physics, map variety, customization, and ease of use. I'm about an hour into TRYP FPV, and while I was feeling a bit put off at first, [b]I am very impressed with this sim.[/b]

First off, the [b]graphics are unmatched[/b]. Being able to fly a simulator that looks like this is incredible. The maps are MASSIVE with small points of interest spread throughout. A grand city skyline turns into a small cafe with chairs and tables on the ground level. [b]Along with the capability to chase objects such as cars, bikes, and parachutes, TRYP gives different types of pilots with differing levels of experience the environments they are looking for.[/b]

Physics are quite good. I would say that right off the rip, the [b]physics feel a bit floaty and the quads seem a bit fast[/b]. I fly a 4S 5in, so maybe that is why. Also, something just doesn't feel right with the camera angle. I adjust the angle to a similar value in other sims and it just feels slightly off, not a big deal. With that being said, the customization provided by the game for the drones, physics, etc allowed me to [b]cater the experience to what I felt was more realistic and closely matched my quads.[/b] One caveat to this is I can't seem to find an Angle Strength option, only limit..slightly annoying.

Users that are looking for a variety of parts for building might be a little let down with TRYP. [b]Due to early access, the builder is really lacking in parts[/b]. As of writing this review, there are about 5 frames (smallest looks 3 inch), 4 motors, 4 props, 2 batteries, and some action cams to choose from. [b]While the variety of the items themselves are limited, each part has a plethora of customization sliders[/b] from color, weight, length, width, etc. However, adjusting dimensions of the parts did not seem to alter the appearance only flight characteristics of the quad.

Overall, if you're looking for a new sim with [b]good physics, a customizable experience, and insane environments and scenes, TRYP is a easy recommend for me.[/b] Be wary of the early access label, as it is just that. I would like to see the sim priced at $15, but compared to $16.99, it is pinching pennies. [b]Good price for a good sim. 7.5/10[/b]

Beneath the thick skin of the vibe lives a humble but effective RPG/Action/Roguelike/Platformer/Adventure hybrid. Various random ability upgrades cause your playthroughs to vary in style and strategy. IE. Magic shot is great for clearing mobs at range, magic rain can delete entire packs and bosses with a well-timed hit, and magic blades are the most efficient for conserving energy.

There's a lot of progression to unlock in-game, with collectable badges able to be invested into a talent tree, and then later a paragon board, to increase your character's various stats. An exhaustive list of items, with effects that alter your gameplay (and which eventually become permanent as you collect souls), adds to the amount of collectables and customization possible in your character. Effects such as explosive kills, meteor summons, gold multipliers, and combo extensions feel great to experiment with, especially after you spend the time to venture off the beaten path to discover them.

There's also collectible cards which I have yet to get all of. I hope these feed into some kind of mini game or something down the line. Overall there's plenty of stuff to chase and pine for, which brings the completionist playtime up to a respectable size considering the price, and also that you will probably tack on a few extra hours just dying needless deaths because you were too busy trying to pull off some dumb maneuver (such as grand slam ground pound an obscenely large pack of enemies into dust).

I knew of this game as early as when it was on Kickstarter, back when I was captivated by the writing style of the demo, and now having bought the game on first launch, I am more than pleased with my purchase.

If you are into romance-focused visual novels, then this game may not be for you.
But if you enjoy plot-heavy stories in a fantasy setting with supernatural powers, then this is your cup of tea.

Not to say the romance is not well written (interactions are wholesome and cute), but with how action filled the story becomes, particularly in the later chapters, romance is usually not on the forefront. But it didn't really matter, because your attention is kept busy alternating between the main cast and the diverse set of side characters.

One thing I love most is that, depending on the route you are on, different side characters get their time to shine. They are crucial to the plot, as well as allowing you to understand more about Sheryl and the guys. Sooner or later, you become as endeared to the secondary cast of characters as the MC and the LIs, so much so I much enjoyed the Common Route (labelled as such by the official guide), aka the friendship route where Sheryl does not end up with any of the characters, but that does not make this route any less interesting than the other routes.

As for our protagonist, Sheryl is a terrific heroine. Not only is she not a damsel in distress, she also fights at the frontlines as one of their strongest. But it is her mental strength that is even more impressive. While she is not without flaws, you see her grow throughout the routes, in which not even her phobia or grief hold her back from what needs to be done.

The good (apart from those already mentioned): Needless to say, the art is beautiful. The music is fitting, especially in fight scenes where it really gets your adrenaline pumping. The pacing is good. The first half of the story is lighthearted to allow you to get a grip of the setting and the characters; while the latter half picks up its pacing and rushes full speed ahead without making it feel forced, with the earlier chapters preparing you for what is to come. The world-building is also wonderful. The background of the LIs is quite diverse as well, so completing each of their route contributed to a rather complete big picture.

The bad: Something minor to nitpick at is that there is a fair amount of grammatical mistakes (in Sin, Hiryuu and Osamu's route in particular). Another thing is that I wished there is a clearer indication of whose route you are on. But that is only because I am used to either having a status screen which shows the affection bar, or seeing the face of the guy whose route you are on at the chapter divider once the story branches. If you use a guide though, then it does not matter.

Lastly, I honestly desperately wish for a sequel/fandisc. I would love to see more of how everyone's shin work. In addition, some routes (e.g. Fraser and Osamu) have a happy ending that didn't seem satisfying at all, so a continuation would be good. And of course, with how attached I became to the side characters, I definitely wish more of them had their own route (even if platonic), like Director Cloise, who ends up becoming my favourite character, and also Tsurugi and Blake. Or it would be nice to have a prequel to before the start of this game, as in the early days of the academy or even before that, like how the senior members each came to meet the Director. It would be interesting if we could know about the CR member that went on missions abroad and the one mentioned to have died early in the game. i also felt like it is a shame there was not a witch LI considering the races mentioned.

I tried to be as vague as possible to avoid spoilers. Some things are better experienced after all (like how the romance developed between Sheryl and each LI and how their relationship dynamic differs accordingly), but if this is the least bit helpful to whoever is reading, then I am glad.

Thank you, Raikon Kitsune, for an amazing game.

It also has 6 Love Interest that all brings something different in their own routes, along with a 'common route' route. Now I will warn you this. This is more plot heavy and actiony and it does not help that Sheryl herself is...herself so do not go to this game expecting lots of romance and lovey dovey stuff. That said, I liked how each route helped nurture Sheryl's relationship with each Love Interest in a natural way. I guess if I have a minor complaint, I do wished the endings for each route, specifically the good endings weren't so open ended (especially for a few) but I am hearing this game might have an epilogue game so I will cross my fingers for it to be a reality.

This game also has a lot of side characters that are prominent and given a chance to shine in each route and some adds to the plot themselves so they don't end up making me wonder "why are you here?". 

Overall, this was a great game and I do hope there's more left after this.

I find the protagonist to be the most important piece of a visual novel for me to enjoy and Sheryl is definitely a protagonist I've absolutely loved going through the story, especially because she is quite unique compared to most visual novel protagonists. She is intelligent, strong minded and scarred from her past but still able to grow, learn and change based on choices and expirience as well as positive and negative influence of NPCs and the love interests. One negative thing I have to mention between all the positive expiriences with this visual novel is, that there are quite some typos and grammar issues within the story, though it diddn't bother me much I know that others might be irritated. 

In the end I highly reccomend this visual novel to everybody that enjoys reading long, eventful fantasy storys with a touch of romance, unexpected twist and turns as well as plenty of choices to be made and great art.

Remei no Gakuen is for sure an amazing game. Background are just stunning and detailed. Music fit very well (Shimmering Star is the best one in this game). Price may be scary in countries that don't use euro/USD every day (including myself) so I recommend to play demo and think about it a little.

Main And Background Characters.
It has a very well written (both, background and main) characters that in each route have time to shine and its very refreshing if you're used to games that are only focused on MC(and LI if chosen). Everyone has their flaws, moments and aren't made to push plot further or development on MC(and LI if chosen) and that is just amazing itself. Heroine
Sheryl isn't that silent, uwu owo girly girl that will let everyone step on her, yet she will still help them. Kotaku's full quote: "Cattails looks like Stardew Valley, except cats."

That review is for the original Cattails, not Cattails: Wildwood Story, I don't know why that quote is used in the review section of this game.

It is pixel art and you can plant a few crops... that does not make it like Stardew Valley. Sadly farming is probably the least engaging part of Cattails: Wildwood Story.

That isn't to say that it's a bad game. It's just not a game that I enjoyed playing for an extended period of time.

Farming- minimal crops, not season dependent. I only grew healing herbs because good luck surviving the dungeon areas, it's brutal at times.

Relationships- befriend cats, get married, have kittens. I got far enough to get married but I couldn't even make it through the first year. I quit the second of Winter.

Soundtrack- some tracks are quite nice and others were very repetitive.

Graphics - the portraits are beautiful. I played the original Cattails and I immediately noticed an improvement. I wasn't a fan of the rest of the artwork in the game though. It wasn't bad it just wasn't for me.

Story - for me it was not strong enough for me to want to replay it

World - the world is huge and I had fun exploring except that it was so empty.

Combat - I did not care for the combat system. I wanted a way to heal myself without having to just grow herbs over and over and over. Or overpay for healing.

Money - I found it a tedious grind to make money.

Mining - I LOVE mining in Stardew, and was looking forward to it here.  I hated that I had to go in 25 level increments for my progress to be saved. I cleared the first mine and 75% of the second mine and it just wasn't fun. A quarter of my inventory was filled with food, another quarter healing items

Buddies - It was cool I could bring a cat along with me but they were kind of dumb and kept running headfirst into the poison. So I had to heal them...over and over.

It's not a terrible game. While it has elements that are similar to Stardew Valley on paper,  it really isn't anything like it once you start playing.

I would highly recommend buying this game when it's on sale.

[h1]Full Review:[/h1]

This is a quick visual novel, but a cute one!

All three romanceable characters are sweethearts. And they all have their own struggles beneath the figurative masks they wore, pain or doubt they don't let show. I especially love Vendel! I was delighted to realize he's a troll, and that he has a TAIL! He's so adorable and charismatic and sweet and has this hidden sadness and loneliness that made me feel for him. But like I said, I liked the others too. Phyllis is kind-hearted and gracious. Lief is a bit obsessive about their work, but a sweet, passionate person.

The romances felt a bit rushed since the game is so short, but still cute enough to make me smile and feel the warm fuzzies.

I also really like that you can choose romance or friendship, so that you can see all the routes in a way that feels genuine to you. And whether you choose romance or friendship, you still get the same story and the same happy ending, just the relationship is different.

There are three routes (one for each romanceable character), and though they share the same intro, the rest is different. They have the same general plot problem that needs solving, but the way you discover and solve the problem is different. So there's not much repeated text, which is nice.

The only choices are which character route to go with, and whether to make it romance or friendship. But that's ok, this is a visual novel that's about getting to know the characters and experiencing a story with them.

The fantasy setting is fun. Not much world-building, but there's magic and trolls and faeries, and I enjoyed the little mentions of how they use magic in their everyday lives.

The music is perfect. It really enhances the emotion, whether it's a cutesy butterflies romantic moment, a serious emotional connection, danger, etc.

The character art is lovely (though you only get art for the main three and one other), and the backgrounds are pretty. There's also a CG to unlock for each route.

It took me 1.5 hours to finish my first playthrough and about 45 minutes to an hour each for the other two. About 4 hours total when you add in going back to see the friendships endings and whatnot.

Overall, quick and simple, but cute with pretty art, nice music, and characters who are sweethearts!

Interesting premise! It's a decent enough game, nice genre-mix but some improvements could take it to the next level.

-Art-
Firstly, I think the art needs a little touch up. As it is, it makes the game feel cheaper than it has to be. The first thing I noticed were the edges, they could be smoother. The UI art sticks out like a sore thumb in the corner, they look like placeholder elements. 

IMO, the ships could have better complementary colors, I can't really say exactly what it is but the colors kind of make it look off and cheap. Maybe slight changes in the color tone would make it feel just right. I can say that when looking at the store page, color decisions kind of put me off but the gameplay ideas drew me in.

I think the ship shapes are great, I had no problems with that.

-Gameplay-
There are great ideas here and it's fine as it is but IMO this game could [b]embrace the shmup[/b] more. In a lot of ways, it could feel faster. I think everything could move faster and it would be fine. Given the stationary position of the player (which is good and what makes it unique) [b]adding a defensive right click option[/b] (e.g. similar to what those green enemies in the first few zones drop off- like a temporary small shield field) would add new depth and allow the game to be faster with more enemies. The only time I felt the game came close to this was the trap event. I think the whole game can be like that and get there faster. I started out with normal which was too easy except for the first boss and the trap event. I tried the hardest difficulty and even that took a while to start up. 

I like the ideas with the population a lot, but I'd like to see more interactivity. For example I'm not sure how much pop health affects anything, I ran most of the game at 0 health but nothing seemed to happen? I assume that's why disease outbreak events happened later on? But they were easily manageable so I never felt it was an issue. Besides, there is no real way to consistently increase it besides the hospital ship which requires an upgrade to increase life, but even then it only happens at increments of 1 with a 40% chance. Maybe I was unlucky but I didn't even get any tech points until like level 30. This is what I mean when the game can be faster, if these points mattered more and we could interact more with them the game would feel faster. I have similar thoughts on happiness.

More abundant and frequent unlocks (besides ships, gun types, flotilla types, defensive options, energy options)  would be nice. What makes a good roguelike is the sense of frequent progress. Hades does this very well, obviously it's an unfair comparison but I think its design philosophy can teach a lot. FTL is the closer inspiration and that has a similar formula for unlocks, but you can also buy guns within a run in that so you get the sense of accomplishment and progress that way.

-Soundtrack-
It's okay and appropriate for what it is. Obviously budget is what it is, but with a more faster gameplay a more upbeat track would complement it nicely but I can't say much on that.

-Conclusion-
Overall I like the ideas, there is fun to be had in the game, but it can do more with what it has. Honestly, this is like a game Ssethtzeentach would review years down the line and make it pop off, but it needs some improvements to make it stand out a bit more.

This game has many problems, technical and mechanically.

For one, the game is locked at 30fps. There is no option to change it, in fact there is absolutely zero graphics options at all. The game runs in window mode, I assume is 1080, and to fullscreen it you have to Alt+Enter. It's not a looker, jagged edges everywhere, jerky controls, no shadows. The animations are alright but the main character (Sachi) moves terribly slow (We'll get to why that matters later).

The game itself is a life sim, much akin to Princess Maker games of old. The issue with this one is it's extremely simplified, so much so that I'd be hesitant to call it a 'sim' at all. There are quite a few endings that are all determined by her stats at the end of the 10th day with one bad ending and one neutral ending. The neutral ending is the all around general ending if you didn't put her stats in a narrow window of points and you'll probably see it a lot. With Princess Maker you had a specific number of actions for the week, in this game though you have a time limit that counts down the moment your intervention begins for the day, which is pretty terrible on it's own but there's more. Not only are you timed, but you also need to pick up 'pages' to even have the ability to get endings, while it is possible to pick up every page and open every ending in a playthrough, you're going to have nearly no time to actually increase her stats because her movement is so extremely slow. She walks to an object, stands there a second, interacts with said object, removes herself from object, stands there a second THEN moves on to the next task. Considering the time limit forcing you to feel rushed, she is not rushed at all. Thankfully her moving to an interaction tallies the stat increase immediately.

The story is pretty good though, Sachi is an endearing character and her struggles are going to be relatable to nearly everyone that has been college age, but the mechanics themselves prevent you from feeling anything for the character and her dilemma after your first playthrough when the game devolves into a numbers game with no emotional connection.
The objects she can use to increase her stats are many, and more unlock as days progress (Under the assumption she buys them and brings them home, like manga books and candy) and nearly all of the objects do a solid increase a stat and more often than not in multiple stats. There are very few objects that actually decrease a stat, and those usually give a hefty increase in something else. You might be thinking, "That's a good thing!" but then you get to the ending requirements. In Princess Maker type of games, the variance in stats required for endings are usually pretty large, which would allow you to play through them twice the same exact way and still get a different ending, here that is not the case. Every ending has a specific set of all five stats with a variance of 20 to achieve, go over? You're not getting that ending. Considering a lot of items increase her stats by 10 or so points and some items increasing up to three stats, it quickly becomes problematic. You find half way in that you're over in points in a certain stat to get an ending you were after, and using the item to lower that stat would raise another stat significantly higher than you could fix so you go "How about another ending" well you missed the page a previous day to unlock the ending you could try for now. That's a common occurance in my time with it.

The lewd portions people may be interested in nearly don't exist. You can peep on her in the shower and see her butt but that's about it, the 'personal massager' is not the type of massager most would assume by it's look. As she's slowly making her way around her room, certain scenerios will happen where she'll do something clumsy and you will get a QTE in order to see her panties, but the issue with this is, since she's so incredibly slow you'll probably be playing at 4x speed (You can change speed with a button) and when the QTE's happen, they'll also play in 4x speed which makes them unenjoyable. You can also do some spectral ghost touching on her, but it only amounts to her being spooked and covering herself.

Overall it's a good story and good idea severely hampered by it's mechanics that fails to reward you for doing well every step of the way by refusing endings for having Sachi 'overqualified'. Zero graphics options. Zero emotional attachment after your first playthrough. Can not recommend.

13 Steps is without a doubt a great indie horror title, full of intrigue and mysteries to uncover. I highly recommend to anyone looking to have a few hours of spooky fun this halloween!

I've put a few hours in now, unlocked three of the endings (so far), and I can say I'm thoroughly enjoying my time. It is spooky, intriguing and rewarding all at the same time. The atmosphere and sound design is very immersive, keeping you on edge as you solve the puzzles and explore the eerie EOS buildings.

The premise centres around tracking your steps as you attempt to escape a time loop in a remote research facility. But it's not as easy as it sounds, you have to use the data-logs you find along the way to point you in the right direction. Not to mention the multiple shark animatronics that stalk the premises. They will appear when you least expect it, leading to a handful of restarted loops (oops). 

Obtaining upgrades and useful tools as you explore, such as the shadowstep device (short range teleport), help you to reach difficult sections of the map and hidden lore or access codes. Hidden plushie shark collectables are dotted around the facility, giving you small boons as you find more. Just make sure to walk by an inventory saving machine, because you might lose some if you find yourself in the jaws of their big brothers!

Be warned, your first time escaping the time loop might be deceiving...

All in all this is a pretty polished little title, I couldn't recommend it more! I'm going to get back to finding all the secrets and alternate endings!

You know when you've made a mistake and you can take either bite the bullet and wildly commit (often very fun & adrenaline fuelled) or take a step back to rethink your approaches (at the cost of limited time :O).
Once the step timer depletes and you start getting desperate/taking risks, that's when the real fun begins.

The whole game runs smooth as hell and I highly recommend everyone give it a go to experience super a new super polished indie release.

So after playing for a few more hours, I wanted to add that this might be my all time favorite indie horror game. The fact that it still only has three reviews feels like a minor injustice.

This game is criminally underrated. Your Spider is undoubtedly one of the best horror-themed puzzle games I have ever tried, maybe even the second best (the first is and will always be DARQ). This game is very slow-paced and very challenging, it requires A LOT of patience, but it offers some of the most clever and brilliant puzzles I have ever seen. And speaking of atmosphere and world design, it is very hard even to describe how good they are. The plot itself is very shallow, maybe even trivial, but the setting, the narration, the colors, the sounds, the scenery, the creatures, the retro and vaguely steampunk technology, everything here screams "masterpiece". It's like... a Tim Burton's movie filtered through the lens of Silent Hill 2. Yes, it's exactly as cool as it sounds. Of course, there are some flaws, even important ones. For example, a few boss fights are unnecessarily long and tedious, with no variation, and the controls of the spider are waaaay too stiff, especially in those situations where speed and accuracy are required. But, dear God, everything else is so damn good! It is literally a shame that, so far, this game has not received an ounce of the visibility it deserves, because, for me, it is as good as the famous LIMBO, or the equally famous Little Nightmares, if not even better. The price is more than honest considering both the length (6-8 hours) and the quality (truly astonishing considering the SOLO dev), so I STRONGLY recommend this game to everyone, even to players who are not much comfortable with horror themes (no cheap and meaningless jumpscares). In particular, I recommend this game to players who like to use their gray cells, and who enjoy simple but very emotional and impactful narration. And of course to all lovers of jumper spiders! <3 :D
Cheers guys!

Alright, this is one of those games that I happened to stumble upon and see some form of potential for it. It also happened to be on sale so of course i bought it and played it. There is an over abundance of problems, but I'll just start with what's entirely  in game for now. 
The first Problem is the complete lack of settings and options for gameplay, movement, and graphics. It's a game that only supports controller based movement which means that it's incredibly disorienting to try and move around at first. Besides that, no audio options? The music is great for ambiance but takes away from the "realistic" style the dev is claiming to go for, on top of the music/ambiance only serving to artificially heighten the tension. As for the gameplay itself, it feels like a bunch of half baked ideas put together. The "pockets" where you can place your items and weapons are horrible to use, usually resulting in the item I try to place in them not registering and falling on the ground at inopportune times, and then couple that with the pockets jumping around trying to follow your character's forward face means that you can't even grab what you're reaching for half the time unless you angle yourself and headset in a weird way. 
The gunplay that they're trying to say is realistic is barely there - pistols have frequent jams, which I genuinely don't know if it's meant to be a mechanic or if it's a bug, but it only happens with the pistols. The other weapons feel pretty standard, albeit inaccurate and cumbersome with how it locks your off hand to the front grip whenever you hold it. 
Another reason i have to call the gameplay lacking is simply due to no melee capabilities at all. I'm not sure if the dev is wanting to implement the mechanic or not? They've responded to a different review asking why they would need to melee since there's enough one handed weapons that are easy to grab? That's barely an argument since if I ran out of ammo I'd gladly use it as a makeshift bludgeoning device if need be. 
Yet another reason is how linear the gameplay feels. There's no real feeling of progress since it's basically just a hallway you go through and then back track occasionally. Besides that the enemies are strange, ranging from genuinely interesting zombie design to Mr. skeleton coughs out skulls at you. That also is kinda of a theme with the enemy attacks, just coughing blood on you by the looks of it. I'd say that I guess it looks like they're biting you, but with how far away they are, no. They just cough on you until you die abruptly since there's not really much in terms of a damage indicator.
And finally, the biggest problem I have is the fact that the developer seems to hate any criticism involving the game. Theres a few other reviews where the dev kinda just insults the reviewer for "not playing it right" or saying things like "this isn't a casual game and you should've known that if you read the store page". Even called one reviewer a liar for addressing a possible bug in the game.

While the concept of a 'realistic and serious' zombie shooter is a good, tried and true idea for virtual reality games, I can't recommend this game when the main idea of handling a firearm accurately and realistically in this game is having to manually fiddle and drop a magazine on a table to get it at the slightly jaunted angle needed to slide it into the magazine well while you're being spat and chewed on. In addition, the overall movement scheme is controller-based locomotion, with no ability to change these settings whatsoever, there's not even a settings menu to lower sound effects, or increase the smooth turning speed, being left at a slow-motion turn when you need it most.

I can understand a game being easy to play, and hard to master, but this game seems to follow the trend of being difficult for the sake of being difficult and even clunky.

In addition, even with a 3060 ROG gaming laptop that runs every other VR title at a smooth, and crisp 90 frames, this game suffers from stutters at the slightest turn of a corner, and the gore effects while absolutely stunning and visceral, seem to play a heavy hand in the loss of performance.

So unfortunately, Putridness VR to me will stay just that. Utterly putrid, and reeking of development-hell.

Perhaps when more ease-of-access options become available and the game becomes better polished and of a higher caliber than a 9x18 bullet, I'll give this game another go.

What can I say about the game.  This was actually a fairly hard game to review.  I fully played through both chapters that are currently available.  

First, the good:  The game runs very smoothly.  There are not many bugs or glitches, which is a very nice aspect for a game.  The atmosphere is nice looking.  For those that complain about reused assets, it just needs to be accepted that not everyone has the time, money or skill to create their own everything from the ground up.  Indie devs need to utilize common assets and I'm cool with that.  The main things for me are story, game play and the overall atmosphere.  Also, how to smartly manage the scares can be a major addition of points or subtraction.

With that being said, as of now, the story is very confusing.  I feel like there really isn't one beyond the guy was on his way home, got into an accident and is now stuck here in this house.  As of writing this, there are only 2 chapters, so it may/will get cleared up later on.  It is early access so I won't be so harsh on that.  There's really nothing explaining what is going on and you have to interpret things from the videos you see at the end of each chapter.  You don't really find any notes or hints as to why this place is so messed up.  The beginning makes no sense, but I can ignore it cause it's just there to get you to the house, but you hit a tree right next to a random alcohol shack that's on the other side of a river, past a cemetery that's attached to a mansion.....why?  Who builds a random shack in the middle of nowhere that is attached to a mansion?  why was there a campfire there?  It just makes no logical sense, but the main story is the house anyway. 

The AI is a bit basic, which makes the evil girl fairly simple to avoid.  As far as chases go, after you figure out how it moves and that you are faster, there's no real tension moving around.  There are a few good jump scares and that aspect of the game is great.  There's some hiccups with things like shooting and such, hiding in areas and moving around, but nothing drastic.  I personally feel like they could have done more with less.  The gun, the camera the lighter the flashlight, I just feel like it was put in cause they could, not that it pertains to the game or story.  It's just too much and it makes no sense why each one shows up at each point.  It's as if they wanted to include it all, cause they could, and really doesn't pertain to much.  

I can't really justify the 15.99 price point at this time.  It's a bit much for this game, but overall it's not bad and it has potential.  At this time I'd have to say I wouldn't recommend it MAINLY because of the price.  An incomplete game with a few quirks and has no real replay-ability.....  If the story was amazing, clear and formed early, then maybe I could, and this has no reflection on the work the devs have done.   It is a promising and good game, just not $16 dollars.  

If there was more promise, maybe, but at this time, I can't justify it at all.  Maybe $7 or even MAYYYYYBBEEE $10, but I've played a lot of Indie horror games,  some good, a lot bad.  The price is just too much for what you are getting.

Outside of that, it really is a pretty fluid game, they did a good job for the most part, but it is a very simple game with very basic gameplay, map, and a very unclear story.  If the game was complete, I may be able to see the price point, but as of now, we don't know where the game is going, have no idea about what is going on now and I can't recommend it for the price.

You can check it out for yourself here with a fuller breakdown and decide if you want to pay and see if it get's better since it is early access, but that is a decision you have to make as a horror gaming fan.

Half an hour into the game, I can tell there is a decent amount of bang for the buck. I have yet to try ObjectN and all the other Russian FPS games on Steam. Chernobyl Trap is pretty self-explanatory: you're in the Chernobyl zone, shooty bang bang.

Pros
* Low-hassle setup; reasonable install size, good default mouse sensitivity and controls
* Shooting feels good
* What may be a compelling story about hazmat guys covering up zombies or something

Cons
* Your dude gets out of breath after sprinting 50 feet and takes a long time to recover
* Rendering seems to be fill-bound with a fair bit of overdraw. Other budget FPS games made in Unity (like Monument) suffer from the same issue, so be prepared for worse performance than the mid-2000s graphics deserve.
* Aiming down the rifle sights seems to be off horizontally by a few pixels.
* First couple areas are deceptively easy, then a significant difficulty spike when you're in the woods surrounded by dead shot hazmat dudes

Overall it's worth playing. I prefer this game's believable setting over a Doom-inspired fever dream, and even a depressing Soviet wasteland can have levity when you knife some dude and he goes splat.

I bought [i]Sand Castle[/i] because it looked cute and other reviews made it sound quite sweet with an emotional element.  It also appealed to me as it was clearly fairly short (I expected around 2-3 hours as I intentionally read VNs much more slowly than I would a book, to ensure I don't miss the opportunity to absorb anything.  It's much easier just to look back again in a book) and would therefore fit well into a personal schedule which provides negligible spare time.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Looking in as a third party upon the interactions between Gilt and Amare, the reader finds them having a date at the beach, during which time they reminisce over (three) dates that they have been on together previously.  Or have they?  And that is the crux of the whole narrative.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
This novel is almost entirely click-and-read, with just one either/or option being presented late on, which will lead you to one of the two possible finishes (making it as straightforward as possible to find them both).  The game does provide an unexpected twist in the later stages which adds a little meat to the dish being served.

[h1]Graphics and Sound [/h1]
I finished the story yesterday and honestly, I can't remember the sound.  Therefore it couldn't have been bad else I'd have felt irritated by it, but neither could it be standout (which, for the price, is fair enough).  Graphically the artwork is quite simple, low on detail but still attractive and pleasing.  I think the sea at the beach looks good, and the rooftop date possesses the most appealing backdrop in the game.  I have chosen not to post a screenshot as if you decide to buy this novel, you should not have the biggest reward offered spoilered for you ahead of time.

[h1]Experience and verdict[/h1]
The extreme brevity of this offering caught me by surprise despite having read several reviews ahead of downloading it.  I assumed the minimal time-played reviewers were skim readers, but apparently not.  To be finished inside half an hour, having taken my time every step of the way, was something of a shock.

The controls available are pretty good for something so small, featuring all of the basics, rollback/forward, skip, save/load, screen size, text speed; with a menu to guide you on how to access them; although there are no frills, such as a CG or backdrop gallery.

Overall, I found the story readable, although as the reviewer [i]Ichigo75[/i] has correctly pointed out; it is simply too short to give the reader time to establish any kind of emotional bond with the players, and therefore as good as impossible to really feel emotionally affected when the twist arrives.

This is yet another offering where Steam's rigid thumb up or down verdict system isn't good enough.  Does it deserve a thumbs down?  No, not really.  The concept is solid and the execution isn't bad, either.  But it's rather like buying an ice cream and getting an empty cone.  There just isn't enough there to leave you feeling satisfied.

For that reason, I cannot give it a thumbs up either, as doing so (to my mind) amounts to recommending a purchase; and despite the very low price, would you really want to buy a blueberry yogurt without the blueberries?  (With apologies to those affected by that analogy).

My review was originally going to say something along the lines if you can handle a little bit of jank that you will enjoy this game, and that is true.... for the first 2 worlds...... but the third world has been one of the most frustrating platforming experiences I have ever played. Each of the 4 characters has a unique ability, but none of them feel like they are working as intended Carl can push and pull boxes.... when the controller decides it registers your button presses, sometimes he will warp around the box in an area where pushing it is impossible, sometimes he will run in place very fast towards the box and nothing else will happen and will not be able to get out of this animation until the game decides it wants to work correctly again. Paperman can throw letters and teleport to them.... except the letters you throw fade away really fast, which would be well and good if you could acutally tell where the letter was , there is a lock mechanic but it only works on enemies and red targets that you need to be extremely close to meaning you don't have acces to it half the time. Scrolly allegedly can float and glide in the air currents that are around most levels... except you pressing the ability button has little to no bearing as to weather or not she will actually float. More often than not she will just drop. Express can run faster than an the other characters with a toggle of the ability button... which would be great... if it actually worked properly, half the time his feet will get caught on the platform he's already standing on and he won't actually run anywhere, which is manageable when you're running in a straight line, but then you throw in the sloped platforms and you might as well just use Paperman's double jump instead. The camera will also lock in specific positions and actively fight you if you try to adjust it, which is an interesting decision for a 3D platformer to say the least..... I played most of it in co-op and my girlfriend and I had many instances where we would re-spawn with the screen too dark to see, or not re-spawn at all, or re-spawn to a checkpoint that was before the boss area we were currently fighting. I was willing to put up with most of those problems for the 1st 2 worlds because we were still having fun, but the 3rd world broke me, it has so many branching paths most of which require pixel perfect platforming, which would be fine, if the game didn't have all the aforementioned issues. Dymension, is a Action Horror game, about a research lab placing human sentience into android mannequins. The player comes into the laboratory as a new worker as the laboratory falls into chaos, the mannequins break out and become hostile to the player abducting them. As of the review Dymension is currently just the first part of the game.

Currently the game comes in two parts, the research labs and the mansion. Both sides of the game have a focus on puzzles and item collection, with there also being simple combat in the mansion. The game is mainly puzzle based, with the need to find door access codes or by completing logic puzzles for fixing control panels. Neither are difficult within the game, and a player can simply spam the control panels to get the answer to them. In the manor there are other puzzles, though none should give the player much challenge, with items being not difficult to find.

The Horror in the game feels lacking, in the Laboratory, we see the mannequins have very dynamic movements. Through accessing the ceiling or monitoring the player, this does not keep up through the rest of the game, with the most terror built in the game is through being overpowered and outnumbered. Even the sounds of Mannequins scuttling through the ceiling are gone.

Combat is a mix, enemies are ever really harmless and slow, or will rush you and quickly kill you if they get close. The player does have access to ranged weaponry and through the first part of the game should not run out of ammo should they just use it on the more aggressive mannequins. Save your ammo till they start charging you, all others are really slow and you can simply bonk them to death.

The game has a few bugs as of the review, like the first mannequin that charges the player in the house, dealt no damage to me and instead just rammed its head into my chest till I disposed of it. Beyond that most of the bugs I found in the demo had been fixed, and I had no other problems.

Overall the game is just the intro, and is a good start of the game, although the laboratory feels a lot more polished than the rest of the game. The cliffhanger at the end is interesting, though it felt stronger at the end of the demo. I hope we will see the rest of the game, as it is an interesting story, it just feels that the narrative was lacking once we were in the manor.

[h1]The Reluctant Forksman[/h1]
TL;DR: A surprisingly well-crafted game that is everything you could want in an indie soulslike. A little easy for the genre, but features creative combat and platforming systems, great comedy writing, and a story that is more touching than a goofy game about crabs has any right to be.[hr][/hr]
I’m wary of trying out new soulslike franchises, especially when they aren’t from a tested studio like From Software. There’s a fine line between challenging and frustrating, and the slightest bit of jank can be a real turnoff in a genre that demands precision. Despite that, [i]Another Crab’s Treasure[/i] got enough affection from people whose opinions I respect that I opted to wade in. What I found was a genuinely funny and enjoyable game that has a few fresh ideas and punches well above its weight.

In [i]Another Crab’s Treasure[/i] you step into the role of Kril, a true hermit of a hermit crab; he lives in a tidepool on the beach, does largely nothing, has no friends, and is perfectly content. He is ushered into utter turmoil after his shell is repossessed to cover back taxes, and he must brave the sea bed in his quest to recover his home. It’s a goofy setup for a story that is unexpectedly grounded, seeing our hero leave his comfort zone to broaden his horizons and find value in things he had previously scarcely considered. Not only relatable, the tale is woven throughout with humor that lands fairly consistently, as well a fair number of groan-worthy marine life puns.

On his odyssey to reclaim his shell, Kril will be forced to take up the fork in self-defense. The melee combat is pretty standard for the genre, but well enough crafted not to feel frustrating except in a few rare situations where footing can be an issue. There are a few variations, like releasing block at the moment of impact to parry, but the real USP comes in the form of shells. Kril can protect himself with a wide variety of found objects, from soda cans to skulls. These have different stats and weights, but the stroke of genius is that different shells enable different spells, and they have their own durability. It’s not uncommon to find yourself scrambling to jump into a new shell in the middle of a boss fight after yours has soaked a few hits. It’s a fun way to tie systems together, and encourages you to try moves you might not otherwise engage with. By the end of the game you’ll probably have a favorite shell, and you can insure it so you always respawn with it, but collecting the different options and trying out the various moves was a lot of fun.

Exploration is a little more lively than most soulslikes, with 3D-platforming eventually bolstered by swimming, climbing, and a grappling hook. Areas start fairly basic and ramp up to some truly impressive levels, ranging from electrified mining rigs to pitch-black abyssal plains. The environs shape the combat, and as mentioned above, this can lead to some slightly wonky encounters, but that is very rare and seemed to happen most in the first handful of levels. The art direction is cartoonish, and fits the tone and humor of the game beautifully. When the surroundings turn inevitably bleak (this [b]is[/b] a soulslike, after all), the loss of light and saturated colors serve to reinforce the severity of the crisis and the depths of Kril’s alienation. This degree of attention to detail is not something I’d expect from a first-time developer, and it’s both impressive and refreshing.

It’s an overused phrase, but this game is a true indie gem, and well worth your time and money if you enjoy the genre. Even if you haven’t in the past, there’s a decent chance you’ll have fun here, and if you get too frustrated, Kril can always bring a gun to any fight and win in one shot. The game’s systems, plot, art direction, humor, and level design have all clearly benefited from a lot of love, are so much better than anticipated, and leave me excited to see what this team puts together in the future.

Each level riffs very well upon the last, there's great sound design, voice acting, the humor really resonated with me, and it has a surprising amount of build potential with unique mechanics that, imo, really refreshed the soulslike experience.

If the difficulty curve is too hard, the game allows for reduced difficulty without punishing potential achievements. This addresses most bugs, because you can reset yourself to the last save and regain your valuables if you felt you ran into an unintended experience. It also addresses feelings of soulslike fatigue. 

It did a good job of keeping to traditional soulslike themes/mechanics that work, while riffing off of that material with genuinely creative ideas.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys souls-like combat. The game is easy enough for beginners while providing a decent challenge for veterans.

[b] Combat [/b]
     The game has a very good spin on traditional souls-like combat. Shops and ways to upgrade your equipment are very easy to find, the game will not hide core features from you. Rolling is included as always, blocking is encouraged, parrying is very satisfying, then add special abilities on top akin to Sekiro prosthetic tools. Additionally, different shells provide different rolling speed, durability, and a special ability, all in all it's a sufficiently fleshed out and fun combat system. Difficulty-wise, combat is not as hard as other souls games but still very satisfying to master.

[b] Music [/b]
     For a game made by 12 people at $30, the music is disgustingly good. It plays very well with sea-themed ambience and several of the boss themes are great and memorable.

[b] Story [/b]
     At first I thought many of the initial jokes and features would be gimmicks just played for a quick joke, but they are readily incorporated into the overarching plot and themes of the game. The humor in this game is really damn good, and being able to balance it with genuine sincerity just makes the game's story a home run for me. My only criticism is that the story starts somewhat slowly, but oh boy, in the final third of the game the story absolutely flies.

[b] Cons? [/b]
     Game has some usual Dark Souls jank, enemies pushing you off ledges, getting slightly stuck above their heads, slight platforming polish issues.

     Overall Another Crab's Treasure has a lot of heart, great humor, great combat systems, and is a steal for $30 (or less if it's on sale).
