As the game currently stands, 100%ing it will take you around 16-19 hours. Possibly longer if you get immensely stuck. This game is overall one of the easier Souls-esque titles I've played and I would not call this a bad thing. There's plenty of exploration to do and you're generally rewarded for it. It has plenty of charm in its writing and world as well. If you're in the market for a game with some Souls combat, give it a shot.

Going into further detail now. It's pretty obvious that they took more inspiration from Sekiro for the game, taking the balance system and grapple. The combat is also much more forgiving compared to other Souls games simply because of one factor: blocking is actually good. Your shells have their own durability bar and you can recover the damage it takes by hitting enemies before it decays. Though they keep the risk and prompt reward when engaging with superior defensive options. Parrying is an option but only when you release block, forcing you to take the brunt of any mistimed parries. Dodging follows the same beats, as well as being needed for grab attacks and heavy attacks that destroy shells. There's only two weapon movesets, and one is temporary (though will last you through most fights). The fork and hammer upgrade. The movesets are perfectly serviceable, are augmented with magic attacks from your shells/boss fights, and they can balance enemies more tightly thanks to this limited weapon pool.

The story is simple, but works well enough. A lot of it is mostly to run into characters and interact with them, and they do a good job at making each character (that has text box art) memorable. My biggest critique for the story primarily comes down to the final boss, as it felt like they had the fight in mind early on but couldn't find a good pathway to reach that point narratively. The rest of the story works fine enough in my opinion, so it's a misstep at the end but they manage to absolutely nail the ending IMO.

With knowledge they're planning to add further content (New Game +, Boss Rush), I think that the core experience is worth buying and playing now while their big update will make it much more worthwhile if you want something with a bit more longevity to sink your teeth into.

[h1]Good[/h1]
[olist]
    [*]Nicely animated intro transitioning from real video footage to game footage with the game’s title in the distance
    [*]Clever idea to have a joke set-up and punchline as the ends of a popsicle stick. You see the set-up, then attack the popsicle stick to get the bottom half out of the ground and see the punchline.
    [*]Clever equipment designs. A long straw with a plastic cup lid is a lance. Bottlecap armor tied together with paperclips. A u-shaped bicycle lock being turned into a guillotine with a razor blade.
    [*]Funny dialogue
    [*]Dying to a boss lets you respawn right at the boss point and collect your plastic
    [*]You can pick up costumes dropped from bosses to wear a piece of their outfit
    [*]The fishing line grappling hook shows a ‘grapple-able’ indicator on the UI even if the grapple point is far from the center of the screen
    [*]Enemies are generous with dropping Heartkelp Pods if you’re not at full capacity
    [*]Accessibility option to equip a gun and 1-shot anything
    [*]The pause menu shows how long it’s been since your last save
[/olist]

[h1]Issues[/h1]
[olist]
    [*]Harvesting a Heartkelp plant is annoying, as after interacting with it, the actual Heartkelp Pod is shot into the air and you either have to wait for it to fall before picking it up or jump and interact.
    [*]No way to skip previously read dialogue when talking to an NPC again. Just have to button mash and wait for the text appearance animation to happen.
    [*]There’s a map, but no minimap. Getting to the map is 2 button presses.
    [*]In game, there’s only a “Return to Menu” option instead of also having a “Quit” option
    [*]There are multiple actions to move and sustain height while in a jump, but you can’t chain all of them together. Jump, air attack, dash, hover. The dash has to be the first thing you do.
    [*]When confirming the microplastics spent levelling up, the screen darkening is only the center 16:9 and doesn’t fill an ultrawide
    [*]It took a while to figure out the significance of pink eyes on some enemies. Those enemies will drop a pink gem if killed, otherwise they seem normal.
[/olist]

Grammer!

recommendation for the developer:
Change the basic RTP and villages; it feels rushed.
Do something with the fishing minigame; it's fun and challenging, but it doesn't add anything more than wasting time on catching fish.
Get the game some more attention so there are more players online at the same time; create some sort of event; this makes the co-op stuff more fun.

This game has too many issues, so I cannot recommend it at all.

The UI has many issues and clunky interactions, such as being unable to type spaces for component names (because it closes the menu) or underscores and other characters (for no reason). Further, general menu navigation is slow and painful, and there appears to be a lot of issues with the resolution and quality of certain assets. The actual UI for creating and managing solutions requires significant polish. And it doesn't give you any hints as for how to achieve optimal solutions on each level (which is required to unlock later levels in the game).

I love the genre, so I was more than willing to look past all that, however...

Levels 11 and 12 are where I really called it on trying to see this game through to the end. These levels introduce obstacles that are randomised each time you play, which is fine, because that's what this type of game is about: creating adaptive solutions. These random elements function as hazards. When functioning as hazards, they play animations. The issue is that these animations are completely disconnected from the game speed, so running a simulation at 1x speed can have completely different outcomes to running the same simulation at 4x speed. As a result, the only way I could pass level 11 was to actually run the simulation at varying speeds, to babysit my robots to avoid the obstacles... That's what the programming is meant to do!

And then, another major problem that both these levels had was... It was never actually explained how the hazards work. On these levels, you're supposed to program the robot to detect the color of a light. The light is tied to the presence of several hazards. However, it's not explained even remotely what the colors of the light mean. They appear to fluctuate randomly, with minimal connection to the actual state of the hazard, producing completely inconsistent results from run to run. And I can't preview or observe the hazards in motion because they don't operate unless there's a robot actually doing something. Add to it that the hazards and the lights appear to change far more rapidly than the robot can detect or respond to, and you're left feeling completely helpless, with no idea how to actually solve the problem.

I spent a good 20 minutes on each of these levels, where I had spent no more than 10 minutes per level up to this point. After barely finishing level 11, and not being able to make a lick of progress son level 12, I had to quit the game.

It is not fair, and it is not fun.

Bending space itself yet again, nothing could be better, right?
BENDING SPACE BY FOLDING PAPER. HELL YEAH!
[b]Plot[/b]
In this game you'll play as a Paige, a budding academic, leaving home for the first time to pursue her studies. On the journey, you learn to fold the world, merging two sides to solve puzzles, explore new areas and uncover long-lost secrets. That's exactly what you should do to get into university nowadays.
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The main mechanic of this game is, of course, paper folding, which allows you to bend space around and reach something you couldn't before. By exploring this wonderful world you'll encounter 7 locations, each having a unique mechanic additionally to the main one. The levels, in my opinion are the perfect size for player not to be bored. Each transition from one location to another is implemented in the form of an interactive cutscene, which tells us more about Paige. And on top of all of that crap you can pet a cat.
[b]Music[/b]
The music in Paper Trail is amazing. It perfectly suits the atmosphere of this colourful, playful and cute world, while reflecting Paige's emotions. Each level has its own soundtrack that sets just the right mood.
[b]Conclusion[/b]
This game is a perfect example of how an amazing and original concept can make a puzzle game even more interesting and enjoyable. Surely, don't [i]fold[/i] on this one.

There's honestly two sides to this game: there's the level design itself and the general physics. The handling in this game is a bit deceptive, in that at first it appears that the precise platforming is almost impossible but then you realise (first somewhat unconsciously, finally objectively) that there are small tricks to make it play more in line with a regular platformer. The level design is once again single screen stages where you advance to a goal platform, but they quickly get rather cramped in terms of obstacles [b]and[/b] tiny platforms to navigate. While a few obstacles do remain "theatre specific", this time around things get significantly reused to create tense situations. Gameplay pacing is a mix of rewarding slow methodical platforming and reckless runs where the ideal timing is actually very close to leaps of faith from the start.

Oh, there's also a minor plot going on, but there's not too much of it. You get one intro cutscene and two sandwiching the final main theatre. I get pixel art is time consuming, but I would have liked at least a bit more context elsewhere, given how I know Jussi (the main person behind Adventure Islands) can deliver satisfying writing.

[b]wordland: let's travel[/b] is pretty much the same as [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1599690]wordland[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1640760]wordland 2[/url] and [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1652650]wordland 3[/url], except it adds a theme, which it should've done after the first game.

it's still a great word game/crossword/tetris hybrid. there are various shapes with letters on a grid and they have to be arranged to form all the words described on the bottom. this is where the [b]educational element[/b] comes in, [b]descriptions assume a bunch of geographical knowledge (or googling skills) from the player[/b]. no diagonals, only left to right or downward, but they don't all have to be connected to each other. in fact, the game accepts layouts that wouldn't fly in a real crossword (e.g. va-tic-anc is accepted even though the answer is vatican).

[b]50 levels[/b] instead of the usual 100, unlocked one by one. the [b]3 difficulty levels[/b] control the amount of revealed letters (more on easy, only the first letter on normal, none on hard), but there's no indication of any of this in the game, so you can't see which levels were completed on which difficulty.

[b]controls are very convenient[/b], left click to pick a piece up, mouse wheel to rotate in either direction, another left click to place. my biggest gripe with the original game was the size of the board, lots of tedium when the word was one letter too long and the entire thing had to be moved a tile to the left piece by piece. plenty of space on the screen, not sure why only a small area is used if it's not a lazy mobile port, but the current size is mostly good enough. towards the end there are way more pieces to move around though, so the grid could still be bigger.

[b]excellent music, but using the same short loop in 4 games now and calling it 'original' is fucking ridiculous.[/b] backgrounds are also nice, some are animated and most are new this time (finally!), but [b]they don't fill the entire screen properly, looks like some lazy mobile crap[/b] instead of the 'artistic choice' they went for. and some are still too dark to be of any use. they change after every restart or new level, and can be changed manually, and also locked so they stay the same all the way. [b]a gallery of them could be a great reward for completing the game.[/b]

settings-wise all the neccessities are present, separate volume settings, windowed mode with a couple resolution options (there could be a few more), and level selection is also a thing. these are all accessible from the main menu and while playing.

[b]it's high time an entry in the series got a more specific coat of paint[/b], the first 3 games are 99% identical, more of exactly the same, music and backgrounds included. besides the traveling aspect there's [b]suitcase decoration[/b] here as an optional extra. not much to it, unlock stickers by solving levels and place them on your luggage that you can also color or draw on, but it's only shown on that screen.

instead of vocabulary, the game is based on geographical information, but difficulty depends on the individual player's knowledge all the same. still, it's really pleasant overall, just like the ones before, but [b]hopefully if there's more coming, they'll all have a theme and more unique features[/b]. I'm always down for food-related stuff, for example.

Thumbs up only for an interesting idea of combining geographical trivia and “sort-of Tetris” (or maybe Tetris-like jigsaw puzzle) in one game. This was a nifty construct, and with proper care it could have been a lovely experience, as it stands – it all kind of stopped just short of that “lovely” line. 

What worked:

-	The initial idea of combining trivia and a puzzle game is brilliant. It’s an all-in-one relaxing gameplay where you get to ponder on the questions, and then ponder on how to put them together correctly – I really enjoyed that. Apparently, this is a geographical spin-off on the previous three installments (which I haven’t tried), but I like the idea of subject-specific trivia, so I can see lots of directions this game can expand in.

-	Gorgeous background images. They invite and entice and tempt to go on the new adventure, aka elicit an emotional response – which is what art is supposed to do. And these are no 8x8 paintings, just static 2D backgrounds in a small game, and yet… Let’s just say I came back from a kayaking trip recently and looking at their image of adventurers in the boats – I immediately planned the next one. 

What was “whatever”:

-	There’s a good soundtrack present, but it becomes repetitive REALLY quick. It screams, begs and cajoles for some variety. 

-	There’s a luggage customization option. Sort of like an additional mini-game/experience you can partake in, which I didn’t care for. If you’re into this kind of thing – there’s your chance to be creative – paint your luggage and put stickers on it, but I didn’t use it all. I’d much rather developers spent whatever this cost towards an additional good track to accompany me on this journey.

What didn’t work:

-	There are a few “kinks” here and there like repeated questions, some answers that bend a rule a bit as far as word placement (as of you can solve the level without connecting them or you can connect them in way that adds an additional letter to word that was already done, making it a word that doesn’t exist), grammar problems. All of these are related to a core gameplay mechanic which makes them stand out a lot more than if they were just a few side issues. 

-	Some questions give away the answer in the way they were asked. When you get a question – you are given a first letter of response and the number of letters in a word. Most of the questions are direct – you need to provide an answer, but some are asked in a way – is it THIS or THIS? When you see something like ‘Is it Japan or Indonesia that…” and your answer shows J_ _ _ _  What was the point of this question??

-	The overall difficulty. For some reason, the default level here is “easy” not “normal”, beware, but if you decide to try your hand at a “hard” setting – you’ll get the same set of questions you just had but with some extra letters mixed-in (not in all cases either – some are the exact same tasks as on “easy” level, with no added letters). This will work as an “increased difficulty” only if you going to start a game with this setting from the get-go, if you going to go for it after playing the game on lower settings, like I did – you’d already have all the responses memorized (there aren’t that many and some of them are pretty unique), so you’ll be flying through levels anyway. I think this is simply not a hard game, regardless of the difficulty level, and it’s a shame, really, because geography trivia has potential of making thousands of levels without a single repeated question.

If “WORDLAND Let’s Travel” would have kept the original concept and art, added more music, went with a fine-toothed comb over all the tangles in their gameplay, and added new/more questions to different difficulty settings (which would have made the game enormously more replayable) – it would have been an excellent puzzle game. As it is – there’s great potential bundled with a wobbly implementation. This is a very tentative “finger pointing upwards”, as it isn’t a bad or broken game, but it’s pretty underbaked. 

Well, at the very least – I’ve got my next kayaking trip planned out of this one, so maybe, if not for smooth puzzle experience, you too can get some inspiration out of it.

So is this a very neat idea for a tower defense? Absolutely! Its one of the freshest ideas I've seen for the genre in a long time! Does it execute it well? I'd have to say it doesn't. Theres also the fact my anti-virus caught the application trying to connect to the internet in a sus way which is.... not a great look.

In a tower defense a lot of the engagement comes from strategic tower placement and the thrill of barely staving off the waves of enemies until you're so powerful that nothing can get past you. Each decision is important and meaningful and you're aware of the choices you're making at all times.

In Quad Dice Defence this is sadly not the case. While yes the scrambling to build a tower out of the dice allotted to you at the time is a VERY good mechanic with some solid choices in there the rest of the game play loop doesn't get very engaging until around the 15th level. The game does cool things to spice it up by having new pathways appear (which can disable your turrets by bisecting them which is VERY cool) but the enemies that appear on the pathways (again I've only played up to the 15th level) always die in one hit from one die damage (the lowest damage you can do) and often only one pathway is sending out enemies at a time. This isn't very engaging on it's own let alone 40 mins into a game. 
It's absolutely possible to plonk one tower next to a goal and have it defend the goal easily without any assistance, there just really isn't any challenge or variety. Nor does it let you sit with your decisions for any length of time. Most of the first levels really only last a wave or two before being finished without any introduction of any new mechanics at all, leaving me with the only thing I'm mastering is turret construction.

Without any enemy variety and all the waves only having enemies that just die in one hit with no real moments that actually try to overwhelm you the game is painfully one note and boring when it has such a cool mechanic going for it. This game needed more time in other parts of it than just more levels. Have less levels, far less levels, and instead give more enemy variety, with ever expanding maps and more powerful enemies so that I have to actually sit with my decisions and so that I'm challenged and surprised with new challenges! In it's current state I could not reccomend it to you as it only gets slightly engaging after 40 minutes of playing and that's simply too long, it should have gotten to that point in the first 5 to 10 minutes.

Ever wondered what happens when Pinball Wizard and Mother Nature decide to have a sleepover? The answer is: Marble Ball Friends - the organic, free-range, gluten-free version of pinball!

Imagine, if you will, you're taking in a deep breath of that sweet, pine-scented forest air while playing pinball in a cozy woodland lodge. But this isn’t just ANY pinball. This is pinball with a twist: launch that shiny orb and pray to the forest spirits that it lands in a prize box. What’s the prize, you ask? Adorable animal statues named "animal friends." And just to clear things up, they're not related to "Kemono Friends," so if you were expecting an exotic trip to Japari Park, well, keep dreaming. (And on a side note, what did they DO to "Kemono Friends" in the sequel?! #NotMyKemonoFriends).

Now, don’t expect any old-school pinball flippers in this game. Once that ball goes, it's on a one-way journey to wherever gravity dictates. It's like sending a text to your crush and realizing autocorrect changed “Hey” to “Heeeyyyyy.”

But fret not! Play with your pals and you might just get... more balls. Which in this game equals profit. Because who doesn't want a higher chance of bonus action?

Score enough nature goodies and you'll hit Jackpot mode! And trust me, this mode is way more thrilling than those "free spins" at the casino slot machines. You know, the ones that are about as "free" as those "free" samples at the mall that have a sales pitch attached?

Feeling a touch lonely? Link up with VRoid Hub, summon your favorite digital avatar, and let them silently judge... I mean, support you during your game. They won’t lift a finger, but hey, sometimes just having someone there while you lose magnificently is comfort enough.

In conclusion: Marble Ball Friends is where zen meditation crashes into a pinball machine. It's chaotic, it's calming, and it's a whole lot of woodland fun. Dive in! 🌲🕹️🌳

I've been waiting for this game since the end of Reliics of the Lost Age. If you've played that game before you will adore this. If you haven't you are still in for a massive treat with this and the start of the game makes it really easy to catch you up. The world tour setting makes for such an expansive and detailed adventure and the romances are so much fun. I enjoyed every minute with these wonderful characters and the ending was so damn satisfying.

I quite liked the first Relics, but this one feels like an improvement in essentially every way. Your decisions feel more consequential, and the tension is vastly increased by the constraints of time and resources. Minor equipment purchases I made at the start of the game had a tangible impact at the very end. Additionally, I really like how this game pays off the decisions and character relationships from the first game. At times, these payoffs can seem a touch contrived, but given the pulp adventure style of the game's writing, this fits the story perfectly. The puzzles are reasonable in difficulty and mostly skippable if they're not your cup of tea. Overall, any gripes I might have are too minor to be worth mentioning.

As with the first game, the attention to detail and historical/mythological research are impeccable. 

I'm really excited to see how this series concludes, especially as WWII looms over the story.

I usually don't write much reviews, but I want to sincerely compliment the author on this one, they did a great job! Everything from Relics of the Lost Age has been expanded upon, and I feel like the romance has improved much more as well.

Speaking about romance, you can date a certain rival from the first book now... You'll be pleasantly surprised if you do. Anything for María.

The characters are great, the story is good, the puzzles are fun, and most puzzles can be skipped too! Please don't hesitate to buy the second book in this series, and buy the first one if you haven't already. Looking forward to the conclusion in the third book!

10/10. As others have said, Relics 2 improves on the previous title on essentially every way. The characters are interesting and likeable, the treasure hunt throughout Europe feels exciting and the time and resource constraints only serve to heighten the feeling. Each chapter feels unique with different tones, atmospheres and challenges, and the choices you make truly feel impactful. This also makes you crave replaying the game and trying out different skills and outcomes. The puzzles were slightly easier this time around, which wasn't a bad thing for me, plus they were skippable if solving ancient riddles isn't your thing. The only problem I had (and it was a very minor one) was that you could only choose one companion to come with you; Though you will get to spend a little time with all of your friends, I picked the threesome romance with Esme and Abdul and I wish I could have taken both of them along for the entire adventure. As always, the archaeological and historical side of the game is impeccable and really immersive.

All in all, if you enjoy the thought of traveling the world, discovering ancient secrets and solving challenges and making remarkable friends while fighting and killing fascists everywhere you go (both the nazis of the German Reich, and other cruel authoritarian groups and individuals), then this series is definitely a must buy. I would recommend you try Relics of the Lost Age first and, if you like it, then know this one is truly even better in every way.
This was better than the first, still adventurous and well written.  Skill checks still punishing but at least now there's ways to recover health or improve skills.

A great follow-up to the first game, full of adventure and mystery! Companions from the previous game return, and interesting new characters appear, as you travel across Europe searching for the resting place of an ancient crusader. The puzzles are challenging but not impossible, and there are new technical aspects to manage, like inventory and budget. The game is packed with content and new locations.

I will definitely play again with a different character -- my altruistic and athletic MC from book 1 wasn't ruthless enough to win the race, though she survived and was content with the overall outcome. I definitely want to try again with a sneaky, more selfish MC. (I want to be more successful at that heist in Venice, though at least I got an achievement for making a mess!)

I really wanted to love Solium Infernum.
As many have said, it's a board game-esque grand strategy game with incredible visuals, soundtrack, and a really intriguing concept. As someone who plays a lot of board games (especially grand strategy games like Eclipse, TI, SE4x, HOLAS, etc), I was all in when it was announced.
Unfortunately, I soon discovered that if I treated SI like a board game... I hated it. The game rewards gambling on chance over good strategy at every possible venture. You just saved up for a big unit? Someone got a random, cheap event to kill that unit. You've taken 3 tribute actions in a row? Sorry, you didn't randomly get enough of the one resource you needed, so you can't buy anything.
I love the idea behind what the game is doing but, unfortunately, every time I think the game is doing something cool or interesting, it craps on itself by introducing some large element of randomness or is overly punishing. 
It calls itself a "grand strategy" game, however you could never feasibly plan beyond 1-2 turns due to the extreme variability baked into the games mechanics (resource gain being a random draw is the most egregious imo).

Overall, I just wanted more from this game than it offers. Most of the game feels mean purely for the sake of being mean and there is rarely any decent payoff for pulling off a long term scheme. The balancing is all over the place and you will often find yourself getting punished for things you had no control over or no way to properly plan for.
However, the aesthetics are fantastic and obviously many people enjoy this game, so if large amounts of chance draws and extreme swinginess don't bother you, than i'm sure you'll enjoy this game. I personally don't think it's anywhere near as strategic as it makes itself out to be.

[code]Not a lot of people know about this game, and probably it should stay this way. This is going to be a rant, and I apologize in advance but I need to vent [b]hard[/b].[/code]

[b]R is for Rachel[/b] is a visual novel about a queer girl Joan who falls in love with her neighbour Rachel. When I've read the name for the first time, I scoffed, to be honest, instantly remembering Life is Strange. But the premise got me, and I thought I should at least try the demo... It was horrible. I hated it so much I needed to complain to everyone. After some time, though, I felt shameful. Maybe I'm being too critical? Maybe I should give this game a chance, it was just a demo. So I bought it.

[h2]Is there anything good in the game?[/h2]
Uhh... no, not really. I honestly can't come up with any praises here.

[h2]Okay. What was bad, then?[/h2]
You really wanna know? First of all, thank you. Second — sit down, babe, we'll be here for a while.

1. The art looks awful. Remember that filter in Photoshop which made everything look as if it was drawn? I think every picture in this game was created with some sort of filter like that. Looks sloppy.

2. You cannot change the text speed, which is a must-have for any VN.

3. Lots of typos/errors. I had a feeling that the writer's first language is not English — this is not a bad thing, of course, but in that case you need to hire someone to edit or translate the text. While we're here, the writing style is no good either, and the dialogues are full of "he/she said" after every phrase.

4. The main schtick of the game is that sometimes you can type your actions. Honestly, the dumbest thing I've ever seen. You can't choose what you're doing, it's always "write the right action to progress", and there are moments when it's not obvious what the game wants. There are like 3 or 4 times when you do need to choose something, but in these cases you usually write "yes" or "no" and that's it. The choices do not impact the plot, btw.

5. The plot is stupid, underdeveloped, and incoherent. I've saved this for last, because you know, if the plot was actually good, I would probably forgive all the bad things. But the characters are shallow, there are constant time skips, even though there [i]should be[/i] time to develop the characters. Every person in this game kinda feels like a parody.

Here's a recap: Joan (MC) has an anxiety disorder and doesn't have any friends because of that. Almost every social interaction is hard for her, she finds it difficult to speak with most people. Joan's mother, Anna, is worried Joan doesn't have friends, so she forces her to meet the neighbours (Rachel and her mother, Samantha) and invite them for dinner. Joan does exactly that, all goes well, and they have a dinner together.

At some point Joan and Rachel go outside, talk for like 5 minutes and then start kissing, even though there wasn't even any spark. Okay. After that they become girlfriends and, as I assume, almost always spend their free time together, but the game doesn't show that, so I don't know for sure. At the same time Joan is getting bullied at school, and her parents are constantly fighting because Anna thinks that James (her husband) is cheating on her.

That's basically most of the story without any boring and unnecessary details. I've told you all of this since I want to share the dumbest plot twist. [spoiler]Turns out, James is actually cheating, and his mistress turns out to be Rachel. Also Rachel apparently wants James to divorce Anna so that they can be together forever. What? Why?? Joan finds out about all of this and decides that she's too tired for this bullshit. (For the first time, I feel you, Joan.) You can probably guess what she wants to do, especially if I tell you her next actions make the whole situation even more dramatic.[/spoiler]

I have so many questions, I still don't know where to start. [spoiler]Why did Rachel date Joan AND her father (stepfather? not sure)?? Why did Rachel lie she has no attraction to men?[/spoiler] 

What's the point of this story? Is it to show that we shouldn't bully anxious depressed teenagers because otherwise they might do something awful to themselves? If yes, was that really the best story you could come up with?

[h2]Let's resume...[/h2]
I honestly don't think that the creators of the game made it so bad on purpose. I can even imagine that [b]R is for Rachel[/b] was created as a cautionary tale. But this tale is cautionary only for the people who create games and stories. You need to make an effort to create a good story. If you do not, you might end with an awful by-product such as this.

Please do not waste your money on this. Even if you want to hate-read, it's a miserable experience.

This genuinely might be one of the worst things I've ever "played." The central conceit of gameplay is clunky, uninspired and it feels like a gimmick. There are no options - only right answers. I have little to say about the authorial tone beyond its juvenile presentation and the artistic presentation is... fine, its not my thing but its more than what most do. Typos and grammatical errors are present (as they often are in these small-scale games. I have no issues with that) but the story - that thing you're paying for - is almost offensively bad.

This is not a love story, this is an odd mish-mash of media. Clearly aping off of Life is Strange but this is not a positive nor a particularly well-written love story. In fact, [spoiler]the game functionally centers around the player character, Joan, falling for another teenaged girl who is sleeping with Joan's father. That's right. The contrived mommy-daddy fight time and mother's concerns about an affair are true because for some reason the plot twist in this game is that Joan's girlfriend is having an affair with her father.[/spoiler] Its such a baffling and asinine twist that it beggars actual belief. I almost regret spoiler tagging it because I think it should stand out as a warning to the poor quality of the story overall, it completely soils what would have otherwise been a mid-tier experience.

Even for free, I wouldn't recommend it. Not as an LGBT story, not as a lesbian story, not even as a zero calorie Life is Strange attempt at emulating messed up Twin Peaksy small town dynamics.

I'll start by saying this game has potential, but it fails in all aspects because it was too ambitious. This game is not a good puzzle game, not a good RPG-maker game, not a good horror game and not a good "game" overall (more on that in the Conclusion).

Bad puzzles
[hr][/hr]

Of the "puzzles" I had, before I ended up quitting, I was told open a red gate with a string of numbers from ... ? The colors of those numbers were arbitrary and had nothing to do with the gate. (So is the game just gonna throw random shit at me and expect me to "solve" it? Maybe this ties into the narrative and horror, maybe numbers/colors are important to our character and this feeling of confusion needs to be conveyed to the player for them to understand the story that's to unfold; let's see.)

The very next "puzzle" told me to do math after it gave me some operators with a red (or should I say yellow) herring [b]and now tells me[/b] the colors are important.

Everything I said in the above paragraph in (parenthesis) for the narrative, is wrong, it's just poor design 🤷🙃, i.e. "go search the environment for arbitrary numbers, do math, and move rocks" does not make for good puzzles, if they serve no other purpose than being a gate, why even include them? Why not use that time for exposition or build puzzles that fit around the idea you want to give to the player. The puzzles were unsatisfying to say the very least.

Bad RPG(-Maker)
[hr][/hr]

The aesthetic of an abstract environment was absolutely great and I loved seeing it (helped with the horror), but the limitations of the underlying engine (RPG-Maker) made it frustrating as hell to deal with. I'm taught at the very beginning that I am a square and I move in 4 directional planes. Great! I'm also taught there are clear boundaries for where I can and can't go (light areas--Good, dark areas--Bad). Great! Next, we're thrown into the abstract world as our character.

Those things you just learned? Throw all that shit out ... Sometimes areas where there's light you can walk on to and move to different areas from. All other times that's not the case (60/40). It's there enough to notice and be frustrated with it.

If you build up the expectation that anywhere there isn't light you cannot tread, well ... "get fucked idiot", because you just missed the first reversed audio recording ruining the story/horror because it will be incomplete in the end, but it's [i]justified[/i] because it's a "mystery" you need to "solve" ... Just like the "puzzles".

So now you as the player are **REQUIRED** to map out every single tile of every single area and then keep that information in your head ... Why? That's not narrative driven, that's not the fault of the Engine, that plays no part in the puzzles, it's just poorly thought out.

Bad Horror
[hr][/hr]

Good horror doesn't rely on jump scares, it relies on making an idea that's otherwise taboo and hard to explain, a reality. Sure, zombies are scary because they're living dead (spoooopy 😨😱), but what's really scary is the idea of losing all faculty of mind and [i]becoming[/i] a mindless drone set out to destroy the very thing that you are and everything that your species has worked to accomplish.

The atmosphere looks good and it stops after that. The OST is non-existent and the jump cuts (which I'm guessing was for cheap jump scares?) were very underwhelming. So when it comes to bad horror (jump scares) it fails and when it comes to good horror (setting up a believable atmosphere and exploring big ideas)

The story [i]had[/i] potential. It's a damn shame I couldn't actually see if there were any big or good ideas to be explored. So I have to go off of what I know.

From as far as I got, there's a child that's gone missing from 2 parents who are (or are getting) divorced and want custody. We could have explored big ideas like feelings of ineptitude (are my parents separating because of me?), abusive/negligent parents, or several other topics.

So when it comes to bad horror (jump scares/shock value) it fails and when it comes to good horror (setting up a believable atmosphere and exploring big ideas) it fails.

Conclusion
[hr][/hr]

I should not have to fight the controls to play the game. I should not have to fight the map to play the game. I should not have to "guess" how TF I solve a puzzle to play the game, and I should not have to reverse an audio recording (???) to understand the game's story.

This video game would have been served much better in a different media. If it were just a video, removing the game, it would  be improved. Working to understand the [b]story outside of the game is bad design[/b]. The reason that works so well in a video is because the viewer isn't required to move around the clunky, hidden map or solve shitty puzzles. They just need to resolve "How do I decipher this message or understand this audio recording?" They feel like an active participant and are more invested in the story. I'm required to do that [b]AND[/b] move around the same areas, no joke, 12 separate times to find nothing has changed, with no direction given and no fucks to give to comb every square inch of every tile of every area for the secret entrance to a new area.

I gave this game a shot after a friend recommend it. I made fun of him for playing a furry game naturally, because of all of its connotations and the repulsive subculture, but I downloaded the demo to try it out.
To my surprise, the writing was good and it was getting better. It has animations and they are good? And the music is great too? No way. Oh no.
Twenty five hours of reading later and I think I just had the most humbling, life changing gaming experiences of my life. Easily the 2024 game of the year, no competition. And while I still can't stand furries this is now one of my favorite games. Are those two things contradictory positions? Yes.

First of all, everything from the colorful style to the name "I Wani Hug That Gator" screams that this is a bad attempt at a self parody, a cringy wifu simulator, or a ♥♥♥♥ post. It completely embraces this expectation, or rather it completely unapologetically embraces its dumb premise and asks itself 'But how do we actually make this kind of game good?'. And the answer is to just tell a compelling romance story, but the impressive part is that they actually managed to pull it off.

The style in a way blindsides the player, the over the top designs make you lower your guard, so when the moment comes, the exploration of more mature themes hits all the harder. And it is masterfully executed.

A big part of the game's charm for me are the multiple endings that give the game real stakes. The main character is not a blank slate, although you couldn't tell by the design. Instead, you guide him in a certain path by picking some choices for him, watch him struggle with his own problems and hopefully by the end of the game he becomes his own person.

To my surprise, there is never a point in the story that feels off tone wise, and the humor is well balanced with the more serious plot points. Despite the fact that a big part of the game is lighthearted banter intermittent with slapstick humor, the game and the story itself never become the punchline. It's so refreshing compared to modern day marvelbrain baby writing today's writers are increasingly afflicted with.

This game is clearly a labor of love, it is what you would call soulfull. In this day and age where products masquerade as art, this is a shining example of what is possible to create when you create with heart.

Everything from the writing, the art, the music, and the animations work wonderfully together to create a cohesive believable world. The music does a lot to elevate the scenes, and there are some real gems in there. You know that a soundtrack is good, when you notice it. "I Dream of a Dance", "Final First Page", "Furious March of Red", "Green Specter", "Teenage Traffic" all stand out as highlights of the original soundtrack. The are fantastic on their own, and paired together with the scenes they are written for they are absolute perfection, and I love them. Even the non original tracks are well picked and add a lot to scenes in which they are used. We are talking about some real tear jerking tracks that will leave even the most grizzled, shriveled up, bonafide crusty sailor complaining about sudden onsets of rain or having some crap stuck in their eyes.

The only questionable parts are the crude pixelated background images that are either passable or stick out like a sore thumb. There was an effort made to make them fit in, but some of them really make the game feel cheap in comparison to the rest of it. The art that is there is great, and while the budget was obviously put into some parts (animations) and not others (background images), there clearly wasn't a lack of effort, because the game is full of details. For example, all over the game there are simple sprite movement animations of the characters visually reacting to something that was said or seen. They add life to the characters and some of them are very cleverly used to convey the story through visuals.

The characters are for the most part well written and very human. They feel as if they are real people, and not just characters there to entertain you or to be a foil to you. While I have given a lot of praise here to the writing, it is not perfect by any means. There are some flaws with the story, but none of them are enough the ruin the good parts. For example not all the characters got the amount of exploration I would have liked. Some parts felt rushed and are left somewhat unfinished, but it's clear that the writers wanted to focus on the two main characters. The reason being, delivering the game's central themes.

The two main characters Inco and Olivia struggle with self actualization, agency and responsibility, and you get two see them at their best or worst depending on your choices.

The game does a beautiful job of presenting those struggles, and it does so consistently, with kindness, and most importantly a real sort of rough sincerity that could have only come from the author's personal experience. The maturity with which the themes and characters are explored makes this one of the best romance stories I've ever seen. If I had to describe the game in two words, it would be unapologetically sincere.

And finally, I don't think a piece of media ever made me cry out of happiness before. I cried like a baby during one of the animations. This wonderful story made me really inspired to create again, something I hadn't felt in a long time. I didn't know how much I needed this game until I got to play it. This piece of art touched me deeply, and it's messages will stick with me forever.

It's okay. Nothing that truly crazed me out. To be honest, I am more indifferent to it then anything. See, because at the start I was super interested. I had hoped that this wasn't going to be a game with a slice of life type of deal. Where there are no issues, and it become bland. Thankfully, there are plenty of issues, situations, and conflicts. Of course, are they actually well written, is the massive picture here. Considering this is a visual novel, the story is front and center, and the rest is dressing. Although, I will admit, that the animations, art, and music are all up to par. Even with the furry stuff (For the record, I do not like this type of material.) I like how it was used to make comedy, but that's about it. 

 I still think their are multiple scenes that can portray the characters emotions well. Inco, is probably my example here. He seems to be more expressive then the rest, and more bombastic. Although, there were multiple moments where I think he was out of character(?) of sorts, and just to play catch-up with the audience, in terms of emotions, and feelings. The scenes with him and Olivia are decently written, I just feel like there was a bit of fluff in the mid-range of this game to delay Iadakhan and the eventual endings. Her disability is fine. Not a lot would've changed if she didn't have it though, which really isn't a good thing. Speaking of, I have not gotten all of the endings, I will admit. I know that this, for some, can mean an invalid review of sorts. I disagree. The ending I got (3) was a slow burner, of sorts. It had boiled down to Olivia coming to terms with her grief, but a year to late. I think it fits, considering what had happened beforehand. She was to scared to face what she needed to move on from, and so it sort of ate at her, until she had thought moving out would fix it. I have seen parts of the other endings, but I just can't be bothered to replay this entire game again for it, sorry. 

One thing that did bother me, however, was a TON of the other characters. Ben, Damien, Liz, and that is pretty much it. Everyone else was a massive blur in the grand scheme of things. I just can't tell if I was retarded or there are genuine writing issues here. I seriously had a massive brain fog mid-way through this game, and started skipping out on texts. Just mindlessly clicking. I don't like when I do that, especially in visual novels. By the end of the game, you and Olivia are pretty much all that matter. I'm not saying that it's a bad thing, that was the whole objective of the game anyway. It didn't help that a lot of the characters were stereotyped. Jock, Dumb Kid, Worried Mom. But I would've loved for a more character oriented decision from Olivia. It focuses so much on her, but I felt so disconnected. What else has she really brought to the table that others haven't? It feels like others are speaking more for her, then she is for herself. Now that I am thinking about it, that was probably intentional. Fair enough, blank slate characters are valid and can be used effectively. I just feel like to much time was wasted on "cheering" her up, instead of making goals or achievements for her. Ben was partially right in a couple of things he said about her. 

Besides that, I don't really know what else to say. This game was a fun time, but holy fuck, I should've slept more during some of those text-boxes. If you want a visual novel, with some cute girl, and some other slice of life narrative shenanigans, pick it up. Otherwise, go for something a bit better.

Unless you live with Patrick (under a rock) or have never paid any attention to a single console game. I find it unlikely that anyone reading this review does not know what Ratchet and Clank is. But I'll tell you anyway.

Rift Apart is the first port of a R&C game to PC. I am unsure of its place in the timeline, but I don't feel that it's relevant as the game can played standalone without any knowledge or understanding of the surrounding lore or mechanics.

[b]Described succinctly[/b] Rift Apart is a third person shooter/action adventure with 3D platforming elements.

[h3]I honestly don't think there's much to say about this game.[/h3]
It's fun, it's relatively simple. Straightforward. The combat can be chaotic given the nature of the weaponry. Coming from Insomniac Games, this developer and series are primarily known for its wacky and obtuse weapons and gadgetry. There is a considerable amount of weapon swapping do to low ammo — I believe this is designed intentionally to give the combat more variety. Using specific weapons also levels them up. Which is a separate leveling system to “Raritainium” used to unlocked nodes at the shop. It's all very [i]standard affair[/i]. 

Typically you'll play as Ratchet in this series, with Clank on his back. But in Rift Apart, you be swapping between Ratchet and a character named Rivet.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3426329129

There are many collectibles and a few side activities in the game.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3426330540

[h3]Deck Specs[/h3]
This is normally where I write how it performs on the Steam Deck. However, I didn't play it there. I tested it briefly — And while it is Verified, I would not call it an ideal experience. It's very much a 720@30ish on low or very low preset type of experience. The game features a TON of effects on weapons and telemetry to forecast enemy shots. The screen is absurdly busy all the time during combat. And there isn't that much exploration. It's playable on Deck, but not where I'd recommend it.

[h3]The Gist[/h3]
It's a great game. Albeit a forgettable one. The last game I played of this series was “Up Your Arsenal” on the PS2. And this game did not strum my nostalgia strings the way I had hoped. It's still very fun, however. Wait for a sale if you're unsure. Or pay full price if you think it'll make Sony bring more stuff faster. The choice is ours, I believe in you.

Originally completed on PS5, replaying here for better graphics/fps. On my 4080/13900k I typically get ~90fps with everything on max, raytracing high/medium, but raytracing ambient occlusion off (it kills fps, although looks nice).

Definitely has more technical issues than the PS5 version:

* Changing graphics settings, especially ray tracing, often kills performance until you restart the game.

* I know RT ambient occlusion is new and PC specific, but it's probably not usable on anything less than a 4090

* DLSS framegen was very buggy for me. Often I'd get lower fps with it on than off, so I just left it off. Game runs well enough without on a 4080 anyway

* Poor performance for first couple hours of play. FPS was generally 20-30fps lower than what it settled to. I assume that it must have been shader compilation or something similar.

* Far more bugs than PS5 version. I've encountered 1 or 2 bugs per world. Sometimes my char gets trapped in a weird waterfall jump when no water is present (just a splashing animation), sometimes npcs fail to animate, etc.. Nothing game breaking but I never encountered a single bug on PS5 so I assume it's the port.


All that said the game looks way better on PC with DLSS and new ray tracing features. Really gorgeous. I disabled in game HDR and use RTX HDR instead, it's better (as is often the case). The new bugs aren't enough to detract from what is really excellent craftmanship of the game beneath.

Definitely worth it, just do restart after changing graphics settings and if your graphics card is 4080 or lower skip RT ambient occlusion. Other settings don't lower performance that much on a 4080, totally worth it there. Also just in case it's useful for someone, I couldn't notice the diff between medium RT shadows and the higher settings.

The first I saw of Rift Apart was on it's initial PS5 launch day, being streamed on Twitch at 60fps in 1080p. It looked pretty amazing graphically even with those restrictions, and the gameplay itself looked pretty great too.

Admittedly, this is my first Ratchet & Clank experience, so I'm not coming into it with my opinions coloured by previous releases. But in absolute terms, this is a great game.  

Graphically speaking, it looks absolutely great. Even at 2K resolution, on a 4K monitor, it's probably the best-looking game I've played. And at 4K it's even better. The art direction is great, capturing the character of the game perfectly, with having fun clearly being at the centre of things.

In terms of gameplay, then we're still on really solid ground. The weapons range from fun variants of classic chooter weapons (pistol, shotgun etc) to completely unique. The enemy types are pretty varied and do encourage use of a good chunk of the player's arsenal, meaning that, whilst a few weapons will be maxed out fully, a good number will be significantly upgraded as well.  Most of the upgraded weapons are good fun to deploy, whether against fodder or heavy adversaries. It's a nice touch that enemies comment on the player's weapon of choice during the heat of battle.

Weapon upgrades are the main reward for exploration, and exploring the environments is pretty enjoyable in and of itself. The map makes things relatively straightforward for collectables, particularly after obtaining the upgraded map.

 The score is cinematic in nature and does a great job complementing the gameplay and story. The story itself isn't particularly deep, but is told with enough humour to keep me engaged.

Difficulty wise, on the second hardest, I did have a few areas of trouble, but the checkpointing meant that giguring out the most successful approach wasn't too bothersome. But overall, it wasn't overbearing to get through the  encounters, especially once I'd gotten used to being on a controller instead of KB&M.

The Challenge Mode, after completing the main campaign, is a nice addition, allowing for a NG+ with tougher enemies to go alongside your upgraded arsenal from the first play-through. New weapons and upgrades are also added, to encourage further experimentation in combat.

I didn't intend on getting 100% completion, but found myself accidentally at 80% and figured it wouldn't be a bother to get the remainder (it wasn't). I'm now working through a Challenge Mode campaign on the hardest difficulty and having just as much fun as the first time around.

All in all, a great game that remembers what the point of video games is - to have some fun!

Alright. [i]Robotherapy[/i] is done and dusted. This is a visual novel with a couple super lite shooter sections, focused on the mental health of robots after killing all humans. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3430744287

You play as Smokes, a delusional megalomaniacal robot who decides he is going to be a robotherapist, and the best one in the world at that. Although he is really about as bad a therapist as you could be, lol. And so anyway, that's what he does. He becomes a robotherapist. A decision he makes while sitting at a cafe. Early on, he meets another robotherapist named Back, who becomes a mentor to Smokes despite Smokes of course acting as if he doesn't need one. Smokes begins taking clients. First a robot named Quantum, then a robot named Whatever. And he also meets a robot named R, whose idea it was to kill all humans to begin with. Throughout the game, while Smokes (and Back) are treating Quantum and Whatever, it really ends up with Smokes receiving some inadvertent treatment himself. And there is of course a big reveal towards the end that has the other robots rallying to help Smokes out.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3430744294

In my opinion, what this game really does well is present mental health issues in a way that treats mental health issues not as something everybody can understand and identify with, but simply as what they are, with no recrimination or people feeling a need to act as if they can identify with said problems. And yet, I think the real message is that you really aren't alone even if you have to be willing to address these issues yourself. IDK. I'm not somebody who identifies with these issues on a personal level, but I think being open to learning about them is important. And the comedy presentation is effective in my opinion.

And so, with that in mind, the dialogue is funny and witty, with a lot of banter, some fourth wall breaking, and a couple other characters that fill out the roster and the game. The graphics and audio are simplistic, but effective in enhancing the game. And I think the developer really had some fun making this game. It shines through.

I recommend this game primarily out of respect for what it represents. It's rare to find a single-player trading card game on Steam that isn't a roguelike, making it a standout in its genre. It brings back nostalgic memories of playing Yu-Gi-Oh! Day of the Duelist and GX Duel Academy on the GBA. While the core gameplay is unique and intriguing, the game suffers from significant progression and balancing issues that detract from the overall experience.

[b]Story (3/10)[/b]
Almost no plot, just a little twist in the end game.

[b]Lore and World Building (2/10)[/b] 
It's there but not interesting enough.

[b]Dialogue (2/10)[/b]
Too flat, no emotion or characters.

[b]Progression system (4/10)[/b]
Feels like playing angry bird where you unlock new stage (NPC) linearly, but with a 5 level difficulty for each of them. Collecting badges from the guardian doesn't feel rewarding. No end game content. 

[b]Economy Design (6/10)[/b]
You can buy booster pack using gold and crafting cards using stardust. And pick a random dark card after battling NPC. The price seems fair enough, but you can easily craft overpowered celestial card or get a random legendary dark card too easily.

[b]Combat System (7/10)[/b]
It's decent. I like the concept of 5 minute card battle. It's interesting that every lane has certain effect that impacting the card placement strategy. And evolving the plano in the field feels satisfying. What I found lacking is the status effect, one card can only has one status at a time, so inflicting status ailment won't override the other based on its stack count, which make it rather confusing.

[b]Visual Style (7/10)[/b]
It's good enough. Cool monster and character design. Just lacking in animation and character expression.

[b]Interface Design (6/10)[/b]
Basic, feels cheap, but works.

[b]Control and Interaction (6/10)[/b]
No Gamepad support, so it cannot be played on Steam Deck. Cannot skip the after battle result which is time consuming. But, it's a good thing that it has options to turn off some animation and display on the battle scene.

[b]Replayability (5/10)[/b]
Very low Replayability. Grinding achievements feels like a chore, it should add other achievement or battle restrictions that will encourage player to use different deck and strategies to play which is the main appeal of the game.

[b]Balance & Difficulty (4/10)[/b]
Despite the advantage of having more than 3 same cards, playing against the CPU impose no challange at all, the game needs most improvement in that area. And the CPU opponent is too dumb, often result in missplay when playing a complex card's effect.

Various Daylife is a very good contender for the worst RPG I have ever played. Its shocking that this was made by the Octopath Traveler devs, in which I consider Octopath Traveler II to be one of my favorite RPGs ever.  If the mostly negative reviews didn't stop you, allow me to share my experience I had with this game. 

[b] The Gameplay/Various Daylife  [/b]
This game really didn't feel like it had any soul in it at all. To start, when traveling to different areas is always 2D, which is not necessarily a bad thing, but the execution is terrible. The characters felt really bland and boring and I had little interest in the overall problem (although I barely remember it). Otherwise you perform "Varous Daylife" tasks to improve your stats. There is no minigame or anything to do. You just upgrade your stats with the tasks given to you and you become stronger. Incredibly bad system. 

[b] The Combat [/b]
The combat overall is the worst part, it felt like regardless of what I did I could always defeat the enemy. There was some interesting combo potential, but it wasn't well executed at all. There were certain times at the beginning where I chose a move and it didn't deduct any SP or HP from my character, and did the powerful move anyway. I also failed to mention that when your exploring, there is no way to control your characters directions or actions except when in battle. In Octopath Traveler, you could go off the main path and find a chest that rewarded you for going a different path, or in some instances you would find a difficult new area where all the enemies would kill you easily. Not here tho! The characters just walk in a straight line and don't do anything until they've walked enough steps to find the boss. The first boss was so easy that he didn't even attack me once and it was a incredibly boring and bland battle. 

Overall, this game is not fun in the slightest. I was actually in pain every moment I was playing this game. I mean look at the title screen its a nearly 1:1 copy of Octopaths, but with a different background and name. AVOID AT ALL COSTS, this game is not even fun as a joke. DO NOT BUY!!!!

I'd change 2 things about this game.

[b]The first would be how the plant works[/b]. As it stands it seems to be either randomly available or open to feeding on a timer.  I would make it so that the plant is only unavailable after you feed it, because it has to chew its food, make it a fixed timer or dynamic relying on the amount of food, and tweak it it so that the plant isn't available until the player is usually over burdened and must choose between waiting and dumping their food. Regardless of what you do; [b]Add sound cues to when the plant opens or closes their mouth.[/b] That extra feedback would allow casual and master players alike good feedback as to when they can feed the plant.

[b]The second would be how garden plants grow[/b], there is a lack of feedback when you feed your plant. Sometimes, especially in missions with slow growth to your garden that you can feed your garden and see no visible change which is unsatisfying to say the least. Adding more growth states or making the plants wiggle or emit some particles a little when they get fed would signal to the player that your action meant something, and would be a touch more satisfying then nothing at all.

I really enjoy this game, I think it's fantastic. I'd be the first negative critic to post a bad review for it which hurts me as much, if not more, then it might hurt the team who made it. This is, as far as I can tell, a 2 man team who crafted something with love.

However, I absolutely can not stand the shoehorned Communist and Lesbian dialogue from the protagonist girl you get in the extra’s menu, it immediately took me out of the game. 

Both of these things are handled in the worst, most lazy way possible.

Maybe you could have shown us an ending scene where the protagonist comes back home to her wife and the two use the fruits to bake a pie or something. You know, something charming and subtle, I'd be characterful and pleasant. Instead of what we got which makes me think about a Dev ham-fistededly pushing in something for bonus points.

And the Communism thing is totally beyond the pale. [i] I’m sorry, am I playing a 5 dollar steam game or attending a Marx lecture? [/i] It brings up world building questions this game isn’t ready to answer. Again, it's cheap brownie point panning.

But worst of all makes me think about the dark history of failed, centuries-old ideology built on the good intentions of people exactly like our protagonist before leading to some of the most horrible atrocities ever committed by man. It’d be like if she threw up her right hand showing a blood red swastika arm band and said, “I’M GROWING FRUIT FOR THE MASTER RACE” or commented on how she’s actually a slave taken from her family, growing fruit under strict quota under the threat of whippings or a impromptu  public hanging in front of her peers. It’s fucked up. I don’t want to think about firing squads, government land seizure, mass psychological manipulation and public humiliation for daring to resist authority, or tyrannical regimes in my cutesy arcade games.

Even if it was removed I’d still be poisoned by this bad juju and not want to play the game because now I associate with all this messed up stuff I think video games should largely try to stray from unless they have a meaningful point to make in their commentary on these subjects.

This, I realize, is way too many words for a review, but I want to make my point clear and explain exactly why I can’t love this otherwise love-able game. 

So bottom line: If your down with Communism and/or are a Lesbian (or like seeing them included) and you don’t mind (or even really like) cheap inclusion name drops of the things you like then this game is going to be right up your alley and you’re going to love it. If I could describe Garden Guardian in two words, they would be "simple" and "effective".

At its core, this is a very easy game to learn and play, while still remaining fun and engaging. The gameplay is inspired by classic Game & Watch LCD games, and it's all about positioning, timing, and managing your flow. The game features a decent selection of difficulty options for the main endless mode, as well as a pretty substantial collection of challenges, each with their own modifiers and conditions to deal with.

The presentation is appealing and very clean. The menus are done in a Smash or Kirby style, and it looks nice and professional, with no unnecessary visual clutter. Seems like a small detail, but it's very appreciated. The art looks nice, and the character designs are cute and interesting. Music also fits the tone of the game very well.

The price is definitely fair for what you get, even if the game itself is rather simple. The level of polish alone makes it well worth the money, and being able to support a new indie developer as well as plant trees is just icing.

Where the game could use improvement is in the settings menu. There are no built-in screen size options, you have to Alt+Enter and resize the window by hand. Definitely not a big deal, the workaround is more than fine, but having those options built-in would just be a bit easier.

All in all, Garden Guardian is a great and polished first effort by a new developer. It knows what it is, and does that very well. Highly recommended to anyone who's nostalgic for LCD games or is looking for a fun time-waster.

Please note that my playtime as of writing this review is low, but that's because I primarily played it on PS5. It got lost in the backlog during my transition back to PC gaming, and I intend to pick it up again. I only got four, maybe five hours into it, but I feel I have a basic grasp of what the game is like, and why it's worth playing.

First off - this is a one man indie project. It's *extremely* janky. The animations in particular are very clunky and odd. But the game reeks with charm from head to toe. The primary game mechanic, while perhaps underutilized, is a unique one - you cannot do anything that you haven't first observed someone else do. The game starts, for instance, with you lying on the ground, unable to walk until you observe a nearby chicken doing so. As you progress in the game, you gain the ability to use magic - shortly before I finished my last play session, I had unlocked the ability to summon a sort of spirit deer, which massively opened up traversal options.

The game doesn't hold your hand. It's not always clear where you should go, and the game is rather merciless and punishing at times. The game world is rather empty as well, and before you unlock new traversal options, it can be a bit of a chore getting from point A to point B. But there's a sort of wonder in unraveling this bizarre game, and a freedom in how you move through it - for instance, at one point I encountered a bunch of neutral mercenary NPCs, and I decided to liberate some of their equipment, causing them to be permanently hostile towards me. (Unfortunately, I had not yet observed anyone using said equipment, and so it was useless in my hands.) My understanding is that how you play the game also affects a sort of morality system, although I have not yet played enough to see the consequences of that.

I'm not sure if I'd call this game a diamond in the rough. It's more like an old, rusted heirloom you find on the side of the road, and while some might ask you to throw it away, you can't help but wonder as to what its story is and who it belonged to. But that mystery in and of itself makes it special.

Also, it might be a metroidvania? Idk, but progress in certain areas is locked behind gaining the ability to perform certain actions, which you gain in other areas. That's kind of like a metroidvania, right?

You have to be very creative in building multiple separate warehouses, each with their own workforce, and the whitelist/blacklist settings, or the warehouse workers will steal all the ropes, fibres and leather scraps from your workshops. Then the craftsmen will grab those items from the warehouse, resulting in a constant tug of war, and production grinding to a standstill. Oh and don't even THINK of building additional stockpiles for stuff like weapons or tools, other than for your personal use- production limits only apply to items in workshop storage. In short, you'll have fun at the start of the game, but once you get further along and try to set up a working village, you'll get burnt. I can't in good conscience recommend this game in this state, it needs serious work on its internals and mechanics.

Really on the fence about this decision as Aska is a very promising game well deserving of "Mostly positive" reviews, with lots of very innovative ideas and it really is a great experience. However currently the game still suffers from many issues which directly affect it's game-play in negative way. Among those are:

-The game appears to be locked at 60FPS which while frustrating, actually doesn't affect experience too much, especially with recently released Nvidia Smooth Motion which can force 120fps output
-There are many cases where NPC get stuck in action and unless you figure out the reason for it, can break the whole production chain
-At times it feels like there's too much micro management due to having manually go and build "work markers" and themselves having less of a radius than idea.
-NPC sometimes stop their work to inform player of non-issue like particular plant not growing in off-season
-Production limits ignore non-building storage and equipped items such as items in warehouse or items stashed in other building leading to overproduction and inability to control desired output.
-Upon destruction, rebuild buildings don't automatically re-open past tasks which can lead to starving village and can end up costing a lot of time.
-UI leaves a lot to be desired, everything is made in form of lists, other than UI nothing is really grid based even when it would greatly benefit usability. It makes interacting with buildings a bit of a chore.
-At times it feels like developers would benefit a lot from exposure to other games in related genres, such as Rimworld where player allocates tasks in time per job rather than per building, or further exploring why Valheim food system worked so well while ASKA's does not.
-Game performance leaves a lot to be desired, on intel i9 12900k, RTX5080 and 64GB RAM game can at times drop to <40fps.

It is a great game and i wish i could give recommendation as "Yes, but..." However with that being the case, i would currently not recommend to try the game unless you're fan of genre and are willing to deal with a lot of inconveniences and bugs.
