Easy to recommend, very nice game. The visuals are wonderful, the gameplay is smart, the design of the different communities is clearly well thought out and consistent. The reveal at the true ending was also very clever, and it was nice to see those 8-11 hours blossom. Having done a little bit of research and seeing some of the comments the devs have written explaining the decisions they made, it's clear that Sennaar was designed with a lot of consideration to exactly how it plays - which shows in the very high positive review count.

If you're reading reviews to decide whether to buy the game, the above is enough: you should! Unfortunately i'm a terminal hater so, for me, there's a couple of things which stop Sennaar from being among the greatest that i'd like to add. 

The first relates to the gameplay itself - I enjoyed walking around and slowly intuiting what each word meant, and I thought the Obra Dinn-like way the game 'locks in' words you've successfully translated was smart (I think a game without that 'lock-in' would be much more frustrating!). However, there are times where it feels a little bit phoned in - I appreciate that you need some way to reintroduce words found in an older language to a new language, but every time i found a 'rosetta stone' (i.e some sign with a message in multiple languages), it felt like cheating. I don't claim to be a game designer so i'm not in any position to suggest how I would have done it different - but there are clear, visceral differences between the delightful 'eureka' moments (such as [spoiler] the glyph on the cutlery informing you about the elements [/spoiler]) and 'oh, it's another sign'. If they were to ever make a sequel, I would love to see a maximal amount of the former and much less of the latter, particularly in the final stretches of the game.

My other comment relates to the overall story - skip this if you haven't played the game yet (it shouldn't discourage you from playing it anyway): 

[spoiler]When it comes to the story, I never really felt a sense of frisson or wonder at any point - but particularly not at the climax of the game, and I found the overall message to be a little saccharine. Yes, the reveal about the links and how they relate to each community's ideals was clever, undeniably. I even agree with that overall message, that communication and language learning breaks down barriers and makes the world a better place. 

The problem is that I would see this sharing of language as a first step, rather than the end in itself; as an indicative example, the idea of communication bringing about total peace is nice, but is soured somewhat by the presence of [i]a literal slave class[/i] (the serfs, who we see serving the bards on the third floor). The relationship between the bards and the serfs is handwaved, even lampooned at one point with the room in the maze dedicated to making anti-serfdom propaganda. This example appears to go entirely against the entire thesis of the game - the bards and the serfs speak the same language, yet they are siloed off into different areas, with one group enjoying beauty and luxury, while the other toiling and sighing at the orders they receive. It doesn't matter how well they communicate with each other, one of them has some sort of hold over the other and will not relinquish it. This is an example, but you could also apply it to the wider tower; are we to expect that the men of the first floor are to feel equal to the warriors, or the bards, or the alchemists (and vice versa)? 

Trying to avoid coming too much across as 'guy who is thinking way too hard about the video game', this is what I mean by 'a little saccharine': it's nice in this fantasy world where everyone apparently sees each other as equal to everyone else (except for where they don't, as with the serfs?); in real life, we have class systems and modes of exploitation and hierarchies and injustices that hinder or prevent this, even with common sharing of language, culture, and interests - shared languages are perhaps necessary, certainly helpful, but simply insufficient for a realistic egalitarian society. To repeat myself and make it unambiguously clear: the game is absolutely right to promote sharing of language and culture, but it does not tackle this idea beyond a fairly cursory 'and then everyone was happy forever'. It's a 'nice' ending, but 'nice' doesn't inspire the awe that I would expect from a 'greatest of all time' game.[/spoiler]

Sennaar was a wonderful way to spend ~8 hours, with a good amount of think about and some very satisfying puzzle moments (except for [spoiler]the minecart on the fourth floor, which i didn't realise you could get in and constituted the only time I had to google what to do next[/spoiler]). I'm very interested to see if the devs release something similar - or indeed something completely different!

It's a beautiful game, with great music, style, visuals, message and compeling gameplay. However, it's definitely not perfect: Stealth sections are awful, it is too easy for most of the game but has some weird difficulty spikes, and there's a lot of blind, slow walking backtracking by the end of the game, when trying to go for achievements.

Definitely worth playing if you like games like Obra Dinn or Tunic, I give it an 8 out of 10.

i want to make it clear that i don't think chants of sennaar is a bad game. i just think it's more of a "very positive" than an "overwhelmingly positive". the language deciphering gameplay and puzzles worked well for the most part, and the themeing and visuals are top notch. but there are a lot of rough edges. the stealth sections, which show up fairly often, are just terrible. although the language deciphering and puzzles work well for the most part, sometimes they really don't make much sense. also, considering the price tag, the game is fairly light on content. those 12.9 hours i spent in chants of sennaar include all the meaningful things there are to do in the game. oh, and the difficulty peaks in the middle for some reason, then it just starts getting easier. that's not really that big of flaw in my book, but it is weird. in conclusion, i would recommend this chants of sennaar, but not at full price

As a language nerd, this game heavily appealed to me. It's a great puzzle game about languages and honestly I think we need more games like it. I really enjoyed the environments and music; the game looks and sounds incredible! As someone who doesn't do too well with chase scenes or stealthing in video games, those parts were a bit difficult, but still fun! I loved learning about the world through the languages, behavior of the inhabitants, and environment. Even if you're not a language nerd, it's still very fun!:)

I've never encountered a puzzle game like this one, it's insanely complex in the best sense. I never imagined I'd enjoy a puzzle game based entirely on languages to be so good. The soundtrack is gorgeous, the puzzles are somehow complex enough to have me thinking about how to solve them for a while (the alchemists' weight puzzle almost made my head explode), but they're still possible to solve eventually. The story itself is insane, it took a twist I didn't see coming. I had so much fun playing this game and I'm sure I'll replay it later even now that I know how it ends :D
Really fun and unique approach to a puzzle game through learning (fictional) languages. The environmental storytelling is incredibly immersive as well.

7.8 out of 10.
This games puzzles are really engaging due to being context based. The contexts in which you must engage are super interesting, this is because of the games really good looking colourful artstyle and also due to the games fantastic world building in which a commentary on culture and societal structure.
I think there were only a handful of puzzles (like one or two iirc) that were a bit misleading, however this is not enough for me to say this game isnt worth a purchase. Another downside of this game is the lack of options if you need to backtrack certain areas, you will have to play long animations to get into some places (however, you wont need to often, and fast travels remove most of this) I would definitely but this game if you are into puzzle games, into games with world building or if you enjoy the interplay of culture and science.

GG really fun game
I love it! A really cool game. More games like this should be made, with a more wide world maybe and DLC to expand on new languages, scripts... Truly one om my favourite games of all time
A very fun puzzle game with amazing storytelling, sound design and visual design. Big recommend for anyone who likes puzzle games
Really fun and interesting game focusing on mechanics around translating languages which is better the less you know.

I just adore this game so much, immediately after playing for my first time I was excited to forget what all the glyphs translated to so i could play it all over again, and after a year and a few months i've played it again and I love it even more, i was familiar with the world, story and some of the 'language rules' but got to have the fun puzzling like the first time. 

I love how much you can learn about each of the peoples and whats important to their culture by what words are seen, learning about how each of them sees each other the same kind of way, the languages are consistent in themselves and some can be worked out by noticing connections in certain kinds of symbols (eg, all location symbols have this feature. the symbol is a part of that symbol and so on)

Aesthetically its gorgeous and i love the music, sound affects and its just beautiful in every way.

And the story, a good amount of it is told by the environment and I'm always a fan of that, helping everyone feels so rewarding and its wonderful seeing the results of you helping them.

Definitely one of my most favourite games, this will forever be special to me.
Really interesting premise, beautiful and charming aesthetic, and fun gameplay! It's always so satisfying to learn a new word or solve a puzzle, and the story and lore is fascinating to watch unfold.
Fun and creative game about languages. Multiple languages to discover and find what each word means. Provides a good level of challenge and difficulty. Highly recommend.

A beautiful puzzle game that successfully strides the line of neither ridiculously hard nor too simple. They have created a challenge where you feel your linguistic skills stretched and it's woven into a thoughtful story. Was hooked from early on.
absolutely brilliant level design. this should be the textbook on how to write games

Saw this and bought it same-day, what a well executed concept of language/symbol puzzle solving. Reminds me partly of Myst except your character is able to take notes themselves, but it's still up to you to solve it all though.

The graphical style of this is very simplistic, obviously, but it keeps your focus on the task at hand which is to resolve the languages of each group of people. I won't spoil why you're tasked with doing this.

I did have some issues remembering where certain places were as many areas look the same in a way. I couldn't remember if there was a path in the next area that went in a certain direction. None of the levels are meant to be mazes, though there is an actual maze in the game, but it was confusing more often than not. Eventually the quick travel made things better.

Overall this was a great game for the price I got it at on sale, it's still worth the $20 base price but your mileage may vary depending on what you get out of it.

Amazing game, wish it was longer but it's basically perfect as-is. The puzzles aren't the hardest but are satisfying to solve and there aren't many frustrating sections. In Phoenix Wright for example sometimes you know the answer but not the right evidence to show- despite being about deciphering languages this game doesn't have much of that frustration.

9.5 / 10

This game takes you on a captivating journey. A point-and-click adventure where you need to litteraly decode the world in order to know what is going on and what to do. On top of all that, you need to solve puzzles while translating and feel smart as hell when you finally get it.  Overall the game is a wonderfull feat of story-telling and an original take on how languages relate to culture and history.

Great fun, short and sweet.

Was a very fun game! Very engaging puzzles and kept me on my toes! Had to really think and apply my mind, but was not frustrating in any way. 
The whole premise of the game is amazing! That you have to "translate" and "learn" new languages. :)
LOVED IT!
Incredibly fun! Try to avoid spoilers if you can, it is a puzzle game after all! I 100%ed it, so it's not too long, but I did most of that in one sitting. Didn't want to put it down!

Great game, creative puzzles, awesome art. It is quite easy to miss something or get lost, and getting stuck can be frustrating, but that made it more fun to eventually figure it out (even if I had to consult a guide here and there).
Highly recommend this game. I absolutely loved it. It got really hard at the end but it was worth it!

I LOVE LOVE LOVE this game. The language learning aspect of it is really unique. I've never been more impressed and engrossed in a game before. The world building was interesting too. I really recommend it if you're interested in linguistics or unique puzzles.

fun, creative, storytelling, puzzle, horror (kind of), never seen before art/graphics, amazing soundtrack... But most of all, It was able to tell me a story, a big amazing story, in 5 languages! never saying a single english word! This story kinda reflects our world, but, that's my opinion. 10/10 would recomend.

Chants of Sennaar is an incredibly charming experience. On the surface level the art style and audio design is delightful! The different areas of the game are all unique yet each one is appealing in its own way. The music and sound effects really sell the experience as well.

The main draw of this game is of course its language based puzzles. I found these to be really enjoyable and thanks to the fairly tight run time I felt it never out stayed its welcome. The puzzles made you feel clever and there were multiple hints scattered around the world to point you in the right direction if you were stuck.

If I had to choose any negatives of the experience there are a few stealth sections that aren't the game's strongest points. It can also sometimes be easy to get lost as there is no in game map. That being said, if you are into word/logic puzzles at all and appreciate a good art style I can't recommend this enough!

Brilliant and aesthetically gorgeous puzzle game. They did a fantastic job of giving you all the pieces and hints to work things out for yourself - and yet you still feel like a genius when you complete a journal page or a language.  I appreciated the occasional non-translation puzzle mechanics like infiltration, they helped to not make the game feel stale. And I really appreciate how interwoven the achievements are, they don't feel like random tasks for no reason, they added to my enjoyment of the story.

This game has successfully made me immersed in the language and social culture of each faction that exists in this game.

Right off the bat, its introduction is pretty simple: something generic to define something i.e. a yes/no kind of glyph and we don't really need to even understand yet what [b]exactly[/b] it's supposed to mean, until we connect the glyphs we find towards an image we note it to. Then it follows by making us learn simple interaction glyphs like when we greet someone or address you/me, that kind of stuff. This game makes us attempt to learn languages in the most natural way possible, and I'm very enlightened to understand more things the more I see each faction behave.

For a game that's very involved with decoding language, I'm surprised how simple (by playtime duration) this game goes, but that's just how efficient its worldbuilding and storytelling is: A lot of the lores are built through stuff you can just look and read, and this game doesn't need to make you listen to people talking, because you've always naturally try to listen to the world you encounter after you've done something anyway, hoping to understand something new of their world they live in. Heck, later in the game you're well rewarded for understanding their language by making OTHERS understand other factions' languages and see how it makes the world change every so slightly every time you connect each dot together. Most of your playtime is well spent fully trying to learn the world within.
Just owsome! briliant puzzels and story telling, beautiful visuals and music, amazing! thank you and well done!

Amazing game, but not for me. Now I finished most of my games on principle and this game just wasn't for me. I still recommend it however since I can see why people would love this game. 

No handholding, you simply move forward and figure your way out, my favourite aspect translating the five different languages with their unique writings make for rather engaging puzzles. The story isn't obvious at first but becomes clear as you progress, learn more of the languages and encounter more people. 

While I did not enjoy this game much I see why people would love a game like this, so if that all sounds interesting then please don't hesitate to buy this game!
Genuinely the best game i ever had the pleasure of playing. Such a great atmosphere and the sound design helps a lot. Such a great premise and I want a sequel/DLC so badly

A solid and enjoyable little puzzler that will mix things up even while all being the same idea of figuring out a language... for the most part. The vibes of the levels are distinct and fit the residents who live there quiet well. I also really enjoyed the ending which (spoiler) [spoiler] reminded me of a Scooby-Doo chase. [/spoiler]

Great game. Deciphering the glyphs is both catching and rewarding. Like it so much that continued unconsciously looking for unknown symbols in real life.

The best part is the languages structure. They are different and getting that is an essential part of the game. Just by looking on a symbol you can get some information, even if you don't jet know nothing about the language! Overall the process is not too easy to catch on the first try, but not to hard to stumble for a long time. Pure fun!

Stealth is a weak point. Though there's not much of it. The worst part of the game is that it's too damn short. Replayability is low. I wish I could play it for like a 100 hours more.

I loved this game, and if you like puzzles you probably will too. It's challenging at times, but very rewarding to figure out on your own. 

Game works well on steam deck, but I'd recommend playing it with a proper keyboard so you can write down your hints more easily.
This is a great game. The language element is unique, challenging at times, and engaging. Aesthetically, it's clean, simple and beautiful. If you like atmospheric puzzle games, this is a can't miss.

An excellent game. It reminded me of Journey, and Heaven's Vault.
Definitely worth it.
Incredible game, very unique. I really loved it and recommend to everyone.

Chants of Sennaar is a pretty enjoyable language/puzzle game. Similar in style to Obra Dinn and Golden idol (matches of 3 objects for translations/answers) but set within the story of the tower of Babel. I found the game to be generally enjoyable with a few annoyances. The stealth sections detract from the game and aren't that great. I don't really get why they were put in to begin with since mechanically they are a bit clunky. The overly large areas lead to a lot of running around that gets a bit tiresome/tedious if you're lost and trying to figure out where to go. I understand they did this to show the vastness of the tower but it hurts the gameplay a bit.

Outside of these minor gripes the game is very fun and a cool spin on the genre since you're using various languages in this one. If you enjoyed other games in this style it's an easy recommend.

I would give this a thumb sideways if I could. The premise is great (Tower of Babel). I loved the mechanic of doing the translations. However, the art is very simple, and it's easy to get lost after you go through the 10th room with a big square thing in the middle. And there is NO MAP despite your toon carting around a journal the whole game. By the third level I started making my own map, which helped a lot, but the game really should record at least major landmarks for you. The ending is also too long; I was ready to be done long before the credits rolled. Overall, my experience tilts toward the negative. With a map and fewer extraneous endings, this game would have been perfect.

A beautiful story told in the most universally human way possible.

Utterly brilliant.

One of the best adventure/riddle games I've ever played. Wonderful theme, great puzzles, well balanced difficulty-wise. Music sets the right mood and doesn't disturb the experience. Very satysfying. Highly recommend for anybody.

Super interesting and fun puzzle and mystery game. If you've played Obrin Dinn then this form of thinking should be familiar - it requires lots of examining, thinking and piecing together. The game will not tell you what to do most of the time so it's all about trial and error and creating the bigger picture. Some of the languages are more challenging than others - only wish the last language wasn't the easiest one to complete! Overall 9/10
very fun, like if monument valley were about linguistics and longer, 10/10

A puzzle game about learning different languages, who would have thought? If you're looking for nail-gnawing puzzles in a vibrant and colorful world, this is the one for you. I only wish there were even more cultures/languages, yet, I think the game bows beautifully and succinctly in its ending. Its theme of overall unity and collaboration also cannot be overstated in current times. Hope to see much more from this developer in the future!
Ending is very unexpected and strange. gameplay is fun and the puzzles are unique and enjoyable
A good language-translation puzzler with an engaging story. On the short side (took me under 12 hours), so I'd recommend getting it on sale.

This is a game that makes you feel clever from putting the clues and contexts together to solve the languages. I got very stuck on the third language though. I really thought of giving into cheating there. The final language is a gimme, so its 4 languages for you to solve. Overall I very much enjoyed this game.

We fixed the [spoiler]tower of babel[/spoiler]. Take that god.

A cool little puzzle adventure game where you wake up in a weird place and deduce people’s languages through context clues, interactions, and world observations. The way that you deduce the language by learning more about the culture of the people and the layout of the land is super well done as you need to pay attention to how they act, label things, and exist. That joy of deducing what a symbol must be, inputting it into your notebook return of obra dinn style and it being accurate is so gratifying. I think like 95% of the deductions made complete sense to me.

The art style is fantastic and that combined with the music and the visuals give a fantastic experience where each level is distinct and yet ties into the greater story. The large towering spires that you have to navigate do convey how big the surroundings are but navigating through them back and forth can get annoying. Adding to the complaints, the adventure game elements are just OK and the stealth is just annoying. The game excels at the deduction and all the extra bits could have been cut imo for a tighter experience. Also also, I wish a greater variety of language styles would have been used as some of them were very similar and I think they ran out of steam by the end.

Good game if you like puzzles. Great hook into world building. Fun little deduction thing.

I absolutely love this game. The way you figure out the languages through puzzles is fantastic, the music is phenomenal, and the designs are amazing. I would highly recommend this game if you love puzzles.

Really neat puzzle point and click with great visual style and artwork. Great soundtrack, creative game design, and unique environments make this one absolutely worth your time.

The backbone of the puzzles here are reading symbols and translating them. You get to write notes for what you think they mean, and then you have to determine the definitive meaning for them via exploration, interactions, and context clues. Truly an original and engaging concept. 

This game absolutely deserves its reviews. However, id still only give it about an 8.5/10. There is quite a lot of guesswork in the translation, which does make it seem immersive, but quite often, there is a lot of guesswork more than logical deduction. Thats fine, its just not quite as enjoyable as it could be. As with all point and clicks, there is a decent bit of backtracking. This one isnt too bad. Took me about 9ish hours for a full 100% initial playthrough.

The design, storytelling, and music in this game is so wonderful. The puzzles were engaging and challenging, but not too frustrating. There is some low risk suspense in parts of the game, I didn't enjoy the parts that involved sneaking around, but that just boils down to my personal preference. Beautiful game, I highly recommend it.

Incredible puzzle game that makes me feel both immersed in the language and lost the city. The game does a great job at maintaining difficulty without losing the allure of discovery. The pieces of culture incorporated into the surroundings add an extra level of depth that makes me feel like I'm more than just translating, I am helping people break down boundaries. The game does a good job at mixing in difficult concepts with easily identifiable things/places. This game was really fun. Very pretty, good puzzles, and longer than I expected! There were a few times where I thought it was about to end but kept going. This is one of the best things I have ever played. The visuals and the art style are just beyond words. The puzzles are really fun and the game keeps you interested.

A charming linguistic based puzzle game. The mechanics may be simple but its always rewarding. Each new area adds its own unique twist to the core mechanic that makes you never feel like your just repeating the same tasks.
The story line is quite engaging and there is even some unexpected twists to keep you guessing.

I love this game with all my heart, I'd love to see a continuation but it maybe better off as is a good sequel is hard to pull of after all If there is a sequel I'd love to see more complex languages My one criticism would be that learning the fairies language was kinda rushed though the mini game to reach it was cool. (maybe you could have done something more with the compound words)

Great game. Very fullfeeling. Puzzles are just good enough so you have to think. Only thing I can suggest to a new player, do not solve things by trying all options, you will get a lot less satisfaction this way, only use analytical method.

The puzzles are unique and were the perfect level of difficulty for me. If you find something is too hard, I'm willing to bet there's something you missed in the area that will make it easier. The plot and lore of the world is intriguing and pulls you in further.

Beautiful game and message behind, really nice puzzles and design for the languages, their equivalences and how to guide you through them. Intuitive enough to let you understand the meaning of the words, but challenging enough to make you think at times. I loved it from beginning to end. If you like puzzle games, I 100% recommend it :)

Great game about discovery and linguistics.

Not too long, not buggy, visually appealing, music is lovely, controls are nice. Anyone who liked Heaven's Vault will like it as well.

This game has a cool story and interesting mechanics. You get attached to the different groups of people you encounter, learning about their vastly different cultures and languages. The ending makes you think and feel, and I absolutely loved it! Not a lot of replay-ability but there are a couple different "endings" and there are a few achievements you can hunt for. Overall a great game, definitely worth it!

I feel confidant reviewing this now that I've 100% completed it including achievements.

This is a really fun language themed puzzle game. It's not super complex but it is complex enough to be fun. At first I assumed it would be 1 to 1 word replacement based on the demo but it does take grammar into account later and does some fun things that really drive home the main point of the game. 

It's well designed, has fun art direction, a relaxing sound track, and sneak sequences that I didn't hate. Normally I do not like sudden sneak mechanics in games. These are easy enough and also puzzle based enough instead of twitch reflex based that I liked them. Usually I only had issues when I hadn't noticed something on the map or made it more complicated than it needed to be.

My play time is not indicative of the length of the game. I often leave games up while doing other things. This is not a particularly long game but I do think it's well worth it for the cost and it's one of the few games I've played recently that I immediately suggested to friends. 

My main criticism is that the drawings in your in game book sometimes are confusing for what they're supposed to represent. I chose not to brute force the translations and as a result ended up with a few where when I figured out what it DID want I was very confused by their choices. Those are easy to brute force without looking up guides if you get stuck however and there's only one or two like this in the whole game. So it's far from a big issue, just something to be aware of. 

I'd love to find another game like this at some point. It's a really well polished experience and enjoyable to complete.

played this game all at once in two settings, and then, weeks later i had still not gotten it out of my head so i replayed again in a language i dont even speak.

Wonderfully beautiful puzzle game. Very much enjoyed figuring out the different languages, alphabets and syntaxes and their respective underlying cultures.
Genuinely a great puzzle game with a good message. A couple of obtuse puzzle solutions, but overall it felt like nothing was bs.

A nice puzzle of language discovery.  You have to guess the meaning of symbols based on the place and context in which they appear, and are able to test your guesses to unlock the verified translation, which allows you to solve puzzles and level up.

really well made, the story is beautiful, the puzzles are language based and  intriguing, i enjoyed the art. The only downside I found is that there is a tad too much walking, Well worth your time and money!

A beautiful story and clever language puzzles, the easy gameplay of Chants of Sennaar is very enjoyable. The game designer actually designed the basis of different written languages, all different and somewhat reflecting their disparate cultures. You are a traveller, and you wake up from a sarcophagus at the bottom of the Tower -- Sennaar being similar to the Hebrew name for Babel. The cultures of the tower are broken and isolated, and your inherent raison d'etre is to find out why these cultures are separate, and the timeless story behind it all.

The gameplay is very smooth and easy, and you simply run around the various levels of the Tower finding clues to each level's pictographic language. Sometimes looking at the characters of the words is enough to deduce a possible meaning, and other times you will find relics lost in forsaken caverns that connect the languages. Most of the time, you will have to put your limited knowledge of the language together with contextual puzzles to both physically and linguistically proceed in the game's universe. The puzzles are usually enjoyable to solve, although sometimes I needed to look-up answers in a walkthrough, as the correct meanings or door passwords were a bit obscure to me. The stealth bits were easy for me, but other reviewers found the opposite (that the language puzzles were easy and the stealth bits were difficult). Overall, the gameplay is solid, relaxing, and enjoyable.

The story is epic, and when you finally get to the top -- and when you finally get to the top -- the feeling of accomplishment and heartwarming beauty feels good, man. I think probably this story is a timeless parable for the dangers of xenophobia and the fear of "others" -- which probably is a very necessary parable for our times.

It's a gorgeous addition to the puzzle genre, and linguistic nerds will love it. Inspired by the Tower of Babel, you play a wanderer traversing different societies and deciphering their languages

There is so much thought and craft in how the languages are constructed. There's absolutely a system here that allows you to pick up and identify similarities, and that is honestly such art
One of the most intellectually rewarding puzzle games I've ever played. This game is to linguistics enthusiasts what Zachtronics games are to programmers.
I am absolutely gobsmacked at how good this game is. Narrative, puzzles, world building. As a translator myself, this spoke to my soul.
Fantastic game, fun puzzles, great visuals, lovely music. Almost cried at the end.

It's nothing fancy, just a point and click adventure where you are piecing together a bunch of languages. It puzzles are engaging and I had fun putting together words and their meaning even though I was wrong most of the time. Probably okay for a play though but then the novelty wears off.

This is such a unique puzzle game. Figuring out a language makes you feel very clever and is incredibly satisfying. If I could say one thing, it is don't use the journal to confirm what you think the symbols mean. I am so glad I read that advice before I started playing. Let me explain what the journal is, and why I think the game is better without using it.

Basically the journal has a list of all the glyphs you've seen, and you can note guesses for the meaning of each glyph. That part is great, use that. However, also, the journal gives you pages with images that are clues to what some glyphs mean and if you drag some correct glyphs over to their matching clue, the game gives you the intended meaning of that glyph.

I much prefer not knowing the intended meaning of the glyph, because it means I could have interpreted a glyph completely wrong, and then later I see a sentence that just doesn't make sense. I then need to evaluate - is there a synonym of my word that would make sense instead? Is my word wrong? I can then go back and revisit old stuff I read and puzzle through. Its so much more satisfying than the first time I see it, note down what I think it is, try it, oops its wrong lets try again till I get it. Being able to check my solution easily kinda takes away the deduction for me.

I also try not to even look at the pictures, as I find they give too much of a clue for me.

This is a completely unique set of puzzle rules, that feel like they should have been invented and published by Nikoli sometime in the 1980s, but that we somehow collectively missed discovering until now.

Rather than a unique solution pencil puzzle however, this game takes those rules and builds an optimization challenge with a surprising amount of depth: the levels, which may look a little intimidating or messy at first, are all carefully designed, full of interesting logical realizations, and incredibly challenging.

They can be approached in two ways: either "chain par" (successfully completing a level at all in no more than a set amount of chains, but possibly using more blocks than needed), or "block par" (successfully completing a level with the minimum amount of placed blocks). The game tries to steer you away from attempting the block par by hiding those targets until you have completed a few levels normally, and I recommend you heed its advice - while finding the "chain par" solutions can already be unexpectedly difficult, finding the "block par" is the absolute true challenge that will keep you up for many hours.

My Main issue: Controls and Flight Mechanics

It is NOT an anti-grav racer ala Whipout, redout, Ballisticng. Even if the vehicle is designed to be similar to those.
This plays more of a zero g jetfighter race in a tube which may occasionally occur a few feet off a road.

Controls cannot be adjusted which is a major Nono for a racer/flight-related sim. Sim racers are /very/ specific about their setups, and this does not give any customizability even through vr steam controller adjustments. I was also expecting a physical HOSAS/HOTAS support but I did not see it.

The game plays through a Virtual HOSAS setup but the left "*virtual* stick'' is not used for anything else than doing hard air brakes , a "slow mo" button, and maybe the initial virtual seat calibration. And even the break is just the trigger. Almost /everything/ is done through the right virtual stick, where the main method of thrust: the trigger finger is obnoxious to do fine precision adjustment of speed: You'll get used to it, but I rather use my left hand for speed, like with other games such as Elite Dangerous, Fly Dangerous, And Redout 2 with controller mods.

While everything is VR, OK, but there are HARD preferences per driver, especially when it comes to flight simmers that most likely would be attracted to this one: Cant even use steams controller bindings to do customization, as it does not differentiate gyro directions that well and you cannot adjust vertical/horizontal sensitivity separately. Its all just “sensitivity”. I cant even believe what would happen to quest users that would look up in a turn and lose tracking of controllers...
 
The controllers can be miscalibrated if you do not put them into an  upright position before the start of a race. Sometimes this occurs even if you have them still due to micro drifts occasionally. I honestly rather use physical HOSAS (or even HOTAS), but this does not give us the option, or something like Tinker Pilot / VTOL VR , where we put hands onto virtual something

I'd also like a method to recenter my position within the game instead of having to restart the game, recenter and then start it again.

Then there is the gameplay:

Gameplay is time trial vs other player ghosts. This is a pretty decent racing formula, similar to Fly Dangerous or Trackmania. This is NOT true multiplayer. It’s just time attack vs leaderboards, it .. is fine. Would like to see Trackmania style multiplayer, but what is present is passable. As you race the track, the next 5 and previous 4 ghosts are loaded into your next attempt on the map, so you always will have a challenge, and something to fly against.  Would like to be able to load my friend list ghosts but thats just me if anyone wants tot try to beat my scores from my groups lol.

The Tracks themselves are a bit eh. The track does not properly indicate the proper direction until you smack into an invisible barrier and get redirected. One always has a track, or something to follow, but it's usually WAY more efficient to fly with that object to your side and pitch up and down than ever roll. You have more room to PITCH on most maps. It's even hard to figure out memory cues because most tracks just look like tubes, and if they do NOT look like tubes, you have invisible walls all along the object they track is aligned by lamps. It is just set dressing without much guidance for the player.

On those sorta maps you can just keep the road to your side and just pitch up and down for corners which is a lot more efficient than rolling per turn that will just disorient.  Sure it can feel like “this is awesome” at the back of the head as if doing a trench run or something like that but after you figure out that technique, it turns into a slog and then the levels start to feel like 3D spaghetti eventually. If only the flight system had a bit more nuance to it (like different pitch rate for up / down, behaviours flat on the surface, etc) or even just “gravity” to discourage just keeping a single roll according to the track axis. There is the slow mo, but I find that I do not use it because its doesnt feel right to the pacing.

Right now one can turn in a dime with some drift depending on initial velocity, and not even have to completely worry about the amount of kinetic energy one has in a turn as the brakes can cancel it out fairly quickly, just releasing the throttle is enough to slow one down quite a lot.

The  Maps themselves feel way more random than actual design. It felt better in Fly Dangerous where you are given a waypoint to reach, and there are obstacles between you and the way point instead of being stuffed into a tube you /must/ fly along. 

Standout maps stuff like Factory, which at least has some interesting obstacles  which can also get annoying as you have to remember them being there, but it also has some of the most annoying collision definitions in a flight game. Every grind on a wall  can stop you on your track, or missing a smaller tube shortcut as well.

The levels end up having  /very/ sharp corners, without any directional heads up like in Redout 2, so learning tracks is not that great of a feel. It's simply just speed control and proactively rolling corners and in a themed tube of various sizes, with “something” on the outside. 

It does however raise the questions why we are limited on roads but can do flips however. The logic sorta goes out the window and it's not anti-grav racing more than racing very close the road in a zero-g star fighter.

Music is track specific and gets… repetitive on the track. For a game that is about polishing track times, having the same beat going on gets tiresome after a bit of time: should have variations, but that's hard when using stock music from audiojungle..

Sound Design feels a bit lacking as there are no audio indicators for when one has boost available. Would be great to hear as the boost tank is filled half way and some sort of audio cue to when it is full, perhaps some sort of pitch changing loop. Some corners it's hard to quickly look down without losing one's current destination. 

The spectator cam... Could be spiced up: Its not that great to watch back honestly. Make it like track cameras in any other racing game etc.  Forexample my headset tends to point a bit upwards due to my face being so weird.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-bKTbfu8fY

So anyone looking at footage will not see my dials, or if id move my head around may make spectators  sick, etc.

 The Ghosts also could be faded out when they are close since they can easilly block ones vision.

So in summary: 
I’d give this a wait to see how the developer continues the game development, but *shrug* It is the price of a pizza, so if you are into this stuff, give it a shot..

This game has a lot of potential but it was never - and will never be - fully realised. As far as I can tell support for this game has been non-existent for years, which would be fine if it still didn't feel like an early access game nearly 2 years later. As far as I can tell, since this game's release the devs have made a whole other VR title and have two more on the way. 

And this game clearly paid a price to make this happen.
 
Honestly, it feels like an overpriced mobile game (and extremely unfinished), which super duper sucks because I genuinely like the bones of it. 

This game feels great to play, its easy to learn yet hard to master, it has crossplay with Quest, Trackmania style multiplayer (and leaderboard) AND realtime mp races WITH VC! Honestly really impressive for what (I assume) is a small VR studio. 

BUT, once you start getting into it you begin to notice all the corners that have been cut to make this happen. 

Map design and variety: 
There are just not that many maps in this game. Half of them are just the first maps played in reverse. Additionally, while they are all visually great, they do not all feel good to play. Most of them are extremely claustrophobic and precise. They don't give you a lot of room to move or to try different racing lines. For a game about going as fast as possible, you sure spend a lot of time slamming into walls. I know this is a skill issue (and you do get much better at it), but it would have been nice to have more space to make mistakes - not every map has to punish you so hard for going too fast.

Many have invisible / janky hitboxes, glitches that allow you get a head start (although some maps appear to have been patched, but not all for some reason?), walls that are basically invisible, and visibility issues to boot. And the actual level design elements themselves need work. The maps that aren't visually just a tunnel (mostly later maps) do a really poor job at indicating the correct path. These just are not fun to play. 

Multiplayer:
Extremely fun when it works. occasionally you will just be unable to finish the race in a live lobby and will be forced to Alt+F4 because you **cant leave or restart a lobby or the game from inside a multiplayer lobby**! Very annoying. 
When actually racing in realtime multiplayer, something about the netcode or timing system just seems broken. Players will appear behind me but still come first and vice versa. Your times aren't even saved in realtime multiplayer, so they won't go on the leaderboard if you beat your PB. This is maybe because they just don't seem to be accurate at all, so better leave them off just in case. 

Asynchronous multiplayer has issues too. WHY. CAN'T. I. TURN. OFF. THE GHOSTS? They are sooo annoying, and on such tight maps (looking at you, Olympus) you are just screwed because you can't see the f**king track. 

Controls: 
The controls are fine, and the tutorial does a decent job at teaching them. Nice! However, it would have been nice to offer more options when it comes to calibrating sensitivity. Personally, I would love to be able to adjust the different axes. Additionally, the option for a virtual joystick (ie Vtol VR) of some kind would have been nice, and would have gone a long way to making this game feel more immersive and - frankly - like some effort went into it. 

Ultimately, I have had a lot of fun with this game. There aren't a lot of games like it - somehow. But actually trying to get better feels more frustrating than fun at this point, and I'm left wishing for a game that is basically this but actually finished. 

To the devs - if you actually read this - please don't give up on this game. I actually think you've struck gold here, but as it stands the opportunity feels squandered. I feel like with some work this could actually be the "Trackmania of VR," but right now it really isn't worth the money or time investment.

With the game out of early access, I'm mostly happy with the end result despite a few gripes. It's a strong overall experience with speedy racing and a unique control scheme—one that takes some time to get used to but leaves an impression for those willing to learn it. Graphically, there's a good balance between realism and stylization, which leads to a good level of immersion inside the cockpit. Issues with controller tracking have been fixed and the UI has been touched up quite a bit since the launch of early access. The asynchronous multiplayer does a good job of adjusting selected opponents to match your skill level, though it may take a few plays on each track for it to find where you're at.

The race tracks, though covering a good range of futuristic styles visually, unfortunately get somewhat repetitive. Flying the vehicles in slightly more open tracks feels great and natural, but a lot of them are tight corridor-type tracks requiring high levels of precision. While a few of these would be welcome, they are the overwhelming majority and overshadow the other kinds. This results in a high difficulty spike early on, as well as struggles with particular tracks where it's easy to constantly run into walls or get stuck on geometry that sticks out. Though the inclusion of a few unique track types, like slalom, is welcome, it would have been nice to see tracks with broader lanes, point-to-point tracks, or even tracks with unique hazards.

Despite the nitpicks, it's a neat enough experience that it's certainly worth looking into.

This could've been an amazing game, sadly a lot of bad decisions make it just exhausting to play.

It feels like no one tested it for balance, rewards, or progression

*Balance of Enemies*
At first, the combat feels challenging but fair. You have to time your attacks and commit to your moves, which kept me hooked early on. But as you progress, the difficulty shifts from being skill-based to just overwhelming you with too many enemies in tight spaces. While it's still possible to win with skill, it just doesn’t feel fun anymore. I kept powering through because why not, but honestly at this point I'm asking "why" a lot more.

*Balance for Bosses*
Boss fights start out enjoyable, with fun mechanics to learn. But around the fourth or fifth boss, things go downhill. They become repetitive, spamming the same moves while taking forever to kill because of their massive health pools (Honestly "The Division" would be proud). At some point, it stops feeling like a fight and starts feeling like a chore.

Some bosses also have attacks that are hard to see coming, but at that point, I just accept the hit and move on (whether it’s my fault or bad design).

*Fast Travel*
You unlock a shop at the base early on, but for some reason, fast travel isn’t available until the third area. Worse, once you enter a new area, you’re locked out of going back to the base until you progress further. Even when fast travel is unlocked, it’s restricted in weird ways. Want to return and spend gold on upgrades? Naaa.

*Rewards*
There are trinkets you can buy, but inventory space is locked behind a weird system, you need to buy a certain number of trinkets just to unlock more slots. Even then, it never feels like you have enough space to use them effectively. So why even bother collecting them?

*Progress*
Despite playing for a long time, I never felt like I was truly progressing. Boss fights drag on forever because of their absurd health, I can’t use the trinkets I collect effectively, and fast travel restrictions make backtracking frustrating. Even basic enemies start taking five hits to kill, making combat feel slow and tedious.

*Overall*
I would try the next game this developer makes, but this just has way too many poor design decisions in my opinion. Obviously I'm not refunding, but I am pretty disappointed as these issues I believe should've been noticed before launch.

The gameplay looks very interesting; the developers had a good and promising idea here. And that’s where the positives end.

The music and environmental design are nothing special. Regular enemies aren’t bad either, but after a while, I found myself skipping entire areas by just running past them to avoid wasting time. Bosses are mediocre at best. They pose no real challenge—you can learn their attack patterns within one or two attempts, and after that, you just spam basic attacks like they’re punching bags.

However, the biggest drawback of the game is how the locations are designed. Progression feels like an endless sequence of unlocking passageways, flipping levers here and there, and then reaching another branching path where you gain a new ability—one that only makes navigation even more confusing by opening yet another set of areas. You often wander around aimlessly, and to make matters worse, there’s no map to guide you.

Overall, while the core concept of the game had potential, its execution leaves much to be desired.

I play about 50 new indie games each year in a quest to find those masterpieces, among those are well known and beloved classics such as the Ori games, Outer wilds, Hyper light drifter, Gris, Subnautica, INSIDE, etc... But also lesser known ones such as Signalis, Carrion, Chants of sennaar, Blasphemous and ofcourse Death's door. It is this last title that Mark of the deep reminds me off in all the best ways! I still prefer the former but not hat much more to be completely honest, which speaks volumes to Mark of the deep's quality! This game is one of those rare indie gems i'm always on the lookout for that make sifting through the worse games all the more worthwhile. I even feel like this can contend with some of the heavy hitters for a spot in my top 25, keeping in mind i've played over 250 including all the masterpieces mentioned above and then some! Ok so i LOVE this game but why? Well, there's many reasons but i'll try to disclose them in detail to hopefully convice you give this underrated & overlooked game a chance. Maybe you'll like it as much as i did, or even more?

Let's start with combat as this is a big focus of soulslike action RPG's and one of Mark of the deep's highlights. The core 3 hit combo and dodge roll are fun & responsive to use on their own but not enough to make a combat system with depth. However, add in a selection of unique firearms that regenerate ammo when you strike enemies akin to Hyper light drifter or Death's door and you've got something better. Then add in a ridiculously fun & versatile hookshot and you're set for an addictive combat system that has even more depth when combined with a few dozen equipable relics that give passive benefits. Finally have a VERY impressive catalogue of uniquely challenging enemies & bosses. The robust & versatile combat system combined with the sheer enemy variety is just magical. I enjoyed every skirmish wether against some roaming enemies, brilliantly designed arena fights or colossal bosses. The difficulty scale on display is also very well paced, gradually getting harder & harder as you get better & better.

On a serious note though Mark of the deep had a perfect challenge for most of it's runtime, it was always challenging without being overly brutal. In no small part because there was no death penalty! I'm eternally gratefull for the devs to have the game this way as it's my biggest pet pieve that can really take all the fun out of an otherwise great game, like nine sols showed. Some enemies will own you the first few times but eventually you can get their attacks down to a T which makes future encounters a lot easier. Bosses also are like this, they may take a few attempts but eventually you'll feel like you can do them hitless with a few more rounds of practice. This is because enemy attacks are well telegraphed and fair in terms of hitboxes. Some people are irked by the fact that their adversaries can change direction mid swing but it's all about timing moreso than positioning. Learning when to weave in attacks and when to dodgeroll away is a satisfying learning experience that made the whole gameplay loop of Mark of the deep immensily addictive.

Bosses especially were a highlight with attacks that got progressively more advanced as their health got lower and lower, really intesifying each fight as their bodies became more cracked. Like death's door, bosses & enemies in Mark of the deep have no health bars but rather show cracks as they get lower health. This really gives you a sense of how strong they are while keeping the fights exciting because you're constantly wondering wether or not to go for one more hit as it might just be the fatal blow. Even if the fatal blow comes from their end you'll respawn very quickly at a nearby respawn point. Another area that Mark of the deep has nailed, no long runbacks at all! There's only one that's a bit longer at about 15 seconds but other than that you can get right back to beating that boss. Arena fights are also a challenging experience that put your skills to the test but just like bosses these stay defeated if you beat them which adds a nice sense of progression to your exploration as you gradually inch forward in each level.

Speaking of levels, the level design in Mark of the deep is just incredible. The way they curve, twist and loop back on themselves is nothing short of outstanding! With tons of satisfying shortcuts to unlock that make the runback from the respawn point that much more convenient. Some people complain about the lack of a map which is something i really did not mind. Isometric games are a whole lot easier to navigate as you can keep track of your relative position a lot more than in a sidescroller. Still though the few items you cannot collect on your first voyage are hard to keep track of in a world this big. Yes, Mark of the deep is a suprisingly lenghty game, much longer than i initally thought but not in a way that outstays its welcome. I was literally blown away that i found yet 2 more huge areas to explore 16 hours in. Each area is also rather big on it's own, completely packed with tons of things to fight and discover. Secrets are shown on screen but the way to them is often cleverly hidden by the terrain.

Finding all these things is a rewarding endaveour as most upgrades felt very worthwhile with tons of different types to discover. From health and damage upgrades, to new relics, stranded allies, quest items or even some suprisingly well written lore entries. Exploration is just an all around blast in this, because of the great level design and rewarding collectibles. I liked this aspect even more than the combat although i also adored the combat! There's not much puzzle solving to be done though and there's not that much platforming gameplay to be had but that's not a suprise given the isometric nature of the game. Still a handfull of puzzles would've added some variety but that's more of a nitpick than a genuine criticism. What you will encounter consistently though is beautiful environments. While there's a lot of reused assets due to indie budget reasons, especially in the 'dungeon levels', what they did with what they had is still impressive. The overworld biomes are all very distinct from one another while all being visually striking. 

The art style for Mark of the deep is beautiful whichever way you look at it. The frozen peaks area especially left me in awe. These gorgeous vistas are accompanied by beautifull music that's worth picking up in the deluxe edition with a sweet art book to boot! I easily got my money's worth out of this game, given the sheer quality AND quantity. I'll get to linger in enjoyment for a lot longer listening to the OST again. It's no masterpiece soundtrack like Ori', Gris or Death's door's are but still a very solid & enjoyable listen. What also was suprsingly fun to listen to where the quirky voice acted characters. While yes, there could've been a few more female voice actors to add some variety, and while not every VA was of equal quality i still find that they did a supreme job bring this swashbuckling cast to life! It's rare for indie games to have voice acting at all, since it's a lot of work, expensive and most often not that good.

So for Mark of the deep to do this aspect so well as well, is just another box this game ticks of to be considered an indie gem in my opinion. It's not only the relative quality of the voice acting but also the absolute quality of the writing that sells this game. The lore as a whole is incredibly coherent, well written & expertly paced. From the lore tablets that slowly click into place to some mysterious NPC's that add to a greater mystery. It's not often i'm engaged with a narrative this much, fervently reading every lore entry/journal to piece it together but it was that good!  The whole game is that good, just play the damn game :D It even consistently ran at a smooth 120 fps on my old GTX1070 with no bugs/crashes either!

Mark of the Deep is profoundly frustrating in a way that makes it less than the sum of its parts. Your attacks are slow, short-ranged, and extremely committal - when you attack you cannot dodge or end the animation early. This means that you will often be punished for attacking by a move that an enemy used after you attacked, and the only way to avoid this is to slowly bait out enemy attacks and exclusively retaliate. However, your dodge is too slow, stiff, and bloated with start and endlag to let you properly position for this sort of bob-and-weave playstyle. Enemies themselves are atrocious HP sponges who are happy to stunlock you and are put in absurdly dense groups even before considering the overly long and overly frequent arena fights. The core of the game's movement comes from its grappling hook, but this too is crippled with problems. It is slow and imprecise to aim, it offers limited invincibility when travelling making its combat utility low for either approaching or escaping, and your travel speed is very slow with a lot of endlag. 

One can scream until they're blue in the face that "Souls-Like elements" means limited healing, mook enemies that kill you easily, complex and punishing bosses, and labyrinthine maps. This isn't anywhere close to having the deftness and clarity of design that justifies that difficulty and rewards mastery of its systems. This is not Hyper Light Drifter. This is not Tunic. This is not even Death's Door. It's an exercise in frustration with game design hiccups that would've been seen as amateurish and clumsy 20 years ago, in a saturated genre where there's no excuse for failing at basic things like "how does it feel to attack" and "can the player see where they are when an enemy is near them". 

It's a shame to be so harsh to the game because despite everything else the love the developers had is clear and the Portuguese voice acting has a lot of character, but the game itself is just not good.

I really wanted to love the game and don't think its objectively bad, just feels a bit... hard for it to stand out in a 'sea' of other similar metroidvania, souls-like isometrics. If there was a neutral review option, I'd choose it but, I'd like to see what else the devs can come up with.

I... WANT... to like this game, but it is very difficult to do so. It has it's redeeming qualities, and I'm going to keep playing it, but it's an utter slog. There are many issues that disrupt the enjoyment, like abysmal guidance, a horribly under-powered player toolkit, and the constant need for grinding memorization. 

If you're going to include a "dodge roll" mechanic in a game, but then design it so that it's essentially ineffective outside a 3-frame window, then snags and catches on every enemy and every minuscule outcropping in the environment (trapping you for repeated hits with no recovery frames), you have not made a dodge roll; you have made a piece of Velcro and thrown it in a jar of syrup lined with hooks. 

If you're going to design REGULAR enemies so that they can breathlessly execute 5-wave AOE power combos in rapid succession, you don't fill the screen with them up to every corner and then give the player a timed pea shooter and a range-less toothpick with the DPS of a mild fart. There is no reason a standard enemy should take 5-6 charged up strong attacks to kill, especially with leveled up weapons and damage-boosting trinkets. And, without any actual numbers, you just basically take the game's word for it when you get a "powerful" new upgrade, because there is no context for comparison between attack types.

If you're going to design an environment within a complex and multi-storied isometric fun house, at least have the courtesy to provide a map. Even Tunic was willing to do this, limited though it was, to give SOME idea of orientation---and that game was literally designed to be confusing. There's a huge and nuanced gap between "hand-holding," and refusing to provide even simple cues about where you're supposed to go next in (at least) the main story line. 

A huge part of this game will be spent wandering, dodging and mindlessly back-tracing, searching for an obscurely hidden access path to something new. There is no XP and you earn far more gold than there are things to buy with it, so the only real incentive to clear out enemies is to look for secrets, but since there is no system to track anything, you have no idea what you're searching for or how much of it is left anywhere. 2 of every 3 chests is a relic, and some of the most cumbersome fights in the game give no reward at all for winning. Almost every active "quest" you are given is along the lines of 'Find 56 of a thing distributed randomly across every region of the game.' Bosses have SO MUCH health, it almost feels like you're being trolled. Battles can take 10 straight minutes of dancing around and attacking.

Even some minor basic additions would have made a huge difference in playability---like location-based quest indicators, a HUD for boss health, or, ffs, an area percent-completion tracker. Most ability upgrades you find are niche, and only really help you navigate an obstacle introduced directly within the area where you found the ability. What was the rationale here? Anything other than being cast in a directionless oblivion is "too easy"?

This game could have had so much more to offer. I just get the feeling that in the 'quest to eradicate hand-holding,' the devs snubbed some obvious quality-of-life mechanics that would have made it a lot more enjoyable along the way.

As someone who loves pirates and pirate themed media and games, the whole vibe of this game really grabbed my attention. And while I would say the game is mostly enjoyable, there are a few notable flaws holding it back from being anything game changing.

To start with the positives, this game has dank, dark atmosphere which plays really well with the overall art style and especially the lore and story you're exposed to over the course of your journey. The characters you meet are all also fully acted, and while some are not as high quality as others, it really does make each character stand out. And the combat, clearly the major focus of the game, is one that isn't overly complex, yet still rewards you for experimenting and mastering it. The bosses also carry that same rewarding feel, with many of them offering some rather difficult, yet engaging challenges.

But now we do get to the notable flaws:
- It wasn't exactly commonplace, (only happening once or twice), but the game does still occasionally crash when trying to load into a new area.
- Despite the convenience of fast travel, the lack of a map can at times prove frustrating. It often makes backtracking, trying to explore new areas or just completing some quests feel tedious and less simple or immediately obvious. -Adorable art style

Negatives:
-Controls are hard to get used too. Found myself drowning most of the time

-Lack of pause menu. Would be nice to have one to change the controls of to adjust the volume. If there is one already in the game, I haven't found it yet. 
-Does not mention that the game is controller compatible. I find the game to be easier with a controller, but the game never mentions you could do this. Interaction buttons are still keyboard keys when a controller is hooked up.

Recommended adjustments:
-Make the water more like water. The physics make it difficult to surf. I'm stuck on the 2nd challenge due to not being able to surf properly. 
-Make some of the ledges taller to allow players to perform tricks easier in the tutorial level. 
-Fix the wave machine on the 2nd photoshoot challenge. It's hard to ride a wave with the current water physics. 
-Maybe have a different jumping sound effect. It's too loud at regular volume and sounds more like a video game jump.

Hope my feedback helps to improve this early access game! I can't wait to see this game in it's full release.

Age of Mythology, a remake of the classic real-time strategy game from 2002, back when RTS was hot and MOBAs were new.

Besides some small drawbacks like questionable voice acting during the campaigns, the main game itself has either stayed the same or improved. Units have better pathing, terrain and textures have been brought ahead a couple years, and some quality of life improvements have been added to make the game more enjoyable.

Some might say that there have been a few things to make it more 'casual' -- being able to automatically create villagers is very different from the RTS games I usually play where you're constantly having to bounce back to whatever worker facility exists, but once you're used to it, it feels like one less chore. Small tweaks like this give more time to dedicate to the fun parts of an RTS: movin' lil' guys around.

This is currently a live game being updated, which means balance patches, which means some things will not be faithful to the original. It's true enough to the original to be the same game, but several buffs have made themselves known since the olden days, the biggest one being reusable God Powers, which were formerly restricted to once-per-game. Some of these changes are light, and some are heavy-handed -- the former Chinese DLC, agreed to have been the most horrible addition to ever grace the game -- is being given a full overhaul, and the original campaign abandoned in favor of a new story.

This is a remake that is not afraid to make changes, being 'true to the original' is taking a back seat in favor of balance and fun. While I'd say they are mostly positive, it's true that fans of the original may find some things out of place here or there (Ulfsarks are called Berserks now? What's a Hirdman, and why did they steal my Swine Array!?), but units that used to be mediocre are now strong -- if you're a returning player, give it a shot, you might find units you never used now have new reasons to go for them.

Overall, this is a remake done right. The game is clearly an improvement over the original in both looks and gameplay, but with enough nostalgia factor to still make you think "this is the game I used to love".

Drifting Kings has the potential for a truly special game, no doubt online personalities like Goosiest will soon showcase this game on their channel once it gets shared around and becomes more well-known.
Only having 30 minutes in Drifting Kings so far, this won't be an in-depth review of the experience, but it was so enjoyable that I needed to share my joy of it. Keep in mind also that I've only played the Touge mode of the game, but there is so much content in it that it could be a game all by itself.
There is a staggering number of tracks and cars to choose from, there's something for everyone in Drifting Kings.
 
Visuals: The style is reminiscent of games like Capcom's 2002 "Auto Modellista" with a strong Japanese influence. Sakura leaves will float through the air, the mountain scenery is just like the Japanese locations, and there are nice little touches of things like other drivers and fans excitedly cheering the racers on, life continuing on far in the background, these things help immersion and make you feel like you're in a real race with your own aspirations and goals. Featured also is visuals like brake lights having a red trail to them, huge puffs of smoke from the tyres, it feels like playing an anime.
There're some aspects of it that are rough around the edges, literally and figuratively, but these things will likely be improved as from the looks of things, the developer is passionate about this new experience and will want to spruce everything up overtime. 

Gameplay: The drifting feels excellent, once you get the hang of it's really satisfying, the car will feel like it's moving in and out of traction unlike some other games with drifting in them, where it feels like you 'glide' through corners. The physics at times remind me of the "Initial D Arcade Stage" games, it's a serviceable combination of arcade and realism. There's both a manual and automatic transmission mode. There's also controller and wheel support, but I haven't tested the wheel support, so I can't speak on it yet. The vibration on the controller feels awesome and helps feed the players imagination.

There are some issues though, there's a lack of speed, you are going very fast at most points yet you still feel slow for some reason, a screen effect of wind flurrying past the player attempts to help this feel of speed but it still doesn't quite hit the mark. The cars feel really light, it's easy to flip your car or turn it on its side, maybe this is intended, but it didn't feel right to me.

AI: The AI is both exciting to race against and troubling to fight. Something that's greatly appreciated is that the AI can make mistakes, and often drive like a real human, which again helps the feeling of immersion and world-structure.

The troubling parts come in with their aggression, a little bump here and there is OK and even could happen in real life, but it is not just slight scrapes. Because of the 'floaty' weight of the cars, it's quite easy to get a car to propel into the air if you hit them from behind. At the start of a race, one of the cars will almost always get hit from behind and get thrown into the air, it breaks immersion and also makes the race frustrating at times, especially considering that there is no physical car damage, so the AI that does this doesn't get any consequences at all. 

Performance: It's... not good, at least in my experience so far, and maybe it's just my computer? So don't get put off from what I say, try it for yourself. I have above the recommended specs for Drifting Kings, yet on anything but low and very low quality mode, the games suffers from constant FPS drop, hovering around 15-25. Instead you can buy a bean which increases 2 random stats. You can easily get two stats you are not using on the characters with your setup, making it a waste. Oh and boss battles are still raise difficulty to 11 like other of their games, but instead of addressing that, this time they have regular enemies do that too. Their fix? Let's just restore your HP after every battle. MP though is not restored so you can easily run low. Or you can buy a premium item to make MP restored after every battle (see a pattern now?)

To top it off the game tells you too much and too little. I got tutorials on how to use a lever and how to navigate the arrow floor puzzle. I never got explained Fatal Moves at all. In fact I never once had an option to even use one.

Over and over. First time, ok shows a little about the characters. Tenth time I was like just shut up already. 

Overall I'd say only get this game if you want something to put on while watching Netflix, or if you don't mind grinding for premium currency for a few hours when starting out. The game will spend a lot of time telling you things that are basic but not explain the stuff that is unique to the game, like the talismans. Or the fatal moves. Or upgrading. Or...

[h1]Easy Sokoban game with blocky but cute cats[/h1]

In Sokoban puzzle games, you typically push blocks to make your 
way through a labyrinth. In [i]Fluffy Milo[/i], you push all milk blocks to blue trays to complete the level.

It starts out with small levels with only one milk block. As you complete levels, they get larger and there are more milk blocks. Regardless, it's quite light and the difficulty never racks up too much.

[h1]Technical stuff[/h1]

There's windowed and fullscreen modes, volume sliders for sounds and music, and a level selection screen.

Arrows/WASD move the cat. If you do a mistake, you can rewind up to three (3) steps, otherwise you have to restart the level.

[h1]Short and cute[/h1]

It's a chill game but quite short: I completed its 60 levels in just over half an hour.

If you like puzzle games and want a quick snack, it's okay, though I'd advice to wait for sale due to its length. Just don't expect it to blow your mind with challenge.

But if you only like your fireballs and goblins and dwarves stick with other games. 

I've read some of the other reviews here. There are some negative ones. I would talk about the issues that they had. But they're so nonsensical I don't even understand them. What does "combat is bad" mean? What "glitches" did you see. 

Instead I'll base this on my own impressions and not comment on what was said in other reviews. 

Combat: It's fast and loose. You can move freely, you can plan attacks and queue up actions. I like turn based games. I like to plan out my actions. This "queue action" system that they have in place let me plan out my moves in advance. I could plan out the following: Guy #1 ran to cover, threw a grenade, then ducked behind cover. Meanwhile. guy #2 stayed behind cover and gunned down an approaching melee enemy. Guy #3 laid down cover fire (while guy #1 was on the move). 

Story: It hits hard from the beginning. You run into unforeseen trouble right away. And you're on the run from the get go. There were also interesting NPCs to meet. I felt bad for the bartender whose wife ran off to the city with another fella. There are choices to be made in dialogs and social skills were needed in many cases. 

Graphics: There were some places where the graphics looked a little rough. But overall what they did came out well. The city has got some very interesting ideas in it that you shouldn't miss. 

Overall: It's worth the money you pay for it. I am enjoying it a lot. There is quite a lot that happens in this game. Enough to keep you entertained.

Edit: Just finished. It ends up in a surprising and cool place. Nice ending to the game. Didn't see that coming. ;)
