[h2]THIS REVIEW IS NEUTRAL! [/h2] 

Please Steam add this option!

THE GOOD:

Ok, the pros, obviously, are many: Beautiful, [u]GORGEOUS graphics [/u] and the [u]Slavic folklore[/u] inspiration is what attracted me to this game. I was not disappointed! The game is stunning, and [u]the plot is just as mesmerizing[/u]: you are plunged into the fairy tale world of Storona, a world that is facing serious problems! From enemy armies waiting to attack the settlements, to a snake demon who is rising in power. From a mysterious disease that has spread along the land, to mythical creatures who are being masacred by humanity. 

There are [u]two stories[/u] that you can go through (visual novel style), with plenty of dialogue options and endings! Both  are connected, but can be played separately. In one of them you are an ambitious servant of the Knyaz (Ruler), with an alcohol problem and a nasty temper on top. During the game you will be able to choose "aggressive" or "cunning"  answers that will affect your future options and ending. In the second one you play a bogatir (Slavic hero) tasked with saving the Knyaz's sick son. You do have some herbs with you that help elevate his pain, but they are limited, and along the way you meet other characters who are suffering. Do you keep the herb for the prince, do you share them with others? It's a tough choice. 

The fairy tale elements are perfectly interwooven with the characters' personal adventures and the world building feels rich and well-thought-out. So what was the problem.

THE BAD:

1. The "many endings" I expected to see weren't... that...many. I found that no matter how I play (I played the first story 5 times) I would always get pretty much the same depressing outcome with a few slight variations. I played all extremes, made different choices both cunning and bold, (yes, I drank every single bottle of vodka in my sight, [spoiler]  I became a forest wanderer, I saved a few of the cities, I tried to be friends with the red-haired guy (don't bother), I even became the servant of the bad guy (which was actually the best outcome so far), but apart from the last one, I would always end up freaking mad, and the majority of the land would be destroyed! Even when I felt like I was picking the right choices!![/spoiler] I even tried a more in-the-middle approach on my first play-through, but the game punished me for not being "extremely" cunning or "extremely" bold. It could be just me, maybe despite my 5 attempts I kept doing something wrong. But whatever the reason I would get super disappointed when I see the same "Results" despite me aggressively trying different routes. I expected far more...variations.

2. The endings sometimes didn't make sense. For instance, a character would die during my playthrough, but he ended up being alive during the outro scenes. (at least something positive happened). 

3. The stories aren't that long, but there is a LOT of text that you can't skip to get to the choices. Meaning I had to go through all the scenes to try something different and by the end I was so frustrated that I tried to be as evil as possible (no apple for you, sis!). And no, there is no "Save" button. The game saves automatically, making it seriously annoying trying to remember all the choices you made. [spoiler] I managed to keep Raven alive, but I made a stupid choice after that and I had to go through the whole game all over again. He died...I couldn't figure out what I did differently. At least he ended up alive during the ending [/spoiler]

4. The second story I enjoyed far more! It felt short, but at least I could see the direct positive and negative outcomes from my decisions. [spoiler] I ended up being super nice to everyone, finished all my ferns midgame because I kept giving them away, helped Baba Yaga and the merfolk, was friendly with the Zmei and promised him everything, didn't betray Maria and sacrificed myself so I can save my country and the prince! And everyone lived happily ever after...except for me. [/spoiler] The story felt a bit hollow. And you might say it's because of my choices, I was playing very passively, letting other characters do some of the tough work for me. I might have to go through it 4 more times to make sure... it felt like the game was punishing me with boredom for being too nice XD   Overall, nothing "unexpected" happened, pretty straight forward and predictable...

Overall, a beautiful game, reasonable price and an enjoyable experience! Just... control your expectations.

I do like the sounds in-game, they're not too obnoxious or loud. I love the graphics and am a fan of the VHS-inspired graphics. The game does allow for changing the VHS intensity but I didn't really see that much of a difference (but I also only messed around with it in the menu). There isn't much of a story--a coworker mentions some disappearances and your boss sends you on an errand to the parking garage. There isn't really much of a reason behind why Lamphead exists (is he in the package you're sent to collect?). The ending was surprisingly pretty good for such a vague storyline. 

One of the first issues I have with the game is that it offers a window mode but with no option to change the resolution. For my laptop, the game's "window" mode is still the same size as fullscreen. If you move or press any other button besides E, the dialogue ends and you'll have to restart the entire dialogue from the beginning again (not a big deal but I do like exploring games and reading NPC dialogues). The game does need some more proofreading, since there are some grammar errors (such as "What are you doing standing in there" when talking to some coworkers). Pressing ESC pulls up a menu but it doesn't actually pause the game. As for the bugs in the game, I only found a couple during my playthroughs. Lamphead can and DOES see you through the wall if you unscrew the vent when he's walking in the hallway by the bathroom door. I also had Lamphead see me right as I was unlocking the HR office and he had followed me into the office but stayed in the front area of the room. I was able to grab the gun and shoot him but it didn't harm him. He eventually turned around and left, walking through the now closed door. For achievement hunters, I had some issues with two achievements not popping (tongue-tied and blabby), which required a few attempts before they popped).

Overall, I did enjoy this game. I don't really see much replay value in the game as there's only one ending and the game is extremely short once you figure out what to do and how to go undetected from Lamphead. The pricetag for the game is pretty high for such little content, no matter how much I enjoy retro graphics. I definitely do recommend this game for those who love short horror games, but I suggest only getting it on sale.

Though the game isn't without some points of criticism. Repositioning the character can be a somewhat difficult task and makes some platforming segments infuriating. In parallel, and for understandable reasons, saving during certain sequences is disabled, which makes for a nasty combination with the aforementioned rigid character repositioning. Another issue I had can be found in regard to direction during levels. No objective arrows and only somewhat specific menu direction led to me getting stuck in some levels and unsure how to progress, especially during a late game segment involving an airship crash. Good level design means in most cases it's easy to figure this out yourself, but those areas where direction is lacking made for a rough time. 

Loved my time with this game despite those flaws in direction: it's bouncy, it's charming, it's fun. Extremely easy to recommend.

[h1]DownTheDead - A Rough Yet Promising Indie Horror[/h1]

[i]“A gritty survival horror set in a dark, underground facility.”[/i]

DownTheDead combines elements reminiscent of [b]Dead Space[/b] and [b]Half-Life[/b] but with its own indie twist. Set in a hidden research facility masquerading as a hospital, it challenges players to navigate the dark corridors filled with zombies and armed foes. While it leans heavily on stealth, players can opt for the guns-blazing approach if they’re skilled enough with movement—though ammo is scarce.

[h2]Storyline and Atmosphere[/h2]

The story is basic and lacks detailed narration. You play as a test subject escaping a zombie-infested research facility. The plot is spontaneous, with minimal exposition, leaving players to piece it together. While the story feels sparse, the eerie setting and dark atmosphere are well-executed, especially with the [b]zombies' red glowing eyes[/b].

[h2]Gameplay Mechanics[/h2]

The mechanics are simple yet functional. Movement includes the usual running, jumping, and crouching, though crouching feels a bit off due to animation issues. Unfortunately, the game lacks control rebinding options, which can inconvenience players who rely on custom setups.

[b]Combat[/b] feels heavily inspired by Half-Life, with a crowbar as the primary weapon and a couple of firearms (a pistol and shotgun) available later. While functional, the gunplay could use refinement; the muzzle flash position, for example, feels misaligned, which can be jarring.

[h2]AI and Special Vision[/h2]

The enemy AI is underwhelming. Both zombies and human enemies can be manipulated with certain movements, making the combat feel almost turn-based at times. The “Special Vision,” akin to heat vision, allows you to detect enemies and items without cooldown but slows down time, adding a strategic element to sneaking.

[h2]Graphics and Sound Design[/h2]

As an indie game, DownTheDead isn’t aiming for AAA visuals, but it does well with the assets it has. Environments recycle elements, and animations are a bit rough, yet the dark aesthetic creates an appropriately ominous vibe. The sound design is minimalistic; more ambient sounds or voice-overs could enhance immersion.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

DownTheDead has its rough edges, but with the developers’ responsiveness to feedback, it shows promise. While it doesn’t introduce new ideas to the horror genre, it’s worth a look for fans of gritty survival horror games. The game’s low price point makes it worth a shot, especially with ongoing updates.

It's got a good interface for a game of this type. If you're familiar with Football Manager or OOTP you'll be able to move around in this game pretty well. The matches look good.

The problem for me is that you don't have enough control over what's going on. Or maybe not that you don't have enough control, but you don't have enough information given to you about why things are they way they are. 

So the players mental state is kind of a big deal in this game. In the matches I played, the player with the best mental state going in always won. That usually matches up with ability but not always. But you're given no indication of why a player feels the way he does.

My one players mental state/morale dropped from 'OK' to 'Rock Bottom' over the course of two days. Why? I don't know. He didn't play a match during that time. I've got no way of turning it around. I just have to shrug and go, OK then, and wait for things to get better.

My other player was in a tournament in which he was one of the strongest players. He destroyed the first two opponents and was in a match against someone who was about as good as he was. He went into the match Troubled and Anxious. Why? I don't know. My pre-match talk was whichever one told him to relax and it had no effect. Talking to him during the match had no effect either. So I'm sitting here watching him blast forehands into the net and miss his shots and I know that's his mental state because he wasn't playing like that before, and there's absolutely nothing I can do about it or avoid whatever caused it next time.

Another thing related to personality is that you'll sign someone and then find out their expectations of what they can do are way out of line with yours. So that second player I mentioned up there with the bad mental state. He's 13, and he insisted that he play in the Mens tour. I had no option not to put him there, and only had the option to turn off Junior tour play and expectations for him.

The match I was talking about up there? That was a Junior tour match. If he's crapping himself on the Junior tour how can he think he's ready for the men's tour? Regardless, that sort of thing should be resolved before you sign a contract.

So basically this is a good game but ruined for me by these two arbitrary mechanics. Unfortunately these mechanics are a major part of gameplay so there's no ignoring them and I can't recommend this at any price.

A weak recommendation as the game plays and looks good, but has short playtime (4h for 100%) and some core design aspects that are not as frictionless as one would hope.

[h1]What worked great[/h1]
* [b]The core mechanic[/b] - it is fun to learn the varied mini-songs for each plant on all the different instruments. I enjoyed practicing my note ear, and by the end of the playthrough I was able to do some of the songs first try
* [b]The simple combat[/b] - While 'random encounters' are a bit pointless, the increasingly complex boss battles went from "alright, let's dispatch you again" to actually enjoyable. The chords for the attack/heal feel a bit awkward on keyboard (attack specifically) but nothing you can't get used to
* [b]The World[/b] - The game uses a simple concept of melodic plants and builds a pretty world off of it. It's not big, it's not complex, but it feels right, as long as you're not bothered by "dark matter" in the game being different to "dark matter" in real life

[h1]What Didn't Work Great[/h1]
* [b]Expeditions[/b] - I have a vague memory of the gameloop being slightly different  back in an early demo I played, and while improvements were made I think some design elements stuck around, being small annoyances here and there, like a pop-up box of whether you want to start an expedition that is largely meaningless, and being sent back to ship after each boss and then having to walk back to the boss area to heal plants there.
* [b]The 'in-betweens' of game design[/b] - So while every element feels great, it feels like they don't fit perfectly well together, kind of like they're puzzle pieces that are just slightly off, but close enough to not realize it. Repeating the song is great (core mechanic), and then assigning a song to a plant is also great (gives it more meaning than if it were to appear only once), But at the same time, with multiple plants per zone you start to need to memorize multiple patterns, or ask every new flower to re-play its song. There is a lot of small situations like that which make what should be fun a little bit tedious or repetitive at times.
* [b]The difficulty selection[/b] - I cannot imagine this game being a good experience if you try and play it on normal. At that point sure, it's still the cute and pretty game it is now, but it loses the core identity and becomes a rhythm game so simple, it would barely be a single easy chart if you combined all the plant songs together. I think overall the difficulty could've increased the toughness of combat-related things, while assigning of keys to music could be an in-game mechanic (e.g. at the botany table in the ship you could mark note sequences for each song, using the note notation from the tutorial, and they would then appear on the notes themselves. Then each plant would over time change from being a by-ear repetition to a reading of 'sheet music'. On top of that it would provide a reason to go back to the ship, and could even improve on the ending experience (not gonna spoil how, but whereas the ending is great if you've got a musical ear, it can fall flat if you need to repeat stuff due to not being a maestro just yet)

Overall this is a slow and simple game which I would probably recommend to younger audiences moreso than adult rhythm fans. It is still extremely different to anything else, so if that's what you want go for it. Though maybe wait for a sale as the price is a bit steep for the playtime available

It is an enjoyable tower defense game and, unlike a lot in the genre, you actually rely on the towers rather than it being essentially a third person shooter that also has towers sometimes.

The main loop is to harvest resources, build towers, refine those resources into higher level variants, build better towers. The resources are all handled manually, meaning you have to pick up and take them where you want them, or throw them at the other player/tower. Everything is done with proximity, so if you throw a resource at a tower that needs it, if it hits that tower it'll be automatically "used".

This is an alright concept but is clunky in practice. At least with 2 players, we ran into issues of thrown resources getting lost in grass, falling into water, or bouncing into the wrong tower. I think this is intended behavior - it's supposed to be a bit of a chaotic mess - and it'd work if the UI and camera controls were more polished.

I haven't tried it with 4P yet but I'm *thinking* it'd be more fun as you can have people working different stations in the supply chain. While I don't think more players is going to make this game perfect, I have a theory it will definitely improve the experience. If I manage to wrangle a 4P game I'll update here.

As is, it's just too rough to recommend. But if you see it for 3 or 4 bucks, it's worth checking out.

The Static is a cozy 3D platformer that delivers a warm sense of nostalgia around every corner. From the use of retro technology, to the familiar-yet-unique soundtrack, this game makes you feel like you're a kid again - playing games like Crash Bandicoot and Super Mario for the first time. 

By far the two strongest aspects of The Static are its beautifully unique art style and its satisfying movement system. When it comes to the characters and the ambiance, there really isn't anything quite like it. As nostalgic as this game feels, it never fails to remind you that this world is its own and you've never seen anything like it.

The player's primary objective is to use a variety of movement abilities and power-ups to traverse a handful of unique levels, all the while defending yourself from dangerous enemies and rescuing your ghostly neighbors. You will find yourself replaying the game just so you can see if there's a faster way to beat a level. No two playthroughs are the same, and that is all because of the games movement system. There's always more than one way to get from point A to point B, and I think that's what keeps me coming back.

The Static is many things: it's cozy, it's humorous, it's smooth and satisfying, and its just the right amount of challenging. I am truly so excited to see where it goes from here. If you're a fan of 3D platformers and colorful worlds then this game is for you. I cannot recommend it enough.

A classic from 2006. This game holds so much nostalgia for me.

I played this game when I was 12 years old, installed from the installation disc borrowed from my local library. Unfortunately this version of the game required the disc to be present in the CD—ROM drive, which meant I could only play it for a limited time until I had to return it.

But now it's on Steam, and while this game was made for windows XP and the likes, I've managed to make it run just fine on Windows 11 by enabling compatibility mode for Windows Vista SP2, and running the game as administrator. If you are having issues (my game crashed when I tried to change graphics settings) I recommend you try that as well. I've heard reports of the game crashing after the first mission, but I cannot confirm this so far. The downside of this compatibility adjustment is that for some reason it will no longer run through Steam, you have to launch the executable manuallly. This is also the reason why I only have 5 minutes playtime, in case you were wondering.

The actual game is a timeless classic—you are a photojournalist, you are sent on numerous missions in the Serengeti of Africa to photograph creatures for a newspaper article. The game is played in first-person mode, and the game world is open (each mission is one map, free for you to explore). There is a special focus on being considerate about the environment, represented in-game by a meter which tells you how much you disturbed the animals, needless to say that running up to them and touching them will give you a penalty. Instead, you have to sneak up to them close enough so you can take those perfect photos but not close enough to disturb them, which is a nice game mechanic I think. The missions are all very varied and teach you a ton about the wildlife of Africa. The music is very epic and really gives you this cool African vibe. Overall the gameplay is incredibly relaxing and very immersive.

In terms of graphics, you can definitely see that the game is from 2006, but in my opinion they have aged very well, don't expect anything super fancy though—you can see the animal models are relatively low poly, textures are not that high res and the shader quality could be better— but I think it still looks very good. The hardware requirements are also minimal and it'll run on practically anything, I've managed to make it run on the Intel chipset family (which is a very low performance integrated GPU, much worse than even Intel HD Graphics) and with a 1.4 GHz processor. 

If you like Indie games, want to learn a bit about our Earth, and would like to immerse yourself in an African Safari adventure, I'd say this game is for you! can definitely recommend.

[h2]First Impressions[/h2]
I say 'No. Absolutely not.' due to the pricetag if you're looking for a game, but 'Yes' if you like playtesting and being a part of the growth process and you have the money to throw around. 

If you're expecting a Star Stable replacement or a completed game, this is not the one. Not yet. 

[h3]Still Here?[/h3]

If, despite the 'No' you still want to play Unbridled at this point in time, please don't go in expecting a completed (partially or in full) game. The base is there in Unbridled, but then a lot of horse games have a 'base' and then kinda stop there and focus on pretty horsies while expecting the playerbase to make their own content. It's still too early to say what this game will become. The multiplayer aspect will bring a whole lot of additional challenges--especially knowing that even AAA games drop the ball on Multiplayer sometimes. It's necessary to keep this in mind, but not have it as an excuse for lack of quality.

The graphics are nothing to brag about. A lot of people value graphics quality. But... I don't personally. [b][i]Pretty graphics will never make a game good. It will just add to surface quality, not the depth and functionality.[/i][/b] Graphics can always be improved later, the gameplay loop and functional features are far more valuable.

[h2]What It Looks Like Now[/h2]

[h3]1. Disjointed Side Features[/h3]
Right now, the current side features--crafting, archery, jobs/questing--when set together with the main loop (which needs work)--get horse, care for horse, train horse--feel disjointed.

[h3]2. Quality of Life Needs a LOT of Work[/h3]
There are a lot of needlessly complicated/ time-consuming things that could use love and improvement, like mining and woodcutting requiring several clicks to complete a harvest, or the low payout for completing jobs, or the tutorials popping up every time I want to restart a jumping course, and the need for me to hide and un-hide the mouse to interact with menu options.
I really don't understand why the hide/un-hide mouse function is necessary at all, so far there is no part of the game that should need that function considering all the games I've played with multiple key inputs.This is just a choice to not tie keyboard controls to interface actions. 

[h3]Overall[/h3]
It's still very early to say whether this game [b][i]will eventually be[/i][/b] good, okay, or bad. What I can say is that the team clearly is working very hard to build and improve Unbridled. So, I give my input and wait patiently to see what will happen.

[h2]What Might Make It Better[/h2]
[h3]More Love for The Game Parts of the Game[/h3]
It needs a lot of adjustments and more in-depth, non-horse, interaction/gameplay focused features, as well as some variety and cleaning up of the material grinding system. 
[h3]Not Hyper-Focusing on Realism First[/h3]
Yes, this game's draw is 'realism', but so are many other simulators. There is a limit to how realistic one can go before the game starts to suffer. Make the game loop solid first, define the ground features so there isn't a feel of 'what now?' I hope they don't focus too much on the aspect of realism, since there's a limit to how much realism should be in a game for the game to remain enjoyable. Oftentimes horse games focus on realism (can't eat this, need to clean that exactly this way, must look this specific way) when the realism doesn't contribute anything helpful to the game itself and is just there to make someone happy. 

[i]"Is it necessary for the horse to raise its head when it sees the jump?"[/i]
[i]'Yes, because it also indicates to the player that the horse sees and is ready to jump and may not refuse it.'[/i]

-This feature is informative and helpful to the player AS WELL AS realistic. There are many realistic features that will simply add tedium, and its extremely important to not make the game tedious. Several tedious features = Tedious Game. 

[h3]Expound Meaningfully On Other Game Features[/h3]
[b]More detailed crafting systems[/b] gives the player more to do when not playing with their horsies. Crafting can be tied into the main game loop helpfully by providing resources the player may not normally get through the shops.

[b]A better archery system[/b] (and an actual usage of archery for sport instead of for cosmetically-fun-pew-pew) would add another facet to the game that is not found in other, more popular horse games. It would also allow the devs to tie in archery to the main game loop and create a challenge that also includes the horses.

[b]A way to customize the ranch[/b] would be perfect for letting the player immerse themselves in the game by making their home, their home. With multiplayer this also adds a level of uniqueness and social interest, as some people will make amazing homes that could be great for rp or just personal creativity. It can ESPECIALLY be helpful for people breeding and training very specific types of horses, to be able to create a space specific to their trade.

[b]Clearer methods of identifying harvestable materials.[/b] [strike]Right now, the lighting system makes everything difficult to see at night.[/strike] In addition to that, harvestable resources are not blatantly obvious outright. Never place unharvestable resources everywhere, then make the harvestable ones blend into the environment. They should stick out with something, be it a specific color, a glow, a shimmer, some stripes or something. 

Hopefully, the team does their homework and gets into a good flow.

After playing the game for several hours, I can definitely recommend it. Is it perfect? Goodness, no. It's early access for a reason. I read through so many reviews and continually see something along the lines of "I know it's early access... but..." which often times the reviewer goes on to complain about all the things that typically plague an early access game. So, do you really understand what early access means? 

Are the textures fantastic? Nope. Are the sounds, models, maps, insert random thing here perfect and polished? Absolutely not. Is it a fully fleshed out game with days worth of content, and a million quests and every feature fully coded into the game already? Uhhh, nope. 

However. 

This game has so much more content packed into it than any other EA horse game I have played (which would pretty much be all of them). Honestly, most EA horse games I am bored in 20 mins or less. This game actually kept my interest throughout the quests that are available, as well as beyond as I enjoyed a bit of job grinding to afford cute tack for my horse. 

The staggering amount of CONTENT this game has already packed in is astounding to me. Jobs, non-annoying horse care, XP system and SKILL TREE, lesson challenges, incredible jump course builder, working saddle, saddle pad and bridle hooks, horses wandering in the pasture, or grabbing a sneaky bite of grass when you dismount, even resource gathering!? I am quite enchanted by this little game. Also, just judging by the way the horses are fleshed out with the genetics and breed mixes, breeding mechanics will likely be a lot of fun once they are added into the game! 

The riding system is beautifully carried out. The HUD is easy to understand and packs a lot of information into a visually pleasing little badge. The riding mechanics are easy to pick up, hard to master - which is perfect! It's not so overly complicated you get frustrated trying to just get your horse to jump, and when things do go sideways and your horse refuses, it's intuitive to figure out why (early, late, etc.). I am very much looking forward to future mechanics, and this dressage nerd can't wait to see what that aspect looks like. 

The jump course builder is very well implemented also. It took a matter of minutes to become comfortable with it, and it works beautifully! My only complaint is that the price of the jumps should be a bit lower in game, since they are individual pieces, it can make it a bit difficult to build out a full course. Maybe have some more worn style jumps that are a fraction of the price until there is a mechanic for making higher amounts of money in the game? 

I am a detail-oriented person, so small details mean the world to me. The way a horse sticks it's tongue out when you hug them, the creaky leather sound when you mount/dismount, etc. Those things add so much charm! 

It definitely has a long way to go, the mining/wood chopping system could be a little more seamless, and it would be nice for the ore rocks to disappear or change once they are harvested so it's easier to keep track of which ones you've already gotten. 

I will say that I came into this completely fresh, I did not watch any trailers, nor was I a beta tester, nor did I play the demo. So to be transparent, my expectations were not super high to begin with, and I found myself pleasantly surprised. I am sure there are other things I am forgetting, but no - it's not finished, it's not polished, and it's not perfect. I never expected it to be in the first place. Unbridled is an exciting new entry in the world of horse games, and even in early access, it shows incredible promise. While there are some bugs (as expected in early development), the developers are actively engaging with the community on Discord, listening to feedback, and working hard to improve the game. It’s clear they are passionate about making Unbridled the best it can be!

One of the unique features is the stride jump counter. Unlike traditional horse games where you just jump an obstacle and get points, Unbridled challenges players to think about their approach, adjust their strides, and time their jumps perfectly. This adds a strategic element that makes game play feel more rewarding and realistic. I also like they've added collective and extended gaits to the game which adds more realism to the game.

Customization is another major highlight. The in-depth coat and marking options allow you to create truly unique horses, giving each one a personal touch. Whether you want to recreate real-life horses or experiment with creative designs, the customization system makes it possible.

Overall, Unbridled has a solid foundation and the potential to become one of the best horse games out there. With time, polish, and continued developer support, this game could be something truly special for equestrian fans. If you love horse games and want to be part of its development, it's definitely worth checking out!

This game was something i decided to try after a youtube video from Shady Cicada, who wrote some of the music in this game. I saw it and wanted to give it a try, and found it to be an enjoyable experience. I wanted to write a review to give some feedback and point out some of the bugs i encountered during my play time in hopes that the developer might notice, and i will update the review to throw in more bugs if i come across them. But now it's time to move on to the actual review.
Mini disclaimer: I have not fully beaten the game as of yet, i am still in my first play through of the Nightmare path, although all i need to do is beat the final boss.

Movement:
The movement in this game is a bit of a mixed bag. it has its moments where it feels clunky and stiff, but it has more moments where it feels good.

You got the typical 2d combat platformer kit of the dash and double jump, but from the little bits i've seen so far, each character gets their own special flavor of dash.

I am going to be completely honest, most of the issues stem from the layout of areas, particularly this one funnel you need to maintain a wall jump climb between two walls that move up and down, AND manage your distance between rows of spikes that can and will send you back to the bottom if you get hit by them.

Combat:
Starting with the controls, combat is relatively simple, you got a melee (bound to J), a gun (bound to K), and a dodge/dash (bound to L). depending on the melee weapon you are using, you can get different moves that require a combination of inputs, typically hitting melee while holding down in the air

Each character has an array of weapons they can purchase using currency you earn in missions. there are also purchasable upgrades that can change aspects about them, and there is an incentive to search levels for Nanotech upgrades, which you can slot up to 3.

The combat in this game is a mixed bag depending on the enemies you are facing. Enemies are diverse in roles with specific purposes that can fundamentally change how you should approach in some cases.
Some of these enemy types do this well and i have no issues with how they are implemented, Some of them are the explodey rolly pollies, who i wish would roll into the fires of hell (I beg of you to lower their health, it shouldn't take 2 shots from the shotgun or an entire melee combo to kill them, especially for how disruptive they are)

Bugs:
I have not run into very many bugs to my pleasant surprise. The game is in a very polished state and runs great. however, i have ran into two bugs, one of which being a somewhat major issue during my playtime so far.

one of these bugs is related to the way some boulders interact with the rafts in Chapter 3, where the boulder gets stuck and keeps spinning on the raft while being locked into place. If you stand next to the spinning boulder on the raft its stuck on, the game will sometimes teleport you backwards in the level. its not a crippling amount of distance, you can get back in less than ten seconds, but this is something that should be looked into.

as for the other bug, it is a lot more serious and can potentially impact the ability to play the game.

in the final boss fight for Nightmare, the boss has a move where they sweep across the bottom of the screen from right to left or vice versa, but sometimes the boss bugs out, and what i assume is a segment of the boss spawns and engulfs the entire lower floor long before it is supposed to, then it goes, which shows the head and rear of the boss, with no connecting body between the two parts.

Overall, this game is an enjoyable experience with a few issues. But the lone Developer has been working on this as a passion project, so it's understandable that some things slipped through the cracks. I personally say it's worth the ten dollar price tag, but ultimately its up to you.

It is very easy to learn, but also very hard to master. The game mechanics are really simple to understand, which is good.

But then you see how brutal it really.  You have 100 health, which is not a lot as enemies do a lot of damage (so expect to die in just a few hits). Each turn also drains 1 health, so you effectively only have 100 turns to beat the game.  

And sometimes it takes several turns to get to one enemy as two enemies are on opposite sides of the map and the enemies are both long range fighters who run away from you.  So you end up taking 3-10+ damage just trying to reach the other enemy at times.  You can use abilities to mitigate this, but they take several turns to recharge and it gets repetitive needing to depend on the same really strong abilities while being forced to ignore weaker, but fun to use ones.

And some maps get you stuck in a lose-lose situation because of the health drain per turn mechanic. You could get a bad map where if you rush in to kill a enemy quickly, you take damage.  But if you take the time needed to not take a hit, you end up taking 3-5+ damage anyways as it moves in a way that makes you have to wait several turns to attack it.

You can heal by killing more then one enemy in the same turn, but because of the health drain per turn mechanic, you can spend several turns setting up a combo...which effectively makes the heal very small.  it means you have to really min-max and do things as perfectly as possible.  Otherwise you will die because you just use too many turns as you are not given much wiggle room for mistakes at all.

Ontop of this, the difficulty ramps up way too fast.  So you may find yourself dying repeatedly over and over again in the first few zones with the same encounters with minor variance.  Which gets old fast.

Of course you could just get better at the game, but you will just fight the same few battles over and over again and that can be said for every game.

It just is not interesting to do those same few battles over and over again. Especially since I could see it getting repetitive even when I get good at the game because of how this.  There are literally only two enemy types in the first three battles and the next zone adds one new type.

The game needs to reduce or outright remove the health drain per turn mechanic, offer more ways to heal or more variety in the first few rounds to keep it more engaging.

If you want to reward the player for using as little turns as possible, just rank the player based on how many turns they used.  

This should make the game much more appealing to many more types of gamers.  Even the youtubers I watched who played it (to try to get some tips) did not get that far before they quit because of how brutal it is. So I know it is not just me.  I could see a niche group of gamers like this, but they would play the same min-max way to get as high of score as possible anyways.

The game itself is fun, just these few things hold it back and suck the fun out of it.

This game is a simple but challenging game that is great for a quick run or two or longer sessions. Essentially it's a chess-like strategy game with a lot of extra factors.

The basic rules are really simple; you lose energy when you're hit, and you also lose 1% of your energy every time you move (100% energy is max). When you get to 0% energy (either by moving with 1% energy or getting hit) you lose and must restart.

When you are standing next to a vactor and move to another tile but are still next to the same enemy, you do a strafe hit (hitting an enemy kills it). When an enemy is two spaces away and you move directly towards it, you also attack, killing it. Killing 2 or more enemies at once restores energy (10% for two).

There are a variety of enemies in the game. The simplest attack when they are next to you and you move but are still next to them. Moving away will prevent them from attacking. So far as I've discovered there are also dash enemies (can move unlimited spaces in a straight line to attack), gun enemies (shoot straight ahead), and grenade enemies, which will throw a grenade next to you that will blow up all surrounding tiles after your turn ends. This can turn a map very challenging very quickly; if there are 5 gun enemies many of the spaces you move to will cause you damage. Vactics will also kill each other in certain circumstances.

There are also special tiles, such as buildings (interrupt line of fire), fire, and others.

Lastly, you also get special abilities and can upgrade these at the end of each zone (3-4 maps). You start off with freeze (freeze enemy for 1 turn) and dash (move 2 spaces forward, destroying anything in the way). I've also unlocked teleport (self-explanatory) and shield (negate 1 attack, goes away after enemy turn). There are at least another 15 to unlock. On top of that, you can upgrade these abilities for further distance, faster recovery time, dashing/teleporting on top of vactic (killing it) and more.

There are 6 pilots (including the starting one) that can be unlocked by completing challenges. I just unlocked the first by destroying all buildings in Vacto housing. The pilot I unlocked can be upgraded as well.

Your score at the end of each run will affect your research points gained. These unlock new abilities as well as color palettes.

As far as the aesthetics go I really enjoy it. You start off with 3 color palettes and will unlock more over time. I enjoy all of them but I can understand if some palettes would bother certain people (one has bright neon blue as the main color).

I really enjoy this game.

- The game advertises itself as a horror game, but it is not. The main picture for the game on Steam is a bloody bucket with very creepy bloody arms stretching out of it. However the game is super light on the horror and doesn't really have any gore in the game except for that one scene. 
- The story is so convoluted that I didn't really invest in any of the characters and I felt no real emotions going through the game. The last half of the game is just one weird nonsensical (story wise) puzzle after another. It all just felt like filler to make the game longer. - In order to figure out the story you will probably have to search the forums, the story is not explained fully in the game properly.
- The game's ending is abrupt and I didn't enjoy it.

- The game is priced high for what you get, wait for a deep sale.

I was fairly hyped for the game, have been for quite a while, played the demo that was briefly available a long time ago. 

It really doesn't seem like much was added from the demo years ago, which is very disappointing. This game is mostly a hodgepodge of isolated mechanics you use in individual puzzles and then move on to the next mechanic for the next puzzle. 
It reminds me of 'SCP: Secret Files,' only in secret files, it made sense for you to get one mechanic/story element and then move on to the next because it was isolated files of isolated SCPs. 
Go Home Annie, is not individual isolated SCPs, it is not isolated stories, it is all one story, one character. 
Why do we start the game using a camera that reveals hidden past events, and the moment we're out of the house, it has no use? 
Why is the only SCP that isn't essentially used in any other SCP game the bathtub and we only interact with it for the story and no other dialogue?
Why are there a bunch of SCPs in a printing room that you can just read about and none of them do anything other than what we use to progress the story? 
Why, OH GOD WHY, do we interact with the clockwork machine, and the only thing we can do with it, is change 1 or 2 items the game leaves in the room, and then the story item. The clockwork machine is something that could be an entire game in and of itself and it is used as a glorified vending machine for a quest item. 

All this is to say, this is an SCP game, that has no real exploration, experimentation, or interaction with any of the SCPs involved, other than to use one at a time as a mechanic for a puzzle and then it is forgotten. 
When it comes to the story, it was ultimately underwhelming, and didn't really conclude in any meaningful way either. The story leaves off with more questions than were answered, and there weren't many questions in the story to begin with.

Everything else I say should be viewed against that background, it's minor niggling and only intended to encourage the creator to create more and even better games in the future!

[hr][/hr]

As a programmer who has dabbled in game-making myself I know first-hand the difficulties of making suitable art and I think the solution of having pre-rendered backgrounds and cel-shaded characters on top works surprisingly well, there's the usual issues with walkable areas and proper z-layering, but nothing I found too annoying.

The game is fully voiced and I applaud leaning into the VAs german accents by setting the game in Germany; However a lot of the minor character voices are synthetic (so probably "AI", but maybe one of the older voice synths) and they neither work particularly well, nor do I like seeing too much "AI art" (or something easily mistaken for it). I think the game would've been better served by simply not voicing those characters, plenty of adventures have taken that path before!

As for the storyline it's certainly suitably cyberpunk, though the ending is not to my personal taste in the genre. There are a few moments where NPCs are ridiculously dense and some where their personality seems to have gone through a big shift (Though it was telegraphed), including some lampshading of Bond Villain Stupidity only to do it anyway. There were a few moments where the PCs do things I would not have chosen, but I feel those were all well in-character; Yelling at the screen because the character is being reckless is par for the course, I think.

This game is very early in development, with barely more than a proof of concept in place.
It shows all the signs of any other game of this type, with a mix of some of the better features from its ancestors.
Players of the Diablo series will be familiar with some of it, Titan Quest for other players, maybe potential for some Sacred inheritance also.

The game is very raw though, nothing about it is clean or polished, and much of it is placeholder (i really hope anyway!!).

As for whether or not I recommend buying it, it really depends on your motivation and expectations.
Buy it only if you consider paying for an early access game an investment, and as such a gamble as much as any investment ever is.
It has potential, but at this point it really could go either way...or just turn out mediocre.

I am crossing my fingers, and happily invested in what I hope becomes a worthy successor of Diablo, Sacred, and Titans Quest.

Nobody Wants to Die is a hidden gem that masterfully blends cyberpunk aesthetics with classic film noir, creating a unique and captivating atmosphere. The game's world, a futuristic New York City where immortality is commonplace, is both stunning and thought-provoking.  What's more, the game beautifully incorporates a layer of art deco inspired architecture and a sense of lavish, yet underlyingly sinister, high elite society.

The gameplay, a clever mix of point-and-click investigation, dialogue choices, and time manipulation mechanics, keeps you constantly engaged. While the puzzles are generally straightforward, achieving a complete understanding of the story and unlocking all the trophies requires at least two playthroughs, adding to the replayability (you can make a few different choices and be a bit of a d**k; drink some whisky and steal some.... spoilers... won't tell you).

The narrative is a standout, with a gripping murder mystery plot, well-developed characters, and sharp, witty dialogue. The story explores themes of transhumanism, morality, and the societal consequences of immortality, leaving a lasting impression long after the credits roll.

And the best part? It's refreshingly short, perfect for those who want a complete and satisfying gaming experience without a massive time commitment.

Overall, Nobody Wants to Die is a must-play for fans of cyberpunk, noir, or anyone looking for a well-crafted and thought-provoking adventure.  Highly recommended! (also thanks ChatGPT for making my words sounds like I know what I am talking about)

This game attempts to channel the spirit of Doom, Rise of the Triad, and Duke Nukem 3D, and at first glance, it seems to succeed with its retro-inspired art style and enemy designs. However, closer inspection reveals inconsistencies—some enemies look like they came from completely different games, as if pulled from various asset packs.

The level design is just as problematic. It’s way too easy to fall through the map, get stuck in terrain, or be trapped between objects due to poorly implemented hitboxes. The controls feel like Catacomb Abyss if your keyboard had been dunked in Mountain Dew, and the motion blur doesn’t help. There’s very little in the way of visual or audio customization, making the experience even more frustrating.

The soundtrack? Imagine My First Dark Synth—repetitive and uninspired. If a five-year-old composed it, I’d be impressed. If anyone older did, I’d suggest leaving music composition to those with actual talent.

With only a handful of maps (about 6-8), you pick one, clear waves, and earn achievements. That’s it. It feels like an asset flip, though I can’t verify it. If it isn’t, that doesn’t really change the outcome. Either way, this one isn’t worth your time.

First of all, I appreciate this game's style and music design. It doesn't feel like the average mobile game-esque vibe that many current year tower defense takes up; It more so feels like a classic flash game which is always an appreciated style in my opinion. It's a simple game, you buy peasants and you give them weapons both bought and crafted. It's an original idea, and I can appreciate some intuitive design in what is otherwise a genre full of copycats of whatever's popular.

However, I do have some criticisms here. 
1. It'd be preferable to be able to see the remaining amount of rounds, I may have missed it, but if it's there then it's not visible enough.
2. The balancing is pretty great, but I think to be able to actually tell what tower is doing and firing what some visual indicators of things like slow down and burning would be ideal. 
3. Generally the particles should be more distinctly visible for the sake of clarity. This could be achieved by brightening the colors or even making the sprites more complex: For example making fire have a range of red, orange, and yellow bits inside the particle's sprite instead of one orangish pixel. 

Overall, I like this game's beginning and I hope it goes farther! Great job.

There are some utterly marvelous, poetic, hard-hitting lines in here too... If you're considering this game, please buy it: it's truly, utterly worth it (and I wish there was an actual fandom too, there's so much good stuff to talk about and not enough people talking about any of it). Honest-to-god one of my favorite visual novels that I've ever experienced.

How do I even begin to describe my obsession with this game?? It teases you with fascinating little tidbits of lore and worldbuilding that constantly leave you wanting more. It has some of the sweetest, most intimate romance scenes I’ve ever seen written. The characters are all interesting and layered, and sometimes they’re annoying and frustrating and that just makes me love them more. I could go on! This game has such delightful attention to detail in every aspect, you can really see how much love and care was poured into it.

I will say though, this game is not for everyone. I understand the people who find it slow and confusing. The game throws you straight into the story without any exposition. Characters often speak in vague, roundabout ways that require some serious reading between the lines, and sometimes they reference things that you won’t have context for unless you’ve played other routes.

This makes your first playthrough somewhat frustrating, as the game makes you feel like an idiot for not understanding things that other characters seem to think are obvious. On the other hand, it makes successive playthroughs incredibly rewarding. As you can tell from my play time, I am utterly addicted to scouring through this game’s dialogue for new insights into the world and characters. This stuff is catnip for me!

In conclusion:
Play Amarantus. Surrender to the brainworms.

not gonna bury the lede, currently [b]nora's adventurescape[/b] is [b]nora's adventure bug-scape[/b], a broken piece of shit. and while it pretends to be the [b]collector's edition[/b], offering all 15 days' worth of content (except stuff you have to skip to continue, see below) and an actual ending, [b]wallpapers and the soundrack are missing[/b].

it starts like every hallmark movie ever. successful lady (ice skater here) moves to small town for a change, to re-invent herself and save a building. everybody's way too nice but also lazy and incompetent (they must be game developers on the side), nora's the only person capable of doing anything. which is mostly playing delivery woman, made all the more tedious with all the slow walking animations from house to house in the cutscenes. and what's with all the hugging?

the 'overworld' is like all those mobile games like [b]gardenscapes[/b], surely there's a construction kit of some kind available, but [b]without any mobile shenanigans[/b]. isometric view, the environment looks great, and [b]lots (LOOOOTS!) of dialog[/b]. loquacious doesn't even begin to describe it. [b]nora's adventure yap-scape[/b] would've been a more apt title, but [b]dialog/cutscenes are skippable[/b] without missing anything of import because see above. no text display sound (woo!) and the typewriter effect is fast enough. sentences can also be clicked to appear immediately but with such phenomenal writing most of them are only a few words and appear faster than you can click.

[b]gameplay is really varied.[/b] sure, there are objects to find, but it's [b]more 1st-person point & click than hidden object game, without the comfort of object highlights and an active mouse cursor, so it's about 50-50[/b]. many different tasks from fixing to decorating and everything in-between, [b]all presented as some sort of puzzle[/b], and they're replayable (not the dialog). would've been nice to have more than 3 on the screen, so as not to have a 36-page level select, or at least quick jumps to different days.

puzzles include finding and using items, memory matching, finding the differences (all in a row, no misclicks, horrible), jigsaw, patterns, match-3, math, lights out, nonogram and pretty much everything under the sun. I passed on a few tedious puzzles and in some cases didn't understand the logic (if there was one) even after looking up the solution, maybe it's just me. [b]3 unexplained difficulty settings[/b] for the game overall, can be changed anytime, and tasks also have a toughness rating, represented by their color.

so far so run-of-the-mill, but what drew me in was the [b]supposedly 100+ door-opening puzzles[/b]. didn't count them but pretty sure it's the total number and not all of them involve a door. still the find items, use them, etc. schtick but with a hint of escape roomism. except it's more [b]escape [i]into[/i] the room, also known as breaking and entering, burglary even[/b]. so despite syrupy appearances you're basically committing felony after felony instead of knocking or asking for a key and the items.

there's a [b]hint and puzzle skip[/b] button, both have a short cooldown but no lives, energy, daily rewards, etc. there's also a [b]24-page help section and a strategy guide (walkthrough)[/b], plus a bunch of 'extra' levels, i.e. the actual ending of the story, scummily always cut from the non-collector's editions (and from what I've read, this one simply says something to the effect of 'buy the ce if you want to see the rest' after day 12, no fake ending or anything, it just stops). also, in-game representation of [b]achievements, half of which are broken[/b] (task-tracking is a mess). and as mentioned above, no wallpapers or soundtrack in the steam version, unlike on big fish.

nice but nothing special mobile/casual graphics, [b]music is beyond repetitive[/b], had to turn it off during day 1. settings are for languages and separate volumes, no player profiles and [b]no windowed mode[/b], alt+enter only produces a non-resizable window, edit the registry if you want a different size. annoyingly, quitting is only possible from the main menu but there's no reason to go back there, with only a new game and continue button besides quit.

all in all, it's a [b]mixed bag but the puzzly gameplay is mostly good[/b], even if the skippable fluff isn't. [b]has a demo[/b] with the first day, not really representative of what's on offer later, basically the tutorial (help is bugged there, works in the full game). the store page is messy and redundant and the [b]promised content updates never happened[/b] (it was originally released in 2021), but I don't expect games appearing on big fish to have endless (or any) updates after restoring cut content in so-called collector's editions to present the whole story. still doesn't mean you should lie on the store page.

"Super Turbo Racing" is an extremely simple drag racer with almost no gameplay to speak of. It also doesn't work properly.

Why people enjoy drag racing has always been a mystery to me, but maybe it's more about the spectactle and the get-together than the actual act of racing. In that regard, [i]simulated[/i] drag racing makes absolutely no sense unless it's only a small part of a racing game. "Super Turbo Racing" however, despite the name promising something else, [i]only[/i] contains drag racing. And that's a problem as there's just not enough gameplay here to make the game any fun, especially since it's a single-player only title.

As expected, you and an AI car race a quarter of a mile on a straight track. Acceleration is automatic, the only thing you have to do is shift the gears at the right time to become faster than the opponent. If that doesn't sound absolutely thrilling it get's better - [i]there's a shift indicator on the screen when you have to shift[/i]. So when the green arrow appears you just tap the shift button and your car becomes faster. Do this five times and A WINNER IS YOU!

And that's really all there is. Yes, there are three different tracks, but two of them require you to purchase new cars - and these cars are expensive. To unlock the second track you need a Ferrari which sets you back a cool virtual $500k, but you only earn $500 per race. The third race - with much cheaper German cars - is also locked and I'm not certain it's even available yet as you don't get told you need a German car to race. You get more money from winning on the different tracks but how does that help you if they are all behind a huge buy-in?

Oh, but there's another problem: you can't unlock the second event on each track as the code handling the buy-in is broken. Would be an easy fix but there has been no update to this game since release so I'm not holding my breath.

The game has exactly zero configuration options; you can't even turn off the sound. You are not even told which key is used for shifting on the keyboard although that's easy as it's Left-Shift or Right-Shift. Visually it's all store-bought assets thrown together and the same goes for the motor sounds. The graphics can only be called basic - there's no post-processing here, not even a skybox. It's all pretty ugly.

Even at the low price point I can't recommend this "game" to anyone.

This game is 50% nostalgic NES-era platforming fun and 50% irritating backtracking designed to frustrate and irritate you. To start with the good, the graphics are very charming and I like the way the gameplay unfolds organically as you progress. The combat is as simple as it gets since all you do is swipe with a knife, but the platforming gets increasingly more complex as you collect things in your inventory like a parachute and duct tape to stick to walls. There's a decent amount of detail to the environments, like blades of grass in the foreground and specific enemy behavior patterns to memorize (You fight a bunch of bugs). As you go along you pick up items to give to specific characters as extremely rudimentary puzzle-solving, e.g. give a violin bow to a grasshopper and he will let you ride his back to the other side of the area. There are also health and attack upgrades that aren't really necessary since the game is so easy but still add a bit of depth.

Now for the bad- it's a lot of backtracking and in areas that are comprised of repetitive linear platforming. There are a couple parts near the end where you need to backtrack about fifteen minutes to get certain items to get a pulley system working- it's extremely irritating. Also you can only hold three inventory items so even if you know what to do you may have left the item somewhere else on the map- and if you forget where you placed the item you might as well start the game over. Lastly, there is no reason to collect extra lives since if you get a game over you restart in the same room you died in. All that doesn't break the game for me and if you stick with it for a couple hours you will probably find it gets a bit addictive picking up the various items and figuring out where to put them to progress. It's reminiscent of old NES Capcom games like Chip and Dale Rescue Rangers, and there's enough content here to make it worth it despite the repetitive backtracking.

Unfortunately, as much as I would love to recommend the game, there are simply too many bugs as of right now. I'm sure that with a good bit of work and some important game-fixing updates it may improve the experience.

Once in a blue moon I look back to the two arcade cabinets I perused on two separate days of my life as a kid and pretend I'm like those boys from Honshu. That I also have the stick itch.

Turn on the vintage visual effects. Pick up the controller. Platform. Attack horizontally. Learn the way of the diagonal kick. Honestly restart the level as my lives run out. Nod in rhythm to the 90s Yamaha samples.

These are games of real place, of community, of good times, of action. In the world of games arcades are cinema.

"Alchemist" is a distilled action-adventure. It is only slightly more complex than the genre originator, "Adventure," on Atari 2600. In Alchemist, the player will explore an open location, search for items, figure out their uses to progress, and then test his abilities and understanding of the game's mechanics against a challenging path leading to a tough boss.

The fun of Alchemist lies in exploration and experimentation. The player is free to traverse from screen to screen and uncover new areas. There are no hard-coded limitations or boundaries as to where he can go. However, there are enemies to prevent him from progressing too far without properly equipping the main character. To progress, the player will have to unravel the functions of items he encounters while exploring. There are no explanations, so it's up to him to figure out where to go and the uses of the items he finds. The more proficient he is with the game's mechanics and the more knowledgeable he is about game items, the more freely he can explore the location.

The goal of the game is to find four pieces of "The Spell of Destruction" and cast the spell on "the Warlock." Finding the pieces will require the player to experiment with the found items. Fortunately, the solutions are not obscure to the point of requiring a walkthrough. After finding the pieces, the player has to locate the Warlock, get close to him, and cast the Spell of Destruction. This, however, is easier said than done, as getting to the Warlock requires careful preparation and planning.

The less you know about the game, the better. This game is not so much about using game mechanics, but rather exploring them. Read the game's manual online and dive in!

If you study game design or are a retro games enthusiast, I recommend playing Alchemist to experience the action-adventure genre in its purest form. Seeing a game genre in isolation can teach you a lot about the game mechanics that define it.

I will continue my review with critique and as such I draw a spoiler-line. Reading beyond this point may be detrimential to your experience of Alchemist.

[b]SPOILER LINE[/b]

The player can traverse the location in either the Alchemist form or Eagle form, between which he can switch freely, provided he has enough Spell Energy. My first assumption was that the Eagle form is for mobility, whereas the Alchemist form is for functionality. However, this has proven to be wrong, as the Alchemist form is redundant and serves no purpose. Alchemist cannot traverse most of the location, whereas Eagle can go anywhere. In the Eagle form, the player can perform every action, such as picking up items, using spells, and fighting enemies, all while being much more mobile than in the Alchemist form. It's a puzzling design decision to allow the Eagle to perform these actions, rendering the Alchemist useless. The only unique ability of Alchemist is shooting lightning from his hands, but as the next paragraph will showcase, this contributes to nothing.

Based on common gaming conventions, the player would reasonably assume that shooting lightning would be the primary way to fend off enemies. However, after applying this theory into practice, the player will inevitably be disappointed. First of all, the enemies struck by lightning will most likely still be alive. Second, the main character's Spell Energy would be quickly depleted to zero. Having no Spell Energy in the Alchemist is bad news. It takes FIVE MINUTES for Spell Energy to regenerate from "00" to "99". Spell Energy, as the name suggests, is needed to execute spells, including switching to the Eagle form. Keep in mind, the enemy might still be there. And the next room will have enemies too. Enemies also randomly respawn upon the player re-entering the room. At this pace, the player won't see the end of Alchemist until retirement!

You can imagine the feeling of despair that comes after seeing how ineffective the lightning is and how long it takes for Spell Energy to regenerate. If this were how combat worked in Alchemist, the game would be borderline unplayable. However, lightning is nothing but a spoof - a beginner's prank, if you may. The most efficient way of dealing with enemies is to face them. Literally. When the main character touches enemies, they receive damage! Of course, the main character also takes damage in return. The touch between the main character and an enemy is supposed to simulate a "physical fight" (the player has to use his imagination!). As in real life, it's best to come prepared for such occasions.

Around the location, there are weapon-shaped items. Carrying such items allows the player to defeat enemies quicker while receiving less damage. The most powerful weapons can trivialize most enemies. However, violence is not always the answer in Alchemist. The main character can carry only one item at a time. While weapons do allow for more freedom in exploring the location, to progress, the player has to find the four pieces of The Spell of Destruction. As such, the player will have to figure out how to use non-weapon items to progress. The one-item-at-a-time limitation provides interesting decisions for the player: should he keep the weapon and explore more? Should he take the item and return to the base? Or should he return to the base with the weapon, restock his health, and then attempt to pick up the item? Although this mechanic may sound arbitrary, it does provide gameplay depth and contributes to the overall enjoyability.

To further assist the player on his journey, there are "lesser spells" all over the location. The main character can carry one lesser spell at a time, and each spell provides a unique ability. This is a cool concept idea, but again, there is an issue with balancing. One spell has only one use, and it's used purely for progression (it's more of a key than a spell). Among the other three spells, there is a clear winner. See if you can spot it:

• Shield - mitigates all enemy damage for some time. Uses 24 Spell Energy points, lasts 3 seconds.
• Bewitch - freezes all enemies on the screen for some time (enemies can still deal damage). Uses 24 Spell Energy points, lasts 3 seconds.
• Regenerate - exchanges Spell Energy points into Stamina points (stamina = health). Uses 1 Spell Energy point per 1 Stamina point.

Two spells prevent damage to health for a ridiculously short amount of time, one spell generously restores health. There is no competition. Perhaps if there were enemies so tough that they could instantly kill you upon touch, then the Shield spell would be useful. Similarly, if there were enemies that chased the main character or were extremely quick, the Bewitch spell might find some utility. However, as it stands, the Regeneration spell is the best pick for any situation in the game.

There are no "situational" nuances in Alchemist; there are only the best solutions. That's precisely why I stated that the game is not so much about using game mechanics, but rather exploring them. Initially, the player does not have knowledge of what is "the best." This knowledge comes from exploration and experimentation. Moreover, this knowledge is not useless; it is essential to defeat the main boss. If the player goes to face the Warlock with anything less than the best spell and the best weapon, he will perish.

That's why I don't think the imbalance in Alchemist is necessarily a bad thing. Yes, most of the items are junk, but that's the point. It's up to the player to find the gold among them. The only way to discover this (aside from going online and cheating yourself out of fun using walkthroughs) is to explore the entire location, find all the items, and determine which is the best through experimentation.

I had a lot of fun doing exactly that: exploring and experimenting. Finding out how to get the four pieces was also fun and exciting when I finally figured it out.

Alchemist provided me with a tough, but rewarding experience. It was fun!

One of my biggest frustrations with modern VR games is how many are visually downgraded ("potato-fied") to accommodate lower-end headsets like the Quest 2. Textures often look mushy, and the overall fidelity suffers.

Boot Strap Island VR, however, says "FU" to the Quest and fully embraces high-end PC hardware. The game looks absolutely stunning, and my immersion in it is higher than in any other VR experience—simply because of how breathtakingly beautiful it is.

That said, I do have one major gripe: the leveling system. On my very first day playing, I managed to survive for 12 days purely on hope and determination—only to unlock a measly three items. Even after making progress and unlocking one or two more, I've hit a wall. Now, I struggle to make it past 10 days, and unlocking anything else feels next to impossible. A very simple game that is made interesting by the fact that items almost always have a pro and a con, you give up one stat to amplify another and it's surprisingly well balanced. Ultimately all you do is run around, gather resources and try to blow up hordes of enemies that come at you throughout the wave, or they try to cut you off, shoot at you from afar or just run arouund aimlessly to form natural barriers. You are a mighty brotato with the ability to carry 6 weapons (most of the time) to take them out or at least keep them away from you and survive until wave 20, then you can choose to carry on in endless mode. Are you locked in with them or are they locked in with you?

There's also 6 difficulty levels so you can take it at your own pace. I've also seen a lot of mods made by a passionate community so it's very flexible. 

There's just a lot of entertainment to be had for a very low price.

Simple addictive fun that's worth your while, I went ahead and got the bundle for like 8 bucks or so and it's definitely worth it. I spent dozens of hours playing out many build styles and had a blast. However, while I do recommend trying it, the fun does end eventually, and it comes crashing down when it does. 

[b] Things I liked:[/b]
Simple controls — All you have to do is run around. There are options for manual aiming, but I found auto-aim to do want you want 99% of the time

Character variety — There's so many potatoes each with their own abilities, it's easy to find one that you like.

Weapon variety — Same deal as with the characters, there's lots of weapons to build out with strengths and weaknesses. 

Quick play — It's super easy to get into a rhythm as the runs are generally short at about 25 minutes. This is great if you just wanna chill out for a bit.

[b] Things that are okay:[/b]
Weapon balancing — Generally, there are weapons that are just better, and you'll find out quickly what they are. This isn't bad per se, but it can leave some runs feeling stale after a while because you end up picking the same weapons to have a chance at winning. This is somewhat mitigated by choice of brotato.

Static enemy waves — Every wave is the same between runs. The only difference is where the enemies spawn, and what bosses spawn. It good for predictability and makes it easy to learn what enemies do, but I really wanted to switch it up sometimes.

[b]The thing that made me quit:[/b]
Enemy bullets — This was the thing that ended my fun. If you play this game, be prepared not to die from bad decision making or poor planning, but a stray enemy bullet that eats 50% of your health. Seriously, these are the worst to deal with and snapped me out of the zone every time I died to them. Not through lack of effort, you will have some awesome runs lose to one bullet making it though your 60% dodge. I've died to them more times than I could count.

Enemies can be stopped, bullets can't, and that's the biggest distinction in what damages you in the game. You either have enough dodge, making dodge mandatory, or you dodge them by moving around them, which is sometimes impossible without wading through a dozen enemy checks. It was this that made me realize how luck-based the end game is and that ultimately, the continued effort was not worth the low low coming off the high of having some fun build come online. I've already uninstalled and probably won't go back. Sink maybe a day or two's worth of hours for the fun then don't turn back.

As one of the weaker, flatter and less creative bullet heaven games available today, Brotato stands out by being an early addition to the genre that focuses on limiting player choices while slogging through it's drawn out 30minute+ rounds where you build out your one-note base characters from limited set of choices — focusing on their one or two specialties. During rounds the game focuses on movement but allows for manual aim as well which comes into handy in some moments on max difficulty. While building out stats in a way that plays out very similar from run to run, the limited item pool doesn't force much creativity and allows for easy and approachable gameplay.

All that said, it's a fun game to play on the steam deck as it's 60 second round timer allows for easy pickup and play and the lack of complex choices makes it easy to keep track of what any given character needs.

These days overshadowed by Halls of Torment, Deep Rock Galactic: Survivors, and even the free HoloCure providing more substance, Brotato stands as a simple classic to enjoy between more demanding games.

------------ ORIGINAL REVIEW (On April 10, 2022) ------------ 

I hate to give this game a "Not Recommend" because after playing it for about a half an hour, it's obvious that a lot of care of work went into making this game.. and it's also obvious that this game is sooo close to being a little gem of an indie game!

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZHefKI7TYAQ

The Developer made a poor decision however to lock the FOV (Field of View) in too low, likely because he didn't want to have to create a hand holding your sword or weapon equipped.  Instead he wanted to simply put the FOV too low (say 70) so the equipped sword asset was only seen and that's a big problem for many people.  Our brain and eyes are used to around a 90 FOV in real life, and when a game locks in a FOV too low, it can make many people start feeling queasy or sick to their stomach just playing the game for any extended amount of time.  In my case with this game, that started being felt only about 10-15 minutes into the game, and it slowly starts making you feel more and more queasy the longer you play.

I also don't like or understand the developers decision to make all the mobs re-spawn just a few seconds after you slay them, because they all drop loot and this could make it way too easy to acquire gold and resources just by running in circles slaying mobs over and over.

Another gripe I have is that this game has NO options at all for audio adjustments or video quality settings.  There's not even any way to change the game from full screen to windowed.  

The developer made a cool little game here, don't get me wrong, but I feel like his laziness with the above mentioned problems is what makes this game a bad game!  ..It could so easily be a great little gem, that is frustrating to me as an indie game critic!

It's so close to being a great little indie adventure game, especially at this $3 price point.  I hope the developer cares enough about his first title to make the changes needed to not make a good percentage of people who play his game feel sick to their stomach just playing it!

NOT Recommended (until the FOV is set to 90 or 95 minimum).  Another great and pretty easy change would be allowing the player to adjust the game volume as there is no current options in the game at all.
