From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game features simple, cartoony 2D graphics, of the type you normally expect to see in low effort mobile apps.  3D graphics programming does require a degree of skill and competence and unfortunately not all developers have the budget or talent to deliver this, despite 3D graphics cards hitting the mainstream in the 1990's.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio.  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but I wasn't able to find it on the app stores.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes this might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 3 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

So, should you buy this asset flip?

Of course not.  Royal Mahjong King's Journey has the ridiculous price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.  Because this is the kind of game you can just play for free on mobile phones, it's impossible to recommend anyone should pay money for the same experience on Steam.

- GREAT Ambient music and sound design
- GREAT level designs
- OK monster / Monster design
- A must play with friends, alone not so much (unless you're a hardcore fan of the genre)

Escape the Backrooms is a pretty good game considering that only 1 developer is working on it (great work, by the way) and I don't think there are any issues that really drag down the game/make you not want to play. I have encountered some bugs, and I'll list them here later, but they only really served as a minor inconvenience. Having the option to restart a level really helps.

I think the game really outshines in graphics and gameplay. What makes the gameplay so special is that they aren't reusing a lot of the gimmicks, and the ones that are reused are reused in a good way. A good example is the chainsaw mechanic. This was introduced back in one of the sub-levels as a way to break down doors to make them openable. This could take a little bit of time, and since there is a creature in the level then increases the paranoia you have when opening doors with your chainsaw. This was reused in the second section of 'Level !" when you had to open a door in a chase scene, making it so if you take too long you die. This turns paranoia into stress as you try your best to open the door and waste as little time to prevent being killed. That's just one example of why the gameplay in this game is smart and unique.

I don't have much to say about the graphics. They are good for a backrooms game. Having the option to adjust the settings  accordingly to whether or not you have a strong or weak PC is something all games need. High graphics have good shaders, and a good bokeh/focus effect.

Bugs I found were primarily in level 9.
The wandering eye was completely broken. The animations sometimes didn't load and it was really easy for the creature to get stuck in place.
The wretches could be clipped out of houses.
In all levels in general, some of the hitboxes are a bit wonky. In co-op, tight hallways make players able to completely block paths.

This doesn't subtract to the game, since this is in early access and bugs are very common.

I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a fun puzzle-exploration experience. I wouldn't play this if your main critique-point is horror. Paranoia is the only non-jumpscare part of the game that can make the experience scary.

Infindustry is a Factory Town clone. If you're ok with that - go ahead. But buy Factory Town first.

I'm sorry to say that, but there's no way around it; it's practically identical, just with fewer things in it. I don't like bashing indie games, but you must have known when building it that it's mostly copying. It's a game about building a little village through automation, conveyor belts and assigning workers to buildings. You provide items to houses to keep them happy, and unlock more technology by producing books. You'll need some patience to play it. Building things and giving instructions to workers is fiddly. That being said, I think I have to recommend it just because I've played 10 hours in 2 days. But I guess you can thank Factory Town for that.

[b]Pros[/b]
- Has an info window so you can find out what buildings produce the item you want
- The peons are nicely detailed, random appearances and much better animated than the little meeples from Factory Town
- Buildings can create multiple things at once (like Factory Town). However, because of the limited number of inputs and outputs to buildings, this is impractical
- Villagers and conveyor belts carry pretty little 3D models of the items
- The developer has been patching it quickly. 5 of my "cons" have been fixed in the 2 days since launch
- Dev replied on Twitter very quickly about an issue I was having with the Forester

[b]Cons[/b]
- You can't change the mouse buttons that control the camera
- The interface has no sound effects
- Peons keep walking into each other and getting stuck
- When you drag the mouse to move the camera, there's a deadzone so it doesn't start moving immediately
- It's a complete clone of Factory Town
- No button to reset keybindings. No ability to remove keybindings. Setting a new key does not remove the duplicate key on another control
- Rather slow paced. I had to sit for 10 minutes at a time waiting for enough resources to research the next thing
- Once the tutorial window has disappeared, there's no way to find out how something functions again without resetting all the tutorials. Like I forgot how to add resources to the top bar, or what the point of upgrading the HQ is - and had no way to find out
- Farms and fields are completely unexplained
- If you want to delete a road, you have to delete every road tile individually, you can't drag over them
- Unlike Factory Town, there is no indication of how many of something you're producing per second, so the only way to optimise your productions is to sit and watch them
- When building conveyor belts, you have to place each straight line, left corner, right corner, slope up and slope down separately instead of being able to drag them
- You can chain peon commands, but if there's a step they can't do they just wait there instead of skipping it - which makes it impossible to use them for more than one job
- You can combine conveyor belts, but if one item isn't needed, the belt will jam. Combined with the fact that buildings have limited inputs, it makes it pretty clunky to use. For example, a workshop making books requires cloth and paper, and outputs wood. The building only has 2 input/output slots which means you can't automate it without having a peon carry the items away
- Unlike Factory Town, houses can only consume one item at a time, which means supplying them with any more than 1 item is pointless. No need to give them food, wood, tools, medicine and luxury goods - they'll only use one of them.

This game is in dire need of balancing, some buildings like the mine are almost useless, as with a mine you can get 2.5x mining speed by using 5 workers, whereas using 5 workers without a mine will give you 5x mining speed. At least the building base values should be higher than a worker base value, since one can get more work done having the right tools.

I in general enjoy automation games, so I also enjoyed playing this, too.

However, compared to the other games I just can't recommend this one. Researches, are done fast, and I don't care about achievements. Hence the "campaign" went quickly.

I love the peons with their brownish waterbender style. But the list of things I wish that would be in game is just too damn long. It starts at not being able to name these peons, goes over not moveable building and ends with missing speedcontrols.

After all, I was kind of confused that this game is released and not in early access. Those points I mentioned would have been detected there.

Like many other suggest, go ahead, play simelar games. Factory Town is a great example, so is Kubifaktorium.


Final words: After writing this I will research the last, which will trgger the hordes. I am not looking forward to it, but I guess I will appreciate the end.

Example: several  field needs watering from a well. One can't program a peon to get water, water a field, but move on if the field does not need watering. Overall, the game is enjoyable and I recommend it. It just needs some better peon logic and QoL upgrades to go from okay to good or great.

Justice League: Cosmic Chaos is a charming and lighthearted game that perfectly captures the spirit of DC’s Trinity—Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman. With its vibrant cartoon-style visuals and quirky dialogue, the game delivers plenty of fun, especially for younger players and longtime DC fans.

The story revolves around Mister Mxyzptlk, one of Superman’s most outrageous and mischievous foes, and as expected, his antics bring plenty of humor and over-the-top situations. The writing is playful, with entertaining banter between Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman, making it enjoyable even for adult fans who appreciate their classic character dynamics.

Since Cosmic Chaos is primarily aimed at kids, the main story is relatively easy to complete. The controls are simple, and the combat mechanics are accessible, making it a great pick for casual players. However, once you dive into the extra content, things take a frustrating turn. Even on the easiest difficulty, some side challenges feel almost impossible. The third-person perspective, combined with somewhat clunky controls, can make these tasks more difficult than they should be.

For longtime DC fans, one of the best aspects of the game is collecting classic Justice League comic books, which unlock new costumes for the main trio. It’s a great nod to DC’s rich history and adds an extra layer of excitement for those familiar with the source material.

While you eventually recruit The Flash, Aquaman, Cyborg, and John Stewart, you can only actively play as Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman. This feels like a missed opportunity, especially considering that fan-favorites like Martian Manhunter and Hal Jordan are absent entirely. Expanding the roster would have made the game even more enjoyable.

One of the game’s biggest highlights is its animated cutscenes. They’re well-crafted, full of energy, and bring the Justice League’s personalities to life in a way that feels true to their comic book roots.

Justice League: Cosmic Chaos is a fun, visually appealing game that delivers plenty of charm, humor, and DC nostalgia. It’s perfect for younger audiences and casual players but may leave completionists frustrated due to a few overly difficult challenges and imprecise controls. Despite some drawbacks, its engaging story, fun character interactions, and comic-inspired collectibles make it a worthwhile experience for DC fans.

Under The Moon is a spin on the hidden object genre, incorporating riddles into finding the hidden objects. The game is relatively short (~1-1.5 hours) and straight-forward, and is thus most appropriate for younger players. There seems to be some minor translation errors making some riddles difficult to understand (particularly given that many incorporate puns, and thus the wordplay is rather important), but you can relaunch the level and hope you don't get that particular riddle again if you can't figure it out. The developers are responsive to feedback as well.

Given the length and complexity of the game, I think the price as-is is too steep. I would recommend the game to younger players at a fairly steep discount (~50+%). If you regularly play puzzle games or are looking for something longer/even moderately difficult, I think you would be disappointed with the game.

I actually bought it without much expectation. I've finished the game several times. It was not easy for me to see the end of the game. Some puzzles can be really challenging at times. The number of chapters and puzzles can be increased and perhaps the difficulty level can be added. Also, apart from a few minor bugs, I haven't come across anything that broke the fun of the game.

I do think that Under The Moon is an interesting and passionate title to look on because it carries over the spirit that can be seen along with the greatest and earliest side-scrollers and point & click puzzles in gaming history such as Monkey Island and Bladerunner. Though that's just something that they theorically have in common. In a practical sense, the gameplay is quite considerably different, compared to these early examples of the genre. It is rather a diffedent game where it doesn't necessarily -unline many others- want to keep the audience in a loop of constant failures and tryings, and shines in a simple and beautifully illustrated way.

The story is developing around the riddles. A short but certainly meaningful story about true love which at some point, is quite a relatable topic for anyone since everyone can feel such emotions towards someone or something at some point in their lives. 

The game is consisting of many levels and has a large scale of riddles. With the updates, there will be 100 or so riddles so that's nice to see that the dev cares about the game. It's not that easy to come by with such a game that's literally full of riddles these days. So, that's a plus in my book. More of a casual, relaxing, undwindy puzzle game I would say. 
 
For the record, I just loved to listening to the environmental sounds, traditional eastern music, sfx and especially cliché -even banal- Turkish words that are spinnin' around like a fidget. Brings me to my childhood. To the good old days. That's just beautiful. And frankly, you can clearly see the effort behind this project. 

Under The Moon is a solid 8 to me. I don't and surely cannot know what you are thinking about it but when you try to give some thought to it, you can see what I was telling you the whole time lies still, in the game, as a fact. That's what gaming is -or was- really about, right? It's all about passion and love because without these, there is no meaning at all. 

All in all, it was an enjoyable adventure to the core.

Plot wise, I'll be brief to avoid any spoilers. You're a mob guy collecting your protection money. Your 'family' has a temporary mob boss in place to handle things. Not everyone seems to like him. Things really ramp up from there. It was a little tricky following what was going on, but the 'memory' section with a family tree and map was useful.

It's up to you how you want to play your guy, you get to decide if you'll try and make nice, or be awful to everyone. If you've played rpg maker games before, there's not a whole lot of active gameplay here, as it's more of a story game. That's what I was looking for personally, but just worth keeping in mind.

The only real caveat I have it that I think I've possibly been softlocked from leaving an office. I think because I spoke to someone in the wrong order. I'll likely restart as this was early on, but worth making a backup save or two. I'll edit this review if I figure out what happened there.

Overall, for £2, get it. If you like rpg maker games like The Deed, or really miss The Sopranos, this is worth your time. I don't know this dev but it's clear they've put some real effort here, and the price point isn't ridiculous. I have a soft spot for these little rpg maker games, and this is another good one to look into if you're into them too.

I also found the battle system surprisingly deep for a simple little game made in Game Maker 2. Reindeer Story is a top down RPG with a TON of Christmassy content and a fairly unique battle system! 

Most enemies feature a Red/Green/Blue colour scheme, with a weakness to one and a resistance to the other. Battles play out in turn based fashion with timed attacks and free movement dodging segments when it becomes the enemies turn. 

One element I've really enjoyed is how the player characters each have some kind of combat specialty. Lux, the titular Reindeer is an all arounder with the highest movement speed, making them best to dodge tricky attacks (and even counter attack). Robin has some support abilities and a spell that can hit almost everything. Whereas the third partner you get seems to deal the most damage by far (and is probably my favourite design of the lot)!

Music, visuals, and writing are all rather adorable, with some nods to its 'Mario & Luigi' inspirations, as well as of course, the holiday season.

Some hitboxes on the environment and enemies can be a bit jank, and I always end up walking away from dialogue conversations accidentally, but as you can see by some of other reviewer's playtime, that certainly doesn't get in the way of experiencing all the many bosses and optional content the game has to offer while i've only scratched the surface. Truly impressive stuff!

TLDR: This game is exactly what I have been waiting for in multiplayer deception games. This is not just a Phasmophobia or an Among Us clone, Masks of Deception takes the simple mechanics from both of those titles and elevates it to something much more complex and gratifying. 

In Depth: 
Welcome to the Game and Scrutinized fans will be welcomed with that special Reflect Studios touch in its menus and starting screen design, but what comes next is something completely new. 

There is a lot to take in with Masks of Deception at first glance and may feel overwhelming, but frequent patches have built in tips for new player onboarding experiences. The community has also been very helpful in assisting new players learn the mechanics when randomly matched up in its dedicated servers. I certainly have been enjoying peeling back the layers and figuring out exactly how things work and get pleasantly surprised learning a new mechanic that is usually only discovered through playtime. 

There is so much to do whether you are the chosen Demon or Purgers, making each match feel robust with unique opportunities and outcomes. Purgers, the main squad looking to identify and expel the sneaky Demon on the team, start off with a table of tools and items picked at the start of the match by a random Item Master. Disperse out to find clues and evidence that will help them identify the Demons Type and Name. The evidence ranges from familiar temperature readings to hidden symbols across the walls. There are even inherent sense based actions a Purger can do to gather evidence, such as smelling the air and checking ones own feelings. All the while making sure not to die to environmental factors like the Butcher or the Shadow people. The last type of evidence the Purgers need to find is who on the team is the actual Demon. By far some of the most hilarious moments is trying to "suss" someone out among all the other actions going on and running "pocket checks" on your team... 

On the Demon side of things, you are tasked with secretly finding Demon Books across the map in order to gain your powers and finally be able to kill your teammates. I've only had a few chances as the Demon, so I am still learning the ropes there, but in my time I have enjoyed being mischievous in stealing items and unlocking Butcher doors :) I think one of the bigger achievements is handling what players do once they are dead. Something I always felt games like Phasmo and Among Us fell short on. In Masks of Deception, dead players have a new objective that solely on their own can win the match for the team, by collecting 10 pages across the map. There are other ways in how the ghosts can help the team, but you will have to figure that out :) 

I am excited to see how the game progresses and I hope to see the community grow. If you enjoy the game spread the word! We need more players!

Game Play:
The game play in this game does feel a bit wonky at first, the running is not smooth, and the controls take a bit to get used to. I had to look at the controls multiple times to get a hang of it. But after you learn it, it isn't that bad. Same with the running thing.
The core game is fine, all the tools work, the map is okay, and the game is not terribly hard to learn, just play a couple games. The GUI's could use a bit of work, they feel a bit odd to use.
The game is nice in the aspect that even when you die, you still have something to do.
IF you do not have a microphone, PLEASE consider getting one. It will make the game 100x more entertaining. If you do not enjoy USING your microphone, please look at "The Community" section.

The Community:
The community for this game is great, I would recommend playing just to get to talk to them! When you queue for a game, please do not be afraid to use your microphone, they are very welcoming. Even if you are SUPER shy, just use it to say what evidence you have. The community will appreciate it. With that said, there is a bit of drama here and there, and it does get dealt with pretty quickly, in ways that you may or may not agree with.

The Developer:
The developer of this game, as I know him is super chill. One of the more down to Earth people I have met. He does not overreact a majority of the time, and he does stream on Twitch, he is super fun to watch, go check him out. (Twitch.tv/IndieHorrorDev) So why is this a negative review just because of the developer? Honestly it really shouldn't even be a negative review, it should be a positive one. But the problem I have with the dev, he does a lot of small things that build up over time, and honestly this review is to blow off some of the frustration. I will not go in-depth, because I do not want to give him a bad reputation, I do think he is a cool guy. Please form your own opinion, and do not base opinions solely off this review. I can list a bunch of stuff he does good as well.
If you like developers that interact with their community a lot, this game/community is for you.

Final Thoughts:
Game play is 8/10, Community is 9.6/10. Get the game, especially on August 15th when the huge sale happens, if you really do not enjoy it, you always have the option to refund it, please do not be scared to take a small investment. I promise it will be worth it.

Just to be really clear, this is the original Escape the Ayuwoki Steam game in third-person, with fixed camera angles and deliberately pixellated graphics, reminiscent of 90s PSX survival horror. I wanted to get that out there as some people have been confused by what a 'demake' is.

So it's not a new storyline (it's still the original protagonist waking up in a dark mansion), but what the game does change is that it adds an inventory system (you can carry up to four items, but each item has a weight value, so you could carry less if the items are too heavy), new puzzles, and, according to the Discord community, some new areas, but as I've only played the first chapter so far, I can't confirm myself.

If you found the original game hard, this is even harder. With the original game, you could see directly in front of you and turn around to see in any direction. With fixed camera angles, you're wholly reliant on the volume of the jangly music that plays when the Ayuwoki is near, which adds to the suspense and terror. To help with this, whenever the Ayuwoki breaks down a door to a room in the mansion (something he didn't do in the first game), the camera pans to his location, so you can see where he is at that moment.

As an older gamer in my 40s, I was a teenager when the PSX survival horror boom took off and grew up on games like Resident Evil, Dino Crisis, Silent Hill etc, so this was a nostalgic trip down memory lane for me and love the pixellated aesthetic. The difference here is those other games had characters with dodge mechanics, weapons to fight back and energy bars - here you can't fight back (don't mistake that crowbar for a weapon!) and if the Ayuwoki catches you, you're greeted with a horrific jumpscare and a one-hit kill.

You can't save your progress manually, but reaching certain stages in the chapters will trigger a checkpoint, so if you die, you'll start back at those positions, but when that happened to me I lost a key item from my inventory. However, the devs are really passionate and committed to improving their games and they've patched the game around ten times since launch based on user feedback, so the experience is really smooth now - I just wish I was better at it!

My favourite of the DeadlyCrow Ayuwoki series is still by far Horror Night with it's unique look and feel, character customisation, and procedurally generated multiplayer gameplay but Demake is still a great game, it's just a little bit too hardcore for me, but I can see that this will be a speedrunner's delight given it's a stealth game where how quickly you complete the game depends on how long you hide under tables and behind boxes where the Ayuwoki can't find you - but don't forget to turn off your flashlight as he can see you as well as hear you.

TL/DR - if you're a fan of old-school PSX survival horror with punishing difficulty, this is right up your street.

I highly recommend this game if you're into old school horror. They've done a great job capturing the essence of 90s gaming, down to the controls, fixed camera angles and graphics. Really scary game with great jumpscares, similar to Devour where it's full screen and loud, 10/10 I fall out my chair every time.

 Only downside at the moment is that there's some bugs which make it difficult to progress, but comparing to the developers other games, they will likely fix this very quickly, so I'd still recommend getting this game.

EDIT: Just finished the game, I'd say 90% of the bugs mentioned before have been fixed, there's a few minor ones but nothing game breaking.

 Had so much fun! I'd say you get kind of used to the jumpscares after a while, since the demake seems a lot harder than the original game - it's on par with a souls-like with how often you die. In spite of this, the suspense was killing me at some points. As someone who often gives up and moves on when I die a lot, this game had me gripped like King Kong's fist. In Chapter 3+ I couldn't take my eyes off the screen.

Highly recommended!

A quick review with a few Bugs and Suggestions for the developers![hr][/hr]Personally I like this version quite a lot, since it's different from the main game by adding a few extra elements that are required to proceed to the next chapter. Different locations are an added bonus and that's what sets this game apart from the original game.

[h1]Bugs:[/h1]

These bugs had occurred during my play through of chapter 2.[hr][/hr]   
- The Ayuwoki was breaking doors I don't believe he should have. He broke the fire hallway doors that lead nowhere, he also broke some of the front doors where the police are.   

- The Ayuwoki broke the White Door after I grabbed the key, even though I hadn't unlocked it and gone through it yet.  (Basically what's the point of the key if the monster breaks the door before I can use it?)   

- During chapter 2, the Ayuwoki was producing a sometimes blinding glow. At first I thought this was intentional since his eyes are now white/pale, however when I entered chapter 3 and the glow was gone, I came to the conclusion it's a bug.

[h1]Suggestions:[/h1]   

- Add another camera angle right by the fire in the hallway of chapter 2 to show the Ayuwoki in the fire (Like the previous game) and provide context to why he is then heard running and breaking a door.   

- In chapter 3 the hallway at the beginning of the train tracks is impossible to judge where he is without heading forwards and dying from him sneaking up, since the camera placement is where you hear audio. I'd also suggest you slow him down a bit more, as trying to sprint down that channel can be deadly 90% of the time.   

-  His AI is definitely different and sometimes not in a good way. My first suggestion is to do with the doors, specifically how instead of breaking every door he sees, he should break it if he hears something from inside. Every now and then I think he should break down a door, but it does become very jarring seeing a camera on him 3 times in a sequence of 0.5 seconds.   

- Another suggestion for his AI would be to make him wander more instead of camping the areas the player is at. This in particular is an issue in Chapter 3, and is what had made my progress near impossible. I think if he was told to wander off into another area and then come back, his AI would be more enjoyable and scary when he comes running round the corner after building a false sense of security.   

- Controller support is almost perfect but is a bit off. When holding the run button it opens the inventory which stops you dead in your tracks. Meaning if he starts chasing you, you can't run and basically surrender yourself to him.   

- When it comes to selecting item choices, (Pick it up y/n) I would suggest making the choice be auto selected and switch between yes and no, instead of dragging a circle around until it selects what you want. This suggestion goes towards other UI elements also.   

- A final suggestion so far would be to make the bedroom on fire in chapter 1 less noisy so you are aware of where the Ayuwoki is!!

[hr][/hr]Anyway! I am enjoying this play style a lot more since it requires a few extra steps. However, if you implement these suggestions I believe it will make the game a lot more user friendly and enjoyable!I will edit this if I find more issues down the line!![hr][/hr]-Ashe

Layers of Fear is a psychological horror game that wraps you in a suffocating blanket of confusion, fear, and eerie beauty. You play as a painter slowly losing his mind, navigating through a constantly shifting mansion that’s as much a character as the protagonist himself. The house twists and warps around you, and with each step, you’re unsure if what you’re seeing is real or just a product of your deteriorating sanity.

The story is told through environmental details—paintings, notes, and disturbing visions—that guide you through the painter’s descent into madness. It's not about combat or action, but the tension comes from the unknown, the unpredictable nature of the environment, and the strange, unsettling occurrences that seem to chase you around every corner. And yes, there are plenty of jump scares, but the true horror lies in the atmosphere and the unraveling of the painter’s tragic past.

If you’re looking for a horror game that digs into the mind rather than just relying on monsters or gore, Layers of Fear nails it. The game doesn’t just want to scare you; it wants to make you feel unsettled, like you’re losing your grip on reality. And, if you’re anything like me, you'll probably finish it with your heart racing and questioning if your house just moved on its own.
Creepy, with just the right amount of psychological, general, and jump scares.

I have been looking for a chill TD game for awhile and this caught my eye. It doesn't disappoint; the gameplay loop is simple, but has the right amount of depth to be really enjoyable. There is enough variety in the different paths, towers, and support blocks to keep your progressing and learning, but not too many where its overwhelming and overly complicated. You also feel like you can get a good grasp on what works best right away, which is nice.

I enjoy that you have to balance your economy, placing the path, and towers. Often what is best for one will be detrimental to another, so its all a balancing act.

The negative reviews all focus on RNG, but from all of my playthroughs I find you can minimise it if you plan ahead. Save money to get interest. Spend a bunch if your power level drops. Map out where your path needs to go so you can get towers in good spots along it. If a card doesn't match that plan, skip it. The game isn't that challenging if you do that, however I can see how easy it is too run into a brick wall if you just place without thinking.

Highly recommend to snag on sale if you want a relaxing, but still strategic TD game with a bit of rougelite progression.

This said, the game is good, and it is a very unique tower defence game for those who love the genre. The achievements are very fun to get, and I think this would make a lovely mobile game actually.

Such a nice little game with... dragons!! I love dragons and riding dragons, and the dragons in this game are honestly pretty cute. I like the way they move and the coloration of each subtype is pretty.

The controls for the dragon are nice and I was really pleasantly surprised to find the controller support was nice. The control scheme was a little awkward and sluggish primarily for the human character, but playing as the dragon is intuitive and nice. Mana (aka what you use for your breath attack) regens a little slowly, meaning fights do have a lot of kiting involved, but navigating the kiting isn't a pain so it's negligible. The dragon is so superior to the human I almost never dismounted once I could fly, only ever dropping down to open cage doors or collect quest items.

The world is a bit empty - the base gameplay loop is go to quest giver, go do quest (typically a fight of some sort), then go to next questgiver, etc. There's little camps of random enemies scattered around and I hope to find some other stuff out there. There's also a little game in the village which I was incredibly charmed by. You can speak to all the villagers, who comment on you depending on your popularity/renown - a nice little detail. It would be nice to have a few more intractables like the game scattered around - maybe a way to find wild dragons? I might've missed some stuff but I did get a sense that what I'd seen of the world was just about it. Still, it's nice and open and gives you a lot of space to ride the dragon - and I was pretty endeared to the fact that the dragon struggles to navigate forests on the ground. It makes sense!

Occasionally, I ran into a few bugs - after defeating the great pirate ship, my dragon got glitched spawning water effects around itself and wouldn't lower himself or let me dismount, but reloading the game fixed it and I didn't run into anything more gamebreaking than that. The translation could use some work but it's clear enough and communicates well what you're supposed to do, so I don't mind at all.

Definitely worth it for the price point.

CONS:
-Game is unoptimized; I can run GTA V on High @60 fps, here I need to lower it to "Good" graphics quality to get even FPS

-Camera/POV: well you can increase POV with the scroll wheel, unfortunately while flying the dragon the crosshair will be hidden by either the head or obstructed by the wings of the dragon.
-Bad collision physics: walking around town you'll know what I mean.
-Weird aiming/fire breathing: up in the sky the Arc of the fireball/breath is weird. On the ground the fire breath is hard to use point blank (when bears are trying to maul your dragon).
-Lack of AI awareness/logic: Deers will stay and be roasted by dragons. Pirates go Kamikaze style and yolo to the village and not dodge and weave.

PROS:
-Graphics: on Fantastic it is okay
-YOU RIDE DRAGONS?

Suggestions:
-For the pov just let it be a shoulder aim type of camera view. So the player can see where the reticle is while flying.
-Weird progression: Using levels to unlock other dragon is fine, but using cash is a bit weird. Use reputation instead for the dragon, and maybe a little bit of cash.
-Awkward map design- I suggest removing the random houses in the forest, and instead group them up just like the home village and scatter 2-3 in and around the forest. Having them scattered around like that is a bit weird. Then you can incorporate the reputation for different villages for the dragon. Icy village = Icy Dragon, Volcano village = Magma dragon, Village in the middle of forest = Forest dragon. And honestly having houses randomly in the forest will destroy the ecosystem of the island, resulting in animals dying out a long time ago (Just saying :P).
-Bad collision: honestly I can live with this since this will take time to smooth out.
-Clunky hand to hand: Not really needed since. Dragons go BRRRRRRRR!!!
-No stable/storage for other dragons: Yes, dragons for me are nothing but objects to be replaced when new, bigger and badder ones are available (JK!).
-Day and Night has no purpose: Have a different animal spawn, boars and foxes in the day, wolves in the night.

Conclusion:
The game is true early access, a few bugs here and there, weird clunkiness are present. The story is nothing more than a modified fetch/destroy quest. Lore is present but you need to squint your eyes for it. It is fun BUT short lived, gameplay loop is just a modified fetch/destroy quests. Ohh and have I meantion YOU RIDE DRAGONS?

It's not trying to do any one thing extremely well, but it does a lot of different things to a satisfactory standard, which is really impressive because the dev has somehow found a way to avoid the seductive but time-wasting lure of perfectionism. First of all, I want to say that I’m a big fan of everything dragon-related, so an open world game that lets you ride a dragon, take to the skies and burn your enemies caught my attention at first glance. However, while it has very good potential, there is work to be done for it to reach a great game status. For that reason, I’ve been thinking, and I wanted to share my recommendations. But before I speak further, I must note that I don’t have even the minimum idea on how to program a game, and I don’t know of the hurdles involved in making one, so if any programmer that sees what I see besides the creator(s) and wants to help (or explain to me how unfeasible these ideas might be), I encourage them to do so. 
Without further ado, let’s begin with…
•	The core mechanics: Okay so, for an RPG open world type game, I would’ve hoped for at least a minimap, an inventory system, and something like a skill tree or a skill point system, where you get to choose your attributes (like the good ’ol Bethesda games). So instead of having some options to your arsenal, you can only carry a sword/axe and a shield, and your gold, which is the only item you can have. And what can you do with the gold? Buy dragons. Each dragon is a little bit more expensive (and powerful) than the one before, and you can only buy them at the Dragon House tower, but I’ll comment this more deeply in The dragons section. For starters, I would suggest adding an inventory system with slots for items, weapons, and armour (if you ask me, I like better when you can combine types of armour, but if you judge easier to start with full, uninterchangeable sets of armour like in The Witcher 3 do so) and adding nothing but three general purpose items: meat, gold, and healing mushroom; for recovering stamina and gaining xp, buy items and recovering health respectively. Then, more refined items could be added for more late purposes, like wood, iron, or materials dropped from specific enemies to craft or upgrade you, your dragons or your equipment.
•	The dragons: Now let’s talk about the dragons, the main thing in this game. If yours dies, you’re dead and stranded, and you must quit and re-enter the game for it to respawn. Now, this will make you lose any progress you might have in your current mission, forcing you to restart it. You have eight dragons in total, and all of them have a melee attack and a fireball attack. The flight controls feel synthetic, and instead of an ascend/descend system like in Ark or Minecraft, I would have gone with something of a accelerate/decelerate system (like Just Cause 3, Century: Age of Ashes, etc), I would also add a Breath attack, and reduce the total of dragons to three, but make each one with special abilities and perks that differentiate them from the rest (for example, a heavy dragon with a shielded cranium that could charge against enemies on land or air, dealing massive damage on contact, or a storm cloud dragon that could summon a lightning bolt… the possibilities are endless really), and then more dragons with different and new abilities could be released. Another thing about the dragons is that you have no option to switch between them, so I would add something like an arcane item capable of storing a dragon and releasing it to the world when you need it, giving you more variety both in combat and exploration (I will discuss further about how to do this in The story section, but if you want references, I would suggest checking the Minecraft mod named Ice and Fire and the dragon horn item). And I would rework completely the function of the Dragon House tower, because I think in its status is wasted potential; instead of simply a dragon shop, that in my opinion ruins the whole dragon trainer thing, how about a dragon item shop? In it, you could buy new saddles with different attributes, weapons (which I will discuss in The enemies/combat section) and magic items for you and your dragons. It could serve as a sort of base or dragon barn, where you could leave the dragons safe from the dangers of the world, store resources, and prepare for the missions. It could even serve as a hub for other players looking to join you in your adventures! And now, the most important thing, how to get new dragons? There are many possible ways: one would be incubating a dragon egg (that could be stole from dragon lairs or given by one after defeating it in combat), or it could be by defeating a dragon while NOT riding a dragon (for proving strength for example). Anyways, if you must add only one thing to the dragons, please make something like a dash in the air or something to gain speed apart from diving.
•	The world: The world is… weird to say the least. In the map there are three main places: your village, the Dragon House, and the Dark rider castle. The rest of the map is divided into two sections, one is either several villages with few distance between them or a city with houses very separated between them; and the other is just plain forest, with a few enemy camps. In this matter I suggest to at least organize the villages, clarify factions and give a recognizable name to the main village, then, I would add verticality, a few more mountains and ravines, since the flying-feeling is so important in a dragon riding game. The day/night cycle is way too fast, and the moon is non-existent, which gives away the passing of time at night. Then, when the map is more organized and less confusing, a second, bigger island could be added, leaving the first one as a sort of tutorial, with the Dark Rider being the tutorial boss.

I recently had the pleasure of immersing myself in the captivating world of On the Dragon Wings, and I must say, it was an exhilarating experience. As a fan of RPG games, I was drawn to the game's unique premise centered around Bruce, a young boy on a quest to save his father. What truly impressed me was the level of realism infused into the game. The lush forest environments were beautifully crafted, each tree and blade of grass rendered with meticulous attention to detail. The dragon itself was awe-inspiring, with its majestic wings and intricately designed scales. The developers truly managed to create a visually stunning world that pulled me in from the moment I started playing.

But it wasn't just the visuals that kept me hooked; the gameplay mechanics were equally engrossing. Navigating through the forest, solving puzzles, and battling foes alongside the dragon companion felt seamless and intuitive. The controls were responsive, allowing for precise movements and engaging combat sequences. The progression system was well-balanced, providing a sense of growth as Bruce became stronger and more skilled in his quest to rescue his father.

The storyline was compelling, and I found myself genuinely invested in Bruce's journey. The emotional depth of his character was portrayed excellently, and I couldn't help but empathize with his determination and courage. The narrative twists and turns kept me on the edge of my seat, always eager to discover what lay ahead.

I must admit, I was so captivated by On the Dragon Wings that I found it difficult to tear myself away from the game. The hours flew by as I immersed myself in its enchanting world, eagerly completing each task and unlocking new areas. It's a testament to the game's quality that I eagerly await the release of new updates and features. I have no doubt that the addition of these enhancements will elevate the already outstanding gameplay to new heights.

In conclusion, On the Dragon Wings is a must-play for any RPG enthusiast. Its compelling storyline, breathtaking visuals, and immersive gameplay make for an unforgettable gaming experience. I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone seeking an adventure that will leave them yearning for more. Embark on this journey with Bruce and his dragon companion, and get ready to be whisked away on the wings of an extraordinary adventure.

This is the kind of gaming experience you can only really get through indie game developers. It's a labor of love, a unique experience that gives you a fresh and different feel which is what indie developers excel at. Highly enjoyable experience quite unlike any other game you've played and not made to the same old formula you tend to see in the mainstream where they won't take risks. Lot of potential here. You'll get served up the big draw to this game pretty quick in the current state, which is cool if you want to jump in and be a MIGHTY DRAGON RIDER asap!

The developer is very good at responding to gaming issues, suggestions and comments on the forum and I've seen fixes appear for reported issues quickly as a result. A good sign and is a win-win for player and developer. There's on-foot segments with sword and axe/sword/etc. combat and flying combat against ground and sky targets. The game comes with a nice tutorial for the EA duration that will do a good job at holding your hand in an unobtrusive way to make sure you know how to fly around the island and do all the basic stuff at the start.

There's a combination of useful quest markers to let you get around to where you are meant to be and a rather useful "return to home" fast travel button that makes sure you can cut out zero-risk travel time heading home after a quest is done. You don't have to use it as it is fun to fly around with the dragon and blast randomly at bears or soldiers for the XP...but it's nice for those who want to speed things up or get lost before they learn the layout of the map. There are times when the point of a mission is to find something and then you won't get the quest marker spoiling it for you, which is a nice balance. 

The difficulty is not high currently, so it's a good time to jump in, try it out and give feed back to the developer if you want to help shape how this game changes.

Without having seen all the endings (but at least the major ones that involve [spoiler]sacrificing yourself or Mollie and either sticking with it or backing out[/spoiler]), I really enjoyed this. I'm not sure I want to see any other endings, though, even for completion, as the former two were difficult enough, to say nothing of the latter (unthinkable!). So, it's probably going to make you cry if you're given to that, as it's majorly bittersweet in most aspects, made more so in how relatable I think most people will find the characters. However, unlike many narrative-heavy games, it earns those moments of joy or sadness by not having any deus ex machinas or last-minute revelations to set things right or wrong — just flawed people trying to make the best of a terrible situation that they aren't responsible for creating. You're given a pretty wide range of decisions — possibly a little too wide at times, as I think the number of choices could be cut down slightly — in guiding Cora through her various challenges.

But, due to the variety of choices you're given, it has high replayability. And the choices you make almost entirely feel that they lead up to a given outcome, making them feel more "real" (i.e. "you got this outcome because that's exactly what you chose"), which fortunately skirts what can often feel like nonsense logic in many VNs (i.e. "you got outcome Z because you chose A! isn't that a great twist?").

The downside to placing such a narrative-heavy game in an RPG engine, instead of a more conventional VN engine like RenPy is that text doesn't skip nearly as quickly, and save for saves (pardon the bad pun), if you wish to see multiple endings or especially to get all achievements, you'll be watching unskippable cutscenes and credits many times over. Fortunately, the quality of writing and pacing makes it worth the minor effort in seeing how your choices affect the story. It never feels like it drags or speeds ahead without time to digest the events.

Speaking of effort, the one real negative I have to give it is the lack of controller support. It's simple enough to re-map controls to make it compatible, but you shouldn't have to. The controls are dead-simple: Accept/Interact, Back, Pause, and move. The B button is already recognized as Back, so I'm not sure why A isn't recognized as Accept/Interact. A relatively small downside, but it's more effort on all players to map controls than for the developer to just support controllers from the start.

On the visuals, the engine is definitely put to good use with lazily moving cloud shadows outdoors, dust motes, dynamic lighting and weather effects, blowing leaves, and foley to match. The tilesets and sprites are pretty much all recognizable at first glance, and don't detract from the gravitas of the story playing out amongst them. However, I did find it a little hard to believe that the inside of Cora's house is as big as it is given how tiny the exterior is. Perhaps it's a House of Leaves situation that is just never pointed out. I'll let it slide, as realism isn't the focus here anyway.

The voiced partial dialogue ("so...", "um...", affirmatives and negatives, etc.) is delivered well, and during a later scene [spoiler]at their last supper when they're crying together after a heated conversation over what to do[/spoiler], quite uncomfortable in the best way. It'd be amazing to play through a fully-voiced version, but also more difficult to experience, I'm sure.

I'm looking forward to playing more titles from this developer, although I think a more typical VN format would serve the story, and how it's experienced, a bit more. The times the RPG movement is utilized for gameplay are very few, although due to the aforementioned quality of visuals, there is a certain nostalgic cuteness to a lot of it. If you're a yuri fan, this is a (bittersweet) must-play, and the bitter is relatively tame compared to other titles I've played (Symbiotic Love, for instance). However, due to the aforementioned wealth of options, I'd say it's a definite ought-to-play for just about any fan of narrative-focused games with fully-realized, humanistic characters who aren't so much tripped up by external circumstances as by their reaction to them.

Mindware continues to revive old, somewhat obscure Japanese indie titles, and bringing awareness to their existence.
Not content with a mere re-release, they usually do their own take on these games, keeping the old spirit and original gameplay mechanics, while adding lots of new content, and the quality of life features one expects from a recent title.

Uootoy 3671 may be their best release yet.
The game is a charming and addictive puzzle platformer, where users must use their creativity to beat the extensive amount of levels available. This is the sort of game where you aren't tied to one solution, you truly have free reign in finding various ways (some surely not even expected by the developers) to reach the goal.

Besides the wonderful retro pixel art presentation, 3 soundtrack variants (one by the great Junko Ozawa), and a very generous amount of content (200+ stages, a number that keeps on growing, with additional stage packs being released), the game has a very easy to use stage editor, which is sure to extend the life of the game, and to pick the curiosity of gamers who enjoy exercising their creativity by doing their own stages.

All in all, Uootoy 3671 is surely the most accessible and polished game Mindware released so far, and an easy recommendation to those who enjoy puzzle games, or retro platformers that test your brain, and not only your reflexes.
Filled to the brim with challenging well designed levels, tight responsive controls, an excellent soundtrack and a level editor so the fun doesn't end. It's peak arcade styled puzzle action.

I'm a fan of Mindware games generally, and have been waiting for this one for a while. It's proving different and interesting.

Not having played the original Uootoy I had assumed it would be somewhat like Solomon's Key or Lode Runner, which on some level it is, but it actually plays like a more cerebral MegaMan/Rockman due to the platforming elements and need to evade surprising projectiles. The level design has, so far, been really good. It's old school - you die, a lot, but with that comes more satisfaction at beating it. 

Mindware has a talent for updating 8 bit graphics. Here rather than arcade mania (like in Alien Field) it's slower and more detailed, which suits the game perfectly. This is how we imagined those home computer games of the 80s to be.

This is probably the Mindware game with the widest appeal. It's also very good, and deserves to get that bigger audience. We should all hope to be real penguins.

A thoroughly enjoyable sokoban puzzler. Polyemisokos utilizes its mechanics in interesting ways and has some tricky levels. 

Basic mechanics:
You control the green square(s). Your goal is to move a green square to a blue square. Pink and cyan squares can be pushed, but will merge into larger shapes when pushed next to squares of their own color. When a block is pushed into a red square, both the red square and the block pushed into it disappear. Yellow squares are "sticky". 

The difficulty curve feels about right. It's worth noting that the game has a significant amount of levels that are not puzzles and can be solved instantly; they instead provide screens with demonstrations of concepts that seem to hint toward hidden messages within the game. I haven't been able to figure out if these screens are set dressing or not, but the store description does claim that the game has "many more secret things". Ignoring non-puzzle screens, the game has closer to 70 puzzles than the 100 mentioned in the store description.

Worth a buy.

This is one of the most innovative nature walking simulators in VR. It has procedurally generated forests which are infinite. Every other "walk in the woods" app that I have played has had an artificial boundary, this app has removed that boundary. You can get lost in the woods. This app has made the dream of the Star Trek holodeck a reality.

Currently, you only have the forest seed. However, there is an almost infinite variation to the forest with different topography (elevations) and vegetation. There are many different tree species and sizes, along with different grass & shrubs, rocks, mushrooms, branches, and even floating pollen & falling leaves. 

Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting an average of 89 fps. You do have full locomotion and snap turning only. I did not experience any serious issues or bugs, however, I did see some graphical glitches. Those graphical glitches included some pop-in, some jaggies in the distance on the edge of objects (poor anti-aliasing?), & a weird glowing white line on the ground.

Despite the issues, walking through the forest was the one of the most immersive experiences I have ever had in VR. I got lost in the woods. I have never experienced that before in VR. While this isn't the best looking or sounding VR relaxation app / nature walking sim, it looks & sounds realistic enough to be totally immersed. 

[b]Rate 9/10. I paid only $2 USD on the steam release sale, turns out this is one of the most innovative apps in VR.[/b]

After spending dozens of hours playing slay the spire, monster train, across the obelisk, vault of the void etc, I have enjoyed seeing how was of my most played genres has continued to evolve. There are many deckbuilder roguelike games out there and the ones mentioned above all put a spin on the traditional formula. There are also a lot of low effort slay the spire clones with a different coat of paint and I can tell you right off of the bat that this is not one of them.

The immediate draw for me and probably you as well was the artwork and animations that are truly unparalleled in this genre. Nothing else really comes close in terms of the presentation and the animation and sound design combining to make a turn based card game feel like each move really has weight and impact. Instead of just the excitement of having a big damage number pop up, you get rewarded with visceral attack animations as well. 

Of course none of this would really matter if the actual gameplay was not engaging or unique. Thankfully that is absolutely not the case here. One thing I have to stress however, is that this game is not a deckbuilder or at least not in the sense that picking what cards to add or remove is equally or even more important than the order you play them in as is the case with many of it's peers. You can add and remove cards from your deck but rather than focusing a build around what cards you have, BTLH emphasizes choosing weapons and artifacts which give passive bonuses to the cards that are already in your deck and many of which drastically change the way you play. 

The game features a combo system where the basic actions you will start each run with, a weapon card that changes depending on what weapon you have equipped, speed strength and pierce cards. 

Alone, a single strength card will ad a flat amount of damage, a single defense card adding a flat amount of damage reduction and so on, but in combination two pierce cards and a strength card will also add the combo effect of adding bleed stacks in addition to  raising the level of that strength card so the next time it is played it will be more powerful. You will start every run with a deck composed of these basic actions and will also end most runs with  a similar deck composition. That might sound like it would lead to a lot of repetitive gameplay, but when making smart decisions about weapons and artifacts you take or leave behind you will significantly alter the interactions those basic cards have with one another and even open up new combinations of cards like strength and speed which do not have any combination benefits if used in  a turn normally.

The biggest game changers are when you equip a legendary weapon which has unlockable nodes like a talent tree that can completely change your approach to combat. For example a weapon that makes weapon cards combine with strength to give you a defense bonus may encourage you to drop defense cards completely in favor of more strength and weapon cards for easier access to those combos that culminate in powerful critical hits with unique gameplay effects and awesome animations as a bonus. 

If you have played the other big names from the genre and you have not been a fan of roguelike deckbuilders before, this game will probably not change your mind, but if you are, I cannot recommend it enogugh.

The game is currently in early access and there are some bugs and unfinished tooltips but In it's current state I have highly enjoyed my time and I am really looking forward to seeing it grow on it's way to it's full release.

Also cannot stress enough how responsive and engaged the developers are in the discord. Both to feedback and addressing bug reports. If you have been burned by early access before by a dev with a promising idea that goes AWOL with maybe a sporadic update every few months, it is really encouraging to see how passionate this team is and how open they are in acknowledging feedback and their transparency so far. 

It is a roguelike so there is not the kind of meta progression that requires grinding enough hours to be able to succeed. This is much more a git gud kind of progression although you will unlock more items and weapons that can appear in your runs, codex entries that expand on the compelling narrative and a few other surprises I won't spoil. The combo system did not click for me for several runs and although I think the tutorial could be improved (which the devs have already acknowledged) once it clicked I could not put it down for an entire weekend. If you are curious I recommend stopping by the discord where there are currently both french and english channels and a very helpful and friendly community.

Although you can click through the story if you choose to see the story, and there is a skip button on it, you have to click ‘skip’ on each section. I don’t know why on these types of games there isn’t a heavier edit button on the story as even one small paragraph before each scene would suffice but they do go on so I do think it’s a great idea to offer this option. So, for a lot of people not wanting a story and just want to play HOS and puzzles they finally addressed it.

They also have added a ‘misclick penalty’ option, and a custom mode which mostly is for how quick your skip or hint is but you can also have ‘minigame locks in correct position’ option as well.

You can zoom in with a scroll or right click to have a magnifying glass. As this is a quality HOG game by a quality developer (Boomzap) there is nothing near pixel hunting even for the collectable but it helps to focus.

The collectable in these games are “?” in each HOS. When you find one it gives you ‘fun fact’ about the place in the theme of the game, here it’s Rome. There was a good bit of research that went into it and made the game a lot more interesting but what’s good if you aren’t interested in it you don’t need to find them.

Gameplay for story mode is a variety of styles of HOS. Once you have played a scene there, it is opened in unlimited mode. Unlimited has each scene with all choices of HOS (although it says there are 8 there are only 7. In the previous game there was a ‘collection’ mode which is find ‘x’ amount of same item which is missing here). These are straight list, missing vowels, find pairs, silhouette, image (which is similar to silhouette) scramble word you are looking for, riddles.

HOS - 19 different original scenes, 11 of them have both night and day options. So 30 different scenes.

Puzzles - 38 main puzzles.

Alright. [i]8/8/88 Needle AL[/i] is done and dusted. I don't know if I bought this at some point or if it was always free to play and I happened to claim it randomly, but I tried playing this previously on my Steam Deck and it was not functional, so I thought I'd give it another go on my desktop. And I'm happy(?) to report that it did in fact function fine on desktop with k/m controls. Anyway, let's dive in:

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3319130851

First off, I want to talk a little about the title itself. In numerology, this is known as [i]Repetition of 8[/i], which is when the number 8 appears multiple times. Its influence is amplified. The date 8/8/88 has four eights, which can be seen as a strong indicator of prosperity and significant positive changes. The number eight represents wealth and success, and when eights are linked together, they are known as [i]angel numbers[/i], whereby, allegedly, they are very powerful messages from your guardian angels telling you that something big is coming soon. [b]I already knew about the number eight in numerology, but I compiled the rest of this via internet searches.[/b] Now, I am very definitely not religious, nor do I give credence to the idea of angels, but this game absolutely does. However, it takes the approach that you should always be careful of what you wish for, lest you actually get the thing you were seeking. And that the positive change you were hoping for might actually be the opposite of what you were seeking.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3319130611

With that out of the way, this is not a fun game. It's actually very serious and very very dark. It features all the things you hope to never witness or experience in life. Rape, torture, pedophilia, murder, being eaten alive, watching your children die, slavery, racism, religious cults, the elite stealing everything from you, and so on. It's all in this game. [b]In fact, I would advise seriously considering this when you are deciding whether or not you would like to play this.[/b] You will not feel good after playing this. And those rewards I mentioned when talking about numerology. Those were doled out to the people in charge, who also took everything from the people who they governed/employed/enslaved. And the punishment for getting what you seek was also meted out amongst the people who had to deal with them. As such, nobody really wins (actually, one character did kind of win by managing to escape, but otherwise, not so much).

As far as the gameplay itself, the game is presented mostly via aged, filtered light photographs with random interactable objects that each advance the story in some way. You play as a brain damaged middle aged to old (this is not exactly specified) janitor who has the hots for a 12-year-old girl and finds himself alone in this town of Needle, Alabama; wondering where everybody went and wandering about trying to find the rest of the townspeople. As he triggers memories (via those random interactable objects), he slowly begins to unlock the mystery of the town. It is implied that other people did manage to leave the town, but not many. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3319130632

Anyway, that is the game. It takes about an hour and twenty minutes to complete, and you probably will wish you hadn't played it for all the sick shit that is presented within. However, the saving grace is that this game does not condone any of these activities. It functions more as a lens by which you can view what life was like in small Southern towns after the Civil War in America, and how people struggled to deal with the integration of black people and the dissolution of legal slavery. Interestingly enough, that does parallel the far-right movement in the U.S. today, where said people struggle with and rail against the integration of women, minorities, secularism, and gender identity in a world that has moved on without them. And for that reason, this game does actually have a strong message about the folly of clinging to hate and divisiveness, despite my warnings about the actual content. And there is merit in experiencing it. You just need to be aware of the incredibly dark content before deciding to do so.

I think people give this 3d platformer a lot of slack because of how cheap it is. The "overwhelming positive" average does not reflect the quality of the game. This is kind of poor, mediocre at best. Super Kiwi 64 is a game. It's a game.

if you were expecting something mind-blowing, this isn't it, but it is an entertaining side-adventure to what will likely be a short yet uneventful afternoon/evening. You'll be reminded of a bygone era of gaming with its N64-era inspired graphics, the vaguely familiar characters with cartoonishly large eyes, and, of course, a soundtrack that has no right being as good as it is on an indie title such as this (for the most part).

Super Kiwi 64 is a classic collect-a-thon, though it's very hands-off in its approach. Don't expect a guide or tutorial here. The icons are fairly straightforward, but some of the collectibles may require a bit of searching through the limited-in-scope levels. I beat the main game and the free update campaign in under an hour and a half, and there's a time trial mode tacked on too if that tickles your fancy.

It's cute. It's a fun distraction. It's so free that it's basically a rounding error on your bank account. Throw the dev some pocket change to vote with your wallet for a small indie dev. You'll be pleasantly whelmed.

"Cyber Bay" is a 2D rhythm-action roguelike game that takes place in a post-apocalyptic world infested with zombies. Players must survive in this perilous setting and eliminate artificial intelligence enemies, all while playing to the beat of the music. Here is my review of the game's most essential features.

First and foremost, the gameplay mechanics in "Cyber Bay" are incredibly engaging. The combination of rhythm-based combat and roguelike elements creates a unique and challenging experience. The ability to synchronize your actions with the music adds an extra layer of excitement and immersion.

The visuals in the game are stunning. The post-apocalyptic setting is brought to life with detailed environments, vibrant colors, and impressive character designs. The attention to detail really enhances the overall atmosphere, making each level feel distinct and captivating.

The soundtrack deserves special mention as it is truly exceptional. The music is not only catchy but also works seamlessly with the gameplay. Every beat and sound effect is perfectly timed to your actions, enhancing the rhythmic combat experience. The variety of tracks keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging, making you want to keep playing for hours.

In terms of difficulty, "Cyber Bay" strikes a good balance. The gradually increasing challenge ensures that players feel a sense of progression, while still providing a satisfying level of difficulty. The roguelike nature of the game adds an element of unpredictability, as each run presents new obstacles and opportunities.

One area that could be improved upon is the game's storyline. While the post-apocalyptic world and AI enemies are intriguing, the narrative lacks depth and fails to fully immerse the player. A more compelling and engaging storyline could have further enhanced the overall experience.

In conclusion, "Cyber Bay" is an excellent 2D rhythm-action roguelike game. Its addictive gameplay, stunning visuals, and exceptional soundtrack make for an engaging and immersive experience. While the storyline may be lacking, the core mechanics and rhythm-based combat more than make up for it. Fans of the genre and those who appreciate unique gameplay experiences will definitely find enjoyment in "Cyber Bay".

For context, I was medically deployed in hospice care during COVID-19. The events of this game are strikingly similar to my own to an extent. Everyone's experiences are certainly different, but there is an idea - the idea that these people, these stories and relationships cut short are all something worth writing about and exploring. For that, I want to commend this game for approaching something that I really haven't seen in the context of video games before. Really awesome approach.

I want to speak earnestly when I suggest that this was poorly delivered. The idea of a nurse moving from patient to patient and working with these people is fantastic, but without attention to authenticity and understanding the implications of not only the treatments but the emotional dynamics at play, it is a struggle to relate and be immersed with the situations being depicted.

For example, the first two deaths are approached abruptly, which isn't a wrong approach at all, but the way the protagonist digests what happened is jarring. In a gamey fashion, the protagonist does not reflect or add any weight to the life of the departed. The game expects the player to feel emotion when there is nothing connecting you to the people you're supposed to care about. It is even harder to care about the situations in the game when the interactions are so goofy and scenarios so bizarre. Having the 2nd patient jump out of bed only to conveniently drop dead is a jarring experience for sure. One way to make this scene more impactful and as emotional as it was intended would be to slow down the scene with introspection, use stronger, realistic dialogue or otherwise conduct itself authentically. Even simply reflecting on the scene in the future would have been fantastic. In the way it was conducted without any reflection, introspection or emotional weight, the player has less of a chance to see this scene outside of a video game and thus the immersion is lost. 

It certainly doesn't help that the player has no reason to care about the characters. Adding some sort of personalization, such as "this person reminds me of my mom" or otherwise putting meaning behind people would give you some sort of care. Vocal tics and quirky attitudes do not do this effectively, at least not by themselves.

The scenes surrounding dementia and grief, especially with regards to the first death, are exceptionally personal to me. I fully expected to be taken off guard or otherwise build a personal connection to what the game was portraying but the manner and speed in which things happened, how the protagonist acted (or did not act), felt almost insulting. 

Having lived through moments akin to what was being portrayed, I yearned to see a proper representation of the complex feelings of grief, of helplessness, of devastation and connection, especially with regards to the first scene. It made complete sense for the protagonist to be taken aback by the low oxygen saturations and diminishing vitals. It made sense for her to have to come to terms with the work environment and how novel things were. It did not, however, make sense for her to not explore her emotions and allow the weight of the moment to settle in. 

Without any emotional significance to the scenes it was simply confusing as to why she cared about any of her patients. Death in any form or exposure is a deeply personal experience, but without any personalization or emotional reaction the game struggles to convey meaning behind the events to the player.

For example, the protagonist says something along the lines of "Oh no! I am sad!" and then later goes "I remember your name! I will work harder now!" 

But what does that sadness mean? How does it manifest within the protagonist? Why is remembering the names of your patients impactful? Why should you resolve to work harder? What good is there to be done when all the good you do is lost with the people who are about to die? Does any of this even matter? 

I struggle with many of these thoughts and questions to this day. In this game I would have loved to have seen these ideas explored, or at the very least, the emotion behind this position the be better expressed to other people, but I am disappointed to be met with the same music on loop and a protagonist too animated to convey anything real.

In my personal opinion, I think this game seemed too scared to put the player in a position where they would have to feel horrible, horrible feelings. The conflict between the intent and what was actually happening was too jarring to be immersive and while I love the idea, I don't find myself able to slog through the rest of the game.

At its heart, Mage and Monsters is all about strategic army-building and watching chaotic battles unfold. Players recruit and position units while their army automatically fights off waves of enemies. The game truly shines in its strategic flexibility, allowing for a variety of playstyles.

The number of characters on screen at any given time is impressive, making fights feel dynamic and intense. Every run presents new choices, and adapting your army composition is key to overcoming challenges. Whether you prefer an aggressive brute-force approach, a defensive turtle strategy, or a ranged build, there’s plenty of room to experiment. Personally, I loved focusing on a range/defense build, which gave a great sense of control over the battlefield.

What makes the game stand out is how adaptable each run is to different playstyles. Whether you prefer ranged attacks, defensive setups, or aggressive strategies, the game allows you to tailor your army accordingly. Personally, I loved focusing on a range/defense build, and it felt incredibly rewarding to see my army thrive.

There’s no sugarcoating it—the presentation is not great. The UI is very basic, and the visuals lack a strong art direction, which can make the game feel a little uninspiring at times. However, the music is surprisingly good and helps enhance the atmosphere.

Despite its lackluster presentation, Mage and Monsters is a solid autobattler that offers engaging and flexible gameplay. It might not be a game you sink dozens of hours into, but for a few solid sessions, it delivers plenty of strategic fun. If you can overlook the basic visuals, you’ll find a well-designed game that’s definitely worth a try!
