CUBEGRID is a fun 3D puzzle with 80 levels to complete. The game revolves round a small cube that interacts with various tiles on the floor and other obstacles as the game progresses. it is simple to learn but maintains a challenging yet achieve-able list of mechanics that gets harder as the game progresses. Each level is setup to be completed within the minimum amount of moves and although it is quite easy to complete every level (most of the time by accident), several play-throughs will be required to perfect each puzzle the game has to offer. 

The music and colour scheme of the game is very ambient and the player can easily lose an hour or two puzzling through each challenge seamlessly whilst relaxing in the evening. I do feel however as the levels progress, the developers could add a few more background tracks to give the player a more deeper feeling of progression, the final level might also provide some feedback or something significant to congratulate the payer for "beating the game" but instead are sent back to the first level as if nothing happened. 

For the most part, the movement and controls were very smooth however it had come to my attention that if I clicked to fast on my arrow keys then the movement wouldn't register and I would come to a halt. This is a very minor detail but it did break the pace of the game on the first play through. (This however might not be an issue on the second time round when I will attempt to reduce my moves per level to obtain three stars. All of the menus are clean and match the overall theme of the game. 

Overall, this is a very clean project and a lovely few hours of game play potentially for the price and definitely a worthwhile purchase for someone looking for a simple game to burn some time or relax in the evening. 

__Suggestions and opinions__

- After the player has the ability to purchase a 'skin' from the shop, notify them and let them change thus adding another layer to the first playthrough. I wasn't aware it was possible to purchase a skin until I had completed the game. 

- Make levels larger, I know this is the first iteration of the game, however the limited space to move means that the overall difficulty of the game is significantly reduced. I would say more than half of the levels I completed through sheer luck which kind of ruined my experience when it became such a recurring situation.

- Add a better loop for the backing track so that the player doesn't hear the abrupt STOP and START of the music which breaks the immersion briefly. 

- Although It's very expensive to do so, this game would be a great mobile release!

I have included a screenshots and posted it to the community hub that shows you one of the examples, in my play through I encountered this BUG around 6 times. Game has two big things going for it. 
The first is how well it can switch up from hilarity to horror. One moment, you're cruising down a dark hallway, laughing away with your buds because the animations look a bit silly or something. Then your buddy dies and suddenly the dark hallway is so much darker, your anxiety shoots through the roof because the (incredible) soundscape made a noise you didn't expect. 

The second is this game is a cinematic moment generator. Perhaps you turn a corner expecting to see something and nothing is there, then you turn back the way you were facing originally and BAM, monster. Or maybe you're with an ally and they heard a noise. They go down the hall to check it out before [i]something[/i] kills them offscreen, their screams being cut off midway through. 

The gameplay loop is simple, which occasionally leaves you wanting a bit more to do, and the maps can feel a bit stale after a while. With that being said, this is still a bargain for what you get out of it.

Got hooked on this immediately and cruised to the highest difficulty level in the game. I am currently running the gauntlet to get all the achievements. Here are my overall thoughts:

Pros:

- It's a fantastic survivors-like that relies on a lot of RNG to keep the gameplay loop engaging (this is also a bad thing that I will elaborate on).
- The art style is refreshing and I love the muted color palette.
- HUGE variety of characters and weapons on top of a lot of permanent upgrades to cycle between and upgrade trees to experiment with. Plenty of different builds to play with.

Cons:

- Once you get to Darkness 15 (highest difficulty) it becomes clear how much the game relies on good RNG. At this point in the game your XP gain is decreased and one of your upgrade options is eliminated everytime you level up, greatly limiting your flexibility if you're going for a specific build. On top of this, each character gets 3 character-specific upgrades each run and a choice of 1 of 3 gun upgrades. Unlike the gun upgrades the character upgrades are completely random and can immediately kill a run if you get a bad one right off the bat. A lot of the time the only way a character can scale their damage fast enough to keep killing enemies and racking up XP is to get their strongest upgrade from the first boss since your build will heavily rely on that buff. If all of the character upgrades were equally powerful and the one you received first determined how to play the rest of the run then it wouldn't be an issue. But as it stands the game does not rely on your skill or knowledge to get you through a run past a certain point and you will find yourself at the mercy of RNG more than you would like. If the game had a banish feature like Vampire Survivors to lock off useless upgrade trees or let you choose your character upgrades the problem would be solved. Again, I've only noticed this problem at Darkness 15 since you need to complete it with every character and weapon for 100% but the problem realistically probably starts happening around Darkness 11-12.
- If you're playing with a summon-heavy character and the screen is filled with a lot of summons it becomes visually confusing to distinguish what are enemies and what are your summons since they are the same color most of the time. This is the only time the art style has been a hindrance to the gameplay, personally, but I imagine everyone will have a different reaction to the repetitive visual stimuli.
- The different maps are nice but the starting one is the only map that doesn't have a boundary so once you complete the other 2 to unlock their characters there's really no point in going back to play them again (unless you like the variety in the enemy types).

Overall, if you plan on 100%-ing the game be prepared to get frustrated and lose a lot of time on dead runs. But if you're looking for a bullet heaven/survivors-like game to play casually then you should have a lot of fun with this.

Before I get to the review, I actually got all the achievements in the game which requires beating the last difficulty with every character and weapon, so I'm pretty sure I am knowledgeable enough to say this game is not that good.

The main issue with 20MTD: Despite runs lasting 20 minutes, you only really get to have fun in the last 4 minutes which is when the game truly embraces its survivor-like essence at max capacity.

Let's get the positives out of the way, because I don't have much comments on these:

+Cool pixel art and character designs if you like tits. The limited color palette gives it enough identity
+Decent amount of upgrades and build variety
+The music is quite good

Everything else, and why this game doesn't work:

20 Minutes Till Dawn takes inspiration from Vampire Survivors in that it is a survivor-roguelike where all you have to do is level up and see shit blow up on the screen, but here the game has a focus on difficulty and balancing while aiming and shooting your starter weapon manually. At first this gives a feeling of participation in the outcome of the run unlike VS where everything happens on auto, but eventually it becomes a pain to hold down LMB for the entire 20 minutes and only drop it between reloads which don't happen so often. This is also worsened by the game's auto aim feature, which only blatantly shows manual aiming isn't a necessity.

The balancing and difficulty aspect are pretty much a joke and only slow down the game. Every upgrade path has a gimmick of focusing exclusively on its effectiveness at the cost of other upgrades. For example, usual summon bonuses reduce bullet damage, and hp bonuses usually reduce dodge chance. I get that the game wants to be balanced and feel difficult, because let's be honest if you know what you are doing the game isn't hard at all, but the real difficulty is only relevant when you first start playing because you still don't know how the characters, weapons and upgrades work, so everything feels new and confusing, but when you learn the mechanics and get to darkness 15, which is when the "real game" truly begins, the fake difficulty is pretty obvious:

Dying almost NEVER feels your fault. The limited palette makes it hard to distinguish your attacks from enemies', which isn't present in the mobile port of the game where you can purchase colors for your bullets. Also, for some reason the mobile version (which is free) has more content than the PC version, where the glossary of upgrade paths is missing. Back to the point, a bad run can usually be blamed at bad level up rng. The difficulty is only present in a) how much time it takes to get the missing peace of your build, and b) actually getting the upgrade choices relevant to your build. To actually start feeling powerful you need almost perfect upgrade choices that truly benefit your build, otherwise spreading upgrades between different damage sources will result in your dps being dogshit and getting overwhelmed before taking control of your run. The gimmick of increasing a damage source at the cost of others becomes extremely annoying when you get upgrades that scale with multiple damage sources, because it remarks another problem with the upgrades: Synergies/Masteries.

When you unlock two to three specific upgrades from their path, Synergies can appear as choices when you level up, these are usually what you pursue as early as possible in the run. Because leveling up is such a chore and the choices are so random, sometimes you spend an entire run without even getting a Synergy even if you take all the steps, so you never feel like your build is truly complete.

Just to name a few, some of the upgrades and balancing choices in the game make no sense and sometimes harm other upgrades completely:

1. Smite (damage surrounding enemies after shooting your last ammo) is by far the worst upgrade in the game, with bad damage, no scaling with significant damage sources other than max HP and a trigger condition that can only be exploited if you sacrifice the potential of the better and easier gun-related upgrades. One of the most common build archetypes in this game is the unlimited ammo builds which synergize with pretty much everything, and Smite goes against that.

2. Tomes, which drop from bosses, always sacrifice a stat to increase another, which does a risk vs reward play that always hurts your build for the sake of making the game feel balanced. The Tome of Stillness can actually disable one of your upgrades by capping walk speed while shooting at 0, basically meaning you can waste an upgrade for nothing.

3. The Tome of Might, which increases HP and damage with the more max HP, CAN'T DROP if you are playing as Diamond, the character whose whole gimmick is having a lot of HP.

4. Almost any type of build is completely outclassed by summon builds. Summons are so busted they can carry you without using your gun, so the game basically plays itself.

5. In higher difficulties the rate at which you level up slows down drastically, making each upgrade very important. More often than it should, the upgrade choices you get don't synergize with anything you are trying to work with and practically feel like a wasted level, making it even harder to get Synergies.

The last one is a common issue that's the whole reason the last 4 minutes, when enemies start spawning like crazy and your build is the strongest it gets, are the only good part of each run: because the game wants to be balanced and doesn't let you abuse broken builds, you are always in one of two situations: you either get overwhelmed because your dps can't keep up with enemy spawns, or you miraculously got the best upgrade paths and enemies don't spawn fast enough to make your build feel strong and get you more upgrades (picking up xp is the most boring loop in the game if you don't get the Magnetism upgrade early).

I didn't expect the review to get this long, so I'll wrap it up briefly: I don't hate this game, I actually did enjoy my time playing it because those last 4 minutes of every run are everything you want the game to be, and it does deliver, even if it's just for a measly 20% of the playtime, making it a dry 7/10 if the other issues aren't so heavy for you. The game is still getting updates and the next patch will overhaul most upgrade systems so I am very excited to see if it changes my opinion on this game.

In regards of everything else, just play Vampire Survivors, it stomps this game and doesn't limit the brokenness of a build to the last 4 minutes of a run. If you want to get this game only to unlock all the achievements, here are some tips to get them fast:

+Dasher is the best character in the game. Every 10 seconds you gain immunity, great damage and higher movement speed, and she works great with summons. If you are struggling with a weapon, just play dasher

+The Flame Cannon should only be used with Scarlett, otherwise your dps will be shit

+The Water Gun and Crossbow are the worst weapons in the game, cheese them with Dasher

+Ethereal, Blessing and Body and Soul are the best Runes, anything else you pick doesn't really matter because Soul Hearts in general are busted as hell and scale with everything (still get the pickup range rune)

+If you get the Dragon Egg early, choose it, the upgrades in its path increase its stats every 60 seconds even if it hasn't hatched yet so the dragon carries when you get more summon bonuses

+Frostbite reduces bosses' max hp by 1% with each freeze effect

From the game's list of key features

"Precise Control: Directional aim and active firing delivers a methodical battle system"

You can press Space in the game and just have it play the exact same as any other survivor-like. Maybe this isn't the case for some weapons, but having auto-aim is obviously far more optimal when the game gets to a level where the game starts spawning massive hordes.

Within a run, haven't seen any enemies that meaningfully interact with either precision aim or movement, even the Vampire Survivors mini-game in Dota 2 was more involved in terms of action element.

Updog is a very cute game with a simple premise - keep your raft going up and have fun doing it. Hop from cloud to cloud and collect the necessary balloons and crates to do so. That simple premise, combined with the wacky physics puzzle-esque aspect of it really appeals to me.

 That said, it is not without its own issues, which is to be expected from a small team's first game. The first thing one might notice is that it's a very floaty game as far as controls go; I've been told this isn't as much of or an issue at all if you go at it with mouse and keyboard, I've been playing with a controller myself. Secondly, it is a tad buggy from time to time, occasionally you might notice a crate spawning inside of a cloud due to the way the map generates, which isn't a big deal but is certainly notable. In addition, it may feel a little opaque at first, with the control scheme not being described to the player outside of the options menu. I do not find that too much of an issue due to the simple control scheme, I picked it up very quickly within one or two attempts.

All in all, despite some rough edges, Updog has a lot of charm and a simple yet fun gameplay loop. Give it a try, it's definitely worth a look!

Mythos is a Diablo like game, that was developed by one or some of the creators of Torchlight, before they went to work on the said game project. This game was built initially to be a mmorpg, but this version was modified to be playable on single player.

To begin with, the game has partial english translation, so part of the game is still in korean. The lack of translation can end up affecting quests, from their texts to objective display, and also classes, including the description of what their skill does. Due to the game not having any kind of translation patch or anything, can be quite troublesome to figure out what something does, or what a quest want you to do.

Due to the game being made to be a mmorpg, it is filled with quests asking you to go do something. That's the primary source of gold and experience in the game, unless you want to grind. Some of the quest texts, like mentioned above, are untranslated, so it can be hard to figure out the objective. Still, this game was made as an mmorpg, so one can try figuring out how to complete the objective on trial and error. Either the objective is acquired by killing monsters on the field, either by destroying rocks or plants on the field, or the objective is in a dungeon (You'll see a ? next to the icon of the dungeon, if any quest objective is in it).

The game features fields, with a few mobs that spawn on it, lots of npcs that will give you quests as they unlock, and a portal where you can select the dungeons on the field. Each dungeon has its level range, monsters, and also may offer loot. Dungeons that are somewhat more complex (has multiple floors), will also feature a locked chest at the end, that will give you lots of loot upon opening.

Beside quests, the main source of gold in the game can be acquired by dismantling items. To unlock the button of dismantling items, you have to go to the airship, and take it to Heaven island, then do part of the Crafting system quest line. After a certain step, a dismantling button will appear on your inventory, and you'll be able to destroy equipments for materials.
The reason why dismantling the equipment is necessary, is because not only equipments takes multiple inventory slots (like in Diablo), but also the equipments only sell for 1 copper on the store, regardless of rarity and level. Meanwhile, the materials sells for more and stacks.

As a diablo like, the gameplay is actually decent. You can find equipments by killing monsters, you can customize your character build, and there's lots of dungeons you can explore. Beside there's a Stamina counter on the game, the value of it is set really high so you can do dungeon as much as you want. And there's also a button above the minimap which allows you to reset dungeons, so you can keep playing them again.

And as mentioned above, the game features a crafting system. The crafting system seems nice, and seems to be able to make quite good gear out of it but... I have no idea where to get some of the materials. Like, I learned a Level 1 Musket recipe, and I have no idea where to get the wood necessary to craft it.

The equipment system reminds a lot of Torchlight, but I kind of miss the level requirement that Torchlight has.
Here, the equipments have stats requirement to allow you to use them. If you don't meet the requirement, you'll need to get the stats required through placing points on it on your build, or by getting gear that increases the stat.
At least on Torchlight, there was a level requirement, which was an extra requirement you could meet to be able to equip the item, so if you passed the level requirement, you don't need the stat requirement to equip it, beside, of course, passing the stat requirement means you equip the item earlier.

Another thing I don't like about this game though, is how some skills requires certain weapon types. For example, I can't use certain skills with my pyromancer character, because they require "Pyromancer Weapons", while my Pyromancer uses guns. I can understand if a melee swipe requires a Melee Weapon, but restricting certain spells to weapon type isn't cool, even more if it's skills to hurl bolts at an enemy.
It's also another thing that was done better on Torchlight, where skills aren't as restrictive of weapon you can use.

So, the game is fine, and might be okay for the price, but I can't recommend for those specific reasons:
* The game could have got a better english translation. I have no idea why this game got partial translation, even more since it rebooted on the west twice by english mmorpg publishers. And I doubt the game changed much from then.
* Probably asking too much, but multiplayer option would be nice. Being able to play with friends could be interesting. But I don't think the early game would be that interesting to play in multiplayer.
* Maybe turn available on the game stores some cash shop items. I believe the game had cosmetics and stuff that one could play with.

I kinda wish somehow that I had spent the money invested on this on better games though.
And if you want a fun Diablo like game that you can also only play solo, maybe better get Torchlight instead.

Double Dragon is one of my favourite franchises from my childhood. I had the first game on NES, the Battletoads crossover on the SNES, and then Neon many years later on Steam. I'm not BIG big fan, but big enough to appreciate that the franchise has continued and gotten this new iteration.

First of all, the character selection is massive in this game, and each character plays very differently from the last. Then second of all, even though there's only four main levels, the order in which you choose approach them changes their length. So whatever you choose as your first level will only have one sector, then the second will have two, and so and so forth.

Another thing I really love about this game is how much it rewards kiting the enemies together for a big combo. If you can kill them all with a big special move, you get awarded varying levels of food that you keep lying around for health pick ups if you so choose, or pick them up for extra cash. And you're gonna WANT a lot of cash.

For each sector and level you complete, you'll have the opportunity to choose different upgrades for your characters' stats, attack, and tagging properties, and you'll want to have a lot of money on hand for potential revivals. Every time I think the game is too easy, I get challenged with very tough terrain with equally tough enemies to challenge my sense of positioning and comboing. You can get away with button mashing in earlier stages, but later on, you really need to know what you're doing.

There's more than enough unique enemy types that all have different attack patterns and behaviours, and any of the 13 playable characters have strengths and weaknesses against each of them. You'll want to be able to take them all out in the biggest cluster you can because a big crowd could easily overwhelm you.

Anyways, the name of the game is collecting as much cash as you can by doing big combos, finishing enemies off with special attacks, and defeating the bosses with as much health left as possible. The more money you get, the more chips you can win at the end of your run that you can then trade for character, tip, art, and music unlocks in the Token Shop.

Nostalgia hits hard with Double Dragon Gaiden. Fans of the classic Beat 'Em Up franchise will feel right at home with Arc System's newest spin on the Lee Brothers saga.

- Classic enemies:
-------------------------
On top of the slew of new opponents the Lee brothers must contend with, many memorable foes from past Double Dragon games also make appearances throughout Gaiden. Iconic adversaries like Abobo, Burnov, Big Boss Willy, and even final boss Duke from Super Double Dragon are just a handful of the recognisable faces encountered in Gaiden's various modes.

Progressing in Story or Survival modes grants players tokens, which can be used to unlock these additional characters for use in Gaiden's various modes; adding incentive and replay value for repeat playthroughs. 


- Music:
-----------
Arguably one of the best features of Gaiden is the game's selection of music. Every track is a newly-composed rendition of classic iconic themes from past Dragon titles. Classics like the original Dragon arcade opening, Abobo's lair/Mission 4, and even an amazingly fleshed out arrangement of Super Double Dragon's Mission 1/Las Vegas theme. Adding a comprehensive touch, there's also new takes on tracks found in the recently-released  Double Dragon IV. 


-Graphics:
--------------
Glancing through other reviews, some players aren't fond of Gaiden's art style. To me, the super-deformed, cartoonish look of Gaiden seems reminiscent of Double Dragon's lesser-known 16-bit 90's spinoff: Combatribes. 

Characters are expressive, animated, and drawn as if they just leaped off of a Saturday morning cartoon show. It's an interesting twist from a developer who's mostly-gravitated to releasing titles from the franchise using the visuals from Double Dragon titles released twenty to thirty years ago. 


Gameplay:
--------------
Far from a typical button masher, Double Dragon Gaiden implements a level of strategy rarely-seen in a Double Dragon title. Special moves are activated with the use of an energy bar. When the bar is filled, players can unleash a character's special moves or special chain combos. Once the move has been activated, the player's energy bar is momentarily depleted.

When swarmed with larger groups of enemies, or facing the end-level bosses, players will have to be mindful of their energy bar; picking the right time to perform their special moves or combos. Take out three or more enemies with a special combo and players are rewarded with food items to help restore their health; adding a level of strategy need to win each fight.

When fully-charged, players can also use a special tag feature to switch out characters when their energy is running low. In two player co-op, the tag feature allows up to four separate characters to be controlled in Gaiden's modes. 


Replay value:
------------------

By collecting tokens via Story or Survival modes, players can use tokens to purchase extra characters, stages, music tracks and even official artwork.

To break up the monotony, players are allowed to choose different paths in story mode with each playthrough. Changing the order of which boss is faced at the end of mission 4 creates new challenges players must deal with before facing the final boss.

For example, choosing to face boss character Anubis on stages 1 to 3 will present Anubis in his regular form. Choose to face Anubis at the end of Stage 4 however, and Anubis's pyramid will contain a plethora of new booby traps before a showdown with Anubis in a giant, transformed state is activated!

It's incentives like these that make players want to challenge each boss at the end of mission 4 - replaying through story mode multiple times in the process. 


Pros:
--------
- Combo-driven battle system that rewards players for strategic thinking.
- Lots of throwbacks to the classic Double Dragon games.
- Familiar enemies and bosses from past Dragon titles.
- Tag Team features adding a new dynamic to playthroughs.
- Online Co-op capability.
- Unlockable characters, artwork, levels, and music tracks.
- Energetic soundtrack featuring redone level themes from throughout the series.
- Multiple challenges, outcomes, and an alternate ending with repeat playthroughs


Cons:
--------
- The cartoonish art style may not appeal to everyone.
- Versus mode does not offer Player vs COM match types.

Ski3 is a modern take on the classic SkiFree game, bringing back the nostalgic gameplay with very good graphics. 
The basic gameplay is very basic and offers a thrilling experience of skiing down a slope while being chased by a yeti(sometimes), all set in a visually stunning environment with a day and night cycle (and snowstorms).
Speaking of graphics, they are very polished and well-done, much better than your average first time indie game. Very immersive snowy mountain setting. 

Back on the gameplay, it is fast-paced and can get challenging, with players having to maneuver through obstacles, trying to score points and also hoping to shrug off the Yeti. Also the map seems to be infinite.
One of the standout features of Ski3 is the hardmode, which offers a very large score multiplier but also ramps up the difficulty, by having to play only during the night with a massive snowstorm to cope with. The yeti also becomes slightly faster(I think). To help with navigation during the night, you are given a lantern. Without it its impossible, so remember to press E to toggle it (i skipped trough the entry message, and didnt know, had to figure it out myself)

On the other side of the spectrum, there is also easy mode, that, from what I've seen, completley disables the yeti and makes the weather mostly mild.

Overall, Ski3 is a fun and exciting game that SkiFree fans will love. The addition of a hard mode with live scores provides a new level of challenge and replayability to the game. Highly recommend for those who love a good arcade-like skiing game, but keep in mind it is still in early access, some things may change or not be fully implement yet. From what I've seen the dev posts updates quite often.

At the moment I will rate it strong 8/10 because of some minor annoying little bugs (i.e. sometimes rarely the character can get stuck and you have to restart)

This is the BEST survival game I've ever played! Forget Subsistence, The Forest, Ark, Green Hell, or dozens of others (excepting Subnautica 1&2, which are just bada$$). This game is AMAZING. You have a story element of being on a ship with Ponce de Leon, looking for the Fountain of Youth. You get to progress along and go through that story line. You also get to learn about the natives and their story line, which adds even more to the exploration and immersion. I love that temperature and weather affect you, which is something many survival games miss. I love that there is sickness and medicine as well. In fact, this is one of the most comprehensive crafting survival games I've ever played. You even build rafts/boats and explore other islands! I've obsessively played for weeks, and still haven't done all of the things there is to do on one island group, when I suddenly discovered that there is a whole other island group, with all new things to do! In fact, it looks like there are FOUR separate island GROUPS to explore and survive in! WOW! It's not enough to harvest resources and explore vast islands to hunt, gather resources, craft and survive, you also get to explore underwater areas, harpoon large fish, fight off sharks and jellyfish, gather underwater resources, and more!

I've recently transitioned to the second island group and I'm pleasantly astonished to find that they are entirely different biomes! The first group is tropical, whereas this one is similar to the Arizona desert. Now, there's a whole different type of survival as you have to find new ways to get water without water sources, and manage the extreme temperature, so that you don't overheat and are left incapable of dragging trees to craft your survival needs. Whew! This got really hard, fast! This is the ONLY game I've ever played that has required you to learn a whole new biome and develop all new strategies to survive, even though games like 7 Days to Die and others have made the attempt to incorporate other biomes. This one really demands all new strategies as you'll seriously struggle to stay alive! If that isn't awesome enough, in the second island group, there are three main islands that are all different versions of desert life. One island is even like a full-blown sand desert, complete with winds and blowing sand! That really gives you a lot of variety and demands you develop new survival strategies. Amazing!

Another thing I love about this game is the immersion. It's 1st person, which is essential for immersion. They've thought of so much. If you get wet, you're soaked for hours and can't rest well., and might also get sick. You get burned by your own fire if you get too close. You get injured when crafting if you're tired and don't have enough light. You can't sleep in rain or windy conditions, which so many games fail to implement, breaking immersion. Your stats deplete when you sail away to different island groups. My favorite immersive detail is that, the temperature increases with the time of day and you will overheat in the height of day, but you can step into shaded areas and you won't overheat. How cool is that??

One thing I will strongly advise is, use the Advanced Settings to adjust the game to your liking. I made mine much harder. Also, once you have easy living on one island group, with your resources stockpiled, leave EVERYTHING behind and start again somewhere new. You won't say that the game is too easy. You'll be surviving by the seat of your pants!

Get this game! You won't be sorry. It was the best $15 I think I've ever spent! I can't wait for this developer to release more games like this one!

Genuine review for once because I respect the devs a lot as people and probably haven't looked forward to a game as much as this one upon hearing its announcement a year or so back.

Anyway, you can tell right from the get-go the passion that went into this. It had a simple story to tell and it told it more subtly, which I find fascinating. 

From a visual standpoint, the elements say more than enough. Polish was a priority and it shows. I wasn't following the development process itself all that closely, but I am very impressed with how the looks of the game came out, especially as a first (and indie) project. Nothing looks rushed and everything blends together extremely well. The atmosphere that is being portrayed hits hard, as I'm sure it does with most of us if the premise wasn't already obvious.

Now for the gameplay. I don't usually seek out platformers, especially given that I'm quite bad at them, but this was a great first experience out of my comfort zone. Every stage adds a new mechanic or a new layer on an already existing mechanic, and I find that type of progression very intuitive. My personal favorite mechanic that I've seen (so far) is the reactive objects, where if you jump then an object moves. It was very fun and challenging to learn the path to either avoid them, or use them to progress. Nothing got stale in this aspect and I loved experiencing a new challenge every time. I also love how the devs instinctively made speedrunning as viable as possible, giving it it's own mode and also designing the stages around that (little waiting sections). Essentially, the way the stages were designed can appeal to everyone. 

I'm still not done with the game at the time of writing this (I accidentally left the game on when I was away from home for 3 days lol), and will probably update this more when I get further, but this well exceeded my expectations. Despite my lack of experience in the platformer genre, I feel confident in saying that this is a game worth looking up to from a development standpoint. This was a great entry into my platforming experience and an excellent first project from the studio. If you take on anymore projects in the future, I very much look forward to seeing them through. ✌️

I love 2D/3D platformers (mainly those that would fall into the category of precision platformers); I went into this game hoping to find another great platformer, and Germinal did not disappoint. There are collectibles hidden throughout each stage, and they each provide engaging challenges. Each stage of the game explores different mechanics with level design, and they all work quite well. The time trial mode was rewarding and enjoyable. The harder versions of each stage were difficult but still fair. The art is wonderful, and the game sounds amazing. I do have a few nitpicks from my experience, though.
[list]
[*]While the art style is great and pleasant to look at, a few of the areas look extremely similar aside from a change in the background color.
[*]The ending of the final stage can easily be cheesed by [spoiler]avoiding the germs that start the chase sequence[/spoiler]
[*]There is a boost that can be performed by holding the hover button on the ground and jumping, but in my experience, it never felt practical to use it often since the stages were not designed around it. Trying to boost immediately after landing will often result in hovering just above the ground.
[*]During the time trial mode (in the first stage), I respawned inside the ground collider, and I was forced to reset the run (this was the only bug I had encountered, though).
[*]While the level design is mostly great, I noticed many curved or diagonal walls. Attempting to jump off of those walls will promptly result in hitting the bottom of a tile. In a game that often utilizes wall jumps to keep the player airborne, the curved walls felt pretty uncomfortable.
[*]You are not able to pause during dialog.
[/list]

Germinal is a good platformer with precise controls, an okay story and mostly good level design. The game is however held back by poor readability, somewhat janky fluid physics and suspicious hitboxes. If I could, I would give this a "sideways thumb". The game itself is decent, but there are many smaller frustrations piling up throughout the game.

The core gameplay itself is solid, and does not overstay its welcome. You have a very high jump, a fast-fall, wallslide and walljump. What makes this game unique is your stamina based abilities to hover and double jump. 

That said, the game suffers from some frustrating moments  which come from either janky gimmicks or visibility issues.

First of all, the biggest offender, the double jump. This shared the same button bind as your jump and wall-jump. With no option to re-bind the boost/double jump, you may find yourself wall-jumping when you mean to boost, and boosting when you mean to wall-jump. The walljump is very sensitive, almost like there is a magnet pulling you to the wall, which is good in most cases, but mixing these items will get you killed as stage gimmicks react differently to your boost and wall jump.

Secondly, the ceiling-climb. The game may require you to climb on the ceiling. The game will often have you climb the ceiling and jump off, often around a corner and on top of the ceiling you were just climbing on. This would be okay if it weren't from the fact that there is no "swing" mechanic to let you gain distance from the ceiling you were just climbing on. You will often find that when attempting to do this action, especially in succession, you will often time "bonk" on the ceiling and fall to your death, or you will climb too far and just fall off. I tried different distances while in a safe area, and it felt rough.

The third problem which sticks out throughout the game is poor visibility. Now, I play many different games, and I have never considered using color or visibility accessibility features in any game before this one. In the end, I decided I wanted to play the game with the default settings, but man it gets rough. There is a lvl where you have a thick, purple outline covering the border of your screen, so you can only see the middle. This "fades" into the lvl. Germs which are green look purple in this mode, and I died many times to thinking I could clean something, but they were a different kind of germ. The lvl design is also not made with this tick outline in mind, as it completely covers and hides important gameplay tiles you will need to finish the lvl. You have to do multiple leaps of faith "off screen" and randomly press the jump button hoping you found a wall, or jump off into the distance hoping the trail of germs the game is showing you will end when you reach the end of the screen. 
While the purple screen smoke is only there for a small part of the game, the game also suffers from boxes in the background sometimes looking like solid platforms, but when you try to land on them they're not, the "trash" in the party lvl sometimes blended so well into the background I could not see them while rushing through a lvl, the "pillows" that jump at you when you use water are sometimes not telegraphed, they will just hit you in the face the first time you try to complete that room like it's a "gotcha" moment. Also, the trails of flying trash have transparent smaller trash flying after it, this also looks like it is just a visual effect, but it is not. Some levels are so dark you just have to guess where to go and hope you land correctly.

You will often have to clean areas where you are landing, this sounds fine, but the jetback water feels inconsistent, especially when cleaning vertical pillars of germs.

Making a game like this, in the artstyle they chose, it cannot avoid getting compared to Celeste. Other than the graphics, the story, and it being a room-based precision platformer, it does not try to be celeste. However, with the comparisons the devs are welcoming making a game like this, I am not sure they do themselves any favours. While the game is good, it simply cannot compete with what it is undeniably going to get compared to. 

So, should you play this game? Maybe. If you are looking for a decent B-grade platformer to play over a weekend and you already played the great ones, this is for you. I enjoyed my time with it, and I am sure you will too. That said, I do not think this is for everyone. There are some rough edges, I found that the music was a mixed bag containing everything from "please turn this annoying music off" to "okay, this is quite pleasant to listen to", I did not care for any of the characters, and I found myself actively disliking the main character. 

This game is made by a small teams of devs, and they should get all the praise in the world for releasing their game in the vision they had. I hope they are successful enough so they get to continue making new experiences for others to enjoy.

Honestly, I have very mixed feelings about this game. I love it, but I hate it as well. These two worlds kept colliding for the whole duration of my playthrough. I played all of this game in one single sitting. It took 5 hours.

So, let's start by why I hate it. This game is basically a Celeste clone, with only different graphics, and some new things. I, unfortunately, couldn't get past this reality while playing Germinal. Next up, the controls. Given that Germinal is a precision platformer, good controls are necessary. The controls are clunky and sometimes don't react that well, walljumping off of sticky surfaces while holding onto them either triggers the double jump or just hover ability by accident, so game over. The movement feels off, it's like playing Super Mario on Nintendo Switch, the character needs a lot of "steering" to control them properly. This issue isn't present in Celeste, however. Madeline moves exactly as you press the keys on your keyboard/tilt your Joy-Con. This is by the way one of the reasons why I love Celeste so much, because the controls are 100% accurate.

I feel like this game was not playtested properly. There are tons of spaces with incredibly strange timing or bad camera. By "incredibly strange timing" I mean those frame perfect cycles that are everywhere in the fifth chapter. And by "bad camera" I mean places where you usually drop down and you see nothing beneath you until you actually hit an obstacle off-screen. The camera certainly needs a lot of improving.

Achievements were, for some weird reason, malfunctioning. I did not earn the achievements for comleting "Crossing the Bridge", chapter one and chapter two. While we are at it, I would also like to note that there are, according to some other player, more bugged achievements like this, to which the developer openly admitted. There is no way one could release their game if they knew major features were broken.

Last, but certainly not least, the collectible exclusive rooms has one massive flaw - usually, you only have to grab the collectible, it gets collected and then, you just are stuck there. The only way out is to either get lucky with leap of faith blind falling down, hoping you don't hit anything or just die. These really mess up the death score. I think there should be something that would return the player to the room start upon grabbing the collectibles in certain rooms.

To summarize things I like, I really liked the story, it was really dark and creepy at times, it was not like Celeste whose story was sad with funny moments at times, Germinal was incredibly dark and it was talking about a very serious problem that certainly needed some attention. One thing I like as well are the notifications when you are about to enter a room that does not allow you to go back. I wished this was a feature in the original Celeste, as I very often found the correct path by accident and missed the oppurtunity to collect the collectibles, meaning I had to go back later. I also liked the Super Mario 64 like thing in fifth chapter (jumping into paintings).

To summarize it, I had fun while playing Germinal, but, like I said, I can't get over the fact that this is basically a clone of Celeste, along with a lot of bugs and inconsistent controls. The soundtrack wasn't anything extraordinary either, it was pretty much average. The only really praisable things are the level design, which is very decent and the story, that's basically everything I can think of. I honestly think that this is a very controversial game. As a standalone game, I think this is solid. Precision platforming built around a double jump and hover mechanic that share the same meter so the game becomes about figuring out which moves to make where while also dealing with whatever platforming puzzle or obstacle lies in your way. And there's a good number of obstacles built around these mechanics, and unique level gimmicks to keep things feeling fresh. It's a fun time that can be challenging, sure, but rarely does it feel "too hard", or thereabouts.

But, also, it is literally impossible to not compare this game to Celeste, because the game is mimicking it almost to a T, to the point where it's kinda frustrating. EVERYTHING must be like celeste. The visual style? Celeste. The plot about anxiety and fear? Celeste. The level structure of linear gauntlets with optional collectibles off to the side? Celeste. The platforming design that's oft as much a puzzle game as it is a platformer? Celeste. A lot of the gimmicks even bear resemblance to gimmicks from Celeste. It's flagrant. It begs the comparison, and it's a comparison it's inevitably going to lose.

And my main frustrations with the game pretty stem from the specific aspect of Celeste it's based most of its gameplay around - stamina management. Everyone's [i]favorite[/i] part of Celeste, I'm sure. No, it really wasn't. And this game's SUPER touchy about stamina management, too. Most of the struggles I had were not because I was failing a jump or platforming challenge, rather, because I just ran short of stamina to make it through a section. Just whittled down my bar slightly too far so now I can't do that last jump input. Don't have quite enough fuel to make the hover. It feels. Bad. To fail in this way. Celeste did have [i]some[/i] stamina management puzzles but they weren't all that frequent and generally were overshadowed by the cooler, movement-based challenges. Not the case here. There's also, towards the end of the game, challenges based around spraying purple blobs, which... feels bad. Especially so with how ungodly huge the hitboxes in this game are compared to its source of inspiration - feel like I had a lot of cheap deaths due to barely clipping a hitbox here (and even sometimes touching a WALL that had a blob atop it would kill me - feels awful!)

The game also generally lacks for, like... fun momentum-based challenges. Aside from the last B-side (oh, btw, this game has Celeste B-sides because of course it does - no C-sides to be found, though, or at least I haven't found any!) you're pretty much gonna be moving at the same speed the whole way through. There [i]is[/i] a boost mechanic that I only vaguely understand how to use, but it's never required at any point in any level and the game never teaches it to you. This kinda feels more like a nitpick, but, hey, it's something I noticed.

I also feel - and forgive me for soapboxing a little, but, this is important - that the narrative is a little... improper. It's obviously something that spawned as a result of covid, but the narrative differs in that... well, the epidemic in this game ends, fairly early on even, and the rest of the game is spent making the main character look like a paranoid freak. Which, in isolation is fine... but I feel like a lot of people don't really understand that covid isn't over, that it's still infectious and ever-evolving, and that we don't fully understand the consequences of long covid yet, either - sure, maybe you survived the initial infection, but at what cost? Sure, it's not as immediately deadly as it used to be, but that doesn't mean it isn't still dangerous. I understand the game's not trying to be about that but it feels like a really bad message to send at this specific point in time, I dunno.

Also, minor nitpick, but the game entirely taking place within a house means there's not much in the way of visual variety - no particularly interesting backgrounds, hell, every room has a wallpaper background with at most some wall hangings because - again, a house. And since every other cue of its visual design is taken from Celeste, well, it's not very interesting to look at.

I dunno. I'd definitely be giving this a "meh" if steam allowed it because, like... there's no reason to play this when you could be playing Celeste or one of the many free Celeste mods (that also often tend to add their own mechanics - someone could probably make this entire game within Celeste with what that mod scene is capable of). But it's a perfectly serviceable precision platformer, and I've certainly played worse - the era of Super Meat Boy and its clones was DIRE, y'all - so I can't say I'd recommend against if it you really need that precision platformer fix. I just. Don't think there's much, like, [i]special[/i] here, just base competence. It's fine.

The simplest description for this is Celeste meets mario sunshine. That's ultimately why I got it so if that's what you want then it is definitely that.

Though with that being said, this game really is inspired by celeste. You can tell looking at it, but the level design and obstacles also feel really similar. Not inherently a negative, but depends on your feelings about that. Personally I think there are a couple design ideas from celeste they borrow that don't particularly work with the system they have. The main one I feel shows this off is they have a refill system like celeste, except this game doesn't have a dash button. it has a double jump and hover. It is used fine here but sometimes you are expected to use it to refresh a double jump quickly and it can get really finicky trying to chain double jumps between normal jumps and movement. 

Also some collisions can be annoying and sometimes I think it prioritizes the wrong actions. It almost feels like wall jumps and wall slides are considered the most important action you  can take and it will make you mess up a lot. This actually also lead to a really weird issue where the game seems to want you to go over a wall with spikes on top but it's inconsistent on if you will go over it or not. And I had issues at the last level where a jump  was on a spiky "stair" shape and I managed to get stuck on the edge. And in this game you can't recover on the same wall like in celeste.

Also the story is the other major part of this game. I didn't particularly care for it. It isn't bad or anything but I wasn't super interested in a pandemic story. Maybe when I'm farther away from the actual pandemic.

Ultimately this is a neat game with some quirks that I wish was a little less similar to celeste.

Parts of this game are excellent, particularly the basic moveset and the controls.  Having the double jump and hover work off of the same resource makes for really interesting and challenging platforming.  Other parts of this game though are pretty flawed.  To address the elephant in the room, yes this game is a bit of a Celeste clone.  Both games have similar movement mechanics and physics, effectively the same art style, similar level design, particle effects, etc.  Not to mention that both are precision platformers with an introspective story centered on mental health featuring LGBTQ characters and themes.  As long as none of that bothers you it doesn't really get in the way of the game.  Maybe with the exception of the art style, like in both games the primary environmental danger are the blobs of black mixed with a colour and they look nearly identical in Germinal as in Celeste.  My main complaint about the game unfortunately is the story, and while that is never the part of a game I gravitate to I couldn't help but feel that Germinal's story was far too much of a focus for how uninterested I was in it.  The characters all aggravated me in some way, so the game pushing me to relate to them at different times was a struggle as I found them (primarily Val and the player character) standoffish and annoying.  Overall though this is a good game, and while it is very short (if you're familiar with Celeste you will probably finish this game in 5-10 hours) I think considering how limited the market is for precision platformers that scratch the itch at all like Celeste or Super Meat Boy it's worth it.  Maybe wait for a sale.

EDIT EDIT EDIT:  I forgot to mention some quirks with the controls and movement mechanics that can be pretty infuriating.  First off (unlike Celeste), Germinal doesn't have much in the way of lee-way or Coyote-time, you double jumped while 1/100 of that platform was behind a jump-activated wall?  Try again.  Also fairly often the game will have you using particle physics to destroy obstacles which (similar to Spelunky 2's liquid physics) introduces too much indeterminacy into what should be a very cut-and-dry physics system.  Finally I would like to point out one of the largest sources of aggravation from this game, the fact that even when facing away from a wall if you press jump mid-air if you are close enough to a wall you will do a wall jump instead of a double jump.  This really felt unintuitive to me and felt limiting to how you could approach the levels and even how the developers could have designed them, though really it is something you should just get used to.

Not a bad game, especially for the price. While I normally don't really review games, I feel I should share thoughts as there doesn't seem to be a whole lot of reviews for this right now and providing some thoughts upfront, both positive and negative, may help inform those who are giving this a look.

So, this is an arcade shooter with roguelike elements, such as procedural level generation, permadeath, and random spawns of items. It also comes with a scoring system (that seems to be mostly from just killing guys, but I can't explain how it calculates it beyond that). You will mainly be running (or should I say sluggishly walking) around office rooms, scavanging for "corporate pills", weapons, and ammo for guns. Your two main weapon types are guns and melee weapons. I always favor guns, and I managed to find a 9mm, revolver, and submachine gun on my first run. They function as you would expect, and headshots deal more damage with decent audio and visual feedback. The hitboxes for the heads do seem a little wonky (particularly for the final boss), but that could purely be a subjective observation on my end. Just a note for the guns: When you come across an ammo box, it will only give ammo for the gun you are currently holding. So, if you have two guns, you will need to switch to what you want to add ammo to before picking up the box. 

It is important to note, that while this game has roguelike elements, there does not seem to be any meta progression between runs. Your progression is solely within the run, and dissipates as soon as you die. I finished a run on normal, and did not unlock anything for the next run. There is also no evidence of any meta progression anywhere else. This is just simply a clarifying point about the game mechanics, and not a positive or negative. 

Your goal is to make it to the elevator, go up a floor, and continue until you either die or beat the game. You take a corporate pill at the beginning of the run, which does some amount of healing, increases movement speed (which is sorely needed), helps to highlight some collectibles (guns, ammo boxes, pills), and perhaps provides some damage reduction (I'm unsure on that last bit, but it seems about right). Now, the catch, is that you're addicted to the pills, and you need to continuously scavenge and take pills or you will succumb to the addiction in some way. I'd tell you what the punishment is, but I never had a problem running out of pills. I was flush with both ammo and pills and was never in any danger of running out of either. Of course, this could be due to both playing on normal, as well as scavenging most/all rooms on every floor for everything. I also could have just been incredibly lucky with the drops as well. At the end of each floor, you can utilize a vending machine right by the elevator exit to buy powerups (that usually have both a benefit and a drawback) with the points you accrued for the level. It is important to note that you do not carry points from floor to floor. So, do not plan to bank on whatever points you got from one floor to the next, because you are starting over in that respect every time you progress to the next level. 

I do have critiques, of course:

1.) The movement is incredibly sluggish. If you're not taking the pill, you walk like you're walking in molasses. Even sprinting doesn't seem to do anything beyond just adding speed lines. The only way you can reliably speed up is taking the pills. While that's not inherently a bad thing, I don't think I like having such slow base movement in general. 

2.) There are some QOL things that I think would be nice. Two are the ability to rebind keys, and ability to adjust the POV. The default controls are fine for the most part, but there's a slide I didn't really use because I find shift+CTRL to be incredibly awkward. If I could rebind that, then I would probably use the slide more. As for POV, I just always like the inclusion of being able to change it. I can tolerate less-than-adequate POV's, and I'm not good at telling you what POV I'm looking at if not being told the number outright. The default POV in this game seemed alright, and I didn't personally have an issue with it. Regardless, for an FPS, a POV option is always nice. 

3.) The AI pathfinding can be quite bad. I've seen instances of running into walls and away from me, as well as being stuck in doorways, particularly if there are multiple enemies. There was also an instance or two of an enemy being able to shoot me through a wall and connecting, causing me to take damage. It was rare, though.

4.) I don't have a problem with the graphics overall. One particular oddity that I get over and over, is that when I'm holding the revolver or semi-auto machine gun, the colors are still inverted when the pill wears off for a short amount of time. Not really an issue, just an observation. I guess more my critique with graphics has to do with the procedural level generation.  What ends up happening is that you get a bunch of rooms deep, and if you like to explore like me, then you end up being unsure if you've been to a room or not when you're backtracking. It's not so much that I got lost, as they literally signpost where the elevator is through certain doorways. But, when I'm exploring, it's hard to tell if I've ransacked the room already because they seem to copy-and-paste just a few basic rooms over and over again. It's hard to landmark where you've been beyond "Okay, this is a kitchen area, this is one of two or three meeting rooms, and this was one of a dozen office cubical areas that I'm having difficulty differentiating". 

That being said, I can really excuse a lot of the critiques because this is literally a $3 game ($2.54 at time of this post). I don't expect polish for this price, just a decent experience. And, honestly, that's what I got. I got a decent experience. There are definitely tweaks that can be made (if I can advocate for anything, it would be increasing base movement). But, beyond that, I had a base amount of fun, which is why I'm giving it a recommend. Again, this is more of an informational post so people have an idea of what they're getting themselves into when looking at this game, rather than an in-depth critique (especially because I don't have lots of time on this game). I'm happy to read comments from devs or people who have more experience with game, especially on points where I'm incorrect in my observations. Happy to discuss and edit if needs be.

This paired with the fact that maps tend to be pretty low-detail and lacking any real way to tell where you've been (all the doors are open by default, corpses don't stick around) and the maps feel maze-y when they aren't one-room kill corridors.

I picked up this game because of its beautiful art style, and it didn’t disappoint. The UI is clean and cozy, and the character designs are fantastic. It’s rare to see a Western indie JRPG that nails the Japanese aesthetic as well as this one does.

The gameplay turned out to be more enjoyable than I expected. On the default difficulty, the early game feels like a classic old-school JRPG- which is slightly challenging, enough to keep you on your toes, but not frustratingly hard. As you progress, you unlock skills that let you build your characters, and the power curve feels great. By the endgame, you're wiping out enemies that gave you trouble earlier with powerful full-screen skills and magic, which is super satisfying and avoids that grindy feeling some JRPGs get when the endgame drags on.

The story is pretty decent— not groundbreaking but still solid. At first, it feels like your typical old-school JRPG setup with a few predictable moments, but there are some unexpected twists later on that bumped it up for me. Predictability isn’t always a bad thing, as some plot points here unfold naturally in the endgame without trying too hard to be shocking or convoluted, which I appreciated, as some games lose their sense of believability and verisimilitude by forcing twists. 

The real highlight for me is the characters. They’re well-written, likeable, and their struggles feel genuine and relatable. The dialogue has some JRPG cliches, but overall it feels natural. The voice acting is top-notch and really brings the emotions to life.

As for romance, I can’t speak for all the pairings, but the Shiori and Suzaku ending was really well-written and heartwarming. If you’re into romances, I’d definitely recommend experiencing it.

Overall, I’d rate the combat a 7.5. It’s not super deep but fun enough that it doesn’t feel like a chore. The story is also a 7.5 for me, with some moments that even hit an 8.0. It’s a short and enjoyable adventure at around 30 hours, so it’s definitely worth the time.

Final score: 7.5

Overall, it's still enjoyable and I'll give a score of 8/10.

It can be an intentional thing, of course, but that must be counteracted by effective tools for the player to use. You do have a flashlight, but it has a very narrow beam, if you shine it too close, it flares up brightly, and it also has a very short effective distance. This wouldn't be a problem in areas designed to be dark, but there were areas there were just too dark for no discernible, justifiable reason. The tutorial area at the very beginning was the most egregious example, with a black-and-glowing-white grid for most of the level construction, but the Distortion castle area (which is when I decided to abandon and refund the game) had that problem a lot as well.

There was also something of an artstyle dissonance. We have ultrasmooth enemy entities, blocky, angular gun models, BSP/Quake Engine/Goldsrc-inspired level design, high-fidelity lighting, and textures that can't seem to decide if they're low-res or not.

It's clear that this game was made by a "first" (Dev has one other game released) time developer. I do admire the effort, but it needed some extra work. I don't know how many worked on it, but I wouldn't be at all surprised if it was less than three guys (plus maybe a music artist).

It was a simple continuation, and that makes it a worthy successor to me. Dadish 3, however, was a bust for me. More funny interactions, recycled spritework, but now with even more boring levels and mechanics that make the game feel unbelievably sluggish. 
Most of the new mechanics are either slow versions of old mechanics with a new coat of paint, or are overused and just make every level significantly longer. Every level feels so much longer and less fun because the game isn't about precision anymore. Every level feels like it's comprised of the same waiting for this platform to move, wait for the water to rise high enough, wait for this enemy to walk away, ect, repeat. This is especially true for the sewage world, where everything is about waiting, waiting, waiting. Not to mention a distinct lack of checkpoints in many levels.
The first two Dadish games were somewhat difficult because they were precise and fast paced. This game was just difficult to sit through, because half the time, that is ALL YOU DO. Sit and wait. The splashes of color and the distinct Dadish charm can't save the lack of quick, precise, action-packed platforming.

If you liked the first two games, and you just wish you could get more, this isn't really going to itch that scratch unless you are inherently super patient. After finishing Dadish 1 & 2 I made the transition to 3.

A bit different experience this time around. The levels are significantly longer and the ramp up in difficulty was notable. The dialog segments are more wordy and the music is still top notch.

Some cons this time around. Despite longer levels, some of them were mirrored. You do your platforming on the left, unlock the right side, and do the same exact thing again. It felt a bit lazy and it came off as a weak method of extending the duration of a level for free.

Secondly, some stages were considerably longer than others, and somehow didn't have a checkpoint. Not game breaking by any means, but this leads into my 3rd issue...

If you're a 100% completion and enjoy getting all those stars, be prepared for frustration and death. There's some levels where you KNOW the star is hidden off screen in a pit somewhere, and there's no method to see the star without taking a gamble on a death or not. You'll find yourself jumping into spike pits or endless voids knowing the outcome is either death or star. Combine this with a lack of checkpoints and you're redoing a stage 4-5 times for no reason.

Despite all this, a solid entry in the series.  I would never NOT recommend it to anyone. If you played 1-2, add this to your collection.

[h1][b]Temple of Starlight[/b][/h1]
[i]Temple of Starlight[/i] is a puzzle game with minimalist and stylized graphics that heavily focuses on mixing colors to complete the puzzles.

[b]Gameplay[/b]

The core gameplay element of [i]Temple of Starlight[/i] is mixing colors by activating pillars that shine primary colors in front of them. Later on, this simple but enjoyable concept is going to get a bit more complex, which makes some of the puzzles a bit more difficult.

[b]Personal Note[/b]

As far as I’m aware, [i]Temple of Starlight[/i] was the first game that Enlit Games made and for that it’s a pretty solid game with a unique setting and gameplay idea. 

The story is easy to follow and the player can influence how the story proceeds throughout the game by making decisions which is neat and is probably enough to play through the game more than once.

Back in August or October, I played the Demo of [i]Temple of Starlight[/i] and I enjoyed it back then already but the voice acting was a bit off, which makes sense because it is the first game this studio made, but I’m glad to see that the voice acting improved since then. 

The overall art style of the game might seem very basic at first glance but the more I thought about it, the more it made sense to choose such a minimalistic and simple art style, since it doesn’t distract the player from the puzzles that heavily focus on mixing colors – so that’s honestly a good thing.

All things considered, the only thing that is somewhat negative in a very subjective way, is the length of the game. Don’t get me wrong, about two hours of playtime is decent for a puzzle game like this. [i]Temple of Starlight[/i] offers 35 levels and some Halloween themed levels too, so there is a lot to do, but I would have loved to have a handful of more levels because I genuinely enjoyed it – so take this “negative point” with a grain of salt, alright?

[b]Rating[/b]
[list][b]Pros[/b]
[*] Unique core gameplay idea
[*] The art style fits to the vibe of the game
[*] Interesting concept and design 
[*] Puzzle difficulty varies
[*] The soundtrack fits
[/list]
[list][b]Cons[/b]
[*] A bit short (1)
[/list]
(1) As stated above, I enjoyed playing through the game and two hours of playtime is decent, I personally would have loved to play through another 35 levels because the puzzles just hit the sweet spot between easy and hard. That’s why it felt a bit short for me personally. 

[b]Conclusion[/b] 

Is [i]Temple of Starlight[/i] worth getting? I’d say so, yes – especially if you are into games that mainly focus on puzzles that vary in difficulty and get more complex later on. 

It took me about two hours to finish the game which is quite alright for a game that focuses on puzzles and for the price of 4€ it was an enjoyable journey. 

[b]7.4 / 10[/b]

Master of War is a turn-based strategy game that draws inspiration from games like Heroes of Might & Magic, albeit with a simplified, slimmed-down approach and some of its own tricks up its sleeve. While the lo-fi presentation is charming and generally well-executed, the game's obtuse tutorials, poor writing, and slew of technical issues prevent it from being an altogether enjoyable experience at this point.

The overarching mechanics are ones you'll be familiar with: build structures to generate resources, increase population capacity, and train the denizens of your tribe. These tribe members all perform distinct combat roles, from the hardy melee warriors to the nimble ranged hunters. The game then becomes a dance between managing your resources and capacity whilst simultaneously spending your turns pursuing your enemy, wiping out their population and destroying their base.

In theory, anyway. Unfortunately, some of the core mechanics here are poorly-explained, and even interactions as simple as left- or right-clicking don't necessarily function in the way you might expect - in some instances, right-clicking brings up a helpful explanatory popup, while in others, it will execute a command, such as converting a building to another type. This wouldn't be such a big issue if the tutorial was concise and well-explained, but between the shoddy writing and difficult-to-read all-caps pixel font, the tutorial itself became a chore rather quickly.

Other technical issues abound, also: my damage numbers while attacking enemies stopped showing up after the first mission, despite that the enemies' would. A* pathfinding paths were visible for the enemies as well, and I couldn't tell if that was intentional or not (either way, it looks broken). The game also crashed multiple times for me, particularly when attempting to load a saved game.

There's something charming with a lot of potential here, but it's hidden under layers of rust right now. With some brushing up, this could become something special, but as it is, there are simply too many technical issues and confusing core mechanics to recommend this title. If it's patched and these issues are addressed, I'll be happy to review again.

I expected to like Bobbi Adventure far more than I did. I enjoyed the original, to an extent. I beat it and felt absolutely no need to continue into Bobbi territory. It was fine, did what it did well, but as a gamer I need more than what was on offer to keep retreading that same territory over and over again. This is something Hades countered exceptionally well; even a terrible run still results in exquisitely voiced dialogue between characters, stories advance, upgrades get upgraded, and there’s a reason to continue once you’ve succeeded.

Here, in Bobbi Adventure, we’ve got loads upon loads, scads upon scads of upgrades you have to incrementally earn with ever-increasing inflation costs. So if you want to feel yourself getting incrementally stronger – and I do mean incremental, here – you’ve got to have good money-making runs. And the best way to earn money is to load yourself up with some negative traits and retread old territory to farm chests and drops. And then you die, and spend your loot, and maybe you get some one-liner or text quip from an NPC to tide you over into the next run. And while, mechanically speaking, Bobbi Adventure is exceptionally competent – combat and platforming are both super tight – there’s not a lot going on gameplay-wise. There’s no depth to it. So expect to spend plenty of time jumping between difficult and easy biomes when you need to heal up, all the while performing the same set of moves for enemies you’ve seen run after run after run. I have no idea how many hours I’ve actually spent on this game, since I often pause and walk away for extended periods, but I want my hours back.

I even googled for advice regarding cutting through the grind, and the best advice was, to paraphrase, “lock down the castle with the Architect and bang your head against the bosses until you git gud against them.” Ugh.

What shot down my interest in the game was that there isn’t a difficulty curve. If you graph out the grinding requirements of this game visually, it’s a staircase of plateaus that reach into the heavens. Sure, you can go up there if you want. You can grind until you’re unstoppable. But you know that life on this rock is finite, right? Hell, I’ve got a baby, so my gaming hours are limited, and if I can find time to play a game, I want to feel like that time was well spent, rejuvenation- and recreation-wise. And there are other games out there that respect your lifespan’s fleeting nature more than Bobbi Adventure does.

I did not finish this game. I played around 40 minutes before getting bored and deciding my time was better spent elsewhere. This wasn't due to the difficulty of the game. I quite like precision platformers and I like a good challenge. The main issue of the game was how bland it is.

The art direction is unique yet greatly uninteresting. I think the idea that the developers were going for was that everything in the foreground is white while background assets were black. This can definitely work, but the only thing to look at besides the platforms are some flowers. It feels lazy, and I felt a headache come on from the harsh contrast of the dark black and bright white.

The gameplay itself is quite simple: jump to the next platform. There isn't much variety besides moving platforms. Once again, I did not witness all that this game had to offer as I did not finish it, but judging from the promotional images, it's more of the same.

The movement is unsatisfying and feels incomplete. When near the edge of a platform, your jump input will often be ignored and you'll go falling to a lower platform. The slippery movement is somewhat annoying but understandable, though I cannot excuse how momentum is kept upon respawning. You'll often slide off the checkpoint platform multiple times before finally slowing down.

There are plenty of little things here that add up to an incomplete game. Moving platforms don't have indicators on how far they go, there are no settings to turn down the sound or remap controls, there is no way to skip or speed up dialogue, the jump sound effect plays every time you press the jump button even when you're midair, etc. 

This game would work as a mobile or web game, but as a $3 release on Steam, I'm quite disappointed. Unless this receives some bug fixes, I recommend staying away.
