Either way, I think my opinion of actually giving this game a positive review is legitimate in both cases for a few reasons that i'll go over quickly. 

I think this game has a really cool and unique idea for a gameplay loop. It's fundamentally very well designed in a lot of ways but has two specific drawbacks that can really sour the experience. 

The first one is that it's kind of buggy. Not in a game crashes losing save file way (Though the game did once crash on me and lost me about 2-3 hours worth of progress at the start, which was a bug at the time, probably fixed by now), but in a general gameplay loop being kind of super buggy. Enemies will ocassionaly just decide to deal damage to you telepathically like we're sending packets to a server that doesn't exist and there's desync between me and the enemy, enemies will ocasionally forget to take damage. One of the worst examples of this is a particular mechanic with the Shuriken. The game explains very early on that it's possible, and usually recommended to throw certain items from the room next door, to avoid taking damage as much as possible. Unfortunately for everyone involved this sometimes results in throwing shurikens into a room you KNOW there are large enemies that will definitely be hit once you've thrown it, only for you to waste your shuriken as the enemy waltzes out of the room as though you just sneezed at it. 

It's small little irritations like that that hamper a lot of the aspects of the gameplay and lead to extremely frustrating moments that add especially because this game's difficulty is brutal. It really doesn't like pulling punches in the way its designed and can sometimes feel like you're just getting screwed over for no other reason than the game's wacky spaghetti code. 

The second complaint is the level designs for some of the later (pre-made levels). The game is split into two halves. There's the pre-made levels which are developer crafted and usually are closer to a sort of puzzle that you as the player need to solve. The second half are randomly-generated dungeons of all shapes and sizes. My problem is the first half, the pre-made levels. The randomly generated dungeons can definitely have a bit of a feast-or-famine situation, but it never feels too frustrating because ultimately you are keenly aware you are at the mercy of the random level generation. But the premade levels, especially the later ones, feel like they were designed specifically to mess with the player and frustrate them. The levels in the latter half start getting into a really nasty and unfun habit of basically having one good solution to the puzzle of the level, and requiring sometimes several hours worth of trial and error deaths that ultimately barely feel like they're of any fault to your own. While there's definitely room for skill expression, especially in the randomly generated dungeons, these puzzles' room for skill expression can sometimes be completely crushed when you don't solve the level in the exact way the developer intended. This is just unfun in a lot of cases, and whats worse is that it never resolves into a feeling of succeeding at a difficult challenge.

You can spend currency to make your wetlands more inviting to frogs with frog furniture, ponds, and plants. I would recommend this game if you like frogs and tic-tac-toe.

"it's first person Hotline Miami!" 
It is, but its more then that. Anger Foot drives hard from the first moment you hear the soundtrack. But the game is silly. While Hotline was gritty and bleak, Anger Foot revels in its stupidity, Running around mowing people down is completely turned into a frantic comedy with goofy character models and Splatoon ink looking pools of blood. This isn't a cop out to sell it to a wider, younger audience, as the rest of the game gleefully runs around with vulgarity and tongue in cheek pokes at all good taste and "gamer" culture. 
The gameplay is smooth and rewarding for the simple concepts it works with, and is one of the most satisfying games to push for completion. You can easily just "finish the game" without any issue, but with the short levels and new shoe powers, you constantly want to see how the game can be changed with more and more unlocked items, and those quickly make what seemed impossible, a cake walk. Even the loop of endlessly restarting and the sting of failure is minimized by the goons all breakdancing to the music as your body flops all the floor from a ruined run.
The game mirrors Hotline in having odd "between episodes" cool downs, but instead of giving us a look into the scattered lore, we get to explore the levels without needing to take down anyone (not that there's a penalty for doing so tho, brilliant) and the chance to just get some fun jokes and talk with the NPCs about the events of the game is a real hoot. 
The game does what every game should aspire to, being a ton of fun and feeling like you've never wasted a minute. I didn't start this review because I love this game, I started this because steam said "hey you wanna write a review? you've played 9 hours" and it honestly didn't feel like more then a couple. That's what makes a game worth recommending. When you can get sucked in and lose yourself for hours at a time and not even feel like time has passed.

The vibes were great, loved the visuals, loved the music, guns were fun, and a good amount of levels were paced well. I liked how they kept introducing new mechanics, it was exciting to see what sort of wacky stuff theyd throw at you next. The core gameplay loop of fast respawns and learning a level is just inherently satisfying in a way similar to watching groundhogs day: you can FEEL yourself getting better at these levels and when it all finally comes together in one perfect execution it is immensely satisfying.

However - there were a bafflingly large amount of macro design decisions that seemed to be encouraging a more cowardly and tactical gameplay style that seems completely antithetical to this game's overall tone/vibe. Regenerating health for example encourages the player to retreat and take cover when faced with larger amounts of enemies, especially towards the end of a longer level. Because of this, a lot of the lategame levels start out fast and exciting, but slow down towards the end in a really anticlimactic and unsatisfying way.

About half of the boss fights force you to wait for a weakpoint to open which I really didnt like, it completely obliterated the pacing especially after restarting the fight several times - the pizza pig fight was AWFUL. Hated it. Hope to never play it again.

This then encourages you to NOT kick them, which sucks, because kicking them is fun.

The unlockable shoes are not balanced at all - some are obviously not meant to be powerful and are just there for the fun factor, but this game gets HARD and after a while. I found myself exclusively using the shoes that let you dash for probably 95% of my playtime.

It's frustrating, because they nailed the core gameplay, and just kind of fumbled at the finish line. I think with a couple tweaks this game could've been a lot better, but it's still definitely worth playing if you're a fan of fast paced FPS games and fast respawn type games.

There are a few reasons why I didn't like the game.

1. This game does [b]not[/b] reward aggressive gameplay. 
What do I mean by this?
You only have very few HP. You can not dodge. There are no heal mechanics except waiting.
This means the easiest way to beat the game is to open a door and wait behind a wall until every opponent runs into your shot.
I often had to play defense because there were too many enemies that would kill me instantly.

I really like to play aggressively in games like this. I don't want to wait until my HP is recovered.
I want mechanics that allow me to heal while killing or at least a solid dodge or bullet time.

Other games did a way better job on this:
Mullet Mad Jack, I Am Your Beast, Warstride Challenges

2. I get it; having a banger on your ears while shooting in a fast-paced game feels great. But the music in this game is all over the place. This is like some techno from the 90's on crack.
Go watch the trailer; this is the exact same song you're going to listen to on repeat for the next couple of hours.

3. In games like this, I usually earn all three stars in a level until I play the next level.
This is [b]not[/b] a speedrun game. You're getting 1 star for beating a level. The 2 remaining stars are for random "challenges". These challenges often force you to play the game in an akward way. For example: Complete the level without killing an enemy. Complete the level using only your feet. Complete the level without jumping.

Sometimes there are time challenges, but there is too much "random" stuff that I don't enjoy.

4. I did not like the artstyle of the game. You're fighting against crocodile humans, rats, and other weird stuff.

5. The bosses are poorly designed, and they were not challenging at all.

6. I frequently had performance issues.

The core shooter mechanics are good and polished, but in my opinion, there are too many flaws and too many games that do a better job.

If you really like games like this, buy it on a huge sale otherwise, leave it alone.

It's like walking through a minefield that's in an apartment complex and the only way forward is through 20 exploding doors, but nobody is allowed to die. It also has missions where the challenge is to complete the mission without being hit, yet all the gun enemies are hitscan and you have no way to dodge other than to wait behind a wall and kick them around the corner. Do I complete the whole game and maybe find that one of the shoes lets me dodge bullets, and then make me go way back to do those challenges later? Maybe! I don't know! Comparing this to "I Am Your Beast" and other similar games, you could always do every challenge before even attempting the next level, which is ideal for completionists.

I've been keeping an eye on this game ever since the developer shared it with me last year. And boy was the wait for it incredibly worth it. 

At the beginning, you can select one of many fantastically designed Vessels. I went with Astrid, the Crystal Fencer who uses Water. The start gives the background and objective right away, which is great for people who wants to explore the places and game mechanics immediately. The gameplay designs of the skill tree and abilities are intricate, so poke through around in order to learn your Vessels' build and understand how combat plays out. 

The music is also a highlight. The pleasant and cheery beats remind me of tunes from classic SNES JRPGs. Overall, the game is very polished. Definitely recommend to give this gem a shot if you like mechanically dense RPGs.

Its a fun game with some flaws.

Pros-
-Combat, the 2 characters (when you aquire the second and upgrade the Vessels) playing off each other is really fun and interesting. I used Astrid and Freya and melted pretty much everything.
-Skills, good variety of builds and how they work, sadly some shine way better than others.
-Interface, easy to navigate.
- Tier 1 vessel upgrades applying to all even if not active, makes getting the ones you don't want to use still worth it.

Mid-
Crafting- requirement are way to high and the benefits are negligible, making the craft of that legendary item impractical at best, a waste of time at worst. Most dropped gear with good augments will be more than enough. Due to this, the feature went largely unused by me.

Cons-
No skill point dump- At the end of the game i was lvl 40 (MAX) and had like 1000+ skill points just sitting there, useless. This also made the skill tomes pointless as well. 
Bugs- extra attacks not working, areas of map glitching, and some aoe occasionally not targeting all enemies.
Some vessels are just bad- plainly weaker than others.
Controller support- Works fine but the lack of a controller overlay for button interactions was confusing, so it took some failed traps and guess work to get it right. I'm sure this wont be an issue to all but it was for me. BTW: for Xbox controller Z = A and X = B RB = Q (reset puzzle).

Over all it is fun to play and worthwhile, but could use some polish to really shine

-Amazing combat animation, especially the bosses and the gods.
-Very fast pacing for battles or grinding.
-Lots of customization with Gemstones, Relics, and Events in the dungeon.

This game focuses on combat, not story, so if you're into combat, this is recommended for you.

This immensely beautiful puzzle adventure is as well done as its demo. I would have liked it to be a bit more "casual" which it's tagged as, but I was glad that it's not much of a platformer and I guess my brain could use the workout. 

I usually have a pretty low tolerance for puzzles that make me think hard for more than a minute or two and have become an avid user of walkthroughs, but something about this game made me continue and even have a (mostly) good time. The pretty background art and contemplative piano music in Amber City create such a calming atmosphere that I stuck around through all the "How?? There's NO WAY this can be solved" until I arrived at "OMG THIS is how... no wait, fuck" and finally at "YESSS" and it was so satisfying when all the right lamps got lit and the way forward unlocked. Though I have a little perfectionist in me that wanted to try and 100% the game, but after a second of considering it I was like NOPE lol. 

There's a sense of progression as you visit newly available areas, get new abilities for more sophisticated puzzles, and pick up pieces of lore. There aren't any elaborate characters or anything mind-blowing, but the story felt like much less of an afterthought than in most other puzzle adventures that I know of. The writing was decent and I should add that the English translation was good as well, I can't remember noticing more than a few minor errors. 
Not to mention that this game had a polished feel with no need for major patches after release. Worked like a charm with Steam Play for Linux too. 

Accessibility info: a certain (mostly low) degree of quick reactions is required, but mechanics are almost always forgiving. Most levels after the first few have a hostile type of robot that you need to avoid getting lasered by, but they didn't stress me much (and I get stressed [i]very[/i] easily). They only have a small radius each and are very predictable. If they do hit you, time just rewinds a few seconds. 
And then one screen towards the end had a sort of "boss" where you had to do sequences of actions very quickly. I struggled a lot with that one and really would have preferred being able to skip it. For the last sequence I ended up taking a screenshot and alt-tabbing out of the game to figure out what to do. I guess it's a non-issue if you're any good at platformers or other dexterity-based gameplay. 
As I mentioned it's not much of a platformer otherwise, no precision jumps or anything of the sort. 

All in all I really enjoyed this one. Easy recommendation if you like mental challenges with a story and nice surroundings and can handle at least one series of Quick Time Events. As the demo is still up, you can check out for free if you vibe with it.

It's a very well made game and I'm impressed at how well it plays for its ridiculously low price.

It's a 8-bit game reminiscent of the old NES games. You basically walk through levels in order to reach the palace to fight the evil samurai who killed you in the first place. The interesting gimmick is that [b]You possess the person who last killed you.[/b] This means that it is impossible for anyone to lose in this game. Each enemy has its own Jump Height, Attack Strength, and Movement Speed. These stats however don't make much of an impact on its gameplay loop. 

You basically move around with your usual WASD, but you have the ability to DEFLECT and ATTACK. Your slash ATTACK is how you kill enemies, it'll take about 3 hits to kill an enemy depending on your character that you possessed. However, enemies can also attack you quickly which is indicated by them flashing blue for a split second before slashing. This is where your DEFLECT comes in handy, press the button to deflect to be blue, yet invincible for a few seconds. You can immediately attack the enemy once you've successfully deflected their attack. So basically, you attack, deflect, attack, deflect, attack until they're dead.

I really liked the retro style of the game, the intro cutscene was well made and the simple sprites are distinguishable enough to discern which enemy is which. If I had a complaint, it would be that you can't bind your mouse clicks to the DEFLECT/ATTACK commands. I was able to bypass this by having a gaming mouse with other buttons to bind the function keys into as I found the default buttons to be a bit uncomfortable.

Anyway, I recommend this game. It's worth the price and the concept of a samurai possessing his killers is well implemented here. Have a nice one, my dudes!

My first impression was very positive, I think the game instantly hits you with an infectious atmosphere and a compelling environment to explore that reminds me of PT and Cube, but in the end, I think the story failed to keep up with the psychological elements and to contextualize its characters, in addition to having some technical issues and glitches. It's very short, like 30-40 minutes, it took me longer because I could not read the numbers properly due to the font. I replayed the game 2 times to get different endings, and to be honest they kinda sucked, like no context or closure at all. To be fair, I think you can end the game on a vague note, and very often it's the way to go because it leaves you wondering about what happened, and I still got that feeling, but I think we needed to spend more time with the character and to know him better. It just kinda feels like that scene from the South Park where they bring you lobster dinner, but you can only eat it for 5 seconds - I like the game, I am invested in it, and then you don't take advantage of it, it feels like you pulled the rug under me. 

Do you ever play short games where you like them, but because they are so short they don't feel satisfying, but then you go back and realize there are some optional secrets, or maybe the game does something different if you replay it - I think this is what this game is lacking the most,  going that extra mile to make the experience more memorable. I would say go back and just add a few secrets, maybe a different event on a second playthrough, or even just a few hidden rooms with more context for the character, maybe you can break the mirror with a rat and there is another hallway, things like that. When I started the game I was enjoying those little cerebral elements like that hallway distance bending, I assumed there would be a lot more of that, but you kind of reuse the same idea of "more than one direction" and never really expand on what is possible in a troubled mind. 

While I like the idea of the entire game essentially taking place in a hallway, I was hoping you would do more unique decorations for the rooms that would reflect the mind of the character, there is just not enough variety to stimulate my interest. Again, the game has an interesting concept, and you have so much opportunity to create some unique psychological effects, but ultimately you did the whole room cycling which is one of the most cliche thing you can do in the genre, I thought the game would expand on that with something original. And for a small bonus nitpick, I just thought the TV dude looked a bit too cartoony, kinda killed the vibe for me a little. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) I thought the game handled the atmosphere very well, you can pretty much feel it from start to finish.  Decent narrative, I like that you are not just explaining everything, but I wish there was more meat on the bone, more exploration. 

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Content [/u] - I think you should add some optional secrets, in a game like this it goes a long way, maybe some hidden rooms, or some new changes if you replay it. I didn't like the lack of closure with both endings, and I am not saying you need to explain the story, I just wanted a little cutscene or something. I wish there was more variety in the room design, maybe something that would reflect the mind of the character.

[u] Technical [/u] - as I already said in the hub, fix the number font (hard to tell the numbers apart), add V-sync if you can, patch the holes in the rooms and the settings reset. 

[b] Overall Thoughts: 5/10 [/b]

It's not so much that I dislike the game, I think in general the story had a good direction, but I need a little more meat on the bone to feel happy about the experience, sandwich the game with some optional secrets, maybe more hidden rooms, more optional context, more cerebral interactions. What I am trying to say is that the game is actually interesting, just not enough of a game here, good ideas, but you need to go that extra mile to make it more memorable.

I was a bit disappointed, personally.  The game length is VERY short (about half an hour to 45 minutes).  The game hints at some explanation (as there are certain reoccuring things mentioned by the various radios you find), but it never really expounds on things.  The "looping" hallways have you trekking back and forth through the same halls.

Occasionally you'll be joined by "something".  You'll have to blow out the candles to hide in the darkness.  Sometimes, you'll be clicking at a candle and it just refuses to want to go out.  Sometimes, you'll feel like you are in darkness but it isn't registered as hidden.  

During my first playthrough, I thought that every time you "died", your vision got a bit worse.  This mean that at a certain point I could no longer read the notes scattered through the hall...and I couldn't reading ANY of the end-game dialogue.   It was a frustrating experience.   Turns out, this was a glitch of some sort and the game was bumping down my "grunge" setting when I died.  If you find the graphics going too grungy and the subtitles unreadable, hit Escape, then options, and look for the "grunge" setting.  You can change it here so you can read notes and dialogue again.

It did the same to me upon completing the game as well...instantly the "Grunge" setting was dropping to it's grungiest setting.

Frustrating glitch aside, this isn't a BAD experience.  But it is definitely a partial experience.  The penalty for failure is low (once you know how to be able to fix the graphics issue), but I didn't feel rewarded either.  No amazing "lore drops" or anything like that.  I'd definitely look at getting another game from these devs again, but other than that I'd say skip this one for now (unless you just want to financially support the devs) and wait for a more fleshed out game in the future.

After playing RWBY: Grimm Eclipse first, i decided i'm gonna take the gamble and try this game out as well. And i can say, without a shadow of a doubt.

This is worse than Grimm Eclipse.

i'm gonna say this, as nicely and politely as i possibly can because when i say this game legit angered me, i truly mean it.

Let's start with the positives, there's a better soundtrack in Arrowfell than what there was in Grimm Eclipse...Doesn't make it good but at least its tolerable, but after a while i just turned the music off and put on the actual soundtracks of RWBY in the background (Which side note: Season 6 Has the best soundtrack, fight me on that i dare you.) so there is that.

And uhh...that's pretty much it for the positives. Now lets go through the negatives.

Lets start with the simple fact that RWBY does NOT WORK AS A METROIDVANIA! the "battle mechanics" if you can even call them that, are so barebones that the entire thing just boils down to spamming one singular button and sometimes using the semblance of the girls, which often times are just for solving puzzles (yes, there are puzzles in the game, i will get to that in a bit.) or just trying to get the most DPS out of it by using Blake's semblance of shadow clone and Yang to pummel the enemies which i did a whopping...one time...on the final boss...because i was too busy maxing out every characters "skill tree", which by the way, can i just ask, who's idea was to put the skill points in treasure chests? 90% of my playthrough boiled down to looking through every single area of the game to make sure i didn't miss a treasure chest because they contained the skill points, you know, the things you need to max out your already weak characters?

But let's go to the puzzle solving mechanics of the game, which is basically Blake's only existence in the game outside of being a DPS character, because guess what, 9 times out of 10 i just resorted to use Ruby because she's the fastest character in terms of going around in areas, but i'm getting side tracked, the puzzles are just a legitimate hassle to get through because they aren't engaging, or even hard, they're just there to be a nuisance for you, a roadblock to prevent you from going further.

Also, can i just ask, why does a huge chunk of the game remain unvoiced, when all the cutscenes (and yes, i will get to the cutscenes too) are fully voice acted, but not the rest of the game? if you gonna commit to a bit, commit to it fully, not half-ass it. because it just comes off as lazy.

To make a comparison, a game by the name of Dust: An Elysian Tail, has full voice acting, even thought that game is also a Metroidvania, and it also has a few cutscenes as well, even though the game was made by a singular guy, the voice acting wasn't half-assed, and the person who made the game committed to it fully.

And speaking of cutscenes...holy crap the cutscenes are bad, it is Season 1-2 levels of grainy and washed out, and i've played this game on a Full HD monitor, and watched the show regularly on it, the cutscenes just do not look good, it is so muddy and dark that i thought my monitor is acting up and crapping itself out, i don't know if Rooster Teeth wasn't paid properly and they half-assed the entire thing but it is so horrid that whenever there was a cutscene i just wanted it to end as soon as they began.

And by the way, by the f-ing way, who's idea was to have the ranged attack of the characters, you know, the entire point of the gun parts to their weapons and in the entire series. HURT YOU, WHEN YOU SHOOT IT?! It actively DRAINS your health bar and the skills to regenerate it is so slow that often times i had to either dash through the enemies or play hide and seek! that is bad game design 101 if i ever seen one. i don't know who's idea was this, but they clearly never played a video game even if it meant saving their goddamn life.

And to top it all off, if that wasn't bad enough, this game costs nearly 30 Euros...again, in comparison to Dust. That game, costs 15 Euros, and is vastly better than this game, with more and engaging skills and combat, and with a better story too, because guess what, the story of RWBY: Arrowfell is...meh, just meh, its not offensively bad, its just, boring, boring and a slog to get through. And THIS, THIS! IS SUPPOSED TO BE CANON TO THE SHOW! never, in the entire 7th season of RWBY was it ever alluded, never hinted at what Arrowfell is, where Arrowfell is, never was it mentioned, never was it even an easter egg, nothing, absolutely nothing ever suggested that this game is canon to the RWBY Universe, and that's the worst part about this entire game, the story practically being non-canon to the RWBY Universe, hell, even Grimm Eclipse is more of a canon to the RWBY universe than this, because at least Grimm Eclipse TRIED, and it was fully backed by Rooster Teeth, while this game was half-assed and given to a team who probably never even saw or cared about RWBY In the first place, they just saw a huge IP and wanted a slice of pie from it.

If i had to sum this game up in a few words, it would be this: rip-off, it is a rip-off, and an even worse attempt at a cashgrab than whatever the hell Grimm Eclipse was. This is one of the most tedious and shallow game i have ever played, nothing about it was engaging, and i loath myself for buying it. But hey, at least i got an easy 100% on the game, so that has to count for something right?......just kill me already.

Tl:Dr; Game's bad, play Dust: An Elysian Tail instead.

oh, and i had to play this game with a controller, because there was no tutorial what keys to press, you know, on a keyboard...that i was playing from...kill me.

Alright. [i]Mystery Solitaire Cthulhu Mythos[/i] is....a very boring game. I only paid 49 cents for this one, so I'm not gonna be too bent out of shape over it, but as cool as the title sounds and as nice as the product page looks, this game does not live up to any of that. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3246916940

With a title like that, you would expect some sort of story to go along with it. Nope. While the actual Solitaire levels are perfectly passable, they aren't particularly noteworthy and get stale pretty quickly.

There are three wrinkles to the game outside of a small variety of Solitaire level designs. You earn credits while playing that can be used to by jokers, which are treated as wild cards, mulligans which roll back your last decision as implied by the name, and shuffle, which shuffles the remaining cards on the table. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3247160678

Rather than match suits or do anything notably solitaire related, your goal is only to stack sequential cards into your discard pile in order to reveal special cards that boost your credits and to reveal and use all gold cards on the table. You have to try and play all the gold cards, at which point you win regardless of how many other cards are left on the table. You can complete a level without using them all by simply using all the cards in your deck, but for a perfect score, that is what is required. Actually, your deck of cards to pull from when you run out of options is this game's main connection to real Solitaire best I can tell.

It has been brought to my attention after buying this game that the developer reskins and resells this exact same game and has many many many many variations of the same game on Steam, with a variety of names. And the publisher promotes many games that employ this same method of development. Although this doesn't factor into my review rating, it is worth noting before you send your cash their way. To me, it is indicative of the lack of imaginative or innovative development you can expect from such games IMO.

That's basically all I have to say about this game. If you are looking for a completely casual experience, that can be found here. If you are looking for anything else at all or have the expectation of some cool factor the title implies exists, don't bother. Personally, I was not impressed. It's barely Solitaire and doesn't even bother trying to live up to its name. There are better and much more fun Solitaire options on Steam that actually respect your time and money.

Don't be fooled by the exciting sounding title. There is no mystery, and yes it is Cthulu themed but that's largely just background. This is a solitaire puzzle through and through. Yes there are lots of different arrangements, and the levels have to be completed by finding all of the special cards rather than clearing the deck, but this is largely all the variations. There are three purchaseable cards (bought through the points you have earned) - a 'mulligan' which allows you to undo your previous move, a shuffle to shuffle all the cards around, and a joker to put down as any card. I played through all levels on the first level of difficulty and it was ok, but there's not much variation. The Cthulu theme is solely restricted to the beautiful background art but that's it - no animations, no story, nothing. If you're just looking for a solitaire game with a little twist, I'd go for Faery Solitaire as it has much more variation.

[i]This blurb is taken from my 2024 Games of the Year list that I posted on GiantBomb.com. HeistGeist was #2.[/i]

I’ve always loved asymmetric co-op games featuring a hacker and an agent on the ground. In these games (Clandestine or Hacktag, for example), you’ll often need to support each other and leapfrog to make progress. The hacker may need to open a door for the agent so the latter can clear a server room of hostiles, so the hacker can then cross an air gap. In Heistgeist you can play both roles, bouncing between two distinct but equally compelling deckbuilding games representing the roles of each operative. There are areas that your ground agent won’t be able to access unless you hack proficiently, and these routes are elegantly represented on each level’s heist map. The combat deck revolves around stringing combos together - cards have a type, A, B, or C, and will gain extra effects if a specific card type was played beforehand. The hacking deck, on the other hand, revolves more around analyzing a server map and targeting specific nodes so that the ones around them are weakened as well. As you progress through the game you’ll unlock new cards for each deck, and you’ll be able to further enhance your strategies. Although I can’t say I found the story tremendously compelling (A shadowrunner named Alexandra is burned on a mission and is trying to get to the bottom of what happened), I liked the game’s visual style and deckbuilding more than enough to compensate.

This is a simple endless score-based game with a unique mechanic where you draw the attack line. This attack has a limit to how much you can draw, and needs to be recharged fully in order to be used again.


There are five characters, two that need to be unlocked, and they all have an different playstyle. While most are cool, Oda, one of them, is just a crutch, where his gimmick is that he has two lives and wipes the screen of enemies when he loses one. While this is fine, it also shows that most characters don't deviate much from eachother, and that feels like a missed oppurtunity for the unique element of this game, the line attack. Like, I don't know, it would be cool if there were more unique characters, like one where you can't draw the line on the enemies or you die, or one where the character needs to draw specific line and they get a bonus for it, or a guy that has a very small draw limit, or can draw only straight lines. But this is just me, the characters are mostly fine.

One thing I don't get though is achievements. There are four achievements per character, and they're all the same for each of them. This is fine, but the amount of achivements and their difficulty is what makes me question them in the first place. I managed to get all achievements for two characters in 14 minutes. I feel like if achievements are gonna be in a game like this, at the very least there should be more of them, aswell as some harder ones. Even if they are basic highscore achievements.

The artsyle is nice, not much to say about it.

Still, this game is fun. Simple and fun. Nothing crazy tho. If you want a nice time waster or are looking for an endless challenge, it's worth it.
For its price, it's worth it, and it's not like a sale is gonna make much of a difference lmao.

I'm so disappointed. I love roller coasters / amusement park rides. I love dinosaurs. This should be a VR game right up my alley. Unfortunately, the quality control is just not there. This game has too many issues for me to recommend it currently as is. This game needs lots of work to be at an acceptable level.

Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, on high graphical settings (everything on high), I was getting variable frame rates from 90 to 30 fps. It was awful. I had to turn off shadows completely and I also lowered the grass texture setting. With that it seems that I was able to get mostly 90 fps.

Unfortunately, the lighting is really bad. The visuals are all over the place. Some parts of the map will look good, some 3D models look good, some of the animations are good. Then there's the rest that look anything from passable to downright putrid. The quality control is just not there. 

This experience has 3 different modes: hunt mode, a dinosaur encyclopedia mode (full of narrated info), and a fun ride mode. The hunt mode is absolutely awful. The encylopedia mode is alright and it does have a lot of narrated info that is even animated, but a lot of the info is very stale, plus it uses a computer voice. Lastly, the rides ... *sigh* there are some rides that are okay. Unfortunately, the quality is all over the place. Plus this is where optimization is really needed.

Overall, I just can't recommend this experience. Buy only to support development, otherwise, wait for a patch that fixes these issues (such patch is unlikely to happen).

Great concept, long ways to go.

The word game itself has lots of problems. You might recognize this core mechanic from Wordscapes, which I've played a bunch. Compared to Wordscapes, there are some problems. I find it unexpected to include proper nouns like "Ben", or obscure words like "et". I am pretty sure that Wordscapes excludes all two-letter words, which is wise because they get tedious very quickly (I see a lots of "et's" in my future should I continue playing). Wordscapes also has a two-tiered dictionary where obscure words are just a bonus rather than required. I recommend adopting all of these changes.

The biggest difference, though, is that every time you get a word, it plays a long, bright, flashy attack animation, which covers the full screen and prevents you from doing anything else. This slows the pace of the game a lot, and I find it grating on the eyes due to the spinning motion. This is probably the main factor in why I haven't played more, because the early stages are very easy but still take a fair bit of time.

The UI is troubled, at least on desktop, where lots of stuff overlaps and can't be clearly seen, especially the blanks that tell you the expected words and their lengths, but also it's unclear what just about every button does, and menus are easy to get lost in. The sound design has a long ways to go; I ended up playing with sound off.

I really don't understand the capture mechanic at all. It just tells you the sequence to input? But then it just fails sometimes anyways? I also kept forgetting to capture at the end of the stage for a while.

So far as I've noticed, you don't have to engage with the RPG mechanics at all if you're good enough at the word game, which seems odd to me. I was excited for what I hoped would be "Puzzle Quest-like" progression and mixing and matching of tools, but I haven't had any reason to engage with it. There also doesn't seem to be a way to view what the creatures or ability buttons do, and collecting them doesn't appear to "add up" to anything like a zoo or diorama, or even unlocks that I can tell. Overall there's also significantly less RPG presence than I expected, which I suppose makes sense since each combat is simply one word puzzle, and completing it is the only win condition that makes sense. I don't expect everyone to want the same things as me, but I would probably make some major mechanical change such as increasing the letter count per puzzle, but not require full completion to win (using stats instead, perhaps), or even changing the letters up regularly so you have to keep adapting to new situations. I was even expecting a timer mechanic where the enemy would take a turn every so many seconds and attack you (since Wordscapes rewards you a lot for playing fast), but enemy actions only seem to happen when you make a bad input, and don't seem to cause any puzzle interference, just life damage.

Going into the game, I was really hoping for "Wordscapes + Puzzle Quest" and I didn't end up enjoying either aspect particularly well. At least there are no ads. I hope its continued development in Early Access can improve on the things that turned me away.

This is a 3d Zelda game about a quaint Austrian ski town that sees a huge boom in tourism when portals to otherworldly dungeons mysteriously appear in the local mountains. Explorers come from all over to brave the dungeons' depths, and the protagonist pushes herself to complete as many as possible before they supposedly vanish at the end of the month. 

The visuals are lovely, with a neat juxtaposition between stark snowy mountains, ultra-saturated fantasy dungeons, and an idyllic European village. Navigating the alpine overworld feels really evocative of hiking out in nature, and the dungeons themselves are all pretty simple, but they're well paced and have fun secrets hidden in dusty corners. There's also a Persona-y time management component that feels a little underbaked, a delicious gooey cube, and a fantastically swoopy hover-snowboard. Definitely recommended!

This game is beautiful. The style is absolutely breathtaking and it never ever looks messed up or janky. The music is also beautiful and adds to the scenery and battles so well. 

I also personally really liked the combat. I feel like some people were talking about it not being engaging, and I guess that's true if you never push yourself, but if you're trying dungeons a little above your level (like 1 or 2) and enemies around the same they're usually decently tough and asking you to really use the mechanics to win. I really like how much you could diversify your playthrough, be it with different gems charms slotted (which are actually really good upgrades, not like 1.5% buff to combat), different special abilities you can unlock and slot onto your hot bar, and different combos that played into each of these systems. This variety was also further enhanced when changing up magical abilities in each different dungeon biome, which was also very fun just alone. I liked going to different biomes and having to remember what abilities I had and figure out how to use them in each dungeon to make it through certain puzzles or enemies. 

Another big part of this game was the story and the NPCs. Basically the main gameplay loops goes like this: 
Wake up in the morning, get ready for dungeon, pick biome to go to and either roam around the map to find a dungeon and complete it or roam around the map to find rest spots or NPCs to pass the time with, then go back home to spend your evening with one of the locals (either a tourist staying there just like you or an actual local that lives there), then go to bed for the night before doing it all over again the next day. 
Maybe that sounds a little boring, but the mixture or story, puzzles, and combat really make it an interesting and fun loop. A big part of that fun, other than the combat which I just described, are the NPC storylines and how your story works off theirs. I really do love the writing in this game -- the plot talking about tourism in a really meaningful and real way and all the NPCs acting and speaking in a very realistic and interesting manner in response to that was just so well done. I loved being able to go hang out with someone at the end of the night, especially after a relatively stressful dungeon. After hanging out with a certain NPC enough times you're given very special upgrades that usually tie in to the personality or story of the person you're hanging out with. This ends up making the rewards highly satisfying, not just because they're unique and good upgrades, but also because it was a reward that meant something to the NPC I was just developing a relationship with. 

With those two together, the combat and the NPC relationships, it ends up making a really satisfying and fun time throughout basically the entire runtime, despite some of it being a little repetitive and there not being a ton of enemy variety. There also feels to be a small amount of bosses, now that I'm thinking back to it, so I think I would have liked some more of that too, but like I said I was having so much fun in the moment it all didn't really matter to me until I started to really think on it.


Now, with all that said, the end of my //checks playtime// HOLY SHIT -- 30 hour playthough ..... o.o ...... was a bit of a slog ((which maybe you'd expect for an indie that can have over 30 hours of content)). I was invested in the story and the NPCs that I really wanted to finish all their storylines before the end of the main game. I felt like that was kinda the point, getting to know everyone around you and their perspectives, even if they didn't seem to make sense at first because all perspectives are worth considering and viewing. But like.. it was fucking impossible to do all the NPC events; and I don't say this to be dramatic it was genuinely starting to ruin my playthrough so I just had to give up on it and end the game. And then there was a final area where all the people you got to know well enough came to see you off and like... that made me so mad? Cause I wanted to do everyone's story and when I saw people missing when I ended up giving up it was like damn did you not want me to give up? Did they expect anyone to do all the NPC stories in one playthrough? If so, then why did they make it so god damn hard? When I say to you that I was done with all dungeons and just burning time before finishing literally the last one for HOURS just so I could pass the days and get better relationship with NPCs I really mean it bro. It was probably like 2 streams worth of content where I was mostly focusing only on NPCs and there were multiple times were I'd do a whole storyline with an NPC and then my relationship wouldn't even go up with them...MULTIPLE TIMES IN A ROW. bruh... It takes me a whole day to talk to one NPC, either give me more dungeons or let me level up the relationship more. Even if I'm not meant to get to know everyone in one playthrough I think the time it takes with some of them is just too long and it really kills the pacing of the game.

Even though I feel that way, that's honestly my only real issue with the game. Some medals were hard to get and it made me a little frustrated because it meant either redo a whole dungeon or just don't get the outfit and when I had really nothing else I wanted to use my copious amount of money on by the end of the game it made me feel a little bad; but really that was a minor issue in the grand scheme of things. 
The battles and dungeons were fun; I loved the puzzles and I usually don't feel that way in games with puzzles as a "side" thing or whatever you want to call it in adventure games like this. The world and every single bit of its design is GORGEOUS, I wish I could live in this world. The music accompanied the world and all the dungeons and battles so well, I was always immersed. All the NPCs were not only well written, like I said, but well designed. I just loved basically everything about this game and I want the studio to make more so desperately. 
**It's like if Zelda and Persona had an indie baby** and while it isn't perfect, it's also this studio's FIRST GAME and I think there is so much promise here. I love this and I will support this studios next project with my dying breath (especially if it's a SEQUEL!!!!!!)

Rolled credits on Dungeons of Hinterberg this evening.

DoH is an action "RPG" of sorts where you are Luisa, vacationing in a village in the Alps where 25 dungeons have mysteriously appeared. The town has embraced this odd event and turned dungeon crawling into a vacation destination. You begin each day visiting a hub area and finding a dungeon. After completing it, you return to town for an afternoon phase where you can buy items and upgrades. Then you can pick one NPC to spend the evening with. You could help the old rich lady find her missing brooch or spend time training with Mr. Intensity or you could just hit the spa and relax. Each evening activity grants some gameplay benefit, so you can either socialize with your favorite people or strategically pick up traits for a "build".

The alpine vibes are immaculate, plenty of beautiful vistas and scenic hikes. The town and the characters are also very wonderfully crafted. I had genuine affection for many of them and I felt a sense of kinship with the town. I think the social-sim-granting-exploration-combat-abilities loop is really interesting to play with. It made me interact with characters I hadn't been interested in, giving me a more well-rounded sense of the world. I thought the plot was a really lovely story about both how tourism can exploit the community and the land but also about how life needs to have more play and joy and camaraderie in it. I even got misty-eyed.

The dungeons are bespoke, Zelda-esque experiences revolving around the hub world's traversal magic and ranged attack magic (which are different in each). There are everything from puzzles about reflecting lasers to getting crates off conveyer belts to snowboarding through a slalom course to big multi-phase boss battles. I felt like across the 25 dungeons, the puzzles stayed mostly fresh and rarely felt like I was just repeating the same busy work. They usually all had little twists to keep it interesting.

What was NOT interesting is the combat. This was a very Death's Door combat system where you wandered into little "combat zones" where you had to defeat waves of enemies to proceed. The enemies draw from German/Swiss folklore which is cute but there really isn't much variety: slow melee, fast melee, slow ranged, fast ranged, repeat. You have a fast swing and a heavy swing but for all the swords and upgrades you can buy, I never really felt like combat had any kind of strategy to it. You kind of just run in circles kiting enemies and trying not to turn your back on projectiles. It was fine for the first half but I came to dread it in the second. You can turn off player death, which I did when I had 5 dungeons left because I just could not stand to care about combat that dull anymore.

But even though most of the game systems revolve around combat skills in someway, I still walked away from the game happy with it. I think it's a clever idea and I think a sequel with some tweaks and innovations (more than one weapon type, more interesting encounter design) would be an instant classic.

I enjoyed playing this, but I must say there are some weird design choices in the game.
Like the summary screen at the end of your day, which isn’t actually at the end of the day. Or the cool art style, where I can’t stop wondering—why do so many people have a mustache?

What I found very frustrating was that it is way too easy to fall off ridges. I died numerous times because of that. It’s a good thing there are no real consequences for dying, because I would have rage-quit 20 hours ago. This could be easily solved by simply preventing the falling, like how many other games handle it.

Another weird choice was the two characters you automatically have a friendship with. Your friend Alex is very pushy and has weird dialogue. I don’t like her at all, which is unfortunate since she is the designated best friend of your character. Another good friend is Klaus, who is twice your age and comes across as a bit of a pervert for my taste. There are a lot of great characters with nice dialogue, and the main character is awesome. That makes it even weirder that two of the worst characters are your first companions, and in Alex’s case, the most frequent one.

The camera view is one of the worst elements in the game. Especially in battles, the camera is one of the biggest monsters to fight. It also sometimes changes perspective in dungeons, which always feels a bit awkward and out of place. And then there are the train carts—my god. I’ve never experienced something like this. They go insanely fast, and you have to pay attention; otherwise, you can’t solve the puzzle and progress. Because of that, it’s no wonder people experience motion sickness and headaches (as you can read in some of the reviews). This is a major flaw.

In the end, I did enjoy playing this but haven’t finished the game and won’t. The dungeons with their puzzles and fights become too similar and boring (I finished half of them). A part of me wants to check out the rest of the story and dialogue with some of the characters, but I can’t be bothered to do more dungeons. But that’s fine, I got my share of fun out of this.

Mixed genre games tend to be something I don't go for too much. I usually prefer when a game is aware of its core gameplay strengths and focuses on refining that. Games that attempt to tackle multiple genres and tie together multiple gameplay loops often end up feeling underdeveloped. Luckily Dungeons of Hinterberg is one of the rare cases that does feel like more than the sum of its parts. It attempts a mix of action combat, puzzle solving, and a social sim, and I think does all of those pretty well.

The gameplay is split into different chunks by the time of day. In the morning you have main story conversations and select which of the four overworld areas you want to spend the afternoon in, during the afternoon you can explore that area and attempt a dungeon, and in the evening you're free to roam the city to shop for upgrades and select a character to spend time with. 

The overworld and dungeon gameplay is a take on the Zelda formula, mixing action combat and light puzzle solving. Overworld exploration is a mix of combat encounters, collecting items for upgrading your equipment (a really satisfying effect where you vacuum in glowing items on the ground with a nice sound), and discovering the paths to dungeons. You also have an option to not do a dungeon for that day and use a rest area to relax and upgrade one of your stats. A minor complaint that feels best to mention here is that while the game controls well generally, there's no run button and every time you move you have to slowly get up to running speed, but the tiniest thing can reset that back to zero. Just an unnecessary annoyance, the game would've been fine if you were just at running speed all the time, the exploration suffers a bit because of this.

The combat portion is very serviceable, while it might not have as much depth as a game focused on this I still found it engaging enough throughout. There's a decent amount of enemy variety, you'll definitely see a lot of repeats but they do really stand out as distinct so the different enemy compositions for different encounters work out well. You'll also be using different builds in combat. While always centered around your basic sword moveset and dodge roll, you can have up to three Attack Conduits which are special attacks that recharge as you deal damage, and can also use your magical abilities in combat. There are also gear upgrades which mostly boils down to prioritizing physical or magical stats in both attack and defense, and a charm system which is mostly standard with a handful of unique effects but I liked that you can upgrade charms you like to take up less slots. 

The magical abilities are the equivalent to items in a Zelda game, but rather than expanding your arsenal as you progress, you unlock two abilities at the start of each overworld area, and those are the only ones you'll have access to for that area and any dungeons in it. This limitation is an interesting choice, and I think mostly works out pretty well. Most of the abilities have a variety of uses which dungeons fully explore, there were one or two that felt sort of single-purpose but I liked them for the most part. Their uses in combat are a bit mixed, I found myself using them much more often in some areas than others, but at least I can say that it keeps the flow of combat smooth without feeling the need to constantly swap them out. 

The dungeons themselves are the center of the game, and I think these are really solid. While they start out a bit on the easy side for my taste, they do increase in complexity as the game goes on, and both the quantity and variety here is really impressive. There are 25 dungeons and they pretty much all manage to stand out as memorable, while a couple do reuse visual styles they usually do something different enough with it to stand out, and I think the game could have easily gotten away with only one dungeon theme for each of the four main zones but I'm glad it didn't. The puzzle complexity isn't too high but does ramp up to be on the upper end of the Zelda series or slightly above, and while it doesn't quite go above and beyond that series like I would say some of its imitators have, there are quite a few dungeons here that I'd put equal to the best ones Zelda has to offer.

The social sim and story part of the game are also solid, I haven't played much Persona but from what I know it takes after that quite a bit. You can choose who you spend time with every evening, and you get to experience side stories with them and level up your friendship which unlocks new gameplay benefits ranging from new charms to shop discounts to exclusive gear upgrades. While not my favorite story or anything like that, I liked the setting and premise well enough, and most of the characters are fun. The pacing of the social sim aspect is probably my biggest complaint with the game though. I ended up liking it enough to want to 100% the game, but felt by the end like that was a mistake. There are just way too many filler social slots that could have been condensed into less per character, and you also simply don't have enough days to get anywhere close to feeling like you did everything you wanted to. There's no time limit, so near the end of the game you can just put off completing it to continue with this aspect, which is what I ended up doing. That was really not a great time though, and I spent several  hours near the end of the game just spamming through the early part of the day, going through multiple loading screens, just to incrementally progress social stuff with one character. I think there really needed to be an option from early on to skip the adventuring for the day and do multiple social actions instead, interspersing this throughout the game would have really helped. It just feels awkward in several ways though, even if you don't want to 100% the game, just with a normal completion you're only going to have maxed out a handful of the characters at most which doesn't feel very good and would have made the ending of the game fall kind of flat I think. On the other hand, progressing towards 100% characters will just disappear after you complete their stuff and the town starts to feel very empty which feels awkward. I think more interactions between the characters and allowing you to increase your status with multiple at once is another avenue they could have gone down, and almost did with the group campfire sessions but these don't actually increase your friendship level with anyone and also feel very optional so they're kind of a waste of time slots. Really any of the above suggestions would have improved this, it really needed something to help with the pacing even if the individual stories are nice on their own.

Overall liked this quite a bit even if I don't feel like any of the individual elements are really excellent. It's a unique feeling game with a cool visual style (a rare game to get me to engage with its photo mode), fun characters, fun gameplay, and even with some complains none of the parts are really bad either. It's really impressive in scope and polish for such a small team, and I'm definitely interested in their work in the future. I can pretty easily recommend this if it looks interesting to you.

Was not a huge fan of this, was glad to have finished.  The concept itself was great the art and the theme/background was good but I personally didn't find flying around at snails pace collecting animal spirits through thorn mazes while being chased by gem stealing mushrooms, competing with dark sprint clouds and having to click through the entire dialogue of each animal repetitively particularly LoFi or chillaxing, quite the opposite.  Overall the game lacked a lot of polish which wouldn't have been difficult to add, even just a different response each time you collected a spirit would have been something.

GOOD:
- MOHAA themed.
- Death animations are pretty cool and varied. It also plays different animations depending on the part of the enemy's body that you shot before he died, like in old FPS games.
- Including an Axis campaign. Though I don't necessarily like that it's the same map but played from the other side.
- Music. Sometimes it's great, sometimes it's pretty monotonous. But overall it's nice.

MEH:
- Some reloading animations are glitchy.
- The melee attack animation is weird. IF that's a melee attack, because I don't really know since there is no tutorial for it, I just happened to hit 'V' on my keyboard by accident.
- Enemy AI is very basic. They go through trees and get alerted as long as you're close by or they are triggered by opening doors. They only go towards you and, once they are in a certain range, they fire. I put this in the MEH category because, even though it's pretty experience-breaking, I know AI is very difficult to get right, especially if you're not an expert and you've developed the game by yourself.
- Invisible walls are way too big. It breaks the experience being stopped by nothing when you are 5 meters from an obstacle.
- Bushes float on slopes and ground bumps. Maybe don't put bushes there :)
- Bushes and trees are rendered weirdly when seen through tree leaves.
- In Winter War, on the Allied campaign, while riding on the tank at the beginning, I was floating behind it instead of sitting on top of it. Or maybe that's a cinamatic for your character walking, but in that case I would remove the ability to move, jump or crouch while it's playing and restrict the camera movement to 120º or so.
- Textures and models are inconsistent. Some models look high-poly while others looks really low-poly. Some textures are picture-based while others are plain colors. Just pick a style and stick with it.
- Tanks at the beginning of Allied Winter War are not textured. I don't mind the low-poly look necessarily, but, come on, at least texture them a bit.

BAD:
- Level design is boring and confusing. I didn't know the red arrow on the compass was marking the objective so I spent 15 minutes going in circles on the first mission after the Finnish ambush. There's a load of nothingness everywhere and enemies sometimes appear randomly and start attacking you from between the trees.
- Tedious long walks with little to no interaction.
- Long cinematics where you just wait in silence because there is no dialog or music or stuff happening for you to watch.
- Optimization issues. I have an RTX 3060 and at one point I was going at 12 fps. I was on ultra settings, yes, but this game is made with Unity and, as I said before, the textures and models are low quality.
- Tree leaves have collision for bullets???
- Voice acting is horrendous. Russians yelling random stuff every quarter of a second on the first ambush with the same voice actor is annoyingly funny.
- Serious lack of juicy feedback when shooting enemies. Sometimes they produce sparks instead of blood when shot (?). In MOHAA, the enemies would play an animation when they got hit and the sound design helped a lot. Here you don't really know if you are hitting them or not.
- Blinding-glowing trees? I get that they're covered in snow, but why are they glowing???
- Enemies are dumped on you from the start of both campaigns and very little health is dropped by them. This becomes unplayable on the Axis campaign where you're alone and enemies have automatic submachine guns. I died 5 times in the same spot because I was at 20 health and I couldn't find any more health. I tried spraying bullets like crazy to the 5-6 enemies thrown at me and I died every time.
- Healthpacks should glow a little, be bigger or have a different color so they can be more easily seen. In MOHAA they were distinctively green or white and they had an animated shader that made them stand out. Here they are small and their color blends with the surrondings, so they are much more difficult to spot.
- Aiming down sides is uncomfortable and doesn't line up to the view correctly. There is too much swing applied to the weapon when looking down the sights and it makes it difficult to actually see what you are shooting at.
- The player should be allowed to change the settings while in game and not have to exit to the main menu first.

Overall, it's a nice try at replicating what for me and many other people is a classic game, but I can't recommend the game at its current state. I'll give it a couple more years and wait for it to implement many of the features it lacks right now that I mentioned previously.

Many either are too easy (though can still be simple fun) or become too complex where minimum moves to complete a puzzle gets to like 50+ moves and it can be impossible to figure out how to match the par moves. Firstly, the gameplay isn't particularly engaging, and the lack of instructions that works for the other games in the bundle doesn't work as much here. The one positive I guess is that managing to construct a full production line is kinda satisfying, especially if you like idle games, or seeing a number go up on the top of the screen. I don't want to be mean, but I wouldn't recommend playing this game even if you got it for free, it's a waste of time.

* Graphics are kinda okay.
* Audio is okay.
* Narrative is very minimal and clearly taken from Dune.
* Game design makes no sense, there aren't strategic challenges.
* Controls are inconvenient.
* Has some bugs

Game Design:
There are almost no meaningful decisions to make:
[spoiler]
* Each building requires a power plant, but power plants can only be connected to a single building, so positioning these power plants is just more tedious clicks, no planning required, it doesn't matter where you place them except for being kinda close to that one building.
* Enemies fly over everything and attack random buildings, there's no planning for that, so the only solution is to try to notice when that happens and quickly place a defensive building (+power plant, of course) next to the enemy - no interesting decision, the only challenge here is to notice when an enemy flies into the screen.
* The lab building increases production by 10%, so at some point it's just effective to keep spamming labs (+power plants, of course) at random positions, it makes absolutely no difference where you put those labs, just place them randomly around the map as fast as you can. (Got the highest possible score this way)
* Goal isn't communicated, what score would be considered a good score?
[/spoiler]

Controls:
* Clickable elements (buttons / buildings) have no hover effects, so it's hard to know if they're clickable, and to bring the mouse to the right position.
* Building buttons' hit areas are smaller than they seem, the square box isn't clickable, only the inner image.
* Building popup-menus require a click to open, should just open on hover. Or maybe avoid a menu altogether, as it always contains just one option.

Bugs found:
* Building popup-menus don't close if you click on another building, only if you click on empty space - very frustrating.
* You can place buildings while the game is paused.

Summary:
This game feels like a half-polished jam game that somehow got released. The developer should mostly focus on improving the game design and UX for future projects.

I was surprised at how engaged I became with this game. 

Developer is responsive.

If I had to distil this game down to just a single word, it would be "Whimsy" this entire game just exudes a relentless aura of whimsy, glee and child-like wonder. And despite this child-like energy and aesthetic, it doesn't feel childish, it's fun and at times can actually be quite challenging. 

Ogu is a game where you can just go where you want to really, it doesn't force you anywhere other than the plot line and intro/tutorial, but after that? You're free to go where you want, you wanna go to the mountains? go for it, wait up you wanna stop in the middle and take a trip to the beach? You can sure as hell do that too, and this map is littered with secrets, mini games, puzzles, boss fights, and all that good stuff.

The just has fun with itself, from drawing pictures to fill out your map, to fighting giant monster in a mech, and even an entire boss battle that's a god damned dance-off, and on the point of dancing, it heals you, need HP? just break out some moves and you're golden! 

The puzzles are also excellent, they take a simple concept, such as pushing a block, and takes it as far as possible, they do as much with as little as possible, which makes for both excellent and challenging puzzles. The puzzles range from logic puzzles, physics puzzles, and even a number of riddles, the riddle regarding the questline for fishing for instance had me genuinely stumped, and I had to go do other stuff and then come back to it once it hit me. 

And on the point of fishing, it's one of SEVERAL mini-games, pretty much all of which are great fun, fishing is my personal favourite, it really takes the classic concept of a fishing mini-game and hones in on the fun stuff, it has effectively no luck based element, other than the raririty of the fish, and even then there's an indicator when its a very rare one, and you even have a sign post at each fishing spot showing you which fish can be caught and even shows which you already have caught, and fighting the rare and very rare fish? Well I won't spoil the hilarity of how it looks.  

The other minigames range from a cooking minigame, which can net you some seriously powerful food, to a gem cutting minigame, to bug catching. Again it's just an adventure, you travel the world and do fun stuff.

It also very much has that metroidvania vibe of "Hey I can't go there" then later you unlock something and you're like "WAIT A SECOND" and immedietly travel back to those places. 

The game also has a geniunely really good story, then simultaneously doesn't take itself too seriously, but also isn't entirely ridiculous, like you end up caring about the world, and the characters, furthermore the story doesn't overstay its welcome, and neither does the game, I 100% completed the game in less than 40 hours. 

Just do yourself a favour and play this absolute gem of a game, it has so much charm and heart, and on top of that some seriously stellar gameplay, each boss fight feels unique and fun, and the few times they do reuse a boss it has a changed mechanic that fundementally changes how you approach the fight.

It's simply absolutely phenomenal and a solid 9,5/10 I have VERY few gripes and they're all extremely minor, the worst being a few annoying lacking control and keybinding options, such as the cooking minigame using F and J, and you cannot change it, BUT even that they have an answer for and item you can buy and you can consume it to skip the entire process.

The clipping actually got so bad that it started to hurt my ears. This was especially bad when multiple people were talking at once via the in-game voice chat.

Another thing we noticed was that the monster AI had trouble getting around terrain. We actually managed to get it stuck, simply by baiting it up the stairs. It was completely unable to move until the player it was following jumped down from the stairs. Lastly, the UI can be somewhat unintuitive. After finishing the first level, we were presented with a button that simply read "Exit". It's not entirely clear what this means, as it could be mistaken to mean something along the lines of "exit the current level and continue with the next", like some of us thought initially.

But honestly, after these issues are ironed out, I can genuinely see this becoming a fun game to play with friends. I've seen the audio issues reported multiple times by other people. Fixing those should definitely be a priority. In its current state however, I can't recommend this game.

What you see is what you get! A fun romp with a couple of quirky kobold buddies. And then tears. Gameplay consists of walking around, searching for and picking up items to help you advance forward, and solving simple puzzles. Standard adventure game fare. But you're not here for that, you're here for the story!

Our kobold heroes are instantly overly attached to Sophie, our protagonist, which is understandable! It's just what kobolds do. The nicer ones, anyway. But I did not expect the same to happen in return, which felt a bit strange. Sophie goes from uncaring to loving very, [i]very[/i] quickly. I suppose it was due to the game being quite short, a little over an hour or so? This makes it somewhat difficult to care about everyone and what is happening to them. What is there is pretty good, but there just isn't enough time to develop the characters and their relationship.

Art is great, gameplay is good, voice acting is quite nice, and the music gets the job done - but I found it to be the one of the weaker parts of the overall presentation.

All in all, good game! Wish there could have been more, and also wish there were more like it!

Graphics: The game's graphics are alright. Not as bad as a unity asset flip, but about rpgmaker quality. The character's sprites are pretty good, but the confused ones are wonky. 

Gameplay: It's nothing too intricate. Just some simple puzzles, deduction, and combining items. But that's not the point of buying this game. 

Setting: You may be asking why this is a category? It's because this game is a weird hybrid of fantasy, that will occasionally throw modern elements such as radios or magazines your way. That's not even including the literal spaceship. 

Story: Oh boy, sit down young chap, because this hopeful to be writer is about to smack down this game so hard, whether that's justified or not. The story is simple, the dragons took a bunch of their kobolds, and left all the others so they could go to space for reasons that are never explained. And since unlike other fantasy settings, these kobolds are summoned creatures, their magical energy reserves are running out. You have Erika, who is clinging onto the faint hope that her "Queen" will come back for her. Niels, who is a stubborn, magic-wielding kobold. And then Bomb, the plucky, chaotic one. So as you progress, the protagonist, Sophie, bonds with these little critters. Erika overcomes her naive thoughts, and decides to follow Sophie. Niels reveals he hid a letter to Bomb from the Queen, which would've told her to get on the ship. Bomb forgives him, stating she never would've abandoned them in the first place. But how does it end? Well, you eventually make it to the vault full of treasure, but the little kobolds are almost out of energy! So, Erika sacrifices herself to reveal...an empty vault. Sophie felt as if she got way too attached to the three strange kobolds that she found, I think she should have came off more unsentimental towards them, since she plays as the greedy treasure hunter, and as the game progressed and the kobolds showed some development towards one another, then she would start to care and feel for them.

Niels is honestly my favorite character in the game. He feels more fleshed out than the other characters and I like the humor in the recurring line: "Kobold Magic!" by him. He seemed a lot more aversion in the dragons, taking a strong disliking in them for going and even hiding an invitation from his friends, refusing to let them go until he realized he was in the wrong in doing so and expressed deep regret for it. 

Bomb is probably my least favorite character, it's not that I find dense but loving characters that speak in third person unlikable but she came off more annoying in the game than cute. Her recurring act in conjuring bombs in cut scenes seemed too repetitive. I know I said that I liked the "Kobold Magic" line from Niels and that was used a lot, but it make Niels hubristic and funny, like there was an ego he had and was proud in showing off his magic towards Sophie. Bomb, however, just conjured bombs and...that's it. I know someone's gonna find it adorable, but for me it was more bothersome. I think it would have been better if I was able to use her bombs in game, perhaps usig her bombs to make a clear path or destroying stuff to get items. I did like the tension she had towards Niels in that one part of the game but, even thought they already pointed it out, it was too rushed.

The gameplay itself was fine too, I thought the puzzles were cool (Although I was pretty lost in that Pipe puzzle, and felt very stupid in not figuring it out and just relied on pressing stuff till something happened). Now the artwork for the game is good, the floating islands looked fine and the character designs were good too.

Overall, it was an okay game, probably not six dollars good but was worth the experience. I just felt there should be more added to it, more tension, more character development, a lot of missed opportunities here and there. If you want a quick story with not a lot to do, then this might be for you. As for the developers, I hope you all don't feel discouraged by this.
