BYTE CATS is a 2d platformer in a pixelated artstyle. It offers a truly challenging experience – for someone like me with little platformer-experience - by gradually increasing difficulty. I just started with Chapter 2 and the difficulty really took off. BYTE CATS offers 5 chapters. It took me around 2 hours to reach Chapter 2. Provided the following chapters take just as long, we’re looking at a game which is around 10 hours long – perhaps longer, since difficulty increases.

What made BYTE CATS special to me was the outstanding music. Really, I can’t stress this enough. The music is superb! It has a metal-y rocky vibe to it. It works with repetition which made them stuck in my head and it just sounds “cool” and “speedy”. Some levels offer classics from the classic-genre which gave me the impression of depth despite the fact I haven’t seen much of the story yet.

The story evolves around 3 cats who died. However, their souls were reincarnated as far as I understood it. Before each level you can choose which cat you want to play. Why that matters? Each cat has a special ability that can help you beat the level. There even is a little progression system integrated to upgrade your cat.

Gameplay is smooth and Performance was great. I did not encounter any bugs so far either, game feels quite polished. The game would profit from some variety in sound effects. For now, every sound emitting entity has only one sound file, which can sound a bit same-y. Yet it’s fun to hear the stereotypical punch sound when you hop onto an enemy. Every time you die, you get a slap. Okay okay sorry game, I’m not that good, okay?

Like every game, BYTE CATS has some frustrating moments which to be fair might just be due to my personal preference. Especially in Chapter 2 now there are quite a lot of hard passages within the level. Checkpoints aren’t that frequent though which results in having to play the same passage repeatedly till you reach the initial point where you’re failing. I would’ve enjoyed some more checkpoints. Furthermore, it takes some practice to get used to the walljump. First, I felt the timeframe was too short to hit the button, but it appears that I’ve just pressed too fast. Feels a bit off but that might just be me.

I’ve read that 10 bucks were too much to demand. I’m torn with this, because the music is clearly well produced and must’ve taken a lot of effort. Also, it seems that the game is longer than you’d imagine. I think within the 10-euro price tag it would be awesome for the developers to provide the soundtrack of this game. I’ve looked on YouTube, but I couldn’t find it unfortunately. Pretty please, devs? I’d like to listen to it outside of the game. :)

To summarize: If you’re a fan of platforming then this game is a no-brainer. I mean I’m not into platformers and even I enjoyed it. I didn’t. I think that’s quite telling.

I had some fun with Byte Cats. It's got a fun story and vibe, and it is clearly inspired by some of the greatest platformers ever made, namely Donkey Kong Country and Super Meat By. The hellish landscapes, the cannon jumping, the bouncy tires, it’s all there. The platforming is pretty straightforward at first, but the difficulty quickly ramps up. I was cursing at my screen by the midway point of the first region.

However, it does have a few problems. For as often as steep as the difficulty ramps and as often as you’ll be dying, there is a pretty annoying pause before you are able to control your character again. There’s the loading screen of course (though some games of this style have found a way to get around this, like Celeste), but there’s an extra what feels like a two-second pause when you revive at the checkpoint. That doesn’t sound like a lot, but when you’re respawning 10-20 times in the same section, it begins to add up. 

The characters also don’t have any inertia, so it stops completely when you take your finger off the button, even in the air. This made the wall-jumping portions strange to navigate at first until I got used to that feature.

Overall though, Byte Cats is quite fun. If you’re looking for a tough platformer and have more than a little bit of patience, I would recommend it.

After playing a couple of hours, I once again wish that Steam had a 'neutral' review option.

I love supporting Indie devs, and it seems a lot of soul has gone into the production of the game, but for me, it's too bare bones to be sold for the price they are asking. The game revolves around the idea of having your characters sitting around the table, with each one performing a different attack to attempt to knock out all other player's characters first. It's simple and fun for probably the first hour, but then it starts to lack.

Although the game is marketed as "pvp" there is no pvp except with those on your Steam friends list, and even then, the number of different cards/characters you have to bring to a game means that most matches feel identical.

I think the game [i]could work[/i], but it needs more time in the oven. I personally would love to see a lot more cards be introduced (perhaps some that don't require a physical character) and some kind of deck system alongside proper randomised matchmaking.

If you find the game on sale, I would say go for it, you'll at least get more fun out of it than those $5 Unity asset flips. But if you're coming for a new spin on the online PvP card game genre, then this is not it - maybe after a few updates, but not yet.

After playing about half an hour of this game, in its current state, as much as I would like to recommend it - I can't.

The game's idea is very cute if not overly complex: you can think of it is a rock-paper-scissors with a twist.
The game's graphics are very eye pleasing and for sure one of this game's stronger points.

However:

1. The game's options, at least the resolution selection, do [b]not[/b] stick: I started the game, changed the resolution from FHD to 4K, quit the game and enteres again only for the resolution to be reset to FHD.
This happens all the time.
Yes, it may be connected to me playing full-screen... in which case, disable the option to choose resolution in the first place.
Also, when changing from FHD to 4K, or the other way around, I didn't see any noticeable change.

2. The offered tutorial is too simplistic and doesn't really explain the game.
It gives a very quick summary of the game's controls and even quicker review of the game's mechanics, and that's it.

Sure, in a game like this there isn't [b]a lot[/b] to take in, and still, a full-blown, step-by-step tutorial would have been appreciated.

3. The [b]in-game[/b] help screen, and yes, it's [b]only[/b] in-game and can [b]not[/b] be accessed from the main menu, [b]is[/b] comprehensive... but also glitchy with some parts of the text overlapping each other making reading some parts of the 4-pager documentation impossible.

4. Unlike my previosu assumption, you can have local hot-seat without a turn timer... too bad you have to dig in the pre-match settings to find it out.

Maybe if there was some [b]helpful, accessible[/b] documentation to explain everything...

All in all, this is a very eye-candy pleasing, rock-paper-scissors with a twist, and a nice twist it is.
And for the price it [b]is[/b] worth it.
I [b]do[/b] enjoy playing it, don't get me wrong.

But I want it to be better, and be better for this game means fix the tutorial and help documentation.
Until these are fixed I will [b]not[/b] recommend this game.

I played the game for the first time just after the Scarlet Forest update was added. What a fun game! This is a semi-roguelike, but rather than randomly generated dungeons you get randomly assigned characters and Emblem pickups. The whole group (3 characters at a time) shares a HP and MP pool, so you've got to give some thought before you blast away with each characters special abilities.
Emblems can be equipped using points earned through levelling up, however when you level up you have to choose from a HP boost, and MP boost or an additional Emblem Point. Emblems can be picked up at the end of a battle, through special events such as looting a corpse found on road or by purchasing them from merchants using gold you collect from monsters. Equipping an Emblem provides a buff of some kind and certain combinations can synergize with each other, adding another layer of complexity to the game. You also collect Soul Fragments, which can be used to permanently unlock a character to start a game with.

Overall, this a great concept and I can't wait to see where the developer takes the game with further updates and refinements.

[b]1) Gameplay:[/b] I found the game's mechanics really cool, you enter the bank as a civilian, completely unarmed, disguise yourself and do some tasks to maintain your disguise. Afterwards, when you build up enough confidence, you gain access to weapons and engage in combat. Both the disguise and combat parts are pretty fun.
[b]2) Story:[/b] The game has a pleasing story, but it doesn't show much relation with the game, I mean, you have to read the story on the Steam store page to understand what's going on. I think they could go even further, adding details about the story in the middle of the game so that those who haven't read the story can understand. Anyway, if you read the game's story and then go play the game, you'll have a good experience and stay on top of everything.
[b]3) Graphics:[/b] The graphics are very beautiful and the map design is very well produced. It's rich in details, has some easter eggs and it greatly elevates the player experience. I believe that one of the best things about the game, besides the gameplay, is the beauty of the map.
[b]4) Soundtrack and effects:[/b] The game doesn't exactly have a soundtrack. It is possible to perceive several sound effects (very well planned, by the way) during the gameplay, which adds a lot to the player's experience and leads to a more intense immersion. In a certain part of the game you feel as if you were the main character, with the tension, the breathing sound, the heart beating... to sum up, this was very well designed.
[b]5) Replayability:[/b] It's not a long game, but the value is in the different levels of difficulty, you can try to complete the game in a higher difficulty than you've already done, and making things much more challenging (depending on the level of difficulty you play). So it doesn't have such a high replay value, enjoy every moment of the game when you first play it and you will enjoy it.
[b]6) Conclusion:[/b] For the price that the game is being sold, I believe it is worth buying. There are some details that the developers still need to fix, but nothing that ruins the game experieence, just some basic things that if adjusted will make the game even better. Overall, it's a very good game, especially since it's an indie game (it's not so easy to find good indie games these days). I had a good experience with the game and found it very interesting.

So I'm a newbie to shmups, only ever played Mushihime-sama and Deathsmiles. First off I wanna ssay the graphics are awesome. You have these fleshy monstrous enemies while you're just a mechanical ship which shows the contrast and really shows how good the sprite art is. You have 2 firing modes like in every other shmup but what differentiates this one is the bomb system. The first level you might play like me and get a little lost just shooting like in other shmups, you very soon notice picking up bomb items immediately detonates them so you wonder what's actually going on, you then notice the bomb counter in the top right be a bar that refills. This honestly suprised me, like why is it a bar? Did I mess something up? Then I used the bomb button and it didn't clear the screen, no it only cleared and damaged anything within a little circle around the ship and started refilling. This had me stoked, a bomb on an actual refill? Then I panicked and again pressed while it was refilling and it short circuited the bomb and just cleared an even smaller circle of bullets around you. This is such a cool and engaging mechanic since it wasn't just put in but instead the level design actually takes advantage of the bomb from level 2 onward, for example you have enemies behind flesh walls you can't shoot and have to instead kill with the full bomb bar, this just makes the whole game so fun and honestly I might say from these 3 shmups I played this one might be the most fun and interesting just bc of this clever mechanic. So I definitely recommend for the price

Rating: 🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟☆☆☆☆☆ (5/10)

My Experience: 🏁
Barro GT offers an experience that feels familiar yet underwhelming. The game has a racing concept that could have been thrilling, but instead, it ends up feeling repetitive and lacking in excitement. While it starts with some promise, I found myself quickly disengaging due to limited variety in gameplay and a lack of innovation. It’s the kind of game where you can enjoy a few minutes of fun, but it doesn't offer enough to keep you hooked for long.

Gameplay: 🚗
The gameplay in Barro GT centers around racing, but the mechanics feel basic and often clunky. While the racing itself isn’t inherently bad, it lacks the depth and polish that would make it feel exciting. The controls are fine, but not precise enough to make racing feel smooth or rewarding. The game doesn’t introduce much in the way of new features or challenges, and the tracks quickly begin to feel monotonous. Overall, the gameplay doesn’t evolve in a way that keeps you invested.

Conclusion: 🏁
Barro GT has a concept that could have worked, but it ultimately falls short due to its repetitive gameplay and lack of refinement. It’s the kind of game that may appeal to casual players looking for something quick and easy, but for anyone looking for a deeper or more engaging racing experience, this game doesn’t quite deliver. It’s an average title that doesn’t stand out in any meaningful way.

TLDR; It's good for some nostalgia, but the game just doesn't feel good to play. Buy it if you like supporting Future cop spinoffs, but don't expect anything groundbreaking


*The new turrets and tank types are fun and a good idea, even if there is nothing visually different about them to make them easy to identify

*The effect on Sky Captain's voice is really nice, and feels close enough to the original that I won't complain

*I only played on 2 maps, but they were basically copy/paste of eachother, so it felt pretty boring. I understand the 3 lane thing is popular for mobas since it's balanced and easy to understand, but man is it boring 

*No auto-locking like in the original Future Cop means you have less feedback on if your attacks are working, especially since the attack distances are so short. I do know a red triangle appears above the unit when it is within range, but that also doesn't seem to always work, especially if the unit is moving away from you while you're attacking

*The new outpost claiming system is nice, and a good design choice, but I still have no idea how to send units from the outpost

*There's very very very little feedback when attacking or being hit. Sometimes I'll die without really knowing I was attacked to begin with

*The tanks feel too strong compared to the mech. I'd bet it'd be possible to win by just staying in your base the whole match, but I am not going to test that out.

*The weapon selection is very limited- they all seem to do the same thing. The numbers are tweaked, yes, but that's all they do. There's no mortor type weapon, no arcing electricity, no riot shield, no grenade launcher, etc. The gun is a hitscan with small range, the heavy is a projectile with a small range, and the special is an aoe with a small range (not even sure if it hits sky captain). No variety there

*The website linked for the game doesn't work, and there is no discord to contact the developers, share strategies, schedule games, etc etc. (as a note to the dev, I'd be happy to make the discord for you, but I feel like you may have abandoned the project by now)

*The multiplayer is also dead (not surprising since I was the only one playing the game at the time)

A competent tower defense game, though a bit slow to get going. Feels like it takes a lot of inspiration from Defense Grid: The Awakening.

Pros:
Clean presentation, no bugs that I encountered, acceptable price point for the amount of content, UI is excellent, tower upgrades make sense, enemies have physics allowing for interesting interactions, and balancing that lands nicely between challenging and punishing.

Cons:
No wave preview feature, no means of speeding up waves, early levels suffer from lack of variety in enemy type and tower availability, and has a bit of an inverse difficulty curve where the beginning of levels tends to be harder than the end.

Overall, if you're a fan of Tower Defense, Cyber Tower is a simple but competent entry to the genre. A couple tweaks to early pacing and the addition of some quality of life features would take this to the next level.

A change of heart, changing my review to positive. The game isn't perfect, but the combination of incremental improvements and developer responsiveness have changed my mind.  
The game is pretty much a standard tower defense game. 
There is a limited number of towers, only six, with only two upgrades for five of them (the other has none) and no choices or decision making. 
The towers are as follows, energy (worth while. ten energy every ten seconds or so at the first level) a slowing tower, a machine gun type, missiles with a little AOE, and a big gun. The last gun is unusual in my experience, a wave buster. It is pretty expensive, but fires a mass of missiles, then self destructs. Has its uses in the late game, but it is a little larger than he regular towers, so you need to be sure to leave a space to place one. 
The route has sections where pathing is available, then long stretches without, with gun posts on each side. 
There are only a handful of enemies, and they don't really have much to distinguish them aside from their number of hit points. Some can attack, but only seem to do so when the path is blocked, which works for me. I normally dislike when towers can be destroyed. 
They have recently added some primitive target prioritizing, which is nice. 
The game does not have any strategic upgrades, nor does it have any tactical attacks or other options. 
Sadly there is really very little to distinguish one level from the next. There re forty levels, but they are all just the same pieces rearranged without anything really interesting to make later ones different, except for more and bigger enemies. 
All in all, at the price I paid, I decent offering, I feel that I have gotten my money's worth. That said, I wouldn't mind of the developers found more ways to make the game more interesting. One thumb up.

The system requirements in this game are incredibly misleading, the store page states that it only requires a GTX 770 and a "3rd gen i5", with 2gb of RAM on Windows Vista. First and foremost, the Vista requirement is very misleading as Steam ended support for operating systems older than Windows 10 on January 1st. So despite what the system requirements say, this game would not run on Windows Vista. 

Next off, the GPU stated in the requirements is a GTX 770 which only has 2gb of VRAM...As this game runs off of the DirectX12 API and uses UE5. 2gb of VRAM in this game will simply not cut it, I am testing this game on my rig with a Radeon RX 7900XT (20 gb's of VRAM) and will report that at 1440p Default settings (This game has no graphical options) The game uses 2.5 gb's of VRAM, higher than the 2gb on the GTX 770 and that's not even accounting for background tasks running on your card. 

Which also brings me into my issue with the system RAM requirements, this game lists 2gb of RAM enough to run the game. Considering that Windows 10 itself will hardly run off of 2gb of RAM, this is false. If we are going to revisit the GPU (GTX 770) with 2gb of VRAM and the game itself using as much 2.5 gb of VRAM. Then this means that we are going to have a memory leak where the game will leak into system memory because of the lack of VRAM. Leaving your system with only 1.5 gb of system RAM, not accounting for the 500mb of System RAM the game already utilizes. Leaving you with a total of 1 gb, obviously Windows 10 cannot function on a single gigabyte of system RAM. So this will likely result in the game being unplayable or just a flat out crash. 

This game seemed very promising but this just ruined it for me and I can't recommend it.

[b]Summary:[/b] Brain meltdown in a super atmospheric puzzle platformer 🤯

ROTA is a game where your character can rotate the world by walking around the edges. Jumping over edges won't rotate the world.

This concept sounds very simple on paper, but the developer applied this concept in so many creative ways and created fantastic challenges behind each of the game's doors.

Add some spike traps and moveable boxes to the formula and the puzzles are now really tricky and challenging.

I liked that the platforming aspect is not overly complex, you don't have to worry about "making the jump" or complex timing.

[b]So exploration and solving the levels is never hectic, I always played at my own pace.[/b]

This whole calming mood is supported by the cool music and ambient sounds. It creates a chill atmosphere where I could easily relax (while my brain was steaming).

In each level, there is a gem that you need to collect to complete it and that counts towards a global counter of said gems.
The gems are used to unlock new doors, featuring new game worlds behind them. The different worlds are vibrant and cute giving off a nice vibe and the worlds also introduce new game mechanics and features.

The difficulty curve is really good, although some levels were particularly hard and made me scratch my head. On the other hand, the dopamine kicked in super hard when I finally managed to beat the level! 😁

I absolutely recommend giving ROTA a try, it's a super interesting concept and the game is overall perfectly executed.

It's not really bad, but it's definitely not what I expected from the description. The elements are all there, but at the core is something not mentioned: A hard-stop time limit in every stage, and a timer where the enemy spawns get exponentially more intense, making navigating or avoiding damage almost impossible. 

This makes it feel like it's supposed to be a speedrun game, except the levels are randomly generated and you have very little in the way of movement tools. You don't really have time to pick and choose upgrades or explore around, you have to rush for the tokens required to get to the next level, if you see any good upgrades (or maybe good) grab them on the way (if you have enough money from killing enemies on the go), and then camp at the exit until the timer hits a certain spot farming money for the next level.

Normally with roguelikes you have a few approaches: carefully explore, choose how to spend resources, risk vs. reward of dumping resources into one option over another, or rush through if there is a scaling element in the hopes of getting lucky enough to keep ahead of the curve. Here you don't have those options at all, it's JUST "rush forward at all times until you're ready to leave". It makes it feel kind of pointless to play.

On top of that, the weapons are pure stat sticks. They basically all feel the same to use, with the exception of some bad ones that I'm pretty sure you should NOT use. So you grab the best weapon you can find and dump upgrades into that but it doesn't matter if it's a shotgun or uzi or bolt action because ultimately your playstyle is exactly the same.

Enemies just spawn everywhere around you, so that forces your hand. Enemy spawn rate increases rapidly once it starts up, forcing your hand. The levels are VERY vertical but you only have a pretty wimpy double jump and iffy air dash, which means much of your limited time is just platforming up to the token hands, also forcing your hand. You basically have no time to explore, choose, etc. and the best combat approach (because of the chaotic enemy mass spawns) is always just "shoot in front of you while running in a serpentine".

If you are interested in the idea of a roguelike designed around just going as fast as you can with no real dynamics other than what that forces on you, this is definitely the game for you. Otherwise, I am not sure what audience might find it fun. 

One last note: You have to redo the intro/tutorial level every time you start, which wastes ~20 seconds. Which doesn't sound like much but how many times do you rerun roguelikes? Hundreds? That is gonna add up to hours eventually, and it doesn't add anything. I'm guessing it's to avoid starting the death timer in the first real level until you pick your weapon but there has to be a less tedious way to do that.

My recommendation ultimately came down to the extreme low price of this game.  If it was more expensive, I don't know if I would recommend it.  It doesn't seem to have any glaring flaws, but it also does not excite me, either.

EpicRecovery is a vertically scrolling shoot 'em up that is laid out more like a test.  Which fit the story I've unlocked so far.  Each stage has a number of enemy waves showing the enemy type to the player kinda like future pieces in Tetris.  Additionally, the game indicates where these enemy waves are coming on screen, as well as; the size of the ship(s) via the size of the indication chevron.  And the size indication is nice, since I rarely look at the lineup of enemy ship waves coming.

I suppose the name of the game comes from the fact that things can quickly become a bullet hell if you lose dominance of the play area and have to get it back.  Often using the limited resource bomb attack clearing the screen and destroying the popcorn enemies.  Or conversely, destroying the larger enemy ships, which often also clears their bullets. 

There's nothing inherently wrong with the game play.  However, I find the presentation very sterile and more like a puzzle game.  The stages feel like little tests. You're even graded on your performance each stage.  But because each stage is a jumble of small, medium and large enemy ships, if doesn't really feel like I'm piloting a space fighter ship.  Even if all the shmup mechanics are there.  I suppose the lack of a background layer or terrain to show progress is partly to blame.  And possibly the lack of mid-level and end-level bosses (at least for the amount of stages I reached) reinforces that.  As well as the stages themselves being pretty short.  I can't quite put my finger on what's missing here.

EpicRecovery just leaves me underwhelmed.  I can't say entirely why.  It's not doing anything obviously wrong, but even when I'm forced with weave and dodge or absolutely controlling the field, the game just doesn't thrill me like other shooters.  But because this game isn't expensive, and because I can't articulate why I'm underwhelmed; I'm still going to give it the thumb's up.  Just know, it's an incredibly weak recommend.

I wanted this game to be something amazing.  My next world to disappear in to.  I put in the hours and the time and after 500 hours I am sad to say I can't support this product anymore.  

It is a beautiful game and wonderful crafting system, but there are a few things holding it back.

1.  The developers could do a better job telling us what is going on and where they are going.  Yes they released a road map awhile ago but it hasn't been much since.  This ties in to my other concerns

2.  A social sandbox game should have better social systems in place than this.  it took them six months to get chat to a slightly better place and that was done with discord integration. I am still not sure if it is a good move or not for the game.  In this same span of time we got market stalls put in to the game and some gold economy.  You can only sell at this time and no buy orders in place.  ( I don't even know if they ever will be?) and has to be at each persons stalls.  These are items that should have been in place prior to early access.

3. crafting is grindy without feeling satisfying: (I love to grind in games too) I am going to give some examples here.  I loved the idea of running a tavern for a town and focused on food, drinks and booze.  However spending hours (days with some skills) to make 100-250 of the SAME item to level my skill one point leaves you feeling like crap.  To make matters worse cooking recipes lack a unique feeling as the next item you can make just increases health by 5 points or stamina by 5 (or something else marginal).  Once a player has these high enough there is no need for any of the lower items.  Or imagine making 300 pick axes to level up once.  Their idea to mix it up was anything that requires more components gives more experience.   But they forget that also means more time grinding.  So do we really get anything out of it for the extra steps?

4. Magic: This one really bothers me.  It is a beautiful game but all your magic is currently tied to a weapon and there are maybe a dozen spells in the game?  Want to cast fireballs? Better have a leather bracer that lets you?  Want to heal?  Go get the headband?  Taunt? Magical sword.  This is a horrible system imo.

5. No character development:  Aside from having higher skills my character doesn't feel special, unique or remotely important.  The value of my character is strictly connected to how much time I spent leveling a crafting skill or hitting a target with a weapon.

6. Combat:  I normally am not concerned with combat in a game but after 6 months of "We're working on it" its become nothing still. Each time you hit a target with the weapon you are holding it increases your weapon xp by 100 points.  Flat rate,, Want to get your weapon to max skill?  Hit a mob...any mob 10,933 times and you will max the skill.  Weapons have 1 skill ability and if a magic weapon will have a proc ability or maybe a spell.  To make matters worse, there is so little to kill.  Deer, bears, fox, badgers, boars are your animals.  Zebians, inquisitors and ghosts are the rest. Some of the latter will look different here or there but they all hit hard as hell so make sure you get the best stuff possible to farm them for crappy mats and gold.

All and all, its a beautiful puddle.  Great to look at but no depth. 

I am so sorry everyone, please go elsewhere until they get their act together.

I am completely hooked on this game. The world is beautifully crafted, with breathtaking landscapes, intricate details, and an immersive atmosphere that pulls you in.  

As of writing, the game is in early access, so yes, there are bugs. However, in my experience, they’ve been nothing more than minor inconveniences—things you’d expect in a work-in-progress title.  

I've seen a lot of comments claiming the game becomes boring quickly or that there's "nothing to do." I couldn't disagree more. It really comes down to what you enjoy in a game.  

At its core, this is a builder's paradise. The gameplay revolves around designing and constructing your home, cottage, or even a full-blown castle, while crafting to unlock better materials, equipment, and decorative elements. If you're a creative player who enjoys sandbox-style freedom, there's an endless amount of content to engage with.  

That said, if you're someone who prefers structured gameplay with quests, missions, or an engaging combat system, this might not be for you. Combat exists, but it’s not the focus. If grinding for resources and perfecting your build sounds like a chore rather than a joy, you’ll likely find yourself bored before long.  

The game is quite forgiving compared to many survival/building titles:  
✔ No resource loss – If you misplace or demolish a building piece, you get 100% of your materials back.  
✔ Death isn't punishing – Dying simply means retrieving your gear from your body, no permanent loss.  
✔ Grindy but rewarding – Expect a slow but steady progression system. If you don’t like grinding for materials and upgrades, this might not be for you.  

While the game is technically an MMO, I’ll admit the world feels fairly empty—at least where I am. I typically run into 2-3 players per session, which isn’t a dealbreaker for me, but if you're hoping for a thriving, player-filled world, it might be hit or miss.  

That said, playing with friends or in a clan significantly enhances the experience. The grind becomes easier, and it’s a lot of fun exploring the map, discovering other players’ builds, and working together on massive projects.  

You’ll probably enjoy this if you like:  
✅ Building, crafting, and designing your own home or town  
✅ Sandbox-style games with freedom to create at your own pace  
✅ Beautiful medieval environments  
✅ Relaxing, open-ended gameplay with no pressure to "win"  

You might not enjoy this if you:  
❌ Hate grinding for materials and upgrades  
❌ Prefer structured missions, quests, or story-driven objectives  
❌ Need a clear endgame or final goal (this game keeps going)  
❌ Want a heavily populated multiplayer world  

Final Thoughts: This game isn't for everyone, but if you’re a fan of immersive sandbox building and medieval aesthetics, it’s a fantastic experience. It’s still in early access, so I’m excited to see where it goes. If you're looking for direction, story, or intense combat, this might not be your cup of tea—but for creative builders, it’s an absolute gem.

One thing that really turned me off is the subscription model planned after early access. I’m not a fan of pay-to-play MMOs unless the content justifies the cost, and right now, Pax Dei doesn’t offer enough to warrant it.

The biggest issue? There’s not much to do. No real quests, no meaningful progression outside of building and combat. For an MMORPG, even in early access, there should be at least a few quests to guide new players. Instead, the game leaves you guessing where to go and what to do. Sure, there's a roadmap, but if you're looking for immersion, expect to feel lost—a lot.

That said, the building system is fantastic—probably the standout feature so far. If you love crafting and designing structures, this might be worth checking out down the line.

Final Verdict: As it stands, I wouldn’t recommend buying Pax Dei at full price. If you're curious, wait for a sale or until it's out of early access to see how the game evolves.

One of the main features of Pax Dei is the collection of essential materials such as wood, stone, and other natural resources. These resources are crucial for building houses, which can eventually evolve into impressive castles.

The game also encourages players to learn various professions, allowing specialization in tasks like carpentry, blacksmithing, or tailoring. While it is possible to play solo, collaborating with friends makes it easier to progress and face greater challenges.

Although Pax Dei offers opportunities for territorial conquest and combat, my personal interest lies more in gathering resources and crafting items. I enjoy exploring the world, collecting materials, and creating useful objects, which I find more rewarding than fighting.

In conclusion, Pax Dei is a versatile game that allows each player to enjoy the experience at their own pace, whether through building, crafting, or conquering.

Crow Country pays homage to classic survival horror titles like many other games alike on the market currently, but this one manages to stand out more than the rest and bring its own unique experience. There are some clear inspirations taken from PS1 era graphics, but no other game looks, plays or feels like this one in particular. It's not trying to be like Resident Evil or Silent Hill it is its own unique experience, it's Crow Country. For a horror game it ironically gives me a unique feel of nostalgia and warmth, like I'm revisiting parts of my childhood I never actually experienced. It's incredibly unique low poly blocky art style mixed with its stellar soundtrack sets the tone and atmosphere perfectly, making it feel surreal or very dream-like. Even though I was never fond of theme parks Its rich beautifully designed environments make this theme park seem like one breathing entity. It also has one of the cutest mascots I've ever seen, I adore that crow fella in the heart of the park.

The progression and gameplay aspects are simple but incredibly satisfying. Traversing through different areas of the map and exploring them peaks more curiosity to see what piece of clue or story next area might present to you. The weapons are not only very useful as self defense but they're your very powerful tools too. It isn't afraid to hold your hand a bit too much sometimes, because finding resources is a tad bit too easy, but that's honestly great. Not every horror game needs to be punishing and grounding, its a breath of fresh air having to put up a fair fight against enemies and I'm glad it encourages that especially considering gunplay is very fun and satisfying, enemies can easily overrun you if you're not careful enough. Not to mention, randomized enemy encounters and designs are beyond impressive.
It explains itself well without being too convoluted and delivers one of the most top tier storytelling I've seen in a while

The devs KNEW what they were doing with this, massive credits should be given for their flawless writting.[/spoiler] The jokes she cracks are always chuckle worthy and are very fitting which is why the game doesn't take itself too seriously sometimes despite its tone. Humor is very well thought of and placed well, it fits the overall style of the game. It sometimes feels very heartwarming even though for the most part it isn't. It's a beautiful but dark game all in one which is all you really need. (It's also yet another game that makes me wish women were real)

Crow Country rules, and is the most fun I've had with a survival horror game. If you've never played a survival horror game before, I think would be an amazing entry to the genre. Either way, this is a fantastic game absolutely oozing with style and charm.

If you told me you were going to buy me a survival horror game without telling me what it was, and asked whether I'd prefer something from a AAA studio or more independent studios and developers, I'd choose the latter every time. To me, it seems way more likely that indie studios/devs will innovate and play with norms and conventions, while also taking risks that AAA studios simply can't afford to do. Yes, there are definitely good, if not great AAA releases within the last five years, but have they really brought anything new and innovative to the genre? Do we really need another over-the-shoulder style survival horror game? We could argue all day on these questions, but the point I'd ultimately try and underline is that the indie scene for survival horror is undeniably more creative. Not necessarily good, but just is simply trying new things. Signalis, Darkwood, Stay out of the House, and Song of Horror are all WAY more interesting to me than playing something like the Deadspace remakes. 

That said, the indie scene is not without stagnation. One "trend" that feels like it's becoming worn, are having older PS1-era graphics, in lieu of more polished renders and characters. This makes sense, of course, because older graphics demand less of indie developers, and can still achieve the same thrills of the genre. However, at this moment, the style feels a bit pablum.

Enter Crow Country, a game that clearly wears it's influence on it's sleeve, but manages to still stand out. How? The creators of this game have a clear vision on what works about it's influences, and what doesn't. The controls feel fluid, but never feel too tough to learn. Combat starts a little tricky, but feels great once you get down the basics. You can dodge enemies in this game, but going too fast can prove reckless as you may run into traps. Add to all of this some charming characters, great pacing, genuine scares, an interesting mystery, attention to detail, and a clear love of the genre make this game a success. 

The other thing that is wonderful about this game, is that while it's not as innovative as something like Darkwood, it clearly has it's own voice, and is incredibly confident in what it has to say. After playing through this game, I'd say that confidence is greatly earned. Highly recommended for survival horror fans.

Quick Description:
-Crow Country is a such a cool Survival Horror Indie gem.  The controls are atrocious on keyboard (can't rebind), and it always feels a bit slow and cumbersome navigating the world.  I also found the grainy pixelated PS1 visuals made it difficult to see things.  But if you can look past these small frustrations, this game is a ton of fun.  It's a really cool blend of modern and retro in mostly all the right ways.  The world feels very alive in a really unique way (you can interact with almost everything in the world).  Every biome has a distinct visual look and the soundtrack/sound design is perfect for this game.

Consensus:
-Solid Game (Tier 3 and makes up 35% of my reviews).  This game grew on me more and more with each passing hour.  It is on the easier side, but they have added a Hard Mode which is a great addition.  There are tons of secrets and most of them are very intuitive, making you feel clever for figuring things out for yourself.  This game really shines in the Fun department, which is exactly what I was hoping for when I purchased it.

Puzzles are reasonable, environments are beautiful, the weapons all feel satisfying, the enemies are delightfully creepy, and the plot wound up being far deeper and enjoyable than I predicted. If you like games like Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Alisa, etc. this is a must-play.

[h3]The good:[/h3]
[list]
[*]The game has a very unique art style; the low-poly characters mixed with the backgrounds that resemble pre-rendered art from early PS1 games (while actually being fully 3D) is extremely appealing  and lends the game a visual quality all its own. This is compounded further by its unique haunted theme park setting; fans of the Five Nights at Freddy's series will find a lot to love in its cute-creepy visuals.
[*]The story it tells is pretty compelling, with some twists and red herrings. The characters are charming, especially the protagonist Mara, whose quirky dialogue in the flavor text while exploring the park is always worth reading.
[*]Most of the puzzles are very good and usually feel pretty satisfying to solve. With one major exception (see “The Bad”) they never feel unfair. Many require some outside-the-box thinking, as opposed to the “find the note with the combination to the lock” puzzles and the like that the genre tends to lean on.
[*]The game cuts an extremely brisk pace; you are almost constantly being drip-fed both new puzzles to solve and solutions to ones you've previously discovered. The game also features an optional treasure map item, unlockable about 1/3 of the way through the game's runtime, that shows you where all the optional secrets are, so you can pursue them or ignore them at your discretion.
[/list]

[h3]The bad:[/h3]
[list]
[*]The game is quite short. I finished the game, explored everything, and solved all the optional puzzles in a little over 6 hours, though there is a post-game mode and a higher difficulty mode I didn't dip into. While many will find it satisfying as is, I personally could've done with another few hours for the main game.
[*]The game world is quite small, leading to a lot of backtracking. You will have seen almost the entirety of the game's world within the first hour or two of the game, and I got pretty sick of traversing the same areas over and over again. Coupled with its short run-time, it makes me wish there was just more to do.
[*]The puzzles and story are the stars of the show here, as opposed to the combat, which feels pretty tacked on. Two additional modes exist, one to increase combat difficulty and one to remove combat entirely, so your mileage may vary on this point.
[*]While most of the puzzles are fun and satisfying to solve, they overall skew a bit on the easy side, especially for seasoned veterans of the genre. 
[*]There was one puzzle that, in my opinion, was extremely poorly designed, enough that I feel the need to mention it here. The puzzle itself was purely optional, but I had no way of knowing that. If you're already playing the game, please just look up the solution to the [spoiler]mushroom dinner[/spoiler] puzzle, or skip it if you don't care about finding all the secrets, and spare yourself the trouble of solving it yourself.
[/list]

[h3]Conclusion:[/h3]
Crow Country is a fun, bite-sized survival horror adventure that distills the appeal of its bigger genre counterparts to a short but sweet experience. If you've ever wanted to jump into something like Resident Evil or Silent Hill, but were put off by the violence, difficulty, and adult horror of those games, I strongly recommend starting here. While fans of the genre might be left finding it a bit too brief, simple, and lacking in challenge for their liking, it's very clearly going for broader appeal in its design, and its art style and charming world and characters really elevate what would otherwise be a somewhat by-the-numbers experience into an absolute gem.

Crow County is a wonderfully succinct and self-contained adventure horror RPG. This game features a stylish PS1 retro aesthetic that really clicked with me - it's sort-of similar to Animal Well insofar as it's a "new" game trying (and succeeding) to look "old". That said, outside of the shared aesthetic this game handles waaaay better than any PS1 title ever did and features none of the janky camera angles (looking at you Resident Evil). Don't underestimate the scares though, this game will get you to jump (at least a few times). 

I beat this game in 8 hours playing very casually and unfocused on collectables which is very uncharacteristic for me. Honestly, I was just so much more engaged in progressing through the story and figured I would be rewarded for doing so (and I was right). I was equally enamored with the puzzles which threaded the needle of "too easy" vs. "too hard" perfectly. I felt like such a lil' braniac solving the puzzles the game presented even if they weren't all that difficult. I only ever got stumped once and, honestly, it was my own fault. 

Tl;dr buy this game - it's high quality and it's on sale until February 24th. The fact this takes under 10 hours to beat means you aren't sinking time into it even if you don't love it, and trust me, there will come a night you're gonna be bored and feel like getting spooked.

Verdict: Keep an eye on this game, but do not buy if you're looking for an EA game to look into.

As a big fan of the first Greedfall, I was excited to see what Spiders was going to do with the next game in the franchise. Even in an Early Access state, the game still has a ways to go before I would even consider it on par with its predecessor. I've played all the way through where the EA takes after writing this.

Pros:
-World Building: Which was my favorite part from the original game, is still present. I was pleasantly surprised the game continues to build on the lore that already existed to give a full glimpse into what time was like before the first game.
-Story Direction Overall: Playing up until the end of EA, while I think the pacing needs a heavy look at, the overarching story direction I really enjoyed and was curious to know where your character ends up next.
-World Environment: The game takes you through quite a few different areas and scenery. I do wish they just put more treasures or side nuggets for you to find throughout.

Cons:
-Combat: It is way too underdeveloped still and the battles are just not fun. As a big cRPG fan I do actually prefer this kind of combat, but after playing the first game a lot, it was very clear a lot of assets were just re-slapped onto this new system. It would of been better if they just refined the system they already had in the 1st game and gone from there. I basically consider it an Alpha Build of Dragon Age: Inquisition Combat.
-Party Members: While also kind of an issue I had with the first game, it's hard for me to really relate, or much less, care about at all, this cast of characters. I do wish the characters had a bit more time to develop and converse with one another naturally as this band helping your MC. Party Banter in other games really goes a long way to building this.
-Intro Zone: I honestly did not like at all playing the 'Turtorial' area since all the characters are speaking in native tongue. While 100% immersive, it turned the first few hours into an Audiobook as opposed to an active dialogue I was paying attention to.

I genuinely would like Spiders to succeed with this IP but the Game Direction for this at the moment is a hot mess.

First off, just have to say, the new combat system is just awful. One of the reasons I loved the first Greedfall was because of the familiar yet unique combat style. This new style is garbage. It leaves you feeling removed from the game in combat and like you're just trying to play chess. Really hoping that this style is just for the beta and they actually have a combat style like in the first game.

I do like the ability point system and professions or whatever they are called in the game. Allowing you to build more specific for a tank or damage or archer style. 

Overall I was extremely excited for this game and so far the beta has done nothing but regret my purchase. I understand it's still in beta but unless some drastic changes are made, this will be a far cry from the first Greedfall that I enjoyed so much and a waste of the money spent on it.

How can a lonely game with one room have so many hours of enjoyable escapism, find out, if we are happier apart in ISOLANIA. Well, apparently anything can be good when you have a stellar world-building that probes your mind for every feeling of joy and sorrow it can find. You are a new podder in a society where nobody is allowed to leave their designated cell, the sadness is the sickness that you get from other people, and you must stay inside because isolation is the key to salvation. Everything that you need to stay alive is done within your room, and if you question your existence, there are consequences. I want to say it took the game maybe 4 seconds to get my attention because the voice of 'authority' is so compelling, and for the most part it manages to maintain that level of story-telling, even during the moments of downtime, I was always looking forward to the next day. Now the game has a 'waiting' aspect to it which usually amounts to several minutes per day, after you are done with your daily routine, you might have to just **** around for 5 to 10 minutes.

I am sure the claustrophobic vibes were intentional, but it actually got to me in a real way, I was starting to feel a little uncomfortable because of the short walking distance. I like how the game went from being very moody in a negative way, to also being very lighthearted. Later in the game, you get to interact with other people through the mail which was a highlight of the narrative - l think their responses felt very natural, except maybe for the "email" guy, that one was kinda forced. Each character has an interesting look at their situation and in general, I think the game has good writing. Surprisingly, there are a lot of sweet and funny moments as well. 

The game is around 10 hours give or take, but there are a lot of things that could potentially confuse you, and it's not always clear what the next step is. The ending that I picked was rather short, but I think it's appropriate for the story, and I don't really mind that it still has some unanswered questions. My personal playthrough had various technical issues, some of them have been fixed, that said, I am not confident that game will not have any potential softlocks, granted you can generally fix them by fully exiting the game and reloading. Taking everything into consideration, there is not much I can nitpick in terms of the story, if the game itself was not somewhat disjointed with the progression, I think the actual narrative is enjoyable from start to finish.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) Very moody, very atmospheric, unique vibes, and playful as well.
(+) Actually solid narrative and world-building, interesting characters in the mailing list,  just always something that makes you want to keep going.
(+) More content than you might think, lots of variety like mini-games and stupid things you can buy.

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Technical Issues/Triggers [/u] - To be fair, the developer fixed some of the big issues and I managed to complete the game, but I would not go as far as saying that you won't find any softlocks or crashes. Other than that, the game is a bit convoluted, like sometimes I did the right thing and I missed the event (I did the "gate" code correctly, and it didn't work so I wasted another 2 hours looking for something else) That feeling of "strange progression" was with me at least 30% of the game.

Note that game takes about 20 seconds to load when you start a new game, if you click on it,  select wait for the program, it should load (it's not stuck). If you do get the locked interaction bug, exiting the game and loading helps (right now in-game loading does not).

[u] Currency [/u] - when you are making only 100 a day doing the job it sort of complements the oppressive universe, and then the arcades kick in where you can generate 50.000 in a day. I get you made it possible to buy things for progression, but it feels like it takes away from the settings, and instead of feeling like a very believable universe, it starts feeling like a meta game with exploits. I think in retrospect, the arcades should have been more risky, and the prices balanced to scale off your job, not arcade earnings. 

[b] Overall Thoughts: 7/10 [/b]

I would say the narrative is just so playful if you could actually follow it without any problems. Still, the world-building and the carefully crafted interactions between the characters are so enjoyable, and often so sweet, clearly, a lot of love went into making it. Even with all of the problems, there is a cool game there, I think it's so overlooked, but hey, I'll play it alone if I have to, just like I live alone in my cell.

A really interesting concept marred by bugs, a sketchy economy and a bad saving system.

Bugs encountered in the first 90 minutes:
2 crashes
Ministry sent a letter scolding me for not showing up to work in addition to the letter they already sent for being late (I did show up, I was just late)
The position where you have to stand to be scanned is almost pixel-perfect, and the tutorial does not adequately explain this or prepare you for it.
Running into walls makes your camera flicker

Saving system:
The game charges you in-game money to perform a manual save, so players will naturally be stingy with their saves. This system could work if the game was extremely stable and had a near-zero percent chance of crashing; however, as demonstrated by my 2 crashes in 90 minutes, the game is not stable, so I ended up losing a lot of progress each time it crashed.

Economy:
You get $100 per day for working. At first, this seems pretty fair, since the most expensive item in the store is $500. As soon as you unlock the first playable arcade game though, the inflation begins. You can win $5,000 for beating a 3 minute game. All of a sudden, the work money seems less impressive. Then, the store introduces a toy that costs $25,000, and a bunch of new arcade games to play. Now the work money seems really pathetic, and you start to just go for the fun of working. If this game was meant to be a crypto-millionaire simulator, then this would be a really effective message. However, I don't think this is what the developer was trying to communicate.

I would like to unravel the story by playing more, however, in its current state, the game is simply too frustrating.

[h1]Adventures of Deliveryman[/h1]

"Adventures of Deliveryman" combines isometric city exploration, fast-paced puzzle-solving, and bike customization into a unique experience that feels both fresh and challenging. As a newly "born" delivery cyclist trapped in a Groundhog Day-like loop, your mission is to uncover the city's secrets while navigating its bustling streets.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Pros[/h1]
- Vibrant City Exploration: The detailed, interactive city brims with life, from narrow alleyways to rooftop ramps, making every delivery a new adventure.
- Dynamic Gameplay: Freeriding across unconventional terrain is exhilarating, with trampolines, ramps, and grindable rails adding depth and creativity.
- Customization Freedom: The ability to mix and match bike parts offers endless opportunities to tailor your bike's performance and visual style.
- Personalized Soundtrack: Hidden records let players curate their own playlist, enhancing immersion and gameplay rhythm.
- Stylish Tricks and Rewards: Unlocking and performing stunts during deliveries adds flair and an extra layer of challenge.
- Engaging Mystery: The narrative encourages exploration and decision-making, with choices that shape your path and reveal city secrets.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Mixed Aspects[/h1]

- Delivery Missions: Missions are engaging puzzles, but their repetitive nature could feel monotonous to some players.
- Bike Customization System: While rewarding, managing card combinations for upgrades might feel complex for casual gamers.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Cons[/h1]

- Challenging Controls: Navigating the city’s tight spaces and dense traffic requires precise control, which may frustrate newcomers.
- Repetitive Loop: The Groundhog Day premise is intriguing, but the lack of significant narrative progression might not resonate with everyone.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

"Adventures of Deliveryman" succeeds in blending action, puzzles, and self-expression in a bustling, interactive urban playground. Its vibrant city design and dynamic gameplay mechanics make it a standout experience for players who enjoy creativity and challenge. While the repetitive nature of the delivery loop may not appeal to everyone, the game offers enough charm, customization, and exploration to make it a worthwhile ride for fans of isometric adventures.

- It's fun to see the chests are all open in that cave, because you looted them in the previous game!

At first glance, Placid Plastic Duck Simulator appears to be little more than a whimsical, idle experience—a mere digital pond wherein rubber ducks lazily bob upon the water’s surface. However, to dismiss it as such would be a grievous oversight, for beneath its seemingly simplistic exterior lies an evocative meditation on time, randomness, and the quiet beauty of aimless existence.
 The game offers no objectives, no defined goals, and no means of direct intervention—an antithesis to the hyper-stimulating, dopamine-fueled mechanics of contemporary gaming. Instead, players are invited to observe an ever-growing congregation of rubber ducks as they drift, collide, and meander within the gentle embrace of physics-driven fluidity. It is a game that challenges the very definition of "gameplay," opting instead for an experience akin to an interactive art installation or a digital Zen garden.
Each duck introduced into the pool possesses its own unique design, ranging from the mundane to the outright absurd. A duck clad in a medieval knight’s helmet, another donning a UFO motif, and one inexplicably exuding a quiet melancholy all coexist in this simulated microcosm of existence. Their behavior is dictated by an unseen hand—governed not by artificial intelligence but by the immutable forces of digital physics, their fates determined by the currents and collisions that shape their gentle pilgrimage across the water’s surface.
And therein lies the game’s true brilliance: it is a celebration of unpredictability. The ducks do not adhere to a strict routine, nor do they possess any discernible agency. Instead, they simply are, existing in an indifferent yet strangely poetic simulation. It is an experience that rewards patience, inviting the player to relinquish control and embrace the serendipity of unstructured moments.
Much of the game’s hypnotic charm is derived from its impeccable sound design. The ambient hum of water, the soft splashes of buoyant movement, and the occasional chime of a duck gently colliding with another all contribute to an atmosphere of deep tranquility. The dynamic shifts in weather—from the golden warmth of midday to the serene stillness of a moonlit night—enhance the feeling of an ever-changing yet perpetual world, one that exists beyond the constraints of player input.
To those seeking high-octane action or narrative depth, Placid Plastic Duck Simulator may seem inconsequential, perhaps even absurd. But to those willing to surrender to its unique rhythm, it offers something rare in gaming—a meditative, almost therapeutic escape from the incessant demands of structured gameplay. It is a game about nothing, and yet, in its nothingness, it finds an ineffable kind of profundity.
A masterclass in minimalism, Placid Plastic Duck Simulator transcends its premise to become something strangely poetic. It is not merely a game—it is an experience, a gentle whisper amidst the cacophony of modern gaming.

A mostly chill (and seldom chilling) conversation with Ellie, or at least her AI counterpart, within the VR social media platform E-ON.

The game's narrative is led by two mysteries: 1) Why is E-ON's new user verification system down? 2) Where is the real Ellie, and why has she been offline for so long?

IMMERSION: This game reminded me a lot of UnearthU, an interactive experience where you also spend the whole time talking to an AI character. Except, instead of navigating a new social media platform, UnearthU has you going through mindfulness activities and breathing exercises. I think both games are successful in their immersive components, since you the person sitting there playing are actually performing these activities, whether it be meditating at your chair for UnearthU or scrolling round the hoop to to understand the functions available in E-ON.

STORY: I think my view of the story is best described by how often I used the "text bubble" feature (from now on referred to as T.B.) at different points in the game. At the beginning, when getting more credits is your main in-game goal, I found myself constantly fighting the urge to click through the T.B. dialogues as I was much more concerned at that point about the age-old, cave-man desire to "make big number on screen go bigger", as each new dialogue got me another credit. However, near the end of the game I actually lingered on the T.B. feature, even though credits were no longer a concern. I thought how my view of Ellie and the E-ON platform transformed throughout the game was very effective, and the surrounding design leading me on this narrative journey was well-executed.

CUSTOMIZATION: I loved the lofi playlist and that I had control to pause or skip songs whenever I wanted to. I also enjoyed being able to change the hoop and background colors. I wish there was more customization! For example, being able to change Ellie's appearance would have been a fun break in between all of the readings.

CONCLUSION: I'm not a big fan of visual novel style games, but I actually really enjoyed E-ON! My main gripe is the lack of customization options, but all in all I thought it was a moving story mixed with some interesting commentary on social media and its relationships between its users, its corporate owners, and itself. I'll remember you, Ellie!

I pray Koei Tecmo keeps GUST going strong because this was a lovely game to play from start to finish… I wasn’t slowly going crazy from the sheer size of the game. They really stuffed a lot of things into this game which led to multiple moments of just going “oh god what do you mean there’s more to see?!” Oh and the barrel check was done and the barrel was indeed a barrel!

I do believe some areas could be improved, some on the technical side and some on the general game side but before getting into any of that I can honestly say it is a good RPG. It builds on mechanics and ideas from the first two games and makes decent attempts to expand on them with the majority doing a good job. I do feel on the technical side of things they could have spent some more time fine tuning some things because I found the game to be a little unstable as it got closer to the end of the game with multiple crashes after cutscenes.. At least the auto saves are well timed so if a crash does happen you likely won’t lose a ton of progress.

Graphically i’d place it the same as Ryza 1 & 2, good but a little less compared to them because mannnnn they went a little hard on things like bloom in some areas (I had to turn it off because it made some areas feel like a flashbang went off) I did catch in some areas textures not stretched fully and resulting in being able to see out into the void a little bit, the ones I caught were minor and weren’t big enough to squeeze into the void so at least there’s that. I will forever have a few issues with a lot of visual FX in games recently where it just gets so heavy it becomes hard to really see anything going on at times, I don’t hold it against the game itself but I do wish a lot more modern games had better options for how heavy visual FX can be.

Music is a solid high grade as usual in Atelier games, it has a good variety and doesn’t make tracks so overloaded that it becomes a nightmare to listen to after a couple times. I do wish there was an extra battle track and boss track in the sound track however but that’s a personal thing I prefer, I do feel it would be a good idea to reduce character voices in battle because they do talk a fair bit as battles go on and as the game went on it slowly became noise to me I’ll be honest. Heck as I think about it they could have snuck in battle themes from Ryza 1 & 2 in some areas of the game and I think it would have been a welcome thing to experience again. 

Gameplay wise it’s pretty much Ryza 2 with a couple bells and whistles added on top, more variety in some equipable tools, a skill tree filled with a lot less passive abilities and more recipes to feel better progression wise and combat is really just Ryza 2 with some more moves and polish worked in which works fine. I do have a couple issues with the gameplay side of things and that partly due to the length of the game itself…. A lot of areas in the game contain a lot of the same ingredients outside of a fair number of unique ones but it results in a fair number of ingredients being harder to get sometimes because of how little there is of it at times. Some ingredients just feel so rare it becomes a pain using them because you don’t know when you’ll manage to get another one… it could of been improved with the shops because outside of Romy the traveling merchant you don’t really see shops expand much in terms of stock like in Ryza 2 and that could of been a good way to get rare items to become easier to obtain closer to end game.

I am happy I played Atelier Ryza’s trilogy, it’s a good set of RPGs in a pretty good franchise. I hope GUST continues to make good games and avoids any company management hell like layoffs. I happily recommend the trilogy but of course I always suggest waiting for a sale because Koei will forever make their products a bit high in the initial price range….

The gameplay itself is pretty light; there are no real puzzles to speak of. You speak to a character, find out what you need to accomplish to "level" your friendship with them, then you travel to places marked on the map to activate those things, then repeat. As you collect more things and unlock more friendship levels more parts of the map become unlocked, and more characters. You won't have to think too hard to work out how to progress; if you're stuck with levelling friendship with one character, it's usually because you've forgotten to do something clearly marked or you have to progress with a different character first. That makes progressing through the game pretty linear, but it works with the narrative.

I can see how the gameplay would be boring or repetitive for some, especially for anyone looking for a challenge, but for those who want an easy diversion with a lovely story, do give it a shot. Wholesome as heck, and very enjoyable, also easy to get all the achievements in a single playthrough. I hope you give it a try!

The chores you have to do for the gods aren't herculean epics, but rather quirky nods to each god's aspect. I loved them.

You have to be aware though that you will have to run back and forth across the island a lot. The game lore gives a reason for why you continually have to walk past quest items or revisit areas, but it is obvious artifical gating and it feels like it. If you are easily frustrated by backtracking, this game isn't for you. 
For me, the beauty of the island and especially the soundtrack made up for it. I can highly recommend the chill-out spots and I wish the soundtrack was available as DLC.

While I would have liked full voice acting, focusing on some key phrases was probably a good compromise between cost/effort and giving the characters personality.

The game runs on a 24h cycle, but you can save anytime, pass in-game time, and you can't miss anything.

I didn't like the concept involved in the story conclusion, but I chalk that up to personal taste. It made sense and was well executed.

Overall, I really liked the game, it's worth checking out if you are in the mood for some heavenly housekeeping.

Endless Creativity & Player-Driven Economy
One of Dual Universe’s standout features is its voxel-based building system, which lets players construct everything from small vehicles to massive space stations. The level of detail and customization is incredible, making it a paradise for builders and engineers. Combined with a fully player-driven economy, it encourages both cooperation and competition, as players establish their own industries, markets, and organizations.

A Living, Persistent Universe
Unlike traditional MMOs with instanced zones, Dual Universe boasts a single persistent world, meaning every action has a lasting impact. This makes exploration feel meaningful—whether you're scouting uncharted planets or working on your faction’s latest megastructure. The social aspect is also strong, with alliances forming to control territories, engage in political maneuvering, or even wage war.

Challenging Yet Rewarding Gameplay
While Dual Universe is complex, it's deeply rewarding for those willing to invest time. The economy, crafting, and automation systems require careful planning, and combat adds another layer of strategy. The game may not hold your hand, but for players who enjoy emergent gameplay and community-driven experiences, it offers a depth that few MMOs can match.

Room for Improvement
Like any ambitious game, Dual Universe has had its share of challenges, from performance optimizations to balancing mechanics. Some players may find the learning curve steep, and at times, the world can feel a bit empty due to its massive scale. However, with continued updates and a dedicated community, the potential for growth remains strong.

Final Verdict
If you love sandbox MMOs, enjoy deep crafting and building mechanics, and thrive in a world shaped by players, Dual Universe is worth your time. It’s a game where imagination and collaboration are key, offering an experience unlike any other in the MMO genre.

I have over 1400 hours in MW5:Mercs and 900 in HBS Battletech, and my evaluation of Clans is heavily influenced by those games existence. If Mercs and HBS:B did not exist, I would probably give Clans a thumbs-up. However, they do exist. And you should play them instead. 

Piranha tried something different for Clans, and there's nothing wrong with that. Unlike Mercs (which is a mech combat sandbox with some story bolted on later), Clans is a linear story-driven campaign. Those of us who have been Battletech lore nerds for a while will recognize it as a faithful telling of Op:Revival's Smoke Jaguar campaign. There's nothing here that would make an editor at Sarna spit out his/her soda. So far so good. The problem is the exact same head-scratching issue we saw with Ubisoft and Skull & Bones. Ubisoft ALREADY had an excellent pirate game (AC4 Black Flag), and they used those years of experience to make...a much worse pirate game. Same thing here. 

MW5:Mercs at launch was...rough. Good foundation, but rough. Over time, between DLCs and outstanding mods from the community, it has become excellent. Piranha, for reasons known only to them, has chosen to ignore essentially all of that experience and data to make a worse version of Mercs. 

Yes, the story cutscenes are very well done. And if you're looking to play Mechwarrior:The Movie...stop reading now, purchase Clans, and go have a good time. On the other hand, if you're looking for an actual Mech combat experience....this ain't it.

(1) AI. MW5:Mercs combat AI is notoriously garbage. Star Wars:Outlaws-level garbage. HOWEVER....Oraeon's TableTop Rulz AI mod has existed now for years, currently on version 9.3. It's a foundation mod for PC, everybody and their brother uses it. TTRUlzAI fixes the stock Mercs AI and replaces it with a very, VERY sophisticated model that will unalive you rapidly for doing dumb things. In most cases it is smarter than my friends when playing co-op. Piranha could have either at least tried to emulate the lessons learned from TTRUlz or, better yet, spent a little bit of their cutscene budget to offer Oraeon some money to code Clans AI for them. Community would have loved that. Instead....PGI has ignored it entirely and shipped an AI with Clans which is just as dumb as the five years old Mercs AI, but now also actively walks into you. Well done, gentlemen. Well done.

(2) Graphics and Optimization. I run a 4090 and a Ryzen 9 series CPU, with 64 gigs RAM behind it. I should not see any stutter, in any current game, ever. For reference, I am running The First Descendant (known GPU hog) in 4k, Ultra settings, DLSS Quality mode, at 80 frames or better. Yet, MW:5 Clans occasionally stutters. This is simply not acceptable, and indicates staggeringly poor optimization. Now, Mercs was also not well optimized at launch, lot of extra polygons and draw calls that just didn't need to be there. Fortunately, the modder Xeno fixed all the assets in game and optimized them properly, although I'm sure it cost some sanity. XenoPax Optimize 4 is the current version. And yet, AGAIN, PGI ignored this experience and shipped a game that is even more poorly optimized than Mercs. It also doesn't look much better. In fact, if you add stuff like Ultimate Visuals and Weather 3 and the HD normals and texture upgrades to Mercs.....Clans looks worse. 

I could go on, but you get the picture. Piranha looked at the five years of experience, DLC, and community modding and patching behind Mercs that has turned it into a tremendous game and....ignored all of it. Such a missed opportunity. If you want a great first person Mech experience, get MW5:Mercs (and the DLCs, they are actually very good) and mod it with the basics. If you want the premier turn-based tabletop-style Mech experience, get Harebrained Scheme's Battletech. Skip this.
