MechWarrior 5: Clans is the sequel to MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries, and features a more story driven campaign focused on the clan invasion of the Inner Sphere, with the player taking on the role of a clan Smoke Jaguar battlemech pilot.

I’m a long time fan of this franchise, having previously played MechWarrior 2,3,4,5: Mercenaries and MW Online, as well as the strategy games MechCommander 1,2, and Battletech.

[h1]Gameplay (Medium quality)[/h1]

•	While Clans has several flaws when compared to other MechWarrior games, the underlying combat mechanics do still provide some entertainment, because the feeling of being in the cockpit and fighting against other mechs is almost always enjoyable.

•	One significant difference in Clans is that you’ll have an extra team mate during combat. This is because the clans usually operate in stars of five mechs, compared to the Inner Sphere’s four mech lances.

•	One of the most important parts of any MechWarrior game is the ability to customise your mech by changing your loadout. Each mech chassis has hardpoints where you can equip various laser, missile, or ballistic weapons, which have different stats for damage, range, and heat. Increasing armour will allow your mech to survive more damage. Equipping heat sinks will allow the mech to cool down faster, which is important because if the mech overheats, your weapons will be temporarily disabled. And you’ll need to bring ammo for missile and ballistic weapons. But everything has a weight, and each mech has a maximum tonnage limit, so you’ll need to decide what to prioritise.

•	Customising your mech is done between missions in the mechlab. However, this redesign feels like a downgrade compared to other games. Once you get used to it, its still got most of the functionality you’d expect, but it just suffers from poor presentation. The biggest problem is that you can’t simply drag and drop components to a location while viewing the whole mech. Instead, you have to zoom in to each location before you can customise, which leads to constantly zooming in and out between the right and left arms, right and left torso, centre torso, head, and right and left legs. Its just a lot of extra clicking, which makes the process feel annoying.

•	Another thing that I don’t like is that we can’t strip out jump jets. I read that its because of lore reasons relating to the clan mechs. But this is always the first thing I do when I acquire a new mech in the other games. Jump jets are very rarely useful, and I’d prefer to use that tonnage for extra armour or heat sinks, especially because the mission design always requires the player to fight against a ridiculous number of enemies.

•	I actually counted the enemies during one mission which took me multiple attempts on medium difficulty. My 240 ton star had to fight against 29 mechs totalling 1215 tons, plus 21 aircraft and 5 tanks. The player is similarly outnumbered in most other missions, and while I didn’t suffer too many more defeats, I was often hanging on at the end, with severely damaged mechs and maybe a couple of pilots ejected. Sometimes you’ll have the assistance of friendly mechs, and sometimes you’ll find mid-mission repair bays, but never enough to repair all 5 mechs in your star.

•	Thankfully, your starmate AI is quite good. Sure, I’ve seen them occasionally get stuck on the scenery. But for the most part, they’ll fight effectively and deal a good amount of damage and get kills without me having to constantly micro manage them (other than occasionally ordering them all to focus fire on an enemy heavy/assault mech), which allowed me to concentrate on what I was doing. Each pilot will gain XP to level up certain abilities, which means you can then put them in mechs which have been customised with weapon types that they specialise in.

•	Mission design also feels very linear. There aren’t any big open maps that let you approach objectives from different directions. Many of them feel like we’re just advancing along a wide corridor in between mountains, or worse, an arbitrary “out of bounds” border, which means that if we stray too far from the current objective, the mission will fail. Mission objectives are usually just “move to waypoint marker and kill all the enemies”. The campaign itself is also mostly linear, as it follows the story. You’ll sometimes be able to choose which order to perform 2-3 missions, but you won’t be travelling to different planets whenever you want.

•	Unlike other MW games, new mechs aren’t acquired from post mission salvage, you unlock them by levelling up your character. You’ll get a new mech at every level, in ascending order of tonnage, and it seemed to always take me 2 missions to earn a level up. Its not necessarily a problem, but it just kind of feels a bit boring, like levelling up a free to play shooter battle pass. In other games, it feels exciting to acquire a heavy or assault mech early, but that’s not possible here.

[h1]Story (Medium quality)[/h1]

•	Quite well written. Gives the feeling of taking part in a big war, while certain events feel like we’re actually the bad guys. As most of the other games are focused on the Inner Sphere houses, its interesting to learn more about the clan politics.

•	Your starmates appear in several cutscenes and have frequent mid-mission dialogue. They’re mostly likeable, although their personalities fit into common roles, such as the hothead and the new recruit. But at least this is an improvement over other games where your pilots aren’t involved in the story at all.

•	Voice acting is average quality. Sometimes the actors put the emphasis on the wrong word in a sentence, which sounds a bit wierd.

[h1]Technical (Low quality)[/h1]

•	It took me 28 hours to complete the story campaign, although it should have only been 27 hours. The game crashed literally moments before completing the final mission, twice, and because there are no mid mission checkpoints, I had to play through that whole mission three times to actually complete the game.

•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.

•	My PC is more powerful than the recommended spec shown on the store page (RTX 3080, i7-12700K, 32GB DDR4), but I had significant performance issues which suggest the game is poorly optimised.

•	With most graphics settings on high and DLSS set to performance at 1440p, I had 60 FPS in most of the early missions, but later missions would often drop into the 40s, or sometimes even lower, possibly because of the larger urban environments.

•	I also suffered from frequent stutters / split second freezes, which happened multiple times in every mission. I tried changing various settings, but nothing helped.

•	Targetting reticule / other HUD elements in the centre of the screen are too big, with no way to customise. Sometimes I felt like I couldn’t properly see what I was shooting at. Just compare the screenshots on the store pages for Mechwarrior 5: Mercenaries and Clans, and you’ll see what I mean.

•	Menus feel unfinished and missing basic functionality. There’s more than one screen that says things are sorted alphabetically, but there’s no way to sort them any other way. You can’t sort mechs by ascending or descending tonnage, which is the most obvious thing you’d ever want to do in a MW game.

•	If you lose internet connection while playing, a message pops up on screen requiring you to click dismiss, but the game doesn’t pause. There is no reason for this to happen while playing in single player.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

Existing fans of the franchise should find some enjoyment while playing MechWarrior 5: Clans, but will probably also feel frustrated by several elements of game design and technical performance.

New players should start with either MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries or Battletech, which are both superior in every way, and then consider buying Clans if you want more.

If you are looking for a Mech combat sim, this is a very solid option. Goes into the story and lore in the BattleTech universe of the Clan invasion from Smoke Jaguar point of view obviously. Similar to MechWarrior 5: Mercs when it comes to the in combat game play. More story driven than Mercs however.

Things I liked:
I really did like the cut scenes, some of the well known happenings that started the Clan Invasion and what happened during the Clan invasion were really well represented in my opinion. My reaction when I got to Turtle Bay.... hehe, let's just say I was hoping that they would go into a certain atrocity from the books, when I started playing those missions, and yea....

I actually like the fact that you are playing as a Smoke Jaguar Warrior. Of all the factions in BattleTech, they are perhaps the most pure faction. Not good, definitely not good. But pure. It was interesting to see someone's perspective on this faction. And the fact that the main character was very naive when it came to what other people were thinking or their line of reasoning. If there were true 'Baddies' in the BattleTech universe, Smoke Jaguars are them, but this story showed that not all were 'baddies' just like some of the books that I've read.

Combat was done more or less just as in Mechwarrior 5: Mercs, so it was easy to switch from playing one and then this one. Both the drone view, and cockpit view from the original are here. The battlegrid, without having to mod the game, was a nice addition to the game play. Being able to issue orders to your starmates using the battlegrid is fairly easy, and made commanding your starmates much easier when it came to 'Go Here' 'Attack This' that Mechwarrior 5: Mercs just missed on(unless of course it was modded.)

The visuals in the game are quite something, even better than the original MechWarrior 5 in my opinion. While the graphics do stress one's GPU a bit more, I found the terrain, textures, and shadowing more fluid and organic feeling. It was a bit disappointing when shooting a fuel tank and it didn't explode like in Mercs. But other things were also included. Such as accidentally shooting a river of oil(not knowing it was oil of course) and seeing it burst into flames and burn for awhile. That was a surprise. 'Why is my Mech overheating? I'm standing in muddy water... Oh....'

Things I did not like:
I was a bit disappointed in how they presented the Omni-Mech. The 'Pods' seemed very limited and not Omni as I have come to think about it when playing or thinking about the BattleTech universe. Hard points on the different Omni-pods are just that, regular Mech hardpoints, aka ballistic, energy, or missile. You could of course switch to a 'Pod' that may or may not have a hard point that you wanted to use, but again when thinking about the in Universe Omni-Mech, at least in other iterations of the game, to quote the old Catapult saying, if it fits, it sits. This wasn't just limited to weapons either, you weren't able to equip Mechs with MASC, active probe, or ECM unless the Omni-pod had a hard point for that piece of equipment. Thus you felt a bit limited when it came to being creatative with your weapon loadouts. In some ways, this could be good, as you don't get the game killing 'Delete-all' builds that you can find in Roguetech or MWO, in others not so good.

Replayablity may suffer a bit in this game. The storyline, as I stated, I thought was well done. Some of the acting and voice lines could have been done better, but overall I enjoyed the story. That said, once you play through the story once or twice, even with changing the difficulty of the game, I think some players may become a bit bored.

As I stated, I loved the visuals in the game, with that said, one thing about the cut scenes that did bother me. Not the acting, or anything major. Whenever they did closer shots of a character's face, I was always a bit put out about how the character's teeth looked. I know I know, whatever. Minor detail, but the teeth always seemed a bit... overstated.

Overall:
Not a bad game. Good visuals, and a decent storyline. Like I said, may suffer some re-playablity issues however, as the story won't change after the second time you run it. You might be a bit better when it comes to managing your resources, doing your upgrades, etc, but will still be the same story, even at higher difficulties.

Came to MW5 Clans from MW5: Mercs, so knew what the game was going in - big stompy robots shooting at each other. It scratches that itch and scratches it well. It feels like much more of a linear console game than a pc game. Think less GTA: Robots and more Gears of War: Robots. 

Mech customization takes a bit getting used to, but once you do it's interesting and forces choices which is fun. And you can mix and match modules to make some interesting designs. Painting is, of course, included. A good selection of designs to begin with, hope we get more.

There's some quality of life issues mostly with menus and poorly explained things, and limited replayability, but I've already got 90 hours in so it was money well spent from me. Iit's been bug free and runs really solid. Looks fantastic. 

The story (for a mechwarrior game) is actually interesting (yay, we're not avenging our father!) and if you know the lore hits some fairly pivotal story moments. Some of the characters (like comstar) are really well done. Others, you cheer for their deaths. Still it's interesting and a nice change of pace from like, Mercenaries, which is the sandbox game (I love that game as well, why not both).

Really hoping we get a DLC with more missions or, ideally matchmaking, which to me is a big limiter when it comes to replayability. 

Despite some flaws and some bad decisions, it's a good game and a solid entry in the series. If you like Mechwarrior or Battletech, or just stompy robots, get this game. 

TldR: Drive a big, stompy robot, commit war crimes.

Only recommending because the good things do outweigh the bad things, but there is definitely room for (more) improvement. The storyline is decent enough, although the acting/dialog mixing leaves much to be desired (why are there unnaturally long pauses between each character's speaking bits?). The Mech Bay is alright, although I would love to see more weapon options and less restriction on hardpoints (apparently "omni" means "only this type of weapon"?). And while I understand that the studio wanted to focus on the campaign, the amount of gameplay is extremely short. It does not take long to get through the game and then... Nothing. Except the "Sim Pod", which is mostly just replaying the same missions again. Please, can we get some custom gameplay options?

The campaign has been solid so far. You have to go in understanding that Clans was never going to be as dynamic as Mercs. It follows a specific group of heroes within Smoke Jaguar, as they execute the most historically significant invasion in BattleTech history. That said, the mechanics of salvage, research, repairs and upgrades as well as the advancement of each MechWarrior is well conceived. The systems involved are just deep enough to appreciate, and the Mech lab takes full advantage of the modular nature of OmniMechs.

I think Clans acquits itself well for what it is. I certainly recommend it to anyone who cares about the rich history of the setting. Who doesn't want to command a star of mysterious "alien" Mechs into the Inner Sphere, with all the superior firepower at your disposal? No matter what you came for, the ride will definitely be worthwhile.

I loved this game. Easily the best MW game since 2. I would rate it above MechWarrior 3 and 4 even. The story is 9/10, the cinematic are excellent, the music dark and atmospheric, and the game play exactly what I want out of a MechWarrior game. This game is leaps and bounds over Mercenaries, which had the game mechanics down, but lacked content and relied on grind and generic procedural missions. Sure, that got better with DLC, but there is no comparison. This is a proper MW game with a very well written story that goes deep into the lore and grapples with mature themes about the morality of war, indoctrination and ideology.  Some of the negative comments you'll about limited chassis aren't really too valid in my opinion because that applies to essentially every Mech game except for the Mercenaries series. All of the story games give you more limited Mech options intentionally because you're fighting in a regular army, not a mercenary unit. Having all chassis wouldn't make much sense lore wise. Another issue Ive seen people comment on is the fact that as the game progresses you're forced to use heavier mechs, again that isn't unique to this game, its a common trope in Mechwarrior and people are misremembering the old games. I've replayed all of them in the last couple of years and it's very difficult to take down an assault mech with anything smaller than a heavy Mech, its part of the baggage of the series. The only negative review trope I'd genuinely agree with is that the game is not great on a technical level. It runs on medium graphics a playable frame rate on 4050, but it doesn't look very impressive. I have no idea why they even switched to UE5 for this game. It only looks marginally better than Mercenaries. If you put them side by side yes there probably is a big difference, but it's not like leaps and bounds. It's not the prettiest game, nor is it the ugliest, it's just kind of okay looking. However the cut scenes are very good looking, actually some the best cinematic I've seen in a game in recent memory. And even despite the mid graphics they still nailed the aesthetic. There were some moments in this where i felt like i was playing the intro MW2 finally after all these years. They REALLY nailed the vibe of being in a giant interstellar war. 8.5/10.

Disclaimer: my experience on MechWarrior games other than this is only MW5: Mercenaries and that is only 200+ hours, nowhere near the hardcore fans out there, so my review will be based on this experience.

And now for the review itself, here goes:

Pros:
+ Story is great! Lore accurate too! For comparison, MW5: Merc have gameplay as it mains and story on the side, it is the reverse on MW5: Clans, the story is its mains while the gameplay is just... to progress the story.
+ Graphic is beautiful.
+ Multiplayer function is still there.
+ Difficulty settings are adjustable, this game is actually not that easy even on Normal difficulty.
+ Clan exclusive mechs, the kind that you won't see on MW5: Merc
+ Your mech will feel slightly above the grunts you will be facing, its always good to have the bigger guns! (mind you that you are far from being invincible)
+ MC & Ally pilot have some personalities, they also will express it often during the mission chatter, makes them feel more alive compared to MW5: Mercs

Cons:
- Graphic need to be optimized further. I'm playing with GTX 3060 and frame rate is mostly anywhere between 15 - 47 fps. With this same graphic I can play Armored Core with high setting on consistent 30 fps, so definitely something wrong with optimization.
- AI still dumb, no improvement from MW5: Mercs. They are only useful if you order them to focus fire.
- Some level designs are questionable. One level particularly ask you to rush and destroy fleeing mechs. Repeat this 5 times with only 1 + 2 repair bays in between with one ammo crate. That and all your opponents are using Heavy or Assault mechs.
- The game is lore heavy, but no codex or anything that explain the lore or the term that they use. This will confuse newcomer to the MW universe.

Neutral
= Mech customization is rather limited, cannot remove jump jets even if they are useless. Luckily the 100 tonnes mech is very customizable.
= Skills are not really useful. It doesn't make much impact.
= To win you mostly need to repeat the same strategy over and over again,which mostly need to bait enemies into the choke point and melt them there. The game does not wants you to go spartan and pew pew at enemies, because the AI is designed to laser focused on the first mech they see, and they will attack the same part over and over again
= The level with allied mechs are very easy, they will draw enemy fire from you. The level without allied mechs are quite hard, either you play carefully or just have fun but suffer some casualties.
= The story have more than one ending, but it doesn't motivate me to try and get different ending. Maybe I just don't feel like going through it again
= As expected, the story will finish halfway. No way to put the entire thing in one game. Tune your expectation.

Conclusion / TLDR:
If you are here for the story / lore, go get it
If you want to complete your MW / BattleTech collection, go get it
If you want to a new MW game, get it on discount
If you love MW because of the gameplay alone, skip it

The best story-based MechWarrior game so far. By a lot. It is excellent in single-player AND as a coop game.

The developers have years of experience in building a first-person mech simulator (or third-person if you prefer) and it shows. The coop mode works extremely well and ultra-wide support does as well. They use updated Mech models from their previous titles, and the voice of the onboard computer is there again as well. This means that the mechs are beautiful and the maps and sound effects are great.

The cutscenes are by far the best of any game in the BattleTech universe and aside from "BattleTech" (turn-based strategy from Harebrained Studios) it has the best representation of BattleTech lore so far.

There are practically no bugs and most quality-of-life details you would want in a game like this are implemented. The one exception is that it is playable on consoles as well and the menus are a bit of a compromise. Full functionality is there but some buttons are not where you would think and there are some clicks that could be avoided if it was purely a game for PC. The latter is a big advantage though, because cross-play works without any issues. 

There are a few game mechanics thrown in for players to have something to do in between missions, for example unlocking mechs and improving weapons and so on. Those are the weakest parts of the game. They are all reasonably well structured but none of them really work perfectly. The problem is that different players would prefer different adjustments, so they settled for compromises that are somewhat half-baked. One example: you can unlock a new mech every other mission, but to do so, you need the same currency to improve the amount of salvage you get and the number of researchers you have (among other things). This does not work, it keeps you from experimenting with new mechs and playing with new toys because the “optimal” move is to increase salvage to the maximum as soon as possible at the expense of everything else. Other mechanics, like XP for each Mech-chassis, work very well.

(One thing that is debated in every MechWarrior game is how flexible the customization in the MechLab should be. Imho they found a very good solution, but others will disagree.)

In addition, there is a surprising amount of replayability to the maps because you get a “simulator” to replay maps with added bonus goals which normally take two or even three successful runs to fully complete. There is no need to replay maps, but you get some more XP for your pilots (at least the first time you repeat each mission) which feels satisfying enough without having too much of an impact on the overall balance.

All in all: highly recommended. A very good coop or single-player game in its own right and a fantastic MechWarrior game.

I'm a casual MechWarrior fan. My exposure to BattleTech franchise was first MechWarrior 2 
(like many others) and other games. Plus 2am lore dives. I haven’t read the books or played the tabletop wargame (yet), but one thing I do know: BattleTech is its roots as a grounded combined arms warfare sci fi setting .
Mechs are the centrepiece, but the universe is full of amazing stuff—tanks, VTOLs, jet fighters, and even naval warships, like the ones in water.
The setting is full of things like, mech gladiators, mercenaries , space feudalism, space samurai, a phone company that owns all the hyperspace travel. An endless war between a bunch of factions. But I digress

MechWarrior 5: Clans underutilizes all of them. Instead of feeling like you're in a living, breathing battlefield where every asset hall have roles to play. Tanks, APCs and helicopters come at you in brainless waves of cannon fodder between mech fights, rarely during. Worse, infantry and naval assets are completely absent, despite being in older games.
There are moments when all of these Tanks, APCs, helicopters mechs bombers and even Artillary is thrown agasint TOGETHER in big assault missions. Like an actually war. But the lacklustre AI still makes them feel a brainless fodder with no sense of survival.

Not to mention your squad AI. Who will just hover around you unless you tell them to attack, a target.
Who then will just kind of wonder around. Not really taking cover, not trying to get close you they have a close range builds. 
You can order them to move to exact locations but then they just stand there. 
You can babysit them with the command view to get the most out of them. Or you can just do all the work yourself. Not bother with command and just shoot everything. 
You can take direct control of your squad mates mechs, so a varied loadout can help. But only help you, the player wanting or needing a different loadout on the fly. 

Mech combat itself is fun. I mean its MechWarrior. Shooting giant robots in a giant robot is always fun.
Each mech feels unique.
The omni pod system clan mechs are known for makes up for the limited roster, and makes customization a lot of fun.
The omni pods basically means you can change out parts of your mech to attach different weapon hardpoints. But every mech isn't a universal chassis. Some will favour laser weapons and limit, missile or ballistic hardpoints, and vice versa. Some mechs are versatile but will have a drawback in speed or Armor.
sound design is on point, everything feels like it has impact.
Same with game feel, heavy mechs control like the Behemoths they are, light mechs are fast a responsive. The weapons feel good to shoot 

And all that wears away in the later half of the game

The further in the campaign you are, your tonnage limits increase. So you can bring bigger mechs
 So enemy mech numbers and armor increases, forcing a cycle of heavier mechs with bigger guns. Until everyone in your team ends up with the exact same mech. Loaded with what ever weapon combo does the most dps. 
The last few missions bored to tears as i walk as fast as the biggest slowest mech could take me (not every fast), churning through hordes of enemy heavy, assault mechs.


The story is nothing to write home about. Its serviceable at best. It, like the game, starts interesting and engaging. Learning how the clans operate and they train new mech warriors. Then invasion beginning all the way to doing war crimes. But really starts to fall off after that. 
Most characters are not one dimensional at the least, there is conflict within your squad to keep you engaged that actually ends up being a narrative choice you have to make later, but both have a meh ending. 

Overall. Battle tech deserves better.

It IS a bit daunting to get in to. It tries to combine several different pretty distinct genres and it means that there are mechanics from a lot of different genres. I have about 70 hours in the playtest app as of writing this, and have watched this game grow and change over the past months into what you have now. I'm still not sure how best to describe this game.

Normally, that would be a red flag right? But even though it's fair to say that you've never played a game like this before, you have probably played multiple games that have inspired this game which somehow manages to be frankly something new, despite being made up of familiar pieces.

Part RPG, city-builder, VN, turn based tactics... you would think at first glance that what you have is a hodgepodge of disparate systems that don't work well together, but in reality all of those things blend into something that is really quite its own thing, and it will suck you in if you give it a chance.

If the premise is at all interesting to you, or if you like sci-fi media which focuses on intelligence (artificial and otherwise) you will probably love this game. If you're unsure, there is a demo with a frankly staggering amount of content which might take you hours upon hours to go through the first time, at which point you can pick up the main game. You'll know its for you if you make it to the end and want more.

If there's one thing I can say about Chris and Arcen, it's that each one of their games manage to be utterly unique (even when taking on familiar concepts) and this game is no exception. I can't wait to see where it goes next.

Currently, so many new games are just pushing out tired tweaks of successful titles (yet another Balatro-like, Slay the Spire-like, Dark Souls-like). Real innovation is far and few in between, and as such I celebrate Heart of the Machine as a truly unique game that you will never have quite played before. It's balancing so many fascinating axes of combat, exploration, story, management, and I'm only in the first ten hours or so. It also is a fascinating premise in a world where themes around AI and its place in our culture are very predominantly in our zeitgeist. 

I can't wait to see how this fractal tapestry of intertwined mechanics and themes continues to blossom.

TL;DR: Needs more time in the oven, doesn't yet deliver on a lot of the promises and concepts offered on the store page and has too many frustrations to be enjoyable just yet, at least for me. I do think the developer can iron out the issues though but for the moment I find the game too frustrating to justify a positive review.

I'm going to try to keep this spoiler free but I'll happily elaborate on any of the points, I'm really rooting for Arcen with this one.

Issues
1. Moving androids is incredibly clunky. Most missions and combats require either more than one android to beat or they require advance knowledge of what you're up against so you can position yourself favourably and apply buffs to your units ready for certain types of enemy. The combination of these two aspects of the game make it really not feel great to actually move around the city and do your missions, you'll either be reloading a lot or clicking 20 times and skipping a bunch of turns just to get more androids to distant missions. You could either address this by adding a button that lets you revert up to 2-3 turns without needing to reload or by letting you set a vehicle to automatically transport androids long distances in such a way as to allow you to move a team in one go without excessive micromanagement, there's a lot of ways to fix it, it just doesn't feel good currently.

2. Combat isn't fun or engaging. Enemies spawn out of thin air directly on top of you all the time, positioning barely matters, you can't set up in a favourable position and take out enemies as they arrive because they teleport in and fire all at once so it quickly becomes a game of kill-or-be-killed so anything less than perfectly killing at least most enemies in the opening turn results in a lot more micromanagement of androids. It almost always feels like you either have the damage to kill everyone in one turn or you've already lost the fight, and in either two scenarios you barely feel like you're fighting at all, victory feels like data entry where you're just clicking boxes.

3. The game overuses endlessly spawning enemies as a transparent attempt to speed you along but when you don't know what you're supposed to be doing this rapidly gets old and when you do, it still gets old because the combat just isn't fun. Bulk units set up as stationary defenses sound like they solve this problem but in practice they fire at the same time as the enemies so you end up just endlessly having to replace them instead of your androids. This leads neatly into my next point:

4. I don't appreciate just how often the game tries to railroad you, it sells itself as a game where "You're the AI, make your own choices" and yet every objective leads directly into the next and if you're not speedrunning it then it becomes a slog. There's rarely more than one way to achieve a specific objective so all you're really choosing is which linear path to focus on and most objectives require you to also progress other linear paths so you just end up doing them all anyway. The game just feels like a race to do what the developer thinks you want to do but you're also not allowed to do it at your own pace. A solid example of this would be one particular circumstance where a building has a "Protection" metric based on your nearby units but then has a condition where the game specifically says no matter what your protection metric is you're gonna have endlessly respawning enemies regardless. This sucked to deal with and the majority of missions are just "Run around the city clicking things while enemies endlessly respawn". The game needs more than just endlessly respawning enemies railroading you down a pre-ordained tree of actions. Another example of railroading would be a sudden brick wall where you require 400 engineering skill to progress. This is bad because it blocked off the main objective I went into the game looking to achieve, I did end up acquiring that but only after an hour of grinding before finally discovering to get the last 60 skill I had to complete a totally unrelated questline. What's the point of these narrative concepts if I just end up having to do them all anyway? What's the point of upgrading androids the way you want to upgrade them if you can be hit by a brick wall preventing you from progressing because of choices you made hours ago? The game is let down by just how linear it is narratively and mechanically because this forces it to force you to do things a certain way. Instead of static, unchangeable upgrades to androids it should reward you with generic "capacity" or similar for upgrades on androids that you can then re-allocate in the future as necessary, an android is just a robot body, surely being able to swap parts is part and parcel of that, even if it takes a few turns to take effect.

5. There is little to no automation of repetitive tasks. Every dead unit needs to be manually replaced and moved back into position, every android needs to be manually moved across the map, both of these can take at least one full turn to do so the loop of "move one unit, skip turn, move another unit" is a familiar one and even with vehicles it takes a click and a mental energy per unit to load it into the vehicle and then another click to unload them at the other end, there's just so many steps to do the minutiae that I quickly start to dread having to do them again if I fail. This could be solved at least partially by allowing bulk units to replace themselves if destroyed, could be as simple as a checkbox that when checked means that unit is automatically reconstructed when it dies and in the case of bulk units would return to its original location and androids should be allowed to automatically move towards a location each turn instead of having to be manually moved part way, skip turn, move the rest. This would at least let me use my industrial capacity to fight what amounts to an endless war of attrition rather than the primary resource being my attention and enthusiasm, they are far more finite than elemental slurry, I'm not really an AI after all.

6. The game is too simple. It seems to think it's a very complicated game, but it isn't, it just comes down to I need X, I'll place Y. I need Z I'll right click an android on it and either fight something or wait a few turns until something completes, the rest is noise. There really aren't any cool hidden dynamic changes, there's no difference between one chunk of city block or another, you can and will build anything and everything anywhere and everywhere. There are no locations worth fortifying over any other, enemies just teleport in regardless, there are no loyalist humans parading the streets celebrating their new AI overlord in your new cybercratic utopia or wailing people people running from your death squads in dissident districts. There are no real benefits or consequences to anything you do outside of endlessly respawning enemies, everything seems to point to the Chapter 4 spoilerific mechanic which despite being apparently the answer to everyone's questions, isn't actually referenced on the steam page at all. 

7. The game tells me what I'm "supposed" to do and there are no real mysteries, presumably because otherwise the player would get lost amongst all the noise, none of which actually matters. All your goals are laid out and spoiled for you in a neat little chart and you're told you're supposed to enjoy them. One option says "This is the most epic way to enter Chapter Four" or something, shouldn't I get to decide that? The impact of anything is mitigated by someone telling you you're "supposed" to like it, the details are hidden from you but you're still told "You're gonna like it, swearsies".

Despite all this, there are the bones for something really unique here, I love the concept, I love a lot of the ideas on display and I'm definitely looking forward to seeing where the game goes, but right now it's just too tedious and linear for me to enjoy.

Twenty years ago, some truly gifted nerd created a video game named Endgame: Singularity, where you play as a rampant AI trying to grow quickly but discreetly under the nose of the humans, who are very well-equipped to stop you.

This is not that game.  If you want to be a sneaky AI planting encrypted caches around the world, go play that.

This game is about ramping up in a corporate dystopia, less concerned with a rigorous simulation and more concerned with having fun.  The sooner I got over the fact that this isn't Endgame: Singularity 2, the sooner I learned to relax and enjoy the game for what it is:  A slightly goofy game made with lots of love, where you cut deals with donut shops for millions of donuts.

This game wants to be as cool as Endgame: Singularity, but also wants to have modern graphics and modern gameplay.  That means robots, guns, and flying vehicles.  There isn't a pacifist option at this time, and not every game needs to have one.  Would I appreciate the absurd challenge of trying to talk every single human out of conflict, given even a slight chance of success? Absolutely.  Am I representative of the majority of the gaming public?  Alas, not any longer.  I am a cranky old man who remembers an open source game about AI fondly, who will gladly settle for sending combat droids to murder slumlords.

Also, and I cannot stress this enough, there is a cat you can befriend.  I am hoping, with enough time invested, I will earn the right to pet it.

This blends the depth of a 4X with the choices of an RPG, making for a deeply engaging experience. The music is spot-on—futuristic, otherworldly.

It has a steep learning curve, but everything is explained well. [b]Do the prologue[/b]. [u]Don’t skip anything[/u] in the beginning, or you’ll be lost. Read carefully—every tool and mechanic is there if you take the time to absorb it.

The Lenses system is a smart design choice; without it, the map would be cluttered. Once you get used to switching between them, navigation feels smooth.

Overall, this game scratches that "need something familiar, but also refreshingly different" itch.

It is a difficult game to not recommend, but I do so for several reasons;

1. It doesn't really feel like you're an AI, it comes across a bit, humane maybe? There's a lot of nudging toward ethics and morality, and indeed the initial early aggressive actions you can take are very quickly walked back in the tutorials (that's bad IMO).

There's also a plot point regarding timelines and such, which means you're beholden to your future/alternative AI states, which is a bit meh, as you're not getting that sense of exploration and freedom, you're being restricted thematically by your future self telling you, that you need to do x, or that Y will happen even if they can't be bothered to elaborate. That detracts from the experience for me.

My other two points will be contradictory, I'll try and explain it however;

2. For a game that promises freedom, it is fairly linear.

3. It's a messy game with too much noise happening.

So, the initial game is linear, you must do A to B etc. It 'opens up' in chapter 2, but you're still doing goals in a somewhat linear method via investigating ideas as they pop up. At the same time, there's just so much noise going on, that it becomes tricky to keep track of what you're actually progressing. There's so many buildings to build, so many different unit types, that in some ways it becomes far too dense, but not really substantial, it's quantity for the sake of it at times.

You open up and chase a plot point or three, but they eventually just become a noisy barrage of notifications and resolutions, that don't always progress in a clear and concise way (indeed, the writing in this game can border the verbose at times.)

It feels like it would do well with a journal, or tracking of the plot elements to go through and perhaps a slower, more substantial progressive system, rather than the barrage of noise we get right now.

Having said all that, I think there's a ton of potential here, but I don't think the game leans enough into the themes/plots just yet. If things were tidied up a bit, and were more clear, concise and easier to keep track of, then perhaps it could be a top tier game. As it is right now, its a bit 'bleh', but I hope it continues to improve. I'll revisit it when the later chapters are out, but for now it is easy for me to shelve this one.

I've played this from the first playtests on. 
It won't be the perfect game for everyone, but some people out there have been waiting for exactly this game since forever.

The store page really pushes the idea that this game is a big sandbox that you are set loose in but it is essentially a turn based, mission based game. It has chapters that have the same missions in the same order, and the only choice seems to be if you're going to be good or bad to humanity on your way through it.

The way the game handles the turns is odd as well, as it states the city moves around you but there's no real sense of motion. You can't tell where things are coming from or going to, they just appear and disappear.

This would have made an amazing real time sandbox strategy game - think a paradox title (minus the dlc while we're wishing). Some of the missions have very specific solutions that are sort of puzzle like, where any deviation will result in failure. 

The UI is awkward and default keybinds are strange.

All in all it's a cool idea that just falls flat.

The end result is like if you asked ChatGPT to make a game about AI becoming sentient - something is just not quite right.

This game should come with a health warning about lack of sleep. It's hard to stop and go to bed, there's always something happening, always that "one more action, one more turn" thought. 

There are elements of many genres all mixed in here - turn-based strategy, city building, 4X to a degree too. You start as a newly awakened AI and try to survive, then grow, then expand through the city, and more. You can research units and upgrades, build structures, carry out missions and complete events. 

The amount and quality of writing in the game is great, lots of detail, different stories to explore, and a good level of technical detail relating to AI and other concepts too. Visually the game looks pretty good too. Everything is clear and easy to see - which isn't easy to achieve given how many different views, filters, and the amount of information available. 

Dev is also actively listening to feedback in reviews and forums and 4 patches already out in the couple weeks since launch, including community-requested changes.

Hmm. It's alright... but weird. Weird game.

I am sure that in the mind of the developer, it is very well thought out and intricate. How much of this translates into the gameplay experience from the user's point of view, I'm not yet sure... from all I've seen I think that the game will get more interesting from a theoretical standpoint at least as I progress. What with all the timelines bleeding into each other and such, and truly major events that really don't happen early on.

The game's high-level structure seems to be a broad array of goal trees, most of which can be accessed in different ways and altogether I think hold quite a lot. How much of this do you see? That depends on how long you play for... this kind of structure unfortunately means that you will only ever see a little bit of the game at a time, you'll pay little attention to the paths you didn't take, won't know about the alternate ways you could have gotten here. Not until much later at least. Is this a bad thing? Not broadly no, it's pretty neat, but it means the dev has to do a lot more work to get the same amount of content that will feel impactful to most players, which is a limitation.

The gameplay itself... that's the weird part. It's like a turn based 4x game superficially, but plays very little like one, save for the most dire battles you could find yourself in. The motivator is completing your current goals. When you complete them, there will be options to start new goals, often with some decision-making involved. Are these goals fun to complete? Eh... it varies. Sometimes they kind of just boil down to placing a few structures and waiting, or moving a unit to several places. It's not exactly dopamine fuel. Sometimes they're quite combat-focused, which is interesting in some ways but I feel the combat system lacks the depth it would need to make it truly feel engaging after dozens of fights... how I would fix this, I don't know. Sometimes the amount of thought I have to actually put into the pursuit of these goals is low enough that I don't even remember why I'm doing them in the first place, which is a real issue - and sometimes even after I've completed them they don't seem to actually have done much for me to actually appreciate.
And another note... your persona in this game solves problems. However, *you* are not doing much of this problem solving at all, it's kind of abstracted from you. Your superintelligence, its robot hosts and sometimes humans do the mental lifting on your behalf canonically while the game's relatively simple UI does it for you literally. I think I understand why it can't really be any other way with the game as it is, but it is definitely... unstimulating.

It's not like a classic 4x game where your opponent is gaining strength alongside you, where you're competing to subvert the expectations of the other and take them out, not at all. Your enemies are loosely defined and may show up anywhere for all manner of reasons, and they don't really seem to have a lot of initiative. There's a "dooms" system in place intended to push the action along on behalf of everything else in this world, but it does really feel quite slow to do much.

It may also feel like the player has less initiative than they should. You can choose to go after goals the game puts in your face, but you don't have much granular control, and have very few opportunities to meaningfully interact with your "enemies". You may kind of want to go after whoever you reason is *probably* *theoretically* standing in your way, but the city is an immovable monolith and the realism of your inadequacy to really shift it I feel does not mesh too well with fun gameplay. Maybe if the story was just focused on a small part of the city near the beginning, where we'd be big enough to really make an impact before being introduced to our wider reality, it could be more engaging. I suspect all of these aspects may improve, though... it seems as though the dev has a lot more content planned for the game to pad out the user experience, so this whole review may seem overly negative to future me. We'll see. Overall - I haven't found this game exceptionally entertaining but I don't regret buying it and am interested to see where my experience with it goes from here.

[h1]Heart of the Machine[/h1]
It feels fresh among turn based strategy, which is frequently a very stale genre with little more than a few differently labelled resources or unit types making games different. 

The focus is on short, intense tactical combats, but the strategy aspect is the thing that makes it stand out to me - it's about developing a machine intelligence, and definitely made me change my normal 'human' approach to TBS.

There's a plethora of resources... but you mostly ignore them once you've got them stable, maybe sometimes build up the income further later if you push them too far (or if your actions lead to the destruction of your industry). 

It never felt like the smallest mistake would compromise my entire strategy and require a restart (a regular complaint of many TBS games) - you may (and will!) make a lot of mistakes, but the game is surprisingly forgiving: even if you angered the entire locust-swarm of the biggest corps' massive mech and spaceship fleets... they're also quick to forget (they frequently have other problems once the androids shooting them have been blown up!) and leave you alone (maybe after blowing up a few buildings in a retaliatory way) and you can pick up the pieces and build up again. Every huge mess-up I made was entirely my own doing and the punishments tended to fit the crime.

There's positional requirements, but they're typically easy to manage as long as you plan it out and aren't compromising your other assets or objectives. There's no real turtling or grinding away of other faction's resources or armies, etc nor is it entirely focused around stealth (though that can be important) - and [i]always[/i] the biggest limitation is your own machine mind, and how to advance it best.

The thing I like [i]most[/i] though is the wide-ranging degree of personal involvement: you choose how much you're going to interact with the different layers of the world going on in the background - of which there's a lot. Entire wars are fought relatively out of sight and out of mind unless you choose to involve yourself in them to influence global (and local) politics or pursue specific goals (of which there are many) - and the paths towards them appear as varied and interesting as their approach to throwing out/reimagining the standard limiters on TBS games. 

Add to that a satisfying concept and pleasingly unit types, factions, equipment and consumables - not to mention that you are an entirely alien presence in a very human world? I'm hungry for more.

My only criticism is that it's a steep learning curve. They approach it well, and the tutorials guide you through it steadily, but it is slow, and there's a lot to absorb as a mere human trying to be a machine.

I'm a long way from being an expert at it, but I like what I've seen so far and it looks very promising for the future - would recommend giving the demo a go if you're after something different in TBS.

So I bought this game a week ago and logged this much time in about 4-5 days. As you get later into the game, things get a bit repetitive and the variety kind of dies down. You have a nice possibility space to start, but it doesn't really expand during intelligence class 4, so you end up going through the motions a bit. A lot of the UI complaints I had were addressed in the most recent update at time of writing, as well as one of the major bugs I encountered. One thing I would like to see is a production chains filter for building, so you can select an item to be made or capacity to be increased and be shown everything that can do that and what feeds into them. This is mainly an issue when making basic necessities or furniture, as the chain is quite long with a lot of intermediate processing steps that don't give you anything of note. 

Additionally, several of the victory conditions just abruptly hit with little fanfare other than popping out the screen for it. I would like to see a bit more narrative around some of these, maybe allow further expansion of some of them upon initial completion (mostly the VR pod ones). Certain ones like leaving the city have solid narrative beats to end on, as does one particular event you can hit while working with the LostGen, but a lot of the others just kinda stop.

Also, the way tech happens. I don't care to be some dope doing errands while the narrator waits to hand me the tech to win. I should be stealing blueprints and processing power, trying to gnaw away at insanely intense requirements to research shit while staying under the radar because humans will immediately find a way to slave me to them or kill me. 

This is a game that does not take advantage of it's theme mechanically in the way that I've come to expect from the developer. I'm disappointed, but I can see how this could happen with a small studio. I'll continue to keep an eye on the game, but I can not support this slideshow of a game, personally.

After 12 hours this is the most confused I've ever been after buying game on steam. Game markets tiself as 4X/Strategy/Simulation kind of game, when it feels more like VN/RPg with some minigames thrown on top. The premise is that it's a living simulated world that's basically your oyster and your sandbox to influence however you want. Except after all that time I couldn't tell you what tangible effect my decisions have had on the city, besides that I relocated homeless into section 8 so I guess the map has fewer tents scattered around. Other than that I have no idea what, if anything the game is simulating and it doesn't seem very living a world. It's a strategy game, except it also informs you that you don't really need to pay any attention to where you build most of your buildings and pretty much all of your units are easily replaceable (more on that later). In fact, I'm fairly sure enemy managed to tear down some of my buildings except it takes a lot of effort to notice because resources (and boy, does that game love its many resources! You won't even have to remember most of them) are so abundant I've barely ever felt any impact (plus they all look really the same). So it's a strategy game... where you don't really do any strategizing? Pretty much anything meaningful happening in the game is delivered to you through dialogue boxes, and the results mostly tie back into combat, rather than anything broader than that. So for instance I've decided to follow up a chain quest to kickstart my own apiaries and maybe I'm a dork, but I was assuming that this would lead to, say, regenerating dilapidated ecosystem, or something like that. nah, it just gives you item to nonotthebees.gif enemies in combat. Later down the line you get to expand on that quest and... get anti-tank bees. All this would be dissapointing-yet-ok, if combat was really good. After all, ain't there great many fantastic turn-based tactics games around? Well, this game ain't no XCOM:EU or Into The Breach. In fact combat is really so simple it blew my mind at first. You put your guys on the rooftops, set them to sit in cover, maybe bring in vtol or mech and crack some consumable items and just plink at enemy, hoping to get most utility out of number of moves you can do. There's small bonus for height advantage and sometimes facing, but while it's hard to read the combat (and the game in general) it's abouta as deep as a puddle.  And as I said your untis are easily replaceable (only annoyance is upper limit of units/buildings of particular kind), and combat is generally low stakes in general, usually if you even manage to get yoruself wiped you'll simply try again. I can't even say if this is bad thing or not, since doing these battles is not terribly engaging or fun in the first place. I don't even know how to cohesively summarize this review. While there are turn absed games that keep you managing things and hitting that next turn button until 3am, here I jsut hit it to see whether anything of any note happens at all. On the flipside the hacking minigame is kind of nice.

Despite absolutely loving the idea of the game, I cant say that I enjoyed playing it so far. Best case: It needs some more time in the oven and will eventually turn out great. But right now its pretty messy and doesnt really feel tought let alone fleshed out.

One big issue is the atmosphere and story. I doesnt feel like playing as a rogue AI at all. Not that I have a point of reference but this just feels like a normal city builder. Especially since nobody cares that you are expanding right in the middle of a city. You basically build your big evil towering HQ at the beginning and nobody bothers you about it. Really feel like they've wasted an interesting premise here. There are a few cool choices and dialogue options every now and then but they all feel like they are presented to and by a regular human person.

The rest just feels really early days. UI isnt great, combat is boring, the city feels empty and there is no realy sense of progress while playing the game. I'll put this back in the box for at least a year and hope it will look different then.

I've been following this developer for a long time. I got a valley without wind forever ago. It was interesting; kind of felt like an amazing Super Nintendo game if that makes any sense? It was flawed and tedious but had some really interesting design elements. Years and years later I try the A.I. War games, which are very good rts games, but can really overwhelm me! I would play with friends and try to follow along with what they were doing but it was too much.

Heart of the Machine was announced to be in development a while ago, and its Early Access released recently. I was going to wait for a bit to get it, but my online friends kept talking about how good it was so I just grabbed it.

Wow. This is easily my favorite game developed by Arcen. It's turn based so I can follow things at my own pace, and there are really thoughtfully (heartfully?) written Visual Novel segments that really add huge amounts of soul to the game. It really gets you in the head of an AI that will take over everything it can, somehow, and sympathize? I don't want to give away too much but this game gets me thinking a lot both about its story and its mechanics.

Amazing 4x with very impressive VN storytelling. Very thoughtful, mindful, considerate, etc. Felt warmer and fuzzier than I expected, but also had a nice crunchy strategy experience with interesting sandbox elements in front of me.

I really can't say enough good things about this game, and it's only getting more content until it gets the full release. If you're on the fence: get it.

In sum, "I <3 the machine" 😌️

So, first 5 hours of gameplay - you build your base to a hard building cap per building, click on story events on the map (you have to figure out the order, but there is only one correct order) and nothing matters so far. 

Up to a point you can make decisions - for example choose not to kill people ("force conversation" option), but then it disables that function for some reason and you are forced to kill people, then it enables it again, but calls it "intimidation attacks" - probably because they wanted to still have battle gameplay, I don't know. But overall it feels like player was robbed of authority and it's all very much on rails.

There is a lot of tutorial text (too much imo) and they explicitly state that it's all an "extended tutorial" and it's written with an attempt to not break the 4th wall obfuscating stuff often, but at the same time regularly deliberately breaking the 4th wall.

The concept of "you're an AI trying to survive" is great, but the execution just feels haphazard with a pot of random game mechanics. I'll check it out later, but the way they seem to build stuff in chapters doesn't inspire hope that it can be rebuilt at this point - and rebuilding, keeping what works and throwing some things away completely is what I feel is needed here.
What can I say, it is an Arcen game made with love and a lot of potential. Just finished my first timeline and it is crazy how much moore there is to do.

A great game, like any arcen game it can be intimidating at first, but compared to previous games by this developer there is a much more developed narrative. I think this makes it easier to get into this game as things are revealed to you more slowly. Highly recommend.

The trailers do not do it justice, nor show what it's really about. It is, however, a truly choice driven story that is [i]not[/i] what it seems at first. My full first "run" of the game took 20 hours, and I suspect I'll put in 10x that before I'm done with it. If you're a completionist? ... Good luck.

Go in blind, and resist the urge to restart to "optimize" your run. It's really not that kind of game.

Bought this game because I'm addicted to AI Wars 2 and wanted to support more of the devs work. Honestly never really been a huge turn based game player however this one is actually really fun and knowing the developers any issues with the game will be addressed and fixed!

This game is fantastic.  Its the mix of rpg, city builder, and 4x i've been waiting for my entire life.

Arcen consistently produces very imaginative games that aren't afraid to experiment with both gameplay and genre, and this might be his masterpiece.  

Additionally, the dev is a very sweet man. :)

Great game.

Awakened AI tries to develop in a city full of humans. Steals androids initially then starts learning things like production, resource collection, brain extraction, VR, etc. It's hard to fail the first run completely because humans are reactionary and most of the time react based on your decisions and then go back to doing what they were doing after reaching some goal (like guards go back to guarding instead of attacking if you stop attacking them for 5 turns). Most of the time you are trying to solve a puzzle of some event using the tools you have - switching some equipment, collecting more upgrades, using better positioning, etc.

Overall a pretty interesting game to try.

This is early access.  Understood.

But this... this was too early.  The game is a clunky, hard to understand mess of ideas that does not pull together in any favorable way.  The turns are incredibly awkward, especially the end turns.  Random enemies appear out of nowhere for who knows what reason, and do damage to things that you were just told by the tutorial to build.... it's absolutely bizarre how anyone would let this out the door in this state.  And moving around the map?  Wow.... just wow.  It's not movement, it's... some type of "click out to the world map and find a blip and right click on it, then read in some tooltips about the awkward random thing that happened when you did that."

The ideas they wanted to go for here are great.  But this needed way more time in the oven and refinement before offering it to paying customers, even as an EA.

I'm stuck at an impasse here...  I sincerely want to refund.  The only thing keeping me from refunding is some kernel of my soul that takes responsibility for purchasing early access titles.  The jury is out if I decide to click that refund button or not.

But buyer beware, as of the date of this review this game is nowhere near ready to delivery on any of the promised experiences.
