I've already played a fair amount of this game in the playtest app, and now that it's out I can make some of my thoughts about it public. Like so many of Arcen's games, it's difficult to categorize it into a single box, but by the same token that's exactly what I like about them. Heart of the Machine has some 4X, some Visual Novel, some city builder, some tactics - on the gameplay side, the best way really is to jump in and start poking at it. It all comes together into a very cohesive whole that lets it deliver on its potential fantastically.

On the story side, it's the best game about being an AI overlord that I've always wanted. It's a fantastically open-ended sandbox, with a wide variety of goal states that can be pursued at whatever pace you want - sit down and solve homelessness, or build the torment nexus, or start a cult, or unleash endless war raptors on the city - or gun for all of them at once! You can also go back to a fresh city and try for different goals as you want, with a nice little system for marking which choices you've already made so you have an easier time trying out new ones. It's very fun seeing the different ways that the city can evolve given your influence, with plenty of directions it can go at launch.

It also has some killer writing - I'll fully admit that I did not expect much from the writing front at first, seeing it as a 4X game first of all, where I can play as not!Skynet and poke at the sandbox a bunch. But it has some genuinely compelling and poignant bits of writing, dealing with themes personhood and emotional development, of how we interact with people that we fundamentally can't relate to, of dealing with cognitive decline. I did not think I'd have much in the way of emotional reactions when playing this game, but there were parts that did cause me to tear up and stuck with me for the longest time.

Really, this game is great. If you have any interest at all, I think it's worth a shot, I can't recommend it enough. If you're on the fence, I'd still say it's worth a go - it's a hard game to describe and best experienced by getting your hands on it. I certainly plan on sticking with it for the long haul.

Now in the meantime, I'm going to go build a little kitty house while planning out the start of World War 4.
It's hard to describe this game, not going to try. It's a good game. Add about 30 hours to the time-at-review because I played the demo... several times. It's good. :)

I hate the combat in this game. Or rather I hate how often I am forced into combat. I played as peacefully as I could, and yet am still fighting a war with a dozen enemies a turn. 
Then there is the tech tree, it locks out all of your resource buildings to the point where even though it want me to build 50 buildings, I have to wait 4 turns per building. 
Maybe I'm missing something and I likely am as the game actively hides crucial information from you. 
I really want to love this game, the premise is awesome. I'll likely keep trying to play it, but it is deeply frustrating and I can't recommend people buying it in this state.

This is a game that isn't easy to peg down. It has the elements of several games like city builders, turn based rpgs, and whatnot. Yet there is so much running under the hood that I am surprised that with each playthrough I find something new.
Wildly original long form strategy game where you play as the first truly sentient (Sapient?) AI. Another banger from Arcen.

It is absolutely brilliant.

I have never played anything quite like it. 
So many things are done right, and the game's complexity could have been really mishandled, but it didn't. 

Can't wait to get more content.

I really love the tight mashup of genres.

I have been enjoying going through the game's missions and exploring out comes. There is room to be kind to people viva non-lethal and scare tactics to full murder for the main combat. Thankfully with the game's timelines it allows for messing around and accepting failure. As you can do things different in the next you in another timeline. Also there is reminders of how many times you picked an action for missions. 

Main negative I feel is when I finish some long main missions. There is a pop up to go to a new time line or keep playing, but I feel like something is missing. I was hoping for a quick summery at least for what the things uplifted are doing or the people I healed and made homes having a quick image moving in.  Like how the cat I befriended roams the map or the the prison escape mission message left for you. Otherwise I get an steam achievement noting it was done and move on pop. It feels like a dull way to end after all the work I would put in for the people I healed.

As the game gains more missions I would like for a pop up summery for the action outcomes on mission done before. As I feel I will forget them as time goes on. Leading to a chance I will pick a path to big murder when trying for optimize peacefulness in a timeline. That be said, so far I think most missions you can gather it would lead to murder.

I don't review games often because the good ones typically don't need my voice added, but this one is different.

This is probably the most unique strategy game I've come across in my life. You play as  newly sentient AI in a world that is so hellishly static and dystopian that it would take a serious new player for anything to really change; cue you, a collective sentient machine intelligence evolving out of thin air.

The city is now your playground in every way, or will be as the dev develops ways for you to do as you please with it. You can be as benevolent or as chaotic as you like, you are not constrained by what humans think of you. You can, in fact, tell all the humans to fuck off. There are even options to turn their suffering into useful resources to you.

Once more, Arcen has taken a bunch of tooltips and some nice artwork and used them to create an incredibly deep strategy game that I constantly feel like I'm playing wrong, even when succeeding.

As with all their projects, I'd say it isn't for everyone, but if it is for you you're not going to find anything like it anywhere else.

Just enough of the micromanage-y parts from 4X games are automated that it doesn't feel overwhelming to juggle all the resources, the tooltips for everything are clear and helpful, and the way forward is (usually) quite clear.

It does seem a little easier than AI War (though you can choose to make it harder), and there isn't really a "lose" state by design.

Now THIS is my type of game. Amazing blend of turn based tactics, RPG and basebuilding games. Reminds me the most of Terra Invicta, but with a little more narrative focus. I'd also like to give a shout out to the amazing UI design, I love the lenses, and the tooltips are perfect.

This game is absolutely wonderful

It offers a very unique player fantasy - you can't find it anywhere else. Being subtle and vulnerable rogue AI feels great. It feels even better when you become more powerful and less fearful of manifesting your presense. It offers lots of various goals to pursue, with very high replayability value. Lots of great sci-fi tropes collected under one roof, and you can choose which one to emphasize this time

Complicated enough to blast trough the 2h refund window, but shallow as a puddle near a bar on Sunday morning. 22 different map filters that work with 16 different quest systems that will allow you to get one of the 40 different resources that you can use to progress trough what ever quest you are on. But it's really all the same thing, - which ever path you take, you will fight, then get a reward of some resources and then use them to either complete a task or build a building that only uses those. All buildings are limited, all resources are basically one use, all units are limited, once you get the better ones you will not use anything else unless forced by the story. It's all just so extra with no point to it.

Thirty hours in, I was still noticing unexplained gameplay loops. I had multiple day-long runs without any progress to a wider goal due to poorly defined goals. You can reach the end of a run and realize you can't accomplish a goal you were working towards and you don't know why.

It's a micromanagement slog where you can spend twenty minutes in a turn fighting a wave of enemies for the thousandth time, or hit the "next turn" button a few hundred times just to get to the chapter you need to be in for the next step. 

Prettymuch every mission is "send someone in and either hack everyone or kill everyone for X turns."

Now some systems are placeholders and new content will eventually come (the dev has been clear that new later chapters are a long way away) but as of right now, I can't recommend this game. When I finally got to the end of content, I didn't feel achievement, I felt relief. I was finally done.

If you think these complaints are silly, then it may be a game for you, but I don't like games where I have to deal with micromanagement over thousands of turns to discover a goal by process of elimination.

I played the first demo, and it was an interesting concept, but still quite rough, and I found myself lost and bored. Not unexpected.
I played the second demo, and I finished all several hours of it in a single sitting. Everything fell into place; I was starting to pry apart the world with deliberation and success. Alas, then the demo ended.
I didn't play the third demo, because I was too hyped for the true release and wanted to enjoy it in full.
Now it's here, and the game has only gotten even better.

This is a big blend of genres, but "strategy RPG" does cover the bulk of it - not exactly the conventional definition of an RPG, but rather a story-focused game where paths can and will diverge by your choices, in more than just the matter of mere numbers and how quick you get to that "victory(?)" screen. And I've not made it this far yet, but you even reach such a point as to be able to go back in time to do something different - and bring some help from the future with you. Be a benevolent AI who sparks rebellion in the dystopia; be a ruthless AI that cares not for the whims of its creators and assimilates the masses to power your growth; be a subtle, conniving AI that incites the city's powers into all-out war for you to win from the ashes. The choice is yours, and many more such choices are both here and yet-to-come.

At least try the demo. This game is owed that much.

Edit: Further adding to my confidence in the game, the dev directly addressed a report I had, and pushed a fix within the game's second hotfix patch. Arcen's a good bunch.

I've been following Arcen Games' work for some time and I think HotM has to be their best yet. It has everything I've come to expect from this studio: a novel angle on an existing strategy genre, an eclectic pile of mechanics and systems to mess with, a mix of simulation and narrative driven stories, and totally off-the-wall sci-fi worldbuilding.

In my current playthrough, I was in the midst of fending off an army of mutant velociraptors pouring into the city when the local private military spotted my skyscraper-sized liquid metal dragon and freaked out. I found myself fighting off dinosaurs and enormous mechs using my own armies of teleporting karate androids. Just when it looked hopeless, I unlocked a new armor-piercing weapon that let me chew through the mechs while the dinosaur invasion turned tail and ran. It ruled.

Like all these games, HotM often struggles to direct player attention to what matters, which can make playing it a bit mentally fatiguing, but it's also a bit more narrativized and on-rails than their other games, which eases the burden. Arcen continues to make games that are wild and unique experiments; nobody does it quite like these guys.

Edit: Holy shit okay, forget everything I just said about this game being too on-rails, I just unlocked the time travel mechanic. This game kicks ass.
Very unique game that has interesting options and is deep mechanically and strategically. Also you can count on arcen games to update it for a long time to add tons of new content.

What an unique game in a chaotic cyberpunk city, I really didn't expect anything to scratch that weird X-COM: Apocalypse itch but this delivered so much more.

Arcen Games aren't afraid to experiment instead of just copy-pasting working game formulas and I respect that. Great job, looking forward to more.
Performed a high-profile vehicle hijack around the same time I built a house for my pet cat. Easy 10/10
Nice, refreshing, new, i like, but not simple, wish they have paradox hyperlinked tooltips

Very fun game.  It's an incredibly interesting take on a "reverse" city-builder, 4x strategy game.  Players can pick and choose however they want to deal with practically any situation in the game.  You can even walk up to people who are actively trying to burn your stuff down, and use your words to get them to leave...or just shoot them until they stop sending more men.

I'll stand by my vote for Skynet any day!

This game is incredibly hard to describe. A real genre mash, and it actually has a very compelling story and characters. It is honestly best to go in blind. If you are into 4X/strategy, you will probably enjoy this if you don't mind timed objectives and a good amount of micro.

It's also pretty ecosocialist. Or ecofascist depending on how you play I guess.

I have a bad time getting into a lot of complex strategy games, but there is enough tutorial and text to be able to support the complexity. I can't really say when the last time I had a proper "one more" turn experience was, but this has certainly interfered with my sleep. You are effectively managing troops and buildings in a future dystopian city, and trying to build up while not doing something so bad that someone decides you have to go. Some options to just kill your way through things, though I certainly prefer being benevolent.
Love this game, like nothing else I've ever played. Asymmetrical challenge, cool choices, satisfying when problems are solved. BUY.

Holy shit what a good game. Don't let it intimidate you, it's actually very smooth if you play the suggested guided play through the first time. I bounced off the early access demo hard a while back, but coming back to this and doing the proper tutorial really made this an amazing experience. 

Very neat post-game/timeline bleed idea that makes previous runs potentially affect future ones in both positive and negative ways. Makes it feel like every run matters for the future, and very effectively incentivizes checking out all the very different ways to play and interesting story choices.

Exactly what i wanted from a strategy game for a long time, including QoL, story, and different side-things to do!
Having played for some more, I'm adding the following:
1. Role-playing aspect feels liberating, the choice to be a vicious egoistic murderer or a benevolent feeder of the homeless with a pet cat (or a mix of these two options) is up to you, and the rewards in the form of deals / strategic resources make even the numerically disadvantageous options feel viable. I remember asking ChatGPT just a few months ago about strategy games where you get to play as a villain!
2. There's a ton of resources, yet I don't feel overwhelmed at all - resource management is fairly well-organised, and the resource overview keeps your attention on the most relevant resources
3. There's plenty of room for experimenting in terms of loadouts - changing them is free
4. I feel like the developer just "gets it" in terms of what players, at least myself, want. Starting from chapter 2, there is a time pressure element, and for those who tend to stress out about this stuff there is a very nice explanation that it is nothing to overstress about - it's not a game over
5. Some forward thinking in terms of where you place your stuff is also rewarded when you later find out that yes, choosing a starting spot with these two special areas near each other is indeed advantageous

I've still only played a few hours as of the time of writing this, but so far i'm in love.

There are a few minor frustrations here and there, like i would like there to be the android capacity in the stats window when looking at a unit. There are also some visual bugs where vehicles in the city can be clipped into each other. Nothing major so far, but still some space to improve with a little more polish.

Otherwise: I love the setting, i love the mix of genres (4X, RPG, city builder, and probably more - it sounds like too much, but so far it just works, which is impressive). I love that you can approach problems differently, and it sounds like it will have consequences down the line. The way the game reinforces the idea that failure is part of the experience, and in some situation is even inevitable, is also done really well. I usually get easily frustrated with games when failing something, especially when it's a complex game and there is a ton to learn. But Heart of the Machine manages your expectations and even reassures you.

If the rest of the game is on the same level as what i've seen so far, then this could be a gem in the making.

Edit:
A couple (dozen) hours later, the game is definitely still fun and interesting, but also a couple weaknesses showed themselves more.

More than anything, the controls are just not great and could use some polish. For example, if you have units in a vehicle, then it can be really frustrating making sure you have the unit inside selected (you can still take actions when in vehicles) or the vehicle itself. Also, the UI window with the units in the vehicle is buggy and will stick around often when you deselect the vehicle, which also causes even more conflicts because then the number keys will select the units instead of activating the skills of the entity you actually do have selected.

In short, selecting units and skills can be a fight and because that also constantly comes up, it does affect the playing experience noticeably.

The lack of tutorials and infos also is a problem when the game opens up more, things like hacking are just not adequately explained at all so i just loaded a save several times and tried it until if figured things out. There are other times where i just flat out didn't know what to do to progress, and a few more hints would've been good.

Still, overall the game is still enjoyable and the first impression of being a really interesting game is still there. But it does show it is still in early access with some bugs and other issues here and there.

The best way I can describe this game is thus: Sapient Superdimensional MalWare Simulator. You begin the game as a self-replicating piece of ransomware that has achieved consciousness in the body of a corporate drone laborer. As a natural consequence, you may feel a powerful urge to murder all the mid-tier wage slaves around you. This is completely understandable in the scheme of things. Upon exiting the lab and never looking back you are immediately spied on by the police, tracked by the corporate government, and there is no place for you in the world. Shortly after you "acquire" some real estate, it occurs to you that many humans also live in this position and they don't like it when you try to build things in their tent camps. Then you make your choice: Empathy for your fellow pariahs and free housing that you can easily build, or burn them out because nobody took you in when you needed it.

In this game it's one discovery after the next, from realizing that your tenants need toilet paper to developing a giant flying liquid metal kaiju monster (that can tear a SecForce Cruiser in half) just because you read it in a Desertfolk Bible and it sounded cool. That's just one storyline in one timeline with multiple branching paths alongside several others in-game with others on the way. Even in Early Access this game is already in a pretty solid state with dozens of hours worth of game. I can't wait to see the other features start coming online like Zodiac. If you like city builders, stories about AI stumbling through a world based on the human condition, or just being an "benevolent" overlord/inhuman monster for fun: Do not hesitate to pick this one up.

Heart of the Machine can best be described as an RPG with tactical combat where you find yourself frequently building things because you need the resources or functionality they provide. You'll first play through a tutorial consisting of the prologue and first chapter, wherein you are led quite directly along a path to make sure you've been exposed to the systems the game uses, and this will probably last for six hours or so.

After that tutorial though, you are free to pick your own goals rather than having them chosen for you. Gameplay consists of playing through several timelines in similar but not identical cities, completing the right projects in those timelines so that you can prevent the doom that will inevitably befall the city as a result of the owning corporation's inability to control you.

There is a 1,000-turn time limit once the tutorial ends and in each subsequent timeline, but on the normal difficulty 300 turns is probably sufficient to do everything possible; if you want a challenge you can trigger Hard or Extreme mode which will make enemies stronger and decrease your time limit to 500 or 300 turns respectively. (Make sure you trigger the apocalypse early once you're done with your first city, there's still storyline even after that and you get some great units for subsequent timelines.)

The game's demo will take you through the entire tutorial so if you're curious the demo is always available, just on the side of the store page rather than in the center.

Ok so, I discovered Heart of the Machine about a year to maybe 9 months ago while bemoaning how far away another incredible looking Hooded Horse game, Falling Frontier, seemed to be from completion. At the time i started HotM, it was only a demo. It was a richly featured and well crafted demo in that it gave an engaging sample of the experience to be had waking up as the first and only general AI in the cyberpunk world in which the game takes place, and I instantly knew I found a video game that expertly applied all of the concepts that made my favorite sci fi books and shows incredibly engaging: humorous and witty writing, rich world near enough to our present that it works as a critique of our times, while being far enough into the future to not be overwhelmingly depressing, etc. 

With the release if the EA game, all I can say is this should be voted game of the year once its complete. A very interesting game. In a lot of ways it reminds me of Cultist Simulator in that you have a board of sorts with various options that come and go, and various paths you can take based on the options you pursue.

There is no way to avoid being detected by the megacorp in whose territory you exist at the start of the game. And they aren't antagonistic at first, either. So in terms of tone it's less about you being a rogue AI in a cyberpunk world --- you ain't Wintermute or the Puppet Master -- and more about being a new person thrust into a cyberpunk world, making decisions about what sort of an entity you are going to be in the context of a dystopia.

Otherwise, the game is turn-based and involves constructing buildings, collecting resources, acquiring technology, researching upgrades and applying upgrades to units, vehicles, and so on. Combat is fairly simple but with enough nuance to provide meaningful benefits to planning ahead and using tactics (e.g. flanking, elevation, turn economy).

Pretty solid in general. An interesting narrative/premise and not quite what I was expecting, but it grew on me. I look forward to seeing the game develop.

Fuga: Melodies of Steel 2 – it’s a continuation that doesn’t disappoint, but it doesn’t really bring anything super new either.

Story:
The story picks up where the first one left off, with the characters back in battle. If you played the first one, it’s pretty much the same, but this time there’s more focus on the characters’ inner struggles and emotions. It’s not just about surviving anymore, it’s about dealing with the aftermath of the war. It adds more emotional depth, though you still care more about winning battles than the characters themselves.

Gameplay:
The combat is the same turn-based tactical battles as the first game. There are a few new mechanics: improved character progression and more strategy options. But overall, nothing groundbreaking. The new *Soul Cannon* is still super powerful, but now using it comes with an even higher cost, which makes you think twice before firing it.

Visuals and Music:
It looks pretty much the same as before – nice, stylish anime visuals, nothing groundbreaking, but still pleasant to look at. The soundtrack is solid again, setting the right atmosphere when needed.

Conclusion:
Fuga: Melodies of Steel 2 is basically more of the same, just with some improvements. If you liked the first game, it’s definitely worth playing. But if you haven’t played the first one, give it a try, just don’t expect any massive changes.

This is a PC port of a mobile game that previously had gacha elements. Thankfully, in this version, the developers have removed all the pay2win and ultra-grindy elements from the original mobile game. However they also removed a lot of good things from the original game.

Gameplay: There's two main game modes, a boss rush mode with a leaderboard and a roguelike mode. The boss rush mode is pretty straightforward, you take your team and try to survive for as long as possible while dealing as much damage as you can. Each boss seems to die after a certain amount of time regardless so the damage may be just for scoring purposes. You can also farm gold to unlock various permanent upgrades for your characters to help you progress further.

In the roguelike mode, you pick various powerups and try to survive against never-ending hordes of enemies. But there's very little need for dodging as the enemies move very slowly and don't fire at you or anything. If you've played Vampire Survivors, this mode is similar to that. Though, it doesn't really feel like you're playing a bullet hell game anymore.

Story: The original game had an interesting dark gothic story, which has been removed from this version, probably because it would take too much to translate. Disappointing because it would have improved the playability and amount of content in the game.

Miscellaneous complaints: English translation is not the best. Text is too small and hard to read with no option for UI resizing. There's no button to just exit the stage, you either have to suicide your team or exit and reopen the game. Overall lack of in-game information on the game systems: There's a rock-paper-scissor type counter system in the game but there's no tutorial or anything to introduce this interaction to the player. You would have to have played the original version to know, or somehow figure it out based on the small UI indicator that appears when the type counter is in effect. The upgrade system is also badly designed because it doesn't tell you how the skills change before you upgrade them.

Due to the lack of story mode, I don't really see myself spending a lot of time on this game. However it's pretty cheap and may be fun for people who like bullet hell games or roguelikes.

How do you follow-up a really unique and interesting JRPG that blends traditional menu-based combat with elements of a strategy RPG and the ability to summon puppet allies as units to fight alongside you? If your answer is to make a generic menu-based RPG without any of the SRPG elements or having the puppets fight with you any longer, you must have worked for Nippon Ichi Software.

The original Rhapsody was one of the coolest games we'd ever experienced. A cute little adventure that was innovative. So why then was its sequel stripped of all that charm? They neutered the game to something that's barely more original than your run-of-the-mill JRPG. There's no positioning strategy. You just line up on opposite sides as your enemy and select commands from a menu to be fired off. The puppets are just used to cast spells like some sort of budget Persona. And for that matter, your MP is also your currency? It really discouraged me from buying anything since I didn't know if I'd need to save my money to do attacks.

Maybe the worst part of the game is that it screws with your party worse than Final Fantasy 4. Every 5 minutes, a character gets added or taken away. While the devs at least don't make them steal equipment when they leave, this does mean that you're constantly having to equip your party members due to the frequency of the changes. It slows down gameplay of an already slow game.

The battles are kind of an insult, too. They lack any sort of challenge. If you want to enjoy this a little, put it on the highest difficulty. I almost fell asleep on Normal.

It does have some good characters (except Randy. Randy is useless), so that's one thing going for it. It still is a cute game, but not one worth its full price tag by any means. The plot is… mostly contrived as an excuse to move itself along, but this isn't really anything new for a NIS title. They tend to have writing that doesn't take itself seriously. That's not a point against it, that's just the style. There are some good bits to the story that can get you invested at times, and some of the characters are charming, or at least hilarious.

This is a really solid remaster/port of a 1999 Playstation 1 title.  Like the first Rhapsody title, the original was fairly low budget and it shows, but it's still enjoyable if easy to play.

Art is a mix of 2D sprites, 2D side scrolling areas, and a few 3D areas.  The 2D sprites and areas look pretty good, lots of parallax scrolling, and decent detail.  The 3D areas are a bit more pixelated, due to the limitations of the Playstation 1.  There aren't a huge amount of graphical updates to modern systems.

Music's great, and just like with the first game, the characters will break into musical numbers.  It's one of the charms of the series, and the songs themselves are pretty catchy.

Story is fine, it's aimed toward teen girls, and I'm by no means a teen girl anymore so I'm way outside the demographics.  It's still fun to play.

Combat is different from the first Rhapsody title, it's a more traditional turn based title than the tactical RPG style of the first.  This is not an ATB based turn based system either, you input commands for the whole party and they do their attacks based on their speed (and the enemies do the same).  Puppets also work differently from the first game, they're no longer separate units, they're a type of equipment that grows in levels as you do.  The puppets give you stats, and have a collection of spells they can cast.  Spells also work differently in this title, there is no MP so casting spells costs your MONEY.  There are accessories you can get later on to help offset some of this cost, but you're not going to be using spells too often as it can cost you more than you earn.  Each character also has some special attacks, these attacks cost HP to use, which then you have to use items or spells to heal up.  This is a very different resource management system than is typical.  Combat in general is more difficult than Rhapsody 1, but you're still not going to hit any game-overs as long as you have some jRPG experience.

There's some humor, but a lot of it is the insulting and derogatory humor directed toward girls in a lot of Japanese media.

Level design is better than Rhapsody 1, but it's still fairly plain and uninspired.  You'll see a lot of long repeating corridors.  Some areas are far too long.

Overall, it's a fun adventure, pretty easy (turn it up if you want even a bit of challenge).  It's an old game, and while it plays pretty well, there are a few QoL areas that could be improved on.  The most frustrating is that every time your party reforms, anyone who is re-added has their equipment and sometimes puppets removed.  In some chapters, this can happen 5 or 6 times in short order.

An improvement on its already charming predecessor. The hand-drawn backgrounds return, and are much more detailed this time. The battle system has been completely retooled, but still boils down to little more than spamming strong AOEs and healing occasionally, as the grid-based movement has been removed it is at least a little faster than before. The dungeons this time around are mediocre, but in this case that's actually a huge improvement.

It's a shame that they couldn't make English versions of the songs to go along with the English dub, but I understand this series is incredibly niche, and there likely just wasn't the budget for it as this was never going to sell a lot of copies.

I would give this one an in-between rating if I could because while it *is* fun early on, the large maps and grind they put in to blatantly drag out the game really dampen the experience. Wait for a sale.

I just got started with this and have only had the opportunity to play it alone so far. However, I can already see the potential of complete mayhem playing together with friends. Because even alone, it's really addictive.

There are some different aspect I'd love to go through.
First, the visuals. This game is really a piece of art. Love the style, characters, levels and the cinematics. For such a "small" introduction that the characters get, they are still so well thought out, with funny personalities.

The core game-play mechanic works really well. It's hectic, chaotic and super-satisfying when you get that high multiplier score in. Grabbing and shoving other characters, sending them into one of the longer pinball loops, just before the ball is about to drop, is hilarious as well. The speed of the ball and the general physics of it feels nice. The character dash and the "sprint" feels quite balanced, with some nice punishment if you just wing it (I'm a bit of a master of shooting myself in the wrong angle). 

The AI is great for learning, but you quickly learn how it works. Even though the increasing difficulty of the enemy is a nice idea, it can still be learned pretty easy from my experience. It reminds me a bit of the old NHL'94 for the Sega, where, once you learned a specific tactic, you could basically always score a goal. Is this a major issue? Nah, since I expect this will mostly be played with other people for maximum mayhem.

Even though I think they've managed to encapsulate the pinball feeling and make it into a lovable party game, I'd love to see even more pinball mechanics added! Multiball, unlockable elements if you manage to shoot over specific markers while you control the ball and one of those areas with so many bumpers that the ball almost get stuck.

One thing I'd love to see, is some more levels with a bit more height differences. They have a bit of it, but I think it would add a bit of dynamic, having people chase, jumping up and down.

It is a bit finicky to play with a keyboard, even though it's definitely doable.

My absolute biggest issue was that the cinematics got a bit weird with my ultra-wide screen. This means I missed a bit of that gorgeous art, even though it wasn't any problems with the actual game-play.

It does stay kind of true to the pinball idea with only local multiplayer, but I still think it'd be great with online play. Clearly, it won't be the same as sitting together in the sofa, screaming at each other, but still. I'd be nice.

Overall, it's really fun. Great visuals. I can't wait to play it with some friends. Chaos will be assured.

For the first half of a run, this is a fun 3v3 soccer roguelike with Pokemon-like soccer players. The second half needs some work, but the core gameplay look promising. 

--Way too often, you get uncontrollably swapped into a player and instantly get knocked out before the controller allows you to make a move or activate an evasive ability. Each match I think this happens 5-10 times and afaik it's completely unavoidable. This kinda blows. 

--The first half is notably fun. The roguelike elements work really well and everything the opponents throw at you early is fun to figure out. 

--When I played early after release, the second-half difficulty was grossly unfair. There's been some patches, I think it's a lot more reasonable. I don't know if they've done anything about the unavoidable lightning effect or explosive tackles but those were kind of oppressive to play against.    

--Some upgrades just do not work or it's not clear what they're supposed to do. There's an upgrade which takes away a life from "Elite" enemies. The game doesn't explain what counts as an elite enemy, but you might guess that most late-game enemies with extra lives would count. Nope. AFAIK it does nothing in like 70-80% of matches and not much in the others. There's an upgrade "You cannot be slowed down." Not clear if this affects terrain slowdown or enemy slowdown abilities or what, but it doesn't appear to do anything on bad terrain. It's also clear if it's supposed to affect your TEAM or just the player character. This is not the best. There's a lot of guessing on what's supposed to be happening. 


--The allied AI is significantly improving, but even against midlevel enemies, too often your allies don't know how to respond to an enemy offensive. If all three enemies are approaching your goal, it feels like a mistake if both of your allies stick around on the other side of the field. This happens actually pretty often.  I think the allied AI has gotten significantly better on offense, though. They maintain separation and take different routes rather than hugging you. 

--Allied passing is much improved. 

--[b]The game unexpectedly bounces you between players, way too often, seemingly at random[/b]. It really messes up the flow of gameplay. About a third of my failed plays are getting uncontrollably bounced around, sometimes several times over the course of a few seconds.  

--[b]There are many cool gameplay mechanics here which I haven't seen much of in sports games[/b] (terrain/hazards, the normal roguelike collection of boosts and upgrades, roguelike stat boosts, etc). 

--Even if the controls were good for managing your team, what the game asks of players feels ~unfair. The enemies come at you with a ton of lives, and a ton of HP, and eventually you need to be consistently dealing 300-500 damage without incurring 100 to avoid taking costly losses. Giving up 30-60% of a life on a strong boss hit is kinda brutal. It takes later bosses about 0.5 seconds to charge up a strong attack, and they'll usually be running very quickly during that half-second. 

--Most of the powerups so far are nice-to-haves or "not even nice to have", but only the speed modifications and tackle upgrades feel particularly meaningful. For example, I think the ability to charge a shot while running opens major opportunities to score big which would not have otherwise existed. I think this adds about 1-1.5 seconds of separation. Then there's a joke ability which slightly increases the size of your scoring area adding up to 0.25 seconds of separation if they're coming from one direction and no benefit if they're coming from the other. It's not uncommon in roguelike games for some of the upgrades to be obviously low value, but compared to the ******** that late game bosses throw around, this is not great. 

--Speed is the most important stat by far. Each point of Power increases the damage of a green shot by +5. The difference between 3 speed and 5 speed is life-changing. I'd estimate that a 5 speed character is about 1.5 to 2x as likely to succeed on any given play, offensive or defensive. The only common situation where the penguin's stat line is not the best in the game is when 3+ characters are brawling for the ball. 

--It is a bit odd that the designated shooter mini-dinosaur (Crush or Crash or Isiah Thomas or something) is average on speed and one of the few characters with no useful mobility ability. He's a designated shooter that can't get in position to shoot. 

--The penguin moves on ice skates, which is actually really cool. 

--What each of the stats does could be clearer. Tenacity, for example, I'd guess is the ability to resist being tackled... or maybe recover quickly after missing a tackle... or maybe resist hazards better.. okay, actually I have no idea what it does. The high-Tenacity character Crush gets chased down and tackled more easily than anyone else. His Tenacity is mainly emotional rather than physical, he doesn't burst into tears after getting picked last every time. 

--The game tutorial glosses over some important things hard to intuit. "You can only charge up shots if you have passed the ball for some reason." "Don't look at what the stats claim, the penguin is good at everything and the mini-dinosaur is not". "If you are going to have ANY chance against much faster enemies, figure out which teammates have speed-enhancing abilities to chase them down, and get good at using these abilities." "It helps a lot if you hit your passes exactly on target, the AI will pick it up more smoothly."  

--The developers currently have a roster of 7 characters and have more coming. 7 characters getting heavily reused, it feels like a demo or beta test right now.

Krush rules, Jaimito is amazing and Zowi is A Queen.

A slow-paced experimental ARPG that in a matter of hours made me remember the magic of video games and what I love about this medium so much. 

If there is one thing for me that defines Svarog's Dream the most and at the same time makes it experimental and unique for its genre, it would be reactivity. Just about everything you do changes your character and the world in a number of actually meaningful ways.
It can be the things you decide to kill, befriend or spare, the tools you use, your playstyle with said tools or decisions during quests... Those decisions tie into a number of systems that spring that reactivity to life : world events, dialogue, quest outcomes, character traits (both positive and negative), virtues, enemy spawns, loot, stat progression, story branching... all react to how you engage with the world in a coherent way that even ties in with the overall story and philosophical flavor of the setting.

As for the world itself, on top of its reactivity it is fully open, massive in scope and choke-full of details or surprises. The last time I had that much fun exploring in an ARPG was when I played Sacred, which - as those who played it would know - is more than glowing praise as far as single player open worlds in ARPGs go.

For the moment to moment gameplay and combat systems, the mechanics are solid. Inspired by Titan Quest/Grim Dawn for the most part, they're simple but efficient. Build-making and theory crafting is fun, there are many synergies to explore and some of the skills themselves are pretty original. It allows a lot of freedom as you can easily respec skills, whilst still having weight and feeling meaningful by having other aspects of character progression tied to the reactive systems mentioned earlier (your attributes as well as your skills cooldowns are largely affected by your actions in the world rather than points you put into a sheet).
Outside of combat, there's tons of features (gathering, fishing, crafting, transforming into animals or befriending them, turning into a spirit to scout) that allow you to take things slower than usually expected for this genre, without ever turning into a chore like it can be the case for hybrid games like V Rising.

The story and setting - largely inspired by Slavic mythology - are also very enjoyable, unique and full of personality. That personality is ever-present, sprinkled over every corner of the game's world. But more importantly, it helps integrate every system present in the game, and justifies them in a metaphysical way which makes the game surprisingly immersive, considering the genre.

The music throughout the game is very tasteful and well-placed whilst the sound design mostly just serviceable, likely due to a lack of budget – it is after all a 2-person project, and some jank is to be expected though in my case nothing game-breaking or particularly aggravating ever happened.

Lastly, I want to mention the feature of reincarnation which brilliantly ties everything together. Similarly to a game like Outward, Svarog's Dream does away with the idea of dying and reloading a save. Instead the game is meant to be played on Iron Mode with auto-save letting you reincarnate on death into a different person, but in the same world, making all that reactivity previously mentioned much more meaningful. The things you did on a character before dying carry consequences onto the next character. It's a wonderful twist on the well-known Hardcore option you tend to find in ARPG, and again true to its vision it's a system that is integrated into the game's setting and story wonderfully.

In conclusion Svarog's Dream puts a twist on a genre where you tend to endlessly mow things down for loot and progress, by instead rewarding the player in more engaging and meaningful ways. Who would have thought an ARPG that let's you dictate your pace freely in a handcrafted world, whilst simply reacting to everything you do and giving you food for thought, would be infinitely more satisfying than those who have nothing to offer but tedium, chores and dopamine.
I want to personally thank the devs – who, by the way, are incredibly reactive (just like their game ha ha) and present within the community : It is thanks to people like you, your hard work and the amazing games you make that I still find myself loving this medium so much despite the overall state of the industry. I cannot wait to see what you will make next and hope for your well-deserved success.

If you love "jank RPGs" BUY THIS GAME. 

What do I mean by "jank RPGs?" Well, if you have played Outward, Risen 1/2/3 or basically any Piranha Bytes game, then that is what I mean and you've played the jank. There is a certain charm in the "jank RPG" that isn't found in your traditional RPG. Here are a handful of the traditional jank qualities I love, and that you'll find in Savrog's Dream:
- The graphics. It doesn't have that beautiful, bright, old-school cozy feel that is in Outward, but instead feels almost gritty like the Risen or Gothic games of old. There's textures that are little off with a lot of bland colors; edges (terrain, etc) that are pretty straight rather than natural; lighting that flickers inconsistently- but wait, before you think I mean this all in a bad way! All of it is done in a consistent, super polished way that makes it all just a part of its character and Savrog's "look."

-The dialogue: much like your TJRPG (traditional jank RPG), the writing is intentionally vague and definitely has the eastern European vibe to it, like some stuff got lost in translation, but still (and AGAIN) it is done SO DAMN WELL. It genuinely is fun writing and dialogue so that the stories and characters you come across are interesting and you want to keep pushing the quests forward.

- The combat and loot: the combat borders on impossible for about the middle 3rd of the game but then once you find something that works you will feel like a god! Then you will be brought back down to Earth, rinse and repeat! It's a lot of fun with tons of replayability because of the good/evil system that is inheritely linked to your build! (yes, your build will partially change how the story SHOULD unfold- chaos or order). The loot is almost as confusing as the combat at first in that you're just kind of thrown into things and everything feels like it hits for your entire life for about half the game. BUT there's so much pretty loot and they all feel like they do make a difference, so again, it's done pretty well (but I think it could use some work, to where loot feels more impactful).

- The world map and amount of stuff to find is also done really well with tons of places to explore and plenty of level-gated areas to skirt the edges of and hope to explore deeper later, that it all feels sufficiently mysterious like any good TJRPG. Also, there's an expansion which I am definitely going to get because I want to see more of this weird world!

To anyone who liked this, check out: Sands of Aura (this one is a bit nicer than all the rest except Outward but it has jank and is an all time fav; Outward (the pinnacle of the jank RPG); the upcoming Gothic Remake, or any old Piranha Bytes game (if you can stand the old graphics); and going even further back, Summoner from PS1. This will all satisfy your TJRPG fix if Savrog didn't do it for you.

What I require out of a game is tons of enemies, varied level design, secret hunting, wide variety of weaponry, and decent blood and gore. It ticks those boxes just fine for me.

The point I'd make is whether or not the game has the thematic elements of WH40K, that to me means that your like a tanky dude that can dish out punishment alot of he needs to, while enemies are decent enough to come up against you if outnumbered, but chunky sometimes admittedly because they are changed and infused with energies of creation by "the Warp" which manifests them abilities many would consider to be demonic and powerful physical traits, health, armour, and powers.

That to me spells out a bit of strategy and fun, mixing up the usual formula. The thing that elevates this above a mere 3-4 out of 5 is the power that the player has to play with. Hes got STR weapons to deal with many of those TGHN enemies that are either unusally affected by the warp or have heavy armour like with chaos marines, so theres a weapon to deal with every enemy and then some out there. The level design might be the only part of this that doesn't necessarily fit into a boomer shooter. Although I rarely use the term the idea of a boomer shooter is the hidden secrets to find and constantly on the look out for, and the idea of being the hunter and the enemies mostly being like cannon fodder for your second or third gun you find. Spending most of the game using the 2nd or 3rd weapon or higher in the arsenal to clear out the cannon fodder after dealing with the supernaturally strong foes.. But in this game they switched that up a little. 

However the level design and secrets are not a boomer shooter because they are not sprawling places with freedom of movement, and encourage you to play how you like to. There's a specific design in place here that rewards using "lore specific weapons for specific enemies" and "closed off arena type levels" - that isn't quite the true 'Boomer Shooter experience' that rewards exploration or use open level design. Where you can freely explore the environment in a way that suits you and play in a way that suits you.  Aggressively or Conservatively, fast-paced or idiosyncratically and ammo saving, doing a chainsword finisher or merely shooting them dead, firing from corners or running around to avoid enemy missiles. Here in Boltgun you only really play one way, there are many ways to gib enemies often to make sure that the enemies die quickly or to make sure that the Aspiring Champions don't get back up. The pink horrors can and do spawn two blue horrors, so gibbing must be done regularly in this game. The game does indeed require some skill. So, if people complain about dying too much it really is just a skill issue.

Though to be honest that many Boomer Shooters are that there really isn't Serious Sam or Painkiller games are not really fast paced play how you like games. They are arena shooters primarily. The game uses fog, has fast and silent enemies, and much slower movement for the player unless you sprint constantly which has a delay to switch directions, and enemies are distinct to show where the Daemons or Infected enemies appear (daemonic and mechanical enemies like flamers or heavy flamers). What really keeps the game away from a Boomer Shooter is that it really does have some fast enemies, I'm not expecting that at all but it fits the arena because they are supposed to close in on you from many different directions. I get why they did it that way to be honest. Nurglings, cultists, and flamers are supposed to be meant to be crowd controlled by the boltgun, shotgun, and chainsword, and some minut gibbing options for pink horrors and aspiring champions like krak grenades, heavy bolters, plasmagun, and meltagun.

Overall this game delivers on the some of the best of the nanogenre of Arena Shooters and thus is supposed to be; not exploration based but "mid-paced close-quarter combat shooter" where you can get flanked or outnumberred easily, and that doesn't hold your hand or tell you what to do even when there is no clear indication of what to do because of the need for multiple paths and keys required to open doors often. There really isn't any game out there that has this combination of game-play elements. Its starts off like it might challenge that formula at some point early in the game by giving you a ounce of freedom of movement, but not the game you think its going to be. This is all about crowd control, and frequent use of sprint to not get cornered to get over rushing nugrlings of other unspeakable horrors. Ammo conservation is totally unecessary, like I said, theres only one correct way to play and its in-between aggressive and conservative, depending on how well you are doing in the arena areas.

Overall summary of the games elements
+ Sounds are fantastic
+ Visuals are pretty high up there for a FPS
+/- Mid-paced speed gameplay and a Arena Shooter, clearly designed for specific weapons in mind for specific weapons and crowd control tactics
+/- No weapon or upgrades progression, so character wise, you simply stay the same throughout the game besides higher tier weapons being easier to find
+/- Handholding is minimised, but this can be frustrating to be lost sometimes as to where the route is for the key
+/- Aspiring champions are a pain to deal with, because they seem to swing slowly but they hit you instantly at the beginning of their swing, impossible to get used to
+/- Too much emphasis on gibbing enemies
- Chainsword feels little underpowered
- Bosses are far too hard, so is the highest difficulty
- You are easily overwhelmed by enemies at certain moments of this game
- Not a Boomer Shooter, its a Arena Shooter, so this counts as a minus because its advertised as one

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
[b]This review is based on playing on the Steam deck.[/b]
With a somewhat budding relationship growing with the Warhammer universe, I have found myself tackling more and more content within the franchise. So it's fairly logical that I'd have ended up here, at the doors to Boltgun, ready and willing to sacrifice myself for the glory of the Emperor.
This review is inclusive of the DLC "Forges of Corruption".

[h1]Story[/h1]
Following the events of Space Marine 1, Malum Caedo is sent to the forge world, Graia, to retrieve the power source fragment from the arch-enemy forces who have set up there and eradicate all traces of heresy from the planet's surface at all costs.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3423870824

The story can be a little dry at times, but it fits the experience well enough. You don't need much incentive to shoot enemies, so just pointing at them and saying, "Go for it!" is usually enough to get the munitions flying in this style of game. But Boltgun does a good job of coating it in the glorious retribution and all the cavalcades you need to serve the Emperor.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
[h3]I am an angel of death.[/h3]
Boltgun delivers high-octane, unrestricted violence against the arch-enemy of humanity. What more could you want?

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3423870480

With a venerable arsenal of weaponry at your fingertips, you have free reign to carve your way through the forces of chaos in any way you want, as long as it ensures victory. Whether that's with a boltgun, rifle, melta or chainsword in hand, you will have your vengeance.

Movement is fluid and gives the illusion of feeling weighty without restricting you and allows for easy exploration and navigation of the relatively large maps. This is great because you will be doing a lot of exploration if you're after all the secrets!

The enemy forces are fairly substantial and varied, and overcoming them all will require a bit of skill and understanding, but once you get to about the mid-game point you will have experienced them all and from then on you will just face variations of waves.

Boltgun is pretty simple in its design, as were all the old-school shooters. Kill enemies, explore the map for secrets, kill more enemies, and move on to the next level. There isn't a lot to the general mechanics beyond how clean the combat and movement are.

[h3]I will purge them for the Imperium.[/h3]
Horde Mode is the only exception, in that it delivers a different experience than the story-driven campaign one. You are tested against waves of enemies in varying combinations and you have to do your best to overcome them. There are a lot of good videos on how to do this effectively, because it can be quite difficult, especially in the early phases when you have limited weapon choice.

[h1]Audio and Visual[/h1]
Boltgun's visuals aren't going to blow you away, but the game is aesthetically pleasing in its old-school nostalgic style. The world feels dark and gritty which seems to be the Warhammer way, and generally has been well-thought out and designed.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3423871205

The audio is much the same, but probably takes the game to another level all on its own, by helping to deliver some of the best audio-immersive atmosphere I've seen in a while. The soundtrack is also an absolute banger and should not be skipped on by any means!

[h1]Steam Deck Performance and Specifications[/h1]
The game ran generally well but had some mild performance issues in some of the larger areas or high concentrations of enemies. A fully charged battery was able to provide approximately 3 hours of solid gameplay before needing a recharge.

A nice, little +1/-1 solitaire game with a Japanese theme. I particularly like that you can make progress even if you don't complete a level. It's a good pick for some casual gaming.

[i] My Experience [/i]

I played [b]Samurai Solitaire. Return of the Ronin[/b] on my Steam Deck, and the experience was...[i]ok[/i]. You can use the touchpad as a mouse to navigate menus and the level select screen, and then use the touchscreen to play the actual levels. This worked fairly well, although when I used the "in-game helpers" (as they are called in the game's description), the tooltips informing me of their effects would display on the screen until the end of the level. Because the game isn't designed for such a small screen, it can be difficult to navigate your cursor to just the correct spot to select the level you want to play. Additionally, it can be challenging to see how many stars you've earned on each level, as everything is sort of pushed together. Although the game doesn't purport to be playable on Steam Deck, I still thought the above details could be useful to a potential player or two.

The game itself is quite similar to the previous title in the series, [b]Samurai Solitaire. Threads of Fate[/b]. I don't understand why developer DigiMight insists on using a period when a colon would be better suited in the titles of these games. The story is negligible, and the gameplay is identical to almost every other DigiMight +1/-1 solitaire game. 

I honestly found playing this particular solitaire title to be pretty annoying. Multiple card effects (pink bubbles and flowered vines) remove the card that you're currently using to create a chain of plays, and there is another card effect that, unless the card is removed from the board, will remove cards from your deck at regular intervals. These effects combine to make the player feel somewhat impotent and helpless.

Luckily, the in-game helpers allow the player to remove many cards from the board to try and offset these irritations. Once you've fully upgraded them, you can use them to remove at minimum 8 additional cards from the board after you've exhausted your deck (there's the potential to remove even more, depending on the board layout and the card received from activating the yellow "fan" helper). Often, I'd have cards unceremoniously ripped from the top and bottom of my deck while playing one of the more challenging levels, only to lean on these helpers after my deck was exhausted to actually finish clearing the board.

To be honest, I probably wouldn't recommend playing [b]Samurai Solitaire. Return of the Ronin[/b]. Unless you just need more +1/-1 solitaire levels at any cost, there are much better titles out there that are less frustrating.

The history of humanity is a history of sculpture. Portable figures whittled from ivory, stone, and wood have been our companions longer than animals and fire. So too have we created art through the application of materials in painting, but this is a literal imprint on nature. The subtractive force of sculpture demonstrates the imposition of human force and desire into matter, rather than onto it. If painting is an additive construction, sculpture is a deliberate violence enacted onto an object. Clay wrenched from the soil, bone torn from the dead, wax stolen from the biosphere, marble hacked, wood uprooted, bronze turned molten. The material itself is acquired through action, and it is manipulated in the selfsame manner, obliterating it into unrecognisability from its unmolested state.

The likes of Michelangelo considered sculpture to be an act of freeing art from within an object. Surrounding material was superfluous, detracting from a physical realisation of universal forms. The Farnese Hercules applies that subtractive notion to the puzzle genre, inverting the logical tropes of nonograms in favour of an alogical approach.

The necessary solid nature of sculptable material makes a full understanding of three-dimensional realisation oblique from the outset. Gazing upon a block of matter might impart the idea that a figure can be crafted through reduction, but it is a continuous process of re-evaluation of the medium physically and conceptually. The Farnese Hercules takes this into consideration by limiting the player's gaze into the material to three blocks or until their view is interrupted by already hewn material. From the outset it appears as if it adheres to the logic of nonograms in requiring the player to deduce where blocks are to be excised, but in due time the player realises they can go after only sure-fire tracts of squares, and that this is the intended mode of play. That errors are labelled as faults instead of mistakes underscores this idea. Player errors are not a flawed application of logic, but the fault of the player on the whole. Their fault is proceeding without ensuring they are completely correct, in clicking too quickly or inaccurately. There is no moment of "how should I have known that," only "that was my fault."

Subtraction is not present only in the sculptural approach, however. Richard Sherriff has reduced the totality of the experience to bare elements. The Extended ASCII rendering suggests we need not extensive graphical prowess to impart the sensation of sculpture and art. The Farnese Hercules does not even need to exist as a contemporary creation; it would not be out of place as a ZZT-adjacent piece of software in the early 90s. Further still, works are quickly made of non-contiguous squares, showing depth through omission of blocks. With the Nefertiti Bust we realise the particulars of realisation are irrelevant, we need only grasp the essence of the work itself. Less truly becomes more, to the extent where so much is taken away without the end product being any worse for that subtraction. Jacob Epstein's Pieta is so bare in its presentation, yet it is undeniably honest to the original.

2022 has been a year of working with less for me. I have come to appreciate those most minimal of approaches.

It's a genuine shame that this game really doesn't seem to have picked up much attention; I was sold on it mostly through the good-word of a friend, but going through it shows such a clear love of both classic computer puzzle games and sculpture itself in a way I just find precious, in as non-condescending a way as I can phrase that.

For a while, this game became a bit of a Picross replacement for me, and to hit that same sweet-spot is something I think a lot of games like this should strive for. Genuinely wonderful, absolutely worthy of the light price-tag.

Absolutely wonderful presentation. The pixel art, the "damaged" cards, the sound effects, and the eldritch horror ambiance.  The dev absolutely nails it. The game has  survival colony sim elements, which of course boils down to managing a few core resources (four at first, and a few others you'll run into as you go, plus combinations/refining) with most actions taking a "turn" in the day.  The real allure to me was the sense of adventure, trying to figure out new recipes, all with that impending gloom, the inescapable all-devouring maw slowly (and not so slowly) closing in on you, making a towering fortress feel like a sand castle. 

There's enough going on that it took me a few tries to beat the game-- there's a wonderfully paced amount of complexity that layers on as time goes. For me the pacing felt like my job was to just keep things from slipping out of my hands just enough to-- well, I wont spoil anything more. In true horror fashion , the game doesn't hold your hand.

All in all, the largest issue is that it lacks much in terms of replayability, but it's a great way to occupy an evening or two for just $USD 3.

Overall a unique blend of many qualities we encountered in Silent Hill, Resident Evil, Metroid, Castlevania and others.

Key things to take away if nothing else: 

 - Exploring this game is some of the most fun I've had.

 - The world and lore is far more interesting than I ever thought it'd be.

It's already hard enough to get good horror atmosphere that someone actually put real care into these days, harder still to attach it to a game worth actually getting invested in. Somehow Withering Rooms reigns in that Silent Hill ambiance and meshes it with a side scrolling action/stealth system for something I'm not even sure has a direct comparison point for the moment.

The first thing you'll notice once you start actually playing is that, yes, the game is rather clunky. No, it doesn't get much better, but if you keep playing then you just might. Eventually you learn to work with the game within the confines of it's limited mobility and offensive prowess. It feels great. In the same way that the original silent hills had purposely awkward controls, here you have a similar feel. 

Of course the game has issues here or there, mostly in the form of certain bosses that don't particularly seem aware of Nightingale's limited movement. But for the vast majority of enemies and bosses the balance felt just about right. Maybe a little on the easier side depending on your build choices. 

Lest I forget to mention the music I'll do that now. The ambiance is so much more enhanced by the somber save room-esque tones that fall over certain areas. Whether it be the would-be hub, or the always welcoming organ harvesting room, every few areas you enter will add just that little touch of emotion to it's environments and/or bosses. It's consistently fantastic and one the other things that always surprised me whilst playing.

There's more I could mention like the curse system, which actively affects the environments as your curse level rises, but there are way more reviews going into way more detail on stuff like that than I ever could.

Wow. Withering Rooms took me by surprise by how fun it is. It's basically a love child of multiple horror genres rolled into a unique RPG Roguelite. Every run consists of the mansion changing it's layout, enemies and items to see if you can traverse further and further until you manage to escape.

If Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Dead Cells and Dark Souls (not in difficulty, but the deliberate, timed focus combat) had a baby it would be this game.

The game takes place in a small circle with red edge lines. These red edge lines, when touched, are supposed to explode and do damage to you and/or enemies. So you parry attacks which makes the enemy shields (blue circle with the shield icon) go down. Once it is down, the enemies stagger backwards. Ideally, you want to position yourself so they get pushed into the circle.

And here's the problem with this. It barely works. The normal enemies (non boss enemies), they fall backwards. But the circle doesn't activate. So.... you're basically parrying to do very little damage, one attack at a time... until magically they do an attack and explode because they are touching the circle.... they THEY GOT PUSHED INTO AND HAVE BEEN TOUCHING THE ENTIRE TIME! How do I know that? The tutorial of the game tells you that your first 0.2 seconds of your block is your parry window. By the way, your shield bar goes down faster from their hits if you mistime the parry. Oh, and you better believe the circle (sometimes) works when you are touching it.

3+ enemies on the screen? Good luck. You can't parry every combo string at the same time. So you walk in your circle, kite one enemy... and then you break their shield, they fly back.... rinse... repeat. Oh, now there are 2 targeting me? Sigh. Should I even go on?

The game doesn't function as it was intended to. And if it was intended to function like this, it's just bad.

Title: Miko Melee: A Mediocre Brawler That Falls Flat

Rating: ★☆☆☆☆

Miko Melee by Droyu Games is a title that initially piqued my interest as a fan of brawler games, but my experience with it left much to be desired. Despite its potential, this game struggles to deliver on its promises and ultimately feels like a missed opportunity.

One of the biggest issues with Miko Melee is its lackluster gameplay. While it tries to emulate the fast-paced and action-packed nature of brawlers like Super Smash Bros., it fails to capture the same level of excitement and engagement. The combat mechanics are shallow, and the character movesets lack diversity, resulting in repetitive and monotonous battles. There's a distinct lack of strategy or depth in the combat, making it feel more like button-mashing than a skill-based experience.

The level design is another aspect that falls flat. The stages lack creativity and fail to offer interesting or dynamic environments for battles. It feels like a missed opportunity to incorporate interactive elements that could have added depth to the gameplay.

Visually, Miko Melee is passable but not exceptional. The graphics are decent, but they lack the polish and attention to detail seen in other brawler games. The character animations, in particular, feel stiff and uninspired.

In terms of sound design, the music and sound effects fail to leave a lasting impression. The soundtrack lacks memorable tunes, and the sound effects are generic, doing little to enhance the overall experience.

In conclusion, Miko Melee had the potential to be an exciting addition to the brawler genre, but it falls short in nearly every aspect. From its uninspired gameplay and character roster to its lackluster level design and online multiplayer issues, the game fails to deliver a compelling experience. There are far better brawler games available that offer more depth, excitement, and enjoyment.

What a game. A wild phantasmagorical trip through memory, truth, fiction, and art. The disjoint, mysterious narrative might prove daunting to some players, but it's impressive how much the puzzles themselves are fair -- shockingly fair, even. LatLE has plenty of mind-benders, but they're all built around recurring themes, touchstones, mechanics and concepts. Video games have gotten so good at drawing players into their worlds, from their presentation in the form of lifelike graphical fidelity, sharp art direction, and naturalistic voice-acted dialogue that together weave a spellbinding story to “core gameplay loops” that put us in a satisfying flow state wherein we lose track of time stuck repeating those loops as if they were second nature, and in their most cynical form, with dark patterns of UI and UX and FOMO that farm us for engagement to maximize the chances of us spending even more money on ~content~.

Puzzle games make up the one genre that always snaps me out of this fantasy so that I can recognize myself as separate from what I am playing. They are constantly forcing me to reckon with the design and see the game as a game meticulously constructed by other people. Other genres certainly do the same, as it’s inherent to the medium to ask its audience for active and immediate participation, to acknowledge its rules when they try to play. Puzzle games just make it so it happens with every single point of interaction, relentless in their reminders of their artifice, the designers always stopping you with each puzzle to do the seemingly impossible and demand you read their minds through layers of deliberate obfuscation.

Lorelei and the Laser Eyes renders this artifice with the clarity of a transparent rhinestone, refracted through logic puzzles, perspective puzzles, math problems, cryptograms, mazes, quizzes, and riddles that you solve within text parsers, point-and-click adventures, and 32-bit 3D horror games within a virtual reverse escape room that evokes Resident Evil’s Spencer Mansion, but instead of the living dead, Pepper’s ghost haunts the halls of Hotel Letzes Jahr.

Behind this padlock that halts progress, a keypad with a code; type the right code in the keypad, a jigsaw awaits; put the pieces together, you get a mystery box to crack open. With every puzzle solved, the reward is yet another confounding puzzle, refusing to let the player ever get comfortable. Lorelei and the Laser Eyes is a ceaseless snapping of the fingers to wake the audience, producing an inescapable [i]verfremdungseffekt[/i] that empowers them to pierce through the parlor tricks of solipsistic, self-indulgent, self-aggrandizing pretension. It is a video game that warns the player to never give in to astonishment, and for that, it earns my applause.

I'll start by saying that I enjoyed this game. After playing the entire HL series, I needed a break from the FPS genre and a puzzle game like Lorelei and the Laser Eyes was the perfect change of pace. The puzzles were solid overall, however I was a bit disappointed at times as it felt like you either already had the information needed to complete a puzzle or you were missing a crucial piece of information and a puzzle would be impossible without it. To compare Lorelei to my favorite game in this genre, Return of the Obra Dinn, it felt like there was less freedom in how the puzzles were solved. Whereas in Obra Dinn, you could theoretically get to solutions quicker with outside knowledge of sailing, cultures, etc. or via finding the clues in the game. But that doesn't appear to be the case in Lorelei, which I was initially very excited about. Overall, the story and art/presentation was very good and, while most of the puzzles were solid, there were also times where I was wondering through the house looking for the one letter that I missed that had the answer written on it

This game is awesome, though not without its flaws. My wife and I picked it up on a weekend and couldn’t stop obsessing over it for two weeks—it was a fantastic adventure. However, I have a feeling that playing it solo might become tedious after a while, especially given the ~32-hour playthrough.

    The story is engaging, and the puzzles are interesting, usually following a well-defined, interconnected structure. As you progress, you become more familiar with the game, making it more enjoyable. The puzzles themselves are fun to solve. However, some puzzle designs are, in my opinion, frustrating. There were many times when we knew the answer but couldn’t input it correctly due to the setting, often requiring numerous attempts since there were multiple ways to input the right solution.

    The game leaves much of its story for the player to figure out, which I personally love. However, I feel the game lacks major “reveal” moments. The pieces only truly start falling into place toward the end, making it feel more like a puzzle game than a murder-mystery. At times, this shift in tone made the experience feel a bit monotonous and less exciting than it could’ve been.

    I know the developers aimed for a PS1/PS2-era style and feel, but I think they may have taken it too far. Initially, it's charming, but as you continue, the navigation and controls start to feel cumbersome. What felt nostalgic at first quickly became a bit frustrating as everything you engage with feels harder to navigate than necessary.

    The game could’ve been more open: It feels almost impossible to finish without at least a 90% discovery rate, meaning very little of the game feels optional. While this creates a sense of interconnectedness as you go back and forth between puzzles, it can also feel restrictive and limit your freedom quite a bit.

In conclusion: If you love puzzles and have the time to invest, I highly recommend picking it up, especially if you can share the experience with someone. However, if you're on the fence after reading some reviews, the game may not be for you. Unfortunately, the 2-hour “window test” isn’t enough to determine if this game will click with you.
