I wouldn't recommend playing this game in short chunks or with large breaks between gaming sessions. Otherwise, if you like a good brain teaser and don't mind getting lost in a maze from time to time, this game is for you.

This is one very special game! A complete new take on puzzle game. Within a limited space, without dungeon/ level designs, an intricate design of intertwined puzzles allow you can keep progressing without feeling bored. I am just some hours into the game and I'm very hooked! 
The atmosphere and graphics manage to convey some eerieness and mystery. A very masterful game! 

Genre: puzzles

Well I had some doubts about this game, but in the end it was fairly interesting...tough though. Couldn't progress without some help at times, also didn't finish the final situation. The program allowed me to miss something in the maze....and I didn't want to go back to get it! Nothing particularly memorable about the game, and as I said I didn't finish it and probably won't care. Your call though. Have fun!
This is a great puzzle game. It's challenging, but rewards you for critical thinking. Some of the puzzles can be obscure, but if you take your time you'll be fine. Highly recommended.

Making progress in Lorelei means exploring the 3D maze-space of the Hotel Letztes Jahr, and piecing together a timeline of events across two centuries, and advancing a half-dozen separate longform puzzles, all at the exact same time, and the combined effect is heady stuff. Possibility unfurls around you in all directions, a flood of doors and mysteries that dares you to keep up, but there's always just enough guidance to prevent frustration from spilling over. The stark, Killer 7-inspired visuals are unimpeachably cool, the constant uptick of the "percent complete" tracker feels great, and the final challenge ties everything together in an immensely satisfying fashion. Just super charming throughout, even if most individual puzzles aren't especially interesting on their own.

This game feels like a large, delicate and intimate digital solo escape room experience. But calling it an escape room might undersell it, depending on how you like those.

Lorelei and the Laser Eyes is definitely a staple in the escape/puzzle genre - every puzzle enjoyer worth their salt should at least give this game a try, not just because of the puzzles but moreso how this whole experience comes together. The atmosphere, visual style and storytelling just hasn't been done before like that/

This game required 18 pages full of notes from me. If that sounds like a good time, you should play this game. Otherwise, I'm sorry you have to miss out on such a beautiful experience.

A great puzzle game with some interesting concepts. I feel like the plot is hit or miss is you're into it or not but you can ignore it completely and still find the game enjoyable IMO.
The puzzles aren't frustrating or needlessly complex and some are very rewarding once you figure them out.

If you like puzzle games or interesting in them, I think this game is a must.

This game is an absolute masterpiece. If you like well-designed puzzle/adventure games and brilliant stories, I can't recommend it enough. The visual design is unique and stunning as well. 

You might get immersed in an enthralling mystery and in some excellent puzzle-solving which will make you want to take notes and scribble some weird symbols and other random stuff on paper or on a touch screen. As the game has auto-pause on focus loss, it works excellent with multiple displays as well if you keep some note-taking software (or a simple graphics software, or a calculator...) handy.

Thanks Billy Basso for recommending this game in some random interview! I gotta pay it forward by praising it as well.

This is a very demanding puzzle game, some minor leaps of logic can be required to eureka your way to a solution for some of them, and this means it's very possible to be stuck for hours! If that's not your cup of tea, this game may not be for you.

I wish anyone else who wishes to beat it without a guide like me the very best of luck, it's possible but VERY DIFFICULT!

Song in the end credits was worth it though.
It is a very enjoyable game, with great atmosphere and puzzles! I definatelly recommend it!

This might be one of the weirdest puzzle games I've ever played but I greatly enjoyed it. Never has a game made me make such unhinged notes. You will need pen and paper for this game but not for the reasons you may think. There are so many fun secrets tucked away that to even  talk about it feels like spoiling it. I loved how many of the puzzles aren't about finding the answer but instead finding the right type of input for the answer. It seems apt then that a game all about input would only have one interaction button and four direction keys. This can lead to problems as the "back" key is also the interact button. Despite this being awkward at first I was able to push through because of this game's entire aesthetic. The use of colour, music, sound effects, patterns . I started seeing the maze in my dreams. I got entirely pulled in. Everything sucked me in.

Do yourself a favour and give this strange ass game a try.

Also excellent writing!

Amazing puzzle game. Incredibly stylish and fiendishly clever. Pays homage to early survival horror games while still blazing its own path. And unusually for a puzzle game, the story is fantastic - primarily in the way that it's told more so than the facts. I'll be thinking about this game for a long time to come and recommending it to everybody who will listen.

This game had me hooked in the first hour and ended with me filling a notebook with insane scribbles like "1979=1973 *series of greek letters*???". For all the things this game does right (there's a lot) it suffers from some issues that whether purposeful or otherwise left me feeling slightly more relieved than satisfied by the time the credits rolled. 
The gameplay loop is incredibly satisfying offering but the occasional "now what do I do?"s and fuzzy expectations on what is required for certain puzzles (multiple times tried to construct elaborate solutions repeatedly only to find out the puzzle was gatekept by an item 10 hours later in the game) end up bogging down an otherwise very good experience. 
The greatest sin this game is that the ui/ux feels very limited and constricting. I understand that this may be a deliberate design choice but the lack of a back button turns some of the later puzzles into an excercise in patience as you scroll back and forth through key items and the close button. A few quick qol improvements (map hotkey, page down key, BACK BUTTON) would have fixed 90% of the issues I had with this game. 
Tldr: very good, loses a lil steam towards the end due to clunky ui and some lack of direction

Also the puzzle randomization making online guides much more limited is such a cool feature.
This might be the best puzzle game ever made.

Great puzzles, great atmosphere, good story, not so great controls and ok mechanics.

Negatives:

I may be dumb, but would have appreciated a "You can solve this puzzle now" indicator, as I was often stumped on if I didn't have enough information or if I was just simple minded. Not a fan of the run mechanics, don't really get why it wears off. this makes back tracking a slog. Having one button makes clicking back a chore, and certain puzzles are a pain if you go one step too far, having to cycle all the way around to get to the correct symbol/letter/number. Probably not a negative, but the money system, just finding them randomly about, as well as the "click on this random item you may not have noticed to proceed" isn't my jam.

Positives:

Having a pen and paper to solve the problems is super fun! You kinda feel like a genius when things click into place. While some of the challenges are quite easy, for the most part it does a good job being just tricky enough to use some of that delicious brain juice. The graphics are great, giving a noir vibe with the stylish black and white but also red every now and then. The music adds to that. There's an old timey technology vibe that really works as well, both in presentation and sound design. Moving around the menus, opening up your purse every time you need to look for items, and just your footsteps as you walk around all sound wonderful. references to video game history, either through the 8 bit esthetic of your inventory or the tank controls and Silent Hill sound effects when playing the in-game console are all top notch. Lorelei doesn't outstay it's welcome, ending at just the point I was like "ok, I'm done correlating the dates of the ketchup packets with the symbols I found in the clogged toilet bowl". I don't know if I'll ever revisit the game, but such is the way of games in this genre.

Nice puzzles, it drags too much at the end.

You need to take notes and after reading them you'll seem schizo.

The setting and ambiance are good.  The story started off intriguing, but eventually wore me out. There was a whole set of puzzles I was praying would be optional, and when it seemed they weren't I gave up.  More "moon logic" than I hoped there would be in some of the puzzles.

A truly great puzzle game, well-balanced in its difficulty and so heavy on atmosphere that it's just about marinating in it.

Collapsing a whole hotel's worth of puzzles and clue-finding down into a singular climax is one heck of a game design and narrative feat, and well worth the price of admission. It's one of those games that you can never really experience twice, which may turn away people who thrive on replay value - but not all games need to be replayed to be great. Sometimes, your first ride is enough.

Quite fun puzzle game with a strange and intriguing vibe. Really worth it for the style and very original story. I am not a great puzzler so I used occasional light hints, but nothing was too frustrating. That said if you are a very hardcore puzzler you might find it too easy, but I don't think most people would.

I enjoyed this more than initially expected. It's almost like playing Alone in the dark or Resident Evil but without any of the monsters, just the puzzles. There are a few to many instances where the "puzzle" is simply a matter of finding the information and then entering it, but overall the quality of the things you actually have to solve easily makes up for those. The atmosphere and graphical style is excellent. Though the lack of any volume controls are a bit baffling.

Overall a decent puzzle game that I'm glad I played. The game is really carried by the stylish setting, visuals, and atmosphere: it has the feel of an old school Resident Evil but with the puzzles only. The puzzles aren't too difficult - I only had to look up hints for maybe 4 or 5. They are of varying quality though: 

- there are simple puzzle book / cereal box type problems which are fine but aren't all that engaging in a video game,

- there are puzzles where you are basically just told the answer in a document later in the game and the only challenge is recognising that this document corresponds to that lock. 

- There are a couple of tedious sequences where you literally just have to look up and type in a name or number from the documents you've collected, no interpretation or puzzling required.

- there are some memory tests, these are actually kinda fun,

- there are some truly interesting puzzles that require creative thinking.and pattern recognition. These are the puzzles that make the game worth playing, but it's a shame there aren't more of these in place of the above.

The story is very cryptic and I didn't really understand it until after I'd finished the game and read up online, but that didn't hurt my enjoyment of the game at all. 

I reached the credits in just under 17 hours but didn't 100% the game.

Simogo is one of the best game developers out there. I first got into their games with Sayonara Wild Hearts a few years ago, and although this game is very different, Simogo's attention to detail that was showcased in SWH is certainly present here. The game is filled with excellent puzzles that will challenge you just enough to make each successful solve feel rewarding, and the game's story is incredibly complex and deep, filled with meaning (although uncertain at times).

I can't wait to see what Simogo comes out with next, although it will probably be several years. I wish more game devs operated like Simogo.

This is a fantastic puzzle game. It oozes with atmosphere and is littered with interesting / clever puzzles.

There's a few puzzles that miss the mark, but I overwhelmingly enjoyed my time with the game. It stumbles a bit towards the end, and the story is a little too obtuse for my taste, but I would day-1 buy a game like this from these guys should they decide to make another.

Cryptic, obtuse, esoteric. A rambling story, a nonsensical atmosphere, a never-ending mystery and a monochromatic fever dream - with hours of puzzles carefully placed throughout a labyrinthine manor that overwhelm you with intrigue, contemplation, frustration, then epiphany. You start to remember the first time you watched the lady masturbating on the couch in Mulholland Drive, Remedios ascending to heaven in a gust of wind grasping onto the sheets, and the circular ruins being consumed in an invincible fire.

Then, as sudden as it started, the game is over - you are now through the maze. As you walk down the crimson path and as the game envelops you in the final stroke of mystery, you wonder to yourself - now what?

This is my kind of video game, and I loved every second of it.

7/10 from me. Quite a good game. I would anticipate people who like pure puzzle games will like this more than I did, but I went in expecting something more like Obra Dinn or Golden Idol. A puzzle game with meta puzzles and layers. Instead, it's essentially an escape room, but it is a good one!

This game has good puzzles and exploring the mansion is fun.
I'd recommend this game to some people, but it has some flaws that prevent me from recommending it in general.
I was stuck at around 40% completion due to [spoiler]an upside down lamp on the second floor[/spoiler] which forced me to use a guide.
The 2 [spoiler]maze[/spoiler] sections of the game are contrived and annoying. I don't mind backtracking in the Hotel, or revisiting the [spoiler]forest video game[/spoiler], but I draw the line at the punishing need for memorization due to threat of small mistakes.
I think the game would be better if you could access what I assume is faster movement earlier on, but I understand the need to have walking pace movement to avoid players running past clues since the Hotel itself is both puzzle and setting. I guess it is a pet peeve of mine that I get annoyed at slow movement when barely less than appropriate.
Relating to the clue collection system (aka memory) in this game, and the backpack [b]tm[/b], I think having additional button utility while on pc or using a controller would be nice. I don't see why back buttons or a bookmark wouldn't be included, I don't want to have to take a photo or write down every detail even if that is the intended experience, because stupid monkey brain that I have would rather just jump back and forth between while trying to memorize details.
Game is best when the flow into and between puzzles is smooth. Game is worst when I've solved a puzzle but need to toil at the finer details in the memory. This problem doesn't happen often at all, but I lost my patience in [spoiler] the 2nd maze [/spoiler].
Game is good overall, but I dislike having my patience tested.

THIS GAME IS ART!

I had to pull out a guide at around 70% and was still lost and frustrated.

3/10 laser my eyes out of my skull.

If you like mind teasers, maybe you'll enjoy the first 60% of the game. 
The last 40% of the game is just not worth it- please save yourself your time and money and go play literally anything else.

This game is a love letter to puzzles and the kind of Lynchian weirdness that we all come to love in classics like Twin Peaks. I absolutely fell for it for in minute one and enjoyed every second of experiencing it. I wish I could start all over again.

- The puzzles are taken seriously and there is no hand-holding. You will need a pen, paper and a good night's sleep for some of these.

 - The plot commits to its weirdness and remains bravely ambiguous and strange even until the end.

- The limited colours and geometric designs create a really bold aesthetic that then, in keeping with the themes of the plot, becomes its own recognisable character in the game. You'll see the same motifs repeatedly and come to understand them and their meanings as the time goes on, allowing the setting to slowly reveal itself to you.

Atmospheric, smart and strange. Really excellent game and a very easy recommendation.

Decent puzzler, though I had to look up a few clues along the way.  Unlike some games, none of the puzzles seemed directly unfair to solve.

Also, you can pet a dog.

Intriguing style, OK puzzles, but the most bafflingly bad control design I've ever seen.

The developers decided there should only be directional controls and a single action control. That is, if you're using a controller, B does the same thing as A. (And X, Y, both shoulder buttons and both triggers.)
[list]
[*]Because there is only one interaction button and that button interacts with items, to open your journal you need to carefully manoeuvre your character to not be facing an interactable item.
[*]There is no "back" button, so the only way to leave a puzzle you don't know how to solve is to deliberately fail it.
[*]Since there's no way to leave a puzzle other than failing it, messing up the input to a puzzle necessarily kicks you out of it, making the retry loop slow.
[*]The journal consists of menus nested 3 levels deep with (eventually) dozens of items. Since there's no back button, leaving the journal is a matter of navigating to the "Back" menu entry several times to use your one interaction button on it.
[*]Most of the puzzles involve numeric input but, again, one is limited by the singular interaction control. Inputting "9999" to a combination lock involves 40 button presses. Other puzzles involve wheels with 100 positions that can only be advanced by one position per use of the singular interaction button.
[/list]

If you find the style and nature of the puzzles sufficiently compelling, there's a mod that can be found in one of the Discussions threads that adds a "Back" button, but it cannot address the other issues. But for me, the control design completely broke the game. I gave up after a puzzle which I knew the solution to in a couple seconds but needed to spend half a minute pressing "A" around 50 times to input it to the game.

A great puzzle game with decent variety of mechanisms to solve these puzzles. The story is a mix of surreal, psychological, and real (in the context of the game), and is a good motivation to continue solving the puzzles, learning the story bit by bit, reading new documents, letters and so on. 

The puzzles are well-designed and the solution is always logical — however, it might take some time occasionally to figure out what is being required of the player. Usually though the clues are right next to the puzzle itself (the only exception I found is the final part of the game, where I had to check the internet to figure out that I needed the very first discovered puzzles to use for the solution). By the way, with almost 100% certainty you will need a pen and paper to make solving puzzles easier. Or you can screenshot the game and solve the puzzles in e.g. Paint.

The stylistic choices are nice, and I especially like the music.

There are, however, some minor things that made the experience not quite perfect: the controls in certain areas ([spoiler]prototypes are the worst offender IMO, and the weird speed ramp due to espresso introduced so late in the game is more conductive to running into walls than quickly navigating the hotel[/spoiler]) were seemingly intentionally frustrating, and navigation in certain places ([spoiler]the labyrinth, especially once the mirror is broken[/spoiler]) was annoying with no valid reason to be like that (again, screenshotting helped). The minimalistic control scheme also made it a bit frustrating to check out the puzzles for the first time (you [i]must[/i] enter some kind of "solution" in each puzzle, backing out is not an option, even if you have zero clue yet of the solution) and fixing mistakes (in most of the puzzles, entering an e.g. wrong digit in the middle means that you must finish entering the combination, see that the solution is wrong, and than start over, which isn't a big deal once, but may become frustrating when happening multiple times).

Overall, I would certainly recommend the game to those who love solving puzzles to uncover a bigger mystery behind it all, and I would advise to be patient, as the game itself is trying to make one to take it slow (one of the achievements being to speedrun the game is kinda confusing in that regard).

The game is atmospheric and intriguing but stupid controls kill it all. It will waste your time like no other game. Most of the time you will spend not solving puzzles, but trying to find a way out of a screen with a list of collected information. The developers did not bother to make a back button in the game, the game has a lot of long lists and to exit the list you need to scroll to the "back" item and sometimes these are dozens of items. For the sake of a strange whim to make one-button control, they completely destroyed the quality of life. In order for this game to be good, the developers just had to listen to the community comments and add Back and Map buttons. But they do not want to do this, and I do not want to support such a derogatory attitude towards the user.

[h1]The Death of the Author[/h1]
TL;DR: A surreal exploration of the meaning of art through puzzles. I came away from this title feeling like it had been tailored specifically to my tastes and abilities, and I absolutely loved it.[hr][/hr]
In [i]Lorelei and the Laser Eyes[/i] you'll be answering a curious invitation to collaborate with an eccentric director on his newest project in a mysterious old European manor-turned-hotel. As the story develops, you (as a player) will likely come to the conclusion that coming here was a terrible idea, but protagonist Lorelei is driven by her passion for art and the opportunity to work with a living legend. What ensues is a multi-layered mystery involving secret societies, a plot spanning decades, and an examination of the act of creation, all through the lens of a potentially unreliable narrator.

Genre here is a little hard to pin down, but I'd describe the game as being a combination of exploration and puzzles. Starting with nothing but the letter that invited her, Lorelei will quickly stumble upon a multitude of puzzles. At first it feels overwhelming, but as you explore more of the hotel and its surroundings, you’ll start a drip-feed of clues that will give you the context you’ll need to start chipping away at the massive tangle of logic, pattern-recognition, and other brain teasers. It’s a slow burn, but also a very satisfying game loop; each time you make some progress you’ll potentially uncover a little more plot, more of the manor, and of course more riddles.

Somehow, the difficulty of the puzzles was pitch perfect for me. I managed to solve everything in the game without feeling like it was ever insultingly easy or so hard I needed to resort to looking up hints. I say that not as a brag, but to point out how well-tuned everything feels. A fair few puzzles required creative approaches to interpreting the puzzle itself, but many more test your ability to make connections between the riddles and information you'll encounter through exploration. There was only a single puzzle that felt like it required outside trivia knowledge not presented within the texts of the game, which leads me to think I missed its related hint.

There are a ton of different books, pictures, and other clues spread across the estate, but it never becomes overwhelming thanks to Lorelei’s photographic memory, represented by having instant access to a categorized list of every piece of meaningful info you've encountered from your inventory. This prevents unnecessary backtracking while giving a glimpse into how our artist-protagonist’s mind works. My only gripe with the design of the system is the very basic control scheme: the entire game is designed to use only one button input. This means that you'll be browsing nested journal entries (for example), and be forced to physically navigate to a “back” or “close” selection repeatedly rather than having a separate button to exit the memory system directly. I love the idea as an inclusive design option for those who need simplified controls, but I hate that it's mandatorily forced on everyone.

Besides that one (admittedly frustrating) choice, I was absolutely taken with the game’s design. Everything looks appropriately mod for the early 1960s setting. The largely monotone color scheme is faithful to the art film aesthetic, and makes the flashes of fuschia feel important and almost otherworldly. Even the bonus currency being “American Dollars” tickled me. The story’s themes and method of slowly unwinding just enough to let you come to your own conclusions felt like David Lynch at his best. If you enjoy slowly picking apart narrative and gameplay puzzle-boxes, aren't put off by the pretense of the presentation, and appreciate stories that leave [i]just[/i] enough to the imagination, you're almost guaranteed to have a really satisfying experience with Lorelei.

Puzzles range from easy enough to "ye gods, how did anyone ever figure that out." Visual design deserves all the awards. Play this if you're a fan of 1960s European avant-garde films and Dutch angles. Lorelei is one of my favorite protagonists, with her chic chignon, her smart little clutch purse, and a walk that's all business. Honestly I'd play a straight-up walking simulator with her. Minor hint for the early game: [spoiler]Solve the document tubes early.[/spoiler]

Despite some weaknesses here and there, not far from a masterpiece. If you enjoy having multiple sheets of papers laid on your desks with various drawings, letters, names, and other symbols, while asking yourself how can these be connected, just buy the game, you will not regret it.

This one is a bit tricky... it's certainly a good game, maybe even a great game, but it left me a bit cold in the end - which was all the more disappointing because I really liked the style/atmosphere/concept of the game.  I got into the story and mystery, but didn't quite enjoy how it all wrapped up.  The puzzles are also somehow creative and overly simple at the same time.

In any case, if you like puzzle games or the sound of "giant escape room" then this is for you. Not quite Obra-Dinn or Outer Wilds or Golden Idol, but few things are.
some of the puzzles can be pretty tough, cool game though

Video games are ART and I won't listen to anyone tell me otherwise.

The longest escape room I've ever done, except there was actually interesting payoff at the end and my friendships are still intact.
Very stylish puzzle game with somewhat frustrating controls.

Been the first time in a while I've enjoyed a game where I've had to take pages of notes that someone without context would think was the scrawlings of a mad man. Just rolled credits and I am extremely satisfied. I think I want to loop back around to discover more things about the game's story that may have went over my head as I was trying to not rip my hair out dealing with some of these puzzles. Strongly recommend.

Este jueguito me hizo sentir un repelotudo, pero después (y ahora) un tremendísimo genio, pero también un increíble disléxico. Hice todo solito, sin ayuda, muy rápido, me sentí un putísimo crack PERO en el último puzzle tenía todas las respuestas bien y correctas y todo pero no me andaba hasta que repelotudo mal me di cuenta que tenía mal copiada una cosa (y no era la primera vez que me pasaba algo similar!!) 

Aún así, el juego es como un increíble y gigante escape room combinado con un test de IQ. Al principio me quejaba de que el juego se sentía como una colección de puzzles de revistas arrojados en el espacio sin ningún orden aparente, pero la verdad es que temáticamente tiene muchísimo sentido. No solo eso, sino que la narrativa del juego es interesante, una especie de metacomentario sobre el arte digital y el arte en general y... whatever the fuck happened to Lorelei. En muchos sentidos es bastante Alan Wakesco, en esto de que las cosas escritas ocurren en el juego pero en realidad no pero en realidad si pero ocurrieron pero no ocurrieron. No sé del todo bien que entendí de la historia y que no, pero no me importa, me gusta quedarme con la sensación de todo. Atmosféricamente es muy rico, temáticamente muy interesante, los puzzles tickean mi cerebro y me hacen sentir cool. Las referencias a Silent Hill o Resident Evil no se me pasaron (y también me hicieron sentir culto). Al principio no tenía muchas ganas de jugar porque no tenía tantas ganas de usar todo el brain power que necesitaba para jugar al jueguito pero admito que me cagó enganchando y siento que salgo del jueguito con al menos un punto de IQ más. Me iba a dormir y seguía pensando en algún que otro puzzle, uno lo resolví mientras iba en el auto y lo pensaba, otro lo resolví sacando una foto del puzzle en el baño y pensando mientras cagaba, son esos juegos que los seguís jugando mientras no estas jugando y después tenes ganas de llegar para entrar y ver si la respuesta que se te ocurrió efectivamente tenía sentido. Esos juegos que te persiguen digamos. Cuando te trabas es una verga (me pasó un par de veces) hasta que logras destrabarte y entrás en el flow de puzzle tras puzzle tras puzzle y todo se vuelve fácil y todo te sale y te sentís un crack. Algunos realmente siento que están bastante oscuros, y lo pasé con un 98.4% Los puzzles de los shortcuts fueron probablemente los que mas pro me hicieron sentir, sobretodo porque todos me salieron muy rápido.

Lo ÚNICO que me molsetó, fue que el puzzle final era... raro. En el sentido de que tenés que poner 3 combinaciones de inputs kinda raro, y si una sola estaba mal nada andaba y no sabías cual estaba mal. Tenía un error en uno de los años porque había copiado mal (dislexia) y estuve como una hora lidiando con eso sin saber cual era el error, fijándome en las 3 combinaciones hasta que tuve que sacar mi amigo el internet y chequear que mis respuestas eran correctas (lo eran) y recién ahí me di cuenta rechequeando todo que efectivamente había puesto una respuesta en otra respuesta. Por esa razón (porque tuve que googlearlo) me sentí un poquito decepcionado del final, podrían confirmarte que una cosa está bien así no entraba en modo paranoia.

I thought people were exaggerating when they said I’d need a pen and paper for this game oh boy, they weren’t. Lorelei and the Laser Eyes is, without a doubt, one of the best puzzle games I have ever played in my life. The level of detail, the intricacy of the puzzles, and the sheer intelligence behind the game design are nothing short of mind blowing. Every puzzle feels deliberate, rewarding, and, at times, absolutely maddening in the best way possible. It challenges you in ways most modern games don’t, making you feel like a detective piecing together a surreal, cryptic mystery. The atmosphere is hauntingly beautiful, the narrative is deeply engaging, and the sense of discovery is unparalleled. If you love puzzles, real, satisfying, mind bending puzzles this game is an absolute must play. A true masterpiece.

Excellent Puzzle game with perfect vibes. The puzzles revolve a lot around pattern recognition than straight up math problems and be aware, these can a bit challenging on occasion (but not impossible). Took me 40-ish hours without getting hard stuck on any puzzle and without rushing it, so don't expect this to be a short jog.
Fantastic game with very clever and meaningful puzzles. Can't wait for the next one!
I love how the puzzles are scrambled so you can't just look up answers.
I really enjoyed it! Maybe not to everyone, but if you're already interested you'll probably enjoy it too.
Masterpiece. I was consistently impressed by the immersive, intelligent design. Hard but rewarding! Don't be ashamed to look up a hint or two.

A short, but [i]intense[/i] and satisfying rougelite experience, They Don't Sleep casts you as the sole surviving parent of an infant child born into a zombie apocalypse. The initial plan is simple: survive long enough to repair your broken truck and escape to the coastline. Problem is, you're just a normal woman who knows how to use a gun and has to keep her child comfortable, clean, and fed, keep [i]yourself[/i] comfortable and fed, [i]and[/i] manage your supplies....

Fortunately for you and unfortunately for your character, tanking you or your baby's stats will merely reboot you to the beginning with your experiences intact. So you'll get stronger alongside getting better at managing your resources and time.

Once you've escaped the nightmare, there's New Game+ mode if you want to continue the nightmare, plus multiple ways of making your experience more difficult, if not more interesting, including [i]ditching the reboot mechanic[/i] for a true Roguelike experience.
Parents don't sleep. The game ain't kidding on that one.

Zaxterian - Space Frezy is the 10th game of ZaxtorGames I've purchased and the 9th I've played. Oddly enough, I've never played Rock'n'Roll. It's one of the next in the queue. All ten games are definitely the work of ZaxtorGames, mostly through his own coding and asset creation or contracting out for unique music, etc. There's the occasional Creative Commons music piece in his games catalog but nothing I could find that's stolen, misappropriated, or otherwise used unethically. If I'm in between recommend and not recommending, I'll typically recommend a unique work and not recommend one that consists of non-unique work.

Zaxterioin - Space Frenzy is a 2D rougelike space shooter. There's permadeth but you carry your currency with you. It's not without progression. There's a working leaderboard too, even if I'm quite terrible at getting anything other than "at least it's not last place" on it. The firing distance, strength of shots, and other weapons / powerups-related variables seem to be appropriately balanced, but it's possible that later in the game it's not (didn't obtain all of the powerups / weapons / etc). The controls are responsive and precise regardless of whether keyboard and mouse or gamepad is used.

The music, sound effects, and graphical assets are surprisingly not super amateurish this time around. I always found the amateurish art of games like Poggers to be a cute selling point for the game, but this game definitely is one of the more professional-looking and sounding of the bunch.

The $8.99 price tag is likely to be an issue for someone randomly perusing Steam. Let's review some of the competition:
- Nova Drift can be obtained for a similar price on sale but is nearly double the price at full price. 
- Asteroids.. But Roguelite has a similar level of artistic design quality but is an inferior game. It's only $1.99. 
- Asteroids Millenium is much more traditional Asteroids than a roguelite. It's $7.99. 
- Aliens & Asteroids is a traditional Asteroids-like experience for only $1.99 and is polished. 
- Bit Blaster XL & Super Bit Blaster XL both share the Asteroids aspects but not the roguelite elements. Both are under $4.
- Asteroids Recharged is $9.99. Better presentation, worse gameplay/controls, and yet another that's missing the rougelite elements.

VERDICT:
This might be my favorite ZaxtorGames title thus far. It's definitely up there with Vektor Z and while lacking the extra gamemodes, this game's single mode is superior to any of the modes in Vektor Z. It's still sub-$10 and for the amount of time and effort put into this title, I have no issue paying $8.99 for it. The controls are responsive and precise, the gameplay is fun, and the various systems in game are balanced appropriately. For someone with no ties to the developer's other games or content, it might be a title to wait for a 25% off or similar sale. That's moreso due to the low cost of Asteroids-based titles on Steam than any issue with the quality of this game.

Relaxing tactical battle / ball game where you play as Desta, who has returned home after a difficult time in their life and is worried how being reunited with their friends and family will go. You play through their anxiety dreams and work through Desta's worries through a metaphorical game of dodgeball representing the difficult conversions ahead.

Thematically it's very sweet. The ball game was a technique used by Desta's father, a youth counsellor, to get kids talking about their problems. You confront each of Desta's friends and family in dreams and learn about Desta's life through the resulting conversations.

Gameplay wise it's a fun little dodgeball-like game. It's tactical combat, but you have to have a ball to attack, so you can try to monopolise the balls, you can pass them around and use skills for added effects, you can try to neatly bounce a ball off of three enemies and back into your hands... there are lots of possibilities. It's fairly casual; it wasn't very hard, and the framing device used by the narrative reassures you that failure is always an option, it's just a dream and you can try again. I think it's meant to have roguelite elements, but I completed the main story on my first try and didn't continue, so I'm not sure how much replay value there is.

It's also fully voiced, and the voice work is pretty good. Personally I think the voice acting and the storytelling are the main positives in this game; it took me on Desta's journey and made me care about their story.

I'd recommend if you like tactical games and you want a fairly casual, story-driven experience.

Nock is definitely one of those "easy to learn, hard to master" kind of games! I think it has the potential to be the next big VR e-sport.

The simple gameplay of using the bow and arrow to hit the ball is extremely fun, and the included cosmetic/season pass levelling system makes the game quite addictive as you level up, collecting new bows, playermodels, and blocks. The movement controls have you gripping the controllers and throwing your hands back, forth, up, and down to move around, and it works really well with the games Rocket-League-esque style, it for sure wouldn't be the same if it just had simple stick-based movement. 

It's got a pretty solid matchmaking system with 1v1, 2v2, and 3v3 options that span across both casual and competitive, each different mode has it's merits and I'll be swapping between them quite a lot! Usually I play 1v1 until I find someone I like and we can party up in 2v2s together!

On the topic of partying up, the game has a great party system! You can basically just think up any code made of a few characters and have that be your party/room code, you can have one you agree with beforehand or make up one on the fly and send it to your mates. I'm not sure if it also integrates with the Steam friends list, but the code system is pretty good, especially because it facilitates crossplay with your friends! Yeah so this game has crossplay and is out on most major VR platforms, the game has a tight-knit but very active community, now spanning across PCVR, Quest, PSVR 2, and Pico headsets. 

As the game has expanded out onto different platforms, the recent addition of crossplay does come with some downsides though. Do be aware that some people playing the game are very sweaty, even in casual matches. As the game has been out for ages on Quest some players have become very good at the game (probably because the Quest has about 3 games worth playing lmao) but I'd say definitely tough it out if you keep getting matched with high level players, because a simple friendly match is really fun and kind of a work out on the arms by the end of it!

Hopefully the cross-play element of it keeps the community thriving. I think if the devs play their cards right in terms of marketing and trailers this game could absolutely blow up. They should definitely make a big boast about being one of the few multiplayer VR games across almost every major VR platform, and really put themselves out more, play to their strengths in terms of what they've got. If it was my game I'd make a trailer showing people across all different platforms picking up their headsets (Valve Indexes, Quests, PSVR, Pico) and all partying up together.

So yeah this game is super fun when played against non-sweaty/toxic players and I think I'm going to sink a lot of hours on it now that it's on PC. Fingers crossed the playerbase grows from here!

Decent game, but a pretty heavy ask for $20. Should've MSRP'd at $10 max (and then gotten sharp discounts). The Quest version is $10, but if this is the "premium PCVR" version, that's even worse. The store page info is laughably non-existent about what the difference is between the two versions of the game and why one cost twice as much.

You're bound to your usual 2020's style battle pass progression for unlocks, insanely uninspired. Furthermore, battle passes don't belong in games you have to pay for. The "premium" tier is included with PCVR, whereas I guess you have to buy it as an add-on if you're on Quest. 

The matchmaking is terrible, even beyond the abysmal player counts (11 peak online players since launch). Game has crossplay with the various other systems, but it doesn't really show. 1v1 is massively boring, same as it is in most 1v1 situations, there's only so much variety, especially if there are skill discrepancies. You can exclude 1v1, but then matchmaking takes eons. 

Thankfully they added some single-player courses with the latest update, but the execution sucks. You need to go from the menu, to the 'training range' area, from where you can wander to the portals for the courses. You can do this while matchmaking, which is nice, but when it finds the players, it pulls you out of the course, into the 'match lobby', before getting all the players connected. So you then sit there waiting for everyone to connect, which I burned a casual half-hour of just getting looped on this. When everyone doesn't join, it kicks you back to the main menu and you restart, disregarding any progress of your course. I get that they're somewhat meant to be small enough to do quickly, but I don't like being rushed along versus a random variable of matchmaking in a game with ~50 players.

Movement is an acquired taste, maybe. It doesn't have much ability to tweak it, and on Index, is less than enjoyable. Even trying community keybinds, I settled on something I liked from making my own, but it still doesn't feel good for me. 

The maps are pretty, but you don't really get to see a lot of them with everything going on, so not much of a win. 

I think it would take a pretty heavy revamp of base systems, and I don't see that happening. Not a bad game, as much as one where most of the systems don't really work, or they suck. Hitting the ball with the arrow works, and the blocking mechanic is cool, but the rest of the game crumbles quickly.

Bonus: their roadmap it looks like they want to add a "store to buy unique items" store? Surely that won't require a premium paid currency.

[h1] FOG...just wow [/h1]

How can I introduce such a title? It's no easy task, that's for sure. There's so much to be said about it but, at the same time, I can't put my finger on where or how to begin. From it's unique and charming art style to it's very much needed take on the roguelike genre as a whole. Innovative, wild, random and full of personality. This is the type of game I want to see. So...let's go ahead and disect it to the best of my ability. 

[h1] Near Vanna [/h1]

What will probably first catch your eye is the visuals of the game. Making use of Unity, the title decides to create a unique set of worlds that can only be described graphically with an example, think of it as some sort of...Soda Drinker Pro. But it goes beyond that simple comparison (which I honestly think underestimates this game itself, but there is no easy way of describing it). It's the subtle, and not so subtle, details that contribute on making FOG's world on of the most interesting to look at and revisit, something that many roguelike games tend to forget. 

We can talk about the NPC's and bosses designs, making use of distorted photographs of human faces and colorful textures that all together give some kind of uncanny feel to it all. Which is specially clever given that these "angels" of sort are pretty much our only shelter on this mad, mad world. Speaking of angels, the symbolism in this game is pretty clear from the get go. Risking to get myself on the terrain of self interpretation a bit much, although one could argue it's one of the game's intentions, I think it's important to also shed light on what FOG might be trying to communicate regarding on how it interprets the afterlife...or, something...you'll see what I mean.

So, we got earth and ten circles of...hell? Heaven? Nirvana? It's hard to tell...and maybe that's intentional. I like to think of this world as a mashup of many religious concepts with the objective of either giving a more bizarre approach on how it all may work or maybe portraying the ridiculousness with which some ideas have been incrusted on the beliefs of so many people. The skill tree, for example, all parts from the image of an apple as a direct reference to the forbidden fruit. The amulet is depicted as a crucifix. And each level is named after a sin of sorts.

[h1] 0 haloes gained [/h1]

Gameplay wise, we also have tons of things to discuss. FOG's core behaves as a roguelike. With each death throwing us back to the previous level. And each complete level awarding us with experience plus 10 haloes, the game's currency, if we found the hidden gray man on the scenario...more on that later. Experience is used on the very well designed skill tree, where we can improve many stats like recoil, attack, move and reload speed, lifesteal, critical hit chance and many others. At the time of writing this review, the maximum level you can achieve is 50. This ultimately means that we can not max out the entire tree and it's designed in a way which makes us think about our decisions on which abilities we want to level up. It is an amazingly well crafted system that ties directly onto the items we can equip.

Haloes, on the other hand, are the currency used to buy all of the items available. This ranges from a full armor set, to different weapons, spells, and many other objects which are meant to upgrade or change the behaviour of certain aspects of our character. Maybe it's a small boost to one of the previous explained skills, maybe we are talking about a very powerful weapon but with a clear downside to it. The twist that comes with these items is that they are all random. We spend 10 haloes to buy an item from a certain type and what stats come packed with that item are up to the game. And while this may seem a bit harsh at first given that getting haloes is not such an easy task, we quickly realize that it's not really about getting the best items. More so about learning to play with what you get and adapting to the different builds. 

That is the key component of FOG's amazingly fun yet simple gameplay. The different builds that you can think of and that the game is willing to give you. You may chose to have a very high chance of explosive damage but a rather tame weapon. Maybe you compensate the obvious downsides of a melee choice like an axe with an absurd amount of movement speed and lifesteal. Maybe you use a totem which allows you to focus more on the objectives rather than the enemies themselves. The game wants, and will, force you to adapt, think and vary the style of your playthroughs. Yes, it is true that you will eventually find a powerful enough weapon that most other items become trivial and your use of the skill tree may be less restrictive, but that's when the high replay value of this game really shines. 

Given that you can find the gray man on all levels, you guarantee yourself 10 haloes per scenario which translates on one item per level. This progress, intentionally, may seem a bit slow. But once you beat the game, you are rewared with 50 haloes. This, from what I can tell, is done in order to encourage the player to go on a shopping spree and test out different equipments. And it does wonders to the game on the long run. FOG is simply, a different kind of roguelike. A very much needed one. On which going for long and extensive runs is not really the point, but rather focusing on the way you play around and face situations on a rather short experience. It is a very fresh addition to the genre in that sense, and I think many other great games could learn a lot from it.

[h1] The way of the fetus [/h1]

There are other comments to be made, but I will try to be as brief as possible. Starting with the soundtrack, or rather the lack of one. It is an...interesting choice, that's for sure. While having a glimpse of what this game may sound like is something I crave for. I dont think FOG needs music. I would say the silence and sound effects are part of what this game is. If you really can't stand the monotony of it, you can always play something in the background. 

It may take you a couple tries to understand how some aspects of the game work. And I understand how the lack of any guides can be a bit underwhelming for you. But, then again, I believe the fact this game remains unknown just improves it's quality. It's up to you to learn it's ways, it's up to you to find all gray man locations, It's up to you to learn how the items work. I was actually considering making a guide for some basic information, but I'm conflicted. I want to help newcomers get the hang of things but I also would like to keep the mistery of it all, and allow people to figure stuff on their own.

[h1] Play FOG [/h1]

I kept on debating if maybe I was attributing a little too much to this videogame. And you know what, maybe I am. But the truth is, I think Happy Art Club knew what they were doing. It has a very unique style that goes beyond what a lot of people may consider just a sh!tpost or an amateur's game. Given the aesthetics and the gray man himself, there's a clear inspiration from LSD: DREAM SIMULATOR. And witnessing that such a piece of art is still being used as a reference by so many talented people warms my heart. 

In the end, this game is simply exceptional and a lot of fun. Happy Art Club have stated that they are already working on new weapons and spells. And having read the many update logs and changes that this game has gone through already, I can't wait for what's to come. Not only on FOG, but from Happy Art Club in general. If anyone from the team gets to read this, thank you! I cannot express how much I was in the need for a game like FOG and I wish you a great future on the gaming industry if that's what you are aiming for. 

Oh, and the game is really cheap, just give it a go already.

Thank you for reading.

I will recommend the game, however I am really mixed on it.

On one side, you have amazing features like an actual top run history (sadly not a historical one on top), as well as your character growing based on how much you played him, but on the other side the game offers very little explanation on pretty much anything. Above actually gives me hope that the game has potential and the developer has good ideas that I haven't seen in games in this genre in a solid way, the advancement by playing is in fact the first time that I saw it being done and it felt rewarding to play a character I would enjoy. However, I can't really say I had a character I enjoyed which I explain further down.

Which skill affects what? What do the values on the character actually mean aside from high or low? How do you unlock new characters? Especially the last one is one that hurt since you have to read the game updates or go to discussions on here, and that should not be necessary.

Further, reaching 30 waves is quite far in - either by play time or in general how far you advanced. A nice progression would be that special bosses drop a key. E.g. I think at 22 minutes in the game itself, I killed 9 bosses. Giving 4 keys at that time would allow me to buy more characters and test out more. I played for 2 hours and haven't gotten a second character, not that it takes you that long if you know what you do, but first without the information and then learning how the game actually works, you can expect it takes more than 2 hours or a lucky run of picking what is good without knowing it.

I don't want all unlocked after 2 hours, but at least that I can play 1-2 more characters, especially if I chose one that I end up disliking - I am just stuck with him.

Talking about unlocks, it may be better to start off with 2 keys instead, or make it 3. And instead, weapons are also locked away that you unlock via playing, or add upgrades into that as well. I see no reason why 1 of 3 elements should be locked away and the rest is fully available.

Now to the game itself. After figuring out what weapon is solid, this was all it needed to get to 22 minutes on insane, after which I died because a boss slowly approached me and I didn't pay attention, so the issue was not being too weak, but simply bored by having nothing to do. You play on the same map with the same character and a very small selection of weapons. A good chunk of the weapons are directional and feel just way worse than the rest of the weapons, but due to the small selection and the easy access to rerolls, you pretty much always end up with the same build if you want the best build. The only difference is a slight delay in which order you get them.

The graphics are meh. The Barbarian/Warrior (Axe guy) I played felt weird. His body and head is 66% of the sprite, if not more, and while the body looks buff, the legs look more like sticks and frantically move around like legs of an insect. The background is nice but repetitive, the map does not simply repeat it's structure but is missing something to fill it out (as in, it doesn't loop forever and feels hand-crafted, but is completely empty and just stone walls and a stone floor).

The monsters are kind of the same. The first thing you face are 3 differently colored slimes, to then face your first boss who is a weirder and bigger slime of one of the 3 colors.

2 of the weapons - poison and skull - use the same (to be fair, wonderful looking) texture but differently colored. Now that I wrote about that, the names further go into the bland aspect. Poison. Skull. Flail. Kunai. Bow. And upgrades like Speed, Damage, Armor. It just feels incredibly boring and lacking character. That actually describes this part including the graphics and stage design the best. It almost feels like you have 2 different people working on this, one coming up with creative and interesting ways and the other being barely motivated enough to do the bare-minimum that it functions.

On the other hand, the achievements are nice and well thought about, which again shows the creativity of the developer that was also shown in the positive things I mentioned, which makes it even more confusing as to why the actual game feels bland. 

Hitboxes: Top, Music: Top - but the music has long gaps in-between playing tracks and it almost feels like their volume is not leveled, Sound: Lacking and overlapping sound kills the sound, also sound is too loud.

Is this better than Virtuoso? Nope, not even close. However, this is a nice app as far as music creation apps go in VR. I would say this is okay & a nice start to Early Access. It's budget-priced, so I can recommend it, but there's other's I would recommend over this one.

Basically, at this time, in Early Access, you're really limited to the synthesizer, the drum kit, & the looper. That's it as far as tools that you can use. It's got some nice things like the automatic in-rhythm option that is also an option in Virtuoso so that you sound better as a beginner. You can set the metronome sound as well or a have your controllers vibrate to keep you in rhythm or you can use lights. You can also have a backing drum kit playing to inspire you.

Within the drum kit & the synth, there's many different sounds you can choose from. You can also bend volume, twist your controllers to get more volume or a different sounding drum kit sound or even bend notes. You can record the different loops and then export them to your PC for your later listening pleasure (or displeasure as was in my case).

Game is running on the Unity engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting a steady 90 fps. I did not experience any serious issues or bugs. The only bug I noticed was that it would not save your volume setting for the synth. 

Overall, this is a simple music creation looping software for VR that is easy to learn. You can definitely make some nice music or terrible music. However, you are limited by the limited nature  of the app in Early Access. You can change volume or delete loops, but you can't create layers for their timing in the final product. So they automatically loop until the overall loop is done. There's no mic. There's no community functions / sharing. 

[b]Rate 6.5/10. I'm scoring this high because it's budget-priced and easy to use, but I would recommend several other VR music apps, such as Virtuoso, before this one.[/b]

Memes aside, [i]Zero Wing[/i] has long been a favorite of mine, and this is a solid, if slightly bare-bones presentation of it. Some may decry that it's "just a rom in an emulator" but Arcade games can be a pain to deal with so having something nicely configured for you with steam implementation is a plus and this does offer some features such as practice mode you can't get from simply running the game in MAME. DIP Switches are easily accessible and there's a respectable variety of display options, though I actually love the CRT Filter they use by default, it looks much better than the hacky bilinear filter a lot of low-end retro-rereleases smear all over the screen.

That said, this is the [i]arcade[/i] version of [i]Zero Wing[/i], which is frankly the least interesting version of the game. If you come in expecting the iconic "All your Base" scene, you'll be disappointed for a second before realizing the game is still pretty awesome. The developers have stated they're looking into adding the scene and if they do I think it would also be cool if they added the completely different Anime intro from the PC Engine CD version as well. The arcade version also has frankly the worst soundtrack, with none of the hard-hitting bass of the Genesis version or the epic orchestration of the CD version. The arcade instruments just sound a bit... [i]farty[/i]? If they add an option to choose which soundtrack or even just add the other versions of the game I think that would go a long way and make a truly comprehensive edition of Zero Wing, though I understand that likely takes additional licensing and may be too costly to be practical.

That said, this is a good presenation of the arcade version and will no doubt become a mainstay of my Steam Deck experience. I'm a huge advocate for retro collections and rereleases with nice Steam-friendly launchers and achievements, so this is a win in my book.

There are not many negative things to say about this release. I was only really mainly hoping that this would also include the Mega Drive version as I vastly prefer that soundtrack. Though what I would like to see more of is:
* More sound options. Allow us to change the frequency rate to more closely gimmick older game systems (22KHz for an example, with different audio-filter options).

* Add different CRT filters or let us customize it more. They can look good if done right.

* Maybe change the way the info menu looks? Not a big fan of how big the text options are, but that's just me being nit-picky.

Old School Taoplan shooters are well know for the unforgiving difficulty like Truxton.  And Zero Wing isn't an exception.  Fortunately, this version of the game offers a number of 'assists' to allow players to practice or see further into the game than they otherwise might not.

The core gimmick with Zero Wing is that the player's ship has a tractor beam that allows them to pull an enemy ship in front of them.  This enemy ship can then be used as shield to protect the player's ship or hurled as a projectile.  Even the medium sized enemy ship can be pulled in, though; it affects the movement of the player's ship.  Zero Wing also has a super bomb pick-up that takes forward spot of a tractor beamed enemy and speed ups.  Though, I find the game practically unplayable with more than 1 or 2 speed ups.  

The graphics, music and sound design are all top notch for the era it came out.  And I think it all holds up.  Zero Wing is definitely my favorite presentation of shoot 'em ups of colorful pixel graphics and rockin' chip tunes.

The raw difficultly of this game isn't for the squeamish.  Fortunately, it offers an autofire assist.  As well as save states and even a rewind feature.  However, only the autofire assist will allow the player to unlock certain achievements.  Personally, I find these assists invaluable.  As much as I enjoy playing Toaplan shooters, I can't make it much further than the third or so boss in most of them without tons of practice.  Unlike Truxton, Zero Wing doesn't seem to have as deep of a power up system.  Which is good and bad.  The good is that's much easier to recover if the player fails.  The bad is, the player can't get a crazy powered up ship that makes the game far easier if they can collect enough power ups.

I'm on the fence about recommending Zero Wing.  I really like it, even if I'm trash at it.  But I can easily see someone getting frustrated with it.  Even with the assists.  Still, I think it is a solid game that looks and plays superbly.  I don't recommend this for anyone dipping their toes into shmups.  However, if you know you like the genre and aren't bothered by classic brutal difficulty, I think it's worth a look.

In addition to this, the play can grab an upgrade that places satellites above and below the player's ship.  These satellites for both more fire power and enemy projectile blockers.  Once that upgrade is obtained, the play can further upgrade their ship with a spread shot, a powerful laser or homing missiles.

Immortal Family is about managing your own clan in a cultivation world. Basically it's Xianxia CK3-lite.

It is surprisingly deep. I suggest you to play the tutorial before doing anything.

My advice is to always use your points on clan creation to get extra members. The initial start is very bumpy otherwise. In addition you should be disabling the celebrity feature. Celebrities are main characters of popular novels such as Reverend Insanity, Battle Through The Heavens etc. they are very OP and make your run feel weird.

Now to the game:
You start with a flying boat on a sea of sand or an actual sea. It can devour Islands to grow. You can also invade and make bases out of other islands. You can vassalize other clans, get captives and assimilate them to your clan, fight demonic beasts out in the sea, make or break alliances with other forces.

All clans, including yours have bloodlines. In addition there are inheritable traits and special cultivation physiques. The key to victory is to channel your inner Hyuuga Hiashi and make the greatest eugenics project ever since your last Crusader Kings run.

There are literally hundreds of cultivation techniques and battle skills. You can get them from adventures, purchase them from merchants, acquire them from your clan's secret inheritance tower and so on...

The battles are quite like Dominions. They are autobattlers but you determine which skills will be used in what order. The AI is decent.

Diplomacy is better than most games. But nothing spectacular. There is a setting that increases AI aggressiveness, shut that down, it is "the hard mode" which is enabled from the start for some reason. Due to its mechanics, it makes diplomacy worse, since it makes everyone aggressive, including your allies. Later on it adds more challenges for a "crapsack world" run.

Building and Plot management becomes a little tedious but there are menus for managing all your holdings from one menu.

You will have to manage a lot of different plants and fishes to make pills or food.

You will have to line up a lot of alchemy furnaces for your clan's needs.

You will have to setup a foundry to make items.

You can turn your island into a resort by putting down inns and markets.

You can raise demonic beasts by getting their eggs/cubs.

I am sure there are some things I have missed. There is a lot to do in this game.

All in all a good buy for its price.

Basically you can fish yourself into riches and even a level 1 fisherman can easily catch fish. Add the minigame with the lady who gives you free bait AND money AND catching nets, and it can pretty much break the game.

My only other gripe with this game is that I can't choose my careers, I only get to choose from 3 randomly selected choices for each of my 4 party members. With all the available new careers, it makes mixing and matching virtually impossible, it's hope that the RNG loves you, basically. And the RNG sometimes does 
REALLY cruel things to you, like make you sick immediately after you're forced to choose whether to toss your last medicine or your last clothes when your wagon is full. You'll definitely get dysentery at some point, it's Oregon Trail, baby!

Other than that, it's basically you against the RNG to see if you can make it to Oregon City with your party intact! I love all the game modes, I love the amount of content vs the price asked, this is a nicely crafted game that pays reverence to the original AND to its subject matter. High YES from me. I don't even know what to call this kind of game. Roguelike with historic voyage theme and inventory management game?

If that doesn't appeal to you, you probably aren't going to buy this. Everyone else, come try out Oregon Trail! It's a classic that I am glad is still with us!

Pedro Land DX is a collection of six retro-themed platformers, in the vein of the original Super Mario Bros. Each game is quite short but is packed with tough platforming and enemies. It's certainly worth the price of admission, and is an entertaining and enjoyable experience, even if it's a short one. However, while it definitely has it's highs, such as the music and some honestly very nice simplistic pixel art, it also has it's lows, namely in a few bugs. Specifically, there are issues with bosses not gaining aggro on the player, which makes the boss rushes more doable but detracts a lot of tension. While these bugs slightly sour the experience, they don't ruin it by any means. 

Additionally, I want to point out that this is one of the dev's first games, which I found to be a very impressive feat. I went in knowing this, and while it shows it, it actually makes it more enjoyable. I specifically want to point to Pedro Land 2, and how the developer expands upon existing content and pushing his skills further with more impressive locations, enemies, and secrets. While it's far from a perfect product, Pedro Land DX is an enjoyable game. My only major complaints are the potentially frustrating bugs, and a lack of power-ups (with one exception), which feel like a classic retro platformer staple that was unfortunately forgotten. The alternative characters modes are a suitable enough replacement, but the mode is hidden away in the options menu, and vary WILDLY in difficulty. Aside from those few issues though, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Pedro Land DX, and would recommend it, especially considering it's low price. 7 out of 10, a fun little platformer with some great moments, but some slightly wasted potential.

Challenge Completion: This game's challenge is merely to complete it, which tests my patience just as much as my skill.
Overall: 1/10

Mr. Hangy (Demo): If this is the demo, there's no need to purchase the entire game, as I've had my fill. A simple game of hangman with common phrase answers.
Challenge Completion: Hardly difficult compared to the previous three games' challenges; you have to find all the solutions.
Overall: 5/10

Blackjack Buddy: A gambler's fantasy, except this time, no money or stakes. Play a round of blackjack with an unknown dealer, or spam the various buttons until you win, whichever you prefer.
Challenge Completion: So far, this is the only game where the required game time of 3 minutes is the tricky part, where the challenges can be achieved easily in the first minute of playing by mashing "HIT ME."
Overall: 2/10

Drawifyer 2000: Be the artist you always dreamed you could be! Brush up on your painting skills with a wide variety of 9 colors on a white background. Click the erase button really fast if you feel a bit of eye strain could add to the fun.
Challenge Completion: The only real challenge here is overcoming the bug that is "Use all colors to make a drawing." When this has happened, the challenge isn't marked as complete.
Overall: 5/10

Survive Squares: Do you want to play a claustrophobic game of unforgiving hit detection as a triangle running away from squares only guided by the cold, uncaring hand of randomness? Well, I can tell you firsthand that Survive Squares is that game.
Challenge Completion: It's not too hard to get more than 15 points if your dodges are good enough and your luck is blessed (My high score is 23).
Overall: 6/10

The Wingless Bee: This is easily the most in-depth game thus far, as it has higher-quality music, all kinds of enemies, and even a boss battle, which caught me by surprise. The only complaint I have with it is that you can't move the bee as fast as you can tap the inputs.
Challenge Completion: The completion marks weren't much of a challenge here, as it just asked to beat the game and pick up all the collectibles you see.
Overall: 9/10

Hunger Strike: Ever wanted to play a game of Pac-Man where the ghosts didn't fight fair? Your wish has been granted. In this game, you'll be clipped around corners, spawn trapped, surrounded, and more. There is no sanctuary or solitude to be found here, no punches pulled.
Completion Challenge: The point challenge was not that bad, and by the time I got 6000 points, I thought the game was fun. HOWEVER, I refuse to complete this game due to how awful it gets and how wonky of a port of Pac-Man this is. Legitimately made me more frustrated than Ship it Like the Mailman.
Overall: 2/10

Number Crawler: A grid of numbers assigned randomly from 1-9; you pick a tile adjacent to you and slide across the board in that direction that many times and if you go off the board or a space you've been on, you lose. I'd rather play minesweeper.
Challenge Completion: The point goal wasn't particularly tough to reach.
Overall: 5/10

Balls at War 2: Install an auto clicker and click on some balls. A truly ballular experience to be had.
Challenge Completion: I'm not sure if the auto clicker counts as cheating to get the best-ending text, but I don't care at this point.
Overall: 8/10

Joseph's Plate Smasher: Toss your hat at plates. Avoid the red ones if you want a positive score, and only hit the red ones if you wish to have a negative score. If only Joseph and his hat could move a little more quickly.
Challenge Completion: Both point goals weren't difficult to hit with a few tries.
Overall: 6/10

Cascading Blocks: I hope you're ready for a version of Tetris with the most touchy, disagreeable controls you've ever experienced.
Challenge Completion: Get a Tetris, and then play marathon mode for an unnecessarily long time.
Overall: 4/10

Fifty Zeroes: Are you a mathematician who also happens to be a tire enthusiast? This game is for you. Count the number of zeroes in the numbers listed in scientific notation and jump over various obstacles. What fun.
Challenge Completion: The challenge is to beat the game. Not much more to say here.
Overall: 7/10

Slither: The simple game compilation wouldn't be complete without a version of Snake. And what a version it is. This version is so stripped back and simple that it would put the Nokia version to shame.
Completion Challenge: Score 25 points. What else am I supposed to say? It's Snake. You've played it before.
Overall: 5/10

Color Invasion: Oh no! Humanity is under attack by odd-shaped, primary color space ships! The only way you take them out is to shoot them with a matching color shot. It's as if Space Invaders required conscious thought while playing.
Challenge Completion: You have to shoot 25 red and yellow ships. I had it done before the required 3 minutes were up.
Overall: 6/10

Desktop Tank: It made me out of breath with laughter and made Greenway Mini Golf 5x more fun.
Challenge Completion: The challenge is just to use it in different places, and I sure did.
Overall: 10/10

Cowboy Lance: Episode One: I really like this one. The dialogue is hilarious, and so are the various things that happen. Super great; I wouldn't mind seeing a full game like this.

Overall: 7/10

My family got a fancy PC in 1993, which came with a stack of cool Aztech shareware discs. I played through a ton of the games over the years, always noticing the lone individuals credited and the registration information. 

Although I never did register any of those games, they really stuck with me. Hugo's House of Horrors, Corn Cob, The Last Half of Darkness, and hundreds of other small, independently developed games shaped my earliest experiences on a computer. 

This nostalgia piece really struck home. Like any real shareware disc, some games are better than others, but most were engaging enough to get me pushing for the optional achievements. While Cowboy Lance was easily the most entertaining, I enjoyed wrapping my head around Fifty Zeros and getting wrecked by Hunger Strike. 

Feel free to ignore the unfocused hot tub story sequences, but stay for the dev's understanding of what made shareware discs so cool!

Voidwrought is very clearly inspired by Hollow Knight, does mostly well in the graphic design and sound department (you can really notice the amount of work that went into those aspects), and somewhat manages to be a decent metroidvania in its collectathon phase. While I'm not a huge fan of creating "somewhat but not really" replayability with branching yet illusory choices, it's not exactly an unusual mechanic, and can be quite fun to explore when you're planning on replaying a game anyways.

But its movement, a central part to the gameplay feel, leaves [i]a lot[/i] of room for improvement: most abilities are much more sluggish than simply walking, and several of them feel redundant and/or overlapping in their use cases - which is supposed to be part of the nonlinear design, I get it, but the way it's done just feels like your controls get more and more bloated with useless moves. (As a side note, contraptions also take way too long to operate. Remember the time in HK when you needed to wait half a minute for an elevator to arrive, and then spend another 30s on the ride? Right, that happened exactly 0 times.) Attacking also feels somewhat monotonous, apart from the standard slash you only get relics that really feel more like utility items - there are hardly any options to use or adapt movement abilities for combat (nothing but [spoiler]a way to turn the dash into a proper i-frame evasion[/spoiler]), and if an enemy floats outside of the range of your tiny poking stick (something that happens quite often especially at earlier points in the game) you can either stare at it, hoping it descends again, or you can leave.
Combat setups, apart from the occasional enemy you engage during exploration, can be broadly divided into two categories:
- Wave fights, where each subsequent wave spawns in as soon as you clear the previous one - the combination of instantaneous spawn and contact damage meaning you either learn the spawn positions of every single enemy, or you'll take a couple of free hits each time. (Remember the floating enemy part? Well, good luck leaving an arena with closed doors.)
- Boss fights, with 1 phase and 3-4 repetitive moves each for the most part (for bosses with more than one phase the transitions seem only loosely bound to the actual health pool, meaning sufficient dps can lead to skipping a phase). Add the occasional broken mechanic that unintentionally punishes playing "by the rules", and those fights turn into pure dps checks where you rather wildly wail on the boss rather than properly facing its attack patterns. The part where several bosses apparently got stat-boosted due to complaints about them being pushovers doesn't solve that issue, instead it makes it even worse (as properly engaging those health-inflated bosses is now even less of an option).

TL;DR: the game looks and sounds pretty - if you're interested in the story it tells, go watch a playthrough; but don't bother playing, the gameplay is anything but fun.
