This is an amazing visual novel. The art is gorgeous, and the story is gripping. All the characters felt distinct, and the world felt lived in.

A Visual Masterpiece… Held Hostage by the Dialogue
Alright, first things first—this game is gorgeous. The art? Stunning. The music? Chef’s kiss. Seriously, more visual novels should aim for this level of quality. The artist absolutely crushed it, nailing everything from character designs to world-building to scenic vibes. Even the costumes had drip.

But then… the dialogue. Oh. My. God.

It’s like someone put the script on slow-motion mode. Every conversation drags, every character sounds the same, and every line feels like it was written to test my patience. I was skipping through chunks of text like I was speedrunning the boredom. What happened to “show, don’t tell”? What happened to variety in character voices? Why does everyone talk like they’re reading off the same teleprompter?

And don’t get me started on the pacing. Why am I spending valuable gaming time making bedsheets? Why are we stuck in a never-ending cycle of crafting, tidying, and other mundane activities? I came here for the juice, not a medieval Home Ec class.

That said, the humor system was great. For the first time, I actually felt like I was the character. A rare win.

Final Verdict:
✅ Drop-dead gorgeous art
✅ Immersive world-building
❌ Dialogue as lively as a tax report
❌ Pacing that makes molasses look fast

I had a lot of fun with this game. It starts out slowly and I almost gave up on it due to the poor early game pacing and apparent lack of depth from that playtime, but it picked up and became much more interesting after about 6 hours. At that point, the game became very fun and satisfying and remained so throughout the remainder of the playtime (51 hours for me).

The sim/management aspects of the game are fairly light but add texture to the game. You basically progress along a set of linear upgrades in terms of equipment, base upgrades, and so on. Each set of upgrades is attributed to a tier which is gated on advancing the main storyline. There are only a few mutually-exclusive choices to make - you can grind and get everything if you take your time.

During play, you'll recruit adventurers, form adventuring parties, manage their relationships, upgrade their gear, level them up, choose their class progression, purchase their abilities, and so on. These parties you form can sometimes be sent on background quests to give small buffs or unlock special boss battle quests. Most of the early game though, you'll be playing a few basic quests in between each main quest. Quests involve walking around a map and exploring, getting loot and fighting a series of tactical battles. Different quest types get unlocked as you play the game, and soon you'll be focusing on special boss battle quests for your progression and the materials you need to craft specialty gear.

Combat can be moderately challenging at times - which is good. Even if you over-level, you'll be looking for advantages to exploit. I only lost 1 character but I came very close to losing several during my playthrough. Only a few lucky death saves prevented several of my characters from dying.

The class abilities in combat are fairly simple but sometimes have interesting combos. Characters can use temporary bravery points to boost their stats or trigger extra actions. Managing your bravery is the core of the game by the time you hit end-game, since it will enable you to trigger multiple team combos and make big moves across the map. As characters developer their relationships, you'll improve their chain attack chance, which has a fun slot-machine-style feeling when it triggers. Proper party composition, skill use, bravery management, etc. will optimize your performance in combat more than positioning will (which also matters but less over time as the game progresses).

The biggest source of customization ultimately stems from classes. Early classes are very basic and a little boring. You can unlock mid-tier classes, which are much more interesting and can build atop your previous class build. By the end-game, you can unlock master classes, and there can only be one character per mastery. The result is that you'll play a couple of rotating parties early on while you learn what compositions work well and how to avoid over-working your adventurers. Eventually you'll settle on an optimal composition for your playstyle and start investing almost solely into your core party and you'll use your other adventuring parties to take care of background quests to support the main party. There are a few named characters with their own stories, but I preferred playing with my custom party and that worked fine. The named characters have quests you can play and unique skill trees they can access.

The story and characters are charming but nothing exceptional. There are a few funny moments that did make me smile. It certainly was interesting enough to keep my attention through most of the game. The art is not to my taste but it is of good quality. The music is similarly fine but will be very repetitive on a longer playthrough. I'd recommend having your own soundtrack ready to switch to while playing.

I think if you like SRPGs like FF:T or similar games, you'll love this game. If you want an RPG or something heavily story-driven, it will be less satisfying. As a management game, it's middling. This is really a tactical strategy RPG at its core and it's quite a good entry in the genre. Congratulations to the developer!

I have really only scratched the surface of this game as you can see from my 15 hrs played at the writing of this review. I love tactical rpgs, in fact I got distracted from playing this game because I started an XCOM 2 Long War of the Chosen playthrough. This game while much smaller and of course far more indie than XCOM 2, does not suffer that much in comparison. Many of the same concepts are here, from forming squads to squad members forming bonds and gaining benefits.

Let me take a step back and explain the premise of this game, you are taking over an adventurer guild after your friend who started it passed away. The story vignettes that you unlock are surprisingly well written and do get you emotionally invested. In this game, you will build up your guild base with buildings to give you benefits such as crafting, alchemy, recruiting adventurers. If you've played any type of XCOM style game, it should be familiar to you.  You recruit team members from the Tavern and they come with their own background of classes and extra traits. Part of this sort of game is always scouting the talent and making sure you hire the members that can show the most potential.  You then form teams from your roster and send them out for missions. Some are procedurally generated and are just there for you to farm experience and resources, other missions are story based to advance the story. Some sidequests unlock additional benefits. The combat is turned based and has some pretty good mechanics around special terrain squares, positioning, and timing. Everything that a fan of this genre is looking for.

I'm not super far into the story yet, I've only done a couple of story missions, but what I've seen so far is challenging boss fights and special battle mechanics that you don't see in the standard missions. That's really good and gives you something to look forward to as you grind up the ranks for your teams.  Overall this is a really good game and well worth your time if you like this genre. I plan on getting back to this game soon, after I am done being distracted. There's too many good games out there.

The permanent death of hero's makes for good stakes but I think the game balances risk and reward well.  I like that the happier your adventurers are the better they start out each quest.

One of my favorite things so far is the party and relationship mechanics.  When you unlock parties if you send them on quests together they will grow closer together and build team work.  The more characters complete quests together the more they will like each other.  The events are a nice touch too.  For example I was trying to get one party to like each other more and two of them became lovers which caused them work together better in battle and have some sweet chats while camping.  A different party failed a quest and two characters started arguing afterwards driving their relationship down.  I even had a moment of friendly fire and the two characters had a lower relationship after the quest as a result.  Another fun character I hired is a pessimist and I end up interacting with her more because she is always needing cheering up.  

There are some story characters you can hire and one of the heroes I love I got from a random encounter.  the little events and quips make me love these little guys and It hurts all the more when they die because they can't truly be replaced.
The only thing this game is missing is a good content creator that focus on each part of the game. Most videos are too long and too advance for a noob.

While its a bit rough around the edges, Robot Revolt has enough unique ideas and fun mechanics to quickly become one of my favorite games in the horde survival genre. 

For starters, the vehicle controls feel great. Boosting for dodging and ramming enemies is a lot of fun. The mini dungeons are simple but a very nice addition. Finding and beating these opens blueprints for a large list traits that can be equipped before the start of a run adding some nice pre-run customization. I really like the shops having a purchasable item called "Directions" Once purchased, an arrow and distance indicator shows up pointing out the next mini dungeon. 

The weapons each feel unique and have a wide variety of build choices. For example, once you get a machine gun, you can choose to upgrade how many guns you have to target multiple enemies or focus on the fire rate or damage, etc. Its fun to explore the different combinations possible for each skill. Other build options like stat books have some great synergy potential and the Recycler is OP. 

I highly recommend RR for player that are looking for a fun and interesting twist on this genre. GG!

‘Cyber Blades’ is a sword-swinging action game in which you have to swipe away at arrows fired by the various ninja-style enemies. With its synth-wave style graphics and sounds it certainly fits in with the ’80s vibe, but sadly it is the action that lets the game down. There is no beat-mapping here, it is just random action in which you can listen to one of two tracks, 3 difficulty levels and that is about it. If you play a single game here you have seen all there is to see and do. Sure, you can ramp up the difficulty and maybe chase your own score, but nothing that is going to hold your interest for very long.

I suppose the good news is the game doesn’t cost a lot, so those who are willing to endure the same gameplay loop over and over will get their money’s worth here. For me it is the lack of any variety that puts me off recommending it. I don’t expect much from a game that only costs £3.99 and the end T-Rex boss fight was cool, but I just didn’t enjoy it quite enough to give it the thumbs up. But as with any review, it is just a personal opinion and might not reflect your own.

I've been waiting for this one since the Origins demo, but so far it's been just a little disappointing. I do like the concept and it's not an expensive game, so I would say this is more of a "neutral" review.

The amount of new die and mechanics is interesting, but it also means your rewards are much more crowded with subpar options. I really don't like the 2 energy die, especially in Act 1 when you usually only have 3 energy. Maybe they should only be offered later. It seems far better to just collect the 0-cost d4s that draw an extra dice than waste moves on energizers, if you even get offered one.

Also more options means RNG becomes a bigger factor and it's also harder to build around a specific strategy. Puzzle-like games get a little tiring when you can make optimal moves and still lose often.

The map is definitely improved from 2nd demo since the paths have more variability, but it could use even more. There's rarely meaningful enough trade-offs beyond elite vs regular fights. For example, short paths that give you more encounters vs. long ones where you sacrifice encounters if you really need to hit a specific spot.

As far as difficulty goes, Act 1 is fine but it doesn't really prepare you for Act 2. Once you get to the honey enemies (overturned IMO), you won't have big enough numbers to block everything or kill in one 1-2 turns unless you get lucky with drops. The game gets significantly easier when you unlock (and find) certain items, which generally means those items are too strong or the base difficulty is too high.

Shop price scaling also seems high?

Since it's in EA I'm sure more balance chances are incoming. I'll check back after the next patch.

1. Cost. The early access launch price was very palatable and feels like a bargain, without ripping off the hard work of the developers.
2. Game design. I am generally hesitant to trust dice-based roguelikes, as it takes a genre filled with rng and usually introduces too much. Through a series of very inventive design decisions and balancing levers, that does not feel like the case here. 
3. You are given dramatic freedom in how you choose to build out your deck and what areas you wish to prioritze. 
4. Incredibly inventive enemy and boss designs. Many enemies introduce mini games and rules to play around. These ensure that different combats and combinations of enemies lead to having to find creative solutions.
5. I really enjoy the art and animation, kudos to the people behind that :)

Cons-
I’d like to start off by acknowledging this is a first early access patch and many things presumably will change. I also don’t consider any of these cons to be particularly meaningful, just weed for improvement.

1. Elite battles. I would like to see mini boss style elite fights as opposed to just two waves of normal enemies. It feels a little underwhelming pathing for elites only to see the same enemies we see in other fights. 
2. Late game hand vomit. I find that the complexity of decisions are at their highest in the early/mid game, where as the last biome has felt like either my deck is strong and I can hand vomit mindlessly, or I don’t have the ability to generate the necessary numbers.
3. I play on steam deck only, so it’s possible this is different on desktop, but late game, when you have 15+ relics, the clarity around where dice values come from feels to be lacking in the UI. I feel as if being able to in the moment know what is making my dice strong would allow me to try and make more strategic decisions.

Conclusions- this game is already a triumph and would be more than worth the price with no further patches. Get it and have fun

If Slay the Spire used dice instead, had frogs, and was inspired by Dicey Dungeons, you'd get Die in the Dungeon.
Its a vibrant, lovely roguelite with a fresh take on "cardbuilders", while providing a challenge despite its "cutesy" appearance.
I thoroughly enjoyed the demo, and the current release does not disappoint. 
At its price point for an early access game, the amount of content and effort put in is worth the price, and I am looking forward to future updates.

The game is incredible for what it is, having an amazing duality of puzzle-like dice rolling and deck building mechanics. As a novice to deck building games, I love this game but also hate it for being punishing for its own RNG but encouraging experimentation and strategic testing while trying to manage your dice deck. 

There may feel like a lack of content as there are only 3 playable heroes so far, and there is a lot of possibilities for other dice ideas, characters, play styles, and relics, but they are very open and honest about the fact this is an early access release that is playable on the spot with the core mechanics well established and some very nuianced and exciting mechanics that totally change around your gameplay.

I would say my biggest problem is that I'm not used to deck builders, and often run off of 'vibe' rather than hard strategy, making most of my runs not last into the 2nd round. If I'm not clearing the first boss in just a few turns, I don't expect to make it far with how fast enemy damage hikes up into the second phase, especially when you need to eventually be balancing perfect sustain with perfect attack. The decks that I have go the furthest in those situations are ones that got early energy increases during the first stretch, and ends up making me reluctant to spend time on other avenues of play since I know how stacked I have to get later.

I'd going to recommend because it's early access and I can't wait to see where this goes, but also be warned that this is not a completed product. Plenty enjoyable the way it is now though, and I think I'll enjoy playing it as it expands with more content and creativity.

This is by far the most I have been invested in the early days of an early access roguelike. 

I really like the gameplay, I find the puzzle of stringing together an elaborate domino chain boosts and dices satisfying, and the game creates a really involved powerdynamic, where you always feel simultaneously in control, yet powerless to the impending attacks.  The joy of finding deviously busted combos is super satisfying, yet soo many of its best mechanics are intertwined in such a way that you often find the loophole that enabled your busted combos also being your downfall.  The game feels just complex enough to me, and from a pure gameplay standpoint is my go to roguelike, and I see that being the case for years to come.

It is not all perfect however.  I find the bad runs to be really bad in this game.  It  is very easy to accidentally clunk up your deck with dice that just cycle in a slow and tedious way.  Defensive play is just boring here, and I have found myself reseting over this multiple times.  On top of that, I find the diffaculty scaling to be very inconsistent.  While some enemies are satisfying to learn, or have funny noob traps which catch up to you, there are multiple enemies that just dont feel inspired or fun to learn.  

Overall, I believe this is a very great start for what I see becoming one of my favorite games.  It has caputed my heart in ways most other games can only dream of, and I really have high hopes for the future of this game

THE GOOD
Innovative mechanics. An interesting puzzle-like dice roguelite where board positioning matters. Decent amount of variety at the moment.

HOPEFULLY WILL IMPROVE
Runs take a loooong time at the moment, and this is probably the biggest downside currently. My completions have been ~2hrs.
This is partly due to loading and animations, which I'd expect to be better optimised and have snappier UI transitions as it continues getting updated. There's a fast mode setting which doesn't seem to do a lot, but turns also generally need a bit of thought and testing out your options as you move dice around, reroll, draw etc. 

BALANCE (early impressions)
I still haven't played a ton of the game, and I'm sure this will change over time so these are just initial feelings: An issue I'm having is some runs end because of an unlucky dice draw, which feels bad when you've got the tools to deal with a situation in your deck. There doesn't seem to be a lot of content available to draw more dice, at least in the base content and early unlocks. The first character has a dice draw mechanic and it makes a huge difference when you lose that.

When you do get the tools needed to reroll I still feel somewhat at the mercy of which enemies spawn, and the endgame seems to have some pretty punishing variance as I'm trying to go up difficulties. Regular battles can be more punishing than elites depending what spawns.

Loved the demo when it was first out and was really excited to get the real thing.

The current version needs a LOT of work still.  Certain enemies simply can't be killed because of needing exact damage, and scaling on the 2nd floor is way off.  You also can't buy half of the items in the store so why are they even there?

Looking forward to these things being cleaned up but until then I won't be playing it.  I'll update my review if things improve.

I would recommend this game for anyone who likes aspects of deck building, dice, and gambling.  Die in the dungeon has always been a solid game since the Itch.io days and surpasses my initial expectations on my first play through.  In my opinion would not suggest to a beginner since it takes a little bit of reading to play well and not everyone can handle that.  Otherwise a great game and would 20/10 buy it again if I could (closest I could to is gift to friends)

This game really grows on you! The main mechanism of this entire game is spatial management where placement of dice on a little board is everything. There is a nice build-up towards ridiculous combos and a godlike end-game status with the right dice and relics found along the way. It is unique enough to have its own identity among other creative games like Dungeon Clawler, and certainly a delectable addition to any board gamer's collection. If only there were more content like additional heroes etc!

I played the Prologue demo for 10 hours, and the Origins demo for 6 hours; the bones of this game are strong!

That being said, this iteration is a bit rough. As others have pointed out:
- Load times are rather poor.
- Run length feels too long.
- Many encounters feel meaningless.
- Current enemies designs are delightful, but too few in number.
- Die drafting after combat is very underwhelming. I liked it better when die acquisition was less common.
- The new map system doesn't add meaningful choices and slows the game down.
- Damage / Health pools are such that by areas two and three you can heal to full in every fight. This eliminates the long term planning that makes map travel in roguelikes interesting.
- Elite combats are very lame and I find that I tend to avoid them, just to make the run go quicker
      - Boss designs are brilliant, so it's a shame not to see more of that in minibosses and such.
- The game is way too easy. With all the relics and upgrades thrown at the player, I only felt threatened in the boss fights.

Despite appearances, I like what's here! It's a charming, attractive, mostly enjoyable roguelike that I think will become something pretty special. However, as a returning player, I can't help but feel that the game has taken a few steps backwards. I'll keep playing and update my review as necessary.

It's satisfying and fun for a while, I don't think it will have the staying power that Slay the Spire has though. Combos are not as absurd as other deck builders, which makes each run feel very similar. It's definitely worth playing, I just think there are other deck builders that offer more combo potential.

Needs Polish.
The game is almost good, and as its early access hopefully it'll get better on release, but as it currently sits, I wouldnt recommend it. 
There needs to be a lot of little things improved with this dicey roguelike, like tooltips, explanations for certain things that make sense, and general QOL fixes. 
All in all its a cutesy roguelike where youre at the whims of your dice rolls. Strangely, the dice rolls seem to be HEAVILY weighted. An example: I had a 6 sided die with 1, 2, 2, 5, 5, 5 which I could reroll up to 3x per turn. Even with 3 rerolls, nearly EVERY time it came up as a 1 across multiple times getting and rolling it. This happened for other die too, where your lowest number will always appear. I dont know if this is intentional or a bug or what, but it really shows that things are rather weighted sometimes.
Some of the dice dont do a very good job of explaining what it really does (like gravity and heavy) which makes some positives seem negative or some negatives seem positive. Of course, once you use those a few times you'll understand, but its important to know what they do CLEARLY. 
I'm starting to lose patience with dice roguelikes as they all seem to have similar issues where what SHOULD happen and what DOES happen are two very different things. 
I got to the last boss on my first run but had to close the game and honestly... I'm not sure I super feel like loading it up until release. 
YMMV but I'd go in with some caution until a proper release can give proper reviews.

Game has upsides, but overall is made to kill the player and frustrating ways with cheap mechanics. Runs last an extremely long time, loading from zone to zone by itself is a huge time waste. The game is "cheap" in that it gives some regular enemiesn abilities that are a nuisance to micromanage. Some of the abilities are fine but others are just unnecessary and will kill you if you don't constantly pay attention to them. Not paying enough attention would be a skill issue, if it wasn't for the fact that it's every battle, and the runs can get up to 3 hours long even playing fairly fast. My biggest example of just getting caught off guard by a dumb mechanic was this encounter on a D1 difficulty run. It was 2 hours in, three rooms away from final boss, had been steamrolling the entire game, get an encounter with two enemies that have 99 health (which is fairly large). The enemies stack poison on you every turn. Bad RNG makes the fight last a while, but I eventually dwindle down the encounter to just one enemy with exactly one health left. I'd been doing this encounter for a while, was a few rooms away from the final boss, and 2 hours into a run. So to just end the encounter I throw down one die and end the fight. The problem? Well all that poison that had been stacking up still attacks you when the fight ends. I had never noticed this until that point and even though I had the resources to defend against it, I didn't, because I was just ending the fight trying to get to the boss. This wasn't an elite encounter, this wasn't some special fight. The poison kills me and ends the run over 2 hours in. That definitely could be seen as a massive skill issue. But in my opinion when you make a game so monotonous and long, having a regular encounter kill you with a poison tick after the fight is already over is irritating. Games are supposed to be fun, that wasn't, it just felt cheap and made me not want to start a new run. Anyway, other general complaints. The relic pools are small in each run, if a relic shows up in your reward choices, it will show up again and again and again. The game has very little run variety across the characters. You can have different builds but they aren't that different from each other. Also most set ups aren't even very viable on the higher difficulty runs. You eventually will find yourself just using some variation of boosting up an attack die, then mirroring it. The characters barely feel different from one another, and your run is basically decided on the first floor. You either will steamroll, get stomped on second floor, or steamroll through until you forget about how a certain enemy needs to get hit for it's exact health to die, or until you die to poison after an encounter has ended. I just really think this stuff is frustrating over fun. What makes roguelikes good, is wanting to get right back into a run and not feeling robbed when you lose a run. This game is probably the least replayable roguelike of all time when it comes to starting a run right when you ended the last one.

This is a must have roguelite game. 

The design of the game is intelligent and charming. Playing your dice on the game board is simple at first, but evolves into a really fun and unique run. You must factor in your relics that you pick up that fundamentally change how and where you play your dice.

Each character feels unique. Tons of different dice and modifiers. You can constantly manipulate the faces on each die to benefit the relics you pick up. You can truly customize each run!

Enemies/bosses are varied and challenging. You can't just blast through every enemy with high damage dice. You need to balance attack, healing, and blocking along with other gimmick dice to ensure victory.

The music is amazing. I haven't heard a track that I haven't been thoroughly enjoying as I'm deciding what dice to play, or what items to buy in the shops. The music is quirky but also really catchy. Really reminds me of a more catchy binding of isaac type of music.

Art is lovely. Each area feels special. Different floors have different vibes and they match the character designs as well. The art in this game is just cool and oozes with charm.

I would heavily recommend this to any roguelite fan that enjoys Binding of Isaac, Slay the spire, or Monster Train. If you are looking for a charming, fun and engaging card/dice builder, pick this up immediately! It's definitely worth the full price. If it's on sale, you should be adding it to your cart right now. Even if you aren't a fan of roguelite games, this one might do the trick to convince you to enjoy the genre. Very well crafted game!

To start my review off I really enjoy the atmosphere this game has presented. The art and music are superb! I played the Demo a ton and loved what they were going for! As a demo I didnt expect it to represent the whole game. What I dislike is the game play. This is a very good Slay the Spire inspired game. its a little too inspired and this results in it feeling like a card game instead of one with dice. Other rogue-likes have shown you can have a good balance of gimmicky mechanics and solid deck building ones. Dice are extremely fun RNG elements in so many games. A huge factor of them being so fun is that you the player throw the dice! Whether its in dungeons and dragons, card games or gambling. In Die in the Dungeon none of what you do or how you play feels like youre playing with dice. 

- You see the numbers right away

- You never actually roll the dice

- There arent any gameplay elements consistent with different types of Dice. It generally feels like you only make number get bigger which imo isnt interesting at all. 

- There arent any dice related rogue-like elements. 
For example we cant rig the dice to have a higher chance of rolling a big number. We dont roll the dice all the relics do is raise numbers or atleast thats how it feels similarly to a Slay the Spire. 

- Theres NO first hand interaction with the RNG elements which is a huge bummer.. Its a lot like Baldurs Gate 3 combat checks where the dice roll automatically and behind the scenes when you attack. But what i want is the conversation checks where you manually role the dice. Imagine a mechanic where you get a bad dice roll in Die in the Dungeon and you can "Cheat" to redo the roll! That would be sick

Its reasons like these that unfortunately kill my enjoyment. Combined with a few other things such as Elite rooms having multiple fights instead of providing a solid challenge from the get go. The boss fights or so what ive fought so far are ok.

TLDR: Die in the Dungeon feels more like a card game than a game played with dice and considering the whole game is based around dice its uninteresting. If you like card games its great but its not what im looking for currently. 

Ill revisit the game several updates from now and I hope it has a better identity. Best Wishes!

This game is cute, but it's really missing a lot of components to be a great game, and it also feels like they released a half baked game with missing features or content while relying on early access play testing to patch things over. Maybe this game will get a thumbs up from me when it's released and has its act together, but in the meantime, here are the good and bad points about this game. 

Good: 
- Cute game
- Music is great and I can jam to it for hours
- Shops have free samples, which is a great feature since every other roguelite never has anything for free and it felt bad if you enter a shop without money  
- Interesting game play with the dice board and their mechanics 
- I like how all the unlocks are achievements as well, but that can be viewed as a negative 
- Has room for breaking the game like I like to do in roguelites where the deck becomes super powerful  

Negatives and Room for Improvement: 
- Relics feel too inconsequential and samey 
- There really are not many ways of getting extra energy for each round 
- Game gets repetitive really quickly
- Elite battles are just literally two waves of regular enemies, so there aren't any unique elite enemies to fight
- Zero lore, like none at all. We don't know why we are here, why the final boss is that particular character, and no follow up afterward 
- There is a lack of variety and interesting dice 
- The rewards you get are usually pretty lack luster, and you will skip plenty of dice because they are just standard dice 
- Poorly written tool tips such as not telling players that regen/barrier will reduce by half after each round, that thorns only last for the damage it reflects (so it's basically an attack with extra steps and that's lack luster), and there seems to be some descriptions of enemies but where to hover over them is difficult to understand  
- You can't see your die numbers and descriptions if it's on the board, which leads to sometimes you having to take it off the board to review its distribution of stats or abilities 
- Board clarity is very messy. A dice over a modified board square will usually obstruct it and make it hard to read 
- Game gets brutal really quickly unless you broken the game in turn, especially in higher difficulties. It just feels extremely unfair and punishing with factors beyond my control. You can easily get a game over on turn one if you don't roll a shield against late game enemies as they will attack hard enough to one shot you  
- Some mechanics are awful and have little room for counter play, especially thorns and relics that damage you on round start. Thorns will hit the player before they use their shield, so it will always deal hp damage unless you had armor at the start of the turn, and that isn't usually possible without very few specific relics or a heavy block dice. Relics that damage you at turn start are literally impossible to prevent taking that first turns' damage, which on paper makes sense, but it's frustrating and not fun.   
- It feels like there are a lack of bosses, enemies, relics, acts, and characters in this game. I don't really know how else to describe this point other than saying it feels incomplete of a game.  
- Your choices don't feel like they matter as many times the following events or rewards will just give you the unselected relics you passed over  
- Not showing total damage the enemy plans on dealing you as a whole. It's not always fun to constantly do math to see how much damage you have to plan for 
- Events are just point and click and have nothing to do with dice like in the demo  
- The map just doesn't feel great compared to the demo where you didn't know what you were getting into next and feels like a total rip off of slay the spire 

Overall at this point in time, I highly advise waiting on purchasing this game, as it sorely feels incomplete and has a lot of quality of life updates that it desperately needs. I really looked forward to this game after playing the demo two years ago, but it seems like this Early Access game is more of a paid demo and not a fully released game. Maybe it will get changes, and maybe this IS the fully released game and there won't be any significant changes or new content for it, and if it is the latter, then I highly advise staying away from it.

- There are not that many plays you can actually make, but this time it's worse. Dice that depend on terrain are a backfire cause there's an abundance of mechanics that not only block their positioning, but punish you for setting them up. 
- The enemy difficulty scaling from the first floor to the second is absurd, and you dont have enough instances to build up your dice. They deal increasing ammounts of damage with no drawbacks, to the point they just bruteforce through you. 
- I wont spoil the game but the final boss is not fun at all, it does not stop making huge damage every turn and penalizing you for even playing, not only that but every single value of effects or attacks keeps increasing with turns. So as it is a damage sponge, I ended up losing even if I was dealing huge ammounts of damage at the same time of tanking hits.
- some effects on enemy attacks are not explained until you already are affected with them.
- the default character you first play with is awful, nothing compared with the one on the demo, the bag is much smaller and gives little to no space for planning or variety.

Look, it's definitely a good game and you get your money's worth, but there are a few flaws that prevent me from truly enjoying this game as much as I thought I would. I usually wouldn't compare this type of game to Slay The Spire, but as it wears its inspiration on its sleeves, I think it's fair. I really hope my comments can help the game improve.

1) The fun of the dice

To put it bluntly, the dice are simply not that interesting to play around with. The basic dice you start with don’t feel that much different from the ones you get later. In Slay, every single time you pick a card you feel like it empowers you and you get excited about what kind of combo and synergies you can do with it. Not so much with the dice in this game. I hope I make sense here, but instead of feeling like you are building towards more power and combos, you feel like you pick the one that is the least detrimental to your game "deck". It really feels like you start bloating your deck with just a few choices into a game. Also, the dice simply lack the personality and variety the Slay cards have. I do understand that this will be an intrinsic issue with  using dice, but visually it all looks the same and it's hard to tell them apart other than the numbers and that makes for some uninteresting choices. I know this can be made better, because I didn't get that feel while playing Dicey Dungeons. 

2) The balance

That can probably be fixed in patches, but at the moment, the pacing and scaling is odd once you start progressing into the game. You will have like 10-15 fights where it feels good and like your choices matter to then die instantly the room after. With the relatively low health pool of your character, when you face 2 or 3 foes that attack at the same time you either die instantly or survive with something like 50 extra shield points. It's all or nothing and the player is left with little control on the outcome of these events. In Slay, once you start getting overwhelmed, you usually have at least 1 or two turns to try to come up with something or can rely on a potion to even out these spikes in difficulty, but you don't quite get that in this game. Once you do get a powerful deck that steamrolls through everything, it doesn't feel like it is because of your choices or even because you got lucky, but instead feels like it is unbalanced. 

3) Pacing

The runs feel a bit too slow for how quick they can end. That issue is exacerbated by the long load times between each room. The loading screens are objectively not that long at all, only about 2-5 seconds, but they are within every single room and really put the brakes on any kind of momentum you were getting. It also feels like there are too many fights before getting to the end of an act for the little variety in enemies you face along the way.

That's my major gripe with the game, but like I said, it is still a very good game  that is worth your time and I think it was a good choice to pre-release to hopefully iron out some kinks.

If you played Outta Gas and enjoyed it, you'll probably really enjoy this game.  The only real problem with this game is that it really explains very little, and it may take a while before someone really enjoys the game, making people not give it the chance it deserves.  First and foremost, this game is HARD.  You'll probably die pretty quickly, so I'll go over some hints and tips that I think would help players starting off.

#1: Kite enemies away from each other to take them out one at a time.  If you engage an enemy close to another one, you'll be fighting every nearby enemy, which can be hard to deal with, and force you to expend a large amount of consumables to complete the fight, where a solo is always easier to deal with.
#2: If you do fight multiple enemies, use any and every item to neutralize as many enemies as quickly as possible.  Some items are clearly meant to damage multiple targets at once, and should be used liberally in these situation.  Experiment with all the items.  You can't take it on your next run anyway.
#3: Save your ammo to stun enemies.  Basically, you can see enemies winding up attacks.  You can press the right mouse button to put up guard, and take 30% or so less damage (I think).  This, however is probably a last ditch solution to the problem.  The better choice is to stun enemies, which happens when the enemy takes enough damage.  Ammo is fairly sparse, but packs quite the punch, and can easily deal enough damage to fulfill the damage requirement to stun as long as you start shooting before the attack gauge has a chance to fill up.  Doing so will help you take significantly less hits, and feels like a key part of lasting a decent amount of time.
#4: Upgrade your weapons.  The mysterious orbs are designed to be used on the empty altar to the left of the healing fountain.  Open your inventory, and drag the weapon you want to upgrade into the square above the altar, then choose whatever upgrade you can afford. My first problem with this game is bugs. NPCs constantly bug out, for example talking/attacking when they're fucking decapitated. Vehicles explode you into gibs instantly if you try to exit one with a wall next to you (or anything else that is mildly solid.) Hell, sitting down in a chair crashed me one time (as well as a server of 14 people.)

Secondly, cross-platform jank. Accounts are tied to your device, not your Steam account, which means that if you, let's say, get a new laptop, you'll have to entirely start over with a new account. This was probably Android users wouldn't have to connect a Steam account to play, but 1. you can just use two different systems for each platform, and 2. Android can't even play multiplayer anymore!

The third problem (by far the worst) is the multiplayer community. I have never seen such horrible, moronic and genuinely hateful people in a community since 2015 COD lobbies (not to say all of them are, there are lovely people I've met on Gorebox, but like 40% of them suck.) I have been called slurs more times than I can count. People spam loud-ass audios constantly. A significant portion of the playerbase plays multiplayer solely to be as obnoxious as possible. It's better now that they've disabled multiplayer for Android, but it's still pretty fucking bad. This problem is magnified by the lack of ability to set extra moderators/admins or permissions for specific players. Oh, and the unusually-large <13 section of the playerbase.

I have good memories with this game, and genuinely want it to thrive, but I struggle to have any interest in recommending it in its current state.

I like Monster Crawl.  It's a good game.  I played it non-stop for over 2 hours.  It pulls you in, and there are unlocks to give you some purpose in completing levels.

However, I also greatly dislike the unlock system.  You have to play as a specific class and reach a specific level, as well as spend gold to unlock a character.  The level requirement is easy to accomplish, but if you don't like playing as that character class you're just being forced to do things you don't enjoy in order to unlock something you might enjoy.

Moving past that though, the characters themselves are alright.  At this point I've played up to the Wizard.  So I have the Warrior, Archer, and Wizard.  The Warrior is the all-around great character from this mix.  Melee attacks are good, great special attacks, and really just a pleasure to play.

The Archer takes a more calculated approach, but their special attacks aren't as great as the Warrior.  This means making my way through the levels really took more time than it did as the Warrior.

The Wizard is the Archer, but shoots magic.  Slightly different specials, but still less great than the Warrior.

Combat is going to feel different based on which character you play as, and despite my dislike of the characters that weren't the Warrior I do think the combat is fun.  It's engaging, typically pretty quick, and feels rewarding with the coins, gems, and health that can drop.

Coins are used for permanent upgrades.  Gems earn you experience to level you up.  Health improves your health.  Easy enough.

Level design is alright.  But in the 2.5 hours I played it definitely felt like I had played the same handful of locations several times.  I knew they were different in many cases, but they certainly felt similar.  Going through dungeon after dungeon just to do the same thing again, knowing I'd have to do it a few more times before facing the boss made it a bit less engaging.

Still, as a big fan of Gauntlet I've enjoyed my time with Monster Crawl so far.  It's a fun experience that's almost certainly a game you'll have fun with when playing with a friend or family member.  Solo is fun too, just find the character you like the most and stick with it.

[b]TL;DR: It's absolutely worth getting.[/b]

[H1]Gun Diversity[/H1]

Currently, there's 9 survivors to choose from. Each character has a passive (i.e. bonus starting health, bonus movement speed, etc.) and a starting ability and weapon. The character selection I think is perfect, each of their starting abilities feels unique and you can make a class fantasy out of any of them.

However, most weapons don't feel particularly unique, except for the 2 melee classes (solely because they are melee) and the Scientist who has 2 of the more unique weapons (a lightning arc gun and an explosive spore shooter with no magazine). I think the guns could use a little more flavor and diversity, such as giving guns various stats like penetration (excluding laser weapons which already penetrate 100% of the time), knockback, damage fall-off, even crit chance would be a fun addition. Right now they only have 3 stats that matter: magazine size, damage,  reload speed, and rate of fire (this aspect cannot be augmented, however, and there is no information readily available on the rate of fire of weapons).

Reload speed mostly seems irrelevant and I personally believe is outclassed by magazine size. I've hardly noticed a difference picking up reload speed passive in game, unless it's for a gun with a very slow reload speed, but that isn't many weapons. Scout's snipers, for instance, reload almost quickly as her rate of fire, or at least fast enough that I never felt downtime in which I needed to retreat and reload. I figured a sniper would have high damage, low rate of fire, small magazine, and long reload, but that doesn't seem to be the case. While she does the most damage per shot by far, there's a few guns that feel as though they have the same impact as her snipers.

I love the guns, I love all the gun designs and their aesthetics and shooting lasers, but I believe they need to be more differentiated.

[H1]Ability Diversity[/H1]

The abilities give about the same feeling of "lacking". For example, the laser ability fires a ray down a straight line, and there's another ability that does exactly the same thing but with bullets (I forgot the same, sorry). Their upgrades are also the same: the laser upgrades into a cone, the gun upgrades into a cone. While it's neat to stack them for maximum AOE, and maybe that was the intention, the lack of other abilities makes this just feel like 2 cloned abilities.

There are 12 abilities, not including starting abilities, and being able to pick 4 per run makes you cycle through build variations pretty quickly. Beyond that, I felt playing solo that I NEEDED to pick up the stim ability for healing, and in higher tiers the shield. Not having access to easier forms of healing or damage reduction gimps build diversity. I feel as though health could regenerate out of combat, by not shooting or taking any damage, by multiplying the current health regen stat by 4x (including upgrades) or something similar. Heals would still be viable because healing mid-fight is always good, but they wouldn't be [i]necessary[/i].

On top of this, if you want to upgrade an ability, you NEED to spec into its respective passive. For example, the lightning arcing ability requires a maxed out bonus health buff into order to be upgraded, and it's a substantial upgrade. But this means that you MUST spec into this health buff, even if you feel like you don't need health, and it doesn't have synergy with the lightning ability in any way. It doesn't scale off of health or arc to more units with bonus health, it's just added because...because?

I think this upgrade system needs to be changed completely. I want to experiment with different passives and abilities, but not being able to upgrade abilities seriously gimps you a lot of the time. Like for the stim ability, sure you can ignore its upgrade when you're playing solo--it just turns into an AoE. I can live without the shield deflect damage, too. But the massive bonus damage on the lightning arc? The wide cones of the gunfire and laser abilities? The massive screen-wide frost debuff of the frost nova? The upgrades are impactful, and skipping them feels so, so bad. Tying them to passives, while I understand the intention and simplicity of it, just ruins build diversity.

Upgrades could come from random chance chest pick-ups, encouraging exploration. They could also be rare level up options, not always guaranteed but exciting when you're lucky enough to get one. There could be some alternative form of currency in each level to spend on these upgrades. Something, something that allows me to build more freely. I think this is probably one of the stronger priorities the dev should work on.

[H1]Monsters[/H1]

The monster designs are all right. They have unique enough identities to know what to look out for, such as one being fast and another being ranged and another being tanky, and the silhouettes of the monsters are easy to learn and understand. They also don't dogpile TOO high on you, which leaves room for kiting and quick thinking. What I would like to see is a few more boss designs (there's currently only two), and [i]maybe[/i] unique enemies on different maps as a stretch goal. The latter is far less important, but boss diversity would be very welcome.

I would also like to be able to dodge roll through enemies. Being pressed into a corner with no way out does not feel good, and sometimes there's instances where you think you can squeeze through a tight area, only to be invisiwall'd. This has happened a few times, and it feels cheesy.

[H1]Maps[/H1]

There are currently 4 maps. A passable amount, but I would welcome more. The balance between their environments is a little off to me, though.

The city map has high chest spawns and a straightforward design. You're walking between big squares with a few obstacles along the road, like cars or spore gunk. It's easy to kite through, getting to objectives is simple [i]most[/i] of the time, and the aesthetic of it I think is my favorite.

But I can't tell you much about the other maps, because chest spawns feel so rare on them it doesn't even feel worth visiting them. Like the forest map, chests seem to only spawn in camps, but you don't really have a direction to go off of to reach any camps. If there were some sort of forest path leading you to them, that would circumvent this nicely, but as it stands finding chests here makes me feel lost. The city just has chests simply on any road you go down.

The desert I have went to the least, and probably can't give chest info on it, so that's my fault.

But the suburbs, oh boy, this map is hell. There's SO many nooks and crannies and corners to get stuck on and wiped out by incoming enemies. If you go inside a house, you're likely going to be blocked in by waves of monsters. If you want to leave the house, finding the exit is weirdly difficult with no strong indicator of where the doors are, and if you want to even leave the [i]lot[/i], you have to find a break in the long rows of white picket fences. Apply this to every house, and you'll never want to enter a home. It feels so inconvenient traveling on this map, you think you found a shortcut to the objective and instead you made your trip twice as long trying to maze your way through. While the map is charming and well designed, its environment is unfortunately a hindrance on gameplay.

First off a word of advice: take the negative reviews with a pinch of salt. I don’t mean to criticize them but most of those were made during the Early Access period and the game has changed a lot during that time. Now then, let’s begin. I’ll start by explaining some of the core points and then summarize the good and bad.

Game: Rift Loopers is a roguelite twin stick shooter. It comes with both passive and active skills and a few classes. There are two games modes, being the self-explanatory wave based endless mode and the scavenger mode.
During scavenger, you have to survive for 20 minutes while completing as many objectives as you can to rail up precious crystals, the in-game currency. You’ll need those to unlock classes, skins, weapons and passive skills.
During a map, your character will level up, allowing you to choose between a pool of 3 (or 4 with the Lucky passive skill) either active or passive skills, up to a limit of 6 passive and 2 active skills. Which you’ll then need to level up by… leveling up. If you can survive the bosses, that is.

Classes: The game features 10 classes, 8 of which are unlockable by completing some achievements and the last one being DLC locked (the Pyro). These 10 classes come with a unique ability and a unique weapon as well as either a healing skill or a shield depending on your choice.

Active and passive skills: As I mentioned before, during a map, you’ll get a total of 4 active skills (one unique ability coming from your class, and the other being either a healing skill or a shield) and 6 passive skills. They range from buffs to huge AoE explosion as well as some touch based skills. Keep in mind, any passive skill you unlock with crystals will always be active whether or not you choose it in your passive skills pool during a map, and they are additive. Meaning if you unlock the health bonus and then choose the health bonus passive, you can get a total of 100% bonus health, as an example.

Maps: There are 4 maps, 2 of which are city based, while the other 2 are more in nature.
Now, let’s sum up the good and a few issues I’d like to mention. Although not dramatic enough to ruin the game which I really enjoyed, I like to make honest reviews.

Let's summarize what I think of the game now!

Good:
+ The classes and the game are pretty well balanced.
+ The unlock system is really good. All the upgrades you get have some meaningful impact on your game performance, meaning by the time you unlock most of the stuff, you’ll have a comfortable time even in the highest difficulty mode.
+ It’s a cheap game. Nowadays, that counts.
+ It’s co-op! You can play with up to 4 players, either online or in LAN.
+ The game looks nice.

Bad:
- There are a few bugs as well as collision issues with the maps. I’ve completed all the achievements and didn’t run into any game breaking issue yet, but there were a few times I should have been able to walk down a certain way and couldn’t despite the fact there was, visually at least, more than enough room for a guy to walk through. Mostly in the urban map.
- This is a bit subjective but some aspects of the game lack a bit of oompf. eg the weapons are too similar, the objectives visual and audio cues aren’t dramatic enough for them to feel varied and the classes all feel the same.
- The game could use a bit of performance optimization.

All in all the issues are quite limited and I really, really had a good time playing this game in co-op. Especially considering how cheap it is. I’ve paid ten times that amount for way worse games. If you liked Helldivers or Red Solstice, you can go right ahead with this one.

This needs to be separated into a different system, it can work the same, but it has to be a unique thing different from the usual skills. Like an implant or a pill that grants a special passive bonus that is different that the others.  Or a weapon upgrade that adds a new effect. Like bullet bouncing or piercing, maybe an elemental effect... If there was a dash move, there could be upgrades for that, same for a melee attack. All of these mechanics offer an opportunity to diversify the upgrade system and increase strategic options for game play styles. 

Games like this are SORELY missing out on the opportunity for a CRAFTING SYSTEM.  When literally the entire form of game play is farming hoards of monsters...but just for meta upgrade gems...that's it.  No materials for crafting anything. Even if only cosmetics, but hopefully more types of guns and armor and equips are going to be added.  And consumables you can use or equip in an active slot (there are at least 2 free buttons) before a run that could be crafted, would support a crafting economy indefinitely, also having weapons with a few random attributes, maybe with chances effected by the grade of crafting material... That would be another cool option.  Four levels of grade for crafting materials with three types.  I am digressing I know but stay with me..   Lowest tier would be like rotten for organic parts, raggedy for textile parts, corroded for component parts.  Then mid tier could be like dried/preserved for organics, clean/intact for textiles, Salvageable for components, and for high tier, Fresh for organics, Pristine for textiles, and Shiny for components.  Each tier would increase the value of the crafting item (higher value means fewer needed for crafting) and the higher tier would increase the chance for additional attributes or maybe certain specific attributes. 

Anyway, this is supposed to be a review and not a rant about all the things I wish I could put in a game I have absolutely zero discipline to ever even approach learning how to make. So thanks to the Devs for trying. [b]I hope they read and consider my ideas.[/b]  I really think these ideas could HUGELY improve the marketability and stand out quality of this game.

Addictive, relentless, swarming alien bugs-type isometric shooter featuring several different classes, very cool special-attack abilities and procedurally generated map(s). Offers a fully-featured 4-player online co-op system (game browser list, session lobby etc.), uses the Unreal game engine and sells for a bargain price. To some extent I'm enjoying it more solo than in co-op, where I think having a good time is just running into players who will remain in fairly close proximity to you.
https://youtu.be/PK5leU8cLGg
[h1] Why do you like it, Mr. Twin-Stix Know It All?[/h1]
For me, the game's diversity in classes, weapons and the special attack abilities you choose on-the-fly while playing help overcome its initial early access limitations in gameplay modes and maps (only one each) and one-note swarming enemy AI behaviors. The latter was alleviated a pinch by introduction of a flying ranged attacker, the Spitter.

I think what keeps the one-note swarming from getting tedious is the city environment with all its cars, corridors, bug nests and other objects. You end up on the fly trying to figure out ways to use these to break up the swarm and not get overwhelmed too quickly. Or you can also just run in circles in the more wide-open areas. There is a little bit of strategy that way. :)
https://youtu.be/luNcjFL0W4U
[h1]What's the Game's Concept? How does it work?[/h1]
Game sessions are essentially 20-minute, gradually wall-to-wall action sessions on a city map battling all matter of swarming alien creatures. Challenges, based on surviving a designated number of minutes, will unlock new weapons and classes. 

Kills earn you purple crystals that you pick up to spend on Enhancements, which improve a variety of passive abilities or your crystal rate. These drop rapidly whether playing solo or co-op, it's not much of a "grind."

Within a session, you rapidly "level," and every time you do so, up pops a screen that lets you pick from several things -- either special abilities (like missile salvo or frost nova) or passives for your class ability or special abilities that you already have chosen. I should note that it takes a while to get used to this screen constantly popping up while you're playing -- once I just accepted it as part of the game, it didn't bother me, but you could argue it sort of interrupts Rift Loopers' "flow" often.
https://youtu.be/L2zTzH_AmNs
[h1]I don't like pointless "swarm shooters," so what else IS there TO DO?[/h1]
While the one initial gameplay mode available is pretty simple, once you reach later minute marks in a session, a couple optional Objectives may appear. Acquring Intel requires putting X amount of time in the radius of the Intel object before successfully acquiring it. Another objective involves destroying alien items in certain areas.

Also, an alien "event" involving toxic spores dropping all over may occur.

A more Objectives-based mode seems to be on the long term dev roadmap, and I look forward to it. :-)

Although it's early in its Early Access, I can attest the devs are so far very aggressive about updating the game frequently with fixes and player-suggested or player-feedback-derived new features. Good to see, and I hope the devs get to see through their dev roadmap, which so far stretches well into 2023.

[h1]Fanboi, you must have some quibbles, right?[/h1]
Well, it's Early Access, and it's Very Early. :)

As far as constructive criticism I or others have submitted feedback on:
[list] [*] Although I think the game is animated brilliantly, the graphics do seem a bit, I guess grainy or a tad blurry? I'm not sure if the game maybe is that way by design, or if there's some sort of filtering at work? It doesn't bother me, but I have noticed other players pointing this out.

[*] The muddy-brown color of the one city map tends to blend in too much with the many brown alien enemies, especially in shadows. Many of us submitted feedback on this, and I suspect devs are reviewing that aspect.

[*] My pet peeve in online co-op is that while your fellow players' character models are very clearly marked by name/health meter, your own player character model is NOT marked, and it's way too easy to just lose sight of him/her when the maps' full of other players and alien enemies. Again, most likely devs will do something about that eventually.

[*] My other co-op pet peeve is currently there is NO way to respawn or be revived if you die in co-op. Other than ensuring you save the crystals you earned, there's no compelling reason to sit around and watch remaining players try to finish the session. It will be interesting to see if this is changed at some point.

[*] With most games in this genre, if all enemies just rush you, I eventually lost interest. See stuff like Tesla vs. Helsing or Solstice Chronices: MIA. I really have more fun battling enemies that have varieties in movement patters, attack patterns, general behaviors. I'm not positive how ambitious the RL devs may get in that direction, but the early addition of the new ranged-attack flying Alien Spitter enemy suggests that some alien enemies diversity is in future cards, at least a bit - i.e., the Spitter flies at ranged distances and spits poison balls, doesn't try to rush to you at melee-range.

[*] Although co-op session lobby has a fine text-chat system, in-game currently you have no means of communicating. I've lobbied (get it???) for a "quick text chat system" with maybe four basic messges (like "follow me," "Let's move to the objective point," "Heal me" etc.), and I'm sure integrating a voice chat system might be in the cards since it's pretty common in Unreal-engine games.
[/list]

While I haven't played much, not even a full hour, I already feel this is too barebones for early access.  

Maybe it'll improve over time, but it has to improve a lot.  It's another early access game that's so barebones that it's more of a tech demo.  A tech demo I get to pay to test, testing that requires grinding long enough for unlocks that I'll disqualify myself for a refund.

Mixing twin-stick combat with active skills and bullet-heaven progression is a decent idea, but it's not enough.  Plenty of games already do one or or the other, or even both, better.

It's not really a competition in this price range, but it's still difficult to justify playing or even holding onto this after considering the options.  I'm a sucker for anything vaguely like this, but I still have standards.

I could do worse for $5, but I can also certainly do better, and I've already bought a whole bunch like this, in this price range, that are more fleshed out, that deserve more attention.

A few observations...

Enemy behavior is limited, with melee enemies charging unceasingly at me.  They also deal damage on contact, at the start of their attack animations.  And they tend to move faster then me, so kiting isn't really an option, I have to kill them fast or damage is guaranteed.

Feedback when dealing damage is limited.  There are effects, but enemies don't react in a way that implies they've been hit by something.  Instead of dying from bullets or an explosion, they die from health loss.

Feedback when taking damage is also limited.  Similar to enemies, I don't react to damage in a way that implies I took it, I just lose health.  While there is a damage number, it's easy to miss that I'm taking damage until I glance at my status in the corner or get surprised by my death.

Leveling up is disorienting.  EXP is gained immediately, which is fine, but the window that pops up for upgrades also happens immediately, and blocks the center of the screen.  After I'm done, gameplay immediately resumes, and it's very easy to take damage from the enemies closest to me.

Player and enemy designs, and the 2 maps, are functional, and that's about it.  Nothing about the visuals gets me hyped to play as or fight against anything.  I get a premade asset vibe, especially considering the player skins that are just simple retextures (and in no way worth that grind).

The retrowave aesthetic of the title graphic is misleading, there is absolutely nothing in the game that matches it.  No bright neon colors (other than the special effects), no 80's vibe, it's a very specific theme that isn't utilized past the title graphic.
I think it's a fun rough game. There's plenty of room for improvement, but I love the aesthetic, and I am always looking for a new game like Heroes of Hammerwatch, so this fits that niche perfectly.

Platboarder is an absolute gem of a puzzle platformer that brings together the best elements of snakes and ladders, chess, and Mario in a truly innovative and captivating way. I've had a blast playing this game, and I can confidently say it's a refreshing addition to the genre that offers a unique and enjoyable experience.

First and foremost, the combination of snakes and ladders, chess, and Mario mechanics creates a gameplay dynamic that is both challenging and addictive. It's a brilliant fusion that keeps you engaged from start to finish. The incorporation of chess-like elements adds a strategic layer, making each move feel like a calculated decision rather than just mindless platforming.

The level design is nothing short of fantastic. Each stage presents a new set of puzzles and obstacles that require careful planning and precise execution. The progression is well-paced, ensuring that the difficulty gradually ramps up as you improve your skills. -Character customisation is quick, while still being able to make yourself unique

-Optimisation: A big ticket to talk about in many games, but there could definitely be some work done here. I was getting ~20fps on low-med settings.
-Some items don't have complete tool tips on how to use (Glass Jars for example)
-Repairing items. I couldn't figure out if there was a way to do so, or if there was another crafting station required.
-Building. Building a base was a little too snappy, requiring more precision to place things the way you would like (fitting walls to foundations)

All in all, it's a game that I sincerely wish to excel. At it's core it intrigues me, and I want to continue playing, but with the current optimisation it's a little tough. In the modern day landscape of gaming, it seems many of the best we've gotten in recent years are remakes of classics (Last of Us, Dead Space, Silent Hill, etc.). Resident Evil has been a recipient of this treatment for a while now, since the release of RE2R in 2019. I haven't played the original 2 and 3, so I can't speak for their quality in terms of that comparison (though I'm told 3 is disappointing in this regard), but both of the remakes are good, overall fun experiences. However, I have played the original 4. This remake manages to capture many of the sections and aspects of the original that made it so fun and engaging, though much like the 2 and 3 remakes, there are a lot of things that have been left out. There was never going to be a chance that this game matched the original in terms of quality or status. That game is simply on another level. But all things considered, this is a good game, a fairly faithful remake, and on its on terms is an absolute blast.

I've played this remake probably 3 or 4 times over now, and each time is just as riveting as the last. While many of the sections from the original are removed (the lake segment is very different, you are no longer chased by a giant stone Salazar, etc.), the way they're set up here work well within their own context and setup. Gunplay is snappy and mimics that classic RE4 feel, while being modernized so that you don't have to stand still like an asshole while aiming (always hated that). Parrying is carried over, the merchant is still awesome, and the atmosphere of the game (while not as thick as the original), is still quite present. Ada Wong[a] is a character in Resident Evil (Biohazard in Japan), a survival horror video game series created by the Japanese company Capcom. Ada was first mentioned in the original Resident Evil (1996), before being introduced as a supporting character and antiheroine in Resident Evil 2 (1998). The character was initially conceived as a researcher named Linda for the prototype of the second game, but her name was changed to Ada and she was rewritten as a spy and mercenary for the final build to connect its story to that of the original. Over the course of the series, Ada is often hired to steal biological weapons for various organizations, although she betrays her employers on numerous occasions to save protagonist Leon S. Kennedy from dire situations.

Resident Evil 4 is the sequel to Leon's story following the events of RE2. It's an amazing experience that builds up on everything previously stabilished while also setting itself apart from other entries in the franchise. The whole game is a marvel of game design, with the changes made to the core gameplay being nothing short of fantastic. It sets itself apart by being a lot more action focused, but overall the gameplay is extremely satisfying. Other gameplay aspects like atmosphere, graphics and sound design are also incredibly well done and the characters really feel alive and real. While the game may not be as horror-like as it was before, it definetly compensates for that with fun new mechanics to explore and new ways to fight the enemy.

The first thing that makes RE4 so different from its predecessors is the main gameplay loop. RE2 had a very deep focus on horror, the game would literally lock you inside an abandoned police station, give you a knife and a gun and hope you came out of it alive. And it was awesome.
RE4, on the other hand, is a lot more focused on combat, since Leon is now actually a trained professional with honed skills and combat experience. One good comparison to make is how in RE2, killing enemies would be very rare. The only way to permanently kill an infected would be to blow their head off, which would take either a lot of luck or a lot of precious resources. So the game plan would usually boil down to [b]crippling[/b] your targets instead of trying to eliminate them. However in RE4, due to the nature of the new virus affecting the people, known as Las Plagas, enemies are a lot less resiliant, so killing them is not just viable, it's actually needed in most situations. To compensate for that, the game gives you every single tool you might need to actually get rid of your enemies, like more ammo, more options when choosing your combat tools and many more ways to deal damage to whatever's bothering you. 
One of those things is Leon's newfound skill to [b]kick the shit out of enemies[/b], or how he figured out that knives are actually pretty useful in most combat situations, so now you can, I dunno, PARRY ATTACKS???

All of these changes make actually [i]playing[/i] the game SO MUCH MORE FUN. You don't just run away anymore, you face that shit HEAD ON. It's entirely possible to be on kissing distance from an enemy and be completely safe as long as you have the tools and the skill to defend yourself. 
The game is also a lot more streamlined, with very little backtracking being required (but still possible and even encouraged sometimes), everything feels more dynamic and rewarding, and the combat just feels so satisfying. Tearing through waves of enemies as you perfectly time a parry, ending the foe with a kick to the face, it's a thing of fucking beauty.
I am genuinely impressed with how awesome all of this feels.

Finally, the game also passes with flying colors on most other aspects. It looks gorgeous, like every other RE Engine game, of course, but it also runs great, with me having literally no performance issues throughout almost 40 hours of gameplay since the start.
Not just that, but the story elements are also amazing. The characters are well done and overall pretty loveable, the story makes sense and forms an interesting tale, and it honestly just feels really good to see Leon as a more mature guy, with real training and experience in the field but still keeping his signature silliness and jokey personality. Also, everyone looks fucking gorgeous and it's kind of insane but no complaints here

Overall, I think RE4 does an amazing job improving on the gameplay mechanics and idea of RE2. It's a completely different game with a completely different feel that basically trades horror for action, but still has some pretty scary moments and DOES NOT dissapoint when it comes to things like enemy design and overall game visuals, which I think are PEAK in this game. Los Illuminados are a really interesting and fascinating cult and Las Plagas feel even more awesome than the G-Virus did, with us facing quite a lot of different enemies throughout the journey. It's an incredible game that I'll definetly be playing again for collectibles and achievements (and because it's fucking fun, let's get real here). Best Resident Evil I've played thus far.

It has been a long time since I wrote my latest review. I'm breaking my long silence because I feel this game deserves much more attention than it is getting. Shadelight is a prominent example of what a talented and passionate dev can obtain with the Unity engine and a bunch of purchased assets. Formally, this game is a classic escape survival horror: scavenge for resources, solve puzzles, avoid monsters, escape. A pretty old formula, isn't it? Well, yes, but I think this game shows its own character, its own style you may say. First, the environment is much larger and much less claustrophobic than usual, there is a lot to explore, even multiple locations to visit, each with its own threats of course. Second, I appreciated the presence of multiple monsters, that all present the same behaviour, but come with different models and above all different moving speed, thus requiring different strategies to be avoided. Speaking of monsters, their AI is very tough, very well designed: they can hear you if you open doors or step on creaking floor boards, they can find you if they see you hide in a locker, and above all they can see you through the fissures of said lockers, if you forget to crouch! Nevertheless, their behaviour is always fair, when you die, you always know WHY you died, so that next time you can do better. Also, you have the possibility to save whenever you want by consuming a certain item, so the mutiple deaths never become frustrating. Finally, what I appreciated the most are the multiple ways at your disposal to deceive the monsters: besides hiding in the lockers, you can crouch in the bushes, you can inject adrenaline shots into your body to get powerful speed bursts, and you can even stun the enemies for a few seconds with a very fun taser gun, which is pretty difficult to find, but gives you an enormous advantage! Furthermore, the dev is very active on the game, constantly adding new content. The only thing I really don't like is the lack of a true plot. Who are we? Why are we here? Who are the monsters? Where do they come from? I would have liked more background, maybe in the form of notes scattered across the large map.
Overall, I think Shadelight is a very well crafted survival horror, challenging but fair. It requires a bit of patience, but it can reward you with a fun and thrilling experience.
Cheers guys!

EDIT: in their latest patch, the dev added a spine-chilling background story that can be learnt through notes scattered across the map. This ENORMOUSLY increases the gloomy atmosphere of the game. Even more recommended now! It is always a pleasure to meet devs that care about their games and listen to the suggestions of their customers!

AND
