I sadly have to leave to leave a bad review, which is something I basically never do.
This game is extremely odd but not fun at all in my opinion.

TL;DR the game has potential, but as it stands, it is extremely exhausting to play, with no accessibility options (or any kind of options) and is downright not fun to play.

The worst part is the movement.
This is a fighting game, which, for as far as I can tell, is focused on punching things, so why would you make the movement also involve punching? Punching the air is how you move and when you hit an enemy it is supposed to prevent you from moving, I think (it still moved me most of the time and I did end up kind of breaking the game, more on that later).
I tried the giant fighting arena for a bit, which looks nice, but that's about it. The hitboxes of objects just don't work or don't exist.
About that giant arena, it said that I'd have to survive for like 20 minutes. This is a fighting game, where punching is both for movement and attacking, 20 minutes of that would have killed my arms. I get that VR games are way more exhausting than pressing some buttons on a keyboard, but it should be taken into account that not everyone has enough stamina to punch for 20 minutes straight, the best I can do is like Beat Saber on Expert+ for 15 and after that I already will have had enough.
Next up is the leveling system, if you want to call it that. After beating enough enemies, you level up I think, which takes you straight out of the combat area to grant you a chest with 3 cards. After selecting your card, you are just brought back into the arena. I have no idea what these things did, I saw a card with Crypt and I love necromancy so I thought perhaps I'd get some zombie or skeleton minions or something. Nothing. I got another card which I don't remember the name of, still nothing. So the cards are confusing and being taken out of combat so abruptly is extremely annoying and kills the flow of the game.
Now, I did say I kind of broke the game, well, let me explain. If you hold one hand forward and one backwards while making a fist, you charge up your attack, up to the point where there are like rainbow beams around your field of vision. However, if you punch and then punch your hands up and down (one hand up, one hand down, and then lower the upper hand and raise the lower hand) and keep repeating that motion, you are just a sort of truck mowing down your enemies. It doesn't move smoothly obviously since you still have to punch every time in order to keep moving, but it does a lot of damage and the AI will not be able to keep up. You can also kind of glitch through walls this way, not much for as far as I could tell, but still a bit.
Now for a couple smaller issues that aren't gamebreaking, but are annoying and since I assume the person/team behind this game will read this review, it'd be good for them to work on these things (if they want to of course)
The skybox is also extremely low, so punching up to just slam down or something is not possible. It'd be really cool to just go up really high and then slam down (with some sort of cooldown of course), it'd really fit this game in my opinion.
When I turned around after selecting the arena gamemode (right after the tutorial), there was text in a different language on the portal, I do not recognize that language.
The voice acting is not great, the first guy you hear is fine (aside from the fact that he doesn't say all the text that is shown in his text box thing), but the rest is just awful, I am sorry, but that is just what it is.
The hands look really weird, not funny weird, just weird.

This game feels like it has great ideas and is extremely weird. It is really unique, it doesn't try to be a realistic fighting game like Blade and Sorcery and also not somewhat realistic but funnier like Gorn, it is just that what it tries to do, it does extremely poorly, by not explaining systems properly, having no accessibility or other kinds of options, expecting that players all have the stamina to punch for 20+ minutes, amongst a bunch of smaller issues.

I do hope that this game someday will become great, VR needs more good fighting games that aren't trying to be realistic (not that that is a bad thing btw) and just be stupid fun. I wish the team or person behind this the best of luck and I might try it again in the future if it is given away in a bundle or if it becomes really good, but for now, I will have to refund this.

This is exactly what I was looking for (TL;DR):
A fun and relaxing casual racing-manager that you can just hop into and start playing without watching any tutorial videos first. Probably wont keep you entertained for hundreds of hours but definitely worth the full price.

Some points to help you decide if this is for you:
Pros: 
-) The menus are self explanatory, everything you need is easy to find and not hidden in sub-menus. You're not ending up playing the game for hours, just to find out, that you've been missing a crucial mechanic. Micro-management is tuned down to a minimum.
-) Looks nice. Everything are pretty and clean. Buttons sound and feel satisfying - typical Funselektor stuff.
-) Instant gratification or punishment. You mess up, you know it - learn and make it better next time.
-) You can play through a season in pretty much one session. So even if you mess up the start of the season because you hired the wrong engineer or gambled too much with your sponsor - it's ok, you dont need to start the career all over again.
-) Addictive gameplay loop. Just one more race - I swear.

Neutral:
-) There are little to no helpers. When to pull your guy in for a pit stop or when to push for that crucial extra gap is pretty much up to your gut feeling (although you could theoretically figure it out yourself). I like it, but you may not.
-) There is very little RNG involved - which is positive if you hate those "BULLSH*T" moments. But on the other hands it makes the outcomes of the races very predictable and is (we are talking about racing here) totally unrealistic.
-) There are no "Are you sure?" boxes. You mindlessly click a button and figure out, you shouldn't have - deal with it.

Cons: 
-) This game is very simple - you want a deep racing-sim, look elsewhere. At least give us a fuel-strategy, it's a game about historic racing, right? Nope, you start with a full tank of gas every race and that's it.
-) Players are complaining, that the "70s F1 racing sim" is false advertising and they are correct. The only accurate 70s aspect is that drivers die - a lot.
-) The music and sound. "Art of Rally" had one of the best soundtracks I can think of and this game is just the same short boring loop and sounds. This is such a disappointment for a "Funselektor" game - probably my biggest complaint.

Absolutely recommend this game if you enjoy nonograms (Picross), and even if you don't. The game has a criminally low price for the features and number of puzzles it provides, a cheap DLC adding a ton more, a random puzzle generator within the game so if you enjoy abstract nonograms you'll never get bored, and workshop support (!!!!!!) to play puzzles other users create. 
There are so many settings to accommodate all sorts of play styles. It has multiple forms of assist including checking if the puzzle is correct (that doesn't spoil to you which specific square is wrong), a line assist to highlight rows that can have at least one square solved (without spoiling the specific square), placeholders for both squares and crosses (and buttons to either clear or replace all placeholders), and even a setting to disable all assists including placeholders if you really want to challenge yourself.
There's also a ton of settings for things like the theme (including allowing custom solid-color themes), what music plays, controls in menus vs in puzzles, lots of graphics settings, and some accessibility settings as well.
The music does become somewhat repetitive after 100 hours, but is overall very enjoyable and relaxing.
The game also appears very stable and I personally have experienced no crashes or bugs of any kind, which is always well appreciated.
Overall Nonozle answers literally every desire I've ever had for a nonogram game and there's a reason it managed to enter my 2nd most played game this year in under ~2 months. Imo, considering the popularity of the Picross franchise, this game is criminally underrated and really deserves more support, which is why I decided to write a review.

I've been having a great time with this, the engine is among the best, this is the one to get if you're looking to nonogram, the level of customisation is unmatched with the insane amount of details you can tweak. Large amounts of puzzles - I managed to get 60 hours off of the premade sets, many more hours to come with the workshop and random generation implemented. It just feels good to play, UX is buttery smooth. Really a good 6 dollars spent for the amount of playtime I've gotten, try this one out for a nice experience.
If you like nonograms then Nonozle is a nobrainer

" A Unique Painting Experience with Colorful Gameplay and Outstanding Audio"

Wetory is a one-of-a-kind game that brings a fresh and creative approach to the world of gaming. This innovative title sets itself apart by offering players a truly unique gameplay experience. In Wetory, the main concept revolves around colors and creativity as players are tasked with coloring their environment in an extraordinary way.

One of the standout features of Wetory is its gameplay mechanic, which involves producing paint directly from your character's feet. Yes, you read that right! Instead of traditional brushes or tools, you'll be using your character's feet to create colorful artwork. This approach adds an element of whimsy and fun to the game that's unlike anything you've seen before. Whether you're painting landscapes, characters, or even abstract designs, the game's mechanics make the process highly enjoyable and engaging.

Another aspect that makes Wetory a standout title is its exceptional background music (BGM) and sound effects. The game's soundtrack is not just an afterthought; it's a crucial part of the overall experience. The BGM sets the mood perfectly for each level, enhancing immersion and providing a delightful auditory backdrop to your painting adventures. Furthermore, the well-crafted sound effects add depth to your actions, making every splash and squish of paint feel satisfying.

In conclusion, Wetory is a game that combines creativity and entertainment in a refreshing way. Its unique gameplay mechanics, which involve painting with your character's feet, provide a fresh take on the gaming experience. Couple that with its exceptional BGM and sound effects, and you have a game that's not only fun to play but also a treat for the ears. If you're looking for a game that offers a unique twist on the traditional painting and platforming genres, Wetory is definitely worth a try.

- Firstly, there's a bug when trying to rewind, where a clone was destroyed immediately as we start a new rewind.
- The puzzle design is not good. It starts off with something immensely hard, coupled with a mechanic that is very counter-intuitive, the rewind aspect. Repetendium – A Fast-Paced and Tactical Action-Roguelike

After playing Repetendium for over 50 hours, I can confidently say it’s a hidden gem in the action-roguelike genre. The game combines fast-paced combat, tactical depth, and a strong sense of progression, making it incredibly addictive.

Gameplay & Mechanics
Repetendium delivers an intense and challenging experience where every run feels unique thanks to a wide variety of weapons, abilities, and upgrades. It requires both quick reflexes and strategic thinking to progress deeper into the game’s levels. The enemies are diverse, forcing players to adapt constantly.

However, there is a noticeable difficulty shift after Depth 10. At this point, the game moves from being a strategic challenge to feeling almost impossible to survive. The sheer number of enemies becomes overwhelming, and survival depends more on luck than skill or strategy.

Strengths +
- Huge variety of characters, weapons, and abilities: Every playable character feels unique, and there are endless combinations of weapons and abilities, providing tons of replayability.

- Great secrets to discover: The game rewards players who explore and uncover hidden areas and mechanics.

- Deep progression: Every run feels rewarding, whether you survive for a long time or die early, as you’re always learning and improving your strategy.

- Challenging but fair (until Depth 10): The first 10 levels strike a great balance between reflex-based combat and planning.

Weaknesses -
- Chaos after Depth 10: The number of enemies skyrockets to the point where strategy almost disappears, and survival is based more on luck than skill.

- Lack of explanations: Some mechanics can be confusing for new players, as the game doesn’t always explain them clearly.

Looking Forward to the Game’s Development
One of the most exciting things about Repetendium is how the developer, "Alex Sollazzo", often adds unexpected but amazing new features to the game. A great example is the latest playable character, a bear, who can call in reinforcements from HQ, control a tank directly, or let it shoot automatically as a turret. Every character in the game feels unique and plays differently, keeping the gameplay fresh.

I’m really looking forward to the official release in 2025 and can’t wait to see what surprises the developer has in store.

⭐ Score: 7/10

Conclusion: 
Fantastic variety and depth, but the balance after Depth 10 could use some improvement.

So, as another reviewer angrily pointed out, these are not really choose-your-own-adventure games.  The author has written a story which has some slight variations to it that have no effect beyond one or two pages of content (or at least, no major ones that I've found) and some gain or loss of points, and your goal is to read the clues in the story to choose the options that give you the most points.  (and avoid death)  This story has notably more chapters (which serve as checkpoints) than Wizard's Choice, making it less frustrating to die and need to backtrack.

But, THE STORY IS GOOD!  It's hard to measure in terms of pages, but there is at least as much story here as your typical 200 page paperback, and it's cheaper, too.  So, if you like fantasy books in the D&D style (like forgotten realms or dragonlance) then by all means, buy this book.  er, game.  The game aspect really acts like miniature mystery solving as you read the story; the narrative almost always gives you the hints you need to make the right choice, like mentioning that someone is immune to fire and then later giving you an option of turning into a dragon to fight them, which ends in failure because they were immune to dragon breath.  I find this fun.  I guess one other reviewer didn't.

One possible detraction, this story is written toward a male audience, moreso than Wizard's Choice.  It has disclaimers at the start of each chapter saying things like "This chapter contains sexual themes, violence " etc etc but there is no way to skip a chapter or opt out of the possibly objectionable parts of the story, so those disclaimers really ought to be on the game as a whole.

Very solid game. The gameplay loop is similar to roguelike deckbuilders where instead of acquiring cards you acquire modules for your ship called units. Units are placed on your ship, and many have directional aspects that require the player to place them strategically. Some units are strong by themselves, while others require synergies with other units or artifacts (called treasures in this game) in order to be effective. There is a limit to how many units you can equip as well as limited space on your ship, and this calls upon the player's creativity to create a good setup.

The enemies in the game are well designed in general and often call for specific strategies. Even if you get very powerful, there are some enemies with special mechanics who are able to use your power against you and this can keep the game challenging. In particular, the final bosses tend to have a unique mechanic that brings its own challenge. The bosses are well designed and all appropriately balanced. I don't feel any particular boss is much stronger or weaker than the others.

There are two ships for the player to choose from, each with their own units and special mechanic. Both are viable, although I found the Shielder ship to be better designed and stronger.

The player gets to choose a pilot who brings a unique perk. There are many pilots to choose from which gives the game decent replay value, but overall units are more impactful. It would be better if there were more units instead, but overall the selection is respectable.

The art, writing, and UI are all solid. There is not much plot, which is completely acceptable for this genre (maybe even preferred!) Overall this is a very respectable addition to the genre at a good price point.

Tons of replayability. Lots of fun, very much in the vein of so many other card battlers. Lots of variety of pilots. We just need some more ships. Lonestar needs an Eagle V! Mel Brooks would be proud. For the price, you can't beat it. I tend to judge games on if I can get 1 hour of enjoyment out of each dollar I spent. At even $10, I've doubled that.

This game has a story that lasts about 10 minutes, if I'm being really generous and it only took me 40 minutes to get every ending and I read it aloud with a friend, so it would have taken me slightly longer. There are only 4 choices in this game, one of which changes literally nothing. There are only really 3 ending, despite there being marginally different versions of one of them, and none of them were particularly satisfying.

Spoilers from this point on.




Now, the storytelling. If I hadn't read the Steam page, I would have been missing [i] a lot [/i] of important context for this story. For example: Kayla is rich, Miles has fallen in with the literal mafia, Luna is Kayla's butler. Of course, it is possible to guess this information from the game itself, however it is never made clear. This wouldn't be too much of a problem if the story was good.

It's not.

I haven't read the book that this game is based on, so perhaps the original story is good, but the story presented in this game is... lacking, to put it mildly. Firstly, due to it never being established that Kayla is rich, she just gets randomly attacked by the mafia for no reason, secondly, after given a choice on whether to return home or not, it is unclear where you actually go, as you end up in a house, no matter what you picked (Although, the latter choice isn't your house). Thirdly, if you choose not to return home, the mafia chases you down and a fight ensues. Kind of. Assuming you're getting the "good" ending, you slap the mafia leader and just run back to your house. That's it. 

Another thing is the actual dialogue, which is confusing. For example, when the mafia arrives at Miles's house, he says "They are pressuring me, but they shouldn't know my address", but, after he turns to look at them, he asks "How did you know my address?". This just sounds odd and unnatural, almost as if it's been lost in translation, but the game is only available in English, so that can't be the case.

Overall, this game is fun to laugh at with a friend for 30 minutes, but you shouldn't buy it if you're looking for a well written serious story. As I mentioned earlier, this game is based on a book which I haven't read, so, if you want to experience this story, that's your best bet.

So, more or less the rest of this review is towards the developer than the players reading it.

Firstly, if a game is this short with the selling point of achieving multiple different endings at least make them interesting or have them reveal some new information for the players to learn. All of the total of the 3 bad endings were particularly the same while the one good ending wasn't that satisfying as we don't get to spend much time with the existing character to feel it's earned or anything. What this game desperately needs is more scenes fleshing out the supporting characters like the butler and our main character's best friend, Mike. Furthermore, it would have been helpful to have an introduction to Kayla (the protagonist) and her relationship to being a part of a rich family, answering a lot of unanswered questions like, why are the mafia after her and for what? We don't get much of an explanation of what's going on from what the summary on the Steam page made it seem making it hard to follow through with what the story is about.

Based on Kayla's body language and facial expression, it seems like she is the type of person who wants to be a 'normal' every-girl character which could be an interesting direction for the story being a commentary that inherited wealth isn't everything going make your life better or be apart of wealthy life isn't for everyone. I know this game is based on a book called Fool Me Twice written by the same creator (from what I could tell) having 300 pages, so I am sure there's enough content to lengthen this game gameplay run unless the source material itself begs a differ. I haven't read it so who knows?

One thing I'm going to give credit for this visual novel (and one of the reasons I'm taking this review seriously in the first place) is the art style. Nothing too complex, something that's a cute and simplistic style that could make the character stand out by having dramatic poses and expressions. 

From what have seen on the creator's website and Twitter this game has potential, but a lot of work is needed to fulfil that requirement for the game to be fun and quirky.

I forget where I first spotted this, but I've had it on the watch-list for a while now, waiting to grab it once it finally released. Didn't know much going into it beyond a singular fixation on ducks, but having played it quite thoroughly, I can say I enjoyed my time with it! About my biggest criticism with this is the difficulty with regards to getting the endings isn't as high as I was expecting from the outset.

The core of the game involves bringing Quark the duck back to the start of the level, the time machine where the game's plot originates. Exploration tools are explained clearly enough, and players are challenged to explore to find lives, duck eggs, and devices that change Quark, affecting where the portal will land them on the next level. Duck eggs give you ducklings, which can give you power boosts, regenerating shields, piercing shots, improved time-stop capabilities and so on - generally a good help to find. On top of that are shields, which are your one saving grace against the enemy; anything and everything can kill you, including your own bullets. Any shots you fire MUST hit something to dissipate, and they don't care if that something is your character.

Dying restarts the level, minus one life - lose all your lives and the run ends. Simple as. But lives scattered around the level regenerate when you die; know where the lives are, and it's very easy to stay equal whilst you learn a level's layout. At that point, a run can be very difficult to lose short of exiting out of the game. Heck, one achievement ties to having 20 lives, so this isn't unexpected behaviour.

The aforementioned changing of Quark lets you access different level types - the Disco and Bathroom stages. The former has you playing bat-and-ball with a glitter-ball whilst doing your best to avoid the chunkier enemies flying around, whilst the latter changes up gameplay by letting you control a duck for a short while! The aim as a duck is to bypass areas that your human self can't access, whilst bringing a time-shifted version of yourself to the same station that changed you to a duck without being hurt or dragged back to the start of the level. It's a fun little change on what's been established, though controlling the duck might be a little finicky at first.

The boss fights... that [i]might[/i] be the weak point of the game, I think? One of them simply spawns guys to bother you whilst following a strict path; a second is more of a challenge on a platforming level as the ground beneath you starts to dissipate if you want to blunt its offence. The third boss works with the usual gameplay model of pitting you against an exponentially-growing horde of horrid waterfowl. Completing these fights gives you unlockable toggles for your gun, either offering traversal or greater power without being tied to the upgrades.

These upgrades are key to completing the game's "Impossible" mode, which disables duckling upgrades. You get no extra defences or offences; simply reach the end of the game with your starting energy and the tools you have to unlock on each run (with the game's one kindness being to let you start with the boss drops, so you only need to get their respective component parts with the standard methods). I expected this to take me a while; [spoiler]I got it on my first run[/spoiler]. This DOES do more than just act as a challenge, so I recommend giving that a go if you grab this game.

The meat of the game's challenge lies in the Survival mode. Shooting gives points, and the Kronits (energy points) the horde drops give points too, IF you're at full time-slowing juice. Points let you buy shielding, duckling eggs, and support ducks with their own firing modes, but the prices go up as you buy them from different areas. Face as many waves of weird ducks as you can before they finally overwhelm you. This is the mode that let me realise I'm not as good at this game as I thought, because my best progress still didn't reach Wave 20...

So in summary: there's some good fun to this game, but the main challenge lies outside of the standard gameplay mode, which can feel like a bit of a cakewalk once you get a proper handle on the controls.

[i](also I like Quark's little "I'm over here! ;_;" sounds)[/i]

EDIT: Forgot to mention, the settings seem quite sparse, and the game doesn't seem to have a frame-rate cap. I don't [i]think[/i] this adversely affected my computer as Steam believed it was trying to render over two thousand frames a second, but it seems odd that the extent of this game's graphical settings are whether it was full-screen or not.

Pine: A Story of Loss is a beautiful game depicting grief and moving on after losing someone you love. The game tells a the love story of the woodworker (the protagonist), and his late wife through memories and flashbacks. While the game is short (I completed it in approximately 90 minutes), and repetitive, it's beautiful and definitely worth a play.

There are quite a few reviews that dislike how short the game is, in addition to disliking how repetitive the minigames are. I personally do not have a problem with either of these issues. For one, going day-by-day into a person's life when they are grieving would not be the most effective, and for another, it would get somewhat depressing after a while. Additionally, the repetitive minigames, I felt, were effective at demonstrating how people can sort of just "go through the motions" after experiencing a loss like the woodworker. Grief is a funny thing, and you can sort of shut down, just doing what you know you need to do in order to survive. Is it healthy? No. Is it fun? Definitely not. But is it real? Absolutely. And I think the creators did a great job at demonstrating this.

Please note: If you have recently experienced the loss of a loved one, this game may not be something you would want to play for a while. Spoken as someone who has recently gone through a great loss, I can personally say that while it did trigger some tears, playing the game was cathartic, and did provide a sense of "peace" at knowing that the process of grief is similar for many. However, I acknowledge that the grieving process is different for everyone, and if you are not in the right head space to play this game, I recommend either looking into another game, or waiting until you are in the right head space to play.

For me personally, this one is a no. Ultimately it just comes down to difficulty. The game absolutely has variety, there are a staggering number of spells and passives available to you can mix and match, but unfortunately the game difficulty ramps up so rapidly each floor that you generally find yourself having to use specific, pre-existing builds in order to make any decent progress, and experimenting will generally just end your run, sometimes as early as the second or third floor. The quantity of enemies, the health, their damage, their abilities, all of it scales up exponentially to the point you kind of have to already know what final build you're going for before you even start.

To make a comparison, if you've played roguelikes with 'ascension' ranks or similar to optionally increase the difficulty every time you win, this feels sort of like playing on one of the much higher ascensions... by default. The game also includes alternate game modes, but each of them from what I've seen are even -harder- than the standard game.

For me at least, I suppose it's just disheartening to have a whole sandbox of possible spells and upgrades and synergies to try out and experiment with, yet feeling like I'm being punished for wanting to try them out. Like if 75% of the spell combinations in Noita killed your wizard as soon as you plugged them into the wand. You wouldn't be encouraged to experiment, you'd be encouraged to just...look up what spell combinations already work to save you time. 

I don't even mean outlandish combinations either, but even ones that seem sensible. "Oh, I can learn fireball, then a flaming eye, then upgrade that flaming eye so it -casts- my fireb-" Nope, even that much veered too far from a reliable build and now I'm surrounded and killed. I've managed to win a select few runs, but only by either using someone else's specific build, or just throwing an army of summons at the screen and then just hitting 'pass turn' until they beat the game for me, and that's not counting the dozens and -dozens- of runs where I'd die on the second/third floor.

It's a shame, I really do want to like this game, but it's just too frustrating an experience to play. If you're not put off by that kind of high difficulty though, then you can consider this a positive review for you.

Edit (2025-02-02):

Just to add, as inspired by others and wanting to add more detail, a suggestion for how to fix the difficulty issue. If there were a hypothetical new game mode added to smooth the difficulty curve, these are some considerations I'd have for it:

- All positive enemy resistances have a flat -25% applied. This way, new players are encouraged to pay attention to resistances and plan around them, without one of the game's many, many fully immune enemies instantly ending their run.
- +1 SP per level. Currently, the amount of SP gain is balanced for if you already know exactly what build you're going for. If you don't, or if you're experimenting...you die in the first floors. Having more SP to go around, thus, encourages experimenting with potential synergies.
- Overall reduction on enemy stats. This could involve reducing HP/damage/range/shield, but it could also involve removing some enemy abilities outright. Not only will this make it less punishing as new modifiers are introduced, but it gives players something new to look forward to when they hear that higher difficulties (current base game) fundamentally change enemies. Imagine a player reading 'In the next difficulty, enemies can spawn as a 'lich' variant, and become immortal'! Incentive for them to push and make their discovered builds work better
- Rare items spawning earlier in the game. This way, players more easily discover what kind of rare tools the game will provide to them and how they affect their builds, so when they become less rare in harder difficulties, they already know what to keep an eye out for.
- +1 items spawned per floor. Instead of just picking between +health or a chest, maybe one floor has two health, while another has wands and a scroll, while another has health and trinkets. Powerful? Sure, but this ties into the last note about teaching players synergies, and giving them the health to live through beginner mistakes.

A game mode, or even general game difficulty options, with settings that can be changed like that, would make the game far, far more approachable to new players.

Unusual game. It's mostly Traditional Roguelike with a splash of old school Gauntlet, but with *tons* of spells and items. 

But the difficulty inadvertently discourages experimenting with spells, which is unfortunate. It's also very unfriendly to new players, bombarding them with a massive list of spells/skills without useful filters for those lists.


[h2]Pros:[/h2]

- Huge spell list, all with upgrades available. One of the biggest spell lists I've ever seen in a game

- Creative items

- Can create just about any specific "Wizard" you could possibly think of. I'm working on an Ice summon / Ice spell hybrid right now that summons Ice Phoenixes while throwing out Blizzards and such. Very fun


[h2]Mehs:[/h2]

- Music isn't bad, but it's not quite good enough or varied enough. The simpler a game's graphics are, the more important the music is

- Graphics are mostly fine, but it's kinda hard to see enemy spawners, Wizards/Liches among all the other stuff... and it's absolutely critical to know where they are

- Summons are a very important part of the game. While it's possible to go without any, the *vast* majority of builds will use at least some. This can be annoying to players looking for more of a "solo wizard" fantasy


[h2]Cons:[/h2]

- Difficulty ramps up really quick. I wish there were some difficulty options or something. It's largely a matter of wasted time in trying new combos that are instantly doomed to fail

- Most choices will result in your death, so the huge spell variety is kind of an illusion

- if you don't specialize enough, your damage is too low to proceed, but if you DO specialize, you'll get screwed by immune/resistant enemies everywhere. There are therefore very limited viable builds

- Summons can get permanently silenced and become useless 

- It's rare, but some enemies and abilities leave out critical information. That can result in a permadeath 

- Filters for the massive list of spells/skills are *horrible*. They filter out extremely important, critical skills you need for your build. New players get screwed as they cannot filter to find critical skills

- Dev seems to be completely silent. No review responses or forum post responses

OK so a bit of background. I came to this game because of Path of Achra, which I absolutely love and honestly cannot get enough of. The guy who made it - Ulfsire - cited Rift Wizard as one of his key influences. Right then, if Ulfsire says it's a massive influence, then surely I will like it, and it will scratch that itch. The bottomline is: I do like this game and I do recommend it. But after spending 4 hours with it, I want to share some thoughts. Not simply to save you the money, but to calibrate your expectations and what you might expect in terms of dumping time into a game like this.

The game is widely regarded (and I guess is meant to be) a kind of theory building power fantasy, where you basically engage in wild combinatorics problem to build 'broken' characters out of the various spells and skills (and items you randomly find) to try and beat the game: get to level 20 (yeah, it's pretty traditional). The thing about this game - unlike Path of Achra - is that it doesn't actually feel like a "power fantasy". Actually, most of the time I feel quite powerless. Now, people might rush to put baby or clown emojis on my review, and that's fine. But I've played a lot of traditional roguelikes, including and especially Rogue. I'm not stranger to difficulty and 'unfairness' (variously defined). I like dying - it's fun. The thing about this game, in its current release at least, is that it doesn't have a sense of progression that feels right or particularly engaging. I am enjoying it but I'm sort of forcing myself to get through this phase of the game where I am memorising literally hundreds of spells and skills, trying to find a path forward for synergies that are fun and rewarding, even if they don't work.

I don't know how to put this: the game is the sort of thing you'd love if you love Path of Achra, and I can see how much of an influence it is on that game. But the progression is just so... off... I don't feel like I'm particularly learning anything from my mistakes, even after googling a lot of Reddit threads and watching YouTube videos about both this game it the first Rift Wizard.

I know that I'll probably get through this stage and start to really hone the synergies and build that knowledge which only comes from experience and failure in roguelikes, but at this stage I can say: yes, buy this especially if it's on sale, but don't expect to be hooked or satisfied straight from the get go. This might be like one of those novels that you need 9 chapters to really start to feel like you're getting the gist of it.

Kudos to the developer - I love the music. I love the art. I love the sensibilities that are in the soul and technical architecture of this game. It is - in principle - exactly what I love and want in a roguelike... especially this new breed of broken build sandbox 'power fantasy' type ones. The game is dripping with style and mood. 

But, I would recommend that the developer tries to find a way to structure the spells and skill trees a bit more, to allow players to get a feel for the learning. Try to scaffold the learning a bit so that you can deduce where you went wrong and backtrack on synergies. Should I have not upgraded that one spell? Did I dump points into the skill tree too early? Am I picking up the wrong items when choosing which realm to rift into? 

I'd also love to see a *search* function built into the spells and skills lists - like in Path of Achra. Sometimes I just want to see which spells mention "summons" or which ones mention "heal". I don't want to just subset the list based on the type of spell or skill. I want to be able to theorycraft the **** out of this and learn as I explore and go in and out of rabbit holes. Giving stats at the end of a run would be nice - whether failure or not. Unless I'm missing something? When you die I am currently confused about what it shows. It has a death screen and then if you click, it shows you random (?) screenshots from each level you were on your run? I can't find more info in the help file on this. Maybe my frustration is causing me to breeze through it too quick. It also takes too long for the tiles to do that disappearing effect after a failed run. Honestly, just let us click to skip it or something.

Overall, this is a really exciting masterpiece in the making, and I recommend it. But I have so many things to say about it that I just had to get out there. Dev, if you're listening, keep going! I look forward to see where this goes to.

There are many games with permadeath, randomly generated challenges/rewards, and upgrade systems for characters and gameplay progresses in a given run.  Rift Wizard 2, however, is one of the rare games that I would call a true Roguelike.  It is simple in its presentation and general gameplay, but complicated by the near-incomprehensible combinations of powers, skills, items, and other features that can make game runs feel unique until the heat death of the universe.  It is also inscrutable and horrifically difficult, often to the point of unfairness.  These features, plus the charming art style evoke the same sense of wonder and dread that a Roguelike should instill in its players.  There is no metaprogression or additional tools to unlock.  The only thing that will progress from game to game is you, as you learn to use the tools that have always been there to their fullest capacities.

If what you want is a punishing yet charming Roguelike with some of the most interesting possibilities of skill progressions, combinations, and upgrades I have seen in the genre, Rift Wizard 2 might be your favourite game.  But, it is not without flaws.  Even by Roguelike standards, its difficulty is, as other reviewers point out, both intense and oddly skewed.  The combination of few early game options and multiple sources of infinitely spawning enemies mean that you might not be able to get a build off the ground before being pulverized.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing for a Roguelike; unfair difficulty is a hallmark of the genre.  But, it is a problem when build and spell variety are so heavily emphasized.  The Discussions are full of complaints that some spell paths and even entire build archetypes (e.g., summoner) are just incompatible with the way the game is balanced.  I don't know yet if I agree or not, but the complaints are certainly plausible even from my limited experience.

This game is very similar to Path of Achra if you're familiar.  You get points to put towards unlocking spells or passives.  You pick then pick "rifts" which are procedurally generated levels with different layouts, enemies, and rewards.  On the surface Rift Wizard 2 has an insane amount of combos and builds.  In reality this is not the case because many spells and passives are simply too weak to use.  For example you might think that getting the eye of fire spell, upgrading it so it casts fireball, and then upgrading your fireball would be a viable strategy.  You would be wrong.  Fireball is very good, especially the meteor upgrade, but eye is terrible and you can't afford to spend the points on it over other better spells.  Plus to add insult to injury the eye can kill you with the fireball by casting it on enemies that manage to get too close.  Once you start to understand what's good and what's not the game becomes a lot more fun.  The second thing you need to learn is how to  pick the best level for your build.  I think a lot of new players get baited into picking levels based off the rewards without considering if their build can even clear it.  The two most important things you need to consider when picking a level are the enemies present (mostly just their resistances) and the map layout.  Many enemies are completely immune to certain damage types.  If you're playing a fire build don't go to the level that gives you fire rewards if there are a bunch of fire immune enemies.  Map layout is just as important because certain spells straight up don't work on certain levels.  Usually wide open levels are significantly easier to clear than the closed in ones.  The other thing about map layout to consider is where the enemy spawners are.  If they're on opposite sides of the map you might kill one and run out of spells before you can kill the next one.  Once you learn how to make decent builds and what levels those builds can clear you'll have a much better time.  If you find figuring that stuff out then Rift Wizard 2 is a fantastic game, if not then it's probably not the game for you.

Do you remember Diablo 2?
 
After 5 long, grueling hours slinging firebolt, you'd finally be rewarded with the iconic spell: Fireball. What a moment, right? You could now deal some area-of-effect damage. A real explosion, nothing too flashy. But back then, it felt unbelievable.
 
For the next 10 hours of playtime, it was you and your trusty Fireball, chipping away at enemies. And then you'd get Meteor. Now that was an upgrade! An explosion AND a bit of damage over time? Revolutionary! At least, that's what we thought.
 
But it's 2025 now, and games have evolved.
 
In Rift Wizards 2, there's no waiting. You start with a mega version of Fireball right from the beginning. No 5-hour grind required. And every 5 minutes, you're rewarded with choices from hundreds of spells: volcanic eruptions, hellhound summons, rainstorms of fire. It's a constant cascade of chaos and creativity.
 
On the surface, you might dismiss it. The graphics are so bad that next to this, Pong looks like Red Dead Redemption 2. But under that rough exterior, it delivers what Diablo 2 could only tease: non-stop excitement without the grind, a spellbook that doesn't make you wait for fun.
 
Some reviews have raised concerns about the difficulty, and honestly, they're not wrong. Other roguelikes, such as Faster Than Light and Slay the Spire are a bit easier to get started. Rift Wizard 2 tosses you straight into the deep end. A few extra difficulty options or ascension levels would’ve been a solid addition. That said, I didn't find the high difficulty to be a dealbreaker and enjoyed the challenge.

So yeah, we're having this conversation again. Is difficulty good?

Because of the nature of videogame discussion, we can't just let people decide for themselves. We enter the discussion with loaded opinions and sweeping statements, and any attempt to have a discussion strands. One side will argue that the game was perfect because it was hard, even though there's a good chance they didn't find it all that hard.

The other side will say that they found the game too hard and it sucked.

Not to be biased or anything, but I think that second group is correct and the first is in the wrong. If a product doesn't meet your expectations as a consumer, if you didn't have fun, complaining is the right thing to do!

So let's talk about Quasimorph. I'd summarize the game like this: do you want to carry food? Or do you want to carry an extra clip of ammo, so you can shoot more people and eat their dismembered limbs instead?

Quasimorph is one of those games known primarily for being difficult, Nintendo Hard. But the difficulty quickly becomes manageable with proper planning and understanding of the mechanics. I seriously question whether the people applauding the game for being hard really had a hard time, or whether they're applauding the game for giving them a sense of accomplishment. 

That's not the same thing.

The game is also a roguelike. Like Rogue, it's a turn based dungeon diving game where any item you find has the potential to save your life and win your mission, and anything you carried with you when you died is lost forever.

Quasimorph is a game that rewards calculated gambling, whereas small oversights or bad rolls will potentially catch players in an death spiral. There's a dozen or more status effects, most of them will kill you if left untreated, and there's usually no treatment available for anything more exotic than a fracture or a laceration.

Is that fun? Well, you have to learn which risks are associated with which enemies, environments and weapons. Mars is different from Earth is different from Venus, etc. Plan accordingly.

The missions are also marathons, with multiple floors, seemingly endless hordes of enemies and enough supplies to maybe deal with half of that. The other half you have to scavenge.

It makes a big difference whether you're going to be in a mission for 300 turns or 1000 turns, or even 2000 turns, and the game gives little indication which one to prepare for. Sometimes you just get lucky with an elevator spawn. I'm ambivalent on this. On one hand I think calculated gambling requires the player have information to calculate.

On the other hand, I've had several long missions where I escaped with barely 10 turns left to live. Running out of supplies isn't fun, but expending all you have left to clutch the win is fun. One mission, I was able to climb into the elevator with a fatal wound. The mission after that, after securing the objective, I had to sprint away from an unstoppable death tide of enemies, desperately blasting my shotgun in all directions as I fled. These were the most memorable moments of the game for me.

While the game can often boil down to a diceroll, I think the gameplay, graphics, sound design and UI do an admirable job creating an atmosphere to contextualize that diceroll and make it interesting.

With that in mind, I give Quasimorph a cautious recommendation.

Alright, originally I wrote a bad review for the game, however, that was not really... correct. There are a lot of things this game does right. And a few it does... not so right. Not that the mechanics themselves arent good, its just in a way they interact with each other that is not good. First this is an extraction game. On one hand, this is good. A well made extraction shooter can be really good. However, this game has a few issues that make the unforgiving extraction shooter element not fun. Examples are: Enemies behind doors that shoot you the moment you open it, painshock you and then shoot you again and then you die. Or when the VIP in escort missions cannot be healed (you physically cannot heal him and he wont heal himself either) and dies you die with him. While the logical outcome would be that your character could just head out again because why not. Or when you accidentally start the mission with the wrong faction and you dont want to complete it because it would hurt you in the long run and you can only cancel the mission by finding a valuable item (which isnt guaranteed) or resetting which means you die. These are all things you can partially avoid or reduce the risk of but its not something I think belongs into the game right now. I am sure these will be ironed out eventually. But fortunately for now, you can make a custom difficulty and just turn it off. Which is good because if you just want a fun casual playthrough, you can have that, if you want a masochistic playthrough you can hav that too.
Next the crafting. Technically good, effectively not so much. The Demo actually had a very good system in place: You can craft anything as often as you want, but you need to find a production chip for it. Aka, you need to win RNG to find the chip, then need RNG to get what you want upon chip activation but if you do, its nice. Good system. In the release its the same system but now you also need time to craft it (not an issue, makes the system better actually) but you also need copious amounts of resources. Which wouldnt be an issue if your inventory size wouldnt be comically small. You typically need some things to start a mission (ammo, weapons and meds) which eat a few slots. Then you find some nice goodies which do not stack typically and/or are insanely huge (take 2 item slots or so) and you NEED these to upgrade your ship, unlock new mercs, classes, items, that stuff. But you typically cant take crafting materials AND valuables out of a mission because your inventory is too small. Not good, cannot be turned off either.
Can be mitigated through turning off drop on death because now you only need to go through the hassle of crafting something once instead of crafting it several times and then stockpiling it. Can also further be mitigated by turning on repair on return which just means you dont need to worry about repair kits or repairing your tools that much.
Honourable mentions also go to the bartering system (Basically your PMC does illegal stuff and because of that they cant trade with corporations, which makes no sense because first: The world is anarcho capitalist. PMCs are openly hired to do stuff so everyone knows that corporations pay people to do illegal stuff. Also ever heard of cash? Nearly untracable but im diverging) so you need to barter items (the stuff we painstakingly grabbed during missions with our very small inventory) to semi-gambling to hope that they give us the stuff we want. Not how bartering works but alright. Its not entirely random but a lot of it is random. Could be done better but will probably not impact anyone that much because of the exchange rates. Your stuff is nearly worthless and everything has pretty big fees (50% additional cost is normal on game start) so bartering is really just your last ditch effort if you REALLY need something and want to trade bad RNG to semi-bad RNG.
And lastly the combat system. Mostly good. But then you get to absolute comedy moments like your chainsaw missing a target four times in a row and then you die because of that. Very infuriating when it happens with extraction mode on, annoying inconvienience without.

With all that said: Its still a fun game. Slightly repetitive but it has a good concept and we have options. If you want pain, gambling and masochism: It has that. If you want gambling and fun: It has that too.
Good choice for giving us the option to customize how fun the game should be.

Quasimorph is simultaneously addictive and very abusive. You will feel the highest highs looting your first buffalo and evacuating the mission with a backpack full of goods...
Only to be brought crashing down when you start the next mission, open a door, and eat a face full of lasers, dying instantly. You curse, alt+f4 the game... and then open it again 30 seconds later.

It rewards careful planning and the occasional risky gamble and can eat up hours of your time just playing mission after mission. The universe and aesthetic is really neat and well implemented. If you enjoy games which reward finding and exploiting a steady gameplay loop, or if you just enjoy being a cannibalistic loot goblin, Quasimorph provides hours of enjoyment.

But... There's a high probability this game isn't for you. If you don't enjoy:
-Very punishing games which can kill you before you realize what happened
-Having to constantly monitor several different resources and understand how to properly use them (food, health, ammo, etc)
-Having to regularly lose and restart hours of progress, from either wiping or updates (every time the game is updated you generally need to delete your old save and start a new one. It's super annoying)
-Playing a very steady gameplay loop (in the late game, you will tend to play most missions the same way once you understand how resistances and combat works, meaning that there isn't a lot of variety besides the big faction missions)

Then the game isn't for you. You won't enjoy it, it'll seem overly difficult and grindy. However, if any part of it appeals to you, I reccomend giving it a try. The game is frequently updated and the devs seem to listen, hopefully one day it'll  receive a proper full release!

A simple top down rogue-like shooter yet with turn-based moves similar to Xcom, and what if Aliens Isolation is taken to next level, where humanity can be just as violent as xenomorphs, along with real time course of events between factions relation based on player's actions.

As you complete missions, you will get reward from the faction you're helping, take a little time to check around each faction's Technology and see what they can offer, or simply be a mediator, keeping factions in balance and in check, play for multiple sides at different time.

Or simply play on the side of factions you like, as you earn coins for taking their contracts after all. Be sure to check out their sector after the conflict in said area is over, so you may trade with factions that have good standing with you, as they may have resource you need to upgrade your ship.

Every resource is useful, not a single thing is useless, a tin can or empty bottle can be made into throwables like bombs and molotov, while rag and plastic are always your go to must-have resource, for you always need as much medicine as possible. Rotten meat is needed to make pain killers with plastic, while rag is needed to make bandage and splint, so you can make first aid kits yourself.

Multiple guns, from pistols and nail guns to high-tech pulse rifles and laser weapons, and melee weapons. Each weapon has different attack type, and it is best you diverse weapons of your choice, for you will always need as many guns and many bullets as possible.

Multiple armor, from plain shirt and jeans to high-tech power armors that each sets offer different protection value and resistance against elements. You surely can wear entirely bullet-proof armor, but you will soon find out that lack of radiation and poison resistance can be your doom against energy weapons and poisons.

Multiple classes, and blueprints for products you can make for yourself. As you play each mission, you may randomly come across chips, and blueprints. ALWAYS take them with you and go home in one piece, as you can get new operatives, give them different classes to fit in your play style, as each operative is unique and has their personal bonus, make it even better with class you pick for them.

Food, EXTREMELY IMPORTANT, you will find out that every move can cost hunger based on how heavy you are. I would advice simply mass produce food with plastic you've been gathering. They're fast to make, 5 stacks at a time, can refill 350 to 400 hunger each bite, returns the plastic, so you can create an infinite food source. Or just cannibalise whoever you killed, you can make smoked meat with flesh from human and alien alike, and they taste DELICIOUS.

Enemies are vary and based on faction you're fighting against. You can check technology and be prepared for upcoming fights, for example, Civil Resistance will always be people armed with plain guns and nail guns, you can then wear armor offer good blunt and pierce resistance to render them harmless against your character, in case they do have the opportunity to pull the first shot. Right click on them to see their overall stats as well, as conventional firearms early game are mostly blunt damage, while at mid to late game, they will be using bullet-proof armor resist against blunt, and you will have to use more guns with armor pierce or fire rounds to set them on fire.

Plan your moves in each combat, as you will always face both gunnery and melee enemies, especially in tight corners and rooms, where opening the door will instantly give them opportunity to fire at you. My recommendation is fire a round to bait enemies out, it is much better deal to fire a shot than taking unnecessary damage, as incoming harm can be really bad, such as causing laceration, bleed, fracture, you name it, and worst case scenario is you may even lose a limb or a leg, and it's always fatal if your head and torso are torn open.

On and all, it's really enjoying if you know how to play around, and take on what you can chew.

[u][h3]Overview[/h3][/u]
As of this review this game is still in development however it already feels like a proper completed sandbox game. Again, the story is still a WiP and in my opinion I think there is a need to readjust its difficulty and scaling as it is almost impossible to complete; be it by design by the developers. 
[b]DO NOTE[/b]: that this is a very difficult game and I strongly recommend players to be very vigilant and compose while playing this game as it is very unforgiving to even the smallest of mistakes.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]Game Play[/h3]
It is a turn base RPG in 2D form, quite literally an interesting mix between X-com with Escape from Tarkov. You are a mercenary travelling through space picking up missions posted by the many available corporate/organisation that exist. You have absolute freedom on what to do and how to go about it, however every mission that help you gain resource and reputation with one faction will inevitably gain notoriety and aversion from the victim. So, take your positions on who you want to support and which hill you want to die on. There is an extensive looting experience to this game as well, which intensify the decision making of “what to keep” and the more agonizing “what should I drop”. Did I mentioned be vigilant and compose? Ah yes, be discipline and use your turns properly to check all those conners, God forbid if you finally fill you bag full of goodies just to be killed for being too complacent to check the path you came from. Enemies can patrol and will catch you off guard. And do not forget, Quasimorphs. Apart from the world you start at, every other world can spawn monsters/demons/Quasimorphs. These creatures usually start spawning from dying humanoid later in missions when the bottom right meter pass 100 and it only get progressively harder from that point. So, the more reason to not loiter around and just “Stick to the mission and bail the hell out ASAP”, unless of course you are adventurous but often that additional risk is not worth the reward as you won’t have the munition and carrying capacity for it.
Knowing all that my advice is:
- Learn the weaknesses of your victim. Play test the game to figure out each faction weakness (you can right click on a visible enemy to check its weapon armor weakness and its move set)
- Have adequate medical kits to deal with injuries that you [b]WILL [/b] sustain. 
- And lastly, unless it is critical to upgrades or an item you want to fabricate, just pick the most expensive item at hand to keep since most resource can be sold and purchased to an assortment of station.

[h3]Did I also mention there are mods on the steam workshop?[/h3] 
Because why play a game that is insufferably difficult? Unless you are a masochist like me, mods will make this game more conducive to your own enjoyment. There is a good number of mods out there as of this review and I hope more will come to add quality of life improvement that fits everyone’s niche. And for that, Quasimorph gets bonus points!

[h1] Early Access Review [/h1]

[u] Summery: [/u] 
I have finished all the quests, though not got the 200 3* hare statue. Really fun game-play, from combat to building, it is all fun and feels nice to use. Elite enemies feel difficult and can still hit hard if you mess up late-game. The building is grindy but look good with a lot of decoration for the stage that the game is in. Hunting can take a bit to get use to and due to damage needed some are capped with their rarities with weapon tiers, though there are some problems but will mention later. Overall, the game feel like valhein with greek mythos.

[u] Building: [/u]
My personal favourite part of the game and where I can give the best opinions and my personal recommendations.
[list]
[*] The basic building parts are very similar to Valheim but has variety in the decorations, though adding more would never be a bad thing and would love to see. A problem I have seen is that the small foundations and floors dont match with the large foundations and floor, leaving them miss-matched around the interior stairs which are only one size. Additionally having 'small' low walls (foundations are 2x2, small foundations are 1x1) that are 1x1 that are thin would add a lot of variety with detailing in builds.
[*] For decorations the potential is there and honestly my favourite part of the building system and I cant wait until the variety of options is larger. More statue variation, with different animals (natural and mythical), humanoid (warriors, Gods). Colour variation to the rugs, and furniture, similar to how the banners work. Adding armour and weapon stands could be cool as well.
[*] Adding the different woods for walls (and other building items) could be cool but would need different crafting methods maybe, and adding minerals into the stone walls to add accents could allow players to add 'prestige' to their builds in later game.
[*] Please add a way to edit terrain when building, or make it so the ground doesnt clip through the foundations (grass, dirt, etc.) and make it so things dont respawn if there is a foundation a certain hight above it (cotton, bushes, etc.)
[/list]

[u] Resource Gathering: [/u]
[list]
[*] Very satisfying progression and can have tool stages skipped if you prefer a faster play style. Progressing through all the tools requires almost full map explorations and when played with others doesnt take too long. Resource amounts are reasonable and throughout the game you will pretty much need lower tier materials as well as upper tier materials making it seem feel more 3D in the design of crafting.
[*] Killing creatures is easy with the right equipment. My only concern is boars are really hard to get a 3 star. Like almost irrationally hard to get the bow shot right (my friend got them all, I couldnt get a single one)
[/list]

[u] Combat: [/u]
[list]
[*] There are 3 Melee weapons and 1 Range; Spear, Sword, Mace (Club), and Bows. I mainly used Maces and Bow while my friend used a Swords and Bow. Melee weapons can be duel wielded with Shields (recommended).
[*] Sword: Short range and Fast swing. Dont know what the dash is as I didnt use them. Single Target.
[*] Spear: Long range and slightly Slower swing. Dash attack is a high jump attack with increased damage. Single Target. Has a signature weapon from shrine drop.
[*] Club: Short range and Slow swing. Dash attack bashes shields away and wider AoE. All attacks can hit multiple Targets.
[*] Bow: Makes fighting easier and recommend using early game primarily. Arc feels pretty good though shooting downwards needs getting use to.
[*] Shield: Blocks damage to health with stamina.

[*] Would like to see signature weapons with other weapons.
[*] The unlockable variety of weapon design could be used to give different buffs? (E.G: faster attack, better attack.)
[*] Make weapons and armour not identify/look the same in the inventory, maybe diff background colours based on tier?
[/list]

If you're not stuck on a nostalgia trip looking for the childhood sense of wonder you had when playing M.I.1 and 2 then this is a great Point and Click adventure game. I love pixel art and could complain about the style and look, but the dialogue, puzzles, sound, world, story, all hit clean as ever. Not to keen on the ending but i had a lot of laughs getting there.
The art style isn't the best, but the story is pretty good.  Not as good as the first two, but still worth playing if you're a fan of the originals.

**MILD SPOILERS**

Much has been said about the art style, but when looking at the screenshots, please ask yourself if the style is capable of being expressive. I see stiff and flat cardboard-cutouts, and regrettably, they feel that way in-game as well -- the strong voice acting helps mitigate this to some extent. I will never understand this art choice over the pixel art of the originals or the art of the remastered editions.

However, the real disappointment lies in the world-building and the story. The game leans heavily on nostalgia, and it works well enough to remain engaging to some extent. But beyond Guybrush and LeChuck, no one in this world seems to care about what's happening. They feel like relics, in a world that left them behind. What we are doing does not seem to matter. As a result, there is little to feel invested in.

And what little there is comes crashing down at the end, with yet another fourth-wall-breaking Thimbleweed-Park-style ending. Even worse, the ending seems unsatisfying by design, a regrettably consistent conclusion to a game that is mocking us throughout for still caring about the franchise. I get it, nothing is real and nothing matters.
It's like a "Déjà vu", a great feeling. A reminiscent of a previous time, in a nostalgic way.

Infested is right. I started out playing on casual mode, and it was wave after wave after wave of impossible to kill monsters. You don't get any time to actually play the game because you're being attacked by massive things that just wipe you out straight away. Even spending all your time just pumping up your characters and ignoring the rest of your base building you can barely make it past the first couple of fights before you've been wiped out. And that's on CASUAL?!?! I dread to think how unplayable the harder levels are....!

I would reccomend you to try the demo before you buy it you get to see the crafting tree so far there are very few quests and even on easy the game significantly slows down after day 10 or so .
